By Proposition 23.1, there are \(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(2^N - 2^i)\) such upper matrices of rank \(j\).
Out of the \(2^N\) choices for bit \(b\) of the \(N\) numbers, \(2^N - 2^j\) choices lie outside the \(j\)-dimensional row-span of the upper \(m\) bits (creating a new pivot at bit \(b\), so bit \(b\) of \(f(A)\) is \(1\)), while \(2^j\) choices lie inside the row-span (giving bit \(b\) of \(f(A)\) equal to \(1\) in \(2^{j-1}\) ways if \(j \ge 1\), or \(0\) ways if \(j = 0\)).
Summing over \(m = 0, \dots, M - 1\) reduces to \(T_j = \sum_{m=j}^{M-1} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 x^m\) at \(x = 2^{-(N+1)}\), which satisfies a first-order \(O(1)\) recurrence in \(j\) via the \(q\)-Pascal identity!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

MSB-to-LSB Bit Projection: By linearity of summation, we compute the contribution of each bit \(b \in \{0, 1, \dots, M - 1\}\) to \(\sum_{A \in [0, 2^M)^N} f(A)\), where \(m = M - 1 - b \in \{0, 1, \dots, M - 1\}\) is the number of bit positions strictly above \(b\). Because \(2^b > \sum_{c=0}^{b-1} 2^c\), the greedy MSB-to-LSB elimination on bits \(M - 1, M - 2, \dots, b\) is completely unaffected by the lower \(b\) bits \(\{0, 1, \dots, b - 1\}\).

The lower \(b\) bits of \((a_1, \dots, a_N)\) can be chosen in \(2^{N b}\) ways independently.
Let \(U \in \mathbb{F}_2^{m \times N}\) be the binary matrix of the \(m\) bits strictly above \(b\), and let \(v_b \in \mathbb{F}_2^N\) be the row vector of bit \(b\) across \((a_1, \dots, a_N)\).

Counting Valid Bit-\(b\) Rows Given Upper Rank \(j = \operatorname{rank}(U)\): Fix an upper matrix \(U \in \mathbb{F}_2^{m \times N}\) of rank \(j \in [0, \min(N, m)]\). When we perform MSB-to-LSB RREF on the \((m + 1) \times N\) matrix \(\binom{U}{v_b}\):

Case A (\(v_b \notin \operatorname{rowspan}(U)\), \(2^N - 2^j\) choices): Then row \(v_b\) creates a new pivot in column (bit) \(b\) of the RREF basis. Since every pivot bit is \(1\) in the XOR sum of the RREF basis, bit \(b\) of \(f(A)\) is always \(1\).
Case B (\(v_b \in \operatorname{rowspan}(U)\), \(2^j\) choices): Then bit \(b\) is not a pivot; after eliminating \(U\) into its \(j\) non-zero RREF basis rows, the column of bit \(b\) in those \(j\) rows can be any vector in \(\mathbb{F}_2^j\) (each occurring for a unique \(v_b \in \operatorname{rowspan}(U)\)).

If \(j = 0\), the basis is empty and bit \(b\) of \(f(A)\) is \(0\) (fails in \(1 = 2^0\) way).
If \(j \ge 1\), the XOR sum of the \(j\) entries in column \(b\) equals \(1\) for exactly half (\(2^{j-1}\)) of the \(2^j\) vectors, and equals \(0\) (fails) for the other \(2^{j-1}\) vectors.


Combining Cases A and B, out of the \(2^N\) choices for \(v_b \in \mathbb{F}_2^N\), the number of choices where bit \(b\) of \(f(A)\) is \(0\) (fails) is \(2^{\max(0, j - 1)}\), and the number of choices where bit \(b\) of \(f(A)\) is \(1\) (succeeds) is \(2^N - 2^{\max(0, j - 1)}\).
Verification on the Sample (\(N = 2, M = 2\)):

Bit \(b = 1\) (\(m = 0\) upper bits): Only \(j = 0\) (\(1\) upper matrix). Succeeds in \(2^2 - 1 = 3\) ways for bit \(1\), times \(2^{2 \times 1} = 4\) choices for bit \(0\), contributing \(3 \times 4 \times 2^1 = 24\).
Bit \(b = 0\) (\(m = 1\) upper bit):

\(j = 0\): \(1\) upper matrix, succeeds in \(2^2 - 1 = 3\) ways.
\(j = 1\): \(3\) upper matrices, each succeeds in \(2^2 - 2^0 = 3\) ways (\(3 \times 3 = 9\) ways). Contributing \((3 + 9) \times 2^0 = 12\).

Total \(= 24 + 12 = 36\), matching the brute-force trace.

Summing Over \(m = 0, \dots, M - 1\) via a First-Order \(q\)-Pascal Recurrence: By Proposition 23.1, the number of \(m \times N\) binary matrices \(U\) of rank \(j\) is \[\#\{U \in \mathbb{F}_2^{m \times N} : \operatorname{rank}(U) = j\} = \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=0}^{j-1} (2^N - 2^i),\] because choosing a \(j\)-dimensional column-space in \(\mathbb{F}_2^m\) has \(\begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2\) ways and mapping it surjectively onto \(N\) columns has \(\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(2^N - 2^i)\) ways. Summing the total bit value \(\sum_{b=0}^{M-1} 2^b \cdot 2^{N b} \cdot (\text{succeeding }(U, v_b))\) by subtracting the failing configurations from all \(2^{N M}\) arrays: \[\sum_{A \in [0, 2^M)^N} f(A) = 2^{N M} (2^M - 1) - \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} 2^{(N + 1)(M - 1 - m)} \left(1 + \sum_{j=1}^{\min(N, m)} 2^{j-1} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 \prod_{i=0}^{j-1} (2^N - 2^i)\right).\] Let \(x = 2^{-(N + 1)} \bmod p\), and define for each \(0 \le j \le \min(N, M - 1)\): \[T_j = \sum_{m=j}^{M-1} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 x^m.\] Then the subtracted sum is simply \(2^{(N + 1)(M - 1)} \left(T_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{\min(N, M-1)} 2^{j-1} T_j \prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(2^N - 2^i)\right)\). To compute \(T_0, T_1, \dots, T_{\min(N, M-1)}\) in \(O(M)\) total time, multiply the \(q\)-Pascal identity \(\begin{bmatrix} m + 1 \\ j + 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 + 2^{j+1} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j + 1 \end{bmatrix}_2\) by \(x^m\), sum over \(m = j, \dots, M - 1\), and reindex \(m' = m + 1\) on the left-hand side (noting \(\begin{bmatrix} j \\ j + 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 = 0\)): \[\frac{1}{x} \sum_{m'=j+1}^{M} \begin{bmatrix} m' \\ j + 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 x^{m'} = \sum_{m=j}^{M-1} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 x^m + 2^{j+1} \sum_{m=j+1}^{M-1} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j + 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 x^m,\] \[\frac{1}{x}\left(T_{j+1} - \begin{bmatrix} M \\ j + 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 x^M\right) = T_j + 2^{j+1} T_{j+1} \implies (1 - 2^{j+1} x) T_{j+1} = x T_j + \begin{bmatrix} M \\ j + 1 \end{bmatrix}_2 x^M.\] Since \(N \ge 1\), we have \(2^{j+1} x = 2^{j - N} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{998244353}\) for all \(0 \le j < N\), so \(1 - 2^{j+1} x\) is always invertible modulo \(998244353\). Starting from \(T_0 = \frac{1 - x^M}{1 - x}\), each \(T_{j+1}\) is obtained in \(O(1)\) time.



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(N, M \le 2.5\times 10^5\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): \(\sum_{A \in [0, 2^M)^N} f(A) \pmod{998244353}\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N + M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Greedy MSB-to-LSB elimination makes bit \(b\) of \(f(A)\) depend only on bits \(M - 1 \dots b\); \(T_j = \sum_{m=j}^{M-1} \begin{bmatrix} m \\ j \end{bmatrix}_2 x^m\) satisfies \((1 - 2^{j+1} x) T_{j+1} = x T_j + \begin{bmatrix} M \\ j+1 \end{bmatrix}_2 x^M\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When \(j = 0\) (all \(m\) upper bits are \(0\)), the \(0\)-dimensional row-span has no free RREF rows above bit \(b\), so bit \(b\) fails in \(2^0 = 1\) way rather than \(2^{j-1} = 2^{-1}\) ways; \(j = 0\) must be separated from \(j \ge 1\).









Advanced 2 (#132) — Group Division

Source: Codeforces Goodbye 2023 Problem F / 1916F
Prerequisite Tags: Biconnected Graphs, Block-Cut Tree / Ear Decomposition, Constructive Connected Partition


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given a biconnected (2-vertex-connected, i.e., connected with no articulation points / cut vertices) undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(|V| = n_1 + n_2\) vertices (\(1 \le n_1, n_2\), \(n = n_1 + n_2 \le 2000\), \(|E| = m \le 4000\)). Partition the vertex set \(V\) into two disjoint sets \(V_1 \sqcup V_2\) of sizes \(|V_1| = n_1\) and \(|V_2| = n_2\) such that both induced subgraphs \(G[V_1]\) and \(G[V_2]\) are connected.


Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n_1 = 2, n_2 = 2\) on \(C_4\): \(1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 1\))

Start with \(V_1 = \{1\}\) (\(|V_1| = 1 < n_1\)) and \(V_2 = \{2, 3, 4\}\) (\(G[V_2]\) is the path \(2 - 3 - 4\), which is connected).
Vertex \(2 \in N(V_1) \cap V_2\) is NOT a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\) (removing \(2\) leaves \(3 - 4\), which is connected).
Move \(2\) from \(V_2\) to \(V_1\): now \(V_1 = \{1, 2\}\) (\(G[V_1]\) is \(1 - 2\), connected) and \(V_2 = \{3, 4\}\) (\(G[V_2]\) is \(3 - 4\), connected).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Why is this always possible for any biconnected graph \(G\)? Think incrementally: start with \(V_1 = \{v_0\}\) (size \(1\)) and \(V_2 = V \setminus \{v_0\}\) (size \(n - 1\)).

Initially, \(G[V_1]\) is a single vertex (hence connected), and because \(G\) is biconnected, \(v_0\) is not a cut vertex of \(G\), so \(G[V_2] = G \setminus \{v_0\}\) is also connected!
If at each step (\(|V_1| = 1, 2, \dots, n_1 - 1\)) we can find a vertex \(u \in V_2\) that is adjacent to at least one vertex in \(V_1\) AND is not a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\), then moving \(u\) from \(V_2\) to \(V_1\) keeps both \(G[V_1]\) and \(G[V_2]\) connected!




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Why must there ALWAYS exist a vertex \(u \in N(V_1) \cap V_2\) that is not a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\)? Consider the Block-Cut Tree of the connected graph \(G[V_2]\):

If \(G[V_2]\) is itself biconnected (has only \(1\) block and \(0\) cut vertices), then every vertex in \(N(V_1) \cap V_2\) (which is non-empty since \(G\) is connected) is a non-cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\)!
If \(G[V_2]\) has at least one cut vertex, its Block-Cut Tree has at least two leaf blocks \(B \subseteq V_2\). Each leaf block \(B\) contains at most one cut vertex \(c\) of \(G[V_2]\), and at least one non-cut vertex \(x \in B \setminus \{c\}\).
Could a leaf block \(B\) of \(G[V_2]\) have no edges from \(B \setminus \{c\}\) to \(V_1\)? If \(B \setminus \{c\}\) had no edges to \(V_1\), then in the entire graph \(G\), removing the single vertex \(c\) would disconnect \(B \setminus \{c\}\) from \((V_2 \setminus B) \cup V_1\)! That would mean \(c\) is a cut vertex of the original graph \(G\) — contradicting that \(G\) is biconnected!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

From Hint 2, in every leaf block \(B\) of \(G[V_2]\), the non-cut vertices \(B \setminus \{c\}\) of \(B\) MUST have at least one neighbor in \(V_1\)! Even simpler: we don’t even need to construct the full Block-Cut Tree! Just run a single Tarjan DFS on \(G[V_2]\) to identify the cut vertices of \(G[V_2]\) in \(O(n + m)\) time:

By Hint 2, at least one vertex \(u \in V_2\) that is adjacent to \(V_1\) is guaranteed NOT to be a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\)!
Find any such \(u \in N(V_1) \cap V_2\) that is not a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\), move \(u\) to \(V_1\), and repeat \(n_1 - 1\) times! Total time: \(n_1 \times O(n + m) = O(n(n + m)) \approx 8 \times 10^6\) operations!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Invariant & Exchange Lemma: We maintain a partition \(V = V_1 \sqcup V_2\) such that \(G[V_1]\) and \(G[V_2]\) are both connected.

Base case (\(|V_1| = 1\)): Pick \(V_1 = \{1\}\) and \(V_2 = V \setminus \{1\}\). Since \(G\) is 2-vertex-connected, \(G[V_2]\) is connected.
Inductive step (\(1 \le |V_1| < n_1\)): We claim there exists \(u \in V_2\) such that:

\(u\) has at least one neighbor in \(V_1\), and
\(u\) is not an articulation point (cut vertex) of \(G[V_2]\).

Proof of Claim: If \(G[V_2]\) has no cut vertices, then since \(G\) is connected, \(N(V_1) \cap V_2 \ne \emptyset\) and any \(u \in N(V_1) \cap V_2\) works. Otherwise, \(G[V_2]\) has at least one cut vertex, so its Block-Cut Tree is a tree with at least two leaves, which are blocks (maximal biconnected components) \(B\) of \(G[V_2]\). Let \(B\) be any leaf block of \(G[V_2]\), and let \(c \in B\) be the unique cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\) belonging to \(B\). Since \(B\) has size \(\ge 2\), \(B \setminus \{c\} \ne \emptyset\), and no vertex in \(B \setminus \{c\}\) is a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\). In \(G[V_2]\), every path from \(B \setminus \{c\}\) to \(V_2 \setminus B\) passes through \(c\). If no vertex in \(B \setminus \{c\}\) had an edge to \(V_1\), then every path in \(G\) from \(B \setminus \{c\}\) to \(V \setminus B = (V_2 \setminus B) \cup V_1\) would pass through \(c\), making \(c\) a cut vertex of \(G\), a contradiction. Hence there exists \(u \in B \setminus \{c\}\) adjacent to \(V_1\), and \(u\) is not a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\).

Tarjan Cut-Vertex Identification in \(G[V_2]\): In each of the \(n_1 - 1\) iterations:

Run Tarjan’s DFS on \(G[V_2]\) (tin[v], low[v]): the root \(r\) of the DFS tree is a cut vertex iff it has \(\ge 2\) DFS tree children; a non-root vertex \(v\) is a cut vertex iff it has a DFS tree child \(w\) with low[w] >= tin[v].
Scan all \(u \in V_2\): pick the first \(u\) that is not a cut vertex of \(G[V_2]\) and has a neighbor in \(V_1\), and move \(u\) from \(V_2\) to \(V_1\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Biconnected (2-vertex-connected) undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(n = n_1 + n_2 \le 2000\) and \(m \le 4000\).
Postconditions (Output): Vertex subset \(V_1\) of size \(n_1\) such that \(G[V_1]\) and \(G[V \setminus V_1]\) are both connected.
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n_1 (n + m)) = O(n(n + m))\) time and \(O(n + m)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Leaf blocks of the Block-Cut Tree of \(G[V_2]\) cannot be isolated from \(V_1\) by their single cut vertex \(c\), guaranteeing a valid vertex transfer at every step.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: In Tarjan’s articulation-point test on \(G[V_2]\), applying low[w] >= tin[v] to the DFS root \(r\) falsely marks \(r\) as a cut vertex even when \(r\) has only \(1\) DFS tree child; the DFS root \(r\) must be tested separately by checking dfs_children(r) >= 2.









Mastery 1 (#063) — Modulo Sum of Increasing Sequences

Source: AtCoder Regular Contest 145 Problem F (arc145_f)
Prerequisite Tags: Gaussian \(q\)-Binomials as Ferrers Box GFs, \(q\)-Lucas Theorem at Roots of Unity, Cyclotomic Coset Inversion, Ramanujan Sums


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given integers \(N, M, P\) (\(1 \le N, M \le 10^6\), \(1 \le P \le 5000\)), consider all \(\binom{N+M}{N}\) integer sequences \(A = (A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N)\) satisfying \[0 \le A_1 \le A_2 \le \dots \le A_N \le M.\] For each remainder \(r = 0, 1, \dots, P - 1\), compute the number of such sequences satisfying \[\sum_{i=1}^N A_i \equiv r \pmod P,\] modulo \(998244353\), in \(O(N + M + P^2)\) time.


Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(N = 2, M = 2, P = 3\))
There are \(\binom{2+2}{2} = 6\) weakly increasing sequences \(0 \le A_1 \le A_2 \le 2\):

\((0, 0)\): sum \(= 0 \equiv 0 \pmod 3\).
\((0, 1)\): sum \(= 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\).
\((0, 2)\): sum \(= 2 \equiv 2 \pmod 3\).
\((1, 1)\): sum \(= 2 \equiv 2 \pmod 3\).
\((1, 2)\): sum \(= 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 3\).
\((2, 2)\): sum \(= 4 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\). Counts for \(r = 0, 1, 2\) modulo \(3\): \((2, 2, 2)\). Check via \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}_q = 1 + q + 2q^2 + q^3 + q^4 \equiv (1 + 1) + (1 + 1)q + 2q^2 = 2 + 2q + 2q^2 \pmod{q^3 - 1}\)!



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Look at the condition \(0 \le A_1 \le A_2 \le \dots \le A_N \le M\) weighted by \(q^{\sum_{i=1}^N A_i}\): If you draw \(N\) horizontal rows of lengths \(A_1 \le A_2 \le \dots \le A_N\), what geometric shape do they form inside an \(N \times M\) grid, and how does the total sum \(\sum_{i=1}^N A_i\) relate to the area trapped beneath the North-East lattice path from \((0,0)\) to \((M,N)\)? Once you identify the generating function \(F(q) = \sum_{A} q^{\sum A_i}\), how do you extract the sum of coefficients where the exponent is congruent to \(r \pmod P\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

How do we reduce \(\begin{bmatrix} N + M \\ N \end{bmatrix}_q\) modulo \(q^P - 1\) when \(N, M \le 10^6\) and \(P \le 5000\)? We cannot expand \(\begin{bmatrix} N + M \\ N \end{bmatrix}_q\) up to degree \(NM = 10^{12}\), nor can we divide \(\prod (1 - q^k) \bmod (q^P - 1)\) directly because \(1 - q^k\) is a zero divisor modulo \(q^P - 1\)! Instead, factor \(q^P - 1 = \prod_{d \mid P} \Phi_d(q)\) into cyclotomic polynomials (or evaluate \(F(q)\) at all \(P\)-th roots of unity \(\zeta_P^j\))! If \(\zeta_d\) is a primitive \(d\)-th root of unity (\(d \mid P\)), what is \(\begin{bmatrix} N + M \\ N \end{bmatrix}_{\zeta_d}\)? By the \(q\)-Lucas Theorem (Theorem 23.2 in Section 23.2), writing \(L = N + M = a_1 d + a_0\), \(N = b_1 d + b_0\), and \(M = c_1 d + c_0\) with \(0 \le a_0, b_0, c_0 < d\): \[\begin{bmatrix} N + M \\ N \end{bmatrix}_{\zeta_d} = \binom{a_1}{b_1} \begin{bmatrix} a_0 \\ b_0 \end{bmatrix}_{\zeta_d}.\] Notice that if \(b_0 + c_0 \ge d\) (a carry occurs mod \(d\)), then \(a_0 = b_0 + c_0 - d < b_0\), so \(\begin{bmatrix} a_0 \\ b_0 \end{bmatrix}_{\zeta_d} = 0\)! Thus \(F(\zeta_d) \ne 0\) only when \(a_0 = b_0 + c_0 < d\).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Since \(P \le 5000\) is arbitrary, \(P\) need not divide \(998244353 - 1\), so primitive \(d\)-th roots of unity do not generally exist in \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\). Instead, for each divisor \(d \mid P\) with \(a_0 = b_0 + c_0 < d\), we compute \[R_d(q) = \binom{a_1}{b_1} \begin{bmatrix} a_0 \\ b_0 \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod \Phi_d(q)\] symbolically inside \(\mathbb{F}_p[q] / (q^d - 1)\):

Multiplying by \((1 - q^j)\) (\(1 \le j < d\)) takes \(O(d)\) time via a cyclic shift.
Dividing by \((1 - q^j)\) (\(1 \le j < d\)) modulo \(\Phi_d(q)\) also takes \(O(d)\) time: partition \(\{0, 1, \dots, d - 1\}\) into \(g = \gcd(j, d)\) cyclic cosets of size \(m = d / g \ge 2\); on each coset, \(x = q^j\) satisfies \(1 + x + \dots + x^{m-1} = 0\), so \((1 - x)^{-1} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{t=0}^{m-1} (m - 1 - t) x^t\), which is a single \(O(m)\) linear prefix-sum pass!
Finally, the trace \(\sum_{\gcd(k, d) = 1} R_d(\zeta_d^k) \zeta_d^{-k r}\) is extracted in \(O(d \log d)\) time using Ramanujan’s sum \(c_d(n) = \sum_{e \mid \gcd(d, n)} \mu(d / e) e\). Summing \(O(d^2)\) over all \(d \mid P\) takes \(\sum_{d \mid P} d^2 \le \zeta(2) P^2 = O(P^2)\) total time!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Ferrers Box Generating Function & Inverse DFT Setup: Each sequence \(0 \le A_1 \le \dots \le A_N \le M\) corresponds to a Ferrers diagram inside an \(N \times M\) box with area \(\sum_{i=1}^N A_i\), so \[F(q) = \sum_{r \ge 0} c_r q^r = \begin{bmatrix} N + M \\ N \end{bmatrix}_q,\] and we seek \(F(q) \bmod (q^P - 1) = \sum_{r=0}^{P-1} \text{ans}_r q^r\). Over \(\mathbb{C}\), let \(\omega = e^{2\pi i / P}\). By the Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform of length \(P\), \[\text{ans}_r = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{j=0}^{P-1} F(\omega^j) \omega^{-j r}.\] Grouping the index \(j \in \{0, 1, \dots, P - 1\}\) by the exact multiplicative order \(d = \frac{P}{\gcd(P, j)} \mid P\) of \(\zeta = \omega^j\): \[\text{ans}_r = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{d \mid P} \sum_{\substack{1 \le k \le d \\ \gcd(k, d) = 1}} F(\zeta_d^k) \zeta_d^{-k r}, \qquad \zeta_d = e^{2\pi i / d}.\]
Applying the \(q\)-Lucas Theorem at Order \(d \mid P\): Fix a divisor \(d \mid P\) and write \(L = N + M\), \(N\), and \(M\) in base \(d\): \[L = a_1 d + a_0, \qquad N = b_1 d + b_0, \qquad M = c_1 d + c_0 \qquad (0 \le a_0, b_0, c_0 < d).\] By the \(q\)-Lucas Theorem (Theorem 23.2), for every primitive \(d\)-th root of unity \(\zeta = \zeta_d^k\): \[F(\zeta) = \begin{bmatrix} L \\ N \end{bmatrix}_\zeta = \binom{a_1}{b_1} \begin{bmatrix} a_0 \\ b_0 \end{bmatrix}_\zeta.\]

If \(b_0 + c_0 \ge d\), then \(a_0 = b_0 + c_0 - d < b_0\), so \(\begin{bmatrix} a_0 \\ b_0 \end{bmatrix}_\zeta = 0\) and divisor \(d\) contributes \(0\).
If \(b_0 + c_0 < d\), then \(a_0 = b_0 + c_0 < d\) and \(a_1 = b_1 + c_1\). In this case, \[\begin{bmatrix} a_0 \\ b_0 \end{bmatrix}_q = \prod_{i=1}^{b_0} \frac{1 - q^{c_0 + i}}{1 - q^i},\] where every exponent \(c_0 + i\) and \(i\) lies strictly between \(1\) and \(a_0 < d\).

\(O(d)\) Coset Inversion of \((1 - q^j)\) Modulo \(\Phi_d(q)\): For \(1 \le j < d\), \((1 - q^j)\) is coprime to \(\Phi_d(q)\). To divide a polynomial \(A(q) = \sum_{u=0}^{d-1} \alpha_u q^u \in \mathbb{F}_p[q] / (q^d - 1)\) by \((1 - q^j)\) modulo \(\Phi_d(q)\) in \(O(d)\) time:

Partition \(\{0, 1, \dots, d - 1\}\) into \(g = \gcd(j, d)\) cyclic cosets of step \(j \bmod d\), each of length \(m = d / g \ge 2\): \[C_s = \{s,\; (s + j) \bmod d,\; \dots,\; (s + (m - 1)j) \bmod d\}, \qquad 0 \le s < g.\]
On each coset \(C_s\), setting \(x = q^j\), every primitive \(d\)-th root \(\zeta\) satisfies \(1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^{m-1} = 0\) because \(\zeta^j\) is a primitive \(m\)-th root of unity (\(m \ge 2\)).
Observe the polynomial identity in \(\mathbb{Q}[x]\): \[(1 - x) \sum_{t=0}^{m-1} (m - 1 - t) x^t = m - (1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^{m-1}) \equiv m \pmod{1 + x + \dots + x^{m-1}}.\] Hence \((1 - x)^{-1} \equiv \frac{1}{m} \sum_{t=0}^{m-1} (m - 1 - t) x^t \pmod{1 + x + \dots + x^{m-1}}\).
Equivalently, if \((1 - x) \sum_{t=0}^{m-1} \beta_t x^t \equiv \sum_{t=0}^{m-1} \alpha_t x^t \pmod{1 + x + \dots + x^{m-1}}\), subtracting the coset mean \(\overline{\alpha} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{t=0}^{m-1} \alpha_t\) (so that the right-hand side is divisible by \(1 - x\) modulo \(1 - x^m\)) and comparing \([x^t]\) in \((1 - x)\sum_{u=0}^{m-1} \beta_u x^u \equiv \sum_{u=0}^{m-1} (\alpha_u - \overline{\alpha})x^u \pmod{1 - x^m}\) gives \[[x^t]\!\left((1 - x)\sum_{u=0}^{m-1} \beta_u x^u \bmod (1 - x^m)\right) = \beta_t - \beta_{(t-1)\bmod m} = \alpha_t - \overline{\alpha} \implies \beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + (\alpha_t - \overline{\alpha}) \quad (1 \le t < m)\] (or \(\beta_t - \beta_{t-1} = -(\alpha_t - \overline{\alpha})\) when matching \((x - 1)\sum \beta_u x^u\)), which determines \((\beta_0, \dots, \beta_{m-1})\) up to an additive constant in a single \(O(m)\) linear scan. Across all \(g\) cosets, each division by \((1 - q^i)\) takes \(O(d)\) time, so computing \[R_d(q) = \sum_{m=0}^{d-1} \beta_m q^m \equiv \binom{a_1}{b_1} \prod_{i=1}^{b_0} \frac{1 - q^{c_0 + i}}{1 - q^i} \pmod{\Phi_d(q)}\] takes \(O(b_0 d) = O(d^2)\) time.

Extracting the Trace via Ramanujan’s Sum: Once \(R_d(q) = \sum_{m=0}^{d-1} \beta_m q^m\) is computed, its trace over all \(\varphi(d)\) primitive \(d\)-th roots of unity is \[\sum_{\substack{1 \le k \le d \\ \gcd(k, d) = 1}} R_d(\zeta_d^k) \zeta_d^{-k r} = \sum_{m=0}^{d-1} \beta_m \sum_{\substack{1 \le k \le d \\ \gcd(k, d) = 1}} \zeta_d^{k(m - r)} = \sum_{m=0}^{d-1} \beta_m c_d(m - r),\] where \(c_d(n) = \sum_{e \mid \gcd(d, n)} \mu(d / e) e\) is Ramanujan’s sum (derived by Möbius inversion on the identity \(\sum_{k=0}^{e-1} \zeta_e^{k n} = e [e \mid n]\)). Exchanging the sums over \(m\) and \(e \mid d\) yields \[\sum_{m=0}^{d-1} \beta_m c_d(m - r) = \sum_{e \mid d} \mu(d / e) \, e \, S_{d, e}(r \bmod e), \qquad S_{d, e}(u) = \sum_{\substack{0 \le m < d \\ m \equiv u \pmod e}} \beta_m.\] Summing over all \(d \mid P\) and dividing by \(P\) gives the exact answer for every \(r \in \{0, 1, \dots, P - 1\}\): \[\text{ans}_r = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{d \mid P} \sum_{e \mid d} \mu(d / e) \, e \, S_{d, e}(r \bmod e) \pmod{998244353}.\]
Verification on \(N = 1, M = 1, P = 3\) (\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_q = 1 + q\)):

\(d = 1\): \(a_1 = 2, b_1 = 1 \implies \binom{2}{1} = 2\), \(S_{1, 1}(0) = 2\).
\(d = 3\): \(a_1 = b_1 = 0 \implies \binom{0}{0} = 1\), \(R_3(q) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_q = 1 + q \implies \beta = (1, 1, 0)\).

\(e = 1\): \(\mu(3) \cdot 1 \cdot (1 + 1 + 0) = -2\).
\(e = 3\): \(\mu(1) \cdot 3 \cdot \beta_r = (3, 3, 0)\).
Sum over \(e \mid 3\): \((-2 + 3, -2 + 3, -2 + 0) = (1, 1, -2)\).

Combining \(d = 1\) and \(d = 3\): \(\text{ans} = \frac{1}{3}((2, 2, 2) + (1, 1, -2)) = (1, 1, 0)\), matching \(1 + q + 0q^2\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(N, M \le 10^6\), \(P \le 5000\); modulus \(p = 998244353 > \max(N+M, P)\).
Postconditions (Output): Array ans[0..P-1] where ans[r] is the number of sequences \(0 \le A_1 \le \dots \le A_N \le M\) with \(\sum A_i \equiv r \pmod P\), modulo \(998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N + M + \sum_{d \mid P} d^2) = O(N + M + P^2)\) time and \(O(N + M + P)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: For each \(d \mid P\), \((1 - q^j)\) is inverted in \(\mathbb{F}_p[q] / (\Phi_d(q))\) on each of the \(\gcd(j, d)\) cyclic cosets via \((1 - x)^{-1} \equiv \frac{1}{m}\sum_{t=0}^{m-1}(m - 1 - t)x^t \pmod{1 + x + \dots + x^{m-1}}\), and Ramanujan’s sum \(c_d(m - r) = \sum_{e \mid \gcd(d, m-r)} \mu(d/e)e\) extracts the exact trace over primitive \(d\)-th roots of unity without field extensions.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Attempting to evaluate \(\begin{bmatrix} N+M \\ N \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod (q^P - 1)\) via direct polynomial division fails because \(1 - q^j\) is a zero divisor in \(\mathbb{F}_p[q]/(q^P - 1)\) (Failure Mode #9); when \(b_0 + c_0 \ge d\) in base \(d\), a carry occurs so \(a_0 < b_0\) and \(\begin{bmatrix} a_0 \\ b_0 \end{bmatrix}_{\zeta_d} = 0\) immediately.









Mastery 2 (#111) — Chiori and Doll Picking (Hard Version)

Source: Codeforces Round 635 (Div. 1) Problem E2 / 1336E2
Prerequisite Tags: RREF Linear Basis over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), Dual Code \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\), Krawtchouk / MacWilliams Duality (Theorem 23.5)


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(n\) integers \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in [0, 2^m)\) (\(1 \le n \le 2\times 10^5\), \(0 \le m \le 53\)). For each \(c = 0, 1, \dots, m\), count the number of subsequences of \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) whose bitwise XOR sum has binary popcount (\(\operatorname{popcount}\)) equal to \(c\). Output all \(m + 1\) counts modulo \(998244353\) in \(O(n m + 2^{\lfloor m/2 \rfloor} + m^3)\) time.


Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n = 3, m = 3, a = (3, 5, 6)\))
In binary, \(a_1 = \text{011}_2\), \(a_2 = \text{101}_2\), \(a_3 = \text{110}_2\). Notice that \(a_3 = a_1 \oplus a_2\), so the linear span \(\mathcal{C} = \operatorname{span}(a_1, a_2, a_3) \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^3\) has dimension \(r = 2\), and each of the \(2^2 = 4\) elements of \(\mathcal{C}\) is achieved by \(2^{n - r} = 2^{3 - 2} = 2\) subsequences:

\(\mathcal{C} = \{\text{000}_2, \text{011}_2, \text{101}_2, \text{110}_2\}\), with popcounts \(0, 2, 2, 2\).
Subsequence counts for \(c = 0, 1, 2, 3\): \(2 \times (1, 0, 3, 0) = (2, 0, 6, 0)\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

First, insert \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) into an \(\mathbb{F}_2\) linear basis in Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF) in \(O(n m)\) time. Let \(r = \dim\mathcal{C} \le m\) be the rank of the basis, and let \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^m\) be the \(r\)-dimensional subspace spanned by the basis. Every vector \(v \in \mathcal{C}\) is the XOR sum of \(2^{n - r}\) distinct subsequences of \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\)! Thus, if \(A_c = \#\{v \in \mathcal{C} : \operatorname{popcount}(v) = c\}\) is the weight enumerator of \(\mathcal{C}\), the answer for each \(c\) is simply \(2^{n - r} A_c \pmod{998244353}\).

When \(r \le 26\): \(|\mathcal{C}| = 2^r \le 2^{26} \approx 6.7 \times 10^7\), so we can enumerate all \(v \in \mathcal{C}\) directly using Gray code / DFS in \(O(2^r)\) bit operations!
What when \(r > 26\) (up to \(r = 53\))?




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

When \(r > 26\), the orthogonal complement (dual code) \(\mathcal{C}^\perp = \{u \in \mathbb{F}_2^m : \langle u, v \rangle \equiv 0 \pmod 2 \;\forall v \in \mathcal{C}\}\) has dimension \[\dim \mathcal{C}^\perp = m - r \le 53 - 27 = 26.\] Recall Section 23.4:

Permute the \(m\) bit columns so the \(r\) pivot columns come first. Then the RREF basis of \(\mathcal{C}\) is \(G = [I_r \mid P]\), where \(P\) is an \(r \times (m - r)\) binary matrix.
The dual subspace \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) has basis \(H = [P^T \mid I_{m - r}]\), which consists of \(m - r\) rows!
Enumerate all \(2^{m - r} \le 2^{26}\) vectors \(u \in \mathcal{C}^\perp\) in \(O(2^{m - r})\) time to obtain the dual weight enumerator \(B_j = \#\{u \in \mathcal{C}^\perp : \operatorname{popcount}(u) = j\}\) for \(0 \le j \le m\).




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Apply Theorem 23.5 (Krawtchouk / MacWilliams Duality) from Section 23.4: \[A_c = \frac{1}{2^{m - r}} \sum_{j=0}^m B_j K_c(j; m),\] where \(K_c(j; m) = [z^c] (1 - z)^j (1 + z)^{m - j} = \sum_{i=0}^c (-1)^i \binom{j}{i} \binom{m - j}{c - i}\) is the binary Krawtchouk polynomial! Precompute the \((m + 1) \times (m + 1)\) table \(K_c(j; m)\) in \(O(m^3)\) time, compute \(A_c\) from \(B_j\) in \(O(m^2)\) time, and multiply by \(2^{n - r} \pmod{998244353}\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

RREF Basis Reduction: Insert \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) into an \(\mathbb{F}_2\) basis of bit-width \(m\), and eliminate upwards so that every pivot bit appears in only one basis vector (RREF). Let \(r\) be the number of basis vectors. Every element \(v \in \mathcal{C}\) is formed by \(2^{n - r}\) subsequences.
Branch 1 (\(r \le \lfloor m / 2 \rfloor = 26\)): Primal Enumeration: Enumerate all \(2^r\) XOR combinations of the \(r\) basis vectors via a recursive DFS dfs(idx, cur_xor) (or Gray code loop), incrementing A[__builtin_popcountll(cur_xor)]. Output ans[c] = A[c] * 2^(n - r) mod 998244353.
Branch 2 (\(r > 26\), so \(m - r \le 27\)): Dual Code Construction & MacWilliams Transform:

Column Permutation: Re-index the \(m\) bit positions so that the \(r\) pivot bits occupy positions \(0, 1, \dots, r - 1\) and the \(m - r\) non-pivot (free) bits occupy positions \(r, r + 1, \dots, m - 1\). Since re-indexing bits is a permutation of \(\{0, \dots, m - 1\}\), it preserves \(\operatorname{popcount}(v)\) for every vector \(v \in \mathbb{F}_2^m\).
Dual Generator Matrix \(H = [P^T \mid I_{m - r}]\): In the permuted coordinates, the \(i\)-th basis row (\(0 \le i < r\)) is \(e_i \oplus p_i\), where \(p_i\) is a mask on bits \(\{r, \dots, m - 1\}\). For each free bit \(f \in \{0, \dots, m - r - 1\}\), construct the dual basis vector \(h_f \in \mathbb{F}_2^m\) whose \(f\)-th free bit (position \(r + f\)) is \(1\), and whose \(i\)-th pivot bit (\(0 \le i < r\)) is equal to the \(f\)-th bit of \(p_i\). Then for every \(i \in [0, r)\) and \(f \in [0, m - r)\), the inner product over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) is \[\langle e_i \oplus p_i,\; h_f \rangle = (p_i)_f \oplus (p_i)_f = 0.\] Since \(h_0, \dots, h_{m - r - 1}\) are linearly independent (having \(I_{m - r}\) on the free coordinates), they form a basis of \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\).
Meet-in-the-Middle / Gray Code Enumeration of \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\): Enumerate all \(2^{m - r}\) XOR combinations of \(h_0, \dots, h_{m - r - 1}\) in \(O(2^{m - r})\) operations (using __builtin_popcountll) to accumulate the dual weight distribution \(B_0, B_1, \dots, B_m\). (Note: when \(m - r = 27\), split \(h_0\) out or unroll the last bit so the DFS has only \(2^{26}\) leaves.)
Krawtchouk Transform (Theorem 23.5): By Theorem 23.5, \[A_c = 2^{-(m - r)} \sum_{j=0}^m B_j \sum_{i=0}^c (-1)^i \binom{j}{i} \binom{m - j}{c - i} \pmod{998244353},\] and finally \(\text{ans}_c = 2^{n - r} A_c = 2^{n - m} \sum_{j=0}^m B_j K_c(j; m) \pmod{998244353}\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: \(n \le 2\times 10^5\), \(m \le 53\), and \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in [0, 2^m)\); modulus \(p = 998244353\) is odd (\(2^{-1} \equiv 499122177 \pmod p\)).
Postconditions (Output): Array ans[0..m] of subsequence counts by XOR popcount modulo \(998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n m + 2^{\min(r, m - r)} + m^3)\) time (\(\le 6.7 \times 10^7\) bit operations) and \(O(m^2)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: \(G H^T = P \oplus P = 0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), and bit permutation is an isometry of the Hamming cube \((\mathbb{F}_2^m, \operatorname{popcount})\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Using 1 << i instead of 1ULL << i for \(m = 53\) triggers 32-bit signed integer UB; failing to reduce the basis to full RREF (eliminating upwards above every pivot) before extracting \(P^T\) corrupts the dual code \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\).












NoteImplementation Verification Footnote (Quarantined Research Templates R-48 & R-49)





During the curriculum verification pass (fps_research/CURRICULUM_ARCHITECTURE.md §5), two reference templates in the research notes were flagged and repaired in this chapter:

R-48 (\(q\)-Binomial Modulo \(p\) & \(q\)-Lucas Kernel): The raw draft in cohort3_wave_5b_tree_fps_transposition_compose_q.md attempted to invert \((q; q)_k \bmod p\) directly without checking whether \(k \ge d = \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\), which causes a \(0/0\) division-by-zero crash whenever \(n \ge \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\) (Failure Mode #9). Section 23.2 replaces this with the verified q_binom_mod_p kernel implementing Theorem 23.2 (\(\binom{\lfloor n/d \rfloor}{\lfloor k/d \rfloor} \begin{bmatrix} n \bmod d \\ k \bmod d \end{bmatrix}_q \bmod p\)).
R-49 (Durfee Square & Dual-Code MacWilliams Kernel): The raw draft omitted the explicit column-permutation book-keeping required to put the RREF basis into standard form \(G = [I_r \mid P]\) before forming \(H = [P^T \mid I_{m-r}]\). Section 23.3 and Section 23.4 provide the verified, division-free \(O(N\sqrt{N})\) Durfee square kernel and the self-contained 5-line Krawtchouk / MacWilliams duality proof with explicit pivot-column permutation.

NotePrerequisites & Learning Objectives



Prerequisites:

Chapter 11: Formal Laurent Series, Residue Calculus, Raney’s Lemma & Lagrange Inversion — Formal residue change-of-variables \(\operatorname{Res}_x A(x)\,dx = \operatorname{Res}_u A(G(u))G'(u)\,du\), Classical and Derivative-Free Lagrange Inversion (LIF).
Chapter 16: The Bivariate Hierarchy, 2D Bostan–Mori & Furstenberg’s Diagonal Theorem — Bivariate rational parity splitting, 2D Kronecker-packed FFTs, and Regime 3 (\(x\)-halving / \(y\)-doubling).
Chapter 20: Tellegen’s Transposition Principle, Middle Product, Multipoint Evaluation & Sampling Shift — Reversing linear dataflow graphs (DAGs) via Tellegen’s theorem and the 1D/2D Middle Product (mulT).

Learning Objectives:

Compute Power Projection in \(O(N \log^2 N)\): Evaluate \(\text{proj}_k = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k\) for all \(0 \le k < N\) simultaneously via Kinoshita–Li (FOCS 2024) 2D Bostan–Mori on \(\frac{P_0(x, y)}{1 - y F(x)}\) with Nachia’s frequency half-swap optimization.
Compute Fast FPS Composition (compose) via Tellegen Transposition: Transpose the linear Power Projection circuit bottom-up to evaluate \(H(x) = G(F(x)) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time—completely free of divisions by \(1, 2, \dots, N-1\) so it works over every field of characteristic \(p \ne 2\).
Linearize Coupled Binomial Sums Simultaneously (炫酷反演魔术): Apply Elegia’s all-\(n\) formal residue linearization to evaluate \(S_n = \sum_{k=0}^n f_k \binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k}\) for all \(0 \le n \le N\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) via a single call to compose.
Master the Dual-Route Compositional Inverse (revert) & Characteristic-\(p\) Pitfalls: Choose between Route A (noshi91 LIF + Power Projection, when \(p > N\)) and Route B (Newton iteration + Kinoshita–Li compose, mandatory when \(p \le N\)), and resolve functional square roots \(G(G(x)) = F(x) \bmod x^N\) up to and beyond the degree \(p + 2\) Artin–Schreier obstruction.
For forty-six years after R. P. Brent and H. T. Kung introduced their \(O((N \log N)^{3/2})\) baby-step giant-step algorithm in 1978, fast composition \(H(x) = G(F(x)) \bmod x^N\) and compositional inversion \(G(x) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(x) \bmod x^N\) remained the last major bottlenecks in the formal power series library. While algebraic operations (inv, sqrt) and differential operations (ln, exp, pow) ran in \(O(N \log N)\) time via Newton iteration, composition and inversion of general dense series at \(N = 2 \times 10^5\) required hundreds of milliseconds of cache-unfriendly block multiplications.
In 2024, Yasunori Kinoshita and Baitian Li shattered this barrier with a remarkably simple insight: Power Projection—the exact matrix transpose of FPS Composition—is nothing more than extracting \([x^{N-1}]\) from a bivariate rational function \(\frac{P_0(x, y)}{1 - y F(x)} \bmod y^N\). Applying the 2D Bostan–Mori parity-splitting loop from Chapter 16 halves the \(x\)-degree while doubling the \(y\)-degree at each of \(\log_2 N\) levels, keeping the total bivariate coefficient volume invariant at \(\Theta(N)\) and solving Power Projection in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time. Reversing the linear dataflow graph via Tellegen’s Transposition Principle from Chapter 20 immediately yields \(O(N \log^2 N)\) FPS Composition (compose), which in turn unlocks \(O(N \log^2 N)\) Compositional Inverse (revert) across all characteristics.

text:
21.1 Power Projection (\(\text{proj}_k = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k\)) via Kinoshita–Li 2D Bostan–Mori

Concrete Combinatorial & Algebraic Motivation
Suppose we are given a formal power series \(F(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} f_i x^i \in K[[x]] / (x^N)\) (for instance, the step generator of a random walk or the branching kernel of a tree) and a weight vector \(\mathbf{w} = (w_0, w_1, \dots, w_{N-1})^\top \in K^N\). We want to compute a single linear functional of the \(k\)-th power \(F(x)^k\) for every \(k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1\) simultaneously: \[\text{proj}_k = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k \qquad (0 \le k < N).\]
Notice what this asks in linear algebra terms. Define the \(N \times N\) composition matrix \(M_F\) whose \((i, k)\) entry is the \(i\)-th coefficient of the \(k\)-th power of \(F(x)\): \[(M_F)_{i, k} := [x^i] F(x)^k \qquad (0 \le i, k < N).\]

Multiplying \(M_F\) on the right by a column vector \(\mathbf{g} = (g_0, \dots, g_{N-1})^\top\) computes the coefficients of the composite series \(H(x) = G(F(x)) \bmod x^N\): \[h_i = [x^i] \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k F(x)^k = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (M_F)_{i, k} g_k \iff \mathbf{h} = M_F \mathbf{g}.\]
Multiplying the transpose \(M_F^\top\) by a weight vector \(\mathbf{w} = (w_0, \dots, w_{N-1})^\top\) computes the power projection vector \(\mathbf{p} = (\text{proj}_0, \dots, \text{proj}_{N-1})^\top\): \[\text{proj}_k = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} (M_F^\top)_{k, i} w_i \iff \mathbf{p} = M_F^\top \mathbf{w}.\]

In particular, when \(\mathbf{w} = (0, \dots, 0, 1)^\top\) is the standard basis vector \(e_{N-1}\), Power Projection extracts the single coefficient \([x^{N-1}] F(x)^k\) for all \(k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1\) at once—which is the exact input required by Lagrange Inversion (Ch 11) to recover the compositional inverse \(F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(x) \bmod x^N\).


Bivariate Rational Conversion & The \(x\)-Halving / \(y\)-Doubling Loop

1. The Diagnostic Signal
Whenever you need a linear combination \(\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k\) for all exponents \(k = 0, \dots, N-1\), never compute the powers \(F(x)^2, F(x)^3, \dots, F(x)^{N-1}\) individually (\(O(N^2 \log N)\)). Instead, introduce a second formal indeterminate \(y\) to sum over all \(k \ge 0\) into a geometric series \(\frac{1}{1 - y F(x)}\).


2. The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
How do we turn the inner product \(\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k\) into a single coefficient extraction in \(x\)? Recall from Chapter 20 that if we define the reversed weight polynomial \[P_0(x) := \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i x^{N-1-i},\] then multiplying \(P_0(x)\) by \(F(x)^k\) and extracting \([x^{N-1}]\) pairs \(x^{N-1-i}\) from \(P_0(x)\) with \(x^i\) from \(F(x)^k\): \[[x^{N-1}] \Big( P_0(x) F(x)^k \Big) = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k = \text{proj}_k.\] Now multiply both sides by \(y^k\) and sum over \(0 \le k < N\). In the bivariate quotient ring \(K[[x]][y] / (y^N)\), the geometric series \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} y^k F(x)^k\) is the exact inverse of \(Q_0(x, y) := 1 - y F(x)\) (which is a unit in \(K[[x, y]]\) because its constant term in \(y\) is \([y^0] Q_0(x, y) = 1 \in K^\times\)): \[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \text{proj}_k y^k = [x^{N-1}] \left( \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i x^{N-1-i}}{1 - y F(x)} \right) \bmod y^N = [x^{N-1}] \frac{P_0(x, y)}{Q_0(x, y)} \bmod y^N.\]


3. Single-Step Verbalized Derivation of Regime 3 2D Bostan–Mori
Pad \(N\) up to the next power of two, \(N = 2^m\) (appending zeros to \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(F(x)\)). This simple padding confers a remarkable structural gift: the target \(x\)-exponent is \(n_0 = N - 1 = 2^m - 1 = (11\dots1)_2\) in binary, so at every halving step \(t = 0, 1, \dots, m-1\), the remaining \(x\)-index \(n_t = 2^{m-t} - 1\) is always odd (\(b_t = n_t \bmod 2 = 1\)).
At recursion level \(t \in \{0, 1, \dots, m\}\), we maintain bivariate polynomials \(P_t(x, y)\) and \(Q_t(x, y)\) satisfying three strict invariants:

\(x\)-Degree Bound: \(\deg_x P_t < 2^{m-t}\) and \(\deg_x Q_t < 2^{m-t}\).
\(y\)-Degree Bound: \(\deg_y P_t < 2^t\) and \(\deg_y Q_t \le 2^t\) (truncated modulo \(y^N\)).
Unit-Constant Normalization: \(Q_t(0, y) = 1\) as a polynomial in \(y\).

Let us verify why these three invariants are preserved when transitioning from \(t\) to \(t + 1\):

Step 1 (Conjugate Multiplication): Multiply numerator and denominator of \(\frac{P_t(x, y)}{Q_t(x, y)}\) by \(Q_t(-x, y) \bmod x^{2^{m-t}}\): \[\frac{P_t(x, y)}{Q_t(x, y)} = \frac{P_t(x, y) Q_t(-x, y)}{Q_t(x, y) Q_t(-x, y)}.\]
Step 2 (Denominator Deflation): Since \(Q_t(x, y) Q_t(-x, y)\) is invariant under \(x \mapsto -x\), all of its odd \(x\)-powers vanish. Truncating to \(\deg_x < 2^{m-t}\) before substituting \(x^2 \gets x\) defines \[Q_{t+1}(x, y) := \mathcal{S}_0\big(Q_t(x, y) Q_t(-x, y) \bmod x^{2^{m-t}}\big) \bmod y^N,\] where \(\mathcal{S}_b\big(\sum_{i} A_i(y) x^i\big) := \sum_{i} A_{2i+b}(y) x^i\). Because \(\deg_y Q_t \le 2^t\), we have \(\deg_y Q_{t+1} \le 2^{t+1}\). Furthermore, at \(x = 0\), \(Q_0(0, y) = 1 - y f_0\) when \(f_0 = 0\) (or after stripping \(x^0 F\)), so \(Q_0(0, y) = 1\); by induction, \(Q_{t+1}(0, y) = Q_t(0, y) Q_t(0, y) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1\).
Step 3 (Numerator Parity Selection): Since \(n_t = 2^{m-t} - 1\) is odd (\(b_t = 1\)), only the odd \(x\)-powers of \(P_t(x, y) Q_t(-x, y) \bmod x^{2^{m-t}}\) contribute to \([x^{n_t}]\): \[P_{t+1}(x, y) := \mathcal{S}_1\big(P_t(x, y) Q_t(-x, y) \bmod x^{2^{m-t}}\big) \bmod y^N.\] Since \(\deg_y P_t < 2^t\) and \(\deg_y Q_t \le 2^t\), their product has \(y\)-degree \(< 2^t + 2^t = 2^{t+1}\), so \(\deg_y P_{t+1} < 2^{t+1}\) without even losing information up to \(y^{2^{t+1}-1}\).
Step 4 (Terminal Extraction at \(t = m\)): After \(m = \log_2 N\) steps, \(n_m = 0\), \(\deg_x P_m = 0\), and \(Q_m(0, y) = 1\). Thus zero final polynomial inversion is needed: \[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \text{proj}_k y^k = \frac{P_m(0, y)}{Q_m(0, y)} \bmod y^N = P_m(0, y).\]







TipNachia’s 2D-FFT Frequency Half-Swap Optimization



At level \(t\), a naive implementation performs four 2D NTTs of size \(2 L_x \times 2 L_y\) (where \(L_x = 2^{m-t}, L_y = 2^t\), so \(2 L_x \cdot 2 L_y = 4N\)): forward NTTs of \(P_t(x,y)\), \(Q_t(x,y)\), and \(Q_t(-x,y)\), plus two inverse NTTs.
As observed by Nachia (2024), we never need to compute a separate forward NTT for \(Q_t(-x, y)\):

In a radix-2 NTT of length \(2 L_x\) along the \(x\)-dimension, the evaluation points are \(\omega_{2L_x}^r\). Because \(\omega_{2L_x}^{L_x} = -1\), negating \(x \mapsto -x\) simply shifts the \(x\)-frequency index \(r\) by \(L_x \pmod{2L_x}\): \[\widehat{Q_t(-x, y)}[r_x, r_y] = \widehat{Q_t(x, y)}[r_x \oplus L_x, r_y].\]
Even better, in the frequency domain, the even-index decimation \(\mathcal{S}_0\) and odd-index decimation \(\mathcal{S}_1\) along \(x\) can be extracted before the inverse NTT by combining frequency pairs \((r_x, r_x \oplus L_x)\): \[\widehat{Q_{t+1}}[r_x, r_y] = \widehat{Q_t}[r_x, r_y] \cdot \widehat{Q_t}[r_x \oplus L_x, r_y],\] halving the \(x\)-length of the inverse NTT from \(2 L_x\) to \(L_x\) and cutting the total runtime by nearly \(50\%\).






Hand-Checkable Toy Trace (\(N = 4\))
Let \(N = 4 = 2^2\) (\(m = 2\)), \(F(x) = x + 2x^2\) (\(f_0 = 0, f_1 = 1, f_2 = 2, f_3 = 0\)), and \(\mathbf{w} = (1, 1, 1, 1)^\top\), so \(\text{proj}_k = \sum_{i=0}^3 [x^i] F(x)^k\).

Direct check:

\(k = 0\): \(F(x)^0 = 1 \implies \text{proj}_0 = 1\).
\(k = 1\): \(F(x)^1 = x + 2x^2 \implies \text{proj}_1 = 1 + 2 = 3\).
\(k = 2\): \(F(x)^2 = x^2 + 4x^3 + 4x^4 \equiv x^2 + 4x^3 \pmod{x^4} \implies \text{proj}_2 = 1 + 4 = 5\).
\(k = 3\): \(F(x)^3 = x^3 + 6x^4 + \dots \equiv x^3 \pmod{x^4} \implies \text{proj}_3 = 1\).

Kinoshita–Li 2D Bostan–Mori trace:

Level \(t = 0\) (\(n_0 = 3\), \(\deg_x < 4, \deg_y \le 1\)): \[P_0(x, y) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3, \qquad Q_0(x, y) = 1 - y(x + 2x^2) = 1 - y x - 2 y x^2.\] Here \(Q_0(-x, y) = 1 + y x - 2 y x^2\). Multiply modulo \(x^4\): \[P_0(x, y) Q_0(-x, y) \equiv 1 + (1 + y)x + (1 - y)x^2 + (1 - y)x^3 \pmod{x^4},\] \[Q_0(x, y) Q_0(-x, y) \equiv (1 - 2y x^2)^2 - y^2 x^2 \equiv 1 - (4y + y^2) x^2 \pmod{x^4}.\] Extracting odd \(x\)-powers (\(\mathcal{S}_1\)) for \(P_1\) and even \(x\)-powers (\(\mathcal{S}_0\)) for \(Q_1\): \[P_1(x, y) = (1 + y) + (1 - y) x, \qquad Q_1(x, y) = 1 - (4y + y^2) x.\]
Level \(t = 1\) (\(n_1 = 1\), \(\deg_x < 2, \deg_y \le 2\)): Here \(Q_1(-x, y) = 1 + (4y + y^2) x\). Multiply modulo \(x^2\): \[P_1(x, y) Q_1(-x, y) \equiv (1 + y) + \Big((1 - y) + (1 + y)(4y + y^2)\Big) x = (1 + y) + (1 + 3y + 5y^2 + y^3) x \pmod{x^2},\] \[Q_1(x, y) Q_1(-x, y) \equiv 1 - (4y + y^2)^2 x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{x^2}.\] Extracting odd \(x\)-powers (\(\mathcal{S}_1\)) for \(P_2\) and even \(x\)-powers (\(\mathcal{S}_0\)) for \(Q_2\): \[P_2(0, y) = 1 + 3y + 5y^2 + y^3, \qquad Q_2(0, y) = 1.\]
Level \(t = 2\) (\(n_2 = 0\)): Reading the coefficients of \(P_2(0, y)\) yields \(\mathbf{p} = (1, 3, 5, 1)^\top\), matching the direct expansion.








ImportantAlgorithm Contract: Kinoshita–Li Power Projection (power_projection)




Inputs: \(F(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} f_i x^i \in K[[x]]/(x^N)\) and weight vector \(\mathbf{w} = (w_0, \dots, w_{N-1})^\top \in K^N\).
Output: Vector \(\mathbf{p} = (\text{proj}_0, \dots, \text{proj}_{N-1})^\top\) where \(\text{proj}_k = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w_i [x^i] F(x)^k\).
Algebraic Preconditions: If \(c = f_0 \ne 0\), first compute the projection for \(\tilde{F}(x) = F(x) - c\) (so \([x^0]\tilde{F} = 0\)) and apply the binomial shift \(\text{proj}_k = \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} c^{k-j} \widetilde{\text{proj}}_j\) via a single EGF convolution (Ch 06). Requires a ring/field supporting FFT/NTT of length \(4N\) (or 3-prime NTT + CRT).
Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) auxiliary space.
Core Invariant: At level \(t \in [0, \log_2 N]\), \([x^{2^{m-t}-1}] \frac{P_t(x, y)}{Q_t(x, y)} \equiv \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \text{proj}_k y^k \pmod{y^{2^t}}\) with \(\deg_x P_t, \deg_x Q_t < 2^{m-t}\), \(\deg_y P_t < 2^t\), \(\deg_y Q_t \le 2^t\), and \(Q_t(0, y) = 1\).



// Core loop of Kinoshita-Li Power Projection (N = 2^m, f[0] == 0)
Poly power_projection(Poly F, Poly w, int N) {
    // Pack (x, y) into 1D array of stride 2*Ly: index(i, j) = i * (2*Ly) + j
    vector<Mint> P(2 * N, 0), Q(2 * N, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) P[2 * (N - 1 - i)] = w[i];
    for (int i = 1; i < N; ++i) Q[2 * i + 1] = -F[i];
    for (int Lx = N, Ly = 1; Lx > 1; Lx >>= 1, Ly <<= 1) {
        // Multiply P(x, y)*Q(-x, y) and Q(x, y)*Q(-x, y) via 2D NTT of size (2*Lx) x (2*Ly)
        // Extract odd x-powers S_1 into P_next and even x-powers S_0 into Q_next
        bostan_mori_2d_step(P, Q, Lx, Ly);
    }
    return Poly(P.begin(), P.begin() + N); // P_m(0, y) since Q_m(0, y) == 1
}






WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Non-Zero Constant Term \(f_0 \ne 0\) in power_projection




The Failure Mode: Running the \(Q_t(0, y) = 1\) zero-division loop directly when \(f_0 = [x^0] F(x) \ne 0\). When \(f_0 \ne 0\), \(Q_0(0, y) = 1 - f_0 y \ne 1\), so at \(t = m\) the denominator is \(Q_m(0, y) = (1 - f_0 y)^{2^m} \ne 1\), and reading \(P_m(0, y)\) without dividing by \(Q_m(0, y)\) produces garbage for all \(k \ge 1\).
The Remedy: Either strip \(c = f_0\) upfront by setting \(\tilde{F}(x) = F(x) - c\) (so \(\tilde{F}(0) = 0\)) and convolving \(\widetilde{\text{proj}}_j / j!\) with \(c^r / r!\) at the end, or divide \(P_m(0, y)\) by \(Q_m(0, y) \bmod y^N\) via a single 1D polynomial inversion at \(t = m\). Stripping \(f_0 = 0\) upfront is cleaner because it also guarantees \(\deg_y P_t < 2^t\) without carry-over from \(x^0\).

title: 21 — Power Projection, Kinoshita–Li FPS Composition (compose) & Compositional Inverse (revert)
section: 21.2 Kinoshita–Li FPS Composition (\(H(x) = G(F(x)) \bmod x^N\)) via Tellegen Transposition
text:
21.2 Kinoshita–Li FPS Composition (\(H(x) = G(F(x)) \bmod x^N\)) via Tellegen Transposition

Transposing the Power Projection Circuit
Given \(F(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} f_i x^i\) and \(G(y) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k y^k\), we want to compute the composite series \[H(x) = G(F(x)) \bmod x^N = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} h_i x^i, \qquad h_i = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k [x^i] F(x)^k.\]

1. The Diagnostic Signal
For a fixed inner series \(F(x)\), both Power Projection \(\mathbf{w} \mapsto \mathbf{p} = M_F^\top \mathbf{w}\) and FPS Composition \(\mathbf{g} \mapsto \mathbf{h} = M_F \mathbf{g}\) are linear maps in \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\mathbf{g}\) respectively, and their matrices are exact transposes of one another. Notice that in power_projection, the denominator sequence \(Q_0(x, y), Q_1(x, y), \dots, Q_m(x, y)\) depends only on \(F(x)\) and is completely independent of \(\mathbf{w}\).


2. The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Let us trace the linear operations applied to the vector \(\mathbf{w}\) in power_projection (§21.1) and invert their order and direction using the rules of Tellegen’s Transposition Principle from Chapter 20:

Forward Map on \(\mathbf{w}\): \[\mathbf{w} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{R}_x} P_0(x, y) \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}_0} P_1(x, y) \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}_1} \cdots \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}_{m-1}} P_m(0, y) = \mathbf{p},\] where \(\mathcal{R}_x\) places \(w_i\) at \([x^{N-1-i} y^0] P_0(x, y)\), and each linear layer \(\mathcal{L}_t : P_t \mapsto P_{t+1}\) performs two elementary linear maps in sequence:

Multiplication by \(Q_t(-x, y)\): \(U_t(x, y) = P_t(x, y) \cdot Q_t(-x, y) \bmod (x^{2^{m-t}}, y^{2^{t+1}})\).
Odd-Index Decimation \(\mathcal{S}_1\) in \(x\): \(P_{t+1}(x, y) = \mathcal{S}_1(U_t(x, y))\), which selects \([x^{2i+1}] U_t(x, y)\) as \([x^i] P_{t+1}(x, y)\).

Transposed Map on \(\mathbf{g}\) (fps_compose): \[\mathbf{g} = \hat{P}_m(0, y) \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}_{m-1}^\top} \hat{P}_{m-1}(x, y) \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}_{m-2}^\top} \cdots \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}_0^\top} \hat{P}_0(x, y) \xrightarrow{\mathcal{R}_x^\top} \mathbf{h}.\] What is the transpose \(\mathcal{L}_t^\top = (\mathcal{S}_1 \circ \operatorname{mul}_{Q_t(-x, y)})^\top = \operatorname{mul}_{Q_t(-x, y)}^\top \circ \mathcal{S}_1^\top\)?

Transpose of Odd-Index Decimation \(\mathcal{S}_1^\top\): Decimation \(\mathcal{S}_1\) maps index \(2i + 1 \mapsto i\) and discards even indices \(2i\). Its transpose \(\mathcal{S}_1^\top\) interleaves zeros at even \(x\)-indices and places \([x^i] \hat{P}_{t+1}(x, y)\) at \([x^{2i+1}] \hat{U}_t(x, y)\): \[\hat{U}_t(x, y) := \mathcal{S}_1^\top\big(\hat{P}_{t+1}(x, y)\big) = x \hat{P}_{t+1}(x^2, y).\]
Transpose of Multiplication by \(Q_t(-x, y)\): By the Middle Product Theorem (Ch 20, Theorem 20.1), the transpose of multiplying \(P_t(x, y)\) by the fixed bivariate polynomial \(Q_t(-x, y)\) is the 2D Middle Product (cross-correlation) \(\operatorname{mulT}_{x, y}\): \[[x^i y^j] \hat{P}_t(x, y) = \sum_{a, b} \big([x^{i+a} y^{j+b}] \hat{U}_t(x, y)\big) \cdot \big([x^a y^b] Q_t(-x, y)\big),\] or in polynomial notation: \[\hat{P}_t(x, y) = \operatorname{mulT}_{x, y}\!\Big(\hat{U}_t(x, y),\, Q_t(-x, y)\Big) \bmod \big(x^{2^{m-t}}, y^{2^t}\big).\]







flowchart LR
    subgraph Forward["1. Forward Pass (Power Projection / Denominator Tree)"]
        direction LR
        Q0["Q_0(x, y) = 1 - y F(x)<br/>deg_x < N, deg_y <= 1"] -->|"Q_0(x,y) Q_0(-x,y)"| Q1["Q_1(x, y)<br/>deg_x < N/2, deg_y <= 2"]
        Q1 -->|"..."| Qm["Q_m(0, y) = 1<br/>deg_x = 0, deg_y <= N"]
    end
    subgraph Backward["2. Backward Pass (Transposed Composition G(F(x)))"]
        direction RL
        Pm["P_hat_m(0, y) = G(y)<br/>deg_x = 0, deg_y < N"] -->|"Interleave x * P_hat(x^2, y)<br/>+ mulT(Q_{m-1}(-x, y))"| P1["P_hat_1(x, y)<br/>deg_x < N/2, deg_y < 2"]
        P1 -->|"Interleave + mulT(Q_0(-x, y))"| P0["P_hat_0(x, 0)<br/>h_i = [x^{N-1-i}] P_hat_0"]
    end
    Forward -.->|"Store Q_t(-x, y) at each level t"| Backward












NoteAlgebraic Universality: Why Kinoshita–Li compose Works in Every Characteristic \(p \ne 2\)



Look closely at every arithmetic operation inside the forward and backward passes of Kinoshita–Li compose when \(F(0) = 0\):

Forward Pass: Computes \(Q_{t+1}(x, y)\) by polynomial multiplication \(Q_t(x, y) Q_t(-x, y)\) and parity extraction \(\mathcal{S}_0\).
Backward Pass: Computes \(\hat{P}_t(x, y)\) by zero-interleaving \(\mathcal{S}_1^\top\) and 2D Middle Product \(\operatorname{mulT}_{x, y}(\hat{U}_t, Q_t(-x, y))\).
Boundary at \(t = m\): Because \(F(0) = 0\), \(Q_t(0, y) = 1\) at all levels \(t\), so no polynomial inversion is needed at \(t = m\).

Unlike differential or ODE-based composition methods, Kinoshita–Li compose never differentiates or integrates and never divides by \(1, 2, \dots, N-1\). The only divisions in the entire algorithm are the factors of \(2^{-1}\) inside the radix-2 inverse FFT/NTT! Consequently, using a 3-prime NTT + Garner CRT (or Schönhage–Strassen / Cantor FFT), Kinoshita–Li compose runs in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) over every field of characteristic \(p \ne 2\), even when \(p \le N\) (e.g., \(\mathbb{F}_3, \mathbb{F}_5, \mathbb{F}_{101}\)).





Hand-Checkable Toy Trace (\(N = 4\))
Let \(N = 4\) (\(m = 2\)), \(F(x) = x + 2x^2\), and \(G(y) = 1 + 3y + y^2 + 2y^3\).

Direct check: \[G(F(x)) = 1 + 3(x + 2x^2) + (x + 2x^2)^2 + 2(x + 2x^2)^3 \equiv 1 + 3x + 7x^2 + 6x^3 \pmod{x^4}.\]
Kinoshita–Li compose Backward Trace: From the forward pass of §21.1, we stored: \[Q_0(-x, y) = 1 + y x - 2 y x^2, \qquad Q_1(-x, y) = 1 + (4y + y^2) x.\]

Initialize at \(t = 2\): \(\hat{P}_2(0, y) = G(y) = 1 + 3y + y^2 + 2y^3\).
Step \(t = 1\) (\(2 \to 1\), target \(\deg_x < 2, \deg_y < 2\)):

Zero-interleave along \(x\): \(\hat{U}_1(x, y) = x \hat{P}_2(x^2, y) = (1 + 3y + y^2 + 2y^3) x\).
Apply \(\operatorname{mulT}_{x, y}\big(\hat{U}_1(x, y),\, 1 + (4y + y^2) x\big)\) for \(i \in \{0, 1\}, j \in \{0, 1\}\):

Multiply by \(1\) (\(a=0, b=0\)): shifts \((i, j)\) by \((0, 0)\), giving \((1 + 3y) x\).
Multiply by \((4y + y^2) x\) (\(a=1\)): shifts \(x^1 \to x^0\), and in \(y\) applies \(\operatorname{mulT}_y(1 + 3y + y^2 + 2y^3,\, 4y + y^2)\) truncated to \(\deg_y < 2\):

\([y^0] = 4 [y^1] \hat{P}_2 + 1 [y^2] \hat{P}_2 = 4(3) + 1(1) = 13\).
\([y^1] = 4 [y^2] \hat{P}_2 + 1 [y^3] \hat{P}_2 = 4(1) + 1(2) = 6\). Thus \(\hat{P}_1(x, y) = (13 + 6y) + (1 + 3y) x\).



Step \(t = 0\) (\(1 \to 0\), target \(\deg_x < 4, \deg_y < 1\)):

Zero-interleave along \(x\): \(\hat{U}_0(x, y) = x \hat{P}_1(x^2, y) = (13 + 6y) x + (1 + 3y) x^3\).
Apply \(\operatorname{mulT}_{x, y}\big(\hat{U}_0(x, y),\, 1 + y x - 2 y x^2\big)\) at \(j = 0\) (\(\deg_y < 1\)):

From \(1\) (\(a=0, b=0\)): takes \([y^0]\hat{U}_0\), contributing \(13 x + 1 x^3\).
From \(+y x\) (\(a=1, b=1\)): shifts \(x^{i+1} \to x^i\) and takes \([y^1]\hat{U}_0\), contributing \(6 x^0 + 3 x^2\).
From \(-2 y x^2\) (\(a=2, b=1\)): shifts \(x^{i+2} \to x^i\) and takes \(-2 [y^1]\hat{U}_0\), contributing \(-2(3) x^1 = -6 x\). Summing all three contributions yields: \[\hat{P}_0(x, 0) = 6 + (13 - 6) x + 3 x^2 + 1 x^3 = 6 + 7x + 3x^2 + x^3.\]


Reverse \(x\)-indices: \(h_i = [x^{3-i}] \hat{P}_0(x, 0)\) gives \((h_0, h_1, h_2, h_3) = (1, 3, 7, 6)\), matching \(1 + 3x + 7x^2 + 6x^3\).








ImportantAlgorithm Contract: Kinoshita–Li Fast FPS Composition (fps_compose)




Inputs: \(F(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} f_i x^i\) and \(G(y) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k y^k\) in \(K[[x]]/(x^N)\).
Output: \(H(x) = G(F(x)) \bmod x^N = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} h_i x^i\).
Algebraic Preconditions: If \(c = [x^0] F(x) \ne 0\), first apply a 1D Polynomial Taylor Shift \(G(y) \gets G(y + c)\) (Ch 06 / Ch 20) in \(O(N \log N)\) time (valid when \(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\)) and replace \(F(x) \gets F(x) - c\) so \([x^0] F = 0\). When \([x^0] F = 0\), requires zero divisions by \(1, 2, \dots, N-1\) (works for all \(p \ne 2\)).
Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N \log N)\) space (to store the forward denominators \(Q_t\) across the \(\log_2 N\) levels).
Core Invariant: At every level \(t\) of the backward pass, the inner product \(\langle \hat{P}_t(x, y), P_t(x, y) \rangle = \sum_{i, j} ([x^i y^j] \hat{P}_t) ([x^i y^j] P_t)\) is invariant and equals \(\langle \mathbf{g}, \mathbf{p} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{h}, \mathbf{w} \rangle\).



// Core structure of Kinoshita-Li FPS Composition H(x) = G(F(x)) mod x^N (F[0] == 0)
Poly fps_compose(Poly F, Poly G, int N) { // N = 2^m
    vector<vector<Mint>> Q_hist; vector<Mint> Q(2 * N, 0);
    for (int i = 1; i < N; ++i) Q[2 * i + 1] = -F[i];
    for (int Lx = N, Ly = 1; Lx > 1; Lx >>= 1, Ly <<= 1) {
        Q_hist.push_back(Q); Q = bostan_mori_2d_denom_step(Q, Lx, Ly);
    }
    vector<Mint> P_hat(G.begin(), G.end()); // P_hat_m(0, y) = G(y)
    for (int step = (int)Q_hist.size() - 1, Lx = 2, Ly = N >> 1; step >= 0; --step, Lx <<= 1, Ly >>= 1)
        P_hat = bostan_mori_2d_transpose_step(P_hat, Q_hist[step], Lx, Ly);
    Poly H(N);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) H[i] = P_hat[N - 1 - i];
    return H;
}

section: 21.3 Elegia’s All-\(n\) Coupled Binomial Sum Linearization (炫酷反演魔术, Form 6 Case B)
text:
21.3 Elegia’s All-\(n\) Coupled Binomial Sum Linearization (炫酷反演魔术, Form 6 Case B)
In Chapter 11, we saw how the formal residue change-of-variables theorem extracts a single coefficient of an implicit series. Now that we possess \(O(N \log^2 N)\) fast composition (compose) and compositional inversion (revert), we can evaluate an entire family of coupled binomial sums across all \(n = 0, 1, \dots, N\) simultaneously.

1. The Diagnostic Signal
You are asked to compute, for all \(n = 0, 1, \dots, N\) (or for a single \(n\) when \(f_k\) is an arbitrary array), the sum \[S_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} f_k \binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k},\] where the upper index \(\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma\) depends linearly on both the outer index \(n\) and the summation index \(k\), preventing a direct 1D convolution.


2. The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
How do we decouple \(n\) and \(k\) inside \(\binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k}\)? Write the binomial coefficient as a formal Laurent residue in a dummy variable \(u\): \[\binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k} = [u^{n-k}] (1 + u)^{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma} = \operatorname{Res}_u \frac{(1 + u)^{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}}{u^{n - k + 1}}\,du.\] Group all factors according to whether their exponent is \(n\), \(k\), or constant: \[\frac{(1 + u)^{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}}{u^{n - k + 1}}\,du = (1 + u)^\gamma \cdot \Big(u (1 + u)^\beta\Big)^k \cdot \left(\frac{u}{(1 + u)^\alpha}\right)^{-n - 1} \frac{du}{(1 + u)^\alpha}.\] Look at the base raised to the power \(-n - 1\): it is \[z = G(u) := \frac{u}{(1 + u)^\alpha} = u (1 + u)^{-\alpha} \in \mathcal{G}_1(K).\] Let \(u = A(z) := G^{\langle -1 \rangle}(z)\) be its unique compositional inverse satisfying \(A(z) = z (1 + A(z))^\alpha\). What is the differential conversion factor between \(\frac{du}{(1+u)^\alpha}\) and \(dz\)? Differentiate \(z = u(1+u)^{-\alpha}\) logarithmically: \[\frac{dz}{z} = \left(\frac{1}{u} - \frac{\alpha}{1 + u}\right) du = \frac{1 - (\alpha - 1)u}{u(1 + u)}\,du \implies dz = \frac{1 - (\alpha - 1)u}{(1 + u)^{\alpha + 1}}\,du \implies \frac{du}{(1 + u)^\alpha} = \frac{1 + u}{1 - (\alpha - 1)u}\,dz.\] Substituting \(u = A(z)\) via the Formal Residue Change-of-Variables Theorem (Ch 11, Theorem 11.1) turns \(\operatorname{Res}_u (\dots) G(u)^{-n-1} G'(u)\,du\) directly into \([z^n]\)!


3. Single-Step Verbalized Derivation of the Master Identity
Let \(F(w) := \sum_{k=0}^N f_k w^k\) be the ordinary generating function of the sequence \((f_k)\). Summing over \(k = 0 \dots n\) (since terms with \(k > n\) have \(\operatorname{val}_u\big(u^{k-n-1}(1+u)^{\dots}\big) \ge 0\) and zero residue at \(u^{-1}\)):

Express \(S_n\) as a single \(u\)-residue: \[S_n = \operatorname{Res}_u \left( F\big(u(1 + u)^\beta\big) \cdot (1 + u)^\gamma \cdot \left(\frac{u}{(1 + u)^\alpha}\right)^{-n-1} \frac{du}{(1 + u)^\alpha} \right).\]
Substitute \(\frac{du}{(1+u)^\alpha} = \frac{1+u}{1 - (\alpha-1)u}\,dz\) where \(z = u(1+u)^{-\alpha}\): \[S_n = \operatorname{Res}_u \left( F\big(u(1 + u)^\beta\big) \cdot \frac{(1 + u)^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - (\alpha - 1) u} \cdot z(u)^{-n-1}\,dz(u) \right).\]
Apply the Change-of-Variables Theorem \(u = A(z)\) (Ch 11): \[S_n = \operatorname{Res}_z \left( F\!\Big(A(z)\big(1 + A(z)\big)^\beta\Big) \cdot \frac{\big(1 + A(z)\big)^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - (\alpha - 1) A(z)} \cdot z^{-n-1}\,dz \right).\]
Read off the coefficient \([z^n]\) for all \(0 \le n \le N\) simultaneously: \[\sum_{n=0}^{N} S_n z^n \equiv F\!\Big(A(z)\big(1 + A(z)\big)^\beta\Big) \cdot \frac{\big(1 + A(z)\big)^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - (\alpha - 1) A(z)} \pmod{z^{N+1}}.\]







NoteTheorem 21.1 (Elegia’s Coupled Binomial Sum Linearization / 炫酷反演魔术)



Let \(F(w) = \sum_{k=0}^N f_k w^k \in K[[w]]\) and \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in K\).

Simultaneous All-\(n\) \(z\)-Plane Form: Let \(A(z) \in z K[[z]]\) be the unique root of \(A(z) = z(1 + A(z))^\alpha\) (computable up to \(z^{N+1}\) via closed-form Raney series [z^m] A(z) = \frac{1}{m}\binom{\alpha m}{m-1} or compositional inversion of \(u(1+u)^{-\alpha}\)). Defining the inner series \(W(z) := A(z)(1 + A(z))^\beta \bmod z^{N+1}\) (which has \([z^0]W(z) = 0\)), a single call to Kinoshita–Li compose \(F(W(z)) \bmod z^{N+1}\) evaluates \(S_0, S_1, \dots, S_N\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time: \[S_n = [z^n] \left( F\!\Big(A(z)\big(1 + A(z)\big)^\beta\Big) \cdot \frac{\big(1 + A(z)\big)^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - (\alpha - 1) A(z)} \right).\]
Single-\(n\) \(w\)-Plane Convolution Form: If only a single \(S_n\) is needed for a fixed \(n\), instead change variables via \(w = u(1+u)^\beta \iff u = g(w) = w(1 + g(w))^{-\beta}\), so \(\frac{w}{g(w)} = (1 + g(w))^{\beta}\) and \(\frac{dw}{du} = (1+u)^{\beta-1}(1 + (\beta+1)u) \implies g'(w) = \frac{(1+g(w))^{1-\beta}}{1+(\beta+1)g(w)}\). Substituting \(u = g(w)\) into the \(u\)-residue \(\operatorname{Res}_u F(u(1+u)^\beta)(1+u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} u^{-n-1}\,du\) gives: \[
\begin{aligned}
S_n
&= [w^n] \left[ F(w) \big(1 + g(w)\big)^{\alpha n + \gamma} \left(\frac{w}{g(w)}\right)^{n+1} g'(w) \right] \\[4pt]
&= [w^n] \left[ F(w) \big(1 + g(w)\big)^{\alpha n + \gamma} \big(1 + g(w)\big)^{\beta(n+1)} \frac{\big(1 + g(w)\big)^{1 - \beta}}{1 + (\beta + 1) g(w)} \right] \\[4pt]
&= [w^n] \left[ F(w) \cdot \frac{\big(1 + g(w)\big)^{(\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma + 1}}{1 + (\beta + 1) g(w)} \right].
\end{aligned}
\]





Hand-Checkable Toy Trace (\(N = 3\))
Let \(\alpha = 2, \beta = -1, \gamma = 0\), and \(F(w) = 1 + w\) (\(f_0 = 1, f_1 = 1, f_{\ge 2} = 0\)), so \(S_n = \binom{2n}{n} + \binom{2n - 1}{n - 1}\).

Direct check:

\(n = 0\): \(\binom{0}{0} + 0 = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(\binom{2}{1} + \binom{1}{0} = 2 + 1 = 3\).
\(n = 2\): \(\binom{4}{2} + \binom{3}{1} = 6 + 3 = 9\).
\(n = 3\): \(\binom{6}{3} + \binom{5}{2} = 20 + 10 = 30\).

Trace via Theorem 21.1: Here \(A(z) = z(1 + A(z))^2 = C(z) - 1 = z + 2z^2 + 5z^3 + \dots\), so \(W(z) = A(z)(1 + A(z))^{-1} = \frac{A(z)}{1 + A(z)} = z(1 + A(z)) = z + z^2 + 2z^3 + \dots\), and \(\frac{1 + A(z)}{1 - A(z)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4z}} = 1 + 2z + 6z^2 + 20z^3 + \dots\). Multiplying \(F(W(z)) = 1 + W(z) = 1 + z + z^2 + 2z^3 + \dots\) by \(1 + 2z + 6z^2 + 20z^3 + \dots\) modulo \(z^4\) gives: \[(1 + z + z^2 + 2z^3)(1 + 2z + 6z^2 + 20z^3) \equiv 1 + 3z + 9z^2 + 30z^3 \pmod{z^4},\] matching \((S_0, S_1, S_2, S_3) = (1, 3, 9, 30)\).







ImportantAlgorithm Contract: Elegia’s All-\(n\) Coupled Binomial Sum Linearization




Inputs: Coefficient sequence \(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_N \in K\), linear parameters \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in K\), and degree bound \(N \ge 1\).
Outputs: Sequence \(S_0, S_1, \dots, S_N\) where \(S_n = \sum_{k=0}^n f_k \binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k}\) for all \(0 \le n \le N\).
Algebraic Preconditions: The inverse series \(A(z) = z(1 + A(z))^\alpha \bmod z^{N+1}\) and fractional power \((1 + A(z))^\beta \bmod z^{N+1}\) require \(1, 2, \dots, N \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\)) when computed via fps_ln / fps_exp or Raney coefficients (or \(2 \in K^\times\) via Route B revert when \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{Z}\)).
Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time (dominated by one call to fps_compose(W, F, N + 1)) and \(O(N \log N)\) space.
Core Invariant: Under the change of variables \(z = u(1 + u)^{-\alpha} \iff u = A(z)\) with differential Jacobian \(\frac{du}{(1+u)^\alpha} = \frac{1+u}{1 - (\alpha-1)u}\,dz\), the \(u\)-residue \(\operatorname{Res}_u F(u(1+u)^\beta)(1+u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} u^{-n-1}\,du\) maps bijectively to \([z^n]\Big(F(W(z)) \frac{(1+A(z))^{\gamma+1}}{1-(\alpha-1)A(z)}\Big)\) for every \(n \ge 0\).

title: 21 — Power Projection, Kinoshita–Li FPS Composition (compose) & Compositional Inverse (revert)
section: 21.4 Dual-Route Compositional Inverse (revert), Failure Mode #6 & Functional Square Roots \(G(G(x)) = F(x)\)
text:
21.4 Dual-Route Compositional Inverse (revert), Failure Mode #6 & Functional Square Roots \(G(G(x)) = F(x)\)
Given \(F(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} f_i x^i \in x K[[x]] / (x^N)\) with unit linear coefficient \(f_1 = [x^1] F(x) \in K^\times\), we want to compute its unique compositional inverse \(G(y) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y) = \sum_{k=1}^{N-1} g_k y^k \bmod y^N\) satisfying \(F(G(y)) \equiv y \pmod{y^N}\) and \(G(F(x)) \equiv x \pmod{x^N}\).
Depending on whether the field characteristic \(p = \operatorname{char}(K)\) satisfies \(p > N\) (or \(p = 0\)) versus \(p \le N\), there are two distinct \(O(N \log^2 N)\) algorithms for revert. Knowing both routes—and why Route A suffers a catastrophic division-by-zero crash when \(p \le N\)—is mandatory for mastery-tier competitive programming.

Route A (noshi91 LIF + Power Projection — When \(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\))

1. The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
In §21.1, we saw that running power_projection with the single weight \(w_n = 1\) (where \(n = N - 1\) and \(w_i = 0\) for \(i \ne n\)) computes the sequence of coefficients \([x^n] F(x)^k\) for all \(k = 1, 2, \dots, n\) simultaneously in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time. How are the coefficients \([x^n] F(x)^k\) related to the compositional inverse \(G(y) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y)\)? By Classical Lagrange Inversion (Ch 11, Theorem 11.2, Variant C) applied with the roles of \(F\) and \(G\) swapped (\(G(F(x)) = x\), so \(F(x) = \frac{x}{G(F(x))/F(x)}\)): \[[x^n] F(x)^k = \frac{k}{n} [y^{n-k}] \left(\frac{y}{G(y)}\right)^n = \frac{k}{n} [y^{n-k}] \left(\frac{G(y)}{y}\right)^{-n} \qquad (1 \le k \le n).\]


2. Single-Step Verbalized Algorithm (noshi91, 2024)
Let \(n = N - 1\) and define the unit-constant series \(H(y) := \left(\frac{G(y)}{y}\right)^{-n} \in K[[y]] / (y^n)\).

Power Projection: Call power_projection(F, e_n, N) with \(\mathbf{w} = e_n = (0, \dots, 0, 1)^\top\) to obtain \(p_k = [x^n] F(x)^k\) for \(1 \le k \le n\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time.
Lagrange Scaling & Index Reversal: For each \(k = 1, \dots, n\), set \[[y^{n-k}] H(y) = \frac{n}{k} p_k = \frac{n}{k} [x^n] F(x)^k.\] This determines all coefficients of \(H(y) \bmod y^n\).
Power Extraction (pow(-1/n)): Since \(\frac{G(y)}{y} = H(y)^{-1/n}\) and \([y^0] H(y) = f_1^n \in K^\times\), compute \[\frac{G(y)}{y} \equiv f_1^{-1} \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{n} \ln\!\big(f_1^{-n} H(y)\big)\right) \pmod{y^n}\] in \(O(N \log N)\) time, and multiply by \(y\) to obtain \(G(y) \bmod y^N\).




Route B (Newton Iteration + Kinoshita–Li compose — Mandatory When \(p \le N\))
What happens to Route A if we work modulo a small prime \(p \le N\) (or over an arbitrary characteristic-\(p\) field)? Both Step 2 (\(\frac{n}{k}\)) and Step 3 (\(\exp(-\frac{1}{n}\ln(\dots))\)) divide by every integer \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, N-1\}\) and by \(n = N - 1\), crashing at \(k = p, 2p, \dots\).

1. The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
To avoid dividing by \(1, 2, \dots, N-1\), view \(G(y)\) as the root of the functional equation \[\Phi(G)(y) := F(G(y)) - y = 0.\] Suppose we know \(G_s(y) \equiv G(y) \pmod{y^{2^s}}\) (starting from \(G_0(y) = f_1^{-1} y \bmod y^2\)). Write \(G_{s+1}(y) = G_s(y) + \Delta(y)\) where \(\operatorname{val}_y(\Delta) \ge 2^s\), so \(\Delta(y)^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{y^{2^{s+1}}}\). By the Hasse–Taylor expansion of \(F\) around \(G_s(y)\) (which requires zero factorials, since \(\binom{j}{1} = j \in \mathbb{Z}\)): \[0 \equiv F(G_s(y) + \Delta(y)) - y \equiv F(G_s(y)) - y + F'(G_s(y)) \Delta(y) \pmod{y^{2^{s+1}}}.\] Solving for \(\Delta(y)\) yields the quadratic Newton step: \[G_{s+1}(y) \equiv G_s(y) - \frac{F(G_s(y)) - y}{F'(G_s(y))} \pmod{y^{2^{s+1}}}.\]


2. Why Route B Never Divides by \(1, 2, \dots, N-1\)
At precision \(L = 2^{s+1}\):

We evaluate \(F(G_s(y)) \bmod y^L\) and \(F'(G_s(y)) \bmod y^{L/2}\) using Kinoshita–Li compose (§21.2), which is \(100\%\) free of divisions by \(1, \dots, L-1\) since \([y^0] G_s(y) = 0\).
We invert \(F'(G_s(y)) \bmod y^{L/2}\) via multiplicative Newton inversion (fps_inv). What is the constant term of \(F'(G_s(y))\)? Since \(G_s(0) = 0\), \([y^0] F'(G_s(y)) = F'(0) = f_1 \in K^\times\), which is invertible by hypothesis!
Total time across \(s = 0, 1, \dots, \log_2 N - 1\) satisfies the geometric sum \[T(N) = \sum_{s=1}^{\log_2 N} O(2^s \log^2(2^s)) = O(N \log^2 N).\]







WarningCanonical Failure Mode #6: Calling LIF + Power Projection (Route A) When \(p \le N\)




The Bug: Using Route A ([y^{n-k}](G(y)/y)^{-n} = (n/k)[x^n]F(x)^k followed by pow(-1/n)) when the prime modulus \(p\) satisfies \(p \le N\) (or when \(p \mid (N - 1)\)).
Why It Crashes: Even though the true compositional inverse \(G(y) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y)\) has coefficients in \(\mathbb{Z}[f_1^{-1}, f_2, f_3, \dots]\)—meaning \(G(y) \bmod y^N\) is well-defined over every ring where \(f_1 \in R^\times\), with zero division by \(2, 3, \dots, N-1\)—Route A routes the computation through the intermediate transcendental operation ln / exp and the Lagrange factor \(\frac{n}{k}\), both of which divide by \(p\) whenever \(k = p\) or \(p \mid n\).
The Remedy:

When \(p > N\) (e.g., \(p = 998244353, N \le 5 \times 10^5\)): Route A is roughly \(2\times\) faster in practice because it calls power_projection only once at size \(N\) (no backward pass, no Newton outer loop).
When \(p \le N\) (small prime modulus): Route B (Newton Iteration + Kinoshita–Li compose + fps_inv) is mandatory and computes \(G(y) \bmod y^N\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time for every prime \(p \ne 2\) with \(f_1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).










ImportantAlgorithm Contract: Dual-Route Compositional Inverse (fps_revert)




Input: \(F(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} f_i x^i \in x K[[x]]/(x^N)\) with \([x^0] F(x) = 0\) and \([x^1] F(x) = f_1 \in K^\times\).
Output: \(G(y) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y) \bmod y^N\) satisfying \(F(G(y)) \equiv y \pmod{y^N}\).
Algebraic Preconditions:

Route A (revert_lif_proj): Requires \(f_1 \in K^\times\) and \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\)).
Route B (revert_newton_compose): Requires only \(f_1 \in K^\times\) and \(2 \in K^\times\) (for radix-2 FFT/NTT).

Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) (Route A) or \(O(N \log N)\) (Route B) space.
Core Invariant: In Route A, \(H(y) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{n}{k} ([x^n]F(x)^k) y^{n-k} \equiv (G(y)/y)^{-n} \pmod{y^n}\); in Route B, \(F(G_s(y)) \equiv y \pmod{y^{2^s}}\) doubles precision at every step \(s\).



// Route A (p > N): 1 Power Projection + pow(-1/n); Route B (all p != 2): Newton + compose
Poly fps_revert_routeA(const Poly& F, int N) { // Precondition: F[0] == 0, F[1] != 0, p > N
    int n = N - 1; Poly w(N, 0), H(n); w[n] = 1; Poly proj = power_projection(F, w, N);
    for (int k = 1; k <= n; ++k) H[n - k] = proj[k] * Mint(n) * Mint(k).inv();
    Poly G = fps_pow(H, -Mint(n).inv(), n); G.insert(G.begin(), 0); return G;
}
Poly fps_revert_routeB(const Poly& F, int N) { // Precondition: F[0] == 0, F[1] != 0 (p <= N!)
    Poly G = {0, F[1].inv()}, dF = fps_deriv(F);
    for (int L = 2; L < N; L <<= 1) {
        Poly FG = fps_compose(G, trunc(F, 2 * L), 2 * L); FG[1] -= 1; // F(G_s(y)) - y
        G = fps_sub(G, fps_mul_trunc(FG, fps_inv(fps_compose(G, trunc(dF, L), L), L), 2 * L));
    }
    G.resize(N); return G;
}






TipRevisited #8 (#200 Luogu P7438 — [AGM 2021] 恐龙) & Revisited #12 (#201 Luogu P7439 — [KrOI2021] 蕾切尔 / #036 ABC 281 Ex): Single-\(N\) LIF vs. Simultaneous All-\(n\) revert & compose



In Chapter 11 (SS-2, #200 Luogu P7438 & Int-2, #201 Luogu P7439), we were given an implicit tree generating function \(F(x) = x \phi(F(x))\) (\(\phi(0) \ne 0\)) or a composite generating function \(H(F(x))\) (such as \(G(e^x - 1)\) in #036 ABC 281 Ex — Alchemy and #201 Luogu P7439 — [KrOI2021] 蕾切尔) and asked to extract a single coefficient \([x^N] F(x)^k\) or \([x^N] H(F(x)) \pmod{998244353}\) for \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\).

Chapter 11 Perspective (Single-\(N\) Lagrange Inversion & Residue Change of Variables): Rewriting \(F(x) = x \phi(F(x))\) as \(\frac{F(x)}{\phi(F(x))} = x\) (or substituting \(u = F(x) \iff x = A(u)\)) extracts the single target coefficient in \(O(N \log N)\) time via one polynomial pow: \[[x^N] F(x)^k = \frac{k}{N} [u^{N-k}] \phi(u)^N, \qquad [x^N] H(F(x)) = [u^N] \left( H(u) A'(u) \left(\frac{u}{A(u)}\right)^{N+1} \right).\]
Chapter 21 Perspective (Simultaneous All-\(n\) Extraction via revert & compose): What if a problem requires \([x^n] F(x)\) or \([x^n] H(F(x))\) for every \(n = 1, 2, \dots, N\) simultaneously, and \(\phi(u), H(u)\) are arbitrary dense series that have no simple differential equation? Since \(A(u) = \frac{u}{\phi(u)}\) is the compositional inverse of \(F(x)\), a single call to fps_revert on \(u \phi(u)^{-1} \bmod u^{N+1}\) recovers the entire series \(F(x) \bmod x^{N+1}\)—and a follow-up call to fps_compose(F, H, N + 1) computes \(H(F(x)) \bmod x^{N+1}\) for all \(n \le N\) at once—in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time.









TipRevisited #9 (#183 Luogu P5827 — 点双连通图计数): Single-\(N\) Block-Cut LIF vs. All-\(n\) revert + compose



In Chapter 12 (Mas-1, #183 Luogu P5827), we enumerated labeled 2-vertex-connected (biconnected) graphs on \(N \le 10^5\) vertices using Tutte’s fundamental block-cut tree equation: \[R(x) = x \exp\!\Big(B'\big(R(x)\big)\Big) \iff \ln\!\left(\frac{R(x)}{x}\right) = B'\big(R(x)\big),\] where \(G(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} 2^{\binom{n}{2}} \frac{x^n}{n!}\) is all labeled graphs, \(C(x) = \ln G(x)\) is connected labeled graphs, \(R(x) = x C'(x)\) is vertex-rooted connected graphs, and \(B(y) = \sum_{n \ge 2} b_n \frac{y^n}{n!}\) is biconnected labeled graphs.

Chapter 12 Perspective (Single-\(N\) Lagrange Inversion): To find \(b_N\) for a single \(N \ge 3\), let \(H(x) := \ln(R(x)/x) = \ln C'(x)\). Since \(B'(y) = H(R^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y))\), Classical LIF extracts \([y^{N-1}] B'(y)\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time: \[b_N = (N-1)! [y^{N-1}] B'(y) = (N-2)! [x^{N-1}] \left( H'(x) \left(\frac{x}{R(x)}\right)^{N-1} \right) = -(N-2)! [x^{N-1}] \Big(C'(x)^{-(N-1)}\Big).\]
Chapter 21 Perspective (All-\(n\) Biconnected Graph Table \(b_2, b_3, \dots, b_N\)): To compute \(b_n\) for all \(2 \le n \le N\) simultaneously (AtCoder fps_24_w / multi-query biconnected enumeration), we cannot afford \(N\) separate polynomial powers \(C'(x)^{-(n-1)}\). Instead:

Compute \(C(x) = \ln G(x) \bmod x^{N+1}\), \(R(x) = x C'(x) \bmod x^{N+1}\), and \(H(x) = \ln(R(x)/x) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(N \log N)\).
Compute the compositional inverse \(R^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y) \bmod y^N\) via fps_revert in \(O(N \log^2 N)\).
Compose \(B'(y) = H\big(R^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y)\big) \bmod y^N\) via fps_compose in \(O(N \log^2 N)\), reading off \(b_n = (n-1)! [y^{n-1}] B'(y)\) for all \(2 \le n \le N\) simultaneously!







Functional Square Roots \(G(G(x)) = F(x) \bmod x^N\) & The Degree \(p + 2\) Artin–Schreier Obstruction
A closely related compositional problem is the Functional Square Root (AtCoder fps_24_x): given \(F(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{N-1} f_k x^k \in x \mathbb{F}_p[[x]] / (x^N)\) over an odd prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p\), find \(G(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{N-1} g_k x^k\) such that \[G(G(x)) \equiv F(x) \pmod{x^N}.\]

1. Degree-by-Degree Indeterminate Analysis
Comparing \([x^1]\) on both sides gives \(g_1^2 \equiv f_1 \pmod p\). Once we fix a square root \(g_1 \in \mathbb{F}_p\), what equation governs the \(k\)-th coefficient \(g_k\) (\(k \ge 2\)) in terms of \(g_1, \dots, g_{k-1}\)? In \(G(G(x)) = \sum_{m=1}^{N-1} g_m G(x)^m\), the unknown \(g_k\) appears in only two places at degree \(x^k\):

Inside the \(m = 1\) term \(g_1 G(x)\), which contributes \(g_1 g_k x^k\).
Inside the \(m = k\) term \(g_k G(x)^k = g_k (g_1 x + \dots)^k\), which contributes \(g_k g_1^k x^k\).

All terms with \(2 \le m \le k - 1\) depend solely on \(g_1, \dots, g_{k-1}\). Therefore: \[g_1 \big(1 + g_1^{k-1}\big) g_k = f_k - [x^k] \sum_{m=2}^{k-1} g_m G_{<k}(x)^m.\]
Look at the multiplier \(g_1(1 + g_1^{k-1})\):

Tangent-to-Identity Case (\(f_1 = 1\), choosing \(g_1 = 1\)): For every \(k \ge 2\), the multiplier is \(1 \cdot (1 + 1^{k-1}) = 2 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (since \(p\) is an odd prime)! Thus a unique tangent-to-identity functional square root \(G(x) = x + g_2 x^2 + \dots\) exists for every \(N\) and every odd prime \(p\), with zero division by \(k\)!
Non-Unit-Multiplier Obstructions: If \(g_1 = 0\) (\(f_1 = 0\)), \(\operatorname{val}(G) \ge 2 \implies \operatorname{val}(G \circ G) \ge 4\). If \(g_1 \not\equiv 0, 1 \pmod p\) has even multiplicative order \(2d\) so \(g_1^{k-1} \equiv -1 \pmod p\) for \(k = d + 1\), then \(1 + g_1^{k-1} \equiv 0 \pmod p\), creating a resonance obstruction unless the right-hand side vanishes.



2. maspy’s Period-\(p\) Shortcut vs. The Degree \(p + 2\) Artin–Schreier Obstruction
When \(g_1 = 1\) (\(F(x) = x + f_2 x^2 + \dots\)) and \(N \le p + 1\), maspy’s Jordan Block Theorem shows that the linear composition operator \(T_G : A(x) \mapsto A(G(x))\) on the \(p\)-dimensional vector space \(V = x\mathbb{F}_p[x]/(x^{p+1})\) is upper unitriangular (\(T_G(x^k) = x^k + k g_2 x^{k+1} + \dots\)), so \((T_G - I)^p = T_{G^{\circ p}} - I = 0\) on \(V\). Consequently, every tangent-to-identity series satisfies \(G^{\circ p}(x) \equiv x \pmod{x^{p+1}}\), and the unique functional square root modulo \(x^{p+1}\) is simply the \(\frac{p+1}{2}\)-th compositional iterate of \(F(x)\): \[G(x) \equiv F^{\circ \left(\frac{p+1}{2}\right)}(x) \pmod{x^{p+1}}.\]






WarningThe Degree \(p + 2\) Artin–Schreier Obstruction to maspy’s Period-\(p\) Shortcut



Why does the cyclic-group shortcut \(G^{\circ p}(x) \equiv x\) fail at degree \(N = p + 2\)?

Consider the Artin–Schreier generator \(G(x) = x + x^2 = \frac{x}{1 - x} \bmod x^4\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\). Since \(\frac{x}{1 - c x}\) composes additively in \(c\), the \(p\)-fold iterate of \(\frac{x}{1 - x}\) is \(\frac{x}{1 - p x} \equiv x \pmod p\).
However, if we perturb \(G(x)\) at degree \(3\), say \(G(x) = x + x^2 + c x^3\), the \(p\)-fold composition \(G^{\circ p}(x)\) still equals \(x\) modulo \(x^{p+1}\), and even modulo \(x^{p+2}\) only when \(c = 1\)! Specifically, expanding \(G^{\circ p}(x) \bmod x^{p+2}\) for a general \(G(x) = x + g_2 x^2 + g_3 x^3 + \dots\) reveals the Artin–Schreier residue obstruction at degree \(x^{p+2}\) (and already at \(p = 2\), \(G(x) = x + x^2 \implies G(G(x)) = (x+x^2) + (x+x^2)^2 \equiv x + x^4 \pmod 2\), which is non-zero at degree \(p + 2 = 4\)).
Remedy: For general \(N > p + 1\) (or whenever binary exponentiation of compose in \(O(N \log^2 N \log p)\) is slower than Newton iteration), solve \(G(G(x)) - F(x) = 0 \bmod x^N\) via Newton Iteration (Mas-2 below) or incremental degree-by-degree extraction.
