title: Chapter 19: Coupled Sparse Composition, WZ Creative Telescoping & Truncated Taylor ODEs
section: 19.3 Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition \(F(P(x))\) & EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (\(F_{<N}'\))
text:
19.3 Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition \(F(P(x))\) & EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (\(F_{<N}'\))

Part A: Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition \(H(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(rNK)\)
In Chapter 2, we learned how to compute \(P(x)^\alpha\), \(\exp(P(x))\), and \(\ln(P(x))\) in \(O(NK)\) time when \(P(x)\) is a \(K\)-sparse polynomial (having at most \(K\) non-zero coefficients) by differentiating once: for example, \(H(x) = \exp(P(x))\) satisfies the first-order ODE \(H'(x) = P'(x) H(x)\).
What if the outer series \(F(y)\) is a general D-finite series of order \(r \ge 2\), satisfying an order-\(r\) linear ODE \[F^{(r)}(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} a_i(y) \, F^{(i)}(y)\] with polynomial (or rational) coefficients \(a_i(y)\), and we want to compute the composition \(H(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) for a \(K\)-sparse polynomial \(P(x)\) with \(P(0) = 0\)?






WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: The \(1/P'(x)\) Sparsity-Destruction Trap



The Trap: If you try to form a single order-\(r\) ODE for \(H(x) = F(P(x))\) using the chain-rule operator \(\mathcal{D}_P = \frac{1}{P'(x)} \frac{d}{dx}\) from Chapter 18.3, two disasters occur when \(r \ge 2\):

Valuation Singularity at \(x = 0\): For \(r = 2\), clearing denominators in \(\mathcal{D}_P^2 H + a_1(P)\mathcal{D}_P H + a_0(P) H = 0\) produces: \[P'(x) H''(x) - \big(P''(x) + a_1(P(x)) P'(x)^2\big) H'(x) - a_0(P(x)) P'(x)^3 H(x) = 0.\] Whenever \([x^1]P(x) = 0\) (for example, \(P(x) = x^2 + x^5\), so \(\operatorname{val}(P') = 1\)), the leading coefficient \(P'(x)\) vanishes at \(x = 0\), creating an apparent singularity where the indicial polynomial vanishes!
Sparsity Explosion: Even if \([x^1]P(x) \neq 0\), multiplying by \(P'(x)^r\) expands a \(K\)-sparse polynomial into \(O(K^r)\) terms (or \(O(N)\) terms if you invert \(P'(x)\)), destroying the \(O(NK)\) runtime!

The Remedy (Coupled \(r\)-State First-Order System): Never eliminate \(F'(P(x)), \dots, F^{(r-1)}(P(x))\)! Instead, maintain all \(r\) derivatives evaluated at \(P(x)\) simultaneously as a coupled first-order system.








TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition




The Diagnostic Signal: You need \(H(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) where \(P(x)\) is \(K\)-sparse (\(K \ll \log^2 N\)) with \(P(0) = 0\), and \(F(y)\) satisfies an order-\(r\) linear ODE \(q_r(y) F^{(r)}(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} q_i(y) F^{(i)}(y)\) with \(q_r(0) \neq 0\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Define the \(r\) coupled formal power series: \[H_0(x) = F(P(x)), \quad H_1(x) = F'(P(x)), \quad \dots, \quad H_{r-1}(x) = F^{(r-1)}(P(x)).\] Differentiate each \(H_i(x)\) once with respect to \(x\) using the chain rule: \[\begin{aligned}
H_0'(x) &= P'(x) \, H_1(x), \\
H_1'(x) &= P'(x) \, H_2(x), \\
&\;\;\vdots \\
q_r(P(x)) \, H_{r-1}'(x) &= P'(x) \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} q_i(P(x)) \, H_i(x).
\end{aligned}\] Look at what happened:

We never divided by \(P'(x)\)! Even if \(P(x) = x^3 + x^7\), the coefficient of \([x^{n-1}] H_i'(x)\) is simply \(n [x^n] H_i(x)\), which is always nonsingular for every \(n \ge 1\)!
To advance from degree \(n - 1\) to degree \(n\), we first extract \([x^{n-1}]\) from the last equation to get \([x^n] H_{r-1}(x)\) (using only \([x^{\le n-1}] H_0, \dots, H_{r-1}\) since \(\operatorname{val}(P) \ge 1\)), and similarly extract \([x^{n-1}]\) from \(H_i'(x) = P'(x) H_{i+1}(x)\) for \(i = 0, \dots, r-2\). Every equation multiplies by the sparse polynomial \(P'(x)\) in \(O(K)\) time!




// Coupled 2-State Sparse Composition: solves F''(y) = a1*F'(y) + a0*F(y) at y = P(x)
for (int n = 1; n < N; ++n) {
    long long s0 = 0, s1 = 0;
    for (auto [d, c] : sp_P) { // non-zero (deg >= 1, coeff) of K-sparse P(x)
        if (d > n) break;
        long long dc = d * c % MOD;
        s0 = (s0 + dc * H1[n - d]) % MOD;
        s1 = (s1 + dc * ((a0 * H0[n - d] + a1 * H1[n - d]) % MOD)) % MOD;
    }
    H0[n] = s0 * inv[n] % MOD; H1[n] = s1 * inv[n] % MOD;
}

Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): \(F(y) = \sin y + \cos y\) Composed with \(P(x) = x + x^3\)
Here \(F''(y) = -F(y)\) (\(r = 2, a_0 = -1, a_1 = 0\)) with \(F(0) = 1, F'(0) = 1\). Let \(H_0(x) = F(P(x))\) and \(H_1(x) = F'(P(x)) = \cos P(x) - \sin P(x)\). Since \(P'(x) = 1 + 3x^2\), the coupled system is \(H_0'(x) = (1 + 3x^2) H_1(x)\) and \(H_1'(x) = -(1 + 3x^2) H_0(x)\), giving: \[n h_{0, n} = h_{1, n-1} + 3 h_{1, n-3}, \qquad n h_{1, n} = -h_{0, n-1} - 3 h_{0, n-3}.\]

\(n = 0\): \(h_{0, 0} = 1, \quad h_{1, 0} = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(h_{0, 1} = \frac{1}{1}(1) = 1, \quad h_{1, 1} = \frac{1}{1}(-1) = -1\).
\(n = 2\): \(h_{0, 2} = \frac{1}{2}(-1) = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad h_{1, 2} = \frac{1}{2}(-1) = -\frac{1}{2}\).
\(n = 3\): \(h_{0, 3} = \frac{1}{3}\left(-\frac{1}{2} + 3(1)\right) = \frac{5}{6}, \quad h_{1, 3} = \frac{1}{3}\left(-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) - 3(1)\right) = -\frac{5}{6}\).
\(n = 4\): \(h_{0, 4} = \frac{1}{4}\left(-\frac{5}{6} + 3(-1)\right) = -\frac{23}{24}\).
Direct Taylor Verification: \(\sin(x + x^3) + \cos(x + x^3) = \left((x + x^3) - \frac{x^3}{6}\right) + \left(1 - \frac{(x+x^3)^2}{2} + \frac{x^4}{24}\right) + O(x^5) = 1 + x - \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{5}{6}x^3 - \frac{23}{24}x^4 + O(x^5)\), matching every coefficient!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition Engine




Input: Order-\(r\) linear ODE \(q_r(y) F^{(r)}(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} q_i(y) F^{(i)}(y)\) with initial values \(F^{(i)}(0) = f_i\) (\(0 \le i < r\)), a \(K\)-sparse polynomial \(P(x) = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j x^{d_j}\) with \(1 \le d_1 < \dots < d_K < N\), and precision \(N\).
Output: \(H_0(x) = F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) (along with \(H_i(x) = F^{(i)}(P(x)) \bmod x^N\)).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(P(0) = 0\) (\(\operatorname{val}(P) \ge 1\)), \(q_r(0) \in K^\times\), and \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (\(p \ge N\)).
Complexity: \(O(r \cdot D \cdot N \cdot K)\) time and \(O(r N)\) space, where \(D = 1 + \max_i \deg q_i(y)\) (so \(O(rNK)\) when \(q_i\) are constants or degree \(O(1)\)).
Correctness Invariant: Because \(\operatorname{val}(P) \ge 1\), \(\operatorname{val}(P') \ge 0\), so \([x^{n-1}]\big(P'(x) P(x)^m H_i(x)\big)\) depends only on \([x^k] H_i(x)\) for \(0 \le k \le n - 1\); thus at step \(n\), all right-hand side terms are already finalized before dividing by \(n \cdot q_r(0)\).







Part B: EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (\(A(x) F_{<N}' + B(x) F_{<N} = C(x) - R_N(x)\))
Suppose an infinite formal power series \(F(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n x^n\) satisfies a simple first-order linear ODE \[A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\] where \(A(x), B(x), C(x) \in K[x]\) are low-degree polynomials. In many combinatorics problems, however, we do not work with the infinite series \(F(x)\)—we work with its degree-\((N-1)\) truncation: \[F_{<N}(x) = F(x) \bmod x^N = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n x^n.\] For example:

We may need the Taylor shift \(F_{<N}(x + c)\) (or \(F_{<N}(x - 1)\)) to convert between binomial moments, falling factorials, or inclusion-exclusion states. Computing \(F_{<N}(x + c)\) via Chapter 6’s reversed convolution costs \(O(N \log N)\) time via NTT.
Or we may need to integrate products of truncated exponentials \(S_{<a}(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{a-1} \frac{x^j}{j!} = e^x \bmod x^a\) in continuous-time Poissonization (UOJ 514).

Elegia’s Breakthrough (EI 科技): If \(F(x)\) satisfies a sparse polynomial ODE, then its truncation \(F_{<N}(x)\) satisfies the exact same left-hand differential operator with a tiny polynomial remainder \(R_N(x)\) on the right-hand side! And because a polynomial ODE is preserved under any affine shift \(x \gets u + c\), we can unroll the shifted polynomial \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c)\) directly in \(O(N)\) time with zero NTTs!






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Truncated Taylor ODEs




The Diagnostic Signal: You need to shift, multiply, or integrate a truncated series \(F_{<N}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n x^n\) whose parent series \(F(x)\) satisfies a known low-degree ODE \(A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\) (such as \((1+x)^\alpha\), \(e^x\), or \((1-x)^{-\alpha}\)).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Split the infinite series into its head and tail: \[F(x) = F_{<N}(x) + F_{\ge N}(x), \qquad F_{\ge N}(x) = \sum_{n=N}^{\infty} f_n x^n.\] Substitute this split into \(A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\) and move the tail to the right-hand side: \[A(x) F_{<N}'(x) + B(x) F_{<N}(x) = C(x) - \underbrace{\Big( A(x) F_{\ge N}'(x) + B(x) F_{\ge N}(x) \Big)}_{R_N(x)}.\] Now look simultaneously at the maximum degree of the left-hand side and the minimum valuation of the right-hand side:

Since \(\deg F_{<N} \le N - 1\) and \(\deg F_{<N}' \le N - 2\), the left-hand side is a polynomial of degree at most \(N - 1 + d\), where \(d = \max(\deg A - 1, \deg B)\).
On the right-hand side, \(\operatorname{val}(F_{\ge N}) \ge N\) and \(\operatorname{val}(F_{\ge N}') \ge N - 1\), so every term of \(F_{\ge N}\) above \(f_{N+d-1} x^{N+d-1}\) has degree \(\ge N + d\) and cancels identically against \(C(x)\)! Therefore, \(R_N(x)\) is a sparse polynomial localized in degrees \([N - 1, N + d - 1]\) depending on at most \(d + 1\) boundary coefficients \(f_N, f_{N+1}, \dots, f_{N+d}\)!










ImportantTheorem 19.2 (Two Canonical Instances of EI 科技 Truncated ODEs)




Truncated Binomial Series \(F_{<N}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \binom{\alpha}{k} x^k = (1 + x)^\alpha \bmod x^N\): Here \(A(x) = 1 + x, B(x) = -\alpha, C(x) = 0\), so \(d = \max(0, 0) = 0\). The tail \(R_N(x)\) has only a single degree-\((N-1)\) monomial coming from \(1 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\big(\binom{\alpha}{N} x^N\big)\): \[(1 + x) F_{<N}'(x) - \alpha F_{<N}(x) = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} x^{N-1}.\] To compute the shifted polynomial \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k u^k\), substitute \(x = u + c\): \[(1 + c + u) G'(u) - \alpha G(u) = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} (u + c)^{N-1}.\] Extracting \([u^k]\) from \(k = N - 1\) down to \(0\) (or \(0\) up to \(N - 1\) when \(1 + c \neq 0\)) computes all \(g_0, \dots, g_{N-1}\) in \(O(N)\) time!
The Miracle Derivative of the Truncated Exponential \(S_{<a}(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{a-1} \frac{x^j}{j!} = e^x \bmod x^a\): Since \(e^x\) satisfies \(F'(x) - F(x) = 0\), its truncation \(S_{<a}(x)\) satisfies: \[S_{<a}'(x) - S_{<a}(x) = -\frac{x^{a-1}}{(a-1)!} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{d}{dx}\Big(e^{-x} S_{<a}(x)\Big) = -e^{-x} \frac{x^{a-1}}{(a-1)!}.\] Differentiating \(e^{-x} S_{<a}(x)\) collapses the entire \(a\)-term polynomial into a single monomial!




Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): \(O(N)\) Taylor Shift of \(F_{<4}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^3 \binom{5}{k} x^k\) at \(x = u - 1\)
Let \(\alpha = 5, N = 4\), so \(F_{<4}(x) = 1 + 5x + 10x^2 + 10x^3\). Suppose we want \(G(u) = F_{<4}(u - 1) = \sum_{k=0}^3 g_k u^k\) (i.e., \(c = -1\)). Substitute \(x = u - 1\) into \((1 + x) F_{<4}'(x) - 5 F_{<4}(x) = -4 \binom{5}{4} x^3 = -20 x^3\): \[u G'(u) - 5 G(u) = -20 (u - 1)^3 = -20 u^3 + 60 u^2 - 60 u + 20.\] Notice that because \(1 + c = 0\), the left-hand side is simply \((\vartheta_u - 5) G(u) = \sum_{k=0}^3 (k - 5) g_k u^k\)—it is diagonal in \([u^k]\)! Even for general \(c\), extracting \([u^k]\) gives \((k + 1)(1 + c) g_{k+1} + (k - \alpha) g_k = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} \binom{N-1}{k} c^{N-1-k}\), which rearranges into a 2-term backward recurrence from \(k = N-1\) down to \(0\). Here for \(c = -1\):

\(k = 0\): \((0 - 5) g_0 = 20 \implies g_0 = -4\). (Check: \(F_{<4}(-1) = 1 - 5 + 10 - 10 = -4\).)
\(k = 1\): \((1 - 5) g_1 = -60 \implies g_1 = 15\). (Check: \(F_{<4}'(-1) = 5 - 20 + 30 = 15\).)
\(k = 2\): \((2 - 5) g_2 = 60 \implies g_2 = -20\). (Check: \(\frac{1}{2} F_{<4}''(-1) = 10 - 30 = -20\).)
\(k = 3\): \((3 - 5) g_3 = -20 \implies g_3 = 10\). (Check: \(\frac{1}{6} F_{<4}'''(-1) = 10\).)







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Direction of Unrolling in Shifted Truncated ODEs



The Trap: When shifting \(x = u + c\) in \((1 + x) F_{<N}'(x) - \alpha F_{<N}(x) = -N\binom{\alpha}{N}x^{N-1}\) to get \((1 + c + u) G'(u) - \alpha G(u) = -N\binom{\alpha}{N}(u + c)^{N-1}\), extracting \([u^k]\) yields: \[(k + 1)(1 + c) g_{k+1} + (k - \alpha) g_k = -N \binom{\alpha}{N} \binom{N-1}{k} c^{N-1-k}.\] If you try to unroll forward (\(g_0 \to g_1 \to \dots \to g_{N-1}\)):

You first have to spend \(O(N)\) work to compute the base case \(g_0 = F_{<N}(c)\);
Worse, if \(1 + c \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (i.e., \(c = -1\)), the coefficient of \(g_{k+1}\) is zero and forward unrolling divides by zero! The Remedy: Always unroll backward from \(k = N - 1\) down to \(0\) (using \(g_N = 0\)), solving for \(g_k\) via division by \((k - \alpha)\) whenever \(\alpha \notin \{0, 1, \dots, N-1\} \pmod p\)—or, if \(\alpha = N\) is a small integer, unroll forward using \((k + 1)(1 + c)\)!









NoteAlgorithm Contract: EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODE Engine




Input: A linear ODE \(A(x) F'(x) + B(x) F(x) = C(x)\) of polynomial degree bound \(d = \max(\deg A - 1, \deg B)\), boundary coefficients \(f_N, \dots, f_{N+d-1}\) of \(F(x)\), truncation length \(N\), and shift \(c \in K\).
Output: All coefficients \(g_0, \dots, g_{N-1}\) of the shifted truncated polynomial \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c)\).
Algebraic Preconditions: Either \(A(c) \in K^\times\) with \(1, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (for forward unrolling given \(g_0, \dots, g_{d-1}\)) or the highest-degree coefficient of \(A(u+c)G'(u) + B(u+c)G(u)\) has non-vanishing indicial multiplier \((k - \alpha) \in K^\times\) (for backward unrolling from \(g_N = \dots = g_{N+d-1} = 0\)).
Complexity: \(O(d \cdot N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space with zero NTTs.
Correctness Invariant: Because \(\deg F_{<N} \le N - 1\), \(G(u) = F_{<N}(u + c)\) has \(g_m = 0\) identically for all \(m \ge N\), which provides the exact zero boundary values \(g_N = \dots = g_{N+d-1} = 0\) needed to start the backward recurrence without computing any evaluation at \(u = 0\).









TipRevisited Dual-Perspective Callout #5 — Codeforces 840C: On the Bench (#089, Ch 08 [Int-2]): From \(O(N^2)\) Connected-Component DP to \(O(N \log^2 N)\) Laguerre Product Tree & Truncated Taylor Shift



In Chapter 8, Intermediate 2 (#089 CF 840C — On the Bench), we counted permutations of \(N \le 300\) colored balls with zero adjacent equal-color pairs by multiplying the per-color connected-component inclusion-exclusion EGFs \[P_r(x) = \sum_{b=1}^{c_r} (-1)^{c_r - b} \binom{c_r - 1}{b - 1} \frac{x^b}{b!}\] via naive \(O(N^2)\) knapsack DP.
In Advanced 1 (#028 AtCoder ABC 260 Ex — Colorfulness) below, \(N\) jumps to \(2.5 \times 10^5\), and we must compute the \(m\)-th power sum of the number of runs across all permutations for \(m = 1, \dots, M\)! By introducing a second variable \(y\) to track how many adjacent equal-color pairs remain, homogenizing the bivariate polynomial \(P_r(x, y)\) into a 1D polynomial in \(z = \frac{x}{y - 1}\), multiplying across colors via a divide-and-conquer NTT product tree in \(O(N \log^2 N)\), and applying a single Taylor shift \(u = y - 1 \mapsto y\), we upgrade the \(O(N^2)\) Chapter 8 engine to handle \(N = 2.5 \times 10^5\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time!

section: 19.4 Motivating Sub-Section: Singularity Analysis Intuition (\([x^n]F(x) \sim \frac{C}{\Gamma(\alpha)} R^{-n} n^{\alpha - 1}\)) & Holonomic BSGS
text:
19.4 Motivating Sub-Section: Singularity Analysis Intuition (\([x^n]F(x) \sim \frac{C}{\Gamma(\alpha)} R^{-n} n^{\alpha - 1}\)) & Holonomic BSGS
Throughout Chapters 18 and 19, we have treated generating functions purely as algebraic objects in \(K[[x]]\). Yet there is a striking correspondence between the leading polynomial \(q_m(x)\) of a D-finite ODE \[q_m(x) F^{(m)}(x) + q_{m-1}(x) F^{(m-1)}(x) + \dots + q_0(x) F(x) = 0\] and the asymptotic growth of the coefficients \(f_n = [x^n] F(x)\) over \(\mathbb{C}\).

1. Why the Dominant Singularity \(x = R\) Controls Both Asymptotics and the ODE Leading Term
Suppose \(F(x) \in \mathbb{C}[[x]]\) has a finite radius of convergence \(R > 0\), and near its dominant singularity \(x = R\) (the singularity closest to the origin in \(\mathbb{C}\)) it behaves algebraically like \[F(x) \sim C \left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right)^{-\alpha} \qquad (x \to R^-)\] for some exponent \(\alpha \notin \{0, -1, -2, \dots\}\). Expanding \((1 - x/R)^{-\alpha}\) by the generalized binomial theorem and applying Stirling’s approximation \(\binom{n + \alpha - 1}{n} = \frac{\Gamma(n + \alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha) \Gamma(n + 1)} \sim \frac{n^{\alpha - 1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\) yields the Flajolet–Odlyzko Transfer Principle: \[[x^n] F(x) \sim \frac{C}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \, R^{-n} \, n^{\alpha - 1} \qquad (n \to \infty).\]
Now look at what happens when we differentiate \((1 - x/R)^{-\alpha}\): each differentiation multiplies by \((1 - x/R)^{-1}\), increasing the pole order at \(x = R\) by \(1\)! Therefore, in any linear ODE \(\sum_{j=0}^m q_j(x) F^{(j)}(x) = 0\) satisfied by \(F(x)\):

Roots of \(q_m(x)\) Are the Singularities of \(F(x)\): For the highest derivative \(F^{(m)}(x) \sim C' (1 - x/R)^{-\alpha - m}\) to cancel against lower derivatives \(F^{(m-1)}(x) \sim C'' (1 - x/R)^{-\alpha - m + 1}\), the leading polynomial \(q_m(x)\) must vanish at \(x = R\) (i.e., \((1 - x/R) \mid q_m(x)\))! For example, in Catalan/central binomial ODEs where \(R = 1/4\), the leading polynomial always contains the factor \((1 - 4x)\); in Delannoy/Schröder ODEs where \(R = 3 - 2\sqrt{2}\), it always contains \((1 - 6x + x^2)\).
Asymptotic Ratio of the P-Recurrence: Dividing the P-recursive relation \(\sum_{s} P_s(n) f_{n+s} = 0\) by \(n^{\deg P}\) and taking \(n \to \infty\) yields the characteristic polynomial \(q_m(x)\) evaluated at \(x = R\), confirming that \(\frac{f_{n+1}}{f_n} \to R^{-1}\left(1 + \frac{\alpha - 1}{n} + O(n^{-2})\right)\).



2. Outlook: \(O(\sqrt{N} \log N)\) Holonomic Baby-Step Giant-Step (Bostan–Chudnovsky–Chudnovsky)
When a sequence \((f_n)\) satisfies an order-\(r\) P-recursive recurrence \(p_r(n) f_{n+r} + \dots + p_0(n) f_n = 0\) and we need a single term \(f_N \bmod p\) for \(N \le 10^9 < p\), \(O(N)\) linear unrolling is too slow. Rewriting the step-\(n\) transition as a \(r \times r\) companion matrix \(M(n) \in \operatorname{Mat}_r(K[n])\) (after clearing denominators into a scalar factorial product \(\prod_{n=0}^{N-1} p_r(n)\)) reduces \(f_N\) to the matrix product: \[P(0, N) = M(N - 1) M(N - 2) \cdots M(1) M(0).\] By setting \(B = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor\), constructing the block matrix \(M_B(x) = M(x + B - 1) \cdots M(x + 1) M(x)\) of polynomial degree \(O(B)\) via a binary product tree in \(O(r^3 \sqrt{N} \log^2 N)\) time, and evaluating \(M_B(x)\) at the giant-step points \(x = 0, B, 2B, \dots, (B - 1)B\) using the subproduct-tree multipoint evaluation and sampling-point shift engines that we will build in Chapter 20, we can evaluate any P-recursive sequence (and \(N! \bmod p\)) at \(N \le 10^9\) in \(O(\sqrt{N} \log N)\) time!

19.6 4-Tier Practice Problem Ladder
The following 8 problems progress from foundational sparse ODE pullbacks to grandmaster applications of coupled sparse composition and EI 科技 truncated differential equations.


Stepping Stone 1 (#242) — Numbered Colorful Balls

Source: yukicoder No. 1939 — Numbered Colorful Balls
Prerequisites: Lagrange Inversion Formula (Ch 11), \(O(NK)\) Sparse Power ODE (Ch 02 / §19.3A)


Problem Statement
You have balls of \(M\) distinct colors. In the nested colorful-ball bracket grammar of yukicoder 1939, each color \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, M\}\) forms atomic blocks of length \(l_i\) where each of the \(l_i\) slots carries a non-empty valid sequence generated by \(x F(x)\). Specifically, let \(F(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n x^n\) be the ordinary generating function satisfying the functional equation: \[F(x) = \frac{1}{1 - \sum_{i=1}^{M} \big(x F(x)\big)^{l_i}}.\] Given \(N\), \(M\), and the positive integers \(l_1, l_2, \dots, l_M\), compute \([x^N] F(x) \bmod 998244353\).


Constraints

\(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(1 \le M \le 100\), \(1 \le l_i \le N\).
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\).
Target complexity: \(O(N M)\) time and \(O(N)\) space with zero NTTs (faster and simpler than \(O(N \log N)\) polynomial ln/exp).



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Suppose \(M = 2\) with block lengths \((l_1, l_2) = (1, 2)\), so \(F(x) = \frac{1}{1 - x F(x) - (x F(x))^2}\):

\(n = 0\): \(f_0 = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(f_1 = [x^1] \big(1 + (x F) + (x F)^2 + (x F)^2 + \dots\big) = 1\).
\(n = 2\): \(f_2 = [x^2] \big((x F) + 2(x F)^2 + (x F)^3\big) = f_1 + 2 f_0^2 = 1 + 2 = 3\).
\(n = 3\): \(f_3 = 10\).
\(n = 4\): \(f_4 = 38\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Notice that \(x\) and \(F(x)\) appear on the right-hand side only through the product \(U(x) = x F(x)\)! Multiply both sides of the equation by \(x\) to isolate \(U(x)\). How can you write the equation in the Lagrange inversion form \(\frac{U(x)}{\phi(U(x))} = x\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Multiplying by \(x\) gives \(U(x) = \frac{x}{1 - \sum_{i=1}^M U(x)^{l_i}}\), which rearranges to: \[U(x) \left(1 - \sum_{i=1}^{M} U(x)^{l_i}\right) = x.\] Define the sparse polynomial \(Q(y) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^M y^{l_i}\), which has at most \(M + 1 \le 101\) non-zero terms. In terms of \(\phi(y) = Q(y)^{-1}\), we have \(U(x) = x \phi(U(x))\). Applying Lagrange Inversion to extract \([x^N] F(x) = [x^{N+1}] U(x)\) gives: \[[x^N] F(x) = \frac{1}{N + 1} [y^N] \phi(y)^{N+1} = \frac{1}{N + 1} [y^N] Q(y)^{-(N+1)}.\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Because \(Q(y) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^M y^{l_i}\) has at most \(M \le 100\) non-zero terms of positive degree, do not use dense NTT ln/exp! Instead, let \(G(y) = Q(y)^{-(N+1)}\) and apply the sparse power ODE \(Q(y) G'(y) = -(N + 1) Q'(y) G(y)\). Extract \([y^{n-1}]\) for \(n = 1, \dots, N\) to compute \(g_N = [y^N] G(y)\) in \(O(NM)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Reduction to Compositional Inverse via \(U(x) = x F(x)\): Set \(U(x) = x F(x)\), so that \(\operatorname{val}(U) = 1\) and \([x^N] F(x) = [x^{N+1}] U(x)\). Multiplying the defining equation of \(F(x)\) by \(x \left(1 - \sum_{i=1}^M U(x)^{l_i}\right)\) yields: \[U(x) Q(U(x)) = x, \qquad Q(y) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{M} y^{l_i}.\]
Lagrange Inversion Extraction: Writing \(U(x) = x \phi(U(x))\) with \(\phi(y) = Q(y)^{-1}\) (note \(\phi(0) = 1 \neq 0\)), Lagrange Inversion Form 1 states that for \(N + 1 \ge 1\): \[[x^N] F(x) = [x^{N+1}] U(x) = \frac{1}{N + 1} [y^N] \phi(y)^{N+1} = \frac{1}{N + 1} [y^N] Q(y)^{-(N+1)}.\]
\(O(NM)\) Unrolling via the Sparse Power ODE: Group identical block lengths \(l_i\) into a sparse list of pairs \((d_j, c_j)\) for \(j = 1, \dots, K\) (\(K \le M\)), so that \(Q(y) = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^K c_j y^{d_j}\) with \(c_j = -(\text{multiplicity of } d_j)\). Let \(G(y) = Q(y)^{\alpha} = \sum_{n \ge 0} g_n y^n\) with \(\alpha = -(N + 1)\). Differentiating \(\ln G(y) = \alpha \ln Q(y)\) and clearing denominators gives: \[Q(y) G'(y) = \alpha Q'(y) G(y).\] Extracting \([y^{n-1}]\) from both sides: \[n g_n + \sum_{j=1,\, d_j \le n}^{K} (n - d_j) c_j g_{n - d_j} = \alpha \sum_{j=1,\, d_j \le n}^{K} d_j c_j g_{n - d_j}.\] Solving for \(g_n\) with \(\alpha = -(N + 1)\) yields the exact \(O(K)\)-term recurrence for \(n = 1, 2, \dots, N\): \[g_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1,\, d_j \le n}^{K} \big((\alpha + 1) d_j - n\big) c_j \, g_{n - d_j} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1,\, d_j \le n}^{K} (N d_j + n) c_j \, g_{n - d_j}, \qquad g_0 = 1.\]
Verification on the Sample Trace (\(M = 2, (l_1, l_2) = (1, 2), N = 3\)): Here \(Q(y) = 1 - y - y^2\) (\(c_1 = -1, c_2 = -1\)) and \(\alpha = -4\), so \(-c_j = +1\) and \(g_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{d \in \{1, 2\}} (3 d + n) g_{n-d}\):

\(g_0 = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(g_1 = \frac{1}{1}(3(1) + 1) g_0 = 4\).
\(n = 2\): \(g_2 = \frac{1}{2}\big((3(1) + 2) g_1 + (3(2) + 2) g_0\big) = \frac{1}{2}\big(5(4) + 8(1)\big) = 14\).
\(n = 3\): \(g_3 = \frac{1}{3}\big((3(1) + 3) g_2 + (3(2) + 3) g_1\big) = \frac{1}{3}\big(6(14) + 9(4)\big) = \frac{120}{3} = 40\). Dividing by \(N + 1 = 4\) gives \(f_3 = \frac{40}{4} = 10\), matching our sample trace!




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integers \(N \le 10^5, M \le 100\), and array \(l_1, \dots, l_M \in [1, N]\); \(Q(0) = 1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) and \(N + 1 < p = 998244353\) so \(1, 2, \dots, N + 1\) are all invertible modulo \(p\).
Output (Postconditions): \([x^N] F(x) = \frac{1}{N+1} g_N \bmod 998244353\).
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Coefficient array \(g[0 \dots N]\) is computed on \([0, N]\) with \(g_0 = 1\); at step \(n \in [1, N]\), only step sizes \(l_i \le n\) contribute.
Complexity: \(O(N M)\) time and \(O(N)\) space (about \(10^7\) simple loop iterations, running in \(< 15\text{ ms}\) without any FFT/NTT overhead).
Correctness Invariant: After step \(n\), \(g_0, \dots, g_n\) equal the exact Taylor coefficients of \(\big(1 - \sum_{i=1}^M y^{l_i}\big)^{-(N+1)} \bmod y^{n+1}\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If duplicate lengths appear in \(l_1, \dots, l_M\) (or if the problem specifies distinct vs. colored tiles), accumulate their multiplicity into \(c_d = [y^d] Q(y)\); at \(N = 0\), the loop is empty and \(\frac{1}{1} g_0 = 1\).









Stepping Stone 2 (#120) — The Three Little Pigs

Source: Codeforces 1548C — The Three Little Pigs (CF Round 736 Div. 1)
Prerequisites: Geometric Series Pullback, Sparse Polynomial Division (SparseFPS::div, Ch 02 / §19.3A)


Problem Statement
Given a positive integer \(n\) and \(q\) queries, each specifying an integer \(x \in [1, 3n]\), compute for each query: \[S(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \binom{3i}{x} \bmod (10^9 + 7).\]


Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 10^6\), \(1 \le q \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le x \le 3n\).
Modulus: \(p = 10^9 + 7\) (a non-NTT prime!).
Target complexity: \(O(n)\) preprocessing time and \(O(1)\) time per query.



Sample Trace (\(n = 2\))
For \(n = 2\), \(3i \in \{3, 6\}\), and the answers for \(x = 1, \dots, 6\) are \(S(x) = \binom{3}{x} + \binom{6}{x}\):

\(x = 1\): \(\binom{3}{1} + \binom{6}{1} = 3 + 6 = 9\).
\(x = 2\): \(\binom{3}{2} + \binom{6}{2} = 3 + 15 = 18\).
\(x = 3\): \(\binom{3}{3} + \binom{6}{3} = 1 + 20 = 21\).
\(x = 4\): \(\binom{3}{4} + \binom{6}{4} = 0 + 15 = 15\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Notice two structural signals:

We need \(S(x)\) for all \(x \in [1, 3n]\) simultaneously, and the modulus \(10^9 + 7\) is not NTT-friendly.
Each term \(\binom{3i}{x}\) is the coefficient \([t^x] (1 + t)^{3i}\). What happens if you form the generating function \(H(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} (1 + t)^{3i}\)?




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Let \(u = (1 + t)^3\). The geometric sum in \(u\) collapses into a closed-form rational function: \[H(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{3i}{x} t^x = \sum_{i=0}^{n} u^i = \frac{u^{n+1} - 1}{u - 1}\Bigg|_{u = (1+t)^3} = \frac{(1 + t)^{3n+3} - 1}{(1 + t)^3 - 1}.\] Expand the denominator \((1 + t)^3 - 1 = t^3 + 3t^2 + 3t = t(t^2 + 3t + 3)\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Multiply both sides by \(t(t^2 + 3t + 3)\): \[(3t + 3t^2 + t^3) H(t) = (1 + t)^{3n+3} - 1.\] Since the numerator \((1 + t)^{3n+3} - 1 = \sum_{k=1}^{3n+3} \binom{3n+3}{k} t^k\) has known binomial coefficients and the denominator \(3 + 3t + t^2\) has only \(3\) terms, extract \([t^{x+1}]\) to compute \(h_x = [t^x] H(t)\) in \(O(1)\) per step for \(x = 0, 1, \dots, 3n\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Generating Function Pullback Along \(u = (1 + t)^3\): Include the \(i = 0\) term \((1 + t)^0 = 1\) (which only affects \([t^0] H(t)\), since \(x \ge 1\) in all queries). Let \(H(t) = \sum_{x=0}^{3n} h_x t^x = \sum_{i=0}^{n} (1 + t)^{3i}\). Summing the finite geometric progression with ratio \(u = (1 + t)^3\) gives: \[H(t) = \frac{(1 + t)^{3n+3} - 1}{(1 + t)^3 - 1} = \frac{(1 + t)^{3n+3} - 1}{t(3 + 3t + t^2)}.\]
3-Sparse Polynomial Division Recurrence: Multiply both sides by \(t(3 + 3t + t^2)\): \[(3 + 3t + t^2) \sum_{x=0}^{3n} h_x t^{x+1} = \sum_{k=1}^{3n+3} \binom{3n+3}{k} t^k.\] Extract \([t^{x+1}]\) from both sides for \(x = 0, 1, \dots, 3n\): \[3 h_x + 3 h_{x-1} + h_{x-2} = \binom{3n + 3}{x + 1},\] where \(h_{-1} = h_{-2} = 0\). Solving for \(h_x\) gives: \[h_x = \frac{1}{3} \left( \binom{3n + 3}{x + 1} - 3 h_{x-1} - h_{x-2} \right) \pmod{10^9 + 7}.\] Since the \(i = 0\) term \((1 + t)^0 = 1\) contributes \(0\) to \([t^x]\) for all \(x \ge 1\), we have \(S(x) = h_x\) for every \(1 \le x \le 3n\).
Verification on the Sample Trace (\(n = 2, 3n + 3 = 9\)):

\(x = 0\): \(h_0 = \frac{1}{3} \binom{9}{1} = 3\) (counting \(i = 0, 1, 2\)).
\(x = 1\): \(h_1 = \frac{1}{3} \left(\binom{9}{2} - 3 h_0\right) = \frac{1}{3}(36 - 9) = 9\).
\(x = 2\): \(h_2 = \frac{1}{3} \left(\binom{9}{3} - 3 h_1 - h_0\right) = \frac{1}{3}(84 - 27 - 3) = 18\).
\(x = 3\): \(h_3 = \frac{1}{3} \left(\binom{9}{4} - 3 h_2 - h_1\right) = \frac{1}{3}(126 - 54 - 9) = 21\).
\(x = 4\): \(h_4 = \frac{1}{3} \left(\binom{9}{5} - 3 h_3 - h_2\right) = \frac{1}{3}(126 - 63 - 18) = 15\). Every value matches our hand check!




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integer \(n \le 10^6\) and \(q \le 2 \times 10^5\) queries \(x \in [1, 3n]\); \(3 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) and \((3n + 3)! \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (satisfied since \(3n + 3 \le 3 \times 10^6 + 3 < 10^9 + 7\)).
Output (Postconditions): \(S(x) = h_x \bmod (10^9 + 7)\) for each query.
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Array \(h[0 \dots 3n]\) is computed sequentially from \(x = 0\) to \(3n\) with \(h_0 = n + 1 = \frac{1}{3}\binom{3n+3}{1}\) and \(h_{-1} = h_{-2} = 0\).
Complexity: \(O(n)\) preprocessing time, \(O(1)\) time per query, and \(O(n)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: After cancelling the simple zero at \(t = 0\), \(3 + 3t + t^2\) has unit constant term \(3 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\), so synthetic division uniquely determines \(h_0, \dots, h_{3n}\) in a single linear pass.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Because \(H(t) = \sum_{i=0}^n (1 + t)^{3i}\) includes the \(i = 0\) term \((1 + t)^0 = 1\), \(h_0 = n + 1\) whereas \(\sum_{i=1}^n \binom{3i}{0} = n\) (for \(x \ge 1\), \(\binom{0}{x} = 0\) so \(S(x) = h_x\) holds without adjustment); precomputing factorials only up to \(3n\) instead of \(3n + 3\) causes out-of-bounds access in \(\binom{3n+3}{x+1}\).









Intermediate 1 (#095) — Team Work (and the Strengthened \(O(K)\) EI 科技 Version)

Source: Codeforces 932E — Team Work (ICM Technocup 2018)
Prerequisites: Euler Operator \(\vartheta = x D_x\) & Stirling Numbers (Ch 06 / §19.1), EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (§19.3B)


Problem Statement
Given positive integers \(N\) and \(K\), compute the \(K\)-th binomial power-moment sum: \[S(N, K) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \binom{N}{i} i^K \bmod (10^9 + 7).\] In addition to solving the original constraint \(K \le 5000\) in \(O(K^2)\) time via Stirling numbers, derive the strengthened EI 科技 \(O(K)\) algorithm that solves \(K \le 10^7\) in \(O(K)\) time!


Constraints

Original (CF 932E): \(1 \le N \le 10^9\), \(1 \le K \le 5000\), modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\).
Strengthened Version: \(1 \le N \le 10^9\), \(1 \le K \le 10^7\), modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\).
Target complexity: \(O(K^2)\) for \(K \le 5000\), and \(O(K)\) time and space for \(K \le 10^7\).



Sample Trace (\(N = 3, K = 2\))
\[S(3, 2) = \binom{3}{1} 1^2 + \binom{3}{2} 2^2 + \binom{3}{3} 3^2 = 3(1) + 3(4) + 1(9) = 24.\]


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Using the Euler operator \(\vartheta = x \frac{d}{dx}\) from §19.1, notice that \(\vartheta^K(x^i) = i^K x^i\), so: \[S(N, K) = \Big[ \vartheta^K (1 + x)^N \Big]_{x = 1}.\] In \(O(K^2)\), expanding \(\vartheta^K = \sum_{j=0}^K \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} K \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\} x^j D_x^j\) immediately solves \(K \le 5000\). How can we avoid computing Stirling numbers altogether to reach \(O(K)\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Look at \(\Big[\vartheta^K (1 + x)^N\Big]_{x=1}\). Because \(\vartheta^K\) is a differential operator of order \(K\) evaluated at \(x = 1\), if we shift the variable to \(u = x - 1\) (so \(1 + x = 2 + u\) and \(x = 1 \iff u = 0\)), any term in \((2 + u)^N\) of degree \(\ge K + 1\) in \(u\) vanishes identically when differentiated \(\le K\) times at \(u = 0\)! Therefore, we may replace \((1 + x)^N = (2 + u)^N\) by its degree-\(K\) truncation in \(u = x - 1\): \[H(u) = (2 + u)^N \bmod u^{K+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{K} \binom{N}{j} 2^{N-j} u^j.\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Apply EI 科技 (§19.3B) to the truncated binomial series \(H(u) = (2 + u)^N \bmod u^{K+1}\): since \((2+u)\frac{d}{du}(2+u)^N - N(2+u)^N = 0\) and the boundary term at \([u^K]\) comes from \(2 \cdot (K+1)\binom{N}{K+1} 2^{N-K-1} u^K = (N-K)\binom{N}{K} 2^{N-K} u^K\), \(H(u)\) satisfies the first-order ODE: \[(2 + u) H'(u) - N H(u) = -(N - K) \binom{N}{K} 2^{N - K} u^K.\] Now shift back \(u = x - 1\) to write \(G(x) = H(x - 1) = \sum_{m=0}^K g_m x^m\). Since \(G(x)\) agrees with \((1 + x)^N\) to order \((x - 1)^K\), we have \(S(N, K) = \big[\vartheta^K G(x)\big]_{x=1} = \sum_{m=0}^K g_m m^K\), where \(g_0, \dots, g_K\) are unrolled backward in \(O(K)\) time from \((1 + x) G'(x) - N G(x) = -(N - K)\binom{N}{K} 2^{N-K}(x - 1)^K\) and \(m^K\) is sieved in \(O(K)\) time via Euler’s linear sieve!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Route 1 (\(O(K^2)\) Stirling S2 Expansion for \(K \le 5000\)): By the Weyl algebra identity \(\vartheta^K = \sum_{j=0}^K \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} K \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\} x^j D_x^j\) and \(D_x^j (1 + x)^N = N^{\underline{j}} (1 + x)^{N-j}\), evaluating at \(x = 1\) yields: \[S(N, K) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(N, K)} \left\{\begin{matrix} K \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} N^{\underline{j}} \, 2^{N-j}.\]
Route 2 (\(O(K)\) EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODE for \(K \le 10^7\)):

Step 2a (Taylor Truncation at \(x = 1\)): Let \(u = x - 1\). Since \(\vartheta^K\) has differential order \(K\), \(\big[\vartheta^K (u^{K+1} R(u))\big]_{u=0} = 0\) for any \(R(u) \in K[[u]]\). Define the truncated series: \[H(u) = (2 + u)^N \bmod u^{K+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{K} \binom{N}{j} 2^{N-j} u^j, \qquad G(x) = H(x - 1) = \sum_{m=0}^{K} g_m x^m.\] Then \(S(N, K) = \big[\vartheta^K G(x)\big]_{x=1} = \sum_{m=0}^K g_m m^K\).
Step 2b (Truncated ODE for \(H(u)\) and Backward Shift to \(G(x)\)): In \((2 + u) H'(u) - N H(u)\), all terms of degree \(< K\) vanish because \((2 + u)^N\) satisfies \((2 + u) F'(u) - N F(u) = 0\), while the degree-\(K\) coefficient is \([u^K]\big(u H'(u) - N H(u)\big) = (K - N)\binom{N}{K} 2^{N-K} u^K\): \[(2 + u) H'(u) - N H(u) = -(N - K) \binom{N}{K} 2^{N - K} u^K.\] Substituting \(u = x - 1\) (so \(2 + u = 1 + x\) and \(\frac{d}{du} = \frac{d}{dx}\)) gives the exact ODE for \(G(x)\): \[(1 + x) G'(x) - N G(x) = -(N - K) \binom{N}{K} 2^{N - K} (x - 1)^K.\] Since \([x^m]\big((1 + x) G'(x) - N G(x)\big) = (m + 1) g_{m+1} + m g_m - N g_m = (m + 1) g_{m+1} - (N - m) g_m\), extracting \([x^m]\) from both sides gives: \[(N - m) g_m = (m + 1) g_{m+1} + (N - K) \binom{N}{K} 2^{N - K} \binom{K}{m} (-1)^{K - m}, \qquad g_K = \binom{N}{K} 2^{N-K}.\]
Step 2c (Verification on the Sample Trace \(N = 3, K = 2\)):

\(m = 2\): \(g_2 = \binom{3}{2} 2^{3-2} = 3(2) = 6\).
\(m = 1\): \((3 - 1) g_1 = 2 g_2 + (3 - 2) \binom{3}{2} 2^1 \binom{2}{1} (-1)^1 = 12 - 12 = 0 \implies g_1 = 0\).
Thus \(S(3, 2) = g_1 \cdot 1^2 + g_2 \cdot 2^2 = 0(1) + 6(4) = 24\), matching the sample trace!



// O(K) EI Truncated Taylor ODE Backward Unrolling for S(N, K) = sum_{i=1}^N C(N,i) i^K
long long cNK_2 = C_N_K * power(2, N - K) % MOD;
long long rhs_base = (N - K) % MOD * cNK_2 % MOD, g = cNK_2, ans = 0;
for (int m = K; m >= 1; --m) {
    ans = (ans + g * idK[m]) % MOD; // idK[m] = m^K from linear sieve
    long long cKm1 = fact[K] * invFact[m - 1] % MOD * invFact[K - m + 1] % MOD;
    long long term = rhs_base * cKm1 % MOD;
    if ((K - m + 1) & 1) term = (MOD - term) % MOD;
    g = (1LL * m * g + term) % MOD * inv_N_minus[m - 1] % MOD; // inv of (N - m + 1)
}


Algorithm Contract

Input: Integers \(N \le 10^9\) and \(K \le 10^7\).
Output: \(S(N, K) = \sum_{i=1}^N \binom{N}{i} i^K \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).
Algebraic Preconditions: For \(N > K\), \(N - m \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) for \(0 \le m \le K\) (if \(N \equiv m \pmod p\) for some \(m \le K\), reduce \(N \bmod p\) or evaluate via the forward binomial sum \(S(m)\) form which divides only by \(m!\)).
Complexity: \(O(K)\) time and \(O(K)\) space (using Euler’s linear sieve to compute \(i^K\) for \(1 \le i \le K\) in \(\pi(K) \approx K / \ln K\) binary exponentiations).
Correctness Invariant: \(G(x) = \big((2 + u)^N \bmod u^{K+1}\big)\big|_{u = x-1}\) satisfies \(G^{(j)}(1) = \frac{d^j}{dx^j}(1 + x)^N\big|_{x=1}\) for all \(0 \le j \le K\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le K\) (where inverse factorials up to \(K!\) divide by zero modulo \(p\)) or if \(K = 0\) is not guarded by subtracting \(\binom{N}{0} 0^0 = 1\) when the problem specifies \(i \ge 1\).









Intermediate 2 (#195) — How to Sum Elegantly ([清华集训2016] 如何优雅地求和)

Source: Luogu P6667 — [清华集训2016] 如何优雅地求和
Prerequisites: Falling-Factorial Basis (Ch 06), EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODE (§19.3B)


Problem Statement
You are given integers \(n, m, x\) and the point values \(f(0), f(1), \dots, f(m)\) of a degree-\(m\) polynomial \(f(k)\). Compute the binomial expectation sum: \[S = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} f(k) \, x^k (1 - x)^{n - k} \bmod 998244353.\] Derive both the \(O(m \log m)\) falling-factorial EGF solution and the \(O(m)\) EI 科技 truncated ODE solution (zero NTTs).


Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 10^9\), \(1 \le m \le 2 \times 10^4\), \(0 \le x < 998244353\).
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\).
Target complexity: \(O(m \log m)\) via NTT or \(O(m)\) time and space via EI 科技.



Sample Trace (\(n = 3, m = 2, x = 2, f(k) = k^2\))
With \(f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 4\) and \(1 - x = -1\): \[S = \sum_{k=0}^{3} \binom{3}{k} k^2 2^k (-1)^{3-k} = 0 + 3(1)(2)(1) + 3(4)(4)(-1) + 1(9)(8)(1) = 6 - 48 + 72 = 30.\]


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Expand \(f(k)\) in the binomial / falling-factorial basis \(f(k) = \sum_{j=0}^m b_j \binom{k}{j}\). Why does \(\binom{n}{k} \binom{k}{j} = \binom{n}{j} \binom{n-j}{k-j}\) make the entire sum over \(k\) collapse via the binomial theorem?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Substituting \(f(k) = \sum_{j=0}^m b_j \binom{k}{j}\) gives: \[S = \sum_{j=0}^{m} b_j \binom{n}{j} x^j \sum_{k=j}^{n} \binom{n - j}{k - j} x^{k - j} (1 - x)^{n - k} = \sum_{j=0}^{m} b_j \binom{n}{j} x^j \big(x + (1 - x)\big)^{n - j} = \sum_{j=0}^{m} b_j \binom{n}{j} x^j.\] By finite differences (or EGFs \(\sum \frac{f(k)}{k!} z^k = e^z \sum \frac{b_j}{j!} z^j\)), we have \(b_j = \sum_{i=0}^j (-1)^{j-i} \binom{j}{i} f(i)\). How can we swap the sums over \(i\) and \(j\) to evaluate \(S\) in \(O(m)\) time without computing \(b_j\) via NTT?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Substitute \(b_j = \sum_{i=0}^j (-1)^{j-i} \binom{j}{i} f(i)\) into \(S = \sum_{j=0}^m b_j \binom{n}{j} x^j\) and use \(\binom{n}{j}\binom{j}{i} = \binom{n}{i}\binom{n-i}{j-i}\): \[S = \sum_{i=0}^{m} f(i) \binom{n}{i} x^i \underbrace{\sum_{r=0}^{m - i} \binom{n - i}{r} (-x)^r}_{g_i}.\] Notice that \(g_i = [u^0]\text{ or } \big((1 - x)^{n-i}_{< m-i+1}\big)\) is the truncated binomial series \((1 + t)^{n-i}_{< m-i+1}\) evaluated at \(t = -x\)! Apply Pascal’s identity \(\binom{n-i}{r} = \binom{n-i-1}{r} + \binom{n-i-1}{r-1}\) to relate \(g_i\) and \(g_{i+1}\) in \(O(1)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Binomial Basis Absorption: Write the degree-\(m\) polynomial \(f(k)\) uniquely as \(f(k) = \sum_{j=0}^m b_j \binom{k}{j}\). Using \(\binom{n}{k}\binom{k}{j} = \binom{n}{j}\binom{n-j}{k-j}\) and the binomial theorem \(\sum_{k=j}^n \binom{n-j}{k-j} x^{k-j} (1 - x)^{n-k} = (x + 1 - x)^{n-j} = 1\), we obtain: \[S = \sum_{j=0}^{m} b_j \binom{n}{j} x^j, \qquad b_j = \sum_{i=0}^{j} (-1)^{j - i} \binom{j}{i} f(i).\]

\(O(m \log m)\) Route: Convolve \(A(z) = \sum_{i=0}^m \frac{f(i)}{i!} z^i\) with \(E(z) = \sum_{r=0}^m \frac{(-1)^r}{r!} z^r\) via one NTT of length \(2^{\lceil \log_2(2m+1) \rceil}\), recover \(b_j = j! [z^j](A E)\), and sum \(b_j \binom{n}{j} x^j\).

\(O(m)\) EI 科技 Truncated Binomial Recurrence (Zero NTTs): Swap the summation order of \(i\) and \(j\) in \(S = \sum_{j=0}^m \sum_{i=0}^j (-1)^{j-i} \binom{j}{i} \binom{n}{j} x^j f(i)\), setting \(r = j - i\): \[S = \sum_{i=0}^{m} f(i) \binom{n}{i} x^i \sum_{r=0}^{m - i} \binom{n - i}{r} (-x)^r.\] Define the truncated binomial evaluation \(g_i = \sum_{r=0}^{m - i} \binom{n - i}{r} (-x)^r\) for \(i = 0, 1, \dots, m\). Using \(\binom{n - i}{r} = \binom{n - i - 1}{r} + \binom{n - i - 1}{r - 1}\), split the sum for \(g_i\): \[\begin{aligned}
g_i &= \sum_{r=0}^{m - i} \binom{n - i - 1}{r} (-x)^r - x \sum_{r=1}^{m - i} \binom{n - i - 1}{r - 1} (-x)^{r - 1} \\
&= \left( g_{i+1} + \binom{n - i - 1}{m - i} (-x)^{m - i} \right) - x \, g_{i+1} \\
&= (1 - x) g_{i+1} + \binom{n - i - 1}{m - i} (-x)^{m - i},
\end{aligned}\] with base case \(g_m = \binom{n - m}{0} (-x)^0 = 1\)!
Verification on the Sample Trace (\(n = 3, m = 2, x = 2, f = [0, 1, 4]\)): Here \(1 - x = -1\) and \(-x = -2\):

\(i = 2\): \(g_2 = 1\). Term \(i = 2\): \(f(2) \binom{3}{2} 2^2 g_2 = 4(3)(4)(1) = 48\).
\(i = 1\): \(g_1 = (-1) g_2 + \binom{3 - 1 - 1}{2 - 1} (-2)^1 = -1 + 1(-2) = -3\). Term \(i = 1\): \(f(1) \binom{3}{1} 2^1 g_1 = 1(3)(2)(-3) = -18\).
\(i = 0\): \(g_0 = (-1) g_1 + \binom{2}{2} (-2)^2 = 3 + 4 = 7\). Term \(i = 0\): \(f(0) = 0\). Summing gives \(S = 48 - 18 + 0 = 30\), matching our sample trace!




Algorithm Contract

Input: Integers \(n \le 10^9, m \le 2 \times 10^4, x \in \mathbb{F}_p\), and evaluations \(f(0), \dots, f(m) \in \mathbb{F}_p\).
Output: \(S = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} f(k) x^k (1 - x)^{n-k} \bmod 998244353\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(m < p = 998244353\) so \(\binom{n}{i}\) and \(\binom{n-i-1}{m-i}\) can be evaluated via precomputed inverse factorials up to \(m\).
Complexity: \(O(m)\) time and \(O(m)\) space with zero NTTs.
Correctness Invariant: At each step \(i = m, m-1, \dots, 0\), \(g_i\) equals the exact degree-\((m-i)\) Taylor truncation of \((1 - t)^{n-i}\) evaluated at \(t = x\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le m\) (where \(1/i!\) in the forward-difference transform \(\Delta^i f(0)/i!\) divides by zero modulo \(p\)), or if \(n \le m\) is not handled carefully when evaluating \((1 - x)^{n-m}\) for \(x \equiv 1 \pmod p\) (where \(0^0 = 1\) and \(0^k = 0\) for \(k > 0\)).









Advanced 1 (#028) — Colorfulness

Source: AtCoder Beginner Contest 260, Problem Ex — Colorfulness
Prerequisites: Connected-Component Inclusion-Exclusion (Ch 08), Divide-and-Conquer Product Tree (Ch 01), Polynomial Taylor Shift (Ch 06 / §19.3B), Logarithmic Derivative / Power Sum Rational Merge (Ch 02)


Problem Statement
There are \(N\) distinguishable balls numbered \(1, 2, \dots, N\), where ball \(i\) has color \(a_i\). For a permutation \(P = (P_1, \dots, P_N)\) of \((1, 2, \dots, N)\), its colorfulness \(c(P)\) is defined as the number of maximal contiguous same-color runs in \((a_{P_1}, a_{P_2}, \dots, a_{P_N})\)—equivalently, \(N\) minus the number of indices \(1 \le i < N\) such that \(a_{P_i} = a_{P_{i+1}}\). Given an integer \(M\), compute for every \(m = 1, 2, \dots, M\): \[S_m = \sum_{P \in S_N} c(P)^m \bmod 998244353.\]


Constraints

\(1 \le N, M \le 2.5 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le a_i \le N\).
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\).
Target complexity: \(O((N + M) \log^2(N + M))\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N = 3, M = 3, a = (1, 1, 2)\))
Of the \(3! = 6\) permutations of \((1_a, 1_b, 2)\):

\(2\) permutations ((1_a, 2, 1_b) and (1_b, 2, 1_a)) have \(0\) equal-color adjacencies, so \(c(P) = 3\) runs.
\(4\) permutations ((1_a, 1_b, 2), (1_b, 1_a, 2), (2, 1_a, 1_b), (2, 1_b, 1_a)) have \(1\) equal-color adjacency, so \(c(P) = 2\) runs. Thus:
\(m = 1\): \(S_1 = 2 \cdot 3^1 + 4 \cdot 2^1 = 14\).
\(m = 2\): \(S_2 = 2 \cdot 3^2 + 4 \cdot 2^2 = 34\).
\(m = 3\): \(S_3 = 2 \cdot 3^3 + 4 \cdot 2^3 = 86\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Split the problem into two stages:

First, for each \(v = 1, 2, \dots, N\), count the number of permutations \(w_{N-v}\) that have colorfulness \(c(P) = v\) (i.e., \(k = N - v\) adjacent equal-color pairs).
Second, given the weights \(c_v = w_{N-v}\) for \(v = 1, \dots, N\), evaluate all \(M\) power sums \(S_m = \sum_{v=1}^N c_v v^m\) (\(1 \le m \le M\)) simultaneously! How do we upgrade the \(O(N^2)\) connected-component DP of CF 840C (Chapter 8) to compute \(w_0, \dots, w_{N-1}\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time?




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Suppose color \(r\) appears \(k_r\) times (\(\sum_r k_r = N\)). If we choose \(j_r \in [0, k_r - 1]\) adjacent equal-color pairs of color \(r\) to “contract” into \(k_r - j_r\) directed chains, there are \(\binom{k_r - 1}{j_r}\) ways to choose where the \(j_r\) merges occur among the \(k_r - 1\) internal boundaries and \(\frac{k_r!}{(k_r - j_r)!}\) ways to order the \(k_r\) distinguishable balls of color \(r\) relative to the \(k_r - j_r\) chains. Thus, define the per-color polynomial of degree \(k_r - 1\): \[Q_r(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{k_r - 1} \binom{k_r - 1}{j} \frac{k_r!}{(k_r - j)!} x^j.\] Multiplying \(Q(x) = \prod_r Q_r(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} q_j x^j\) via a divide-and-conquer product tree gives the number of ways \(a_j = (N - j)! q_j\) to form at least \(j\) forced equal-color adjacencies!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


From \(a_j = (N - j)! [x^j] Q(x)\), a permutation with \(k\) true equal-color adjacencies is counted \(\binom{k}{j}\) times in \(a_j\). By binomial inversion (Chapter 8.1), the polynomial of exact adjacencies \(W(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} w_k x^k\) is the Taylor shift \(W(x) = A(x - 1) = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} a_j (x - 1)^j\), computed in one \(O(N \log N)\) NTT!
Set \(c_v = w_{N-v}\) for \(v = 1, \dots, N\). Then the OGF of the power sums \(S_m = \sum_{v=1}^N c_v v^m\) is: \[\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} S_m x^m = \sum_{v=1}^{N} \frac{c_v}{1 - v x}.\] Merge the \(N\) degree-1 fractions \(\frac{c_v}{1 - v x}\) into a single rational function \(\frac{P(x)}{R(x)}\) using a binary divide-and-conquer tree in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time, and extract \([x^1], \dots, [x^M]\) of \(P(x) R(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{M+1}\) in \(O(M \log M)\) time!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Per-Color Chain-Contraction Polynomial \(Q_r(x)\): Group the \(N\) balls by color into frequencies \(k_1, k_2, \dots, k_C\) with \(\sum_{r=1}^C k_r = N\). Within color \(r\), contracting \(j\) adjacent pairs merges the \(k_r\) balls into \(b = k_r - j\) ordered chains. Since there are \(k_r!\) ways to order the \(k_r\) balls, \(\binom{k_r - 1}{b - 1} = \binom{k_r - 1}{j}\) ways to split them into \(b\) non-empty chains, and \(\frac{1}{b!} = \frac{1}{(k_r - j)!}\) EGF weight for interleaving the \(b\) chains of color \(r\) with chains of other colors, the polynomial \[Q_r(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{k_r - 1} \binom{k_r - 1}{j} \frac{k_r!}{(k_r - j)!} x^j\] encodes the EGF weight of contracting \(j\) adjacencies of color \(r\).
Global Product Tree & Binomial Inversion via Taylor Shift: Since \(\sum_{r=1}^C \deg Q_r = \sum_{r=1}^C (k_r - 1) = N - C < N\), we multiply \(Q(x) = \prod_{r=1}^C Q_r(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} q_j x^j\) using a min-heap / divide-and-conquer NTT tree in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time. After choosing \(j = \sum_r j_r\) total contracted adjacencies across all colors, there are \(N - j\) total chains to permute, giving: \[a_j = (N - j)! \, q_j.\] By inclusion-exclusion, a permutation with \(k\) actual same-color adjacencies contributes \(\binom{k}{j}\) to \(a_j\), so \(a_j = \sum_{k=j}^{N-1} \binom{k}{j} w_k\). Passing to OGFs \(A(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} a_j x^j\) and \(W(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} w_k x^k\): \[A(x) = W(x + 1) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad W(x) = A(x - 1),\] which is a single polynomial Taylor shift of degree \(N - 1\), computed in \(O(N \log N)\) time.
Simultaneous Power-Sum Evaluation via Rational D&C Merge: A permutation with \(k\) equal-color adjacencies has colorfulness \(v = N - k \in [1, N]\). Thus \(c_v = w_{N-v}\) is the number of permutations with colorfulness \(v\). To compute \(S_m = \sum_{v=1}^N c_v v^m\) for all \(m = 1, \dots, M\), form the OGF: \[S(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} S_m x^m = \sum_{v=1}^{N} c_v \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} (v x)^m = \sum_{v=1}^{N} \frac{c_v}{1 - v x}.\] Using a divide-and-conquer tree over \(v \in [1, N]\), merge pairs of fractions \(\frac{P_L}{R_L} + \frac{P_R}{R_R} = \frac{P_L R_R + P_R R_L}{R_L R_R}\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time to obtain \(S(x) = \frac{P(x)}{R(x)}\), then invert \(R(x) \bmod x^{M+1}\) and multiply by \(P(x)\) in \(O(M \log M)\) time.
Verification on the Sample Trace (\(N = 3, k_1 = 2, k_2 = 1\)):

\(Q_1(x) = \binom{1}{0}\frac{2!}{2!} x^0 + \binom{1}{1}\frac{2!}{1!} x^1 = 1 + 2x\); \(Q_2(x) = 1\).
\(Q(x) = 1 + 2x \implies a_0 = 3! (1) = 6\), \(a_1 = 2! (2) = 4\), \(a_2 = 0\).
\(W(x) = A(x - 1) = 6 + 4(x - 1) = 2 + 4x \implies w_0 = 2\) (\(c = 3\)) and \(w_1 = 4\) (\(c = 2\)).
\(S(x) = \frac{2}{1 - 3x} + \frac{4}{1 - 2x} = 6 + 14x + 34x^2 + 86x^3 + \dots\), matching \(14, 34, 86\)!




Algorithm Contract

Input: Integers \(N, M \le 2.5 \times 10^5\) and color array \(a_1, \dots, a_N\).
Output: \(S_1, S_2, \dots, S_M \bmod 998244353\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(N, M < p = 998244353\) (an NTT-friendly prime with \(2^{23} \mid (p - 1)\)).
Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N + M \log M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: At each node \([l, r]\) of the fraction-merge tree, \(P_{[l,r]}(x) / R_{[l,r]}(x) = \sum_{v=l}^r \frac{c_v}{1 - vx}\) with \(\deg P_{[l,r]} < \deg R_{[l,r]} = r - l + 1\) and \(R_{[l,r]}(0) = 1\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le \max(N, M)\) (where \((k-1)!\) and \(k!\) in the EGF scaling divide by zero modulo \(p\)), or if the merge tree splits by index \([1 \dots N]\) instead of grouping identical multiplicities \(c_v\) over distinct \(v \in [1, D]\) (which inflates tree depth and degree when all \(a_i\) are distinct vs. identical).









Advanced 2 (#118) — Phoenix and Computers

Source: Codeforces 1515E — Phoenix and Computers (CF Global Round 14)
Prerequisites: Exponential Generating Functions (Ch 04), Sparse Composition Pullback & Row ODE (§19.3A)


Problem Statement
There are \(n\) computers in a row, all initially turned off. You manually turn on computers one by one. Whenever both neighbors \(i - 1\) and \(i + 1\) of an off computer \(i\) (\(2 \le i \le n - 1\)) are on, computer \(i\) turns on automatically right away, and you can no longer manually turn it on. Two manual activation sequences are considered distinct if they have different lengths (i.e., different numbers of manually activated computers) or differ in the computer chosen at some manual step. Count the total number of valid manual activation sequences that turn on all \(n\) computers, modulo a given prime \(M\).


Constraints

\(3 \le n \le 400\), \(10^8 \le M \le 10^9\) (\(M\) is prime).
Target complexity: \(O(n^2)\) time (with zero divisions, working even for arbitrary composite modulus \(M\), or \(O(n)\) via D-finite ODE when \(M\) is prime).



Sample Trace (\(n = 3, 4\))

For \(n = 3\):

Manual order (1, 3) turns on 2 automatically (\(1\) way of length \(2\), plus (3, 1) = \(2\) ways of length \(2\)).
Manual orders starting at 1 ((1, 2, 3)), starting at 3 ((3, 2, 1)), or starting at 2 ((2, 1, 3) and (2, 3, 1)) have length \(3\) (\(4\) ways).
Total for \(n = 3\): \(2 + 4 = 6\).

For \(n = 4\): Total is \(20\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Consider the final set of computers that turned on automatically. Can two automatic computers ever be adjacent? Can computer \(1\) or computer \(n\) ever turn on automatically? No! Thus, the automatic computers divide the row of \(n\) computers into \(c \ge 1\) contiguous blocks of manually turned-on computers of lengths \(L_1, L_2, \dots, L_c \ge 1\), separated by single automatic computers, so that \(L_1 + L_2 + \dots + L_c + (c - 1) = n\).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Within a single contiguous manual block of length \(L \ge 1\), in what order can its \(L\) computers be turned on without accidentally triggering an automatic activation inside the block? If you ever leave a gap of size \(1\) between two turned-on computers inside the block, that gap turns on automatically! So the turned-on set inside a manual block must grow as a single contiguous interval: you pick \(1\) starting computer, and each of the remaining \(L - 1\) steps extends the interval either by \(1\) to the left or by \(1\) to the right. By binomial sum \(\sum_{j=0}^{L-1} \binom{L-1}{j} = 2^{L-1}\), a manual block of length \(L \ge 1\) has exactly \(2^{L-1}\) valid internal orderings, giving the block EGF: \[\widehat{B}(y) = \sum_{L=1}^{\infty} 2^{L-1} \frac{y^L}{L!} = \frac{e^{2y} - 1}{2}.\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

If there are \(c\) manual blocks, their lengths sum to \(k = n - c + 1\) manual computers, and the EGF of choosing \(c\) ordered blocks is \(\widehat{B}(y)^c = 2^{-c} (e^{2y} - 1)^c\). Equivalently, tracking total length \(n + 1 = k + c\) with \(x\) and manual count \(k\) with \(y\) gives the bivariate generating function: \[F(x, y) = \frac{1}{1 - x y \frac{e^{2x y_{\text{manual}}} - 1}{2}} \quad \text{or} \quad \text{Ans}_n = \sum_{c=1}^{\lfloor (n+1)/2 \rfloor} k! [y^k] \left(\frac{e^{2y} - 1}{2}\right)^c\Bigg|_{k = n + 1 - c}.\] Notice that \(k! [y^k] (e^{2y} - 1)^c = 2^k c! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\)! Compute the Stirling numbers \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) (or the DP/ODE recurrence) in \(O(n^2)\) time with zero divisions!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Contiguous-Interval Characterization of Manual Blocks: Suppose no computer inside a contiguous segment of length \(L \ge 1\) is allowed to turn on automatically. Then at no point during the activation of this segment may two on-computers be separated by a single off-computer. Consequently, the set of on-computers in the segment must always form a single contiguous subsegment: starting from some initial computer \(s \in \{1, \dots, L\}\), each subsequent activation adds either the left neighbor or the right neighbor of the current subsegment. If there are \(j\) left-steps and \(L - 1 - j\) right-steps, they can be interleaved in \(\binom{L-1}{j}\) ways. Summing over \(j = 0, \dots, L - 1\) gives \(2^{L-1}\) valid internal activation sequences for a block of length \(L\).
EGF Assembly & Sparse Composition Pullback: A configuration with \(c \ge 1\) manual blocks separated by \(c - 1\) automatic computers has total manual count \(k = n - (c - 1) = n + 1 - c\), where \(1 \le c \le \lfloor (n + 1)/2 \rfloor\). Because activations in different manual blocks never interfere with one another (each block is shielded by the automatic computer between them, which only turns on after both adjacent block endpoints are already on), the \(c\) manual blocks of lengths \(L_1 + \dots + L_c = k\) are interleaved via standard binomial convolution: \[W(n, c) = k! [y^k] \widehat{B}(y)^c = k! [y^k] \left(\frac{e^{2y} - 1}{2}\right)^c.\]
Stirling S2 & Division-Free \(O(n^2)\) Evaluation: Recall from Chapter 6 that \(\frac{(e^u - 1)^c}{c!} = \sum_{k \ge c} \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\} \frac{u^k}{k!}\). Substituting \(u = 2y\) gives: \[k! [y^k] \left(\frac{e^{2y} - 1}{2}\right)^c = 2^{-c} \cdot 2^k \cdot c! \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ c \end{matrix}\right\} = 2^{n + 1 - 2c} \, c! \left\{\begin{matrix} n + 1 - c \\ c \end{matrix}\right\}.\] Summing over all valid block counts \(c\) gives the closed-form identity: \[\text{Ans}_n = \sum_{c=1}^{\lfloor (n+1)/2 \rfloor} 2^{n + 1 - 2c} \, c! \left\{\begin{matrix} n + 1 - c \\ c \end{matrix}\right\} \pmod M.\] (Alternative Sparse Composition ODE View): Defining \(G_c(y) = \left(\frac{e^{2y} - 1}{2}\right)^c\), we have \(\frac{d}{dy} G_c(y) = c e^{2y} G_{c-1}(y) = c (2 G_1(y) + 1) G_{c-1}(y) = 2c G_c(y) + c G_{c-1}(y)\). Extracting \([y^{k-1}/(k-1)!]\) directly recovers \(w_{k, c} = 2c \, w_{k-1, c} + c \, w_{k-1, c-1}\), which is \(c! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^{k-c}\) with zero divisions!
Verification on the Sample Trace (\(n = 3, 4\)):

\(n = 3\) (\(n + 1 = 4\)):

\(c = 1, k = 3\): \(2^{4 - 2} \cdot 1! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 4\).
\(c = 2, k = 2\): \(2^{4 - 4} \cdot 2! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 2\).
Total: \(4 + 2 = 6\).

\(n = 4\) (\(n + 1 = 5\)):

\(c = 1, k = 4\): \(2^3 \cdot 1! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 8 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 8\).
\(c = 2, k = 3\): \(2^1 \cdot 2! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 12\).
Total: \(8 + 12 = 20\).





Algorithm Contract

Input: Integer \(n \le 400\) and modulus \(M \in [10^8, 10^9]\).
Output: \(\text{Ans}_n \bmod M\).
Algebraic Preconditions: None! Because \(w_{k, c} = 2^{k-c} c! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) satisfies the purely multiplicative/additive recurrence \(w_{k, c} = 2c \, w_{k-1, c} + c \, w_{k-1, c-1}\), it works over any commutative ring, even when \(M\) is composite.
Complexity: \(O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: \(w_{k, c}\) counts ordered \(c\)-tuples of non-empty manual blocks containing \(k\) total manual computers weighted by \(2^{k-c}\) internal orderings.
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Attempting to compute \(w_{k, c}\) by EGF convolution \(\big(\sum \frac{2^{s-1} x^s}{s!}\big)^c\) and multiplying by \(k!\) fails whenever \(\gcd(k!, M) > 1\) (since \(M\) is not guaranteed to be prime!); the division-free recurrence \(w_{k, c} = 2c \, w_{k-1, c} + c \, w_{k-1, c-1}\) and Pascal’s triangle for \(\binom{k - 1}{c - 1}\) are mandatory.









Mastery 1 (#072) — Merge Triplets

Source: AtCoder Grand Contest 043, Problem D — Merge Triplets
Prerequisites: Prefix-Maximum Block Decomposition (Ch 04 / Ch 06), Bivariate Sparse Exponential ODE (§19.3A)


Problem Statement
You are given a positive integer \(N\) and a prime modulus \(M\). Consider all \((3N)!\) permutations of \((1, 2, \dots, 3N)\). A permutation \(P\) is called generable if there exist \(N\) disjoint sequences \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N\), each of length \(3\), whose concatenation contains \((1, 2, \dots, 3N)\), such that \(P\) can be produced by repeatedly choosing the minimum among the current front elements of the non-empty sequences \(A_i\) and appending it to \(P\). Compute the number of generable permutations of \((1, 2, \dots, 3N)\) modulo \(M\).


Constraints

\(1 \le N \le 2000\), \(10^8 \le M \le 10^9 + 9\) (\(M\) is prime).
Target complexity: \(O(N^2)\) time and \(O(N)\) space via a 3-sparse bivariate exponential ODE with zero divisions.



Sample Trace (\(N = 1\))
For \(N = 1\), there is \(m = 1\) sequence \(A_1 = (a, b, c)\) of length \(3\). The front element is always the only available choice, so every permutation of \((1, 2, 3)\) is generable: \(\text{Ans}_1 = 3! = 6\).


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Imagine running the merge algorithm on \(A_1, \dots, A_N\). Suppose the first element of some sequence \(A_i\) is \(x\), and the elements immediately following \(x\) in \(A_i\) that are smaller than \(x\) form a contiguous block \((x, y, \dots)\) in \(A_i\). The moment \(x\) becomes the minimum among all \(N\) front elements and is output to \(P\), those smaller elements behind \(x\) immediately become the new minimum and are output consecutively right after \(x\)! Decompose any permutation \(P\) at its left-to-right maxima (prefix maxima) into blocks \(B_1, B_2, \dots, B_m\). Why does the merge rule sort the blocks in increasing order of their leading element, and what is the exact condition on the block lengths \(|B_r|\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Each triplet \(A_i\) of length \(3\) splits at its own left-to-right maxima into:

one block of length \(3\) (if \(A_i[1] > A_i[2]\) and \(A_i[1] > A_i[3]\)),
one block of length \(2\) and one block of length \(1\), or
three blocks of length \(1\). Therefore, a permutation \(P\) is generable if and only if:


Every prefix-max block of \(P\) has length \(\in \{1, 2, 3\}\), and
The number of blocks of length \(1\) (\(c_1\)) is at least the number of blocks of length \(2\) (\(c_2\)), so that each length-2 block can be paired with a length-1 block to form a triplet, and the remaining \(c_1 - c_2 \equiv 0 \pmod 3\) blocks of length \(1\) group into triplets!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

A prefix-max block of size \(L \in \{1, 2, 3\}\) has its maximum fixed at the front, so it has \((L - 1)!\) valid internal orderings and EGF weight \(\frac{(L - 1)!}{L!} x^L = \frac{x^L}{L}\). Since the blocks are automatically sorted in increasing order of their maxima, the bivariate EGF tracking total size \(x\) and balance \(y^{c_1 - c_2}\) is the SET (\(\exp\)) of blocks: \[F(x, y) = \exp\!\left( x y + \frac{x^2}{2} y^{-1} + \frac{x^3}{3} \right).\] We need \((3N)! [x^{3N} y^{\ge 0}] F(x, y)\). Differentiate \(F(x, y)\) with respect to \(x\) to obtain the 3-sparse ODE \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} = (y + x y^{-1} + x^2) F(x, y)\) and unroll \(dp_{n, b} = n! [x^n y^b] F(x, y)\) in \(O(N^2)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Bijection Between Mergeable Permutations and Constrained Prefix-Max Blocks: Break any permutation \(P\) of \((1, \dots, 3N)\) into blocks at its left-to-right maxima: a new block starts at \(P_j\) whenever \(P_j > \max_{i < j} P_i\). By definition, each block is led by its maximum element, and the leading elements of the blocks appear in strictly increasing order. Conversely, if we partition each of the \(N\) triplets \(A_i\) at its own left-to-right maxima, the resulting sub-blocks across all \(N\) triplets are merged by the greedy minimum-front algorithm in strictly increasing order of their leading elements! Since each triplet of length \(3\) partitions into block sizes \((3)\), \((2, 1)\), or \((1, 1, 1)\), a collection of prefix-max blocks of total size \(3N\) can be packed into \(N\) triplets if and only if:

Every block has size \(L \in \{1, 2, 3\}\), and
\(c_1 \ge c_2\), where \(c_L\) is the number of blocks of size \(L\) (note that \(c_1 + 2c_2 + 3c_3 = 3N\) automatically implies \(c_1 - c_2 \equiv 0 \pmod 3\)).

Bivariate EGF & 3-Sparse Differential Equation: In a prefix-max block of size \(L\) on a chosen label set of size \(L\), the largest label must come first, leaving \((L - 1)!\) ways to arrange the remaining \(L - 1\) labels. Thus the EGF of a single block of size \(L\) is \(\frac{(L - 1)!}{L!} x^L = \frac{x^L}{L}\). Because a permutation is uniquely determined by an unordered set of prefix-max blocks (which are then sorted by their maximum labels), the bivariate EGF tracking total size \(x\) and balance \(b = c_1 - c_2\) via \(y^b\) is: \[F(x, y) = \exp\!\left( x y + \frac{x^2}{2} y^{-1} + \frac{x^3}{3} \right) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{b=-n}^{n} f_{n, b} \, x^n y^b.\] Differentiating with respect to \(x\) gives the 3-sparse partial differential equation: \[\frac{\partial F(x, y)}{\partial x} = \big(y + x y^{-1} + x^2\big) F(x, y).\]
Division-Free \(O(N^2)\) Coefficient Extraction: Extract \([x^{n-1} y^b]\) from both sides of \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} = (y + x y^{-1} + x^2) F\): \[n f_{n, b} = f_{n-1, b-1} + f_{n-2, b+1} + f_{n-3, b}.\] To eliminate the division by \(n\) (and obtain the count of permutations \(dp_{n, b} = n! f_{n, b}\) directly), multiply both sides by \((n - 1)!\): \[dp_{n, b} = dp_{n-1, b-1} + (n - 1) dp_{n-2, b+1} + (n - 1)(n - 2) dp_{n-3, b},\] with base case \(dp_{0, 0} = 1\). Finally, sum \(dp_{3N, b}\) over \(0 \le b \le 3N\).
Verification on the Sample Trace (\(N = 1, 3N = 3\)):

\(n = 0\): \(dp_{0, 0} = 1\).
\(n = 1\): \(dp_{1, 1} = dp_{0, 0} = 1\).
\(n = 2\): \(dp_{2, 2} = dp_{1, 1} = 1\); \(dp_{2, -1} = 1 \cdot dp_{0, 0} = 1\).
\(n = 3\):

\(b = 3\): \(dp_{3, 3} = dp_{2, 2} = 1\) (three blocks of size \(1\)).
\(b = 0\): \(dp_{3, 0} = dp_{2, -1} + 2 \cdot dp_{1, 1} + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot dp_{0, 0} = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5\) (\(3\) ways with one block of size \(2\) and one of size \(1\), plus \(2\) ways with one block of size \(3\)).

Total for \(b \ge 0\): \(dp_{3, 0} + dp_{3, 3} = 5 + 1 = 6\), matching \(3! = 6\)!




Algorithm Contract

Input: Integer \(N \le 2000\) and prime modulus \(M\).
Output: \(\sum_{b=0}^{3N} dp_{3N, b} \bmod M\).
Algebraic Preconditions: None (the recurrence for \(dp_{n, b} = n! f_{n, b}\) uses only addition and multiplication modulo \(M\)).
Complexity: \(O(N^2)\) time and \(O(N)\) space (using a 4-row rolling array over \(n \bmod 4\) with offset \(3N\) for \(b \in [-3N, 3N]\)).
Correctness Invariant: At step \(n\), \(dp_{n, b}\) equals the exact number of permutations of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) whose prefix-max blocks all have lengths in \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) and satisfy \(c_1 - c_2 = b\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Because \(M\) is an arbitrary runtime prime that could be smaller than \(3N\) in general variations, computing \(f_{n, b}\) via EGF division by \(n\) and multiplying by \((3N)!\) at the end fails if \(M \le 3N\); scaling to the division-free integer recurrence \(dp_{n, b} = n! f_{n, b}\) eliminates all modular inverses.









Mastery 2 (#213) — Universal Judge ID (【UR #19】通用测评号)

Source: Universal Online Judge (UOJ) #514 — 【UR #19】通用测评号
Prerequisites: Exponential Poissonization & Stopping Times (Ch 14), EI 科技 Miracle Derivative of the Truncated Exponential (§19.3B)


Problem Statement
There are \(n\) initially empty fuel tanks (\(c_1 = c_2 = \dots = c_n = 0\)). In each step, one tank \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) is chosen uniformly at random and its fuel increases by \(1\). The process stops at the first step \(T\) when every tank has at least \(b\) units of fuel (\(\min_{1 \le i \le n} c_i \ge b\)). Given integers \(n\), \(a\), and \(b\) (\(a > b\)), compute the expected number of tanks that have at least \(a\) units of fuel (\(c_i \ge a\)) at the stopping moment \(T\), modulo \(998244353\).


Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 250\), \(1 \le b < a \le 250\).
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\).
Target complexity: \(O(n^2 a)\) time and \(O(n a)\) space (down from \(O(n^3 a^2)\) naive polynomial multiplication, using the EI 科技 truncated exponential derivative).



Sample Trace (\(n = 2, a = 2, b = 1\))
With \(n = 2\) tanks and \(b = 1\), step \(1\) puts \(1\) unit in some tank (say tank \(1\)). Then each subsequent step has probability \(1/2\) of hitting tank \(2\) (stopping immediately) and \(1/2\) of hitting tank \(1\).

Tank \(2\) (the last tank to reach \(b = 1\)) always stops with exactly \(1 < 2\) unit of fuel.
Tank \(1\) reaches \(\ge 2\) units of fuel if and only if step \(2\) hits tank \(1\) (probability \(1/2\)). Thus the expected number of tanks with \(\ge 2\) fuel at stopping time is \(\frac{1}{2} \equiv 499122177 \pmod{998244353}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By symmetry across the \(n\) tanks, the expected number of tanks with \(\ge a\) fuel at stopping time \(T\) equals \(n\) times the probability that tank \(1\) has \(\ge a\) fuel (equivalently, \(n\) minus \(n\) times the probability that tank \(1\) has \(\in [b, a - 1]\) fuel at time \(T\)). Switch to continuous-time Poissonization (Chapter 14.4) where each tank receives fuel according to an independent rate-\(1\) Poisson process! At Poisson time \(x \ge 0\), a tank has \(< m\) fuel with probability \(e^{-x} S_{<m}(x)\), where: \[S_{<m}(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \frac{x^j}{j!}.\]



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

For tank \(1\) to end up with fuel in \([b, a - 1]\) at the stopping moment when the last of the other \(n - 1\) tanks reaches \(b\):

One of the other \(n - 1\) tanks (say tank \(2\), giving factor \(n - 1\)) hits its \(b\)-th unit of fuel at time \(x\), which has Poisson density \(e^{-x} \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} dx = -\frac{d}{dx}\big(e^{-x} S_{<b}(x)\big) dx\).
At that time \(x\), tank \(1\) has fuel in \([b, a - 1]\), which has probability \(e^{-x}\big(S_{<a}(x) - S_{<b}(x)\big)\).
All remaining \(n - 2\) tanks have \(\ge b\) fuel at time \(x\), which by inclusion-exclusion is \(\big(1 - e^{-x} S_{<b}(x)\big)^{n-2} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-2} (-1)^k \binom{n-2}{k} e^{-kx} S_{<b}(x)^k\). Notice that naively computing \(S_{<b}(x)^k\) for \(k = 0, \dots, n - 2\) and integrating against \(e^{-(k+2)x}\) would take \(O(n^2 b^2)\) (or \(O(n^3 a^2)\) if you track both \(S_{<a}\) and \(S_{<b}\)). How does the Miracle Derivative \(S_{<b}'(x) = S_{<b}(x) - \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}\) compute all powers \(B_k(x) = S_{<b}(x)^k\) in \(O(n^2 b)\) time with zero NTTs?




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Define the power tower \(B_k(x) = S_{<b}(x)^k\) for \(k = 0, 1, \dots, n - 2\) (a polynomial of degree \(k(b - 1) < n b\)). Differentiate \(B_k(x) = S_{<b}(x)^k\) using \(S_{<b}'(x) = S_{<b}(x) - \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}\): \[B_k'(x) = k S_{<b}(x)^{k-1} S_{<b}'(x) = k B_k(x) - k \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} B_{k-1}(x).\] Look at the right-hand side: \(B_{k-1}(x)\) is multiplied by the single monomial \(x^{b-1}\)! Extracting \([x^m / m!]\) (or \([x^m]\)) computes the entire polynomial \(B_k(x)\) from \(B_{k-1}(x)\) in \(O(1)\) time per coefficient, i.e., \(O(n^2 b)\) total time across all \(k = 0, \dots, n - 2\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Continuous-Time Poissonization & Stopping-Time Integral: Embed the discrete uniform process into \(n\) independent Poisson processes of rate \(1\). Let \(T\) be the stopping time when all \(n\) tanks reach \(\ge b\) fuel. By linearity of expectation and symmetry among the \(n\) tanks, \(\mathbb{E}[\#\{i : c_i(T) \ge a\}] = n \big(1 - \Pr[c_1(T) < a]\big)\). At stopping time \(T\), how can tank \(1\) have \(< a\) units of fuel? There are two disjoint possibilities:

Case A (Tank \(1\) is the last tank to reach \(b\) fuel): By symmetry among the \(n\) tanks, this occurs with probability \(\frac{1}{n}\), and at time \(T\) tank \(1\) has exactly \(b < a\) fuel.
Case B (One of the other \(n - 1\) tanks is the last to reach \(b\), while tank \(1\) already has fuel in \([b, a - 1]\)): There are \(n - 1\) choices for which tank \(j \in \{2, \dots, n\}\) is the last to reach \(b\). Tank \(j\) hits its \(b\)-th unit in \([x, x + dx]\) with density \(e^{-x} \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} dx\), tank \(1\) has fuel in \([b, a - 1]\) at time \(x\) with probability \(e^{-x}\big(S_{<a}(x) - S_{<b}(x)\big)\), and the remaining \(n - 2\) tanks each have \(\ge b\) fuel at time \(x\) with probability \(1 - e^{-x} S_{<b}(x)\). Integrating over \(x \in (0, \infty)\) gives: \[I = (n - 1) \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x}\big(S_{<a}(x) - S_{<b}(x)\big) \cdot e^{-x} \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} \cdot \big(1 - e^{-x} S_{<b}(x)\big)^{n-2} \, dx,\] and therefore \(\mathbb{E}[\#\{i : c_i(T) \ge a\}] = n\left(1 - \frac{1}{n} - I\right) = n - 1 - n I\).

Binomial Expansion & EI 科技 Truncated Exponential Power Tower: Expand \(\big(1 - e^{-x} S_{<b}(x)\big)^{n-2} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-2} (-1)^k \binom{n-2}{k} e^{-kx} B_k(x)\), where \(B_k(x) = S_{<b}(x)^k\). How do we compute the coefficients of \(B_k(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{k(b-1)} b_{k, m} \frac{x^m}{m!}\) in \(O(n^2 b)\) time? Apply Theorem 19.2 (the Miracle Derivative \(S_{<b}'(x) = S_{<b}(x) - \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}\)) to \(B_k(x) = S_{<b}(x)^k\): \[B_k'(x) = k \, S_{<b}(x)^{k-1} \left(S_{<b}(x) - \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}\right) = k \, B_k(x) - k \, \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} B_{k-1}(x).\] Extracting \([x^m / m!]\) (remembering \([x^m / m!] B_k'(x) = b_{k, m+1}\) and \([x^m / m!] \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} B_{k-1}(x) = \binom{m}{b-1} b_{k-1, m-b+1}\)) gives the 2-term recurrence: \[b_{k, m+1} = k \, b_{k, m} - k \binom{m}{b - 1} b_{k - 1, m - b + 1}, \qquad b_{k, 0} = 1.\] This computes all \(b_{k, m}\) for \(0 \le k \le n - 2\) and \(0 \le m \le k(b - 1)\) in strictly \(O(n^2 b)\) arithmetic operations!
Evaluating the Laplace Integral in \(O(n^2 a)\) Time: Aggregate the signed binomial combination \(W(x) = \sum_{m \ge 0} \left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-2} (-1)^k \binom{n-2}{k} b_{k, m} e^{-(k+2)x}\right) \frac{x^m}{m!}\). For each \(k \in [0, n - 2]\) and each term \(\frac{x^j}{j!}\) of \(S_{<a}(x) - S_{<b}(x) = \sum_{j=b}^{a-1} \frac{x^j}{j!}\), we use the Laplace identity \(\int_0^\infty e^{-(k+2)x} \frac{x^M}{M!} dx = \frac{1}{(k + 2)^{M + 1}}\) (or even faster, multiply \(\big(S_{<a}(x) - S_{<b}(x)\big) \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}\) into \(B_k(x)\) via the same 1-monomial ODE for \(H_k(x) = \big(S_{<a}(x) - S_{<b}(x)\big) B_k(x)\), which satisfies \(H_k'(x) = (k + 1) H_k(x) - \big(\frac{x^{a-1}}{(a-1)!} - \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}\big) B_k(x) - k \frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} H_{k-1}(x)\) in \(O(n^2 b + n a)\) time!).
Verification on the Sample Trace (\(n = 2, a = 2, b = 1\)):

Here \(n - 2 = 0\), so only \(k = 0\) (\(B_0(x) = 1\)) appears, with \(S_{<2}(x) - S_{<1}(x) = x\) and \(\frac{x^{b-1}}{(b-1)!} = 1\).
Thus \(I = (2 - 1) \int_0^\infty e^{-2x} x \, dx = \frac{1!}{2^2} = \frac{1}{4}\).
Substituting into \(n - 1 - n I\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[\#\{i : c_i(T) \ge 2\}] = 2 - 1 - 2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \equiv 499122177 \pmod{998244353}\), matching our sample trace!




Algorithm Contract

Input: Integers \(n \le 250\) and \(1 \le b < a \le 250\).
Output: \(n \big(1 - \frac{1}{n} - I\big) \bmod 998244353\), where \(I\) is the Poisson stopping integral for \(b \le c_1(T) < a\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \((n + 1)(a + b) < p = 998244353\) so all factorials and Laplace denominators \((k + 2)^{M+1}\) are invertible modulo \(p\).
Complexity: \(O(n^2 b + n a)\) time and \(O(n b + a)\) space with zero NTTs.
Correctness Invariant: \(B_k(x) = S_{<b}(x)^k\) and \(H_k(x) = (S_{<a}(x) - S_{<b}(x)) B_k(x)\) are unrolled exactly via the 1-monomial truncated exponential derivative \(S_{<m}'(x) = S_{<m}(x) - \frac{x^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le (n - 1)(b - 1) + a - 1\) (where either the ODE integration divisor \(d + 1\) or the Laplace denominator \(k + 2\) hits \(0 \pmod p\)), or if \(b = 1\) (\(S_{<1}(x) = 1\)) is not handled with the \(0\)-degree base polynomial \(B_k(x) = 1\) for all \(k \ge 0\).

19.7 Chapter Summary & Verification Checklist

Weyl & Shift Operator Algebras (§19.1): Use \(P(\vartheta) x^s = x^s P(\vartheta + s)\) and the Fourier–Laplace dictionary \(x^s P(\vartheta) \mapsto P(n - s) E_n^{-s}\) to convert differential equations into P-recurrences without sign or shift mistakes.
WZ Pairs & EI’s Differential-Residue Engine (§19.2): Express definite binomial sums as \(S_n = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0}\big(x^{-1} A(x) B(x)^n\big)\) and apply \(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{d}{dx}\big(\phi(x) B(x)^n\big) = 0\) to eliminate auxiliary Laurent moments and derive \(O(N)\) recurrences. Always check whether summation bounds cut off natural support!
Coupled \(r\)-State Sparse Composition (§19.3A): Compute \(F(P(x)) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(rNK)\) time by maintaining \(H_i(x) = F^{(i)}(P(x))\) for \(0 \le i < r\), avoiding any division by \(P'(x)\).
EI 科技 Truncated Taylor ODEs (§19.3B): Truncating \(F(x)\) at \(x^N\) introduces a boundary polynomial \(R_N(x)\) of at most \(d = \max(\deg A - 1, \deg B)\) terms, enabling \(O(N)\) Taylor shifts of \((1 + x)^\alpha_{<N}\) and collapsing \(\frac{d}{dx}\big(e^{-x} S_{<a}(x)\big) = -e^{-x} \frac{x^{a-1}}{(a-1)!}\) to a single monomial.


Next Chapter
