Advanced 2 (#225) — LibreOJ 6503: Magic (魔术)

Source: LibreOJ #6503 (雅礼集训 2018 Day 4)
Prerequisite Tags: [Connected-Component Run-Length IE, EGF Block Assembly, Divide-and-Conquer NTT]
Problem Statement: A magician has \(m\) colors of magic cards, where color \(i\) (\(1 \le i \le m\)) has \(a_i \ge 1\) identical cards, and the total number of cards is \(n = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i\). Two cards of the same color are indistinguishable. Given an integer \(k\) (\(0 \le k < n\), with \(k = 0\) requiring no two adjacent cards to share the same color), compute the number of card sequences of length \(n\) in which exactly \(k\) adjacent indices \(1 \le r \le n - 1\) have card \(r\) and card \(r + 1\) of the same color, modulo \(998244353\). (Note: If cards of the same color are instead treated as distinguishable, simply multiply the final answer by \(\prod_{i=1}^m a_i! \bmod 998244353\).)
Constraints: \(1 \le m \le 10^5\), \(1 \le n = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i \le 4 \times 10^5\), \(0 \le k < n\). Modulus \(p = 998244353\). Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(n \log^2 n)\).
Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(m = 2\) colors with counts \(a = (2, 1)\) (\(n = 3\) indistinguishable cards per color: two 1s and one 2), the \(\binom{3}{2,1} = 3\) arrangements are (1, 2, 1) (\(0\) monochromatic adjacent pairs) and (1, 1, 2), (2, 1, 1) (\(1\) monochromatic adjacent pair each). Thus \(f_0 = 1\) for \(k = 0\) and \(f_1 = 2\) for \(k = 1\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By Chapter 08’s Connected-Component Inclusion-Exclusion (连续段容斥), suppose the \(a_i\) identical cards of color \(i\) are partitioned into \(j\) non-empty contiguous blocks (\(1 \le j \le a_i\)).

Using Stars and Bars, in how many ways can \(a_i\) identical cards be split into an ordered sequence of \(j\) non-empty blocks? \(\binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1}\) ways.
How many adjacent monochromatic pairs are forced inside these \(j\) blocks? Since fusing two blocks of the same color creates \(1\) monochromatic adjacency, splitting \(a_i\) cards into \(j\) blocks forces at least \(a_i - j\) monochromatic adjacencies.




Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

First consider the \(k = 0\) case (zero adjacent monochromatic pairs): If color \(i\) is split into \(j\) blocks (\(a_i - j\) forced violations), its Inclusion-Exclusion sign is \((-1)^{a_i - j}\), and because the \(j\) blocks of color \(i\) are indistinguishable when interleaved with blocks of other colors, its Exponential Generating Function (EGF) is \[
P_i(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{a_i} (-1)^{a_i - j} \binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1} \frac{x^j}{j!}.
\] When we multiply \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m P_i(x) = \sum_{B=m}^n p_B x^B\), what does \(B! [x^B] P(x)\) represent? It sums over all ways to interleave \(B = \sum_{i=1}^m j_i\) total blocks across all \(m\) colors. And for general \(k \ge 0\) (exact \(k\) adjacent monochromatic pairs), replace the sign \((-1)^{a_i - j}\) with \((y - 1)^{a_i - j}\) via Binomial Inversion (\(y \mapsto y - 1\)).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Notice that \(\sum_{i=1}^m (a_i - j_i) = n - \sum_{i=1}^m j_i = n - B\) depends only on the total number of blocks \(B = \sum_{i=1}^m j_i\), NOT on the individual \(j_i\)’s. Therefore, even for general \(k \ge 0\), we DO NOT need 2D polynomials. Define the 1D polynomial of degree \(a_i\): \[
Q_i(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{a_i} \binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1} \frac{x^j}{j!}.
\] Multiply \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m Q_i(x) = \sum_{B=m}^n q_B x^B\) using a Divide-and-Conquer Product Tree (Ch 01.4) in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time. Then \(g_{n - B} = B! \, q_B\) is the number of ways to force \(v = n - B\) monochromatic adjacencies:

For \(k = 0\): \(\text{Ans} = \sum_{B=m}^n (-1)^{n - B} B! \, q_B\).
For general \(k\): \(\text{Ans}_k = \sum_{v=k}^{n-m} (-1)^{v - k} \binom{v}{k} g_v\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Per-Color Block Decomposition & Binomial Inversion): Consider color \(i \in \{1, \dots, m\}\), which has \(a_i\) indistinguishable cards. In any arrangement of the \(n\) cards, there are \(a_i - 1\) potential internal boundaries between consecutive occurrences of color \(i\) if they are placed adjacent to each other. If we select \(v_i = a_i - j_i\) of these internal boundaries to be forced adjacent pairs (\(1 \le j_i \le a_i\)), the \(a_i\) cards of color \(i\) fuse into \(j_i\) contiguous blocks. There are \(\binom{a_i - 1}{a_i - j_i} = \binom{a_i - 1}{j_i - 1}\) ways to choose which boundaries are fused. Now suppose color \(i\) is fused into \(j_i\) blocks for each \(i = 1, \dots, m\), giving \(B = \sum_{i=1}^m j_i\) total blocks and \(v = \sum_{i=1}^m (a_i - j_i) = n - B\) total forced monochromatic adjacencies. Since cards of the same color are indistinguishable, two interleavings of the \(B\) blocks produce the same sequence of fused blocks if and only if they permute the \(j_i\) blocks of color \(i\) among themselves. Thus there are \[
\frac{B!}{j_1! \, j_2! \cdots j_m!}
\] ways to arrange the \(B\) blocks in a line.
Step 2 (Factoring into 1D EGFs & Divide-and-Conquer NTT): Summing over all tuples \((j_1, \dots, j_m)\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m j_i = B\), the number of relaxed configurations \(g_{n - B}\) with \(v = n - B\) forced monochromatic adjacencies is \[
g_{n - B} = B! \sum_{j_1 + \dots + j_m = B} \prod_{i=1}^{m} \binom{a_i - 1}{j_i - 1} \frac{1}{j_i!} = B! \, [x^B] \prod_{i=1}^{m} Q_i(x),
\] where each \(Q_i(x)\) is a polynomial of degree \(a_i\): \[
Q_i(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{a_i} \binom{a_i - 1}{j - 1} \frac{x^j}{j!}.
\] Since \(\sum_{i=1}^m \deg Q_i = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i = n \le 4 \times 10^5\), we compute \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m Q_i(x)\) in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time using a binary divide-and-conquer product tree (multiply_all(l, r)) or a min-heap (Huffman) NTT merge.
Step 3 (Final Inclusion-Exclusion / Binomial Inversion Extraction): Once \(g_{n - B} = B! [x^B] Q(x)\) is computed for all \(B = m, m + 1, \dots, n\) (so \(v = n - B \in [0, n - m]\)):

By Binomial Inversion (Chapter 08.1), the number of sequences with exactly \(k\) monochromatic adjacent pairs is \[
f_k = \sum_{v = k}^{n - m} (-1)^{v - k} \binom{v}{k} g_v = \sum_{B = m}^{n - k} (-1)^{n - B - k} \binom{n - B}{k} B! \, [x^B] Q(x) \pmod{998244353}.
\]
In particular, for \(k = 0\) (no two adjacent cards of the same color), this simplifies to the single linear pass \[
f_0 = \sum_{B = m}^{n} (-1)^{n - B} B! \, [x^B] Q(x) \pmod{998244353}.
\]
Hand-Check for \(m = 2, a_1 = 2, a_2 = 1\) (\(n = 3, k = 0\)):

\(Q_1(x) = x + \frac{x^2}{2}\), \(Q_2(x) = x \implies Q(x) = x^2 + \frac{x^3}{2}\).
\(B = 2\): \((-1)^{3-2} \cdot 2! \cdot 1 = -2\).
\(B = 3\): \((-1)^{3-3} \cdot 3! \cdot \frac{1}{2} = +3\).
\(f_0 = -2 + 3 = 1\) (corresponding to the unique valid sequence 1 2 1). Matches!









NoteAlgorithm Contract: LibreOJ 6503 (#225)




Preconditions: Positive color counts \(a_1, \dots, a_m \ge 1\) with \(n = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i \le 4 \times 10^5\), and target adjacency count \(0 \le k < n\).
Postconditions: Returns \(f_k \bmod 998244353\), the number of arrangements with exactly \(k\) monochromatic adjacent pairs.
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Each polynomial \(Q_i(x)\) has degree \(a_i\) with \([x^0] Q_i(x) = 0\); the product \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m Q_i(x)\) has non-zero coefficients only on \([m, n]\).
Complexity: \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.
1-Sentence Loop Invariant: At node \([l, r]\) of the divide-and-conquer product tree, multiply_all(l, r) returns the exact polynomial \(\prod_{i=l}^r Q_i(x)\) of degree \(\sum_{i=l}^r a_i\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le n\) (since inverse factorials \(1/c!\) in \(Q_i(x)\) and \(c!\) in the EGF extraction divide by zero modulo \(p\)), or if \(k > n - m\) (where \(c = n - k < m\), so no valid block decomposition exists and the output must be \(0\)).









Mastery 1 (#206) — UOJ 50: [UR #3] 链式反应 (Chain Reaction)

Source: Universal Online Judge #50 (UOJ Round #3)
Prerequisite Tags: [Riccati Nonlinear ODE, Self-Convolution CDQ NTT, Failure Mode #13, Relaxed Convolution]
Problem Statement: In a nuclear chain reaction, atoms are labeled \(1, 2, \dots, m\). A valid reaction tree of size \(m\) (\(1 \le m \le n\)) is a rooted labeled structure constructed as follows:

If \(m = 1\), the single atom \(1\) forms a trivial tree on its own (\(1\) way).
If \(m \ge 2\), the root must be atom \(1\) (the minimum label among all atoms in its subtree). When the root fires, it simultaneously produces:

An unordered pair of two active child reaction trees (which are themselves non-empty valid reaction trees on disjoint subsets of labels, each rooted at its own minimum label), and
A set of \(i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m - 3\}\) passive leaf atoms (allowed if and only if \(a_i = 1\) in a given binary string \(a_0 a_1 \dots a_{n-1}\)). Given \(n\) and the binary string \(a_0 a_1 \dots a_{n-1} \in \{0, 1\}^n\), compute the number of valid reaction trees \(f_m\) for every \(m = 1, 2, \dots, n\) modulo \(998244353\).


Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(a_i \in \{0, 1\}\). Modulus \(p = 998244353\). Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(n \log^2 n)\) via CDQ NTT / RelaxedConvolution (or \(O(n \log n)\) via Integrating-Factor Newton in Chapter 10).
Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): Suppose \(n = 4\) and \(a = (1, 1, 0, 0)\) (\(a_0 = 1, a_1 = 1\)). Then \(f_1 = 1\) (single root atom \(1\)); \(f_2 = 0\) (two active child trees require at least \(1 + 1 + 1 = 3\) atoms); \(f_3 = a_0 = 1\) (root \(1\) plus an unordered pair of size-\(1\) active children \(\{2\}, \{3\}\) and \(0\) passive leaves); and \(f_4 = 3 a_1 = 3\) (root \(1\), \(1\) passive leaf chosen in \(\binom{3}{1} = 3\) ways from \(\{2, 3, 4\}\), and the remaining \(2\) atoms forming two size-\(1\) active child subtrees).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(F(x) = \sum_{m=1}^n \frac{f_m}{m!} x^m\) be the Exponential Generating Function (EGF) of valid reaction trees, and let \(A(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{a_i}{i!} x^i\) be the EGF of the passive leaf set. By Chapter 04’s Boxed Product (\(C' = A' B\)) (Section 4.2), removing the minimum-labeled root from a labeled structure of size \(m\) corresponds to taking the formal derivative \(F'(x)\). What remains after removing the root? Either the tree had size \(m = 1\) (leaving the empty set, EGF \(1\)), or the remaining \(m - 1\) labels are partitioned into an unordered pair of active subtrees (\(\operatorname{SET}_2(F) = \frac{1}{2} F(x)^2\)) and a passive leaf set (\(A(x)\)).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By the EGF product rule, \(F(x)\) satisfies the non-autonomous Riccati differential equation: \[
F'(x) = \frac{1}{2} A(x) F(x)^2 + 1, \qquad F(0) = 0.
\] Extracting \([x^{m-1}]\) for \(m \ge 1\) gives \[
m \cdot \tilde{f}_m = [m = 1] + \frac{1}{2} [x^{m-1}] \big( A(x) F(x)^2 \big), \qquad \text{where } \tilde{f}_m = \frac{f_m}{m!} = [x^m] F(x).
\] Notice that because \(F(0) = 0\), \([x^{m-1}]\big(A(x) F(x)^2\big)\) only involves \(\tilde{f}_j\) and \(\tilde{f}_k\) with \(j + k \le m - 1\) (\(1 \le j, k \le m - 2\)). How can we solve this in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time using two RelaxedConvolution instances (or via CDQ NTT while applying the Failure Mode #13 factor-of-2 symmetry fix)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


Method A (Two RelaxedConvolution Instances — 10 Lines, Zero Edge Cases): Define \(S(x) = F(x)^2\) and \(P(x) = A(x) S(x)\), so \(F'(x) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} P(x)\). At step \(q = m - 1\) (\(q = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1\)), since \(\tilde{f}_q\) was already finalized at the end of step \(q - 1\):

s_q = rc_S.next(f_tilde[q], f_tilde[q]); (computes \([x^q] F(x)^2\)).
p_q = rc_P.next(a_tilde[q], s_q); (computes \([x^q](A(x) F(x)^2)\)).
f_tilde[q + 1] = ((q == 0 ? 1 : 0) + inv2 * p_q % MOD) * inv[q + 1] % MOD;

Method B (Semi-Online CDQ NTT): In solve(l, r) on \([0, n - 1]\), maintain \(s_q = [x^q] F(x)^2\) and \(p_q = [x^q](A(x) S(x))\) using the Failure Mode #13 multiplier (l == 0 ? 1 : 2) on \(\tilde{f} \times \tilde{f}\) and accounting for the \(k = 0\) term \(\tilde{a}_0 s_q\) at the leaf \(l = r = q\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Translating the Chain-Reaction Grammar into a Riccati ODE): For a reaction tree of size \(m \ge 2\), the root must receive label \(1\) (the smallest of the \(m\) labels). The remaining \(m - 1\) labels are partitioned into three parts: two active subtrees of sizes \(j \ge 1\) and \(k \ge 1\) (unordered, so we divide by \(2! = 2\)), and one set of passive leaves of size \(i \ge 0\) (\(i + j + k = m - 1\)). Since the \(i\) passive leaves have only \(a_i \in \{0, 1\}\) ways to be formed on a given label subset of size \(i\), their EGF is \(A(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{a_i}{i!} x^i\). The unordered pair of active subtrees has EGF \(\frac{1}{2} F(x)^2\). Including the base tree of size \(m = 1\) (whose derivative is \(1\)), the EGF \(F(x) = \sum_{m=1}^n \tilde{f}_m x^m\) (\(\tilde{f}_m = \frac{f_m}{m!}\)) satisfies \[
F'(x) = \frac{1}{2} A(x) F(x)^2 + 1, \qquad F(0) = 0.
\]
Step 2 (Solution 1: Chained RelaxedConvolution in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) — Recommended for Contest Implementation): Let \(S(x) = F(x)^2 = \sum_{q \ge 0} s_q x^q\) and \(P(x) = A(x) S(x) = \sum_{q \ge 0} p_q x^q\). Extracting \([x^q]\) from \(F'(x) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} P(x)\) for \(q = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1\) gives \[
(q + 1) \tilde{f}_{q+1} = [q = 0] + \frac{1}{2} p_q.
\] Notice the strict causality: at step \(q\), \(\tilde{f}_0, \tilde{f}_1, \dots, \tilde{f}_q\) are already known (starting with \(\tilde{f}_0 = 0\)). Therefore:

Feeding \((\tilde{f}_q, \tilde{f}_q)\) into rc_S.next immediately yields \(s_q = [x^q] F(x)^2\).
Feeding \((\tilde{a}_q, s_q)\) (where \(\tilde{a}_q = a_q / q!\)) into rc_P.next immediately yields \(p_q = [x^q](A(x) S(x))\).
Dividing \([q = 0] + \frac{1}{2} p_q\) by \(q + 1\) immediately produces \(\tilde{f}_{q+1}\), ready for step \(q + 1\). Let us trace \(q = 0, 1, 2\) by hand:
\(q = 0\): \(\tilde{f}_0 = 0 \implies s_0 = 0 \implies p_0 = 0 \implies 1 \cdot \tilde{f}_1 = 1 + 0 = 1 \implies f_1 = 1! \tilde{f}_1 = 1\).
\(q = 1\): \(\tilde{f}_1 = 1 \implies s_1 = [x^1] F^2 = 0 \implies p_1 = 0 \implies 2 \cdot \tilde{f}_2 = 0 \implies f_2 = 0\).
\(q = 2\): \(\tilde{f}_2 = 0 \implies s_2 = [x^2] F^2 = \tilde{f}_1^2 = 1 \implies p_2 = \tilde{a}_0 s_2 = a_0 \implies 3 \cdot \tilde{f}_3 = \frac{1}{2} a_0 \implies f_3 = 3! \frac{a_0}{6} = a_0\). (Indeed, a tree of size \(m = 3\) has \(1\) root and \(2\) active child leaves of size \(1\), leaving \(i = 0\) passive leaves, so there is \(a_0\) way to form it.)

Step 3 (Solution 2: Asymmetric Semi-Online CDQ NTT & Preview of Ch 10.2 Newton ODE): If implemented via CDQ NTT solve(l, r) on \(q \in [0, n - 1]\) without RelaxedConvolution, we maintain \(s_q = [x^q] F(x)^2\) and \(p_q = [x^q](A(x) S(x))\):

Leaf Base Case (\(l = r = q\)): If \(q = 0\), set \(\tilde{f}_0 = 0, s_0 = 0, p_0 = 0, \tilde{f}_1 = 1\). If \(q \ge 1\), all pairs \((j, k)\) with \(j + k = q\) (\(1 \le j, k \le q - 1\)) have already been accumulated into \(s_q\) by ancestor cross-transfers, so \(s_q\) is finalized. Now add the instantaneous \(k = 0\) contribution p[q] = (p[q] + s[q] * a_tilde[0]) % MOD (since \(p_q = \sum_{j=0}^q s_j \tilde{a}_{q-j}\) includes \(j = q\), which cannot come from \(j \le m < q\)), so \(p_q\) is finalized, and finalize \(\tilde{f}_{q+1} = \frac{p_q}{2(q + 1)} \bmod p\).
Cross-Transfer (\([l, m] \to [m + 1, r]\)): After solve(l, m) returns, both \(\tilde{f}[l \dots m]\) and \(s[l \dots m]\) are finalized. We perform two NTT convolutions into \([m + 1, r]\):

Convolve \(\tilde{f}[l \dots m] \times \tilde{f}[0 \dots (l == 0 ? m : r - l)]\) with multiplier (l == 0 ? 1 : 2) (Failure Mode #13) and add to \(s[m + 1 \dots r]\);
Convolve \(s[l \dots m] \times \tilde{a}[1 \dots r - l]\) with multiplier 1 and add to \(p[m + 1 \dots r]\) (using \(\tilde{a}[1 \dots r - l]\) since \(\tilde{a}_0\) is applied at the leaf).

Cross-Reference to Chapter 10.2: In Chapter 10, we will see how to solve \(F' - \frac{1}{2} A F^2 - 1 = 0\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time via Integrating-Factor Newton Iteration: linearizing \(F = F_k + \Delta\) gives \(\Delta' - (A F_k) \Delta = \frac{1}{2} A F_k^2 + 1 - F_k'\), which is solved by multiplying by the integrating factor \(\mu(x) = \exp\!\left(-\int A(x) F_k(x)\,dx\right)\).








NoteAlgorithm Contract: UOJ 50 (#206)




Preconditions: Integer \(n \ge 1\) and binary array \(a[0 \dots n - 1] \in \{0, 1\}^n\), converted to EGF coefficients \(\tilde{a}_q = a_q / q! \bmod 998244353\).
Postconditions: Returns \(f_m = m! \, \tilde{f}_m \bmod 998244353\) for all \(1 \le m \le n\).
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Step index \(q\) runs over \([0, n - 1]\) with \(\tilde{f}_0 = 0\); step \(q\) computes \(s_q = [x^q] F(x)^2\) and \(p_q = [x^q](A(x) S(x))\) and writes \(\tilde{f}_{q+1} = ([q = 0] + \frac{1}{2} p_q) / (q + 1)\).
Complexity: \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space via two RelaxedConvolution instances or CDQ NTT.
1-Sentence Loop Invariant: At the beginning of step \(q \in [0, n - 1]\), \(\tilde{f}[0 \dots q]\), \(s[0 \dots q - 1]\), and \(p[0 \dots q - 1]\) are finalized, allowing rc_S.next and rc_P.next to produce \(s_q, p_q\), and \(\tilde{f}_{q+1}\) in strict causal order.
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le n\) or \(p = 2\) (since integrating \(F'(x)\) divides by \(q + 1 \in [1, n]\) and the unordered child-pair factor divides by \(2\) modulo \(p\)), or if \(s_0 = \tilde{f}_0^2 = 0\) is not pushed into rc_P at \(q = 0\) before advancing to \(q = 1\).









Mastery 2 (#075) — AtCoder AGC 060 D: Same Generating Function (Same Descent Set)

Source: AtCoder Grand Contest 060, Problem D
Prerequisite Tags: [Coupled Permutation Descent IE, Hadamard-Square Super-Block EGF, CDQ NTT / Online Inversion]
Problem Statement: Given an integer \(N\), count the number of ordered pairs of permutations \((P, Q) \in S_N \times S_N\) of \((1, 2, \dots, N)\) that have the exact same descent set—that is, for every index \(1 \le i \le N - 1\), \[
(P_i < P_{i+1}) \iff (Q_i < Q_{i+1}).
\] Output the number of such pairs modulo \(998244353\).
Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5\). Modulus \(p = 998244353\). Time limit: \(5.0\text{ s}\). Required complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) via coupled CDQ NTT or \(O(N \log N)\) via Hadamard-square super-block EGF inversion.
Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\)): For \(N = 1\), \(\text{Ans}_1 = 1^2 = 1\). For \(N = 2\), \(D(1, 2) = \emptyset\) (\(1\) perm) and \(D(2, 1) = \{1\}\) (\(1\) perm), so \(\text{Ans}_2 = 1^2 + 1^2 = 2\). For \(N = 3\), the four subsets of \(\{1, 2\}\) have counts \(f(\emptyset) = 1, f(\{1\}) = 2, f(\{2\}) = 2, f(\{1, 2\}) = 1\), so \(\text{Ans}_3 = 1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 10\) (and \(\text{Ans}_4 = 88\)).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(D(P) = \{i \in [1, N - 1] : P_i > P_{i+1}\}\) be the descent set of \(P\). For any fixed subset \(S \subseteq [1, N - 1]\), let \(f(S)\) be the number of permutations \(P \in S_N\) with \(D(P) = S\). Then we want to compute \[
\text{Ans}_N = \sum_{S \subseteq [1, N - 1]} f(S)^2.
\] By Inclusion-Exclusion on a single permutation \(P\), if we instead fix a subset \(A \subseteq [1, N - 1]\) of positions forced to be ascents (\(P_i < P_{i+1}\)), then \(A\) partitions \([1, N]\) into contiguous increasing runs of lengths \(s_1, \dots, s_k\), and the number of such permutations is the multinomial coefficient \(\frac{N!}{s_1! \, s_2! \cdots s_k!}\). How does squaring \(f(S)\) couple the run lengths of \(P\) and \(Q\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Using the algebraic identity on the Boolean hypercube \(\{+1, -1\}^{N-1}\) (or expanding \(f(S)\) via Inclusion-Exclusion over forced ascent runs for both \(P\) and \(Q\)), at each boundary \(i \in \{1, \dots, N - 1\}\), there are four possibilities for the IE relaxation states of \((P, Q)\):

Both \(P\) and \(Q\) are cut (start a new run) at \(i\);
\(P\) continues its run across \(i\), while \(Q\) is cut at \(i\);
\(Q\) continues its run across \(i\), while \(P\) is cut at \(i\);
Both \(P\) and \(Q\) continue their runs across \(i\). Key observation: if we group the sequence \([1, N]\) at the positions where both \(P\) and \(Q\) are simultaneously cut (forming super-blocks of length \(M \ge 1\)), inside a single super-block of length \(M\), \(P\)’s cuts and \(Q\)’s cuts never need to synchronize until the end of the super-block.




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let us compute the weight of a super-block of length \(M\) (noshi91’s Super-Block Decomposition):

Encode the ascent/descent pattern of \(P\) as \(\sigma_i(P) = 2[P_i < P_{i+1}] - 1 \in \{+1, -1\}\). Inside a super-block of length \(M\), \(P\) chooses a composition \(s_1 + \dots + s_r = M\) of increasing run lengths where each run of length \(s\) has EGF weight \(2^{s-1} \frac{x^s}{s!} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{(2x)^s}{s!}\) and each of the \(r - 1\) internal cuts has weight \(-1\), giving the single-permutation super-block EGF \[
U(x) = \sum_{r \ge 1} (-1)^{r - 1} \left(\frac{e^{2x} - 1}{2}\right)^r = \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^{2x} + 1} = \tanh(x) = \sum_{M=1}^{N} u_M x^M.
\]
Because \(P\) and \(Q\) choose their internal runs on \([1, M]\) independently, the combined weight on a super-block of length \(M\) between two simultaneous cuts is the Hadamard square \(w_M = u_M^2\).
Summing over all compositions of \([1, N]\) into super-blocks via SEQ inversion gives: \[
\text{Ans}_N = \frac{(N!)^2}{2^{N - 1}} [x^N] \frac{1}{1 - W(x)}, \qquad W(x) = \sum_{M=1}^{N} u_M^2 x^M.
\]








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1 (Boolean Fourier / Inclusion-Exclusion Expansion of \(\sum_S f(S)^2\)): For a permutation \(P \in S_N\), encode its ascent/descent pattern as a sign vector \(\sigma(P) \in \{+1, -1\}^{N-1}\), where \(\sigma_i(P) = +1\) if \(P_i < P_{i+1}\) and \(-1\) if \(P_i > P_{i+1}\). Notice that for any pair \((P, Q) \in S_N^2\) and each \(i \in [1, N - 1]\): \[
\frac{1 + \sigma_i(P) \sigma_i(Q)}{2} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \sigma_i(P) = \sigma_i(Q), \\ 0 & \text{if } \sigma_i(P) \neq \sigma_i(Q). \end{cases}
\] Summing over all \((P, Q) \in S_N^2\) and expanding the product over \(i = 1, \dots, N - 1\) gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Ans}_N
&= \sum_{P, Q \in S_N} \prod_{i=1}^{N-1} \frac{1 + \sigma_i(P)\sigma_i(Q)}{2} = \frac{1}{2^{N-1}} \sum_{P, Q \in S_N} \sum_{T \subseteq [1, N - 1]} \prod_{i \in T} \sigma_i(P)\sigma_i(Q) && \text{(expanding } \prod_{i=1}^{N-1}(1 + x_i) = \sum_{T} \prod_{i \in T} x_i\text{)} \\
&= \frac{1}{2^{N-1}} \sum_{T \subseteq [1, N - 1]} \sum_{P \in S_N} \sum_{Q \in S_N} \left(\prod_{i \in T} \sigma_i(P)\right) \left(\prod_{i \in T} \sigma_i(Q)\right) && \text{(swapping }\sum_{P,Q}\text{ and }\sum_T\text{ and factoring }\prod_{i \in T}\text{)} \\
&= \frac{1}{2^{N-1}} \sum_{T \subseteq [1, N - 1]} \left( \sum_{P \in S_N} \prod_{i \in T} \sigma_i(P) \right)^2. && \text{(factoring independent sums over } P \text{ and } Q\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\] Look at the inner sum \(g(T) = \sum_{P \in S_N} \prod_{i \in T} \sigma_i(P)\) for a fixed subset \(T \subseteq [1, N - 1]\).
Step 2 (Evaluating \(g(T)\) via Alternating EGF \(U(x) = \tanh(x)\)): In \(g(T) = \sum_{P \in S_N} \prod_{i \in T} \sigma_i(P)\), the positions \(i \notin T\) have weight \(1\) (meaning \(P\) is cut at \(i\): there is no relation between \(P_i\) and \(P_{i+1}\)). Thus the complement \([1, N - 1] \setminus T\) partitions \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) into contiguous super-blocks of lengths \(M_1, M_2, \dots, M_k\) (\(M_1 + \dots + M_k = N\)), where inside each super-block of length \(M\), every adjacent step \(i\) has weight \(\sigma_i(P) = 2[P_i < P_{i+1}] - 1\). Expanding \(\prod_{i=1}^{M-1} (2[P_i < P_{i+1}] - 1)\) splits the block of length \(M\) into \(r \ge 1\) increasing runs of lengths \(s_1 + \dots + s_r = M\), where each internal ascent edge contributes \(+2\) (total \(2^{(s_1 - 1) + \dots + (s_r - 1)} = 2^{M - r}\)) and each of the \(r - 1\) cut edges contributes \(-1\) (total \((-1)^{r - 1}\)). Thus a single increasing run of length \(s \ge 1\) has EGF weight \(2^{s - 1} \frac{x^s}{s!} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{(2x)^s}{s!}\), so summing over \(r \ge 1\) runs with sign \((-1)^{r - 1}\) gives the single-block EGF \(U(x) = \sum_{M \ge 1} u_M x^M\): \[
U(x) = \sum_{r \ge 1} (-1)^{r - 1} \left( \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{2} \right)^r = \frac{\frac{1}{2}(e^{2x} - 1)}{1 + \frac{1}{2}(e^{2x} - 1)} = \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^{2x} + 1} = \tanh(x).
\] Let us check \(M! [x^M] \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^{2x} + 1}\) for \(M = 1, 2, 3\):

\(M = 1\): \(1! [x^1] (x - \frac{1}{3} x^3 + \dots) = 1\) (since \(S_1\) has \(1\) permutation with weight \(1\)).
\(M = 2\): \(2! [x^2] \frac{e^{2x}-1}{e^{2x}+1} = 0\) (since in \(S_2\), (1,2) has \(\sigma_1 = +1\) and (2,1) has \(\sigma_1 = -1\), summing to \(+1 - 1 = 0\)).
\(M = 3\): \(3! [x^3] \left(x - \frac{1}{3}x^3\right) = 6 \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = -2\) (in \(S_3\), (1,2,3) gives \(+1\), (3,2,1) gives \(+1\), and the \(4\) alternating permutations (1,3,2), (2,3,1), (2,1,3), (3,1,2) each have one ascent and one descent so \(\sigma_1 \sigma_2 = -1\), summing to \(1 + 1 - 4 = -2\)).

Step 3 (Hadamard Square & Final SEQ Inversion / CDQ NTT): For any subset \(T \subseteq [1, N - 1]\) whose complement \([1, N - 1] \setminus T\) partitions \([1, N]\) into super-blocks of lengths \(M_1 + M_2 + \dots + M_k = N\), the multinomial choice of labels across blocks gives \[
g(T) = N! \prod_{r=1}^{k} u_{M_r}, \qquad \text{where } U(x) = \sum_{M=1}^{N} u_M x^M = \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^{2x} + 1}.
\] Squaring \(g(T)\) and summing over all \(2^{N-1}\) subsets \(T \subseteq [1, N - 1]\) (which is in bijection with all compositions \(M_1 + \dots + M_k = N\)) yields: \[
\text{Ans}_N = \frac{(N!)^2}{2^{N - 1}} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \sum_{M_1 + \dots + M_k = N} \prod_{r=1}^{k} u_{M_r}^2 = \frac{(N!)^2}{2^{N - 1}} [x^N] \frac{1}{1 - W(x)},
\] where \(W(x) = \sum_{M=1}^{N} u_M^2 x^M\) is the Hadamard square of \(U(x)\). (Note: Because \(U(-x) = -U(x)\) is an odd function, \(u_M = 0\) for all even \(M\), so \(W(x) = x + \frac{1}{9}x^3 + \frac{4}{225}x^5 + \dots\) has only odd powers \(x^{2k+1}\).)

Hand-Check for \(N = 1, 2, 3\):

\(u_1 = 1, u_2 = 0, u_3 = -1/3 \implies W(x) = x + \frac{1}{9} x^3 + \dots\).
\(N = 1\): \(\frac{1^2}{2^0} [x^1] \frac{1}{1 - x} = 1\).
\(N = 2\): \(\frac{2^2}{2^1} [x^2] \frac{1}{1 - x} = 2 \cdot 1 = 2\) (pairs ((1,2),(1,2)) and ((2,1),(2,1))).
\(N = 3\): \(\frac{6^2}{2^2} [x^3] \big(W(x) + W(x)^2 + W(x)^3\big) = 9 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{9} + 0 + 1\right) = 10\) (in \(S_3\), descent set sizes are \(1, 2, 2, 1\), and \(1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 10\)).

Algorithm:

Construct \(E(x) = e^{2x} \bmod x^{N+1}\) in \(O(N)\) time (\([x^m] E(x) = 2^m / m!\)).
Compute \(U(x) = (E(x) - 1)(E(x) + 1)^{-1} \bmod x^{N+1}\) via polynomial inversion (or online inv via CDQ / RelaxedConvolution).
Square coefficients pointwise: \(w_M = u_M^2 \bmod p\) for \(1 \le M \le N\).
Compute \((1 - W(x))^{-1} \bmod x^{N+1}\) via polynomial inversion (or online inv via CDQ / RelaxedConvolution) and multiply \([x^N]\) by \((N!)^2 \cdot 2^{-(N-1)} \bmod p\).









NoteAlgorithm Contract: AGC 060 D (#075)




Input & Preconditions: Integer \(N \ge 1\) (\(N \le 2 \times 10^5\)) and prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > N\).
Output & Postconditions: Returns \(\text{Ans}_N = \frac{(N!)^2}{2^{N-1}} [x^N](1 - W(x))^{-1} \bmod 998244353\), the number of pairs \((P, Q) \in S_N^2\) sharing the same descent set.
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Both \(U(x)\) and \((1 - W(x))^{-1}\) are truncated at \(\bmod x^{N+1}\); \([x^0](e^{2x} + 1) = 2 \not\equiv 0\) and \([x^0](1 - W(x)) = 1 \not\equiv 0\) are invertible modulo \(998244353\).
1-Sentence Loop Invariant: After doubling precision to \(2^k\) in Newton inversion, the truncated inverse satisfies \((1 - W(x)) G_k(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{x^{2^k}}\).
Complexity & Failure Modes: \(O(N \log N)\) time via offline Newton inv (or \(O(N \log^2 N)\) via online RelaxedConvolution / CDQ NTT) and \(O(N)\) space. Squaring the ordinary coefficients \((M! u_M)^2\) instead of the EGF coefficients \(u_M^2\) before applying SEQ \((1 - W(x))^{-1}\) destroys the multinomial block assembly \(\binom{N}{M_1, \dots, M_k}^2\), and forgetting the normalization factor \(2^{-(N-1)}\) at \(N = 1\) (\(2^0 = 1\)) vs \(N \ge 2\) shifts the result by a power of \(2\).

9.6 Implementation Verification Benchmark & Self-Assessment Checklist






NoteQuarantined Library Verification Footnote (R-45)



Before tackling the 8-problem ladder above, unit-test your Semi-Online CDQ NTT (solve(l, r)) and 0-Indexed RelaxedConvolution implementations on the quarantined bare-template problem below:

R-45 — Luogu P4721: 【模板】分治 FFT (CDQ Divide-and-Conquer FFT) (Luogu P4721): Given \(g_1, g_2, \dots, g_{n-1}\) (\(n \le 10^5\)), compute \(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{n-1} \bmod 998244353\) where \(f_0 = 1\) and \(f_k = \sum_{i=1}^k f_{k-i} g_i\). (Pedagogical Note: As emphasized in Section 9.1, because this bare template has no non-linear wrapper \(\psi_k\), it is simply \(F(x) = (1 - G(x))^{-1}\) in disguise! Use it purely to benchmark the speed and indexing of your solve(l, r) and RelaxedConvolution::next engines against your \(O(n \log n)\) Newton inv.)




Chapter 09 Self-Assessment Checklist

Can you state the four structural obstacles (pointwise division by \(n\), non-autonomous multipliers \(w_n\), pointwise \(\min/\max\) envelopes, and self-referential products) that prevent offline \((1 - G(x))^{-1}\) inversion?
Can you prove the LCA Partition Invariant for solve(l, r) and trace all \(6\) causal pairs for \(N = 4\)?
Can you explain Failure Mode #13 (why self-convolution CDQ NTT requires multiplying f[l..m] * f[0..r-l] by 2 when \(l > 0\), and why \(r - l < l\) holds on a dyadic grid)?
Can you implement the 15-line RelaxedConvolution struct using \(d = \operatorname{lowbit}(q)\) and apply the 3-Step Self-Referential Protocol (Read c[q] \(\to\) Solve \(\to\) Push)?

title: Chapter 07: Point-Value Duality, Roots-of-Unity Filters, Chirp Z-Transform & Arbitrary-Modulus NTT

NotePrerequisites & Learning Objectives



Prerequisites:

Chapter 01 (Ch 01): Formal power series rings \(K[[x]]\), polynomial rings \(K[x]\), units vs. zero divisors in commutative rings, and formal residue arithmetic.
Chapter 02 (Ch 02): Truncated quotients \(K[x]/(x^N)\), the algebraic Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) over prime fields \(\mathbb{F}_p\), and the standard radix-2 Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT).

Learning Objectives:

View the Discrete Fourier Transform not just as an \(O(L \log L)\) multiplication black box, but as an explicit Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) ring isomorphism \(K[x]/(x^L - 1) \cong \prod_{r=0}^{L-1} K[x]/(x - \omega_L^r)\) that diagonalizes cyclic shift operators.
Convert multiplicative group convolutions modulo a prime \(P\) (\(i \cdot j \bmod P\)) into cyclic additive convolutions modulo \(P-1\) via discrete logarithms (\(\operatorname{ind}_g\)), while cleanly isolating the absorbing element \(0 \bmod P\).
Execute Arbitrary-Modulus Convolution (MTT) over any integer modulus \(M \le 10^9 + 9\) with zero floating-point precision loss using 3-Prime NTT and Garner’s Mixed-Radix CRT reconstruction.
Derive Bluestein’s Chirp Z-Transform (CZT) to evaluate polynomials on arbitrary geometric progressions \(x_i = a \cdot c^i\) and execute arbitrary-length DFTs (\(L\) not a power of \(2\)) in \(O((n+m)\log(n+m))\) operations—avoiding Failure Mode #12 (\(c^{1/2} \notin \mathbb{F}_p\) and \(c=0\)).
Apply Roots-of-Unity Index Filters (单位根反演) to extract arithmetic progressions \(\sum_{k \equiv r \pmod m} f_k\) and floor sums \(\sum_i f_i \lfloor i/m \rfloor\), and resolve Failure Mode #11 (when \(m \nmid (p-1)\) so \(\omega_m \notin \mathbb{F}_p\)) using either the cyclic quotient ring \(K[x]/(x^m - 1)\) or the cyclotomic quotient ring \(\mathbb{F}_p[\omega]/(\Phi_m(\omega))\).

section: 7.1 DFT as Vandermonde Evaluation–Interpolation, Cyclic Wrap-Around & Multiplicative Convolutions
text:
7.1 DFT as Vandermonde Evaluation–Interpolation, Cyclic Wrap-Around & Multiplicative Convolutions
In Chapter 02, we used the Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT) primarily as an algorithmic engine to compute truncated products \(A(x)B(x) \bmod x^N\) by zero-padding both inputs to a power of two \(L \ge 2N - 1\) so that indices never wrap around. In this chapter, we invert our perspective: cyclic wrap-around is not a bug to be padded away, but an exact algebraic tool for counting problems governed by modular arithmetic, cyclic shifts, and group homomorphisms.

7.1.1 The Algebraic Meaning of the DFT: CRT Isomorphism on \(K[x]/(x^L - 1)\)
Suppose we want to track a combinatorial quantity—such as the sum of chosen elements or the position of a random walk—modulo a fixed period \(L \ge 1\). In polynomial language, two monomials \(x^a\) and \(x^b\) represent the same residue class modulo \(L\) whenever \(a \equiv b \pmod L\), which is equivalent to imposing the relation \(x^L = 1\).
The natural algebraic home for sequences indexed by \(\mathbb{Z}_L = \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}\) is the cyclic quotient ring \[
\mathcal{R}_L = K[x]/(x^L - 1).
\] An element of \(\mathcal{R}_L\) is represented uniquely by a polynomial \(A(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{L-1} a_i x^i\) of degree \(< L\). Multiplication in \(\mathcal{R}_L\) is cyclic convolution of length \(L\): for \(A(x), B(x) \in \mathcal{R}_L\), their product \(C(x) = A(x)B(x) \bmod (x^L - 1)\) has coefficients \[
c_k = \sum_{\substack{0 \le i, j < L \\ i + j \equiv k \pmod L}} a_i b_j \qquad (0 \le k < L).
\]
When can we diagonalize this ring so that cyclic convolution becomes pointwise multiplication? Suppose \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) is a prime field (or a commutative ring) satisfying two local algebraic hypotheses:

\(L\) is a unit in \(K\) (\(L \in K^\times\), i.e., \(p \nmid L\) when \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\)).
\(K\) contains a primitive (or principal) \(L\)-th root of unity \(\omega_L\): over a field \(K\) (or an integral domain), this means \(\omega_L\) has multiplicative order \(L\), so \(\omega_L^L = 1\) and \(\omega_L^d \ne 1\) for all proper divisors \(d \mid L, d < L\) (over \(\mathbb{F}_p\), this holds if and only if \(L \mid (p-1)\), where \(\omega_L = g^{(p-1)/L} \bmod p\) for a primitive root \(g\) of \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\)); over a general commutative ring \(K\), \(\omega_L\) is a principal \(L\)-th root of unity, meaning \(\omega_L^L = 1\) and \(\sum_{j=0}^{L-1} \omega_L^{jt} = 0\) for all \(1 \le t < L\) (which guarantees \(\omega_L^r - \omega_L^s \in K^\times\) for all \(0 \le r < s < L\)).

Under these two hypotheses, the polynomial \(x^L - 1\) factors completely into \(L\) pairwise coprime linear factors in \(K[x]\): \[
x^L - 1 = \prod_{r=0}^{L-1} (x - \omega_L^r).
\] By the Chinese Remainder Theorem for polynomial rings, reducing \(A(x) \bmod (x - \omega_L^r)\) is simply evaluating \(A(\omega_L^r)\). Thus, we obtain an explicit ring isomorphism: \[
\operatorname{DFT}_L : K[x]/(x^L - 1) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \prod_{r=0}^{L-1} K[x]/(x - \omega_L^r) \cong K^L, \qquad A(x) \longmapsto \bigl(A(\omega_L^0),\, A(\omega_L^1),\, \dots,\, A(\omega_L^{L-1})\bigr).
\]
In matrix form, \(\operatorname{DFT}_L\) multiplies the coefficient vector \(\mathbf{a} = (a_0, \dots, a_{L-1})^\top\) by the \(L \times L\) Vandermonde matrix \(V(\omega_L)\) with entries \(V_{r, j} = \omega_L^{rj}\): \[
\hat{a}_r = A(\omega_L^r) = \sum_{j=0}^{L-1} a_j \omega_L^{rj} \qquad (0 \le r < L).
\] Its inverse \(\operatorname{IDFT}_L\) reconstructs the unique polynomial \(A(x) \in K[x]/(x^L - 1)\) from its \(L\) point values via the inverse Vandermonde matrix \(V(\omega_L)^{-1} = \frac{1}{L} V(\omega_L^{-1})\): \[
a_j = \frac{1}{L} \sum_{r=0}^{L-1} \hat{a}_r \omega_L^{-rj} \qquad (0 \le j < L).
\]






TipWhy Exploiting Cyclic Wrap-Around Saves Work



Whenever a problem asks for coefficients of \(A(x)^n \bmod (x^L - 1)\) (for instance, counting length-\(n\) sequences whose sum modulo \(L\) equals \(k\)), we never compute the full degree-\(n(L-1)\) polynomial and reduce afterward. Instead:

Case 1 (\(L \mid (p-1)\) and \(L = 2^k\)): Apply a single length-\(L\) forward NTT to obtain \(\hat{a}_r = A(\omega_L^r)\), raise each point value to the \(n\)-th power \(\hat{a}_r^n \bmod p\) in \(O(L \log n)\) field operations, and apply a single length-\(L\) inverse NTT. Total time: \(O(L \log L + L \log n)\) instead of \(O(L \log L \log n)\).
Case 2 (\(L\) is not a power of 2 or \(\omega_L \notin \mathbb{F}_p\)): Maintain polynomials of degree \(< L\) during binary exponentiation, reducing modulo \((x^L - 1)\) after each polynomial multiplication by folding the upper half into the lower half: for \(i \ge L\), add the coefficient of \(x^i\) into \(x^{i \bmod L}\) in \(O(L)\) time.






7.1.2 Multiplicative Group Convolution \(\bmod P\) (Ind_g Reduction)
Up to now, every convolution we have studied combines indices additively (\(i + j\) or \((i + j) \bmod L\)). What if a combinatorial process combines states by modular multiplication?
Suppose \(P\) is a prime number, and we are given two arrays \(a, b\) indexed by residues modulo \(P\). We want to compute the multiplicative convolution modulo \(P\): \[
c_k = \sum_{\substack{0 \le i, j < P \\ i \cdot j \equiv k \pmod P}} a_i b_j \qquad (0 \le k < P),
\] or, more generally, we are given a subset \(S \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, P-1\}\) and asked how many length-\(n\) sequences \((s_1, \dots, s_n) \in S^n\) have product \(s_1 s_2 \cdots s_n \equiv x \pmod P\).

The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Diagnostic Signal: The transition or convolution index combines via multiplication modulo a prime \(P\): \(i \cdot j \equiv k \pmod P\), or \(\prod_{t=1}^n s_t \equiv x \pmod P\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

How do we turn multiplication into addition? Over the positive reals, the logarithm satisfies \(\ln(i \cdot j) = \ln(i) + \ln(j)\). What is the exact finite-field analogue of the logarithm for residues modulo a prime \(P\)?
Be careful: \(0 \bmod P\) is not invertible! In \(\mathbb{Z}_P\), the element \(0\) is an absorbing element (\(0 \cdot j \equiv 0 \pmod P\)). However, the remaining \(P-1\) nonzero residues \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times = \{1, 2, \dots, P-1\}\) form a cyclic group of order \(P-1\) under multiplication modulo \(P\).
Because \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times\) is cyclic of order \(P-1\), there exists a primitive root \(g \in \{1, \dots, P-1\}\) whose powers \(g^0, g^1, \dots, g^{P-2} \bmod P\) visit every nonzero residue in \(\{1, \dots, P-1\}\) exactly once, with \(g^{P-1} \equiv 1 \pmod P\).
Define the discrete logarithm (index) map \(\operatorname{ind}_g : \{1, \dots, P-1\} \to \{0, 1, \dots, P-2\}\) by the unique exponent \(u = \operatorname{ind}_g(x) \in \{0, \dots, P-2\}\) such that \(g^u \equiv x \pmod P\).
For any two nonzero residues \(i = g^u \bmod P\) and \(j = g^v \bmod P\), their product modulo \(P\) is \[
i \cdot j \equiv g^u \cdot g^v \equiv g^{(u + v) \bmod (P-1)} \pmod P.
\] Under the bijection \(x \leftrightarrow \operatorname{ind}_g(x)\), multiplication in \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times\) becomes cyclic addition modulo \(P-1\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_{P-1}\)!




Single-Step Verbalized Derivation (Separating \(0\) from \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times\))
Let us write out the complete reduction of \(c_k = \sum_{i \cdot j \equiv k \pmod P} a_i b_j\) into two clean pieces:

Isolate the absorbing element \(k = 0\): Since \(P\) is prime, \(\mathbb{F}_P\) is an integral domain, so a product \(i \cdot j \equiv 0 \pmod P\) if and only if \(i = 0\) or \(j = 0\). Counting all pairs \((i, j) \in \{0, \dots, P-1\}^2\) where at least one index is \(0\) gives \[
c_0 = a_0 \sum_{j=0}^{P-1} b_j + b_0 \sum_{i=0}^{P-1} a_i - a_0 b_0 = a_0 \sum_{j=0}^{P-1} b_j + b_0 \sum_{i=1}^{P-1} a_i.
\]
Re-index the nonzero group \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times = \{1, \dots, P-1\}\) via \(\operatorname{ind}_g\): Define new arrays \(\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}\) of length \(L = P-1\) indexed by \(u \in \{0, 1, \dots, P-2\}\): \[
\tilde{a}_u = a_{g^u \bmod P}, \qquad \tilde{b}_v = b_{g^v \bmod P} \qquad (0 \le u, v \le P-2).
\]
Perform cyclic additive convolution of length \(P-1\): Form the polynomials \(\tilde{A}(z) = \sum_{u=0}^{P-2} \tilde{a}_u z^u\) and \(\tilde{B}(z) = \sum_{v=0}^{P-2} \tilde{b}_v z^v\), and compute their product in the cyclic quotient ring \(K[z]/(z^{P-1} - 1)\): \[
\tilde{C}(z) = \tilde{A}(z)\tilde{B}(z) \bmod (z^{P-1} - 1) = \sum_{w=0}^{P-2} \tilde{c}_w z^w, \qquad \text{where } \tilde{c}_w = \sum_{u + v \equiv w \pmod{P-1}} \tilde{a}_u \tilde{b}_v.
\] In practical NTT implementations where the transform length \(N_{\text{ntt}} = 2^{\lceil \log_2(2(P-1)-1) \rceil}\) exceeds \(P-1\), we simply multiply \(\tilde{A}(z)\) and \(\tilde{B}(z)\) as ordinary polynomials of degree \(\le 2P - 4\) and then fold the upper coefficients back into the lower half: for each \(w \in \{0, \dots, P-2\}\), set \(\tilde{c}_w \leftarrow [z^w](\tilde{A}\tilde{B}) + [z^{w + P - 1}](\tilde{A}\tilde{B})\).
Map exponents back to nonzero residues: For each \(w \in \{0, \dots, P-2\}\), set \[
c_{g^w \bmod P} = \tilde{c}_w.
\]



Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(P = 5\))
Let \(P = 5\), and suppose we want to compute the multiplicative self-convolution \(c_k = \sum_{i \cdot j \equiv k \pmod 5} a_i a_j\) for the indicator polynomial of \(S = \{1, 2, 3\} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_5\), so \((a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4) = (0, 1, 1, 1, 0)\).

Absorbing element \(0\): Since \(a_0 = 0\), \(c_0 = 0\).
Primitive root and index table for \(\mathbb{F}_5^\times\): Let \(g = 2\) be our primitive root modulo \(5\). The powers of \(2\) modulo \(5\) are:

\(u = 0 : 2^0 \equiv 1 \pmod 5 \implies \operatorname{ind}_2(1) = 0\)
\(u = 1 : 2^1 \equiv 2 \pmod 5 \implies \operatorname{ind}_2(2) = 1\)
\(u = 2 : 2^2 \equiv 4 \pmod 5 \implies \operatorname{ind}_2(4) = 2\)
\(u = 3 : 2^3 \equiv 3 \pmod 5 \implies \operatorname{ind}_2(3) = 3\)

Re-indexed polynomial \(\tilde{A}(z)\) of length \(P-1 = 4\): \[
\tilde{a}_0 = a_1 = 1, \quad \tilde{a}_1 = a_2 = 1, \quad \tilde{a}_2 = a_4 = 0, \quad \tilde{a}_3 = a_3 = 1 \implies \tilde{A}(z) = 1 + z + z^3.
\]
Ordinary square and cyclic folding \(\bmod (z^4 - 1)\): \[
\tilde{A}(z)^2 = (1 + z + z^3)^2 = 1 + 2z + z^2 + 2z^3 + 2z^4 + z^6.
\] Folding \(z^4 \equiv z^0\) and \(z^6 \equiv z^2 \pmod{z^4 - 1}\) gives \[
\tilde{C}(z) = (1 + 2)z^0 + 2z^1 + (1 + 1)z^2 + 2z^3 = 3 + 2z + 2z^2 + 2z^3.
\]
Map back via \(w \mapsto 2^w \bmod 5\):

\(w = 0 \implies k = 2^0 \bmod 5 = 1 : c_1 = 3\) (pairs \((1,1), (2,3), (3,2)\))
\(w = 1 \implies k = 2^1 \bmod 5 = 2 : c_2 = 2\) (pairs \((1,2), (2,1)\))
\(w = 2 \implies k = 2^2 \bmod 5 = 4 : c_4 = 2\) (pairs \((2,2), (3,3)\))
\(w = 3 \implies k = 2^3 \bmod 5 = 3 : c_3 = 2\) (pairs \((1,3), (3,1)\))

The total number of pairs is \(3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9 = |S|^2\), matching every ordered pair in \(\{1, 2, 3\}^2\).







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Non-Cyclic Multiplicative Groups Modulo Composite \(M\) & Prime Powers \(p^k\)



The Trap: What if a problem asks for multiplicative convolution \(i \cdot j \bmod M\) where \(M\) is not prime? A common mistake is assuming that \(\mathbb{Z}_M^\times\) always has a primitive root \(g\), or assuming that non-units simply collapse to \(0\) in a single step.
Why It Fails:

Zero divisors: When \(M\) is composite, \(i \cdot j \equiv 0 \pmod M\) can occur even when \(i \not\equiv 0\) and \(j \not\equiv 0 \pmod M\) (e.g., \(2 \cdot 2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4\), or \(2 \cdot 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 6\)). Non-coprime residues (\(\gcd(i, M) > 1\)) do not belong to the unit group \(\mathbb{Z}_M^\times\).
Non-cyclic unit groups: By Gauss’s theorem, \(\mathbb{Z}_M^\times\) is cyclic (possesses a single primitive root \(g\) of order \(\varphi(M)\)) if and only if \(M \in \{1, 2, 4, p^k, 2p^k\}\) for an odd prime \(p\). For \(M = 2^k\) (\(k \ge 3\)) or any \(M\) divisible by two distinct odd primes (such as \(M = 15\) or \(M = 12\)), no single generator \(g\) exists!

The Exact Algebraic Remedy:

Case 1 (Odd prime power \(M = p^k\)): The unit group \((\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z})^\times\) is cyclic of order \(\varphi(p^k) = p^{k-1}(p - 1)\) (if \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\) and \(g^{p-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}\), then \(g\) is also a primitive root modulo \(p^k\) for all \(k \ge 1\)). For non-units, factor every residue \(x \in \mathbb{Z}_{p^k} \setminus \{0\}\) uniquely as \(x = p^v \cdot u\) with \(0 \le v < k\) and \(u \in (\mathbb{Z}/p^{k-v}\mathbb{Z})^\times\); stratify by the \(p\)-adic valuation \(v = v_p(x)\) (which adds via \(v_p(i \cdot j) = \min(k, v_p(i) + v_p(j))\)) and apply cyclic discrete-log convolution on the unit part \(u\).
Case 2 (Power of two \(M = 2^k\) with \(k \ge 3\)): The unit group \((\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z})^\times\) is isomorphic to the 2-dimensional abelian group \(\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_{2^{k-2}}\), generated by \(-1\) (of order \(2\)) and \(5\) (of order \(2^{k-2}\)). Every odd residue \(u \in (\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z})^\times\) has a unique representation \(u \equiv (-1)^a \cdot 5^b \pmod{2^k}\) with \(a \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(b \in \{0, 1, \dots, 2^{k-2}-1\}\). Multiplication of odd residues becomes a 2D cyclic convolution of size \(2 \times 2^{k-2}\)!
Case 3 (General composite \(M = \prod_{r=1}^s p_r^{k_r}\)): By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, \(\mathbb{Z}_M \cong \prod_{r=1}^s \mathbb{Z}_{p_r^{k_r}}\), so the unit group \(\mathbb{Z}_M^\times \cong \prod_{r=1}^s (\mathbb{Z}/p_r^{k_r}\mathbb{Z})^\times\) decomposes into a direct product of cyclic groups, transforming multiplicative convolution on units into a multidimensional cyclic DFT across the prime-power factors.









ImportantAlgorithm Contract: dft_cyclic_exp(A, L, n) & mult_conv_mod_p(a, b, P)




Input:

For dft_cyclic_exp(A, L, n): Polynomial \(A \in K[x]/(x^L - 1)\) of length \(L\), and exponent \(n \ge 0\).
For mult_conv_mod_p(a, b, P): Prime \(P \ge 2\) and coefficient arrays \(a, b \in K^P\) indexed by \(\{0, 1, \dots, P-1\}\).

Output:

dft_cyclic_exp: Coefficient array of \(A(x)^n \bmod (x^L - 1)\) of length \(L\).
mult_conv_mod_p: Array \(c \in K^P\) where \(c_k = \sum_{i \cdot j \equiv k \pmod P} a_i b_j\) for \(0 \le k < P\).

Preconditions:

In mult_conv_mod_p, \(P\) must be prime so that \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times = \{1, \dots, P-1\}\) is cyclic of order \(P-1\).
The coefficient ring \(K\) (e.g., \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\) or \(\mathbb{F}_{1004535809}\)) must support length-\((2P-3)\) polynomial multiplication (via standard NTT or 3-Prime MTT).

Core Invariant:

Zero index \(k = 0\) is isolated before taking discrete logarithms: \(c_0 = a_0 \sum_{j=0}^{P-1} b_j + b_0 \sum_{i=1}^{P-1} a_i\).
For \(1 \le x < P\), \(\operatorname{ind}_g(x) \in \{0, \dots, P-2\}\) is a group isomorphism \((\mathbb{F}_P^\times, \cdot) \xrightarrow{\sim} (\mathbb{Z}_{P-1}, +)\), and folding index \(w + (P - 1)\) into \(w\) for \(0 \le w \le P - 3\) after degree-\((2P-4)\) Cauchy multiplication preserves exact cyclic wrap-around modulo \(P - 1\).

Complexity:

dft_cyclic_exp: \(O(L \log L + L \log n)\) time if \(L = 2^k \mid (p-1)\), or \(O(L \log L \log n)\) via binary exponentiation with cyclic folding; \(O(L)\) space.
mult_conv_mod_p: \(O(\sqrt{P})\) (or \(O(P)\)) to find primitive root \(g\) and build \(\operatorname{ind}_g\), plus \(O(P \log P)\) for one cyclic convolution of length \(P - 1\); \(O(P)\) space.

section: 7.2 Arbitrary-Modulus Convolution (MTT) via 3-Prime NTT & Garner’s CRT
text:
7.2 Arbitrary-Modulus Convolution (MTT) via 3-Prime NTT & Garner’s CRT
In Chapter 02, our NTT engine required the modulus \(p\) to be an NTT-friendly prime of the form \(p = c \cdot 2^k + 1\) with \(2^k \ge L\). What happens when a problem asks for polynomial convolution or formal power series inversion modulo \(M = 10^9 + 7\), modulo \(M = 999999999\), or modulo an arbitrary prime \(p\) given at runtime (as we will face in Mas-2: Luogu P5293)?

7.2.1 Why 3-Prime NTT Beats Floating-Point FFT (MTT)
Two competing families of algorithms go by the name MTT (Modulus Transform Technique) in competitive programming:

Split-Radix Complex FFT: Splitting each coefficient into \(15\)-bit halves \(a_i = a_{i,\text{hi}} \cdot 2^{15} + a_{i,\text{lo}}\) and running 4 to 7 complex FFTs in double or long double. While fast in wall-clock time, floating-point MTT is notorious for subtle rounding errors when \(N \ge 2^{18}\) and \(M \approx 10^9\), especially if std::polar or naive trigonometric recurrences drift by \(10^{-12}\) ULPs.
3-Prime NTT + Garner’s Mixed-Radix CRT: Performing exact integer NTTs modulo three distinct NTT-friendly primes \(p_1, p_2, p_3\) and reconstructing the exact integer convolution coefficients via the Chinese Remainder Theorem before reducing modulo \(M\).

Because 3-Prime NTT uses 100% exact integer arithmetic, it suffers zero floating-point precision loss and reuses your existing NTT library verbatim.


7.2.2 Choosing the Three Canonical NTT Primes
Suppose we convolve two sequences \(A, B\) of length \(N \le 5 \times 10^5\) with coefficients in \(\{0, 1, \dots, M-1\}\), where \(M \le 10^9 + 9\). Over the integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) (before any modular reduction), each exact convolution coefficient \(C_k = \sum_{i+j=k} A_i B_j\) satisfies the strict upper bound \[
0 \le C_k \le N (M - 1)^2 \approx 5 \times 10^5 \times 10^{18} = 5 \times 10^{23}.
\] Therefore, if we compute \(C_k \bmod p_1\), \(C_k \bmod p_2\), and \(C_k \bmod p_3\) for three distinct primes whose product \(P = p_1 p_2 p_3\) exceeds \(N(M-1)^2\), the Chinese Remainder Theorem uniquely determines the exact integer \(C_k \in [0, p_1 p_2 p_3)\)!
The standard triad of NTT primes with primitive root \(g = 3\) for all three is:









Prime \(p_i\)
Factorization \(c \cdot 2^k + 1\)
Max Power-of-2 Length \(2^k\)
Primitive Root \(g\)




\(p_1 = 998244353\)
\(119 \cdot 2^{23} + 1\)
\(2^{23} = 8{,}388{,}608\)
\(3\)


\(p_2 = 1004535809\)
\(479 \cdot 2^{21} + 1\)
\(2^{21} = 2{,}097{,}152\)
\(3\)


\(p_3 = 469762049\)
\(7 \cdot 2^{26} + 1\)
\(2^{26} = 67{,}108{,}864\)
\(3\)



Their product is \[
p_1 p_2 p_3 \approx 4.71 \times 10^{26} > 5 \times 10^{23} \ge N (M - 1)^2,
\] which safely covers all convolution lengths up to \(N = 2^{20}\) and moduli up to \(M \le 2 \times 10^9\).



7.2.3 Step-by-Step Derivation of Garner’s Mixed-Radix CRT Reconstruction
How do we reconstruct \(X = C_k \bmod M\) from its three remainders \[
r_1 = X \bmod p_1, \qquad r_2 = X \bmod p_2, \qquad r_3 = X \bmod p_3
\] without needing 128-bit or arbitrary-precision big-integer division by \(p_1 p_2 p_3 \approx 4.71 \times 10^{26}\) (which exceeds \(2^{64} \approx 1.84 \times 10^{19}\))?

The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Diagnostic Signal: We know \(X \bmod p_1, X \bmod p_2, X \bmod p_3\) with \(0 \le X < p_1 p_2 p_3\), and we want \(X \bmod M\), where \(p_1 p_2 p_3 > 2^{64}\) overflows standard 64-bit unsigned integers.
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

Instead of writing \(X\) in the standard CRT sum \(\sum_{i=1}^3 r_i M_i (M_i^{-1} \bmod p_i) \bmod (p_1 p_2 p_3)\)—which requires reducing a huge sum modulo the 89-bit integer \(p_1 p_2 p_3\)—let us write \(X\) in mixed-radix representation with base \((1, p_1, p_1 p_2)\): \[
X = x_1 + x_2 p_1 + x_3 p_1 p_2,
\] where the “digits” satisfy \(0 \le x_1 < p_1\), \(0 \le x_2 < p_2\), and \(0 \le x_3 < p_3\).
Notice that every integer \(X \in [0, p_1 p_2 p_3)\) has a unique mixed-radix tuple \((x_1, x_2, x_3)\) in those ranges!
How do we find \(x_1, x_2, x_3\) one by one using only arithmetic modulo \(p_1, p_2, p_3\)?

Take the equation modulo \(p_1\): since \(p_1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p_1}\), the \(x_2 p_1\) and \(x_3 p_1 p_2\) terms vanish! We immediately get \[
x_1 = r_1 \bmod p_1.
\]
Now take the equation modulo \(p_2\): the \(x_3 p_1 p_2\) term vanishes! We get \(x_1 + x_2 p_1 \equiv r_2 \pmod{p_2}\). Subtracting \(x_1\) and multiplying by the modular inverse \(inv_{1,2} = p_1^{-1} \bmod p_2\) gives \[
x_2 = (r_2 - x_1) \cdot (p_1^{-1} \bmod p_2) \bmod p_2.
\]
Finally, take the equation modulo \(p_3\): \(x_1 + x_2 p_1 + x_3 p_1 p_2 \equiv r_3 \pmod{p_3}\). Subtracting \((x_1 + x_2 p_1) \bmod p_3\) and multiplying by \(inv_{12,3} = (p_1 p_2)^{-1} \bmod p_3\) gives \[
x_3 = \bigl((r_3 - x_1 - x_2 p_1) \bmod p_3\bigr) \cdot \bigl((p_1 p_2)^{-1} \bmod p_3\bigr) \bmod p_3.
\]

Once the exact bounded digits \(x_1 \in [0, p_1)\), \(x_2 \in [0, p_2)\), and \(x_3 \in [0, p_3)\) are known, the identity \(X = x_1 + x_2 p_1 + x_3 p_1 p_2\) holds as an exact equality of integers in \(\mathbb{Z}\)! Therefore, we can project it directly modulo our target modulus \(M\): \[
X \bmod M = \Bigl(x_1 + x_2 (p_1 \bmod M) + x_3 (p_1 p_2 \bmod M)\Bigr) \bmod M.
\] Every multiplication in this final projection is between two numbers \(< 2 \times 10^9\), which fits comfortably inside a standard 64-bit integer (uint64_t / long long)!








WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Premature Modulo-\(M\) Reduction During Garner’s CRT



The Trap: A frequent bug when implementing Garner’s CRT is computing \(X_{12} = (x_1 + x_2 p_1) \bmod M\) first and then trying to compute \(x_3\) from \(X_{12}\), or forgetting to reduce \(x_3\) into \([0, p_3)\) before multiplying by \((p_1 p_2 \bmod M)\).
Why It Fails:

To compute \(x_3\), we need \((x_1 + x_2 p_1) \bmod p_3\), not \((x_1 + x_2 p_1) \bmod M\). Since \(x_1 + x_2 p_1 < p_1 p_2 \approx 10^{18}\) fits inside a signed 64-bit integer (int64_t), you should store the exact 64-bit integer \(X_{12} = x_1 + x_2 p_1\) first.
In Step 3, \(x_3\) must be reduced modulo \(p_3\) into the canonical range \([0, p_3)\) before we transition to modulo-\(M\) arithmetic. This is because the equality \(X = X_{12} + x_3 p_1 p_2\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) holds only for the unique representative \(x_3 \in [0, p_3)\). If \(x_3\) is off by a multiple of \(p_3\), then \(X\) changes by a multiple of \(p_1 p_2 p_3\), which is not a multiple of \(M\)!

The Exact 64-Bit Reconstruction Snippet:
// Precomputed constants:
// inv1_2 = qpow(p1, p2 - 2, p2);
// inv12_3 = qpow(1ULL * p1 * p2 % p3, p3 - 2, p3);
// p12_mod_M = (1ULL * p1 * p2) % M;

uint64_t x1 = r1; // in [0, p1)
uint64_t x2 = (r2 + p2 - x1 % p2) * inv1_2 % p2; // in [0, p2)
uint64_t X12 = x1 + x2 * p1; // Exact integer in [0, p1*p2), < 1.003e18
uint64_t x3 = (r3 + p3 - X12 % p3) * inv12_3 % p3; // Exact digit in [0, p3)
uint64_t ans = (X12 % M + x3 * p12_mod_M) % M;








ImportantAlgorithm Contract: 3-Prime Arbitrary-Modulus Convolution mtt_3prime_conv(A, B, M)




Input:

Coefficient arrays \(A \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}^n\) and \(B \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}^m\), and arbitrary integer modulus \(1 \le M \le 2 \times 10^9\).

Output:

Array \(C \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}^{n + m - 1}\) where \(C_k = \left(\sum_{i+j=k} A_i B_j\right) \bmod M\) for \(0 \le k < n + m - 1\).

Preconditions:

Transform length \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(n + m - 1) \rceil}\) must satisfy \(L \le 2^{21} = 2{,}097{,}152\) (the maximum power-of-2 divisor of \(p_2 - 1 = 479 \cdot 2^{21}\)).
Unreduced integer coefficients must satisfy \(\min(n, m) \cdot (M - 1)^2 < p_1 p_2 p_3 \approx 4.71 \times 10^{26}\).

Core Invariant:

After three independent NTT convolutions modulo \(p_1 = 998244353\), \(p_2 = 1004535809\), and \(p_3 = 469762049\), the mixed-radix digits \((x_1, x_2, x_3) \in [0, p_1) \times [0, p_2) \times [0, p_3)\) satisfy the exact integer equality \(\sum_{i+j=k} A_i B_j = x_1 + x_2 p_1 + x_3 p_1 p_2\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) before reducing modulo \(M\).

Complexity:

Time: \(9\) NTT passes of length \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(n + m - 1) \rceil}\) plus \(O(n + m)\) Garner reconstruction steps, totaling \(O((n + m) \log(n + m))\) operations.
Space: \(O(n + m)\) words of auxiliary memory.

title: Chapter 07: Point-Value Duality, Roots-of-Unity Filters, Chirp Z-Transform & Arbitrary-Modulus NTT
section: 7.3 The Chirp Z-Transform (Bluestein’s Algorithm) & Failure Mode #12
text:
7.3 The Chirp Z-Transform (Bluestein’s Algorithm) & Failure Mode #12
In Chapter 02, our general multipoint evaluation algorithm evaluated a degree-\(n\) polynomial \(F(x)\) at \(m\) arbitrary points \(x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}\) in \(O((n + m) \log^2(n + m))\) time with a heavy constant factor (requiring a product tree of polynomials and transposed remainders).
However, in a vast range of generating function problems—including arbitrary-length DFTs (\(L\) not a power of \(2\)), \(q\)-analogues, and root-of-unity filters—the evaluation points are not arbitrary: they form a geometric progression \[
x_i = a \cdot c^i \qquad (0 \le i < m),
\] where \(a, c \in K\) are fixed scalars. Given \(F(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j x^j\), how fast can we compute all \(m\) values \[
y_i = F(a \cdot c^i) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j a^j c^{ij} \qquad (0 \le i < m)?
\] Bluestein’s Chirp Z-Transform (CZT) solves this entire multipoint evaluation in a single polynomial convolution—taking just \(O((n + m) \log(n + m))\) field operations!

7.3.1 Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Diagnostic Signal: A double sum or evaluation features a bilinear exponent \(c^{i \cdot j}\) (or \(\omega^{i \cdot j}\) where the length \(L\) is not a power of \(2\)), coupling the output index \(i \in [0, m)\) with the summation index \(j \in [0, n)\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

Why can’t we apply a convolution directly to \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (f_j a^j) c^{ij}\)? Because in a convolution, the kernel must depend only on the sum \(i + j\) (or difference \(i - j\)) of the two indices, whereas \(c^{ij}\) depends on their product \(i \cdot j\).
How can we rewrite a product \(i \cdot j\) as a linear combination of functions of \(i + j\), \(i\), and \(j\) alone?
Over the complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\), textbook signal processing uses the identity \(ij = \frac{1}{2}\bigl((i+j)^2 - i^2 - j^2\bigr)\) (or \(ij = -\frac{1}{2}(i-j)^2 + \frac{1}{2}i^2 + \frac{1}{2}j^2\)).
Finite-field stress test over \(\mathbb{F}_p\): If \(i + j\) is odd, then \(\frac{1}{2}(i+j)^2\) is a half-integer! Raising \(c\) to a half-integer power requires choosing a square root \(c^{1/2} \in \mathbb{F}_p\). What if \(c\) is a quadratic non-residue modulo \(p\)? Then \(c^{1/2}\) does not even exist in \(\mathbb{F}_p\)!
Can we write \(i \cdot j\) using a quadratic function of \(k\) that is always an integer for every integer \(k\), with no \(\frac{1}{2}\) outside? Yes! The binomial coefficient \(\binom{k}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2}\) is an integer for every \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\), and expanding \(\binom{i+j}{2}\) gives: \[
\binom{i+j}{2} = \frac{(i+j)(i+j-1)}{2} = \frac{i(i-1)}{2} + \frac{j(j-1)}{2} + ij = \binom{i}{2} + \binom{j}{2} + ij.
\] Rearranging this identity gives Bluestein’s Binomial Identity: \[
i \cdot j = \binom{i+j}{2} - \binom{i}{2} - \binom{j}{2},
\] and for negative products \(-i \cdot j\) (needed in inverse DFTs), flipping the sign gives: \[
-i \cdot j = \binom{i}{2} + \binom{j}{2} - \binom{i+j}{2}.
\]
Note on Sum-Index \(\binom{i+j}{2}\) vs. Difference-Index \(\binom{i-j}{2}\) Conventions: Some references write \(i \cdot j = \binom{i}{2} + \binom{j}{2} - \binom{i-j}{2}\) (using \(\binom{-k}{2} = \binom{k+1}{2}\) for negative arguments \(i - j < 0\)). Both identities are algebraically valid, but the sum-index identity \(i \cdot j = \binom{i+j}{2} - \binom{i}{2} - \binom{j}{2}\) is cleaner in competitive programming: since \(i \ge 0\) and \(j \ge 0\), the argument \(k = i + j\) is always non-negative (\(0 \le i + j \le n + m - 2\)), avoiding negative index offsets entirely and requiring only a single reversal \(\tilde{u}_{n-1-j} = u_j\) to align \((n - 1 - j) + (i + j) = n - 1 + i\).








WarningFailure Mode #12: Bluestein Square-Root Failure (\(c^{1/2} \notin \mathbb{F}_p\)) & The \(c = 0\) Edge Case



Failure Mode 12A (The \(c^{1/2}\) Quadratic Non-Residue Trap): Never implement CZT over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) using \(ij = \frac{1}{2}\bigl((i+j)^2 - i^2 - j^2\bigr)\). Half the elements of \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\) are quadratic non-residues, so \(\sqrt{c}\) does not exist in \(\mathbb{F}_p\) half the time (for instance, when \(c = g\) is a primitive root of \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\)!). By contrast, Bluestein’s Binomial Identity \[
c^{ij} = c^{\binom{i+j}{2}} \cdot c^{-\binom{i}{2}} \cdot c^{-\binom{j}{2}}
\] uses exclusively integer exponents \(\binom{k}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) and works unconditionally for every nonzero element \(c \in K^\times\) in any commutative ring \(K\).
Failure Mode 12B (The \(c = 0\) and \(a = 0\) Non-Unit Trap): Notice that \(c^{-\binom{i}{2}}\) divides by powers of \(c\). If \(c = 0\), \(c\) is not invertible! Before running the binomial substitution, always guard the two degenerate boundary cases explicitly:

If \(a = 0\): Every evaluation point is \(x_i = 0 \cdot c^i = 0\), so \(y_i = F(0) = f_0\) for all \(0 \le i < m\).
If \(c = 0\) (with \(0^0 := 1\)):

For \(i = 0\), \(x_0 = a \cdot 0^0 = a\), so \(y_0 = F(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j a^j\) (evaluated in \(O(n)\) time via Horner’s rule).
For all \(i \ge 1\), \(x_i = a \cdot 0^i = 0\), so \(y_i = F(0) = f_0\).







7.3.2 Single-Step Verbalized Derivation of Bluestein’s CZT
Assume \(a \ne 0\) and \(c \in K^\times\) is invertible. Let us transform \(y_i = F(a \cdot c^i)\) into a standard polynomial convolution step by step:

Write out the point evaluation: For each \(0 \le i < m\), \[
y_i = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j (a \cdot c^i)^j = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j a^j c^{ij}.
\]
Substitute Bluestein’s Binomial Identity \(c^{ij} = c^{\binom{i+j}{2}} c^{-\binom{i}{2}} c^{-\binom{j}{2}}\): \[
y_i = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j a^j \left(c^{\binom{i+j}{2}} c^{-\binom{i}{2}} c^{-\binom{j}{2}}\right).
\]
Factor the \(i\)-only term outside the sum and group the \(j\)-only terms: \[
y_i = c^{-\binom{i}{2}} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \underbrace{\left(f_j a^j c^{-\binom{j}{2}}\right)}_{u_j} \cdot \underbrace{\left(c^{\binom{i+j}{2}}\right)}_{v_{i+j}}.
\]
Reverse the array \(u\) to convert the correlation index \(i + j\) into a standard Cauchy convolution: Define the reversed sequence \(\tilde{u}\) of length \(n\) by \(\tilde{u}_{n - 1 - j} = u_j = f_j a^j c^{-\binom{j}{2}}\) for \(0 \le j < n\), and define the chirp sequence \(v_k = c^{\binom{k}{2}}\) for \(0 \le k < n + m - 1\). Then as \(j\) runs from \(0\) to \(n-1\), the sum of the two indices in \(\tilde{u}_{n - 1 - j}\) and \(v_{i + j}\) is \[
(n - 1 - j) + (i + j) = n - 1 + i,
\] which depends only on \(i\)! Therefore, the sum is the exact coefficient of \(x^{n - 1 + i}\) in the ordinary polynomial product \(\tilde{U}(x) V(x)\): \[
y_i = c^{-\binom{i}{2}} \cdot [x^{n - 1 + i}] \bigl(\tilde{U}(x) V(x)\bigr) \qquad (0 \le i < m).
\]







Tip\(O(n + m)\) Precomputation of \(c^{\binom{k}{2}}\) Without qpow Inside the Loop



Notice that \(\binom{k+1}{2} - \binom{k}{2} = k\). Therefore, the powers \(p_k = c^{\binom{k}{2}}\) and \(s_k = c^k\) satisfy the first-order recurrences \[
p_0 = 1, \quad s_0 = 1, \qquad p_{k+1} = p_k \cdot s_k, \quad s_{k+1} = s_k \cdot c \qquad (k \ge 0).
\] Similarly, putting \(c^{-1} = 1/c\) in place of \(c\) generates all negative powers \(q_k = c^{-\binom{k}{2}}\) in \(O(n + m)\) multiplications using only one modular inverse \(c^{-1} \bmod p\) overall!





7.3.3 Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace of Bluestein’s CZT
Let us trace Bluestein’s CZT by hand over \(\mathbb{Q}\) (or \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\)) for \[
F(x) = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 \quad (n = 3, \; f = [1, 2, 3]), \qquad a = 1, \quad c = 2, \quad m = 4.
\] We want to evaluate \(F(x)\) at \(x_i = 1 \cdot 2^i \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2, 3\). Directly:

\(y_0 = F(1) = 1 + 2(1) + 3(1) = 6\),
\(y_1 = F(2) = 1 + 2(2) + 3(4) = 17\),
\(y_2 = F(4) = 1 + 2(4) + 3(16) = 57\),
\(y_3 = F(8) = 1 + 2(8) + 3(64) = 209\).

Now trace the CZT algorithm step by step:

Chirp sequence \(v_k = 2^{\binom{k}{2}}\) for \(0 \le k < n + m - 1 = 6\): Since \(\binom{0}{2} = 0, \binom{1}{2} = 0, \binom{2}{2} = 1, \binom{3}{2} = 3, \binom{4}{2} = 6, \binom{5}{2} = 10\), we have \[
V(x) = \sum_{k=0}^5 2^{\binom{k}{2}} x^k = 1 + 1x + 2x^2 + 8x^3 + 64x^4 + 1024x^5.
\]
Weighted reversed coefficients \(\tilde{u}_{2-j} = f_j \cdot 1^j \cdot 2^{-\binom{j}{2}}\) for \(j = 0, 1, 2\):

\(j = 0 : u_0 = 1 \cdot 2^{-0} = 1 \implies \tilde{u}_2 = 1\)
\(j = 1 : u_1 = 2 \cdot 2^{-0} = 2 \implies \tilde{u}_1 = 2\)
\(j = 2 : u_2 = 3 \cdot 2^{-1} = \frac{3}{2} \implies \tilde{u}_0 = \frac{3}{2}\) Thus \(\tilde{U}(x) = \frac{3}{2} + 2x + x^2\).

Multiply \(\tilde{U}(x) V(x)\) and read coefficients at \(x^{n - 1 + i} = x^{2 + i}\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2, 3\):

\(i = 0\) (\([x^2](\tilde{U}V)\)): \(\tilde{u}_0 v_2 + \tilde{u}_1 v_1 + \tilde{u}_2 v_0 = \frac{3}{2}(2) + 2(1) + 1(1) = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6\). Multiply by \(2^{-\binom{0}{2}} = 1 \implies y_0 = 6\).
\(i = 1\) (\([x^3](\tilde{U}V)\)): \(\tilde{u}_0 v_3 + \tilde{u}_1 v_2 + \tilde{u}_2 v_1 = \frac{3}{2}(8) + 2(2) + 1(1) = 12 + 4 + 1 = 17\). Multiply by \(2^{-\binom{1}{2}} = 1 \implies y_1 = 17\).
\(i = 2\) (\([x^4](\tilde{U}V)\)): \(\tilde{u}_0 v_4 + \tilde{u}_1 v_3 + \tilde{u}_2 v_2 = \frac{3}{2}(64) + 2(8) + 1(2) = 96 + 16 + 2 = 114\). Multiply by \(2^{-\binom{2}{2}} = \frac{1}{2} \implies y_2 = \frac{114}{2} = 57\).
\(i = 3\) (\([x^5](\tilde{U}V)\)): \(\tilde{u}_0 v_5 + \tilde{u}_1 v_4 + \tilde{u}_2 v_3 = \frac{3}{2}(1024) + 2(64) + 1(8) = 1536 + 128 + 8 = 1672\). Multiply by \(2^{-\binom{3}{2}} = \frac{1}{8} \implies y_3 = \frac{1672}{8} = 209\).


Every single value \([6, 17, 57, 209]\) matches!



7.3.4 Algorithm Contract: czt(f, a, c, m)






ImportantAlgorithm Contract: Chirp Z-Transform czt(f, a, c, m)




Input:

Coefficient array \(f = [f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{n-1}] \in K^n\) representing \(F(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j x^j\).
Starting point \(a \in K\), geometric ratio \(c \in K\), and number of evaluation points \(m \ge 0\).

Output:

Array \(y = [y_0, y_1, \dots, y_{m-1}] \in K^m\) where \(y_i = F(a \cdot c^i)\) for \(0 \le i < m\).

Algebraic Preconditions:

If \(n = 0\) or \(m = 0\), return \(m\) zeros immediately.
If \(a = 0\), return \([f_0, f_0, \dots, f_0]\).
If \(c = 0\), return \([F(a), f_0, f_0, \dots, f_0]\).
For \(a \ne 0\) and \(c \ne 0\), \(c\) must be a unit in \(K\) (\(c \in K^\times\)), and the underlying convolution engine (standard NTT if \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) is NTT-friendly, or 3-Prime MTT from §7.2 otherwise) must support polynomial multiplication of degree \((n - 1) + (n + m - 2) = 2n + m - 3\).

Index Boundaries & Core Invariant:

Array \(\tilde{U}\) has length \(n\) with \(\tilde{U}_{n - 1 - j} = f_j a^j c^{-\binom{j}{2}}\) for \(0 \le j < n\).
Array \(V\) has length \(n + m - 1\) with \(V_k = c^{\binom{k}{2}}\) for \(0 \le k < n + m - 1\).
Core Invariant: For every \(0 \le i < m\) and \(0 \le j < n\), the index \(k = i + j\) satisfies \(0 \le k \le n + m - 2\), so \(V_{i+j}\) is always in bounds, and the unique pair of indices in \(\tilde{U}\) and \(V\) summing to \(n - 1 + i\) with \(0 \le n - 1 - j < n\) is \((n - 1 - j, i + j)\). Thus \([x^{n - 1 + i}](\tilde{U}V)\) sums over all \(j \in [0, n-1]\) without omission or wrap-around contamination.

Complexity:

\(O(n + m)\) time for the recurrence precomputation of \(c^{\pm\binom{k}{2}}\) plus one polynomial multiplication of length \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(2n + m - 2) \rceil}\), giving \(O((n + m) \log(n + m))\) time and \(O(n + m)\) space.










NoteRevisited Dual-Perspective Cross-Reference: Additive Power Sums (Ch 04 Mas-2, #154 Luogu P4705) vs. Multiplicative Geometric Evaluations (§7.3 Bluestein CZT)



Compare the bilinear sum in Chapter 04 (Mas-2, #154 Luogu P4705 — 玩游戏) with Bluestein’s Chirp-\(Z\) Transform in this section:

Additive Base + Fixed Exponent (Ch 04 Mas-2, Luogu P4705): To evaluate \(\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m (a_i + b_j)^k\) for \(1 \le k \le t\), the coupling is additive inside the base. Expanding \((a_i + b_j)^k = k! \sum_{r=0}^k \frac{a_i^r}{r!} \frac{b_j^{k-r}}{(k-r)!}\) in the EGF ring reduces the problem to computing power sums \(P_r(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^r = [x^r]\Big(n - x \frac{d}{dx}\ln \prod_{i=1}^n (1 - a_i x)\Big)\) via Newton’s logarithmic derivative (Ch 04), followed by a single 1D EGF convolution.
Multiplicative Exponent + Geometric Base (Ch 07 §7.3, Bluestein CZT): When the coupling moves into the exponent as \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j a^j c^{ij}\) (or \(\sum_{i, j} a_i b_j c^{i^2 j^3}\) in Int-2 #100), the binomial theorem on the base no longer applies. Instead, Bluestein’s identity \(ij = \binom{i+j}{2} - \binom{i}{2} - \binom{j}{2}\) acts as the exponent-space analogue of EGF binomial decoupling, factoring the coupled weight \(c^{ij}\) into \(c^{\binom{i+j}{2}} \cdot c^{-\binom{i}{2}} \cdot c^{-\binom{j}{2}}\) and reducing multipoint geometric evaluation to a single 1D Cauchy convolution!
