3. Flagship Dual-Perspective Cross-Reference Index (12 Problems Solved Two Ways)
To prevent technique silos, 12 flagship problems are designated as cross-chapter dual-perspective bridges. Each problem is counted exactly once in the 254-problem partition (in its Primary Home Slot in Column 2) and is explicitly revisited from a second algebraic angle in the Secondary Chapter (Column 5):



#
Primary Home Slot
Problem ID & Title
First Perspective (Primary Chapter)
Second Perspective (Revisited Chapter)
Pedagogical Takeaway




1
Ch 02 [Int-1] (#101)
CF 1096G — Lucky Tickets
Ch 02 (2.4): \(O(NK)\) Sparse Power ODE \((1-x)(1-x^{10})G' = k P' G\) (zero NTTs).
Ch 01 / Ch 07: Direct NTT cyclic power \(\bmod (x^N - 1)\) via roots of unity.
Shows when a 10-line \(O(NK)\) formal derivative recurrence beats \(O(N \log N)\) NTT by \(10\times\).


2
Ch 02 [Adv-2] (#084)
CF 438E — The Child and Binary Tree
Ch 02 (2.5): Quadratic closed form \(F(x) = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4C(x)}}\) using 1D Newton sqrt and inv.
Ch 10 (10.2): Direct 1D Fréchet Newton iteration on \(\Phi(F) = C(x)F(x)^2 - F(x) + 1 = 0\) without radicals.
Bridges explicit radical extraction (Ch 02) with general implicit Fréchet Newton iteration (Ch 10).


3
Ch 05 [Adv-1] (#040)
ABC 300 Ex — Fibonacci: Revisited
Ch 05 (5.3): Standard \(O(K \log K \log N)\) Bostan–Mori on \(Q(x) = 1 - x - \dots - x^K\).
Ch 02 (2.4): Multiply top/bottom by \((1-x)\) so \((1-x)Q(x) = 1 - 2x + x^{K+1}\) becomes 3-sparse!
Teaches students to check if \((1-x)Q(x)\) collapses a dense denominator into a sparse polynomial.


4
Ch 06 [Adv-1] (#094)
CF 923E — Perpetual Subtraction
Ch 06 (6.3): Two Taylor shifts \(P(x-1) \to (k+1)^{-M} \to A(x+1)\) diagonalizing transition matrix in \(O(N \log N)\).
Ch 13 (13.3): Explicit upper-triangular eigenbasis factorization \(T = V \Lambda V^{-1}\) with \(V_{i,j} = \binom{i}{j}\).
Reveals why Taylor shift diagonalizes binomial transitions: \(x \mapsto x+1\) is the group action of \(\exp(D)\)!


5
Ch 08 [Int-2] (#089)
CF 840C — On the Bench
Ch 08 (8.3): Connected-Component IE (连续段容斥) with signed per-color EGF \(\sum (-1)^{c_i-b}\binom{c_i-1}{b-1}\frac{x^b}{b!}\).
Ch 19 (19.3): Laguerre polynomial / Truncated Taylor-shift D&C NTT (#028 ABC 260 Ex, \(N \le 2.5 \times 10^5\)).
Connects \(O(N^2)\) DP inclusion–exclusion directly to \(O(N \log^2 N)\) D&C NTT + Taylor shift.


6
Ch 09 [Int-2] (#023)
ABC 230 Ex — Bullion
Ch 09 (9.4): Fully Online Relaxed Convolution updating harmonic multiples \(d f_d \to g_{kd}\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\).
Ch 10 (10.3): Offline Pólya Newton Iteration treating \(F(x^2), F(x^3), \dots\) as constants in \(O(N \log N)\).
Contrasts 15-line simplicity of Online Relaxed Convolution (Ch 09) against \(O(N \log N)\) Pólya Newton (Ch 10).


7
Ch 10 [Int-1] (#244)
yukicoder 3029 — Colored Tree (FPS 24)
Ch 10 (10.2): \(2 \times 2\) Coupled Jacobian Newton Iteration on \((F(x), G(x))\) in \(O(N \log N)\).
Ch 09 (9.3): Coupled Online Relaxed Convolution solving the same system in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) without Jacobians!
Shows Online Relaxed Convolution as a bug-free fallback when Jacobians are tedious under contest pressure.


8
Ch 11 [SS-2] (#200)
Luogu P7438 — [AGM 2021] 恐龙
Ch 11 (11.2): Lagrange–Bürmann Inversion extracting single coefficient \([x^N] F(x)^k = \frac{k}{N}[u^{N-k}]\phi(u)^N\) in \(O(N \log N)\).
Ch 21 (21.3): Kinoshita–Li compositional_inverse computing \([x^n] F(x)\) for all \(1 \le n \le N\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\).
Clarifies the boundary between single-coefficient LIF (Ch 11) and all-coefficients revert (Ch 21).


9
Ch 12 [Mas-1] (#183)
Luogu P5827 — 点双连通图计数
Ch 12 (12.3): Pointed Block-Cut Tree \(\ln(R(x)/x) = B'(R(x))\) inverted at single degree \(N\) via LIF in \(O(N \log N)\).
Ch 21 (21.3) & Ch 24 (24.3): All-\(n\) extraction via compose_inv (#016 fps_24_w), and fixed-graph biconnected subgraphs via Pointed SPS \(\mathcal{R}_n\) (#207 UOJ 94)!
3-way bridge uniting Labeled Graph Theory (Ch 12), Transposed Composition (Ch 21), and Set Power Series (Ch 24).


10
Ch 14 [Int-1] (#156)
Luogu P4548 — [CTSC2006] 歌唱王国
Ch 14 (14.2): Stopping-time PGF \(F(z) + (1-z)G(z) = 1\) + KMP border identity \(G(1) = \sum_{k \in \text{Borders}} m^k\).
Ch 08 (8.4) & Ch 14 (14.5): Goulden–Jackson cluster inversion at \(z = 1/m\), and Martingale casino betting game.
Connects deterministic string avoidance (Ch 08), PGF differentiation at \(z=1\) (Ch 14.2), and Martingales (Ch 14.5).


11
Ch 15 [Int-1] (#220)
Luogu P3266 — [JLOI2015] 骗我呢
Ch 15 (15.1): André’s Reflection Principle & Kelvin alternating image sum across parallel walls in \(O(N/(a+b))\).
Ch 15 (15.3) & Ch 05: Bivariate Kernel Method \((u - tuS(u))F(t,u) = \dots\) and rational transfer matrix \(P(x)/Q(x)\).
Shows why symmetric steps \(\{-1, +1\}\) admit reflection while general steps require the algebraic Kernel Method.


12
CP-IV.6 (#058)
ARC 136 F — Flip Cells
Ch 16 (16.3–16.4): Bivariate rational / exponential parity walk reduced to algebraic residue extraction.
Ch 18 (18.2): Differentiating the algebraic diagonal into a D-finite ODE and unrolling the P-recursive recurrence in \(O(N)\) time!
Completes \(\text{2D Rational} \xrightarrow{\text{Diag}} \text{1D Algebraic} \xrightarrow{\text{ODE}} \text{D-Finite } O(N) \text{ P-Recursive}\)!

4. Complete Quarantined Template Verification Guide (R-01–R-67)






WarningThe Anti-Template-Bloat Quarantine Rule



A common failure mode of competitive programming polynomial notes is treating bare library-checker unit tests (e.g., “Given \(F(x)\), output \(\exp(F(x)) \bmod x^N\)”) as if they were combinatorial practice problems. In this textbook, all 67 bare-template problems (R-01–R-67) are strictly quarantined from the 192 Chapter Ladders, 48 Blind Checkpoints, and 14 Synthesis Reserve problems. Use them solely as implementation unit tests to verify that your C++ polynomial library handles valuation shifts, degree truncation, and modular edge cases before starting each chapter’s 8-problem combinatorial ladder.

title: Multilingual Bibliography & Terminology Rosetta Stone
text: Competitive programming flow modelling has evolved across three semi-independent traditions:

title: Multilingual Bibliography & Terminology Rosetta Stone
text:
1. Foundational [EN] Academic Papers & Textbooks

Ford, L. R., & Fulkerson, D. R. (1956, 1962). Maximal flow through a network (Canadian Journal of Mathematics, 8, 399–404) & Flows in Networks (Princeton University Press). — Establishes the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem, augmenting paths, and the Integrality Theorem (Ch 01).
Dinitz (Dinic), E. A. (1970) & Even, S., & Tarjan, R. E. (1975). Algorithm for solution of a problem of maximum flow in a network with power estimation (Soviet Math. Doklady, 11, 1277–1280) & Network flow and testing graph connectivity (SIAM J. Comput., 4(4), 507–518). — Proves blocking-flow level-graph bounds \(O(V^2 E)\), \(O(E \min(V^{2/3}, E^{1/2}))\) on unit-capacity networks, and \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) on unit networks (Ch 01, Ch 05).
Picard, J.-C. (1976) & Picard, J.-C., & Queyranne, M. (1980). Maximal closure of a graph and applications to combinatorial problems (Management Science, 22(11), 1268–1272) & On the structure of all minimum cuts in a network and applications (Mathematical Programming Study, 13, 8–16). — Proves the Maximum Weight Closure reduction (Ch 09) and the bijection between all minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cuts and ideals of the residual SCC condensation DAG (Ch 02).
Hoffman, A. J. (1960) & Hoffman, A. J., & Kruskal, J. B. (1956). Some recent applications of the theory of linear inequalities to extremal combinatorial analysis & Integral boundary points of convex polyhedra. — Establishes Hoffman’s Circulation Theorem (Ch 04) and the Totally Unimodular (TU) matrix characterization of integral polyhedra (Ch 21).
König, D. (1931), Hall, P. (1935), Dilworth, R. P. (1950), & Dulmage, A. L., & Mendelsohn, N. S. (1958). Foundational duality theorems for bipartite vertex covers (Ch 05), neighborhood marriage conditions (Ch 08), poset chain decompositions (Ch 08), and canonical bipartite vertex/edge partitions (Ch 06).
Birkhoff, G. (1946) & von Neumann, J. (1953). Decomposition of doubly stochastic and \(k\)-regular bipartite matrices into permutation matchings (Ch 07).
Kolmogorov, V., & Zabin, R. (2004). What energy functions can be minimized via graph cuts? (IEEE TPAMI, 26(2), 147–159). — Proves that a pairwise pseudo-Boolean function is graph-representable if and only if every pairwise term satisfies submodularity \(E(0,0) + E(1,1) \le E(0,1) + E(1,0)\) (Ch 10).
Boros, E., & Hammer, P. L. (2002). Pseudo-Boolean optimization (Discrete Applied Mathematics, 123, 155–225). — Establishes Quadratic Pseudo-Boolean Optimization (QPBO), roof duality, half-integrality, and bipartite variable flipping (Ch 11).
Ishikawa, H. (2003). Exact optimization for Markov random fields with convex priors (IEEE TPAMI, 25(10), 1333–1336). — Introduces multi-state ordered chains with reverse \(\infty\)-arcs and cross-difference capacities \(-\Delta_a \Delta_b \Phi(a,b) \ge 0\) (Ch 12, Ch 13).
Chambolle, A. (2004) & Darbon, J., & Sigelle, M. (2006). * Exact total variation minimization and the discrete coarea formula via parametric level-set minimum cuts* (Ch 13, CF 1427 G).
Dinkelbach, W. (1967) & Goldberg, A. V. (1984). On nonlinear fractional programming (Management Science, 13(7), 492–498) & Finding a maximum density subgraph (UC Berkeley Tech Report UCB/CSD-84-171) (Ch 14).
Hassin, R. (1981), Reif, J. H. (1983), Stoer, M., & Wagner, F. (1997), Gomory, R. E., & Hu, T. C. (1961), & Gusfield, D. (1990). Planar \(s\)-\(t\) cycle-cut duality (Ch 15), global minimum cut, and \(N-1\) all-pairs min-cut tree construction (Ch 16).
Edmonds, J., & Karp, R. M. (1972) & Suurballe, J. W. (1974). Johnson vertex potentials \(\pi(v)\) for non-negative reduced costs in MCMF and edge-disjoint shortest paths (Ch 17, Ch 20).
Edmonds, J. (1965, 1970) & Tutte, W. T. (1947, 1954). Paths, trees, and flowers (Blossom contraction and Tutte–Berge duality, Ch 22), The factorization of linear graphs (Tutte skew-symmetric matrix and \(f\)-factors, Ch 22), and Submodular functions, matroids, and certain polyhedra (Ch 21, Ch 24).
Ahuja, R. K., Magnanti, T. L., & Orlin, J. B. (1993) & Schrijver, A. (2003). Network Flows: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications (Prentice Hall) & Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency (3 vols., Springer). — Comprehensive reference monographs across Parts I–VI.

title: Multilingual Bibliography & Terminology Rosetta Stone
section: 2. Landmark [ZH] Chinese Competitive Programming Treatises (国家集训队论文 & Classics)
text:
2. Landmark [ZH] Chinese Competitive Programming Treatises (国家集训队论文 & Classics)

Hu Botao (胡伯涛, 2007). 《最小割模型在信息学竞赛中的应用》 (Applications of Minimum Cut Models in Olympiad in Informatics), IOI 2007 Chinese National Training Team Paper. — The seminal Chinese CP monograph introducing Picard’s Maximum Weight Closure (最大权闭合子图, Ch 09) and Goldberg/Amber’s Maximum Density Subgraph (最大密度子图, Ch 14), with canonical proofs of vertex-only degree-sum reductions.
Zhou Dong (周冬, 2009). 《浅析最大最小定理在信息学竞赛中的应用》 (Applications of Min-Max Theorems in OI), IOI 2009 Chinese National Training Team Paper. — Systematizes planar cycle-cut duality (平面图最小割转对偶图最短路, Ch 15), König’s theorem, and Dilworth’s theorem.
Jiangind / NOI 2008 Committee ([NOI2008] 志愿者招募, 2008) & Subsequent National Team Treatises on LP Duality (LP对偶转网络流). — Introduces the Algebraic Equation-Difference Method (流守恒差分建模法) (Ch 19) and explicit primal–dual LP compilation (Ch 21).
Zkw (张昆玮, Tsinghua University, 2009). 《统计的力量 — 费用流与zkw算法》. — Introduces the primal–dual multi-augmenting-path MCMF algorithm (zkw费用流) and analyzes its performance on dense unit-length networks vs. long zero-cost paths (Ch 17).
Xu Haoran / National Team Papers on Simulated Cost Flow (2017–2019). 《模拟费用流问题综述》 (A Survey of Simulated Min-Cost Flow Problems). — Formalizes the bijection between Successive Shortest Path augmenting paths and priority-queue regret greedy (反悔贪心), 1D mouse-to-hole (UOJ #455), tree LCA merge, and 5-queue coupled bipartite state machines ([NOI2019] 序列, Ch 23).

title: Network Flows, Minimum Cuts, Matching, Duality & Non-Graph Modelling
text:
Welcome to the Network Flows, Minimum Cuts, Matching, Duality & Non-Graph Modelling textbook.
Unlike domains such as Formal Power Series (where dozens of distinct algebraic algorithms must be mastered), network flows in competitive programming rely on a remarkably small algorithmic kernel: blocking-flow maximum flow (Dinic), Successive Shortest Path / primal–dual Min-Cost Max-Flow (MCMF), and Edmonds’ blossom algorithm for general matching. Consistent with the repository’s editorial policy, this textbook assumes your competitive programming library already contains tested implementations of Dinic, Hopcroft–Karp, and MCMF.
Why, then, are flow and minimum-cut problems among the hardest tasks on AtCoder (ARC/AGC), Codeforces (Div. 1), ICPC World Finals, and the Chinese NOI/集训队 circuit? Because over 90% of the difficulty lies in recognition and graph construction (modelling):
Every chapter in this textbook enforces the 4-Step “Zero Magic Gadgets” Compilation Standard:
\[\text{1. English Constraint} \longrightarrow \text{2. Algebraic Intermediate Model} \longrightarrow \text{3. Normal-Form Graph Gadget} \longrightarrow \text{4. Broken-Gadget Counterexample}\]
No graph edge or capacity is ever introduced “by magic”: every vertex, directed arc, \(\infty\)-constraint, and constant offset is derived algebraically from first principles, accompanied by a concrete counterexample proving how the model fails when a hypothesis (such as bipartite parity, submodularity \(A + D \le B + C\), or cost convexity) is violated.

title: Network Flows, Minimum Cuts, Matching, Duality & Non-Graph Modelling
text:
Entry Contract & Prerequisites
Before starting Chapter 1, we assume you have:

Tested Black-Box Solvers:

A blocking-flow maximum-flow solver (Dinic(V, E) supporting residual graph inspection e.cap and s-reachability queries after termination).
A Min-Cost Max-Flow solver (MCMF(V, E) supporting Johnson potentials \(\pi(v)\), Successive Shortest Path with Dijkstra, and slope inspection \((f_k, C(f_k))\)).

Foundational Graph & Data-Structure Fluency:

Breadth-First Search (BFS), Depth-First Search (DFS), topological sorting, and strongly connected components (Tarjan / Kosaraju).
Dijkstra’s algorithm, Bellman–Ford / SPFA on small DAGs or negative-weight initialization, and segment trees with lazy propagation.

No Prior University LP or Combinatorial Optimization Required:

Every mathematical tool—from residual skew-symmetry, Hoffman’s circulation theorem, König–Hall–Dilworth duality, and submodular pseudo-Boolean polynomials to LP primal–dual compilation, totally unimodular (TU) matrices, and \(L_p\) isotonic regression—is developed from scratch with self-contained proofs and small hand-worked traces.


Start with Notation & Conventions for canonical symbols and the 24-item Failure Mode taxonomy (FM-01–FM-24), and consult the Study Plan & Diagnostic Protocol to choose your track.

The curriculum comprises 24 chapters, 6 Part-End Blind Recognition Checkpoints (CP-I–CP-VI), and 2 Grandmaster Capstone volumes, anchored by a bijective, zero-duplicate pool of 320 curated problems (256 fully solved non-template problems #001–#256 + 64 quarantined bare-template problems R-01–R-64).

title: Checkpoint V — Part V Blind Recognition: Min-Cost Max-Flow, Equation Differencing, Hubs & LP Duality
text:
When you solve an exercise at the end of Chapter 18 (“Separable Convex Marginal Splitting, Degree Penalties, and Tournament Orientation”) or Chapter 19 (“\(K\)-Interval Coverage and the Consecutive Equation Difference Method”), the chapter heading itself hands you the critical modelling transformation. Before reading the constraints, you already expect to split a quadratic cost \(\Phi(f) = a f^2 + b f\) into parallel unit-capacity arcs of marginal cost \(\Delta\Phi(k) = a(2k-1) + b\), or to subtract adjacent prefix equations \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) so each interval column \([l_j, r_j]\) collapses to a single \(+1\) inflow at \(l_j\) and \(-1\) outflow at \(r_j + 1\).
In a live ICPC World Finals, NOI, Codeforces, or AtCoder contest, problems arrive completely untagged—and worse, problem setters deliberately disguise simple binary-search bottlenecks, \(O(N)\) difference arrays, or NP-hard fixed-charge traps inside “cost flow” narratives. Your decisive competitive advantage in Part V is blind algebraic-to-graph recognition: looking at a multi-period inventory schedule, a two-tree quota system, a subtask-waiting queue, or a linear program and immediately knowing whether to compile it into a Min-Cost Max-Flow (MCMF) network, dualize it into a closed-form sweep, or reject MCMF altogether before falling into any of the five Part V failure modes (FM-17–FM-21).

section: 1. Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills (FM-17–FM-21 & Decoy Elimination)
text:
1. Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills (FM-17–FM-21 & Decoy Elimination)
Before tackling the eight full checkpoint slots in Section 2, test your diagnostic reflexes on six short modelling scenarios. Each scenario either contains a fatal Part V modelling bug (FM-17–FM-21) or tests decoy discrimination (CURRICULUM_ARCHITECTURE.md Stage 1–2). Formulate your diagnosis before expanding the answer callout.


Drill 1.1 — The Stale Johnson Potential & Negative-Arc Saturation Trap (FM-17)
A contestant implements Primal–Dual Successive Shortest Path (SSP) with Dijkstra and Johnson potentials \(\pi_v\). 1. In each phase, after running Dijkstra on reduced costs \(c^\pi(u, v) = c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v \ge 0\) to obtain shortest-path distances \(d_v\), they update \(\pi_v \gets \pi_v + d_v\) only for vertices \(v\) lying on the chosen augmenting path \(P\), claiming that vertices outside \(P\) did not have their flow changed. 2. On a second problem where the input directed graph has cycles and some edges have negative costs \(c(u, v) < 0\) (CF 708D Incorrect Flow), they initialize \(\pi_v\) with SPFA; when SPFA loops infinitely on a negative cycle, they conclude the problem is unsolvable.
Identify both bugs (FM-17), construct a 3-vertex counterexample for Bug 1, and state the exact mechanical protocol for Bug 2.






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.1






Failure Mode: FM-17 (Stale Johnson Potentials & Un-Saturated Negative Cycles, Chapter 17).
Bug 1 Counterexample (Updating \(\pi\) Only on \(P\)): Suppose \(S = 1, T = 3\) with edges \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 2\), \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, 2)} 3\), and \(2 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 3\), starting at \(\pi = (0, 0, 0)\).

Shortest distances from \(1\) are \(d_1 = 0, d_2 = 0, d_3 = 0\) via \(P = (1 \to 2 \to 3)\), and wait: suppose there is also a side vertex \(4\) with \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 4\) and \(4 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 2\), so \(d_4 = 0\), or suppose \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, 5)} 2\), \(2 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 3\) (\(d_2 = 5, d_3 = 5\)) and another vertex \(4\) has \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 4\) (\(d_4 = 0\)) and \(2 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 4\)!
If we augment along \(P = (1 \to 2 \to 3)\) and update \(\pi\) only on \(P\) (\(\pi_1 \gets 0, \pi_2 \gets 5, \pi_3 \gets 5\)) while leaving \(\pi_4 = 0\) untouched, then the forward residual edge \(2 \to 4\) now has reduced cost \(c^\pi(2, 4) = 0 + \pi_2 - \pi_4 = +5\), Wait: what if edge \((4 \to 2)\) had cost \(2\) (\(d_4 = 0, d_2 = 2, d_3 = 2\)), and \(P = (1 \to 2 \to 3)\) came from \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, 2)} 2 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 3\)? After augmenting \(1 \to 2 \to 3\), the reverse residual arc \((2 \to 1)\) opens with cost \(-2\). For \((4 \to 2)\), if \(\pi_2\) is updated to \(2\) while \(\pi_4\) was \(0\) (okay), what if \(d_4 = 1\) (via \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, 1)} 4\)) and \(4 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 2\) gave \(d_2 = 1\)? If we update \(\pi_2 \gets 1\) on \(P = (1 \to 4 \to 2 \to 3)\) vs. if \(P = (1 \to 2 \to 3)\) (cost \(1\)) is chosen and \(\pi_4\) is not updated (\(\pi_4 = 0\) instead of \(d_4 = 1\)), then the reverse arc \((2 \to 4)\) or forward arc \((4 \to 2)\) violates \(c^\pi \ge 0\)! Specifically, if \(2 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} 4\) exists, \(d_2 = 1 \implies d_4 = 1\); leaving \(\pi_4 = 0\) while setting \(\pi_3 = 1\) on \(P=(1\to 2\to 3)\) and then opening reverse arc \((3 \to 2)\) or \((4 \to 3)\) with cost \(0\) creates \(c^\pi(4, 3) = 0 + \pi_4 - \pi_3 = -1 < 0\)!
Invariant (Ch 17.1): You must update \(\pi_v \gets \pi_v + d_v\) for every vertex \(v\) reachable from \(S\) in \(G_f\) during Dijkstra so that \(d_v \le d_u + c^\pi(u, v) \iff c^{\pi'}(u, v) \ge 0\) holds across the entire residual network, including newly opened reverse arcs \((v \to u)\) along shortest-path trees where \(d_v = d_u + c^\pi(u, v) \implies c^{\pi'}(v, u) = 0\).

Bug 2 Fix (Mandatory Negative-Arc Pre-Saturation Ch 17.3): When an edge \(e = (u \to v)\) has capacity \([0, u(e)]\) and negative cost \(c(e) < 0\) inside a potentially cyclic graph, pre-saturate it before running MCMF:

Force \(f(e) = u(e)\), adding \(u(e) \cdot c(e)\) to the base cost and incrementing nodal balance \(M(v) \mathrel{+}= u(e), M(u) \mathrel{-}= u(e)\).
Replace \(e\) with its reverse cancellation arc \(v \xrightarrow{\text{cap } u(e),\; \text{cost } -c(e) > 0} u\).
Now every arc in the network has non-negative cost \(-c(e) \ge 0\), so \(\pi \equiv 0\) is immediately valid for Dijkstra, and super-terminal rebalancing \(S^* \to T^*\) (Ch 04 + Ch 17.3) cancels any unprofitable flow around non-negative cycles!








Drill 1.2 — Convex Quadratic Shipping vs. The Concave Fixed-Charge Setup Trap (FM-18)
Compare two factory-to-warehouse shipping problems (\(N, M \le 50\), maximum road capacity \(U = 10\)): - Scenario A (#227 Stage 1): Shipping \(f \in \{0, 1, \dots, 10\}\) units along road \(e\) costs \(\Phi_A(f) = a_e f^2 + b_e f\) where \(a_e > 0, b_e \ge 0\). - Scenario B (#228 Stage 1): Shipping \(f \in \{0, 1, \dots, 10\}\) units along road \(e\) costs \(0\) if \(f = 0\), and costs a fixed setup fee plus linear shipping \(\Phi_B(f) = F_e + b_e f\) if \(f \ge 1\), where \(F_e > 0, b_e \ge 0\).
A contestant compiles both scenarios into MCMF by replacing each road \(e\) with \(10\) parallel unit-capacity arcs where the \(k\)-th arc (\(k = 1, \dots, 10\)) has cost \(\Delta\Phi(k) = \Phi(k) - \Phi(k-1)\). Why does Scenario A succeed while Scenario B fails catastrophically?






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.2






Failure Mode: FM-18 (Unrolling Non-Convex / Concave Marginals into Parallel Arcs, Chapter 18).
Scenario A (Genuine Ch 18.1 — Strictly Convex Marginals): The \(k\)-th marginal cost is: \[\Delta\Phi_A(k) = a_e\big(k^2 - (k-1)^2\big) + b_e = a_e(2k - 1) + b_e.\] Because \(a_e > 0\), the second difference \(\Delta^2 \Phi_A(k) = \Delta\Phi_A(k+1) - \Delta\Phi_A(k) = 2a_e > 0\) is positive: \[\Delta\Phi_A(1) < \Delta\Phi_A(2) < \dots < \Delta\Phi_A(10).\] A minimum-cost flow solver greedily saturates the cheapest parallel arcs between \(u\) and \(v\) first, so sending \(f\) units is guaranteed to use precisely arcs \(1, 2, \dots, f\), whose costs telescope to \(\sum_{k=1}^f \Delta\Phi_A(k) = \Phi_A(f)\).
Scenario B (Decoy — Concave Fixed-Charge Network Flow is NP-Hard): For \(\Phi_B(f) = F_e \cdot [f \ge 1] + b_e f\), the marginal costs are: \[\Delta\Phi_B(1) = F_e + b_e, \qquad \Delta\Phi_B(2) = \Delta\Phi_B(3) = \dots = \Delta\Phi_B(10) = b_e.\] Because \(F_e > 0\), \(\Delta\Phi_B(1) > \Delta\Phi_B(2)\) (concave!). If you place parallel arcs of costs \((F_e + b_e, b_e, b_e, \dots)\) in an MCMF network, the shortest-path solver will route the first unit of flow through the second arc of cost \(b_e\), completely dodging the setup fee \(F_e\)! Fixed-charge network flow contains Steiner Tree / Set Cover as a special case and is NP-Hard.







Drill 1.3 — The Off-by-One Interval Endpoint Trap & Doubly-Bounded Coverage (FM-19)
Consider two interval problems: 1. Doubly-Bounded Interval Coverage: Given \(M \le 400\) intervals \(I_j = [l_j, r_j] \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) with profit \(w_j > 0\), select a subset \(x_j \in \{0, 1\}\) such that each point \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) is covered at least \(A_i\) and at most \(B_i\) times (\(0 \le A_i \le B_i\)), maximizing \(\sum_j w_j x_j\). A contestant writes \(E_i - E_{i-1}\) and wires each interval \(I_j = [l_j, r_j]\) as an arc \(l_j \to r_j\) instead of \(l_j \to r_j + 1\), and says doubly-bounded constraints \([A_i, B_i]\) cannot be handled by equation differencing. 2. Contiguous \(\pm 1\) Subarray Zeroing: Given \(a_1, \dots, a_N\) (\(N \le 2 \cdot 10^5\)), each operation adds \(+1\) or \(-1\) to any \([l, r]\) at cost \(1\); find the minimum cost to make all \(a_i = 0\).
Fix both flaws in Problem 1 (FM-19) and explain why Problem 2 is an \(O(N)\) decoy.






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.3






Failure Mode: FM-19 (Off-by-One \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) Interval Endpoint & Unbounded-Only Slack Assumption, Chapter 19).
Problem 1 Fix (Doubly-Bounded Equation Differencing Ch 19.1–19.2):

For each point \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), the double bound \(A_i \le \sum_{j: i \in [l_j, r_j]} x_j \le B_i\) becomes an exact equality by subtracting a bounded slack variable \(y_i \in [0, B_i - A_i]\): \[E_i : \quad \sum_{j:\, l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j - y_i = A_i \qquad (i = 1, \dots, N),\] with boundary dummy equations \(E_0 : 0 = 0\) and \(E_{N+1} : 0 = 0\).
Take consecutive differences \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) for \(i = 1, \dots, N+1\):

Variable \(x_j\) (covering \(i \in \{l_j, \dots, r_j\}\)) enters at \(i = l_j\) with coefficient \(+1\) (in \(\Delta E_{l_j}\)) and exits at \(i = r_j + 1\) with coefficient \(-1\) (in \(\Delta E_{r_j+1}\))! Wiring \(l_j \to r_j\) instead of \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) drops point \(r_j\) from the interval (FM-19).
Slack variable \(y_i \in [0, B_i - A_i]\) has coefficient \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_i\) and \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_{i+1}\), which compiles directly to a capacitated backward spine arc \(i + 1 \xrightarrow{[0, B_i - A_i],\; \text{cost } 0} i\)!


Problem 2 Diagnosis (\(O(N)\) Difference-Array Decoy): When every interval \([l, r]\) is available at uniform cost \(1\) with unbounded capacity, setting \(b_i = a_i - a_{i-1}\) (\(i = 1, \dots, N+1\), with \(a_0 = a_{N+1} = 0\)) means one operation on \([l, r]\) changes \((b_l, b_{r+1})\) by \((\pm 1, \mp 1)\). Pairing positive and negative entries of \(b\) takes zero graph search: the minimum cost is simply \(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N+1} |a_i - a_{i-1}|\) in \(O(N)\) time!







Drill 1.4 — Merged Dirty/Clean Inventory Nodes & Forward Queue Indexing (FM-20)
Audit two classic Chapter 20 compilations: 1. Napkin Laundering (餐巾计划): Day \(i\) requires \(r_i\) clean napkins. A solver creates a single vertex \(v_i\) per day, wires \(S \xrightarrow{r_i} v_i \xrightarrow{r_i} T\), and adds laundry arcs \(v_i \to v_{i+d}\)! Why does this always output cost \(0\)? 2. Multi-Machine Total Completion Time (修车): \(N\) cars and \(M\) technicians (\(T_{i,j}\) = time for technician \(j\) to fix car \(i\)). A solver splits each technician \(j\) into \(N\) slots \((j, 1), \dots, (j, N)\) where \((j, p)\) denotes the \(p\)-th car repaired from the start of technician \(j\)’s shift, and assigns edge cost \(p \cdot T_{i,j}\) to \(\text{Car}_i \to (j, p)\). Why is this weight formula wrong?






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.4






Failure Mode: FM-20 (Merged Dirty/Clean State Nodes & Forward vs. Reverse Queue Indexing, Chapter 20).
Bug 1 (Merged Dirty/Clean Node Short-Circuit): If day \(i\) is a single node \(v_i\) with \(S \xrightarrow{r_i, 0} v_i \xrightarrow{r_i, 0} T\), flow injected from \(S\) into \(v_i\) (representing used/dirty napkins generated on day \(i\)) immediately exits \(v_i \to T\) (satisfying day \(i\)’s clean napkin demand) at cost \(0\) without ever buying a single napkin or waiting for laundry! You must split day \(i\) into two disjoint states:

Dirty Supply Node \(D_i\) (\(S \xrightarrow{r_i, 0} D_i\), emitting dirty napkins to \(D_{i+1}\) or to clean nodes \(C_{i+d}\) via laundry);
Clean Demand Node \(C_i\) (\(C_i \xrightarrow{r_i, 0} T\), receiving clean napkins only from fresh purchases \(S \to C_i\) or completed laundry \(D_{i-d} \to C_i\)).

Bug 2 (Forward vs. Reverse Queue Position Indexing): Suppose technician \(j\) repairs \(k\) cars in order \(i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k\).

The \(1\)-st car \(i_1\) delays all \(k\) cars (\(i_1, \dots, i_k\)) on technician \(j\), contributing \(k \cdot T_{i_1, j}\) to total waiting time—which depends on the unknown total number \(k\) of cars assigned to technician \(j\)!
Conversely, if we index slots backward from the end of technician \(j\)’s schedule (\(p = 1\) = last car repaired, \(p = 2\) = second-to-last car repaired, etc.), then the \(p\)-th car from the end delays exactly \(p\) cars (itself and the \(p-1\) cars after it), so its contribution to total completion time is statically \(p \cdot T_{i,j}\) regardless of how many cars precede it!








Drill 1.5 — Dual Sign Orientation & Non-TU Odd Cycles (FM-21)

DAG Project Crashing (#229 Stage 1): Given a DAG \(G = (V, E)\) with edge lengths \(w_e\), you can pay \(c_e > 0\) per unit to increase edge \(e\)’s length by \(x_e \ge 0\) (Wait: or pay \(c_e > 0\) per unit to shorten edge \(e\)’s length to \(w_e - x_e\)) so that every \(S \leadsto T\) path has length \(\le D\) (i.e., potential difference \(\pi_T - \pi_S \le D\) with \(\pi_v - \pi_u \ge w_e - x_e\)). Derive the LP Dual and explain why getting a single inequality sign wrong destroys Kirchhoff flow conservation.
Non-TU Odd Cycle Trap: Why can you not solve Minimum Vertex Cover on a triangle \(C_3 = \{1, 2, 3\}\) by compiling its LP relaxation into an MCMF / Min-Cut network without Bipartite Variable Inversion failing?







TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.5






Failure Mode: FM-21 (LP Dual Sign Inversion & Non-TU Odd-Cycle Half-Integrality, Chapter 21).
Part 1 (Exact LP Dual of DAG Crashing Ch 21.2): Set \(\pi_S = 0\). The Primal LP minimizes \(\sum_{e \in E} c_e x_e\) subject to: \[\pi_u - \pi_v + x_e \ge -w_e \quad (\forall e = (u \to v) \in E), \qquad -\pi_T \ge -D, \qquad x_e \ge 0.\] Introduce non-negative dual flow variables \(f_e \ge 0\) for each edge constraint and \(F \ge 0\) for \(-\pi_T \ge -D\):

Dual constraint for \(x_e \ge 0\): \(0 \le f_e \le c_e\) (edge capacity \(c_e\)!).
Dual constraint for unconstrained \(\pi_v\) (\(v \notin \{S, T\}\)): \(\sum_{e \in \delta^+(v)} f_e - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} f_e = 0\) (exact Kirchhoff flow conservation!).
Dual constraint for \(\pi_T\): \(\sum_{e \in \delta^+(T)} f_e - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(T)} f_e - F = 0 \implies \text{net flow into } T \text{ equals } F\).
Dual objective: \(\max \big(-D \cdot F + \sum_{e \in E} w_e f_e\big) = -\min_{F \ge 0} \big(D \cdot F + \sum_{e \in E} (-w_e) f_e\big)\), which is a parametric Minimum-Cost \(S\)-\(T\) Flow with edge capacities \(c_e\) and edge costs \(-w_e\)! Reversing \(\pi_u - \pi_v\) on a single edge turns \(\delta^+(v) - \delta^-(v)\) into \(\delta^+(v) + \delta^-(v)\), which has two \(+1\)s in one column and breaks flow conservation.

Part 2 (Odd Cycle Non-TU Determinant \(\pm 2\)): The vertex-edge incidence matrix of the triangle \(C_3\) is: \[A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \det(A) = 1(1) + 1(1) = 2 \notin \{-1, 0, +1\}.\] Because \(\det(A) = \pm 2\) on every odd cycle \(C_{2k+1}\), \(A\) is not Totally Unimodular, and its LP relaxation has the unique fractional optimum \(x^* = (1/2, 1/2, 1/2)\) of cost \(1.5 < 2\).







Drill 1.6 — Decoy Discrimination: Minimum Mean Cycle vs. Minimum-Cost Circulation (#226 Stage 1)
You are given a directed graph \(G = (V, E)\) (\(N \le 300, M \le 2000\)) with edge weights \(w_e \in \mathbb{R}\) and asked to find a single directed cycle \(C\) minimizing the average edge weight \(\mu(C) = \frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{e \in C} w_e\). A contestant binary searches \(\lambda\), assigns shifted edge costs \(w'_e = w_e - \lambda\) and unit capacities \(c_e = 1\), and runs Minimum-Cost Circulation (Ch 17.3) to check if the minimum circulation cost is \(< 0\).
Is this overkill, and what happens if they instead ask for the cycle \(C\) with the smallest total shifted weight \(\sum_{e \in C} (w_e - \lambda)\)?






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.6






Verdict: Decoy (Ch 17 vs. Karp’s Algorithm / Binary Search + Bellman–Ford).
Why MCMF Is Wrong / Overkill Here:

For fixed \(\lambda\), \(\min_C \frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{e \in C} w_e < \lambda \iff \exists \text{ cycle } C \text{ with } \sum_{e \in C} (w_e - \lambda) < 0\). Testing whether \(G\) contains at least one negative cycle under edge weights \(w_e - \lambda\) requires only Bellman–Ford / SPFA negative-cycle detection in \(O(VE)\) (or Karp’s Minimum Mean Cycle DP \(\mu^* = \min_{v \in V} \max_{0 \le k < N} \frac{d_N(v) - d_k(v)}{N - k}\) in \(O(VE)\) without binary search!).
Furthermore, a Minimum-Cost Circulation solver saturates the disjoint union of all negative cycles simultaneously, whereas finding a single minimum-weight simple cycle is NP-hard in general and only the sign of the minimum cycle weight (\(\ge 0\) vs. \(< 0\)) is needed for the binary search predicate \(\mu^* \le \lambda\).

2. Blind Checkpoint Problems (#225–#232)
The eight canonical slots below (#225–#232) test every modelling pillar of Part V (Ch 17–Ch 21). To ensure complete coverage of both problem_archive.md and PROBLEM_CURATION.md, several slots pair a foundational 网络流 24 题 diagnostic benchmark with its contest-level companion problem. Write down your Step 1 (Diagnostic Signal) and Step 2 (Algebraic Model) before opening Hint 1.


Problem #225 — Luogu P4016: 负载平衡问题 (24题 #17) & Luogu P2770: 航空路线问题 (24题 #18) [ZH]

Judge URLs: Luogu P4016 (LOJ #6015) · Luogu P2770 (LOJ #6017)
Constraints:

Part A (Luogu P4016 负载平衡问题): \(N \le 100\) (and up to \(N \le 10^6\) in its strengthened version Luogu P2512 [HAOI2008] 糖果传递) circularly arranged warehouses with initial stocks \(A_1, \dots, A_N\) whose sum is divisible by \(N\). Moving \(1\) unit of stock between adjacent warehouses \(i\) and \((i \bmod N) + 1\) costs \(1\). Find the minimum total cost to make all stocks equal to \(\bar{A} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N A_i\).
Part B (Luogu P2770 航空路线问题): \(N \le 100\) cities ordered strictly West-to-East (\(1 = \text{westmost}, N = \text{eastmost}\)) and \(M\) undirected flight routes. Find a closed tour \(1 \leadsto N \leadsto 1\) that starts at city \(1\), travels strictly West-to-East to city \(N\), and then returns strictly East-to-West from \(N\) back to \(1\), visiting each intermediate city at most once, maximizing the total number of distinct cities visited, and print the tour (or No Solution!).








NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal) (#225)






Target Chapters:

Part A (P4016 / P2512): Chapter 17 (Supply-Demand Balancing MCMF) upgraded by Chapter 21 (§21.3 Cycle-Space / Tree-Flow Offset Duality & \(L_1\) Median). At \(N \le 100\), MCMF passes easily, but recognizing that a cycle has corank \(1\) (\(|E| - |V| + 1 = 1\) free circulation parameter \(x_1\)) collapses the entire MCMF into an \(O(N \log N)\) median sort (which is why P4016 is quarantined as R-37 in pure flow lists!).
Part B (P2770): Chapter 17 + Chapter 20 (§20.1 Bitonic Tour \(\equiv\) Two Vertex-Disjoint DAG Paths). Reversing the East-to-West return leg \(N \leadsto 1\) turns it into a second West-to-East path \(1 \leadsto N\) that is internally vertex-disjoint from the first path!











NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#225)






Part A (P4016 Algebraic Cycle Parametrization): Let \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}\) be the net signed flow from warehouse \(i\) to \((i \bmod N) + 1\) (\(x_i < 0\) means flow moves backward). Nodal conservation at warehouse \(i \in \{2, \dots, N\}\) reads: \[x_{i-1} - x_i = \bar{A} - A_i \implies x_i = x_1 - \sum_{k=2}^i (\bar{A} - A_k) = x_1 - c_i,\] where \(c_1 = 0\) and \(c_i = c_{i-1} + \bar{A} - A_i\). Thus the total transportation cost is the 1D \(L_1\) objective: \[\min_{x_1 \in \mathbb{R}} \sum_{i=1}^N |x_1 - c_i|,\] which is minimized at \(x_1^* = \operatorname{median}(c_1, \dots, c_N)\)!
Part B (P2770 Two-Path Vertex-Split Model): Orient every flight \(\{u, v\}\) with \(u < v\) from West to East: \(u \to v\). Split each city \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) into \(i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}\):

Endpoints \(1\) and \(N\) are shared by both paths: \(1_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 2,\; \text{cost } -1} 1_{\text{out}}\) and \(N_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 2,\; \text{cost } -1} N_{\text{out}}\).
Intermediate cities \(i \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}\) can be visited at most once: \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } -1} i_{\text{out}}\).
Each flight \(u < v\) compiles to \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } 0} v_{\text{in}}\) (except if \((1, N) \in E\), give \(1_{\text{out}} \to N_{\text{in}}\) capacity \(2\) to allow the degenerate 2-city tour \(1 \to N \to 1\)).

Run MCMF from \(S = 1_{\text{in}}\) to \(T = N_{\text{out}}\) (or cap \(S \to 1_{\text{in}}\) at \(2\)).

NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#226)






Part A (P4015 Primal Model): Variables \(f_{i,j} \ge 0\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=1}^N f_{i,j} = a_i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^M f_{i,j} = b_j\), optimizing \(\min \sum c_{i,j} f_{i,j}\) and \(\max \sum c_{i,j} f_{i,j} = -\min \sum (-c_{i,j}) f_{i,j}\).
Part B (CF 164C Consecutive Equation Differencing): Let \(p_1 < p_2 < \dots < p_V\) (\(V \le 2N\)) be the sorted distinct values of \(\{s_j, s_j + t_j\}_{j=1}^N\), and replace each interval by its compressed index range \([l_j, r_j)\) (\(1 \le l_j < r_j \le V\)). At each elementary segment \(i \in \{1, \dots, V-1\}\), at most \(K\) active intervals can overlap: \[E_i : \quad \sum_{j:\, l_j \le i < r_j} x_j + y_i = K \qquad (x_j \in \{0, 1\},\; y_i \ge 0).\] Taking \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) (or routing \(K\) units of machine capacity left-to-right along the spine):

Spine arc \(i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } K,\; \text{cost } 0} i + 1\) carries the \(y_i\) idle machines across segment \([p_i, p_{i+1})\).
Task detour arc \(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } -c_j} r_j\) carries \(x_j \in \{0, 1\}\) (one machine leaves the spine at \(l_j\), executes task \(j\) for profit \(c_j\), and rejoins the spine at \(r_j\)!).











TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #226 (Luogu P4015 & CF 164C)






Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Part A (Luogu P4015 — Dual-Run Bipartite MCMF):

Wire \(S \xrightarrow{(a_i, 0)} W_i\), \(W_i \xrightarrow{(\infty, +c_{i,j})} R_j\), and \(R_j \xrightarrow{(b_j, 0)} T\). Run MCMF for min_cost.
For max_cost: restore every arc’s residual capacity to its initial value (cap[id] += cap[id ^ 1]; cap[id ^ 1] = 0;) and negate the cost of every forward/backward pair (cost[id] = -cost[id]; cost[id ^ 1] = -cost[id ^ 1];). Re-run MCMF and output -min_cost.

Part B (Codeforces 164C — Coordinate-Compressed Interval Spine):

Collect all \(2N\) endpoints \(\{s_j, s_j + t_j\}\), sort and deduplicate into \(p_1 < \dots < p_V\) (\(V \le 2000\)).
Wire \(S \xrightarrow{(K, 0)} 1\), spine arcs \(i \xrightarrow{(K, 0)} i + 1\) for \(i = 1, \dots, V - 1\), and \(V \xrightarrow{(K, 0)} T\).
For each task \(j \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), find compressed indices \(l_j = \text{id}(s_j)\) and \(r_j = \text{id}(s_j + t_j)\), and add arc \(e_j = (l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } -c_j} r_j)\), recording its edge index edge_id[j].
DAG Potential Initialization (Ch 17.1): Because all arcs go from smaller index to larger index (\(l_j < r_j\) and \(i < i + 1\)), the initial graph is a topological DAG! Initialize Johnson potentials \(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_V\) in \(O(V + N)\) via a single forward DP: \[\pi_1 = 0, \qquad \pi_v = \min\big(\pi_{v-1},\; \min_{j:\, r_j = v} (\pi_{l_j} - c_j)\big).\]
Then run at most \(K \le 50\) phases of Dijkstra in \(O(K(V + N)\log V)\) time!
Solution Readout: Task \(j\) is selected (\(x_j = 1\)) iff its forward arc edge_id[j] has residual capacity \(0\).




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (CF 164C, \(N = 3, K = 1\)): Tasks \([1, 4)\) profit \(5\), \([1, 2)\) profit \(3\), \([2, 4)\) profit \(4\).

Compressed points: \(p_1 = 1, p_2 = 2, p_3 = 4\) (\(V = 3\)).
Spine: \(1 \xrightarrow{(1,0)} 2 \xrightarrow{(1,0)} 3\). Task arcs: \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, -5)} 3\), \(1 \xrightarrow{(1, -3)} 2\), \(2 \xrightarrow{(1, -4)} 3\).
Path \(1 \to 2 \to 3\) via tasks 2 and 3 has cost \(-3 + (-4) = -7 < -5\), so \(1\) unit of flow takes the two-task detour, outputting 0 1 1 with profit \(7\).

Broken-Gadget Warning (FM-19 — Half-Open \([s_j, s_j + t_j)\) vs. Closed \([l_j, r_j]\)): In CF 164C, task \(j\) ends at \(s_j + t_j\) and another task can start at the exact same timestamp \(s_{j'} = s_j + t_j\). Therefore you connect \(l_j = \text{id}(s_j)\) directly to \(r_j = \text{id}(s_j + t_j)\) (NOT \(\text{id}(s_j + t_j) + 1\)!). Always distinguish half-open \([L, R)\) intervals (connect \(\text{id}(L) \to \text{id}(R)\)) from discrete inclusive integer intervals \([L, R]\) (connect \(\text{id}(L) \to \text{id}(R+1)\)).
Complexity: P4015 takes \(O(NM(N+M)\log(N+M))\); CF 164C takes \(O(K(N + V)\log V)\) with \(K \le 50, V \le 2000\) (\(\approx 10^5\) operations).

Each technician repairs their assigned cars sequentially one at a time, and a customer’s waiting time is the total time from \(t = 0\) until their own car finishes repair. Find the minimum average customer waiting time (to 2 decimal places).








NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal) (#227)






Target Chapters:

Part A (P4014): Chapter 17 (Unit-Capacity Bipartite Assignment)—the special case \(a_i = b_j = 1\) of #226 (P4015, quarantined as R-33 in standalone lists).
Part B (P2053 修车): Chapter 20 (§20.3 Reverse Queue-Position Bipartite Expansion). If you only create one vertex per technician \(j\), the waiting time of the \(k\)-th car depends on which earlier cars were assigned to technician \(j\). Splitting each technician \(j\) into \(N\) reverse queue-position slots \((j, p)\) (\(p = 1, \dots, N\) from the end of technician \(j\)’s schedule) makes every edge cost completely independent and linear!











NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#227)





In Part B (P2053), suppose technician \(j\) repairs \(k_j\) cars in chronological order \(i_1, i_2, \dots, i_{k_j}\). The sum of completion times on technician \(j\) is: \[\sum_{r=1}^{k_j} \sum_{q=1}^r T_{i_q, j} = \sum_{q=1}^{k_j} (k_j - q + 1) \cdot T_{i_q, j} = \sum_{p=1}^{k_j} p \cdot T_{i_{k_j - p + 1},\, j},\] where \(p = k_j - q + 1 \in \{1, 2, \dots, k_j\}\) is the car’s reverse position from the end of technician \(j\)’s queue (\(p = 1\) is the last car repaired by \(j\), \(p = 2\) is the second-to-last, etc.). Introduce binary matching variables \(x_{i, j, p} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicating that car \(i\) is placed in reverse slot \((j, p)\): \[\min \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^M \sum_{p=1}^N (p \cdot T_{i,j})\, x_{i, j, p} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{j, p} x_{i, j, p} = 1 \;\; (\forall i), \quad \sum_{i=1}^N x_{i, j, p} \le 1 \;\; (\forall j, p).\] Notice that because \(p \cdot T_{i,j}\) is strictly increasing in \(p\) (\(1 \cdot T_{i,j} < 2 \cdot T_{i,j} < \dots\)), an optimal matching automatically packs slots \(p = 1, 2, \dots, k_j\) contiguously without gaps!

Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Problem #228 — Luogu P4012: 深海机器人问题 (24题 #22) & Luogu P3967: [TJOI2014] 匹配 [ZH]

Constraints:

NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal) (#228)






Target Chapters:

Part A (P4012): Chapter 18 (§18.1 Diminishing Marginal Edge-Reward Splitting \((1, -w_e) \parallel (\infty, 0)\)). Unlike Luogu P2045 方格取数加强版 (Ch 20, where rewards sit on vertices), here rewards sit directly on grid edges.

What is the exact weighted MCMF analogue?











NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#228)






Part A (P4012 Concave Reward = Convex Cost): If \(f_e \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) robots traverse grid edge \(e\), the reward is \(R_e(f_e) = w_e \cdot \min(f_e, 1)\), so the cost \(\Phi_e(f_e) = -R_e(f_e)\) has marginal differences: \[\Delta\Phi_e(1) = -w_e \le 0 = \Delta\Phi_e(2) = \Delta\Phi_e(3) = \dots\] Because \(-w_e \le 0\), \(\Phi_e\) is convex! It splits into one reward arc \((u \to v, \text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -w_e)\) and one free transit arc \((u \to v, \text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0)\).
Part B (P3967 Zero-Reduced-Cost Residual Cycle Criterion): Let \(M^*\) be a maximum-weight perfect matching (minimum-cost flow of value \(N\) under costs \(c_{i,j} = -w_{i,j}\)) with optimal potentials \(\pi\). By Complementary Slackness (Ch 17.1 / Ch 21.2), every residual arc \(a \in G_{f^*}\) satisfies \(c^\pi(a) \ge 0\), and another perfect matching \(M'\) has the exact same maximum weight if and only if the symmetric difference \(M^* \triangle M'\) is a vertex-disjoint union of directed cycles in \(G_{f^*}\) consisting exclusively of zero-reduced-cost residual arcs (\(c^\pi(a) = 0\), equivalently \(\sum_{a \in C} c(a) = 0\))! Therefore, a matched edge \(e = (L_i \to R_j) \in M^*\) belongs to every optimal perfect matching if and only if its reverse residual arc \((R_j \to L_i)\) does not lie on any directed cycle inside the zero-reduced-cost residual subgraph \(G_{f^*}^{(0)} = \{a \in G_{f^*} : c_{f^*}(a) > 0 \text{ and } c^\pi(a) = 0\}\)—equivalently, \(\operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}^{(0)}}(L_i) \neq \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}^{(0)}}(R_j)\)!










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #228 (Luogu P4012 & P3967)






Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Part A (Luogu P4012 深海机器人问题):

Create \((P+1)(Q+1)\) grid vertices \(\text{id}(r, c) = r(Q+1) + c\).
For every East edge \((r, c) \to (r, c+1)\) with value \(w\) and every North edge \((r, c) \to (r+1, c)\) with value \(w\), add two parallel arcs: \[\text{id}(u) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } -w} \text{id}(v) \quad \text{and} \quad \text{id}(u) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty,\; \text{cost } 0} \text{id}(v).\]
Connect \(S \xrightarrow{(k_i, 0)} \text{id}(r_i, c_i)\) for each start base and \(\text{id}(r'_j, c'_j) \xrightarrow{(l_j, 0)} T\) for each destination base. Run MCMF and output \(-\text{MinCost}\).

Part B (Luogu P3967 [TJOI2014] 匹配):

Method 1 (\(O(N^3)\) Residual \(c^\pi = 0\) Tarjan SCC — Recommended):

Build bipartite network \(S \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} L_i\), \(L_i \xrightarrow{(1, -w_{i,j})} R_j\), \(R_j \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} T\) and run MCMF to find the optimal matching \(M^*\) (value \(N\), weight \(W^* = -\text{MinCost}\)) and final Johnson potentials \(\pi\).
Construct the zero-reduced-cost residual subgraph \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\): include a directed edge \(u \to v\) in \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\) iff there is a residual arc \(u \to v\) with cap > 0 and \(c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v == 0\) (or simply run Tarjan / Floyd / BFS on \(G_{f^*}\) restricted to zero-reduced-cost arcs!).
Run Tarjan’s SCC algorithm on \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\). A matched edge \((L_i \to R_j) \in M^*\) is mandatory (belongs to every max-weight perfect matching) iff \(\operatorname{scc}(L_i) \neq \operatorname{scc}(R_j)\) in \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\)!

Method 2 (Surgical Rollback / Edge Deletion for \(N \le 80\)): For each of the \(N\) matched edges \(e = (L_i \to R_j) \in M^*\), temporarily forbid \(e\) and check if a shortest path from \(L_i\) to \(R_j\) in \(G_{f^*} \setminus \{R_j \to L_i\}\) has length \(\le w_{i,j}\) (if \(> w_{i,j}\) or unreachable, \(e\) is mandatory!). Notice this shortest-path test on \(G_{f^*}\) is mathematically identical to checking whether \(L_i \leadsto R_j\) has a zero-reduced-cost path in \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\)!




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (P3967, \(N = 2\)): \[W = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{vs.} \quad W' = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ 5 & 5 \end{pmatrix}.\]

For \(W'\), the alternating cycle has cost \((-5) + 5 + (-5) + 5 = 0\), so \(L_1, R_1, L_2, R_2\) form a single SCC in \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\) and neither edge is mandatory!

NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal) (#229)

NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#229)






Part A (P3355 König Complement): Partition non-forbidden squares \(V_{\text{valid}}\) (\(|V_{\text{valid}}| = N^2 - M\)) into \(L = \{(r, c) : (r+c) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\}\) and \(R = \{(r, c) : (r+c) \equiv 1 \pmod 2\}\). By König’s Theorem (Ch 05.2), \(\alpha(G) = |V_{\text{valid}}| - \nu(G)\).
Part B (P4553 Exact-Bound Affine Slack Decomposition): Split each country \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) into \(i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}\) with exact flow requirement: \[V_i \le f(i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}) \le V_i, \qquad \text{cost} = 0.\] Let source \(S_0\) emit up to \(M\) travelers (\(S \xrightarrow{[0, M],\; 0} S_0\)), where each traveler can start at any country (\(S_0 \xrightarrow{[0, \infty),\; 0} i_{\text{in}}\)), fly along DAG edges (\(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{[0, \infty),\; c_{i,j}} j_{\text{in}}\) for \(i < j\)), and terminate at any country (\(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{[0, \infty),\; 0} T\)), with circulation feedback arc \(T \xrightarrow{[0, \infty),\; 0} S\). Substituting \(f(e) = l(e) + \tilde{f}(e)\) sets \(M(i_{\text{in}}) = \text{in}_l(i_{\text{in}}) - \text{out}_l(i_{\text{in}}) = -V_i\) and \(M(i_{\text{out}}) = +V_i\), wiring super-source \(S^* \xrightarrow{(V_i, 0)} i_{\text{out}}\) and \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{(V_i, 0)} T^*\)!










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #229 (Luogu P3355 & P4553)






Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Part A (Luogu P3355 骑士共存问题):

Mark the \(M\) forbidden squares in a boolean grid bad[r][c].
For each valid square \((r, c)\) with \((r + c) \bmod 2 == 0\): add \(S \xrightarrow{1} \text{id}(r, c)\), and for each of the \(8\) knight moves \((nr, nc)\) that is inside \([1, N]^2\) and not bad, add \(\text{id}(r, c) \xrightarrow{1} \text{id}(nr, nc)\).
For each valid square \((r, c)\) with \((r + c) \bmod 2 == 1\): add \(\text{id}(r, c) \xrightarrow{1} T\).
Run Dinic and output \((N^2 - M) - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)\).

Part B (Luogu P4553 80人环游世界):

Create ordinary terminals \(S, T\), dispatch gate \(S_0\), split country nodes \(i_{\text{in}}, i_{\text{out}}\) (\(i = 1, \dots, N\)), and super-terminals \(S^*, T^*\).
Zero-Lower-Bound Arcs (\(\tilde{f} \in [0, u]\), remaining in \(G\)):

\(S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } M,\; \text{cost } 0} S_0\) (caps total travelers at \(M\)).
\(S_0 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty,\; \text{cost } 0} i_{\text{in}}\) and \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty,\; \text{cost } 0} T\) for all \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).
\(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty,\; \text{cost } c_{i,j}} j_{\text{in}}\) for each valid flight \(i < j\) (\(c_{i,j} \ne -1\)).
Circulation feedback arc: \(T \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty,\; \text{cost } 0} S\).

Exact-Bound Arcs (\(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{[V_i, V_i], 0} i_{\text{out}}\)):

Because \(u(e) - l(e) = V_i - V_i = 0\), the residual arc \(i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}\) has capacity \(0\) (omitted!), and the lower-bound balance \(M(i_{\text{out}}) = +V_i, M(i_{\text{in}}) = -V_i\) wires: \[S^* \xrightarrow{\text{cap } V_i,\; \text{cost } 0} i_{\text{out}} \quad \text{and} \quad i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } V_i,\; \text{cost } 0} T^*.\]

Run a single pass of MCMF from \(S^*\) to \(T^*\) and output min_cost! (Because every traveler path starts at \(S_0\) at cost \(0\) and ends at \(T\) at cost \(0\), and \(c_{i,j} \ge 0\), no Stage 2 adjustment is needed—the minimum-cost feasible circulation on \(S^* \to T^*\) directly minimizes total flight cost!).




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (P4553, \(N = 2, M = 2, V = [1, 1], c_{1,2} = 5\)):

Super-source \(S^*\) sends \(1\) unit to \(1_{\text{out}}\) and \(1\) unit to \(2_{\text{out}}\); \(1_{\text{in}}\) and \(2_{\text{in}}\) each send \(1\) unit to \(T^*\).
Option 1 (1 traveler \(1 \to 2\)): \(1_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{c_{1,2}=5} 2_{\text{in}} \to T^*\), while \(2_{\text{out}} \to T \to S \to S_0 \to 1_{\text{in}} \to T^*\) uses \(1\) unit on \(S \to S_0\), costing \(5\).
Option 2 (2 travelers, one visiting \(1\) only and one visiting \(2\) only): \(1_{\text{out}} \to T\) and \(2_{\text{out}} \to T\) both loop through \(T \to S \to S_0\) (using \(2 \le M\) units on \(S \to S_0\)) to \(1_{\text{in}}, 2_{\text{in}} \to T^*\) at total cost \(0\)! If \(c_{1,2} < 0\), Option 1 would beat Option 2.

If you output \(N^2 - \text{MaxFlow}\) instead of \((N^2 - M) - \text{MaxFlow}\), every forbidden square is falsely counted as containing a knight!

Problem #230 — Codeforces 818 G: Four Melodies & Codeforces 802 C: Heidi and Library (medium) [EN]

Judge URLs: Codeforces 818 G · Codeforces 802 C
Constraints:

Part A (Codeforces 818 G — Four Melodies): Given an array \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_N\) (\(N \le 3000\), \(1 \le a_i \le 10^5\)), choose 4 disjoint increasing-index subsequences (melodies) such that in each subsequence, every pair of adjacent elements \(a_i, a_j\) (\(i < j\)) satisfies \(|a_i - a_j| = 1\) or \(a_i \equiv a_j \pmod 7\). Maximize the sum of lengths of the 4 subsequences.
Part B (Codeforces 802 C — Heidi and Library (medium)): Over \(N \le 80\) days, day \(i\) requests book \(a_i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) (purchasing book \(b\) costs \(c_b\)). The library holds at most \(K \le 80\) books at a time; if \(a_i\) is already in the library on day \(i\), no purchase is needed; otherwise you must buy \(a_i\) (discarding an existing book if the library Already holds \(K\) books). Minimize total purchase cost.








NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal) (#230)






Target Chapters:

Part A (CF 818G): Chapter 20 (§20.4 Auxiliary Relay Chain / Hub Sparsification for MCMF). Splitting \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{(1, -1)} i_{\text{out}}\) and adding direct edges \(i_{\text{out}} \to j_{\text{in}}\) for all \(i < j\) with \(|a_i - a_j| = 1\) or \(a_i \equiv a_j \pmod 7\) creates \(\binom{3000}{2} \approx 4.5 \cdot 10^6\) edges (TLE/MLE). Because \(K = 4\) is tiny and all valid transitions depend only on the residue \(a_j \bmod 7\) or exact value \(a_j \in \{a_i - 1, a_i + 1\}\), we can route transitions through two linear relay chains (mod_chain[i] and val_chain[i]), shrinking the edge count from \(4.5 \cdot 10^6\) to \(7N \le 21,000\)!
Part B (CF 802C): Chapter 19 + Chapter 20 (§20.3 Book-Caching Interval Saving Detours). Pre-pay \(\sum_{i=1}^N c_{a_i}\) (assuming you buy book \(a_i\) fresh every single day \(i\) and throw it away at night). If the same book recurs at \(i < j\) (where \(j = \text{next}(i)\) is the next request for book \(a_i\)), keeping that book on the shelf from the end of day \(i\) until day \(j\) occupies \(1\) of the \(K - 1\) spare shelf slots across days \([i+1, j-1]\) and saves \(-c_{a_i}\)!











NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#230)






Part A (CF 818G Relay Chain Factorization): For each index \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), let:

\(\text{next\_mod}(i) = \min\{j > i : a_j \equiv a_i \pmod 7\}\),
\(\text{next\_val}(i, v) = \min\{j > i : a_j = v\}\). Introduce two auxiliary relay nodes per index \(i\): \(M_i\) (representing the stream of melodies currently waiting for any element \(\equiv a_i \pmod 7\) at index \(\ge i\)) and \(V_i\) (representing the stream of melodies currently waiting for exact value \(a_i\) at index \(\ge i\)):
\(M_i\) can either enter \(i_{\text{in}}\) (\(M_i \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} i_{\text{in}}\)) or pass forward to the next index of the same residue (\(M_i \xrightarrow{(4, 0)} M_{\text{next\_mod}(i)}\)).
\(V_i\) can either enter \(i_{\text{in}}\) (\(V_i \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} i_{\text{in}}\)) or pass forward to the next index of the exact same value (\(V_i \xrightarrow{(4, 0)} V_{\text{next\_val}(i, a_i)}\)).
Now \(i_{\text{out}}\) only needs at most 3 outgoing edges: to \(M_{\text{next\_mod}(i)}\), to \(V_{\text{next\_val}(i, a_i - 1)}\), and to \(V_{\text{next\_val}(i, a_i + 1)}\)!

Part B (CF 802C Interval Saving Formulation): On day \(d\), the active book \(a_d\) occupies \(1\) slot, leaving \(K - 1\) slots for cached books carried over from earlier days. Let \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether we cache book \(a_i\) from day \(i\) to its next occurrence \(j = \text{next}(i)\): \[\text{Total Cost} = \sum_{i=1}^N c_{a_i} - \max \sum_{i:\, \text{next}(i) \text{ exists}} c_{a_i} x_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i < d < \text{next}(i)} x_i \le K - 1 \;\; (\forall d).\]










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #230 (CF 818G & CF 802C)






Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Part A (Codeforces 818G — Four Melodies):

Create \(S, S_0, T\), and for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) create 4 nodes: \(i_{\text{in}}, i_{\text{out}}, M_i, V_i\) (\(4N + 3 \le 12,003\) vertices).
Wire \(S \xrightarrow{(4, 0)} S_0\). For each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\):

\(S_0 \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} i_{\text{in}}\) (start a melody at \(i\)) and \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} T\) (end a melody at \(i\)).
\(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{(1, -1)} i_{\text{out}}\) (visiting index \(i\) adds \(+1\) to length, i.e., cost \(-1\)).
\(M_i \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} i_{\text{in}}\) and \(V_i \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} i_{\text{in}}\).
If \(j = \text{next\_mod}(i)\) exists: add \(M_i \xrightarrow{(4, 0)} M_j\) and \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} M_j\).
If \(j = \text{next\_val}(i, a_i)\) exists: add \(V_i \xrightarrow{(4, 0)} V_j\).
If \(j_- = \text{next\_val}(i, a_i - 1)\) exists: add \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} V_{j_-}\).
If \(j_+ = \text{next\_val}(i, a_i + 1)\) exists: add \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} V_{j_+}\).

Initialize potentials \(\pi\) in \(O(N)\) by topological DP (since all edges go from \(i\) to \(j > i\), or \(M_i / V_i \to i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}\) within layer \(i\)!), then run 4 iterations of Dijkstra in \(O(N \log N)\)! Output \(-\text{MinCost}\).

Part B (Codeforces 802C — Heidi and Library):

Compute base_cost \(= \sum_{i=1}^N c_{a_i}\).
Build a 1D spine \(1 \xrightarrow{(K-1, 0)} 2 \xrightarrow{(K-1, 0)} \dots \xrightarrow{(K-1, 0)} N\) (or split day \(i\) if \(a_i = a_{i+1}\): if \(j = i + 1\), keeping \(a_i\) to day \(i + 1\) uses \(0\) spare slots during intermediate days, so simply subtract \(c_{a_i}\) directly whenever \(a_i = a_{i+1}\), and for \(j = \text{next}(i) > i + 1\) add interval detour arc \((i + 1) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } -c_{a_i}} j\) across spine segments \((i+1) \to \dots \to j\)!).
Wire \(S \xrightarrow{(K-1, 0)} 1\) and \(N \xrightarrow{(K-1, 0)} T\), run MCMF, and output base_cost + min_cost.




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (CF 818G, \(N = 4, K = 1\) melody): \(a = [1, 8, 15, 2]\).

Notice \(1 \equiv 8 \equiv 15 \pmod 7\). Instead of connecting \(1_{\text{out}}\) to both \(2_{\text{in}}\) and \(3_{\text{in}}\), \(1_{\text{out}}\) connects only to \(M_2\); \(M_2\) connects to \(2_{\text{in}}\) and forwards to \(M_3 \to 3_{\text{in}}\), and \(1_{\text{out}}\) also connects to \(V_4\) (\(a_4 = 2 = a_1 + 1\)). The longest 1-melody is \(1 \to 8 \to 15\) of length \(3\).

Broken-Gadget Warning (CF 802C — Adjacent Duplicate \(a_i = a_{i+1}\)): If book \(a_i\) is requested on two consecutive days (\(j = i + 1\)), it is already the active book on day \(i\) and remains the active book on day \(i + 1\) without occupying any of the \(K - 1\) background cache slots on an intermediate day! Even when \(K = 1\) (\(K - 1 = 0\) spine capacity), \(a_i = a_{i+1}\) saves \(c_{a_i}\) for free. Handling \(j = i + 1\) as a free saving (or splitting each day \(d\) into \(d_{\text{in}} \to d_{\text{out}}\)) prevents \(K = 1\) from failing on adjacent identical books.
Complexity: CF 818G takes \(4\) Dijkstra runs on \(12,000\) vertices and \(21,000\) edges (\(\approx 3 \cdot 10^5\) ops, < 50 ms); CF 802C takes \(O(K N^2 \log N)\).








Problem #231 — Codeforces 1061 E: Politics & ICPC World Finals 2015 C: Catering [EN]

NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal) (#231)

NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#231)






Part A (CF 1061E Subtree Equation Differencing): In tree \(T_1\), let \(U_1 \subseteq V\) be the set of constrained vertices (if root \(r_1 \notin U_1\) or \(r_2 \notin U_2\), or if \(k^{(1)}_{r_1} \neq k^{(2)}_{r_2}\), how do we know the total size? TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #231 (CF 1061E & ICPC WF 2015 C)






Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Part A (Codeforces 1061E — Politics):

Check \(k^{(1)}_{r_1} == k^{(2)}_{r_2}\); if not, output -1.
Run a DFS on \(T_1\) from \(r_1\) passing down the nearest constrained ancestor anc1[i], and for each \(u \in U_1\) compute \(c_1(u) = k^{(1)}_u - \sum_{v \in \text{ch}^*(u)} k^{(1)}_v\). Repeat on \(T_2\) from \(r_2\) to find anc2[i] and \(c_2(w)\).
Early Infeasibility Guard: If any \(c_1(u) < 0\) or \(c_2(w) < 0\) (or \(c_1(u) > |R_1(u)|\)), immediately output -1.
Build Bipartite MCMF:

\(S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } c_1(u),\; \text{cost } 0} R_1(u)\) for each \(u \in U_1\).
\(R_2(w) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } c_2(w),\; \text{cost } 0} T\) for each \(w \in U_2\).
For each vertex \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), add \(R_1(\text{anc}_1(i)) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } -a_i} R_2(\text{anc}_2(i))\).

Run MCMF from \(S\) to \(T\). If \(\text{MaxFlow} < k^{(1)}_{r_1}\), output -1; otherwise output \(-\text{MinCost}\).

Part B (ICPC World Finals 2015 C — Catering):

Using Lower-Bound MCMF (Ch 17.3): wire \(S \xrightarrow{(K, 0)} 0_{\text{out}}\), \(0_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{(K, 0)} T\) (unused teams stay at depot \(0\)), \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{(1, c_{i,j})} j_{\text{in}}\) (\(0 \le i < j \le N\)), \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} T\) (\(1 \le i \le N\)), feedback \(T \xrightarrow{(\infty, 0)} S\), and for each mandatory request \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{[1, 1], 0} i_{\text{out}}\) wire \(S^* \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} i_{\text{out}}\) and \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{(1, 0)} T^*\). Run MCMF from \(S^*\) to \(T^*\) and output min_cost!

Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (CF 1061E, \(N = 3\)):

\(T_1\): \(1\) is root with children \(2, 3\); constraints \(k^{(1)}_1 = 2, k^{(1)}_2 = 1 \implies R_1(2) = \{2\}\) (\(c_1(2) = 1\)) and \(R_1(1) = \{1, 3\}\) (\(c_1(1) = 2 - 1 = 1\)).
\(T_2\): \(3\) is root with children \(1, 2\); constraints \(k^{(2)}_3 = 2, k^{(2)}_1 = 1 \implies R_2(1) = \{1\}\) (\(c_2(1) = 1\)) and \(R_2(3) = \{2, 3\}\) (\(c_2(3) = 2 - 1 = 1\)).
Vertex \(2 \in R_1(2) \cap R_2(3)\) is forced (\(x_2 = 1\)), saturating \(R_1(2)\) and \(R_2(3)\); then vertex \(1 \in R_1(1) \cap R_2(1)\) is forced (\(x_1 = 1\)), selecting \(\{1, 2\}\) with profit \(a_1 + a_2\).

Broken-Gadget Warning (CF 1061E — Subtracting All Descendants Instead of Highest Constrained Descendants): When computing \(c_1(u)\), you must subtract \(k^{(1)}_v\) only for constrained descendants \(v \in U_1 \setminus \{u\}\) whose path to \(u\) contains no other constrained vertex (\(\text{anc}_1(\text{parent}(v)) = u\)). Subtracting all constrained descendants double-subtracts nested subtrees (FM-19)!
Complexity: CF 1061E has \(\le 1002\) vertices and \(1500\) edges, running in \(O(N^2 \log N)\) (< 30 ms).








Problem #232 — AtCoder ARC 125 E: Snack & Luogu P3305: [SDOI2013] 费用流 [EN]/[ZH]

Judge URLs: AtCoder ARC 125 E · Luogu P3305 · Companion LP Dual Audit: Luogu P3337 [ZJOI2013] 防守战线
Constraints:

Part A (AtCoder ARC 125 E — Snack): There are \(N \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) types of snacks (type \(i\) has \(A_i \le 10^{12}\) pieces available) and \(M \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) children. Child \(j\) can receive at most \(B_j\) pieces of snack \(i\) (for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\)) and at most \(C_j\) pieces of snack in total across all types (\(B_j, C_j \le 10^{12}\)). Find the maximum total number of snack pieces that can be distributed.
Part B (Luogu P3305 [SDOI2013] 费用流 — The Ultimate Diagnostic Decoy): Given a directed flow network \(G = (V, E)\) (\(N \le 100, M \le 1000\)) with source \(1\), sink \(N\), edge capacities \(c_e\), and a price multiplier \(P\): the cost of routing a flow \(f\) is defined as \(P \cdot \max_{e \in E} f_e\) (you pay \(P\) times the single largest flow value on any edge). First find the maximum \(1\)-\(N\) flow \(F^*\), and then find the minimum possible cost \(P \cdot \max_{e \in E} f_e\) among all maximum flows of value \(F^*\)!








NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal) (#232)






Target Chapters:

Part A (ARC 125E): Chapter 21 (§21.1 / Chapter 16 Complete Bipartite Max-Flow Eliminated via Min-Cut Cardinality Sweep). Building the bipartite flow graph \(S \xrightarrow{A_i} L_i \xrightarrow{B_j} R_j \xrightarrow{C_j} T\) requires \(N \cdot M = 4 \cdot 10^{10}\) edges (TLE/MLE). By Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality, every cross-edge into \(R_j\) depends only on \(j\) (\(B_j\)), so if we fix the number \(k = |L \cap S_{\text{cut}}| \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) of left vertices placed on the \(S\)-side of the cut, the optimal cut choices for all \(L_i\) and all \(R_j\) decouple completely!
Part B (Luogu P3305): Diagnostic Decoy (Ch 01 + Ch 14 Bottleneck Binary Search + Dinic, NOT Ch 17 MCMF!). Even though the problem title literally says 费用流 (“Min-Cost Flow”), the objective \(P \cdot \max_{e \in E} f_e\) is an \(\ell_\infty\) bottleneck norm, NOT a linear sum \(\sum_e c_e f_e\)! Never try to run MCMF here: simply compute \(F^* = \operatorname{MaxFlow}(1, N)\), then binary search the maximum single-edge flow ceiling \(B \in [0, \max c_e]\), clamping every edge’s capacity to \(\min(c_e, B)\) and checking if \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}_B(1, N) == F^*\)!











NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation (#232)






Part A (ARC 125E Min-Cut Parametrization by \(k = |L \cap S_{\text{cut}}|\)): In any \(S\)-\(T\) cut \((S_{\text{cut}}, T_{\text{cut}})\) of the bipartite network \(S \xrightarrow{A_i} L_i \xrightarrow{B_j} R_j \xrightarrow{C_j} T\):

Suppose \(|L \cap S_{\text{cut}}| = k \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\). For the \(N - k\) left vertices \(L_i \in T_{\text{cut}}\), we pay \(\sum_{L_i \in T_{\text{cut}}} A_i\). To minimize this sum for a fixed \(k\), we must put the \(N - k\) snacks with the smallest \(A_i\) into \(T_{\text{cut}}\) (and the \(k\) snacks with the largest \(A_i\) into \(S_{\text{cut}}\))!
Once \(|L \cap S_{\text{cut}}| = k\) is fixed, each right vertex \(R_j\) (\(j = 1, \dots, M\)) has two choices:

Put \(R_j \in S_{\text{cut}}\): cuts \(R_j \xrightarrow{C_j} T\) at cost \(C_j\).
Put \(R_j \in T_{\text{cut}}\): cuts the \(k\) cross-edges from \(L \cap S_{\text{cut}}\) to \(R_j\), at total cost \(k \cdot B_j\).

Therefore, by the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem: \[\text{MaxFlow} = \min_{0 \le k \le N} \left( \sum_{i=1}^{N-k} A_{(i)} + \sum_{j=1}^M \min(k \cdot B_j,\; C_j) \right),\] where \(A_{(1)} \le A_{(2)} \le \dots \le A_{(N)}\)!

Part B (Luogu P3305 Real-Valued Bottleneck Feasibility): Because the clamped capacity \(B \in [0, \max c_e]\) can be fractional (e.g., splitting \(1\) unit of flow equally across \(2\) parallel paths gives \(B = 0.5\)), binary search \(B \in [0, \max c_e]\) over double for \(60\) iterations, running Dinic with edge capacities \(\min(c_e, B)\) and checking MaxFlow(B) >= F* - 1e-8.










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #232 (ARC 125E & Luogu P3305)






Step 1–3: Mechanical Compilation & Sweep Algorithm

Part A (AtCoder ARC 125E — Snack in \(O((N+M)\log(N+M))\)):

Sort \(A\) ascending: \(A_{(1)} \le A_{(2)} \le \dots \le A_{(N)}\), and compute prefix sums \(P_A[r] = \sum_{i=1}^r A_{(i)}\).
For each child \(j \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), \(\min(k \cdot B_j, C_j)\) equals \(k \cdot B_j\) when \(k \le \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\) and equals \(C_j\) when \(k > \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\).
Bucket or sort the children by their threshold \(\tau_j = \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\). Maintain the sum of \(B_j\) for children with \(\tau_j \ge k\) (active_B_sum) and the sum of \(C_j\) for children with \(\tau_j < k\) (capped_C_sum).
Sweep \(k = 0, 1, \dots, N\) in \(O(N + M)\) time: \[\text{ans} = \min_{0 \le k \le N} \big( P_A[N - k] + k \cdot \text{active\_B\_sum}(k) + \text{capped\_C\_sum}(k) \big).\]

Part B (Luogu P3305 [SDOI2013] 费用流):

Step 1: Run integer Dinic on original capacities \(c_e\) to get \(F^* = \operatorname{MaxFlow}(1, N)\) and print \(F^*\).
Step 2: Binary search real ceiling \(B \in [0, \max_{e} c_e]\) for \(60\) iterations:

Rebuild the graph with capacities \(c'_e = \min(\text{double}(c_e), B)\).
Run Dinic (EPS = 1e-8). If \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}_B(1, N) \ge F^* - 10^{-8}\), set hi = B; else lo = B.

Step 3: Output \(P \cdot \text{lo}\) formatted to \(4\) decimal places.
(Companion Audit — Luogu P3337 [ZJOI2013] 防守战线 Ch 21.3): When the primal problem asks for the minimum cost to place towers (\(c_i\) per tower at \(i\)) so that every interval \([l_j, r_j]\) contains at least \(d_j\) towers, its LP Dual maximizes \(\sum_j d_j f_j\) where \(f_j \ge 0\) is flow on interval arc \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) and the spine arc \(i \to i + 1\) has capacity \(c_i\)—the exact dual mirror of Luogu P3980 志愿者招募!




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (ARC 125E, \(N = 2, M = 2\)): \(A = [2, 5]\), \(B = [2, 3]\), \(C = [3, 4]\).

Thresholds: \(\tau_1 = \lfloor 3/2 \rfloor = 1\), \(\tau_2 = \lfloor 4/3 \rfloor = 1\).
\(k = 0\): \(P_A[2] + 0 = (2 + 5) + 0 = 7\).
\(k = 1\): \(P_A[1] + \min(2, 3) + \min(3, 4) = 2 + 2 + 3 = 7\).
\(k = 2\): \(P_A[0] + \min(4, 3) + \min(6, 4) = 0 + 3 + 4 = 7\). Maximum snacks \(= 7\).

Broken-Gadget Warning (Luogu P3305 — Integer-Only Binary Search Trap): In Luogu P3305, edge flows in the second question are not restricted to integers! For example, if \(F^* = 1\) and there are \(2\) parallel edges from \(1\) to \(N\) each of capacity \(1\), the optimal flow sends \(0.5\) on each edge (max_e f_e = 0.5). Binary searching only over integers \(B \in \mathbb{Z}\) outputs \(1.0000 \cdot P\) instead of \(0.5000 \cdot P\)!
Complexity: ARC 125E runs in \(O((N+M)\log(N+M))\) time and \(O(N+M)\) space; Luogu P3305 runs in \(60 \cdot O(M \sqrt{N})\) time.

3.2 Part V Failure Mode Self-Audit (FM-17–FM-21)



Code
Failure Mode Name
Broken Habit / Symptom
Mathematical Root Cause
Mandatory Defensive Guard & Chapter Reference




FM-17
Stale Johnson Potentials & Un-Saturated Negative Cycles
Updating \(\pi_v \gets \pi_v + d_v\) only along the augmenting path \(P\), forgetting to negate reverse arc costs cost[id ^ 1] = -cost[id], or running SPFA/Dijkstra directly on a cyclic graph with negative-cost edges (Drill 1.1).
Leaving \(\pi_v\) un-updated on off-path reachable nodes violates \(c^{\pi'}(u, v) = c^\pi(u, v) + d_u - d_v \ge 0\); negative cycles cause infinite SPFA loops unless pre-saturated.
Update \(\pi_v \gets \pi_v + d_v\) for every node \(v\) with \(d_v < \infty\) after each Dijkstra; on cyclic networks with \(c(e) < 0\), pre-saturate \(f(e) = u(e)\), adjust \(M(u), M(v)\), and add reverse arc \((v \to u, u(e), -c(e) > 0)\) (Ch 17 §17.1–17.3).


FM-18
Concave Fixed-Charge Parallel Arc Trap & Un-Complemented Tournament Triples
Splitting a concave or fixed-charge cost \(\Phi(f) = F_e \cdot [f > 0] + b_e f\) (\(F_e > 0\)) into parallel unit arcs (Drill 1.2), or trying to count transitive tournament triples directly without complementing via out-degrees \(d_i^+\).
When \(\Delta\Phi(1) > \Delta\Phi(2)\), MCMF routes the first unit of flow along the cheaper second arc (\(b_e\)), bypassing the first arc (\(F_e + b_e\)); transitive triples involve 3 edges, whereas non-transitive triples depend only on \(\sum_i \binom{d_i^+}{2}\).
Always verify convexity \(\Delta\Phi(1) \le \Delta\Phi(2) \le \dots \le \Delta\Phi(U)\) before unrolling parallel arcs; for tournaments, use Kendall–Babington Smith \(T_{\text{trans}} = \binom{N}{3} - \sum_{i=1}^N \binom{d_i^+}{2}\) with marginal costs \(0, 1, 2, \dots\) (Ch 18 §18.1–18.4).


FM-19
Off-by-One Interval Differencing (\(l_j \to r_j\) vs. \(l_j \to r_j + 1\)) & Nested Subtree Double-Subtraction
Wiring closed integer interval \([l_j, r_j]\) as \(l_j \to r_j\) instead of \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) (Drill 1.3), or subtracting all constrained descendants instead of only highest constrained descendants in tree differencing (#231).
In \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\), an indicator covering \(i \in \{l_j, \dots, r_j\}\) has \(+1\) at \(i = l_j\) and \(-1\) at \(i = r_j + 1\); subtracting nested descendants \(w \prec v \prec u\) subtracts \(E_w\) multiple times.
For closed integer intervals \([l_j, r_j]\), always wire \(l_j \leftrightarrow r_j + 1\) (with dummy node \(N+1\)); for half-open \([s_j, t_j)\), wire \(\text{id}(s_j) \leftrightarrow \text{id}(t_j)\); on trees, subtract only \(v \in \text{ch}^*(u)\) with \(\text{anc}(\text{parent}(v)) = u\) (Ch 19 §19.1–19.3).


FM-20
Merged Dirty/Clean Inventory Nodes & Forward Queue-Slot Indexing
Using a single node \(v_i\) per day in 餐巾计划 (Drill 1.4), or indexing machine queue slots forward from the start of shift instead of backward from the end (#227 修车 / 美食节).
A single day node lets dirty inflow from \(S \to v_i\) exit directly to clean demand \(v_i \to T\) at cost \(0\); forward position \(q\) delays \(k_j - q + 1\) jobs where \(k_j\) is unknown beforehand.
Split day \(i\) into Dirty Supply \(D_i\) (\(S \to D_i\)) and Clean Demand \(C_i\) (\(C_i \to T\)); index machine slots by reverse position \(p \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) from the end with static cost \(p \cdot T_{i,j}\), and spawn slot \((j, p+1)\) lazily when \((j, p)\) saturates (Ch 20 §20.2–20.3).


FM-21
LP Dual Sign Inversion & Non-TU Odd-Cycle Half-Integrality
Mixing \(\ge\) and \(\le\) constraints when taking the LP dual of path-crashing or covering LPs (Drill 1.5), or assuming vertex-edge incidence LP relaxations are integral on general graphs with odd cycles.
Flipping a primal inequality sign turns a \([-1, +1]\) conservation column into \([+1, +1]\); odd cycles \(C_{2k+1}\) have submatrix determinant \(\pm 2\), producing \(1/2\)-integral optima.
Normalize all primal constraints to standard form before dualizing so each potential difference \(\pi_v - \pi_u\) produces exact Kirchhoff conservation \(\delta^+(v) - \delta^-(v) = 0\); verify Total Unimodularity (bipartite / network matrix) before asserting LP integrality (Ch 21 §21.1–21.3).









NoteSelf-Audit Rapid Check — 5 Diagnostic Questions (Verify Before Proceeding)






(FM-17) In an MCMF network with negative edge costs on a DAG (#226 CF 164C, #230 CF 818G), why can you initialize \(\pi_v\) in \(O(V + E)\) without SPFA, and why does that fail if the initial graph contains a directed cycle?

Check: On a DAG, topological order guarantees no cycles exist and computes shortest distances \(d_v\) in a single linear pass; on a cyclic graph, a negative cycle has \(-\infty\) shortest path and must be eliminated via mandatory arc pre-saturation (\(f(e) = u(e)\)).

(FM-18) Given edge cost \(\Phi(f) = c_e \cdot f^2\) vs. \(\Phi(f) = c_e \cdot \sqrt{f}\) for integer flow \(f \in \{0, 1, \dots, U\}\) (\(c_e > 0\)), which one can be compiled into \(U\) parallel unit-capacity MCMF arcs?

Check: Only \(\Phi(f) = c_e f^2\) (\(\Delta\Phi(k) = c_e(2k-1)\) is strictly increasing). The square-root cost \(\Phi(f) = c_e \sqrt{f}\) has strictly decreasing marginals (\(\sqrt{1}-0 > \sqrt{2}-\sqrt{1} > \dots\), concave!), so MCMF would pick the \(U\)-th arc before the \(1\)-st arc.

(FM-19) In Consecutive Equation Differencing \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) (Ch 19.2), how does changing a point coverage constraint from \(\ge A_i\) to an interval \([A_i, B_i]\) modify the spine arc between \(i\) and \(i+1\)?

Check: Instead of an unbounded slack variable \(y_i \ge 0\) (capacity \(\infty\) on \(i+1 \to i\)), the slack variable is bounded by \(y_i \in [0, B_i - A_i]\), which simply changes the capacity of the backward spine arc \(i+1 \to i\) from \(\infty\) to \(B_i - A_i\)!

(FM-20) In Luogu P2050 [NOI2012] 美食节 (\(N \le 40\) dishes, total orders \(P = \sum p_i \le 800\), \(M \le 100\) chefs), why do we not pre-allocate all \(M \times P = 80,000\) chef-slot vertices before running MCMF?

Check: Because for any chef \(j\), \(\text{Slot}(j, p)\) has strictly smaller cost \(p \cdot T_{i,j}\) than \(\text{Slot}(j, p+1)\) for every dish \(i\). Thus Dijkstra will never augment through \(\text{Slot}(j, p+1)\) until \(\text{Slot}(j, p)\) is saturated! Lazily adding \(\text{Slot}(j, p+1)\) (and its \(N\) incoming dish edges) only when \(\text{Slot}(j, p)\) is matched keeps the active graph at \(\le M + P = 900\) slot nodes instead of \(80,000\).

(FM-21) After solving a Maximum-Weight Bipartite Perfect Matching via MCMF (#228 Luogu P3967), how do you determine in \(O(N^2)\) time which matched edges belong to every optimal perfect matching?

Check: Build the zero-reduced-cost residual subgraph \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\) containing all positive-capacity residual arcs with \(c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v = 0\), and run Tarjan’s SCC algorithm; a matched edge \((L_i, R_j) \in M^*\) is mandatory iff \(\operatorname{scc}(L_i) \neq \operatorname{scc}(R_j)\) in \(G_{f^*}^{(0)}\).
