section: 4. Readiness Bridge to Part IV: Fractional Programming, Planar Duality, Min-Cut DP & Gomory–Hu Cut Trees
text:
4. Readiness Bridge to Part IV: Fractional Programming, Planar Duality, Min-Cut DP & Gomory–Hu Cut Trees
In Part III (Ch 09–Ch 13), you mastered the compilation half of minimum-cut theory: translating non-graph algebraic objectives into a single static directed network \(G = (V, E, c, s, t)\) and calling Dinic once. In Part IV (Ch 14–Ch 16), we ask what happens when a single static Dinic call is no longer enough—either because the objective is a nonlinear ratio of two cut polynomials, or because \(V\) and \(E\) are too large or queried too many times for standard max-flow:

From Static Project Selection (Ch 09) to Parametric Cuts & Maximum Density Subgraphs (Ch 14):

In #209 (Gold Mine) and #216 (Strange Set), you maximized a linear sum \(\sum_{i \in C} b_i - \sum_{e \in \text{cut}} c_e\).
In Chapter 14, you will maximize ratios of closure quantities—such as Dinkelbach’s 0-1 Fractional Programming \(\max_C \frac{\sum_{i \in C} p_i}{\sum_{i \in C} w_i}\) and Goldberg’s Maximum Density Subgraph \(\max_{S \subseteq V} \frac{|E(S)|}{|S|}\)—by embedding a Ch 09 / Ch 10 cut network inside a parametric binary search on \(\lambda\) where node capacities vary continuously as \(c_v(\lambda) = \lambda w_v - p_v\).

From Grid Partition Cuts (Ch 10–Ch 13) to \((s, t)\)-Planar Cycle–Cut Duality & Shortest Paths (Ch 15):

In #210 (Wolves and Sheep) and #214 (Cross), you ran Dinic on \(100 \times 100\) grids (\(V = 10^4\)). What if the grid is \(1000 \times 1000\) (\(V = 10^6\)), where Dinic times out?
In Chapter 15, when the cut network is \((s, t)\)-planar (or general planar), every minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut bijects with a shortest path in the planar dual graph \(G^*\), replacing \(O(V^{1.5})\) Dinic with \(O(V \log V)\) Dijkstra ([ICPC-Beijing 2006] 狼抓兔子 and [NOI2010] 海拔).

From Explicit Cut Graphs (Ch 09–Ch 13) to Min-Cut DP, Stoer–Wagner & Gomory–Hu Cut Trees (Ch 16):

Whenever a Ch 10–Ch 13 cut graph has bounded treewidth, small corridor width, or complete-bipartite cardinality symmetry (like ARC 125 E Snack or CF 724 E Goods Transportation), Chapter 16 shows how to eliminate the flow solver altogether and compute \(\text{MinCut}(S, T)\) directly via Dynamic Programming over the \(S/T\) partition. Finally, for undirected graphs queried across all \(\binom{N}{2}\) terminal pairs, Gusfield’s Gomory–Hu Cut Tree compresses all \(\binom{N}{2}\) minimum cuts into \(N - 1\) Dinic calls.



4.1 Part III Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation Cheat Sheet
Keep this master compilation table beside you as you enter Parts IV–VI:








Pseudo-Boolean / Multi-State Clause (\(x_u = [u \in T] \in \{0,1\}\))
Submodularity / Structural Condition
Mechanical \(s\)-\(t\) Cut Gadget




Maximize \(\sum_{u} w_u (1 - x_u)\) s.t. \(u \in S \implies v \in S\) (Ch 09, #209, #216)
Any directed graph (prune cycles if sequential order required)
\(\text{Base} = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u\); \(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u\) (\(w_u > 0\)), \(u \xrightarrow{-w_u} T\) (\(w_u < 0\)), \(u \xrightarrow{\infty} v\)


Pairwise asymmetric penalty \(c_{01}(1 - x_u)x_v + c_{10}x_u(1 - x_v)\) (Ch 10, #210, #214)
Submodular: \(c_{01} + c_{10} \ge c_{00} + c_{11}\)
Add directed arc \(u \xrightarrow{c_{01}} v\) and reverse arc \(v \xrightarrow{c_{10}} u\)


Edge-compressed pairwise bonus \(E_A(1-x_u)(1-x_v) + E_B x_u x_v\) (Ch 10.4)
Always submodular (\(E_A, E_B \ge 0\))
Add \(\frac{1}{2}E_A\) to \(S \to u, S \to v\); add \(\frac{1}{2}E_B\) to \(u \to T, v \to T\); add \(u \xleftrightarrow{\frac{1}{2}(E_A+E_B)} v\)


All-\(S\) subset bonus \(+W \prod_{u \in A} (1 - x_u)\) (Ch 10.3)
\(W \ge 0\), arbitrary subset \(A \subseteq V\)
Add \(+W\) to base; create hub \(B_A\) with \(S \xrightarrow{W} B_A\) and \(B_A \xrightarrow{\infty} u\) (\(\forall u \in A\))


All-\(T\) subset bonus \(+W \prod_{u \in A} x_u\) (Ch 10.3, Drill 1.2)
\(W \ge 0\), arbitrary subset \(A \subseteq V\)
Add \(+W\) to base; create hub \(B_B\) with \(u \xrightarrow{\infty} B_B\) (\(\forall u \in A\)) and \(B_B \xrightarrow{W} T\)


Supermodular conflict \(\infty \cdot x_u x_v\) or same-state penalty \(w[x_u = x_v]\) (Ch 11, #211)
Conflict graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) must be bipartite
Invert \(R\): \(y_u = 1 - x_u\) (\(u \in L\)), \(y_v = x_v\) (\(v \in R\)); wire \(L \xrightarrow{\infty} R\) (or \(L \xleftrightarrow{w} R\))


Destroy all 4-vertex patterns across a 4-colorable grid (Ch 11+Ch 12, #212)
Every forbidden pattern maps to \(C_1 \to C_2 \to C_3 \to C_4\)
Split \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{w_i} i_{\text{out}}\) and wire \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} C_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} C_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} C_3 \xrightarrow{\infty} C_4 \xrightarrow{\infty} T\)


Multi-state choice \(h_u \in \{1..K\}\) with \(h_u - h_v \le D\) (Ch 12, Drill 1.4)
Arbitrary \(w(u, k) \ge 0\), integer offset \(D \in \mathbb{Z}\)
Chain \((u, 1) \xrightarrow{w(u,1)} \dots \xrightarrow{w(u,K)} T\), reverse \((u, k+1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, k)\), diagonal \((u, k) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, k-D)\)


Convex difference penalty \(\phi(h_u - h_v)\) (Ch 13.1, Drill 1.5)
Discrete convex: \(\Delta^2 \phi(d) = \phi(d+1) - 2\phi(d) + \phi(d-1) \ge 0\)
Unary chains with cross-arcs \((u, i) \to (v, j)\) of capacity \(\frac{1}{2}\Delta^2 \phi(i - j)\)


Large-range \(L_1\) Coarea \(\sum c_u |h_u - b_u| + \sum w_{uv}|h_u - h_v|\) (Ch 13.2, Drill 1.6)
\(b_u \in [0, 10^9]\), \(c_u, w_{uv} \ge 0\)
Slice by sorted targets \(b_{(1)} < \dots < b_{(K)}\); solve decoupled binary cuts \(z_u(t) = [h_u > t]\)

title: Checkpoint I — Foundations, Residual Anatomy, Vertex Splitting, and Bounded Circulations
text:
When you solve an exercise at the end of Chapter 2 (“Residual Graph Geometry and Cut Edge Classification”) or Chapter 4 (“Flows with Demands and Lower-Bound Circulations”), the chapter heading itself hands you half the solution. Before reading a single word of the problem statement, you already know whether to run Tarjan’s SCC algorithm on \(G_{f^*}\), split vertices into \(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\), or introduce super-terminals \(S^*, T^*\) for affine slack variables \(\tilde{f}(e) = f(e) - l(e)\).
In a live ICPC, NOI, Codeforces, or AtCoder contest, problems arrive completely untagged. You are given an English, Chinese, or Japanese narrative, a set of numerical constraints (\(N, M, K, V_{\max}\)), and a two-second time limit. Your most decisive competitive skill is blind diagnostic recognition: translating non-graph surface clues into an algebraic conservation law or cut polynomial, and then compiling that algebra into an exact capacity network without falling into any of the six foundational failure modes (FM-01–FM-06).

title: Checkpoint I — Foundations, Residual Anatomy, Vertex Splitting, and Bounded Circulations
text:
1. Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills (FM-01–FM-06)
Before tackling the eight full contest problems in Section 2, test your diagnostic reflexes on six short modelling scenarios. Each scenario either contains a subtle modelling bug (FM-01–FM-06) or asks you to identify the minimal graph compilation fix. Formulate your diagnosis before expanding the answer callout.


Drill 1.1 — The Greedy Shortest-Path Deletion Trap
You are given a directed unit-capacity graph \(G = (V, E)\) (\(N \le 500, M \le 1000\)) and asked to find the maximum number of edge-disjoint directed paths from \(1\) to \(N\). A teammate proposes the following \(O(M^2)\) algorithm:

Run BFS from \(1\) to \(N\) to find a shortest directed path \(P\).
If no path exists, stop and return the count of paths found.
Delete all edges of \(P\) from \(G\) and repeat from Step 1.

Construct a 4-vertex counterexample where this algorithm fails, identify the exact Part I failure mode, and state how the residual graph fixes it.






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.1






Failure Mode: FM-01 (Greedy Path Deletion without Reverse Residual Cancellation, Chapter 1).
4-Vertex Counterexample: Let \(V = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) with five directed unit edges: \((1 \to 2)\), \((2 \to 3)\), \((3 \to 4)\), \((1 \to 3)\), and \((2 \to 4)\).

Suppose Step 1 finds the 3-edge path \(P_1 = (1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4)\) and deletes its three edges.
The remaining graph has only \((1 \to 3)\) and \((2 \to 4)\), which are disconnected! The greedy algorithm halts and reports \(1\) path, whereas \(2\) edge-disjoint paths exist: \((1 \to 2 \to 4)\) and \((1 \to 3 \to 4)\).

Exact Residual Fix: Instead of deleting \((2 \to 3)\), skew-symmetric flow conservation (Ch 01.2) sets \(c_f(2 \to 3) = 0\) and opens a backward residual arc \((3 \to 2)\) with capacity \(c_f(3 \to 2) = 1\). The second augmenting path \((1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 4)\) traverses \((3 \to 2)\), which algebraically cancels \(f(2 \to 3)\) from \(1\) back to \(0\) and splices the two prefixes and suffixes into \((1 \to 3 \to 4)\) and \((1 \to 2 \to 4)\).







Drill 1.2 — The Saturated-Edge Cut Illusion
After running Dinic’s algorithm to completion on a directed network \(G = (V, E, c, s, t)\), a contestant wants to list all edges \(e = (u \to v)\) that belong to at least one minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut (可行割边). They output every original edge \(e = (u \to v)\) that is saturated (\(f^*(e) = c(e)\), i.e., \(c_{f^*}(u \to v) = 0\)).
Why is saturation insufficient, what is the smallest counterexample, and what exact \(O(V + E)\) test on \(G_{f^*}\) is required?






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.2






Failure Mode: FM-02 (The Saturated \(\implies\) Cut Edge Fallacy, Chapter 2).
Counterexample: Consider \(s \xrightarrow{1} u \xrightarrow{1} v \xrightarrow{1} t\) with an alternate parallel bypass \(u \xrightarrow{1} w \xrightarrow{1} v\).

The maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow is \(1\). Suppose Dinic routes \(1\) unit along \(s \to u \to v \to t\).
Then edge \((u \to v)\) is saturated (\(f^*(u, v) = 1 = c(u, v)\)), yet the total capacity between \(u\) and \(v\) is \(2\) while the minimum cut of the network is \(1\) (either \((s \to u)\) or \((v \to t)\)).
In \(G_{f^*}\), the forward bypass \(u \xrightarrow{1} w \xrightarrow{1} v\) and the backward arc \(v \xrightarrow{1} u\) form a directed residual cycle \(u \to w \to v \to u\), so \(u\) and \(v\) belong to the same Strongly Connected Component (\(\operatorname{scc}(u) = \operatorname{scc}(v)\)) and can never be separated by any minimum cut!

Exact Residual SCC Criterion ([AHOI2009] 最小割 Theorem, Ch 02.2): Run Tarjan’s SCC algorithm on \(G_{f^*}\). A saturated edge \(e = (u \to v)\) belongs to at least one minimum cut iff \(\operatorname{scc}(u) \neq \operatorname{scc}(v)\), and belongs to every minimum cut iff \(\operatorname{scc}(u) = \operatorname{scc}(s) \land \operatorname{scc}(v) = \operatorname{scc}(t)\).







Drill 1.3 — The Unsplit Middle Bottleneck & Undirected Bridge Trap
In a 3-stage matching problem (Luogu P1402 酒店之王), each guest \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) must be assigned one compatible room \(r \in \{1, \dots, P\}\) and one compatible dish \(d \in \{1, \dots, Q\}\). A contestant wires \(S \xrightarrow{1} \text{Room}_r \xrightarrow{1} \text{Guest}_i \xrightarrow{1} \text{Dish}_d \xrightarrow{1} T\) using a single vertex for \(\text{Guest}_i\). Later, on an undirected vertex-cut problem, they split each vertex \(v\) into \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\), and for each undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) they add an undirected capacity-\(\infty\) edge between \(u_{\text{out}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}}\) (i.e., both \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}\)).
What goes wrong in both constructions?






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.3






Failure Mode: FM-03 (Unsplit Internal Vertex Capacities & Undirected Bridge Short-Circuiting, Chapter 3).
Bug 1 (Unsplit Guest Vertex): If Guest \(i\) likes two available rooms \(r_1, r_2\) and two available dishes \(d_1, d_2\), a single vertex \(\text{Guest}_i\) can absorb \(2\) units of flow from \(r_1, r_2\) and emit \(2\) units to \(d_1, d_2\), counting one guest as two satisfied people! Every middle bottleneck entity must be split into \(\text{Guest}_{i,\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} \text{Guest}_{i,\text{out}}\).
Bug 2 (Reversed \(\infty\)-Arc on Split Vertices): Adding \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}\) allows flow arriving at \(v_{\text{in}}\) (say from some \(w_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}\)) to immediately exit through \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}\) without ever crossing the internal bottleneck arc \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\)! An undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) between vertex-split nodes must always be compiled as two separately directed \(\infty\)-bridges: \[u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}} \quad \text{and} \quad v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}.\]







Drill 1.4 — The Time-Expanded Infinite Loop & Missing Holdover Bug
In a discrete-time evacuation problem (Luogu P2754 家园), \(K\) astronauts at station \(0\) must reach the Moon (\(N+1\)) using periodic shuttles. A solver loops \(T = 1, 2, 3, \dots\), adding shuttle transit arcs \((u_{t-1}, T-1) \xrightarrow{H_i} (u_t, T)\) and running Dinic from scratch at each step \(T\) until \(\text{MaxFlow} \ge K\). However, they do not add arcs \((v, T-1) \to (v, T)\) for stations \(v\), and their code gets Time Limit Exceeded on an instance where the Moon is unreachable.
Identify all three defects in this time-expanded compilation.






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.4






Failure Mode: FM-04 (Time-Expanded Horizon Traps, Chapter 3).
Three Required Fixes:

Missing Station Holdover Arcs: Without \((v, T-1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, T)\), astronauts who disembark at station \(v\) at time \(T-1\) vanish unless another shuttle leaves \(v\) at the exact same instant! Holdover arcs allow inventory/passengers to wait at station \(v\) across time steps.
Unchecked Unreachability (Infinite Loop): Before starting the incremental time loop \(T = 1, 2, \dots\), you must verify via DSU or BFS on the static union of shuttle routes whether \(0 \leadsto N+1\) is reachable at all.
Rebuilding Dinic from Scratch: Because adding layer \(T\) only appends new vertices and forward arcs to an existing network, you should keep the persistent residual network \(G_{f_{T-1}}\) and call dinic(S, T_sink) incrementally to augment only the newly unlocked flow!








Drill 1.5 — The Feedback-Arc Leakage Bug in Bounded \(s\)-\(t\) Max-Flow
To solve a Maximum \(s\)-\(t\) Flow problem with edge lower bounds \(l(e) \le f(e) \le u(e)\), a contestant adds the feedback arc \(e_{\text{fb}} = (t \to s, [0, \infty))\), computes \(M(v) = \text{in}_l(v) - \text{out}_l(v)\), and runs Phase 1 dinic(S*, T*). After verifying that Phase 1 saturates \(\Sigma^+\), they read off \(f_0 = \tilde{f}(t \to s)\) and immediately call Phase 2 dinic(s, t) on the residual network without modifying \(e_{\text{fb}}\). Their Phase 2 call returns \(\infty\). Why?






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.5






Failure Mode: FM-05 (Feedback-Arc Leakage & Slack Offset Omission, Chapter 4).
Why Phase 2 Returns \(\infty\): In the residual network after Phase 1, the feedback arc \(t \to s\) has residual capacity \(\infty - f_0 = \infty\), and its reverse companion arc \(s \to t\) has residual capacity \(f_0\)! Worse, if any \(s \leadsto t\) path exists, or directly along the reverse residual arc \(s \xrightarrow{f_0} t\), Phase 2 interacts with the artificial feedback edge. Specifically, if you leave the reverse residual arc \(s \to t\) active (or if you run dinic(t, s) for minimum flow while \(t \xrightarrow{\infty} s\) is still open), flow circulates around the artificial feedback loop!
Exact Protocol (Ch 04.2): After recording \(f_0 = \tilde{f}(t \to s) = \text{cap}[e_{\text{fb}} \oplus 1]\), you must zero out both half-edges of the feedback arc (cap[e_fb] = cap[e_fb ^ 1] = 0) before calling Phase 2 dinic(s, t) (for \(F_{\max} = f_0 + \Delta^+\)) or dinic(t, s) (for \(F_{\min} = f_0 - \Delta^-\)). Finally, reconstruct each edge’s physical flow as \(f(e) = l(e) + \tilde{f}(e)\).







Drill 1.6 — The Mixed-Graph Eulerian Orientation Trap
You are given a connected mixed graph \(G = (V, E_{\text{dir}} \sqcup E_{\text{undir}})\) (POJ 1637 Sightseeing Tour) and asked whether every undirected edge can be oriented so the resulting directed graph has an Eulerian circuit (\(\text{in}(v) = \text{out}(v)\) for all \(v \in V\)). A solver arbitrarily orients each undirected edge as \(u \to v\), computes \(D(v) = \text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)\), wires \(S \xrightarrow{D(v)} v\) (for \(D(v) > 0\)) and \(v \xrightarrow{-D(v)} T\) (for \(D(v) < 0\)), and puts capacity \(1\) on each reversible edge \(u \to v\).
Why does this fail even on a single 2-vertex, 2-edge graph?






TipAnswer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.6






Failure Mode: FM-06 (Mixed Eulerian Parity Omission & Unit-vs-Two Delta Bug, Chapter 4).
Two Compounding Bugs:

Each Reversal Changes \(\text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)\) by \(2\), Not \(1\): When an initially oriented edge \(u \to v\) is reversed to \(v \to u\), \(\text{out}(u)\) decreases by \(1\) and \(\text{in}(u)\) increases by \(1\), so \(D(u) = \text{in}(u) - \text{out}(u)\) changes by \(+2\) (and \(D(v)\) changes by \(-2\)).
Mandatory Parity Pre-Check: Because every reversal changes \(D(v)\) by \(\pm 2\), a valid orientation is immediately impossible if any vertex \(v \in V\) has \(D(v) \not\equiv 0 \pmod 2\) (equivalently, if the total degree \(\deg(v)\) is odd)!

Exact Compilation (Ch 04.3): First check that \(D(v) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\) for all \(v \in V\). Then divide by \(2\): wire \(S \xrightarrow{-D(v)/2} v\) when \(D(v) < 0\) (excess out-degree) and \(v \xrightarrow{D(v)/2} T\) when \(D(v) > 0\) (excess in-degree), with unit capacity \(1\) on each reversible undirected arc \(u \to v\), and check if \(\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) = \sum_{D(v) > 0} D(v)/2\).

title: Checkpoint I — Foundations, Residual Anatomy, Vertex Splitting, and Bounded Circulations
text:
2. Blind Checkpoint Problems (#193–#200)
The following eight problems span the full toolkit of Part I (Ch 01–Ch 04). Remember: read the statement, inspect the constraints, and write down your Step 1 (Diagnostic Signal) and Step 2 (Algebraic Model) before opening Hint 1.


Problem #193 — CSES 1711: Distinct Routes ([EN])

Judge URL: https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1711
Constraints: \(2 \le N \le 500\) rooms, \(1 \le M \le 1000\) one-way teleporters, Time Limit \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Untagged Problem Statement: A game consists of \(N\) rooms and \(M\) one-way teleporters between rooms. You start in room \(1\) and must reach room \(N\) each day. Every teleporter \(e = (u \to v)\) can be used at most once across the entire game. Determine the maximum number of days \(K\) you can play, and explicitly output the room sequence of each of the \(K\) routes.







NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal)






Target Chapter: Chapter 1 (§1.4 Flow Decomposition Theorem & Menger’s Edge-Disjoint Connectivity).
Diagnostic Clue: “Each directed teleporter used at most once” + “maximize the number of \(1 \leadsto N\) routes and print them.” As we saw in Drill 1.1 (FM-01), greedily extracting shortest paths fails because an early path can straddle a bridge edge and block two disjoint paths. You must first compute the global maximum unit flow \(f^*\), and only after all residual cancellations have settled, decompose \(f^*\) into \(K = |f^*|\) directed \(1 \leadsto N\) paths.










NoteHint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model





For each teleporter \(e = (u \to v) \in E\), introduce a binary flow variable \(f(e) \in \{0, 1\}\). Enforce Kirchhoff nodal conservation at every interior room:
\[\sum_{e \in \delta^+(v)} f(e) - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} f(e) = 0 \qquad \forall v \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}\]
and maximize \(|f| = \sum_{e \in \delta^+(1)} f(e) - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(1)} f(e)\). By the Flow Decomposition Theorem (Ch 01.4), any integral \(1\)-\(N\) flow \(f^*\) with \(f^*(e) \in \{0, 1\}\) is the edge-disjoint sum of \(K = |f^*|\) directed \(1 \leadsto N\) paths and zero or more directed cycles.









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #193 (CSES 1711)






Step 1 & Step 2: Recognition & Algebraic Formulation
Each teleporter \(e = (u \to v)\) has capacity \(c(e) = 1\). In any converged integral maximum flow \(f^*\), an original forward teleporter \(e = (u \to v)\) is active (\(f^*(e) = 1\)) if and only if its forward residual capacity is \(c_{f^*}(u \to v) = 0\) (equivalently, its companion backward arc \(v \to u\) has residual capacity \(1\)).


Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation & Path Extraction Contract

Network Construction: Create vertices \(1, \dots, N\). For each input teleporter \((u, v)\), add a directed arc \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\) (keeping a flag or checking edge_idx % 2 == 0 to distinguish original forward arcs from synthetic reverse residual arcs).
Blocking-Flow Solve: Run K = dinic(1, N). By Dinic’s unit-capacity complexity theorem (Ch 01.3), this takes \(O(M \min(N^{2/3}, M^{1/2})) \le 3 \cdot 10^4\) operations.
Constructive Path Peeling (Ch 01.4):

Consider the subgraph \(E_{\text{active}} = \{e = (u \to v) \in E : f^*(e) = 1\}\). At every interior vertex \(v \notin \{1, N\}\), \(\deg^+_{\text{active}}(v) = \deg^-_{\text{active}}(v)\), while \(\deg^+_{\text{active}}(1) - \deg^-_{\text{active}}(1) = K\).
Repeat \(K\) times: start at \(u = 1\), and greedily follow any active original forward arc \(e = (u \to v)\) with \(f^*(e) = 1\), immediately setting \(f^*(e) \gets 0\) (marking it consumed) until reaching \(N\).
Subtlety (What if \(E_{\text{active}}\) contains a directed cycle?): In a unit network solved by Dinic from \(f \equiv 0\), augmenting along shortest level-graph paths rarely creates isolated flow cycles, but if a vertex \(v\) on the current walk has both an \(s \leadsto t\) path and a directed cycle through \(v\), a naive walk that enters the cycle simply loops back to \(v\) and then continues to \(N\)! To print strictly simple paths (or avoid any dead-end if a cycle touches \(1\)), either run a standard Eulerian/DFS post-order walk that splices out cycles, or walk \(1 \leadsto N\) via DFS and only record the simple stack path when \(N\) is reached.




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (\(N = 4, M = 5\)): Edges \(e_1=(1\to 2), e_2=(2\to 3), e_3=(3\to 4), e_4=(1\to 3), e_5=(2\to 4)\).

Augmentation 1 pushes \(1\) unit along \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4\). Now \(c_f(2\to 3)=0\) and reverse arc \(c_f(3\to 2)=1\).
Augmentation 2 pushes \(1\) unit along \(1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 4\), traversing the reverse arc \(3 \to 2\).
After Dinic terminates (\(K = 2\)), check original forward arcs with \(c_{f^*}(e) = 0\): they are \(e_1(1\to 2), e_3(3\to 4), e_4(1\to 3), e_5(2\to 4)\)—notice \(e_2(2\to 3)\) now has \(c_{f^*}(2\to 3) = 1\) (\(f^*(2\to 3) = 0\))!
Peeling \(2\) paths from \(E_{\text{active}}\) yields 1 -> 2 -> 4 (length 3) and 1 -> 3 -> 4 (length 3).

Broken-Gadget Warning: When scanning the adjacency list during path reconstruction, never allow the walk to traverse odd-indexed reverse residual arcs! A reverse residual arc \(3 \to 2\) with \(c_{f^*}(3\to 2) = 0\) just means the forward arc \(2 \to 3\) is unused (\(f^*(2\to 3) = 0\)). Only original forward arcs (id % 2 == 0 with cap[id] == 0) represent physical teleporters used in the solution.
Complexity: Time \(O(M\sqrt{N} + K \cdot N)\), Space \(O(N + M)\).








Problem #194 — Luogu P1345: [USACO 5.4] Telecowmunication (奶牛的电信, [EN]/[ZH])

Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P1345
Constraints: \(2 \le N \le 100\) computers, \(1 \le M \le 600\) bidirectional cables, two distinct hub computers \(c_1, c_2 \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), Time Limit \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Untagged Problem Statement: Farmer John’s \(N\) computers are connected by \(M\) bidirectional cables so that data can travel between any two computers through a sequence of intermediate computers. An accident may destroy some computers (together with all cables attached to them), but cables themselves never fail on their own, and the two endpoint computers \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) can never be destroyed. Find the minimum number of computers that must be destroyed so that \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) can no longer communicate.







NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal)






Target Chapter: Chapter 3 (§3.1 Internal Vertex Capacity Splitting \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c(v)} v_{\text{out}}\) & Vertex-Disjoint Menger Duality).
Diagnostic Clue: “Cables never fail; computers fail.” We are looking for a Minimum \(c_1\)-\(c_2\) Vertex Cut on an undirected graph. Standard edge-cut capacities on the original graph fail because destroying one degree-\(d\) computer simultaneously breaks all \(\binom{d}{2}\) pairs of paths passing through it at a single unit cost of \(1\).










NoteHint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model





By Menger’s Vertex-Connectivity Theorem (Ch 03.1), the minimum number of intermediate vertices whose removal disconnects \(c_1\) from \(c_2\) equals the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths between \(c_1\) and \(c_2\). Split every computer \(v \in V\) into an entry port \(v_{\text{in}}\) and an exit port \(v_{\text{out}}\) with cut indicators \(x_{v,\text{in}}, x_{v,\text{out}} \in \{0, 1\}\): - Destroying computer \(v \notin \{c_1, c_2\}\) corresponds to placing \(v_{\text{in}} \in S\) (\(x_{v,\text{in}} = 1\)) and \(v_{\text{out}} \in T\) (\(x_{v,\text{out}} = 0\)) at cost \(1\). - An invulnerable bidirectional cable \(\{u, v\}\) forbids both \((u_{\text{out}} \in S \land v_{\text{in}} \in T)\) and \((v_{\text{out}} \in S \land u_{\text{in}} \in T)\) at cost \(\infty\).









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #194 (Luogu P1345)






Step 1 & Step 2: Recognition & Algebraic Formulation
Let each vertex \(v \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) be mapped to \(v_{\text{in}} = v\) and \(v_{\text{out}} = v + N\) in a \(2N\)-vertex directed network. In the primal flow view, any path visiting \(v\) must enter \(v_{\text{in}}\), traverse the internal bridge \(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\), and leave from \(v_{\text{out}}\). Setting the capacity of \(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\) to \(1\) limits vertex \(v\) to at most \(1\) unit of throughput.


Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Internal Vertex Arcs:

For each \(v \in \{1, \dots, N\} \setminus \{c_1, c_2\}\), add a directed arc \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\).
For \(v \in \{c_1, c_2\}\), either add \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{out}}\) or directly set the flow source to \(S = (c_1)_{\text{out}}\) and the flow sink to \(T = (c_2)_{\text{in}}\).

Bidirectional Cable Arcs:

For each undirected cable \(\{u, v\}\), add two separate directed \(\infty\)-arcs: \[u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}} \quad \text{and} \quad v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}.\]

Solve: Output dinic(c1 + N, c2). Since every internal vertex has unit capacity (Ch 01.3 Unit-Vertex Regime), Dinic runs in \(O(M \sqrt{N})\) time.



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (\(N = 4\), \(c_1 = 1, c_2 = 4\), cables \(\{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}, \{2,4\}, \{3,4\}\)):

Vertices \(2\) and \(3\) have internal arcs \(2_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 2_{\text{out}}\) and \(3_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 3_{\text{out}}\).
Path 1 routes \(1_{\text{out}} \to 2_{\text{in}} \to 2_{\text{out}} \to 4_{\text{in}}\) (saturating \(2_{\text{in}} \to 2_{\text{out}}\)).
Path 2 routes \(1_{\text{out}} \to 3_{\text{in}} \to 3_{\text{out}} \to 4_{\text{in}}\) (saturating \(3_{\text{in}} \to 3_{\text{out}}\)).
Total flow \(= 2\), matching the minimum vertex cut \(\{2, 3\}\).

Broken-Gadget Warning (FM-03): Never compile the undirected cable \(\{u, v\}\) by giving the reverse residual arc of \(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}\) an initial capacity of \(\infty\)! The reverse residual arc of \(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}\) goes from \(v_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}\); if it starts with positive capacity, flow entering \(v_{\text{in}}\) from \(1_{\text{out}}\) can immediately escape to \(u_{\text{out}}\) without ever passing through \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\)! You must create two distinct directed edges: \((u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}, \text{cap}=\infty, \text{rev\_cap}=0)\) and \((v_{\text{out}} \to u_{\text{in}}, \text{cap}=\infty, \text{rev\_cap}=0)\).
Complexity: Time \(O(M\sqrt{N})\), Space \(O(N + M)\).








Problem #195 — Luogu P2763: 试题库问题 (网络流 24 题 #07, [ZH])

Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2763
Constraints: \(2 \le K \le 20\) categories, \(K \le N \le 1000\) problems in the bank, total required problems \(M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j \le N\), Time Limit \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Untagged Problem Statement: An exam paper must be assembled from a test bank of \(N\) problems spanning \(K\) categories. Category \(j \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) requires exactly \(c_j\) problems, so the exam contains \(M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j\) problems in total. Each problem \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) is tagged with a subset of categories \(S_i \subseteq \{1, \dots, K\}\) to which it belongs. A problem may be included on the exam at most once, and if included, it can count toward only one of the categories in \(S_i\). Determine whether a valid exam paper can be assembled; if so, output the exact list of problem IDs assigned to each category \(j = 1, \dots, K\), or print No Solution! otherwise.







NoteHint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal)






Target Chapter: Chapter 1 (§1.1 Supply-Demand Quota Conservation) & Chapter 3 (§3.3 Rank-2 Binary Constraint Factorization).
Diagnostic Clue: Every individual selection decision (“assign problem \(i\) to category \(j \in S_i\)”) simultaneously consumes \(1\) unit from problem \(i\)’s usage limit (\(\le 1\)) and \(1\) unit from category \(j\)’s quota (\(= c_j\)). Whenever each decision touches at most two constraint families (one Problem and one Category), the constraint matrix is a bipartite incidence matrix!










NoteHint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model





Introduce binary decision variables \(f_{i, j} \in \{0, 1\}\) for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and \(j \in S_i\):
\[\sum_{j \in S_i} f_{i, j} \le 1 \quad (\forall i \in \{1, \dots, N\}), \qquad \sum_{i : j \in S_i} f_{i, j} = c_j \quad (\forall j \in \{1, \dots, K\}).\]
Relaxing \(\sum_{i : j \in S_i} f_{i, j} = c_j\) to \(\le c_j\) and maximizing \(\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j \in S_i} f_{i, j}\) achieves value \(M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j\) if and only if all \(K\) category quotas are simultaneously met with equality.









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #195 (Luogu P2763)






Step 1 & Step 2: Recognition & Algebraic Formulation
Why does greedy assignment fail? If Problem 1 has tags \(\{A, B\}\), Problem 2 has tag \(\{A\}\), and Categories \(A, B\) each need \(1\) problem, greedily assigning Problem 1 to Category \(A\) leaves Category \(B\) starved; residual cancellation is required to reroute Problem 1 to \(B\) and Problem 2 to \(A\).


Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation & Assignment Recovery

Vertices: Source \(S = 0\), Problem nodes \(\text{Prob}_i = i\) (\(i = 1, \dots, N\)), Category nodes \(\text{Cat}_j = N + j\) (\(j = 1, \dots, K\)), and Sink \(T = N + K + 1\).
Directed Arcs:

Per-Problem Single-Use Cap: \(S \xrightarrow{1} \text{Prob}_i\) for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).
Tag Compatibility Bridges: \(\text{Prob}_i \xrightarrow{1} \text{Cat}_j\) for each \(j \in S_i\).
Category Quotas: \(\text{Cat}_j \xrightarrow{c_j} T\) for each \(j \in \{1, \dots, K\}\).

Feasibility Check & Residual Extraction:

Compute \(F^* = \text{dinic}(S, T)\).
If \(F^* < M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j\), output No Solution!.
Otherwise, for each category \(j = 1, \dots, K\), iterate over all incident arcs connecting \(\text{Cat}_j\) to \(\text{Prob}_i\): whenever the forward arc \(\text{Prob}_i \to \text{Cat}_j\) is saturated (cap == 0, i.e., its companion reverse arc \(\text{Cat}_j \to \text{Prob}_i\) has residual capacity \(1\)), append \(i\) to category \(j\)’s output list.




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit

Toy Trace (\(N = 3, K = 2, c_1 = 1, c_2 = 1\), \(S_1 = \{1, 2\}, S_2 = \{1\}, S_3 = \emptyset\)):

Path 1 pushes \(S \to \text{Prob}_1 \to \text{Cat}_1 \to T\).
Path 2 pushes \(S \to \text{Prob}_2 \to \text{Cat}_1 \xrightarrow{\text{rev}} \text{Prob}_1 \to \text{Cat}_2 \to T\), using the reverse residual arc \(\text{Cat}_1 \to \text{Prob}_1\) to reassign \(\text{Prob}_1\) from Category 1 to Category 2!
Final saturated bridges: \(\text{Prob}_2 \to \text{Cat}_1\) and \(\text{Prob}_1 \to \text{Cat}_2\).

Broken-Gadget Warning: Never omit the capacity-\(1\) bound on \(S \to \text{Prob}_i\) (or set it to \(|S_i|\))! If \(S \to \text{Prob}_i\) had capacity \(> 1\), a single multi-tagged problem \(i\) would be duplicated across several categories on the same exam paper.
Complexity: Since every \(\text{Prob}_i\) has in-degree \(1\) of capacity \(1\), the network is a unit-vertex network (Ch 01.3), so Dinic runs in \(O(NK \sqrt{N + K})\) time and \(O(NK)\) space.

Target Chapter: Chapter 3 (§3.1 Vertex Splitting + §3.3 Row/Column Hub Virtualization).
Diagnostic Clue: If 'S' and 'T' share the same row (\(r_S = r_T\)) or the same column (\(c_S = c_T\)), the frog jumps directly in \(1\) step and the answer is -1. Otherwise, we want a Minimum Vertex Cut of 'o' leaves. However, connecting every pair of leaves in the same row or column directly creates \(O(HW(H + W)) \approx 2 \cdot 10^6\) edges on \(2HW \approx 2 \cdot 10^4\) split vertices! NoteHint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model

TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #196 (ARC 074 D / F)






Step 1 & Step 2: From \(O(HW(H+W))\) Clique Edges to a \(200\)-Vertex Bipartite Hub Cut
Let us see how both the Explicit Vertex-Split View (Ch 03.1) and the Contracted Row-Column Hub View (Ch 03.3) produce the exact same network: - View A (Explicit Leaf Splitting): Create row hubs \(R_1, \dots, R_H\) and column hubs \(C_1, \dots, C_W\). Split each leaf 'o' at \((r, c)\) into \(\ell_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} \ell_{\text{out}}\), and wire \(\infty\)-edges \(R_r \xrightarrow{\infty} \ell_{\text{in}}, C_c \xrightarrow{\infty} \ell_{\text{in}}\) and \(\ell_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} R_r, \ell_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} C_c\). - View B (Algebraic Contraction to Row/Column Hubs): Notice that in View A, \(\ell_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} \ell_{\text{out}}\) is simply a unit-capacity switch between \(R_r\) and \(C_c\)! Because any \(s\)-\(t\) cut places \((R_r, C_c)\) in one of the four states \((S, S), (T, T), (S, T), (T, S)\), replacing the 2-node gadget \((\ell_{\text{in}}, \ell_{\text{out}})\) with a single undirected unit-capacity edge \(R_r \xleftrightarrow{1} C_c\) (i.e., \(R_r \xrightarrow{1} C_c\) and \(C_c \xrightarrow{1} R_r\)) assigns cut cost \(0\) when \(x_{R_r} = x_{C_c}\) and cut cost \(1\) when \(x_{R_r} \neq x_{C_c}\)! This shrinks the entire graph from \(2HW + H + W \approx 20{,}200\) vertices down to \(H + W + 2 \le 202\) vertices!


Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Direct-Jump Guard: Locate 'S' at \((r_S, c_S)\) and 'T' at \((r_T, c_T)\). If \(r_S == r_T\) or \(c_S == c_T\), output -1 and terminate.

Wire \(R_{r_T} \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{snk}}\) and \(C_{c_T} \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{snk}}\).
For every intermediate leaf 'o' at \((r, c)\), add two directed unit-capacity arcs: \[R_r \xrightarrow{1} C_c \quad \text{and} \quad C_c \xrightarrow{1} R_r.\]

. o .
. o T

Problem #197 — ZOJ 2587: Unique Attack [EN]

Judge & Bounds: ZOJ 2587 · \(N \le 800\) vertices, \(M \le 10^4\) undirected communication links with positive integer disruption costs \(w_e \ge 1\), source terminal \(A\), sink terminal \(B\).
Untagged Statement: A saboteur wants to disconnect terminal \(A\) from terminal \(B\) in an undirected network by severing a subset of links of minimum total disruption cost. Determine whether the set of links severed in a minimum-cost disconnection is strictly unique — that is, whether there exists only one subset of edges whose removal disconnects \(A\) from \(B\) at the minimum possible total cost. Output "UNIQUE" or "AMBIGUOUS".







NoteHint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#197)






Target Chapter & Archetype: Ch 02 — Residual Graph Anatomy, Minimum-Cut Structure & Dynamic Edge Updates (§2.1 Extremal Minimum Cuts \(S_{\min}\) vs. \(S_{\max}\) and the Submodular Cut Lattice).
Diagnostic Signal: Asking whether the minimum \(A\)-\(B\) cut is unique (\(N \le 800, M \le 10^4\)) cannot be answered by checking whether each individual cut edge is saturated, nor by re-running Dinic \(M\) times. You must inspect the distributive lattice of all minimum cuts inside the final residual graph \(G_{f^*}\) using a single forward reachability pass from \(A\) and a single reverse reachability pass from \(B\).










NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Lattice Representation (#197)






Replace each undirected link \(\{u, v\}\) of cost \(w_e > 0\) with two directed arcs \(u \to v\) and \(v \to u\) of capacity \(w_e\) (or initialize a single antiparallel residual pair with cap[e] = cap[e^1] = w_e). Since \(w_e > 0\), every minimum edge cut is induced by a vertex partition \((S, V \setminus S)\) with \(A \in S, B \notin S\).
By the submodularity of the cut capacity function \(C(S) + C(S') \ge C(S \cup S') + C(S \cap S')\), the family of all minimum \(A\)-\(B\) cuts forms a distributive lattice with a unique source-minimal cut set \[S_{\min} = \{v \in V : A \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} v\}\] and a unique source-maximal cut set \[S_{\max} = V \setminus T_{\min}, \quad \text{where } T_{\min} = \{v \in V : v \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} B\}.\]
Uniqueness Criterion: Every minimum cut \(S\) satisfies \(S_{\min} \subseteq S \subseteq S_{\max}\). Therefore, the minimum cut is unique if and only if \(S_{\min} = S_{\max} = V \setminus T_{\min}\), which is equivalent to: \[S_{\min} \cup T_{\min} = V \iff |S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = N\] (since \(S_{\min} \cap T_{\min} = \emptyset\) at maximum flow).










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — ZOJ 2587 (#197)






Step 1–3: Residual Lattice Compilation & Algorithm

Graph Construction: For each undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) with weight \(w_e\), insert directed arc \(u \to v\) with capacity \(w_e\) and reverse arc \(v \to u\) with initial residual capacity \(w_e\). Run Dinic from \(A\) to \(B\) to reach a maximum flow \(f^*\).
Forward Reachability (\(S_{\min}\)): Run a BFS/DFS from \(A\) in \(G_{f^*}\), traversing directed arcs \(x \to y\) only when their remaining residual capacity satisfies \(c_{f^*}(x, y) > 0\). Mark all visited vertices as belonging to \(S_{\min}\).
Reverse Reachability (\(T_{\min}\)): Run a reverse BFS/DFS starting from \(B\) to find all vertices \(x\) that can reach \(B\) via a path of positive residual capacity in \(G_{f^*}\). When stepping backward from a visited vertex \(y\) along an adjacency list edge to neighbor \(x\), you must check that the arc entering \(y\) from \(x\) has positive residual capacity: \[c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0 \quad (\text{i.e., } \texttt{edges[id \^{} 1].cap > 0}\text{ when traversing }\texttt{id: } y \to x).\]
Decision: Since \(f^*\) is maximum, \(S_{\min} \cap T_{\min} = \emptyset\). If \(|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = N\), every vertex belongs to either \(S_{\min}\) or \(T_{\min}\), so \(S_{\min} = V \setminus T_{\min} = S_{\max}\) and the cut is "UNIQUE". Otherwise, any vertex \(v \notin S_{\min} \cup T_{\min}\) lies in an intermediate zero-net-cost SCC of \(G_{f^*}\), yielding at least two distinct minimum cuts (\(S_{\min}\) and \(S_{\max}\)), so output "AMBIGUOUS". Total post-processing time: \(\mathcal{O}(N + M)\).



Step 4: Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (FM-02)

Toy Trace: Let \(A = 1, B = 4\) with undirected path \(1 - 2 - 3 - 4\) where \(w_{12} = 5, w_{23} = 7, w_{34} = 5\).

Max flow is \(5\). In \(G_{f^*}\), arcs \(1 \to 2\) and \(3 \to 4\) are saturated (\(c_{f^*}(1, 2) = 0, c_{f^*}(3, 4) = 0\)), while \(c_{f^*}(2, 3) = 7 - 5 = 2 > 0\) and \(c_{f^*}(3, 2) = 7 + 5 = 12 > 0\).
Forward from \(A=1\): \(S_{\min} = \{1\}\) (representing cut \(\{1\} \mid \{2, 3, 4\}\), severing edge \((1, 2)\)).
Backward from \(B=4\): \(T_{\min} = \{4\}\) (representing \(S_{\max} = V \setminus T_{\min} = \{1, 2, 3\}\), severing edge \((3, 4)\)).
Since \(|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = 1 + 1 = 2 < 4\), vertices \(\{2, 3\}\) lie outside \(S_{\min} \cup T_{\min}\), immediately certifying "AMBIGUOUS".

Broken Gadget Counterexample 1 (FM-02 — Reverse BFS Residual Direction Bug): Suppose during the reverse BFS from \(B\), you check edges[id].cap > 0 (\(c_{f^*}(y \to x) > 0\)) instead of edges[id ^ 1].cap > 0 (\(c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0\)). In the trace above, when \(y = 4\), the backward residual arc \(4 \to 3\) has capacity \(c_{f^*}(4 \to 3) = 5 + 5 = 10 > 0\)! Checking \(c_{f^*}(4 \to 3) > 0\) would falsely pull vertices \(3\) and \(2\) into \(T_{\min}\), reporting \(|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| > 2\) and hallucinating uniqueness.
Broken Gadget Counterexample 2 (Counting Saturated Edges): Testing whether the number of saturated edges equals \(1\) fails whenever the unique minimum cut consists of two parallel/series-parallel edges (e.g., \(A=1, B=2\) connected by two edges of weight \(3\) each: unique cut severs both edges, yet \(2\) edges are saturated). Conversely, an extra saturated edge with both endpoints inside \(S_{\min}\) does not create cut ambiguity.








Problem #198 — AtCoder ABC 285 G: Tatami [JA]

Untagged Statement: You want to tile an \(H \times W\) grid with \(1 \times 1\) monominoes (tatami of size \(1\)) and \(1 \times 2\) / \(2 \times 1\) dominoes (tatami of size \(2\)) so that every cell is covered by exactly one tile, and:

Every cell labeled '2' is covered by a \(1 \times 2\) or \(2 \times 1\) domino;

NoteHint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#198)






Target Chapter & Archetype: Ch 04 — Flows with Lower Bounds, Circulations & Matrix Rounding (§4.1 Feasible \(s\)-\(t\) Circulation with Lower Bounds 上下界可行流 on a Chessboard Bipartite Graph, also achievable via Ch 02 §2.1 compulsory vertex matching or Ch 04 parity demand transformation).

For each adjacent pair of non-'1' cells \((u, v) \in L \times R\), introduce a binary variable \(x_{uv} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicating whether a domino covers \(\{u, v\}\).

For \(u \in L\): arc \(S \to u\) has capacity interval \([1, 1]\) if \(u = \text{'2'}\), or \([0, 1]\) if \(u = \text{'?'}\).
For \(v \in R\): arc \(v \to T\) has capacity interval \([1, 1]\) if \(v = \text{'2'}\), or \([0, 1]\) if \(v = \text{'?'}\).
For adjacent non-'1' cells \((u, v) \in L \times R\): arc \(u \to v\) has capacity interval \([0, 1]\).
Add feedback arc \(T \xrightarrow{[0, \infty)} S\) to form a sourceless lower-bound circulation network!











TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — AtCoder ABC 285 G (#198)






Step 1–3: Lower-Bound Circulation Compilation

Pre-filtering & Bipartition: Delete all '1' cells. Partition remaining cells into \(L\) (\((r+c)\) even) and \(R\) (\((r+c)\) odd). Create source \(S\), sink \(T\), super-source \(S^*\), and super-sink \(T^*\).
Lower-Bound Arc Table & Net Balances \(M(w) = \text{in}_{\text{low}}(w) - \text{out}_{\text{low}}(w)\):

Mandatory '2' cell \(u \in L\): Arc \(S \xrightarrow{[1, 1]} u\) has \(l = u_{\text{cap}} = 1\), so residual capacity \(u_{\text{cap}} - l = 0\), \(M(S) \mathrel{-}= 1\), and \(M(u) \mathrel{+}= 1\) (giving arc \(S^* \to u\) of capacity \(1\)).
Optional '?' cell \(u \in L\): Arc \(S \xrightarrow{[0, 1]} u\) has \(l = 0, u_{\text{cap}} = 1\), so add arc \(S \to u\) of capacity \(1\) (\(M\) unchanged).
Mandatory '2' cell \(v \in R\): Arc \(v \xrightarrow{[1, 1]} T\) has \(l = u_{\text{cap}} = 1\), so residual capacity \(0\), \(M(v) \mathrel{-}= 1\) (giving arc \(v \to T^*\) of capacity \(1\)), and \(M(T) \mathrel{+}= 1\).
Optional '?' cell \(v \in R\): Arc \(v \xrightarrow{[0, 1]} T\) has \(l = 0, u_{\text{cap}} = 1\), so add arc \(v \to T\) of capacity \(1\).
Grid adjacency \((u, v) \in L \times R\): Add arc \(u \to v\) of capacity \(1\).
Feedback arc: Add \(T \to S\) of capacity \(\infty\).
Balances at \(S\) and \(T\): If there are \(k_L\) cells of type '2' in \(L\) and \(k_R\) cells of type '2' in \(R\), then \(M(S) = -k_L\) (so add \(S \to T^*\) of capacity \(k_L\)) and \(M(T) = +k_R\) (so add \(S^* \to T\) of capacity \(k_R\)).

Feasibility Check & Complexity:

Total positive balance is \(\sum_{w : M(w) > 0} M(w) = k_L + k_R = \#(\text{'2'})\).
Run Dinic from \(S^*\) to \(T^*\). Output "Yes" if and only if \(\text{MaxFlow}(S^*, T^*) = k_L + k_R\).
Since the network is a unit-capacity bipartite-like DAG with \(\mathcal{O}(HW)\) vertices and edges, Dinic runs in \(\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{HW} \cdot HW) \approx 2.7 \cdot 10^7\) operations, well within \(2.0\text{ s}\).

\(S^*\) supplies \(1\) unit to \(c_1\) and \(1\) unit to \(c_3\) (total demand \(2\)).
However, both \(c_1\) and \(c_3\) only have edges to \(c_2 \in R\), and \(c_2\) is an optional '?' cell with only a single unit-capacity arc \(c_2 \to T \to S \to T^*\).

Diagnostic Signal: Two coupled constraints immediately point to Ch 03 + Ch 04:

Each cell \((i, j)\) independently increments \(\text{row}_i\) and \(\text{col}_j\) (Ch 03 bipartite row-column factorization \(R_i \to C_j\)), with 'C' forcing lower bound \(1\) and '.' allowing \([0, 1]\).
The equality \(\text{row}_i = \text{col}_i \le D\) for an unknown variable load \(\text{row}_i \in [0, D]\) appears to couple \(R_i\) and \(C_i\) non-locally — until you introduce a slack bypass arc \(R_i \xrightarrow{[0, D]} C_i\) carrying the unused quota \(y_i = D - \text{row}_i\)!











NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Slack-Bypass Representation (#199)






Fix the maximum allowed load per row/column \(D \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) by exhaustive enumeration (\(N \le 40\)).
For each \((i, j)\), let \(x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether cell \((i, j)\) has a component (\(x_{ij} = 1\) if 'C', \(x_{ij} = 0\) if '/', \(x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) if '.'). Then \(\text{row}_i = \sum_j x_{ij}\) and \(\text{col}_i = \sum_j x_{ji}\).
Introduce a slack variable \(y_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, D\}\) for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and enforce: \[\text{row}_i + y_i = D \quad \text{and} \quad \text{col}_i + y_i = D \qquad (\forall i = 1, \dots, N).\] Notice the algebraic magic: subtracting the two equations immediately forces \(\text{row}_i = \text{col}_i = D - y_i \in [0, D]\)!
Summing over all \(i = 1, \dots, N\) yields total components \[W = \sum_{i=1}^N \text{row}_i = N D - \sum_{i=1}^N y_i.\] To maximize \(W\) for a fixed cap \(D\) (which both maximizes our objective and makes the threshold condition \(B \cdot D \le A \cdot W\) easiest to satisfy), we must minimize total slack \(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\) (or equivalently give each cell arc \(R_i \to C_j\) cost \(0\) and each slack arc \(R_i \to C_i\) cost \(+1\), or give cell arcs reward \(+1\)).










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — ICPC WF 2007 Chips Challenge (#199)






Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation & Slack-Minimization Loop
For each candidate maximum load \(D \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\):

Vertices & Fixed Supplies: Create source \(S\), sink \(T\), row nodes \(R_1, \dots, R_N\), and column nodes \(C_1, \dots, C_N\).

Every row node \(R_i\) must receive exactly \(D\) units of flow from \(S\): arc \(S \xrightarrow{[D, D]} R_i\).
Every column node \(C_i\) must send exactly \(D\) units of flow to \(T\): arc \(C_i \xrightarrow{[D, D]} T\).

Cell Arcs & Slack Bypass Arcs:

If cell \((i, j)\) is 'C': mandatory arc \(R_i \xrightarrow{[1, 1], \text{cost } 0} C_j\) (consumes \(1\) unit of \(R_i\)’s supply and \(C_j\)’s demand).
If cell \((i, j)\) is '.': optional arc \(R_i \xrightarrow{[0, 1], \text{cost } 0} C_j\).
If cell \((i, j)\) is '/': no arc.
Slack Bypass Gadget: For each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), add arc \(R_i \xrightarrow{[0, D], \text{cost } +1} C_i\). Flow \(y_i\) on this arc simultaneously absorbs \(y_i\) units of \(R_i\)’s supply \(D\) and \(y_i\) units of \(C_i\)’s demand \(D\), enforcing \(\text{row}_i = D - y_i = \text{col}_i \le D\).

Why Cost Distinction Between Cell Arcs and Slack Arcs Is Required:

In a pure unweighted lower-bound feasibility check, a cycle of '?'/'.' cells \((R_i \to C_j, R_j \to C_i)\) vs. slack arcs \((R_i \to C_i, R_j \to C_j)\) carries identical net terminal flow \(N D\) from \(S\) to \(T\), so an unweighted circulation solver might route flow through the slack bypass arcs \(y_i\) instead of placing components on '.' cells!
By assigning cost \(+1\) to slack arcs \(R_i \to C_i\) (and cost \(0\) to cell arcs \(R_i \to C_j\)), or equivalently running a minimum-cost feasible circulation (previewing Ch 17), we find a valid circulation that minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\), thereby maximizing \(W = N D - \sum_{i=1}^N y_i\).
If a feasible circulation exists for cap \(D\) and the resulting maximum \(W\) satisfies \(B \cdot D \le A \cdot W\), update the best answer with \(W - \#(\text{'C'})\).




Step 4: Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (FM-03 / FM-05)

Toy Trace: Let \(N = 2\), \(A/B = 1/2\), and grid: \[\begin{pmatrix} \text{C} & \text{.} \\ \text{.} & \text{.} \end{pmatrix}\]

Test \(D = 1\): Since \(B \cdot D = 2 \cdot 1 = 2\), we need \(W \ge 2\) components so that \(1 \cdot W \ge 2\).
With \(D = 1\), mandatory cell \((1, 1) = \text{'C'}\) forces \(x_{11} = 1\), saturating \(R_1\) and \(C_1\) (\(y_1 = 0\)).
For \(R_2\) and \(C_2\), the flow of \(D = 1\) unit can go either through the cell arc \(R_2 \to C_2\) (cost \(0\), placing a component at \((2, 2)\) so \(y_2 = 0, W = 2\)) or through the slack bypass \(R_2 \to C_2\) (cost \(+1\), \(y_2 = 1, W = 1\)).
Minimizing slack cost selects \(x_{22} = 1, y_2 = 0\), giving \(W = 2\), \(\text{row}_1 = \text{col}_1 = \text{row}_2 = \text{col}_2 = 1 \le \frac{1}{2}(2)\), and \(W - \#(\text{'C'}) = 2 - 1 = 1\) new component.

Broken Gadget Counterexample (FM-05 — Unweighted Slack Routing): In the exact \(2 \times 2\) trace above, if you give the slack bypass arc \(R_2 \to C_2\) the same priority/cost as the cell arc \(R_2 \to C_2\), Dinic may saturate the slack bypass \(y_2 = 1\) first, yielding \(W = 1\), failing the ratio check \(2 \cdot 1 \le 1 \cdot 1\), and falsely declaring \(D = 1\) infeasible!








Problem #200 — Codeforces 611 H: New Year and Forgotten Tree [EN]

Judge & Bounds: Codeforces 611 H · \(N \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) vertices labeled \(1, \dots, N\); \(N - 1\) lines describing the edges of a hidden tree where each endpoint label has been replaced by a string of '?' characters of the same decimal digit length (so vertex lengths lie in \(\{1, \dots, L\}\) with \(L = \lfloor \log_{10} N \rfloor + 1 \le 6\)).
Untagged Statement: You are given \(N\) and the multiset of \(N - 1\) pairs of digit lengths \((\text{len}(u), \text{len}(v))\) of the edges of a tree on vertices \(\{1, 2, \dots, N\}\). Reconstruct any valid tree on \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) whose edges match the given digit-length pairs, or output -1 if no such tree exists.







NoteHint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#200)






Target Chapters & Archetype: Ch 01 — Conservation, Residual Networks & Max-Flow Min-Cut + Ch 03 — Vertex Splitting, Time-Layered DAGs & Path Decomposition (§3.3 Rank-2 Pair-to-Bucket Supply-Demand Network) + Ch 04 — Flows with Lower Bounds & Circulations (Cayley Spanning Tree Enumeration \(L^{L-2} \le 6^4 = 1296\) + Parent-Orientation Supply-Demand Feasibility).
Diagnostic Signal: \(N \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) looks huge, but vertices of the same decimal digit length \(c \in \{1, \dots, L\}\) are completely interchangeable, and \(L \le 6\)! A graph on \(N\) vertices with \(N - 1\) edges is a tree if and only if we can choose one representative (boss) vertex \(r_c\) in each bucket \(V_c\), connect \(\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}\) via a spanning tree \(T_{\text{rep}}\) of size \(L - 1\), and orient every remaining edge \((u, v)\) away from the bosses so that every non-boss vertex \(v \in V_c \setminus \{r_c\}\) receives indegree exactly \(1\) from a vertex already connected to \(T_{\text{rep}}\).










NoteHint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Tree-Orientation Representation (#200)






Partition \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) into \(L \le 6\) buckets \(V_1, \dots, V_L\) by decimal length, with sizes \(s_c = |V_c|\) and fixed boss vertex \(r_c = 10^{c-1} \in V_c\). Let \(\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2]\) (\(1 \le c_1 \le c_2 \le L\)) be the given number of edges between \(V_{c_1}\) and \(V_{c_2}\).
Self-Bucket Edges (\(c_1 = c_2 = c\)): Any edge with both endpoints in \(V_c\) must connect \(r_c\) to a fresh non-boss vertex \(v \in V_c \setminus \{r_c\}\) (avoiding cycles inside \(V_c\)). If \(\text{cnt}[c][c] > s_c - 1\), no tree can exist (-1). Otherwise, we immediately greedily assign all \(\text{cnt}[c][c]\) self-edges as \((r_c, v)\) for distinct \(v \in V_c \setminus \{r_c\}\), reducing the remaining unmatched non-boss count in bucket \(c\) to: \[\text{rem}_c = (s_c - 1) - \text{cnt}[c][c] \ge 0.\]
Cross-Bucket Decomposition: Enumerate all \(L^{L-2} \le 6^4 = 1296\) labeled spanning trees \(T_{\text{rep}}\) on the \(L\) bosses \(\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}\) (via Prüfer sequences or DFS). For a fixed \(T_{\text{rep}}\):

Each tree edge \((r_{c_1}, r_{c_2}) \in T_{\text{rep}}\) consumes \(1\) unit from \(\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2]\) (if any \(\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2] < 0\), skip \(T_{\text{rep}}\)).
Every remaining cross-bucket edge of type \((c_1, c_2)\) (\(c_1 < c_2\)), say \(rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2]\) of them, must have one endpoint at a boss (\(r_{c_1}\) or \(r_{c_2}\)) and the other endpoint at a fresh non-boss vertex (\(v \in V_{c_2} \setminus \{r_{c_2}\}\) or \(u \in V_{c_1} \setminus \{r_{c_1}\}\)).
That is a pure bipartite supply-demand flow problem: split \(rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2] = f_{c_1, c_2 \to c_1} + f_{c_1, c_2 \to c_2}\) so that each bucket \(c\) receives \(\sum_{c' \ne c} f_{\{c, c'\} \to c} = \text{rem}_c\)!











TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Codeforces 611 H (#200)






Step 1–3: Rank-2 Pair-to-Bucket Flow Network & Reconstruction

Pre-Processing Self-Bucket Edges:

Compute \(s_c = |V_c|\) and boss \(r_c = 10^{c-1}\) for \(c = 1, \dots, L\).
Check \(\sum_{c_1 \le c_2} \text{cnt}[c_1][c_2] = N - 1\). For each \(c\), if \(\text{cnt}[c][c] > s_c - 1\), output -1. Otherwise, pop \(\text{cnt}[c][c]\) non-boss vertices from \(V_c \setminus \{r_c\}\), connect each directly to \(r_c\), and set \(\text{rem}_c = (s_c - 1) - \text{cnt}[c][c]\).

Enumerating Boss Spanning Trees \(T_{\text{rep}}\) (\(L^{L-2} \le 1296\)):

Generate all spanning trees \(T_{\text{rep}}\) on \(\{1, \dots, L\}\).
Subtract \(1\) from \(\text{cnt}[\min(u, v)][\max(u, v)]\) for each edge \((u, v) \in T_{\text{rep}}\). If all remaining counts \(rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2] \ge 0\), build the following miniature flow network (\(\le 1 + \binom{6}{2} + 6 + 1 = 23\) vertices):

Source \(S\), sink \(T\), \(\binom{L}{2} \le 15\) pair nodes \(P_{c_1, c_2}\) (\(1 \le c_1 < c_2 \le L\)), and \(L \le 6\) bucket nodes \(B_1, \dots, B_L\).
For each pair \(1 \le c_1 < c_2 \le L\): add \(S \to P_{c_1, c_2}\) with capacity \(rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2]\), and add \(P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_1}\) and \(P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_2}\) with capacity \(\infty\).
For each bucket \(c \in \{1, \dots, L\}\): add \(B_c \to T\) with capacity \(\text{rem}_c\).


Flow Check & Acyclic Edge Materialization:

Note that \(\sum_{c_1 < c_2} rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2] = (N - 1) - (L - 1) - \sum_{c=1}^L \text{cnt}[c][c] = \sum_{c=1}^L \text{rem}_c\).
Run Dinic on this \(23\)-node network. If \(\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) = \sum_{c=1}^L \text{rem}_c\), a valid tree exists!
Edge Materialization:

Output \((r_{c_1}, r_{c_2})\) for each \((c_1, c_2) \in T_{\text{rep}}\).
Output all pre-assigned self-bucket edges \((r_c, v)\).
For each pair \((c_1, c_2)\) (\(c_1 < c_2\)):

For each of the \(f(P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_1})\) units of flow into \(B_{c_1}\), pop a fresh unused non-boss vertex \(u \in V_{c_1} \setminus \{r_{c_1}\}\) and connect it to boss \(r_{c_2}\): output \((u, r_{c_2})\).
For each of the \(f(P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_2})\) units of flow into \(B_{c_2}\), pop a fresh unused non-boss vertex \(v \in V_{c_2} \setminus \{r_{c_2}\}\) and connect it to boss \(r_{c_1}\): output \((r_{c_1}, v)\).

Because every non-boss vertex in \(V_c \setminus \{r_c\}\) is attached as a degree-\(1\) leaf directly to some boss \(r_{c'}\), and the bosses \(\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}\) form the spanning tree \(T_{\text{rep}}\), the resulting \(N\)-vertex graph is guaranteed to be connected and acyclic!





Step 4: Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples

Toy Trace: Suppose \(N = 12\) (\(L = 2\): \(V_1 = \{1, \dots, 9\}\) with \(s_1 = 9, r_1 = 1\); \(V_2 = \{10, 11, 12\}\) with \(s_2 = 3, r_2 = 10\)). Given \(\text{cnt}[1][1] = 6, \text{cnt}[2][2] = 1, \text{cnt}[1][2] = 4\).

Self-edges: connect \(r_1 = 1\) to \(\{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}\) (\(\text{rem}_1 = 8 - 6 = 2\)), and \(r_2 = 10\) to \(\{11\}\) (\(\text{rem}_2 = 2 - 1 = 1\)).
Boss tree \(T_{\text{rep}}\) on \(\{r_1, r_2\}\) has the single edge \((1, 10)\), leaving \(rem\_cnt[1][2] = 4 - 1 = 3\).
Flow routes \(2\) units \(P_{1,2} \to B_1\) (connecting remaining \(V_1\) vertices \(\{8, 9\}\) to boss \(r_2 = 10\)) and \(1\) unit \(P_{1,2} \to B_2\) (connecting remaining \(V_2\) vertex \(\{12\}\) to boss \(r_1 = 1\)). All \(11\) edges form a valid tree!

Broken Gadget Counterexample (Connecting Non-Boss to Non-Boss Without Boss Backbone): If you try to satisfy degree counts without fixing a spanning tree \(T_{\text{rep}}\) on \(\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}\) (or if you connect non-boss vertices to each other arbitrarily), you can easily satisfy all pair counts \(\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2]\) while producing a disconnected graph consisting of a cycle in \(V_1 \cup V_2\) and an isolated component in \(V_3\). Grounding every non-tree edge at a boss \(r_{c'}\) guarantees acyclicity and connectivity simultaneously.

section: 3. Part I Diagnostic Mastery Rubric & Failure Mode Self-Audit (FM-01–FM-06)
text:
3. Part I Diagnostic Mastery Rubric & Failure Mode Self-Audit (FM-01–FM-06)
Before moving on to Part II (Bipartite Matching, König–Hall–Dilworth Duality & Decomposition), score your blind recognition performance across the 6 rapid-fire drills and 8 checkpoint problems above, and verify that every Part I failure mode is permanently eliminated from your implementation habits.

3.1 Quantitative Scoring & Remediation Protocol
Score each of the 8 blind checkpoint problems (#193–#200) on a 3-point scale (maximum 24 points):

3 points (Contest-Ready Compilation): Identified the correct Part I structural archetype and wrote down the intermediate algebraic/conservation formulation within 10 minutes without opening Hint 1 or Hint 2, and avoided all FM-01–FM-06 traps.
2 points (Assisted Compilation): Needed Hint 1 to identify the chapter archetype or vertex-splitting / lower-bound gadget, then completed the algebraic compilation and residual extraction independently.
1 point (Guided Reconstruction): Needed Hint 2 to set up the conservation equations, intermediate hub factorization (#196, #200), or slack bypass (#199).
0 points (Consulted Full Solution): Opened the full solution before writing down a complete graph specification, or fell into a broken-gadget trap (FM-01–FM-06).




Total Score
Readiness Tier
Actionable Remediation Plan




20 – 24 pts
Part I Mastery
Proceed immediately to Ch 05 — Bipartite Matching, König’s Theorem, MVC & MIS. Your English-to-Graph compilation reflex for conservation, residual anatomy, vertex splitting, and circulations is contest-solid.


15 – 19 pts
Solid with Blind Spots
Review the specific Part I chapter(s) where you opened Hint 1/2 (typically Ch 02 residual SCC/lattice classification or Ch 04 slack/feedback circulation arcs), re-solve the missed problem(s) cold after 48 hours, and advance to Part II.


10 – 14 pts
Gadget Fragility
Do not skip ahead yet. Re-work the 4-Step Compilation Scratchpads in Ch 01–Ch 04 alongside the Failure Mode Self-Audit Table below.


< 10 pts
Foundational Rebuild Required
Re-study Part I sequentially (Ch 01 \(\to\) Ch 04), tracing every small \(N \le 4\) numerical example by hand before re-attempting this checkpoint.





3.2 Part I Failure Mode Self-Audit (FM-01–FM-06)



Code
Failure Mode Name
Broken Habit / Symptom
Mathematical Root Cause
Mandatory Defensive Guard & Chapter Reference




FM-01
Greedy Path Deletion & Unpruned Dinic DFS
Finding 1 shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path and deleting its edges (#193), or omitting cur[u] / level[u] = 0 in Dinic (Drill 1.1).
Destroys the skew-symmetric cancellation arc \(v \to u\) of capacity \(+f(u, v)\) required by the Augmenting Path Theorem; re-scans dead residual subtrees in \(\mathcal{O}(V^2 E)\).
Always augment along a residual network with edges[id ^ 1].cap += pushed; advance cur[u] by reference and set level[u] = 0 on dead ends (Ch 01 §1.2–1.5).


FM-02
Saturated \(\implies\) Cut Edge Fallacy & Misdirected \(T_{\min}\) BFS
Assuming \(c_{f^*}(u, v) = 0\) implies \((u, v)\) is in some/every min-cut (Drill 1.2), or checking cap[id] > 0 instead of cap[id ^ 1] > 0 during reverse BFS from \(t\) (#197).
A saturated arc can have both endpoints inside the same residual SCC or inside \(S_{\min}\); reverse reachability to \(t\) requires positive residual capacity entering the current node.
Run Tarjan SCC on \(G_{f^*}\): Always-Cut iff \(u \in S_{\min}, v \in T_{\min}\); At-Least-One-Cut iff \(\text{scc}(u) \ne \text{scc}(v)\). In reverse BFS from \(t\), test edges[id ^ 1].cap > 0 (Ch 02 §2.1–2.2).


FM-03
Unsplit Vertex Capacities & Undirected Bridge Short-Circuiting
Placing node capacities on incident edges (#194), or adding undirected edge \(u_{\text{in}} \leftrightarrow u_{\text{out}}\) (Drill 1.3), or connecting \(R_i \leftrightarrow C_j\) pairwise (#196).
Edge capacities constrain per-neighbor flow rather than \(\sum_v f(v, u) \le c(u)\); an undirected internal bridge lets flow enter \(u_{\text{out}}\) and exit \(u_{\text{in}}\), bypassing \(c(u)\).
Split every capacitated internal vertex into \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c(u)} u_{\text{out}}\) (directed!) and wire external edges as \(x_{\text{out}} \to y_{\text{in}}\) (Ch 03 §3.1, §3.3).


FM-04
Time-Expanded Horizon Traps
Omitting waiting arcs \((u, t) \to (u, t+1)\), rebuilding \(G(\mathcal{T})\) from scratch at every timestamp, or binary searching \(\mathcal{T}\) without an unreachability guard (Drill 1.4).
Entities forced to move at every step can collide or oscillate; rebuilding wastes \(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{T}^2)\) work; disconnected destinations cause infinite horizon loops.
Always ask if entities can wait in place (holdover arc capacity \(c_{\text{wait}}(u)\)); append layers incrementally in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) Dinic phases per step up to a proven reachability bound \(\mathcal{T}_{\max}\) (Ch 03 §3.2).


FM-05
Lower-Bound Sign Inversion, Feedback Leakage & Slack Omission
Computing \(M(v) = \text{out}_{\text{low}} - \text{in}_{\text{low}}\) (Drill 1.5), leaving \(t \to s\) active during Stage 2 adjustment, or forgetting to add \(+l(e)\) / minimize slack (#198, #199).
Reversing \(M(v)\) swaps supply and demand; leaving \(t \to s\) open during \(s\)-\(t\) adjustment creates an \(\infty\)-capacity loop; unweighted slack arcs absorb flow meant for real cells.
Memorize In minus Out: \(M(v) = \text{in}_{\text{low}}(v) - \text{out}_{\text{low}}(v)\); read \(f_0 = \text{flow}(t \to s)\), zero both e_fb and e_fb ^ 1 before Stage 2, and reconstruct \(f(e) = l(e) + f'(e)\) (Ch 04 §4.1–4.3).


FM-06
Mixed Eulerian Parity Omission & Unit-vs-Two Degree Delta
Running Dinic on mixed Eulerian graphs without checking \(D(v) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\), or setting edge capacity to \(2\) instead of \(1\) (Drill 1.6).
Reversing one undirected edge changes \(\text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)\) by \(\pm 2\), so odd \(D(v)\) is algebraically impossible and \(1\) unit of flow represents \(1\) reversed edge (\(2\) degree units).
Pre-orient undirected edges arbitrarily, abort immediately if \(D(v) = \text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)\) is odd for any \(v\), and wire node demands \(|D(v)| / 2\) with unit-capacity (\(1\)) arcs (Ch 04 §4.4).

title: Checkpoint I — Foundations, Residual Anatomy, Vertex Splitting, and Bounded Circulations
section: 4. Readiness Bridge to Part II: Bipartite Matching, König–Hall–Dilworth Duality & Decomposition
text:
4. Readiness Bridge to Part II: Bipartite Matching, König–Hall–Dilworth Duality & Decomposition
Every technique you mastered in Part I serves as the direct algebraic and algorithmic foundation for Part II (Ch 05–Ch 08):

From Unit-Capacity Networks & Residual Reachability (Ch 01–Ch 02) to König’s Theorem & Dulmage–Mendelsohn (Ch 05–Ch 06):

In #195 (Test Paper Library) and #196 (Lotus Leaves), you compiled matching and row-column hitting problems into unit-capacity \(S \to L \to R \to T\) flow networks.
In Ch 05 — Bipartite Matching, König’s Theorem, Minimum Vertex Cover & Maximum Independent Set, the source-minimal cut set \(S_{\min}\) you extracted in Ch 02 (#197) directly constructs the Minimum Vertex Cover \(\text{MVC} = (L \setminus S_{\min}) \cup (R \cap S_{\min})\) and Maximum Independent Set \(\text{MIS} = V \setminus \text{MVC}\) via alternating reachability trees.
In Ch 06 — Grid Parity, Domino Tilings, Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition & Matching Games, the 3-way residual edge/vertex classification of Ch 02 specializes to the Dulmage–Mendelsohn canonical partition \(V = \mathcal{D} \sqcup \mathcal{A} \sqcup \mathcal{C}\), characterizing winning strategies in two-player walk games on graphs.

From Bounded Row-Column Circulations (Ch 04) to Birkhoff–von Neumann & Bipartite Edge Coloring (Ch 07):

In #198 (Tatami) and #199 (Chips Challenge), you used lower-bound circulations to construct 0-1 matrices with prescribed row and column degree intervals.
In Ch 07 — Birkhoff–von Neumann Decomposition, Row-Column Matrices & Bipartite Edge Coloring, you will decompose \(k\)-regular bipartite graphs and doubly stochastic matrices into \(\Delta\) disjoint matchings (color classes), combining Ch 04 degree-splitting with Eulerian halve-splitting in \(\mathcal{O}(M \log \Delta)\).

From DAG Path Extraction (Ch 03) to Dilworth’s Poset Width & Hall Marriage Elimination (Ch 08):

In Ch 03, you decomposed \(s\)-\(t\) flows into paths and split vertices into \(u_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}\).
In Ch 08 — Poset Chain Covers, Dilworth’s Theorem, Hall’s Marriage Theorem & Sports Elimination, splitting each poset element \(u\) into \((u_{\text{out}}, u_{\text{in}})\) turns Minimum Disjoint Path Cover on a DAG into a simple bipartite matching correction \(N - \text{MaxMatching}\), while Ch 01 cut capacity bounds yield Hall’s Marriage Theorem and Sports Elimination certificates (#200 pair-to-bucket supply-demand networks).



4.1 Part I Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation Cheat Sheet
When entering Part II (and later Parts III–VI), keep the following four canonical Part I compilation signatures at your fingertips:








English Constraint / Question
Intermediate Algebraic Equation
Mechanical Graph Gadget




Pack \(K\) edge-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths (Ch 01, #193)
\(\sum_{v} f(u,v) - \sum_{v} f(v,u) = 0\), \(f(e) \in \{0, 1\}\)
Unit capacity \(1\) on each directed arc; run residual Dinic + positive-flow DFS path peel


Is edge \(e=(u,v)\) in every / some min-cut? (Ch 02)
\(u \in S_{\min}, v \in T_{\min}\) vs. \(\text{scc}(u) \ne \text{scc}(v)\) in \(G_{f^*}\)
Saturated (\(c_{f^*}(e)=0\)) + Tarjan SCC & terminal reachability on \(G_{f^*}\)


Is the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut unique? (Ch 02, #197)
\(S_{\min} = S_{\max} \iff S_{\min} \cup T_{\min} = V\)
Forward BFS from \(s\) (\(c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0\)) + reverse BFS from \(t\) (\(c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0\)); check \(|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = |V|\)


Destroy / cap internal vertex \(u\) at cost \(c(u)\) (Ch 03, #194, #196)
\(f_{\text{thru}}(u) = \sum_{x} f(x, u) \le c(u)\)
Split \(u\) into \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c(u)} u_{\text{out}}\) (directed!); route external edges as \(x_{\text{out}} \to y_{\text{in}}\)


All-to-all transfer inside row \(R_i\) or column \(C_j\) (Ch 03, #196)
Hub variable \(r_i, c_j\) mediating cell incidence
Create hub nodes \(R_i, C_j\) with \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} R_i \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}\) (\(\mathcal{O}(HW)\) edges total)


Edge flow must lie in \([l(e), u(e)]\) (Ch 04, #198)
\(f(e) = l(e) + f'(e)\), \(M(v) = \text{in}_{\text{low}}(v) - \text{out}_{\text{low}}(v)\)
Residual arc \(u(e)-l(e)\); \(S^* \to v\) if \(M(v)>0\), \(v \to T^*\) if \(M(v)<0\); feedback \(t \xrightarrow{\infty} s\)


Equal row/column load \(\text{row}_i = \text{col}_i \le D\) (Ch 04, #199)
\(\text{row}_i + y_i = D = \text{col}_i + y_i\) (\(y_i \in [0, D]\))
Fixed \(S \xrightarrow{[D,D]} R_i\), \(C_i \xrightarrow{[D,D]} T\), and slack bypass \(R_i \xrightarrow{[0, D], \text{cost } +1} C_i\)


Mixed graph Eulerian orientation (Ch 04, Drill 1.6)
\(\text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v) = D(v) - 2\Delta_{\text{rev}}(v) = 0\)
Check \(D(v) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\); wire demand \(|D(v)|/2\) and unit-capacity (\(1\)) arcs on undirected edges

NotePrerequisites



Before studying this chapter, make sure you are comfortable with:

Chapter 17 (Minimum-Cost Flow Fundamentals): The Successive Shortest Path (SSP) algorithm, reduced costs \(c^\pi(u, v) = c(u, v) + \pi(u) - \pi(v)\), and the discrete convexity of the minimum-cost flow function \(C(f)\) with respect to the total flow \(f\).
Chapter 18 (1D Interval & Spine MCMF): Consecutive equation differencing (\(E_t - E_{t-1}\)) and why 1D interval covering or matching problems compile into flows along a directed spine.
Chapter 20 & Chapter 21 (Bipartite MCMF & Linear Programming Duality): Complementary slackness, potential variables, and why dualizing a constrained optimization problem exposes a flow or cut network.









TipLearning Objectives



By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Prove and apply the Regret-Heap Residual Isomorphism Theorem: Translate every reverse residual arc \(j \to i\) of cost \(-(c_j - c_i)\) created during an SSP augmentation into an explicit regret key stored inside a priority queue (反悔贪心 \(\equiv\) 模拟费用流).
Eliminate cardinality constraints via WQS / Aliens Binary Search (CF 802 O): Combine the convexity of \(C(K)\) with a per-unit Lagrangian penalty \(-\lambda\) so that an offline \(K\)-step SSP problem reduces to a single left-to-right sweep with a two-candidate regret heap in \(O(N \log N \log V)\).
Simulate SSP on 1D ranges and trees (CF 280 D, ICPC WF 2018 Conquer the World, UOJ #455): Replace Bellman-Ford/Dijkstra with a Segment Tree that flips subarray signs upon augmentation, or with mergeable subtree heaps that decompose tree distances \(d(u, v) = \operatorname{dep}(u) + \operatorname{dep}(v) - 2\operatorname{dep}(\operatorname{lca}(u, v))\) at each Lowest Common Ancestor.
Compile multi-state residual automata ([NOI2019] 序列): Enumerate all elementary augmenting paths and cycles on a constant-state vertex automaton, maintain each transition family in a lazy-deletion priority queue, and guard against missing cross-swap regret paths (FM-23).

title: Chapter 23 — Simulated Cost Flow: Regret Greedy, Priority Queues, and Segment-Tree Augmentation
section: 23.1 Direction B for MCMF — Why Successive Shortest Paths Collapses to a Data Structure When \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\)
text:
23.1 Direction B for MCMF — Why Successive Shortest Paths Collapses to a Data Structure When \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\)
In Chapter 13, we saw that when a Maximum Flow or Minimum Cut problem has \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) vertices, running Dinic’s algorithm on an explicit graph is hopeless; instead, we use Direction B (Graph \(\to\) Data Structure) to simulate the minimum cut via dynamic programming, segment trees, or greedy sweeps.
The exact same phenomenon occurs—with even greater frequency in modern contests—for Minimum-Cost Maximum Flow (MCMF). Suppose a problem has \(N = 2 \times 10^5\) items, days, or tree vertices. Even if the underlying MCMF network is sparse (\(|V|, |E| = O(N)\)), running the explicit Successive Shortest Path (SSP) algorithm requires \(F = \Theta(N)\) augmentations, each taking \(\Omega(N)\) or \(\Omega(N \log N)\) time via SPFA or Dijkstra with Johnson potentials—a fatal \(\Theta(N^2 \log N)\) bottleneck.
Yet in competitive programming, huge-scale MCMF networks are never arbitrary graphs. Their topology is almost always one of four structured families:

A 1D Directed Spine (Time / Prefix Order): Supply arrives at index \(i\) and can only travel rightward to demand at index \(j \ge i\).
A 1D Doubly-Linked Adjacency Chain or Interval Line: Augmenting paths correspond to flipping the selection state of a contiguous subarray or alternating chain.
A Weighted Tree Metric: Flow moves between subtrees, and the cost between \(u\) and \(v\) telescopes at \(w = \operatorname{lca}(u, v)\) as \(\operatorname{dep}(u) + \operatorname{dep}(v) - 2\operatorname{dep}(w)\).
A Constant-Size Hub or Vertex-State Automaton: All \(N\) items interact only through \(O(1)\) global hub nodes (such as a shared token pool of capacity \(K - L\)).

In Chinese competitive programming literature, the technique of executing the exact steps of SSP or Cycle Cancelling on these structured graphs using priority queues, segment trees, or mergeable heaps—without ever instantiating adjacency lists—is known as Simulated Cost Flow (模拟费用流). Its priority-queue specialization is known as Regret Greedy (反悔贪心) or Buy-Back Greedy.

The Regret-Heap Residual Isomorphism Theorem
Why do “regret heaps” work, and why do ad-hoc greedy intuition attempts so often fail on edge cases? Because Regret Greedy is not a heuristic at all: it is an exact, step-by-step algebraic encoding of the residual graph in the Successive Shortest Path algorithm.






ImportantTheorem 23.1 (The Regret-Heap Residual Isomorphism Theorem)



Consider a 1D prefix bipartite transportation network on indices \(1, 2, \dots, N\) where:

Every supply node \(i\) can inject \(1\) unit of flow from the source \(S\) at cost \(-c_i\) (or acquisition cost \(+c_i\)).
Every demand node \(j \ge i\) can absorb \(1\) unit of flow into the sink \(T\) at cost \(+c_j\).
Thus, matching supply \(i\) to demand \(j\) (\(i \le j\)) along the forward spine costs \(c_j - c_i\).

Suppose that at step \(j\), a unit of flow from \(i\) is matched to \(j\), contributing \(c_j - c_i\) to the objective. In the MCMF residual network \(G_f\), saturating the path \(S \to i \to j \to T\) creates a reverse residual arc \(T \to j \to i\) of residual cost \(-(c_j - c_i)\).
If a later demand node \(k > j\) augments \(1\) unit of flow by traversing this reverse residual arc \(j \to i\) and continuing forward along \(i \to k \to T\), the net change in total cost is:
\[
\Delta \text{Cost}(j \mapsto k) = \underbrace{-(c_j - c_i)}_{\text{reverse arc } j \to i} + \underbrace{(c_k - c_i)}_{\text{forward arc } i \to k} = c_k - c_j.
\]
Notice that the original supply cost \(c_i\) cancels out identically! After this augmentation, the total accumulated cost is:
\[
(c_j - c_i) + (c_k - c_j) = c_k - c_i,
\]
which is the exact cost of having matched \(i\) directly to \(k\) in the first place. Therefore, inserting a matched demand \(j\) back into the candidate supply priority queue with a “regret key” equal to \(c_j\) is \(100\%\) isomorphic to exposing the reverse residual path \(T \to j \to i\) in \(G_f\).


Proof. In the explicit residual network \(G_f\) on the 1D spine \(1 \to 2 \to \dots \to N\):

Before matching \((i, j)\), the arc \(S \to i\) has capacity \(1\) and cost \(-c_i\), the spine arcs \(t \to t+1\) have capacity \(\infty\) and cost \(0\), and the arc \(j \to T\) has capacity \(1\) and cost \(+c_j\).
Pushing \(1\) unit of flow along \(S \to i \to \dots \to j \to T\) saturates \(S \to i\) and \(j \to T\), and sends \(1\) unit of positive flow along the spine segment \([i, j]\).
Consequently, in \(G_f\), the arc \(T \to j\) (or equivalently, a virtual source arc \(S_{\text{regret}} \to j\) representing the ability to un-match \(j\) from \(T\)) appears with capacity \(1\) and cost \(-c_j\), while reverse spine arcs \(t+1 \to t\) carry cost \(0\) on \([i, j]\).
Any future demand \(k > j\) looking for the cheapest available supply in \([1, k]\) sees two classes of residual paths from \(S\):

Fresh supplies \(i' \le k\) via \(S \to i' \to \dots \to k \to T\) at cost \(c_k - c_{i'}\).
Regret supplies (redirected demands) \(j \le k\) via \(S \to i \to \dots \to j \xrightarrow{\text{cancel } j \to T} j \to \dots \to k \to T\) at incremental cost \((c_j - c_i) - (c_j - c_i) + (c_k - c_j) = c_k - c_j\).

Both classes have the exact functional form \(c_k - \text{key}\), where \(\text{key} = c_{i'}\) for a fresh supply and \(\text{key} = c_j\) for a regret supply. A single min-heap (for minimization of \(c_i\), or max-heap for maximization of \(c_i\)) over all active keys in \([1, k]\) therefore returns the exact shortest augmenting path in \(G_f\) in \(O(\log N)\) time. \(\blacksquare\)

    I -->|"flow = 1"| J(("Node j"))
    J -->|"+c_j (saturated)"| T(("T"))
