title: Chapter 21 — Total Unimodularity, Linear Programming Duality & Dual Flow Compilation
section: 3. Dual Compilation (LP 对偶转网络流 — Direction A): When the Primal LP Is Not a Flow, Dualize It
text:
3. Dual Compilation (LP 对偶转网络流 — Direction A): When the Primal LP Is Not a Flow, Dualize It
In Chapter 19, we saw that whenever a Primal LP has the Column Consecutive-Ones Property (Column-C1P) — each decision variable \(x_j\) appears with coefficient \(+1\) on a contiguous interval of constraints \([L_j, R_j]\) — consecutive row differencing \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) compiles the Primal LP directly into a flow network.
What if the Primal LP has the Row Consecutive-Ones Property (Row-C1P), or involves differential inequalities \(\pi_v - \pi_u + x_e \ge w_e\) where variables appear in arbitrary cycles or overlapping constraints?






ImportantThe Fundamental Law of Dual Compilation (Direction A)



Because transposition swaps rows and columns (\(A \mapsto A^T\)):

Row-C1P Primal \(\xrightarrow{\text{LP Dual}}\) Column-C1P Dual \(\xrightarrow{\text{Ch 19 Differencing}}\) Directed Flow Network!
Differential Potential Primal (\(\pi_v - \pi_u + x_e \ge w_e\)) \(\xrightarrow{\text{LP Dual}}\) Node-Arc Incidence Dual (\(\nabla \cdot f = b\)) with Cost and Capacity Swapped!



flowchart TD
    P1["Primal LP has Row-C1P<br/>N variables, M interval constraints (M >> N)<br/>e.g. [ZJOI2013] Defense Line (#161)"]
    P2["Primal LP has Potential Differences<br/>π_v - π_u + x_e >= w_e or x_e + y_f >= w_e - w_f<br/>e.g. Project Crashing (#163), Inverse MST (#166)"]
    D1["Take LP Dual: A -> A^T<br/>Now Column-C1P with N rows and M columns!"]
    D2["Apply Ch 19 Row Differencing ΔE_i = E_i - E_{i-1}<br/>Builds N-node Spine Flow Network (NOT M nodes!)"]
    D3["Take LP Dual: Potentials π_v -> Flow Conservation<br/>Primal Money Cost c_e -> Dual Arc Capacity!<br/>Primal Duration/Weight w_e -> Dual Arc Cost!"]
    SOL["Solve via MCMF & Extract Dual Potentials π* from G_{f*}"]

    P1 --> D1 --> D2 --> SOL
    P2 --> D3 --> SOL


3.1 Row-C1P vs. Column-C1P Transposition ([NOI2008] 志愿者招募 vs. [ZJOI2013] 防守战线)
Comparing NOI 2008 Volunteer Recruitment (#148, Ch 19) with ZJOI 2013 Defense Line (#161) reveals why LP Duality is indispensable when the roles of items and intervals are transposed:








Feature
[NOI2008] 志愿者招募 (#148, Ch 19)
[ZJOI2013] 防守战线 (#161, Ch 21)




Positions / Days \(N\)
\(N \le 1,000\) constraints (days)
\(N \le 1,000\) variables (positions \(x_1, \dots, x_N\))


Intervals \(M\)
\(M \le 10,000\) variables (volunteer types)
\(M \le 10,000\) constraints (\(\sum_{i=L_j}^{R_j} x_i \ge D_j\))


Position Cap \(x_i \le C_i\)
None (\(x_j \ge 0\) unbounded)
Upper bound \(0 \le x_i \le C_i\) on each position \(i\)


Primal Matrix \(A\)
\(N \times M\) Column-C1P
\(M \times N\) Row-C1P (with \(N \times N\) identity for \(x_i \le C_i\))


Direct Primal Differencing?
Works directly: \(N+1\) vertices, \(M\) arcs
Fails: \(M\) rows are arbitrary intervals; differencing rows does NOT yield two non-zeros per column!


Dual Compilation Fix
Not needed (already Column-C1P)
Dualize first! Dual LP has \(N\) constraints (positions) and \(M\) interval variables \(y_j \ge 0\) (Column-C1P), giving an \((N+1)\)-vertex MCMF!




Step-by-Step Algebraic Derivation of Row-C1P Dual Compilation
In ZJOI 2013 Defense Line (#161), we choose \(x_i \in [0, C_i]\) towers at position \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) at cost \(W_i\) per tower, subject to \(M\) interval covering demands:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{\textbf{Primal LP (Row-C1P):}} \quad \min_{x} \quad & \sum_{i=1}^N W_i \, x_i \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{i=L_j}^{R_j} x_i \ge D_j && \forall j = 1, \dots, M \quad &\text{(Dual variable: } y_j \ge 0 \text{)} \\
& -x_i \ge -C_i && \forall i = 1, \dots, N \quad &\text{(Dual variable: } z_i \ge 0 \text{)} \\
& x_i \ge 0 && \forall i = 1, \dots, N
\end{aligned}
\]
Look at the column for primal variable \(x_i\): it appears in every interval constraint \(j\) that covers position \(i\) (\(L_j \le i \le R_j\)) and in its own capacity constraint \(-x_i \ge -C_i\). Taking the LP Dual immediately transposes the system into \(N\) rows (one per position \(i\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{\textbf{Dual LP (Column-C1P):}} \quad \max_{y, z \ge 0} \quad & \sum_{j=1}^M D_j \, y_j - \sum_{i=1}^N C_i \, z_i \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{j: L_j \le i \le R_j} y_j - z_i \le W_i && \forall i = 1, \dots, N
\end{aligned}
\]
Now add a non-negative slack variable \(s_i \ge 0\) to the \(i\)-th dual inequality to make it an equality \(E_i\):
\[
E_i : \quad \sum_{j: L_j \le i \le R_j} y_j - z_i + s_i = W_i \qquad (i = 1, \dots, N)
\]
Notice that in the Dual system \(E_1, \dots, E_N\), each interval dual variable \(y_j \ge 0\) appears with coefficient \(+1\) in the contiguous block of rows \(i \in [L_j, R_j]\) — it is Column-C1P! Applying Chapter 19 consecutive equation differencing \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) (with \(E_0 \equiv 0\) and \(E_{N+1} \equiv 0\)):
\[
\Delta E_i : \quad \sum_{j: L_j = i} y_j - \sum_{j: R_j + 1 = i} y_j + (s_i - s_{i-1}) - (z_i - z_{i-1}) = W_i - W_{i-1} \qquad (i = 1, \dots, N+1)
\]
Every dual variable now appears once with \(+1\) (outflow) and once with \(-1\) (inflow) on an \((N+1)\)-vertex graph (even though \(M = 10,000 \gg N = 1,000\)):

Interval Dual Variable \(y_j \ge 0\): Directed arc \(L_j \to R_j + 1\) with capacity \(\infty\) and cost \(-D_j\) (to turn \(\max \sum D_j y_j\) into min-cost).
Slack Variable \(s_i \ge 0\): Directed spine arc \(i \to i + 1\) with capacity \(\infty\) and cost \(0\).
Capacity Penalty Variable \(z_i \ge 0\): Appears with \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_i\) and \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_{i+1}\), so it is a backward spine arc \(i + 1 \to i\) with capacity \(\infty\) and cost \(+C_i\)!
Node Supplies: Node \(i\) has net outflow demand \(b_i = W_i - W_{i-1}\) (where \(W_0 = W_{N+1} = 0\)).





3.2 Differential Potential & Schedule Crashing Duals (Cost–Capacity Role Reversal)
A second major family of contest problems optimizes node timestamps / potentials \(\pi_v\) together with edge modification variables \(x_e\):

Project Schedule Crashing (Fulkerson 1961, Luogu P5295, #163): Given a project DAG \(G = (V, E)\) where task \(e = (u, v)\) has normal duration \(w_e\), can be crashed (shortened) by \(x_e \in [0, d_e]\) days at money cost \(c_e\) per day, minimize total money \(\sum_{e \in E} c_e x_e\) so that all tasks finish by deadline \(K\) (\(\pi_T - \pi_S \le K\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\pi, x} \quad & \sum_{e \in E} c_e \, x_e \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \pi_v - \pi_u + x_{uv} \ge w_{uv} && \forall (u, v) \in E \quad &\text{(Dual flow variable: } f_{uv} \ge 0 \text{)} \\
& \pi_S - \pi_T \ge -K && &\text{(Dual return flow: } F \ge 0 \text{)} \\
& -x_{uv} \ge -d_{uv}, \;\; x_{uv} \ge 0 && \forall (u, v) \in E \quad &\text{(Dual bound multiplier: } r_{uv} \ge 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]

Look at what happens when we take the LP Dual:

Free Potential Variables \(\pi_v \in \mathbb{R}\) Become Flow Conservation! In the Primal LP, \(\pi_v\) is unrestricted in sign (free). By the Primal–Dual Dictionary (Section 2.1), the dual constraint corresponding to \(\pi_v\) is an exact equality:
\[
\sum_{u: (u,v) \in E} f_{uv} - \sum_{w: (v,w) \in E} f_{vw} = \begin{cases} -F & \text{if } v = S \\ +F & \text{if } v = T \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\]
The dual variables \(f_{uv} \ge 0\) literally form an \(S\)-\(T\) flow of value \(F\)!
Primal Money Cost \(c_{uv}\) Becomes Dual Arc Capacity! The primal crashing variable \(x_{uv} \ge 0\) has objective coefficient \(c_{uv}\) and appears in \(\pi_v - \pi_u + x_{uv} \ge w_{uv}\) (dual \(f_{uv}\)) and \(-x_{uv} \ge -d_{uv}\) (dual \(r_{uv}\)). Its dual constraint is:
\[
f_{uv} - r_{uv} \le c_{uv} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad r_{uv} \ge \max(0, \; f_{uv} - c_{uv})
\]
Two-Regime Parallel Arc Gadget: The Dual LP maximizes \(\sum_{e \in E} w_e f_e - K F - \sum_{e \in E} d_e r_e\), which is equivalent to minimizing:
\[
\min_{f, F \ge 0} \; K \cdot F + \sum_{e \in E} \Big( -w_e f_e + d_e \max(0, \; f_e - c_e) \Big)
\]
This piecewise-linear convex cost on \(f_e \ge 0\) splits each DAG edge \(e = (u, v)\) into two parallel directed arcs \(u \to v\):

Crashable Arc \(e_{\text{crash}}\): Capacity \(c_e\), unit cost \(-w_e\) (the first \(c_e\) units of flow earn slope \(-w_e\)).
Fully-Crashed Rigid Arc \(e_{\text{rigid}}\): Capacity \(\infty\), unit cost \(-(w_e - d_e)\) (any flow beyond \(c_e\) pays the penalty \(+d_e\), earning slope \(-(w_e - d_e)\)).








TipDiagnostic Signal: Cost–Capacity Role Reversal in Potential LPs



Whenever a problem gives linear costs \(c_e\) for modifying edge lengths \(w_e \gets w_e \pm x_e\) to control shortest or longest path distances \(\pi_v\):

In the Dual Flow Network, the primal modification cost \(c_e\) becomes an arc capacity, and the original edge length \(w_e\) becomes an arc cost!






3.3 Matroid / Spanning Tree Swap Inequalities (Inverse MST #163, #166)
Suppose we are given an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with initial edge weights \(w_e\), together with a designated spanning tree \(T \subseteq E\). We can decrease the weight of any tree edge \(e \in T\) by \(x_e \ge 0\) (at cost \(c_e\) per unit) and increase the weight of any non-tree edge \(f \notin T\) by \(y_f \ge 0\) (at cost \(c_f\) per unit). What is the minimum cost \(\sum_{e \in T} c_e x_e + \sum_{f \notin T} c_f y_f\) so that \(T\) becomes a Minimum Spanning Tree of \(G\)?

Step 1: Cycle Optimality Characterization of MST
By the cycle optimality theorem for MSTs, \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree under the modified weights \(w'_e = w_e - x_e\) (\(e \in T\)) and \(w'_f = w_f + y_f\) (\(f \notin T\)) if and only if for every non-tree edge \(f = (u, v) \notin T\) and every tree edge \(e \in \text{Path}_T(u, v)\) on the unique fundamental cycle of \(f\):
\[
w_e - x_e \le w_f + y_f \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \boxed{x_e + y_f \ge w_e - w_f} \qquad \forall f \notin T, \;\; \forall e \in \text{Path}_T(u_f, v_f)
\]


Step 2: Bipartite Incidence & Dual Compilation
Construct a bipartite dependency graph \(\mathcal{B} = (T, E \setminus T, \mathcal{E}_{\text{pair}})\) where the left side is the set of tree edges \(e \in T\) (\(|T| = N - 1\)), the right side is the set of non-tree edges \(f \notin T\) (\(|E \setminus T| = M - N + 1\)), and there is a bipartite edge \((e, f) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{pair}}\) with requirement \(W_{ef} = \max(0, w_e - w_f)\) whenever \(e \in \text{Path}_T(u_f, v_f)\) and \(w_e > w_f\).
The Primal LP is a Weighted Bipartite Vertex Cover (Potential) Problem on \(\mathcal{B}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{\textbf{Primal (Inverse MST):}} \quad \min_{x, y \ge 0} \quad & \sum_{e \in T} c_e \, x_e + \sum_{f \notin T} c_f \, y_f \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & x_e + y_f \ge W_{ef} && \forall (e, f) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{pair}} \quad &\text{(Dual flow: } \phi_{ef} \ge 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(\mathcal{B}\) is a bipartite graph, its incidence matrix is Family 2 Totally Unimodular! Taking the LP Dual immediately yields:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{\textbf{Dual (Bipartite Flow / Matching):}} \quad \max_{\phi \ge 0} \quad & \sum_{(e, f) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{pair}}} W_{ef} \, \phi_{ef} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{f: (e,f) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{pair}}} \phi_{ef} \le c_e && \forall e \in T \\
& \sum_{e: (e,f) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{pair}}} \phi_{ef} \le c_f && \forall f \notin T
\end{aligned}
\]

Special Case 1: Unit Modification Costs \(c_e = c_f = 1\) ([SHOI2004] 最小生成树, #163): The Dual LP is literally Maximum-Weight Bipartite Matching (by Egerváry’s Theorem, 1931)! Running the Hungarian / Kuhn–Munkres (KM) algorithm in \(O(V_{\mathcal{B}}^3)\) solves both the Dual matching \(\phi^*\) and the Primal vertex potentials \((x^*_e, y^*_f)\) simultaneously.
General Case 2: Arbitrary Linear Costs \(c_e, c_f\) (BZOJ 3118 Orz the Immortal, #166): The Dual LP is a Maximum-Weight Bipartite \(b\)-Matching (Min-Cost Flow):

Source \(S \to e \in T\) with capacity \(c_e\), cost \(0\).
Bipartite arc \(e \to f\) for \((e, f) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{pair}}\) with capacity \(\infty\), cost \(-W_{ef}\).
Sink arc \(f \to T_{\text{sink}}\) with capacity \(c_f\), cost \(0\).
Furthermore, if explicit primal modifications \((x^*_e, y^*_f)\) are needed, they are extracted directly from the optimal dual potentials \(\pi^*_e, \pi^*_f\) of \(G_{f^*}\) via Section 2.5!






3.4 Polymatroid Intersection, Dilworth Reachability & Total Dual Integrality (TDI)
Why do Matroid Intersection (Ch 22), Polymatroids, and Dilworth’s Chain Decomposition (Ch 9, #167) also enjoy exact integer LP relaxations?






NoteTheorem 21.4: Edmonds’ Polymatroid Intersection Integrality Theorem (1970)



A function \(\rho : 2^E \to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) with \(\rho(\emptyset) = 0\) is a submodular rank function if it is monotone (\(\rho(A) \le \rho(B)\) for \(A \subseteq B\)) and satisfies the diminishing-returns inequality:
\[
\rho(A) + \rho(B) \ge \rho(A \cup B) + \rho(A \cap B) \qquad \forall A, B \subseteq E
\]
For any two submodular functions \(\rho_1, \rho_2 : 2^E \to \mathbb{Z}\), the Polymatroid Intersection Polyhedron
\[
\mathcal{P}(\rho_1, \rho_2) = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^E \;\middle|\; \sum_{e \in S} x_e \le \rho_1(S) \;\; \text{and} \;\; \sum_{e \in S} x_e \le \rho_2(S) \quad \forall S \subseteq E \right\}
\]
is Total Dual Integral (TDI) and has strictly integral vertices \(x^* \in \mathbb{Z}^E\), with minimax duality:
\[
\max_{x \in \mathcal{P}(\rho_1, \rho_2)} \sum_{e \in E} x_e = \min_{S \subseteq E} \Big( \rho_1(S) + \rho_2(E \setminus S) \Big)
\]


Why does Theorem 21.4 hold? For any fixed vector \(x^*\), the family of tight sets \(\mathcal{F}_i = \{S \subseteq E \mid x^*(S) = \rho_i(S)\}\) is closed under intersection and union (by submodularity: \(\rho_i(A) + \rho_i(B) \ge \rho_i(A \cup B) + \rho_i(A \cap B) \ge x^*(A \cup B) + x^*(A \cap B) = x^*(A) + x^*(B) = \rho_i(A) + \rho_i(B)\)). Therefore, any linearly independent basis of tight constraints from \(\mathcal{F}_1\) can be uncrossed into a nested chain \(\emptyset \subset S_1 \subset S_2 \subset \dots \subset S_k \subseteq E\). Reordering elements along the chain makes the incidence matrix of \(\mathcal{F}_1\) an Interval (C1P) matrix, and subtracted consecutive differences turn \(\mathcal{F}_1\) into disjoint sets (one \(+1\) per column) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) into one \(-1\) per column — a Family 1 Totally Unimodular matrix!
(By contrast, the intersection of three matroids/polymatroids \(\mathcal{P}(\rho_1, \rho_2, \rho_3)\) is NOT TU and is NP-hard, e.g. 3D Matching or Hamiltonian Path.)

title: Chapter 21 — Total Unimodularity, Linear Programming Duality & Dual Flow Compilation
section: 4. Direction B Dual Elimination (网络流转对偶 DP): Replacing Flow with \(O(N)\) Dual Potential DP
text:
4. Direction B Dual Elimination (网络流转对偶 DP): Replacing Flow with \(O(N)\) Dual Potential DP
So far, we used LP Duality in Direction A (\(N \le 1,000\)): taking a non-flow Primal LP and dualizing it so we can run an MCMF solver.
What if the problem has \(N, M \le 10^5\) or \(5 \times 10^5\), where even the fastest MCMF solver is orders of magnitude too slow? Then we reverse the compiler and execute Direction B (Dual Elimination):

Write the Primal Flow / Covering LP (or recognize that the problem is a huge-scale flow/cut/covering LP).
Take the LP Dual to pass to vertex potentials \(\pi_i\).
Use Total Unimodularity + Complementary Slackness to prove that optimal dual potentials \(\pi^*_i\) lie in a tiny bounded discrete set (such as \(\pi_i \in \{0, 1\}\) or \(\pi_i \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\)) or obey a 1-Lipschitz constraint \(|\pi_i - \pi_{i+1}| \le 1\).
Solve the Dual LP in \(O(N)\) via Dynamic Programming or \(O(N \log N)\) via Sorting / Median without ever building a graph!



4.1 Archetype 4.1: 1D Cycle Nullspace & Dual 1-Lipschitz Median ([HAOI2008] 糖果传递, #162)
Consider \(N \le 10^6\) people sitting in a circle, where person \(i\) initially has \(a_i\) candies and needs \(\bar{a} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N a_i\) candies. Passing \(1\) candy between adjacent neighbors \(i\) and \(i+1 \pmod N\) costs \(1\).

Flow View: This is a Min-Cost Circulation on an undirected cycle \(C_N\) with node supplies \(b_i = a_i - \bar{a}\) (\(\sum b_i = 0\)) and unit edge costs \(c_e = 1\), capacities \(\infty\).
Primal Nullspace Elimination: On a single cycle of \(N\) vertices and \(N\) undirected edges, the node-arc incidence matrix \(M\) has rank \(N - 1\), so the circulation space \(\{f \in \mathbb{R}^N \mid M f = b\}\) has dimension \(N - (N - 1) = \mathbf{1}\)! Parametrizing by the single flow variable \(x = f_N \in \mathbb{R}\) (flow from \(N\) to \(1\)) forces every other edge flow to be \(f_i = x - C_i\), where \(C_i = \sum_{k=1}^i (\bar{a} - a_k)\). The total cost \(\sum_{i=1}^N |x - C_i|\) is minimized in \(O(N \log N)\) by setting \(x^* = \operatorname{median}(C_1, \dots, C_N)\).
Dual Potential View (Kantorovich–Rubinstein 1-Wasserstein Duality): The Dual of uncapacitated Min-Cost Circulation with unit edge costs \(|c_{i,i+1}| \le 1\) is:
\[
\max_{\pi \in \mathbb{R}^N} \sum_{i=1}^N b_i \, \pi_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad |\pi_{i+1} - \pi_i| \le 1 \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, N\}
\]
Substituting \(b_i = C_{i-1} - C_i\) and summing by parts (Abel summation) transforms the dual objective into \(\sum_{i=1}^N C_i (\pi_{i+1} - \pi_i)\) where \(\delta_i = \pi_{i+1} - \pi_i \in [-1, +1]\) satisfies \(\sum_{i=1}^N \delta_i = 0\). To maximize \(\sum C_i \delta_i\) subject to \(\delta_i \in [-1, +1]\) and \(\sum \delta_i = 0\), we assign \(\delta_i = +1\) to the top \(N/2\) largest \(C_i\) and \(\delta_i = -1\) to the bottom \(N/2\) smallest \(C_i\) — which is the exact dual certificate of the \(\ell_1\) median!




4.2 Archetype 4.2: Continuous Bipartite Flow-Cut Dual Elimination (AtCoder ARC 125 E — Snack, #165)
Suppose \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) snacks and \(M \le 2 \times 10^5\) children form a complete bipartite network:

Source \(S \to \text{snack } i\) has capacity \(A_i\).
Snack \(i \to \text{child } j\) has capacity \(B_j\) (every snack \(i\) can give at most \(B_j\) to child \(j\)).
Child \(j \to \text{Sink } T\) has capacity \(C_j\).

Building the \(N \times M\) bipartite graph requires \(4 \times 10^{10}\) edges — completely impossible!

Dual Elimination (Min-Cut / Dual LP): By Max-Flow Min-Cut (Section 2.2), the maximum flow equals the minimum over all subsets \(X \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) of snacks placed on the \(T\)-side (so \(S \to i\) is cut for \(i \notin X\)). Suppose \(|X| = k\) snacks remain on the \(S\)-side (\(0 \le k \le N\)).

To minimize the cut of \(S \to i\) for \(i \notin X\), we should pick \(X\) to be the \(k\) snacks with the largest \(A_i\), cutting the \(N - k\) smallest \(A_i\).
For each child \(j \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), either child \(j\) is on the \(S\)-side (cutting \(j \to T\) at cost \(C_j\)) or child \(j\) is on the \(T\)-side (cutting all \(k\) edges from \(X\) to \(j\) at cost \(k \cdot B_j\)). Thus child \(j\)’s minimum cut contribution is \(\min(C_j, k \cdot B_j)\)!


\[
\text{Max-Flow} = \min_{0 \le k \le N} \left( \underbrace{\sum_{i \notin X_k} A_i}_{\text{Sum of } N-k \text{ smallest } A_i} + \sum_{j=1}^M \min(C_j, \; k \cdot B_j) \right)
\]
Sorting \(A_i\) and sorting children by threshold \(C_j / B_j\) evaluates all \(k \in \{0, \dots, N\}\) in \(O((N + M) \log(N + M))\) time!



4.3 Archetype 4.3: Bounded-Alphabet Dual Potential DP ([ZJOI2020] 序列, #168)
What if the constraint matrix is not a complete bipartite graph and not a single C1P family, but a combination of three different interval/parity operations on an array \(a_1, \dots, a_N\) (\(N \le 10^5\))?
In Luogu P6631 [ZJOI2020] — 序列 (Sequence) (#168), we are given \(a_1, \dots, a_N \ge 0\) and want the minimum number of operations to reduce all \(a_i\) to \(0\), where each operation chooses a contiguous range \([L, R]\) and decrements by \(1\) either:

Type 1 (All): Every index \(i \in [L, R]\).
Type 2 (Odd): Every odd-indexed element in \([L, R]\).
Type 3 (Even): Every even-indexed element in \([L, R]\).


Why Primal Flow Fails & Why Dual Potential DP Triumphs
Notice that Type 1 intervals cover \([L, R]\) continuously, while Type 2 and Type 3 intervals cover \([L, R]\) with stride \(2\). Together, their incidence matrix is neither Column-C1P nor Row-C1P, and \(N \le 10^5\) forbids any flow solver!
Yet watch what happens when we write the Dual LP (assigning a dual potential \(\pi_i\) to each position \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) to maximize \(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \pi_i\)):

Every allowed subset \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) (any interval \([L, R]\), any odd-subset of \([L, R]\), any even-subset of \([L, R]\), and singleton decrements) has primal cost \(1\), so it imposes the dual constraint:
\[
\sum_{i \in S} \pi_i \le 1
\]
In Section 6 (#168), we prove using Total Unimodularity and prefix-sum bounds that:

There exists an optimal integer dual potential vector with \(\pi_i \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\) for every \(i\)!
Tracking three prefix-sum potentials — the running max subarray sum of all elements \(s_{\text{all}} \in \{0, 1\}\), odd elements \(s_{\text{odd}} \in \{0, 1\}\), and even elements \(s_{\text{even}} \in \{0, 1\}\) — compresses all \(O(N^2)\) dual constraints into a local transition automaton with at most \(27\) states, solved in \(O(N)\) linear time!

5. The 4-Step LP Duality & TU Compilation Protocol
Whenever a problem involves linear objectives, covering/packing constraints, differential inequalities, or modification costs, execute the following 4-Step LP Duality & TU Compilation Protocol before writing a single line of graph code:








Step
Action
Key Diagnostic Questions & Algebraic Checks




Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Inspect \(N, M\) bounds and why Greedy/DP fails
- Are there \(M \gg N\) overlapping interval constraints (\(N \le 10^3, M \le 10^4\))? \(\to\) Row-C1P Dual Compilation (#161).- Are edge weights modified at linear cost to control shortest paths or MSTs? \(\to\) Potential / Swap Inequality Dual (#163, #166).- Are \(N, M \le 10^5\) too large for MCMF? \(\to\) Direction B Dual Elimination (#162, #165, #168).


Step 2: Primal LP & TU Audit
Write the exact Primal LP and check the constraint matrix \(A\)
- Is \(A\) Column-C1P? \(\to\) Apply Ch 19 row differencing \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) directly.- Is \(A\) Row-C1P? \(\to\) Dualize first (\(A \mapsto A^T\) is Column-C1P), then difference (#161).- Does \(A\) have \(\pi_v - \pi_u + x_e \ge w_e\)? \(\to\) Dualize free \(\pi_v\) into flow conservation \(\nabla \cdot f = 0\) (#163).- Does \(A\) contain odd cycles? \(\to\) Check if parity coloring (#164, #167) makes it bipartite; otherwise TU fails (FM-21A).


Step 3: Mechanical Dual / Graph Compilation
Translate each dual variable/constraint into arcs or DP states
- Direction A (Flow): Map \(+1\) to tail (outflow), \(-1\) to head (inflow), primal cost \(c_e\) to dual capacity, and primal RHS \(w_e\) to dual cost.- Direction B (Dual DP): Bound the integer alphabet of \(\pi_i \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\) and build a local prefix-sum DP (#168).


Step 4: Complementary Slackness & Toy Trace
Verify signs on a 3-node toy graph and extract \(\pi^*\) if required
- Audit FM-21B: verify \(\pi_v - \pi_u \le c_{uv}\) (never \(\pi_u - \pi_v \le c_{uv}\)).- If primal potentials \(\pi^*_v\) are needed, run SPFA on active residual edges (\(\text{cap}_{\text{res}} > 0\)) from a virtual super-source \(S_{\text{pot}}\) (Section 2.5).

7. Pre-Submission Checklist (FM-21 Audit)
Before submitting any problem compiled via LP Duality, Total Unimodularity, or Dual Potential Extraction, run through this 8-point audit:









#
Audit Item
Failure Mode Prevented
Verification Rule




1
TU / Odd-Cycle Audit
FM-21A (Half-integrality gap \(1.5\) vs \(1.0\))
For undirected edge incidence or V-paths on trees, verify bipartiteness (#164 \(\Omega(a_i) \bmod 2\), #167 role split) before trusting LP integrality.


2
Dual Potential Sign Lock
FM-21B (Flipped edges \(v \to u\) vs \(u \to v\))
Always write \(\pi_v - \pi_u \le c_{uv}\) (Head minus Tail \(\le\) Cost) for a directed edge \(u \to v\).


3
Row-C1P vs. Column-C1P Orientation
Building an \(M\)-vertex graph when \(N \ll M\) (#161)
If \(M\) constraints are intervals over \(N\) variables, take the LP Dual first so the graph has \(N+1\) vertices instead of \(M+1\).


4
Cost–Capacity Role Reversal
Swapping \(c_e\) and \(w_e\) in Schedule Crashing (#163, #166)
In potential LPs (\(\pi_v - \pi_u + x_e \ge w_e\) with objective \(\sum c_e x_e\)), primal money rate \(c_e\) becomes dual capacity, and duration \(w_e\) becomes dual cost.


5
Disconnected Residual Components in \(\pi^*\)
Missing unreachable negative cycles or wrong \(\pi^*_v\) (#162)
When extracting \(\pi^*_v\) from \(G_{f^*}\) or checking feasibility of difference constraints, initialize SPFA from a virtual super-source \(S_{\text{pot}}\) connected to all vertices with cost \(0\).


6
Active Residual Capacity Filter
Relaxing along saturated \(0\)-capacity edges in \(G_{f^*}\)
In extract_dual_potentials, relax \((u \to v)\) only if e.cap > 0 in \(G_{f^*}\).


7
Persistent Hub Bypass Capacity
Blocking relay chains in path packing (#164 CF 818G)
Separate the unit-capacity vertex-split arc \(i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}\) from the persistent hub relay \(H_i \to H_{\text{next}}\) so other paths can bypass used vertices.


8
Direction B Scale Cutoff (\(N \ge 10^5\))
TLE from running MCMF on \(N = 10^5\) (#162, #165, #168)
When \(N \ge 10^5\), pass to the Dual LP and solve via sorting/median (#162, #165), 0-1 BFS (#166), or bounded-state Kadane DP (#168).

8. Chapter Summary, Quarantined Template Problems & Bridge to Part V Checkpoint (CP-V)

8.1 Synthesis of Part V (Chapters 16–21)
Chapter 21 completes our Algebraic Flow Compilation Engine:

Chapter 16 (MCMF) & Chapter 17 (Circulations) gave us the algorithmic machinery for solving min-cost flows with demands and lower bounds.
Chapter 19 (Equation Differencing) showed that Column-C1P LPs compile into directed flow networks via consecutive row differencing \(U A_{\text{C1P}} = M_{\text{flow}}\).
Chapter 20 (Convex Split & Dynamic Simulation) extended linear flows to separable convex costs and online slope-DP simulation.
Chapter 21 (TU & LP Duality) proved why all of these relaxations are integral (Hoffman–Kruskal + Ghouila–Houri), showed how to compile Row-C1P and Differential Potential LPs by transposing \(A \mapsto A^T\) via Direction A Dual Compilation, and showed how to eliminate the flow solver altogether when \(N \le 10^5\) via Direction B Dual Potential DP.

Next, in Part V Checkpoint (CP-V), you will face mixed diagnostic drills where the problem statement gives zero hint as to whether it requires direct Ch 19 equation differencing, Ch 20 convex marginal splitting, Ch 21 Direction A Dual Compilation, or Ch 21 Direction B Dual Potential DP — testing your ability to classify and compile from raw English constraints alone.



8.2 Quarantined Template Problems
The following standard difference-constraint and textbook verification problems are quarantined from the main ladder to prevent template memorization; use them only as warm-up syntax checks:

Problem Title
Reason for Quarantine

Direct textbook difference-constraint \(\pi_v - \pi_u \le c_{uv}\) template check.

Direct 3-case translation of \(\pi_a - \pi_b \ge c\), \(\pi_a - \pi_b \le c\), and \(\pi_a = \pi_b\) into SPFA negative-cycle detection.


POJ 1201 / Luogu P1250

Standard prefix-sum interval difference constraint \(\pi_{R} - \pi_{L-1} \ge C\) with \(0 \le \pi_i - \pi_{i-1} \le 1\).

title: Chapter 19 — Disjoint K-Interval Coverage & The Algebraic Equation-Difference Method
text:
Before studying this chapter, make sure you are comfortable with:

Chapter 01 (Flow Conservation, Residual Networks & Max-Flow Min-Cut): Interpreting nodal flow conservation \(\text{OutFlow}(u) - \text{InFlow}(u) = b_u\) as a linear system \(A \mathbf{f} = \mathbf{b}\) where every column of the node-arc incidence matrix \(A\) contains at most one \(+1\) (at the arc’s tail) and at most one \(-1\) (at the arc’s head).
Chapter 04 (Lower-Bound Flows & Feasibility Circulations): Compiling nodal supplies/demands \(b_u \in \mathbb{R}\) and edge capacity intervals \([l_e, u_e]\) into a standard \(S^*\)-\(T^*\) auxiliary network, and using Mandatory Initial Saturation (负权边强制满流消圈法) to eliminate negative-cost cycles.
Chapter 17 (Minimum-Cost Max-Flow, Johnson Potentials & Slope Convexity): Running Primal-Dual / Successive Shortest Path (SSP) with Dijkstra, initializing potentials \(\pi_0\) via \(O(V + E)\) topological dynamic programming when the initial support is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), and reconstructing discrete decisions from optimal integer flows.
Chapter 18 (Circulation Cost-Scaling & Separable Convex Cost Flows): Bundling piecewise-linear convex cost brackets into parallel arcs and reasoning about marginal cost increments.




By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Compile Contiguous Interval Linear Programs Mechanically via Consecutive Equation Differencing (流守恒差分建模法, \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\)): Starting from a pure algebraic system of interval covering inequalities with zero graphs mentioned, introduce explicit slack/surplus variables \(y_i \ge 0\), pad boundary equations \(E_0: 0 = 0\) and \(E_{n+1}: 0 = 0\), and take consecutive row differences \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) to transform every Consecutive-Ones (C1P) column into a single \(+1\) and a single \(-1\).
Eliminate Off-by-One Endpoint & Slack-Polarity Bugs (FM-19 / H-21): Prove from first principles why a closed interval \([l_j, r_j]\) compiles into the directed arc \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) (requiring vertex \(n+1\)), why a lower-bound surplus slack \(-y_i\) compiles into a backward spine arc \(i + 1 \to i\) ([NOI2008] Volunteer Recruitment #148), and why an upper-bound slack \(+y_i\) compiles into a forward spine arc \(i \to i + 1\).
Compile Doubly-Bounded Sliding Windows via Capacitated Slack Arcs: Transform two-sided window constraints \(L_i \le \sum_{j \in W_i} x_j \le R_i\) into exact equations using a single bounded slack variable \(y_i \in [0, R_i - L_i]\), and reconcile the Forward-DAG Upper-Slack compilation with the Backward-Spine Lower-Slack compilation ([NEERC 2016] Delight for a Cat #151).
Unify \(K\)-Overlapping Interval Selection (最长k可重区间集) and 2D Segment Coordinate Doubling (\(x \mapsto (2x, 2x+1)\)): Prove the exact algebraic isomorphism between the intuitive “backbone \(i \to i+1\) with bypass chords \(l_j \to r_j\)” model and the equation-difference model, and resolve the vertical-segment self-loop degeneracy \(x_1 = x_2\) in [网络流24题] 最长k可重线段集 (#147) via coordinate doubling.
Generalize Equation Differencing to Rooted Trees (树上流守恒差分): Extend linear differencing \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) to tree-path coverings via \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u = E_u - \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} E_v\) ([ICPC 2018 Nanjing] #152).

title: Chapter 19 — Disjoint K-Interval Coverage & The Algebraic Equation-Difference Method
section: 1. The Algebraic Equation-Difference Compiler (流守恒差分建模法: \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\))
text:
1. The Algebraic Equation-Difference Compiler (流守恒差分建模法: \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\))

1.1 Why Traditional Interval-Flow Editorials Violate the “Zero Magic Gadgets” Mandate
Open almost any traditional editorial for the classic [NOI2008 / Luogu P3980] 志愿者招募 (Volunteer Recruitment, #148) and you will be greeted by a baffling recipe presented out of thin air:

“Create \(n + 1\) vertices \(1, 2, \dots, n + 1\). Connect \(S \to i\) with capacity \(A_i - A_{i-1}\) if \(A_i - A_{i-1} > 0\), or connect \(i \to T\) with capacity \(A_{i-1} - A_i\) if \(A_i - A_{i-1} < 0\). Add a backward edge \(i + 1 \to i\) of capacity \(\infty\) and cost \(0\) for each \(i = 1, \dots, n\). For each volunteer type \([l_j, r_j]\), add a forward edge \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) of capacity \(\infty\) and cost \(c_j\). Run Min-Cost Max-Flow.”

A programmer meeting this construction for the first time asks four completely legitimate questions:

Why are there \(n + 1\) vertices when the problem only has \(n\) days?
Where did the finite difference \(A_i - A_{i-1}\) come from?
Why does a volunteer working on days \([l_j, r_j]\) connect to \(r_j + 1\) instead of \(r_j\)?
Why do the free spine edges point backward (\(i + 1 \to i\)) in lower-bound coverage, whereas they point forward (\(i \to i + 1\)) in upper-bound interval packing?

The answer is not a clever geometric picture of people walking along a corridor. It is pure linear algebra—specifically, the Algebraic Equation-Difference Method (流守恒差分建模法), formalized in Chinese competitive programming by Bushu Zhou (周冬) in the 2009 National Training Team Papers (国家集训队论文).
Once you understand this four-step algebraic compiler, you will never guess a vertex count, an arc orientation, or a right-hand-side supply again.


1.2 Step 1 — Starting from Pure Linear Inequalities (Zero Graphs Mentioned)
Suppose a problem gives us a discrete timeline of \(n\) positions (days, hours, or elementary segments) indexed by \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\), and \(m\) decision variables \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m\). Each decision variable \(x_j \in [0, u_j]\) (with unit cost \(c_j \in \mathbb{R}\) and upper bound \(u_j \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \cup \{\infty\}\)) is active across a contiguous closed interval of positions \([l_j, r_j] \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) (\(1 \le l_j \le r_j \le n\)).
On each position \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\), the total number of active variables covering position \(i\) must be at least \(A_i\):
\[
\min_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{Z}^m} \sum_{j=1}^m c_j x_j \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{j \,:\, l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j \ge A_i \quad (i = 1, 2, \dots, n), \qquad 0 \le x_j \le u_j.
\]
Why isn’t this linear program already a network flow problem?
Recall from Chapter 01 that in any directed network \(G = (V, E)\), the flow conservation equations at the vertices \(i \in V\):
\[
\text{OutFlow}(i) - \text{InFlow}(i) = \sum_{e \in \delta^+(i)} f_e - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(i)} f_e = b_i
\]
have a very rigid matrix structure: each flow variable \(f_e\) (corresponding to a directed arc \(e = (u \to v)\)) appears in the entire system of equations at most twice—once with coefficient \(+1\) in the equation for its tail vertex \(u\), and once with coefficient \(-1\) in the equation for its head vertex \(v\).
In our interval covering system, by contrast, variable \(x_j\) appears with coefficient \(+1\) in every inequality \(i \in \{l_j, l_j + 1, \dots, r_j\}\). If we stack the \(n\) constraints as rows of an \(n \times m\) matrix \(M\), the \(j\)-th column of \(M\) is a contiguous block of \(r_j - l_j + 1\) ones:
\[
M_{*, j} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \cdots & 0 & \underbrace{1 \quad 1 \quad \cdots \quad 1}_{\text{rows } l_j \text{ through } r_j} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{bmatrix}^T.
\]
A \(\{0, 1\}\)-matrix whose ones in every column form a single contiguous block is said to satisfy the Consecutive-Ones Property (连续 1 性质, C1P) on columns.


1.3 Step 2 — Slack Variables \(y_i \ge 0\) and Consecutive Row Differencing (\(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\))
How do we transform a column containing a contiguous run of ones \((0, \dots, 0, 1, 1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0)^T\) into a column containing only a single \(+1\) and a single \(-1\)?
First, we cannot subtract two inequalities \(\ge\) from one another directly (if \(\alpha \ge A_2\) and \(\beta \ge A_1\), it does not follow that \(\alpha - \beta \ge A_2 - A_1\)). Therefore, we must first convert every inequality into an exact linear equation by introducing an explicit non-negative surplus (slack) variable \(y_i \ge 0\) for each position \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\):
\[
y_i := \left(\sum_{j \,:\, l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j\right) - A_i \ge 0 \qquad (i = 1, 2, \dots, n).
\]
Physically, \(y_i \ge 0\) counts the excess coverage at position \(i\) above the required threshold \(A_i\), and incurs zero cost (\(0 \cdot y_i\)) in the objective function. Rewriting the \(n\) constraints as exact equalities \(E_1, E_2, \dots, E_n\):
\[
E_i : \quad \sum_{j \,:\, l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j - y_i = A_i \qquad (i = 1, 2, \dots, n, \quad y_i \ge 0).
\]
Second, to ensure that intervals starting at \(l_j = 1\) and intervals ending at \(r_j = n\) both have a clean boundary when we take row differences, we pad the system at the top and bottom with two trivial dummy equations \(E_0\) and \(E_{n+1}\) (defining \(A_0 := 0\), \(A_{n+1} := 0\), \(y_0 \equiv 0\), and \(y_{n+1} \equiv 0\)):
\[
E_0 : \quad 0 = 0, \qquad\qquad E_{n+1} : \quad 0 = 0.
\]
Now, replace the system \((E_1, E_2, \dots, E_n, E_{n+1})\) by the \(n + 1\) consecutive difference equations:
\[
\Delta E_i := E_i - E_{i-1} \qquad \text{for } i = 1, 2, \dots, n + 1.
\]
Why is this replacement lossless? Because for any \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, n+1\}\), the prefix sum of the first \(k\) difference equations telescopes back to \(E_k\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \Delta E_i = \sum_{i=1}^k (E_i - E_{i-1}) = E_k - E_0 = E_k.
\]
In matrix terms, premultiplying by the \((n+1) \times n\) first-difference operator \(D\) maps the solution space bijectively onto the subspace of \((\Delta E_1, \dots, \Delta E_{n+1})\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} \Delta E_i = E_{n+1} - E_0 = 0\).


1.4 Step 3 — The Consecutive-Ones Telescoping Theorem (Why Every Column Becomes an Arc)
Let us compute the exact coefficient of each interval variable \(x_j\) and each slack variable \(y_k\) across the \(n + 1\) differenced equations \(\Delta E_1, \Delta E_2, \dots, \Delta E_{n+1}\).






ImportantTheorem 19.1 (The Consecutive-Ones Telescoping Law)



Let \(E_i : \sum_{j : l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j - y_i = A_i\) (\(i = 1, \dots, n\)) be a Consecutive-Ones linear system padded with \(E_0: 0 = 0\) and \(E_{n+1}: 0 = 0\). In the differenced system \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) for \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n + 1\):

Interval Variable \(x_j\) (active on \([l_j, r_j] \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\)):

For \(1 \le i < l_j\): \(x_j\) appears in neither \(E_i\) nor \(E_{i-1}\), so its coefficient in \(\Delta E_i\) is \(0 - 0 = 0\).
At \(i = l_j\): \(x_j\) appears in \(E_{l_j}\) (coefficient \(+1\)) and does not appear in \(E_{l_j - 1}\) (coefficient \(0\)), so its coefficient in \(\Delta E_{l_j}\) is \(+1 - 0 = +1\).
For \(l_j < i \le r_j\): \(x_j\) appears in both \(E_i\) (\(+1\)) and \(E_{i-1}\) (\(+1\)), so its coefficient in \(\Delta E_i\) cancels identically: \(+1 - 1 = 0\)!
At \(i = r_j + 1\): \(x_j\) does not appear in \(E_{r_j + 1}\) (\(0\)) and does appear in \(E_{r_j}\) (\(+1\)), so its coefficient in \(\Delta E_{r_j + 1}\) is \(0 - 1 = -1\).
For \(r_j + 1 < i \le n + 1\): \(x_j\) appears in neither equation, so its coefficient is \(0\).

Surplus Slack Variable \(y_k\) (\(1 \le k \le n\), appearing only in \(E_k\) with coefficient \(-1\)):

At \(i = k\): in \(\Delta E_k = E_k - E_{k-1}\), \(y_k\) has coefficient \(-1 - 0 = -1\).
At \(i = k + 1\): in \(\Delta E_{k+1} = E_{k+1} - E_k\), \(y_k\) has coefficient \(0 - (-1) = +1\).
For all \(i \notin \{k, k + 1\}\): \(y_k\) has coefficient \(0\).

Right-Hand Side Nodal Demand \(b_i\):

The right-hand side of \(\Delta E_i\) is \(b_i := A_i - A_{i-1}\) (with \(A_0 = A_{n+1} = 0\)), satisfying total balance \(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} b_i = A_{n+1} - A_0 = 0\).




Look at the column for \(x_j\) before and after differencing:
\[
\text{Before } (\text{rows } 1 \dots n): \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ \vdots \\ l_j - 1 \\ l_j \\ l_j + 1 \\ \vdots \\ r_j \\ r_j + 1 \\ \vdots \\ n \end{array}
\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ +1 \\ +1 \\ \vdots \\ +1 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad \xrightarrow{\quad \Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1} \quad} \qquad
\text{After } (\text{rows } 1 \dots n+1): \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ \vdots \\ l_j - 1 \\ \mathbf{l_j} \\ l_j + 1 \\ \vdots \\ r_j \\ \mathbf{r_j + 1} \\ \vdots \\ n + 1 \end{array}
\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ \mathbf{+1} \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ \mathbf{-1} \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Every single column in the entire differenced system \(\Delta E_1, \dots, \Delta E_{n+1}\) now has literally one \(+1\) and one \(-1\)!


1.5 Step 4 — Mechanical Graph Compilation from \(\Delta E_i\)
Writing out the \(i\)-th difference equation \(\Delta E_i\) (\(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n+1\}\)) and grouping the \(+1\) terms (outflow) and \(-1\) terms (inflow) gives:
\[
\Delta E_i : \quad \underbrace{\left(\sum_{j \,:\, l_j = i} x_j + y_{i-1}\right)}_{\text{OutFlow}(i) \text{ (coeff } +1\text{)}} - \underbrace{\left(\sum_{j \,:\, r_j + 1 = i} x_j + y_i\right)}_{\text{InFlow}(i) \text{ (coeff } -1\text{)}} = A_i - A_{i-1} =: b_i,
\]
where \(y_0 \equiv 0\) and \(y_{n+1} \equiv 0\).
Now create \(n + 1\) timeline vertices \(V_{\text{time}} = \{1, 2, \dots, n + 1\}\), plus a super-source \(S\) and super-sink \(T\). Under the standard nodal conservation law \(\text{OutFlow}(i) - \text{InFlow}(i) = b_i\):

Any non-negative variable \(z \in [0, U]\) with unit cost \(c\) that has \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_u\) (outflow from \(u\)) and \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_v\) (inflow to \(v\)) is compiled into a directed arc:
\[
u \xrightarrow{\text{cap } U, \;\text{cost } c} v.
\]

Applying this rule mechanically to every term in \(\Delta E_i\) produces the complete network specification:

Row with \(-1\) (Head \(v\))

Every mystery from Section 1.1 is now completely resolved:

Why \(n + 1\) vertices? Because an interval \([l_j, r_j]\) covering day \(r_j = n\) is still active in \(E_n\) and only drops out in \(E_{n+1}: 0 = 0\), placing its \(-1\) coefficient in \(\Delta E_{n+1}\) (vertex \(n + 1\)).
Why \(A_i - A_{i-1}\)? Because the right-hand side of \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) is literally \(A_i - A_{i-1}\).
Why \(l_j \to r_j + 1\)? Because \(x_j\) enters at row \(l_j\) (\(E_{l_j} - E_{l_j - 1}\)) and leaves at row \(r_j + 1\) (\(E_{r_j + 1} - E_{r_j}\)).
Why does the slack edge point backward (\(i + 1 \to i\)) for \(\ge A_i\) but forward (\(i \to i + 1\)) for \(\le K_i\)? Because in \(\sum x_j - y_i = A_i\), the slack variable has sign \(-y_i\) in \(E_i\), giving \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_i\) and \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_{i+1}\) (\(i + 1 \to i\)); whereas in \(\sum x_j + y_i = K_i\), the slack variable has sign \(+y_i\) in \(E_i\), giving \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_i\) and \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_{i+1}\) (\(i \to i + 1\))!







WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexample FM-19 (↔︎ H-21): Off-by-One Interval Wiring (\(l_j \to r_j\) vs. \(l_j \to r_j + 1\)) & Missing Vertex \(n + 1\)



Suppose \(n = 2\) days with requirements \(A_1 = 1, A_2 = 1\), and we have a volunteer type covering the closed interval \([l_1, r_1] = [1, 2]\) at cost \(c_1 = 5\), plus single-day volunteers \([1, 1]\) (cost \(4\)) and \([2, 2]\) (cost \(4\)).

What breaks if you wire \([l_j, r_j]\) as \(l_j \to r_j\) instead of \(l_j \to r_j + 1\)?

The single-day volunteers \([1, 1]\) and \([2, 2]\) become self-loops \(1 \to 1\) and \(2 \to 2\) that cannot carry any net flow between vertices!
Meanwhile, the two-day volunteer \([1, 2]\) becomes the arc \(1 \to 2\), which only has \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_1\) and \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_2\). Undifferencing \(+1\) at row \(1\) and \(-1\) at row \(2\) corresponds to covering only day \(1\) (\([1, 2 - 1] = [1, 1]\)), leaving day \(2\) completely uncovered!

What breaks if you wire \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) but only allocate \(n\) vertices (omitting \(\Delta E_{n+1}\))?

In \(E_1, \dots, E_n\), \(b_1 = A_1 - 0 = +1\) and \(b_2 = A_2 - A_1 = 0\), so \(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i = A_n = 1 \ne 0\)! There is no sink demand \(b_{n+1} = 0 - A_n = -1\) at vertex \(n + 1\), so the flow network has \(0\) sink capacity and outputs cost \(0\)!

Audit Rule (H-21): Whenever an interval \([l_j, r_j]\) is closed on integer indices \(1 \dots n\), its half-open span is \([l_j, r_j + 1)\), its arc is \(l_j \to r_j + 1\), and the timeline requires \(n + 1\) vertices.

section: 2. Flagship Deep-Dive Case Studies: [NOI2008] 志愿者招募 (#148) & Doubly-Bounded Sliding Windows ([NEERC 2016] Delight for a Cat #151)
text:
2. Flagship Deep-Dive Case Studies: [NOI2008] 志愿者招募 (#148) & Doubly-Bounded Sliding Windows ([NEERC 2016] Delight for a Cat #151)
Let us now apply the Equation-Difference Compiler to two flagship problems: first, a complete numerical walkthrough of [NOI2008] Volunteer Recruitment (#148), and second, the two-sided sliding-window generalization [NEERC 2016] Delight for a Cat (#151).

2.1 Hand-Checkable Toy Trace of [NOI2008 / Luogu P3980] 志愿者招募 (#148)
Consider a \(n = 3\) day project with daily volunteer requirements:
\[
A_1 = 2, \qquad A_2 = 3, \qquad A_3 = 1 \qquad (\text{with boundary } A_0 = 0, \; A_4 = 0),
\]
and \(m = 3\) volunteer types (\(x_1, x_2, x_3 \in [0, \infty)\)):

Type 1: works days \([l_1, r_1] = [1, 2]\), cost \(c_1 = 4\).
Type 2: works days \([l_2, r_2] = [2, 3]\), cost \(c_2 = 2\).
Type 3: works days \([l_3, r_3] = [1, 3]\), cost \(c_3 = 5\).


Step-by-Step Algebraic Compilation

Equality System \(E_0, \dots, E_4\) with Surplus Slacks \(y_1, y_2, y_3 \ge 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_0 &: & 0 &= 0 \\
E_1 &: & x_1 \phantom{{}+ x_2} + x_3 - y_1 &= 2 \\
E_2 &: & x_1 + x_2 + x_3 - y_2 &= 3 \\
E_3 &: & \phantom{x_1 +{}} x_2 + x_3 - y_3 &= 1 \\
E_4 &: & 0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Consecutive Equation Differences \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) (\(i = 1, 2, 3, 4\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta E_1 = E_1 - E_0 &: & +x_1 \phantom{{}+ x_2} + x_3 - y_1 \phantom{{}+ y_2 - y_3} &= 2 - 0 = +2 \\
\Delta E_2 = E_2 - E_1 &: & \phantom{+x_1} + x_2 \phantom{{}+ x_3} + y_1 - y_2 \phantom{{}- y_3} &= 3 - 2 = +1 \\
\Delta E_3 = E_3 - E_2 &: & -x_1 \phantom{{}+ x_2 + x_3 + y_1} + y_2 - y_3 &= 1 - 3 = -2 \\
\Delta E_4 = E_4 - E_3 &: & \phantom{-x_1} - x_2 - x_3 \phantom{{}+ y_1 + y_2} + y_3 &= 0 - 1 = -1
\end{aligned}
\]
Reading Off the Flow Graph (\(V = \{S, T, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\)):

Source / Sink Supplies & Demands:

\(b_1 = +2 \implies S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 2, \text{cost } 0} 1\)
\(b_2 = +1 \implies S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} 2\)
\(b_3 = -2 \implies 3 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 2, \text{cost } 0} T\)
\(b_4 = -1 \implies 4 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} T\)

Volunteer Arcs (\(l_j \to r_j + 1\)):

\(x_1\): \(1 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 4} 3\)
\(x_2\): \(2 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 2} 4\)
\(x_3\): \(1 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 5} 4\)

Backward Surplus Spine Arcs (\(i + 1 \to i\)):

\(y_1\): \(2 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0} 1\)
\(y_2\): \(3 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0} 2\)
\(y_3\): \(4 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0} 3\)








flowchart LR
    S(["Source S"])
    T(["Sink T"])
    v1["Node 1 (b1 = +2)"]
    v2["Node 2 (b2 = +1)"]
    v3["Node 3 (b3 = -2)"]
    v4["Node 4 (b4 = -1)"]

    S -- "cap 2, cost 0" --> v1
    S -- "cap 1, cost 0" --> v2
    v1 -- "x1: cap inf, cost 4" --> v3
    v2 -- "x2: cap inf, cost 2" --> v4
    v1 -- "x3: cap inf, cost 5" --> v4
    v2 -- "y1: cap inf, cost 0" --> v1
    v3 -- "y2: cap inf, cost 0" --> v2
    v4 -- "y3: cap inf, cost 0" --> v3
    v3 -- "cap 2, cost 0" --> T
    v4 -- "cap 1, cost 0" --> T







Tracing SSP Augmentations and the Physical Meaning of Slack Flow:

Total supply leaving \(S\) is \(b_1 + b_2 = 2 + 1 = 3\) units. Notice that all initial edge costs are non-negative (\(c_j \ge 0\) and \(0\)), so \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\) is immediately a valid Johnson potential even though the graph contains directed cycles such as \(1 \xrightarrow{x_1} 3 \xrightarrow{y_2} 2 \xrightarrow{y_1} 1\)!
Candidate Flow 1: Route \(2\) units along \(S \to 1 \xrightarrow{x_1} 3 \to T\) (cost \(2 \times 4 = 8\)) and \(1\) unit along \(S \to 2 \xrightarrow{x_2} 4 \to T\) (cost \(1 \times 2 = 2\)), for a total cost of \(8 + 2 = 10\).
Candidate Flow 2 (Using \(x_3\) and a Backward Slack Arc): Wait—what if we route \(1\) unit along \(S \to 1 \xrightarrow{x_3 \text{ (cost 5)}} 4 \xrightarrow{y_3 \text{ (cost 0)}} 3 \to T\), \(1\) unit along \(S \to 1 \xrightarrow{x_1 \text{ (cost 4)}} 3 \to T\), and \(1\) unit along \(S \to 2 \xrightarrow{x_2 \text{ (cost 2)}} 4 \to T\)?

Here \((x_1, x_2, x_3) = (1, 1, 1)\) and \((y_1, y_2, y_3) = (0, 0, 1)\), with total cost \(4 + 2 + 5 = 11 > 10\).
Look at what the \(1\) unit of flow on the backward slack arc \(4 \xrightarrow{y_3} 3\) means algebraically: on day \(3\), both \(x_2 = 1\) and \(x_3 = 1\) are working, giving \(1 + 1 = 2\) volunteers when only \(A_3 = 1\) is needed. That \(1\) extra volunteer on day \(3\) is the surplus \(y_3 = 2 - 1 = 1\), which flows backward from \(4 \to 3\) so that \(x_3\)’s endpoint at \(4\) can satisfy node \(3\)’s demand!

Thus the minimum cost is \(10\), achieved uniquely by \((x_1, x_2, x_3) = (2, 1, 0)\) and \((y_1, y_2, y_3) = (0, 0, 0)\).





2.2 Doubly-Bounded Sliding Windows ([NEERC 2016] Delight for a Cat #151)
Now suppose a problem imposes both a lower bound \(L_i\) and an upper bound \(R_i\) on each constraint row \(i\):
\[
L_i \le \sum_{j \,:\, l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j \le R_i \qquad (i = 1, 2, \dots, W).
\]
This exact structure arises in [ICPC NEERC 2016 D / Luogu P6967] Delight for a Cat (#151) (and [ONTAK 2010] Vacation):

Across \(n\) hours \(j \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\), a cat must choose either to sleep (gaining \(s_j\) happiness) or to eat (gaining \(e_j\) happiness) in each hour \(j\).
In every contiguous sliding window of \(k\) hours \([i, i + k - 1]\) (\(i = 1, 2, \dots, n - k + 1\)), the cat must sleep for at least \(m_s\) hours and eat for at least \(m_e\) hours (\(m_s + m_e \le k\)).
Maximize the cat’s total happiness across the \(n\) hours.


Step 1: Dualizing Point Decisions into Interval Columns
If the cat sleeps in all \(n\) hours, its baseline happiness is \(S_{\text{base}} = \sum_{j=1}^n s_j\). Let \(x_j \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether the cat switches hour \(j\) from sleeping to eating, which changes happiness by \(w_j = e_j - s_j\) (equivalent to minimizing cost \(c_j = -w_j = s_j - e_j\)).
Let \(W = n - k + 1\) be the number of sliding windows. In window \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, W\}\) (spanning hours \(j \in [i, i + k - 1]\)):

Eating at least \(m_e\) hours means \(\sum_{j=i}^{i+k-1} x_j \ge m_e =: L\).
Sleeping at least \(m_s\) hours means eating at most \(k - m_s\) hours: \(\sum_{j=i}^{i+k-1} x_j \le k - m_s =: R\).

Now ask: Which window constraints \(E_i\) (\(1 \le i \le W\)) contain the decision variable \(x_j\)?
\[
x_j \text{ appears in } E_i \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad i \le j \le i + k - 1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad j - k + 1 \le i \le j.
\]
Intersecting with \(1 \le i \le W\), variable \(x_j\) appears with coefficient \(+1\) in the single contiguous interval of window indices \([l_j, r_j]\) given by:
\[
l_j = \max(1, \; j - k + 1), \qquad r_j = \min(W, \; j) \qquad (1 \le l_j \le r_j \le W)!
\]
Thus, the sliding-window constraint matrix has the Consecutive-Ones Property on columns!


Step 2: Turning Two-Sided Inequalities \(L_i \le \text{sum}_i \le R_i\) into a Single Bounded Slack Variable
At first glance, \(L_i \le \sum_{j : l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j \le R_i\) looks like two separate inequalities per window \(i\). If we wrote two separate rows per window, each variable \(x_j\) would appear in two non-adjacent blocks of rows, destroying the Consecutive-Ones Property!
Instead, observe that a two-sided inequality \(L_i \le S_i \le R_i\) is 100% equivalent to a single equality with a capacity-bounded slack variable of range \([0, R_i - L_i]\)! Moreover, we have two dual choices for how to define that slack variable:











Compilation Variant
Slack Variable Definition
Equality \(E_i\) (\(i = 1, \dots, W\))
Differenced Arc for \(x_j\)
Differenced Arc for Slack
Nodal Balance \(b_i\) (when \(L_i \equiv L, R_i \equiv R\))




Variant A: Upper-Slack Forward-DAG
\(y_i := R_i - \sum x_j \in [0, R_i - L_i]\) (unused upper capacity)
\(\sum_{j : l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j + y_i = R_i\)
\(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -w_j} r_j + 1\)
\(i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } R_i - L_i, \text{cost } 0} i + 1\) (forward!)
\(b_1 = +R\), \(b_{W+1} = -R\), \(b_2 = \dots = b_W = 0\)


Variant B: Lower-Slack Backward-Spine
\(z_i := \sum x_j - L_i \in [0, R_i - L_i]\) (surplus above lower bound)
\(\sum_{j : l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j - z_i = L_i\)
\(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -w_j} r_j + 1\)
\(i + 1 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } R_i - L_i, \text{cost } 0} i\) (backward!)
\(b_1 = +L\), \(b_{W+1} = -L\), \(b_2 = \dots = b_W = 0\)









TipWhy Both Compilations Are Algebraically Isomorphic — And When to Prefer Variant A vs. Variant B



Notice that \(y_i + z_i = R_i - L_i\): sending \(z_i\) units backward on \(i + 1 \to i\) is literally the residual reverse of sending \(y_i = (R_i - L_i) - z_i\) units forward on \(i \to i + 1\)!

Why Variant A (Upper-Slack Forward-DAG) is Magical: In Variant A, both the decision arcs \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) and the slack arcs \(i \to i + 1\) point strictly from smaller index to larger index (\(u < v\)). Therefore, the initial network on vertices \(1, 2, \dots, W + 1\) is a strictly topological DAG! Even though \(-w_j = s_j - e_j\) can be negative when \(e_j > s_j\), there are zero directed cycles at \(f = 0\), so we can compute initial Johnson potentials \(\pi_0\) in \(O(n + W)\) time via a single left-to-right DAG DP pass and run \(R = k - m_s\) steps of pure Dijkstra without SPFA or pre-saturation!
How Variant B (Lower-Slack Backward-Spine) Works: In Variant B, the total flow from \(1\) to \(W+1\) is only \(L = m_e\) units (which is smaller when \(m_e \ll k - m_s\)), and the negative-cost arcs \(l_j \to r_j + 1\) (\(e_j > s_j\)) can be handled in \(O(n)\) setup via Mandatory Initial Saturation (Ch 04 / Ch 17) so that \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\) works for Dijkstra!

title: Chapter 19 — Disjoint K-Interval Coverage & The Algebraic Equation-Difference Method
section: 3. \(K\)-Overlapping Interval Selection (最长k可重区间集) — Backbone Bypass vs. Equation Differencing
text:
3. \(K\)-Overlapping Interval Selection (最长k可重区间集) — Backbone Bypass vs. Equation Differencing
We now turn to the packing dual of NOI2008 志愿者招募: instead of covering each point \(i\) at least \(A_i\) times at minimum cost, we are given \(m\) weighted intervals \(I_j\) with profits \(w_j > 0\) and must select a subset of intervals of maximum total weight such that no point on the real line is covered by more than \(K\) selected intervals ([Luogu P3358] 最长k可重区间集问题 (#145), [POJ 3680] Intervals (#146), [CF 164C] Machine Programming).

3.1 The 4-Step Compilation of Maximum-Weight \(K\)-Interval Packing

Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Why Greedy and Standard DP Fail for \(K \ge 2\):

When \(K = 1\) and \(w_j \equiv 1\), classic earliest-deadline-first greedy runs in \(O(m \log m)\) time.
When \(K = 1\) and weights \(w_j\) are arbitrary, sorting by right endpoint and running 1D DP with binary search runs in \(O(m \log m)\) time because the last chosen interval completely summarizes the suffix compatibility state.
When \(K \ge 2\) and weights \(w_j\) are arbitrary, a naive DP from left to right must remember the right endpoints of all \(K\) currently active intervals, blowing up the state space to \(O(m^K)\). Yet the constraint “at every coordinate \(x\), at most \(K\) chosen intervals cover \(x\)” is a system of linear upper-bound inequalities where each interval covers a contiguous range of coordinates!




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation & Half-Open Normalization
Before writing down linear equations, we must normalize the geometry of intervals so that endpoint touching semantics match the problem statement:

Open Intervals \(I_j = (L_j, R_j)\) (e.g., Luogu P3358, POJ 3680, CF 164C): Two intervals \((1, 3)\) and \((3, 5)\) do not overlap at \(x = 3\). After coordinate-compressing the distinct endpoint values into \(1 < 2 < \dots < n\), the real line between \(1\) and \(n\) is partitioned into \(n - 1\) elementary half-open segments \(S_i = [i, i + 1)\) for \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n - 1\). An open interval \((l_j, r_j)\) (in compressed indices \(1 \le l_j < r_j \le n\)) covers the contiguous range of elementary segments \(S_i\) for \(i \in \{l_j, l_j + 1, \dots, r_j - 1\}\).
Closed Intervals \(I_j = [L_j, R_j]\) (Integer Points): Two intervals \([1, 3]\) and \([3, 5]\) do overlap at the integer point \(x = 3\). By shifting the right endpoint \(R_j \gets R_j + 1\), every closed integer interval \([L_j, R_j]\) becomes the half-open interval \([L_j, R_j + 1)\), reducing immediately to the open-interval case!

Now let \(x_j \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether interval \(I_j = [l_j, r_j)\) is selected, and introduce unused-capacity slack variables \(y_i \ge 0\) for each elementary segment \(S_i = [i, i + 1)\) (\(i = 1, 2, \dots, n - 1\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Maximize} \quad & \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j x_j \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{j=1}^{m} (-w_j) x_j \\
\text{subject to} \quad & E_i : \quad \sum_{j \,:\, l_j \le i \le r_j - 1} x_j + y_i = K, \qquad i = 1, 2, \dots, n - 1, \\
& x_j \in [0, 1], \quad y_i \in [0, \infty).
\end{aligned}
\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Equation Differencing vs. Backbone Bypass)
Attach boundary equations \(E_0 : 0 = 0\) and \(E_n : 0 = 0\), and take consecutive differences \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) for \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\):

Decision Variable \(x_j \in [0, 1]\) (covering rows \(i \in \{l_j, \dots, r_j - 1\}\)):

Enters at \(\Delta E_{l_j}\) with coefficient \(+1\) and exits at \(\Delta E_{(r_j - 1) + 1} = \Delta E_{r_j}\) with coefficient \(-1\).
Compiles to a forward bypass arc:
\[
e_{x_j} = (l_j \to r_j), \qquad \text{cap} = 1, \qquad \text{cost} = -w_j.
\]

Unused-Capacity Slack Variable \(y_i \in [0, \infty)\) (appearing in row \(E_i\) with coefficient \(+1\)):

Enters at \(\Delta E_i\) with coefficient \(+1\) and exits at \(\Delta E_{i+1}\) with coefficient \(-1\).
Compiles to a forward backbone arc:
\[
e_{y_i} = (i \to i + 1), \qquad \text{cap} = \infty \text{ (or } K\text{)}, \qquad \text{cost} = 0.
\]

Right-Hand Side Supplies & Demands \(b_i = K_i - K_{i-1}\):

Since \(K_0 = 0\), \(K_1 = K_2 = \dots = K_{n-1} = K\), and \(K_n = 0\):
\[
b_1 = K - 0 = +K, \qquad b_2 = b_3 = \dots = b_{n-1} = K - K = 0, \qquad b_n = 0 - K = -K.
\]
Only vertex \(1\) receives supply \(+K\) from \(S\) (\(S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } K, \text{cost } 0} 1\)), and only vertex \(n\) sends demand \(K\) to \(T\) (\(n \xrightarrow{\text{cap } K, \text{cost } 0} T\))!








ImportantTheorem 19.2: Exact Isomorphism Between the Intuitive ‘Backbone + Bypass’ Model and Equation Differencing



In competitive programming folklore, Luogu P3358 (最长k可重区间集) is often taught using two seemingly unrelated explanations:

The Intuitive “Flow Conservation / Ticket Bypass” Story: Imagine \(K\) parallel tracks running from coordinate \(1\) to coordinate \(n\) along the zero-cost backbone \(1 \to 2 \to \dots \to n\). Selecting interval \([l_j, r_j)\) means pulling \(1\) unit of flow off the backbone at \(l_j\), routing it through the bypass arc \(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -w_j} r_j\), and returning it to the backbone at \(r_j\). While that \(1\) unit of flow is in flight on the bypass \(l_j \to r_j\), only \(K - 1\) units remain on the backbone segments \(i \to i + 1\) for \(l_j \le i < r_j\). Because the backbone flow \(y_i\) on \(i \to i + 1\) satisfies \(y_i \ge 0\), at most \(K\) units can be in flight across cut \(( \{1, \dots, i\}, \{i+1, \dots, n\} )\) at any segment \(i\)!
The Algebraic Equation-Difference Story: Write \(\sum_{l_j \le i < r_j} x_j + y_i = K\) and take \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\).

Theorem 19.2: These two models produce the exact same graph, vertex for vertex, edge for edge, and flow unit for flow unit. Specifically, the flow \(y_i\) on the backbone edge \(i \to i + 1\) in the intuitive story is literally the slack variable \(y_i = K - \sum_{l_j \le i < r_j} x_j\) in equation \(E_i\), and the cut conservation equation across \((\{1, \dots, i\}, \{i+1, \dots, n\})\) is literally the prefix sum \(\sum_{t=1}^i \Delta E_t = E_i\)!





3.2 \(O(N + M)\) DAG DP Potential Initialization (Anti-SPFA Guardrail)
Notice a crucial structural property of the Luogu P3358 / POJ 3680 / CF 164C network (and Variant A of NEERC 2016 Delight for a Cat):

Every backbone edge \(i \to i + 1\) satisfies \(i < i + 1\).
Every interval bypass edge \(l_j \to r_j\) satisfies \(l_j < r_j\).
Therefore, at initial flow \(f = 0\), the entire network is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in topological order \(1, 2, \dots, n\)!

Even though every interval bypass edge has a negative cost \(-w_j < 0\), there are zero negative cycles in the initial graph. Instead of running \(O(NM)\) Bellman-Ford / SPFA to initialize Johnson potentials \(\pi_0\), or even pre-saturating negative edges, we can compute the exact shortest-path potentials \(\pi_0(1), \pi_0(2), \dots, \pi_0(n)\) in \(O(n + m)\) linear time via a single left-to-right sweep:
\[
\pi_0(1) = 0, \qquad \pi_0(v) = \min\!\left( \pi_0(v - 1), \; \min_{j \,:\, r_j = v} \bigl(\pi_0(l_j) - w_j\bigr) \right) \quad \text{for } v = 2, 3, \dots, n.
\]
After this \(O(n + m)\) initialization, we run at most \(K\) iterations of Dijkstra’s algorithm (Ch 17), giving an optimal total time complexity of:
\[
T(n, m, K) = O\bigl((n + m) + K (n + m) \log n\bigr).
\]
When \(K \le 10\) and \(n, m \le 2000\) (as in CF 164C — Machine Programming), this \(K\)-step DAG-initialized Dijkstra finishes in under \(5\text{ ms}\), whereas naive SPFA-based MCMF risks TLE on adversarial anti-SPFA DAGs!

section: 4. 2D Segment Projection & The Coordinate Doubling Trick \(x \mapsto (2x, 2x+1)\) (最长k可重线段集 #147)
text:
4. 2D Segment Projection & The Coordinate Doubling Trick \(x \mapsto (2x, 2x+1)\) (最长k可重线段集 #147)
What happens when the objects we are selecting are 2D line segments in the plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and the constraint forbids any vertical line \(x = x_0\) (\(x_0 \in \mathbb{R}\)) from intersecting more than \(K\) selected segments? This is the classic [Luogu P3357] 最长k可重线段集问题 (#147):

We are given \(m\) line segments in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), where segment \(j\) connects \((x_{j,1}, y_{j,1})\) to \((x_{j,2}, y_{j,2})\) with integer coordinates and weight \(w_j = \lfloor \sqrt{(x_{j,1} - x_{j,2})^2 + (y_{j,1} - y_{j,2})^2} \rfloor > 0\).
No vertical line \(x = x_0\) (\(x_0 \in \mathbb{R}\)) may intersect more than \(K\) selected segments.


4.1 Why Naive \(x\)-Projection Fails Catastrophically (FM-19b)
A tempting first thought is: “Since the constraint only cares about vertical lines \(x = x_0\), the \(y\)-coordinates only affect the weight \(w_j\)! Let’s project every 2D segment onto its \(x\)-interval \([\min(x_{j,1}, x_{j,2}), \max(x_{j,1}, x_{j,2})]\) and run Luogu P3358!”
If you do this naively by adding an edge \(x_{j,1} \to x_{j,2}\) (assuming \(x_{j,1} \le x_{j,2}\)), two fatal bugs occur simultaneously:

The Vertical Segment Self-Loop Bug (\(x_{j,1} = x_{j,2}\)):

A vertical segment from \((x, y_1)\) to \((x, y_2)\) (\(y_1 \ne y_2\)) has positive length \(w_j = |y_1 - y_2| > 0\), yet its \(x\)-projection is the degenerate single point \([x, x]\) (\(x_{j,1} = x_{j,2} = x\)).
If you add an edge \(x_{j,1} \to x_{j,2}\), it becomes a self-loop \(x \to x\) with negative cost \(-w_j < 0\)!
A flow unit on \(S \to \dots \to x \to \dots \to T\) does not need to traverse a self-loop \(x \to x\) to satisfy flow conservation, so SSP Dijkstra ignores it; conversely, in a circulation solver, a negative self-loop is a negative cycle of length \(1\) whose capacity does not interact with the backbone capacity \(K\) at all! Thus \(K + 1\) vertical segments at the same \(x\) could all be selected simultaneously, or none of them could ever be selected along an \(S \to T\) path!

The Closed-Endpoint Collision Bug (\(x_{a,2} = x_{b,1}\)):

Even if there are no vertical segments, if segments are closed (so \((1, 0)\text{--}(2, 0)\) and \((2, 1)\text{--}(3, 1)\) both intersect the vertical line \(x = 2\)), mapping them to \(1 \to 2\) and \(2 \to 3\) allows the same single unit of flow to traverse \(1 \to 2 \to 3\), counting them as only \(1\) segment at \(x = 2\) when in fact two segments intersect the vertical line \(x = 2\)!




4.2 The Coordinate Doubling Compiler: Splitting Points vs. Unit Intervals
To distinguish intersection with a vertical line \(x = c\) at an integer coordinate from intersection with a vertical line \(x = c + 0.5\) strictly between integers, we split every integer coordinate \(x \in \mathbb{Z}\) into two points:
\[
x \quad \longmapsto \quad \bigl(2x, \; 2x + 1\bigr),
\]
where we think of \(2x\) as \(x^-\) (just to the left of \(x\)) and \(2x + 1\) as \(x^+\) (just to the right of \(x\)):

The elementary step \(2x \to 2x + 1\) represents crossing the exact integer vertical line \(x\) (the singleton closed interval \([x, x]\)).
The elementary step \(2x + 1 \to 2(x + 1)\) represents crossing the open unit interval \((x, x + 1)\) between integers \(x\) and \(x + 1\).

This gives a clean, mechanical compilation table for both endpoint conventions encountered on online judges:









Endpoint Convention
Geometric Meaning of Segment \(j\) with \(x_1 \le x_2\)
Vertical Segment (\(x_1 = x_2 = x\))
Non-Vertical Segment (\(x_1 < x_2\))




Convention 1: Closed Segments (every segment includes both endpoints \([x_1, x_2]\))
Covers all \(x_0 \in [x_1, x_2]\), including \(x_0 = x_1\) and \(x_0 = x_2\)
\(\mathbf{2x \to 2x + 1}\) (covers \([x, x]\))
\(\mathbf{2x_1 \to 2x_2 + 1}\) (covers \([x_1, x_2]\))


Convention 2: Open Segments (Luogu P3357 Judge Convention) (non-vertical segments are open \((x_1, x_2)\), vertical segments occupy point \(x\))
Non-vertical covers \(x_0 \in (x_1, x_2)\); vertical covers \(x_0 = x\)
\(\mathbf{2x \to 2x + 1}\) (covers point \(x\))
\(\mathbf{2x_1 + 1 \to 2x_2}\) (covers \((x_1, x_2)\))









WarningJudge Convention Alert for Luogu P3357 (最长k可重线段集问题)



In Luogu P3357 (from the classic Network Flow 24 Problems suite), the problem statement says “segments are open segments (开线段)”, which creates a famous logical paradox if taken literally: an open vertical segment \(((x, y_1), (x, y_2))\) still intersects the vertical line \(x_0 = x\) on the open \(y\)-interval \((y_1, y_2)\), whereas an open non-vertical segment \(((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2))\) with \(x_1 < x_2\) intersects vertical lines \(x_0 \in (x_1, x_2)\) but not \(x_0 = x_1\) or \(x_0 = x_2\)!
Coordinate doubling \(x \mapsto (2x, 2x+1)\) resolves this paradox effortlessly:

Under Convention 2 (Open Segments, P3357):

A vertical segment at \(x_1 = x_2 = x\) intersects the vertical line \(x_0 = x\), so it spans \(\mathbf{2x \to 2x + 1}\).
An open non-vertical segment with \(x_1 < x_2\) intersects vertical lines \(x_0 \in (x_1, x_2)\) (strictly after \(x_1\) and strictly before \(x_2\)), so it starts at \(x_1^+ = \mathbf{2x_1 + 1}\) and ends at \(x_2^- = \mathbf{2x_2}\)!
Check: Can a vertical segment at \(x\) (\(2x \to 2x + 1\)) and an open non-vertical segment starting at \(x\) (\(2x + 1 \to 2x_2\)) share the same unit of flow? Yes, at node \(2x + 1\), because the open segment \((x, x_2)\) does not contain \(x\), so no single vertical line intersects both!
Can two vertical segments at \(x\) (both \(2x \to 2x + 1\)) share the same unit of flow? No, because both traverse the segment \([2x, 2x+1)\) in parallel!
Can a vertical segment at \(x\) (\(2x \to 2x + 1\)) and an open non-vertical segment \((x_1, x_2)\) that straddles \(x\) (\(x_1 < x < x_2\), i.e., \(2x_1 + 1 \to 2x_2\) with \(2x_1 + 1 < 2x < 2x + 1 < 2x_2\)) share the same unit of flow? No, because both intervals cover the elementary slice \([2x, 2x + 1)\)!






4.3 Concrete Toy Trace: Coordinate Doubling in Action
Suppose \(K = 1\) and we have three segments around \(x \in \{1, 2\}\):

Segment 1 (Vertical at \(x = 1\)): \((1, 0)\text{--}(1, 5)\), weight \(w_1 = 5\).
Segment 2 (Vertical at \(x = 1\)): \((1, 2)\text{--}(1, 6)\), weight \(w_2 = 4\).
Segment 3 (Non-vertical from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 2\)): \((1, 0)\text{--}(2, 0)\), weight \(w_3 = 1\).

Compare how the two conventions compile these three segments onto the doubled coordinate spine \(2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 5\) (representing \(1^- \to 1^+ \to 2^- \to 2^+\)):

Under Convention 1 (Closed Segments — endpoints count as intersections):

Segment 1 (\(x = 1\)): arc \(2 \to 3\), cap \(1\), cost \(-5\).
Segment 2 (\(x = 1\)): arc \(2 \to 3\), cap \(1\), cost \(-4\).
Segment 3 (\([1, 2]\) closed): arc \(2 \to 5\), cap \(1\), cost \(-1\).
Notice that all three segments cover the elementary slice \([2, 3)\) (the vertical line \(x = 1\)). With \(K = 1\), at most one of \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) can be chosen, and the optimal flow of \(1\) unit chooses \(2 \xrightarrow{\text{Seg 1}} 3 \to 4 \to 5\) of weight \(5\).

Under Convention 2 (Open Segments — Luogu P3357):

Segment 1 (\(x = 1\)): arc \(2 \to 3\), cap \(1\), cost \(-5\).
Segment 2 (\(x = 1\)): arc \(2 \to 3\), cap \(1\), cost \(-4\).
Segment 3 (\((1, 2)\) open): arc \(3 \to 4\), cap \(1\), cost \(-1\).
Now Segments 1 and 2 still compete on slice \([2, 3)\) (line \(x = 1\)), so we cannot pick both. However, Segment 1 (\(2 \to 3\)) and Segment 3 (\(3 \to 4\)) touch at node \(3\) (\(x = 1^+\)) without overlapping on any slice! The single unit of flow routes \(2 \xrightarrow{\text{Seg 1}} 3 \xrightarrow{\text{Seg 3}} 4 \to 5\), achieving total weight \(5 + 1 = 6\).
