section: 5. Advanced Equation-Difference Compilers: LP Dual Transposition, Rooted Trees, and Tractability Boundaries
text:
5. Advanced Equation-Difference Compilers: LP Dual Transposition, Rooted Trees, and Tractability Boundaries

5.1 Master Reference Table of Equation-Difference Archetypes
Before tackling advanced variations, let us consolidate the six canonical compilation patterns of the Consecutive-Ones & Equation-Difference framework:











Archetype
Primal Linear System
Transformation to Column Consecutive-Ones
Differenced Decision Arc \(e_{x_j}\)
Differenced Slack Arc
Representative Problems




1. Lower-Bound Interval Covering
\(\sum_{l_j \le i \le r_j} x_j \ge A_i\), \(\min \sum c_j x_j\)
Subtract surplus \(y_i \ge 0\): \(\sum x_j - y_i = A_i\), take \(E_i - E_{i-1}\)
\(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } u_j, \text{cost } c_j} r_j + 1\)
\(i + 1 \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0} i\) (backward)
NOI2008 志愿者招募 (#148), Luogu P4311


2. Upper-Bound Interval Packing
\(\sum_{l_j \le i < r_j} x_j \le K_i\), \(\max \sum w_j x_j\)
Add unused slack \(y_i \ge 0\): \(\sum x_j + y_i = K_i\), take \(E_i - E_{i-1}\)
\(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -w_j} r_j\)
\(i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0} i + 1\) (forward)
Luogu P3358 (#145), POJ 3680 (#146), CF 164C


3. Two-Sided Sliding Window
\(L_i \le \sum_{j=i}^{i+k-1} x_j \le R_i\), \(\max \sum w_j x_j\)
Add bounded slack \(y_i \in [0, R_i - L_i]\): \(\sum x_j + y_i = R_i\), take \(E_i - E_{i-1}\)
\(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -w_j} r_j + 1\)
\(i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } R_i - L_i, \text{cost } 0} i + 1\) (forward)
NEERC 2016 Delight for a Cat (#151), BZOJ 1283 (#150)


4. 2D Segment Vertical-Stab Packing
Vertical line \(x = x_0\) stabs \(\le K\) segments
Double coordinates \(x \mapsto (2x, 2x+1)\) before taking \(E_i - E_{i-1}\)
Vertical: \(2x \to 2x+1\); Open non-vert: \(2x_1+1 \to 2x_2\)
\(i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0} i + 1\) (forward)
Luogu P3357 (#147)


5. Row-Interval Covering with Large Point Capacities
\(\sum_{i=l_j}^{r_j} d_i \ge D_j\), \(0 \le d_i \le C_i\), \(\min \sum a_i d_i\)
Take LP Dual (\(A \mapsto A^T\)) to move intervals from rows to columns, then take \(E_i - E_{i-1}\)
Dual variable \(y_j\): \(l_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } -D_j} r_j + 1\)
Dual slack \(z_i\): \(i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } C_i} i + 1\)
ZJOI2013 防守战线 (Luogu P3337)


6. Rooted Tree Ancestor-Chain Covering
\(\sum_{j : u \in \text{path}(p_j, q_j)} x_j \ge A_u\) (\(p_j\) ancestor of \(q_j\))
Subtract subtree equations: \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u = E_u - \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} E_v\)
\(q_j \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } c_j} \text{parent}(p_j)\)
\(u \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0} \text{parent}(u)\)
LOJ #6405 (#152)





5.2 LP Dual Transposition: When Intervals Live on Rows ([ZJOI2013 / Luogu P3337] 防守战线)
Suppose we are given \(n\) positions \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\), where placing a defense tower at position \(i\) costs \(a_i\) per tower (up to \(C_i\) towers, or \(C_i = 1\)), and \(m\) interval requirements stating that the total number of towers in interval \([l_j, r_j]\) must be at least \(D_j\):
\[
\text{Minimize} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i d_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i=l_j}^{r_j} d_i \ge D_j \quad (j = 1, \dots, m), \qquad 0 \le d_i \le C_i.
\]

When \(n\) is small (\(n \le 1000\)) and \(m \le 1000\): Notice that variable \(d_i\) appears in constraint \(j\) iff \(l_j \le i \le r_j\). If \(m\) constraints have arbitrary intervals \([l_j, r_j]\), the columns \(d_i\) do not have consecutive ones unless the intervals \([l_j, r_j]\) have fixed length \(k\) (sliding windows)! Instead, the rows \(j\) have consecutive ones over the columns \(i \in [l_j, r_j]\)!
Can we use Prefix Sums \(P_i = \sum_{t=1}^i d_t\) (Difference Constraints)? Only when \(a_i\) is uniform! When each position \(i\) has an arbitrary unit cost \(a_i\), shortest-path difference constraints cannot express \(\min \sum_{i=1}^n a_i (P_i - P_{i-1})\).
The LP Dual Transposition Trick: Because a matrix \(A\) is Totally Unimodular if and only if its transpose \(A^T\) is Totally Unimodular (Ch 18), taking the Linear Programming Dual transposes the constraint matrix \(A \mapsto A^T\), moving the consecutive-ones intervals \([l_j, r_j]\) from the rows to the columns!

Specifically, associating dual variables \(y_j \ge 0\) with the interval constraints \(\sum_{i=l_j}^{r_j} d_i \ge D_j\) and dual variables \(z_i \ge 0\) with the upper-bound constraints \(-d_i \ge -C_i\), the LP Dual of the above problem is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Maximize} \quad & \sum_{j=1}^{m} D_j y_j - \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i z_i \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \sum_{j \,:\, l_j \le i \le r_j} y_j - z_i \le a_i, \qquad i = 1, 2, \dots, n, \\
& y_j \ge 0, \quad z_i \ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Look at the dual constraint for each position \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\): the dual variable \(y_j\) appears in row \(i\) iff \(i \in [l_j, r_j]\)—which is a contiguous range of rows! Adding an unused-slack variable \(s_i \ge 0\) gives \(\sum_{l_j \le i \le r_j} y_j - z_i + s_i = a_i\), which compiles via \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) directly into a \(n+1\)-vertex MCMF network!


5.3 Rooted Tree Equation Differencing (树上流守恒差分: \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u = E_u - \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} E_v\))
The Consecutive-Ones equation-difference method is not restricted to 1D lines! Suppose we have a rooted tree \(T\) with root \(r\) (append a virtual super-root \(0 = \text{parent}(r)\) with equation \(E_0 : 0 = 0\)), where each node \(u \in V(T)\) has a coverage requirement \(E_u : \sum_{j : u \in P_j} x_j - y_u = A_u\), and each available operation \(j\) covers a vertical ancestor-descendant chain \(P_j = \text{path}(p_j, q_j)\) where \(p_j\) is an ancestor of \(q_j\) ([LOJ #6405] 无源汇有上下界最小流 / 树上志愿者招募 (#152)).
If we tried to order the tree nodes linearly and take \(E_i - E_{i-1}\), a vertical path \(p_j \to q_j\) would break into \(\Theta(n)\) disjoint pieces. Instead, what is the natural tree generalization of \(E_i - E_{i-1}\)?






ImportantTheorem 19.3: Rooted Tree Equation Differencing (树上流守恒差分)



For every node \(u \in V(T) \cup \{0\}\) in a rooted tree (with virtual super-root \(0 = \text{parent}(r)\) and \(E_0 : 0 = 0\)), define the tree-differenced equation at node \(u\) by subtracting the sum of the equations of all direct children of \(u\) from \(E_u\):
\[
\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u \;:=\; E_u - \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} E_v \qquad \bigl(\forall u \in V(T) \cup \{0\}\bigr).
\]
Then for any vertical ancestor-descendant chain \(P_j = \text{path}(p_j, q_j)\) (where \(p_j\) is an ancestor of \(q_j\)):

If \(u = q_j\) (the bottom endpoint of the chain), \(x_j\) appears in \(E_{q_j}\) (\(+1\)) and in none of \(q_j\)’s children (\(0\)), so its net coefficient in \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_{q_j}\) is \(+1\).
If \(u \in P_j \setminus \{q_j\}\) (any interior node or \(p_j\) on the chain), \(x_j\) appears in \(E_u\) (\(+1\)) and in exactly one child \(v \in \text{child}(u)\) on the chain (\(+1\)), so its net coefficient in \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u\) is \(1 - 1 = \mathbf{0}\)!
If \(u = \text{parent}(p_j)\) (the strict parent of the top endpoint), \(x_j\) does not appear in \(E_{\text{parent}(p_j)}\) (\(0\)) but appears in the single child \(p_j \in \text{child}(\text{parent}(p_j))\) (\(+1\)), so its net coefficient in \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_{\text{parent}(p_j)}\) is \(0 - 1 = \mathbf{-1}\)!
For all other nodes \(u\), \(x_j\) has coefficient \(\mathbf{0}\).

Therefore, under \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u = E_u - \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} E_v\):

Every vertical path variable \(x_j\) on \(\text{path}(p_j, q_j)\) compiles to a single directed arc from the bottom endpoint to the parent of the top endpoint:
\[
e_{x_j} = \bigl(q_j \to \text{parent}(p_j)\bigr), \qquad \text{cap} = u_j, \qquad \text{cost} = c_j.
\]
Every surplus slack variable \(-y_u\) (a chain of length \(1\) with \(p = q = u\), appearing as \(-y_u\) in \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u\) and \(+y_u\) in \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_{\text{parent}(u)}\)) compiles to a downward tree arc:
\[
e_{y_u} = \bigl(\text{parent}(u) \to u\bigr), \qquad \text{cap} = \infty, \qquad \text{cost} = 0.
\]
Every node \(u \in V(T) \cup \{0\}\) has net supply/demand:
\[
b_u = A_u - \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} A_v \qquad (A_0 = 0).
\]



Look how clean Theorem 19.3 is: when the tree \(T\) is a 1D chain \(0 \gets 1 \gets 2 \gets \dots \gets n\) (where \(\text{parent}(i) = i - 1\) and \(\text{child}(i - 1) = \{i\}\)), Theorem 19.3 reduces immediately to \(\Delta E_{i-1} = E_{i-1} - E_i\) (the exact sign-flipped form of Theorem 19.1)!


5.4 The Tractability Boundary: Multi-Period Coupling ([ONTAK 2010] Vacation) vs. Equal-Flow NP-Hardness (FM-19d)
What happens if a decision variable \(x_j\) appears in two or more disjoint contiguous blocks of equations \([l_{j,1}, r_{j,1}] \cup [l_{j,2}, r_{j,2}]\)?

In General: NP-Hard (The Equal-Flow Boundary FM-19d): If \(x_j\) covers \([l_{j,1}, r_{j,1}]\) and \([l_{j,2}, r_{j,2}]\) (\(r_{j,1} + 1 < l_{j,2}\)), taking \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) leaves four non-zero coefficients for \(x_j\): \(+1\) at \(l_{j,1}\), \(-1\) at \(r_{j,1} + 1\), \(+1\) at \(l_{j,2}\), and \(-1\) at \(r_{j,2} + 1\). In graph terms, \(x_j\) would have to simultaneously send equal flow along two separate arcs \((l_{j,1} \to r_{j,1} + 1)\) and \((l_{j,2} \to r_{j,2} + 1)\). This is the Integer Equal-Flow Problem, which is strongly NP-hard (reducing from 3-SAT / Exact Cover).
The Remarkable Exception — Coupled Two-Scale Sliding Windows ([ONTAK 2010 / BZOJ 3550] Vacation #152): Suppose \(N = 3K\) days are divided into \(3\) consecutive blocks of length \(K\) (\([1, K]\), \([K+1, 2K]\), \([2K+1, 3K]\)), and we must satisfy both:

Every sliding window of length \(K\) contains at most \(L_1\) chosen elements: \(\sum_{t=i}^{i+K-1} x_t \le L_1\) for \(i = 1, \dots, 2K + 1\).
The entire \(3K\)-day horizon \([1, 3K]\) contains at most \(L_2\) chosen elements: \(\sum_{t=1}^{3K} x_t \le L_2\).

Even though this looks like two different window sizes (\(K\) and \(3K\)), notice that for the middle block \(t \in [K+1, 2K]\), variable \(x_t\) affects windows \(i \in [t - K + 1, t]\), whereas for \(t \in [1, K]\) and \(t \in [2K+1, 3K]\), pairing \(x_t\) (\(t \le K\)), \(x_{t+K}\) (\(K < t+K \le 2K\)), and \(x_{t+2K}\) (\(2K < t+2K \le 3K\)) along residue classes modulo \(K\) allows the global constraint \(\sum_{t=1}^{3K} x_t \le L_2\) to act as a single \(L_2\)-capacity choke edge in the flow network! We will derive the exact algebraic compilation of BZOJ 3550 (#152) in Section 6.8 below.

7. Pre-Submission Checklist (FM-19 Audit) & Quarantined Template Problems
Before submitting any interval-covering, interval-packing, or equation-differencing MCMF solution, run through this 6-point verification checklist:

Off-by-One Endpoint Audit (r_j + 1 vs. r_j, FM-19a):

Did you write out the discrete equation indices \(E_i\) (\(i = 1, \dots, n\)) that contain \(x_j\)?
If \(x_j\) appears in equations \(i \in \{l_j, l_j + 1, \dots, r_j\}\) (inclusive), then in \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) the \(-1\) coefficient appears at row \(\mathbf{r_j + 1}\), so the arc is \(l_j \to \mathbf{r_j + 1}\) and the graph has \(\mathbf{n + 1}\) equation nodes (\(1, \dots, n + 1\)) with \(A_0 = A_{n+1} = 0\).
If \(x_j\) is an open interval \((L_j, R_j)\) over compressed coordinates \(1 \dots M\), it covers elementary segments \(i \in \{l_j, \dots, r_j - 1\}\), so the \(-1\) coefficient appears at \((r_j - 1) + 1 = \mathbf{r_j}\).

Slack Arc Orientation Audit (FM-19, H-21):

Lower-bound covering (\(\sum x_j \ge A_i \iff \sum x_j - y_i = A_i\)): slack \(-y_i\) has coefficient \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_i\) and \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_{i+1}\), so the slack arc points backward (\(i + 1 \to i\)).
Upper-bound packing (\(\sum x_j \le K_i \iff \sum x_j + y_i = K_i\)): slack \(+y_i\) has coefficient \(+1\) in \(\Delta E_i\) and \(-1\) in \(\Delta E_{i+1}\), so the slack arc points forward (\(i \to i + 1\)).

Two-Sided Sliding Window Capacity Audit (FM-19c):

For \(L_i \le \sum x_j \le R_i\), did you bound the slack arc capacity by \(\mathbf{R_i - L_i}\)? Leaving the slack capacity as \(\infty\) drops the lower bound \(L_i\) (in Variant A) or drops the upper bound \(R_i\) (in Variant B).

2D Vertical Segment Self-Loop Audit (FM-19b):

In 2D segment projection problems (Luogu P3357), did you double coordinates \(x \mapsto (2x, 2x + 1)\) so vertical segments \(x_1 = x_2 = x\) map to \(2x \to 2x + 1\) instead of zero-length self-loops \(x \to x\)?

DAG DP vs. \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\) Potential Initialization Audit:

In lower-bound covering (NOI2008 志愿者招募), all initial edge costs are \(\ge 0\), so \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\) is immediately valid for Dijkstra despite directed cycles.
In upper-bound packing (P3358, POJ 3680, CF 164C, NEERC 2016 Delight for a Cat Variant A), initial edge costs \(-w_j < 0\) are negative, but all edges satisfy \(u < v\) (a topological DAG), so a single \(O(N + M)\) left-to-right DP pass computes exact initial Johnson potentials \(\pi_0\) without SPFA!

Consecutive-Ones Contiguity Audit (FM-19d):

Does every variable \(x_j\) appear in a single contiguous interval of equations? If a variable spans two disjoint intervals of equations, stop—that is the NP-hard Equal-Flow problem unless a global block sum telescopes onto slack variables.

text:
8. Chapter Summary, Bridge to Chapter 20, and Multilingual Bibliography

Key Takeaways of Chapter 19

The Consecutive-Ones Property is the Soul of Interval Flow: Any linear program whose constraint matrix \(A \in \{0, 1\}^{n \times m}\) has contiguous \(1\)s in every column reduces mechanically via consecutive row subtraction \(\Delta E_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\) (流守恒差分建模法) to a node-arc incidence matrix of a directed flow network on \(n + 1\) vertices.
No More Guessing Edge Directions: Slack sign dictates arc direction—surplus slack \(-y_i\) in \(\ge A_i\) constraints compiles to backward arcs \(i + 1 \to i\), unused slack \(+y_i\) in \(\le K_i\) constraints compiles to forward arcs \(i \to i + 1\), and two-sided bounds \(L_i \le \text{sum}_i \le R_i\) compile to capacity-bounded slack arcs of capacity \(R_i - L_i\).
Coordinate Doubling & Tree Differencing: Coordinate doubling \(x \mapsto (2x, 2x+1)\) resolves 2D vertical segment self-loops (Luogu P3357), and subtree equation differencing \(\Delta^{\text{tree}} E_u = E_u - \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} E_v\) extends the compiler from 1D intervals to vertical ancestor-descendant chains on rooted trees.



Bridge to Chapter 20: Convex Cost Scaling, Incremental Slope Arrays, and Non-Linear MCMF
Throughout Chapters 17–19, every decision variable \(x_j\) had a linear unit cost \(c_j x_j\). What happens when the cost of routing \(x_j\) units of flow along an edge—or the penalty of a degree imbalance, project tardiness, or worker fatigue—is a nonlinear convex function \(\Phi_j(x_j)\) such as \(a x_j^2 + b x_j\), \(x_j \ln x_j\), or an arbitrary convex piecewise-linear curve? In Chapter 20, we open the Convex Cost & Non-Linear MCMF toolkit:

The Incremental Finite-Difference / Parallel-Edge Gadget (拆边费用流): How discrete convexity \(\Delta^2 \Phi(k) = \Phi(k+1) - 2\Phi(k) + \Phi(k-1) \ge 0\) guarantees that SSP Dijkstra greedily saturates parallel unit-capacity edges in exact order \(k = 1, 2, \dots, u\).
Dynamic On-the-Fly Edge Generation (动态加边): How to avoid \(O(U)\) parallel edges by inserting the \((k+1)\)-th marginal edge \(\Delta \Phi(k+1) = \Phi(k+1) - \Phi(k)\) only when the \(k\)-th edge becomes saturated.
Capacity-Scaling MCMF (\(O(M^2 \log U \log V)\)): How binary bit-scaling handles huge capacities \(U \le 10^9\) when explicit parallel edges are impossible.




Multilingual Bibliography & Seminal References

[ZH]刘汝佳 (Liu, R.), 陈锋 (Chen, F.) (2012), 《算法竞赛入门经典：训练指南》(AOAPC II: Training Guide), Chapter 6 (Network Flows — Linear Programming and Consecutive Equation Differencing).
[ZH] 李煜东 (Li, Y.) (2018), 《算法竞赛进阶指南》(Advanced Guide to Algorithm Competitions), Sections 0x68–0x69 (Bipartite Matching & Network Flow / Min-Cost Max-Flow Models).
[EN] Ahuja, R. K., Magnanti, T. L., & Orlin, J. B. (1993), Network Flows: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications, Prentice Hall — Chapter 9 (Minimum Cost Flows) & Section 19.3 (Transformations of Consecutive-Ones Linear Programs to Network Flow Problems).
[EN] Fulkerson, D. R., & Gross, O. A. (1965), “Incidence matrices and interval graphs”, Pacific Journal of Mathematics, 15(3), 835–855 (foundational theorem connecting Consecutive-Ones matrices, Total Unimodularity, and interval network incidence matrices).

text:
Prerequisites:

Chapter 1 (Residual Graphs \(G_f\), Skew-Symmetry, and the Flow Decomposition Theorem into \(s\text{--}t\) Paths and Directed Cycles).
Chapter 4 (Bounded-Demand Circulations [l, u], Nodal Excess Balances \(M(v) = \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} l_e - \sum_{e \in \delta^+(v)} l_e\), and Super-Terminal Feasibility \(S^* \to T^*\)).
Standard Shortest Paths: Dijkstra’s algorithm on non-negative edge weights in \(O((V + E)\log V)\) time, and topological dynamic programming on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) in \(O(V + E)\) time.

Learning Objectives:

Master the Cycle-Optimality & Complementary Slackness Theorems: Prove that a feasible flow \(f\) has minimum cost among all flows of the same value \(F\) if and only if its residual network \(G_f\) contains no negative-cost directed cycle, and equivalently if and only if there exist Johnson node potentials \(\pi: V \to \mathbb{R}\) making every residual reduced cost \(c^\pi(u, v) = c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v \ge 0\).
Execute Primal–Dual MCMF Without SPFA Timeouts: Implement the Successive Shortest Path (SSP) and Zkw Primal–Dual engines using Dijkstra on non-negative reduced costs, apply the Early-Exit Capping Update \(\pi'_v \gets \pi_v + \min(d^\pi(v), d^\pi(t))\) to prevent INF overflow (H-18), and select the exact initial potential regime \(\pi_0\) (Zero, \(O(V + E)\) DAG Topological DP, Fixed-Hop Bipartite Shift, or Bellman–Ford) to immune your code against exponential SPFA traps (H-17).
Exploit Cost-vs-Flow Slope Convexity (atcoder::mcf_graph::slope): Prove that the minimum cost function \(C(F)\) is piecewise-linear and convex with marginal slopes \(\lambda_k = \pi_k(t) - \pi_k(s)\), distinguish the Four Augmentation Stopping Regimes (Max-Flow, Min-Cost Feasible Flow stopping at \(\lambda_k \ge 0\), Budget-Threshold Fractional Stopping, and Full Slope Profile Extraction), diagnose the Variable-Hop \(+M\) Cost-Shift Fallacy, and bridge slope convexity to 1D/2D WQS Binary Search (Aliens Trick).
Eliminate Initial Negative Cycles via Mandatory Saturation (强制满流, H-19): Resolve networks containing negative-cost arcs or negative-cost cycles before running a single shortest-path search by pre-saturating every arc \((u \to v, u_e, c_e < 0)\) to full capacity \(f_e = u_e\), reversing it into a positive-cost residual refund arc \((v \to u, u_e, -c_e > 0)\), and restoring nodal conservation via Ch 04 super-terminals \(S^* \to T^*\).
Compile Bounded-Demand Min-Cost Circulations ([l, u], c): Combine lower-bound shifts \(l_e\) and negative-arc pre-saturation into a unified two-phase Primal–Dual architecture (BoundedMCMF).

title: Chapter 17 — Min-Cost Max-Flow Foundations: Johnson Potentials, Convex Slope Curves & Negative Cycles
section: 1. The Residual Cost Landscape, Cycle-Optimality & Johnson Potentials
text:
1. The Residual Cost Landscape, Cycle-Optimality & Johnson Potentials
In Chapters 1 through 16, every flow and matching problem asked a purely volumetric or structural question: how much flow can cross from \(s\) to \(t\), what is the minimum capacity of a disconnecting cut, or what is the maximum size of a valid matching? Even when weights appeared (as in Project Selection in Ch 05 or Closure Cuts in Ch 07), a single capacity \(c_e\) encoded the weight directly because each arc was either cut or uncut.
Many combinatorial optimization problems, however, impose two independent numerical parameters on every decision:

A volumetric bound (Capacity \(u_e\)): How many times can a resource, transition, or path segment \(e = (u \to v)\) be used?
A unit rate (Cost \(c_e\)): What is the marginal price (or negative reward) paid per unit of flow routed across \(e\)?

This decoupling produces the Minimum-Cost Flow (MCF) and Minimum-Cost Maximum-Flow (MCMF) paradigm.

1.1 Formal Setup & Residual Cost Skew-Symmetry
Let \(G = (V, E)\) be a directed multigraph with source \(s \in V\) and sink \(t \in V\). Each directed arc \(e = (u \to v) \in E\) is equipped with:

a non-negative capacity \(u(e) = u(u, v) \ge 0\), and
a real-valued unit cost \(c(e) = c(u, v) \in \mathbb{R}\) (which may be positive, zero, or negative).

A function \(f: E \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is a feasible \(s\text{--}t\) flow of value \(F\) if it obeys capacity bounds \(0 \le f(e) \le u(e)\) for all \(e \in E\) and flow conservation \(\sum_{e \in \delta^+(v)} f(e) - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} f(e) = 0\) for all internal nodes \(v \in V \setminus \{s, t\}\), with net outflow \(F\) from \(s\). The total cost of \(f\) is the linear functional:
\[
C(f) = \sum_{e \in E} c(e) \, f(e)
\]
How does \(C(f)\) change when we push \(\delta > 0\) units of flow in the residual network \(G_f = (V, E_f)\)? Recall from Chapter 1 that each original arc \(e = (u \to v)\) with current flow \(0 \le f(e) \le u(e)\) induces up to two residual arcs in \(E_f\):

Forward residual arc \(e = (u \to v)\) with residual capacity \(r_f(u, v) = u(e) - f(e) > 0\). Pushing \(\delta\) units along \(e\) increases \(f(e)\) by \(\delta\), increasing total cost by \(\delta \cdot c(u, v)\). Thus, its residual cost is \(+c(u, v)\).
Backward (reverse) residual arc \(e^{\text{rev}} = (v \to u)\) with residual capacity \(r_f(v, u) = f(e) > 0\). Pushing \(\delta\) units along \(e^{\text{rev}}\) cancels (refunds) \(\delta\) units of existing flow on \(e\), decreasing \(f(e)\) by \(\delta\) and changing total cost by \(-\delta \cdot c(u, v)\). Thus, its residual cost MUST be the exact negation:

\[
c(v, u) = -c(u, v) \quad \text{(Residual Cost Skew-Symmetry)}
\]






ImportantThe Fundamental Law of Residual Costs



In every MCMF adjacency list, forward edge e and reverse edge e ^ 1 form a coupled pair:

Forward arc \(u \to v\): cap = u_e, cost = +c_e
Reverse arc \(v \to u\): cap = 0, cost = -c_e

Whenever \(\delta\) units of flow traverse a residual walk \(W\) (whether an \(s \to t\) path or a closed cycle), the new flow \(f' = f \oplus \delta \chi(W)\) satisfies the exact linear identity:
\[
C(f') - C(f) = \delta \sum_{a \in W} c(a) = \delta \, c(W)
\]




1.2 The Circulation Decomposition Lemma & Cycle-Optimality Theorem
Suppose we have already constructed a feasible flow \(f\) of value \(|f| = F\). How can we certify whether \(f\) achieves the minimum possible cost \(C(F)\) among all feasible flows of the same value \(F\)?






TipLemma 17.1 (Circulation Decomposition of Equal-Value Flow Differences)



Let \(f\) and \(f^*\) be two feasible \(s\text{--}t\) flows in \(G\) of the exact same value \(|f| = |f^*| = F\). Then their difference \(\Delta f = f^* - f\) is a feasible circulation in the residual network \(G_f\), and decomposes into a collection of at most \(|E|\) directed simple cycles \(W_1, W_2, \dots, W_k \subseteq G_f\) with positive weights \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k > 0\) such that:
\[
f^* = f + \sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i \chi(W_i) \quad \text{and} \quad C(f^*) - C(f) = \sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i \, c(W_i)
\]
Proof: Because both \(f\) and \(f^*\) satisfy flow conservation at every \(v \in V \setminus \{s, t\}\) and have identical net outflow \(F\) at \(s\) and inflow \(F\) at \(t\), their difference \(\Delta f = f^* - f\) has net divergence \(0\) at every vertex \(v \in V\) (including \(s\) and \(t\)). For each original arc \(e = (u \to v)\):

If \(f^*(e) > f(e)\), then \(0 < f^*(e) - f(e) \le u(e) - f(e) = r_f(u, v)\), so \(\Delta f\) routes \(f^*(e) - f(e)\) units along the forward residual arc \((u \to v) \in E_f\) at unit cost \(+c(u, v)\).
If \(f^*(e) < f(e)\), then \(0 < f(e) - f^*(e) \le f(e) = r_f(v, u)\), so \(\Delta f\) routes \(f(e) - f^*(e)\) units along the backward residual arc \((v \to u) \in E_f\) at unit cost \(-c(u, v)\).

By the Flow Decomposition Theorem (Ch 01) applied to a divergence-free circulation in \(G_f\), \(\Delta f\) is a non-negative linear combination of directed simple cycles \(\sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i \chi(W_i)\) in \(G_f\). By linearity of cost and skew-symmetry, \(C(f^*) - C(f) = \sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i \, c(W_i)\). \(\blacksquare\)


Lemma 17.1 immediately yields the master optimality criterion of minimum-cost flow theory:






ImportantTheorem 17.2 (The Residual Cycle-Optimality Theorem — Klein 1967)



A feasible flow \(f\) of value \(F\) has minimum cost among all feasible flows of value \(F\) if and only if its residual network \(G_f = (V, E_f)\) contains no directed cycle \(W\) of strictly negative cost \(c(W) < 0\).
Proof:

(\(\Rightarrow\) Necessity): Suppose \(G_f\) contains a directed cycle \(W\) with \(c(W) < 0\). Let \(\delta = \min_{a \in W} r_f(a) > 0\) be the bottleneck residual capacity of \(W\). Routing \(\delta\) units of flow around \(W\) produces \(f' = f \oplus \delta \chi(W)\), which preserves all vertex divergences (\(|f'| = |f| = F\)), obeys all capacities, and achieves \(C(f') = C(f) + \delta \, c(W) < C(f)\), contradicting the optimality of \(f\).
(\(\Leftarrow\) Sufficiency): Suppose \(c(W) \ge 0\) for every directed cycle \(W \subseteq G_f\). Let \(f^*\) be any feasible flow with \(|f^*| = F\). By Lemma 17.1, \(C(f^*) - C(f) = \sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i \, c(W_i)\) with \(\alpha_i > 0\) and \(W_i \subseteq G_f\). Since every \(c(W_i) \ge 0\), we have \(C(f^*) \ge C(f)\), proving \(f\) is globally cost-optimal for flow value \(F\). \(\blacksquare\)





1.3 LP Duality, Complementary Slackness & Johnson Node Potentials \(\pi_v\)
How does the combinatorial absence of negative residual cycles connect to Linear Programming duality and fast shortest-path algorithms?
Consider the primal LP for minimum-cost circulation (or fixed-value flow \(F\), which adds divergence constraints \(\text{div}_f(s) = F, \text{div}_f(t) = -F\)):
\[
\min \sum_{(u,v) \in E} c(u, v) f(u, v) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{v} f(u, v) - \sum_{v} f(v, u) = b_u \;\; (\forall u \in V), \quad 0 \le f(u, v) \le u(u, v)
\]
Assigning an unrestricted dual variable \(\pi_u \in \mathbb{R}\) (called the Johnson node potential) to the flow conservation constraint at vertex \(u\), and a non-negative dual variable \(z_{uv} \ge 0\) to the capacity upper bound \(f(u, v) \le u(u, v)\), the dual constraint corresponding to primal variable \(f(u, v)\) is \(\pi_v - \pi_u - z_{uv} \le c(u, v)\), or \(z_{uv} \ge \pi_v - \pi_u - c(u, v)\). Defining the reduced cost \(c^\pi(u, v)\) of any directed arc \((u \to v)\) with respect to potential vector \(\pi\) as:
\[
c^\pi(u, v) \triangleq c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v
\]
LP Complementary Slackness states that a primal feasible flow \(f\) and dual potentials \((\pi, z)\) are simultaneously optimal if and only if for every original arc \(e = (u \to v) \in E\):

If \(f(u, v) < u(u, v)\) (so forward arc \((u \to v) \in E_f\)), then \(z_{uv} = 0\), which forces \(c^\pi(u, v) = c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v \ge 0\).
If \(f(u, v) > 0\) (so primal variable \(f(u,v) > 0\) is slack and reverse arc \((v \to u) \in E_f\)), then the dual constraint is tight (\(\pi_v - \pi_u - c(u, v) = z_{uv} \ge 0\)), which means \(-c(u, v) + \pi_v - \pi_u \ge 0\), i.e., \(c^\pi(v, u) \ge 0\).

Notice that these two conditions collapse into a single, breathtakingly clean invariant on the residual graph \(G_f\):
\[
c^\pi(a) = c(a) + \pi_{\text{tail}(a)} - \pi_{\text{head}(a)} \ge 0 \quad \text{for every residual arc } a \in E_f
\]
Why do potentials \(\pi\) alter individual edge costs without corrupting the shortest paths or cycle costs of \(G_f\)? Because \(\pi_u - \pi_v\) is a potential difference (discrete gradient), which telescopes along any walk!






TipLemma 17.3 (Telescoping Path Identity & Cycle Invariance of Reduced Costs)



For any potential assignment \(\pi: V \to \mathbb{R}\):

Path Telescoping: Along any directed walk \(P = (v_0 \to v_1 \to \dots \to v_k)\), the total reduced cost differs from the true cost solely by the endpoint potentials \(\pi_{v_0} - \pi_{v_k}\):
\[
c^\pi(P) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \bigl(c(v_i, v_{i+1}) + \pi_{v_i} - \pi_{v_{i+1}}\bigr) = c(P) + \pi_{v_0} - \pi_{v_k}
\]
In particular, because \(\pi_{v_0} - \pi_{v_k}\) is a constant independent of the internal vertices of \(P\), a path \(P\) is a shortest \(s \to t\) path under reduced costs \(c^\pi\) if and only if \(P\) is a shortest \(s \to t\) path under true costs \(c\).
Cycle Invariance: Around any closed directed cycle \(W = (v_0 \to v_1 \to \dots \to v_k = v_0)\), all potential terms cancel identically:
\[
c^\pi(W) = c(W) + \pi_{v_0} - \pi_{v_0} = c(W)
\]
Reverse-Arc Skew-Symmetry: Reduced costs obey the exact same skew-symmetry as true costs:
\[
c^\pi(v, u) = c(v, u) + \pi_v - \pi_u = -\bigl(c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v\bigr) = -c^\pi(u, v)
\]
Consequently, any arc \((u \to v)\) on a shortest path tree where \(c^\pi(u, v) = 0\) immediately creates a reverse residual arc \((v \to u)\) of reduced cost \(c^\pi(v, u) = -0 = 0 \ge 0\)! \(\blacksquare\)





1.4 Successive Shortest Path (SSP) vs. Zkw Primal–Dual Engines
Lemma 17.3 and Theorem 17.2 unlock the Successive Shortest Path (SSP) algorithm (Jewell 1958; Iri 1960; Busacker–Gowen 1961) accelerated by Johnson–Edmonds–Karp potentials (Edmonds & Karp 1972; Tomizawa 1971):
Suppose flow \(f\) is cost-optimal for value \(F\), evidenced by potentials \(\pi\) satisfying \(c^\pi(a) \ge 0\) on all \(a \in E_f\).

Shortest-Path Search via Dijkstra: Since \(c^\pi(a) \ge 0\) everywhere in \(G_f\), run Dijkstra from \(s\) using edge weights \(w(u, v) = c^\pi(u, v) \ge 0\) to compute reduced shortest-path distances \(d^\pi(v)\) for all \(v \in V\).
Potential Shift: Define updated potentials \(\pi'_v \gets \pi_v + d^\pi(v)\) (or its capped variant below). For every residual arc \((u \to v) \in E_f\), the triangle inequality of shortest paths guarantees \(d^\pi(v) \le d^\pi(u) + c^\pi(u, v)\), which rearranges to:
\[
c^{\pi'}(u, v) = c(u, v) + (\pi_u + d^\pi(u)) - (\pi_v + d^\pi(v)) = c^\pi(u, v) + d^\pi(u) - d^\pi(v) \ge 0
\]
Zero-Cost Tight Augmentation: Along any shortest \(s \to t\) path \(P^*\) (or across the entire tight zero-reduced-cost subgraph \(E_0 = \{a \in E_f : c^{\pi'}(a) = 0\}\)), every arc satisfies \(d^\pi(v) = d^\pi(u) + c^\pi(u, v)\), meaning \(c^{\pi'}(u, v) = 0\). When we augment flow along \(P^*\), the newly created backward residual arcs \((v \to u)\) receive reduced cost:
\[
c^{\pi'}(v, u) = -c^{\pi'}(u, v) = 0 \ge 0
\]
Therefore, no negative reduced costs are created, and the updated flow \(f'\) is immediately certified as cost-optimal for its new value \(F + \delta\)!


Single-Path SSP vs. Zkw Multi-Augmentation (Primal–Dual Blocking DFS)
Once Dijkstra updates \(\pi'\) so that all shortest \(s \to t\) paths consist exclusively of zero-reduced-cost arcs (\(c^{\pi'}(u, v) = 0\)), we have two ways to push flow:

Standard SSP (1-Path Augmentation): Record parent pointers pv[v], pe[v] during Dijkstra, find bottleneck capacity \(\delta = \min_{e \in P^*} r_f(e)\) along a single shortest \(s \to t\) path, and augment \(\delta\) units. Best when total flow \(F\) is small or when each augmentation changes the shortest-path tree topology rapidly (long sparse chains).
Zkw Primal–Dual (Dinic-Style Multi-Path Augmentation): Perform a Dinic-style DFS (cur[u] pointer + vis[u] boolean flag) over the tight subgraph \(E_0 = \{(u \to v) \in E_f : r_f(u, v) > 0 \text{ and } c^{\pi'}(u, v) = 0\}\) to push as much flow as possible at the current marginal price \(\pi'_t - \pi'_s\) before running the next Dijkstra.







WarningCrucial Zkw Implementation Rule: Why vis[u] Must Guard Against Zero-Cost Cycles



Unlike Dinic’s level graph in Ch 01 (where \(d(v) = d(u) + 1\) strictly increases along every edge, guaranteeing a DAG), the zero-reduced-cost subgraph \(E_0\) in MCMF can contain zero-cost directed cycles (or back-and-forth \(0\)-cost antiparallel arcs \((u \to v)\) and \((v \to u)\)).
Therefore, Zkw’s DFS MUST maintain an active boolean array vis[u]:

Set vis[u] = true upon entering dfs(u, pushed).
Only traverse to neighbor \(v\) if !vis[v] && cap > 0 && cost + pi[u] - pi[v] == 0.
Dead-End Retention Rule: If dfs(u, pushed) finishes its adjacency loop and still has total_pushed < pushed (meaning \(u\) is now saturated/blocked from reaching \(t\) in \(E_0\)), leave vis[u] = true for the remainder of the current DFS phase so later branches do not waste \(O(E)\) time re-exploring dead-end zero-cost components! Only clear vis[u] = false when u successfully saturates its incoming push (total_pushed == pushed), or at the very start of the next Dijkstra phase.






1.5 The Four Regimes of Initial Potential \(\pi_0\) Initialization
Before the very first Dijkstra call at \(f \equiv 0\), we need a valid initial potential vector \(\pi_0: V \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(c^{\pi_0}(u, v) = c(u, v) + \pi_0(u) - \pi_0(v) \ge 0\) for every original forward arc \((u \to v) \in E\) with \(u(u, v) > 0\). Calling SPFA blindly on every problem is unnecessary—and on dense graphs with \(N \approx 2 \cdot 10^5\), fatal (H-17). Always classify the initial network into one of four structural regimes:










Regime
Initial Network Condition (\(f \equiv 0\))
Initialization Formula for \(\pi_0(v)\)
Preprocessing Time
Canonical Contest Archetypes




1. Non-Negative Costs
\(\forall e \in E,\; c(e) \ge 0\)
\(\pi_0(v) = 0\) for all \(v \in V\)
\(O(V)\)
Routing costs, Euclidean distances, convex penalty pieces (Luogu P2153, CF 708 D post-saturation)


2. DAG with Negative Costs
\(G = (V, E)\) is a DAG (even after SCC condensation)
Topological DP from \(s\): \(\pi_0(s) = 0\), \(\pi_0(v) = \min_{(u \to v) \in E} \{\pi_0(u) + c(u, v)\}\)
\(O(V + E)\)
Grid / trapezoid path harvesting (POJ 3422, Luogu P4013), condensed SCC graphs (ABC 214 H)


3. Fixed-Hop Bipartite / Layered
\(s \to L \to R \to t\) with negative rewards on \(L \to R\)
\(\pi_0(s) = 0, \pi_0(\ell) = 0\), \(\pi_0(r) = \min_{\ell \to r} c(\ell, r)\), \(\pi_0(t) = \min_{r} \pi_0(r)\)
\(O(V + E)\)
Maximum-weight bipartite matching, ABC 247 G — Dream Team, assignment problems


4. Cyclic Graph with Negative Arcs (No Negative Cycles)
Directed cycles exist, \(c(e) < 0\) possible, but \(c(W) \ge 0\)
Single initial SPFA / Bellman–Ford pass from a virtual super-source \(q_0 \to \forall v\)
\(O(V \cdot E)\)
General cyclic state-transition graphs without negative cycles



(Note: If the initial graph contains negative-cost directed cycles \(c(W) < 0\), no valid potential \(\pi_0\) exists at \(f \equiv 0\)! We resolve this in Section 3 via Mandatory Saturation 强制满流, which eliminates all negative arcs and reduces the graph directly to Regime 1 with \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\).)


1.6 The Early-Exit Capping Update (H-18): Preventing Potential Overflow
In competitive programming, Dijkstra often terminates early as soon as \(t\) is popped from the priority queue—or even after a full run, some vertices \(v \in V\) may have \(d^\pi(v) > d^\pi(t)\) or be completely unreachable (\(d^\pi(v) = \infty\)).
If you naively write if (d[v] < INF) pi[v] += d[v]; when stopping Dijkstra early, or if you add INF to unreachable nodes, two disasters occur:

Integer Overflow (INF + INF): Unreachable nodes with \(d^\pi(v) = \infty\) overflow int64_t on the next iteration when computing cost + pi[u] - pi[v].
Negative Reduced Cost Creation on Unsettled Frontiers: If you break out of Dijkstra the instant \(t\) is popped, any node \(v\) still sitting in the priority queue with \(d^\pi(v) > d^\pi(t)\) has not yet relaxed its outgoing edges \((v \to w)\), so \(d^\pi(w) \le d^\pi(v) + c^\pi(v, w)\) may be violated if \(d^\pi(v)\) is left un-capped!

The universal, mathematically airtight potential update formula that supports both full Dijkstra and early-exit Dijkstra (breaking when \(u = t\) is popped) is the Capped Distance Shift:
\[
\pi'_v \gets \pi_v + \min\bigl(d^\pi(v),\, d^\pi(t)\bigr) \quad \forall v \in V
\]






TipLemma 17.4 (Correctness of the Capped Potential Shift \(\pi'_v = \pi_v + \min(d^\pi(v), d^\pi(t))\))



Suppose Dijkstra runs from \(s\) on non-negative reduced costs \(c^\pi \ge 0\) and terminates as soon as \(t\) is popped (so every node \(u\) with \(d^\pi(u) < d^\pi(t)\) has already been popped and fully relaxed all its outgoing residual arcs). Set \(\tilde{d}(v) = \min(d^\pi(v), d^\pi(t))\) and \(\pi'_v = \pi_v + \tilde{d}(v)\). Then for every residual arc \((u \to v) \in E_f\):

Non-Negativity Preserved: If \(d^\pi(u) < d^\pi(t)\), then \(u\) was popped before \(t\), so relaxation guaranteed \(d^\pi(v) \le d^\pi(u) + c^\pi(u, v)\). Taking \(\min(\cdot, d^\pi(t))\) on both sides preserves the inequality \(\tilde{d}(v) \le \tilde{d}(u) + c^\pi(u, v)\) (since \(c^\pi(u, v) \ge 0\) and \(\tilde{d}(u) = d^\pi(u)\)). If instead \(d^\pi(u) \ge d^\pi(t)\), then \(\tilde{d}(u) = d^\pi(t) \ge \tilde{d}(v)\), so \(c^{\pi'}(u, v) = c^\pi(u, v) + \tilde{d}(u) - \tilde{d}(v) \ge c^\pi(u, v) \ge 0\).
Shortest \(s \to t\) Paths Remain Zero-Cost: For every node \(v\) on a shortest \(s \to t\) path \(P^*\), \(d^\pi(v) \le d^\pi(t)\) (since edge weights \(c^\pi \ge 0\)), so \(\tilde{d}(v) = d^\pi(v)\) and \(c^{\pi'}(e) = 0\) for all \(e \in P^*\).
Bounded Growth: Because \(\tilde{d}(v) \le d^\pi(t) < \infty\) whenever \(t\) is reachable, even completely unreachable vertices (\(d^\pi(v) = \infty\)) receive a finite shift \(d^\pi(t)\), making INF overflow impossible! \(\blacksquare\)





1.7 Hand-Checkable 4-Node Negative-Cost DAG Trace
Let us trace Regime 2 (\(O(V + E)\) DAG Topological DP initialization) followed by two Primal–Dual Dijkstra passes on a concrete 4-node DAG where naive Dijkstra without \(\pi_0\) would fail or loop.
flowchart LR
    s(("1 (s)")) -->|cap=2, cost=-5| u(("2"))
    s -->|cap=2, cost=-1| v(("3"))
    u -->|cap=1, cost=+2| v
    u -->|cap=1, cost=-2| t(("4 (t)"))
    v -->|cap=2, cost=-4| t

Vertices: \(V = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) in topological order, \(s = 1, t = 4\), target flow \(F = 2\).
Arcs (u -> v, cap, cost): \(e_1 = (1 \to 2, 2, -5)\), \(e_2 = (1 \to 3, 2, -1)\), \(e_3 = (2 \to 3, 1, +2)\), \(e_4 = (2 \to 4, 1, -2)\), \(e_5 = (3 \to 4, 2, -4)\).

Step 0: DAG Topological DP for \(\pi_0\) (\(O(V + E)\)):

\(\pi_0(1) = 0\).
\(\pi_0(2) = \pi_0(1) + c(1, 2) = 0 + (-5) = -5\).
\(\pi_0(3) = \min\bigl(\pi_0(1) + c(1, 3),\, \pi_0(2) + c(2, 3)\bigr) = \min(0 - 1, -5 + 2) = -3\).
\(\pi_0(4) = \min\bigl(\pi_0(2) + c(2, 4),\, \pi_0(3) + c(3, 4)\bigr) = \min(-5 - 2, -3 - 4) = -7\).

Let us verify that all 5 forward reduced costs \(c^{\pi_0}(u, v) = c(u, v) + \pi_0(u) - \pi_0(v)\) are non-negative:

\(c^{\pi_0}(1, 2) = -5 + 0 - (-5) = 0\)
\(c^{\pi_0}(1, 3) = -1 + 0 - (-3) = +2\)
\(c^{\pi_0}(2, 3) = +2 + (-5) - (-3) = 0\)
\(c^{\pi_0}(2, 4) = -2 + (-5) - (-7) = 0\)
\(c^{\pi_0}(3, 4) = -4 + (-3) - (-7) = 0\)

Pass 1 (Flow \(0 \to 2\)):

Dijkstra #1: Since \(c^{\pi_0}(1, 2) = c^{\pi_0}(2, 3) = c^{\pi_0}(2, 4) = c^{\pi_0}(3, 4) = 0\), Dijkstra finds \(d^{\pi_0} = [0, 0, 0, 0]\).
Potential Update: \(\pi_1 = \pi_0 + d^{\pi_0} = [0, -5, -3, -7]\). Marginal unit cost of flow in Pass 1 is \(\lambda_1 = \pi_1(4) - \pi_1(1) = -7\).
Augmentation along \(E_0\): Both \(P_A = (1 \to 2 \to 4)\) (bottleneck \(\min(2, 1) = 1\)) and \(P_B = (1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4)\) (bottleneck \(\min(2-1, 1, 2) = 1\)) consist entirely of \(0\)-reduced-cost edges! Pushing \(1\) unit on \(P_A\) and \(1\) unit on \(P_B\) saturates \(e_1 = (1 \to 2)\), \(e_3 = (2 \to 3)\), and \(e_4 = (2 \to 4)\), delivering \(F = 2\) units of flow at total cost \(C(2) = 2 \times (-7) = -14\).

Pass 2 (Suppose we also had 1 extra unit of supply, testing \(F = 3\)):

Now \(e_1 = (1 \to 2)\) is saturated (\(r_f(1, 2) = 0\)), while backward arcs \((2 \to 1)\), \((3 \to 2)\), \((4 \to 2)\), \((4 \to 3)\) appear in \(G_f\) with reduced cost \(0\).
Dijkstra #2: From \(1\), the only available forward arc is \(e_2 = (1 \to 3)\) with \(c^{\pi_1}(1, 3) = +2\). Thus \(d^{\pi_1}(1) = 0\), \(d^{\pi_1}(3) = 2\). From \(3\), we can reach \(4\) via \(e_5 = (3 \to 4)\) with \(c^{\pi_1}(3, 4) = 0\) (\(d^{\pi_1}(4) = 2\)) and reach \(2\) via backward arc \((3 \to 2)\) with \(c^{\pi_1}(3, 2) = 0\) (\(d^{\pi_1}(2) = 2\)).
Potential Update: \(\pi_2 = \pi_1 + [0, 2, 2, 2] = [0, -3, -1, -5]\). The new marginal cost is \(\lambda_2 = \pi_2(4) - \pi_2(1) = -5 > \lambda_1 = -7\) (convex slope increase!). Pushing \(1\) unit along \(1 \to 3 \to 4\) costs \(-1 + (-4) = -5\), bringing \(C(3) = -19\).



1.8 Broken-Gadget Counterexamples & Implementation Traps (FM-17)
Every competitive programmer who has written MCMF under contest pressure has encountered at least one of the following four failure modes. Understanding why they break mathematically makes your code immune to them:

The SPFA Exponential Grid Trap (H-17 / FM-17a): If you replace the Johnson potential + Dijkstra loop with repeated SPFA calls (while (spfa(s, t)) augment();), a maliciously constructed \(K \times K\) grid or layered halving-cost gadget forces SPFA to relabel vertices \(\Omega(2^{V/2})\) or \(\Theta(V^2 E)\) times per augmentation. On graphs with \(N \ge 2000\) (such as AtCoder ABC 214 H with \(N = 2 \cdot 10^5\)), repeated SPFA receives an instant TLE, whereas topological DP \(\pi_0\) + Dijkstra runs in \(O(K (V + E) \log V) \approx 40\text{ ms}\).
Uncapped Early-Exit Potential Corruption (H-18 / FM-17b): Suppose Dijkstra stops as soon as \(t\) is popped at distance \(d^\pi(t) = 5\), while another vertex \(x\) sits in the priority queue with tentative distance \(d^\pi(x) = 20\) and has an unrelaxed outgoing arc \((x \to y)\) of reduced cost \(c^\pi(x, y) = 0\) to an unreachable vertex \(y\) (\(d^\pi(y) = \infty\)). If you update \(\pi'_x \gets \pi_x + 20\) and leave \(\pi'_y \gets \pi_y\) (because \(d^\pi(y) = \infty\)), the new reduced cost becomes \(c^{\pi'}(x, y) = 0 + 20 - 0 = +20\); worse, if \(x\) had an incoming arc \((z \to x)\) from an unreachable node \(z\) (\(d^\pi(z) = \infty\)) with \(c^\pi(z, x) = 2\), leaving \(\pi'_z = \pi_z\) while shifting \(\pi'_x \gets \pi_x + 20\) makes \(c^{\pi'}(z, x) = 2 + 0 - 20 = -18 < 0\), injecting a negative reduced cost into \(G_f\) and crashing the next Dijkstra! Using \(\pi'_v \gets \pi_v + \min(d^\pi(v), d^\pi(t))\) guarantees every node with \(d^\pi(v) \ge d^\pi(t)\) receives the identical shift \(+d^\pi(t)\), keeping \(c^{\pi'}(z, x) = 2 + 5 - 5 = 2 \ge 0\).
Zero or Positive Reverse-Arc Cost (FM-15 / FM-17c): In max-flow (Ch 01), reverse edges only carry capacity 0 and have no cost. When adapting a Dinic add_edge helper to MCMF, setting the reverse edge cost to 0 or +cost instead of -cost destroys skew-symmetry \(c(v, u) = -c(u, v)\):

If rev.cost = +cost > 0, any forward augmentation along \((u \to v)\) makes \(c^{\pi'}(v, u) = +c(u, v) + \pi'_v - \pi'_u = +2 c(u, v) \ne 0\), preventing flow cancellation when a cheaper alternate crossover path is discovered (violating Suurballe’s path-rerouting mechanism in Luogu P2153).
If rev.cost = +cost < 0 on a reward arc, the forward and reverse arcs form a 2-cycle \(u \to v \to u\) of negative cost \(2c < 0\) immediately after the first push!

The Undirected Edge Negative-Cycle Trap (FM-17d): In max-flow (Ch 01), an undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) of capacity \(u_e\) can be stored cleanly by initializing both halves of a single edge pair with cap = u_e. In MCMF, you can NEVER initialize a single forward/reverse edge pair with f.cap = u_e, f.cost = +c and rev.cap = u_e, rev.cost = -c! Doing so gives the reverse arc \((v \to u)\) both positive initial capacity \(u_e > 0\) and negative cost \(-c < 0\), creating an immediate negative cycle \(u \xrightarrow{+c} v \xrightarrow{-c} u\) (or unusable negative arc) at \(f \equiv 0\). Rule: An undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) of capacity \(u_e\) and traversal cost \(c \ge 0\) in MCMF MUST be compiled as two independent directed edge pairs (4 adjacency entries total):

Directed pair 1: \((u \to v, \text{cap} = u_e, \text{cost} = +c)\) with reverse \((v \to u, \text{cap} = 0, \text{cost} = -c)\).
Directed pair 2: \((v \to u, \text{cap} = u_e, \text{cost} = +c)\) with reverse \((u \to v, \text{cap} = 0, \text{cost} = -c)\).

section: 2. Convexity of the Cost-vs-Flow Slope Curve (atcoder::mcf_graph::slope)
text:
2. Convexity of the Cost-vs-Flow Slope Curve (atcoder::mcf_graph::slope)
For any flow network \(G\), let \(F_{\max}\) be the maximum \(s\text{--}t\) flow value, and for each \(F \in [0, F_{\max}]\), define the minimum-cost profile function:
\[
C(F) \triangleq \min\bigl\{\, C(f) : f \text{ is a feasible } s\text{--}t \text{ flow of value } |f| = F \,\bigr\}
\]
One of the deepest structural truths in combinatorial optimization—and the mathematical engine behind atcoder::mcf_graph::slope, fractional budget stopping, and WQS Binary Search (Aliens Trick)—is that \(C(F)\) is piecewise-linear and globally convex on \([0, F_{\max}]\).

2.1 Two Independent Proofs of Slope Convexity
Why does every successive unit of flow cost at least as much as the previous unit (\(\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_{F_{\max}}\))? We give two complementary proofs: one purely geometric (via residual decomposition) and one algorithmic (via Johnson potential monotonicity).






ImportantTheorem 17.5 (Convexity of the Minimum-Cost Flow Function \(C(F)\))



Let \(G = (V, E, u, c)\) have integer capacities. For every integer flow value \(F \in \{1, 2, \dots, F_{\max} - 1\}\), the marginal unit cost \(\lambda_F \triangleq C(F) - C(F - 1)\) satisfies the discrete convexity inequality:
\[
\lambda_F \le \lambda_{F+1} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad C(F - 1) + C(F + 1) \ge 2 C(F)
\]
Moreover, in the Successive Shortest Path algorithm, the \(k\)-th unit augmentation pushes flow at marginal unit cost \(\lambda_k = \pi_k(t) - \pi_k(s)\), and the sequence of marginal slopes is monotonically non-decreasing:
\[
\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_{F_{\max}}
\]
Proof 1 (Midpoint Residual Decomposition — Combinatorial): Let \(f_{F-1}\) and \(f_{F+1}\) be minimum-cost feasible flows of values \(F - 1\) and \(F + 1\), respectively, so \(C(f_{F-1}) = C(F-1)\) and \(C(f_{F+1}) = C(F+1)\). Consider their difference \(\Delta f = f_{F+1} - f_{F-1}\).
Because \(\Delta f\) has net divergence \((F + 1) - (F - 1) = +2\) at \(s\), \(-2\) at \(t\), and \(0\) at all internal vertices, and respects residual capacities in \(G_{f_{F-1}}\), the Flow Decomposition Theorem (Ch 01) decomposes \(\Delta f\) into two unit \(s \to t\) paths \(P_1, P_2 \subseteq G_{f_{F-1}}\) plus a collection of directed cycles \(\sum_{j} \alpha_j \chi(W_j) \subseteq G_{f_{F-1}}\):
\[
f_{F+1} - f_{F-1} = \chi(P_1) + \chi(P_2) + \sum_{j} \alpha_j \chi(W_j)
\]
Since \(f_{F-1}\) is optimal for value \(F - 1\), Theorem 17.2 guarantees \(c(W_j) \ge 0\) for every residual cycle \(W_j \subseteq G_{f_{F-1}}\). Furthermore, both \(f^{(1)} \triangleq f_{F-1} + \chi(P_1)\) and \(f^{(2)} \triangleq f_{F-1} + \chi(P_2)\) are valid feasible flows of value \(F\) (since \(P_1, P_2\) are disjoint or share capacity within \(r_{f_{F-1}}\)), so each has cost at least \(C(F)\):
\[
C(F - 1) + c(P_1) = C(f^{(1)}) \ge C(F) \quad \text{and} \quad C(F - 1) + c(P_2) = C(f^{(2)}) \ge C(F)
\]
Summing these and adding the non-negative cycle costs gives:
\[
C(F + 1) - C(F - 1) = c(P_1) + c(P_2) + \sum_j \alpha_j c(W_j) \ge 2\bigl(C(F) - C(F - 1)\bigr) \implies C(F - 1) + C(F + 1) \ge 2 C(F)
\]
Proof 2 (Primal–Dual Potential Monotonicity — Algorithmic): Assume without loss of generality that \(\pi_k(s) = 0\) at every step \(k\) (since \(d^{\pi_{k-1}}(s) = 0\)). Before step \(k\), every residual arc \(a \in E_{f_{k-1}}\) has non-negative reduced cost \(c^{\pi_{k-1}}(a) \ge 0\). Consequently, Dijkstra from \(s\) on \(G_{f_{k-1}}\) produces a non-negative shortest distance \(d^{\pi_{k-1}}(t) \ge 0\). Updating \(\pi_k(t) = \pi_{k-1}(t) + d^{\pi_{k-1}}(t)\) immediately yields:
\[
\lambda_k = \pi_k(t) = \pi_{k-1}(t) + d^{\pi_{k-1}}(t) = \lambda_{k-1} + d^{\pi_{k-1}}(t) \ge \lambda_{k-1} \quad \blacksquare
\]




2.2 The Four Augmentation Stopping Regimes
Because SSP traces the convex curve \((F, C(F))\) from left to right in order of non-decreasing marginal slope \(\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_{F_{\max}}\), we can solve four distinct optimization problems simply by changing the while-loop termination condition of Dijkstra:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Curve["Convex Cost-vs-Flow Curve C(F)"]
        direction LR
        P0["(0, 0)"] -->|"λ₁ = -8 (Reward)"| P1["(F₁, C₁)"]
        P1 -->|"λ₂ = -3 (Reward)"| P2["(F*, C_min)  ◀ Regime 2: Stop at λ ≥ 0"]
        P2 -->|"λ₃ = +2 (Cost)"| P3["(F_budget, B) ◀ Regime 3: Budget Cap"]
        P3 -->|"λ₄ = +9 (Cost)"| P4["(F_max, C_max) ◀ Regime 1: Max Flow"]
    end

Regime 1 — True Min-Cost Max-Flow (Fixed Volume \(F_{\max}\) or Target \(K\)):

Goal: Maximize total flow \(F\) first; among all flows of value \(F_{\max}\) (or fixed \(K\)), minimize \(C(F)\).
Stopping Rule: Run Dijkstra until \(t\) is unreachable in \(G_f\) (d[t] == INF) or until flow == K, regardless of whether the marginal slope \(\lambda_k = \pi_k(t) - \pi_k(s)\) is negative or positive.

Regime 2 — Minimum-Cost Feasible Flow / Maximum-Profit Optional Flow (最小费用可行流):

Goal: Find \(F^* \in [0, F_{\max}]\) that globally minimizes \(C(F)\) (equivalently, maximizes net profit \(-C(F)\) when negative-cost reward arcs compete against positive-cost penalty arcs).
Stopping Rule: Because \(\lambda_k\) is non-decreasing, \(C(F)\) decreases strictly while \(\lambda_k < 0\), plateaus while \(\lambda_k = 0\), and increases strictly once \(\lambda_k > 0\). Thus, terminate the SSP loop the instant \(\lambda_k = \pi_k(t) - \pi_k(s) \ge 0\)!

Regime 3 — Budget-Threshold Fractional or Integral Stopping (\(C(F) \le B\)):

Goal: Maximize the total flow \(F\) subject to a hard total cost budget \(C(F) \le B\) (where costs are non-negative or once we are on the rising \(\lambda_k > 0\) branch of \(C(F)\)).
Stopping Rule: Suppose the current flow \(F_{\text{cur}}\) has cost \(C_{\text{cur}} \le B\), and the next shortest augmenting path (or tight \(E_0\) blocking flow) can push up to \(\delta\) units at marginal unit cost \(\lambda_k > 0\).

If \(C_{\text{cur}} + \delta \cdot \lambda_k \le B\), push all \(\delta\) units and continue.
If \(C_{\text{cur}} + \delta \cdot \lambda_k > B\), we can afford only a partial prefix of this slope segment: push \(\delta_{\text{take}} = \lfloor (B - C_{\text{cur}}) / \lambda_k \rfloor\) integer units (or \((B - C_{\text{cur}}) / \lambda_k\) fractional units) and terminate immediately! Convexity guarantees no later path can have a cheaper marginal rate than \(\lambda_k\).


Regime 4 — Full Parametric Slope Profile Extraction (atcoder::mcf_graph::slope):

Goal: Answer \(Q\) offline or online queries asking for \(C(F)\) at arbitrary flow values \(F\), or inspect every breakpoint \((F_i, C(F_i))\) of the piecewise-linear curve.
Rule: Record a new polyline vertex \((F_{\text{cur}}, C_{\text{cur}})\) at the end of each Zkw phase (or coalesce consecutive SSP pushes sharing the same marginal slope \(\lambda_k\)). By Theorem 17.5, the number of distinct slope breakpoints is bounded by \(\min(F_{\max}, \text{number of distinct path costs}) + 1\).




2.3 The Variable-Hop \(+M\) Cost-Shift Fallacy & Three Exact Remedies
Suppose a problem gives a directed graph with negative edge weights \(c(e) < 0\) (representing rewards \(w_e = -c(e) > 0\)) and asks for the maximum-weight \(s\text{--}t\) flow. A classic beginner temptation is:

“To avoid negative edge weights and skip \(\pi_0\) initialization, can I just add a large constant \(+M\) (say \(M = 10^9\)) to every arc’s cost so all \(c'(e) = c(e) + M \ge 0\), and then subtract \(M\) at the end?”







WarningFM-17e: The Variable-Hop \(+M\) Cost-Shift Fallacy



Adding \(+M\) to every edge’s cost is MATHEMATICALLY INVALID unless every \(s \to t\) path in the residual network has the exact same number of edges (hops)!
Why? Along a path \(P\) consisting of \(|P|\) edges, shifting every edge cost by \(+M\) changes the path cost to:
\[
c'(P) = \sum_{e \in P} (c(e) + M) = c(P) + |P| \cdot M
\]
Because \(M\) is multiplied by the hop count \(|P|\), a short 2-hop path with poor reward easily beats a 3-hop path with much better true reward!



Concrete 4-Node Counterexample to \(+M\) Shifting
Consider the 4-node DAG \(s = 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4 = t\) where we want 1 unit of flow of minimum true cost:

Path \(P_{\text{long}} = (1 \xrightarrow{-4} 2 \xrightarrow{-4} 3 \xrightarrow{-4} 4)\) has \(3\) hops and true cost \(c(P_{\text{long}}) = -12\) (optimal!).
Path \(P_{\text{short}} = (1 \xrightarrow{-5} 3 \xrightarrow{-5} 4)\) has \(2\) hops and true cost \(c(P_{\text{short}}) = -10\) (suboptimal by \(2\)).

If we shift every edge cost by \(M = +5\) so all edges become non-negative (\(c'(e) = c(e) + 5 \ge 0\)):

\(c'(P_{\text{long}}) = (-4 + 5) + (-4 + 5) + (-4 + 5) = 1 + 1 + 1 = +3\).
\(c'(P_{\text{short}}) = (-5 + 5) + (-5 + 5) = 0 + 0 = 0\).

Dijkstra on the \(+M\)-shifted graph picks \(P_{\text{short}}\) (cost \(-10\)) instead of \(P_{\text{long}}\) (cost \(-12\)), returning a wrong answer! Worse still, after pushing 1 unit on a path of length \(k\), backward residual edges must have cost \(-c'(e) = -c(e) - M < 0\), so even after shifting by \(+M\), backward arcs immediately become negative anyway!


The Three Exact Remedies
Whenever you have negative edge costs \(c(e) < 0\):

Remedy 1 (Johnson Potentials \(\pi_0\) — Universal for DAGs & Fixed-Hop Graphs): Keep the true costs \(c(e)\) untouched and compute \(\pi_0\) in \(O(V + E)\) via Topological DP (Regime 2) or single-layer minimum (Regime 3). Because \(c^{\pi_0}(P) = c(P) + \pi_0(s) - \pi_0(t)\) adds a constant \(\pi_0(s) - \pi_0(t)\) that depends only on the endpoints \(s, t\) and NOT on the hop count \(|P|\), path rankings are 100% preserved!
Remedy 2 (Per-Vertex / Per-Unit-Flow Shift — Valid ONLY on Fixed-Charge Transitions): If a reward \(-W\) happens exactly once per unit of flow (e.g., only on edges directly leaving \(s\) or only on the unique bipartite bridge layer \(L \to R\)), adding \(+M\) only to that single mandatory cut layer adds exactly \(+1 \cdot M\) to every \(s \to t\) path regardless of internal detours.
Remedy 3 (Mandatory Saturation 强制满流 — Universal for Cyclic Graphs): Pre-saturate all negative-cost arcs as derived in Section 3, turning every negative arc into a positive-cost reverse refund arc with \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\).




2.4 Worked Slope-Extraction Model: AtCoder ABC 247 G — Dream Team
Let us see how Regime 3 (\(\pi_0\) Fixed-Hop Bipartite Initialization), Regime 4 (slope profile extraction), and Remedy 2 (Per-Unit-Flow Shift) work together on a canonical AtCoder problem.

Problem (AtCoder ABC 247 G — Dream Team): You are given \(N \le 3 \cdot 10^4\) candidates. Candidate \(i\) belongs to university \(A_i \in [1, 150]\), specializes in subject \(B_i \in [1, 150]\), and has power \(C_i \in [1, 10^9]\). A team of size \(k\) is valid if no two members share the same university \(A_i\) and no two share the same subject \(B_i\). Output the maximum possible team size \(k_{\max}\), and for every \(k = 1, 2, \dots, k_{\max}\), output the maximum total power of a valid team of size \(k\).
Why Naive Greedy Fails: Picking the globally strongest pair \((A_i, B_i)\) for \(k = 1\) may block two slightly weaker candidates who share \(A_i\) and \(B_i\) separately and yield a much larger sum for \(k = 2\).
Algebraic & Graph Formulation:

For each pair \((a, b) \in \{1, \dots, 150\}^2\), only the single candidate with the maximum \(C_i\) in cell \((a, b)\) can ever be used (since at most one person can have university \(a\) and subject \(b\)). Let \(W_{a,b} = \max_{A_i=a, B_i=b} C_i\).
Create left vertices \(L = \{1, \dots, 150\}\) (universities) with \(s \xrightarrow{\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=0} a\), right vertices \(R = \{1, \dots, 150\}\) (subjects) with \(b \xrightarrow{\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=0} t\), and bridge arcs \(a \xrightarrow{\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=-W_{a,b}} b\).
Because every \(s \to t\) augmenting path crosses the \(L \to R\) cut a net total of \(+1\) time (each forward \(L \to R\) arc adds \(+1\) to flow, and each backward \(R \to L\) arc subtracts \(1\) from flow), the number of net \(L \to R\) crossings per unit of \(s\text{--}t\) flow is strictly invariant (\(= 1\))!
Therefore, either we initialize \(\pi_0(s) = \pi_0(a) = 0\), \(\pi_0(b) = \min_a (-W_{a,b})\), \(\pi_0(t) = \min_b \pi_0(b)\) in \(O(V + E)\), or we shift only the \(L \to R\) bridge costs to \(c'(a, b) = M - W_{a,b} \ge 0\) (with \(M = 10^9\)) while keeping \(s \to a\) and \(b \to t\) at cost \(0\).
Running SSP and recording \(C(k)\) after each unit augmentation \(k = 1, 2, \dots, k_{\max}\) prints the exact answers \(\text{ans}(k) = k \cdot M - C'(k) = -C(k)\) in \(O(k_{\max} (V + E) \log V)\) time with \(|V| = 302, |E| \le 150^2 + 300\).




2.5 Bridging Slope Convexity to WQS Binary Search (Aliens Trick)
Theorem 17.5 guarantees that the minimum cost \(C(F)\) (or maximum profit \(P(F) = -C(F)\)) as a function of the number of augmenting paths \(F = K\) is convex (or concave for maximization).
What happens when \(N\) and \(K\) are so large (e.g., \(N, K \le 3 \cdot 10^5\) on a tree, or \(N = 2000\) in a 2-resource DP) that we cannot afford to run \(K\) steps of SSP or maintain a \(O(N \cdot K)\) DP state?
We invoke Lagrangian Relaxation (WQS Binary Search / Aliens Trick) on the convex slope curve \(C(F)\):

Dualizing the Flow-Volume Constraint \(F = K\): Instead of forcing the flow (or path count) to equal \(K\) via a hard capacity \(s_0 \xrightarrow{K, 0} s\), we relax the constraint \(F = K\) with a Lagrange multiplier (per-unit penalty/tax) \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\):
\[
g(\lambda) \triangleq \min_{F \in [0, F_{\max}]} \bigl(\, C(F) - \lambda F \,\bigr)
\]
In the flow network, subtracting \(\lambda F\) is equivalent to adding \(-\lambda\) to the cost of every arc leaving \(s\) and transitions directly into Regime 2 (Unconstrained Min-Cost Feasible Flow)! Even better, once the global count constraint \(F = K\) is removed, the problem often decouples into a fast \(O(N)\) tree DP or greedy evaluation for any fixed \(\lambda\).
Recovering \(C(K)\) and Handling Collinear Slope Plateaus: By Theorem 17.5, the optimal unconstrained count \(F^*(\lambda) = \arg\min_F (C(F) - \lambda F)\) is monotone in \(\lambda\). Binary searching for the threshold slope \(\lambda^*\) where \(F^*(\lambda^*) \ge K\) (always breaking ties consistently—e.g., maximizing \(F^*\) among equal-cost states) identifies the tangent line of slope \(\lambda^*\) supporting \(C(F)\) at \(F = K\). Even if \((K, C(K))\) lies strictly in the interior of a flat collinear plateau where multiple values \(F \in [F_L, F_R]\) share the exact same marginal slope \(\lambda^*\), the supporting hyperplane identity recovers \(C(K)\) from \(g(\lambda^*)\) via:
\[
C(K) = g(\lambda^*) + K \cdot \lambda^*
\]


Two Canonical Contest Bridges (CF 739 E & Luogu P4383)

Bridge 1 — 2D Slope Convexity (Codeforces 739 E — Gosha is hunting, \(N, A, B \le 2000\)): We have \(N\) Pokémon, \(A\) Pokéballs (catch probability \(p_i\)), and \(B\) Ultra Balls (catch probability \(u_i\), combined probability \(1 - (1 - p_i)(1 - u_i) = p_i + u_i - p_i u_i\)).

Pure MCMF View: Source \(s\) sends cap \(A\) to node \(P\) (Pokéballs) and cap \(B\) to node \(U\) (Ultra Balls). For each Pokémon \(i\), \(P \xrightarrow{1, -p_i} i\) and \(U \xrightarrow{1, -u_i} i\). Since \(p_i + u_i - p_i u_i < p_i + u_i\), using both balls on Pokémon \(i\) has diminishing marginal returns (concavity): the first ball arriving at \(i\) gains its full probability, while the second ball loses \(-p_i u_i\), modeled by two parallel arcs from \(i \to t\): arc 1 with \((\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=0)\) and arc 2 with \((\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=+p_i u_i)\).
Why WQS Replaces MCMF at \(N = 2000\): Because the graph is a concave flow network in both supplies \((A, B)\), the optimal profit function \(P(A, B)\) is jointly concave in \(A\) and \(B\). Replacing the two supply caps \(A\) and \(B\) with Lagrange multipliers \(\lambda_A, \lambda_B\) reduces the inner problem to \(N\) independent \(O(1)\) four-way choices per Pokémon ({none, P, U, both}), solving the problem in \(O(N \log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) time (\(50 \times 50 \times 2000\) operations \(\approx 15\text{ ms}\))!

Bridge 2 — Vertex-Disjoint Path Cover Slope on Trees (Luogu P4383 [八省联考2018] 林克卡特树, \(N, K \le 3 \cdot 10^5\)): Selecting \(K + 1\) vertex-disjoint simple paths in a weighted tree to maximize total edge weight is equivalent to a minimum-cost flow of volume \(K + 1\) where each vertex has capacity \(1\) (splitting \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1, 0} v_{\text{out}}\)). By Theorem 17.5, the maximum weight \(P(k)\) as a function of path count \(k = K + 1\) is concave! Relaxing the path count \(k\) with a per-path penalty \(\lambda\) reduces each slope probe to an \(O(N)\) tree DP with state dp[u][deg in {0, 1, 2}], reducing \(O(N K)\) to \(O(N \log(\sum |w_e|))\).

section: 3. Eliminating Initial Negative Cycles via Mandatory Saturation (强制满流, H-19)
text:
3. Eliminating Initial Negative Cycles via Mandatory Saturation (强制满流, H-19)
What happens when a flow network \(G = (V, E, u, c)\) contains negative-cost directed cycles \(c(W) < 0\) at \(f \equiv 0\)—or when you simply want a universal, zero-SPFA method that eliminates all negative-cost arcs \((u \to v, u_e, c_e < 0)\) before running a single shortest-path search?

3.1 Why Standard SSP & SPFA Fail on Initial Negative Cycles
By Lemma 17.3(2), potential transformations \(\pi: V \to \mathbb{R}\) leave the cost of every directed cycle completely invariant:
\[
c^\pi(W) = \sum_{(u,v) \in W} \bigl(c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v\bigr) = c(W)
\]
Consequently, if the initial residual network \(G_0 = G\) contains a directed cycle \(W\) with \(c(W) < 0\):

No Valid Initial Potential Exists: Since \(\sum_{a \in W} c^\pi(a) = c(W) < 0\), at least one arc \(a \in W\) must have \(c^\pi(a) < 0\) for every possible potential vector \(\pi \in \mathbb{R}^V\).
SPFA Enters an Infinite Negative-Cycle Loop: Attempting to compute \(\pi_0\) via Bellman–Ford or SPFA loops forever around \(W\).
Why Naive Cycle-Cancelling (Klein 1967) Is Too Slow: Detecting negative cycles via Bellman–Ford and saturating them one by one takes \(O(V E \cdot F \cdot C)\) time in the worst case and requires complex cycle-detection bookkeeping.

Instead, the Chinese competitive programming literature (强制满流 / Mandatory Pre-Saturation, H-19) resolves all negative-cost arcs and all negative-cost cycles simultaneously in \(O(E)\) preprocessing by reducing the problem to a non-negative-cost circulation with nodal demands (Ch 04)!


3.2 Algebraic Derivation of Mandatory Pre-Saturation (强制满流)
Consider any original arc \(e = (u \to v)\) whose unit cost is strictly negative: \(c_e < 0\), with capacity bound \(0 \le f_e \le u_e\).
Why would an optimal flow ever want to route flow along \(e\)? Because \(c_e < 0\), every unit routed along \(e\) reduces total cost! Rather than starting at \(f_e = 0\) and waiting for a shortest-path algorithm to discover \(e\), let us greedily pre-saturate \(e\) to its full capacity \(u_e\) by defining the refund variable \(\bar{f}_e \triangleq u_e - f_e\):
\[
f_e = u_e - \bar{f}_e, \quad \text{where } 0 \le \bar{f}_e \le u_e
\]
Substitute \(f_e = u_e - \bar{f}_e\) into both the objective function and the nodal flow conservation equations:

Objective Cost Transformation (Negative Cost \(\to\) Positive Refund Cost): The contribution of arc \(e\) to the total cost \(C(f)\) becomes:
\[
c_e f_e = c_e (u_e - \bar{f}_e) = \underbrace{u_e c_e}_{\text{fixed constant } (< 0)} + \underbrace{(-c_e)}_{> 0} \bar{f}_e
\]
Here \(u_e c_e\) is a fixed constant added to base_cost, while the decision variable \(\bar{f}_e \in [0, u_e]\) has a strictly positive unit cost \(-c_e = |c_e| > 0\)!
Nodal Conservation Transformation (Forward Arc \(u \to v\) \(\to\) Reverse Refund Arc \(v \to u\)): Sending \(f_e = u_e - \bar{f}_e\) units from \(u\) to \(v\) means:

A fixed mandatory flow of \(u_e\) leaves \(u\) and enters \(v\), updating the nodal excess balance (Ch 04):
\[
M(u) \mathrel{-}= u_e, \qquad M(v) \mathrel{+}= u_e
\]
Choosing \(\bar{f}_e\) units of refund decreases outflow from \(u\) by \(\bar{f}_e\) and decreases inflow to \(v\) by \(\bar{f}_e\)—which is mathematically identical to routing \(\bar{f}_e \in [0, u_e]\) units of flow in the REVERSE direction from \(v\) to \(u\) at unit cost \(-c_e > 0\)!


flowchart LR
    subgraph Before["1. Original Negative-Cost Arc (c_e < 0)"]
        direction LR
        u1(("u")) -->|"f_e ∈ [0, u_e], cost = c_e < 0"| v1(("v"))
    end
    subgraph After["2. Pre-Saturated Refund Gadget (-c_e > 0)"]
        direction LR
        u2(("u\nM(u) -= u_e"))
        v2(("v\nM(v) += u_e"))
        v2 -->|"f̄_e ∈ [0, u_e], cost = -c_e > 0"| u2
    end
    Before ==>|"Pre-saturate f_e = u_e - f̄_e\nbase_cost += u_e · c_e"| After

Restoring Nodal Conservation via Super-Terminals \(S^* \to T^*\) (Ch 04): After applying this replacement to every negative-cost arc \(e \in E\) (and adding unlimited feedback arc \(t \xrightarrow{\infty, 0} s\) if solving an \(s\text{--}t\) flow problem), the transformed graph \(G^+\) contains ONLY non-negative edge costs (\(c \ge 0\))! To reconcile the nodal imbalances \(M(w)\) induced by pre-saturation:

Create super-source \(S^*\) and super-sink \(T^*\).
For each vertex \(w \in V\) with \(M(w) > 0\), add arc \(S^* \xrightarrow{\text{cap} = M(w), \text{cost} = 0} w\).
For each vertex \(w \in V\) with \(M(w) < 0\), add arc \(w \xrightarrow{\text{cap} = -M(w), \text{cost} = 0} T^*\).
Run standard Primal–Dual MCMF from \(S^*\) to \(T^*\) with zero initial potentials \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\)!








ImportantTheorem 17.6 (Why Mandatory Saturation Correctly Resolves Negative Cycles)



Suppose \(G\) contains a negative-cost directed cycle \(W\) with bottleneck capacity \(\delta\) and cost \(c(W) < 0\). How does the \(S^* \to T^*\) MCMF run behave on \(W\)?

Suppose every arc on \(W\) had negative cost (\(c_e < 0\)). When we pre-saturate every \(e \in W\) by \(\delta\) units, the inflow and outflow at every vertex \(w \in W\) increase by the exact same amount \(\delta\), leaving \(M(w)\) unchanged! Even better, the reverse refund cycle \(W^{\text{rev}}\) has strictly positive cost \(-c(W) > 0\), so the \(S^* \to T^*\) MCMF leaves \(\bar{f}_e = 0\) on \(W^{\text{rev}}\) and keeps the negative cycle \(W\) saturated in \(O(1)\) time without pushing a single unit of flow from \(S^*\)!
Suppose \(W\) is a mixed negative cycle: e.g., two negative arcs \(1 \xrightarrow{-4} 2 \xrightarrow{-3} 3\) and one positive arc \(3 \xrightarrow{+2} 1\) (total cycle cost \(c(W) = -4 - 3 + 2 = -5 < 0\)). Pre-saturating the two negative arcs creates excess \(M(3) > 0\) at node \(3\) and deficit \(M(1) < 0\) at node \(1\). Then in the \(S^* \to T^*\) MCMF, \(S^* \to 3\) compares two competing ways to route flow from \(3\) to \(1\):

Option A (Complete the cycle forward): Route along the positive forward arc \(3 \xrightarrow{+2} 1\) at cost \(+2\).
Option B (Cancel/Refund the negative arcs): Route backward along the refund arcs \(3 \xrightarrow{+3} 2 \xrightarrow{+4} 1\) at cost \(+7\). Because \(+2 < +7\), Dijkstra from \(S^*\) automatically picks Option A (\(3 \xrightarrow{+2} 1\)), completing the negative cycle \(W\) at net cost \((-4 - 3) + 2 = -5\)!

Conversely, if the positive arc had cost \(+10\) (so \(c(W) = -4 - 3 + 10 = +3 > 0\), a positive cycle that should NOT be taken), Option B (refunding at cost \(+7\)) is strictly cheaper than Option A (completing the cycle at cost \(+10\)), so Dijkstra automatically refunds the pre-saturated arcs (\(-7 + 7 = 0\) net cost)! \(\blacksquare\)





3.3 Hand-Checkable 3-Node Negative-Cycle Trace
Let us verify Theorem 17.6 by hand on a 3-node circulation network \(V = \{1, 2, 3\}\) with no external source/sink:

\(e_1 = (1 \to 2, \text{cap} = 2, \text{cost} = -4)\)
\(e_2 = (2 \to 3, \text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = -3)\)
\(e_3 = (3 \to 1, \text{cap} = 2, \text{cost} = +2)\)

By inspection, the optimal circulation routes \(1\) unit around the negative cycle \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1\) (limited by bottleneck \(u(e_2) = 1\)) for a minimum cost of \(1 \times (-4 - 3 + 2) = -5\).
Now let us execute Mandatory Pre-Saturation (强制满流):

Initialize: base_cost = 0, \(M = [0, 0, 0]\).
Process \(e_1 = (1 \to 2, 2, -4)\) (\(c < 0\)):

Pre-saturate \(f(e_1) = 2\): base_cost += 2 * (-4) = -8.
Update balances: \(M(1) \mathrel{-}= 2 \implies -2\), \(M(2) \mathrel{+}= 2 \implies +2\).
Add reverse refund arc \(e_1^{\text{ref}} = (2 \to 1, \text{cap} = 2, \text{cost} = +4)\).

Process \(e_2 = (2 \to 3, 1, -3)\) (\(c < 0\)):

Pre-saturate \(f(e_2) = 1\): base_cost += 1 * (-3) = -11.
Update balances: \(M(2) \mathrel{-}= 1 \implies +1\), \(M(3) \mathrel{+}= 1 \implies +1\).
Add reverse refund arc \(e_2^{\text{ref}} = (3 \to 2, \text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = +3)\).

Process \(e_3 = (3 \to 1, 2, +2)\) (\(c \ge 0\)):

Keep as normal forward arc \(e_3 = (3 \to 1, \text{cap} = 2, \text{cost} = +2)\).

Connect Super-Terminals \(S^* \to T^*\):

Final balances: \(M(1) = -2\), \(M(2) = +1\), \(M(3) = +1\).
Since \(M(2) = 1 > 0\) and \(M(3) = 1 > 0\), add \(S^* \xrightarrow{1, 0} 2\) and \(S^* \xrightarrow{1, 0} 3\).
Since \(M(1) = -2 < 0\), add \(1 \xrightarrow{2, 0} T^*\).

Run Primal–Dual MCMF from \(S^*\) to \(T^*\) with \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\):

Unit 1: Shortest path from \(S^*\) to \(T^*\) is \(S^* \xrightarrow{0} 3 \xrightarrow{+2} 1 \xrightarrow{0} T^*\) of cost \(+2\) (using 1 unit of \(e_3\)).
Unit 2: Node \(3\)’s supply from \(S^*\) is now exhausted; the remaining supply is at node \(2\). Shortest path from \(S^* \to 2 \to \dots \to T^*\) compares:

\(S^* \xrightarrow{0} 2 \xrightarrow{+4} 1 \xrightarrow{0} T^*\) (refunding 1 unit of \(e_1^{\text{ref}}\) at cost \(+4\)), vs.
no forward arc from \(2 \to 3\) (already pre-saturated). Thus Unit 2 takes \(S^* \to 2 \xrightarrow{+4} 1 \to T^*\) at cost \(+4\), setting \(\bar{f}(e_1) = 1 \implies f(e_1) = 2 - 1 = 1\).

Total Cost: base_cost + mcmf_cost = -11 + (2 + 4) = -5.
Recovered True Flows: \(f(e_1) = 2 - \bar{f}(e_1) = 1\), \(f(e_2) = 1 - \bar{f}(e_2) = 1\), \(f(e_3) = 1\). Every vertex has exact conservation, and the negative cycle is optimally saturated!




3.4 Flagship Case Study: Codeforces 708 D — Incorrect Flow
Let us see how Mandatory Saturation unlocks one of the most celebrated Division 1 network flow problems on Codeforces: CF 708 D — Incorrect Flow (also featured in full implementation detail in Problem #135).

Problem Statement: You are given a directed graph with \(N \le 100\) vertices (\(s = 1, t = N\)) and \(M \le 100\) edges. Each edge \(e = (u \to v)\) has a true capacity \(c_e\) and a corrupted flow value \(f_e\) produced by a buggy program. Both flow conservation at internal vertices \(v \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}\) and capacity bounds \(f_e \le c_e\) may currently be violated! In one operation of cost \(1\), you may increment or decrement any \(f_e\) by \(1\), or increment \(c_e\) by \(1\) (capacities \(c_e\) can never be decreased, and \(f_e \ge 0\) always). Find the minimum total operations needed to transform \((f, c)\) into a valid \(s\text{--}t\) flow (of ANY valid flow value).


Step-by-Step Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation
Let \(f'_e \ge 0\) be the final repaired flow on edge \(e = (u \to v)\).

Step 1 — Lock In the Pre-Injected Base Flow \(f_e\): Initially, each edge \(e = (u \to v)\) already carries \(f_e\) units of flow. This pre-injected flow contributes \(+f_e\) to \(M(v)\) and \(-f_e\) to \(M(u)\). Also add the unlimited return arc \(t \xrightarrow{\infty, 0} s\) because the final \(s\text{--}t\) flow value is unconstrained.
Step 2 — Plot the Marginal Cost Curve of Changing \(f'_e\) Relative to \(f_e\) and \(c_e\): To reach a final flow \(f'_e \ge 0\), the minimum new capacity required is \(c'_e = \max(c_e, f'_e)\), so the total repair cost on edge \(e\) as a function of \(f'_e\) is:
\[
\text{cost}_e(f'_e) = |f'_e - f_e| + \max(0, f'_e - c_e)
\]
This splits into two cases depending on whether the initial flow \(f_e\) already violates the capacity \(c_e\):

Case A (\(f_e \le c_e\) — Initially Within Capacity): Starting from \(f'_e = f_e\) (base cost \(0\)), we have three convex decision regimes around \(f_e\):

Decrease flow (\(0 \le f'_e \le f_e\)): We can send up to \(f_e\) units backward along \((v \to u)\) at unit cost \(+1\) per unit.
Increase flow up to \(c_e\) (\(f_e \le f'_e \le c_e\)): We can send up to \(c_e - f_e\) units forward along \((u \to v)\) at unit cost \(+1\) per unit (only paying \(|f'_e - f_e|\)).
Increase flow beyond \(c_e\) (\(f'_e > c_e\)): Every additional unit sent forward along \((u \to v)\) requires incrementing both \(f'_e\) and \(c'_e\), costing \(+2\) per unit with capacity \(\infty\).

Case B (\(f_e > c_e\) — Initially Overflowing Capacity!): If we keep \(f'_e = f_e\), we must already pay a mandatory base penalty of \(f_e - c_e\) to raise the capacity \(c'_e\) up to \(f_e\)! Thus, add \(f_e - c_e\) to base_cost, and examine the marginal cost of changing \(f'_e\) from \(f_e\):

Decrease flow from \(f_e\) down to \(c_e\) (\(c_e \le f'_e \le f_e\)): For each unit we reduce \(f'_e\) inside \([c_e, f_e]\), our flow-change penalty \(|f'_e - f_e|\) goes up by \(+1\), while our capacity-overflow penalty \(f'_e - c_e\) goes down by \(-1\)! The two changes cancel to net marginal cost \(0\)! Thus, we add a backward refund arc \((v \to u, \text{cap} = f_e - c_e, \text{cost} = 0)\).
Decrease flow below \(c_e\) (\(0 \le f'_e < c_e\)): Once \(f'_e\) drops below \(c_e\), capacity overflow is already \(0\), so reducing \(f'_e\) further costs \(+1\) per unit along backward arc \((v \to u, \text{cap} = c_e, \text{cost} = +1)\).
Increase flow above \(f_e\) (\(f'_e > f_e\)): Increasing \(f'_e\) further increments both flow and capacity, costing \(+2\) per unit along forward arc \((u \to v, \text{cap} = \infty, \text{cost} = +2)\).



Notice the miracle: every single arc in both Case A and Case B has non-negative cost (\(\text{cost} \in \{0, 1, 2\}\))! Connecting \(S^* \to T^*\) via the nodal balances \(M(v)\) and running standard Primal–Dual MCMF with \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\) solves the entire problem in \(O(M (N + M) \log N)\) time!

text:
5. The 4-Step MCMF & Negative-Arc Compilation Protocol
Whenever a problem asks you to optimize a linear cost or profit objective over capacity-constrained routes, schedules, or circulations, follow this deterministic 4-step compilation checklist before writing a single line of code:

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic & Complexity Audit:

Identify the flow carrier (travelers, paths, time units, net color balance) and verify that the number of augmenting units \(F\) or vertices \(V\) permits Primal–Dual MCMF (\(O(F (V + E) \log V)\)).
If \(V, F \ge 10^5\) on a tree or constant-resource DP, check whether Theorem 17.5 (Slope Convexity + WQS Binary Search) eliminates the flow graph entirely (or whether Ch 20 Simulated MCMF applies).

Step 2 — Algebraic Conservation, Disjointness & Multi-Rate Splitting:

Write down the exact capacity interval \([l_e, u_e]\) and unit cost \(c_e\) for every transition.
If an element (vertex or edge) yields a reward \(w_v > 0\) on its first visit and \(0\) on subsequent visits (POJ 3422), split \(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\) into parallel arcs: a harvest arc (cap = 1, cost = -w_v) and a bypass arc (cap = K - 1, cost = 0).
If a problem tests multiple disjointness levels (Luogu P4013), isolate vertex capacity on \(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\) and transition capacity on \(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}\).

Step 3 — Negative-Cost & Potential Regime Selection (\(\pi_0\) vs. Mandatory Saturation):

Never call SPFA inside the augmentation loop (H-17), and never shift variable-hop edge costs by \(+M\) (FM-17e).
Choose your exact preprocessing weapon from the 4 regimes:

Non-negative costs (\(c_e \ge 0\)): Set \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\).
DAG with negative rewards (\(c_e < 0\)): Condense SCCs if needed (ABC 214 H) and run an \(O(V + E)\) Topological DP for \(\pi_0\).
Fixed-hop bipartite graph: Set \(\pi_0\) in \(O(V + E)\) by taking column minima (or apply per-unit-flow \(+M\) shift solely on the single mandatory cut layer).
Cyclic graph with negative cycles or lower bounds \([l_e, u_e]\): Use BoundedMCMF (Sec 3–4) to pre-saturate all negative arcs (\(f_e = u_e - \bar{f}_e\)) and lower bounds (\(f_e = l_e + \tilde{f}_e\)), reducing directly to \(\pi_0 \equiv 0\)!


Step 4 — Stopping Rule & Capped Update Audit:

Select the exact stopping regime (Sec 2.2): Max-Flow (\(\text{d}[t] < \infty\)), Min-Cost Feasible Flow (\(\pi_t - \pi_s < 0\)), Budget Cap (\(C + \delta \lambda_k \le B\)), or Full Slope Extraction.
Always update potentials via the Capped Shift \(\pi'_v \gets \pi_v + \min(d^\pi(v), d^\pi(t))\) (H-18).

7. Pre-Submission Checklist & FM-17 Diagnostic Audit
Before submitting any Min-Cost Flow or Bounded Min-Cost Circulation solution, run through this 6-point diagnostic audit:









Audit ID
Failure Mode / Bug Pattern
Symptom on Judge
Exact Mathematical Fix




FM-17a (H-17)
Calling SPFA inside the augmentation loop (while (spfa()))
TLE on grids, dense bipartite graphs, or \(N \ge 2000\) (ABC 214 H)
Maintain Johnson potentials \(\pi_v\) and run Dijkstra in \(O((V + E) \log V)\) per phase.


FM-17b (H-18)
Uncapped potential update pi[v] += d[v] when Dijkstra exits early or \(d[v] = \infty\)
WA (negative reduced costs created on unpopped frontier) or int64 overflow
Always use the Capped Shift: \(\pi'_v \gets \pi_v + \min(d^\pi(v), d^\pi(t))\).


FM-17c (FM-15)
Setting reverse edge cost to 0 or +cost instead of -cost
WA on any instance requiring flow cancellation (Luogu P2153) or infinite negative 2-cycle
Enforce strict skew-symmetry: rev.cost = -fwd.cost.


FM-17d
Encoding an undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) as a single MCMF edge pair with rev.cap = u_e, rev.cost = -c
Immediate negative cycle \(u \to v \to u\) of cost \(-c < 0\) at \(f \equiv 0\)
Compile every undirected edge into two independent directed edge pairs (4 adjacency entries).


FM-17e
Shifting variable-hop negative edge costs by \(+M\) (c'(e) = c(e) + M)
WA (short low-reward paths beat long high-reward paths due to \(\|P\| \cdot M\) bias)
Keep true costs \(c(e)\) and compute \(\pi_0\) via \(O(V + E)\) DAG DP (Regime 2) or use Mandatory Saturation (Sec 3).


FM-17f (H-19)
Running standard SSP/SPFA on a network with initial negative cycles or forgetting base_cost in BoundedMCMF
Infinite loop in SPFA or missing \(\sum l_e c_e + \sum_{c_e < 0} u_e c_e\) in final answer
Pre-saturate all \(c_e < 0\) arcs to \(u_e\), reverse them to \((v \to u, u_e - l_e, -c_e > 0)\), and add base_cost.
