title: Chapter 09 — Minimum Cut as Binary Variable Assignment & Project Selection
section: 1. The Paradigm Shift — From Physical Pipes to Logical Binary Variables (\(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\))
text:
1. The Paradigm Shift — From Physical Pipes to Logical Binary Variables (\(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\))
In Parts I and II of this textbook, flow networks represented physical movement or explicit matching: units of fluid travelling along pipes from \(S\) to \(T\), trajectories stitching across a DAG, or disjoint pairings between left and right vertices.
Beginning in Part III (Chapters 09–13), we abandon the physical pipe metaphor entirely. Whenever we invoke a minimum \((S, T)\)-cut solver in this part of the book, no physical commodity is flowing through the problem’s domain. Instead, the directed network \(G = (V, E)\) is a compiled algebraic circuit whose \((S, T)\)-partitions \((V_S, V_T)\) are in one-to-one correspondence with truth assignments to \(N\) binary decision variables \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_N) \in \{0, 1\}^N\).
In the Japanese competitive programming literature (noshi91, maspypy, tatyam), this paradigm is celebrated as 燃やす埋める (Burn or Bury): every decision item \(i\) must ultimately be thrown into either the \(S\)-furnace (“burn”) or the \(T\)-pit (“bury”), and each directed edge \((u \to v, c)\) acts as a tax collector that charges penalty \(c \ge 0\) if and only if \(u\) lands in \(S\) while \(v\) lands in \(T\).


1.1 Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
How do you recognize a Minimum-Cut Binary Assignment or Project Selection problem when the English problem statement mentions no graphs, no pipes, and no flows?

Binary Decision Universe: Every decision entity \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) must be assigned to one of two mutually exclusive states:

Select vs. Abandon, Build vs. Skip, Keep vs. Smash, Assign to Group A vs. Group B, or Fire vs. Retain.

Overlapping Prerequisites or Coupled Pairwise Penalties:

Choosing entity \(u\) forces you to also choose (or pay for) entity \(v\) (\(x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1\)), or choosing \(u\) without \(v\) incurs a penalty \(c_{uv} > 0\).
Why Tree / Bitmask DP Fails: In a general dependency DAG or interaction hypergraph, two projects \(u_1, u_2\) can share a common prerequisite instrument \(v\) (forming diamond subgraphs \(u_1 \to v \leftarrow u_2\)). A subtree DP cannot merge the profit of \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) without either double-counting the cost of \(v\) or tracking the entire frontier of already-purchased instruments (\(2^N\) states).
Why Greedy Fails: An instrument \(v\) may be unprofitable for any single experiment \(u_1\) (\(p_{u_1} < c_v\)), so a local greedy check rejects \(u_1\); yet when five experiments \(u_1, \dots, u_5\) share \(v\), their combined profit \(\sum_{k=1}^5 p_{u_k} \gg c_v\) makes the bundle overwhelmingly profitable.

Constraint Bound Signature: \(N, M \in [50, 5 \cdot 10^4]\) entities/interactions with arbitrary large weights \(V_{\max} \le 10^9\).

Even when weights are \(10^9\), if finite capacities appear primarily on \(S\)-incident and \(T\)-incident arcs while internal dependency arcs carry capacity \(+\infty\), Dinic’s algorithm runs in strongly polynomial time (\(O(V^2 E)\) in general and \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) on bipartite closure networks), completely independent of \(V_{\max}\).





1.2 Step 2: The Cut Monomial \(c \cdot x_u (1 - x_v)\) & The Dual-Convention Rosetta Stone
Let \(G = (V, E)\) be a directed network with source \(S\), sink \(T\), decision vertices \(U = V \setminus \{S, T\}\), and non-negative edge capacities \(c: E \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \cup \{+\infty\}\).
An \((S, T)\)-cut is a partition \(V = V_S \sqcup V_T\) satisfying \(S \in V_S\) and \(T \in V_T\). By definition (Chapter 1), its capacity is the sum of capacities of all directed edges whose tail lies in \(V_S\) and whose head lies in \(V_T\):
\[\text{cap}(V_S, V_T) = \sum_{\substack{(u \to v) \in E \\ u \in V_S, \, v \in V_T}} c(u \to v).\]
Crucially, because the cut is directed, an edge \((u \to v)\) with \(u \in V_T\) and \(v \in V_S\) (crossing backward from \(V_T\) to \(V_S\)) contributes \(0\) to \(\text{cap}(V_S, V_T)\).
To turn \(\text{cap}(V_S, V_T)\) into an algebraic polynomial, we assign each vertex \(v \in V\) a binary indicator variable. In the global literature, two opposite conventions exist for mapping \(V_S\) and \(V_T\) to \(\{0, 1\}\). Mixing them up is the single most common source of reversed edges in contest implementations, so we state both explicitly and establish a permanent translation dictionary.

Convention A ([ZH] Selection / Closure Convention — Primary Convention of This Chapter)
For every vertex \(v \in V\), define \(x_v \in \{0, 1\}\) as the membership indicator of \(V_S\):
\[x_v = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } v \in V_S \quad (\text{"selected / active / kept on the } S\text{-side"}), \\ 0 & \text{if } v \in V_T \quad (\text{"abandoned / inactive / relegated to the } T\text{-side"}), \end{cases}\]
with fixed boundary constants \(x_S = 1\) and \(x_T = 0\).
Under Convention A, when does a directed edge \((u \to v)\) of capacity \(c \ge 0\) cross the cut from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\)? Precisely when \(u \in V_S\) (\(x_u = 1\)) and \(v \in V_T\) (\(x_v = 0\)). Over \(\{0, 1\}^2\), the unique polynomial that evaluates to \(1\) at \((x_u, x_v) = (1, 0)\) and \(0\) on the other three states \((0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)\) is the product \(x_u (1 - x_v)\):
\[\boxed{\text{Directed Edge } (u \xrightarrow{c} v) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{Cut Monomial } c \cdot x_u (1 - x_v)}\]
Substituting \(x_S = 1\) and \(x_T = 0\) into this single rule immediately yields all three atomic building blocks of a minimum-cut network:

Source-to-Vertex Edge \((S \xrightarrow{c} u)\): Since \(x_S = 1\), the cut monomial is \(c \cdot x_S (1 - x_u) = c(1 - x_u)\). It charges penalty \(c\) if and only if \(x_u = 0\) (\(u \in V_T\)).
Vertex-to-Sink Edge \((u \xrightarrow{c} T)\): Since \(x_T = 0\), the cut monomial is \(c \cdot x_u (1 - x_T) = c x_u\). It charges penalty \(c\) if and only if \(x_u = 1\) (\(u \in V_S\)).
Internal Directed Edge \((u \xrightarrow{c} v)\): Charges penalty \(c \cdot x_u(1 - x_v)\) if and only if \(x_u = 1 \land x_v = 0\) (\(u \in V_S, v \in V_T\)).

Summing over all edges of \(G\), the capacity of the cut \((V_S, V_T)\) induced by \(\mathbf{x} \in \{0, 1\}^U\) is the Quadratic Pseudo-Boolean Cut Polynomial (a quadratic posiform in literals \(x_u\) and \(\bar{x}_v = 1 - x_v\)):
\[\Phi_G(\mathbf{x}) = \underbrace{\sum_{u \in U} c(S \to u)\,(1 - x_u)}_{\text{severed } S \to u \text{ when } x_u = 0} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{u \in U} c(u \to T)\,x_u}_{\text{severed } u \to T \text{ when } x_u = 1} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{(u \to v) \in E(U)} c(u \to v)\,x_u(1 - x_v)}_{\text{severed } u \to v \text{ when } x_u = 1, \, x_v = 0}.\]


Convention B ([JA] 燃やす埋める / Kolmogorov–Zabih Convention)
In Japanese treatises (noshi91, maspypy) and computer vision papers (Kolmogorov–Zabih 2004), the binary variable \(y_v \in \{0, 1\}\) is defined as the membership indicator of \(V_T\) (\(y_v = 1 - x_v\)):
\[y_v = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } v \in V_S \quad (y_S = 0), \\ 1 & \text{if } v \in V_T \quad (y_T = 1). \end{cases}\]
Under Convention B, an edge \((u \to v)\) is severed iff \(y_u = 0\) and \(y_v = 1\), producing the cut monomial \(c \cdot (1 - y_u) y_v\). Both conventions compile the exact same directed graph when we identify “selected” with \(V_S\) (\(x_v = 1 \iff y_v = 0\)).








Modelling Concept
Convention A (\(x_S = 1, x_T = 0\): \(x_v = [v \in V_S]\))
Convention B (\(y_S = 0, y_T = 1\): \(y_v = [v \in V_T]\))




State Meaning of \(v \in V_S\) (Selected)
\(x_v = 1\)
\(y_v = 0\) (\(y_v = 1 - x_v\))


State Meaning of \(v \in V_T\) (Abandoned)
\(x_v = 0\)
\(y_v = 1\)


Internal Edge \((u \xrightarrow{c} v)\)
\(c \cdot x_u (1 - x_v)\) (penalizes \(x_u = 1, x_v = 0\))
\(c \cdot (1 - y_u) y_v\) (penalizes \(y_u = 0, y_v = 1\))


Source Edge \((S \xrightarrow{c} u)\)
\(c \cdot (1 - x_u)\) (cut when \(u \in V_T\))
\(c \cdot y_u\) (cut when \(u \in V_T\))


Sink Edge \((u \xrightarrow{c} T)\)
\(c \cdot x_u\) (cut when \(u \in V_S\))
\(c \cdot (1 - y_u)\) (cut when \(u \in V_S\))


Implication (\(u \in V_S \implies v \in V_S\))
\(\infty \cdot x_u(1 - x_v) \iff (u \xrightarrow{\infty} v)\)
\(\infty \cdot (1 - y_u)y_v \iff (u \xrightarrow{\infty} v)\)







1.3 Step 3: The Optimistic Baseline Transformation (先拿后退) & Unary Normalization
A minimum \((S, T)\)-cut solver computes \(\min_{\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^U} \Phi_G(\mathbf{x})\) with non-negative edge capacities \(c(e) \ge 0\). Yet project selection and closure problems almost always ask to maximize a net profit function \(\Psi(\mathbf{x})\) containing both positive rewards and negative costs.
How do we turn \(\max_{\mathbf{x}} \Psi(\mathbf{x})\) into \(\min_{\mathbf{x}} \Phi_G(\mathbf{x})\) without introducing negative edge capacities? Through the two-step accounting identity known in Chinese OI literature (Hu Botao 2007) as 先拿后退 (Pre-Claim Positive Gains, Then Subtract Regret):

1. The Optimistic Baseline Identity (先拿后退)
Suppose each variable \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\) has a weight \(w_i \in \mathbb{R}\) gained when \(x_i = 1\) (and \(0\) when \(x_i = 0\)). Partition the index set \(U\) into positive-weight items \(U^+ = \{i \in U : w_i > 0\}\) and non-positive-weight items \(U^- = \{i \in U : w_i \le 0\}\).
For every positive item \(i \in U^+\), apply the elementary identity \(x_i = 1 - (1 - x_i)\):
\[w_i x_i = \underbrace{w_i}_{\text{Optimistic Baseline}} - \underbrace{w_i (1 - x_i)}_{\text{Forfeited Profit (Regret)}}.\]
For every negative item \(j \in U^-\) (\(w_j \le 0\)), write \(w_j = -|w_j|\), so its contribution is already a non-negative subtraction:
\[w_j x_j = -\underbrace{|w_j| x_j}_{\text{Incurred Cost}}.\]
Summing over all \(i \in U\) yields the Fundamental Optimistic Baseline Identity:
\[\sum_{i \in U} w_i x_i = \underbrace{\sum_{i \in U^+} w_i}_{\text{Baseline } W^+} \;-\; \left(\underbrace{\sum_{i \in U^+} w_i (1 - x_i)}_{\text{Edges } S \xrightarrow{w_i} i} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{j \in U^-} |w_j| x_j}_{\text{Edges } j \xrightarrow{|w_j|} T}\right).\]
Because \(W^+ = \sum_{w_i > 0} w_i\) is a constant independent of \(\mathbf{x}\), maximizing the net gain \(\sum_{i \in U} w_i x_i\) is 100% equivalent to minimizing the non-negative regret-plus-cost sum inside the parentheses:
\[\boxed{\max_{\mathbf{x}} \text{NetGain}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{w_i > 0} w_i - \min\text{Cut}(S, T)}\]
Every term inside the minimum cut now has a strictly non-negative capacity and a crystal-clear economic meaning:

Pre-claim \(W^+ = \sum_{w_i > 0} w_i\) upfront: Pretend we simultaneously collect every positive reward in the problem.
Severing \((S \xrightarrow{w_i} i)\) when \(x_i = 0\) (\(i \in V_T\)): We decided not to select positive project \(i\), so we refund (forfeit) its pre-claimed reward \(w_i > 0\).
Severing \((j \xrightarrow{|w_j|} T)\) when \(x_j = 1\) (\(j \in V_S\)): We decided to select cost-bearing item \(j\), so we pay its purchase cost \(|w_j| \ge 0\).



2. General Two-State Unary Normalization (差値正規化 vs. ゲタを履かせる)
What if an item \(i\) has non-zero payoffs in both states: gaining \(u_i(1) \in \mathbb{R}\) when \(x_i = 1\) and \(u_i(0) \in \mathbb{R}\) when \(x_i = 0\) (or equivalently in minimization, paying unary penalty \(A_i(1 - x_i) + B_i x_i\) where \(A_i\) or \(B_i\) might be negative)? Two algebraic normalization recipes reduce any unary expression to non-negative cut edges:

Recipe 1 — Minimum Extraction / \(O(1)\) 2-Edge Path Pre-Flow (差値正規化, Recommended Default): In minimization of \(U_i(x_i) = A_i(1 - x_i) + B_i x_i\), let \(m_i = \min(A_i, B_i)\). Since \((1 - x_i) + x_i = 1\), extract \(m_i\) into the global constant offset:
\[A_i(1 - x_i) + B_i x_i = m_i + (A_i - m_i)(1 - x_i) + (B_i - m_i)x_i.\]
Now both \(A_i - m_i \ge 0\) and \(B_i - m_i \ge 0\), and at least one of the two capacities is zero!

In maximization of \(u_i(1)x_i + u_i(0)(1 - x_i)\), let \(M_i = \max(u_i(1), u_i(0))\), add \(M_i\) to \(W_{\text{base}}\), and wire either \(S \to i\) of capacity \(u_i(1) - u_i(0)\) (if \(u_i(1) \ge u_i(0)\)) or \(i \to T\) of capacity \(u_i(0) - u_i(1)\) (if \(u_i(0) > u_i(1)\)).
Flow-Theoretic Meaning: If \(A_i > 0\) and \(B_i > 0\) are both positive, wiring both \(S \xrightarrow{A_i} i\) and \(i \xrightarrow{B_i} T\) creates an immediate 2-edge augmenting path \(S \to i \to T\) of capacity \(m_i = \min(A_i, B_i)\). Recipe 1 simply pre-pushes \(m_i\) units of flow along \(S \to i \to T\) in \(O(1)\) time before Dinic even starts!

Recipe 2 — Uniform Constant Pedestal Shift (ゲタを履かせる / “Putting on Geta Clogs”): Add a large constant \(M > \max_i(|A_i|, |B_i|)\) via \(0 = -M + M(1 - x_i) + M x_i\), shifting both capacities to \(A_i + M > 0\) and \(B_i + M > 0\). While Recipe 1 is superior for routine unary normalization (avoiding capacity inflation), Recipe 2 is an indispensable theoretical weapon when we want to force a cardinality invariant across a bipartite graph (as we will see in Section 4.3 on CF 103 E — Buying Sets).





1.4 Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Counterexamples

Concrete Numerical Trace (\(N = 3\) Binary Variables)
Suppose we wish to maximize the score \(\Psi(x_1, x_2, x_3)\) over \(x_1, x_2, x_3 \in \{0, 1\}\) subject to the following rules:

Variable 1: \(x_1 = 1\) yields \(+10\); \(x_1 = 0\) yields \(-4\).
Variable 2: \(x_2 = 1\) costs \(-6\); \(x_2 = 0\) yields \(+5\).
Variable 3: \(x_3 = 1\) yields \(+8\); \(x_3 = 0\) yields \(0\).
Coupling Rules:

Hard logical implication: if \(x_1 = 1\), then we must have \(x_2 = 1\) (\(x_1 = 1 \implies x_2 = 1\)).
Soft directional penalty: if \(x_3 = 1\) while \(x_2 = 0\), we pay a penalty of \(9\).


Let us compile \(\Psi(x_1, x_2, x_3)\) mechanically using Step 2 and Step 3:

Normalize Unary Terms via 先拿后退 (Recipe 1):

Vertex \(1\): \(10 x_1 - 4(1 - x_1) = 10 - 14(1 - x_1) \implies\) add \(+10\) to \(W_{\text{base}}\), wire \(S \xrightarrow{14} 1\).
Vertex \(2\): \(-6 x_2 + 5(1 - x_2) = 5 - 11 x_2 \implies\) add \(+5\) to \(W_{\text{base}}\), wire \(2 \xrightarrow{11} T\).
Vertex \(3\): \(8 x_3 + 0(1 - x_3) = 8 - 8(1 - x_3) \implies\) add \(+8\) to \(W_{\text{base}}\), wire \(S \xrightarrow{8} 3\).
Total Optimistic Baseline: \(W_{\text{base}} = 10 + 5 + 8 = 23\).

Compile Coupling Terms:

Hard implication \(x_1 = 1 \implies x_2 = 1\) forbids \((x_1, x_2) = (1, 0)\), compiled as \(\infty \cdot x_1(1 - x_2) \iff\) directed arc \(1 \xrightarrow{\infty} 2\).
Soft penalty \(9\) when \(x_3 = 1 \land x_2 = 0\) is \(9 x_3(1 - x_2) \iff\) directed arc \(3 \xrightarrow{9} 2\).

[!WARNING] Two Classic Broken-Gadget Errors in Binary Cut Compilation:

section: 2. Picard’s Maximum-Weight Closure Theorem (最大权闭合子图)
text:
2. Picard’s Maximum-Weight Closure Theorem (最大权闭合子图)
We now formalize the cornerstone theorem of Part III, introduced by Jean-Claude Picard in 1976 (“Maximal Closure of a Graph and Applications to Combinatorial Problems”, Management Science) and popularized in competitive programming by Hu Botao’s 2007 national team thesis.

2.1 Definition of a Closed Subgraph & Implication Compilation






ImportantDefinition 2.1 (Closed Subset / Closure of a Directed Graph)



Let \(G_{\text{dep}} = (U, E_{\text{dep}})\) be a directed dependency graph with vertex weights \(w: U \to \mathbb{R}\) (where \(w_u > 0\) represents a net profit and \(w_u < 0\) represents a net cost). A subset of vertices \(C \subseteq U\) is called closed (闭合子图) if no directed edge of \(E_{\text{dep}}\) leaves \(C\):
\[\forall (u \to v) \in E_{\text{dep}}, \qquad u \in C \implies v \in C.\]
The Maximum-Weight Closure Problem (最大权闭合子图) asks for a closed subset \(C^* \subseteq U\) maximizing the total vertex weight:
\[w(C^*) = \max_{\substack{C \subseteq U \\ C \text{ is closed}}} \sum_{u \in C} w_u.\]


Notice that \(C = \emptyset\) is always a valid closed subset with \(w(\emptyset) = 0\), so the maximum closure weight is always \(\ge 0\).

Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation of Picard’s Network \(\mathcal{N}(G_{\text{dep}}, w)\)
Let \(x_u = [u \in C] \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether vertex \(u \in U\) is included in the closed subset \(C\).

Logical Implication Compilation: For each dependency edge \((u \to v) \in E_{\text{dep}}\), the closure condition \(u \in C \implies v \in C\) is the boolean implication \(x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1\). Its unique forbidden state is \((x_u, x_v) = (1, 0)\), which is algebraically equivalent to:
\[x_u(1 - x_v) = 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{Penalty } +\infty \cdot x_u(1 - x_v) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{Directed Arc } (u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v).\]
Unary Weight Compilation (先拿后退): Partition \(U\) into \(U^+ = \{u \in U : w_u > 0\}\), \(U^0 = \{u \in U : w_u = 0\}\), and \(U^- = \{u \in U : w_u < 0\}\), and let \(W^+ = \sum_{u \in U^+} w_u\).

For each \(u \in U^+\) (\(w_u > 0\)): wire \(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u\) (monomial \(w_u(1 - x_u)\), severed if \(u \notin C\)).
For each \(v \in U^-\) (\(w_v < 0\)): wire \(v \xrightarrow{|w_v|} T\) (monomial \(|w_v| x_v\), severed if \(v \in C\)).
For each \(z \in U^0\) (\(w_z = 0\)): no edge to \(S\) or \(T\) is needed (capacity \(0\)).






2.2 Complete Double-Inequality Proof of Picard’s Theorem (1976)






ImportantTheorem 2.1 (Picard’s Maximum-Weight Closure Theorem, 1976)



In the compiled network \(\mathcal{N}(G_{\text{dep}}, w)\) with vertex set \(V = \{S, T\} \cup U\):

Bijection between Closed Sets and Finite Cuts: A subset \(C \subseteq U\) is closed in \(G_{\text{dep}}\) if and only if the partition \((V_S, V_T) = (\{S\} \cup C, \{T\} \cup (U \setminus C))\) is an \((S, T)\)-cut of finite capacity \(\text{cap}(V_S, V_T) < +\infty\).
Exact Cut-Weight Identity: For every closed subset \(C \subseteq U\), the capacity of its corresponding cut \((V_S, V_T)\) satisfies:
\[\text{cap}(V_S, V_T) = W^+ - \sum_{u \in C} w_u, \qquad \text{where } W^+ = \sum_{u \in U^+} w_u.\]
Min-Cut Duality: Consequently, the maximum weight of a closed subset \(C^* \subseteq U\) equals:
\[\max_{C \text{ closed}} \sum_{u \in C} w_u = W^+ - \text{MinCut}(S, T) = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T).\]




Complete Proof
Let \((V_S, V_T)\) be any \((S, T)\)-cut in \(\mathcal{N}(G_{\text{dep}}, w)\), and define \(C = V_S \setminus \{S\} \subseteq U\) (so \(U \setminus C = V_T \setminus \{T\}\)). Every edge of \(\mathcal{N}(G_{\text{dep}}, w)\) belongs to one of three disjoint families:

Dependency arcs \(E_{\text{dep}} = \{(u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v)\}\): An arc \((u \to v) \in E_{\text{dep}}\) crosses from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\) if and only if \(u \in C\) and \(v \notin C\).

\((\implies)\) If \(C\) is closed, no edge \((u \to v) \in E_{\text{dep}}\) has \(u \in C\) and \(v \notin C\), so zero \(\infty\)-capacity arcs cross from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\). Since all other edges have finite capacity, \(\text{cap}(V_S, V_T) < +\infty\).
\((\Longleftarrow)\) Conversely, if \(\text{cap}(V_S, V_T) < +\infty\), then no \(\infty\)-capacity arc can cross from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\), which means \(\neg\exists (u \to v) \in E_{\text{dep}}\) with \(u \in C \land v \notin C\); hence \(C\) is closed.

Source-incident arcs \(\{(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u) : u \in U^+\}\): Since \(S \in V_S\), the arc \((S \to u)\) crosses from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\) if and only if \(u \in V_T\), i.e., \(u \in U^+ \setminus C\).
Sink-incident arcs \(\{(v \xrightarrow{|w_v|} T) : v \in U^-\}\): Since \(T \in V_T\), the arc \((v \to T)\) crosses from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\) if and only if \(v \in V_S\), i.e., \(v \in C \cap U^-\).

For any closed subset \(C \subseteq U\), summing the capacities of the severed edges across these three families yields:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{cap}(\{S\} \cup C, \{T\} \cup (U \setminus C))
&= 0 + \sum_{u \in U^+ \setminus C} w_u + \sum_{v \in C \cap U^-} |w_v| \\
&= \left(\sum_{u \in U^+} w_u - \sum_{u \in C \cap U^+} w_u\right) + \sum_{v \in C \cap U^-} (-w_v) - \sum_{z \in C \cap U^0} 0 \\
&= W^+ - \left(\sum_{u \in C \cap U^+} w_u + \sum_{v \in C \cap U^-} w_v + \sum_{z \in C \cap U^0} w_z\right) \\
&= W^+ - \sum_{u \in C} w_u.
\end{aligned}\]
From this exact identity, we establish the double inequality:

Direction 1 (\(\max_{C \text{ closed}} w(C) \le W^+ - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\)): For every closed subset \(C \subseteq U\), its induced partition \((V_S, V_T)\) is a valid \((S, T)\)-cut, so \(\text{MinCut}(S, T) \le \text{cap}(V_S, V_T) = W^+ - w(C)\), which rearranges to \(w(C) \le W^+ - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\).
Direction 2 (\(\max_{C \text{ closed}} w(C) \ge W^+ - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\)): Since \(C = \emptyset\) gives a finite cut of capacity \(W^+ < +\infty\), the minimum cut \((V_S^*, V_T^*)\) has finite capacity \(\text{MinCut}(S, T) \le W^+ < +\infty\). By Part 1, \(C^* = V_S^* \setminus \{S\}\) is a valid closed subset of \(U\) with \(w(C^*) = W^+ - \text{cap}(V_S^*, V_T^*) = W^+ - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\).

Combining both inequalities completes the proof. \(\blacksquare\)




2.3 Constructive Closure Extraction via \(S_{\min}\) & Zero-Weight Tie-Breaking
In many problems (such as #065 Luogu P2762 — Space Flight Planning and #066 POJ 2987 — Firing), we must output not only the maximum net profit \(w(C^*)\), but also the explicit list of vertices in \(C^*\)—and in POJ 2987, if multiple closed subsets achieve the maximum weight \(w(C^*)\), we must output one with the minimum number of vertices \(|C^*|\)!
How do we extract \(C^*\) from Dinic’s final residual network \(G_{f^*}\)?






ImportantCorollary 2.1 (Canonical Minimal Closure via Residual Reachability \(S_{\min}\))



Let \(f^*\) be any maximum \((S, T)\)-flow in \(\mathcal{N}(G_{\text{dep}}, w)\), and let \(S_{\min}\) be the set of vertices reachable from \(S\) via directed paths of strictly positive residual capacity (\(c_{f^*}(e) > 0\)) in \(G_{f^*}\):
\[S_{\min} = \big\{v \in V : S \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} v\big\}, \qquad C_{\min}^* = S_{\min} \setminus \{S\}.\]
Then:

\(C_{\min}^*\) is an optimal maximum-weight closed subset of \(G_{\text{dep}}\).
Unique Inclusion-Minimal Property: For every maximum-weight closed subset \(C^* \subseteq U\), we have \(C_{\min}^* \subseteq C^*\). In particular, \(C_{\min}^*\) is the unique minimum-cardinality maximum-weight closure (automatically excluding all optional zero-net-gain bundles and isolated \(w_z = 0\) vertices without requiring any weight perturbation!).




Why \(C_{\min}^* \subseteq C^*\) Holds
By Chapter 2 (The Lattice of Minimum Cuts), the family of minimum \((S, T)\)-cuts is closed under intersection \(V_S^{(1)} \cap V_S^{(2)}\), and the residual reachability set \(S_{\min}\) is the unique inclusion-minimal source side among all minimum \((S, T)\)-cuts. Since Theorem 2.1 establishes a bijection \(C \leftrightarrow \{S\} \cup C\) between maximum-weight closures and minimum \((S, T)\)-cuts, \(C_{\min}^* = S_{\min} \setminus \{S\}\) is contained in every maximum-weight closure \(C^*\)!

[!CAUTION] Critical Implementation Trap in Closure Reconstruction (#065 Luogu P2762): Never attempt to reconstruct the chosen projects \(u \in U^+\) or instruments \(v \in U^-\) by checking whether the single edge \((S \to u)\) is unsaturated (\(c_{f^*}(S \to u) > 0\)) or whether \((v \to T)\) is saturated (\(c_{f^*}(v \to T) = 0\))!

A project \(u \in C_{\min}^*\) can have its direct arc \((S \to u)\) 100% saturated (\(c_{f^*}(S \to u) = 0\)) and still belong to \(S_{\min}\) by being reached from \(S\) through another project \(u'\) and a backward residual arc on \((u \to v, \infty)\)!
Conversely, an instrument \(v \notin C_{\min}^*\) can have \((v \to T)\) 100% saturated (\(c_{f^*}(v \to T) = 0\)) if the projects that pushed flow through \(v\) were ultimately cut on the \(S\)-side!

Golden Rule: Always reconstruct \(C_{\min}^*\) by running a full BFS/DFS from \(S\) in \(G_{f^*}\) traversing edges with e.cap - e.flow > 0 and collecting {v in U : vis[v] == true}.





2.4 Step 4: Hand-Checkable Diamond Closure Trace (\(N = 4\))
Consider \(2\) experiments \(E_1, E_2\) and \(2\) instruments \(I_1, I_2\):

Profits: \(w(E_1) = +10\), \(w(E_2) = +12\). (Optimistic baseline \(W^+ = 10 + 12 = 22\).)
Costs: \(w(I_1) = -8\), \(w(I_2) = -9\).
Dependencies: \(E_1\) requires \(\{I_1, I_2\}\); \(E_2\) requires \(\{I_2\}\).


Compiled Network \(\mathcal{N}\):

Source arcs: \(S \xrightarrow{10} E_1\), \(S \xrightarrow{12} E_2\).
Sink arcs: \(I_1 \xrightarrow{8} T\), \(I_2 \xrightarrow{9} T\).
Dependency arcs: \(E_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} I_1\), \(E_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} I_2\), \(E_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} I_2\).

Trace of Dinic’s Augmenting Paths:

Path 1: \(S \to E_1 \to I_1 \to T\), bottleneck \(\min(10, \infty, 8) = 8\). Residual on \(S \to E_1\) is \(2\); \(I_1 \to T\) is saturated (\(0\)).
Path 2: \(S \to E_1 \to I_2 \to T\), bottleneck \(\min(2, \infty, 9) = 2\). Now \(S \to E_1\) is completely saturated (\(0\))! Residual on \(I_2 \to T\) is \(7\).
Path 3: \(S \to E_2 \to I_2 \to T\), bottleneck \(\min(12, \infty, 7) = 7\). Residual on \(S \to E_2\) is \(5\); \(I_2 \to T\) is saturated (\(0\)).
Total Max-Flow / Min-Cut: \(8 + 2 + 7 = 17 \implies\) Maximum Net Profit \(= W^+ - 17 = 22 - 17 = \mathbf{5}\).

Trace of Residual Reachability \(S_{\min}\) (Revealing the Saturation Trap!):

Look at \(S \to E_1\): its residual capacity is \(0\)! A naive check c_f(S -> E_1) > 0 would falsely conclude that \(E_1\) was NOT selected!
Instead, follow the BFS from \(S\) in \(G_{f^*}\):

\(S \to E_2\) has residual capacity \(12 - 7 = 5 > 0 \implies E_2 \in S_{\min}\).
\(E_2 \to I_2\) has residual capacity \(\infty - 7 = \infty > 0 \implies I_2 \in S_{\min}\).
Because Path 2 pushed \(2\) units of flow along \(E_1 \to I_2\), the reverse residual edge \(I_2 \to E_1\) has residual capacity \(2 > 0\)! Thus \(I_2\) reaches \(E_1 \implies E_1 \in S_{\min}\)!
From \(E_1\), the arc \(E_1 \to I_1\) has residual capacity \(\infty - 8 = \infty > 0 \implies I_1 \in S_{\min}\).

Therefore, \(C_{\min}^* = \{E_1, E_2, I_1, I_2\}\) with true profit \(10 + 12 - 8 - 9 = \mathbf{5}\)!

section: 3. Pre-Flow Topological Cycle Pruning & Mutual Dependency Traps
text:
3. Pre-Flow Topological Cycle Pruning & Mutual Dependency Traps
What happens when the prerequisite graph \(G_{\text{dep}} = (U, E_{\text{dep}})\) is not a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), but contains directed cycles \(u_1 \to u_2 \to \dots \to u_k \to u_1\)?
Before writing a single line of Dinic code, you must ask a fundamental modelling question about the physical rules of the problem: Are decisions made simultaneously as a static set, or sequentially one step at a time?


3.1 Simultaneous Set Bundles (Semantics A) vs. Sequential Causal Unlocking (Semantics B)

Semantics A: Simultaneous Set Selection (Cycle = Equivalence Super-Node)
Suppose the problem states: “Select a subset of items \(C \subseteq U\) all at once such that if \(u \in C\) and \((u \to v) \in E_{\text{dep}}\), then \(v \in C\).”
Under Semantics A, a directed cycle \(u_1 \to u_2 \to \dots \to u_k \to u_1\) of \(\infty\)-capacity arcs simply enforces the chain of implications \(x_{u_1} \implies x_{u_2} \implies \dots \implies x_{u_k} \implies x_{u_1}\), which is logically equivalent to:
\[x_{u_1} = x_{u_2} = \dots = x_{u_k} \in \{0, 1\}.\]
Either every vertex in the strongly connected component (SCC) is placed in \(V_S\), or every vertex in the SCC is placed in \(V_T\). Under Semantics A, Picard’s network \(\mathcal{N}(G_{\text{dep}}, w)\) works without any modification: if the cycle’s combined weight \(\sum_{i=1}^k w_{u_i}\) exceeds the cost of its external prerequisites, placing the entire cycle in \(V_S\) severs zero internal \(\infty\)-edges and is completely valid.


Semantics B: Sequential / Causal Unlocking ([NOI2009] 植物大战僵尸 — Cycle = Permanent Deadlock)
Now contrast Semantics A with #070 Luogu P2805 — [NOI2009] 植物大战僵尸 (Plants vs. Zombies):

Zombies enter each row from the right edge and walk left: to eat plant \((r, c)\), a zombie must first eat plant \((r, c + 1)\).
Furthermore, each plant \(v\) can shoot fireballs protecting a set of squares \(u_1, u_2, \dots\); to eat a protected square \(u\), zombies must first eat the protector plant \(v\)!

Here, eating a subset of plants \(C \subseteq U\) is valid if and only if there exists a sequential linear ordering (topological ordering) \((v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{|C|})\) of \(C\) such that when \(v_t\) is eaten at step \(t\), all prerequisites of \(v_t\) have already been eaten at steps \(< t\).
What if Plant \(u\) protects Plant \(v\) AND Plant \(v\) protects Plant \(u\) (\(u \leftrightarrow v\))?

Physical Reality (Semantics B): To eat \(u\), you must first eat \(v\); to eat \(v\), you must first eat \(u\). Neither plant can ever be eaten first! Furthermore, any third plant \(w\) that stands behind \(u\) (or is protected by \(u\)) can never be reached either, even if \(w\) has a positive score of \(+10^9\) and does not belong to any cycle itself!
Mathematical Closure Fallacy (Semantics A): As a static set, \(C = \{u, v\}\) has zero outgoing dependency edges leaving \(\{u, v\}\)! If \(w_u + w_v > 0\), Picard’s unmodified min-cut network happily places \(\{u, v\} \subseteq V_S\), severing zero \(\infty\)-arcs and collecting phantom points from an invincible mutual-protection loop!





3.2 Broken-Gadget Counterexample FM-09 & Why Tarjan’s SCC Deletion Also Fails

[!WARNING] Broken-Gadget Counterexample FM-09 — Unpruned Prerequisite Cycles & The Tarjan SCC Trap:
Consider a \(1 \times 4\) single-row lawn with cells \(u_1 = (0, 0), u_2 = (0, 1), u_3 = (0, 2), u_4 = (0, 3)\) (zombies enter from the right at \(u_4\)), with scores:
\[w(u_1) = +1000, \qquad w(u_2) = -10, \qquad w(u_3) = -10, \qquad w(u_4) = +50.\]

Row-entry prerequisites: \(u_4\) must be eaten before \(u_3\); \(u_3\) before \(u_2\); \(u_2\) before \(u_1\).
Attack protection: Plant \(u_2\) attacks square \(u_3\), so \(u_2\) must be eaten before \(u_3\).

Thus \(u_2\) and \(u_3\) form a deadlocked 2-cycle (\(u_2 \leftrightarrow u_3\)), while \(u_1\) (worth \(+1000\)!) is an acyclic singleton SCC that depends on \(u_2\). Look at what happens under three implementation attempts:









Implementation Attempt
Vertices Fed to Dinic
Claimed Profit
Why It Fails / Succeeds




1. Raw Picard Closure (No Pruning)
\(\{u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4\}\)
\(+1030\) (WA)
Places \(\{u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4\} \subseteq V_S\); internal cycle \(u_2 \leftrightarrow u_3\) never crosses \((V_S, V_T)\), paying only \(10+10=20\) to claim \(1050\).


2. Tarjan SCC (delete if |SCC| >= 2)
\(\{u_1, u_4\}\)
\(+1050\) (WA)
Deletes the 2-cycle \(\{u_2, u_3\}\), which erases the edge separating \(u_1\) from \(u_2\)! Now \(u_1\) appears to have zero prerequisites and is falsely claimed for \(+1000\)!


3. Kahn’s In-Degree-\(0\) BFS on \(G_{\text{pre}}\)
\(\{u_4\}\) only
\(+50\) (AC)
Starts from \(\text{in-deg}=0\) node \(u_4\); when \(u_4\) is popped, \(\text{in-deg}(u_3)\) drops from \(2\) to \(1 > 0\). Queue terminates, pruning both \(\{u_2, u_3\}\) AND downstream \(u_1\)!







3.3 The Two-Phase Causal Pruning Algorithm (Kahn’s BFS + Picard Closure)
To solve any Sequential Causal Closure problem (Semantics B), always execute the following two-phase pipeline:

Phase 1 — Build the Causal Prerequisite Graph \(G_{\text{pre}}\) (Protector -> Protected): Orient edges in the direction of physical unlocking order: add a directed edge \((v \xrightarrow{\text{unlocks}} u) \in E_{\text{pre}}\) whenever \(v\) must be activated/eaten before \(u\). Record in_deg[u] = number of prerequisites of \(u\).

Push all vertices with in_deg[v] == 0 into a queue \(Q\).
While \(Q\) is non-empty, pop \(v\), mark reachable[v] = true, and for each \((v \to u) \in E_{\text{pre}}\), decrement in_deg[u]; if in_deg[u] == 0, push \(u\) into \(Q\).

Phase 2 — Build Picard’s Closure Network on reachable Vertices Only: Discard every vertex \(u\) with reachable[u] == false. On the surviving Induced DAG \(U_{\text{valid}} = \{u \in U : \text{reachable}[u]\}\):

Wire \(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u\) for \(u \in U_{\text{valid}}\) with \(w_u > 0\) (adding \(w_u\) to \(W^+\)).
Wire \(u \xrightarrow{|w_u|} T\) for \(u \in U_{\text{valid}}\) with \(w_u < 0\).
For every \((v \xrightarrow{\text{unlocks}} u) \in E_{\text{pre}}\) with \(u, v \in U_{\text{valid}}\), reverse the edge to form the logical implication \((u \xrightarrow{\text{requires}, \, +\infty} v)\) in the cut network!

section: 4. Non-Graph Closure Archetypes — Divisibility, Interval-Triangle, and Hall-Shifted Closures
text:
4. Non-Graph Closure Archetypes — Divisibility, Interval-Triangle, and Hall-Shifted Closures
The true power of Picard’s theorem in competitive programming is that the dependency graph \(G_{\text{dep}}\) rarely comes given in the input. Instead, it lies hidden inside number-theoretic divisibility, contiguous array intervals, or Hall’s Marriage Theorem. Let us dissect the three canonical non-graph closure archetypes.


4.1 Archetype 1: Divisibility Poset Closure & Complemented Conventions (ARC 085 E — MUL)
In #068 AtCoder ARC 085 E — MUL, we are given \(N \le 100\) gems indexed \(1, \dots, N\) with signed values \(a_i \in [-10^9, 10^9]\). We may perform the following operation any number of times:

Choose a positive integer \(d \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and smash all gems whose index is a multiple of \(d\) (\(d, 2d, 3d, \dots\)).
Maximize the sum of values of the remaining (unsmashed) gems.


Step 1 & Step 2: Why Transitivity of Divisibility Turns Button Choices into Gem Closure
At first glance, the decisions are which buttons \(d \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) to press, while the payoffs belong to which gems \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) survive. Why don’t we need separate vertices for buttons and gems?
Suppose gem \(i\) is smashed by pressing some divisor button \(d \mid i\). Because divisibility is transitive (\(d \mid i \land i \mid j \implies d \mid j\)), that very same button \(d\) already smashes every multiple \(j = k i\) of \(i\)! Conversely, if gem \(i\) is not smashed, then button \(i\) was certainly not pressed. Therefore:
\[\text{A subset of gems } D \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\} \text{ can be the set of smashed gems} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \forall i \in D, \; \forall k \ge 2 \text{ with } ki \le N, \; ki \in D.\]
Taking the contrapositive for the complementary set of kept (surviving) gems \(K = \{1, \dots, N\} \setminus D\):
\[\boxed{j \text{ is kept } (j \in K) \;\land\; i \mid j \quad \Longrightarrow \quad i \text{ is kept } (i \in K)}\]

[!IMPORTANT] Sanity-Checking the Implication Direction in ARC 085 E: Can we keep gem \(1\) and smash gem \(2\)? Yes—just press button \(2\)! So \(1 \in K\) does not imply \(2 \in K\). Can we smash gem \(1\) and keep gem \(2\)? No—pressing button \(1\) smashes every gem! Thus keeping a multiple \(j\) (\(x_j = 1\)) requires keeping all of its divisors \(i \mid j\) (\(x_i = 1\)).

Convention 1 (\(x_i = 1 \iff i \in V_S\) means Gem \(i\) is KEPT):

Implication \(x_j = 1 \implies x_i = 1\) for \(i \mid j\) compiles to directed arc \(j \xrightarrow{+\infty} i\).
Positive gem \(a_i > 0\): wire \(S \xrightarrow{a_i} i\) (pre-claim \(a_i\) in \(W^+\); forfeited if \(i \in V_T\) is smashed).
Negative gem \(a_i < 0\): wire \(i \xrightarrow{|a_i|} T\) (paid if \(i \in V_S\) is kept).

Convention 2 (\(y_i = 1 \iff i \in V_S\) means Gem \(i\) is SMASHED):

Implication \(y_i = 1 \implies y_j = 1\) for \(i \mid j\) compiles to directed arc \(i \xrightarrow{+\infty} j\).
Positive gem \(a_i > 0\): wire \(i \xrightarrow{a_i} T\) (paid if \(i \in V_S\) is smashed).
Negative gem \(a_i < 0\): wire \(S \xrightarrow{|a_i|} i\) (forfeited if \(i \in V_T\) is kept).


Notice that Convention 2 is the exact graph transpose (with \(S\) and \(T\) swapped) of Convention 1, so both networks have the exact same minimum cut capacity! Moreover, by transitivity, we only need \(\infty\)-edges between \(i\) and \(i \cdot p\) for primes \(p\), reducing the edge count from \(O(N \log N)\) to \(O(N \log \log N)\).





4.2 Archetype 2: Interval-Triangle Inclusion DAGs ([SHOI2017] 寿司餐厅)
In #071 Luogu P3749 — [SHOI2017] 寿司餐厅 (Sushi Restaurant), \(N \le 100\) sushi plates sit in a row with type codes \(a_1, \dots, a_N \in [1, 1000]\).

Choosing a contiguous interval of plates \([l, r]\) (\(1 \le l \le r \le N\)) grants a signed satisfaction score \(d_{l,r} \in \mathbb{Z}\), and automatically includes all sub-intervals \([l', r'] \subseteq [l, r]\).
Eating \(c \ge 1\) plates of sushi type \(x\) incurs a total cost of \(m x^2 + c x\) (where \(m \in \{0, 1\}\) is a constant).

How do we compile this seemingly nonlinear, \(O(N^4)\)-dependency problem into a fast closure network?

Transitive Pyramid Compression (\(O(N^4) \to 2\) Edges per Interval): There are \(\binom{N+1}{2} \approx 5050\) intervals \([l, r]\). If we wired \([l, r] \xrightarrow{\infty} [l', r']\) for every sub-interval \([l', r'] \subseteq [l, r]\), we would create \(\approx \frac{N^4}{24} > 4 \cdot 10^6\) edges. Instead, observe that for any interval \([l, r]\) of length \(\ge 2\) (\(l < r\)), every proper sub-interval \([l', r'] \subsetneq [l, r]\) is contained in either \([l + 1, r]\) or \([l, r - 1]\)! By induction on interval length \(L = r - l + 1\):
\[x_{l, r} = 1 \implies x_{l', r'} = 1 \; (\forall [l', r'] \subseteq [l, r]) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \begin{cases} [l, r] \xrightarrow{+\infty} [l + 1, r], \text{ and} \\ [l, r] \xrightarrow{+\infty} [l, r - 1]. \end{cases}\]
Just two \(\infty\)-arcs per interval compress the entire inclusion poset into \(2\binom{N}{2} \approx 10^4\) directed edges!
Decoupling the Cost \(m x^2 + c x\) into Singleton Intervals \([i, i]\) and Type Hubs \(\text{Type}_x\):

Linear term \(c \cdot x\) (\(a_i\) per plate): Plate \(i\) is eaten if and only if the length-\(1\) singleton interval \([i, i]\) is selected! Thus we simply absorb the per-plate cost \(-a_i\) directly into the singleton node’s net weight: \(w([i, i]) = d_{i, i} - a_i\).
Fixed activation tax \(m \cdot x^2\) (paid once if \(c \ge 1\)): Create one auxiliary vertex \(\text{Type}_x\) of weight \(-m x^2\) (wired as \(\text{Type}_x \xrightarrow{m x^2} T\)) for each distinct sushi code \(x\), and wire every singleton interval \([i, i]\) to its type hub:
\[[i, i] \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{Type}_{a_i}.\]

If any plate \(i\) of type \(x\) is eaten (\([i, i] \in V_S\)), the \(\infty\)-arc forces \(\text{Type}_x \in V_S\), severing \(\text{Type}_x \xrightarrow{m x^2} T\) exactly once regardless of how many plates \(c\) of type \(x\) are eaten!

4.3 Archetype 3: Hall-Shifted Bipartite Closures (CF 103 E — Buying Sets)
In #072 Codeforces 103 E — Buying Sets, we are given \(N \le 300\) subsets \(A_1, \dots, A_N \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) with purchase costs \(w_i \in [-10^6, 10^6]\) (note that \(w_i < 0\) means buying set \(A_i\) yields a net profit of \(-w_i > 0\)). The problem guarantees a crucial structural property:

Hall Guarantee: For every \(k \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and every subcollection of \(k\) sets \(I \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) (\(|I| = k\)), their union \(N(I) = \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) has size at least \(k\): \(|N(I)| \ge |I|\).
Task: Choose a subcollection \(I \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) whose union has size exactly \(|I|\) (\(|N(I)| = |I|\)), minimizing the total cost \(\sum_{i \in I} w_i\) (or maximizing the net profit \(\sum_{i \in I} (-w_i)\)).

Why is the equality constraint \(|N(I)| = |I|\) tractable here when exact-cardinality union problems are normally NP-hard? Because the Hall guarantee \(|N(I)| \ge |I|\) means that no subset \(I\) can ever have \(|N(I)| < |I|\)! Every subset \(I \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) satisfies:
\[|N(I)| - |I| \ge 0, \qquad \text{with equality } |N(I)| - |I| = 0 \iff |N(I)| = |I|!\]
This unlocks two dual compilations into Picard’s Maximum-Weight Closure:

Method 1: Uniform Pedestal Shift +M (ゲタを履かせる on \(2N\) Vertices)
Model the natural bipartite closure where choosing set \(i \in I\) forces choosing all elements \(j \in A_i\) (\(i \xrightarrow{+\infty} j\)). To forbid any closed selection \((I, J)\) (\(N(I) \subseteq J\)) with \(|J| > |I|\), choose a huge constant pedestal \(M = 10^9 > N \max_i |w_i|\):

Shift every set \(i\)’s closure weight by \(+M\): \(W(\text{Set}_i) = M - w_i > 0\) (wired as \(S \xrightarrow{M - w_i} \text{Set}_i\)).
Assign every element \(j \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) a closure weight of \(-M < 0\) (wired as \(\text{Elem}_j \xrightarrow{M} T\)).

For any closed selection of sets \(I \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) and elements \(J \supseteq N(I)\), the total closure weight is:
\[W(I, J) = \sum_{i \in I} (M - w_i) - \sum_{j \in J} M = -\underbrace{\big(|J| - |I|\big)}_{\ge |N(I)| - |I| \ge 0} M + \sum_{i \in I} (-w_i).\]
Because \(|J| \ge |N(I)| \ge |I|\) by Hall’s condition:

If \(|J| > |I|\), then \(|J| - |I| \ge 1\), so \(W(I, J) \le -M + N \max |w_i| < 0 = W(\emptyset, \emptyset)\)!
Therefore, any maximum-weight closure \((I^*, J^*)\) must have \(|J^*| = |N(I^*)| = |I^*|\), where the \(-M(|J^*| - |I^*|)\) penalty vanishes to \(0\) and \(W(I^*, J^*) = \sum_{i \in I^*} (-w_i)\)!



Method 2: Hall Perfect-Matching Bijection (\(N\)-Vertex Closure)
By Hall’s Marriage Theorem (Chapter 8), \(|N(I)| \ge |I|\) for all \(I\) implies the existence of a perfect matching \(M: \{1, \dots, N\} \to \{1, \dots, N\}\) with \(M(i) \in A_i\) for each \(i\).
If we first find \(M\) via Hopcroft–Karp / Dinic and identify each element \(e = M(j)\) with its matched set \(j\), then for any subset of sets \(I \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\), the matched partners \(\{M(i) : i \in I\}\) already contribute \(|I|\) distinct elements to \(N(I)\). Hence \(|N(I)| = |I|\) holds if and only if \(N(I)\) contains no elements matched outside \(I\):
\[|N(I)| = |I| \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \forall i \in I, \; \forall e \in A_i, \quad M^{-1}(e) \in I!\]
This collapses the problem to an ordinary unweighted-pedestal Maximum-Weight Closure on just \(N \le 300\) vertices with weights \(-w_i\) and dependency arcs \(i \xrightarrow{+\infty} M^{-1}(e)\) for all \(e \in A_i\)!

5. The 4-Step “Zero Magic Gadgets” Recognition & Compilation Protocol for Closure Models
Whenever you suspect a problem reduces to Project Selection or Maximum-Weight Closure, execute the following 4-Step Compilation Protocol before coding:

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition & Cycle Semantics Check):

Identify the binary decision universe \(U\) and ask: Does selecting \(u \in U\) force selecting (or paying for) a set of prerequisites \(v \in \text{Req}(u)\)?
Check the Cycle Semantics (Section 3.1): Is the selection a simultaneous static set (Semantics A, where cycles contract into equivalence classes) or a sequential causal process (Semantics B, where cycles and their downstream dependents deadlock and must be pruned via Kahn’s BFS on \(G_{\text{pre}}\))?

Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation:

Define \(x_u = [u \in V_S] \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(x_S = 1, x_T = 0\)) and write the net objective using Optimistic Baseline + Regret Accounting (先拿后退):
\[\max_{\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^U} \sum_{u \in U} w_u x_u = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u - \min_{\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^U} \left(\sum_{w_u > 0} w_u(1 - x_u) + \sum_{w_v < 0} |w_v| x_v + \sum_{(u \to v) \in E_{\text{dep}}} c_{uv}\,x_u(1 - x_v)\right),\]
where \(c_{uv} = +\infty\) for hard prerequisites (\(x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1\)) or \(c_{uv} = r_{uv} < +\infty\) if \(u\) can rent \(v\) for single-use at fee \(r_{uv}\) ([CEOI 2008] Order).

Step 3 — Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation):

Compile each monomial \(c \cdot x_a(1 - x_b)\) into a directed edge \(a \xrightarrow{c} b\):

Step 4 — Toy Trace, Residual Reconstruction & Overflow Audit:

Trace a 3-to-4 vertex instance by hand to verify that the intended forbidden state \((x_u = 1, x_v = 0)\) crosses forward from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\) (and not backward from \(V_T\) to \(V_S\)).
Ensure INF and flow accumulators use 64-bit integers (long long) whenever \(W^+ = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u > 2 \cdot 10^9\).
Reconstruct the explicit minimum-cardinality optimal closure via \(C_{\min}^* = \{v \in U : S \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} v\}\).

7. Pre-Submission Verification Checklist (FM-09 Audit)
Before submitting any Binary Assignment, Project Selection, or Maximum-Weight Closure solution, audit your code against these six failure-mode guards:

Sequential vs. Simultaneous Cycle Semantics (FM-09 / [NOI2009] 植物大战僵尸):

Does the problem require a valid sequential unlocking order (Semantics B)?
If yes, did you run Kahn’s in-degree-\(0\) BFS on the causal graph \(G_{\text{pre}}\) (protector -> protected) and discard all unvisited vertices before building the flow network? (Never use Tarjan’s SCC deletion |SCC| >= 2, which fails to prune acyclic vertices downstream of a cycle!)

Implication Arc Orientation (x_u = 1 => x_v = 1):

Under Convention A (\(x_u = 1 \iff u \in V_S\), where \(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u\) for \(w_u > 0\) and \(v \xrightarrow{|w_v|} T\) for \(w_v < 0\)), the forbidden state is \((u \in V_S, v \in V_T)\), so the \(\infty\)-arc always points from dependent to prerequisite: \(u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v\).
Did you verify on a 2-vertex trace (like Gem \(1\) and Gem \(2\) in ARC 085 E) that the legal asymmetric state crosses backward from \(V_T\) to \(V_S\) (cost \(0\)) while the illegal state crosses forward from \(V_S\) to \(V_T\) (cost \(+\infty\))?

Constructive Closure Extraction (S_min vs. Single-Edge Saturation):

When reconstructing the chosen subset \(C^*\) (Luogu P2762, POJ 2987), did you run a residual BFS from \(S\) traversing edges with cap - flow > 0 (get_S_min()) instead of checking whether individual \(S \to u\) or \(v \to T\) edges are saturated?

Optimistic Baseline Inclusion (W^+ Sum):

Did you add only strictly positive weights (\(w_u > 0\)) into \(W^+\)?
For singleton intervals with linear costs (like \(\tilde{w}_{i,i} = d_{i,i} - a_i\) in [SHOI2017] 寿司餐厅), did you compute the net weight \(\tilde{w}_{i,i}\) first, and only then test if (w > 0) vs. if (w < 0)?

Transitive DAG Sparsification:

In interval inclusion (寿司餐厅) or divisibility posets (ARC 085 E), did you wire only Hasse/adjacent transitions (\([l, r] \to [l+1, r], [l, r-1]\)) instead of all \(O(N^4)\) sub-interval pairs?

64-Bit Integer Overflow Guard:

Is INF strictly greater than \(W^+ = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u\) (e.g., INF = 1e16 in long long), while still satisfying INF + INF < LLONG_MAX?

text:
8. Chapter Summary & Bridge to Chapter 10

Key Takeaways

Minimum Cut as a Pseudo-Boolean Compiler: Identifying \(x_v = [v \in V_S] \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(x_S = 1, x_T = 0\)) compiles every directed edge \((u \xrightarrow{c} v)\) into the quadratic cut monomial \(c \cdot x_u(1 - x_v)\).
Optimistic Baseline Accounting (先拿后退): Any profit maximization \(\max \sum_{u} w_u x_u\) converts into a non-negative minimum cut via \(\sum_{w_u > 0} w_u - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\), where severing \(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u\) forfeits a pre-claimed reward and severing \(v \xrightarrow{|w_v|} T\) pays an incurred cost.
Picard’s Maximum-Weight Closure Theorem (1976): Compiling \(x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1\) as \(u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v\) establishes an exact bijection between closed subsets \(C \subseteq U\) and finite-capacity \((S, T)\)-cuts, with \(S_{\min} \setminus \{S\}\) constructively recovering the unique minimum-cardinality optimal closure.
Causal Cycle Pruning (FM-09): When prerequisites represent sequential physical unlocking (Semantics B), Kahn’s topological BFS on \(G_{\text{pre}}\) must precede Dinic to eliminate both deadlocked cycles and their acyclic causal descendants.



Bridge to Chapter 10: From One-Sided Closure to All-\(S\) / All-\(T\) Synergy Hubs and General Submodular Potentials
In this chapter, every project reward \(+w_u\) lived on a single side of the cut (\(V_S\)), and every dependency \(x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1\) pointed in one direction.
What happens when a problem grants bonuses on both sides of the partition simultaneously—for instance, in [国家集训队] 文理分科 (Luogu P4313) or CF 311 E — Biologist, where a group of students \(A \subseteq U\) earns a synergy bonus \(B_A > 0\) if all of them choose Arts (\(x_i = 1\) for all \(i \in A\), an All-\(S\) clause \(\prod_{i \in A} x_i\)) AND another bonus \(B'_A > 0\) if all of them choose Science (\(x_i = 0\) for all \(i \in A\), an All-\(T\) clause \(\prod_{i \in A} (1 - x_i)\))? And what if two variables \(x_i, x_j \in \{0, 1\}\) interact via a general \(2 \times 2\) payoff matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}\) without creating auxiliary vertices?
In Chapter 10, we generalize Picard’s closure network to High-Arity All-\(S\) / All-\(T\) Synergy Hubs, derive Hu Botao’s Symmetric Vertex-Edge Merging (合并点边法), and lays the foundation for the Kolmogorov–Zabih Submodularity Theorem (\(A + D \le B + C\)) and Bipartite Variable Inversion (二部グラフの片側反転).

NotePrerequisites




Chapter 2: Dinic’s algorithm on unit networks (\(O(E\sqrt{V})\) complexity) and capacity-constrained \(S\)-\(T\) flow compilation.
Chapter 5: Maximum Bipartite Matching, König’s Minimum Vertex Cover Theorem (\(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\)), Maximum Independent Set (\(\alpha(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\)), and Minimum Edge Cover (\(\rho(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\)).
Chapter 6: Weighted König duality, Dulmage–Mendelsohn canonical decomposition, and alternating-path reachability.









TipLearning Objectives



After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Compile 2D grids and dual-attribute systems into Row–Column bipartite graphs: Recognize when grid cells \((r, c)\) or two-attribute items must be modeled as edges between row vertices \(L = \{R_1, \dots, R_H\}\) and column vertices \(R = \{C_1, \dots, C_W\}\) rather than as spatial vertices.
Handle obstacle segmentation, shared-border dualization, and 3D slice collapse: Split rows and columns at hard obstacles (#) while ignoring soft obstacles (*), dualize unit grid borders for rectangular brick tilings (CF 1404E), and collapse NP-hard 3D plane-cover instances (\(A \cdot B \cdot C \le 5000\)) into \(O(2^{\min(A,B,C)})\) 2D König instances ([HNOI2013] 消毒).
Model degree-constrained \(b\)-matchings and degree-regularity subgraphs: Compile per-vertex degree bounds \(b_v\) and fixed-center degree constraints (Luogu P2071, CF 387D) into capacitated bipartite networks without vertex-cloning blowup.
Apply the Birkhoff–von Neumann Theorem to \(k\)-regular bipartite multigraphs: Prove via Hall’s condition that every \(k\)-regular bipartite multigraph decomposes into \(k\) edge-disjoint perfect matchings, and apply iterative matching peeling to multi-phase matrix routing (ABC 317 G, AGC 037 D).
Color bipartite multigraph edges using \(\Delta\) colors via König’s Line Coloring Theorem: Choose the right algorithmic engine for \(\chi'(G) = \Delta\)—from \(O(\Delta E\sqrt{V})\) Dinic peeling to \(O(VE)\) online Kempe-chain recoloring (CF 600 F) and \(O(E \log \Delta)\) Eulerian circuit halving.

NotePrerequisites




Chapter 2: Dinic’s algorithm on unit networks (\(O(E\sqrt{V})\) complexity) and capacity-constrained \(S\)-\(T\) flow compilation.
Chapter 5: Maximum Bipartite Matching, König’s Minimum Vertex Cover Theorem (\(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\)), Maximum Independent Set (\(\alpha(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\)), and Minimum Edge Cover (\(\rho(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\)).
Chapter 6: Weighted König duality, Dulmage–Mendelsohn canonical decomposition, and alternating-path reachability.









TipLearning Objectives



After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Compile 2D grids and dual-attribute systems into Row–Column bipartite graphs: Recognize when grid cells \((r, c)\) or two-attribute items must be modeled as edges between row vertices \(L = \{R_1, \dots, R_H\}\) and column vertices \(R = \{C_1, \dots, C_W\}\) rather than as spatial vertices.
Handle obstacle segmentation, shared-border dualization, and 3D slice collapse: Split rows and columns at hard obstacles (#) while ignoring soft obstacles (*), dualize unit grid borders for rectangular brick tilings (CF 1404E), and collapse NP-hard 3D plane-cover instances (\(A \cdot B \cdot C \le 5000\)) into \(O(2^{\min(A,B,C)})\) 2D König instances ([HNOI2013] 消毒).
Model degree-constrained \(b\)-matchings and degree-regularity subgraphs: Compile per-vertex degree bounds \(b_v\) and fixed-center degree constraints (Luogu P2071, CF 387D) into capacitated bipartite networks without vertex-cloning blowup.
Apply the Birkhoff–von Neumann Theorem to \(k\)-regular bipartite multigraphs: Prove via Hall’s condition that every \(k\)-regular bipartite multigraph decomposes into \(k\) edge-disjoint perfect matchings, and apply iterative matching peeling to multi-phase matrix routing (ABC 317 G, AGC 037 D).
Color bipartite multigraph edges using \(\Delta\) colors via König’s Line Coloring Theorem: Choose the right algorithmic engine for \(\chi'(G) = \Delta\)—from \(O(\Delta E\sqrt{V})\) Dinic peeling to \(O(VE)\) online Kempe-chain recoloring (CF 600 F) and \(O(E \log \Delta)\) Eulerian circuit halving.

title: Chapter 7 — Row–Column Grid Duality, Birkhoff–von Neumann Decomposition, and Bipartite Edge Coloring
section: 1. Motivation: When Grid Cells Are Edges, Not Vertices
text:
1. Motivation: When Grid Cells Are Edges, Not Vertices
When a competitive programmer sees an \(H \times W\) grid, the most natural reflex is spatial graph compilation: treat every cell \((r, c)\) as a vertex and connect up/down/left/right neighbors \((r \pm 1, c), (r, c \pm 1)\), using chessboard parity \((r + c) \bmod 2\) to form a bipartite graph.
That spatial reflex works when operations are local—dominoes covering adjacent cells \((r, c)\) and \((r, c+1)\), knights jumping by \((\pm 1, \pm 2)\), or a game token sliding to an orthogonal neighbor. However, a huge class of grid, matrix, and permutation problems features non-local, axis-aligned interactions:

Selecting at most one cell per row and at most one cell per column (rooks, permutation transversals, or matrix diagonalization).
Paying cost \(1\) to clear an entire row \(r\) or an entire column \(c\).
Rearranging elements within rows so that every column becomes a permutation of \(\{1, \dots, H\}\).
Pairing elements that simultaneously belong to one equivalence class in structure \(\mathcal{A}\) and another equivalence class in structure \(\mathcal{B}\) (such as cycle decompositions of two permutations \(a\) and \(b\)).

In all of these problems, two cells \((r, c_1)\) and \((r, c_2)\) in the same row interact even when \(|c_1 - c_2| = W - 1\). If you treat cells as vertices, every row becomes a clique \(K_W\) and every column becomes a clique \(K_H\), destroying bipartiteness and blowing the edge count up to \(O(HW(H + W))\).
The cure is Row–Column Incidence Duality:
\[\boxed{\text{Row } r \;\longleftrightarrow\; \text{Left Vertex } R_r \in L, \qquad \text{Column } c \;\longleftrightarrow\; \text{Right Vertex } C_c \in R, \qquad \text{Cell } (r, c) \;\longleftrightarrow\; \text{Edge } e_{r,c} = (R_r, C_c) \in E.}\]
Under this primal-dual lens, a grid of \(H W\) cells is not a planar graph on \(HW\) vertices—it is a bipartite graph on only \(H + W\) vertices with at most \(HW\) edges!
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                   SPATIAL PARITY GRAPH vs. ROW-COLUMN INCIDENCE DUALITY                           |
|                                                                                                   |
|   [A] Spatial Grid Graph (Local Adjacency)         [B] Row-Column Bipartite Graph (Global Axis)   |
|       Vertices: Cells (r, c)  (|V| = H*W)              Vertices: Rows R_r in L, Cols C_c in R     |
|       Bipartition: (r + c) mod 2 in {0, 1}             (|V| = H + W, |E| <= H*W)                  |
|       Edges: 4-neighbors (|r1-r2| + |c1-c2| = 1)       Edges: Active cells e_{r,c} = (R_r, C_c)   |
|       Use when: Dominoes, knight jumps, grid walk      Use when: Rooks, line covers, row/col      |
|                 games, local cell-to-cell conflicts.             swaps, matrix decompositions.    |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

title: Chapter 7 — Row–Column Grid Duality, Birkhoff–von Neumann Decomposition, and Bipartite Edge Coloring
text:
2. Row–Column Bipartite Duality & Degree-Constrained \(b\)-Matchings

2.1 The Four Step-by-Step Compilations of Row–Column Duality
Let us systematically apply our 4-Step Zero-Magic-Gadgets Compilation to the four foundational variations of Row–Column Duality.

Archetype 2.1A: Matrix Permutation Invariance & The Conjugation Trap ([ZJOI2007] 矩阵游戏)

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal: We are given an \(N \times N\) binary matrix \(A_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(N \le 200\)) and may swap any two rows or swap any two columns any number of times. We want to know whether we can make all main-diagonal entries \(A_{i,i} = 1\) for \(1 \le i \le N\). Notice that swapping rows or columns permutes the row indices and column indices globally. We are looking for \(N\) cells containing \(1\)s that can be moved simultaneously onto the positions \((1, 1), (2, 2), \dots, (N, N)\)—meaning no two chosen \(1\)-cells may share a row or share a column.
Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Applying a row permutation \(\sigma \in S_N\) and an independent column permutation \(\tau \in S_N\) transforms \(A\) into \(A'_{i,j} = A_{\sigma(i), \tau(j)}\) (matrix equivalence \(P A Q\)). Achieving \(A'_{i,i} = 1\) for all \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) is equivalent to finding a binary selection matrix \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\) such that:
\[x_{r,c} \le A_{r,c}, \qquad \sum_{c=1}^N x_{r,c} = 1 \;\; (\forall r), \qquad \sum_{r=1}^N x_{r,c} = 1 \;\; (\forall c).\]
Step 3 — Mechanical Graph Compilation: Introduce left vertices \(L = \{R_1, \dots, R_N\}\) and right vertices \(R = \{C_1, \dots, C_N\}\). For each \((r, c)\) with \(A_{r,c} = 1\), add edge \((R_r, C_c)\) carrying decision variable \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\). The degree constraints \(\sum_c x_{r,c} = 1\) and \(\sum_r x_{r,c} = 1\) define a Perfect Matching (\(\nu(G) = N\)). Row and column swaps merely relabel the vertices in \(L\) and \(R\), which is a graph isomorphism preserving \(\nu(G)\)!
Step 4 — Concrete Toy Trace & The Conjugation Counterexample: Consider the \(2 \times 2\) anti-diagonal matrix:
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\]
In \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\), we have edges \((R_1, C_2)\) and \((R_2, C_1)\), forming a perfect matching of size \(\nu(G) = 2\). Swapping row \(1\) and row \(2\) (\(\sigma = (1\;2), \tau = \mathrm{id}\)) yields \(A' = I_2\) with ones on the main diagonal.







WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexample — Decoupled Swaps (\(PAQ\)) vs. Coupled Conjugation (\(PAP^T\))



What if a problem modifies the operation so that whenever you swap row \(i\) and row \(j\), you are forced to simultaneously swap column \(i\) and column \(j\) (\(\sigma = \tau\), i.e., symmetric conjugation \(A' = P A P^T\))?
In that coupled setting, the new diagonal entries are \(A'_{i,i} = A_{\sigma(i), \sigma(i)}\)—which is simply a permutation of the original diagonal entries \(\{A_{1,1}, \dots, A_{N,N}\}\)! On \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), \(\nu(G) = 2\), yet coupled swaps leave the diagonal \((0, 0)\) forever. Rule: Row–Column bipartite matching applies if and only if row operations and column operations are decoupled (\(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) chosen independently).





Archetype 2.1B: Hard vs. Soft Obstacles & Maximal Strip Segmentation (POJ 2226, [HEOI2016] 游戏)

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal: Suppose a grid contains three types of cells:

Active / Target cells (. or *): cells where a rook may be placed (or muddy cells that must be covered by planks).
Soft obstacles (x or grass): cells where a rook cannot be placed (or planks may pass through / cannot cover), without blocking line-of-sight (or Conversely, in POJ 2226 Muddy Fields, grass . blocks planks while mud * must be covered!).
Hard walls (#): impenetrable barriers that terminate a rook’s attack ray or a plank’s span.

Whenever an obstacle breaks a row or column into independent line-of-sight zones, a single row \(r\) can now hold multiple non-attacking rooks (one in each zone separated by #).
Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Instead of indexing constraints by full rows \(r\) and full columns \(c\), decompose every row into maximal contiguous #-free horizontal segments \(\mathcal{H} = \{H_1, \dots, H_p\}\) and every column into maximal contiguous #-free vertical segments \(\mathcal{V} = \{V_1, \dots, V_q\}\). Each active cell \((r, c)\) belongs to a unique horizontal segment \(\mathrm{id}_H(r, c) \in \mathcal{H}\) and a unique vertical segment \(\mathrm{id}_V(r, c) \in \mathcal{V}\):

Non-Attacking Rook Placement ([HEOI2016] 游戏): Select maximum active cells \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\) such that each \(H_i\) and each \(V_j\) contains at most one selected cell (\(\implies\) Maximum Matching \(\nu(G)\)).
Minimum Plank / Laser Cover (POJ 2226 Muddy Fields): Select minimum segments \(u_{H_i}, v_{V_j} \in \{0, 1\}\) such that \(u_{\mathrm{id}_H(r,c)} + v_{\mathrm{id}_V(r,c)} \ge 1\) for every muddy cell \((r, c)\) (\(\implies\) Minimum Vertex Cover \(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\)).

Step 3 — Mechanical Graph Compilation: Put \(L = \mathcal{H}\) and \(R = \mathcal{V}\). Iterate over all cells \((r, c)\):

If \((r, c)\) is a hard wall #: it already served to split segments during preprocessing; add no edge.
If \((r, c)\) is a soft obstacle x (in rook placement, cannot hold a rook but doesn’t split segments): add no edge, and do not split the current segment!
If \((r, c)\) is an active cell .: add a unit edge \((\mathrm{id}_H(r, c), \mathrm{id}_V(r, c))\) between \(L\) and \(R\).


+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|          OBSTACLE-SPLIT MAXIMAL SEGMENTS: HARD WALL '#' vs. SOFT OBSTACLE 'x'                     |
|                                                                                                   |
|   Row r:   [  .  |  x  |  .  |  #  |  .  ]                                                        |
|            \_______ H_1 _______/     \_H_2_/                                                      |
|                                                                                                   |
|   * Soft obstacle 'x' at (r, 2): DOES NOT split H_1, and adds NO EDGE at (r, 2).                  |
|     Cells (r, 1) and (r, 3) still share vertex H_1 in L (cannot both hold rooks!).                |
|   * Hard wall '#' at (r, 4): SPLITS row r into H_1 = {(r,1)..(r,3)} and H_2 = {(r,5)}.            |
|     Cells (r, 3) and (r, 5) have DIFFERENT left vertices H_1 != H_2 (can both hold rooks!).       |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+



Archetype 2.1C: Shared-Border Dualization for Rectangular Brick Tilings (CF 1404E — Bricks)

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal: We are given an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 200\)) of black (#) and white (.) cells. We want to partition all black # cells into the minimum number of non-overlapping \(1 \times k\) or \(k \times 1\) rectangular bricks (\(k \ge 1\)). Why does standard cell-as-edge compilation fail here? Because a \(1 \times k\) brick covers \(k\) cells at once (\(k\) can be \(1, 2, 3, \dots\)), and bricks may not overlap!
Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Count merges across shared unit borders instead of bricks! Initially, treat every black # cell as an isolated \(1 \times 1\) brick, giving \(|\#|\) bricks.

Whenever we glue two horizontally adjacent black cells \((r, c)\) and \((r, c+1)\) across their vertical unit border \(h_{r,c}\), the number of bricks decreases by \(1\).
Whenever we glue two vertically adjacent black cells \((r, c)\) and \((r+1, c)\) across their horizontal unit border \(v_{r,c}\), the number of bricks decreases by \(1\).

When is a subset of chosen glues valid (producing only \(1 \times k\) and \(k \times 1\) rectangles, never an L-shaped tromino)? If and only if no black cell \((r, c)\) participates in BOTH a horizontal glue (\(h_{r,c-1}\) or \(h_{r,c}\)) AND a vertical glue (\(v_{r-1,c}\) or \(v_{r,c}\))! Thus, if \(x_h \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(y_v \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate chosen horizontal and vertical glues:
\[\text{Min Bricks} = |\#| - \max \left( \sum_{h \in L} x_h + \sum_{v \in R} y_v \right) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_h + y_v \le 1 \;\;\text{whenever } h \text{ and } v \text{ touch the same cell } (r, c).\]
Step 3 — Mechanical Graph Compilation:

Left Vertices \(L\): All horizontal glues \(h_{r,c}\) between \((r, c) = \text{'\#'}\) and \((r, c+1) = \text{'\#'}\).
Right Vertices \(R\): All vertical glues \(v_{r,c}\) between \((r, c) = \text{'\#'}\) and \((r+1, c) = \text{'\#'}\).
Conflict Edges \(E\): For each black cell \((r, c)\), connect each incident horizontal glue in \(\{h_{r,c-1}, h_{r,c}\} \cap L\) to each incident vertical glue in \(\{v_{r-1,c}, v_{r,c}\} \cap R\) (at most \(2 \times 2 = 4\) conflict edges per cell).
By König’s Maximum Independent Set formula, the maximum number of compatible glues is \(\alpha(G) = |L| + |R| - \nu(G)\), so:
\[\boxed{\text{Min Bricks} = |\#| - \Big(|L| + |R| - \operatorname{MaxMatching}(G)\Big).}\]

Step 4 — Concrete Toy Trace: Consider a \(2 \times 2\) all-# square (\(|\#| = 4\)). There are \(|L| = 2\) horizontal glues (\(h_{1,1}, h_{2,1}\)) and \(|R| = 2\) vertical glues (\(v_{1,1}, v_{1,2}\)). Every \(h_i\) shares a corner cell with every \(v_j\), so \(G = K_{2,2}\) with \(\nu(G) = 2\). Then \(\alpha(G) = 2 + 2 - 2 = 2\) glues, and \(\text{Min Bricks} = 4 - 2 = 2\) (either two \(1 \times 2\) horizontal bricks or two \(2 \times 1\) vertical bricks).




Archetype 2.1D: 3D Grid NP-Hardness vs. Pigeonhole Dimension Collapse ([HNOI2013] 消毒)

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal: Suppose we must cover all marked cells \((x, y, z)\) in an \(A \times B \times C\) 3D grid using axis-aligned planes \(x = x_0\), \(y = y_0\), or \(z = z_0\) of cost \(1\) each, given the volume constraint \(A \cdot B \cdot C \le 5000\). In 3D, each marked cell \((x, y, z)\) requires \(u_x + v_y + w_z \ge 1\). This is Minimum Vertex Cover on a 3-Partite 3-Uniform Hypergraph, which is dual to 3-Dimensional Matching (3DM) and is NP-hard! Why is this problem solvable in polynomial/exponential-slice time? Because \(A \cdot B \cdot C \le 5000\) forces the shortest dimension to satisfy:
\[\min(A, B, C) \le \lfloor 5000^{1/3} \rfloor = 17!\]
Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Assume without loss of generality that \(A = \min(A, B, C) \le 17\) (rotate axes if necessary). Any optimal cover chooses some subset \(M \subseteq \{1, \dots, A\}\) of \(x\)-planes (paying \(|M| = \operatorname{popcount}(M)\)), and must cover all remaining marked cells \((x, y, z)\) with \(x \notin M\) using only \(y\)-planes and \(z\)-planes:
\[\min_{M \subseteq \{1, \dots, A\}} \left( |M| + \min_{\substack{v_y, w_z \in \{0, 1\} \\ v_y + w_z \ge 1 \;\forall (x, y, z) \text{ with } x \notin M}} \left( \sum_{y=1}^B v_y + \sum_{z=1}^C w_z \right) \right).\]
Step 3 — Mechanical Graph Compilation: For each fixed bitmask \(M \in [0, 2^A)\), the inner minimization has eliminated \(x\) completely: projecting all surviving marked cells \(\{(y, z) : \exists x \notin M \text{ s.t. } (x, y, z) \text{ is marked}\}\) onto the 2D \((y, z)\) plane yields a standard 2D bipartite graph \(G_M = (Y \sqcup Z, E_M)\) whose Minimum Vertex Cover is \(\nu(G_M)\) by König’s Theorem! Total runtime: \(O(2^{\min(A,B,C)} \cdot \text{Matching}(B, C))\).





2.2 Degree-Constrained \(b\)-Matchings & Capacitated Bipartite Networks
In standard bipartite matching, every vertex \(u \in L\) and \(v \in R\) can be incident to at most \(1\) matched edge. In Degree-Constrained \(b\)-Matching, each left vertex \(u \in L\) can match up to \(a_u \ge 1\) edges (or must match within \([l_u, u_u]\)), and each right vertex \(v \in R\) can match up to \(b_v \ge 1\) edges:
\[\max_{x_e \in \{0, 1\}} \sum_{e=(u,v) \in E} x_e \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{v \in N(u)} x_{u,v} \le a_u \;\; (\forall u \in L), \qquad \sum_{u \in N(v)} x_{u,v} \le b_v \;\; (\forall v \in R).\]

Compilation Rule (Direct Terminal Capacities vs. Vertex Cloning): Never clone a vertex \(v \in R\) into \(b_v\) separate copies if \(b_v\) is large—that multiplies the edge count by \(b_v\)! Instead, in your Dinic network:

Wire \(S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } a_u} u\) for all \(u \in L\).
Wire \(u \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1} v\) for all \((u, v) \in E\) (or capacity \(c_{uv}\) if multiple parallel edges between the same \((u, v)\) are allowed).
Wire \(v \xrightarrow{\text{cap } b_v} T\) for all \(v \in R\).

Because all middle edges \((u \to v)\) have unit capacity \(1\), the network is a unit-edge-capacity network (even when \(a_u, b_v > 1\)), on which Dinic’s algorithm still runs in \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) time (or \(O(E \sqrt{\sum b_v})\))!

title: Chapter 7 — Row–Column Grid Duality, Birkhoff–von Neumann Decomposition, and Bipartite Edge Coloring
section: 3. The Birkhoff–von Neumann Theorem & \(k\)-Regular Bipartite Decomposition
text:
3. The Birkhoff–von Neumann Theorem & \(k\)-Regular Bipartite Decomposition
What happens when every vertex on both sides of a bipartite multigraph has the exact same degree \(k\)? This structure arises whenever an \(N \times M\) grid contains each of \(N\) labels (or target row destinations) exactly \(M\) times.

3.1 Hall’s Regularity Guarantee & Inductive Matching Peeling






ImportantTheorem 7.1 — Regular Bipartite Decomposition & Birkhoff–von Neumann Theorem




Discrete \(k\)-Regular Decomposition (König 1916): Every \(k\)-regular bipartite multigraph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) (\(k \ge 1\)) has a perfect matching \(M_1\) with \(|L| = |R| = N\). Consequently, peeling \(M_1, M_2, \dots, M_k\) one by one decomposes the edge set \(E\) into \(k\) edge-disjoint perfect matchings:
\[E(G) = M_1 \sqcup M_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup M_k.\]
Continuous Polyhedral Form (Birkhoff 1946, von Neumann 1953): An \(N \times N\) non-negative real matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{N \times N}\) is doubly stochastic (all row sums equal \(1\) and all column sums equal \(1\)) if and only if \(X\) is a convex combination of \(N \times N\) permutation matrices \(P_\sigma\):
\[X = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i P_{\sigma_i}, \qquad \lambda_i \ge 0, \quad \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i = 1.\]




Proof of Discrete Decomposition via Double Counting (Cut / Hall Argument)
First, count total edges from both sides: \(|E| = \sum_{u \in L} \deg(u) = k|L|\) and \(|E| = \sum_{v \in R} \deg(v) = k|R|\), which immediately forces \(|L| = |R| = N\).
To prove that a perfect matching exists (equivalently, that the maximum \(S\)-\(T\) flow in the unit-capacity network equals \(N\)), consider any subset \(A \subseteq L\) and let \(N(A) \subseteq R\) be the set of neighbors of \(A\) in \(R\). Let \(E(A, N(A))\) be the multiset of all edges incident to \(A\).

Exact count from \(A \subseteq L\): Since every vertex \(u \in A\) has degree exactly \(k\) and all its incident edges land inside \(N(A)\) by definition of \(N(A)\), we have:
\[|E(A, N(A))| = \sum_{u \in A} \deg_G(u) = k |A|.\]
Upper bound from \(N(A) \subseteq R\): Every edge in \(E(A, N(A))\) is incident to some vertex \(v \in N(A)\), and each \(v \in N(A)\) has total degree \(k\) in \(G\) (some of its edges might even go to \(L \setminus A\)). Therefore:
\[|E(A, N(A))| \le \sum_{v \in N(A)} \deg_G(v) = k |N(A)|.\]

Combining the two relations and dividing by \(k \ge 1\) yields Hall’s Marriage Condition for every \(A \subseteq L\):
\[k |A| = |E(A, N(A))| \le k |N(A)| \implies \boxed{|N(A)| \ge |A| \quad \forall A \subseteq L.}\]
In the standard \(S\)-\(T\) flow network (Chapter 5), any finite \(S\)-\(T\) cut \((S_{\text{cut}}, T_{\text{cut}})\) with \(A = L \cap S_{\text{cut}}\) must satisfy \(N(A) \subseteq R \cap S_{\text{cut}}\) to avoid cutting \(\infty\)-capacity middle edges, so its cut capacity is at least \(|L \setminus A| + |N(A)| = N - |A| + |N(A)| \ge N\). By the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem, a perfect matching \(M_1\) of size \(N\) exists!
Deleting the \(N\) edges of \(M_1\) reduces the degree of every vertex in \(L \cup R\) by exactly \(1\), leaving a \((k - 1)\)-regular bipartite multigraph. By induction on \(k\), \(E(G)\) partitions into \(k\) edge-disjoint perfect matchings \(M_1, \dots, M_k\). \(\blacksquare\)
(For the continuous Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem, build the bipartite support graph with edge \((r, c)\) whenever \(X_{r,c} > 0\). By the exact same sum argument \(\sum_{r \in A} 1 = |A| = \sum_{r \in A, c \in N(A)} X_{r,c} \le \sum_{c \in N(A)} 1 = |N(A)|\), the support graph has a perfect matching \(P_{\sigma_1}\). Letting \(\lambda_1 = \min_{(r,c) \in P_{\sigma_1}} X_{r,c} > 0\) and subtracting \(\lambda_1 P_{\sigma_1}\) zeroes out at least one positive entry while keeping row and column sums equal to \(1 - \lambda_1\), terminating in at most \(N^2 - N + 1\) steps!)




3.2 Worked Flagship 1: AtCoder ABC 317 G — Rearranging

Judge URL: https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc317/tasks/abc317_g
Constraints: \(N, M \le 100\). Given an \(N \times M\) grid \(A\) where each integer \(1, 2, \dots, N\) appears exactly \(M\) times across the entire grid, permute the elements within each row independently so that every column becomes a permutation of \(\{1, 2, \dots, N\}\).


4-Step Compilation

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal: We may reorder elements arbitrarily within each row \(r \in \{1, \dots, N\}\). Thus row \(r\) is simply a multiset of \(M\) available values. Placing one value from each row into Column \(1\) so that Column \(1\) contains \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) is choosing one value per row to cover all \(N\) values—a Perfect Matching between Rows and Values!
Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Construct a bipartite multigraph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) where:

\(L = \{\text{Row}_1, \dots, \text{Row}_N\}\) represents the \(N\) rows.
\(R = \{\text{Val}_1, \dots, \text{Val}_N\}\) represents the \(N\) distinct values \(\{1, \dots, N\}\).
Each cell \((r, c)\) of the input matrix with value \(v = A_{r,c}\) creates one multigraph edge \(e_{r,c} = (\text{Row}_r, \text{Val}_v)\).

Look at the degrees in \(G\):

Every row \(r \in L\) has \(M\) cells \(\implies \deg_G(\text{Row}_r) = M\).
Every value \(v \in R\) appears \(M\) times in \(A \implies \deg_G(\text{Val}_v) = M\).

Hence \(G\) is an \(M\)-regular bipartite multigraph!
Step 3 — Mechanical Graph Compilation: By Theorem 7.1, \(G\) decomposes into \(M\) edge-disjoint perfect matchings \(M_1, M_2, \dots, M_M\). For \(c = 1, 2, \dots, M\):

Run Dinic / Hopcroft–Karp on the remaining edges of \(G\) to find a perfect matching \(M_c\) of size \(N\).
For each matched edge \((\text{Row}_r, \text{Val}_v) \in M_c\), set the output cell \(B_{r, c} = v\) and delete that single edge instance from \(G\).

Step 4 — Concrete Toy Trace: Take \(N = 3, M = 2\) with input matrix:
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}.\]

\(\text{Row}_1\) has edges to \(\{1, 1\}\); \(\text{Row}_2\) has edges to \(\{2, 3\}\); \(\text{Row}_3\) has edges to \(\{2, 3\}\). Every vertex in \(L \cup R\) has degree \(2\).
Column 1 (\(c = 1\)): Peel perfect matching \(M_1 = \{(\text{Row}_1, 1), (\text{Row}_2, 2), (\text{Row}_3, 3)\}\), setting Column 1 of \(B\) to \([1, 2, 3]^T\).
Column 2 (\(c = 2\)): The remaining edges form \(M_2 = \{(\text{Row}_1, 1), (\text{Row}_2, 3), (\text{Row}_3, 2)\}\), setting Column 2 of \(B\) to \([1, 3, 2]^T\).
Output \(B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\): each row is a rearrangement of \(A\)’s row, and both columns are permutations of \(\{1, 2, 3\}\).
Complexity: \(M\) calls to Dinic on \(2N\) vertices and \(\le NM\) edges takes \(O(M \cdot NM\sqrt{N}) = O(N^{1.5} M^2) \approx 10^7\) operations (\(< 0.05\text{ s}\)).






3.3 Worked Flagship 2: AtCoder AGC 037 D — Sorting a Grid (3-Phase Row–Col–Row Benes Routing)

Judge URL: https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc037/tasks/agc037_d
Constraints: \(N, M \le 100\). You are given an \(N \times M\) matrix \(A\) containing a permutation of \(\{1, 2, \dots, NM\}\). You must sort \(A\) into standard row-major order \(D_{r,c} = (r - 1)M + c\) in three phases:

Phase 1 (\(A \to B\)): Permute elements within each row independently.
Phase 2 (\(B \to C\)): Permute elements within each column independently.
Phase 3 (\(C \to D\)): Permute elements within each row independently.

Output the intermediate matrices \(B\) and \(C\).


4-Step Compilation

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Working Backwards from Phase 3): Why can any permutation of \(1 \dots NM\) be routed to its exact destination in Row -> Col -> Row (the classic 3-stage Clos / Beneš network architecture)? Work backwards from the final sorted matrix \(D\):

Phase 3 (\(C \to D\)) only permutes within rows. Therefore, at the end of Phase 2 (in matrix \(C\)), every number \(x \in \{1, \dots, NM\}\) must already sit in its final target row:
\[\operatorname{dest}(x) := \left\lceil \frac{x}{M} \right\rceil \in \{1, \dots, N\}!\]
Phase 2 (\(B \to C\)) only permutes within columns. For column \(c\) of \(B\) to be rearranged into column \(c\) of \(C\) where every element sits in its target row \(\operatorname{dest}(x)\), the \(N\) numbers placed into column \(c\) of \(B\) during Phase 1 must have \(N\) pairwise distinct target rows \(\{1, 2, \dots, N\}\)!

Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Replace each number \(x\) in the initial matrix \(A\) by its target row color \(\operatorname{dest}(x) \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).

Each current row \(r \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) contains \(M\) numbers.
Across the entire matrix \(A\), exactly \(M\) numbers belong to each target row \(d \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) (namely \((d-1)M + 1, \dots, dM\)).

This reduces Phase 1 (\(A \to B\)) to the exact same problem as ABC 317 G!
Step 3 — Mechanical Graph Compilation:

Build a bipartite multigraph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) between Current Rows \(L = \{1, \dots, N\}\) and Target Rows \(R = \{1, \dots, N\}\).
For each cell \((r, c)\) of \(A\) with value \(x = A_{r,c}\), add a labelled edge \(e_x = (r, \operatorname{dest}(x))\) carrying payload \(x\).
Since \(\deg_G(r) = M\) for all \(r \in L\) and \(\deg_G(d) = M\) for all \(d \in R\), \(G\) is \(M\)-regular.
Peel \(M\) perfect matchings \(M_1, \dots, M_M\) from \(G\):

Matrix \(B\) (after Phase 1): For each column \(c \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) and each edge \(e_x = (r, \operatorname{dest}(x)) \in M_c\), set \(B_{r, c} = x\).
Matrix \(C\) (after Phase 2): Within each column \(c \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), sort the \(N\) elements \(x = B_{1,c}, \dots, B_{N,c}\) by their target row by setting \(C_{\operatorname{dest}(x), c} = x\).
(Phase 3 then sorts each row of \(C\) into \(D\) automatically!)


Step 4 — Concrete Toy Trace: Take \(N = 2, M = 2\) with reversed matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\).

Target rows: \(\operatorname{dest}(1) = \operatorname{dest}(2) = 1\), and \(\operatorname{dest}(3) = \operatorname{dest}(4) = 2\).
In \(G\): Current Row \(1\) has two edges to Target Row \(2\) (payloads \(4, 3\)); Current Row \(2\) has two edges to Target Row \(1\) (payloads \(2, 1\)).
Matching \(M_1\) (Column 1): Picks \(e_4 = (1 \to 2)\) and \(e_2 = (2 \to 1) \implies\) Col 1 of \(B\) is \([4, 2]^T\).
Matching \(M_2\) (Column 2): Picks \(e_3 = (1 \to 2)\) and \(e_1 = (2 \to 1) \implies\) Col 2 of \(B\) is \([3, 1]^T\).
Construct \(B\) and \(C\):
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{\text{Phase 1 (Rows)}} B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{\text{Phase 2 (Cols)}} C = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{\text{Phase 3 (Rows)}} D = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.\]
