text:
6. Curated 4-Tier Practice Ladder
Each problem below is engineered to build a distinct layer of the Chapter 5 modelling pipeline. Try to formulate the algebraic indicator variables and bipartition on your own before opening the progressive hints and the full 4-step compilation.


#033 — [CF 1423B] Valuable Paper

Tier: Stepping Stone 1 (SS-1) | Judge URL: https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1423/B
Constraints: \(N \le 10^4\) factories, \(N \le 10^4\) airports, \(M \le 10^5\) candidate bidirectional roads \((u_e, v_e)\) with construction times \(d_e \in [1, 10^9]\). Time limit: 2.0s.
Problem Summary: You are given \(N\) factories, \(N\) airports, and \(M\) candidate roads connecting factories to airports. All chosen roads are built in parallel, so the completion time of a subset of roads is the maximum construction time \(\max_{e \in M^*} d_e\) among the chosen roads. Each factory must be connected to a distinct airport (\(1\)-to-\(1\) pairing). Find the minimum possible completion time \(T\), or output -1 if no perfect matching exists.







NoteHint 1 — Monotonicity of the Bottleneck Threshold





Whenever an objective minimizes the maximum edge weight (\(\min_{M^*} \max_{e \in M^*} d_e\)) rather than the sum of edge weights, convert the optimization problem into a decision problem: “Given a time budget \(T\), does there exist a matching of size \(N\) using only roads with \(d_e \le T\)?” Since increasing \(T\) only adds edges to the graph, this predicate is monotone in \(T\).









NoteHint 2 — Complexity Trap at \(N = 10^4, M = 10^5\)





Sort the distinct road weights \(d_e\) and binary search over the index \(k \in [0, M-1]\) (\(\le 17\) checks). At each step, why does a standard \(O(NM)\) DFS-based Kuhn matching algorithm Time Limit Exceed (TLE), and which \(O(M\sqrt{N})\) unit-network algorithm must you use instead?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — CF 1423B: Valuable Paper






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Signal: We must pair \(N\) factories with \(N\) airports (\(1\)-to-\(1\) disjoint assignment between two disjoint classes \(L\) and \(R\)) while minimizing the bottleneck edge weight \(\max_{e \in M^*} d_e\).
Why Greedy & Kuhn Fail: Sorting edges by weight and greedily pairing endpoints fails whenever an early cheap edge blocks the only valid partner of another factory. Furthermore, at \(N = 10^4, M = 10^5\), running \(O(NM) \approx 10^9\) Kuhn DFS per binary search step takes \(\sim 1.7 \times 10^{10}\) operations (TLE). Hopcroft–Karp (Dinic on unit networks, Ch 04) runs in \(O(M\sqrt{N})\) per check.



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For a fixed threshold \(T\), let \(E_{\le T} = \{e = (u, v) \in E : d_e \le T\}\). Introduce binary decision variables \(f_{uv} \in \{0, 1\}\) for each \((u, v) \in E_{\le T}\):
\[\nu(G_{\le T}) = \max_{f \in \{0,1\}^{|E_{\le T}|}} \sum_{(u,v) \in E_{\le T}} f_{uv} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{v : (u,v) \in E_{\le T}} f_{uv} \le 1 \ \ (\forall u \in L), \quad \sum_{u : (u,v) \in E_{\le T}} f_{uv} \le 1 \ \ (\forall v \in R).\]
The threshold \(T\) is feasible if and only if \(\nu(G_{\le T}) = N\). Since \(E_{\le T_1} \subseteq E_{\le T_2}\) for \(T_1 \le T_2\), \(\nu(G_{\le T})\) is monotonically non-decreasing in \(T\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Sort the \(M\) roads in non-decreasing order of \(d_e\): \(d_{e_1} \le d_{e_2} \le \dots \le d_{e_M}\).
Binary search the road index \(mid \in [1, M]\):

Construct the unit bipartite network \(\mathcal{N}(mid)\) on \(\{s, t\} \cup L \cup R\) where \(|L| = |R| = N\):

Source arcs: \(s \xrightarrow{1} u\) for all \(u \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).
Middle arcs: \(u_{e_i} \xrightarrow{1} v_{e_i}\) for all \(1 \le i \le mid\).
Sink arcs: \(v \xrightarrow{1} t\) for all \(v \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).

Run Hopcroft–Karp / unit Dinic to compute \(\nu(G_{\le d_{e_{mid}}})\). If \(\nu = N\), move the upper bound \(hi \gets mid\); otherwise move \(lo \gets mid + 1\).




Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: Suppose \(N = 2\) and roads are \((u_1, v_1, d=3)\), \((u_1, v_2, d=5)\), \((u_2, v_1, d=4)\).

For \(T = 3\): \(E_{\le 3} = \{(u_1, v_1)\}\), \(\nu = 1 < 2\) (infeasible).
For \(T = 4\): \(E_{\le 4} = \{(u_1, v_1), (u_2, v_1)\}\), both factories compete for \(v_1\), so \(\nu = 1 < 2\) (infeasible; König MVC is \(\{v_1\}\) of size \(1\)).
For \(T = 5\): \(E_{\le 5}\) adds \((u_1, v_2)\); augmenting path \(u_2 \to v_1 \Rightarrow u_1 \to v_2\) yields \(M^* = \{(u_2, v_1), (u_1, v_2)\}\) of size \(\nu = 2 = N\) (feasible, optimal \(T^* = 5\)).

Failure-Mode Guard: Always check if \(mid = M\) achieves \(\nu = N\) (or search over \([1, M+1]\)); if even all \(M\) roads have \(\nu(G) < N\), output -1. Never use \(O(VE)\) single-path Kuhn on \(N = 10^4, M = 10^5\)—Hopcroft–Karp’s multi-path blocking flow phase in \(O(M\sqrt{N} \log M) \approx 1.7 \times 10^8\) operations is mandatory.








#034 — [Luogu P1640 / SCOI2010] 连续攻击游戏 (Continuous Attack Game)

Tier: Stepping Stone 2 (SS-2) | Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P1640
Constraints: \(N \le 10^6\) equipment items; each item \(i\) has two integer attribute values \((a_i, b_i) \in [1, 10^4]^2\). Time limit: 1.0s.
Problem Summary: You have \(N\) equipment items. Each item \(i\) can be used at most once, and when used it provides either attribute \(a_i\) or attribute \(b_i\) (not both). You must attack sequentially with attribute values \(1, 2, 3, \dots, K\) without skipping any integer. Find the maximum consecutive prefix length \(K\) (\(0 \le K \le 10^4\)) that can be simultaneously covered by distinct items.







NoteHint 1 — Which Side Goes on \(L\), and Why Can We Augment Greedily?





If you put the \(N = 10^6\) items on \(L\), you don’t know which subset of items should be matched. Instead, put the attribute values \(1, 2, \dots, 10^4\) on \(L\) and the items \(1, \dots, N\) on \(R\)! Because augmenting paths in Kuhn’s algorithm never unmatch a previously matched left vertex (the Transversal Matroid property), you can try matching \(u = 1, 2, 3, \dots\) in order and stop at the very first attribute \(u = K + 1\) where dfs(u) fails!









NoteHint 2 — The memset TLE Trap & The \(O(N \alpha(V))\) Pseudoforest Dual View






In Kuhn’s algorithm: If you call memset(vis, 0, sizeof(vis)) inside the loop \(u = 1 \dots 10^4\), clearing an array of size \(10^4\) or \(10^6\) takes \(10^8 \sim 10^{10}\) operations (TLE). How do you clear vis in \(O(1)\) time using an integer timestamp vis[u] == timer?
Even Faster (\(O(N \alpha(V))\) without Flow): View each item \(i\) not as a vertex, but as an undirected edge \((a_i, b_i)\) between attribute vertices \(a_i\) and \(b_i\)! When can a connected component \(C\) of \(V_C\) vertices and \(E_C\) edges orient its edges to cover all \(V_C\) vertices vs. \(V_C - 1\) vertices?










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P1640: Continuous Attack Game






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Signal: Each item \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) covers one of two attributes \(\{a_i, b_i\} \subseteq \{1, \dots, V\}\) (\(V = 10^4\)), and we want the longest matchable prefix \(\{1, 2, \dots, K\} \subseteq L\).
Two Dual Formulations:

Bipartite Transversal Matroid View: \(L = \{1, \dots, V\}\) (attributes), \(R = \{1, \dots, N\}\) (items), with edges \((a_i, i)\) and \((b_i, i)\). By Theorem 2.2 (Edmonds–Fulkerson Transversal Matroid), matchable subsets of \(L\) form a matroid, and augmenting from \(u = K+1\) never unmatches \(\{1, \dots, K\}\). Thus we sequentially run dfs(u) for \(u = 1, 2, \dots, V\) and halt at the first \(u\) where dfs(u) returns false, outputting \(K = u - 1\).
2-Choice Edge-Orientation / Pseudoforest View: Since each item \(i\) touches at most two attributes \((a_i, b_i)\), view \(V = \{1, \dots, 10^4\}\) as vertices and each item \(i\) as an undirected edge \(e_i = (a_i, b_i)\)! Matching item \(i\) to attribute \(a_i\) or \(b_i\) is equivalent to orienting edge \(e_i\) toward one of its endpoints so that each vertex receives in-degree \(\le 1\).




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation

In the Bipartite View: For each prefix \(K\), we require binary assignments \(x_{i, a_i}, x_{i, b_i} \in \{0, 1\}\) with \(x_{i, a_i} + x_{i, b_i} \le 1\) (\(\forall i \in [1, N]\)) and \(\sum_{i : a_i = u} x_{i, a_i} + \sum_{i : b_i = u} x_{i, b_i} = 1\) (\(\forall u \in [1, K]\)).
In the Pseudoforest View: By Hall’s Theorem applied to each connected component \(C = (V_C, E_C)\) of the attribute graph:

If \(E_C = |V_C| - 1\) (\(C\) is a tree), at most \(|V_C| - 1\) vertices in \(C\) can be covered (by rooting the tree at the single uncovered vertex and orienting all edges away from the root). To maximize the covered prefix \(1, 2, \dots, K\), we must leave the maximum-numbered vertex \(\max(V_C)\) uncovered, covering all other \(|V_C| - 1\) vertices in \(C\)!
If \(E_C \ge |V_C|\) (\(C\) contains at least one cycle / unicyclic / multicyclic), we can orient the cycle cyclically and orient all attached trees away from the cycle, covering all \(|V_C|\) vertices in \(C\)!




Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Both Algorithms)

Method A (Sequential Kuhn with Timestamp Guard): Build adjacency list adj[u] from each attribute \(u \in [1, 10^4]\) to its incident items \(i \in [1, N]\). Maintain match_item[i] (which attribute item \(i\) is currently matched to) and vis_attr[u]. For \(u = 1, 2, \dots, 10^4\): increment ++timer and run dfs(u, timer). If dfs(u, timer) fails, return \(u - 1\).
Method B (\(O(N \alpha(V))\) Disjoint Set Union): Maintain for each DSU root \(r\): max_val[r] (maximum attribute ID in component \(r\)) and has_cycle[r] (boolean, true iff \(E_C \ge |V_C|\)). When processing item \((a_i, b_i)\):

Find \(u = \text{find}(a_i)\) and \(v = \text{find}(b_i)\).
If \(u == v\): set has_cycle[u] = true.
If \(u \ne v\): merge \(u\) and \(v\), set max_val to \(\max(\text{max\_val}[u], \text{max\_val}[v])\), and set has_cycle to has_cycle[u] | has_cycle[v].

Finally, the first uncovered attribute is the minimum of max_val[find(u)] over all components where !has_cycle[find(u)] (or \(10^4 + 1\) if none).



Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: Items are \((1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 3), (4, 5)\).

Component \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) has \(3\) vertices and \(3\) edges (has_cycle = true), so all three attributes \(1, 2, 3\) are covered.
Component \(\{4, 5\}\) has \(2\) vertices and \(1\) edge (has_cycle = false), so it covers \(\min(4, 5) = 4\) and leaves \(\max(4, 5) = 5\) uncovered.
First uncovered attribute is \(5 \implies\) maximum prefix is \(K = 4\).

Failure-Mode Guard: In Method A, calling memset(vis, 0, sizeof(vis)) inside the \(10^4\) loop resets \(10^6\) item booleans \(10^4\) times (\(10^{10}\) ops \(\to\) instant TLE). Always put vis on the smaller side (\(V = 10^4\)) AND use vis[u] == timer so each step only touches visited vertices!








#035 — [UVA 11419] SAM I AM

Tier: Intermediate 1 (Int-1) | Judge URL: https://onlinejudge.org/external/114/11419.pdf
Constraints: \(R, C \le 1000\) rows and columns; \(N \le 10^6\) enemy locations \((r_i, c_i)\). Multiple test cases terminated by 0 0 0.
Problem Summary: Enemies are located at grid coordinates \((r_i, c_i)\) in an \(R \times C\) temple grid. Firing a cannon along row \(r\) (r<r>) destroys all enemies in row \(r\); firing along column \(c\) (c<c>) destroys all enemies in column \(c\). Output the minimum total number of cannon shots required to destroy all enemies, followed by the exact space-separated list of row and column shots (rX and cY).







NoteHint 1 — From 2D Grid Lasers to König’s Minimum Vertex Cover





Every enemy at \((r_i, c_i)\) imposes the logical clause: “Row \(r_i\) must be fired OR Column \(c_i\) must be fired.” What graph has Rows \(L = \{1, \dots, R\}\) on the left, Columns \(R_{\text{col}} = \{1, \dots, C\}\) on the right, and an edge \((r_i, c_i)\) for each enemy?









NoteHint 2 — Reconstructing the Exact Shots via Alternating Reachability (\(Z\))





After computing a maximum matching \(M^*\) via Hopcroft–Karp, how do you identify which rows rX and which columns cY belong to the Minimum Vertex Cover? Recall Theorem 5.4 and FM-05: which left vertices seed the alternating BFS/DFS, and which direction do unmatched vs. matched edges go?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — UVA 11419: SAM I AM






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Signal: Each enemy at \((r_i, c_i)\) is an incidence constraint between Row \(r_i \in L\) and Column \(c_i \in R_{\text{col}}\). We need the minimum number of rows and columns covering all enemies, plus constructive vertex-cover recovery.
Why Naive Degree Greedy Fails: Greedily shooting the row or column with the most remaining enemies fails on simple trees (e.g., row \(1\) has \(2\) enemies in columns \(1, 2\), while columns \(1, 2\) each have \(1\) additional enemy in rows \(2, 3\): greedy shoots row \(1\) first and then needs \(2\) more shots for total \(3\), whereas shooting columns \(1\) and \(2\) covers everything in \(2\) shots).



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Introduce indicator variables \(x_r \in \{0, 1\}\) for firing row \(r \in \{1, \dots, R\}\) and \(y_c \in \{0, 1\}\) for firing column \(c \in \{1, \dots, C\}\):
\[\min \sum_{r=1}^R x_r + \sum_{c=1}^C y_c \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_{r_i} + y_{c_i} \ge 1 \quad \forall (r_i, c_i) \in E, \quad x_r, y_c \in \{0, 1\}.\]
By König’s Theorem (Theorem 5.2), this minimum equals \(\nu(G)\), and by Theorem 5.4, the optimal cover is recovered from the alternating reachability set \(Z\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation & Recovery)

Network / Bipartite Graph Construction: Create left vertices \(L = \{1, \dots, R\}\) and right vertices \(R_{\text{col}} = \{1, \dots, C\}\). For each enemy \((r_i, c_i)\), add directed arc \(r_i \to c_i\) of capacity \(+\infty\), with \(s \xrightarrow{1} r\) and \(c \xrightarrow{1} t\).
Compute Maximum Matching \(M^*\): Run Hopcroft–Karp / unit Dinic in \(O(N\sqrt{R + C})\) time.
Constructive Set Recovery (\(Z = S_{\min} \setminus \{s\}\)):

Seed a BFS queue with all unmatched rows \(U_L = \{r \in L : \text{match}_L[r] == 0\}\). Mark visL[r] = true for \(r \in U_L\).
From each reached row \(r \in L\), traverse every incident enemy edge \((r, c) \in E\) to reach column \(c \in R_{\text{col}}\). If !visR[c], mark visR[c] = true and immediately traverse its matched edge backward to \(r' = \text{match}_R[c] \in L\) (marking visL[r'] = true and pushing \(r'\) to the queue).
Output \(|M^*|\), then output r<r> for every row \(r\) with !visL[r] (\(r \in L \setminus Z\)), and c<c> for every column \(c\) with visR[c] (\(c \in R_{\text{col}} \cap Z\)).




Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: \(R = C = 3\), enemies at \((1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 2)\).

Maximum matching: \(M^* = \{(2, 1), (3, 2)\}\) of size \(2\).
Unmatched row: \(U_L = \{1\}\).
Alternating BFS from \(r = 1\): reaches columns \(c = 1, 2\) via unmatched edges \((1, 1), (1, 2)\); from \(c = 1, 2\), steps backward along matched edges \((2, 1), (3, 2)\) to reach rows \(r = 2, 3\).
Final visited sets: \(\text{visL} = \{1, 2, 3\}\), \(\text{visR} = \{1, 2\}\).
Output cover: \((L \setminus \text{visL}) \cup (R_{\text{col}} \cap \text{visR}) = \emptyset \cup \{\text{c1}, \text{c2}\} = \{\text{c1}, \text{c2}\}\) (2 shots, destroying all 4 enemies!).

Failure-Mode Guard (FM-05): Never start the alternating search from matched rows, and never include unmatched right vertices in \(Z\) unless reached from \(U_L\).








#036 — [POJ 1466] Girls and Boys

Tier: Intermediate 2 (Int-2) | Judge URL: http://poj.org/problem?id=1466
Constraints: \(N \le 500\) students (\(0, \dots, N-1\)); symmetric “romantically involved” adjacency list guaranteed to be bipartite (no odd cycles), though the bipartition \((L, R)\) is not given in the input.
Problem Summary: Given a group of \(N\) students and a symmetric binary relation of romantic involvement (forming a bipartite graph whose left/right gender labels are hidden), find the size of the Maximum Independent Set—the largest subset of students such that no two chosen students are romantically involved.







NoteHint 1 — Maximum Independent Set via Gallai + König





By Gallai’s First Identity and König’s Theorem (Theorem 5.3), in any bipartite graph \(G = (V, E)\), the Maximum Independent Set size is \(\alpha(G) = |V| - \tau(G) = N - \nu(G)\). How do we compute \(\nu(G)\) when the input does not tell us which vertices belong to \(L\) and which belong to \(R\)?









NoteHint 2 — Two Ways to Handle an Unpartitioned Bipartite Graph





Compare two approaches:

Explicit 2-Coloring: Run a BFS/DFS 2-coloring across all connected components to partition \(V = L \sqcup R\), then run matching from \(L\) to \(R\).
The Bipartite Double Cover (\(G \times K_2\)): Create \(N\) left copies \(V_L\) and \(N\) right copies \(V_R\), add directed arc \(u_L \to v_R\) for every ordered pair \((u, v)\) in the symmetric input, and compute maximum matching \(M_{\text{double}}\). Why does \(\nu(G) = |M_{\text{double}}| / 2\) hold here, and why would it fail if \(G\) had an odd cycle?










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — POJ 1466: Girls and Boys






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Signal: We want the largest conflict-free subset (Maximum Independent Set, \(\alpha(G)\)) in a graph guaranteed to be bipartite (boys vs. girls), where the input already lists both \((u, v)\) and \((v, u)\) without specifying each student’s side.



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(x_v \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether student \(v \in V\) is selected in the independent set \(I\):
\[\alpha(G) = \max_{x \in \{0,1\}^N} \sum_{v \in V} x_v \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_u + x_v \le 1 \quad \forall \{u, v\} \in E.\]
By Gallai’s First Identity (\(\bar{x}_v := 1 - x_v\)) and König’s Theorem on the underlying bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\):
\[\alpha(G) = N - \tau(G) = N - \nu(G).\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (2-Coloring vs. Double Cover \(G \times K_2\))

Approach 1 (Canonical 2-Coloring): Run a linear-time \(O(N + M)\) BFS to 2-color each connected component into color \(0\) (\(L\)) and color \(1\) (\(R\)). Direct edges from \(L \to R\) and compute \(\nu(G)\) directly, outputting \(N - \nu(G)\).
Approach 2 (Bipartite Double Cover \(G \times K_2\)): Because the input already gives each undirected edge \(\{u, v\} \in E\) in both directions \((u, v)\) and \((v, u)\), consider the doubled bipartite graph \(G \times K_2\) on \(V_L \sqcup V_R\) (\(|V_L| = |V_R| = N\)). Since \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) is bipartite, the edges of \(G \times K_2\) partition into two completely vertex-disjoint copies of \(G\):

Copy 1 between \(L_{\text{left}} \subseteq V_L\) and \(R_{\text{right}} \subseteq V_R\), and
Copy 2 between \(R_{\text{left}} \subseteq V_L\) and \(L_{\text{right}} \subseteq V_R\).

Therefore, \(\nu(G \times K_2) = \nu(\text{Copy 1}) + \nu(\text{Copy 2}) = 2\nu(G)\), and hence:
\[\alpha(G) = N - \frac{\nu(G \times K_2)}{2}.\]



Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: \(N = 4\) with romantic pairs \(\{0, 1\}, \{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\}\) (path \(P_4\)).

2-Coloring puts \(L = \{0, 2\}\), \(R = \{1, 3\}\), giving \(\nu(G) = 2\) and \(\alpha(G) = 4 - 2 = 2\) (e.g., \(\{0, 3\}\)).
Double cover \(G \times K_2\) matches \((0_L, 1_R), (2_L, 3_R), (1_L, 0_R), (3_L, 2_R)\) of size \(4\), giving \(4 - 4/2 = 2\).

Failure-Mode Guard (FM-07): Never apply the formula \(N - \nu(G \times K_2)/2\) unless \(G\) is proven bipartite! On the odd triangle \(K_3\) (\(N = 3\)), \(\alpha(K_3) = 1\) and \(\nu(K_3) = 1\), but \(K_3 \times K_2 = C_6\) has a perfect matching of size \(\nu(K_3 \times K_2) = 3\), so \(3 - 3/2 = 1.5\) is fractional (FM-07)!








#037 — [CF 808F] Card Game

Tier: Advanced 1 (Adv-1) | Judge URL: https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/808/F
Constraints: \(N \le 100\) cards, target power \(K \le 10^5\); each card \(i\) has power \(p_i \in [1, 1000]\), magic number \(c_i \in [1, 10^5]\), and level \(l_i \in [1, N]\). Time limit: 2.0s.
Problem Summary: At player level \(L\), you may select any subset of cards having \(l_i \le L\), subject to the rule that no two selected cards \(i, j\) may have a prime sum of magic numbers (\(c_i + c_j \notin \mathbb{P}\)). Find the minimum level \(L\) such that there exists a valid subset of cards with total power \(\sum_{i \in I} p_i \ge K\), or output -1 if impossible.







NoteHint 1 — Why Is a Prime-Sum Conflict Graph Almost Bipartite?





Every prime number greater than \(2\) is odd, and the sum of two integers \(c_i + c_j\) is odd if and only if one integer is odd and the other is even! What is the only even prime number, and which magic number \(c_i\) can sum with another \(c_j\) of the same parity to produce \(2\)?









NoteHint 2 — Resolving the \(1 + 1 = 2\) Odd-Cycle Trap & Compiling to MWIS





Because \(1 + 1 = 2 \in \mathbb{P}\), all cards with \(c_i = 1\) mutually conflict with one another (forming a clique!), so any valid subset can include at most one card with \(c_i = 1\). Among all available cards with \(c_i = 1\) and \(l_i \le L\), which single card dominates all others? Once you discard all other \(c_i = 1\) cards, the remaining conflict graph is 100% bipartite (Odd vs. Even)!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — CF 808F: Card Game






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Signal: Monotone level threshold \(L \in [1, N]\) combined with a Maximum-Weight Independent Set (MWIS) problem under pairwise conflicts \(c_i + c_j \in \mathbb{P}\).
Hidden Bipartition & The \(1 + 1 = 2\) Trap:

For any two cards with \((c_i, c_j) \ne (1, 1)\), their sum is \(c_i + c_j > 2\). Since every prime \(> 2\) is odd, a conflict \(c_i + c_j \in \mathbb{P}\) can only occur between an odd magic number (\(u \in L\)) and an even magic number (\(v \in R\)).
However, for cards with \(c_i = 1\), \(1 + 1 = 2 \in \mathbb{P}\) creates odd-to-odd conflicts (and triangles \((1, 1, 2)\) since \(1 + 2 = 3 \in \mathbb{P}\)), destroying bipartiteness (FM-07)!
Dominance Reduction: Every card with \(c_i = 1\) has the exact same conflict neighborhood (\(c_j\) such that \(1 + c_j \in \mathbb{P}\)), and at most one \(c_i = 1\) card can ever be chosen. Therefore, for a fixed level \(L\), we simply keep the single \(c_i = 1\) card with maximum power \(p_i\) (among \(l_i \le L\)) and discard all other \(c_i = 1\) cards! Now the conflict graph is strictly bipartite.




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For a fixed level \(L\), let \(V(L) = L_{\text{odd}} \sqcup R_{\text{even}}\) be the filtered card set (after deduplicating \(c_i = 1\)). Introduce binary selection variables \(\bar{x}_u \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(u \in L_{\text{odd}}\)) and \(\bar{y}_v \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(v \in R_{\text{even}}\)). By Gallai’s First Identity (\(\text{MWIS} = \sum w - \text{MWVC}\), Theorem 5.3):
\[\alpha_p(G_L) = \sum_{z \in V(L)} p_z - \min_{x, y \in \{0,1\}} \left\{ \sum_{u \in L_{\text{odd}}} p_u x_u + \sum_{v \in R_{\text{even}}} p_v y_v \;\middle|\; x_u + y_v \ge 1 \ \ \forall (u, v) \text{ with } c_u + c_v \in \mathbb{P} \right\}.\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Precompute primes up to \(2 \cdot 10^5\) using a linear sieve.
Binary search the level threshold \(L \in [1, N]\):

Filter cards with \(l_i \le L\); among those with \(c_i = 1\), keep only the one with maximum \(p_i\).
Build the canonical MWVC cut network \(\mathcal{N}(L)\) on \(\{s, t\} \cup L_{\text{odd}} \cup R_{\text{even}}\):

For each \(u \in L_{\text{odd}}\): add \(s \xrightarrow{p_u} u\).
For each \(v \in R_{\text{even}}\): add \(v \xrightarrow{p_v} t\).
For each \((u, v) \in L_{\text{odd}} \times R_{\text{even}}\) with \(c_u + c_v \in \mathbb{P}\): add \(u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v\).

Compute \(\alpha_p(G_L) = \sum_{z \in V(L)} p_z - \operatorname{MaxFlow}_{\mathcal{N}(L)}(s, t)\). Check if \(\alpha_p(G_L) \ge K\).




Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: Cards at level \(\le L\) are \(A = (p=5, c=1)\), \(B = (p=8, c=1)\), \(C = (p=10, c=2)\).

Deduplicating \(c=1\) discards \(A\) and keeps \(B = (p=8, c=1) \in L_{\text{odd}}\) alongside \(C = (p=10, c=2) \in R_{\text{even}}\).
Since \(1 + 2 = 3 \in \mathbb{P}\), edge \(B \xrightarrow{+\infty} C\) exists.
\(\operatorname{MinCut}(s, t) = \min(8, 10) = 8\), so \(\alpha_p = (8 + 10) - 8 = 10\) (pick card \(C\)).

Failure-Mode Guard: Never put \(+\infty\) middle arcs with capacity \(1\), and never forget to deduplicate \(c_i = 1\) before building the network (otherwise two \(c_i = 1\) cards both sit in \(L_{\text{odd}}\) with no conflict edge between them, allowing the flow model to illegally pick both!).








#038 — [Luogu P6268 / SHOI2002] 舞会 (Dance Party)

Tier: Advanced 2 (Adv-2) | Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P6268
Constraints: \(N \le 1000\) students (\(0, \dots, N-1\)), \(M \le 2000\) pairs \((u, v)\) who have danced together. Time limit: 1.0s.
Problem Summary: At a school dance, \(M\) pairs of students have danced together. Every dance pair consists of one boy and one girl (so the underlying graph is guaranteed to be bipartite), but the input neither reveals which students are boys/girls nor guarantees that pairs are listed as (boy, girl). Find the maximum number of students who can be invited to a party such that no two invited students have ever danced together.







NoteHint 1 — Why Naive Directed Matching on Input Pairs Fails





Suppose student \(1\) (boy) danced with student \(2\) (girl) and student \(3\) (girl), and the input lists the pairs as 1 2 and 3 1. If you naively treat the first column of input as \(L\) and the second column as \(R\), student \(1\) is split into two independent copies on \(L\) and \(R\), corrupting the matching! How must you preprocess the edges first?









NoteHint 2 — Symmetrization + 2-Coloring into \(L \sqcup R\)





First add undirected edges \(u \leftrightarrow v\) for all \(M\) input pairs. Then run a BFS/DFS across all connected components to assign each vertex a color \(\text{col}[v] \in \{0, 1\}\). Once \(V = L \sqcup R\) is partitioned by color, orient every edge from color \(0\) (\(L\)) to color \(1\) (\(R\)) and apply Gallai + König!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P6268: Dance Party






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Signal: Maximum Independent Set (\(\alpha(G) = N - \nu(G)\)) on a bipartite graph where both the vertex partition \(V = L \sqcup R\) and the edge orientations in the input file are unstandardized.



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For the underlying undirected bipartite graph \(G = (V, E)\), let \(x_v \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether student \(v\) is invited:
\[\alpha(G) = \max_{x \in \{0,1\}^N} \sum_{v=0}^{N-1} x_v \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_u + x_v \le 1 \quad \forall \{u, v\} \in E.\]
Since \(G\) contains no odd cycles, \(V\) admits a valid 2-coloring \(c : V \to \{0, 1\}\) such that every edge \(\{u, v\} \in E\) has \(c(u) \ne c(v)\). Defining \(L = c^{-1}(0)\) and \(R = c^{-1}(1)\) reduces the problem to \(\alpha(G) = N - \tau(G) = N - \nu(G)\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Symmetrize & Deduplicate: For each of the \(M\) input pairs \((u, v)\), insert \(v\) into undir_adj[u] and \(u\) into undir_adj[v].
Component-Wise 2-Coloring: Initialize col[0..N-1] = -1. Loop \(i = 0 \dots N-1\): if col[i] == -1, set col[i] = 0 and run BFS/DFS, setting col[nxt] = col[cur] ^ 1 for every neighbor.
Build Unit Network \(\mathcal{N}\):

For each \(u\) with col[u] == 0: add \(s \xrightarrow{1} u\), and for each neighbor \(v \in \text{undir\_adj}[u]\) (which has col[v] == 1), add \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\).
For each \(v\) with col[v] == 1: add \(v \xrightarrow{1} t\).

Solve: Compute \(\nu(G) = \operatorname{MaxFlow}_{\mathcal{N}}(s, t)\) and output \(N - \nu(G)\).



Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: \(N = 3\) with input edges (0, 1) and (1, 2).

If we naively wired \(0_L \to 1_R\) and \(1_L \to 2_R\), both arcs would be matched independently (flow = 2), wrongly outputting \(3 - 2 = 1\)!
Symmetrizing and 2-coloring assigns \(\text{col}[0] = 0, \text{col}[1] = 1, \text{col}[2] = 0\), so \(L = \{0, 2\}, R = \{1\}\) with arcs \(0 \to 1\) and \(2 \to 1\). Now \(\nu(G) = 1\), and \(\alpha(G) = 3 - 1 = 2\) (invite \(\{0, 2\}\)).

Failure-Mode Guard: Always symmetrize the adjacency list before 2-coloring, and remember to loop the 2-coloring seed over all \(i \in [0, N-1]\) because \(G\) may have multiple disconnected components!








#039 — [Luogu P3731 / HAOI2017] 新型城市化 (New Urbanization)

Tier: Mastery 1 (Mas-1) | Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3731
Constraints: \(N \le 10^4\) cities, \(M \le 1.5 \cdot 10^5\) non-friendship pairs (or complement edges); the cities can be partitioned into at most two cliques (urban clusters). Time limit: 1.0s.
Problem Summary: A country has \(N\) cities that can be partitioned into two urban clusters (each cluster is a clique of mutually connected cities), plus some inter-cluster edges. The government can build one new road between a currently unconnected pair of cities. Find all candidate missing roads \(\{u, v\} \notin E(G)\) whose addition strictly increases the size of the Maximum Clique \(\omega(G)\) of the country, output in lexicographical order.







NoteHint 1 — Complement Graph Dualization: From 2 Cliques to Bipartite MIS





Finding a Maximum Clique \(\omega(G)\) in a general graph is NP-hard, and network flow cannot model cliques directly. Take the complement graph \(\bar{G} = (V, \bar{E})\) (where \(\{u, v\} \in \bar{E} \iff \{u, v\} \notin E(G)\))!

Since \(V\) is the union of two cliques in \(G\), what is the structure of \(\bar{G}\)?
What does a Maximum Clique in \(G\) correspond to in \(\bar{G}\)?
What does adding a missing road \(\{u, v\}\) to \(G\) correspond to in \(\bar{G}\)?










NoteHint 2 — Critical Edges of Maximum Matching via Residual Tarjan SCC





In the bipartite complement graph \(\bar{G} = (L \sqcup R, \bar{E})\), the maximum clique size of \(G\) is \(\omega(G) = \alpha(\bar{G}) = N - \nu(\bar{G})\). Adding a missing road to \(G\) deletes an edge \(e = (u, v) \in \bar{E}\) from \(\bar{G}\), which strictly increases \(\alpha(\bar{G})\) if and only if deleting \(e\) strictly decreases the maximum matching \(\nu(\bar{G})\)!
How do you find all edges \(e \in \bar{E}\) that belong to every maximum matching of \(\bar{G}\) in a single \(O(V + \bar{E})\) pass after running Dinic? (Hint: run Tarjan’s Strongly Connected Components (SCC) algorithm on the residual network \(G_{f^*}\)!)









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P3731: New Urbanization






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Signal: The graph \(G\) is a union of two cliques \(K_A \sqcup K_B\), and we want to identify all non-edges whose addition increases \(\omega(G)\) by \(1\).
Complement Dualization:

In the complement graph \(\bar{G} = (V, \bar{E})\), there are no edges inside \(K_A\) and no edges inside \(K_B\), so \(\bar{G}\) is bipartite!
A clique in \(G\) is an independent set in \(\bar{G}\), so \(\omega(G) = \alpha(\bar{G}) = N - \nu(\bar{G})\) by Gallai + König.
Adding a missing road \(e\) to \(G\) is equivalent to deleting edge \(e \in \bar{E}\) from \(\bar{G}\). Thus \(\omega(G \cup \{e\}) = \omega(G) + 1 \iff \nu(\bar{G} \setminus \{e\}) = \nu(\bar{G}) - 1\): edge \(e \in \bar{E}\) must an essential / critical edge that appears in every maximum matching of \(\bar{G}\)!




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Residual Characterization
Let \(f^*\) be an integral maximum flow in the unit bipartite network \(\mathcal{N}(\bar{G})\), corresponding to a maximum matching \(M^*\) of size \(\nu(\bar{G})\). When does an edge \(e = (u, v) \in \bar{E}\) (\(u \in L, v \in R\)) belong to every maximum matching of \(\bar{G}\)?

First, \(e\) must belong to our current maximum matching \(M^*\), i.e., \(f^*(u, v) = 1\) (if \(f^*(u, v) = 0\), then \(M^*\) itself avoids \(e\)!).
Second, there must not exist any other maximum matching \(M'\) avoiding \(e\). In the symmetric difference \(M^* \triangle M'\), any replacement of \((u, v) \in M^*\) while preserving matching size \(\nu(\bar{G})\) corresponds to either:

An alternating cycle in \(G_{f^*} \setminus \{s, t\}\) containing the backward residual arc \(v \to u\), OR
An even-length alternating path through \(s\) or \(t\) in \(G_{f^*}\) (which, because \(s \to u\) and \(v \to t\) are saturated and have backward residual arcs \(u \to s\) and \(t \to v\), closes into a directed cycle through \(s\) or \(t\) in the full residual graph \(G_{f^*}\) containing \(v \to u\)!). In both cases, an alternative maximum matching avoiding \(e = (u, v)\) exists if and only if there is a directed residual path from \(u\) to \(v\) in \(G_{f^*}\), which together with the backward residual arc \(v \to u\) (\(c_f(v, u) = 1 > 0\)) puts \(u\) and \(v\) in the same Strongly Connected Component (SCC) of \(G_{f^*}\)!


\[\boxed{e = (u, v) \in \bar{E} \text{ is critical} \iff f^*(u, v) = 1 \ \land \ \operatorname{scc}(u) \ne \operatorname{scc}(v) \text{ in } G_{f^*}.}\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

2-color the complement graph \(\bar{G}\) into \(L \sqcup R\) (looping over all connected components).
Build the unit network \(\mathcal{N}(\bar{G})\) on \(\{s, t\} \cup L \cup R\) with \(s \xrightarrow{1} u\), \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\) (\(\forall (u, v) \in \bar{E}\)), and \(v \xrightarrow{1} t\).
Run Dinic (Hopcroft–Karp) in \(O((N + |\bar{E}|)\sqrt{N})\) to obtain the residual network \(G_{f^*}\).
Run Tarjan’s SCC algorithm in \(O(N + |\bar{E}|)\) on all arcs of \(G_{f^*}\) that have positive residual capacity \(c_f > 0\) (including \(s\) and \(t\)!).
Collect all original middle arcs \(u \to v\) (\(u \in L, v \in R\)) such that \(f^*(u, v) = 1\) (saturated) and \(\operatorname{scc}[u] \ne \operatorname{scc}[v]\). Sort pairs \((\min(u,v), \max(u,v))\) and output.



Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: \(\bar{G}\) has \(L = \{1, 2\}, R = \{3, 4\}\) with edges \((1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 4)\).

Unique maximum matching is \(M^* = \{(1, 3), (2, 4)\}\) of size \(2\)!
In \(G_{f^*}\), \(1 \to 4\) has \(c_f(1, 4) = 1\), \(4 \to 2\) has \(c_f(4, 2) = 1\), and \(3 \to 1\) has \(c_f(3, 1) = 1\), but \(2\) has no outgoing residual arc to \(3\), so there is no residual cycle!
Thus \(\operatorname{scc}[1] \ne \operatorname{scc}[3]\) and \(\operatorname{scc}[2] \ne \operatorname{scc}[4]\): both \((1, 3)\) and \((2, 4)\) are critical!

Failure-Mode Guard: Only inspect middle arcs \((u, v) \in L \times R\) with \(f^*(u, v) = 1\) (never source/sink arcs \(s \to u\) or \(v \to t\)), and make sure \(s\) and \(t\) (along with their residual arcs \(s \leftrightarrow u\) and \(v \leftrightarrow t\)) are included in the Tarjan SCC graph so that even-length alternating paths starting at unmatched vertices \(U_L\) or \(U_R\) properly form cycles through \(s\) or \(t\)!








#040 — [CF 1404C] Fixed Point Removal

Tier: Mastery 2 (Mas-2 — Decoy / Structural Elimination) | Judge URL: https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1404/C
Constraints: Array \(a_1, \dots, a_N\) (\(N \le 3 \cdot 10^5\)), \(Q \le 3 \cdot 10^5\) offline queries \((x_q, y_q)\) restricting removals to the subarray \([L_q, R_q] = [x_q + 1, N - y_q]\). Time limit: 3.0s.
Problem Summary: In a 1-indexed array \(a\), you may repeatedly choose an element currently at position \(p\) that satisfies \(a_p = p\), remove it from the array, and shift all elements to its right one position to the left. For each query \((x_q, y_q)\), the first \(x_q\) elements and last \(y_q\) elements are nailed down and cannot be removed; find the maximum number of elements that can be removed from the remaining active range \([L_q, R_q] = [x_q + 1, N - y_q]\).







NoteHint 1 — Why Is This in Chapter 5? Recognizing Monotone Precedence Closure





An element originally at index \(i\) with value \(a_i\) can eventually land at index \(a_i\) and be removed if and only if:

\(d_i := i - a_i \ge 0\) (since elements only shift left, never right!), and
At least \(d_i = i - a_i\) elements in \([L_q, i - 1]\) are removed before \(i\)!

At \(N, Q = 3 \cdot 10^5\), building an explicit dependency DAG or flow network per query is impossible. What monotonicity property holds as we vary the left boundary \(L\)?









NoteHint 2 — The Critical Left-Boundary Threshold \(L_{\max}(i)\) & Fenwick Binary Lifting





Decreasing the left boundary \(L\) (allowing more elements on the left to be removed) can only help element \(i\) become removable! Therefore, for each index \(i \in [1, N]\), there is a single maximum threshold \(L_{\max}(i) \in [0, i]\) such that element \(i\) is removable in \([L, R]\) if and only if \(L \le L_{\max}(i)\) and \(i \le R\). How can you sweep \(i = 1 \dots N\) and compute \(L_{\max}(i)\) in \(O(\log N)\) using a Fenwick tree?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — CF 1404C: Fixed Point Removal






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition & Flow-Elimination)

Surface Signal: Precedence-constrained selection on \([L_q, R_q]\) where element \(i\) requires \(d_i = i - a_i\) predecessors in \([L_q, i - 1]\) to be selected first.
Why Explicit Graph / Flow Modelling Is Eliminated:

First, if a set of elements is removable, removing them in right-to-left order of their current fixed points never hurts any element to the right, so the maximal removable set is unique (greedy closure)!
Second, for a fixed \(i\), let \(C(L, i - 1)\) be the number of removable elements in \([L, i - 1]\) when the left barrier is \(L\). As \(L\) decreases from \(i\) down to \(1\), \(C(L, i - 1)\) is monotonically non-increasing in \(L\). Thus the feasibility condition \(C(L, i - 1) \ge i - a_i\) holds on a contiguous prefix of left boundaries \(L \in [1, L_{\max}(i)]\).




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For each index \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), define its critical left-barrier threshold \(L_{\max}(i) \in \{0, 1, \dots, i\}\) recursively:
\[L_{\max}(i) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i - a_i < 0 \text{ or } \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \mathbb{I}[L_{\max}(j) \ge 1] < i - a_i, \\[6pt] \max \left\{ L \in [1, i] : \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \mathbb{I}[L_{\max}(j) \ge L] \ge i - a_i \right\} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\]
Once \(L_{\max}(1), \dots, L_{\max}(N)\) are known, a query \([L_q, R_q]\) simply asks for the 2D orthogonal range count:
\[\text{Ans}(L_q, R_q) = \sum_{i = L_q}^{R_q} \mathbb{I}[L_{\max}(i) \ge L_q] = \sum_{i = 1}^{R_q} \mathbb{I}[L_{\max}(i) \ge L_q] \quad (\text{since } L_{\max}(i) \le i < L_q \text{ for } i < L_q).\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Offline Sweep + Fenwick Tree Binary Lifting)

Group all queries \((L_q, R_q)\) by their right endpoint \(R_q\).
Maintain a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) bit[1..N] where after processing prefix \(1 \dots i\), query_suffix(L) returns the count of \(j \le i\) with \(L_{\max}(j) \ge L\) (implemented as a prefix Fenwick tree by storing total_inserted - bit.sum(L - 1)).
Sweep \(i = 1 \dots N\):

Let \(d_i = i - a_i\). If \(d_i \ge 0\) and total_inserted >= d_i:

Use binary lifting on the Fenwick tree in \(O(\log N)\) time to find the largest index \(pos \le i\) such that bit.sum(pos - 1) <= total_inserted - d_i. That \(pos\) is \(L_{\max}(i)\)!
Insert \(L_{\max}(i)\) into the Fenwick tree (bit.add(L_max[i], 1), total_inserted++).

For every query \((L_q, R_q)\) with \(R_q = i\), the answer is total_inserted - bit.sum(L_q - 1).




Step 4: Concrete Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

Toy Trace: \(a = [2, 1, 2]\) (\(N = 3\)).

\(i = 1\): \(d_1 = 1 - 2 = -1 < 0 \implies L_{\max}(1) = 0\) (not inserted).
\(i = 2\): \(d_2 = 2 - 1 = 1 > \text{total\_inserted} = 0 \implies L_{\max}(2) = 0\).
Now suppose instead \(a = [1, 1, 2]\):

\(i = 1\): \(d_1 = 1 - 1 = 0 \implies L_{\max}(1) = 1\) (inserted at \(1\)).
\(i = 2\): \(d_2 = 2 - 1 = 1 \implies\) needs \(1\) prior removal; \(L_{\max}(1) = 1 \ge 1 \implies L_{\max}(2) = 1\) (inserted at \(1\)).
\(i = 3\): \(d_3 = 3 - 2 = 1 \implies\) at \(L = 2\), \(L_{\max}(2) = 1 < 2\) so \(0\) removals; at \(L = 1\), \(2 \ge 1\) removals \(\implies L_{\max}(3) = 1\).


Failure-Mode Guard: Never insert \(L_{\max}(i) = 0\) into the Fenwick tree (otherwise total_inserted counts unremovable elements!). Always guard \(d_i = i - a_i \ge 0\) AND \(\min(L_{\max}(i), i)\) so \(L_{\max}(i)\) never exceeds \(i\). Total complexity: \(O((N + Q)\log N)\) time and \(O(N + Q)\) space.

section: 7. Chapter 5 Verification Checklist, Quarantined Templates & Failure Modes
text:
7. Chapter 5 Verification Checklist, Quarantined Templates & Failure Modes

7.1 Pre-Submission 5-Point Verification Checklist
Before submitting any Bipartite Matching, König Vertex Cover, or Maximum Independent Set solution in a contest, run through this 5-point verification checklist:

Have you proved the conflict graph is bipartite (FM-07)?

Check for hidden odd cycles! In prime-sum conflicts (#037), \(1 + 1 = 2\) creates a clique among \(1\)s; deduplicate to at most one \(c_i = 1\) card first.
If the bipartition \((L, R)\) is not given in the input (#036, #038), symmetrize the edges and run a 2-coloring BFS across all connected components before building the flow network.

Did you use capacity \(+\infty\) on middle arcs \(u \to v\) when extracting cuts or solving weighted problems?

Setting \(c(u, v) = 1\) is only valid when \(w \equiv 1\) and you only need \(\nu(G)\) or the matched pairs \(M^*\). Whenever you extract MVC/MIS via \(S_{\min}\) or have vertex weights \(w_u, w_v\), middle arcs must have capacity \(+\infty\).

Did you seed König’s alternating DFS/BFS strictly from unmatched left vertices \(U_L\) (FM-05)?

In residual terms, \(s \to u\) has \(c_f(s, u) > 0 \iff u \in U_L\). Starting from matched left vertices or forgetting to follow matched arcs backward from \(R \to L\) corrupts \(Z\) and outputs an invalid cover.

Did you apply Bipartite Variable Inversion in the right direction when reading off MVC and MIS?

\(\operatorname{MVC} = (L \setminus S_{\min}) \cup (R \cap S_{\min})\) (severed source arcs \(s \to u\) plus severed sink arcs \(v \to t\)).
\(\operatorname{MIS} = (L \cap S_{\min}) \cup (R \setminus S_{\min})\) (intact source arcs \(s \to u\) plus intact sink arcs \(v \to t\)).

Did you check the complexity regime (\(O(E\sqrt{V})\) vs. \(O(VE)\) vs. Timestamp Reset)?

When \(V \sim 10^4, E \sim 10^5\) (especially inside a binary search, #033), use Hopcroft–Karp / unit Dinic in \(O(E\sqrt{V})\).
When running sequential Kuhn on a Transversal Matroid (#034), never call memset(vis, 0, sizeof(vis)) inside the loop; use vis[u] == timer or DSU.

title: Chapter 5 — Bipartite Matching, König’s Theorem, Minimum Vertex Cover, and Maximum Independent Set
text:
8. Chapter Revision Summary

Bipartite Variable Inversion & Cut Compilation: Encoding \(x_u = 1 - s_u\) on \(L\) and \(y_v = s_v\) on \(R\) compiles the covering disjunction \(x_u + y_v \ge 1\) into a directed middle arc \(u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v\) whose cut term \(+\infty \cdot s_u(1 - s_v)\) forbids the uncovered state \((x_u = 0, y_v = 0)\).
König–Egerváry Theorem & Total Unimodularity: Because the incidence matrix of a bipartite graph is Totally Unimodular, LP duality holds over the integers with zero integrality gap: \(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\) and \(\tau_w(G) = \operatorname{MinCut}_{\mathcal{N}}(s, t) = \operatorname{MaxFlow}_{\mathcal{N}}(s, t)\).
Gallai’s Dual Identities: In all graphs, \(\alpha(G) + \tau(G) = |V|\) and (without isolated vertices) \(\nu(G) + \rho(G) = |V|\). In bipartite graphs, \(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\) locks all four invariants together: \(\alpha(G) = \rho(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\).
Constructive Set Recovery in \(O(V + E)\): The residual source-reachable set \(Z = S_{\min} \setminus \{s\}\) equals the set of vertices reachable from unmatched left vertices \(U_L\) via alternating paths, yielding \(\operatorname{MVC} = (L \setminus Z) \cup (R \cap Z)\) and \(\operatorname{MIS} = (L \cap Z) \cup (R \setminus Z)\).
Looking Ahead to Chapter 6: In Chapter 6, we extend alternating reachability from \(U_L\) and \(U_R\) to the full Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) Canonical Decomposition (\(V = V^+ \sqcup V^- \sqcup V^0\)), unlocking linear-time winning-strategy analysis for Two-Player Impartial Bipartite Walk Games and weighted poset / grid models.

title: Chapter 3 — Vertex Splitting, Time-Expanded Layered DAGs, and Path Decomposition
text:
NotePrerequisites



Before starting this chapter, verify that you are fluent with the following concepts from Chapters 1 and 2:

Skew-Symmetric Conservation & Residual Cancellation (Chapter 1): Every flow \(f: E \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) satisfies \(0 \le f(u, v) \le c(u, v)\) and Kirchhoff conservation \(\sum_{u} f(u, v) = \sum_{w} f(v, w)\) for all \(v \notin \{s, t\}\). Pushing \(\Delta > 0\) units along a reverse residual arc \((v, u)\) in \(G_f\) cancels \(\Delta\) units of previously committed forward flow on \((u, v)\) and splices two crossing paths into two non-crossing paths.
Dinitz’s Three Complexity Regimes (Chapter 1): On general networks, Dinic runs in \(O(V^2 E)\); on unit-capacity networks (\(c(e) = 1\)), Dinic runs in \(O(E \min(V^{2/3}, E^{1/2}))\); and on unit vertex networks (\(\min(\deg^-(v), \deg^+(v)) \le 1\) with unit capacities), Dinic runs in \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) by Even and Tarjan’s theorem (1975).
Canonical Extremal Cuts \(S_{\min}\) and Residual Incrementalism (Chapter 2): The source-reachable set \(S_{\min} = \{v \in V : s \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} v\}\) identifies the unique source-minimal minimum cut, and adding new vertices or arcs to \(G_{f^*}\) allows incremental re-augmentation without rebuilding the network from scratch.









TipLearning Objectives



By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Decompose Flows Constructively: Prove the Flow Decomposition Theorem (流分解定理) and implement an \(O(V E)\) path-and-cycle stripping algorithm to recover explicit \(s\)-\(t\) trajectories from residual capacities—while diagnosing why naive greedy shortest-path stripping without residual uncrossing fails on the 6-Vertex Diamond-Bridge counterexample.
Compile Vertex Capacities & Multi-Stage Decisions via Node Splitting: Transform vertex throughput bounds \(F(v) \le C_v\) into internal bridge arcs \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_v} v_{\text{out}}\) under the strict \(\text{out} \to \text{in}\) port invariant, establish the exact bijection between node cuts and arc cuts, avoid the FM-04 Undirected Vertex-Split Bypass Trap, and prove all Four Variants of Menger’s Connectivity Theorem.
Unroll Discrete Time Horizons & DP Subgraphs: Construct Time-Expanded Layered Networks (分层图) over \(V \times \{0, 1, \dots, T\}\) with holdover and transit arcs, apply Incremental Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层) to find minimum completion times without binary search, and layer optimal DP / Shortest-Path DAGs to count disjoint optimal structures.
Sparsify Dense Transition Cliques via Hub Vertices: Collapse \(\Theta(H W (H + W))\) row/column jump cliques into \(O(H + W)\) bipartite hub networks ([ARC 074 D] Lotus Leaves) and eliminate interior grid vertices via perimeter Cut-DP ([CF 1368H1]).

title: Chapter 3 — Vertex Splitting, Time-Expanded Layered DAGs, and Path Decomposition
section: 1. Motivation: Compiling Node Bottlenecks, Multi-Stage Decisions, and Time Horizons into Arcs
text:
1. Motivation: Compiling Node Bottlenecks, Multi-Stage Decisions, and Time Horizons into Arcs
In Chapters 1 and 2, every capacity constraint lived directly on a directed arc \(e = (u \to v)\):
\[0 \le f(u, v) \le c(u, v).\]
Vertices \(v \notin \{s, t\}\) were treated as frictionless, infinite-bandwidth junctions whose only role was to enforce Kirchhoff flow conservation:
\[\sum_{u : (u, v) \in E} f(u, v) = \sum_{w : (v, w) \in E} f(v, w).\]
Real contest problems, however, rarely hand you a pre-built edge-capacitated graph. Instead, the problem statement hides the flow structure behind three non-arc bottlenecks:

Physical Node Bottlenecks: Routers overheat after forwarding \(C_v\) packets ([CQOI2015] 网络吞吐量), stone pillars crumble after \(h_{r,c}\) lizard jumps ([SCOI2007] 蜥蜴), or thin ice floes sink after a single survivor steps off them ([UVa 11380] Down Went The Titanic). Here, the limit constrains the total flow passing through a vertex \(v\), regardless of which incoming edge it arrives on or which outgoing edge it leaves on.
Multi-Stage Entity Coupling: A hotel guest is satisfied only if assigned both a liked room \(r \in \mathcal{R}\) and a liked dish \(d \in \mathcal{D}\) ([Luogu P1402] 酒店之王). If we model the guest as a single vertex \(g\) between rooms and dishes (\(r \to g \to d\)), conservation at \(g\) guarantees that the number of rooms assigned to \(g\) equals the number of dishes assigned to \(g\), but it does not stop a single guest with two liked rooms and two liked dishes from absorbing \(2\) units of flow!
Temporal & Sequential Coupling: Space shuttles cycle periodically between stations over discrete time steps \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) ([CTSC1999] 家园). An edge that exists at \(t = 1\) may vanish at \(t = 2\), and passengers can wait at stations across time steps. On a static graph, flow is instantaneous: a unit of flow entering \(u\) at \(t = 5\) could illegally depart along an edge that was only available at \(t = 1\).

All three phenomena share a single mathematical cure: state-space expansion. Rather than modifying Dinic’s solver to track vertex budgets or timestamps, we compile vertex capacities, multi-stage roles, and discrete time horizons into ordinary directed arcs by splitting each logical entity into fine-grained state vertices:

Vertex Capacity Splitting: \(v \mapsto (v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_v} v_{\text{out}})\) turns node throughput into an internal arc capacity.
Time-Expanded Layering (分层图): \(v \mapsto (v, 0) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, 1) \xrightarrow{\infty} \dots \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, T)\) turns temporal causality into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
Hub Sparsification: Replacing an \(m\)-clique of valid jumps with a shared hub vertex \(H_{\text{row}}\) turns \(\Theta(m^2)\) transitions into \(2m\) arcs.

Before we build these state-expanded graphs, however, we need a rigorous bridge back from aggregate arc flows \(f(e)\) to individual physical trajectories (paths of lizards, survivors, astronauts, or subsequences). That bridge is the Flow Decomposition Theorem.

title: Chapter 3 — Vertex Splitting, Time-Expanded Layered DAGs, and Path Decomposition
section: 2. The Flow Decomposition Theorem & Constructive Path Extraction
text:
2. The Flow Decomposition Theorem & Constructive Path Extraction
A maximum-flow solver computes a single scalar \(f(e) \in [0, c(e)]\) on each arc \(e \in E\). Yet many problems ask not merely for the scalar throughput \(|f|\), but for the explicit trajectories of the \(|f|\) agents, or rely on the equivalence between an aggregate flow of value \(k\) and \(k\) mutually disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths.

2.1 Statement and Constructive Proof of the Flow Decomposition Theorem






ImportantTheorem 3.1 (Flow Decomposition Theorem — Ford & Fulkerson, 1962; 流分解定理)



Let \(G = (V, E, c)\) be a directed network with source \(s\) and sink \(t\), and let \(f: E \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) be any feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(|f| \ge 0\). Then there exists a collection of simple directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths \(\mathcal{P} = \{P_1, \dots, P_p\}\) and simple directed cycles \(\mathcal{C} = \{C_1, \dots, C_q\}\) with positive weights \(\alpha(P_i) > 0\) and \(\beta(C_j) > 0\) such that:

Arc-wise Decomposition: For every directed arc \(e \in E\),
\[f(e) = \sum_{i : e \in P_i} \alpha(P_i) + \sum_{j : e \in C_j} \beta(C_j).\]
Value Conservation: The weights of the \(s\)-\(t\) paths sum to the total flow value:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{p} \alpha(P_i) = |f|.\]
Sparsity Bound: The total number of paths and cycles satisfies
\[p + q \le |E|.\]
Integrality Preservation: If \(f(e) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) for all \(e \in E\), then every path weight \(\alpha(P_i)\) and cycle weight \(\beta(C_j)\) can be chosen as a positive integer. In particular, an integer flow of value \(|f|\) decomposes into \(|f|\) unit-weight \(s\)-\(t\) paths (possibly repeating) plus integer-weighted directed cycles.




Constructive Proof via Bottleneck Stripping
Define the support of \(f\) as the active arc set \(\operatorname{supp}(f) = \{e \in E : f(e) > 0\}\). We proceed by induction on \(|\operatorname{supp}(f)| \le |E|\).
If \(\operatorname{supp}(f) = \emptyset\), then \(|f| = 0\) and the empty collection \(\mathcal{P} = \emptyset, \mathcal{C} = \emptyset\) satisfies all claims.
Otherwise, pick any active arc \(e_0 = (u_0 \to u_1) \in \operatorname{supp}(f)\) and extend a walk forward \(u_0 \to u_1 \to u_2 \to \dots\) along active arcs whenever possible:

Case 1 (Positive net outflow at \(s\), i.e., \(|f| > 0\)): Start the walk at \(u_0 = s\). For every intermediate vertex \(v \notin \{s, t\}\) reached by the walk, Kirchhoff conservation guarantees
\[\sum_{w} f(v, w) = \sum_{u} f(u, v) \ge f(u_{\text{prev}}, v) > 0,\]
so \(v\) must possess at least one outgoing active arc \((v \to w)\) with \(f(v, w) > 0\). Thus the walk can never get stuck at an internal vertex \(v \notin \{s, t\}\). Since \(V\) is finite, the walk either:

reaches \(t\) without repeating a vertex, yielding a simple directed \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\), or
repeats a vertex \(v\) before reaching \(t\), in which case the sub-walk between the two visits to \(v\) forms a simple directed cycle \(C\).

Case 2 (\(|f| = 0\) but \(\operatorname{supp}(f) \neq \emptyset\)): Start from any active arc \((u_0 \to u_1) \in \operatorname{supp}(f)\). Since every vertex now has zero net excess, the walk can never get stuck and must eventually repeat a vertex, extracting a simple directed cycle \(C\).

In either case, we obtain a simple structure \(\Gamma \in \{P, C\}\) (either a simple \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) or a simple directed cycle \(C\)) contained entirely in \(\operatorname{supp}(f)\). Define its bottleneck weight:
\[\delta(\Gamma) = \min_{e \in \Gamma} f(e) > 0.\]
Subtract \(\delta(\Gamma)\) from \(f(e)\) for every \(e \in \Gamma\) to obtain a residual flow \(f'\):
\[f'(e) = \begin{cases} f(e) - \delta(\Gamma) & \text{if } e \in \Gamma, \\ f(e) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\]
Observe that:

If \(\Gamma = P\) is an \(s\)-\(t\) path, subtracting \(\delta(P)\) decreases both the inflow and outflow of every internal vertex of \(P\) by \(\delta(P)\), preserves conservation everywhere, and reduces \(|f'|\) to \(|f| - \delta(P)\).
If \(\Gamma = C\) is a directed cycle, subtracting \(\delta(C)\) decreases both the inflow and outflow of every vertex on \(C\) by \(\delta(C)\), leaving \(|f'| = |f|\) unchanged.
Because \(\delta(\Gamma) = \min_{e \in \Gamma} f(e)\), at least one bottleneck arc \(e^* \in \Gamma\) drops to \(f'(e^*) = 0\), strictly decreasing the support size:
\[|\operatorname{supp}(f')| \le |\operatorname{supp}(f)| - 1.\]

Since \(|\operatorname{supp}(f)| \le |E|\) initially and each step extracts one path or cycle while zeroing out at least one active arc, the process terminates in \(p + q \le |E|\) steps. If \(f\) is integral, \(\delta(\Gamma) = \min_{e \in \Gamma} f(e)\) is an integer at every step, proving (4). \(\blacksquare\)



2.2 Constructive \(O(V E)\) Path & Cycle Stripping Algorithm
First, how do we recover \(f(e)\) from our Dinic adjacency list after termination?

Standard Directed Arc \(e = (u \to v)\) stored at half-edge index 2k (forward) and 2k+1 (reverse, initialized to capacity \(0\)): the net flow pushed along \(e\) is stored directly in the reverse residual capacity:
\[f(u \to v) = c_f(\text{rev}(e)) = \text{cap}[2k + 1].\]
Compact Undirected Pair \(\{u, v\}\) stored at 2k and 2k+1 (both initialized to capacity \(C\)): as derived in Chapter 1, \(\text{cap}[2k] + \text{cap}[2k+1] = 2C\), and at most one direction carries positive net physical flow:
\[f_{\text{phys}}(u \to v) = \max(0, C - \text{cap}[2k]), \qquad f_{\text{phys}}(v \to u) = \max(0, C - \text{cap}[2k+1]).\]

Once the active positive flows \(f(e) > 0\) are extracted, we strip \(s\)-\(t\) paths in \(O(V E)\) time by maintaining a stack of visited vertices vis_stack and an on-stack boolean flag on_stack[u]:

Walk forward from \(s\) along any active arc \(e = (u \to v)\) with \(f(e) > 0\) (using a cur[u] pointer to skip zeroed arcs).
If the walk hits a vertex \(v\) with on_stack[v] == true, pop the cycle \(C\) above \(v\) from the stack, compute \(\delta(C) = \min_{e \in C} f(e)\), subtract \(\delta(C)\) from all \(e \in C\), and resume the walk from \(v\).
When the walk reaches \(t\), the stack holds a simple \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\); subtract \(\delta(P) = \min_{e \in P} f(e)\) and record \((P, \delta(P))\).

Each step advances at most \(V\) times before either hitting \(t\) or closing a cycle, and every path or cycle extraction zeroes at least one arc (or in the unit-capacity case, consumes \(1\) unit of flow per arc in \(O(|E|)\) total time).






NoteShortcut When the Active Support Is Already a DAG



On unit-capacity networks after shortest-path Dinic augmentation, or on Time-Expanded Layered DAGs (分层图) and Shortest-Path DAGs, the active support \(\operatorname{supp}(f^*)\) contains no directed cycles (or any residual cycle can be ignored because \(|f^*|\) paths are guaranteed to reach \(t\)). In that case, a simple DFS from \(s\) that decrements \(f(e) \gets f(e) - 1\) on each traversed arc extracts all \(|f^*|\) unit \(s\)-\(t\) paths in \(O(|f^*| \cdot V)\) time.




2.3 Why Naive Greedy Path Stripping Without Residual Uncrossing Fails
A classic beginner mistake is to confuse decomposing an already-computed maximum flow \(f^*\) (where \(f^*\) was found using reverse residual arcs) with greedily stripping shortest \(s\)-\(t\) paths directly from the original graph \(G\).






WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexample FM-01 — The 6-Vertex Diamond-Bridge Greedy Failure



Suppose we want to find the maximum number of edge-disjoint directed paths from \(s\) to \(t\), and we try the following “Greedy Shortest-Path Stripping” heuristic:

Repeat until \(t\) is unreachable from \(s\): find a shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) in \(G\) via BFS, output \(P\), and delete all edges of \(P\) from \(G\).

Why does this fail even when we pick the unique shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path at Step 1? Consider the 6-Vertex Diamond-Bridge Graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(V = \{s, a, b, u, v, t\}\) and \(7\) unit-capacity directed edges:

Top entry and bottom exit of the bridge: \(s \xrightarrow{1} u\) and \(v \xrightarrow{1} t\).
Central bridge: \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\).
Two length-2 bypasses: \(u \xrightarrow{1} b \xrightarrow{1} t\) (upper right) and \(s \xrightarrow{1} a \xrightarrow{1} v\) (lower left).






flowchart LR
    s(("s")) -->|"1"| u(("u"))
    s -->|"1"| a(("a"))
    u -->|"1 (bridge)"| v(("v"))
    u -->|"1"| b(("b"))
    b -->|"1"| t(("t"))
    a -->|"1"| v
    v -->|"1"| t






Let us trace Naive Greedy BFS vs. Dinic Residual Uncrossing + Flow Decomposition:

Step 1 (Both Algorithms): What are the \(s\)-\(t\) path lengths in \(G\)?

\(P_{\text{bridge}} = (s \to u \to v \to t)\) has length \(3\).
\(P_{\text{upper}} = (s \to u \to b \to t)\) has length \(3\) (or \(4\) if we subdivide \(b \to b_1 \to b_2\) so \(P_{\text{bridge}}\) is the strictly unique shortest path of length \(3\), while \(P_{\text{upper}}\) and \(P_{\text{lower}}\) have length \(4\)).
Even without subdivision, suppose BFS discovers the length-\(3\) path \(P_{\text{bridge}} = (s \to u \to v \to t)\) first.

Naive Greedy Deletion Terminates with \(1\) Path:

Greedy deletes the three edges \((s \to u)\), \((u \to v)\), and \((v \to t)\).
In the remaining graph \(G \setminus P_{\text{bridge}}\), the only edge leaving \(s\) is \(s \to a \to v\), and the only edge entering \(t\) is \(u \to b \to t\). Vertex \(v\) is a dead end (its only outgoing edge \(v \to t\) was deleted), and vertex \(u\) is unreachable from \(s\) (its only incoming edge \(s \to u\) was deleted).
Thus \(t\) is unreachable from \(s\), and Naive Greedy outputs \(1\) path instead of \(2\)!

How Residual Uncrossing + Flow Decomposition Recovers \(2\) Disjoint Paths:

After Dinic pushes \(1\) unit along \(s \to u \to v \to t\), the residual graph \(G_f\) activates the reverse residual arc \(v \xrightarrow{1} u\).
In Phase 2, Dinic finds the augmenting path
\[P_{\text{aug}} = (s \to a \to v \xrightarrow{\text{rev}} u \to b \to t).\]
Pushing \(1\) unit along \(v \to u\) cancels the flow on the central bridge \(u \to v\) (\(f(u \to v) = 1 - 1 = 0\)), leaving the active support \(\operatorname{supp}(f^*)\) as:
\[f^*(s \to u) = f^*(u \to b) = f^*(b \to t) = 1, \qquad f^*(s \to a) = f^*(a \to v) = f^*(v \to t) = 1, \qquad f^*(u \to v) = 0.\]
Running Flow Decomposition (Theorem 3.1) on \(\operatorname{supp}(f^*)\) immediately extracts the \(2\) edge-disjoint paths \(P_1 = (s \to u \to b \to t)\) and \(P_2 = (s \to a \to v \to t)\)!


Takeaway: Never strip paths greedily before finishing all augmentations. Always compute the full maximum flow \(f^*\) using residual reverse arcs first, and only run Flow Decomposition on the final support \(\operatorname{supp}(f^*)\) after Dinic terminates.

3. Vertex Capacity Splitting (\(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\)), Multi-Stage Chains, and Menger’s Four Connectivity Theorems
We now apply our 4-Step English-to-Graph Compilation framework to our first major non-arc constraint: vertex throughput and destruction capacities.

3.1 The 4-Step Compilation of Vertex Throughput (\(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_v} v_{\text{out}}\))

Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
The problem statement restricts the throughput, durability, or destruction cost of locations / entities (vertices) rather than transitions (edges):

“At most \(C_v\) paths, packets, or agents may pass through vertex \(v\).”
“Destroying vertex \(v\) costs \(w_v\); find the minimum-cost set of vertices whose removal disconnects \(s\) from \(t\).”
“Each entity \(g\) must be matched to one left resource \(a \in \mathcal{A}\) AND one right resource \(b \in \mathcal{B}\), and each \(g\) can be used at most \(C_g = 1\) time.”

Why can’t we simply place capacity \(C_v\) on all incoming edges \((u \to v)\) or all outgoing edges \((v \to w)\)? Because if \(v\) has \(\deg^-(v) = 2\) incoming edges and \(\deg^+(v) = 2\) outgoing edges, giving each incident edge capacity \(C_v = 1\) still allows \(2\) units of flow to pass through \(v\) in parallel!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
In a standard edge-capacitated flow network, Kirchhoff conservation at any internal vertex \(v \notin \{s, t\}\) states that the total throughput \(F(v)\) traversing \(v\) is equal to both its total inflow and its total outflow:
\[F(v) := \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} f(e) = \sum_{e \in \delta^+(v)} f(e).\]
A vertex capacity constraint requires that for every \(v \in V\),
\[0 \le F(v) \le C_v.\]
To enforce \(0 \le F(v) \le C_v\) using a solver that only understands arc capacities \(0 \le f(e) \le c(e)\), we must introduce a single dedicated arc \(e_v\) whose flow \(f(e_v)\) is algebraically forced by Kirchhoff’s law to equal the entire sum \(F(v) = \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} f(e)\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
How do we force every unit of flow entering \(v\) to cross a single dedicated arc \(e_v\) before leaving \(v\)? We separate the arrival event at \(v\) from the departure event from \(v\) by splitting each vertex \(v \in V\) into two half-vertices:

an in-port \(v_{\text{in}}\) that collects all incoming flow \(\delta^-(v)\), and
an out-port \(v_{\text{out}}\) that distributes all outgoing flow \(\delta^+(v)\),

connected by a single directed internal bridge arc:
\[e_v = (v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}), \qquad c(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}) = C_v.\]
Now let us check how original transitions must be wired:

The Strict \(\text{out} \to \text{in}\) Port Invariant: Every original directed edge \(e = (u \to v)\) with edge capacity \(c(u, v)\) represents a departure from \(u\) followed by an arrival at \(v\). Therefore, it must leave \(u\)’s out-port and enter \(v\)’s in-port:
\[(u \to v) \quad\longmapsto\quad \big(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{c(u, v)} v_{\text{in}}\big).\]
If original edges have no capacity limit of their own (pure vertex-cut problems), set \(c(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}) = \infty\).
Proof of Algebraic Equivalence: Because the only outgoing arc from \(v_{\text{in}}\) is the internal bridge \((v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}})\), Kirchhoff conservation at \(v_{\text{in}}\) forces:
\[f(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}) = \sum_{u : (u, v) \in E} f(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}) = F(v).\]
Similarly, because the only incoming arc to \(v_{\text{out}}\) is \((v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}})\), conservation at \(v_{\text{out}}\) forces \(\sum_{w} f(v_{\text{out}} \to w_{\text{in}}) = f(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}) = F(v)\). Thus the arc capacity \(0 \le f(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}) \le C_v\) is 100% equivalent to the vertex throughput constraint \(0 \le F(v) \le C_v\)!
Source and Sink Conventions:

If the source \(s\) and sink \(t\) cannot be destroyed / have infinite vertex capacity (\(C_s = C_t = \infty\)), we can either set \(c(s_{\text{in}} \to s_{\text{out}}) = c(t_{\text{in}} \to t_{\text{out}}) = \infty\) and route from \(s_{\text{in}}\) to \(t_{\text{out}}\), or simply route directly from \(s_{\text{out}}\) to \(t_{\text{in}}\).
If \(s\) and \(t\) do have finite vertex capacities \(C_s, C_t < \infty\), route from \(s_{\text{in}}\) to \(t_{\text{out}}\) so that all flow must cross both \(s_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_s} s_{\text{out}}\) and \(t_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_t} t_{\text{out}}\).




Exact Cut Bijection & Recovering the Minimum Vertex Cut from \(S_{\min}\)
Suppose every original edge \((u \to v)\) is compiled to \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\) and each vertex \(v \notin \{s, t\}\) has internal bridge \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_v} v_{\text{out}}\). Let \((S, \bar{S})\) be any finite-capacity \(s_{\text{out}}\)-\(t_{\text{in}}\) cut in the split network \(G_{\text{split}}\).

Because every transition arc \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\) has infinite capacity, a finite cut \((S, \bar{S})\) can never satisfy \(u_{\text{out}} \in S \land v_{\text{in}} \in \bar{S}\).
Consequently, the only arcs crossing from \(S\) to \(\bar{S}\) are internal vertex bridges \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_v} v_{\text{out}}\) where
\[v_{\text{in}} \in S \quad\text{and}\quad v_{\text{out}} \in \bar{S}.\]
Define the cut vertex set \(U(S) := \{v \in V \setminus \{s, t\} : v_{\text{in}} \in S \text{ and } v_{\text{out}} \in \bar{S}\}\). Along any original \(s\)-\(t\) path \(s = v_0 \to v_1 \to \dots \to v_k = t\), we have \((v_0)_{\text{out}} = s_{\text{out}} \in S\) and \((v_k)_{\text{in}} = t_{\text{in}} \in \bar{S}\). Since no transition arc \((v_i)_{\text{out}} \to (v_{i+1})_{\text{in}}\) can cross from \(S\) to \(\bar{S}\) (otherwise the cut capacity would be \(\infty\)), there must be at least one index \(i \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}\) where \((v_i)_{\text{in}} \in S\) and \((v_i)_{\text{out}} \in \bar{S}\), meaning \(v_i \in U(S)\)!

Conversely, any vertex cut \(U \subseteq V \setminus \{s, t\}\) induces a valid finite cut \((S_U, \bar{S}_U)\) of capacity \(\sum_{v \in U} C_v\) by placing in \(S_U\) all half-vertices reachable from \(s_{\text{out}}\) after deleting \(\{v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}} : v \in U\}\).






TipRecovering the Canonical Source-Minimal Vertex Cut



After running Dinic from \(s_{\text{out}}\) to \(t_{\text{in}}\), let \(S_{\min}\) be the set of half-vertices reachable from \(s_{\text{out}}\) in the final residual graph \(G_{f^*}\). Then the canonical source-minimal minimum vertex cut is:
\[U_{\min} = \big\{v \in V \setminus \{s, t\} \;\big|\; v_{\text{in}} \in S_{\min} \;\land\; v_{\text{out}} \notin S_{\min}\big\}.\]





3.2 Step 4: Broken-Gadget Counterexample FM-04 — The Undirected Vertex-Split Bypass Trap
What happens when the underlying graph \(G = (V, E)\) is undirected and vertices have capacities \(C_v\)?
In Section 5.2 of Wave 1A (and Chapter 1), we saw that on an edge-capacitated undirected graph, an undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) of capacity \(C\) can be represented by a single compact pair of half-edges (2k, 2k+1) between \(u\) and \(v\) with \(\text{cap}[2k] = \text{cap}[2k+1] = C\).
When vertices are split into \((u_{\text{in}}, u_{\text{out}})\) and \((v_{\text{in}}, v_{\text{out}})\), one of the deadliest bugs in competitive programming is trying to connect \(u\) and \(v\) with a single undirected pair (such as \(u_{\text{in}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{in}}\), \(u_{\text{out}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{out}}\), or \(u_{\text{out}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{in}}\))!






CautionBroken-Gadget Counterexample FM-04 — Why Undirected Edges on Split Vertices Require TWO Directed Arcs (\(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}\) AND \(v_{\text{out}} \to u_{\text{in}}\))



Consider a 4-vertex undirected path \(s - u - v - t\) where internal vertices \(u\) and \(v\) each have vertex capacity \(C_u = C_v = 1\), and edges have capacity \(\infty\). Obviously, at most \(1\) unit of flow can travel from \(s\) to \(t\).
Now watch how three common mis-wirings of the undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) catastrophically fail:

Bug A (Connecting in-ports: \(u_{\text{in}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{in}}\) with cap \(\infty\)): Flow travels \(s_{\text{out}} \to u_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}} \to t_{\text{in}}\). Notice that flow arrived at \(u_{\text{in}}\) and immediately jumped to \(v_{\text{in}}\) without ever crossing the internal bridge \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} u_{\text{out}}\)! Vertex \(u\)’s capacity constraint is completely bypassed (\(C_u\) might as well be \(\infty\)).
Bug B (Using a bidirectional undirected edge between \(u_{\text{out}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}}\): \(u_{\text{out}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{in}}\) with cap \(\infty\) in both directions): Suppose we also have edges \(s - v\) and \(u - t\), and we wire \(\{u, v\}\) as an undirected edge \(u_{\text{out}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{in}}\) (so both \(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}\) have initial capacity \(\infty\)). Then flow can travel:
\[s_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{via } v_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}} u_{\text{out}} \to t_{\text{in}}!\]
This path carries \(\infty\) flow from \(s\) to \(t\) while bypassing BOTH \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\) AND \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} u_{\text{out}}\), yielding MaxFlow \(= \infty\) when the true answer is \(2\)!

        v_in1["v_in"] -->|"C_v = 1"| v_out1["v_out"]
        u_out1 -->|"cap = inf"| v_in1
        v_out1 -->|"cap = inf"| u_in1
    end
    subgraph BugB["FM-04 Bug: Undirected u_out <-> v_in"]

        v_in2["v_in"] -->|"C_v = 1"| v_out2["v_out"]
        u_out2 <-->|"BOTH dirs inf (BYPASS!)"| v_in2
    end






The Ironclad Rule for Undirected Edges on Split Vertices: Every undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) of capacity \(c_{uv}\) on a vertex-split graph must be compiled into two independent directed arcs (4 half-edges total in your adjacency list):

Forward transition \(u \to v\): add_edge(u_out, v_in, c_uv) (whose reverse residual arc v_in -> u_out starts with capacity \(0\), so it can only cancel previously committed flow from u_out to v_in).
Backward transition \(v \to u\): add_edge(v_out, u_in, c_uv) (whose reverse residual arc u_in -> v_out starts with capacity \(0\)).

Never violate the \(\text{out} \to \text{in}\) port invariant: every physical transition arc in \(G_{\text{split}}\) must originate at an out-port and terminate at an in-port.




3.3 Menger’s Four Connectivity Theorems (1927) & The \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) Unit-Vertex Regime
By combining the Integrality Theorem, the Flow Decomposition Theorem (Theorem 3.1), and Vertex Capacity Splitting (§3.1), Ford–Fulkerson duality immediately yields all four classical connectivity theorems proved by Karl Menger in 1927:






ImportantTheorem 3.2 (Menger’s Four Connectivity Theorems — Menger, 1927)



Let \(G = (V, E)\) be a directed or undirected graph and let \(s, t \in V\) be two distinct vertices.

Directed Edge-Connectivity (\(\lambda_{\text{dir}}(s, t)\)): The maximum number of arc-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum number of directed arcs whose removal destroys all directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths.
Undirected Edge-Connectivity (\(\lambda_{\text{undir}}(s, t)\)): The maximum number of edge-disjoint undirected \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum number of undirected edges whose removal disconnects \(s\) and \(t\).
Directed Vertex-Connectivity (\(\kappa_{\text{dir}}(s, t)\), assuming \((s \to t) \notin E\)): The maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum number of vertices in \(V \setminus \{s, t\}\) whose removal destroys all directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths.
Undirected Vertex-Connectivity (\(\kappa_{\text{undir}}(s, t)\), assuming \(\{s, t\} \notin E\)): The maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint undirected \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum number of vertices in \(V \setminus \{s, t\}\) whose removal disconnects \(s\) and \(t\).




Mechanical Graph Compilation and Asymptotic Complexity Table

3. Directed Vertex-Disjoint (\((s \to t) \notin E\))
Split \(v \notin \{s, t\}\) into \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\); compile \((u \to v)\) to \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\) (or cap \(1\)). Route \(s_{\text{out}} \to t_{\text{in}}\).
\(\deg^+(v_{\text{in}}) = 1\) and \(\deg^-(v_{\text{out}}) = 1\)!
\(O(E \sqrt{V})\)


4. Undirected Vertex-Disjoint (\(\{s, t\} \notin E\))
Split \(v \notin \{s, t\}\) into \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\); compile \(\{u, v\}\) to two directed arcs \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\) and \(v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}\). Route \(s_{\text{out}} \to t_{\text{in}}\).
\(\deg^+(v_{\text{in}}) = 1\) and \(\deg^-(v_{\text{out}}) = 1\)!
\(O(E \sqrt{V})\)



Why do Variants 3 and 4 run in \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) rather than \(O(E V^{2/3})\)? Because after splitting every internal vertex \(v\) into \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\), every single vertex \(x\) in \(G_{\text{split}} \setminus \{s_{\text{out}}, t_{\text{in}}\}\) satisfies \(\min(\deg^-(x), \deg^+(x)) = 1\):

\(v_{\text{in}}\) has out-degree \(1\) (only \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\)), and
\(v_{\text{out}}\) has in-degree \(1\) (only \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\)).

Thus \(G_{\text{split}}\) is a unit vertex network, and by Even and Tarjan’s theorem (Chapter 1, §1.3), Dinic terminates in at most \(2\sqrt{V}\) blocking-flow phases and \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) total time!



3.4 Multi-Stage Chains: Compiling Three-Way Coupling (\(A \to V_{\text{in}} \to V_{\text{out}} \to B\))
In bipartite matching, an edge \((a, b) \in \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{B}\) couples two types of entities. What if each agent \(v \in \mathcal{V}\) must simultaneously consume one resource \(a \in \mathcal{A}_v\) from Stage 1 AND one resource \(b \in \mathcal{B}_v\) from Stage 2?
Examples include:

[Luogu P1402] 酒店之王 (#017): Guest \(g\) needs \(1\) liked Room \(r \in \mathcal{R}_g\) and \(1\) liked Dish \(d \in \mathcal{D}_g\).
[USACO07OPEN / Luogu P2891] Dining: Cow \(i\) needs \(1\) liked Food \(f \in \mathcal{F}_i\) and \(1\) liked Drink \(d \in \mathcal{D}_i\).

Why can’t we put the agents on the left (\(S \to g\)) and connect \(g \to r \to T\) and \(g \to d \to T\) in parallel? Because then a guest could send \(1\) unit of flow to a room and \(0\) units to a dish (or \(2\) units to rooms and \(0\) to dishes)! To force a logical AND (1 Room AND 1 Dish per unit of flow), the Room and the Dish must lie in series along the same \(s\)-\(t\) path, with the Guest \(g\) placed in the middle as the bridge between them:
\[S \xrightarrow{1} r \xrightarrow{1} g_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} g_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} d \xrightarrow{1} T.\]

Because \(r\) and \(d\) are in series, every unit of \(s\)-\(t\) flow simultaneously saturates one room \(r\), one guest \(g\), and one dish \(d\).
Because \(g\) is split into \(g_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} g_{\text{out}}\), no single guest can absorb two room-dish pairs!
