section: 4. Time-Expanded Layered Networks (分层图) & Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层)
text:
4. Time-Expanded Layered Networks (分层图) & Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层)

4.1 The 4-Step Compilation of Discrete Time Horizons

Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Agents move across a physical graph \(G = (V, E)\) over discrete time steps \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots, T\):

Traversing an edge \(e = (u \to v)\) takes \(\tau_e \ge 1\) seconds and admits at most \(c_e\) agents per step.
Agents can wait (hold inventory) at vertex \(v\) from time \(t\) to \(t+1\) (up to capacity \(h_v\), typically \(\infty\)).
The available edges or their endpoints may vary with \(t\) (e.g., periodic shuttles moving between space stations in [CTSC1999] 家园).
We want either the maximum number of agents delivered by a fixed deadline \(T\), or the minimum time \(T^*\) required to deliver \(K\) agents.



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Because flow conservation in a static graph has no memory of when flow arrived at \(v\), we must promote time \(t \in \{0, 1, \dots, T\}\) into the vertex index itself. Let \(f_{\text{hold}}(v, t)\) denote the number of agents waiting at location \(v\) across the interval \([t, t+1]\), and let \(f_{\text{trans}}(e, t)\) denote the number of agents departing along transition \(e = (u \to v)\) at time \(t\) (arriving at \(v\) at time \(t + \tau_e\)).
At every spacetime coordinate \((v, t) \in V \times \{0, 1, \dots, T\}\), spacetime Kirchhoff conservation requires:
\[\underbrace{f_{\text{hold}}(v, t-1)}_{\text{waited at } v} + \sum_{e=(u \to v)} \underbrace{f_{\text{trans}}(e, t - \tau_e)}_{\text{arrived at } v \text{ at time } t} = \underbrace{f_{\text{hold}}(v, t)}_{\text{stays at } v} + \sum_{e=(v \to w)} \underbrace{f_{\text{trans}}(e, t)}_{\text{departs } v \text{ at time } t}.\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
This spacetime balance equation compiles directly into a Time-Expanded Layered DAG (分层图) \(G_T = (V_T, E_T)\):

Spacetime Vertices: For each location \(v \in V\) and each discrete timestamp \(t \in \{0, 1, \dots, T\}\), create a state vertex \((v, t)\). Add a super-source \(S\) and super-sink \(T_{\text{sink}}\).
Initial Supply (\(t = 0\)): If \(a_v\) agents start at location \(v\) at \(t = 0\), add arc \(S \xrightarrow{a_v} (v, 0)\).
Holdover / Waiting Arcs (滞留边): For each \(v \in V\) and \(0 \le t < T\), add a directed arc representing agents waiting at \(v\) from time \(t\) to \(t+1\):
\[(v, t) \xrightarrow{h_v} (v, t+1) \qquad (\text{usually } h_v = \infty).\]
Transit Arcs (转移边): Whenever a road or shuttle allows up to \(c_e\) agents to depart \(u\) at time \(t\) and arrive at \(v\) at time \(t + \tau_e \le T\), add:
\[(u, t) \xrightarrow{c_e} (v, t + \tau_e).\]
Destination Sink Collection: If \(v_{\text{dest}}\) is the target location, connect \((v_{\text{dest}}, t) \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{sink}}\) for every \(t \in \{0, 1, \dots, T\}\) (or simply connect \((v_{\text{dest}}, T) \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{sink}}\) if holdover arcs at \(v_{\text{dest}}\) have capacity \(\infty\)).






flowchart LR
    subgraph Layer0["Time t = 0"]
        u0["(u, 0)"]
        v0["(v, 0)"]
    end
    subgraph Layer1["Time t = 1"]
        u1["(u, 1)"]
        v1["(v, 1)"]
    end
    subgraph Layer2["Time t = 2"]
        u2["(u, 2)"]
        v2["(v, 2)"]
    end
    S(("S")) -->|"K"| u0
    u0 -->|"hold (inf)"| u1
    v0 -->|"hold (inf)"| v1
    u1 -->|"hold (inf)"| u2
    v1 -->|"hold (inf)"| v2
    u0 -->|"transit c_e"| v1
    v1 -->|"transit c_e"| u2
    v1 -->|"inf"| Tsink(("T_sink"))
    v2 -->|"inf"| Tsink












WarningStep 4: Broken-Gadget Guard — Omitting Holdover Arcs (FM-03)



If you forget to add the holdover arcs \((u, t) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, t+1)\), an agent arriving at station \(u\) at time \(t = 1\) is forced to immediately board an outgoing shuttle at \(t = 1\) or vanish! Whenever agents are allowed to wait at vertices for later connections, holdover arcs \((u, t) \to (u, t+1)\) are mandatory. Furthermore, if vertices also have a simultaneous occupancy limit at time \(t\), split \((u, t)\) into \((u, t)_{\text{in}} \to (u, t)_{\text{out}}\).





4.2 Incremental Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层) vs. Binary Search on \(T\)
Suppose a problem asks for the minimum time \(T^*\) needed to route \(K\) agents from \(s\) to \(t\) (as in [CTSC1999] 家园 / 星际转移问题, #020).
A naive approach binary searches \(T \in [1, T_{\max}]\) and rebuilds the entire \(T\)-layer graph from scratch at each midpoint, costing \(O(\log T_{\max})\) full Dinic executions.
Instead, notice that adding layer \(t\) to \(G_{t-1}\) only appends new vertices \(V \times \{t\}\) and new forward arcs from layer \(t-1\) to layer \(t\) (and from \((v_{\text{dest}}, t)\) to \(T_{\text{sink}}\)). Every flow pushed in \(G_{t-1}\) remains a valid feasible flow in \(G_t\)!






TipAlgorithmic Invariant — Incremental Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层)



Maintain a single persistent residual network \(G_f\) and a running scalar total_flow = 0:

Pre-Check Reachability: Before unrolling time, use Disjoint Set Union (DSU) or BFS on the static union of all transitions to verify that \(v_{\text{dest}}\) is reachable from \(v_{\text{start}}\). If not, immediately return Impossible (preventing an infinite loop!).
Incremental Unrolling (\(t = 1, 2, 3, \dots\)):

Allocate new vertex IDs for \((u, t)\) (\(u \in V\)).
Add holdover arcs \((u, t-1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, t)\), transit arcs \((u, t-1) \xrightarrow{c_e} (v, t)\), and sink collection \((v_{\text{dest}}, t) \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{sink}}\) directly into the existing adjacency list of \(G_f\).
Execute total_flow += dinic(S, T_sink) on the existing residual graph \(G_f\).
Stop at the first timestamp \(t = T^*\) where total_flow >= K.


Because previous flow is preserved in \(G_f\) and reverse residual arcs in layers \(0 \dots t-1\) allow Dinic to seamlessly reroute earlier trajectories to exploit newly opened shuttles at time \(t\), the total work across all layers \(t = 1 \dots T^*\) is roughly a single Dinic run on \(G_{T^*}\)!

section: 5. DP-Subgraph Layering (Luogu P2766 LIS) & Hub Sparsification (ARC 074 D)
text:
5. DP-Subgraph Layering (Luogu P2766 LIS) & Hub Sparsification (ARC 074 D)

5.1 Packing Disjoint Optimal Trajectories on Shortest-Path & DP DAGs
Many problems ask: “How many mutually disjoint optimal paths (or optimal subsequences) can be packed simultaneously?”

Shortest-Path DAG Extraction ([CQOI2015] 网络吞吐量, #024): Suppose packets from \(1\) to \(N\) may only travel along shortest paths with respect to edge weights \(w_e > 0\), while vertices have throughput capacities \(C_v\).

First, run Dijkstra from vertex \(1\) to compute shortest-path distances \(d[1 \dots N]\).
An edge \((u \to v)\) of weight \(w_{uv}\) belongs to at least one shortest path from \(1\) if and only if it is tight:
\[d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v].\]
Because \(w_{uv} > 0\), the subgraph \(E_{\text{DAG}} = \{(u \to v) : d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v]\}\) is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)! Combining \(E_{\text{DAG}}\) with vertex splitting \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_v} v_{\text{out}}\) immediately compiles the problem into standard Max-Flow.

DP Layering ([Luogu P2766] 最长不下降子序列问题, #021): Given an array \(x_1, \dots, x_n\), let \(dp[i]\) be the length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence (LNDS) ending at index \(i\), and let \(s = \max_{1 \le i \le n} dp[i]\) be the global LNDS length. We want the maximum number of index-disjoint non-decreasing subsequences of length \(s\).

Notice that \(dp[i] \in \{1, 2, \dots, s\}\) naturally partitions the indices \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) into \(s\) sequential DP layers!
A pair \((i, j)\) can serve as consecutive elements of a valid LNDS if and only if:
\[i < j, \qquad x_i \le x_j, \qquad \text{and} \qquad dp[j] = dp[i] + 1.\]
Every directed path from a layer-\(1\) vertex (\(dp[i] = 1\)) to a layer-\(s\) vertex (\(dp[i] = s\)) along these admissible transitions has length exactly \(s\) and forms a valid LNDS of maximum length!
Splitting each index \(i\) into \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{out}}\) and wiring \(S \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{in}}\) (for \(dp[i]=1\)), \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} j_{\text{in}}\) (for admissible transitions), and \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} T\) (for \(dp[i]=s\)) reduces disjoint LNDS packing to unit-vertex-network Max-Flow in \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) time!




5.2 Row/Column Hub Sparsification ([AtCoder ARC 074 D] Lotus Leaves)
Suppose a frog on an \(H \times W\) pond (\(H, W \le 100\)) can jump between any two lotus leaves in the same row or the same column. Destroying a lotus leaf at \((r, c)\) costs \(1\), except for the start leaf \(S\) and target leaf \(T\), which cannot be destroyed. Find the minimum number of leaves to remove to disconnect \(S\) from \(T\).

Why Naive Vertex Splitting Is Too Dense—and How Hub Vertices Collapse the Graph
If we split every lotus leaf \((r, c)\) into \((r, c)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} (r, c)_{\text{out}}\) and add directed edges between all pairs of leaves in the same row or column, each row of length \(W\) induces a directed clique of \(W(W-1)\) edges, creating \(\Theta(H W (H + W))\) edges (\(\approx 2 \times 10^6\) edges).
We can sparsify this by introducing auxiliary Hub Vertices (中介点 / 行列虚点):

Step 1 (Introduce Row and Column Hubs): Create \(H\) Row Hubs \(R_1, \dots, R_H\) and \(W\) Column Hubs \(C_1, \dots, C_W\). Since rows and columns are abstract geometric lines that cannot themselves be destroyed, their vertex capacity is \(\infty\).
Step 2 (Route Leaves Through Hubs): Instead of connecting leaf \((r, c)\) directly to all other leaves in row \(r\) and column \(c\), connect \((r, c)\) to its Row Hub \(R_r\) and Column Hub \(C_c\):
\[(r, c)_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} R_r \xrightarrow{\infty} (r, c)_{\text{in}}, \qquad (r, c)_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} C_c \xrightarrow{\infty} (r, c)_{\text{in}}.\]
Now any jump from \((r, c_1)\) to \((r, c_2)\) simply travels \((r, c_1)_{\text{out}} \to R_r \to (r, c_2)_{\text{in}}\) in two hops! The edge count drops from \(\Theta(HW(H+W))\) to \(4HW\).
Step 3 (The Ultimate Bipartite Collapse — Eliminating Cell Vertices Entirely!): Look closely at a lotus leaf \((r, c)\) in the hub graph. Why would a frog ever visit \((r, c)\)? Only to switch from Row \(r\) to Column \(c\), or from Column \(c\) to Row \(r\)! (Jumping from Row \(r\) to \((r, c)\) and back to Row \(r\) is redundant since the frog was already at \(R_r\)). Therefore, each destroyable leaf \((r, c)\) is nothing more than an undirected bridge of capacity \(1\) between Row Hub \(R_r\) and Column Hub \(C_c\):
\[R_r \xleftrightarrow{\text{cap } = 1} C_c!\]

For the start leaf \((r_S, c_S)\), connect \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} R_{r_S}\) and \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} C_{c_S}\).
For the target leaf \((r_T, c_T)\), connect \(R_{r_T} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\) and \(C_{c_T} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\).
For every other leaf \((r, c)\), add an undirected edge of capacity \(1\) between \(R_r\) and \(C_c\).

        Rr1(("R_r")) -->|"inf"| cin["(r,c)_in"]
        Cc1(("C_c")) -->|"inf"| cin
        cin -->|"cap = 1"| cout["(r,c)_out"]
        cout -->|"inf"| Rr1
        cout -->|"inf"| Cc1
    end
    subgraph Collapsed["Step 3: Direct Bipartite Bridge (1 undirected edge/cell!)"]
        Rr2(("R_r")) <-->|"cap = 1 (leaf (r,c))"| Cc2(("C_c"))
    end






This algebraic simplification collapses a \(2HW\)-vertex, \(HW(H+W)\)-edge vertex-cut network into a \(200\)-vertex, \(10^4\)-edge unit-capacity bipartite graph, solving [ARC 074 D] in under \(1\) millisecond in \(O(H W \sqrt{H + W})\) time!

6. Curated 4-Tier Practice Ladder (#017–#024)
The eight problems below progress systematically from 3-stage node splitting (#017) and heterogeneous grid cell capacities (#018–#019) to incremental time-expanded layered DAGs (#020), 3-subtask LIS DP-layering (#021), BFS horizon compaction (#022), perimeter Cut-DP elimination (#023), and shortest-path DAG router bottlenecks (#024).

3-Stage Chain \(S \to \text{Room} \to \text{Guest}_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} \text{Guest}_{\text{out}} \to \text{Dish} \to T\)
Unit Vertex Network: \(O\big((NP + NQ)\sqrt{N+P+Q}\big)\)

[UVa 11380] Down Went The Titanic ([EN])
Grid Vertex Splitting \((r,c)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_{r,c}} (r,c)_{\text{out}}\) with \(C_{r,c} \in \{1, \infty\}\)
Unit-Dominated Grid: \(O\big((XY)^{3/2}\big)\)

#019
[SCOI2007 / Luogu P2472] 蜥蜴 (Lizards) ([ZH])
Euclidean Jump Graph + Pillar Durability Split \((r,c)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{h_{r,c}} (r,c)_{\text{out}}\)
Small Integer Cap (\(h \le 3\)): \(O\big((RC)^{3/2} d^2\big)\)


I2
#020
[CTSC1999 / Luogu P2754] 家园 / 星际转移问题 ([ZH])
Periodic Shuttle Time-Expanded DAG + Incremental Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层)
Incremental Residual: \(O\big(T^* (N+M) \sqrt{T^* N}\big)\)

#021
[Luogu P2766] 最长不下降子序列问题 (LNDS) ([ZH])
3-Subtask LIS DP-Layering (\(dp[j] = dp[i]+1\)) + Endpoint \(\infty\)-Multiplicity
Incremental Unit / Cap Update: \(O\big(n^2 \sqrt{n}\big)\)


A2
#022
[CF 78E] Evacuation ([EN])
Reactor Multi-Source BFS + Scientist Time-Bounded Escape BFS \(\implies\) Bipartite Flow
Compacted Bipartite Network: \(O(N^4)\)


M1
#023
[CF 1368H1] Breadboard Capacity (Easy) ([EN])
\(N \times M = 10^{10}\) Grid Perimeter Port Routing \(\implies\) Monochromatic Line Cut-DP
Dual- eliminated Cut-DP: \(O(N + M)\)


M2
#024
[CQOI2015 / Luogu P3171] 网络吞吐量 ([ZH])
Dijkstra Shortest-Path DAG (\(d[u]+w_{uv}=d[v]\)) + Router Split \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c_u} u_{\text{out}}\)
General Capacities (int64_t): \(O(M \log N + N^2 M)\)





#017 [Stepping Stone 1] — [Luogu P1402] 酒店之王 (King of the Hotel)

Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P1402 ([ZH], practically identical to [USACO07OPEN / Luogu P2891] Dining [EN])
Constraints: \(N \le 100\) guests, \(P \le 100\) rooms, \(Q \le 100\) dishes. Time Limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: A hotel has \(N\) guests, \(P\) rooms, and \(Q\) signature dishes. Each room can accommodate at most \(1\) guest, and each dish can be served to at most \(1\) guest. You are given two boolean preference matrices: \(A_{i, r} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicating whether guest \(i\) likes room \(r\), and \(B_{i, d} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicating whether guest \(i\) likes dish \(d\). A guest is satisfied if and only if they receive both one room they like and one dish they like. Compute the maximum number of guests that can be simultaneously satisfied.







NoteHint 1 — Why Parallel Matching Fails and Why Rooms & Dishes Must Be in Series





Suppose we connect \(S \xrightarrow{2} \text{Guest}_i\), and from \(\text{Guest}_i\) we add edges to liked rooms \(r \to T\) and liked dishes \(d \to T\). Why does this fail? Because a guest could push \(2\) units of flow into two rooms and \(0\) dishes! To force \(1\) room AND \(1\) dish per unit of flow, every \(s\)-\(t\) path must traverse a room first and a dish second, with the guest acting as the intermediate bridge between them:
\[S \to \text{Room}_r \to \text{Guest}_i \to \text{Dish}_d \to T.\]









NoteHint 2 — The Unsplit Central Entity Bug





If you place a single unsplit vertex \(\text{Guest}_i\) between \(\text{Room}_r\) and \(\text{Dish}_d\) with all edge capacities equal to \(1\), what happens when Guest \(1\) likes two rooms \(\{r_1, r_2\}\) and two dishes \(\{d_1, d_2\}\)? Two units of flow can pass through \(\text{Guest}_1\) simultaneously (\(S \to r_1 \to g_1 \to d_1 \to T\) and \(S \to r_2 \to g_1 \to d_2 \to T\)), counting Guest \(1\) twice! How do you cap the total throughput of \(\text{Guest}_i\) at \(1\)?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [Luogu P1402] 酒店之王






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
We have a three-way matching \((\text{Room } r, \text{Guest } i, \text{Dish } d)\) with \(N, P, Q \le 100\). Unlike general 3D Matching (which is NP-hard when preferences are arbitrary triples \((r, i, d)\)), here the preference factors independently into \((r, i)\) and \((i, d)\) with Guest \(i\) as the central hinge. Greedy matching of rooms first can assign a room to a guest who has no available dish left, while residual augmentation can reassign rooms and dishes simultaneously.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(x_{r, i} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether room \(r\) is assigned to guest \(i\) (allowed only if \(A_{i, r} = 1\)), and \(y_{i, d} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether dish \(d\) is assigned to guest \(i\) (allowed only if \(B_{i, d} = 1\)). Let \(F_i \in \{0, 1\}\) be the indicator that guest \(i\) is satisfied. The constraints are:
\[\sum_{i=1}^N x_{r, i} \le 1 \quad (\forall r), \qquad \sum_{i=1}^N y_{i, d} \le 1 \quad (\forall d),\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^P x_{r, i} = F_i = \sum_{d=1}^Q y_{i, d}, \qquad 0 \le F_i \le 1 \quad (\forall i).\]
Notice that \(\sum_r x_{r,i} = F_i = \sum_d y_{i,d}\) is literally Kirchhoff flow conservation at Guest \(i\), and \(0 \le F_i \le 1\) is a vertex throughput capacity of \(1\) on Guest \(i\)!


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
We construct a 4-layer unit-capacity network with \(|V| = 2 + P + 2N + Q\) vertices:

Stage 1 (Rooms): For each room \(r \in \{1, \dots, P\}\), add \(S \xrightarrow{1} r\) (enforcing \(\sum_i x_{r,i} \le 1\)).
Stage 2 (Split Guests): Split each guest \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) into \(i_{\text{in}}\) and \(i_{\text{out}}\) connected by internal bridge \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{out}}\) (enforcing \(F_i \le 1\)).
Room-to-Guest Transitions: For each \((i, r)\) with \(A_{i, r} = 1\), add \(r \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{in}}\).
Guest-to-Dish Transitions: For each \((i, d)\) with \(B_{i, d} = 1\), add \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} d\).
Stage 3 (Dishes): For each dish \(d \in \{1, \dots, Q\}\), add \(d \xrightarrow{1} T\) (enforcing \(\sum_i y_{i,d} \le 1\)).



Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(N = 1\) guest, \(P = 2\) rooms \(\{r_1, r_2\}\), \(Q = 2\) dishes \(\{d_1, d_2\}\), and Guest \(1\) likes everything (\(A_{1,1}=A_{1,2}=B_{1,1}=B_{1,2}=1\)).

With \(1_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 1_{\text{out}}\): Both \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) send capacity \(1\) into \(1_{\text{in}}\), but the bridge \(1_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 1_{\text{out}}\) bottlenecks the total flow to \(1\) (correct).
Without splitting (Failure Guard): Flow \(S \to r_1 \to 1 \to d_1 \to T\) (\(1\) unit) and \(S \to r_2 \to 1 \to d_2 \to T\) (\(1\) unit) both pass, giving \(2\) satisfied guests when only \(1\) guest exists!

Solver Contract: \(|V| = P + 2N + Q + 2 \le 402\), \(|E| = P + Q + N + NP + NQ \le 20300\). Every internal vertex has either in-degree \(1\) or out-degree \(1\) with unit capacities, so Dinic runs in \(O(E \sqrt{V}) \approx 4 \times 10^5\) operations.







#018 [Stepping Stone 2] — [UVa 11380] Down Went The Titanic

Judge URL: https://onlinejudge.org/external/113/11380.pdf ([EN])
Constraints: Grid dimensions \(X, Y \le 30\), lifeboat capacity \(P \le 1000\). Time Limit: \(3.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: After the Titanic strikes an iceberg, survivors are scattered on an \(X \times Y\) grid with 5 cell types:

~ (Water): Cold and impassable; no one can enter.
. (Floating Ice): Thin ice that vanishes after \(1\) person steps off it.
* (Person on Floating Ice): Contains \(1\) survivor initially, resting on thin . ice (so the cell itself also vanishes as soon as that survivor steps off it; no other survivor may pass through it!).
@ (Large Iceberg): Thick ice; infinitely many people may step on and off it.
# (Lifeboat): Thick ice (infinite pass-through capacity), and up to \(P\) people can permanently board the lifeboat at this cell to be rescued. People move 4-directionally (N, S, E, W). Compute the maximum number of survivors who can reach a lifeboat.








NoteHint 1 — Classifying Cell Durability as Vertex Capacities





Every cell \((r, c)\) restricts how many times people can pass through it—a pure vertex capacity \(C_{r, c}\):

~: \(C_{r, c} = 0\) (skip).
. and *: \(C_{r, c} = 1\) (thin ice collapses after 1 person leaves).
@ and #: \(C_{r, c} = \infty\) (never collapses).










NoteHint 2 — Where Should \(S\) Connect for a * Cell: \((r, c)_{\text{in}}\) or \((r, c)_{\text{out}}\)?





A survivor starting at a * cell is standing on thin ice of capacity \(1\). If you connect \(S \xrightarrow{1} (r, c)_{\text{out}}\), then the starting survivor bypasses the internal bridge \((r, c)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} (r, c)_{\text{out}}\), allowing a second survivor from an adjacent cell to enter \((r, c)_{\text{in}}\), cross the bridge, and also use the * cell! Which port must \(S\) connect to so that the starting survivor immediately consumes the * cell’s capacity \(1\)?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [UVa 11380] Down Went The Titanic






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Survivors move along grid paths to # cells, constrained by cell collapse limits (\(1\) for . and *, \(\infty\) for @ and #) and lifeboat boarding limits (\(P\) per # cell). Because multiple survivors’ paths compete for shared thin-ice cells and lifeboats, and \(X, Y \le 30\) (\(XY \le 900\)), this is a vertex-capacitated multi-source multi-sink max-flow problem.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For each non-water cell \(u = (r, c)\), let \(F(u)\) be the total number of survivors who ever occupy and depart (or get rescued at) cell \(u\). Then:
\[F(u) = \mathbb{I}[u \text{ is } \text{'*'}] + \sum_{v \in N_4(u)} f(v \to u) = \text{rescued}(u) + \sum_{w \in N_4(u)} f(u \to w),\]
subject to the vertex durability constraint:
\[0 \le F(u) \le C_u, \qquad C_u = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } grid[u] \in \{\text{'.'}, \text{'*'}\}, \\ \infty & \text{if } grid[u] \in \{\text{'@'}, \text{'\#'}\}, \end{cases}\]
and the lifeboat boarding constraint \(0 \le \text{rescued}(u) \le P\) if \(grid[u] = \text{'\#'}\) (and \(0\) otherwise).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
Split every non-water cell \(u = (r, c)\) into \(u_{\text{in}}\) and \(u_{\text{out}}\):

Internal Cell Durability Bridge: Add \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_u} u_{\text{out}}\) where \(C_u = 1\) for . and *, and \(C_u = \infty\) for @ and #.
Initial Survivors (*): If \(grid[u] = \text{'*'}\), add \(S \xrightarrow{1} u_{\text{in}}\). (By entering \(u_{\text{in}}\), the survivor starting at \(u\) immediately saturates \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} u_{\text{out}}\), blocking any other survivor from stepping onto \(u\)!)
Lifeboat Boarding (#): If \(grid[u] = \text{'\#'}\), add \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{P} T\). (Note that because \(C_u = \infty\) for #, any number of survivors can walk through a # cell to reach other cells, while at most \(P\) can exit to \(T\) at this lifeboat.)
4-Directional Grid Transitions: For every pair of 4-adjacent non-water cells \((u, v)\), add two directed arcs \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\) and \(v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}\).



Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Consider a \(1 \times 3\) row * * # with \(P = 2\):

Cell \(1\) (*) has \(S \xrightarrow{1} 1_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 1_{\text{out}}\).
Cell \(2\) (*) has \(S \xrightarrow{1} 2_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 2_{\text{out}}\).
Because \(2_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 2_{\text{out}}\) has capacity \(1\) and is already saturated by Survivor \(2\), Survivor \(1\) at \(1_{\text{out}} \to 2_{\text{in}}\) cannot pass through Cell \(2\)! Total rescued \(= 1\).
Failure Guard: If we had wired \(S \xrightarrow{1} 2_{\text{out}}\) instead of \(2_{\text{in}}\), Survivor \(2\) would leave from \(2_{\text{out}} \to 3_{\text{in}}\) while Survivor \(1\) simultaneously traversed \(1_{\text{out}} \to 2_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 2_{\text{out}} \to 3_{\text{in}}\), falsely rescuing \(2\) people across a thin-ice cell that can only support \(1\)!

Solver Contract: \(|V| \le 2XY + 2 \le 1802\), \(|E| \le 6XY \le 5400\). Dinic runs in \(O((XY)^{3/2}) \approx 8 \times 10^4\) operations per testcase.







#019 [Intermediate 1] — [SCOI2007 / Luogu P2472] 蜥蜴 (Lizards)

Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2472 ([ZH])
Constraints: Grid \(R, C \le 20\), jump distance \(d \le 4\), pillar heights \(h_{r, c} \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}\). Time Limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: In an \(R \times C\) maze, each cell \((r, c)\) (\(1 \le r \le R, 1 \le c \le C\)) has a stone pillar of height \(h_{r, c} \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}\) (\(0\) means no pillar). Some pillars initially have a single lizard standing on them. In one jump, a lizard can leap to any pillar (or outside the boundary of the \(R \times C\) grid) whose Euclidean distance from its current cell is at most \(d\). Every time a lizard jumps off a pillar \((r, c)\), that pillar’s height decreases by \(1\); once \(h_{r, c} = 0\), the pillar collapses and no lizard can land on it anymore. At most one lizard may stand on any remaining pillar at a time (though pillars only block lizards when they collapse to height \(0\)). Find the minimum number of lizards that cannot escape outside the grid.







NoteHint 1 — Complement Objective & Pillar Durability





Let \(L_{\text{total}}\) be the initial number of lizards. Then:
\[\min(\text{trapped lizards}) = L_{\text{total}} - \max(\text{escaped lizards}).\]
Since a pillar at \((r, c)\) loses \(1\) unit of height each time a lizard jumps off it, at most \(h_{r, c}\) lizards can ever pass through (land on and jump off) cell \((r, c)\). How do we model this?









NoteHint 2 — Boundary Escape Condition vs. Pillar-to-Pillar Euclidean Distance






When can a lizard on pillar \((r, c)\) (\(1 \le r \le R, 1 \le c \le C\)) jump directly outside the grid in a single leap of length \(\le d\)? Whenever \((r, c)\) is within distance \(d\) of Row \(0\), Row \(R+1\), Col \(0\), or Col \(C+1\):
\[r \le d \quad\lor\quad R + 1 - r \le d \quad\lor\quad c \le d \quad\lor\quad C + 1 - c \le d.\]
When can a lizard jump from \((r_1, c_1)\) to another pillar \((r_2, c_2)\)? Whenever \((r_1 - r_2)^2 + (c_1 - c_2)^2 \le d^2\) (Euclidean distance, not Manhattan distance!).










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [SCOI2007 / Luogu P2472] 蜥蜴






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Each pillar \((r, c)\) has a finite jump-off durability \(h_{r, c} \in \{1, 2, 3\}\), and \(R, C \le 20\) (\(RC \le 400\)). Because pillars only restrict how many total jumps can originate from \((r, c)\), the order in which lizards move does not matter: any set of path-flows satisfying the vertex throughput bounds \(F(r, c) \le h_{r, c}\) can be scheduled sequentially without collisions.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For every pillar \(u = (r, c)\) with \(h_u > 0\), let \(F(u)\) be the total number of lizards that jump off \(u\):
\[F(u) = \mathbb{I}[\text{lizard starts at } u] + \sum_{v : \|v - u\|_2 \le d} f(v \to u) = f(u \to T) + \sum_{w : \|u - w\|_2 \le d} f(u \to w),\]
subject to \(0 \le F(u) \le h_u\). We want to maximize \(|f| = \sum_u f(u \to T)\) and output \(L_{\text{total}} - |f^*|\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
Create source \(S\), sink \(T\), and for each cell \(u = (r, c)\) with \(h_{r, c} > 0\), split \(u\) into \(u_{\text{in}}\) and \(u_{\text{out}}\):

Pillar Durability Bridge: Add \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{h_{r, c}} u_{\text{out}}\).
Initial Lizards: If a lizard starts at \(u = (r, c)\), add \(S \xrightarrow{1} u_{\text{in}}\) and increment \(L_{\text{total}}\).
Boundary Escape Arcs: If \(\min(r, R + 1 - r, c, C + 1 - c) \le d\), the lizard can leap off the grid in one jump: add \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\).
Pillar-to-Pillar Jump Arcs: For every ordered pair of distinct pillars \(u = (r_1, c_1)\) and \(v = (r_2, c_2)\) with \(h_u > 0, h_v > 0\), and \((r_1 - r_2)^2 + (c_1 - c_2)^2 \le d^2\), add \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\).



Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(R = 1, C = 3, d = 1\), heights are 1 2 1, and lizards start at \((1, 1)\) and \((1, 2)\). Since \(R = 1\) and \(d = 1\), every cell has \(r = 1 \le d\), so every pillar can jump directly outside to \(T\) ((1,1) jumps north to row \(0\), (1,2) jumps north to row \(0\)). Both lizards escape immediately (\(L_{\text{total}} - |f^*| = 2 - 2 = 0\)).

Failure Guard 1 (Manhattan vs. Euclidean Distance): When \(d = 2\), a diagonal jump of \((\Delta r, \Delta c) = (1, 1)\) has Manhattan distance \(2 \le 2\) AND Euclidean distance \(\sqrt{2} \le 2\), whereas \((\Delta r, \Delta c) = (2, 1)\) has Euclidean distance \(\sqrt{5} > 2\). Always check dr * dr + dc * dc <= d * d!
Failure Guard 2 (Connecting \(S \to u_{\text{out}}\)): Just as in #018, a lizard starting on \(u\) uses up \(1\) unit of \(u\)’s height when it jumps off \(u\). Thus \(S\) must connect to \(u_{\text{in}}\), not \(u_{\text{out}}\).

Solver Contract: \(|V| \le 2RC + 2 \le 802\), \(|E| \le RC(2 + \pi d^2) \approx 2 \times 10^4\), max flow \(\le RC = 400\). Dinic terminates in \(< 5\text{ ms}\).







#020 [Intermediate 2] — [CTSC1999 / Luogu P2754] 家园 / 星际转移问题 (网络流 24 题 #16)

Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2754 ([ZH])
Constraints: \(N \le 13\) space stations, \(M \le 20\) periodic space shuttles, \(K \le 50\) people. Time Limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: There are \(N\) space stations numbered \(1 \dots N\), plus Earth (numbered \(0\)) and the Moon (numbered \(-1\), which we remap to \(N + 1\)). There are \(M\) space shuttles. Shuttle \(i\) has passenger capacity \(H_i\) and cyclically visits a sequence of \(r_i\) stations \((S_{i, 0}, S_{i, 1}, \dots, S_{i, r_i - 1})\):

At time \(t = 0\), shuttle \(i\) is at \(S_{i, 0}\).
In general, at time \(t \ge 0\), shuttle \(i\) is at station \(\operatorname{pos}_i(t) := S_{i, \, t \bmod r_i}\), and travels from \(\operatorname{pos}_i(t - 1)\) to \(\operatorname{pos}_i(t)\) during the interval \([t - 1, t]\) (taking \(1\) unit of time).
Stations can hold infinitely many waiting passengers across time steps. At each integer timestamp \(t\), shuttles at the same station can exchange passengers instantaneously. Initially at \(t = 0\), all \(K\) people are on Earth (\(0\)). Find the minimum time \(T^*\) at which all \(K\) people can reach the Moon (\(N + 1\)), or output 0 if it is impossible.








NoteHint 1 — Why You Must Check Reachability Before Unrolling Time





What if Earth (\(0\)) and the Moon (\(N + 1\)) belong to completely disconnected components of shuttle routes? If you dynamically add layers \(t = 1, 2, 3, \dots\) until total_flow >= K, an unreachable instance will loop forever! How can you check in \(O(M \cdot \max r_i)\) time whether all \(K\) people can eventually reach the Moon?









NoteHint 2 — Incremental Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层)





Once reachability is verified with a DSU (unioning all stations on each shuttle’s cyclic route), do not binary search on \(T\). Instead, maintain a single Dinic residual graph \(G_f\):

At \(t = 0\), connect \(S \xrightarrow{K} (0, 0)\) and \((N+1, 0) \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{sink}}\).
In a loop \(t = 1, 2, 3, \dots\), allocate layer-\(t\) vertices \((u, t)\) for \(u \in \{0, \dots, N+1\}\), add holdover arcs \((u, t-1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, t)\), add shuttle transit arcs \((\operatorname{pos}_i(t-1), t-1) \xrightarrow{H_i} (\operatorname{pos}_i(t), t)\) for \(i = 1 \dots M\), connect \((N+1, t) \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{sink}}\), and call flow += dinic(S, T_sink) on the existing residual network!










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [CTSC1999 / Luogu P2754] 家园






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Shuttles move deterministically as a function of \(t \bmod r_i\), passengers can wait at stations across time steps, and we seek the earliest timestamp \(T^*\) where cumulative arrivals at the Moon reach \(K \le 50\). This is the canonical archetype for a Time-Expanded Layered DAG (分层图) with Incremental Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层) (§4.1–4.2).


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(V = \{0, 1, \dots, N, N+1\}\) where \(0\) is Earth and \(N+1\) is the Moon. For each station \(u \in V\) and timestamp \(t \ge 0\):

Let \(f_{\text{hold}}(u, t-1 \to t) \in [0, \infty)\) be the number of passengers waiting at station \(u\) from \(t - 1\) to \(t\).
Let \(f_{\text{shuttle}}(i, t-1 \to t) \in [0, H_i]\) be the number of passengers aboard shuttle \(i\) during \([t - 1, t]\), moving from \(u_i(t-1) = S_{i, (t-1)\bmod r_i}\) to \(v_i(t) = S_{i, t \bmod r_i}\).

Spacetime conservation at \((u, t)\) requires:
\[f_{\text{hold}}(u, t-1 \to t) + \sum_{i : v_i(t) = u} f_{\text{shuttle}}(i, t-1 \to t) = f_{\text{hold}}(u, t \to t+1) + \sum_{j : u_j(t) = u} f_{\text{shuttle}}(j, t \to t+1).\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Step 0 (DSU Reachability Guard): Initialize a DSU over \(\{0, 1, \dots, N+1\}\). For each shuttle \(i\) and each \(j \in \{0, \dots, r_i - 1\}\), union \(S_{i, j}\) with \(S_{i, (j+1) \bmod r_i}\). If find(0) != find(N + 1), output 0 and terminate immediately.
Base Layer (\(t = 0\)): Define vertex ID encoding id(u, t) = 2 + t * (N + 2) + u (reserving 0 for \(S\) and 1 for \(T_{\text{sink}}\)). Add:

\(S \xrightarrow{K} \operatorname{id}(0, 0)\) (all \(K\) people start on Earth at \(t = 0\); or simply \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} \operatorname{id}(0, 0)\) and check when total_flow >= K).
\(\operatorname{id}(N + 1, 0) \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{sink}}\).

Incremental Layer Loop (\(t = 1, 2, 3, \dots\)):

Station Holdover Arcs: For every \(u \in \{0, \dots, N\}\), add \(\operatorname{id}(u, t - 1) \xrightarrow{\infty} \operatorname{id}(u, t)\).
Shuttle Transit Arcs: For each shuttle \(i \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), let \(u = S_{i, (t-1) \bmod r_i}\) and \(v = S_{i, t \bmod r_i}\). Add \(\operatorname{id}(u, t - 1) \xrightarrow{H_i} \operatorname{id}(v, t)\).
Moon Collection Arc: Add \(\operatorname{id}(N + 1, t) \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{sink}}\).
Incremental Augmentation: Run total_flow += dinic(S, T_sink) on the current residual network without resetting previous flows. If total_flow >= K, return \(t\)!




Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(N = 1\) station, \(K = 2\) people, Shuttle \(1\) (\(H_1 = 1\)) cycles \((0 \leftrightarrow 1)\) with period \(2\), and Shuttle \(2\) (\(H_2 = 1\)) cycles \((1 \leftrightarrow 2)\) (where \(2\) is the Moon) with period \(2\), starting at \(S_{2,0} = 2, S_{2,1} = 1\):

\(t = 1\): Shuttle \(1\) moves \(0 \to 1\) (\(1\) person reaches Station \(1\)); Shuttle \(2\) moves \(2 \to 1\) (empty). Moon flow \(= 0\).
\(t = 2\): Shuttle \(1\) moves \(1 \to 0\); Shuttle \(2\) moves \(1 \to 2\) (\(1\) person reaches Moon!). Moon flow \(= 1 < 2\).
\(t = 3\): Person \(2\) (who waited on Earth via holdover arcs \((0,0) \to (0,1) \to (0,2)\)!) takes Shuttle \(1\) from \(0 \to 1\) at \(t=3\), and Shuttle \(2\) from \(1 \to 2\) at \(t=4\). Total time \(T^* = 4\).
Failure Guard: If you omit holdover arcs \((u, t-1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, t)\), Person \(2\) cannot wait on Earth from \(t=0\) to \(t=2\), and the flow gets stuck at \(1\)!

Solver Contract: On Luogu testdata, \(T^* \le 100\) whenever reachable, so \(|V_{T^*}| \le 1500\) and incremental Dinic finishes in \(< 3\text{ ms}\).







#021 [Advanced 1] — [Luogu P2766] 最长不下降子序列问题 (网络流 24 题 #06)

Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2766 ([ZH])
Constraints: Sequence length \(n \le 500\). Time Limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: Given an integer sequence \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\):

Compute the length \(s\) of its longest non-decreasing subsequence (LNDS).
Compute the maximum number of non-decreasing subsequences of length \(s\) that can be extracted simultaneously if each index \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) may be used at most once.
Compute the maximum number of non-decreasing subsequences of length \(s\) if indices \(1\) and \(n\) (\(x_1\) and \(x_n\)) may be used infinitely many times (while every other index \(i \in \{2, \dots, n-1\}\) is still used at most once, and all extracted subsequences use distinct index tuples).








NoteHint 1 — Layering the Sequence by DP Value \(dp[i]\)





First compute \(dp[i] = 1 + \max(\{0\} \cup \{dp[k] : 1 \le k < i, x_k \le x_i\})\) in \(O(n^2)\) time, and let \(s = \max_{1 \le i \le n} dp[i]\).
When can index \(i\) be immediately followed by index \(j\) in a valid LNDS of length \(s\)? If and only if:
\[i < j, \qquad x_i \le x_j, \qquad \text{and} \qquad dp[j] = dp[i] + 1!\]
Why does restricting edges to \(dp[j] = dp[i] + 1\) guarantee that every path from \(\{i : dp[i] = 1\}\) to \(\{i : dp[i] = s\}\) has length exactly \(s\)?









NoteHint 2 — Incremental Update for Subtask 3 & The Deadly \(s = 1\) Corner Case





For Subtask 2, split every index \(i\) into \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{out}}\), connect \(S \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{in}}\) if \(dp[i] = 1\), connect \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} T\) if \(dp[i] = s\), and connect \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} j_{\text{in}}\) if \(i < j, x_i \le x_j, dp[j] = dp[i] + 1\).
For Subtask 3, we allow index \(1\) and index \(n\) to be used \(\infty\) times. Which 4 arcs need their capacity upgraded to \(\infty\)? And what goes catastrophically wrong when \(s = 1\) if you upgrade \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} 1_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} 1_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\)?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [Luogu P2766] 最长不下降子序列问题






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Subtask 1 is standard \(O(n^2)\) DP. Subtasks 2 and 3 ask for the maximum number of vertex-disjoint paths across the \(s\) layers of the DP transition DAG! Why does greedy LNDS extraction fail? Because just like the 6-Vertex Diamond-Bridge counterexample (§2.3), greedily deleting one LNDS can sever two other disjoint LNDSs that residual uncrossing would decouple.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(dp[i] \in \{1, \dots, s\}\) be the longest non-decreasing subsequence ending at index \(i\), and define the admissible transition set:
\[\mathcal{E}_{\text{DP}} = \big\{(i \to j) \;\big|\; 1 \le i < j \le n,\;\; x_i \le x_j,\;\; dp[j] = dp[i] + 1\big\}.\]
Every directed path \(i_1 \to i_2 \to \dots \to i_s\) in \(\mathcal{E}_{\text{DP}}\) starting at \(dp[i_1] = 1\) and ending at \(dp[i_s] = s\) steps strictly from layer \(k\) to layer \(k+1\), so it automatically contains \(s\) indices and satisfies \(x_{i_1} \le x_{i_2} \le \dots \le x_{i_s}\).
Let \(F(i)\) be the number of chosen subsequences passing through index \(i\). In Subtask 2, \(0 \le F(i) \le 1\) for all \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\). In Subtask 3, \(F(1), F(n) \in [0, \infty)\) while \(F(i) \le 1\) for \(2 \le i \le n - 1\), and each transition \((i \to j) \in \mathcal{E}_{\text{DP}}\) still has capacity \(1\) (since \(i\) and \(j\) cannot both be in \(\{1, n\}\) unless \(s = 2\), and even then the subsequence \((1, n)\) can only be chosen once if distinct index tuples are required, or we keep transition capacities at \(1\)).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Corner Case Guard (\(s = 1\)): If \(s = 1\) (the sequence is strictly decreasing), every single element \((x_i)\) is already an LNDS of length \(1\). Even if \(x_1\) and \(x_n\) can be reused, a subsequence of length \(1\) is uniquely determined by its single index (or in Luogu’s testdata convention for \(s = 1\), both Subtask 2 and Subtask 3 output \(n\)). Always check if (s == 1) { print(1, n, n); return; } first!
Subtask 2 Network (\(s \ge 2\)):

Split each \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) into \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{out}}\).
If \(dp[i] = 1\), add \(S \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{in}}\).
If \(dp[i] = s\), add \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} T\).
For all \(1 \le i < j \le n\) with \(x_i \le x_j\) and \(dp[j] = dp[i] + 1\), add \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} j_{\text{in}}\).
Run ans2 = dinic(S, T).

Subtask 3 Incremental Upgrade (\(s \ge 2\)): Without rebuilding the graph, append capacity \(\infty\) to the existing residual network on:

\(1_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} 1_{\text{out}}\), and if \(dp[1] = 1\), \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} 1_{\text{in}}\).
\(n_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} n_{\text{out}}\), and if \(dp[n] = s\), \(n_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\).
(Note: Keep all transition arcs \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} j_{\text{in}}\) at capacity \(1\)!)
Run ans3 = ans2 + dinic(S, T) on the updated residual network!




Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Consider \(n = 4\) and \(X = [3, 6, 2, 5]\):

\(dp = [1, 2, 1, 2]\), so \(s = 2\).
Layer \(1\) (\(dp = 1\)): indices \(\{1, 3\}\). Layer \(2\) (\(dp = 2\)): indices \(\{2, 4\}\).
Admissible transitions (\(i < j, x_i \le x_j, dp[j] = dp[i]+1\)):

From \(i = 1\) (\(x_1 = 3\)): \((1 \to 2)\) (\(3 \le 6\)) and \((1 \to 4)\) (\(3 \le 5\)).
From \(i = 3\) (\(x_3 = 2\)): \((3 \to 4)\) (\(2 \le 5\)).

Subtask 2: Both \((1 \to 2)\) and \((3 \to 4)\) are disjoint! ans2 = 2.
Subtask 3: Index \(1\) and Index \(4\) get \(\infty\) capacity on \((S \to 1_{\text{in}} \to 1_{\text{out}})\) and \((4_{\text{in}} \to 4_{\text{out}} \to T)\). Now the unused transition \(1_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{1} 4_{\text{in}}\) unlocks a third subsequence \((x_1, x_4) = (3, 5)\)! ans3 = 3.
Failure Guard: When \(s = 1\) (e.g., \(X = [5, 4, 3]\)), \(dp[1] = 1 = s\), so Index \(1\) connects both to \(S\) and to \(T\). Upgrading \(S \to 1_{\text{in}} \to 1_{\text{out}} \to T\) to \(\infty\) creates an \(\infty\)-capacity path from \(S\) to \(T\), outputting INF instead of \(n\)! That is why guarding s == 1 upfront is mandatory.

Solver Contract: \(|V| = 2n + 2 \le 1002\), \(|E| \le n^2 / 2 + 3n \le 1.3 \times 10^5\). Unit-vertex network runs in \(O(n^2 \sqrt{n}) \approx 2.5 \times 10^6\) operations.







#022 [Advanced 2] — [CF 78E] Evacuation

Judge URL: https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/78/E ([EN])
Constraints: Grid size \(N \times N\) with \(N \le 10\), evacuation time limit \(T \le 60\). Time Limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: On an \(N \times N\) laboratory grid, some cells are impassable walls (Y), exactly one cell is a malfunctioning nuclear reactor (Z), and the remaining cells contain \(A_{r, c} \in \{0, \dots, 9\}\) scientists initially and \(B_{r, c} \in \{0, \dots, 9\}\) rescue capsules.

At \(t = 0\), the reactor at Z explodes. Every \(1\) second, radiation spreads 4-directionally to all adjacent non-wall cells.
Scientists also move 4-directionally at up to \(1\) cell per second (any number of scientists may occupy or pass through the same corridor cell simultaneously).
A scientist cannot step onto a cell \((r, c)\) at time \(t\) if radiation reached \((r, c)\) at time \(< t\).
Crucial Boundary Rule: If a scientist reaches cell \((r, c)\) at the exact second \(t = \operatorname{rad}(r, c)\) when radiation hits \((r, c)\) (with \(t \le T\)), the scientist can immediately board an available rescue capsule at \((r, c)\) and survive, but cannot walk out of \((r, c)\) at time \(t + 1\)! Compute the maximum number of scientists who can board rescue capsules within \(T\) seconds.








NoteHint 1 — Why We Don’t Need a \(60 \times 100\) Time-Expanded Flow Network





Notice that corridor cells have infinite walking capacity—scientists never block one another while walking! Only the starting scientist counts \(A_{r_1, c_1}\) and the final rescue capsule capacities \(B_{r_2, c_2}\) are finite. What does this imply about the time-expanded DAG between starting cells and capsule cells?









NoteHint 2 — Precomputing Safe Reachability via Two BFS Passes






First, run a BFS from the reactor Z to compute \(\operatorname{rad}(r, c)\), the earliest time radiation hits \((r, c)\).
Second, from each starting cell \(u = (r_1, c_1)\), run a BFS to find all capsule cells \(v = (r_2, c_2)\) that a scientist starting at \(u\) can reach by time \(\le T\).
When expanding the scientist BFS from \(x\) at time \(d\) to a neighbor \(y\) at time \(d + 1 \le T\):

If \(d + 1 < \operatorname{rad}(y)\), the scientist can both board a capsule at \(y\) and continue walking from \(y\) (push \(y\) into the BFS queue).
If \(d + 1 == \operatorname{rad}(y)\), the scientist can board a capsule at \(y\), but must NOT push \(y\) into the BFS queue!











TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [CF 78E] Evacuation






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
At first glance, radiation spreading over \(T \le 60\) steps on an \(N \times N\) grid looks like a time-expanded DAG with \(T N^2 \le 6000\) vertices. However, because intermediate corridor transitions have \(\infty\) capacity, a group of scientists at \(u\) can reach a capsule at \(v\) before the deadline if and only if there exists at least one safe spacetime walk from \((u, 0)\) to \((v, t)\) with \(t \le \min(T, \operatorname{rad}(v))\). Thus the entire time horizon collapses via BFS precomputation into a tiny 2-layer Bipartite Flow Network!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(\operatorname{rad}(v) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \cup \{\infty\}\) be the shortest-path distance from the reactor Z to cell \(v\) avoiding walls Y. For each cell \(u\), let \(\operatorname{Reach}(u)\) be the set of cells \(v\) reachable by a walk \(u = w_0 \to w_1 \to \dots \to w_k = v\) of length \(k \le T\) such that:
\[t < \operatorname{rad}(w_t) \quad \forall t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k - 1\}, \qquad \text{and} \qquad k \le \operatorname{rad}(w_k).\]
Once \(\operatorname{Reach}(u)\) is known, let \(f(u \to v) \ge 0\) be the number of scientists starting at \(u\) who evacuate in capsules at \(v \in \operatorname{Reach}(u)\), subject to \(\sum_v f(u \to v) \le A_u\) and \(\sum_u f(u \to v) \le B_v\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Pass 1 (Reactor BFS): Run BFS from Z (with rad[Z] = 0, walls impassable) to compute \(\operatorname{rad}(v)\) for all cells \(v\).
Pass 2 (Scientist Safe-Horizon BFS from each \(u\)): For each cell \(u\) with \(A_u > 0\) and \(\operatorname{rad}(u) > 0\):

Initialize dist[u] = 0, can_board[u] = true, and push \(u\) into a queue \(Q\).
While \(Q\) is non-empty, pop \(x\). If dist[x] == T, continue.
For each 4-neighbor \(y\) of \(x\) (not a wall):

Let \(nt = \operatorname{dist}[x] + 1\).
If \(nt \le \operatorname{rad}(y)\), mark can_board[y] = true (a scientist from \(u\) can reach and board a capsule at \(y\) at time \(nt\)).
If \(nt < \operatorname{rad}(y)\) and \(y\) has not been pushed to \(Q\) yet, set \(\operatorname{dist}[y] = nt\) and push \(y\) into \(Q\).


Pass 3 (Bipartite Max-Flow):

Create left vertices \(u_{\text{sci}}\) for all cells \(u\) with \(A_u > 0\): add \(S \xrightarrow{A_u} u_{\text{sci}}\).
Create right vertices \(v_{\text{cap}}\) for all cells \(v\) with \(B_v > 0\): add \(v_{\text{cap}} \xrightarrow{B_v} T_{\text{sink}}\).
Whenever can_board[v] == true from source \(u\), add \(u_{\text{sci}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{cap}}\).
Output dinic(S, T_sink).




Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose u -- x -- v where \(u\) has \(1\) scientist, \(v\) has \(1\) capsule, and \(\operatorname{rad}(x) = 1, \operatorname{rad}(v) = 2\):

At \(t = 1\), the scientist reaches \(x\) at the exact moment \(1 = \operatorname{rad}(x)\).
Can the scientist board a capsule at \(x\)? Yes (nt <= rad[x]).
Can the scientist continue walking from \(x\) to \(v\) at \(t = 2\)? No (nt < rad[x] is false, because \(x\) is already flooded with radiation at \(t = 1\)!).
Failure Guard: If you push \(y\) into the BFS queue whenever nt <= rad[y] instead of strictly nt < rad[y], scientists will illegally walk through irradiated cells! Conversely, if you only record can_board[y] = true when nt < rad[y], you miss capsules boarded at the exact second \(t = \operatorname{rad}(y)\).

Solver Contract: BFS takes \(O(N^4) \le 10^4\) operations; the bipartite flow network has \(|V| \le 202, |E| \le 10^4\), solving in \(< 2\text{ ms}\).







#023 [Mastery 1] — [CF 1368H1] Breadboard Capacity (Easy Version)

Judge URL: https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1368/H1 ([EN])
Constraints: Grid dimensions \(N, M \le 10^5\) (\(N \times M \le 10^{10}\) internal nodes!). Time Limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: A breadboard is an \(N \times M\) undirected grid of internal junctions \((r, c)\) (\(1 \le r \le N, 1 \le c \le M\)), where adjacent internal junctions are connected by unit-capacity undirected wires. Along the four outer boundaries of the grid sit \(2(N + M)\) ports:

\(N\) ports on the Left (L[1..N]), each wired with capacity \(1\) to \((r, 1)\);
\(N\) ports on the Right (R[1..N]), each wired with capacity \(1\) to \((r, M)\);
\(M\) ports on the Top (U[1..M]), each wired with capacity \(1\) to \((1, c)\);
\(M\) ports on the Bottom (D[1..M]), each wired with capacity \(1\) to \((N, c)\). Each of the \(2(N + M)\) boundary ports is colored either Red (R) or Blue (B). Each wire (internal or port-to-grid) has capacity \(1\), and internal junctions have infinite vertex capacity (only wires are unit-capacitated). Compute the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths connecting Red ports to Blue ports.








NoteHint 1 — From \(10^{10}\)-Vertex Max-Flow to Planar Grid Min-Cut





With \(N \times M = 10^{10}\) vertices, running Dinic on the grid is impossible. Switch immediately to Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality: every \(S\)-\(T\) cut assigns each internal grid cell \((r, c)\) a color \(x_{r, c} \in \{\text{Red}, \text{Blue}\}\), and pays \(1\) for every wire (internal horizontal, internal vertical, or boundary port wire) whose two endpoints have different colors!









NoteHint 2 — Structural Geometry Lemma: Why an Optimal Grid Cut Is Either Row-Monochromatic or Column-Monochromatic





Suppose a cut colors the \(N \times M\) grid so that neither does any monochromatic horizontal stripe span all the way across, nor do all rows/columns stay monochromatic.
Consider any connected component \(C\) of Red cells. If \(C\) does not touch all four sides, smoothing its boundary into straight horizontal or vertical lines across the entire grid never increases the internal perimeter length! Specifically, one can prove that there always exists a minimum cut on the \(N \times M\) grid where either:

Every row \(r \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) is monochromatic (all \(M\) cells in row \(r\) have the same color \(c_r \in \{\text{R}, \text{B}\}\)), OR
Every column \(c \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) is monochromatic (all \(N\) cells in column \(c\) have the same color \(d_c \in \{\text{R}, \text{B}\}\))!










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [CF 1368H1] Breadboard Capacity






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
The problem asks for the maximum edge-disjoint routing between Red (\(S\)) and Blue (\(T\)) boundary ports on an \(N \times M\) grid with \(N, M \le 10^5\). This is our first glimpse of Cut-DP Elimination (explored systematically in Part IV): when a flow network is a highly regular geometric grid of size \(10^{10}\), we dualize Max-Flow to Min-Cut and optimize the cut partition \((S, T)\) directly via Dynamic Programming!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(x_{r, c} \in \{0, 1\}\) denote the cut side of cell \((r, c)\) (\(0 = \text{Red}, 1 = \text{Blue}\)). The capacity of the cut \(x\) is:
\[\operatorname{Cut}(x) = \sum_{r=1}^N \sum_{c=1}^{M-1} |x_{r,c} - x_{r,c+1}| + \sum_{r=1}^{N-1} \sum_{c=1}^M |x_{r,c} - x_{r+1,c}| + \text{BoundaryMismatch}(x).\]
Geometric Rectification Theorem: Suppose row \(r\) is not monochromatic, so \(\sum_{c=1}^{M-1} |x_{r,c} - x_{r,c+1}| \ge 1\). Each non-monochromatic row pays at least \(1\) internal horizontal cut edge, plus at most \(2\) boundary mismatches (L[r] and R[r]) can be saved by making row \(r\) bichromatic instead of monochromatic—and only when L[r] != R[r], where a monochromatic row also pays \(1\) boundary mismatch! By submodular cut uncrossing and boundary projection, any minimum cut can be rectified without increasing its cost so that either all rows are monochromatic (\(x_{r, 1} = \dots = x_{r, M} = c_r\)) OR all columns are monochromatic (\(x_{1, c} = \dots = x_{N, c} = d_c\)).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Two 1D Sweeping DPs)

Case 1: Row-Monochromatic Cut (\(x_{r, c} = c_r \in \{0, 1\}\) for all \(c\)):

Within row \(r\), horizontal internal wires cost \(0\).
Left and right ports of row \(r\) cost \([L_r \neq c_r] + [R_r \neq c_r]\).
At row \(1\), top ports cost \(\sum_{c=1}^M [U_c \neq c_1]\). At row \(N\), bottom ports cost \(\sum_{c=1}^M [D_c \neq c_N]\).
Between row \(r-1\) and row \(r\), all \(M\) vertical wires are cut if \(c_r \neq c_{r-1}\) (cost \(M\)), or \(0\) if \(c_r = c_{r-1}\).
Define dp_row[r][col] for \(r = 1 \dots N, \text{col} \in \{0, 1\}\):
\[\text{dp\_row}[1][\text{col}] = \sum_{c=1}^M [U_c \neq \text{col}] + [L_1 \neq \text{col}] + [R_1 \neq \text{col}],\]
\[\text{dp\_row}[r][\text{col}] = [L_r \neq \text{col}] + [R_r \neq \text{col}] + \min\big(\text{dp\_row}[r-1][\text{col}],\;\; \text{dp\_row}[r-1][1 - \text{col}] + M\big),\]
and add \(\sum_{c=1}^M [D_c \neq \text{col}]\) at \(r = N\).

Case 2: Column-Monochromatic Cut (\(x_{r, c} = d_c \in \{0, 1\}\) for all \(r\)): By exact \(90^\circ\) symmetry (swapping \(N \leftrightarrow M\), \((L, R) \leftrightarrow (U, D)\)), run the identical 2-state DP dp_col[c][col] across columns \(c = 1 \dots M\) with transition penalty \(N\).
Final Answer: \(\min(\text{ans}_{\text{row}}, \text{ans}_{\text{col}})\).



Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(N = 2, M = 3\), all U ports are Red (R), all D ports are Blue (B), and all L, R ports are Red (R).

If we assign Row \(1\) all Red (\(c_1 = \text{R}\)) and Row \(2\) all Blue (\(c_2 = \text{B}\)):

Row \(1\) pays \(0\) (U, L[1], R[1] are all Red).
Transition \(c_1 \neq c_2\) cuts \(M = 3\) vertical internal wires.
Row \(2\) pays \(2\) (L[2] and R[2] are Red vs. \(c_2 = \text{B}\), while D is all Blue). Total cost \(= 3 + 2 = 5\).

If instead we make the entire grid Red (\(c_1 = c_2 = \text{R}\)), we only cut the \(3\) bottom D port wires! Total cost \(= 3\). Both states are explored automatically by dp_row.
Failure Guard: Only running dp_row and forgetting dp_col fails whenever \(N \ll M\) and the optimal cut runs vertically across \(N\) wires instead of horizontally across \(M\) wires! Always take \(\min(\text{ans}_{\text{row}}, \text{ans}_{\text{col}})\).

Solver Contract: Two linear passes of length \(N\) and \(M\) run in \(O(N + M)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space (\(< 10\text{ ms}\) for \(N, M = 10^5\)).







#024 [Mastery 2] — [CQOI2015 / Luogu P3171] 网络吞吐量 (Network Throughput)

Judge URL: https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3171 ([ZH])
Constraints: \(N \le 500\) routers, \(M \le 10^5\) undirected bidirectional links, link distances \(w_e \in [1, 10^9]\), router capacities \(c_u \in [1, 10^9]\). Time Limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Problem Statement: A communication network consists of \(N\) routers and \(M\) undirected fiber links. Each link \(\{u, v\}\) has a propagation delay \(w_{uv} > 0\) (and infinite bandwidth). By routing protocol rules, all data packets traveling from the source router \(1\) to the destination router \(N\) must follow shortest paths with respect to total propagation delay. However, each router \(u \in \{2, \dots, N - 1\}\) has a finite CPU forwarding capacity \(c_u\) (routers \(1\) and \(N\) have infinite CPU capacity). Compute the maximum total throughput that can be routed from \(1\) to \(N\).







NoteHint 1 — Extracting the Directed Shortest-Path DAG from an Undirected Graph





Run Dijkstra’s algorithm starting from vertex \(1\) to compute the shortest-path delay \(d[u]\) for every \(u \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).
Given an undirected link \(\{u, v\}\) of delay \(w_{uv} > 0\), when can packets travel along \(\{u, v\}\) in the direction \(u \to v\) as part of a shortest path from \(1\) to \(N\)? Whenever:
\[d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v]!\]
And because \(w_{uv} > 0\), can both \(d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v]\) and \(d[v] + w_{uv} = d[u]\) hold simultaneously? No! So orienting all tight edges produces a strict Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).









NoteHint 2 — Combining Shortest-Path DAG Orientation with Router Vertex Splitting





Once you identify all directed tight transitions \((u \to v)\) satisfying \(d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v]\), how do you enforce the CPU forwarding limit \(c_u\) on each intermediate router \(u \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}\)? And what integer type must you use when \(c_u \le 10^9\)?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — [CQOI2015 / Luogu P3171] 网络吞吐量






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
The problem combines two independent structural constraints:

Routing Policy Constraint: Packets only traverse shortest paths from \(1\) to \(N\) (with respect to delays \(w_e\)).
Hardware Bottleneck Constraint: Intermediate routers \(u \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}\) have vertex throughput capacities \(c_u \le 10^9\).

As established in §5.1, a shortest-path restriction on an undirected weighted graph compiles via Dijkstra’s tightness condition \(d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v]\) into a directed DAG, and router CPU limits compile via vertex splitting \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c_u} u_{\text{out}}\).


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(d: V \to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) be the unique shortest-path distance vector from vertex \(1\):
\[d[1] = 0, \qquad d[v] = \min_{\{u, v\} \in E} (d[u] + w_{uv}).\]
Define the directed Shortest-Path Admissibility Set:
\[E_{\text{SP}} = \big\{(u \to v) \;\big|\; \{u, v\} \in E \;\land\; d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v]\big\}.\]
Any directed path from \(1\) to \(N\) using only arcs in \(E_{\text{SP}}\) has total length \(\sum_{(u \to v) \in P} w_{uv} = \sum_{(u \to v) \in P} (d[v] - d[u]) = d[N] - d[1] = d[N]\), which is a shortest \(1\)-\(N\) path! Conversely, any shortest \(1\)-\(N\) path uses only arcs in \(E_{\text{SP}}\). Thus we seek a maximum \(1\)-\(N\) flow supported on \(E_{\text{SP}}\) subject to vertex throughput \(F(u) \le c_u\) for \(u \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Phase 1 (Dijkstra from Vertex \(1\)): Compute d[1..N] in \(O((N + M) \log N)\) time using int64_t distances.
Phase 2 (Vertex Splitting): Split each router \(u \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) into \(u_{\text{in}} = u\) and \(u_{\text{out}} = u + N\):

For \(u \in \{1, N\}\), add \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}\).
For \(u \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}\), add \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c_u} u_{\text{out}}\).

Phase 3 (Wiring Tight Shortest-Path Arcs): For each original undirected link \(\{u, v\}\) with delay \(w\):

If \(d[u] + w == d[v]\), add directed arc \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\).
If \(d[v] + w == d[u]\), add directed arc \(v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}\).

Phase 4 (Max-Flow): Run Dinic from \(S = 1_{\text{in}}\) (or \(1_{\text{out}}\)) to \(T = N_{\text{out}}\) (or \(N_{\text{in}}\)) using 64-bit integer capacities (long long / int64_t, with \(\infty = 10^{18}\)).



Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(N = 4\), links are \(\{1, 2\}\) (\(w=2\)), \(\{2, 4\}\) (\(w=2\)), \(\{1, 3\}\) (\(w=1\)), \(\{3, 2\}\) (\(w=1\)), \(\{3, 4\}\) (\(w=5\)), and router capacities are \(c_2 = 10, c_3 = 4\):

Dijkstra distances from \(1\): \(d[1] = 0\), \(d[3] = 1\), \(d[2] = 2\) (via both \(1 \to 2\) and \(1 \to 3 \to 2\)!), \(d[4] = 4\) (via \(2 \to 4\); note \(3 \to 4\) has \(d[3] + 5 = 6 > 4\), so \(3 \to 4\) is not tight!).
Tight DAG arcs: \(1_{\text{out}} \to 2_{\text{in}}\), \(1_{\text{out}} \to 3_{\text{in}}\), \(3_{\text{out}} \to 2_{\text{in}}\), and \(2_{\text{out}} \to 4_{\text{in}}\).
Notice that even though \(1 \to 2\) and \(1 \to 3 \to 2\) can together supply \(10 + 4 = 14\) units into \(2_{\text{in}}\), router \(2\)’s internal bridge \(2_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{10} 2_{\text{out}}\) caps total throughput at \(10\).
Failure Guard (int32_t Overflow): Because \(c_u \le 10^9\) and up to \(N = 500\) routers can contribute in parallel, the maximum flow and \(\infty\) constants exceed \(2^{31} - 1\). Using int instead of long long overflows immediately!

Solver Contract: \(|V| = 2N \le 1000\), \(|E| \le N + M \le 10^5\). Because \(E_{\text{SP}}\) is a sparse DAG, Dinic terminates in \(< 20\text{ ms}\).

text:
7. Chapter 3 Verification Checklist & Failure Mode Summary
Before submitting any problem involving path extraction, vertex capacities, multi-stage chains, or time-expanded DAGs, run through the following diagnostic checklist:









Failure Mode ID
Anti-Pattern / Bug
Root Cause
Ironclad Fix




FM-01
Greedy Shortest-Path Stripping Before Full Augmentation
Deleting a shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path from \(G\) without reverse residual arcs strands crossing paths (6-Vertex Diamond-Bridge, §2.3).
Run Dinic to completion first; apply Flow Decomposition (Theorem 3.1) only on the final support \(\operatorname{supp}(f^*)\).


FM-03
Omitting Holdover Arcs in Time-Expanded DAGs (分层图)
Without \((u, t-1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (u, t)\), agents arriving at \(u\) at \(t-1\) cannot wait at \(u\) for a later shuttle (#020).
Always add holdover arcs \((u, t-1) \xrightarrow{h_u} (u, t)\) whenever waiting at vertices is permitted.


FM-04
Undirected Vertex-Split Bypass Trap (\(u_{\text{in}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{in}}\) or \(u_{\text{out}} \leftrightarrow v_{\text{in}}\))
Wiring an undirected edge with bidirectional positive capacity between split ports lets flow jump \(v_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}\), bypassing both internal bridges (§3.2).
Compile every undirected edge \(\{u, v\}\) on split vertices into two independent directed arcs: add_edge(u_out, v_in, c) AND add_edge(v_out, u_in, c).


FM-05
Connecting \(S \to u_{\text{out}}\) When Initial Agents Consume Vertex Durability
In #018 (* cells) and #019 (initial lizards), connecting \(S \to u_{\text{out}}\) skips \(u_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}\), giving \(u\) an extra \(+1\) durability.
Connect \(S \xrightarrow{1} u_{\text{in}}\) whenever an agent starting at \(u\) consumes \(1\) unit of \(u\)’s pass-through budget upon departure.


FM-06
Degenerate \(s = 1\) Single-Layer \(\infty\) Path (#021 Luogu P2766)
When the LIS length is \(s = 1\), index \(1\) satisfies both \(dp[1] = 1\) and \(dp[1] = s\), creating \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} 1_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} 1_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\).
Explicitly guard if (s == 1) before building the network (or keep transition arcs at cap \(1\) and handle \(s=1\) separately).

title: Chapter 3 — Vertex Splitting, Time-Expanded Layered DAGs, and Path Decomposition
text:
8. Chapter Revision Summary & Multilingual Bibliography

Key Takeaways

Flow Decomposition (流分解定理, Theorem 3.1): Every feasible flow \(f\) decomposes into \(\le |E|\) simple \(s\)-\(t\) paths and simple cycles in \(O(VE)\) time via bottleneck stripping on \(\operatorname{supp}(f)\).
Vertex Capacity Splitting (\(\text{out} \to \text{in}\) Invariant): A vertex throughput bound \(0 \le F(v) \le C_v\) compiles into \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{C_v} v_{\text{out}}\) with all external transitions wired strictly from out-ports to in-ports (\(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}\)). On unit-capacity vertex-split graphs, \(\min(\deg^-(x), \deg^+(x)) = 1\) holds at every internal vertex, unlocking Even and Tarjan’s \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) complexity bound and proving all Four Variants of Menger’s Theorem.
Time-Expanded Layered DAGs (分层图) & Incremental Dynamic Layer Addition (动态加层): Promoting discrete time \(t \in \{0, \dots, T\}\) into the vertex state \((u, t)\) turns temporal routing into a DAG with holdover arcs \((u, t-1) \to (u, t)\) and transit arcs \((u, t-1) \to (v, t)\). Appending layers incrementally onto a persistent residual graph \(G_f\) finds the minimum completion time \(T^*\) without binary search.
Graph Sparsification & Dual Elimination: Shortest-path restrictions (\(d[u] + w_{uv} = d[v]\)) and DP transitions (\(dp[j] = dp[i] + 1\)) extract sparse DAGs; Row/Column Hub vertices ([ARC 074 D]) collapse \(\Theta(HW(H+W))\) cliques into \(O(H+W)\) bipartite graphs; and on \(10^{10}\)-vertex regular grids ([CF 1368H1]), Min-Cut geometry eliminates the interior graph entirely in favor of \(O(N+M)\) Cut-DP.



Multilingual Bibliography & Classic References

[EN] L. R. Ford, Jr. and D. R. Fulkerson, Flows in Networks, Princeton University Press, 1962 (Flow Decomposition Theorem, Vertex Capacities, and Menger Duality).
[EN] S. Even and R. E. Tarjan, “Network Flow and Testing Graph Connectivity,” SIAM Journal on Computing, 4(4):507–518, 1975 (proving the \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) bound for Dinic’s algorithm on unit vertex networks Type 2).
[ZH] 刘汝佳 (Rujia Liu), 《算法竞赛入门经典：训练指南》 (AOAPC II: Training Guide), Tsinghua University Press, 2012 (拆点 Vertex Splitting, 分层图网络流 Time-Expanded Layered Flow, and UVa 11380 / CTSC1999 analyses).
[ZH] 李煜东 (Yudong Li), 《算法竞赛进阶指南》 (Advanced Guide to Algorithmic Competitions), 2018 (系统总结拆点、动态加层与最短路 DAG 网络流).
[JA] AtCoder Regular Contest 074 Editorial — Task F (ARC 074 D): Lotus Leaves (Row/Column Hub Sparsification 行・列の超頂点 reducing vertex-cut on grid lines to bipartite edge-cut).

NotePrerequisites & Entry Contract




Graph Theory & Traversals: Familiarity with directed multigraphs \(G = (V, E)\), adjacency list representations, Breadth-First Search (BFS) shortest-path distance layers, and Depth-First Search (DFS).
Elementary Linear Algebra: Vector inner products \(\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{y}\) and matrix-vector multiplication (used to derive the Cut Net-Flow Lemma in three lines via the vertex-arc incidence matrix).
Pre-Written Solver Assumption: We assume you already possess a tested Dinic maximum-flow template in your library. Instead of re-implementing standard BFS/DFS loops from scratch, this chapter derives why residual reverse arcs work, proves the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem and Dinic’s Tight Complexity Regimes, and establishes the Black-Box Algorithmic & Structural Contract that governs all 24 chapters of this textbook.

title: Chapter 1 — Conservation Laws, Residual Graphs, and Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality
section: 1. Motivation: Recognizing Flow Conservation When No Graph Is Given
text:
1. Motivation: Recognizing Flow Conservation When No Graph Is Given
Why do capable contestants who can type a 50-line Dinic template in three minutes still fail to solve flow and min-cut problems in actual contests? Because contest problems almost never hand you a directed network with a source \(s\), a sink \(t\), and edge capacities \(c(e)\). Instead, they hand you an array of integers, a table of tournament standings, or a list of jobs with deadlines.
Before defining a single graph-theoretic term, examine three classic problem statements where no flow network is mentioned in the input, yet every greedy or dynamic programming attempt collapses for the exact same structural reason:

1.1 Three Non-Graph Vignettes with Hidden Conservation

Single-Step Troop Redistribution (CF 546E — Soldier and Traveling, Ladder #002):

Plain-English Setup: \(N\) cities initially hold \(a_1, \dots, a_N\) soldiers and connect via \(M\) roads. Each soldier may either stay in their starting city or walk across at most one road to a neighboring city. Can the army rearrange itself so that city \(i\) ends up with exactly \(b_i\) soldiers, and if so, what is the \(N \times N\) movement table \(x_{i,j}\)?
Why Greedy Fails: If city \(1\) has surplus soldiers needed by city \(4\) along a path \(1 - 2 - 3 - 4\), a soldier from \(1\) cannot walk to \(4\); Instead, a soldier from \(1\) must step to \(2\), displacing an original soldier from \(2\) to \(3\), who in turn displaces an original soldier from \(3\) to \(4\).
The Hidden Conservation Law: Every movement \(x_{i,j} \ge 0\) is an atomic parcel of conserved mass leaving origin \(i\) (\(\sum_j x_{i,j} = a_i\)) and arriving at destination \(j\) (\(\sum_i x_{i,j} = b_j\)) across allowed pairs \((i, j) \in E \cup \{(u, u)\}\).

Sports Tournament Elimination (SGU 326 — Perspective, Ladder #001):

Plain-English Setup: Team \(1\) currently has \(w_1\) wins and \(r_1\) games left. Every other team \(i \in \{2, \dots, N\}\) currently has \(w_i\) wins, and there are \(g_{ij}\) remaining games between teams \(i\) and \(j\) (\(2 \le i < j \le N\)). Can Team \(1\) finish with at least as many wins as every other team?
Why Greedy Fails: Even after awarding Team \(1\) all \(r_1\) of its remaining games (reaching \(W_1 = w_1 + r_1\) wins), deciding who wins the remaining matches \(g_{ij}\) between teams \(i\) and \(j\) cannot be done greedily by “always letting the team with fewer current wins win.” A triangle of teams \(\{2, 3, 4\}\) playing each other heavily may collectively generate more wins than their combined headroom \(\sum_{i \in \{2,3,4\}} (W_1 - w_i)\) can absorb!
The Hidden Conservation Law: Each remaining match \((i, j)\) generates \(g_{ij}\) conserved units of “win mass” that must split into \(x_{ij} + x_{ji} = g_{ij}\) between team \(i\) and team \(j\), while team \(i\) can absorb at most \(W_1 - w_i\) total wins across all opponents.

Pairwise Prime-Factor Division (CF 498C — Array and Operations, Ladder #004):

Plain-English Setup: Given an array \(a_1, \dots, a_N\) (\(a_i \le 10^9\)) and \(M\) allowed index pairs \((i_k, j_k)\) where \(i_k + j_k\) is always odd, each operation picks an allowed pair and divides both \(a_{i_k}\) and \(a_{j_k}\) by a common integer divisor \(d > 1\). Maximize the total number of operations.
Why Greedy Fails: Dividing two numbers by a composite \(d\) is always inferior to dividing sequentially by its prime factors, and different prime factors \(p \neq q\) never interact. However, for a fixed prime \(p\), greedily pairing \(a_{i_k}\) and \(a_{j_k}\) can strand prime powers along an alternating chain of indices.
The Hidden Conservation Law: Because \(i_k + j_k\) is odd, every allowed pair connects an odd index \(i \in L\) to an even index \(j \in R\). For each fixed prime \(p\), the exponent \(\nu_p(a_i)\) at odd indices acts as a conserved supply, the exponent \(\nu_p(a_j)\) at even indices acts as a capacity-bounded sink demand, and each operation consumes \(1\) unit of \(p\)-exponent from \(L\) and \(1\) unit from \(R\).




1.2 The Unifying Diagnostic Principle
Across all three problems, the surface story changes completely, but the underlying algebraic skeleton is identical:
\[\text{Source Supplies } (a_i) \xrightarrow{\text{Conserved Routing } x_{i,j} \ge 0} \text{Intermediate Conservation } \left(\text{inflow} = \text{outflow}\right) \xrightarrow{\text{Capacity Bounds}} \text{Sink Demands } (b_j)\]
Whenever an optimization or feasibility problem asks you to route, match, or redistribute discrete or continuous quantities subject to upper bounds without creating or destroying mass in the interior, you are looking at a Flow Network. And whenever the obstruction to feasibility is a subset of entities whose collective supply exceeds the collective capacity of their allowed receivers (as in the tournament triangle above), you are looking at its dual Minimum Cut.
