1.2 Difficulty Tier Calibration (SS / Int / Adv / Mas)
Every chapter ladder (Ch 01–Ch 24) contains exactly 8 curated problems ordered strictly across four calibrated difficulty tiers:

SS — Stepping Stone (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints): Clean, canonical non-template problems that isolate a single modelling transformation (e.g., translating a 2D grid conflict into parity bipartite MIS, or differencing a linear inequality system into conservation equations). Typical rating: CF 1700–2000 / AtCoder ABC-F,G / Luogu 提高+/省选-.
Int — Intermediate (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints): Requires combining the chapter’s core transformation with a secondary structural invariant (e.g., binary search on bottlenecks, residual SCC edge classification, or Tarjan topological pruning before project selection). Typical rating: CF 2100–2400 / AtCoder ARC-E,F / Luogu 省选/NOI-.
Adv — Advanced (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints): Non-obvious algebraic compilation where the problem statement contains zero graph terminology, or requires rescuing a broken submodularity/convexity condition via variable inversion, complement counting, or persistent data structures. Typical rating: CF 2500–2800 / AtCoder AGC-C,D,E / NOI / Provincial Selection.
Mas — Mastery (2 per chapter, 48 total + 12 in Checkpoints + 16 Synthesis): Research-grade or Olympiad flagship benchmarks (CF 2900–3500, AtCoder AGC-F, ICPC World Finals, NOI / CTSC / WC) requiring multi-layer compilation, continuous Coarea decomposition, simulated MCMF on trees/segment trees, or \(L_p\) Isotonic Regression.



1.3 Master Failure Mode Taxonomy (FM-01 to FM-25)
Throughout the textbook, every gadget construction is paired with an explicit Broken Gadget Counterexample. The table below indexes all 25 canonical failure modes referenced across Sections 2–5:



Code
Failure Mode Name
What Goes Wrong in the Naive Graph / Algorithm
Canonical Fix & Home Chapter




FM-01
Directed vs. Undirected Residual Trap
Adding an undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\) of capacity \(c\) as two independent directed arcs without shared residual coupling, or setting reverse capacity to \(0\) instead of \(c\).
Couple \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) in the residual pair (e and e^1), initializing both forward capacities to \(c\) (Ch 01).


FM-02
Greedy / Naive “\(S\)-Reachable = All Min-Cut” Fallacy
Assuming every edge crossing from the \(S\)-reachable residual set \(R_S\) to \(V \setminus R_S\) is mandatory in every minimum cut, or that any saturated edge is a cut edge.
Run Tarjan SCC on \(G_f\): \((u,v)\) is in some min-cut iff \(f(u,v)=c(u,v)\) and \(\text{scc}(u) \neq \text{scc}(v)\); in all min-cuts iff \(\text{scc}(u)=\text{scc}(S)\) and \(\text{scc}(v)=\text{scc}(T)\) (Ch 02).


FM-03
Un-Split Vertex / Two-Commodity Merging Trap
Placing vertex capacity on incident edges, or testing two-commodity routing by only checking \(S_1 \to T_1, S_2 \to T_2\) without testing the swapped \(S_1 \to T_2, S_2 \to T_1\) run.
Split \(v \to (v_{\text{in}}, v_{\text{out}})\) (Ch 03); run second max-flow with \(S_2 \leftrightarrow T_2\) swapped ([CQOI2014] 危桥, Ch 02).


FM-04
Missing Companion Edge \((t, s, \infty)\) in Lower-Bound Flow
Running max-flow from \(S^*\) to \(T^*\) in a lower-bound \(s\)-\(t\) network without adding the feedback arc \((t, s, \infty)\), violating conservation at \(s\) and \(t\).
Add \((t, s, \infty)\) to convert \(s\)-\(t\) flow into a closed circulation before saturating \(S^* \to T^*\) (Ch 04).


FM-05
König Duality on Non-Bipartite Graphs (Odd-Cycle Trap)
Applying \(\text{MVC} = \text{MaxMatching}\) or \(\text{MIS} = |V| - \text{MaxMatching}\) to a graph containing an odd cycle \(C_{2k+1}\), where \(\text{MVC} > \nu(G)\).
Verify bipartiteness first, or pass to the complement of a two-clique graph / use general Blossom matching (Ch 05, Ch 22).


FM-06
Un-Reset Visited Array in Alternating-Path Game Simulation
Failing to unmatch or update Dulmage–Mendelsohn status dynamically as multi-move grid games progress ([NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋).
Treat each move as moving the blank token along an alternating path and re-test augmenting paths from the current vertex after deleting the previous node (Ch 06).


FM-07
Unreachable Positive-Weight Cycles in Project Selection
Feeding a dependency graph with directed cycles (or nodes reachable from cycles) directly into a closure min-cut ([NOI2009] 植物大战僵尸), allowing the solver to “buy” mutually deadlocked positive-weight nodes.
Prune all vertices with in-degree \(>0\) after Kahn’s topological sort on the prerequisite graph before building the closure network (Ch 09).


FM-08
Submodularity Violation (\(A + D > B + C\)) on Un-Flipped Graphs
Attempting to compile a pairwise reward/penalty table with \(A + D > B + C\) directly into \(s\)-\(t\) cut arcs, producing negative edge capacities \(c_{uv} < 0\).
Check if the interaction graph is bipartite; if so, apply Bipartite Variable Inversion \(y_v = 1 - x_v\) on one side to negate the cross-difference into \(B+C-A-D \ge 0\) (Ch 10, Ch 11).


FM-09
Odd-Cycle Collision in Bipartite Variable Inversion
Attempting to rescue a supermodular penalty (\(A+D > B+C\)) when the conflict graph contains an odd cycle (e.g., a triangle of “same-color bonus” edges).
Recognize that same-state penalties on non-bipartite graphs are NP-hard (Max-Cut); either reformulate via complement / line graph or dualize if planar (Ch 11).


FM-10
Missing Reverse \(\infty\)-Constraint Arcs in Multi-State Chains
Omitting the backward \((z_{i,t}, z_{i,t-1}, \infty)\) monotonicity arcs in a unary chain ([HNOI2013] 切糕), allowing an \(s\)-\(t\) cut to sever multiple edges of the same variable and create fractured indicator states \(z_{i,1}=0, z_{i,2}=1\).
Always wire \((v_{i,t}, v_{i,t-1}, \infty)\) so any finite cut intersects each variable’s chain in at most one transition edge (Ch 12).


FM-11
Non-Convex Interaction Function in Ishikawa / Coarea Compilation
Applying the Ishikawa cross-edge formula \(w = \frac{1}{2}\Delta_i \Delta_j g < 0\) when \(g(a_i - a_j)\) is concave rather than convex, producing negative capacities.
Verify discrete convexity \(g(d+1) - 2g(d) + g(d-1) \ge 0\) before compiling cross-edges (Ch 13).


FM-12
Empty-Subgraph (\(S' = \emptyset\)) Zero-Cut Trap in Density Subgraph
Formulating \(\max |E(S')|/|S'|\) as a standard closure cut without shifting by a large constant \(U\), where the trivial cut \(S' = \emptyset\) has cost \(0\) and masks whether a positive-excess non-empty subgraph exists.
Use the shifted degree-Regularization cut or enforce \(|S'| \ge 1\) via binary search validation (Ch 14).


FM-13
Un-Split Exterior Face in Planar \(s\)-\(t\) Dual Shortest Path
Dualizing a planar graph into faces when \(s\) and \(t\) do not both lie on the outer boundary face, or forgetting to split the outer face into \(F_{\text{top}}\) and \(F_{\text{bottom}}\) along the \((t \to s)\)虛arc.
Embed \(s, t\) on the outer boundary, add virtual arc \((t,s)\), and split the unbounded face into \(S^*\) and \(T^*\) (Ch 15).


FM-14
Adding Residual Edges Instead of Rebuilding in Gomory–Hu Gusfield
Running Gusfield’s \(N-1\) max-flows on the modified residual graph from the previous iteration instead of resetting flow values to zero before each pair.
Reset all edge flows to \(0\) before each of the \(N-1\) \(s\)-\(t\) max-flow calls (Ch 16).


FM-15
Un-Initialized Negative Costs in Dijkstra SSP without Johnson Potentials
Running Dijkstra directly on an MCMF network with initial negative-cost edges, or failing to saturate negative-cost edges / cycles via lower-bound initialization.
Compute initial potentials \(\pi\) via Bellman–Ford/DAG DP, or pre-saturate negative-cost arcs \((u,v,c,w<0)\) and balance excesses via \(S^* \to T^*\) (Ch 17).


FM-16
Concave Edge Cost Splitting / Zero-Length Vertical Segment Loop
Splitting a concave cost function (\(\Delta c_1 > \Delta c_2\)) into parallel arcs (where MCMF greedily picks the second unit before the first!), or adding a zero-length interval \([x, x]\) with \(w > 0\) (最长k可重线段集) creating a positive-weight self-loop.
Only convex costs split into parallel arcs; for vertical segments \(x_1 = x_2\), double coordinates \(x \gets 2x\) and map vertical segments to \([2x, 2x+1]\) vs. open intervals \((2x_1, 2x_2)\) (Ch 18, Ch 19).


FM-17
Sign Inversion in Consecutive Equation Differencing (\(\Delta_i = E_i - E_{i-1}\))
Getting the orientation of slack variables \(s_i \ge 0\) or interval variables \(x_j\) backwards when subtracting consecutive linear equations \(E_i - E_{i-1}\).
Strictly enforce conservation \(\sum_{\text{in}} - \sum_{\text{out}} = b_i - b_{i-1}\): an interval covering \([l_j, r_j]\) enters at \(+x_j\) in \(\Delta_{l_j}\) and exits at \(-x_j\) in \(\Delta_{r_j+1}\), hence forms an arc \(r_j+1 \to l_j\) (or \(l_j \to r_j+1\) under reversed sign convention) (Ch 19).


FM-18
Upfront \(O(NM^2)\) Graph Materialization in Dynamic Scheduling
Building all \(M \times P\) chef-position vertices and \(N \times M \times P\) edges before running MCMF ([NOI2012] 美食节), causing TLE during SPFA/Dijkstra scans.
Materialize only the first reverse-position slot \((j, 1)\) per chef initially; dynamically spawn \((j, k+1)\) only after the augmenting path saturates \((j, k)\) (Ch 20).


FM-19
Contaminated vs. Clean Resource Confusion in Napkin Reuse
Allowing “dirty” resources at day \(i_{\text{out}}\) to flow directly to “clean” demand at day \((i+1)_{\text{in}}\) without passing through a wash delay edge (餐巾计划问题).
Separate each day into dirty supply (\(S \to i_{\text{dirty}}\)) and clean demand (\(i_{\text{clean}} \to T\)); only dirty nodes can postpone for free (\(i_{\text{dirty}} \to (i+1)_{\text{dirty}}\)) or wash (\(i_{\text{dirty}} \to (i+d)_{\text{clean}}\)) (Ch 20).


FM-20
Missing Regret Push (反悔边) in Simulated MCMF Heaps
Pushing only the raw item cost into a greedy heap without pushing the residual cancellation cost \(2\text{val}_{\text{chosen}} - \text{val}_{\text{prev}}\) after matching (Buy Low Sell High, CF 802 O).
Maintain the exact residual cycle invariant: every match \((u, v)\) must insert the reverse residual marginal cost into the opposite priority queue (Ch 23).


FM-21
Shared Mutable Nodes Across Versions in Persistent Segment Tree Flow
Linking historical prefix queries directly to an in-place mutated segment tree (BZOJ 3218), allowing flow from time \(t\) to leak backward and reach targets inserted at time \(t' > t\).
Allocate new persistent tree nodes along the updated path at step \(i\), linking \(\text{new\_node} \to \text{old\_node}\) with capacity \(\infty\) so flow only travels to earlier indices \(j < i\) (Ch 22).


FM-22
Bipartite Assumption on Odd-Cycle General Matching Graphs
Running Hopcroft–Karp or Dinic on a general matching problem ([WC2016] 挑战 NPC, CF 1089 B), where odd alternating cycles cause augmenting paths to self-intersect.
Contract odd cycles via Edmonds’ Blossom algorithm (带花树) or test algebraic rank via the skew-symmetric Tutte matrix (Ch 22).


FM-23
Incomplete 5-Queue Cross-Cancel Transitions in Bipartite Simulated Flow
Maintaining only direct match heaps when simulating a \(K\)-bounded common-element constraint ([NOI2019] 序列), missing the 3-hop augmenting paths that free a shared slot by swapping an already-paired element.
Enumerate all elementary augmenting path types in the constant-size residual gadget and maintain a dedicated priority queue for each valid state transition (Ch 23).


FM-24
Non-Convex or Discontinuous Derivative Split in \(L_p\) Isotonic Regression
Attempting to binary search a single threshold \([f_i > \text{mid}]\) for \(L_p\) Isotonic Regression when the node weight functions \(w_i(x)\) are non-convex, violating the nested cut-tree monotonicity property.
Ensure each penalty \(w_i(x)\) is convex so its discrete derivative \(w_i(\text{mid}+\epsilon) - w_i(\text{mid})\) is monotone in \(\text{mid}\), enabling Divide-and-Conquer + Closure Min-Cut (Ch 24).


FM-25
Forcing Network Flow Onto a Non-Flow Lookalike Problem
Building an exponential or malformed flow network for a problem that lacks flow conservation or submodularity—such as bitmask shortest paths (孤岛营救), DAG DP, or greedy exchange—simply because it appeared in 网络流 24 题.
Audit conservation and TU/submodularity first; see the Non-Flow Decoys in Sections 4 and 5 (CP-I–CP-VI).

text:
2. Complete Master Index of Accepted Problems (#001–#256)
This section provides the complete bijective directory of all 256 accepted non-template problems, organized by textbook chapter (#001–#192), blind checkpoint (#193–#240), and grand synthesis reserve (#241–#256).

2.1 Part I: Flow Foundations, Residual Anatomy, Time-Layered DAGs & Circulations (#001–#032)

Chapter 1 — Flow Conservation, Residual Networks & Max-Flow Min-Cut (#001–#008)











ID
Tier
Problem & Judge Code
Primary Modelling Archetype

Failure Mode




#001
SS
SGU 326 / CF Gym — Perspective (alt: Luogu P2756 飞行员配对方案)
Elimination Feasibility via Remaining Game Allocation
Sports league: fix team 1’s max wins \(W_1\); check if remaining match points can be distributed without any team \(i\) exceeding \(W_1\).
FM-01


#002
SS
CF 546 E — Soldier and Traveling (alt: Luogu P3254 圆桌问题)
1-Step Bipartite Conservation & Flow Reconstruction
\(N \le 100\): soldiers move at most 1 edge from \(a_i\) to \(b_i\); check \(\sum a_i = \sum b_i = \text{MaxFlow}\) and print adjacency matrix \(f(u, v')\).
FM-01

Int
CF 653 D — Delivery Bears (alt: Luogu P2763 试题库问题)
Binary Search on Unit Weight + Scaled Integer Capacity
\(X \le 10^5\) bears move along \(s \to t\) paths carrying equal weight \(w\); binary search \(w\) and assign capacity \(\lfloor c_e / w \rfloor\).
FM-01


#004
Int
CF 498 C — Array and Operations
Prime-Factor Decoupled Bipartite Matching Flow
Array \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) (\(n \le 100\)) with good pairs \((i, j)\) of opposite parity (\(i+j\) odd); decouple by each prime \(p \mid a_i\) into independent flow runs.
FM-05


#005
Adv
POJ 3498 / UVA 12125 — March of the Penguins
Enumerating Sink + Vertex-Capacity Splitting
\(N \le 100\) ice floes with jump limit \(b_i\); split \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{b_i} i_{\text{out}}\) and test all \(N\) floes as the meeting sink \(T\).
FM-03


#006
Adv
AtCoder ABC 239 G — Builder Takahashi
Minimum-Weight Vertex Cut & \(S\)-Reachable Reconstruction
Undirected graph \(N \le 100\) with vertex removal costs \(c_i\); split \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c_v} v_{\text{out}}\) and extract \(v_{\text{in}} \in R_S, v_{\text{out}} \notin R_S\).
FM-02, FM-03


#007
Mas
CF 510 E — Fox And Dinner
Parity Bipartite Degree-2 Factor & Cycle Extraction
Arrange \(N \le 200\) integers into circular tables where adjacent sums \(a_i + a_j\) are prime; odd+even \(= \text{odd prime}\) forces bipartite degree-2 flow \(= N\).
FM-05


#008
Mas
CF 1383 F — Special Edges
\(2^K\) Dynamic Residual Rollback + Gray-Code DFS
\(K \le 10\) special edges with \(Q \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) capacity queries; precompute base max-flow once and maintain \(2^K\) residual states in \(O(2^K m)\) via FF augmentations.
FM-01





Chapter 2 — Residual Graph Anatomy, Cut-Edge Classification & Rollback (#009–#016)











ID
Tier
Problem & Judge Code
Primary Modelling Archetype

Failure Mode




#009
SS
USACO 4.4 / Luogu P1344 — Polluted Milk (追查坏牛奶)
Base \(\text{ BASE } = M+1\) Scaling for Lexicographical Min-Edge Min-Cut
Find minimum cut with fewest edges: replace capacity \(c_e\) with \(c_e' = c_e \cdot (M+1) + 1\) so \(\lfloor C'/(M+1) \rfloor = C\) and \(C' \bmod (M+1) = |E_{\text{cut}}|\).
FM-02


#010
SS
UVA 11248 — Frequency Hopping
Single-Edge Bottleneck Upgrade along Residual \(S\)-\(T\) Cuts
Check if increasing one saturated cut edge \((u,v)\) (\(u \in R_S, v \notin R_S\)) to capacity \(C\) can achieve target flow \(F\).
FM-02


#011
Int
Luogu P4126 — [AHOI2009] 最小割
Tarjan SCC Residual Classification (“Some” vs. “All” Min-Cuts)
Canonical classification theorem: run Tarjan SCC on \(G_f\); \((u,v)\) is feasible iff \(\text{scc}(u) \neq \text{scc}(v)\) and mandatory iff \(\text{scc}(u)=\text{scc}(S), \text{scc}(v)=\text{scc}(T)\).
FM-02


#012
Int
CF 1139 E — Maximize Mex
Offline Reverse Deletion + Incremental Residual Augmentation
Students leave clubs over \(D\) days; reverse time so edges are only added, and increment the \(\text{mex}\) pointer \(k\) via residual augmenting paths.
FM-01


#013
Adv
CF 727 D — T-shirts Distribution
6-Size Contiguous Interval Flow & Assignment Extraction
Participants request size \(s\) or adjacent \((s, s+1)\); model as small bipartite flow and extract actual allocations from positive edge flows.
FM-01


#014
Adv
Luogu P3163 — [CQOI2014] 危桥
Two-Commodity Undirected Routing via Swapped Sink Verification
Route \(a_n\) trips \(a_1 \leftrightarrow a_2\) and \(b_n\) trips \(b_1 \leftrightarrow b_2\) on an undirected graph; run max-flow twice—once with \((b_1, b_2)\) and once with \((b_2, b_1)\)—to cancel cross-flow.
FM-03


#015
Mas
Luogu P3308 — [SDOI2014] LIS
Lexicographically First Min-Cut via Reverse Residual Un-Pushing
Find lexicographically smallest index set of vertices whose removal destroys all LIS paths; sort by \(c_i\), test residual reachability \(u_{\text{in}} \not\leadsto u_{\text{out}}\), and rollback flow.
FM-02, FM-03


#016
Mas
CF 269 C — Flawed Flow
Constructive Orientation from Known Conservation Sums
Given undirected edges with capacities and the promise that a saturating flow exists without cycles, orient edges greedily like topological Kahn’s algorithm as \(\text{in}(v) = \frac{1}{2}\text{deg}(v)\).
FM-01

#017
SS
Luogu P1402 — 酒店之王
Three-Layer bottleneck Vertex Splitting (\(R \to G_{\text{in}} \to G_{\text{out}} \to D\))
Guests require both a room and a dish; placing Guests in the middle without splitting \(G_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} G_{\text{out}}\) allows one guest to consume multiple rooms/dishes.

#018
SS
UVA 11380 — Down Went The Titanic
2D Grid Multi-Capacity Vertex Splitting
Icebergs have survival counts \(1\) or \(\infty\); split \((r,c)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap}} (r,c)_{\text{out}}\) and connect 4-neighbors \((r,c)_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} (r',c')_{\text{in}}\).
FM-03


#019
Int
Luogu P2472 — [SCOI2007] 蜥蜴
Stone-Pillar Jump Survival via Vertex-Capacity Splitting
Lizards jump Euclidean distance \(\le d\) on pillars of height \(h_{r,c}\); pillar durability \(= h_{r,c}\) is a vertex capacity \((r,c)_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{h_{r,c}} (r,c)_{\text{out}}\).
FM-03


#020
Int
Luogu P2754 — [CTSC1999] 家园 / 星际转移问题 (24题 #16, Rev-01)
Incremental Time-Expanded Network (\(V \times T\))
Spaceships cycle periodically; expand layer \((u, t)\) for \(t = 1, 2, \dots\), adding hold edges \((u, t-1) \to (u, t, \infty)\) and ship edges until cumulative residual flow \(\ge K\).
FM-03


#021
Adv
Luogu P2766 — 最长不下降子序列问题 (24题 #06)
DP-Subgraph Layering & Boundary Endpoint Capacity Modification
Compute \(dp[i]\) first; build layered DAG on \(dp[j]+1 = dp[i]\) with \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} i_{\text{out}}\), then relax \(1_{\text{in}} \to 1_{\text{out}}\) and \(n_{\text{in}} \to n_{\text{out}}\) to \(\infty\) for Part 3.
FM-03


#022
Adv
CF 78 E — Evacuation
Dual-BFS Spreading Fire + Time-Bottleneck Bipartite Matching
Reactor meltdown spreads via BFS in \(T \le 60\) steps; precompute earliest safe arrival times before fire hits each cell and match scientists to capsules.
FM-03


#023
Mas
CF 1368 H1 — Breadboard Capacity (Easy Version)
Grid-Boundary \(S\)-\(T\) Cut to 1D State Transition DP
\(N, M \le 10^5\) grid with red/blue ports on 4 borders; observe any minimal cut is a monochrome horizontal or vertical strip DP (\(O(N+M)\)).
FM-02


#024
Mas
Luogu P3171 — [CQOI2015] 网络吞吐量
Shortest-Path DAG Extraction + Vertex-Capacity Max-Flow
Packets only follow shortest paths from \(1\) to \(n\): run Dijkstra first to extract edges with \(d[u] + w(u,v) = d[v]\), then split vertices \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c_v} v_{\text{out}}\).
FM-03





Chapter 4 — Lower-Bound Flows, Circulations & Matrix Rounding (#025–#032)

#025

ZOJ 2314 — Reactor Cooling (alt: LOJ #115)
Feasible Circulation with Lower Bounds (\([l_e, u_e]\), No Source/Sink)
Pipes have min/max cooling rates \([l_e, u_e]\); compute \(M(v) = \sum l_{\text{in}} - \sum l_{\text{out}}\) and verify \(S^* \to T^*\) saturates \(\sum_{M(v)>0} M(v)\).

#026
SS
POJ 2396 — Budget
Bounded Row-Column Matrix Cell Constraints via \(s\)-\(t\) Lower Bounds
Matrix \(R \times C\) with given row sums, column sums, and cell inequality bounds (\(=, <, >\)); intersect cell intervals \([l_{ij}, u_{ij}]\) and add \((t, s, \infty)\).

#027
Int
Luogu P4843 — 清理雪道
Minimum \(s\)-\(t\) Flow with Edge Lower Bounds \([1, \infty)\)
Cover every directed trail at least once (\([1, \infty)\)) using the minimum number of snowplows; find feasible flow via \((t,s,\infty)\), delete \((t,s)\), and push \(t \to s\) backward.
FM-04


#028
Int
POJ 1637 / UVA 10735 — Sightseeing Tour
Mixed-Graph Eulerian Circuit via Degree Parity Balance Flow
Orient undirected edges so \(\text{in}(v) = \text{out}(v)\): arbitrarily orient undirected edges first, check if \((\text{in}(v)-\text{out}(v))\) is even, and push \(\frac{|\text{in}-\text{out}|}{2}\) reversal units.
FM-01, FM-04


#029
Adv
Luogu P5192 — [ZJOI2010] Shoot the Bullet (拍照)
Maximum \(s\)-\(t\) Flow with Daily & Cumulative Lower Bounds
\(D\) days, \(M\) girls; cumulative photos \(\ge G_j\) (\(j \to T\) in \([G_j, \infty)\)), daily cap \(C_i\) (\(S \to i\) in \([0, C_i]\)), daily girl bounds \([L_{ij}, R_{ij}]\).
FM-04


#030
Adv
CF 704 D — Captain America
Red-Blue Row/Column Discrepancy Bounds (\(|r_i - b_i| \le d_i\))
\(N \le 10^5\) points on lines \(x=x_i, y=y_j\); \(|c_{\text{red}} - c_{\text{blue}}| \le d \iff \lceil \frac{\text{tot}-d}{2} \rceil \le c_{\text{red}} \le \lfloor \frac{\text{tot}+d}{2} \rfloor\), solved via lower-bound max/min flow.
FM-04


#031
Mas
CF 628 F — Bear and Fair Set
Prefix Bucket Disjointness + Remainder-Mod-5 Lower Bounds
Hints specify how many elements in \([1, up_i]\) are \(\le up_i\); sort hints into disjoint intervals \((up_{i-1}, up_i]\) and require exactly \(n/5\) per residue mod \(5\).
FM-04


#032
Mas
BZOJ 3698 — XWW 的难题
Real-Valued Matrix Rounding (\(\lfloor a_{ij} \rfloor\) vs. \(\lceil a_{ij} \rceil\))
Round an \(N \times N\) real matrix with integer row/column sums while keeping row/col sums invariant; subtract \(\lfloor a_{ij} \rfloor\) and route \(\{0,1\}\) fractional residuals via lower-bound max-flow.
FM-04







2.2 Part II: Bipartite Matching, König Duality, Grid Parity & Poset Dilworth (#033–#064)

Chapter 5 — Bipartite Matching, König’s Theorem, MVC & MIS (#033–#040)

#033
SS
CF 1423 B — Valuable Paper
Binary Search Bottleneck + Hopcroft–Karp Perfect Matching
\(N \le 10^4, M \le 10^5\): find min max-edge weight for a perfect matching; binary search edge threshold \(W\) and run \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) Hopcroft–Karp.
FM-05


#034
SS
Luogu P1640 — [SCOI2010] 连续攻击游戏
Sequential Value-to-Item Prefix Bipartite Matching
\(N \le 10^6\) items each have two attributes \((a_i, b_i) \in [1, 10^4]\); match attribute \(1, 2, 3, \dots\) sequentially to items until the first unmatched integer.
FM-05


#035
Int
UVA 11419 — SAM I AM
König Minimum Vertex Cover + Alternating-Tree Set Construction
Shoot all enemies on an \(R \times C\) grid using minimum row/column laser shots, and print the exact rows (\(L \setminus Z\)) and columns (\(R \cap Z\)) via alternating reachability \(Z\).
FM-02, FM-05


#036
Int
POJ 1466 — Girls and Boys
Bipartite Maximum Independent Set (\(|V| - \text{MaxMatching}\))
Romantic conflict graph is bipartite (boys vs. girls); maximum mutually non-romantically-involved subset is \(|V| - \nu(G)\) (remembering to divide undirected double-counted matching by 2).
FM-05


#037
Adv
CF 808 F — Card Game
Binary Search Level + Odd-Even Prime-Sum Bipartite MIS
Cards with power \(p_i\), magic \(c_i\), level \(l_i\); two cards conflict if \(c_i + c_j\) is prime. Filter \(c_i = 1\) cards (keep only the highest \(p_i\)), then remaining conflicts are strictly odd+even bipartite!
FM-05


#038
Adv
Luogu P6268 — [SHOI2002] 舞会
Bipartite MIS on Past-Dance Conflict Graph
Students who danced before cannot both attend if we want a conflict-free group; since dances only occur between boy and girl, conflict graph is bipartite.
FM-05


#039
Mas
Luogu P3731 — [HAOI2017] 新型城市化
Complement of Two-Clique Graph \(\to\) Bipartite Essential Cut Edges
Maximize largest clique after adding 1 edge to a union of two cliques: pass to complement graph \(\bar{G}\) (which is bipartite!), find max independent set, and classify mandatory MVC edges via Tarjan SCC.
FM-02, FM-05

Mas
CF 1404 C — Fixed Point Removal
Prefix Deletion Dependency Analysis (Decoy Contrast vs. Flow)
Demonstrates when an apparent dependency cascade on arrays reduces to offline Fenwick binary-lifting rather than bipartite flow.

Grid with soft rocks * and hard walls #: split each row/col into maximal #-bounded segments and intersect at empty cells . for König matching.
FM-05


#042
SS
Luogu P3355 — 骑士共存问题 (24题 #23, Rev-02)
Chessboard \((r+c) \bmod 2\) Parity Bipartite MIS
Knight move \((\pm 1, \pm 2)\) changes \((r+c)\) by \(\pm 1\) or \(\pm 3\) (always flips parity!); maximum non-attacking knights \(= |V_{\text{valid}}| - \text{MaxMatching}\).
FM-05


#043
Int
CF 1773 D — Dominoes
Grid Parity Domino Matching + Alternating Path Augmentation
Dominoes cover all but 2 cells; slide dominoes to expose two adjacent cells = finding alternating paths from the two exposed opposite-parity cells.
FM-06


#044
Int
CF 1198 E — Rectangle Painting 1
Coordinate-Compressed Elementary Strip König Min-Cut
\(N \le 10^9\) grid with \(M \le 50\) black rectangles; compress \(X\) and \(Y\) coordinates into \(\le 100\) elementary strips with capacities \(\Delta x_i, \Delta y_j\).
FM-05


#045
Adv
LOJ #6062 / POJ 3692 — Kindergarten
Maximum Clique in Two-Part Graph via Bipartite Complement MIS
All girls know each other, all boys know each other; find largest mutually acquainted group = Maximum Independent Set in the bipartite non-acquaintance complement graph \(\bar{G}\).
FM-05


#046
Adv
AtCoder ARC 074 F — Lotus Leaves
Row-Column Shared Hub Virtualization (2H + 2W Sparsification)
Frog jumps along any shared row or column: instead of \(O(HW(H+W))\) cell-to-cell edges, introduce row hubs \(R_r\) and column hubs \(C_c\) connected via \((r,c)\) with capacity \(1\).
FM-03


#047
Mas
Luogu P4055 — [JSOI2009] 游戏
Dulmage–Mendelsohn Essential vs. Non-Essential Starting Cells
Token moves to unvisited 4-neighbors on a grid: starting cell \(u\) is a first-player win iff \(u\) belongs to every maximum matching (testable via alternating reachability from unmatched nodes).
FM-06


#048
Mas
Luogu P1971 — [NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏
Multi-Turn Sliding Puzzle \(\to\) Dynamic Bipartite Matching Blunders
Sliding black/white tiles into the single blank cell is isomorphic to moving the blank along alternating paths; detect player blunders when they move from a mandatory matching node to a non-mandatory one.
FM-06





Chapter 7 — Birkhoff–von Neumann, Row-Column Incidence & Bipartite Edge Coloring (#049–#056)

#049
SS
Luogu P1129 — [ZJOI2007] 矩阵游戏
Row/Column Permutation Invariance of Bipartite Matching
Swapping rows/columns only relabels vertices in the row-to-column bipartite graph; diagonal of all \(1\)s exists iff \(\nu(G) = N\).
FM-05


#050
SS
Luogu P2071 — 座位安排
Capacity-2 Bench Bipartite Matching
\(2N\) passengers, \(N\) rows of 2 seats each; give each row vertex capacity \(2\) (\(r_j \to T\) cap \(2\)).
FM-05


#051
Int
CF 387 D — George and Interesting Graph
Center Enumeration + Remaining \((N-1)\)-Regular Bipartite Completion
Fix center \(c \in \{1..N\}\) (enforce all self-and-center arcs), then remaining \(N-1\) vertices need in-degree \(1\) and out-degree \(1\) = min edge edits to form a perfect matching: \((E_{\text{rem}} - \nu) + (N - 1 - \nu)\).
FM-05


#052
Int
Luogu P3231 — [HNOI2013] 消毒
\(2^{\min}\) Bitmask Dimension Enumeration + 2D König MVC
3D box \(A \times B \times C\) with \(ABC \le 5000\): since \(\min(A,B,C) \le \sqrt[3]{5000} \le 17\) (whilst general 3D MVC is NP-hard!), brute-force the \(2^{\min}\) subset of slices in the shortest dimension and run 2D König MVC on the remaining two.
FM-05


#053
Adv
CF 512 E — Fox And Polygon
Triangulation Flip Canonicalization (Structural Contrast)
Contrasts combinatorial flip invariance on polygons against row-column bipartite permutation invariance.
FM-25


#054
Adv
AtCoder AGC 029 F — Construction of a Tree
Hall’s Marriage Condition + BFS Orientation from Root \(1\)
Given \(N-1\) vertex subsets \(E_1, \dots, E_{N-1}\), pick \(u_i \neq v_i \in E_i\) to form a tree: match \(E_1, \dots, E_{N-1}\) to \(V \setminus \{1\}\) (size \(N-1\)), then orient edges outward via BFS from \(1\).
FM-05


#055
Mas
CF 1592 F1 — Alice and Recoloring 1
Bottom-Right 2D XOR Suffix Transform \(\to\) 4-Cell Corner Matching
Transform grid via \(b_{i,j} = a_{i,j} \oplus a_{i+1,j} \oplus a_{i,j+1} \oplus a_{i+1,j+1}\); then top-left flip costs \(1\) for 1 bit in \(b\), whereas bottom-right flip costs \(3\) to flip \((i,j),(i,m),(n,j),(n,m)\) (saves 1 unit!).
FM-05


#056
Mas
CF 1783 F — Double Sort II
Disjoint Permutation Cycle Intersection Minimum Vertex Cover
Decompose both permutations \(a, b\) into disjoint cycles \(C^a_u, C^b_v\); keeping element \(i\) un-operated requires picking neither its \(a\)-cycle nor its \(b\)-cycle = Bipartite Maximum Matching of saved operations!
FM-05





Chapter 8 — Partially Ordered Sets, Dilworth’s Theorem & Hall’s Condition (#057–#064)











ID
Tier
Problem & Judge Code
Primary Modelling Archetype
Diagnostic Trigger & Key Constraint
Failure Mode




#057
SS
Luogu P2172 — [SCOI2010] 部落战争
Minimum Disjoint Path Cover on Forward-Move DAG
Forward-only jumps \((+r,+c), (+c,+r)\) form a strict DAG; min armies to visit all open cells \(= |V| - \text{MaxMatching}(V_{\text{out}}, V_{\text{in}})\).
FM-05


#058
SS
Luogu P2765 — 魔术球问题 (24题 #04, Rev-04)
Incremental DAG Path Cover (\(u+v = k^2\)) & Chain Extraction
Add balls \(v = 1, 2, \dots\) incrementally with edges \(u \to v\) if \(u < v\) and \(u+v = k^2\); stop when \(v - \text{MaxFlow}\) exceeds \(N\) pillars.
FM-05


#059
Int
Luogu P3974 — [TJOI2015] 组合数学
Weighted Grid Dilworth Equivalence (Max Antichain DP)
Minimum bottom-right-moving passes to collect all treasures \(w_{i,j}\) on a grid equals the maximum weight of a top-right-to-bottom-left antichain DP!
FM-25


#060
Int
CF 1009 G — Allowed Letters
Lexicographical Construction via \(2^6 = 64\) Hall Subset Inequalities
Place smallest valid character at index \(i\) and verify whether remaining counts \(cnt[c]\) satisfy Hall’s Marriage Condition \(\sum_{c \in S} cnt[c] \ge \sum_{m \subseteq S} \text{pos}[m]\) for all \(64\) masks \(S \subseteq \{a..f\}\).

#061
Adv
Luogu P4298 — [CTSC2008] 祭祀

text:
3. The Four Flagship Benchmarks & Non-Graph-to-Flow Recognition Matrix

3.1 Deep-Dive Cross-Reference: The Four User-Highlighted Flagship Benchmarks
These four flagship problems represent the pinnacle of modern non-graph-to-cut compilation. Each appears in its home chapter in Part III and in the cross-paradigm synthesis comparison in Capstone I:



Flagship Benchmark
Canonical ID & Home Chapter
Non-Graph English Surface Statement
Why DP / Greedy Fails
Key Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation Breakthrough




1. AtCoder AGC 038 FTwo Permutations
#087 (Ch 11) & Syn-03 (Capstone I)
Given two permutations \(P, Q\) of \(\{0..N-1\}\) (\(N \le 10^5\)), form \(A_i \in \{i, P_i\}\) and \(B_i \in \{i, Q_i\}\) so \(A, B\) are valid permutations maximizing \(|\{i : A_i \neq B_i\}|\).
\(P\)-cycles and \(Q\)-cycles intersect arbitrarily, creating a general bipartite hypergraph of cycle-shift decisions with no treewidth bound.
1. Cycle Locking: Every cycle \(c\) of \(P\) has a single binary state \(x_c \in \{0,1\}\) (\(A_i = i\) vs. \(A_i = P_i\)).2. Bipartite Variable Inversion: Flip \(Q\)-cycle indicators \(y_d = 1 - x'_d\) so the 5 collision cases (\(i = P_i = Q_i\), \(P_i = Q_i \neq i\), etc.) all compile into submodular \(x_c(1-y_d)\) and \(y_d(1-x_c)\) cut edges!


2. AtCoder ARC 107 FSum of Abs
#095 (Ch 12) & Syn-04 (Capstone I)
Delete a subset of vertices (paying \(A_v\)) so remaining connected components \(C\) maximize \(\sum_C |\sum_{v \in C} B_v|\) (\(N, M \le 300\)).
Absolute value \(|\sum_{v \in C} B_v|\) depends globally on component connectivity; general graphs cannot be solved by tree DP.
1. Linearizing \(|X|\): Replace \(|\sum_{v \in C} B_v|\) by choosing a uniform sign \(\sigma_v \in \{+1, -1\}\) for every vertex in \(C\).2. 3-State Split Chain: Assign each vertex \(v\) state \(\sigma_v \in \{+1, 0 (\text{deleted}), -1\}\) via a 2-node split \((v_{\text{in}}, v_{\text{out}})\), and forbid \(+1\) adjacent to \(-1\) via \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{out}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}\)!


3. AtCoder ARC 142 EPairing Wizards
#096 (Ch 12) & Syn-05 (Capstone I)
Increment \(a_i\) (+1 costs 1) so every pair \((u,v)\) satisfies \(\min(a_u,a_v) \ge \min(b_u,b_v)\) and \(\max(a_u,a_v) \ge \max(b_u,b_v)\) (\(N \le 100, b_i \le 100\)).
\(\max(a_u, a_v) \ge B\) is a logical OR constraint (\(a_u \ge B \lor a_v \ge B\)), which on a general graph is NP-hard Vertex Cover!
1. Deterministic Floor: Force \(a_u \gets \max(a_u, \min(b_u,b_v))\) immediately.2. Hidden Bipartiteness: After floor raising, if \(\max(a_u,a_v) < B = \max(b_u,b_v)\), one endpoint has \(a_u \ge b_u\) (“satisfied”) and the other has \(a_v < b_v < B\) (“unsatisfied”). Thus all OR-edges strictly cross between two disjoint vertex sets \(V_{\text{sat}}\) and \(V_{\text{unsat}}\)!


4. Codeforces 1427 GOne Billion Shades of Grey
#103 (Ch 13) & Syn-06 (Capstone I)
Fill interior cells of an \(N \times N\) grid (\(N \le 200\)) with fixed border values \(\le 10^9\) to minimize \(\sum_{(u,v) \in E} |x_u - x_v|\).
Value domain \(V_{\max} = 10^9\) makes unary chains (\(200^2 \times 10^9\) vertices) impossible by 7 orders of magnitude.
1. Coarea Decomposition: \(\sum |x_u - x_v| = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \sum |[x_u > \lambda] - [x_v > \lambda]| d\lambda\), which is constant on each interval \((v_k, v_{k+1})\) between sorted boundary values.2. Parametric Rollback: Sweep \(\lambda\) across \(4N\) boundary values, flipping one border tile from \(S\) to \(T\) by un-pushing \(\le 4\) units of flow and re-augmenting in \(O(N^3)\) total!





3.2 The Non-Graph-to-Flow Recognition Matrix
One of the hardest skills in competitive programming is recognizing a flow or min-cut problem when the English problem statement contains zero graph terminology. The table below indexes all major non-graph problem domains in our archive and shows how their algebraic structures compile into flow networks:



Non-Graph Surface Domain
Tell-Tale Algebraic / Combinatorial Clues
Canonical Archive Problems (#001–#256)
Target Compilation Paradigm




Permutations & Cycles
Choosing between \(A_i = i\) and \(A_i = P_i\); swapping elements in two permutations \(P, Q\); bounding frequency \(cnt_v\) of values in \([L_i, R_i]\).
#087 (AGC 038 F), #056 (CF 1783 F Double Sort II), #137 (CF 863 F Almost Permutation), #094 (CF 1662 J)
Cycle-level indicator variables + Bipartite Variable Inversion (Ch 11), or Cycle-Intersection MVC (Ch 07).


Number Theory (Primes, Divisibility, XOR)
Pair conflicts when \(a_i + a_j = \text{prime}\) (odd + even!); divisibility implication \(i \mid j \implies x_i \le x_j\); bitwise XOR edge sum \(\sum (a_u \oplus a_v)\); ratio \(a_i/a_j = p\) (\(\Omega(a_i)\) parity).
#004 (CF 498 C), #007 (CF 510 E), #037 (CF 808 F), #058 (P2765 魔术球), #068 (ARC 085 E MUL), #079 (CF 1473 F), #100 (BZOJ 2400), #164 (P4068)
Parity bipartite split (\(\text{odd}+\text{even}=\text{odd prime}\), Ch 05), or Divisibility Poset Closure (Ch 09).


Linear Algebra & Matrices
Bilinear form \(\max (x B x^T - x C)\); real matrix rounding preserving row/col sums; 2D XOR suffix flips; linear basis replacement \(a_i \preceq b_j\).
#071 (P3973 线性代数), #026 (POJ 2396), #032 (BZOJ 3698), #049 (P1129), #055 (CF 1592 F1), #176 (Tutte Matrix), #189 (P6621 魔法商店)
Quadratic-to-Closure reduction (Ch 09), Lower-Bound Matrix Rounding (Ch 04), or Basis Poset Isotonic Cut (Ch 24).


Strings & Substring Posets
Choosing an antichain of mutually non-substring patterns; matching dictionary words along a text with overlap \(\le k\); Hall’s condition on character masks \(2^{|\Sigma|}\).
#060 (CF 1009 G Allowed Letters), #063 (CF 590 E Birthday), #148 (CF 717 G Underfail)
Aho–Corasick Poset + Dilworth Antichain (Ch 08), or Interval Coverage Spine (Ch 19).


1D Arrays, Intervals & Linear Inequalities
\(\sum_{j: i \in [s_j, t_j]} x_j \ge a_i\); sliding window of length \(M\) has sum \(\in [L, R]\); \(L_p\) monotonicity \(b_1 \le b_2 \le \dots \le b_n\) minimizing \(\sum w_i |b_i - a_i|^p\); LIS removal.

section: 4. The 64 Quarantined Problems (R-01–R-64) — Bare Templates, Duplicate Models, and Non-Flow Traps
text:
4. The 64 Quarantined Problems (R-01–R-64) — Bare Templates, Duplicate Models, and Non-Flow Traps
To enforce the No Boilerplate Library Code and Zero Magic Gadgets mandates of our curriculum, 64 problems from the 320-problem research pool were quarantined from the primary chapter ladders (#001–#192). Every quarantined problem falls into one of three pedagogical categories:

Category Q-A — Bare Solver Templates (AGENTS.md Exclusion): The input already specifies raw directed/undirected edges, capacities, lower bounds, or costs, testing only copy-pasted Dinic, MCMF, Hopcroft–Karp, or Edmonds’ Blossom syntax with zero modelling transformation.
Category Q-B — Structural Duplicates: Classic problems whose exact English-to-graph compilation is strictly subsumed by a richer problem in #001–#256 (e.g., POJ 3041 Asteroids is an unweighted subset of UVA 11419 SAM I AM #035, which additionally requires reconstructing the König vertex cover via alternating reachability).
Category Q-C — Non-Flow Lookalike Decoys & NP-Hard Boundary Traps: Problems that either (a) were historically misclassified in flow problem sets (most notoriously the 4 non-flow problems inside Chinese 网络流 24 题) and are actually solved by Bitmask BFS/Dijkstra, Layered Shortest Path, or Dynamic Programming, or (b) cross a mathematical boundary (concave edge costs, 3D matching, non-bipartite supermodular penalties) that makes the flow compilation NP-hard.

NoteDeep-Dive Audit: Why the 4 Classic Boundary Traps (R-61 to R-64) Break Network Flow






Why Concave / Fixed-Charge Edge Costs (R-61) Fail MCMF (FM-16): Suppose transporting \(f \ge 1\) units along edge \(e\) costs \(C(f) = 100 + 2f\) (a fixed opening fee of \(100\) plus \(2\) per unit), while \(C(0) = 0\). The marginal increments are:
\[
\Delta_1 = C(1) - C(0) = 102, \qquad \Delta_2 = C(2) - C(1) = 2, \qquad \Delta_3 = 2, \dots
\]
Because \(\Delta_1 > \Delta_2\), if you place two parallel arcs \(e_1 = (\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 102)\) and \(e_2 = (\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 2)\), any shortest-path augmentation in MCMF will greedily route flow along \(e_2\) (cost \(2\)) without ever saturating \(e_1\) (cost \(102\))! Even worse, Fixed-Charge Network Flow subsumes the Directed Steiner Tree problem (send 1 unit to each terminal \(t_i\), paying \(F_e\) per used edge and \(0\) per additional unit), which is NP-hard.

When CAN a fixed setup cost be modelled? Only when it is a 0-1 decision without volume conservation, compiled as a Maximum Weight Closure (Ch 09) where selecting project \(i\) forces paying fixed cost \(F_j\) (\(i \xrightarrow{\infty} j \xrightarrow{F_j} T\), as in #069 [六省联考2017] 寿司餐厅).

Why 3-Part Chaining \(S \to X \to Y \to Z \to T\) (R-62) Fails 3D Matching (FM-03): Suppose valid triples are \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) and \((x_2, y_1, z_2)\). If you build directed edges \(x_1 \to y_1\), \(x_2 \to y_1\) and \(y_1 \to z_1\), \(y_1 \to z_2\) (even splitting \(y_{1,\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} y_{1,\text{out}}\)), a unit of flow from \(x_1\) can enter \(y_1\) and exit to \(z_2\), hallucinating the invalid triple \((x_1, y_1, z_2)\)! Flow networks are memoryless at intermediate vertices.

When CAN a 3-layer hypergraph be solved?

If every valid choice pairs one resource from \(A\) and one from \(B\) independently for a middle agent \(G\) (i.e., \(G_k\) is compatible with \(A_i\) and independently compatible with \(B_j\)), place the agent in the middle: \(A_i \to G_{k,\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} G_{k,\text{out}} \to B_j\) (#017 酒店之王).
If \(A \times B \times C \le 5000\) in a 3D grid cover, \(\min(A,B,C) \le 17\): brute-force the \(2^{\min}\) bitmask of slices in the shortest dimension and solve 2D König MVC on the other two (#052 [HNOI2013] 消毒).


Why Non-Bipartite Same-Color Penalties (R-63) Fail Min-Cut (FM-08, FM-09): Penalizing \(x_u = x_v\) (or rewarding \(x_u \neq x_v\)) has \(A = C(0,0) > 0, D = C(1,1) > 0, B = C = 0\), so \(A + D > B + C\) (strictly supermodular). On a bipartite graph \(V = L \cup R\), substituting \(y_v = 1 - x_v\) for \(v \in R\) converts \(x_u \neq x_v\) into \(x_u = y_v\) (submodular!). On a graph with an odd cycle (such as \(K_3\)), minimizing same-color edges is equivalent to Maximum Cut, which is APX-hard on general graphs (and solvable via dual matching only if planar).
Why General 2-SAT (R-64) Is Not an \(s\)-\(t\) Min-Cut (FM-25): In an \(s\)-\(t\) cut, an \(\infty\)-capacity arc \(u \xrightarrow{\infty} v\) encodes the implication \(x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1\) (equivalently \(\bar{x}_u \lor x_v\), a Horn / 2-monotone clause). A clause \((x_u \lor x_v)\) is \(\bar{x}_u \implies x_v\), which requires flipping one variable (\(y_u = 1 - x_u\)). If the clause graph of \((x_u \lor x_v)\) and \((\bar{x}_u \lor \bar{x}_v)\) is not bipartite, no global variable flip can turn all clauses into \(z_u \implies z_v\) Simultaneously! Thus pure feasibility of mixed 2-CNF clauses belongs to Tarjan SCC (2-SAT), whereas weighted optimization of 2-CNF requires the conflict graph of same-polarity clauses to be bipartite (as rescued in Flagship Benchmark #3, ARC 142 E Pairing Wizards #096).

title: Capstone II — The 320-Problem Master Archive, Quarantine Ledger & Classic 24-Problem Audit
section: 5. Complete Pedagogical Audit of the Classic Chinese “24 Network Flow Problems” (网络流 24 题)
text:
5. Complete Pedagogical Audit of the Classic Chinese “24 Network Flow Problems” (网络流 24 题)
Compiled in the early 2000s for Chinese NOI/CTSC training and hosted on LibreOJ (LOJ #6000–#6023) and Luogu, the “24 Network Flow Problems” (网络流 24 题) is the single most famous problem collection in competitive programming flow literature. However, studying the raw list in numerical order without a pedagogical map is notoriously hazardous for two reasons:

Four of the 24 Problems Are Not Network Flow Problems (FM-25): Because the list was originally assembled around “Linear Programming and Network Flow” broadly, four problems (孤岛营救问题, 汽车加油行驶问题, 软件补丁问题, and one variant slot) have zero multi-unit flow conservation and are actually solved by Bitmask 0-1 BFS, Layered Fuel-State Dijkstra, or Bitmask Shortest Path. Generations of students have wasted hours trying to force Dinic or MCMF onto bitmask state transitions!
Seven Problems Are Bare Templates or Near-Identical Clones: Problems like 分配问题 (P4014), 运输问题 (P4015), and 飞行员配对 (P2756) hand the bipartite graph directly to the solver, while 圆桌问题 (P3254) and 试题库问题 (P2763) are word-for-word isomorphic.

5.2 Forensic Deconstruction of the Non-Flow Impostors (R-51, R-52, R-53)
Why did these three problems appear in 网络流 24 题, and how do you immediately recognize in a contest that Dinic / MCMF is the wrong tool?

R-51 — Luogu P4011 孤岛营救问题 (Island Rescue, 24题 #14):

Statement: An \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 10\)) has walls, doors of types \(1 \dots P\) (\(P \le 10\)), and keys of types \(1 \dots P\) scattered on cells. Find the shortest time from \((1,1)\) to \((N,M)\).
Why Network Flow Fails: Once you pick up a key of type \(k\), you retain that key forever and can open any number of type-\(k\) doors. In a standard flow network, a unit of flow cannot “remember” which vertices it previously visited without expanding the vertex space by \(2^P\). Once you expand the state space to \((r, c, \text{mask} \in [0, 2^P))\), you only need 1 path of minimum length—which is a standard shortest-path problem, not a multi-unit flow problem!
Correct Algorithm: 0-1 BFS (or BFS) on the layered state graph \((r, c, \text{mask})\) with \(10 \times 10 \times 2^{10} \approx 10^5\) states in \(O(NM 2^P)\) time.

R-52 — Luogu P4009 汽车加油行驶问题 (Car Refueling, 24题 #13):

Statement: Drive a single car from \((1,1)\) to \((N,N)\) (\(N \le 100\)) with fuel tank capacity \(K \le 10\). Moving decreases fuel by \(1\); moving left/up costs \(B\); gas stations force refuel for \(A\); building a new station costs \(C + A\).
Why Network Flow Is Redundant Overhead: Although a single shortest path is technically a 1-unit min-cost flow (\(\text{flow} = 1\)), there are no edge capacity bottlenecks shared across multiple cars. Running SPFA/Dijkstra MCMF on \((r, c, k)\) with capacity \(1\) does the exact same work as 1 run of Dijkstra on the layered state graph \((r, c, k \in [0, K])\) with \(100 \times 100 \times 11 = 1.1 \cdot 10^5\) states!

R-53 — Luogu P2761 软件补丁问题 (Software Patches, 24题 #22):

Statement: A program has \(N \le 20\) bugs (initial mask \(2^N - 1\)). Each of \(M \le 100\) patches requires certain bugs to be present (\(B_1\)) and absent (\(B_2\)), takes time \(t_j\), and fixes subset \(F_1\) while introducing subset \(F_2\):
\[
\text{mask}_{\text{next}} = (\text{mask} \setminus F_1) \cup F_2
\]
Why Network Flow Fails: Bitwise set-union and set-difference on \(N\) coupled bits cannot be expressed as additive flow conservation \(\sum f_{\text{in}} - \sum f_{\text{out}} = 0\) on \(O(N)\) vertices. Instead, the state space is the \(2^{20} \approx 10^6\) hypercube of bug masks, solved by Dijkstra’s Algorithm on \(2^N\) states from \(\text{mask} = 2^N - 1\) to \(\text{mask} = 0\).

Look back across the twenty-four chapters of this textbook and a single unifying principle governs the transition from divisional templates to grandmaster problem solving: at the level of the ICPC World Finals, AtCoder Grand Contests (AGC), and NOI/IOI/CTT, a hard combinatorial optimization problem rarely lives inside a single chapter’s silo. Instead, a contest setter composes two to four distinct theoretical mechanisms into a single pipeline:

section: How to Use This Grand Synthesis Capstone
text:
How to Use This Grand Synthesis Capstone
To extract maximum training value from this capstone, treat every problem in Section 2 as a live 30-minute diagnostic drill before reading any callout:

Read the Untagged Statement and Constraints First: Look closely at \(N, M\), and the cost/weight structure. Ask yourself: Can a single explicit Dinic or SSP solver pass within the time limit, or do the bounds force either graph compression (\(N, M \sim 10^4\text{–}10^5\) with structured geometry/trees) or complete flow elimination (\(N \sim 2 \cdot 10^5\text{–}10^6\))?
Draft the Intermediate Algebraic Model Before Drawing Edges: Write down the indicator variables \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\), degree/flow conservation equations, or Hall deficiency inequalities on scratch paper. Identify where two chapters meet: Which part of the algebra defines the feasible domain (e.g., shortest-path DAG, perfect matching basis, matroid exchange, or circular conservation), and which part defines the objective cut or flow cost?
Open Hint 1 Only When Stuck on the Bridge: Hint 1 reveals the non-graph diagnostic signal and the specific two-chapter interface without giving away the exact edge capacities or DP transitions.
Open Hint 2 to Verify Your Interface Invariants: Hint 2 provides the algebraic-to-graph compilation blueprint and capacity/cost orientation rules.
Study the Full 4-Step Compilation & Failure-Mode Guard: Compare your scratchpad against the four-step derivation, paying special attention to the Broken Gadget Counterexample / Failure-Mode Guard and the Companion Dual-Perspective Bridge at the end of each solution.

title: Capstone I — Multi-Technique Synthesis Reserve & Dual-Perspective Bridges
text:
1. The Multi-Technique Synthesis Architecture
When two or more chapters of this textbook are composed into a single algorithm, the coupling is never arbitrary. Across modern competitive programming, multi-technique synthesis problems follow four recurring Architectural Composition Patterns:
flowchart LR
    subgraph P1["Pattern I: Structural Pre-Extraction -> Core Flow/Cut"]
        A1["Dijkstra DAG / Hopcroft-Karp Witness / XOR Basis / Kruskal Tree"] --> B1["Min-Cut / Closure / Bounded Flow / Tree DP"]
    end
    subgraph P2["Pattern II: Implicit Graph -> Range/CDQ Compression -> Solver"]
        A2["Tree Path / 1D-2D Distance / Prefix Order"] --> B2["HLD SegTree / CDQ Value Spine / 4-Sign Hubs"] --> C2["Dinic / MCMF + Residual Witness Recovery"]
    end
    subgraph P3["Pattern III: Primal Flow Model -> Convexity Proof -> Fast Elimination"]
        A3["MCMF / Hall / Cut Polynomial"] --> B3["Slopes / Unimodularity / Symmetry Invariant"] --> C3["WQS DP / Deque Greedy / Slope Trick / O(1) Formula"]
    end
    subgraph P4["Pattern IV: Level-Set Reduction -> Parallel D&C -> Closure"]
        A4["L_p Isotonic / Parametric Ratio"] --> B4["Coarea / Dinkelbach Thresholding"] --> C4["Parallel Binary Search + Project Selection"]
    end

1.1 The Four Canonical Synthesis Pipelines

Pattern I — Structural Witness Pre-Extraction \(\to\) Constrained Flow / Closure Core: Before a single flow edge can be capacities-assigned, a structural combinatorial theorem must extract a canonical backbone from the input. Examples include running Dijkstra to isolate the shortest-path DAG (Syn-08), finding a reference Perfect Matching via Hopcroft–Karp so that Hall’s condition converts set-union cardinality bounds into Project Selection implications (Syn-05), building a Kruskal Reconstruction Tree to turn min-cut/max-internal-edge cluster conditions into subtree clique counts (Syn-10), or extracting two 64-bit Gaussian XOR linear bases to define the directed matroid exchange poset (Syn-15).
Pattern II — Implicit Dense Graph \(\to\) Data-Structure Sparsification \(\to\) Witness Reconstruction: The natural bipartite or DAG model has \(O(N^2)\) or \(O(NM)\) edges, which TLEs. You insert a layer of auxiliary relay nodes—via Heavy-Light Decomposition + Segment Tree (Syn-01) or CDQ Divide-and-Conquer + coordinate-compressed value spines (Syn-11)—shrinking the edge count to \(O(M \log^2 N)\) or \(O(N \log N)\) while strictly preserving every \(S\)-\(T\) cut capacity and path cost.
Pattern III — Primal Flow Formulation \(\to\) Convexity / Symmetry Certificate \(\to\) Graph Elimination (Direction B): You first write down the exact Bipartite Matching, Bounded Circulation, or Min-Cost Flow model to prove a deep structural property—such as rotational conservation on a phantom-augmented circle (Syn-02), game-theoretic pairing gap minimization (Syn-09), unimodularity of total purchased resources (Syn-12), or concavity of the \(k\)-path objective (Syn-13, Syn-14). Armed with that theorem, you throw away the graph solver and evaluate the answer in \(O(\log M)\), \(O(N \log W)\), or \(O(N \log^2(1/\epsilon))\) via combinatorics, WQS binary search, or FIFO/LIFO deque simulation.
Pattern IV — Beyond Total Unimodularity (General LP Duality & Simplex Pivot Engine): When a problem’s constraint matrix violates Total Unimodularity (more than two non-zero entries per column without bipartite sign-flipping or interval consecutively-ones structure) and \(N, M \le 50\), you step across the boundary of network flows into the general Two-Phase Simplex Algorithm (Syn-16), seeing firsthand why TU flow networks are the ultra-fast combinatorial specialization of Linear Programming.
