Problem #030 — [Codeforces 704D] Captain America ([EN])

Judge URL: Codeforces 704D
Constraints: \(N \le 10^5\) shields on a 2D plane at integer coordinates \((x_i, y_i)\) (\(1 \le x_i, y_i \le 10^9\)). Painting a shield Red costs \(r\), and painting it Blue costs \(b\). You are given \(M \le 10^5\) constraints of two types:

1 l d: On the vertical line \(x = l\), the absolute difference between the number of Red shields and Blue shields must not exceed \(d\).
2 l d: On the horizontal line \(y = l\), the absolute difference between the number of Red shields and Blue shields must not exceed \(d\). Find the minimum total cost to paint all \(N\) shields, and print the color assignment string (r/b), or output -1 if impossible.








NoteHint 1 — Turning Absolute Difference \(|n_R - n_B| \le d\) into a Box Interval





Assume without loss of generality that \(r \le b\) (if \(r > b\), swap \(r \leftrightarrow b\) and swap output characters 'r' \(\leftrightarrow\) 'b'). Then total cost is \(N \cdot b - (b - r) \cdot (\#\text{Red})\), so minimizing cost is equivalent to maximizing the total number of Red shields! Now suppose a line \(L\) contains \(c_L\) shields in total, of which \(k_L\) are painted Red and \(c_L - k_L\) are painted Blue. Rewrite \(|k_L - (c_L - k_L)| \le d_L\) as a lower and upper bound on \(k_L\).









NoteHint 2 — Bipartite Point-as-Edge Graph & \(O((N+M)\sqrt{N})\) Complexity





Since \(|2k_L - c_L| \le d_L \iff \frac{c_L - d_L}{2} \le k_L \le \frac{c_L + d_L}{2}\) and \(k_L \in \mathbb{Z}\), we have: \[\left\lceil \frac{c_L - d_L}{2} \right\rceil \le k_L \le \left\lfloor \frac{c_L + d_L}{2} \right\rfloor.\] Model each occupied vertical line \(x\) as a left node, each occupied horizontal line \(y\) as a right node, and each shield \(i = (x_i, y_i)\) as a directed unit edge \(x_i \to y_i\) with bounds \([0, 1]\) (where flow \(1\) means Red and \(0\) means Blue). Why does Dinic run in \(O((N+M)\sqrt{N})\) even though the capacities on \(s \to x\) and \(y \to t\) can be larger than \(1\)?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Codeforces 704D






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Each shield \((x_i, y_i)\) belongs to one vertical line \(x_i\) and one horizontal line \(y_i\) (Rank-2 Factorization, Chapter 3.3). The discrepancy constraint \(|n_R - n_B| \le d\) on each line translates into a two-sided box interval on the number of Red shields on that line. With \(N, M \le 10^5\), we need Variant 3 (Max s-t Flow with Lower Bounds) on a bipartite graph where all internal edges have unit capacity \([0, 1]\).


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation

If \(r > b\), swap \(r \leftrightarrow b\) and remember to flip 'r' \(\leftrightarrow\) 'b' at the end. Now \(r \le b\), and we want to maximize \(\sum_{i=1}^N z_i\), where \(z_i \in \{0, 1\}\) indicates whether shield \(i\) is painted the cheaper color (Red).
Coordinate-compress the distinct \(x\)-coordinates and \(y\)-coordinates that actually appear among the \(N\) shields (at most \(N\) rows and \(N\) columns). Let \(c_x\) be the number of shields on vertical line \(x\), and let \(d_x\) be the minimum \(d\) among all type-1 constraints on line \(x\) (\(d_x = c_x\) if unconstrained).
On line \(x\), the number of Red shields \(k_x = \sum_{i : x_i = x} z_i\) must satisfy: \[L_x \triangleq \max\!\left(0, \left\lceil \frac{c_x - d_x}{2} \right\rceil\right) \le k_x \le \min\!\left(c_x, \left\lfloor \frac{c_x + d_x}{2} \right\rfloor\right) \triangleq R_x\] (using integer arithmetic: \(\lceil (c_x - d_x)/2 \rceil = (c_x - d_x + 1) / 2\) when \(c_x - d_x > 0\)). Similarly, on horizontal line \(y\), \(L_y \le k_y \le R_y\).

Immediate Parity / Feasibility Check: If \(L_x > R_x\) for any line \(x\) (for instance, when \(c_x\) is odd and \(d_x = 0\), giving \(\lceil c_x/2 \rceil > \lfloor c_x/2 \rfloor\)), output -1 immediately!




Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Graph Compilation)
Build a Variant 3 network with \(s\), \(t\), compressed row nodes \(\text{Row}_x\), and compressed column nodes \(\text{Col}_y\): - Add \(s \to \text{Row}_x\) with bounds \([L_x, R_x]\). - Add \(\text{Col}_y \to t\) with bounds \([L_y, R_y]\). - For each shield \(i = 1, \dots, N\), add \(\text{Row}_{x_i} \to \text{Col}_{y_i}\) with bounds \([0, 1]\), storing the reverse edge index rev_edge[i]. - Add feedback arc \(t \to s\) with \([0, \infty)\). Run Phase 1 dinic(S*, T*). If \(F_1 < \Sigma^+\), output -1. Otherwise, zero out both half-edges of \(t \to s\), run Phase 2 dinic(s, t), compute \(F_{\max} = f_0 + f_{\text{add}}\), and output minimum cost: \[\text{Cost} = F_{\max} \cdot r + (N - F_{\max}) \cdot b.\] For each shield \(i\), if edges[rev_edge[i]].cap == 1, shield \(i\) receives the cheaper color; otherwise the more expensive color.
// Core parity bound calculation for each compressed line v:
long long L_v = max(0LL, (c_v - d_v + 1) / 2);
long long R_v = min((long long)c_v, (c_v + d_v) / 2);
if (L_v > R_v) { cout << -1 << "\n"; return 0; }


Step 4: Toy Trace & Complexity Proof

Why does Dinic run in \(O(N\sqrt{N})\) on \(N = 10^5\)? Even though the boundary edges incident to \(s, t, S^*, T^*\) have capacities \(> 1\), every internal edge between the bipartite layers \(\{\text{Row}_x\}\) and \(\{\text{Col}_y\}\) has unit capacity \(1\)! Any simple path in the residual network alternates between \(\text{Row}\) and \(\text{Col}\) vertices along unit-capacity edges, so by Even–Tarjan’s Theorem (Chapter 1), Dinic terminates in \(O(E\sqrt{V}) = O(N\sqrt{N})\) time (\(\approx 80\text{ ms}\)).
Failure-Mode Guard: Ignore any constraint (type, l, d) whose line \(l\) contains zero shields (\(c_l = 0\))—allocating vertices for \(10^9\) empty coordinates or applying \((0 - d + 1)/2\) carelessly wastes memory or corrupts bounds.

NoteHint 2 — Bipartite Quota Flow & \(2^5\) Hoffman/Hall Certificate





After differencing, the intervals \(I_k = (u_{k-1}, u_k]\) are pairwise disjoint! Each interval \(I_k\) must contribute exactly \(\Delta q_k\) integers, each remainder class \(r \in \{0..4\}\) must receive exactly \(N/5\) integers, and interval \(I_k\) contains a known number \(c_{k,r}\) of integers congruent to \(r \pmod 5\). You can either run Dinic or check Hall/Hoffman’s condition across all \(2^5 = 32\) subsets of remainders!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Codeforces 628F






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Overlapping prefix sum constraints \(|S \cap [1, u_k]| = q_k\) become disjoint interval quotas \(|S \cap (u_{k-1}, u_k]| = q_k - q_{k-1}\) upon sorting and taking consecutive differences. Each chosen number belongs to one interval \(I_k\) and one remainder class \(r \in \{0..4\}\)—a Rank-2 Contingency Table with exact row sums \(\Delta q_k\), exact column sums \(N/5\), and cell bounds \([0, c_{k,r}]\).


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation

Append \((0, 0)\) and \((B, N)\) to the list of hints and sort by \(u_k\).
For each adjacent pair \((u_{k-1}, q_{k-1})\) and \((u_k, q_k)\):

If \(u_k == u_{k-1}\) and \(q_k \neq q_{k-1}\), output unfair (contradictory hints).
If \(q_k < q_{k-1}\) or \(q_k - q_{k-1} > u_k - u_{k-1}\), output unfair (negative quota or quota exceeds interval length).

For each non-empty interval \(I_k = (u_{k-1}, u_k]\) and each \(r \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\), the number of integers in \((u_{k-1}, u_k]\) congruent to \(r \pmod 5\) is: \[c_{k,r} = \text{count}(u_k, r) - \text{count}(u_{k-1}, r), \qquad \text{where } \text{count}(x, r) = \left\lfloor \frac{x + (5 - r) \bmod 5}{5} \right\rfloor.\]
We need non-negative integers \(x_{k,r} \in [0, c_{k,r}]\) such that \(\sum_{r=0}^4 x_{k,r} = \Delta q_k\) (\(\forall k\)) and \(\sum_{k} x_{k,r} = N/5\) (\(\forall r\)).



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Two Equivalent Compilations)

Method A (Flow Network): Add \(s \to I_k\) with capacity \(\Delta q_k\), \(I_k \to \text{Rem}_r\) with capacity \(c_{k,r}\), and \(\text{Rem}_r \to t\) with capacity \(N/5\). Output fair \(\iff \text{MaxFlow}(s, t) == N\).
Method B (\(O(2^5 \cdot Q)\) Closed-Form Hoffman/Hall Certificate): By Theorem 3.1 (Hoffman’s Circulation Theorem / Hall’s Marriage Theorem), since there are only \(5\) remainder vertices on the right, a flow of value \(N\) exists if and only if for every subset of remainders \(R \subseteq \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\) (\(32\) masks), the maximum capacity available to \(R\) across all intervals is at least \(|R| \cdot (N / 5)\): \[\sum_{k} \min\!\left(\Delta q_k, \sum_{r \in R} c_{k,r}\right) \ge |R| \cdot \frac{N}{5} \qquad \forall R \subseteq \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}.\]



Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(N = 5, B = 10\), and hint \((u_1, q_1) = (3, 3)\). - Intervals: \(I_1 = (0, 3]\) with \(\Delta q_1 = 3\), and \(I_2 = (3, 10]\) with \(\Delta q_2 = 2\). - Notice \(I_1 = \{1, 2, 3\}\) has zero elements congruent to \(4 \pmod 5\) or \(0 \pmod 5\), and we must pick all \(3\) elements \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) from \(I_1\). That leaves only \(\Delta q_2 = 2\) picks in \(I_2\) to cover the remaining two remainders \(\{4, 0\}\), which is feasible! Had the hint been \((3, 3)\) and \((4, 4)\), then \(\{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) would force \(4\) picks with \(0\) elements \(\equiv 0 \pmod 5\), and \(I_{\text{last}}\) has \(\Delta q = 1\), still feasible; but if \(I_1 = \{1, 6\}\) had \(2\) elements \(\equiv 1 \pmod 5\) forced, subset \(R = \{0, 2, 3, 4\}\) fails! - Complexity: \(O(Q \log Q + 32 Q)\) with Method B, or \(O(Q\sqrt{Q})\) with Dinic (\(< 10\text{ ms}\)).







Problem #032 — [BZOJ 3698] XWW 的难题 (XWW’s Puzzle — Matrix Rounding) ([ZH])

Judge URL: DarkBZOJ 3698 / Hydro BZOJ 3698
Constraints: You are given an \(N \times N\) real matrix \(A\) (\(N \le 100\)) where:

\(A_{N,N} = 0\);
For \(1 \le i \le N-1\), the last column entry \(A_{i,N} = \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} A_{i,j}\) equals the sum of the first \(N-1\) entries in row \(i\);
For \(1 \le j \le N-1\), the last row entry \(A_{N,j} = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} A_{i,j}\) equals the sum of the first \(N-1\) entries in column \(j\). You must construct an \(N \times N\) integer matrix \(B\) by rounding every entry \(A_{i,j}\) either down (\(B_{i,j} = \lfloor A_{i,j} \rfloor\)) or up (\(B_{i,j} = \lceil A_{i,j} \rceil\)) such that \(B\) still satisfies \(B_{i,N} = \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} B_{i,j}\) and \(B_{N,j} = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} B_{i,j}\). Among all valid roundings, maximize the sum of all \(N^2\) entries of \(B\) (equivalently, maximize the number of entries rounded up), or print No if impossible.








NoteHint 1 — Interpreting the Last Row and Last Column as Flow Margins





Separate the \((N-1) \times (N-1)\) interior matrix \(B_{i,j}\) (\(1 \le i, j \le N-1\)) from its row sums \(B_{i,N}\) and column sums \(B_{N,j}\). In the Rank-2 Matrix Rounding network (Section 4.1), which edges carry flow \(B_{i,j}\), which edges carry flow \(B_{i,N}\), and which edges carry flow \(B_{N,j}\)?









NoteHint 2 — The Factor-of-3 Coupling Between \(s\)-\(t\) Flow and Total Matrix Sum





Notice that for every unit of \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(|f| = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} B_{i,N} = \sum_{i,j=1}^{N-1} B_{i,j} = \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} B_{N,j}\), the total sum of all \(N^2\) entries of \(B\) is: \[\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N B_{i,j} = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} B_{i,N}}_{|f|} + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} B_{i,j}}_{|f|} + \underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{N-1} B_{N,j}}_{|f|} + B_{N,N} = 3 |f|!\] What Variant of lower-bound flow maximizes \(3 |f|\)?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — BZOJ 3698






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
We are rounding a real contingency table \(A\) to \(\lfloor A \rfloor\) or \(\lceil A \rceil\) while preserving row and column margin sums and maximizing the total rounded value. By Archetype A (Section 4.1, Baranyai’s Matrix Rounding Theorem), this compiles directly to Variant 3 (有源汇上下界最大流).


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For every entry \((i, j)\), \(B_{i,j} \in [\lfloor A_{i,j} \rfloor, \lceil A_{i,j} \rceil]\). Furthermore, the margin equations: \[B_{i,N} = \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} B_{i,j} \quad (1 \le i < N), \qquad B_{N,j} = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} B_{i,j} \quad (1 \le j < N)\] mean that the net \(s\)-\(t\) flow value \(|f| = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} B_{i,N}\) simultaneously equals the sum of all interior cells and the sum of all column margins. Therefore, the sum of all \(N^2\) entries in \(B\) is identically \(3 |f|\)! Maximizing \(\sum_{i,j} B_{i,j}\) (or maximizing the number of entries rounded up beyond \(\lfloor A_{i,j} \rfloor\)) is 100% equivalent to maximizing the \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(|f|\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Graph Compilation)
Build a Variant 3 network with \(s\), \(t\), row vertices \(R_1 \dots R_{N-1}\), and column vertices \(C_1 \dots C_{N-1}\): 1. For \(1 \le i \le N-1\): add \(s \to R_i\) with \([l, u] = [\lfloor A_{i,N} \rfloor, \lceil A_{i,N} \rceil]\). 2. For \(1 \le j \le N-1\): add \(C_j \to t\) with \([l, u] = [\lfloor A_{N,j} \rfloor, \lceil A_{N,j} \rceil]\). 3. For \(1 \le i, j \le N-1\): add \(R_i \to C_j\) with \([l, u] = [\lfloor A_{i,j} \rfloor, \lceil A_{i,j} \rceil]\). 4. Add feedback arc \(t \to s\) with \([0, \infty)\). Run Phase 1 dinic(S*, T*). If \(F_1 < \Sigma^+\), output No (in case the input floats violate exact sum conservation). Otherwise, zero out \(t \to s\), run Phase 2 dinic(s, t) to obtain \(F_{\max} = f_0 + f_{\text{add}}\), and output \(3 \cdot F_{\max}\) (or if the problem variant asks for the sum of fractional parts rounded up, \(3 \cdot F_{\max} - \sum_{i,j} \lfloor A_{i,j} \rfloor\)).


Step 4: Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Consider \(N = 3\) with a \(2 \times 2\) interior of all \(0.5\)s: \[A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 & 1.0 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 & 1.0 \\ 1.0 & 1.0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\] - Row/col margin bounds are \([1, 1]\) on \(s \to R_i\) and \(C_j \to t\); interior cell bounds are \([0, 1]\) on \(R_i \to C_j\). - Phase 1 saturates \(\Sigma^+ = 2\) with \(f_0 = 2\), and Phase 2 adds \(0\), giving \(F_{\max} = 2\) and total matrix sum \(3 \cdot F_{\max} = 6\) (two \(1\)s in the interior, two \(1\)s in the last column, two \(1\)s in the last row). - Floating-Point Guard: Read floating-point numbers with eps = 1e-8 when computing floor(x + eps) and ceil(x - eps) so that exact integers like 1.000000 do not get rounded to \([0, 1]\) or \([1, 2]\) due to IEEE-754 representation noise! - Complexity: \(|V| = 2N + 2 \le 202\), \(|E| = O(N^2) \le 10^4\); Dinic runs in \(O(N^3)\) time (\(< 5\text{ ms}\)).

8. Quarantined Template Problems, Chapter Summary & Multilingual References

8.1 Quarantined Pure-Template Verification Benchmarks
To keep our 8-problem practice ladder focused on genuine modelling and structural insights, pure bare-metal implementation drills are quarantined in the table below for rapid template testing:



Benchmark ID
Judge & Title
Variant Tested & Verification Purpose




T-04.1
LOJ #115 — 无源汇有上下界可行流
Direct verification of BoundedFlow::solve_circulation() and get_edge_flow(k) (Variant 1).


T-04.2
LOJ #116 — 有源汇有上下界最大流
Direct verification of BoundedFlow::solve_st_flow(s, t, +1) (Variant 3).


T-04.3
LOJ #117 — 有源汇有上下界最小流
Direct verification of BoundedFlow::solve_st_flow(s, t, -1) (Variant 4).






8.2 Chapter Revision Summary

The Affine Slack Shift: Substituting \(f(e) = l(e) + \tilde{f}(e)\) converts \(l(e) \le f(e) \le u(e)\) and \(\text{div}_f(v) = b(v)\) into standard box bounds \(0 \le \tilde{f}(e) \le u(e) - l(e)\) with nodal divergence \(\text{div}_{\tilde{f}}(v) = M(v) \triangleq \text{in}_l(v) - \text{out}_l(v) - b(v)\).
The Four Variants of 上下界网络流:

Variant 1 (Feasible Circulation): Saturate \(S^* \to T^*\) (\(\text{MaxFlow}(S^*, T^*) = \Sigma^+\)).
Variant 2 (Feasible \(s\)-\(t\) Flow): Add feedback arc \(t \xrightarrow{[0, \infty)} s\) and run Variant 1; initial flow is \(f_0 = \tilde{f}(t \to s)\).
Variant 3 (Maximum \(s\)-\(t\) Flow): Run Variant 2, zero out \(t \to s\) and \(s \to t\), and compute \(F_{\max} = f_0 + \text{MaxFlow}(s, t)\).
Variant 4 (Minimum \(s\)-\(t\) Flow): Run Variant 2, zero out \(t \to s\) and \(s \to t\), and peel back excess flow via \(F_{\min} = f_0 - \text{MaxFlow}(t, s)\).

Hoffman’s Circulation Theorem (1960): A circulation exists \(\iff \sum_{e \in \delta^-(X)} l(e) \le \sum_{e \in \delta^+(X)} u(e)\) for all \(X \subseteq V\), proved via the exact cut identity \(\Sigma^+ - \kappa_{\tilde{\mathcal{N}}}(S^* \sqcup X) = \sum_{e \in \delta^-(X)} l(e) - \sum_{e \in \delta^+(X)} u(e)\). When Phase 1 fails, \(X^* = S_{\min}^* \setminus \{S^*\}\) is the maximum-violation witness subset.
Canonical Non-Graph Compilations: Contingency-table / real-matrix rounding (Baranyai's Theorem), mixed-graph Eulerian circuit orientation (parity + half-discrepancy flow), and minimum-fleet mandatory DAG edge/vertex covers (Variant 4).




8.3 Multilingual Bibliography ([EN], [ZH], [JA])

[EN] Hoffman, A. J. (1960). Some recent applications of the theory of linear inequalities to extremal combinatorial analysis. In Proceedings of Symposia in Applied Mathematics (Vol. 10, pp. 113–127). American Mathematical Society. (Original proof of Hoffman’s Circulation Theorem.)
[EN] Baranyai, Z. (1975). On the factorization of the complete uniform hypergraph. Infinite and Finite Sets, 91–108. (Introduces the matrix rounding lemma via integral bounded circulations.)
[EN] Schrijver, A. (2003). Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency (Vol. A, Chapters 11–12: Circulations, Hoffman’s Theorem, and Matrix Rounding). Springer.
[ZH] 刘汝佳, 陈锋 (2012). 《算法竞赛入门经典：训练指南》 (Chapter 6: 上下界网络流与混合图欧拉回路). 清华大学出版社.
[ZH] OI-Wiki. 上下界网络流 (Flows with Lower and Upper Bounds). https://oi-wiki.org/graph/flow/bound/ (Standard Chinese competitive programming reference for Variants 1–4).

text:
NotePrerequisites



Before studying this chapter, you should be fluent in:

Chapter 1–2 (Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality & Residual Graphs): Forward vs. backward residual arcs, \(s\)-\(t\) cut reachability \(V_S\) and \(V_T^{\text{rev}}\), and Tarjan’s Strongly Connected Components (SCC) algorithm on residual graphs.
Chapter 5 (Bipartite Matching, König’s Theorem & Minimum Vertex Cover): Unit-capacity bipartite networks \(s \to L \to R \to t\), Hopcroft–Karp \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) complexity, König’s identity \(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\), and Maximum Weight Independent Set \(\alpha_w(G) = \sum_{v \in V} w_v - \text{MinCut}(s, t)\).









TipLearning Objectives



By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Compile Non-Graph Problems into Bipartite Networks: Uncover hidden bipartitions in 2D/3D grids, arithmetic conflict sets, and geometric point clouds using chessboard parity \((r+c) \bmod 2\), leaper parity, 2-adic Euclidean distance valuations (AtCoder AGC 025 D), prime-sum parity (CF 808 F), popcount parity \(\operatorname{popcount}(x) \bmod 2\), maximal obstacle-split strips (POJ 2226, [HEOI2016] 游戏, ABC 274 G), and shared-border dualization (CF 1404 E).
Construct the Canonical Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) Decomposition: Partition any bipartite graph into its coarse \(V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\) vertex blocks (or six-block oriented refinement \(L_1 \sqcup L_0 \sqcup L_2\) and \(R_1 \sqcup R_0 \sqcup R_2\)) and fine SCC blocks in \(O(V + E)\) time after a single maximum matching run.
Classify Vertices and Edges Across All Maximum Matchings: Determine in \(O(V + E)\) time which vertices are essential (in every maximum matching) vs. avoidable (omitted by at least one maximum matching), and which edges are mandatory/\(\nu\)-critical ([HAOI2017] 新型城市化), admissible, or forbidden.
Solve Impartial Token Walk Games on Bipartite Graphs: Prove and apply the theorem that a starting vertex \(v_0\) is winning for the first mover if and only if \(v_0 \in V_O \cup V_U\) belongs to every maximum matching ([JSOI2009] 游戏, [NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏), while avoiding the \(O(V \cdot E\sqrt{V})\) per-vertex rematching TLE trap.

title: Chapter 6 — Hidden Bipartitions, Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition, and Matching Games
section: 1. Motivation: Finding Bipartite Structure in Grids, Number Theory, and Impartial Games
text:
1. Motivation: Finding Bipartite Structure in Grids, Number Theory, and Impartial Games
In Chapter 5, the bipartite conflict or incidence graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) was handed to us explicitly, or emerged directly from a two-sided matching narrative (workers vs. tasks, boys vs. girls). In advanced competitive programming, however, the hardest bipartite matching problems never mention a bipartite graph in the problem statement. Instead, they present:

A geometric or grid packing puzzle: “Place the maximum number of non-attacking knights or bombs on a board with walls” (Luogu P3355, [HEOI2016] 游戏), “Tile all black cells with the minimum number of \(1 \times k\) or \(k \times 1\) bricks” (CF 1404 E), or “Select \(N^2\) grid points from a \(2N \times 2N\) lattice so that no two selected points lie at Euclidean distance \(\sqrt{D_1}\) or \(\sqrt{D_2}\)” (AGC 025 D).
An arithmetic subset-selection problem: “Choose a maximum-weight subset of integers such that no two chosen integers sum to a prime number” (CF 808 F) or “differ in a single bit” (Hamming cube games).
A universal quantifier over all optimal matchings or an impartial two-player game: “Which edges, if deleted, strictly shrink the maximum matching?” ([HAOI2017] 新型城市化), or “Two players alternately slide a token or blank tile across a grid to unvisited squares; find every winning starting square or every blunder in a recorded game log” ([JSOI2009] 游戏, [NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏).

On general graphs, Maximum Independent Set (MIS) is NP-hard, and testing whether a vertex belongs to every maximum matching or whether a game position is winning requires Edmonds’ Blossom algorithm and the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition. Yet whenever a hidden invariant forces every conflict edge to cross a binary partition \(V = L \sqcup R\), or splits each 2D constraint into a rank-2 incidence between a horizontal object and a vertical object, the problem collapses into polynomial time.
Moreover, once a bipartite graph is solved via Dinic or Hopcroft–Karp, its residual network \(G_{f^*}\) encodes every maximum matching and every minimum vertex cover simultaneously. The Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) Decomposition (Dulmage & Mendelsohn, 1958; Gallai, 1963) extracts this complete structural map in a single \(O(V + E)\) breadth-first search and Tarjan SCC pass—turning quantifier queries and impartial game analyses into linear-time post-processing.

section: 2. The Hidden Bipartition Compiler: Chessboard Parity, Prime Sums, Popcount, and Obstacle-Split Segments
text:
2. The Hidden Bipartition Compiler: Chessboard Parity, Prime Sums, Popcount, and Obstacle-Split Segments
To adhere to the Zero Magic Gadgets Mandate, we first systematize how non-graph problem statements compile into bipartite graphs \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) before any flow network is drawn.

2.1 Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Whenever a problem asks to maximize selected items without pairwise conflicts (Independent Set), minimize covering primitives (Vertex Cover), or pack non-overlapping pairs (Matching) under \(N, M \le 200\) (or \(V \le 5 \cdot 10^4\)), test for two canonical bipartite signatures:

Signature A — Parity-Flipping Binary Conflicts (Vertices \(=\) Elements, Edges \(=\) Conflicts): Every forbidden pair \(\{u, v\} \in E\) changes a binary valuation \(\phi: V \to \{0, 1\}\), i.e., \(\phi(u) \ne \phi(v)\). Because no edge can connect two vertices of the same color \(\phi\), odd cycles are impossible and \(G\) is bipartite with \(L = \phi^{-1}(0)\) and \(R = \phi^{-1}(1)\).
Signature B — Orthogonal Rank-2 Incidence (Edges \(=\) Grid Cells, Vertices \(=\) Maximal Strips): Every target cell or choice \((r, c)\) lies at the intersection of exactly two covering primitives—one horizontal (\(H \in L\)) and one vertical (\(V \in R\)).

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                   THE HIDDEN BIPARTITION COMPILER: TWO CANONICAL PIPELINES                        |
|                                                                                                   |
|  PIPELINE A: PARITY-FLIPPING CONFLICT GRAPH        PIPELINE B: ORTHOGONAL STRIP INCIDENCE         |
|  (Vertices = Objects, Edges = Forbidden Pairs)     (Vertices = Maximal Strips, Edges = Cells)     |
|                                                                                                   |
|   * Grid step / Knight jump: (r + c) mod 2          * Standard Grid: Row r in L, Col c in R       |
|   * Euclidean dist D = 4^k m: 2-adic coloring       * Hard walls '#': Split rows/cols at '#'      |
|   * Prime sum a_i + a_j in P: a_i mod 2               into maximal segments H_a in L, V_b in R    |
|     (Deduplicate 1 + 1 = 2 first!)                  * Soft obstacles 'x': Do NOT split strips,    |
|   * Bit-flip / Hamming dist: popcount(x) mod 2        but omit edge (H_a, V_b) at 'x'!            |
|   * Shared-border bricks: Horiz in L, Vert in R     * Discretized 10^9 rects: Elementary strips   |
|                                                                                                   |
|   Target: Bipartite MIS alpha(G) = |V| - nu(G)      Target: Max Matching nu(G) or MVC tau(G)      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+



2.2 Step 2 & Step 3 — Algebraic Parity & 2-Adic Valuation Colorings
Suppose we must choose a maximum-weight conflict-free subset \(I \subseteq V\), modeled by indicator variables \(x_u \in \{0, 1\}\) with pairwise conflict constraints \(x_u + x_v \le 1\) for \((u, v) \in E\). To compile this into a bipartite minimum cut (Chapter 5), we must exhibit an explicit 2-coloring \(\phi: V \to \{0, 1\}\) such that \((u, v) \in E \implies \phi(u) \ne \phi(v)\).

1. Chessboard Parity \((r + c) \bmod 2\) and Generalized \((p, q)\)-Leapers
On a 2D integer grid, let a move vector be \((\Delta r, \Delta c)\).

Orthogonal Grid Steps (\(|\Delta r| + |\Delta c| = 1\)): Every step changes \(r + c\) by \(\pm 1\), flipping \(\phi(r, c) = (r + c) \bmod 2\). Thus any subgraph of the 4-connected grid is bipartite.
Standard Knight Moves (\(\{|\Delta r|, |\Delta c|\} = \{1, 2\}\), Luogu P3355): Since \(\pm 1 \pm 2 \in \{\pm 1, \pm 3\}\) is always odd, \(\Delta(r + c) \equiv 1 \pmod 2\). Every knight attack connects a Black square (\(\phi = 1\)) to a White square (\(\phi = 0\)).
Generalized \((p, q)\)-Leapers (Luogu P5030 — Giraffe Placement): Suppose pieces jump by \((\pm p, \pm q)\) or \((\pm q, \pm p)\). Let \(g = \gcd(p, q)\):

First decouple the grid into \(g^2\) independent sublattices by residue classes \((r \bmod g, c \bmod g)\), replacing \((r, c) \gets (\lfloor r/g \rfloor, \lfloor c/g \rfloor)\) and \((p', q') = (p/g, q/g)\) with \(\gcd(p', q') = 1\).
Case 1 (\(p' + q'\) is odd): One of \(p', q'\) is odd and the other is even. Then \(\Delta(r' + c') \equiv p' + q' \equiv 1 \pmod 2\), so \(\phi(r', c') = (r' + c') \bmod 2\) is a valid 2-coloring!
Case 2 (\(p'\) and \(q'\) are both odd, e.g., \((1, 3)\)-Giraffes in Luogu P5030): Here \(p' + q'\) is even, so chessboard coloring \((r' + c') \bmod 2\) fails (every jump stays on the same chessboard color!). However, because \(\Delta r' \in \{\pm p', \pm q'\}\) is always odd, the row parity \(\phi(r', c') = r' \bmod 2\) (or column parity \(c' \bmod 2\)) strictly flips on every jump!




2. Two-Grid-Coloring at Euclidean Distances \(D_1, D_2\) via 2-Adic Valuation (AtCoder AGC 025 D)
In AtCoder AGC 025 D — Choosing Points, we are given a \(2N \times 2N\) grid of \(4N^2\) points (\(N \le 300\)) and two squared distances \(D_1, D_2 \le 2 \cdot 10^5\). We must select \(N^2\) points such that no two selected points lie at squared Euclidean distance \(D_1\) or \(D_2\). Why does no flow solver even need to be called? Because every Euclidean distance graph on \(\mathbb{Z}^2\) is bipartite!

Theorem 1 (Theorem 2.1 (Universal Bipartiteness of Lattice Distance Graphs \(G_D\))) For any integer \(D \ge 1\), let \(G_D = (\mathbb{Z}^2, E_D)\) have an edge between \(\mathbf{p} = (x_1, y_1)\) and \(\mathbf{q} = (x_2, y_2)\) if and only if \((x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2 = D\). Then \(G_D\) is bipartite, and an explicit \(O(1)\)-time 2-coloring \(\phi_D: \mathbb{Z}^2 \to \{0, 1\}\) is constructed from the 2-adic valuation of \(D\): Write \(D = 4^k m\) where \(k \ge 0\) and \(4 \nmid m\) (by repeatedly dividing \(D\) by \(4\) while \(D \equiv 0 \pmod 4\)). Define rescaled coordinates \((x', y') = (\lfloor x / 2^k \rfloor, \lfloor y / 2^k \rfloor)\). Then:
\[
\phi_D(x, y) = \begin{cases}
(x' + y') \bmod 2 & \text{if } m \equiv 1 \text{ or } 3 \pmod 4 \quad (m \text{ is odd}), \\
x' \bmod 2 & \text{if } m \equiv 2 \pmod 4.
\end{cases}
\]


Proof. Let \(\Delta x = x_1 - x_2\) and \(\Delta y = y_1 - y_2\) satisfy \((\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2 = D = 4^k m\). Recall that for any integer \(z\), \(z^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4\) if \(z\) is even, and \(z^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4\) if \(z\) is odd. If \(k \ge 1\), then \((\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4\). Since the sum of two values in \(\{0, 1\}\) is \(0 \pmod 4\) only when both are \(0\), both \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) must be even. Dividing by \(2\) gives \((\Delta x / 2)^2 + (\Delta y / 2)^2 = 4^{k-1} m\). By induction on \(k\), both \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) are multiples of \(2^k\)!
Consequently, any two points \(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}\) connected by an edge in \(G_D\) satisfy \(x_1 \equiv x_2 \pmod{2^k}\) and \(y_1 \equiv y_2 \pmod{2^k}\), meaning their rescaled differences \(\Delta x' = \Delta x / 2^k = x'_1 - x'_2\) and \(\Delta y' = \Delta y / 2^k = y'_1 - y'_2\) are exact integers satisfying \((\Delta x')^2 + (\Delta y')^2 = m\) with \(4 \nmid m\):

Case 1 (\(m \equiv 1, 3 \pmod 4\), i.e., \(m\) is odd): Since \((\Delta x')^2 + (\Delta y')^2 = m\) is odd, one of \(\Delta x', \Delta y'\) is odd and the other is even. Thus \(\Delta x' + \Delta y' = (x'_1 + y'_1) - (x'_2 + y'_2)\) is odd, so \(\phi_D(x_1, y_1) \ne \phi_D(x_2, y_2)\).
Case 2 (\(m \equiv 2 \pmod 4\)): Since \((\Delta x')^2 + (\Delta y')^2 \equiv 2 \pmod 4\), both \((\Delta x')^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4\) and \((\Delta y')^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4\). Hence \(\Delta x' = x'_1 - x'_2\) is odd, so \(x'_1 \bmod 2 \ne x'_2 \bmod 2\) and \(\phi_D(x_1, y_1) \ne \phi_D(x_2, y_2)\). \(\square\)


In AGC 025 D, assigning each of the \(4N^2\) grid points the combined 4-color label \(c(x, y) = (\phi_{D_1}(x, y), \phi_{D_2}(x, y)) \in \{0, 1\}^2\) partitions the \(4N^2\) vertices into \(4\) color classes, each of which is an independent set in \(G_{D_1} \cup G_{D_2}\). By the Pigeonhole Principle, the largest color class has size \(\ge 4N^2 / 4 = N^2\), solving the problem in \(O(N^2)\) time!


3. Prime-Sum Parity (CF 510 E, CF 808 F) & Popcount / Arithmetic Parities
When conflicts arise from number-theoretic or bitwise predicates on integers, three universal bipartitions recur across contests:

Prime Sums \(a_i + a_j \in \mathbb{P}\) (CF 510 E — Fox And Dinner, CF 808 F — Card Game): Every prime number \(p > 2\) is odd. Since \(a_i + a_j\) is odd if and only if one number is odd and the other is even, all prime-sum edges with \(a_i + a_j > 2\) strictly cross the parity bipartition \(L = \{i : a_i \text{ is odd}\}\) and \(R = \{j : a_j \text{ is even}\}\).

The 1 + 1 = 2 Clique Trap: The number \(2\) is the unique even prime! For positive integers \(a_i, a_j \ge 1\), \(a_i + a_j = 2 \iff a_i = a_j = 1\). Thus multiple 1s in the input form a complete clique inside \(L\) (destroying bipartiteness!). In Maximum Independent Set problems (CF 808 F), you can select at most one 1—so simply discard all 1s except the single 1 with the maximum weight/power before building the bipartite graph!

Popcount Parity \(\operatorname{popcount}(x) \bmod 2\) (Hamming Cube \(Q_d\) & Bit-Flip Games): If two bitmasks \(x, y \in \{0, 1\}^d\) are adjacent whenever they differ in an odd number of bits (\(\operatorname{popcount}(x \oplus y) \equiv 1 \pmod 2\), such as single-bit flips \(x \oplus y = 2^k\)), then since \(\operatorname{popcount}(x \oplus y) \equiv \operatorname{popcount}(x) + \operatorname{popcount}(y) \pmod 2\), coloring by \(\phi(x) = \operatorname{popcount}(x) \bmod 2\) makes the graph bipartite.
Power-of-2 Sums \(a_i + a_j = 2^k\) & Primitive Pythagorean Pairs (\(a_i^2 + a_j^2 = c^2, \gcd(a_i, a_j) = 1\)):

For primitive Pythagorean legs, two odd numbers satisfy \(a_i^2 + a_j^2 \equiv 1 + 1 = 2 \pmod 4\) (never a square \(c^2\)), and two even numbers violate \(\gcd(a_i, a_j) = 1\); thus \(\phi(a_i) = a_i \bmod 2\) is a valid bipartition.
For distinct positive integers with \(a_i + a_j = 2^k\), every integer \(y\) has at most one smaller neighbor \(x = 2^{\lfloor \log_2 y \rfloor + 1} - y < y\), so the conflict graph on distinct integers is a forest (hence bipartite, 2-colorable via \(v_2(a_i)\) and \(((a_i / 2^{v_2(a_i)}) - 1)/2 \bmod 2\)).






2.3 Step 2 & Step 3 — Obstacle-Split Maximal Segments & Boundary Dualization
When a 2D grid problem does not involve parity jumps, it almost always compiles via Maximal Strip Incidence or Shared-Border Dualization.

1. Obstacle-Split Maximal Horizontal & Vertical Segments (POJ 2226, [HEOI2016] 游戏, ABC 274 G)
Suppose a grid of size \(N \times M\) contains three types of cells:

Target / Empty Cells (. or *): Where rooks/bombs can be placed, or mud must be covered by planks/cameras.
Soft Obstacles (x): Cannot hold a bomb or do not need to be covered, but blasts/planks/camera rays pass straight through them.
Hard Obstacles (#): Impenetrable walls that block blasts, planks, or camera rays.

Step 2 (Algebraic Formulation): A hard wall # cuts a row or column into independent line-of-sight intervals. Define:

\(\mathcal{H} = \{H_1, H_2, \dots, H_p\}\): the set of maximal contiguous #-free horizontal segments across all rows (each segment is broken only by # or the grid boundary, never by x).
\(\mathcal{V} = \{V_1, V_2, \dots, V_q\}\): the set of maximal contiguous #-free vertical segments across all columns.

Every target cell \((r, c)\) (where grid[r][c] is a target cell, excluding both # and x) belongs to a unique horizontal segment \(H(r, c) \in \mathcal{H}\) and a unique vertical segment \(V(r, c) \in \mathcal{V}\):

Pack Non-Attacking Bombs ([HEOI2016] 游戏, Problem #041): Select maximum target cells \((r, c)\) such that each \(H_a \in \mathcal{H}\) and each \(V_b \in \mathcal{V}\) contains at most one bomb \(\iff\) Maximum Bipartite Matching \(\nu(G)\) where each target cell \((r, c)\) is a directed edge \(H(r, c) \to V(r, c)\)!
Cover All Target Cells with Minimum Planks / Cameras (POJ 2226 — Muddy Fields, AtCoder ABC 274 G — Security Camera 3): Assign binary indicators \(x_a \in \{0, 1\}\) to each horizontal strip \(H_a \in \mathcal{H}\) and \(y_b \in \{0, 1\}\) to each vertical strip \(V_b \in \mathcal{V}\) such that every target cell \((r, c)\) satisfies \(x_{H(r,c)} + y_{V(r,c)} \ge 1\). By König’s Theorem, \(\min \sum x_a + \sum y_b = \tau(G) = \nu(G)\)!



2. Shared-Border Dualization (CF 1404 E — Bricks)
In CF 1404 E — Bricks, we must partition all black # cells of an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 200\)) into the minimum number of non-overlapping \(1 \times k\) or \(k \times 1\) bricks.
Step 2 (Algebraic Formulation via Unit-Border Merges): Start with every black # cell as an isolated \(1 \times 1\) brick, giving \(|\#|\) initial bricks. Whenever we merge two adjacent # cells across their shared unit grid border, the total number of bricks decreases by \(1\):
\[
\min (\text{Number of Bricks}) = |\#| - \max (\text{Number of Valid Unit-Border Merges}).
\]
Let \(L\) be the set of all horizontal unit merges \(h_{r,c}\) (merging # at \((r, c)\) with # at \((r, c+1)\)), and let \(R\) be the set of all vertical unit merges \(v_{r,c}\) (merging # at \((r, c)\) with # at \((r+1, c)\)). When is a subset of merges valid (forming only \(1 \times k\) and \(k \times 1\) bricks)? If and only if no black cell \((r, c)\) participates in both a horizontal merge and a vertical merge (which would create a forbidden L-tromino corner)!
Step 3 (Graph Compilation): Create one left vertex for each \(h_{r,c} \in L\) and one right vertex for each \(v_{r,c} \in R\). For each black cell \((r, c)\), add a conflict edge between every horizontal merge touching \((r, c)\) (\(h_{r,c-1}\) and \(h_{r,c}\)) and every vertical merge touching \((r, c)\) (\(v_{r-1,c}\) and \(v_{r,c}\)). By König’s Theorem, the maximum number of non-conflicting merges is the Bipartite Maximum Independent Set \(\alpha(G) = |L| + |R| - \nu(G)\), so the minimum number of bricks is:
\[
\text{Ans} = |\#| - \big( |L| + |R| - \nu(G) \big).
\]




2.4 Step 4 — Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Counterexamples
Let us trace CF 1404 E — Bricks on a \(2 \times 2\) L-shaped black tromino: cells \((1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1)\) are # (\(|\#| = 3\)), and \((2, 2)\) is ..

There is \(|L| = 1\) horizontal merge \(h_{1,1}\) (joining \((1,1) \leftrightarrow (1,2)\)) and \(|R| = 1\) vertical merge \(v_{1,1}\) (joining \((1,1) \leftrightarrow (2,1)\)).
Both \(h_{1,1}\) and \(v_{1,1}\) touch corner cell \((1, 1)\), inducing the single conflict edge \((h_{1,1}, v_{1,1})\).
Thus \(\nu(G) = 1\), \(\alpha(G) = 1 + 1 - 1 = 1\), and \(\min(\text{Bricks}) = 3 - 1 = 2\) (either one \(1 \times 2\) brick plus one \(1 \times 1\) brick, or one \(2 \times 1\) brick plus one \(1 \times 1\) brick).







WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexamples FM-06A — Three Classic Grid Compilation Traps




Trap 1: Splitting Strips at Soft Obstacles x or Adding Edges at x ([HEOI2016] 游戏): If you split horizontal/vertical segments at soft obstacles x, two bombs placed on the same row on opposite sides of x get assigned different horizontal IDs \(H_1 \ne H_2\) and blast each other! Conversely, if you add an edge \((H(r,c), V(r,c))\) when (r, c) == 'x', Dinic will place a bomb on a forbidden soft obstacle. Rule: Hard walls # split segment IDs; soft walls x neither split segment IDs nor generate edges.
Trap 2: Making Cells Vertices Instead of Shared Borders (CF 1404 E — Bricks): If you put # cells as vertices and try to match pairs of adjacent cells, a \(1 \times 3\) brick covers 3 cells (which cannot be represented by a matching of size-2 edges!). Making shared unit borders the vertices reduces a \(1 \times k\) brick to \(k - 1\) independent horizontal merges that have zero conflicts with one another.
Trap 3: Coupled Row–Column Permutations ([ZJOI2007] 矩阵游戏 vs. Matrix Conjugation): Swapping rows \(\sigma \in S_N\) and columns \(\tau \in S_N\) independently to put \(1\)s on the main diagonal is equivalent to finding a perfect matching \(\nu(G) = N\). However, if a problem requires the same permutation \(\sigma = \tau\) on both rows and columns (\(P A P^T\)), the diagonal entries \(A_{\sigma(i), \sigma(i)}\) are merely permuted among themselves! On \(A = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}\), \(\nu(G) = 2\), yet coupled swaps leave the diagonal \((0, 0)\) forever.

section: 3. Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) Coarse & Fine Decomposition (\(V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\))
text:
3. Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) Coarse & Fine Decomposition (\(V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\))
A single run of Dinic’s or Hopcroft–Karp’s algorithm returns one maximum matching \(M^*\) of size \(\nu(G)\). Yet contest problems frequently ask quantified structural questions over the space \(\mathcal{M}^*(G)\) of all maximum matchings and the space \(\mathcal{C}^*(G)\) of all minimum vertex covers.

3.1 Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Reach for the Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) Decomposition whenever you see:

Universal or Existential Vertex Quantifiers: “Which vertices belong to every maximum matching?”, “Which vertices can be left unmatched in at least one maximum matching?”, or “Which vertices belong to every minimum vertex cover?”
Edge Criticality & Admissibility ([HAOI2017] 新型城市化): “Find all edges \(e \in E\) whose removal strictly decreases \(\nu(G)\) (or strictly increases \(\alpha(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\))”, or “Classify each edge as appearing in all, some, or no maximum matchings.”
Why Naive Re-Solving Fails (FM-06B): Deleting each vertex \(v \in V\) or edge \(e \in E\) one by one and re-running Dinic costs \(O(V \cdot E\sqrt{V})\) or \(O(E^2\sqrt{V})\), which TLEs for \(V \ge 2000, E \ge 10^4\). The DM decomposition answers all vertex and edge queries in \(O(V + E)\) total time after a single maximum flow computation.




3.2 Step 2 & Step 3 — Coarse DM Partition (\(V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\)) and Canonical Invariance
Let \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) be a bipartite graph, and let \(M^*\) be any fixed maximum matching found by Dinic on the standard unit network \(N\) (\(s \xrightarrow{1} u \xrightarrow{\infty} v \xrightarrow{1} t\) for \(u \in L, v \in R\)). Let \(U_L = L \setminus V(M^*)\) and \(U_R = R \setminus V(M^*)\) be the sets of unmatched vertices in \(L\) and \(R\).
An \(M^*\)-alternating path from \(U = U_L \cup U_R\) is a path that starts at an unmatched vertex \(u_0 \in U\) and alternates between unmatched edges in \(E \setminus M^*\) and matched edges in \(M^*\).

1. Equivalence of Alternating Parity (\(V_E, V_O, V_U\)) and Residual \(s\)-\(t\) Reachability (\(V_S, V_T^{\text{rev}}\))
In the residual network \(G_{f^*}\) of \(N\):

An unmatched left vertex \(u_0 \in U_L\) has residual arc \(s \to u_0\) of capacity \(1\). Moving from \(L\) to \(R\) traverses an unmatched edge \((u, v) \in E \setminus M^*\) (odd step from \(U_L\)), and moving from \(R\) back to \(L\) traverses a reversed matched edge \((v, u)\) with \((u, v) \in M^*\) (even step from \(U_L\)).
Symmetrically, an unmatched right vertex \(v_0 \in U_R\) has residual arc \(v_0 \to t\) of capacity \(1\). Tracing residual arcs backward from \(t\) moves from \(R\) to \(L\) along unmatched edges \((u, v) \in E \setminus M^*\) (odd step from \(U_R\)) and from \(L\) to \(R\) along matched edges \((u, v) \in M^*\) (even step from \(U_R\)).

Because \(M^*\) is maximum, there is no augmenting path from \(U_L\) to \(U_R\) (\(V_S \cap V_T^{\text{rev}} = \emptyset\)). This induces both the six-block oriented DM partition \((L_1 \sqcup L_0 \sqcup L_2, R_1 \sqcup R_0 \sqcup R_2)\) and the three-block parity DM partition \(V = V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\) (Dulmage & Mendelsohn, 1958; Lovász & Plummer, 1986):
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_1 &= L \cap V_S, & R_1 &= R \cap V_S \qquad &&(\text{Forward reachable from } s \text{ in } G_{f^*}), \\
L_2 &= L \cap V_T^{\text{rev}}, & R_2 &= R \cap V_T^{\text{rev}} \qquad &&(\text{Can reach } t \text{ in } G_{f^*}, \text{ i.e., backward reachable from } t), \\
L_0 &= L \setminus (V_S \cup V_T^{\text{rev}}), & R_0 &= R \setminus (V_S \cup V_T^{\text{rev}}) \qquad &&(\text{Unreachable residual core}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Grouping across both sides by the parity of the alternating distance from \(U_L \cup U_R\) gives:

\(V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\) (Even-Alternating-Distance / Avoidable Vertices): Vertices reachable from \(U_L \cup U_R\) via an even-length \(M^*\)-alternating path (including length \(0\), so \(U_L \subseteq L_1\) and \(U_R \subseteq R_2\)).
\(V_O = R_1 \cup L_2\) (Odd-Alternating-Distance / Bottleneck Vertices): Vertices reachable from \(U_L \cup U_R\) via an odd-length \(M^*\)-alternating path. Every \(w \in V_O\) is matched in \(M^*\) to a partner in \(V_E\) (\(M^*\) pairs \(R_1\) bijectively with \(L_1 \setminus U_L\), and \(L_2\) bijectively with \(R_2 \setminus U_R\)).
\(V_U = L_0 \cup R_0\) (Unreachable / Perfectly Matched Core): Vertices not reachable from \(U_L \cup U_R\) by any \(M^*\)-alternating path. \(M^*\) restricts to a perfect matching between \(L_0\) and \(R_0\) (\(|L_0| = |R_0|\)).

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|             COARSE DULMAGE-MENDELSOHN BLOCK UPPER-TRIANGULAR STRUCTURE (V_E, V_O, V_U)            |
|                                                                                                   |
|                  R_1 in V_O                 R_0 in V_U                 R_2 in V_E                 |
|             (Essential in M* & MVC;    (Perfectly matched core;   (Avoidable in M*, Never in MVC; |
|              matched into L_1 \ U_L)    |L_0| = |R_0|, Essential)  contains U_R; |R_2| > |L_2|)   |
|            +--------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+     |
|  L_1 in V_E|  MATCHED: L_1\U_L <=> R_1|         0 EDGES          |         0 EDGES          |     |
| (Avoidable |  (+ unmatched U_L)       |  (Blocked by S-reach!)   |  (Would augment S -> T!) |     |
|  in M*)    |  Surplus |L_1| > |R_1|   |                          |                          |     |
|            +--------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+     |
|  L_0 in V_U|  Unmatched edges         |  MATCHED: L_0 <===> R_0  |         0 EDGES          |     |
| (Core;     |  L_0 ---> R_1 allowed    |  (Fine DM: Tarjan SCCs   |  (Blocked by T-reach!)   |     |
|  Essential)|  (FORBIDDEN in all M*!)  |   of core G_{f*}^\circ)  |                          |     |
|            +--------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+     |
|  L_2 in V_O|  Unmatched edges         |  Unmatched edges         |  MATCHED: L_2 <=> R_2\U_R|     |
| (Essential |  L_2 ---> R_1 allowed    |  L_2 ---> R_0 allowed    |  (+ unmatched U_R)       |     |
|  in M*&MVC)|  (FORBIDDEN in all M*!)  |  (FORBIDDEN in all M*!)  |  Surplus |R_2| > |L_2|   |     |
|            +--------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+     |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Theorem 2 (Theorem 3.1 (Canonical Invariance & Structural Laws of the Coarse DM Decomposition)) The partition \(V = V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\) (and its six-block refinement \(L_1, L_0, L_2, R_1, R_0, R_2\)) depends only on the graph \(G\), and is completely independent of which maximum matching \(M^*\) was used to construct it. Furthermore:

Zero-Edge Block Upper-Triangularity: The original graph \(G\) contains zero edges in \(L_1 \times R_0\), \(L_1 \times R_2\), and \(L_0 \times R_2\). Equivalently, in terms of \((V_E, V_O, V_U)\), there are no edges in \(V_E \times V_E\) or in \(V_E \times V_U\); every neighbor of any \(w \in V_E\) lies strictly inside \(V_O\) (\(N_G(V_E) \subseteq V_O\)).
Vertex Classification Across All Maximum Matchings \(\mathcal{M}^*(G)\):

Avoidable Vertices (\(\exists M' \in \mathcal{M}^*(G)\) leaving \(w\) unmatched, i.e., \(\nu(G \setminus \{w\}) = \nu(G)\)): Exactly \(V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\). (Moreover, \(w \in V_E\) is Never-Matched iff \(\deg_G(w) = 0\), and Optionally-Matched iff \(\deg_G(w) \ge 1\).)
Essential / Always-Matched Vertices (\(\forall M' \in \mathcal{M}^*(G), w \in V(M')\), i.e., \(\nu(G \setminus \{w\}) = \nu(G) - 1\)): Exactly \(V_O \cup V_U = R_1 \cup L_2 \cup L_0 \cup R_0\).

Vertex Classification Across All Minimum Vertex Covers \(\mathcal{C}^*(G)\):

Always in MVC (\(\forall C^* \in \mathcal{C}^*(G), w \in C^*\)): \(V_O = R_1 \cup L_2\).
Never in MVC (\(\forall C^* \in \mathcal{C}^*(G), w \notin C^*\)): \(V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\).
Optionally in MVC: \(V_U = L_0 \cup R_0\) (specifically, \(C_{\min\text{-}R} = R_1 \cup L_0 \cup L_2\) uses \(L_0\), while \(C_{\min\text{-}L} = R_1 \cup R_0 \cup L_2\) uses \(R_0\)).

Cross-Block Forbidden Edges: Every maximum matching \(M' \in \mathcal{M}^*(G)\) matches \(R_1\) into \(L_1\), \(L_0\) bijectively with \(R_0\), and \(L_2\) into \(R_2\). All edges in \((L_0 \times R_1) \cup (L_2 \times R_1) \cup (L_2 \times R_0)\) (i.e., edges in \(V_O \times V_O\) and \(V_O \times V_U\)) are forbidden (never appear in any maximum matching).



Proof. Step 1 (Zero-Edge Blocks): In \(G_{f^*}\), every unmatched edge \((u, v) \in E \setminus M^*\) is directed \(u \to v\) (\(L \to R\)) with residual capacity \(1\), and every matched edge \((u, v) \in M^*\) is directed \(v \to u\) (\(R \to L\)) with residual capacity \(1\). If any edge \((u, v) \in E\) existed with \(u \in L_1 \subseteq V_S\) and \(v \in R_0 \cup R_2\), then \((u, v)\) could not be in \(M^*\) (else \(v \to u\) would be in \(G_{f^*}\), and \(u \in V_S\) is only entered from \(R_1\) via \(M^*\)). Thus \((u, v) \in E \setminus M^*\) has residual arc \(u \to v\), forcing \(v \in V_S \cap R = R_1\), a contradiction! Symmetrically, no edge can exist in \(L_0 \times R_2\) (as \(u \to v\) would pull \(u\) into \(V_T^{\text{rev}} \cap L = L_2\)). Hence \(N_G(L_1) \subseteq R_1\) and \(N_G(R_2) \subseteq L_2\), proving \(N_G(V_E) \subseteq V_O\).
Step 2 (Every \(w \in V_E\) is Avoidable): Let \(w \in L_1\) (the case \(w \in R_2\) is symmetric). By construction of \(L_1 = L \cap V_S\), there is an even-length \(M^*\)-alternating path \(P\) from some unmatched vertex \(u_0 \in U_L\) to \(w\). The symmetric difference \(M' = M^* \triangle E(P)\) has the exact same size \(|M'| = |M^*| = \nu(G)\) and shifts the unmatched endpoint from \(u_0\) to \(w\), leaving \(w\) unmatched in \(M'\)! Furthermore, if \(\deg_G(w) \ge 1\), pick any neighbor \(v \in N_G(w) \subseteq R_1\); since \(v \in R_1\), flipping the alternating path from \(U_L\) to \(v\) frees \(v\) so \((w, v)\) can be matched if \(w\) was initially in \(U_L\).
Step 3 (Every \(w \notin V_E\) is Essential, Cross-Block Edges are Forbidden, and Canonical Invariance): Notice that \(C_1 = R_1 \cup L_0 \cup L_2\) and \(C_2 = R_1 \cup R_0 \cup L_2\) are both valid vertex covers of \(G\) (since \(L_1 \times (R_0 \cup R_2)\) and \(L_0 \times R_2\) are empty!) of size \(|R_1| + |L_0| + |L_2| = |M^*| = \nu(G)\). By Complementary Slackness (König Duality, Chapter 5), every maximum matching \(M' \in \mathcal{M}^*(G)\) must saturate every vertex of any minimum vertex cover \(C^*\), and every edge \(e \in M'\) must contain at least one endpoint in \(C^*\) and at most one endpoint in \(C^*\):

Applying this to \(C_1 = R_1 \cup L_0 \cup L_2\) and \(C_2 = R_1 \cup R_0 \cup L_2\): every \(M' \in \mathcal{M}^*(G)\) must cover every vertex in \(C_1 \cup C_2 = R_1 \cup L_2 \cup L_0 \cup R_0 = V_O \cup V_U\)! Thus every vertex in \(V_O \cup V_U\) is matched in all maximum matchings, proving that \(V_E = V \setminus (V_O \cup V_U)\) is the exact invariant set of Avoidable vertices!
Because no edge of \(M'\) can have both endpoints inside the minimum vertex cover \(C_1 = R_1 \cup L_0 \cup L_2\), no edge of \(M'\) can lie in \(L_0 \times R_1\) or \(L_2 \times R_1\). Applying the same rule to \(C_2 = R_1 \cup R_0 \cup L_2\) forbids \(L_2 \times R_0\).
Finally, \(V_O\) is uniquely determined as \(N_G(V_E)\) (the neighbors of Avoidable vertices, or equivalently the intersection of all minimum vertex covers), and \(V_U = V \setminus (V_E \cup V_O)\). Hence \((V_E, V_O, V_U)\) is 100% independent of \(M^*\). \(\square\)






3.3 Fine DM Decomposition via Tarjan SCC: Allowed, Forbidden, and \(\nu\)-Critical Edges
How do we classify individual edges \(e = (u, v) \in E\) across all maximum matchings \(\mathcal{M}^*(G)\)? By Theorem 3.1, any maximum matching \(M'\) differs from \(M^*\) via \(M^* \triangle M'\), which is a vertex-disjoint collection of:

Even-length alternating paths starting at \(U_L\) (entirely inside \(L_1 \cup R_1\), which correspond to directed cycles through \(s\) in \(G_{f^*}\)!),
Even-length alternating paths ending at \(U_R\) (entirely inside \(L_2 \cup R_2\), which correspond to directed cycles through \(t\) in \(G_{f^*}\)!), and
Even alternating cycles (which correspond to directed cycles in \(G_{f^*}^\circ = G_{f^*} \setminus \{s, t\}\)!).


Theorem 3 (Theorem 3.2 (Unified Fine DM Edge Classification via Tarjan SCC on \(G_{f^*}\))) Run Tarjan’s Strongly Connected Components algorithm once in \(O(V + E)\) time on the full residual graph \(G_{f^*}\) (including \(s\) and \(t\)), where a directed arc \(x \to y\) exists iff \(c_{f^*}(x, y) > 0\). Then for every original bipartite edge \(e = (u, v) \in E\) (\(u \in L, v \in R\)):

Allowed / Admissible Edge (可行边, in at least one maximum matching \(M' \in \mathcal{M}^*(G)\)):
\[
e = (u, v) \text{ is Admissible} \iff e \in M^* \;\lor\; \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) = \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v).
\]
Mandatory / Essential / \(\nu\)-Critical Edge (必须边, in every maximum matching, i.e., \(\nu(G \setminus \{e\}) = \nu(G) - 1\)):
\[
e = (u, v) \text{ is Mandatory ($\nu$-Critical)} \iff e \in M^* \;\land\; \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) \ne \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v).
\]
Forbidden Edge (不可行边, in no maximum matching):
\[
e = (u, v) \text{ is Forbidden} \iff e \notin M^* \;\land\; \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) \ne \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v).
\]



Proof. An unmatched edge \(e = (u, v) \notin M^*\) has forward residual arc \(u \to v\) in \(G_{f^*}\). It can be swapped into \(M^*\) without reducing the flow value if and only if there is a residual return path \(v \leadsto u\) in \(G_{f^*}\) (forming a zero-net-change circulation cycle through \(u \to v \leadsto u\), possibly passing through \(s\) or \(t\)), which holds iff \(\operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) = \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v)\). Symmetrically, a matched edge \(e = (u, v) \in M^*\) has backward residual arc \(v \to u\) in \(G_{f^*}\). It can be removed from \(M^*\) while preserving \(|M^*| = \nu(G)\) if and only if there is an alternative augmenting path \(u \leadsto v\) in \(G_{f^*}\), which together with \(v \to u\) forms a directed cycle in \(G_{f^*}\), i.e., \(\operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) = \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v)\). Notice that for every \((u, v) \in M^*\) inside \(L_1 \times R_1\), we have \(s \leadsto u\), \(v \to u\), and \(s \to u_0 \leadsto v \to u\), wait: in \(L_1 \times R_1\), \(u \in L_1\) has residual arc \(u \to s\) (since \(s \to u\) is saturated!), so \(s \to u_0 \leadsto v \to u \to s\) is a directed cycle in \(G_{f^*}\) containing \(s, u, v\)! Thus including \(s\) and \(t\) in Tarjan’s SCC graph automatically places all matched and unmatched edges of \(L_1 \times R_1\) into \(\operatorname{scc}(s)\) and all of \(L_2 \times R_2\) into \(\operatorname{scc}(t)\), unifying the coarse and fine DM rules into a single SCC test! \(\square\)


Application to [HAOI2017] 新型城市化 (Increasing Maximum Clique by Deleting One Conflict Edge)
In [HAOI2017 / Luogu P3731] 新型城市化, a country’s cities partition into two cliques (so the complement graph \(\bar{G} = (L \sqcup R, \bar{E})\) is bipartite). By König’s Theorem, the maximum clique of \(G\) equals the Maximum Independent Set of \(\bar{G}\):
\[
\omega(G) = \alpha(\bar{G}) = |V| - \nu(\bar{G}).
\]
Adding one road \(e\) in \(G\) (i.e., deleting one conflict edge \(e \in \bar{E}\) from \(\bar{G}\)) strictly increases \(\omega(G)\) by \(1\) if and only if deleting \(e\) strictly decreases \(\nu(\bar{G})\) by \(1\)—that is, iff \(e \in \bar{E}\) is a Mandatory (\(\nu\)-Critical) Edge of \(\bar{G}\) (\(e \in M^* \land \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) \ne \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v)\))!

Theorem 4 (Theorem 3.3 (Unique Perfect Matching & \(O(V + E)\) Degree-1 Leaf Peeling)) For a balanced bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) with \(|L| = |R| = N\), \(G\) has a unique perfect matching if and only if \(G\) has a perfect matching \(M^*\) and \(G_{f^*}^\circ\) is a DAG (no alternating cycles), which holds if and only if iterative degree-1 leaf peeling (repeatedly matching a vertex \(z\) of current degree \(1\) with its unique neighbor \(w\) and deleting \(\{z, w\}\)) matches all \(2N\) vertices in \(O(V + E)\) time without ever running Dinic.

section: 4. Impartial Walk Games on Bipartite Graphs ([JSOI2009] 游戏, [NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏)
text:
4. Impartial Walk Games on Bipartite Graphs ([JSOI2009] 游戏, [NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏)
We now connect the Dulmage–Mendelsohn decomposition \(V = V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\) to one of the most celebrated theorems in competitive programming game theory.

4.1 Step 1 & Step 2 — The Bipartite Self-Avoiding Walk Game
Game Rules: Given a bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) and a starting vertex \(v_0 \in V\), a token is initially placed on \(v_0\) (marking \(v_0\) as visited). Two players (First Mover and Second Mover) alternately move the token along an edge of \(G\) from its current vertex \(v_t\) to an unvisited neighbor \(v_{t+1} \in N_G(v_t)\). Under Normal Play convention, the first player unable to move loses.
Step 1 (Diagnostic Signal): A grid or graph game where a single piece, king, or blank space . steps to adjacent cells without ever revisiting a cell (\(N, M \le 100\)), and the problem asks for all winning starting cells or asks to evaluate moves in a game transcript.
Step 2 (Intermediate Logical Representation): Instead of computing Sprague–Grundy (SG) values on the exponential state space \((v_t, \text{VisitedMask}) \in V \times 2^V\), we pair vertices using a maximum matching \(M^*\) of \(G\).



4.2 Complete Proof of the Bipartite Walk Game Theorem

Theorem 5 (Theorem 4.1 (Bipartite Self-Avoiding Walk Game Characterization)) In any bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\), the First Mover from \(v_0\) has a winning strategy if and only if \(v_0\) belongs to every maximum matching of \(G\)—that is, \(v_0 \in V_O \cup V_U\) is an Essential vertex (\(v_0 \notin V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\)). Equivalently, the Second Mover from \(v_0\) has a winning strategy if and only if \(v_0 \in V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\) is an Avoidable vertex (reachable from \(s\) in \(G_{f^*}\) if \(v_0 \in L\), or able to reach \(t\) in \(G_{f^*}\) if \(v_0 \in R\)).


Proof. We prove both directions by explicit strategy construction on the DM blocks.
Direction 1 (\(v_0 \in V_E \implies\) Second Mover has a winning strategy): Since \(v_0 \in V_E\) is Avoidable (Theorem 3.1(2)), there exists a maximum matching \(M^*\) of \(G\) that leaves \(v_0\) unmatched (\(v_0 \notin V(M^*)\)). Second Mover adopts the following simple pairing strategy: whenever First Mover moves the token to a vertex \(y\), Second Mover immediately moves the token along the matched edge \((y, M^*(y)) \in M^*\). Why is Second Mover guaranteed to have a legal move at every turn? Suppose at step \(2k + 1\), First Mover moves the token from \(x_{2k}\) to an unvisited neighbor \(y = x_{2k+1}\):

Could \(y\) be unmatched in \(M^*\)? Suppose for contradiction that \(y \notin V(M^*)\). Look at the trajectory of the token so far:
\[
P = (v_0 = x_0 \to x_1 \to x_2 \to \dots \to x_{2k} \to x_{2k+1} = y).
\]
Because the game forbids revisiting vertices, \(P\) is a simple path in \(G\). In \(P\), every odd-indexed edge \((x_{2j-1}, x_{2j})\) was chosen by Second Mover from \(M^*\), and every even-indexed edge \((x_{2j}, x_{2j+1})\) was chosen by First Mover outside \(M^*\). Furthermore, both endpoints \(v_0\) and \(y\) are unmatched in \(M^*\)! Thus \(P\) is a simple \(M^*\)-augmenting path between two \(M^*\)-unmatched vertices, contradicting that \(M^*\) is a maximum matching of \(G\)!
Could \(y\)’s partner \(z = M^*(y)\) already have been visited earlier in the game? No! Every previously visited matched vertex entered at an odd step \(x_{2j-1}\) was immediately paired with its unique \(M^*\)-partner \(x_{2j} = M^*(x_{2j-1})\) at the very next step, and \(v_0\) was unmatched. Since \(y\) itself was unvisited prior to step \(2k+1\), its unique partner \(z = M^*(y)\) could never have been visited either!

Therefore, \(y\) is always matched in \(M^*\) to an unvisited partner \(M^*(y)\), so Second Mover can always reply. Since \(V\) is finite, First Mover eventually runs out of moves and loses.
Direction 2 (\(v_0 \in V_O \cup V_U \implies\) First Mover has a winning strategy): Suppose \(v_0 \notin V_E\) belongs to every maximum matching of \(G\). Fix any maximum matching \(M^*\); then \(v_0\) is matched to some partner \(w_0 = M^*(v_0)\). First Mover makes the opening move \(v_0 \to w_0\). Once \(v_0\) is visited and permanently deleted from the board, consider the remaining bipartite graph \(G' = G \setminus \{v_0\}\) where the token now sits at \(w_0\) and Second Mover is now the player who must move first from \(w_0\) in \(G'\)!

Because \(v_0\) belonged to every maximum matching of \(G\), removing \(v_0\) strictly reduces the maximum matching size: \(\nu(G') = \nu(G) - 1\).
Consequently, \(M' = M^* \setminus \{(v_0, w_0)\}\) is a matching of size \(\nu(G) - 1 = \nu(G')\) in \(G'\)—that is, \(M'\) is a maximum matching of \(G'\) that leaves \(w_0\) unmatched!
Hence \(w_0 \in V_E(G')\) is an Avoidable vertex of \(G'\). By Direction 1 applied to \(G'\) from \(w_0\), the player who moves second from \(w_0\) in \(G'\) (which is our First Mover!) wins by replying along \(M'\) for the rest of the game! \(\square\)





4.3 Step 3 & Step 4 — Linear-Time All-Starts Testing, Role Inversion, and Counterexamples
How do we find all winning starting vertices \(v_0 \in V\)?

The \(O(V + E)\) Residual BFS Algorithm:

Run Dinic once on \(s \to L \to R \to t\) in \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) time.
Run a single forward BFS from \(s\) along positive residual arcs (\(c_{f^*} > 0\)) to mark \(L_1 = L \cap V_S\).
Run a single backward BFS from \(t\) along positive residual arcs (\(c_{f^*} > 0\) into \(t\)) to mark \(R_2 = R \cap V_T^{\text{rev}}\).
Then \(V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\) are the Avoidable vertices (Second Mover wins), and \(V \setminus V_E\) are the Essential vertices (First Mover wins)!








WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexamples FM-06B — Role Inversion, O(VE) Rematching TLE, and Odd Cycles




The Role-Inversion Trap ([JSOI2009] 游戏 vs. [NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏): Read the opening protocol with extreme care!

In [JSOI2009 / Luogu P4055] 游戏 (#047), Player 1 (YY) places the token on \(v_0\), and then Player 2 (HH) makes the first move out of \(v_0\)! Because Player 2 is the First Mover in the walk game from \(v_0\), Player 1 (YY) wins if and only if Second Mover wins from \(v_0\), i.e., \(v_0 \in V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\) is Avoidable!
In [NOI2011 / Luogu P1971] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏 (#048), the blank space . is already at \(v_0\) and the current player slides a tile (moving . out of \(v_0\) first), so the current player wins iff \(v_0 \in V_O \cup V_U\) is Essential!

The \(O(V \cdot E\sqrt{V})\) Per-Vertex Rematching Trap: Deleting each \(v_0 \in V\) and re-running Dinic from scratch to check \(\nu(G \setminus \{v_0\}) = \nu(G) - 1\) takes \(10^4 \times 10^6 = 10^{10}\) operations on a \(100 \times 100\) grid—an instant TLE. The residual BFS above finds \(V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\) for all \(10^4\) vertices in a single \(O(V + E)\) pass (\(< 1\text{ ms}\))!
Why Naive Bipartite DM BFS Fails on Non-Bipartite Graphs (The Bull Graph Counterexample): Notice that the proof of Theorem 4.1 actually shows \(\text{First Mover wins from } v_0 \iff \nu(G \setminus \{v_0\}) = \nu(G) - 1\) on any graph (since an alternating path between two unmatched vertices is augmenting even in non-bipartite graphs!). What fails on a non-bipartite graph is computing Avoidable vertices via naive bipartite alternating BFS without shrinking odd-cycle blossoms! For example, on the 5-vertex Bull Graph (triangle \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) plus pendant leaves \((2, 4)\) and \((3, 5)\)) with \(M^* = \{(2, 4), (3, 5)\}\) and unmatched apex \(1\), an alternating path \(1 \to 2 \to 4\) (odd) cannot continue, whereas around the triangle \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 5\) is not alternating; conversely, if \(M^* = \{(1, 2), (3, 5)\}\) with \(4\) unmatched, the alternating path \(4 \to 2 \to 1 \to 3 \to 5\) traverses the odd cycle \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) and reaches \(1\) in even steps (\(4 \to 2 \to 1\)) AND reaches \(3\) in odd steps (\(4 \to 2 \to 1 \to 3\)), requiring Edmonds’ Blossom (Gallai–Edmonds) decomposition instead of bipartite BFS.
