title: Chapter 6 — Hidden Bipartitions, Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition, and Matching Games
text:
6. Curated 4-Tier Practice Ladder
We now work through eight carefully selected problems (#041–#048) spanning our 4-Tier Practice Ladder (Stepping Stone, Intermediate, Advanced, and Mastery). Every problem follows the 4-Step “Zero Magic Gadgets” Compilation Framework.


#041 — [HEOI2016 / TJOI2016] 游戏 (Game — Bombs with Soft & Hard Walls)

Tier: Stepping Stone 1 (SS-1) | Judge URL: Luogu P2825
Problem Summary: Given an \(N \times M\) grid (\(1 \le N, M \le 50\)) where each cell is an empty space *, a soft obstacle x (cannot place a bomb here, but bomb blasts pass right through it), or a hard wall # (cannot place a bomb here, and blocks bomb blasts). A bomb blasts all cells in its row and column until hitting a hard wall #. Compute the maximum number of bombs that can be placed on * cells so that no two bombs blast each other.







NoteHint 1 — Why Standard Row-Column Bipartite Matching Breaks





On an obstacle-free board, each row holds at most one bomb and each column holds at most one bomb, so rows form \(L\), columns form \(R\), and * cells form edges. When a hard wall # sits at \((r, c)\), how many bombs can Row \(r\) hold? One to the left of # and one to the right of #! What are the true independent conflict units?









NoteHint 2 — Maximal Contiguous #-Free Segments





Scan each row from left to right and assign a new Horizontal Segment ID \(H_{r,c}\) whenever you pass a hard wall # (do not start a new ID at a soft obstacle x!). Symmetrically, scan each column from top to bottom and assign a Vertical Segment ID \(V_{r,c}\) split only by #.









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P2825






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
We want to pack the maximum number of non-conflicting items on a 2D grid (\(N, M \le 50\)) where conflicts propagate horizontally and vertically until hitting #. Because each valid cell (r, c) == '*' lies at the intersection of one maximal horizontal blast interval and one maximal vertical blast interval, every * cell has degree \(1\) in the horizontal family and degree \(1\) in the vertical family. This is an exact Rank-2 Orthogonal Strip Incidence (Pipeline B), which compiles to Maximum Bipartite Matching.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Let \(\mathcal{H} = \{H_1, \dots, H_p\}\) be the set of maximal contiguous #-free horizontal segments across all \(N\) rows, and let \(\mathcal{V} = \{V_1, \dots, V_q\}\) be the set of maximal contiguous #-free vertical segments across all \(M\) columns. For every empty cell \((r, c)\) with \(\text{grid}[r][c] = \texttt{'*'}\), let \(h(r, c) \in \mathcal{H}\) and \(v(r, c) \in \mathcal{V}\) be the unique horizontal and vertical segments containing \((r, c)\), and assign a binary decision variable \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicating whether a bomb is placed at \((r, c)\). The non-blasting constraints are:
\[
\max \sum_{(r,c) = \texttt{'*'}} x_{r,c} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \forall a \in \{1, \dots, p\}, \sum_{(r,c) \in H_a} x_{r,c} \le 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \forall b \in \{1, \dots, q\}, \sum_{(r,c) \in V_b} x_{r,c} \le 1.
\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Left Partite Set \(L\): One vertex for each horizontal segment \(H_a \in \mathcal{H}\) (\(p \le NM\)). Connect \(s \to H_a\) with capacity \(1\).
Right Partite Set \(R\): One vertex for each vertical segment \(V_b \in \mathcal{V}\) (\(q \le NM\)). Connect \(V_b \to t\) with capacity \(1\).
Incidence Edges: For each cell \((r, c)\) with \(\text{grid}[r][c] = \texttt{'*'}\), add a directed arc \(h(r, c) \to v(r, c)\) of capacity \(1\). (Soft obstacles x and hard walls # generate zero edges!)

int p = 0, q = 0;
vector<vector<int>> hid(N, vector<int>(M, -1)), vid(N, vector<int>(M, -1));
for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r) {
    for (int c = 0; c < M; ++c) {
        if (grid[r][c] == '#') continue;
        if (c == 0 || grid[r][c - 1] == '#') ++p;
        hid[r][c] = p;
    }
}
for (int c = 0; c < M; ++c) {
    for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r) {
        if (grid[r][c] == '#') continue;
        if (r == 0 || grid[r - 1][c] == '#') ++q;
        vid[r][c] = q;
    }
}
int S = 0, T = p + q + 1;
Dinic dinic(T + 1);
for (int a = 1; a <= p; ++a) dinic.add_edge(S, a, 1);
for (int b = 1; b <= q; ++b) dinic.add_edge(p + b, T, 1);
for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r)
    for (int c = 0; c < M; ++c)
        if (grid[r][c] == '*')
            dinic.add_edge(hid[r][c], p + vid[r][c], 1);
cout << dinic.max_flow(S, T) << "\n";


Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
On a \(1 \times 4\) row * x # *:

Cells \((0, 0)\) (*) and \((0, 1)\) (x) share \(H_1\); cell \((0, 2)\) is #; cell \((0, 3)\) (*) gets \(H_2\).
Only \((0, 0)\) and \((0, 3)\) are *, creating edges \((H_1, V_1)\) and \((H_2, V_3)\), giving \(\nu(G) = 2\).
Failure Guard: Never split \(H\)-segments at x (which would falsely give \((0, 0)\) and a cell at \((0, 2)\) different segment IDs if # were *), and never add edges for x.
Complexity: \(|V| \le 2NM + 2 \le 5002\), \(|E| \le 3NM \le 7500\); Dinic runs in \(O((NM)^{3/2})\) (\(< 5\text{ ms}\)).








#042 — [Luogu P3355 / 网络流 24 题 #22] 骑士共存问题 (Knights Coexistence)

Tier: Stepping Stone 2 (SS-2) | Judge URL: Luogu P3355
Problem Summary: Given an \(N \times N\) chessboard (\(1 \le N \le 200\)) with \(M\) forbidden squares where knights cannot be placed. Two knights attack each other if \(|\Delta r| = 1, |\Delta c| = 2\) or \(|\Delta r| = 2, |\Delta c| = 1\). Find the maximum number of non-attacking knights that can be placed on the non-forbidden squares.







NoteHint 1 — Why the Knight Conflict Graph Has No Odd Cycles





Look at the sum of coordinates \(r + c\) before and after a knight jump \((\pm 1, \pm 2)\) or \((\pm 2, \pm 1)\). What is the parity of \(\Delta r + \Delta c\)?









NoteHint 2 — From Conflict Graph to Maximum Independent Set





Since \(\Delta(r + c) \in \{\pm 1, \pm 3\}\) is always odd, every knight move connects a Black square (\((r+c) \bmod 2 = 1\)) to a White square (\((r+c) \bmod 2 = 0\)). Apply König’s complement identity \(\alpha(G) = |V_{\text{valid}}| - \nu(G)\).









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P3355






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
We want the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) of a pairwise conflict graph on \(V_{\text{valid}} \le 40{,}000\) grid squares. General MIS is NP-hard, which signals that the knight conflict graph must be bipartite via a parity invariant.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Let \(V_{\text{valid}}\) be the set of non-forbidden squares, and let \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether a knight is placed at \((r, c) \in V_{\text{valid}}\). We maximize \(\sum_{(r,c) \in V_{\text{valid}}} x_{r,c}\) subject to \(x_{r,c} + x_{r',c'} \le 1\) whenever \(\{|\Delta r|, |\Delta c|\} = \{1, 2\}\). Define the chessboard coloring \(\phi(r, c) = (r + c) \bmod 2\). For any knight jump:
\[
(r' + c') - (r + c) = \Delta r + \Delta c \in \{\pm 1 \pm 2\} = \{-3, -1, +1, +3\} \equiv 1 \pmod 2.
\]
Thus every conflict edge strictly crosses between \(L = \{(r, c) \in V_{\text{valid}} : (r+c) \text{ is odd}\}\) and \(R = \{(r, c) \in V_{\text{valid}} : (r+c) \text{ is even}\}\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Vertices: Source \(s\), sink \(t\), and all valid squares \((r, c) \in V_{\text{valid}} = L \sqcup R\).
Capacities:

For each \(u \in L\): add arc \(s \to u\) of capacity \(1\).
For each \(v \in R\): add arc \(v \to t\) of capacity \(1\).
For each \(u = (r, c) \in L\) and each of the \(8\) knight jumps \(v = (r + \Delta r, c + \Delta c) \in R\) (if \(v\) is in-bounds and not forbidden): add directed arc \(u \to v\) of capacity \(\infty\) (or \(1\)).

Output: \(|V_{\text{valid}}| - \operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\).



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
On a \(3 \times 3\) board with \(0\) forbidden cells (\(|V_{\text{valid}}| = 9\)):

Center \((2, 2)\) is isolated from all knight jumps. The remaining \(8\) boundary squares form a single alternating 8-cycle \((1,1) - (2,3) - (3,1) - (1,2) - (3,3) - (2,1) - (1,3) - (3,2) - (1,1)\) of 4 White and 4 Black squares.
The 8-cycle has maximum matching \(\nu(G) = 4\), giving \(\alpha(G) = 9 - 4 = 5\) knights (e.g., center \((2, 2)\) plus all 4 even squares on the cycle).
Failure Guard: Always mark forbidden squares in a boolean grid blocked[r][c] and compute \(|V_{\text{valid}}|\) by counting blocked[r][c] == false, rather than trusting \(N^2 - M\) blindly in case the input lists a forbidden square twice!
Complexity: \(|V| \le 4 \cdot 10^4\), \(|E| \le 2 \cdot 10^5\); Hopcroft–Karp / Dinic runs in \(O(E\sqrt{V}) \approx 4 \cdot 10^7\) ops.








#043 — [Codeforces 1773 D] Dominoes

Tier: Intermediate 1 (Int-1) | Judge URL: CF 1773D
Problem Summary: An \(N \times M\) grid (\(NM \le 2 \cdot 10^5\)) is tiled with \(1 \times 2\) and \(2 \times 1\) dominoes (L/R and U/D), leaving some empty . cells. You may repeatedly slide any domino lengthwise by \(1\) cell into an adjacent empty . cell (which shifts the empty . cell by \(2\) units along that domino). Count the number of unordered pairs of grid cells \(\{a, b\}\) that can simultaneously be empty . cells after some sequence of domino slides.







NoteHint 1 — Sliding a Domino is an \(M^*\)-Alternating Path Step!





Color the grid like a chessboard into Black (\(L\)) and White (\(R\)). Every domino \((u, v)\) is a matched edge in \(M^*\), and every . cell is an unmatched vertex! When you slide a domino \((u, v)\) lengthwise so that \(u\) covers an adjacent empty cell \(w\), what happens to the empty cell? It jumps from \(w\) to \(v\)—a distance-2 step between two cells of the same chessboard color!









NoteHint 2 — Why the Reverse Reachability Graph Has Out-Degree \(\le 1\) (A Directed Forest!)





Consider how a covered cell \(v\) can become empty: the unique domino \((u, v)\) covering \(v\) must slide into the cell \(w\) immediately adjacent to \(u\) on the side opposite to \(v\)! That requires \(w\) to become empty first. Thus every covered cell \(v\) has at most one parent \(w\) from which it can receive a hole!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — CF 1773D






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
With \(NM \le 2 \cdot 10^5\), we cannot run an \(O(V\sqrt{V})\) flow solver. Instead, we are given an already-matched bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) (where dominoes are matched edges \(M^*\)) and allowed only collinear augmenting walks. The key structural insight is that each domino \((u, v)\) can only slide along its own axis, restricting the DM alternating graph so that every vertex has in-degree \(\le 1\)!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Let \((u, v)\) be a domino covering cell \(u\) and cell \(v\). To expose cell \(v\) (make \(v\) empty), we must slide domino \((u, v)\) by \(1\) unit in the direction \(\vec{d} = u - v\) into cell \(w = u + (u - v) = 2u - v\):

Notice that \(w = 2u - v\) has the exact same chessboard parity as \(v\): \((r_w + c_w) \equiv 2(r_u + c_u) - (r_v + c_v) \equiv r_v + c_v \pmod 2\)!
Moreover, because \(v\) is covered by a unique domino \((u, v)\), \(w = 2u - v\) is the unique cell whose emptiness allows \(v\) to become empty in one slide!



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
Add a directed edge \(w \to v\) for every domino \((u, v)\) where \(w = 2u - v\) is inside the \(N \times M\) grid.

Because every covered cell \(v\) has in-degree at most \(1\) (from \(w = 2u - v\)) and every initial . cell has in-degree \(0\), and no cycle of slides can exist on a finite grid (each edge steps by \(\pm 2\) along a coordinate), the graph decomposes into disjoint directed trees (an out-forest) rooted at the initial . cells (plus isolated components unable to reach any . root)!
Even better: since \(w\) and \(v\) always have the same chessboard parity, the forest splits completely into a Black Forest \(\mathcal{F}_L\) (on cells with \((r+c)\) odd) and a White Forest \(\mathcal{F}_R\) (on cells with \((r+c)\) even)!
Any cell \(x\) in the subtree of an initial . root \(r_0\) can be made empty by sliding the unique path of dominoes from \(r_0\) to \(x\). Because Black slides and White slides never share intermediate cells (actually, if \((u, v)\) is a domino, sliding \(w \to v\) moves \(u\) onto \(w\), which never disturbs any orthogonal tree path, and within the forest two cells \(a, b\) can be simultaneously empty iff they lie in subtrees of distinct . roots!).
Specifically, let \(K\) be the total number of cells in all trees rooted at . cells across the board, and for each . root \(r_i\), let \(s_i\) be the size of its tree:

Any two cells in different .-rooted trees can be made empty simultaneously (since their slide paths from their respective . roots are completely vertex-disjoint!):
\[
\text{Ans} = \binom{K}{2} - \sum_{i} \binom{s_i}{2}.
\]




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Consider a \(1 \times 4\) board . L R .:

Cells \(1\) and \(4\) are . roots (\(r_1 = 1, r_2 = 4\)). Domino \((2, 3)\) gives edges \(1 \to 3\) (sliding L R left into \(1\) exposes \(3\)) and \(4 \to 2\) (sliding L R right into \(4\) exposes \(2\)).
Tree at root \(1\) is \(\{1, 3\}\) (\(s_1 = 2\)); tree at root \(4\) is \(\{4, 2\}\) (\(s_2 = 2\)). Total reachable cells \(K = 4\).
Pairs of cells in distinct trees: \(\binom{4}{2} - \binom{2}{2} - \binom{2}{2} = 6 - 1 - 1 = 4\) pairs: \(\{1, 4\}, \{1, 2\}, \{3, 4\}, \{3, 2\}\).
Failure Guard: A covered cell \(v\) whose predecessor \(w = 2u - v\) lies inside a disconnected cycle of dominoes that never reaches a . root is unreachable—only run DFS/BFS starting from the actual . cells!
Complexity: \(O(NM)\) time and space via a single linear forest traversal from all . cells.








#044 — [Codeforces 1198 E] Rectangle Painting 1

Tier: Intermediate 2 (Int-2) | Judge URL: CF 1198E
Problem Summary: You are given an \(N \times N\) grid (\(N \le 10^9\)) that is initially all white, except for \(M\) black rectangles \([x_{i,1}, x_{i,2}] \times [y_{i,1}, y_{i,2}]\) (\(0 \le M \le 50\), rectangles may overlap). You can paint any sub-rectangle of size \(w \times h\) white for a cost of \(\min(w, h)\). Find the minimum total cost to paint all black cells white.







NoteHint 1 — Reducing Arbitrary \(w \times h\) Rectangles to Full Strips





If you pay \(\min(w, h) = w\) to whiten a \(w \times h\) rectangle, you could instead whiten the entire vertical strip of width \(w\) and height \(N\) (\(w \times N\)) for the exact same cost \(\min(w, N) = w\)! What does this imply about the shapes of all operations in an optimal solution?









NoteHint 2 — Coordinate Discretization & Weighted König Min-Cut





Collect all \(x\)-boundaries \(x_{i,1}\) and \(x_{i,2} + 1\) (half-open intervals!) and sort/deduplicate them into \(K_x \le 2M \le 100\) elementary vertical strips of width \(\Delta X_a = X_{a+1} - X_a\). Do the same for \(y\)-boundaries into \(K_y \le 100\) elementary horizontal strips of height \(\Delta Y_b\). Now how must each black elementary block \((a, b)\) be covered?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — CF 1198E






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
\(N \le 10^9\) rules out per-row/per-column vertices directly, while \(M \le 50\) is tiny. Furthermore, the cost function \(\min(w, h)\) satisfies full-strip dominance: replacing \([x_1, x_2] \times [y_1, y_2]\) with \([x_1, x_2] \times [1, N]\) (if \(w \le h\)) or \([1, N] \times [y_1, y_2]\) (if \(h < w\)) never increases the cost and covers a superset of cells. Thus every cell is covered by either a vertical strip or a horizontal strip—a Weighted Bipartite Minimum Vertex Cover after coordinate compression!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Represent each input black rectangle as a product of half-open integer intervals \([x_{i,1}, x_{i,2} + 1) \times [y_{i,1}, y_{i,2} + 1)\). Let \(X_0 < X_1 < \dots < X_{K_x}\) be the sorted unique endpoints \(\bigcup_{i=1}^M \{x_{i,1}, x_{i,2} + 1\}\), and let \(Y_0 < Y_1 < \dots < Y_{K_y}\) be the sorted unique endpoints \(\bigcup_{i=1}^M \{y_{i,1}, y_{i,2} + 1\}\), where \(K_x, K_y \le 2M \le 100\). For each elementary vertical strip \(I_a = [X_a, X_{a+1})\) of width \(w_a = X_{a+1} - X_a\) and elementary horizontal strip \(J_b = [Y_b, Y_{b+1})\) of height \(h_b = Y_{b+1} - Y_b\), let \(x_a \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(y_b \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether strip \(I_a\) or \(J_b\) is whitened:
\[
\min \sum_{a=0}^{K_x-1} w_a x_a + \sum_{b=0}^{K_y-1} h_b y_b \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_a + y_b \ge 1 \;\;\forall (a, b) \text{ covered by some black rectangle}.
\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
Build a Weighted König Minimum Cut network on \(\{s, t\} \cup \{I_0, \dots, I_{K_x-1}\} \cup \{J_0, \dots, J_{K_y-1}\}\):

For each \(a \in [0, K_x)\): add directed arc \(s \to I_a\) with capacity \(w_a = X_{a+1} - X_a\).
For each \(b \in [0, K_y)\): add directed arc \(J_b \to t\) with capacity \(h_b = Y_{b+1} - Y_b\).
For each pair \((a, b)\) such that \([X_a, X_{a+1}) \times [Y_b, Y_{b+1})\) lies inside at least one black rectangle \(i\): add directed arc \(I_a \to J_b\) with capacity \(\infty\).
Output: \(\operatorname{MinCut}(s, t) = \operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\).

vector<long long> xs, ys;
for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i) {
    xs.push_back(x1[i]); xs.push_back(x2[i] + 1);
    ys.push_back(y1[i]); ys.push_back(y2[i] + 1);
}
sort(xs.begin(), xs.end()); xs.erase(unique(xs.begin(), xs.end()), xs.end());
sort(ys.begin(), ys.end()); ys.erase(unique(ys.begin(), ys.end()), ys.end());
int kx = (int)xs.size() - 1, ky = (int)ys.size() - 1;
int S = 0, T = kx + ky + 1;
Dinic<long long> dinic(T + 1);
for (int a = 0; a < kx; ++a) dinic.add_edge(S, 1 + a, xs[a + 1] - xs[a]);
for (int b = 0; b < ky; ++b) dinic.add_edge(1 + kx + b, T, ys[b + 1] - ys[b]);
for (int a = 0; a < kx; ++a) {
    for (int b = 0; b < ky; ++b) {
        bool black = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i)
            if (x1[i] <= xs[a] && xs[a + 1] - 1 <= x2[i] &&
                y1[i] <= ys[b] && ys[b + 1] - 1 <= y2[i]) { black = true; break; }
        if (black) dinic.add_edge(1 + a, 1 + kx + b, INF);
    }
}
cout << dinic.max_flow(S, T) << "\n";


Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(M = 1\) with black rectangle \([2, 4] \times [3, 3]\).

Using half-open intervals \([2, 5) \times [3, 4)\), we get \(X = [2, 5]\) (\(w_0 = 5 - 2 = 3\)) and \(Y = [3, 4]\) (\(h_0 = 4 - 3 = 1\)).
MinCut is \(\min(w_0, h_0) = \min(3, 1) = 1\).
Failure Guard: If you compress closed endpoints \(\{x_{i,1}, x_{i,2}\}\) instead of half-open \(\{x_{i,1}, x_{i,2} + 1\}\), a \(1\)-wide interval \([3, 3]\) collapses to \(3 - 3 = 0\) width and gives a wrong answer of \(0\)! Always use \([L, R + 1)\).
Complexity: \(|V| \le 202, |E| \le 10^4\); Dinic runs in \(O(M^3)\) (\(< 2\text{ ms}\)).








#045 — [POJ 3692 / LOJ #6062] Kindergarten (& [HAOI2017] 新型城市化 \(\nu\)-Critical Extension)

Tier: Advanced 1 (Adv-1) | Judge URL: POJ 3692 / Luogu P3731 ([HAOI2017] 新型城市化)
Problem Summary:

Base Problem (POJ 3692): In a kindergarten, there are \(G \le 200\) girls (who all know each other) and \(B \le 200\) boys (who all know each other). Among the girls and boys, \(M\) pairs \((g_i, b_i)\) know each other. Find the maximum number of children who can be chosen so that every pair of chosen children knows each other (Maximum Clique).
Fine DM Extension ([HAOI2017 / Luogu P3731] 新型城市化): Given a graph \(G\) of \(N \le 10^4\) cities whose complement \(\bar{G}\) is bipartite (partitioned into two cliques \(L\) and \(R\)), find the maximum clique size \(\omega(G)\) and list all missing roads \(e \in \bar{E}\) whose addition to \(G\) strictly increases \(\omega(G)\)!








NoteHint 1 — Complement Graph Duality: From Two-Clique Union to Bipartite MIS





A subset of vertices \(S \subseteq V\) is a clique in \(G\) (every pair is connected) if and only if \(S\) is an independent set in the complement graph \(\bar{G}\) (no pair is connected in \(\bar{G}\)). Since all girls know each other and all boys know each other, what edges exist in \(\bar{G}\)?









NoteHint 2 — When Does Deleting One Edge of \(\bar{G}\) Increase \(\alpha(\bar{G})\)? ([HAOI2017])





Because \(\bar{G}\) has zero edges inside \(L\) and zero edges inside \(R\), \(\bar{G}\) is bipartite! By König’s Theorem, \(\omega(G) = \alpha(\bar{G}) = |V| - \nu(\bar{G})\). Adding a missing road \(e\) to \(G\) deletes edge \(e\) from \(\bar{G}\). By Theorem 3.2, which edges \(e \in E(\bar{G})\) satisfy \(\nu(\bar{G} \setminus \{e\}) = \nu(\bar{G}) - 1\)?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — POJ 3692 & Luogu P3731






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Maximum Clique is NP-hard on general graphs, but whenever the vertex set partitions into two cliques \(L\) and \(R\) (such as Girls and Boys in POJ 3692, or the 2-colored complement graph \(\bar{G}\) in Luogu P3731), all missing edges lie strictly between \(L\) and \(R\). Thus the complement graph \(\bar{G} = (L \sqcup R, \bar{E})\) is bipartite!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Let \(x_u \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(u \in L\)) and \(y_v \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(v \in R\)) indicate whether child/city \(u\) or \(v\) is selected into the clique. Two vertices conflict if and only if \((u, v) \notin E(G) \iff (u, v) \in \bar{E}\):
\[
\omega(G) = \max \left( \sum_{u \in L} x_u + \sum_{v \in R} y_v \right) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_u + y_v \le 1 \;\;\forall (u, v) \in \bar{E}.
\]
By König’s Theorem on the bipartite complement graph \(\bar{G}\):
\[
\omega(G) = \alpha(\bar{G}) = |L| + |R| - \nu(\bar{G}).
\]
Furthermore, for [HAOI2017] 新型城市化, adding road \(e = (u, v) \in \bar{E}\) to \(G\) removes \(e\) from \(\bar{G}\), which increases \(\omega(G)\) by \(1\) if and only if \(\nu(\bar{G} \setminus \{e\}) = \nu(\bar{G}) - 1\)—meaning \(e\) is a Mandatory (\(\nu\)-Critical) Edge of \(\bar{G}\)!


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Complement Bipartite Network (POJ 3692):

Build boolean matrix know[g][b], initialized to false, and set know[g][b] = true for all \(M\) input pairs.
Connect \(s \to g\) (cap \(1\)) for \(g \in \{1, \dots, G\}\), \(b \to t\) (cap \(1\)) for \(b \in \{1, \dots, B\}\), and \(g \to b\) (cap \(1\)) whenever !know[g][b].
Output \(G + B - \operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\).

Fine DM \(\nu\)-Critical Edge Extraction (Luogu P3731):

2-color the complement graph \(\bar{G}\) into \(L \sqcup R\) (any isolated vertex can be placed in \(L\)).
Run Dinic on \(s \to L \to R \to t\) for \(\bar{G}\), then run DMDecomposition::build (Tarjan SCC on the full residual graph \(G_{f^*}\) including \(s\) and \(t\)).
A conflict edge \(e = (u, v) \in \bar{E}\) (\(u \in L, v \in R\)) is \(\nu\)-critical iff e is saturated in M* and scc[u] != scc[v].




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(G = 2\) girls \(\{g_1, g_2\}\), \(B = 2\) boys \(\{b_1, b_2\}\), and only \((g_1, b_2)\) and \((g_2, b_1)\) know each other.

The missing edges \(\bar{E}\) are \((g_1, b_1)\) and \((g_2, b_2)\), which form two disjoint edges of size \(\nu(\bar{G}) = 2\).
Maximum clique size is \(2 + 2 - 2 = 2\). Both \((g_1, b_1)\) and \((g_2, b_2)\) are Mandatory (\(\nu\)-critical) in \(\bar{G}\): adding either acquaintance creates a clique of size \(3\)!
Failure Guard: In POJ 3692, the input often lists the same \((g, b)\) pair multiple times! Always deduplicate via know[g][b] = true before complementing. In Luogu P3731, remember to include \(s\) and \(t\) inside Tarjan’s residual graph so that edges in \(L_1 \times R_1\) and \(L_2 \times R_2\) are recognized as non-critical via cycles through \(s\) or \(t\)!
Complexity: \(O((G+B)^{2.5})\) for POJ 3692; \(O(E\sqrt{V} + V + E)\) for Luogu P3731.








#046 — [AtCoder ARC 074 F (D)] Lotus Leaves

Tier: Advanced 2 (Adv-2) | Judge URL: AtCoder ARC 074 F
Problem Summary: A pond is an \(H \times W\) grid (\(2 \le H, W \le 100\)) containing a start leaf S, a target leaf T, lotus leaves o, and water .. A frog starts on S and can jump between any two leaves located in the same row or the same column. Find the minimum number of o leaves that must be removed so the frog cannot reach T from S (or output -1 if T is still reachable even after removing all o leaves).







NoteHint 1 — Why Naive Leaf-to-Leaf Vertex Cut Has Too Many Edges





If you make each o leaf a vertex and add edges between all pairs of leaves in the same row or column, each row/column becomes a clique (\(O(HW(H+W))\) edges). Instead, what are the \(H + W\) shared communication buses of the grid?









NoteHint 2 — Row Hubs and Column Hubs: Turning Vertex Deletion into Edge Cut!





Create \(H\) Row Hubs \(R_1, \dots, R_H\) and \(W\) Column Hubs \(C_1, \dots, C_W\). When the frog lands on a lotus leaf o at \((r, c)\), it can switch from moving along Row \(r\) to moving along Column \(c\) (or vice versa)! Thus what is a lotus leaf o at \((r, c)\) in the bipartite graph of Row Hubs and Column Hubs?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — ARC 074 F






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
We want a Minimum Cut disconnecting S from T on an \(H \times W\) grid where transitions occur along full rows and full columns. Instead of modeling cells as vertices (requiring vertex-splitting), Row–Column Hub Dualization makes the \(H\) rows and \(W\) columns the vertices (\(|V| = H + W \le 200\)), and turns every lotus leaf o at \((r, c)\) into an undirected capacity-1 edge \(\{R_r, C_c\}\)!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Assign a binary potential \(p(R_r) \in \{0, 1\}\) to each row \(r \in \{1, \dots, H\}\) and \(p(C_c) \in \{0, 1\}\) to each column \(c \in \{1, \dots, W\}\), denoting whether that row or column is reachable from S (\(0\)) or disconnected toward T (\(1\)):

Starting leaf S at \((r_S, c_S)\) forces \(p(R_{r_S}) = p(C_{c_S}) = 0\).
Target leaf T at \((r_T, c_T)\) forces \(p(R_{r_T}) = p(C_{c_T}) = 1\). (Immediate Feasibility Check: if \(r_S = r_T\) or \(c_S = c_T\), then \(0 = 1\) is impossible, so output -1!)
Every lotus leaf o at \((r, c)\) allows jumping between Row \(r\) and Column \(c\) in either direction unless removed (cost \(1\)):

\[
\min \sum_{(r,c) = \texttt{'o'}} |p(R_r) - p(C_c)|.
\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Vertices: Source \(s\), sink \(t\), Row Hubs \(R_1, \dots, R_H\), Column Hubs \(C_1, \dots, C_W\).
Infinite-Capacity Anchors:

Connect \(s \to R_{r_S}\) and \(s \to C_{c_S}\) with capacity \(\infty\).
Connect \(R_{r_T} \to t\) and \(C_{c_T} \to t\) with capacity \(\infty\).

Bidirectional Leaf Edges:

For every cell \((r, c)\) with \(\text{grid}[r][c] = \texttt{'o'}\), add a directed arc \(R_r \to C_c\) of capacity \(1\) and a directed arc \(C_c \to R_r\) of capacity \(1\).


if (rS == rT || cS == cT) { cout << -1 << "\n"; return 0; }
int S = 0, T = H + W + 1;
Dinic<int> dinic(T + 1);
dinic.add_edge(S, 1 + rS, INF);
dinic.add_edge(S, 1 + H + cS, INF);
dinic.add_edge(1 + rT, T, INF);
dinic.add_edge(1 + H + cT, T, INF);
for (int r = 0; r < H; ++r) {
    for (int c = 0; c < W; ++c) {
        if (grid[r][c] == 'o') {
            dinic.add_edge(1 + r, 1 + H + c, 1);
            dinic.add_edge(1 + H + c, 1 + r, 1);
        }
    }
}
cout << dinic.max_flow(S, T) << "\n";


Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Suppose \(H = W = 3\), S at \((1, 1)\), T at \((3, 3)\), and o at \((1, 3)\) and \((3, 2)\) and \((1, 2)\).

Path 1: \((1, 1) \xrightarrow{R_1} (1, 3) \xrightarrow{C_3} (3, 3)\) uses leaf \((1, 3)\).
Path 2: \((1, 1) \xrightarrow{R_1} (1, 2) \xrightarrow{C_2} (3, 2) \xrightarrow{R_3} (3, 3)\) traverses \(R_1 \to C_2 \to R_3\)!
Failure Guard: Notice that Path 2 traverses \(C_2 \to R_3\) via leaf \((3, 2)\)! If you wired leaf edges only one-way \(R_r \to C_c\) instead of bidirectionally \(R_r \leftrightarrow C_c\), the graph could never take \(2\) hops \(R_1 \to C_2 \to R_3\) and would miss Path 2 completely!
Complexity: \(|V| = H + W + 2 \le 202\), \(|E| \le 2HW \le 2 \cdot 10^4\); Dinic runs in \(O(HW\sqrt{H+W})\) (\(< 1\text{ ms}\)).








#047 — [JSOI2009] 游戏 (Bipartite Grid Token Walk Game)

Tier: Mastery 1 (Mas-1) | Judge URL: Luogu P4055
Problem Summary: Given an \(N \times M\) grid (\(1 \le N, M \le 100\)) of . (empty squares) and # (obstacles). First, Player 1 (YY) chooses an initial empty square \(v_0\) and places a token on it. Then, starting with Player 2 (HH), the two players alternately move the token to a 4-connected adjacent . square that has never been visited before. The player who cannot make a valid move loses. Determine whether Player 1 (YY) has a winning strategy, and if so, output all winning starting squares \((r, c)\) in lexicographical order.







NoteHint 1 — Check Who Moves First After \(v_0\) Is Chosen!





Player 1 (YY) only places the token on \(v_0\); Player 2 (HH) makes the first move \(v_0 \to v_1\)! In the terminology of Theorem 4.1, is Player 1 the First Mover or the Second Mover in the walk game starting from \(v_0\)?









NoteHint 2 — Avoidable Vertices \(V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\) via Residual BFS





Because Player 2 moves first from \(v_0\), Player 1 (YY) is the Second Mover from \(v_0\)! By Theorem 4.1, Second Mover wins from \(v_0\) if and only if \(v_0 \in V_E = L_1 \cup R_2\) is an Avoidable vertex (omitted by at least one maximum matching). How do you find all \(v_0 \in L_1 \cup R_2\) in \(O(NM)\) time after a single Dinic run?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P4055






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
This is the canonical Impartial Self-Avoiding Walk Game on a Bipartite Graph (§4). Every orthogonal grid step flips chessboard parity \(\phi(r, c) = (r + c) \bmod 2\), so the grid of . cells is bipartite. Furthermore, we must classify all \(\le 10^4\) starting cells, requiring the \(O(V + E)\) Coarse Dulmage–Mendelsohn BFS rather than \(O(V \cdot E\sqrt{V})\) per-vertex rematching.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Partition the . cells into \(L = \{(r, c) = \texttt{'.'} : (r + c) \text{ is odd}\}\) and \(R = \{(r, c) = \texttt{'.'} : (r + c) \text{ is even}\}\). Since YY places the token on \(v_0\) and HH moves first from \(v_0\), YY is the Second Mover in the walk game from \(v_0\). By Theorem 4.1:
\[
\text{YY wins by choosing } v_0 \iff \exists M^* \in \mathcal{M}^*(G) \text{ such that } v_0 \notin V(M^*) \iff v_0 \in V_E = L_1 \cup R_2.
\]
In particular, YY has at least one winning starting square if and only if \(G\) does not have a perfect matching (\(V_E \ne \emptyset\))!


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Build the unit bipartite matching network \(N\):

\(s \to u\) (cap \(1\)) for each \(u \in L\), \(v \to t\) (cap \(1\)) for each \(v \in R\), and \(u \to v\) (cap \(1\)) for adjacent . cells \(u \in L, v \in R\).

Run Dinic to obtain maximum flow \(f^*\).
Run Coarse DM Reachability (DMDecomposition from §5.1):

Forward BFS from \(s\) along residual arcs with \(c_{f^*} > 0\) marks \(V_S\), giving \(L_1 = L \cap V_S\).
Backward BFS from \(t\) along residual arcs with \(c_{f^*} > 0\) marks \(V_T^{\text{rev}}\), giving \(R_2 = R \cap V_T^{\text{rev}}\).

Collect all . cells \((r, c)\) in \(L_1 \cup R_2\). If empty, print LOSE; otherwise print WIN followed by all \((r, c) \in L_1 \cup R_2\).

// After running Dinic on S -> L -> R -> T:
vector<int> vis_S(T + 1, 0), vis_T(T + 1, 0);
queue<int> q;
q.push(S); vis_S[S] = 1;
while (!q.empty()) {
    int u = q.front(); q.pop();
    for (const auto& e : dinic.adj[u])
        if (e.cap > 0 && !vis_S[e.to]) { vis_S[e.to] = 1; q.push(e.to); }
}
q.push(T); vis_T[T] = 1;
while (!q.empty()) {
    int u = q.front(); q.pop();
    for (const auto& e : dinic.adj[u]) {
        // Backward arc v -> u has positive residual capacity iffdinic.adj[v][e.rev].cap > 0
        int v = e.to;
        if (dinic.adj[v][e.rev].cap > 0 && !vis_T[v]) { vis_T[v] = 1; q.push(v); }
    }
}
vector<pair<int, int>> ans;
for (int r = 1; r <= N; ++r)
    for (int c = 1; c <= M; ++c)
        if (grid[r][c] == '.') {
            int id = node_id(r, c);
            bool in_L = ((r + c) % 2 == 1);
            if ((in_L && vis_S[id]) || (!in_L && vis_T[id]))
                ans.emplace_back(r, c);
        }


Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Consider a \(1 \times 3\) path . . . at \((1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3)\):

\(L = \{(1, 2)\}\) (odd sum \(3\)), \(R = \{(1, 1), (1, 3)\}\) (even sums \(2, 4\)).
Maximum matching size is \(\nu(G) = 1\), say \(M^* = \{((1, 2), (1, 1))\}\), leaving \((1, 3) \in U_R\) unmatched.
Backward BFS from \(t\): \(t \leftarrow (1, 3) \leftarrow (1, 2) \leftarrow (1, 1)\) marks \(R_2 = \{(1, 1), (1, 3)\}\) and \(L_2 = \{(1, 2)\}\).
Thus \(V_E = L_1 \cup R_2 = \{(1, 1), (1, 3)\}\): YY wins by placing the token on either endpoint \((1, 1)\) or \((1, 3)\) (HH is forced to step to \((1, 2)\), and YY steps to the other endpoint and wins!).
Failure Guard: Role-inversion (FM-06B)—outputting \(V \setminus V_E\) instead of \(V_E\) confuses YY (who places the token and moves second) with HH (who moves first).
Complexity: Dinic in \(O((NM)^{3/2})\) plus \(O(NM)\) BFS (\(< 15\text{ ms}\)).








#048 — [NOI2011] 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏 (Rabbit and Egg Sliding-Tile Game)

Tier: Mastery 2 (Mas-2) | Judge URL: Luogu P1971
Problem Summary: An \(N \times M\) board (\(1 \le N, M \le 40\)) contains white stones O, black stones X, and exactly one blank space .. Rabbit and Egg play \(K \le 1000\) turns (\(2K\) half-moves): on Rabbit’s turn, Rabbit slides an orthogonally adjacent white stone O into the blank space .; on Egg’s turn, Egg slides an orthogonally adjacent black stone X into the blank space .. Given the transcript of \(2K\) moves actually played, identify how many times Rabbit made a blunder (i.e., before Rabbit’s move, Rabbit had a winning strategy from the current board state, AND after Rabbit’s move, Egg now has a winning strategy from the resulting board state) and list their turn indices.







NoteHint 1 — Why the Blank Space . Can NEVER Revisit a Square!





Track the movement of the single blank space .! Let the initial blank space at \((r_0, c_0)\) have chessboard parity \(p_0 = (r_0 + c_0) \bmod 2\).

On Move 1 (Rabbit), . swaps with an adjacent O at parity \(1 - p_0\), leaving O at \((r_0, c_0)\) (parity \(p_0\)).
On Move 2 (Egg), . swaps with an adjacent X at parity \(p_0\), leaving X at parity \(1 - p_0\).

Notice that whenever . leaves a square of parity \(p_0\), it leaves an O behind; whenever . leaves a square of parity \(1 - p_0\), it leaves an X behind! What stone color is required to enter a square of parity \(p_0\) vs. \(1 - p_0\)?









NoteHint 2 — Filtering the Board to the Valid Bipartite Graph & Online Vertex Deletion





To enter a square of parity \(1 - p_0\) (Rabbit’s move), that square must hold O; once . leaves it on Egg’s move, it forever holds X, so . can never enter it again! Symmetrically, to enter a square of parity \(p_0\) (Egg’s move), that square must hold X; once . leaves it on Rabbit’s move, it forever holds O, so . can never enter it again! Thus if we keep only:

\(L\): the initial blank \((r_0, c_0)\) plus all squares of parity \(p_0\) that initially hold X, and
\(R\): all squares of parity \(1 - p_0\) that initially hold O,

the sliding-tile game is 100% isomorphic to a Self-Avoiding Walk Game on the bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\)!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Luogu P1971






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
At first glance, sliding stones changes the board configuration dynamically, which looks like PSPACE-hard Rush Hour / 15-Puzzle. However, tracking the blank space . reveals a strict parity-color alternation: . alternates between \((p_0, \texttt{'X'})\) squares and \((1 - p_0, \texttt{'O'})\) squares, and overwriting a square with the opposite stone color permanently locks that square out of future moves! This compiles the entire game into an online Bipartite Self-Avoiding Walk Game where vertices are deleted one by one along the game transcript.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic & Logical Representation
Let \((r_0, c_0)\) be the initial blank ., and let \(p_0 = (r_0 + c_0) \bmod 2\). Define the active vertex sets:
\[
L = \{(r_0, c_0)\} \cup \big\{ (r, c) : (r+c) \bmod 2 = p_0 \;\land\; \text{grid}[r][c] = \texttt{'X'} \big\},
\]
\[
R = \big\{ (r, c) : (r+c) \bmod 2 = 1 - p_0 \;\land\; \text{grid}[r][c] = \texttt{'O'} \big\}.
\]
At the start of turn \(t \in \{1, \dots, K\}\), the blank sits at \(u_t \in L\), and Rabbit moves the blank to an unvisited neighbor \(v_t \in R\) (permanently deleting \(u_t\) from the graph); then Egg moves the blank from \(v_t \in R\) to an unvisited neighbor \(u_{t+1} \in L\) (permanently deleting \(v_t\) from the graph). By Theorem 4.1 (since the current player moves . first out of its current cell!):

Before Rabbit’s move at turn \(t\): Rabbit has a winning strategy from \(u_t\) in the current remaining graph \(G_t\) if and only if \(u_t\) is Essential in \(G_t\) (\(\nu(G_t \setminus \{u_t\}) = \nu(G_t) - 1\)).
After Rabbit’s move \(u_t \to v_t\): The remaining graph is \(G'_t = G_t \setminus \{u_t\}\) with the blank at \(v_t\). Rabbit’s move was a losing blunder if and only if Rabbit could have won before the move (\(u_t\) was Essential in \(G_t\)) and Egg now has a winning strategy from \(v_t\) in \(G'_t\) (\(v_t\) is Essential in \(G'_t\))!



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Incremental Online DM Maintenance)
How do we test whether the current vertex \(x\) is Essential, and then permanently delete \(x\) from the maintaining maximum matching match[], in \(O(VE)\) time per step?

Initial Matching: Build the bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) between adjacent active cells and compute an initial maximum matching match[] via Hungary / Kuhn’s DFS.
Testing Essentiality + Deleting \(x\) in One Step (del_and_check(x)):

Mark removed[x] = true.
If match[x] == -1 (\(x\) was already unmatched in our current maximum matching!), then \(x\) is trivially Avoidable (not Essential), and deleting \(x\) leaves the remaining matching maximum! Return essential = false.
If match[x] = w != -1, unmatch w (match[w] = -1, match[x] = -1) and run a single Kuhn augmenting-path DFS starting from w in the remaining graph (!removed[.]):

If an augmenting path from w is found, the maximum matching size of \(G \setminus \{x\}\) did not drop (\(\nu(G \setminus \{x\}) = \nu(G)\)), so \(x\) was Avoidable (essential = false)!
If no augmenting path from w exists, \(\nu(G \setminus \{x\}) = \nu(G) - 1\), so \(x\) was Essential (essential = true)!



// Returns true iff x was Essential in the current graph, and permanently deletes x
bool del_and_check(int x) {
    removed[x] = true;
    int w = match_partner[x];
    if (w == -1) return false; // Already unmatched -> Avoidable!
    match_partner[x] = match_partner[w] = -1;
    fill(vis.begin(), vis.end(), 0);
    // If w can re-augment in G \ {x}, then x was Avoidable; else x was Essential!
    return !dfs_augment(w);
}

// For each turn t = 1 .. K:
// Blank is currently at u_t (Rabbit's turn):
bool win_before = del_and_check(u_t); // Deletes u_t and checks if Rabbit could win
int v_t = cell_id(rabbit_r[t], rabbit_c[t]); // Blank moves to v_t
bool egg_wins_after = del_and_check(v_t);    // Deletes v_t and checks if Egg wins from v_t
if (win_before && egg_wins_after) blunders.push_back(t);
int u_next = cell_id(egg_r[t], egg_c[t]);    // Blank moves to u_{t+1}
u_t = u_next;


Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
Look at how clean del_and_check is: when Rabbit moves \(u_t \to v_t\), del_and_check(u_t) tests whether \(u_t\) was Essential in \(G_t\) and updates the maximum matching to \(G'_t = G_t \setminus \{u_t\}\). Immediately after, when Egg is about to move from \(v_t\) in \(G'_t\), del_and_check(v_t) tests whether \(v_t\) is Essential in \(G'_t\) and updates the maximum matching to \(G_{t+1} = G'_t \setminus \{v_t\}\) for the next turn!

Failure Guard: Only include cells matching the invariant (parity == p0 && grid == 'X') || (parity != p0 && grid == 'O') || initial_blank. Including (parity == p0 && grid == 'O') adds unreachable vertices that corrupt the matching size!
Complexity: Initial matching plus \(2K\) incremental DFS augmentations on \(|V| \le 1600, |E| \le 3200\) runs in \(O((NM + K) \cdot NM) \approx 5 \cdot 10^6\) operations (\(< 10\text{ ms}\)).

7. Chapter 6 Verification Checklist & Failure Mode Summary
Before submitting any Hidden Bipartition, Dulmage–Mendelsohn, or Bipartite Game solution, run through this diagnostic checklist:

Bipartition Invariant Audit:

Grid Leapers \((p, q)\): Did you divide by \(g = \gcd(p, q)\) first? If \((p/g + q/g)\) is odd, color by \((r' + c') \bmod 2\); if both \(p/g\) and \(q/g\) are odd (Luogu P5030), color by \(r' \bmod 2\)!
Prime Sums \(a_i + a_j \in \mathbb{P}\): Did you deduplicate \(1\)s so at most one \(1\) remains (1 + 1 = 2 clique trap)?

Obstacle-Split Strip & Coordinate Compression Audit:

Soft (x) vs. Hard (#) Obstacles: Do hard walls # split row/column segment IDs while soft obstacles x neither split segment IDs nor generate edges (#041)?
Discretized Grids (#044): Did you compress half-open intervals \([x_1, x_2 + 1)\) so unit widths are preserved?
Hub Dualization (#046): Are leaf edges wired bidirectionally (\(R_r \leftrightarrow C_c\), cap \(1\) each way)?

Dulmage–Mendelsohn & Game Role Audit:

Tarjan SCC Domain: When classifying \(\nu\)-critical edges via \(\operatorname{scc}(u) \ne \operatorname{scc}(v)\), did you include both \(s\) and \(t\) inside the residual graph passed to Tarjan?
Walk Game Role-Inversion: Did you check whether Player 1 moves first from \(v_0\) (wins \(\iff v_0 \notin V_E\) is Essential, #048) or places the token on \(v_0\) while Player 2 moves first (wins \(\iff v_0 \in V_E\) is Avoidable, #047)?

title: Chapter 6 — Hidden Bipartitions, Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition, and Matching Games
text:
8. Chapter Revision Summary & Multilingual Bibliography

Key Formulas & Structural Invariants

Coarse DM Partition (\(V = V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\)):

\(V_E = (L \cap V_S) \cup (R \cap V_T^{\text{rev}})\): Avoidable vertices (omitted by at least one \(M^*\); never in any MVC; Second Mover wins in Bipartite Walk Game).
\(V_O = (R \cap V_S) \cup (L \cap V_T^{\text{rev}})\): Bottleneck Essential vertices (in every \(M^*\) and in every MVC).
\(V_U = V \setminus (V_S \cup V_T^{\text{rev}})\): Core Essential vertices (in every \(M^*\) and in some MVC).

Fine DM Edge Classification (Tarjan SCC on \(G_{f^*}\) including \(s, t\)):

Mandatory (\(\nu\)-Critical): \(e \in M^* \land \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) \ne \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v)\).
Admissible (Allowed): \(e \in M^* \lor \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) = \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v)\).
Forbidden: \(e \notin M^* \land \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(u) \ne \operatorname{scc}_{G_{f^*}}(v)\).




Multilingual Bibliography

[EN] Dulmage, A. L., & Mendelsohn, N. S. (1958). Coverings of bipartite graphs. Canadian Journal of Mathematics, 10, 517–534. (Foundational paper introducing the canonical \(V_E \sqcup V_O \sqcup V_U\) coarse and fine block triangular decomposition.)
[EN] Lovász, L., & Plummer, M. D. (1986). Matching Theory. AMS Chelsea Publishing. (Chapters 3–4 develop the Dulmage–Mendelsohn and Gallai–Edmonds decompositions in full generality.)
[ZH] 胡伯涛 [Amber] (2007). 《最小割模型在信息学竞赛中的应用》 (Applications of Minimum Cut Models in OI). 国家集训队 2007 论文集. (Standard Chinese reference on bipartite conflict compilation, grid parity, and extremal minimum cuts.)
[ZH] 贾志鹏 (2011). 《二分图博弈及其在 NOI2011 兔兔与蛋蛋游戏中的应用》. (Introduces the online bipartite walk game reduction and incremental augmenting-path blunder check.)
[JA] noshi91 & maspy (2020–2023). Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition (DM分解) and Maximum Matching Criticality. (Japanese algorithmic competitive programming treatises on \(G_{f^*}\) SCC decomposition and lattice distance 2-adic coloring in AGC 025 D.)

NotePrerequisites



Before studying this chapter, you should be fluent in:

Chapter 2 (Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality & Canonical Cut Extraction): Residual graph reachability \(S_{\min} = \{v \in V : S \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} v\}\) and finite-capacity cut isolation.
Chapter 5 & Chapter 6 (Bipartite Matching, König’s Theorem, and Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition): Hopcroft–Karp \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) matching, König’s minimum vertex cover extraction \(C^* = (L \setminus S_{\min}) \cup (R \cap S_{\min})\), and essential/avoidable vertex classification.









TipLearning Objectives



By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Compile DAG Path Covers into Bipartite Split Graphs: Distinguish Minimum Vertex-Disjoint Path Cover (MDPC) on a raw DAG \(G\) from Minimum Overlapping Path Cover (Poset Chain Cover) on its transitive closure \(\text{TC}(G)\), and extend both to weighted costs and Greene–Kleitman \(k\)-chain partial covers via MCMF.
Prove and Apply the Transitivity Non-Overlap Lemma (FM-08): Explain algebraically why transitive closure prevents a minimum vertex cover \(C^*\) of \(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\) from picking both \(v_{\text{out}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}}\) for the same poset element \(v\), and extract explicit Maximum (Weight) Antichains via \(A^* = \{v \in V : v_{\text{out}} \in S_{\min} \land v_{\text{in}} \notin S_{\min}\}\).
Derive Hall’s Marriage Theorem and Ore’s Defect Formula from Min-Cut: Translate capacitated bipartite matching directly into the cut-defect optimization \(\nu_{a,b}(G) = \sum_{u \in L} a_u - \max_{S \subseteq L} \big(\sum_{u \in S} a_u - \sum_{v \in N(S)} b_v\big)\).
Eliminate Explicit Flow Solvers via Hall’s Theorem (Direction B): Collapse \(2^{|L|}\) Hall subset checks into \(O(N \log N)\) Segment Tree range queries (ARC 076 F, POI 2009 LYZ), \(O(N)\) circular unrolling (CF 981 F), \(O(N 2^N)\) Fast Zeta Transform / SOS DP (ARC 106 E), and \(O(V + E)\) Hall–Kotzig leaf-peeling (AGC 029 F).

title: Chapter 8 — DAG Path Covers, Dilworth’s Poset Duality, and Hall’s Theorem Flow Elimination
section: 1. Motivation: From Chain Decompositions to \(O(N \log N)\) Flow Elimination
text:
1. Motivation: From Chain Decompositions to \(O(N \log N)\) Flow Elimination
Chapters 5 through 7 developed Direction A of bipartite modelling: taking a non-graph problem (grid rooks, L-corner brick tilings, prime-sum conflicts), discovering a hidden bipartition \(V = L \sqcup R\), and running Hopcroft–Karp or Dinic in \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) time.
In competitive programming at the ICPC World Finals and AtCoder Grand/Regular Contest level, two structural barriers break standard bipartite matching:

Directional Sequentiality (Trajectories & Posets): What if an agent does not merely pair one \(u \in L\) with one \(v \in R\), but traverses an arbitrarily long directed chain \(v_1 \to v_2 \to \dots \to v_k\) in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) or Partially Ordered Set (Poset)? How do we minimize the number of trajectories needed to visit every vertex, or dualize that trajectory cover into the largest subset of mutually incomparable objects (Dilworth’s Theorem)?
Scale Explosion (\(N, M \ge 2 \cdot 10^5\) or \(D \ge 10^6\)): What if the bipartite graph is easy to spot—say, \(N = 2 \cdot 10^5\) people matching to \(M = 2 \cdot 10^5\) chairs along contiguous intervals, or \(N = 18\) workers matching to \(D = 3.6 \cdot 10^6\) workdays—so that even constructing the edges or running \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) Dinic exceeds the time and memory limits by three orders of magnitude?

This chapter resolves both barriers through a unified algebraic lens:

In Section 2, we compile sequential chains on a DAG into a bipartite split graph \(G_{\text{split}} = (V_{\text{out}} \sqcup V_{\text{in}}, E_{\text{split}})\) where every matched edge merges two chains and reduces the path count by \(1\). We then prove the Transitivity Non-Overlap Lemma, showing how taking the transitive closure turns König’s vertex cover into a constructive Maximum Antichain engine.
In Sections 3 and 4, we reverse the direction of reduction (Direction B: Flow Elimination). Instead of turning an algebraic problem into a flow network, we use Hall’s Marriage Theorem and Ore’s Defect Formula to convert a massive bipartite flow network back into a combinatorial optimization problem over subsets \(S \subseteq L\), which we then crush using Segment Trees, Monotone Queues, and Sum-Over-Subsets (SOS) DP.

title: Chapter 8 — DAG Path Covers, Dilworth’s Poset Duality, and Hall’s Theorem Flow Elimination
section: 2. Minimum Disjoint DAG Path Cover vs. General Overlapping Path Cover (Dilworth’s Theorem)
text:
2. Minimum Disjoint DAG Path Cover vs. General Overlapping Path Cover (Dilworth’s Theorem)

2.1 Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Reach for DAG Path Covers or Poset Duality (Dilworth / Mirsky) whenever a problem exhibits one of the following signatures:

Sequential Reuse / Trajectory Stitching (Min Chain / Path Cover): You must cover all vertices (or treasures/tasks) of a directed acyclic process using the minimum number of agents, hands, pegs, or monotone trajectories.

Vertex-Disjoint Rule (each vertex may be entered and exited by at most one trajectory) \(\implies\) Minimum Disjoint Path Cover (MDPC) on the raw DAG \(G\).
Vertex-Overlapping Rule (trajectories may share intermediate vertices, or the underlying reachability relation is transitive) \(\implies\) Transitive Closure + Dilworth Chain Cover on \(\text{TC}(G)\).

Pairwise Incomparable Selection (Max Antichain): Select the largest (or maximum-weight) subset \(A \subseteq V\) such that no two selected elements satisfy \(u \prec v\) (e.g., no chosen string is a substring of another in CF 590 E — Birthday, or no two shrines can reach each other in [CTSC2008] 祭祀).
Why Naive Greedy Longest-Chain Peeling Fails: It is tempting to repeatedly extract the longest directed path in a DAG and delete it. This fails catastrophically! Consider the 6-vertex DAG with spine \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4\) and two side branches \(2 \to 5\) and \(6 \to 3\):

Greedy Longest Path: Picks the 4-vertex spine \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4\) first, leaving vertices \(\{5\}\) and \(\{6\}\) completely isolated. Greedy uses \(3\) paths: \((1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4)\), \((5)\), and \((6)\).
True Optimum: Reroutes at the middle edge \(2 \to 3\) to form \(2\) paths of length \(3\): \((1 \to 2 \to 5)\) and \((6 \to 3 \to 4)\), covering all \(6\) vertices! Bipartite matching augmenting paths exist precisely to undo greedy edge commitments like \(2 \to 3\).





2.2 Step 2 & Step 3: Algebraic Compilation of the Split Graph \(G_{\text{split}}\)

1. The Dual Quartet on a Finite Poset \(\mathcal{P} = (V, \prec)\)
Before writing down indicator variables, always verify which of the four poset quantities the problem asks for—two of them require zero flow (\(O(V + E)\) topological DP), while the other two require bipartite matching:








Primal Packing Problem
Dual Covering Problem
Exact Algorithmic Engine & Complexity




Maximum Chain (longest chain \(c_1 \prec c_2 \prec \dots \prec c_L\), height)
Minimum Antichain Partition (Mirsky’s Theorem, 1971)
\(O(V + E)\) Topological DP: \(dp[v] = 1 + \max_{u \prec v} dp[u]\) partitions \(V\) into \(L\) antichain level sets \(A_k = \{v : dp[v] = k\}\).


Maximum Antichain (largest pairwise incomparable \(A \subseteq V\), width)
Minimum Chain Cover (Dilworth’s Theorem, 1950)
\(O(E\sqrt{V})\) Bipartite Matching on the transitively closed split graph \(G_{\text{split}}(\text{TC}(G))\).





2. Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation of Disjoint Path Cover
Let \(G = (V, E)\) be a DAG with \(|V| = N\). A vertex-disjoint path cover \(\mathcal{P} = \{P_1, \dots, P_k\}\) partitions \(V\) into \(k\) directed paths. Let \(x_{uv} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether directed edge \((u \to v) \in E\) is traversed by one of the paths in \(\mathcal{P}\).
What algebraic constraints on \(x_{uv}\) characterize a valid vertex-disjoint path cover?

Out-degree at most \(1\): Each vertex \(u \in V\) has at most one successor in its path:
\[\sum_{v : (u, v) \in E} x_{uv} \le 1 \qquad \forall u \in V.\]
In-degree at most \(1\): Each vertex \(v \in V\) has at most one predecessor in its path:
\[\sum_{u : (u, v) \in E} x_{uv} \le 1 \qquad \forall v \in V.\]
Cycle-Freeness via Acyclicity: In a general directed graph, degree-\(\le 1\) subgraphs can contain directed cycles. Because \(G\) is a DAG, no directed cycles exist in \(E\), so every edge subset \(M = \{(u, v) \in E : x_{uv} = 1\}\) satisfying (1) and (2) is a disjoint union of directed paths!
Path Counting Identity: Initially, when \(M = \emptyset\) (\(x_{uv} = 0\)), every vertex \(v \in V\) is a trivial path of length \(0\), giving \(N\) paths. Each selected edge \((u, v) \in M\) concatenates the path ending at \(u\) with the path starting at \(v\), reducing the total number of paths by exactly \(1\):
\[\text{Number of Paths}(M) = |V| - \sum_{(u, v) \in E} x_{uv} = |V| - |M|.\]



3. Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (\(G_{\text{split}}\))
Look at constraints (1) and (2): each edge variable \(x_{uv} \in \{0, 1\}\) consumes at most \(1\) unit of “exit capacity” at \(u\) and at most \(1\) unit of “entry capacity” at \(v\). Since \(u\) can simultaneously have an incoming path edge \((w \to u)\) and an outgoing path edge \((u \to v)\), we must decouple \(u\)’s role as a path tail from its role as a path head:

Split each vertex \(v \in V\) into two bipartite nodes: an outgoing port \(v_{\text{out}} \in V_{\text{out}}\) (left side \(L\)) and an incoming port \(v_{\text{in}} \in V_{\text{in}}\) (right side \(R\)).
For every directed edge \((u \to v) \in E\), add a bipartite edge \((u_{\text{out}}, v_{\text{in}}) \in E_{\text{split}}\).
Constraints (1) and (2) state that \(M \subseteq E_{\text{split}}\) is a bipartite matching in \(G_{\text{split}}(G) = (V_{\text{out}} \sqcup V_{\text{in}}, E_{\text{split}})\)! Minimizing \(|V| - |M|\) maximizes \(|M|\), yielding the fundamental formula:

\[\boxed{\text{MDPC}(G) = |V| - \nu\big(G_{\text{split}}(G)\big).}\]

Explicit Path Reconstruction: After finding a maximum matching \(M^*\) in \(G_{\text{split}}(G)\), a vertex \(v \in V\) is the start of a path iff its incoming port \(v_{\text{in}} \in V_{\text{in}}\) is unmatched. From each unmatched \(v_{\text{in}}\), repeatedly follow the unique matched partner \(v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{M^*} w_{\text{in}}\) until reaching an unmatched outgoing port \(z_{\text{out}}\).
Weighted / Cost Extension: Suppose starting a new path at \(v\) costs \(s_v\) and traversing \((u \to v)\) costs \(c_{uv}\). Then choosing edge \((u \to v) \in M\) replaces the start cost \(s_v\) at \(v\) with the transition cost \(c_{uv}\), changing the total cost by \(c_{uv} - s_v\):
\[\text{Total Cost}(M) = \sum_{v \in V} s_v + \sum_{(u, v) \in M} (c_{uv} - s_v),\]
which compiles immediately to Minimum-Weight Bipartite Matching (MCMF) on \(G_{\text{split}}(G)\)!





2.3 Dilworth’s Theorem, Overlapping Path Covers & The Transitivity Non-Overlap Lemma
What if trajectories are allowed to share vertices (Minimum Overlapping Path Cover), or we want to find the Maximum-Weight Antichain of a poset \(\mathcal{P} = (V, \prec)\) where each element \(v \in V\) has positive weight \(w_v > 0\)?

1. Why Transitive Closure Eliminates Vertex Sharing (Path Jumping)
Suppose two trajectories \(P_1 = (a \to v \to b)\) and \(P_2 = (c \to v \to d)\) share an intermediate vertex \(v\). Because \(P_1\) already covers \(v\), \(P_2\) does not need to physically step on \(v\)—it only uses \(v\) as a stepping stone to get from \(c\) to \(d\). If we replace the raw DAG \(G\) with its transitive closure \(G^{\text{tc}} = \text{TC}(G)\) (adding a direct shortcut edge \(u \to w\) whenever \(u \leadsto_G w\) via a path of length \(\ge 1\)), then \(P_2\) can jump directly across \(v\) via the shortcut edge \(c \to d \in E(G^{\text{tc}})\)!
By uncrossing shared vertices one by one, any collection of \(k\) potentially overlapping paths covering \(V\) in \(G\) converts into \(k\) strictly vertex-disjoint chains covering \(V\) in \(G^{\text{tc}}\), and vice versa (replacing each transitive jump \(c \to d\) by its underlying path \(c \leadsto d\) in \(G\)). Hence:
\[\boxed{\text{MinOverlappingPathCover}(G) = \text{MDPC}\big(\text{TC}(G)\big) = |V| - \nu\Big(G_{\text{split}}\big(\text{TC}(G)\big)\Big).}\]


2. Resolving the Double-Cover Paradox: The Transitivity Non-Overlap Lemma
Now let us connect \(\text{MDPC}(\text{TC}(G))\) to Dilworth’s Theorem and Constructive Antichain Recovery. In \(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P}) = (V_{\text{out}} \sqcup V_{\text{in}}, E_{\text{split}})\) where \((u_{\text{out}}, v_{\text{in}}) \in E_{\text{split}} \iff u \prec v\), assign weight \(w_v > 0\) to both \(v_{\text{out}} \in V_{\text{out}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \in V_{\text{in}}\).
By König’s Theorem (Chapter 6), the maximum matching size (or minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in the weighted split network) equals the minimum vertex cover \(\tau_w\big(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\big)\). Suppose \(C^* \subseteq V_{\text{out}} \sqcup V_{\text{in}}\) is a minimum vertex cover of \(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\).
Wait: each poset element \(v \in V\) was split into two vertices \(v_{\text{out}}\) and \(v_{\text{in}}\)! For \(A^* \subseteq V\) to be a valid antichain in \(\mathcal{P}\), we can only pick \(v \in A^*\) if neither \(v_{\text{out}}\) nor \(v_{\text{in}}\) is needed to cover any comparability edge—that is, we must define:
\[A^* := \big\{\, v \in V \;\big|\; v_{\text{out}} \notin C^* \;\land\; v_{\text{in}} \notin C^* \,\big\}.\]
Why does \(A^*\) have size \(|V| - |C^*|\) (or weight \(\sum_{v \in V} w_v - \tau_w(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P}))\))? What if \(C^*\) selects both \(v_{\text{out}} \in C^*\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \in C^*\) for some element \(v \in V\), paying twice for \(v\) while deleting only one element from \(V\)? The following fundamental lemma proves that transitivity of \(\prec\) makes double-covering impossible!






ImportantLemma 2.1 (The Transitivity Non-Overlap Lemma)



Let \(\mathcal{P} = (V, \prec)\) be a strict poset (irreflexive and transitive), and let \(C^* \subseteq V_{\text{out}} \sqcup V_{\text{in}}\) be any minimal (or canonical minimum-cut) vertex cover of \(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\). Then no element \(v \in V\) has both \(v_{\text{out}} \in C^*\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \in C^*\):
\[v_{\text{out}} \in C^* \implies v_{\text{in}} \notin C^* \qquad \forall v \in V.\]
Consequently, the sets \(C^*_{\text{out}} = \{v \in V : v_{\text{out}} \in C^*\}\) and \(C^*_{\text{in}} = \{v \in V : v_{\text{in}} \in C^*\}\) are disjoint subsets of \(V\), and the complement
\[\boxed{A^* = \big\{\, v \in V \;\big|\; v_{\text{out}} \notin C^* \;\land\; v_{\text{in}} \notin C^* \,\big\} = \big\{\, v \in V \;\big|\; v_{\text{out}} \in S_{\min} \;\land\; v_{\text{in}} \notin S_{\min} \,\big\}}\]
is a Maximum-Weight Antichain of weight \(\sum_{v \in A^*} w_v = \sum_{v \in V} w_v - \tau_w\big(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\big)\) (and cardinality \(|A^*| = |V| - \nu(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P}))\) when \(w_v = 1\)).


Proof: Suppose for contradiction that for some \(v \in V\), both \(v_{\text{out}} \in C^*\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \in C^*\) (and in the canonical min-cut \(C^* = (V_{\text{out}} \setminus S_{\min}) \cup (V_{\text{in}} \cap S_{\min})\) or any minimal cover, neither can be dropped without uncovering an edge):

Because \(v_{\text{out}} \in C^*\) is essential to the cover (or in the canonical min-cut \(v_{\text{out}} \notin S_{\min}\)), there exists at least one outgoing edge \((v_{\text{out}}, y_{\text{in}}) \in E_{\text{split}}\) (\(v \prec y\)) whose right endpoint is not in \(C^*\): \(y_{\text{in}} \notin C^*\) (in the canonical min-cut, \(v_{\text{in}} \in S_{\min}\) means some \(x_{\text{out}} \in S_{\min}\) has an \(\infty\)-edge \((x_{\text{out}}, v_{\text{in}})\) to \(v_{\text{in}}\), so \(x_{\text{out}} \notin C^*\)).
Symmetrically, because \(v_{\text{in}} \in C^*\), there exists at least one incoming edge \((x_{\text{out}}, v_{\text{in}}) \in E_{\text{split}}\) (\(x \prec v\)) whose left endpoint is not in \(C^*\): \(x_{\text{out}} \notin C^*\).
By transitivity of the poset relation \(\prec\), \(x \prec v\) and \(v \prec y\) force \(x \prec y\), which means the shortcut edge \((x_{\text{out}}, y_{\text{in}})\) must exist in \(E_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\)!
Yet \(x_{\text{out}} \notin C^*\) and \(y_{\text{in}} \notin C^*\), meaning the edge \((x_{\text{out}}, y_{\text{in}})\) has neither endpoint in \(C^*\)—contradicting that \(C^*\) is a valid vertex cover! (In the canonical min-cut, \(x_{\text{out}} \in S_{\min}\) and \((x_{\text{out}}, y_{\text{in}}) \in E_{\text{split}}\) with capacity \(\infty\) forces \(y_{\text{in}} \in S_{\min}\), so \(y_{\text{in}} \in C^*\) for every \(y \succ v\), meaning removing \(v_{\text{out}}\) from \(C^*\) leaves zero uncovered edges and strictly decreases the cut cost by \(w_v > 0\)!)

Finally, for any two distinct elements \(u, v \in A^*\), neither \(u_{\text{out}}\) nor \(v_{\text{in}}\) belongs to \(C^*\). Since \(C^*\) covers all edges of \(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\), \((u_{\text{out}}, v_{\text{in}}) \notin E_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\), so \(u \not\prec v\) and \(v \not\prec u\). Thus \(A^*\) is a valid antichain of weight \(\sum_{v \in V} w_v - \sum_{v \in C^*_{\text{out}} \sqcup C^*_{\text{in}}} w_v = \sum_{v \in V} w_v - \tau_w\big(G_{\text{split}}(\mathcal{P})\big)\). Since every chain can contain at most one element of any antichain, no antichain can exceed the minimum chain cover weight, proving optimality. \(\blacksquare\)




2.4 Step 4: Broken-Gadget Counterexample FM-08 (Missing Transitive Closure & OR vs. AND Bug)






WarningFailure Mode FM-08: Omitting Transitive Closure & Using OR Instead of AND in Antichain Extraction



Two fatal bugs account for over 90% of Wrong Answers on Dilworth and DAG path cover problems:

Bug 1 — Omitting Transitive Closure Before Matching (X-Bottleneck Counterexample): Consider the 5-vertex X-shaped DAG \(G\) with edges \(1 \to 2\), \(4 \to 2\), \(2 \to 3\), and \(2 \to 5\) (vertex \(2\) is a central hub; there are no direct edges from \(\{1, 4\}\) to \(\{3, 5\}\)).

True Overlapping Path Cover / Max Antichain: \(2\) chains (\(1 \to 2 \to 3\) and \(4 \to 2 \to 5\), sharing hub \(2\)), and the maximum antichain has size \(2\) (e.g., \(\{1, 4\}\) or \(\{3, 5\}\)).
What Happens If You Forget \(\text{TC}(G)\): In the raw split graph \(G_{\text{split}}(G)\), \(E_{\text{split}} = \{(1_{\text{out}}, 2_{\text{in}}), (4_{\text{out}}, 2_{\text{in}}), (2_{\text{out}}, 3_{\text{in}}), (2_{\text{out}}, 5_{\text{in}})\}\). Because \(2_{\text{in}}\) can match at most one of \(\{1_{\text{out}}, 4_{\text{out}}\}\) and \(2_{\text{out}}\) can match at most one of \(\{3_{\text{in}}, 5_{\text{in}}\}\), the maximum matching size is \(\nu = 2\), falsely reporting \(5 - 2 = \mathbf{3}\) chains! Worse still, the minimum vertex cover of \(G_{\text{split}}(G)\) is \(C^* = \{2_{\text{out}}, 2_{\text{in}}\}\) (size \(2\)), which violates Lemma 2.1 by picking both halves of vertex \(2\), and outputs \(A^* = V \setminus \{2\} = \{1, 3, 4, 5\}\) of size \(4\) (not even an antichain, since \(1 \leadsto 3\))!
How \(\text{TC}(G)\) Fixes It: Adding transitive shortcut edges \(1 \to 3, 1 \to 5, 4 \to 3, 4 \to 5\) allows matching \((1_{\text{out}}, 2_{\text{in}})\), \((2_{\text{out}}, 3_{\text{in}})\), and the shortcut \((4_{\text{out}}, 5_{\text{in}})\), raising \(\nu\) to \(3\) (\(5 - 3 = 2\) chains) and forcing \(C^* = \{2_{\text{in}}, 3_{\text{in}}, 5_{\text{in}}\}\) so \(A^* = \{1, 4\}\) has size \(2\).

Bug 2 — Extracting \(A^*\) with OR (\(\notin C^*_{\text{out}} \lor \notin C^*_{\text{in}}\)) Instead of AND (H-06): On a simple 2-vertex chain \(1 \to 2\), \(M^* = \{(1_{\text{out}}, 2_{\text{in}})\}\) and \(C^* = \{2_{\text{in}}\}\). Here \(1_{\text{out}} \notin C^*, 1_{\text{in}} \notin C^*\) (both out), while for vertex \(2\), \(2_{\text{out}} \notin C^*\) is true even though \(2_{\text{in}} \in C^*\)! Using OR (\(\neg C^*_{\text{out}} \lor \neg C^*_{\text{in}}\)) selects \(\{1, 2\}\) (comparable!), whereas AND (\(\neg C^*_{\text{out}} \land \neg C^*_{\text{in}}\)) selects the true antichain \(\{1\}\).




Reference Implementation Pattern: Constructive Dilworth Maximum Antichain (CF 590 E, [CTSC2008] 祭祀)
// Given a transitively closed, irreflexive poset P on 0..N-1 (reach[u][v] == true iff u < v)
// and residual reachability vis_S[] from Source S after running Dinic on S -> u_out -> v_in -> T:
//   u_out = u (0 .. N-1), u_in = u + N (N .. 2N-1)
vector<int> extract_max_antichain(int N, const vector<bool>& vis_S) {
    vector<int> antichain;
    for (int v = 0; v < N; ++v) {
        // v_out not in C*  <==>  vis_S[v] == true
        // v_in  not in C*  <==>  vis_S[v + N] == false
        if (vis_S[v] && !vis_S[v + N]) {
            antichain.push_back(v);
        }
    }
    return antichain; // Guaranteed size == N - MaxFlow (or weight == Sum(w) - MinCut)
}




2.5 Extension: Partial \(k\)-Chain Covers, Greene–Kleitman Duality (1976) & MCMF Compilation
What if a problem gives us a budget of at most \(k\) chains (or \(k\) paths on a DAG) where \(k < \text{width}(\mathcal{P})\), and asks for the maximum number (or maximum total weight) of vertices we can cover using at most \(k\) chains?






NoteTheorem 2.2 (Greene–Kleitman Theorem, 1976 — \(k\)-Dilworth Duality)



In any finite poset \(\mathcal{P} = (V, \prec)\) and for any integer \(k \ge 1\), the maximum cardinality of a \(k\)-chain family (a subset \(U \subseteq V\) that can be partitioned into at most \(k\) chains) equals:
\[\max_{\substack{C_1, \dots, C_k \text{ chains}}} \left|\bigcup_{i=1}^k C_i\right| = \min_{\substack{A_1 \sqcup \dots \sqcup A_q = V \\ \text{antichain partition}}} \sum_{j=1}^q \min\big(|A_j|, \; k\big) = \min_{U \subseteq V} \Big(|V \setminus U| + k \cdot \text{width}(\mathcal{P}[U])\Big).\]


When each vertex \(v \in V\) of a DAG \(G = (V, E)\) offers a reward \(w_v \ge 0\) upon its first visit by one of at most \(k\) paths, we compile this directly to Min-Cost Max-Flow (MCMF) of flow value \(k\):

Split each vertex \(v \in V\) into \(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\) with:

A reward edge \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{ cost } -w_v} v_{\text{out}}\) (for vertex-disjoint paths).
If paths are allowed to overlap (share vertices without collecting \(w_v\) twice), add a parallel bypass edge \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{ cost } 0} v_{\text{out}}\).

Wire \(S_{\text{sub}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{ cost } 0} v_{\text{in}}\), \(v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{ cost } 0} T\), and for each \((u \to v) \in E\), wire \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{ cost } 0} v_{\text{in}}\).
Throttle total trajectories to \(\le k\) via \(S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } k, \text{ cost } 0} S_{\text{sub}}\) and a slack bypass \(S_{\text{sub}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } \infty, \text{ cost } 0} T\). The negated min-cost of pushing \(k\) units from \(S\) to \(T\) is the exact Greene–Kleitman maximum \(k\)-chain weight!

3. Hall’s Marriage Theorem, Ore’s Defect Formula, and Supply–Demand Hall

3.1 Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (When to Eliminate Flow via Hall’s Theorem)
When a bipartite matching or capacitated supply–demand problem has \(N, M \ge 2 \cdot 10^5\) (or \(D \sim 3.6 \cdot 10^6\) days in ARC 106 E), explicit Dinic or Hopcroft–Karp requires \(O(E\sqrt{V})\) time and TLEs! Reach for Hall’s Marriage Theorem or Ore’s Defect Formula (Direction B: Flow Elimination) whenever:

Geometric Neighbourhood Convexity: Each \(u \in L\) connects to a contiguous interval \([l_u, r_u] \subseteq R\) (POI 2009 LYZ-Ice Skates), a prefix–suffix union \([1, l_u] \cup [r_u, M]\) (ARC 076 F — Exhausted?), or a circular arc of radius \(d\) (CF 981 F — Round Marriage).
Extreme Cardinality Asymmetry (\(|L| \le 18, |R| \ge 10^5\), or vice versa): One side of the bipartite graph has \(\le 20\) vertices (CF 1009 G with \(|\Sigma| = 6\), ARC 106 E with \(N \le 18\)), allowing \(O(N 2^N)\) Sum-Over-Subsets (SOS) DP over all \(2^{|L|}\) subsets \(S \subseteq L\).
Hyperedge-to-Vertex Tree Realization (AGC 029 F): Given \(N - 1\) subsets \(E_1, \dots, E_{N-1} \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\), choosing one representative endpoint \(u_i \in E_i\) per hyperedge to form a spanning tree is equivalent to Hall’s condition \(\left|\bigcup_{i \in S} E_i\right| \ge |S| + 1\) for all \(\emptyset \neq S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N-1\}\).




3.2 Step 2: Deriving Ore’s Defect Formula & Supply–Demand Hall from König / Min-Cut
Let \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) be a bipartite graph where each left vertex \(u \in L\) has supply \(a_u \ge 0\) and each right vertex \(v \in R\) has demand capacity \(b_v \ge 0\) (in unweighted matching, \(a_u = b_v = 1\)). Consider the standard \(S\)-\(T\) flow network \(\mathcal{N}\) with capacities:
\[c(S, u) = a_u \quad (\forall u \in L), \qquad c(u, v) = \infty \quad (\forall (u, v) \in E), \qquad c(v, T) = b_v \quad (\forall v \in R).\]
Let \((V_S, V_T)\) be any finite-capacity \(S\)-\(T\) cut, with \(S_L := L \cap V_S\) and \(S_R := R \cap V_S\).

Infinite-Edge Constraint: For the cut capacity \(\text{cap}(V_S, V_T)\) to be finite, no edge \((u, v) \in E\) with \(u \in S_L\) and \(v \in R \setminus S_R\) may be severed. Thus every neighbor of \(S_L\) must also lie in \(S_R\):
\[N(S_L) \subseteq S_R, \qquad \text{where } N(S_L) := \bigcup_{u \in S_L} N(u).\]
Optimal Right-Side Choice: For any fixed subset \(S_L \subseteq L\), the cut severs \(S \to u\) for \(u \in L \setminus S_L\) and \(v \to T\) for \(v \in S_R\). Since \(b_v \ge 0\), minimizing \(\sum_{v \in S_R} b_v\) over all \(S_R \supseteq N(S_L)\) sets \(S_R = N(S_L)\) exactly!
Cut Capacity as Supply Minus Defect: Substituting \(S_R = N(S_L)\) into the cut capacity gives:
\[\text{Cut}(S_L) = \sum_{u \in L \setminus S_L} a_u + \sum_{v \in N(S_L)} b_v = \sum_{u \in L} a_u - \underbrace{\left(\sum_{u \in S_L} a_u - \sum_{v \in N(S_L)} b_v\right)}_{\text{Defect } \text{def}(S_L)}.\]

Minimizing \(\text{Cut}(S_L)\) over all \(S_L \subseteq L\) maximizes the defect \(\text{def}(S_L)\). By the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem (and König’s Theorem when \(a_u = b_v = 1\)), we immediately obtain the three fundamental pillars of Hall–Ore Duality:






ImportantTheorem 3.1 (Ore’s Defect Formula, Hall’s Marriage Theorem & Complement Zeta Identity)



For any bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) with supplies \(a_u \ge 0\) (\(u \in L\)) and capacities \(b_v \ge 0\) (\(v \in R\)):

Ore’s Defect Formula (1955): The maximum \(a\)-\(b\) flow (or maximum matching \(\nu(G)\) when \(a_u = b_v = 1\)) equals total supply minus the maximum subset defect:
\[\boxed{\nu_{a, b}(G) = \sum_{u \in L} a_u - \max_{S \subseteq L} \left(\sum_{u \in S} a_u - \sum_{v \in N(S)} b_v\right), \qquad \nu(G) = |L| - \max_{S \subseteq L} \big(|S| - |N(S)|\big).}\]
(Note: Choosing \(S = \emptyset\) always yields \(\text{def}(\emptyset) = 0\), so the maximum defect is always \(\ge 0\).)
Hall’s Marriage Theorem (1935) / Supply–Demand Feasibility: A matching saturating all left supplies \(\sum_{u \in L} a_u\) exists if and only if \(\max_{S \subseteq L} \text{def}(S) \le 0\), i.e.:
\[\boxed{\forall S \subseteq L, \qquad \sum_{v \in N(S)} b_v \ge \sum_{u \in S} a_u.}\]
Set-Complement Rewrite for Fast Zeta Transform (ARC 106 E, CF 1009 G): A right vertex \(v \in R\) does not belong to \(N(S)\) if and only if its entire neighborhood \(N(v)\) lies inside the complement \(L \setminus S\). Defining the upward subset-sum \(g[T] := \sum_{v \in R : N(v) \subseteq T} b_v\) for each mask \(T \subseteq L\), we have:
\[\boxed{\sum_{v \in N(S)} b_v = \sum_{v \in R} b_v - g[L \setminus S], \qquad \text{where } g[T] = \sum_{M \subseteq T} \left(\sum_{v \in R : N(v) = M} b_v\right).}\]

Partial \(k\)-Path / \(k\)-Chain Cover (Greene–Kleitman Duality)
\(\max_{|\mathcal{C}| \le k} \sum_{v \in \bigcup \mathcal{C}} w_v\)
Split \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1, -w_v} v_{\text{out}}\) (plus \(\infty, 0\) bypass if overlapping), \(k\)-flow MCMF
\(O(k \cdot E \log V)\)


Dynamic Contiguous Interval Hall Feasibility (POI 2009 LYZ)
\(\forall [l, r], \sum_{i=l}^r (a_i - k) \le d \cdot k\) (Lemma 4.1 Rule A)
Segment Tree maintaining Maximum Contiguous Subarray Sum
\(O((N + Q) \log N)\)


Prefix–Suffix Interval Defect (ARC 076 F, \(N(i) = [1, L_i] \cup [R_i, M]\))
Complement \((L_i, R_i)\) is contiguous \(\implies\) single pair \((L, R)\) suffices (Rule C)
Sweep-Line + Lazy Segment Tree over \(0 \le L < R \le M + 1\)
\(O((N + M) \log M)\)

Unroll \(a\) to \(2N\), \(b\) to \(4N\); check \((r_j - j) \ge (l_i - i)\)

\(O(N \log L)\)


Asymmetric Small-Side Matching (\(|L| \le 18, |R| \ge 10^5\))
Complement identity \(|N(S)| = |R| - g[L \setminus S]\) (Theorem 3.1(3))
Fast Zeta Transform (SOS DP) in \(O(|L| 2^{|L|})\) (CF 1009 G, ARC 106 E)
\(O(|L| 2^{|L|} \log D)\)

\(\forall \emptyset \neq S, |\bigcup_{i \in S} E_i| \ge |S| + 1\)
Match \(\mathcal{E} \leftrightarrow V \setminus \{1\}\) via Hopcroft–Karp + Alternating BFS from root \(1\)
\(O(\sum |E_i| \sqrt{N})\)

section: 7. Chapter 8 Verification Checklist, Failure Mode Summary & Blind Checkpoint CP-II
text:
7. Chapter 8 Verification Checklist, Failure Mode Summary & Blind Checkpoint CP-II

7.1 Pre-Submission Verification Checklist (FM-08 & Hall Guards)
Before submitting any DAG Path Cover, Poset Antichain, or Hall Flow-Elimination solution, run through these five structural checks:

Disjoint vs. Overlapping Path Cover (FM-08 Part 1): Can two paths share an intermediate vertex? If yes (or if you are finding an antichain of a reachability poset), did you compute the Transitive Closure \(\text{TC}(G)\) (with zero diagonal reach[u][u] = 0) before building \(G_{\text{split}}\)?
AND vs. OR in Constructive Antichain Recovery (FM-08 Part 2 / H-06): When extracting a Maximum Antichain from the residual reachability set \(S_{\min}\) of \(G_{\text{split}}(\text{TC}(G))\), did you require both \(v_{\text{out}} \notin C^*\) and \(v_{\text{in}} \notin C^*\), i.e., vis_S[v_out] && !vis_S[v_in]?
Feasibility (\(\le 0\)) vs. Positive Defect (\(> 0\)) on Contiguous Intervals (Lemma 4.1):

If testing feasibility (\(\text{def}(I) \le 0\)), checking single intervals \([l, r]\) is 100% exact (POI 2009 LYZ, CF 981 F).
If computing positive maximum defect (\(\nu(G) < \sum a_u\)) for interior intervals \(N(u) = [l_u, r_u]\), did you use multi-interval DP \(dp[r] = \max(dp[r-1], \max_l (dp[l-2] + \text{def}([l, r])))\) instead of a single interval? (For prefix–suffix unions \([1, L_u] \cup [R_u, M]\) in ARC 076 F, the complement \((L_u, R_u)\) is contiguous, so a single \((L, R)\) query in a Lazy Segment Tree is exact!)

Complement Direction in SOS DP (ARC 106 E, CF 1009 G): In Theorem 3.1(3), \(|N(S)| = |R| - g[L \setminus S]\) where \(g[T] = \sum_{M \subseteq T} \text{cnt}[M]\) sums over subsets of \(T = L \setminus S\) (not supersets!).
Cycles vs. Trees in Hyperedge Realization (AGC 029 F): Finding a perfect matching between \(N - 1\) hyperedges and \(V \setminus \{1\}\) is necessary but not sufficient for tree connectivity; did you run the alternating BFS from root \(1\) (u -> incident e -> match_v[e]) and verify visited_count == N?




7.2 Part II Mastery: Two-Stage Blind Diagnostic Checkpoint (CP-II: #201–#208)
In a real contest, problems do not come labeled with chapter numbers. Test your Part II recognition reflexes on these 8 scrambled problem statements (5 genuine flow/matching/Hall problems from Chapters 5–8 + 3 non-flow decoys):

#201 (CP-II-1): Given \(N \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) brides and \(N\) grooms on a circle of circumference \(L\), minimize the maximum circular distance between matched pairs.
#202 (CP-II-2): Given a tree \(T = (V, E)\) with vertex weights \(w_v > 0\) (\(N \le 2 \cdot 10^5\)), select a maximum-weight independent set of vertices.
#203 (CP-II-3): Given a DAG with \(N \le 200\) vertices where each vertex \(v\) must be visited by at least \(1\) and at most \(c_v\) paths, minimize the number of paths needed to cover all vertices.
#204 (CP-II-4): Given \(N \le 3000\) integers \(a_1, \dots, a_N\), select the maximum-size subset such that no two selected integers satisfy \(a_i + a_j = 2^k\) for any integer \(k \ge 1\).
#205 (CP-II-5): Given \(N \le 500\) intervals \([l_i, r_i]\) with weights \(w_i > 0\), select a subset of pairwise overlapping intervals of maximum total weight.
#206 (CP-II-6): Two players play on an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 100\)) where a token starts at \((r_0, c_0)\) and moves to an orthogonal neighbor \((r', c')\) with strictly larger value \(A_{r', c'} > A_{r, c}\). Determine if the first player has a winning strategy.
#207 (CP-II-7): Given an \(N \times M\) board (\(N, M \le 50\)) where lasers can be placed on . cells and shoot until hitting # walls (passing harmlessly through x pits), place the maximum number of mutually non-attacking lasers and output all . cells that must contain a laser in every optimal placement.
#208 (CP-II-8): Given a bipartite graph \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\) (\(|L|, |R| \le 500\)) with vertex weights \(w_v > 0\), find a minimum-weight subset of vertices covering every edge, and output the subset.







TipStage 2: Diagnostic Resolution & Decoy Elimination Key (Click to Reveal)













ID
Verdict
Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Explanation




#201
Genuine (Ch 08.4)
CF 981 F — Round Marriage: Unroll the circle (\(2N\) brides, \(4N\) grooms), binary search distance \(D\), and check contiguous intervals \((r_j - j) \ge (l_i - i)\) in \(O(N)\) via Lemma 4.1!


#202
DECOY (Tree DP)
Tree MWIS: Although every tree is bipartite, \(N = 2 \cdot 10^5\) is solved in \(O(N)\) time via dp[u][0/1] Tree DP, not Dinic!


#203
Genuine (Ch 04 + Ch 08)
Capacitated DAG Path Cover via Bounded Min-Flow: Split \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{[1, c_v]} v_{\text{out}}\) and run Bounded \(s\)-\(t\) Min-Flow (Chapter 4).


#204
Genuine (Ch 07 + Ch 05)
2-Adic Valuation Bipartite Conflict: Write \(a_i = 2^{v_2(a_i)} m_i\) (\(m_i\) odd). If \(a_i + a_j = 2^k\) (\(a_i \neq a_j\)), then \(v_2(a_i) = v_2(a_j) = t < k - 1\) and \(m_i + m_j = 2^{k-t} \equiv 0 \pmod 4\), so one odd part is \(\equiv 1 \pmod 4\) (\(L\)) and the other is \(\equiv 3 \pmod 4\) (\(R\))!


#205
DECOY (Helly’s Property)
Pairwise Intersecting Intervals: By Helly’s Theorem on \(\mathbb{R}\), a family of intervals is pairwise intersecting iff they all share a common point \(x^* \in \mathbb{R}\)! Sweep endpoints in \(O(N \log N)\).


#206
DECOY (DAG Game DP)
Strictly Increasing Grid Moves: Because \(A_{r', c'} > A_{r, c}\) is a strict DAG (not an undirected bipartite matching walk game!), win/loss is computed in \(O(NM)\) topological DP (win[u] |= !win[v]), not Dulmage–Mendelsohn!


#207
Genuine (Ch 06 + Ch 07)
Obstacle-Split Strips + DM Essential Edges: Split rows/cols only at hard # walls (Ch 07), find max matching \(M^*\), and run Tarjan SCC on \(G_{f^*}\) (Ch 06) to find essential matched edges \((u, v) \in M^*\) with \(\text{scc}(u) \neq \text{scc}(v)\)!


#208
Genuine (Ch 06)
Weighted König Minimum Vertex Cover: Construct \(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u \xrightarrow{\infty} v \xrightarrow{w_v} T\) and extract \(C^* = (L \setminus S_{\min}) \cup (R \cap S_{\min})\).
