#089 (SS-1) — Luogu P3227 [HNOI2013]: 切糕 (Cake Cutting)

Judge URL: Luogu P3227 | LOJ #2314
Constraints: \(P, Q, R \le 40\), \(0 \le D \le R\), \(0 \le c_{p,q}(r) \le 1000\), Time Limit \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Statement: You are given a 3D grid of dimensions \(P \times Q \times R\) where each voxel \((p, q, r)\) has a non-negative cost \(c_{p,q}(r) \ge 0\). For each column \(i = (p, q)\) (\(1 \le p \le P, 1 \le q \le Q\)), you must select a single cutting height \(x_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, R\}\), paying \(c_i(x_i)\), such that for any two 4-adjacent columns \(u \sim v\), their chosen heights satisfy \(|x_u - x_v| \le D\). Minimize the total cost \(\sum_{i} c_i(x_i)\).


Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Each of the \(N = PQ \le 1600\) columns chooses an integer state \(x_i \in \{1, \dots, R\}\) (\(R \le 40\)) with an arbitrary non-convex cost table \(c_i(r)\) and pairwise Lipschitz difference bounds \(x_u - x_v \le D\) and \(x_v - x_u \le D\). Because \(PQ R \le 6.4 \times 10^4\), this is the canonical Form A Series Unary Threshold Chain of Section 1.2–1.3.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Introduce unary threshold indicators \(z_{i,k} = [x_i \ge k] \in \{0, 1\}\) for \(k \in \{1, \dots, R+1\}\) with \(z_{i,1} = 1\) (\(S\)) and \(z_{i,R+1} = 0\) (\(T\)). The objective and constraints compile to the pseudo-Boolean cut polynomial:
\[\mathcal{P}(z) = \sum_{i=1}^{PQ} \sum_{k=1}^{R} c_i(k) z_{i,k}(1 - z_{i,k+1}) + \sum_{i=1}^{PQ} \sum_{k=2}^{R-1} \infty \cdot z_{i,k+1}(1 - z_{i,k}) + \sum_{(u, v) \in E_{\text{grid}}} \sum_{k=D+2}^{R} \infty \cdot z_{u,k}(1 - z_{v,k-D}).\]






Note3-Tier Progressive Hints for #089






Hint 1: Represent each column \(i\)’s choice \(x_i \in \{1, \dots, R\}\) as severing one edge along a directed path of \(R\) edges from \(S\) to \(T\) through \(R-1\) internal threshold vertices \(v_{i,2}, \dots, v_{i,R}\).
Hint 2: What stops a minimum cut from severing two cheap edges along column \(i\)’s chain when cross-edges pull an earlier node into \(T\) and push a later node into \(S\)? Add reverse \(\infty\)-locks \(v_{i,k+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k}\)!
Hint 3: Express \(x_u - x_v \le D\) as \(x_u \ge k \implies x_v \ge k - D\), and wire \(v_{u,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{v,k-D}\) for all \(k \in \{D+2, \dots, R\}\) in both directions \((u, v)\) and \((v, u)\).










NoteComplete 4-Step Solution & Failure-Mode Guard for #089






Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation
For each column \(i \in \{1, \dots, PQ\}\), create \(R - 1\) internal vertices \(v_{i,2}, \dots, v_{i,R}\) (identifying \(v_{i,1} \equiv S\) and \(v_{i,R+1} \equiv T\)):

Forward Series Cost Edges: For \(k = 1, \dots, R\), wire \(v_{i,k} \xrightarrow{c_i(k)} v_{i,k+1}\).
Reverse Monotonicity Locks (FM-12 Guard): For \(k = 2, \dots, R-1\), wire \(v_{i,k+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k}\).
Cross-Column Lipschitz Arcs: For every ordered pair of 4-adjacent columns \((u, v)\) and every threshold \(k \in \{D + 2, \dots, R\}\), wire \(v_{u,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{v,k-D}\).

Run Dinic’s algorithm from \(S\) to \(T\) and output \(\text{MinCut}(S, T)\).


Step 4: Complexity & Failure-Mode Guard

Graph Size: \(|V| = PQ(R - 1) + 2 \le 62,402\) vertices and \(|E| \approx 6 PQR \le 3.8 \times 10^5\) directed edges. Dinic runs in \(< 0.1\text{ s}\).
Failure-Mode Guard (FM-12): Never omit the vertical reverse arcs \(v_{i,k+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k}\) when \(D < R\). Also handle \(D = 0\) cleanly: when \(D = 0\), \(k\) ranges over \(\{2, \dots, R\}\) and wires \(v_{u,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{v,k}\), forcing all columns to choose the exact same height \(x_u = x_v\).









#090 (SS-2) — Codeforces 1517 G: Starry Night Camping

Judge URL: Codeforces 1517 G (Companion 3-state grid boundary cut: Luogu P2598 [ZJOI2009] 狼和羊的故事)
Constraints: \(N \le 1000\) tents at integer coordinates \((x_i, y_i) \in [-10^9, 10^9]^2\), weights \(1 \le w_i \le 10^9\), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\).
Statement: Given \(N\) tents on the 2D integer grid, a tent is called special if it has both a horizontal neighbor (at distance \(1\)) and a vertical neighbor (at distance \(1\)) among the surviving tents, and the problem forbids any configuration where two special tents with even \(y\)-coordinates (specifically, horizontal neighbors \((2a+1, 2b)\) and \((2a, 2b)\)) both survive along with their vertical neighbors. Maximize the total weight of surviving tents.


Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
We want to delete a minimum-weight subset of tents \(D \subseteq V\) so that no forbidden 4-tent walk survives. As shown in Section 3, classifying tents into \(K = 4\) layers by their 2D coordinate parity \((x \bmod 2, y \bmod 2)\) orients every undirected forbidden 4-tent configuration into a directed path across a 4-layer DAG.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Partition the \(N\) tents into four disjoint parity layers:
\[L_1 = (\text{odd}, \text{odd}), \quad L_2 = (\text{odd}, \text{even}), \quad L_3 = (\text{even}, \text{even}), \quad L_4 = (\text{even}, \text{odd}).\]
Every forbidden configuration consists of four tents \((v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4) \in L_1 \times L_2 \times L_3 \times L_4\) with \(\|v_1 - v_2\|_1 = \|v_2 - v_3\|_1 = \|v_3 - v_4\|_1 = 1\).






Note3-Tier Progressive Hints for #090






Hint 1: Classify every tent \((x, y)\) into one of 4 types according to (x & 1) and (y & 1).
Hint 2: Check the parity types of the 4 tents in any forbidden configuration: the two central tents have \(y\) even and differ by \(1\) in \(x\), so one is \((\text{odd}, \text{even})\) and the other is \((\text{even}, \text{even})\). Their vertical neighbors have \(y\) odd, so they are \((\text{odd}, \text{odd})\) and \((\text{even}, \text{odd})\)!
Hint 3: Split each tent \(i\) into \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{w_i} i_{\text{out}}\), wire \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} L_1 \xrightarrow{\infty} L_2 \xrightarrow{\infty} L_3 \xrightarrow{\infty} L_4 \xrightarrow{\infty} T\) between grid-adjacent tents in consecutive layers, and output \(\sum_{i=1}^N w_i - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\).










NoteComplete 4-Step Solution & Failure-Mode Guard for #090






Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation

Split each tent \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) into two vertices \(i_{\text{in}}\) and \(i_{\text{out}}\) connected by a directed edge \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{w_i} i_{\text{out}}\).
Assign each tent \(i\) a layer index \(\text{layer}(i) \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\):

\((x_i \text{ odd}, y_i \text{ odd}) \mapsto 1\): wire \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} i_{\text{in}}\).
\((x_i \text{ odd}, y_i \text{ even}) \mapsto 2\).
\((x_i \text{ even}, y_i \text{ even}) \mapsto 3\).
\((x_i \text{ even}, y_i \text{ odd}) \mapsto 4\): wire \(i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\).

For every pair of tents \((u, v)\) with Manhattan distance \(|x_u - x_v| + |y_u - y_v| = 1\) and \(\text{layer}(v) = \text{layer}(u) + 1\), wire \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\).
Output \(\sum_{i=1}^N w_i - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\).



Step 4: Complexity & Failure-Mode Guard

Graph Size: \(|V| = 2N + 2 \le 2002\), \(|E| \le 5N \le 5000\). Dinic finishes in \(< 5\text{ ms}\).
Failure-Mode Guard: Because coordinates \((x_i, y_i)\) can be negative in C++, never test parity with x % 2 == 1 (which evaluates to -1 for odd negative numbers!). Always use bitwise (x & 1)!
Companion Problem (#090b — Luogu P2598 [ZJOI2009] 狼和羊的故事): On an \(N \times M\) grid with Wolves (1), Empty (0), and Sheep (2), wire \(S \xrightarrow{\infty} \text{Wolf}\), \(\text{Sheep} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\), and bidirectional unit edges \(u \xleftrightarrow{1} v\) between 4-adjacent grid cells so empty cells naturally side with whichever partition minimizes fence perimeter.









#091 (Int-1) — AtCoder ARC 125 E: Snack

Judge URL: AtCoder ARC 125 E (Companion 3-layer hex-parity cut: Luogu P5458 [BJOI2016] 水晶)
Constraints: \(N, M \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le A_i \le 10^{12}\), \(1 \le B_j, C_j \le 10^{12}\), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\).
Statement: There are \(N\) types of snacks (type \(i\) has \(A_i\) pieces) and \(M\) children. Child \(j\) can receive at most \(B_j\) pieces of any single snack type \(i\), and at most \(C_j\) pieces in total across all snack types. Find the maximum total number of snack pieces that can be distributed.


Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Distributing snacks from \(N\) supply types to \(M\) children subject to per-type caps \(A_i\), per-child caps \(C_j\), and pairwise \((i, j)\) caps \(B_j\) is a textbook bipartite maximum flow on \(S \xrightarrow{A_i} u_i \xrightarrow{B_j} v_j \xrightarrow{C_j} T\). Because \(N, M \le 2 \times 10^5\), materializing \(NM = 4 \times 10^{10}\) edges is impossible. However, notice that every cross-edge \((u_i \to v_j)\) has capacity \(B_j\) depending only on \(j\), not on \(i\)! This symmetry allows us to dualize to Minimum \(S\)-\(T\) Cut and parameterize the cut by the unary count \(k = |S \cap U| \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) of snack vertices kept on the \(S\)-side.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(1\) if snack \(i \in S\), \(0\) if \(i \in T\)) and \(y_j \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(1\) if child \(j \in S\), \(0\) if \(j \in T\)). The cut capacity is:
\[\text{Cut}(x, y) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} A_i (1 - x_i) + \sum_{j=1}^{M} C_j y_j + \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{M} B_j x_i (1 - y_j).\]
Suppose we fix the number of snack types in \(S\) to be \(k = \sum_{i=1}^N x_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\). Then \(\sum_{i=1}^N B_j x_i (1 - y_j) = k \cdot B_j (1 - y_j)\), so each child \(j\)’s optimal choice \(y_j \in \{0, 1\}\) decouples completely and pays \(\min(C_j, \; k \cdot B_j)\)! Meanwhile, to minimize \(\sum_{i=1}^N A_i (1 - x_i)\) subject to \(\sum_{i=1}^N x_i = k\), we greedily set \(x_i = 1\) for the \(k\) snack types with the largest \(A_i\):
\[\text{MinCut}(S, T) = \min_{k=0}^{N} \left( \sum_{i=k+1}^{N} A_{(i)} + \sum_{j=1}^{M} \min\big(C_j, \; k \cdot B_j\big) \right),\]
where \(A_{(1)} \ge A_{(2)} \ge \dots \ge A_{(N)}\) are the snack supplies sorted in descending order.






Note3-Tier Progressive Hints for #091






Hint 1: Model the problem as Max-Flow (\(S \xrightarrow{A_i} u_i \xrightarrow{B_j} v_j \xrightarrow{C_j} T\)) and apply Max-Flow Min-Cut duality.
Hint 2: Notice that if \(k\) snack vertices \(u_i\) lie in \(S\), then for every child \(v_j\), putting \(v_j \in S\) costs \(C_j\) while putting \(v_j \in T\) cuts \(k\) edges of capacity \(B_j\), costing \(k \cdot B_j\).
Hint 3: Sort \(A_i\) descending and sort children by threshold \(t_j = \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\). Sweep \(k = 0 \dots N\) using prefix sums of \(B_j\) and \(C_j\) to evaluate all \(N+1\) candidate cuts in \(O((N+M)\log(N+M))\) time!










NoteComplete 4-Step Solution & Failure-Mode Guard for #091






Step 3: Mechanical Evaluation of the Closed-Form Cut

Sort \(A_1 \ge A_2 \ge \dots \ge A_N\) in descending order and compute suffix sums \(\text{suf}_A[k] = \sum_{i=k+1}^N A_i\).
For each child \(j \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), \(\min(C_j, k B_j)\) equals \(k B_j\) when \(k \le \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\) and equals \(C_j\) when \(k > \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\). Bucket children by \(t_j = \min\big((long\;long)N, \; \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\big)\) so that for each \(k = 0, \dots, N\), we maintain the sum of \(B_j\) for children with \(t_j \ge k\) and the sum of \(C_j\) for children with \(t_j < k\).
Return \(\min_{0 \le k \le N} \big(\text{suf}_A[k] + k \cdot \sum_{t_j \ge k} B_j + \sum_{t_j < k} C_j\big)\).



Step 4: Complexity & Failure-Mode Guard

Complexity: \(O(N \log N + M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space—solving a \(4 \times 10^5\)-vertex dense flow network in \(40\text{ ms}\)!
Failure-Mode Guard: Total capacity can reach \(2 \times 10^{17}\), so accumulate all sums in 64-bit long long (or __int128 if computing products \(k \cdot B_j\) before clamping \(t_j = \lfloor C_j / B_j \rfloor\)).
Companion Problem (#091b — Luogu P5458 [BJOI2016] 水晶): Canonicalize 3D hex coordinates \((x, y, z) \mapsto (x - z, y - z)\) and color cells by \(p(x, y, z) = ((x + y + z) \bmod 3 + 3) \bmod 3 \in \{1, 0, 2\}\) into a 3-layer vertex-split chain \(S \to \{p \equiv 1\} \to \{p \equiv 0\} \to \{p \equiv 2\} \to T\) (Section 3).









#092 (Int-2) — Codeforces 434 D: Nanami’s Power Plant

Judge URL: Codeforces 434 D (Companion layered DAG problem: Luogu P2766 最长不下降子序列问题)
Constraints: \(N \le 50\) generators, \(M \le 100\) constraints, \(-100 \le l_i \le r_i \le 100\), \(|a_i| \le 100, |b_i| \le 1000, |c_i| \le 10^4\), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\).
Statement: Each generator \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) must be assigned an integer operating level \(x_i \in [l_i, r_i]\), producing output \(f_i(x_i) = a_i x_i^2 + b_i x_i + c_i\). There are \(M\) constraints of the form \(x_u \le x_v + d\). Maximize the total output \(\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x_i)\).


Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Each generator \(i\) chooses from \(K_i = r_i - l_i + 1 \le 201\) integer states with an arbitrary quadratic reward \(f_i(x_i)\) (where \(a_i\) can be positive, making \(f_i\) convex and non-concave!) subject to pairwise difference bounds \(x_u - x_v \le d\). Since \(\sum K_i \le 50 \times 201 \approx 10^4\), this compiles directly into a Form A Series Unary Threshold Chain ([HNOI2013] 切糕) with a pedestal shift \(M_{\text{ped}} - f_i(k) \ge 0\).


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For each generator \(i\), index its valid levels \(k \in [l_i, r_i]\) and introduce threshold bits \(z_{i,k} = [x_i \ge k] \in \{0, 1\}\) for \(k \in [l_i, r_i + 1]\) with \(z_{i, l_i} = 1\) (\(S\)) and \(z_{i, r_i + 1} = 0\) (\(T\)). Choose a uniform pedestal \(M_{\text{ped}} = 2 \times 10^6 > \max_{i, k} |f_i(k)|\) and define non-negative series capacities \(c_i(k) = M_{\text{ped}} - f_i(k) > 0\).






Note3-Tier Progressive Hints for #092






Hint 1: Create a series chain of \(r_i - l_i + 1\) edges for each generator \(i\), corresponding to choosing \(x_i = k \in [l_i, r_i]\).
Hint 2: Because \(f_i(k) = a_i k^2 + b_i k + c_i\) is being maximized and can be positive or negative, set each edge capacity to \(M_{\text{ped}} - f_i(k)\) where \(M_{\text{ped}} = 2 \times 10^6\), and subtract \(\text{MinCut}(S, T)\) from \(N \cdot M_{\text{ped}}\)!
Hint 3: Add reverse \(\infty\)-locks \(v_{i,k+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k}\), and compile \(x_u \le x_v + d\) by wiring \(v_{u,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{v,\text{clamp}(k-d)}\) for all \(k \in [l_u + 1, r_u]\).










NoteComplete 4-Step Solution & Failure-Mode Guard for #092






Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation
For each generator \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), create internal threshold nodes \(v_{i,k}\) for \(k \in [l_i + 1, r_i]\), identifying \(v_{i, l_i} \equiv S\) and \(v_{i, r_i + 1} \equiv T\):

Shifted Series Edges: For each \(k \in [l_i, r_i]\), wire \(v_{i,k} \xrightarrow{M_{\text{ped}} - f_i(k)} v_{i,k+1}\).
Reverse Monotonicity Locks (FM-12): For each \(k \in [l_i + 1, r_i - 1]\), wire \(v_{i,k+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k}\).
Difference Constraints (\(x_u \le x_v + d\)): For each constraint \((u, v, d)\) and each \(k \in [l_u + 1, r_u]\):

If \(k - d \le l_v\): the target \(v_{v, l_v} \equiv S\) is always \(1\), so no edge is needed.
If \(l_v + 1 \le k - d \le r_v\): wire \(v_{u,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{v, k-d}\).
If \(k - d \ge r_v + 1\): wire \(v_{u,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\) (since \(x_v\) can never reach \(k - d \ge r_v + 1\), forcing \(x_u < k\)).


Output \(N \cdot M_{\text{ped}} - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\).


Step 4: Complexity & Failure-Mode Guard

Graph Size: \(|V| \le 10,002\), \(|E| \le 40,000\). Dinic runs in \(< 15\text{ ms}\).
Failure-Mode Guard: Do not forget the boundary case \(k - d > r_v\)! If a constraint says \(x_u \le x_v + d\) and \(k - d > r_v\), then \(x_u \ge k\) is impossible because \(x_v \le r_v < k - d\), so \(v_{u,k}\) must be wired directly to \(T\) with capacity \(\infty\)!









#093 (Adv-1) — Luogu P3973 [TJOI2015]: 线性代数 (Linear Algebra)

Judge URL: Luogu P3973 | LOJ #2130 (Companion shortest-path Lipschitz chain: TopCoder SRM 590 Div1 Hard — FoxAndCity)
Constraints: \(N \le 500\), \(0 \le B_{ij}, C_i \le 10^3\), Time Limit \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Statement: Given an \(N \times N\) non-negative matrix \(B\) and a \(1 \times N\) vector \(C\), choose a binary row vector \(A = (x_1, \dots, x_N) \in \{0, 1\}^N\) to maximize \(D(x) = (A B - C) A^T = A B A^T - C A^T\).


Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Expanding the matrix product reveals a quadratic pseudo-Boolean maximization objective:
\[D(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} B_{ij} x_i x_j - \sum_{i=1}^{N} C_i x_i, \qquad x_i \in \{0, 1\}.\]
With \(N = 500\), creating \(N^2 = 250,000\) auxiliary project nodes \(p_{ij}\) for every pair \((i, j)\) builds a large graph. Instead, applying the 1D/2D Abel identity \(x_i x_j = x_i - x_i(1 - x_j)\) eliminates all \(N^2\) auxiliary vertices and compiles the entire matrix game onto just \(N\) vertices!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Substitute \(x_i x_j = x_i - x_i(1 - x_j)\) into \(D(x)\):
\[D(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(\sum_{j=1}^{N} B_{ij}\right) x_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N} C_i x_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} B_{ij} x_i(1 - x_j).\]
Let \(R_i = \sum_{j=1}^N B_{ij}\) be the \(i\)-th row sum of \(B\). Subtracting from the baseline \(\Phi = \sum_{i=1}^N R_i\) using \(x_i = 1 - (1 - x_i)\) gives the exact cut polynomial:
\[\Phi - D(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} R_i (1 - x_i) + \sum_{i=1}^{N} C_i x_i + \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j \ne i} B_{ij} x_i(1 - x_j).\]






Note3-Tier Progressive Hints for #093






Hint 1: Expand \((A B - C) A^T = \sum_{i,j} B_{ij} x_i x_j - \sum_i C_i x_i\) using \(x_i^2 = x_i\) for \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\).
Hint 2: Use the identity \(x_i x_j = x_i - x_i(1 - x_j)\) to rewrite each pairwise reward as a unary row-sum reward \(B_{ij} x_i\) minus a cut penalty \(B_{ij} x_i(1 - x_j)\)!
Hint 3: Wire \(S \xrightarrow{\sum_j B_{ij}} i \xrightarrow{C_i} T\) and directed arcs \(i \xrightarrow{B_{ij}} j\) on just \(N + 2\) vertices!










NoteComplete 4-Step Solution & Companion Breakdown (FoxAndCity) for #093






Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation ([TJOI2015] 线性代数)
Create \(N + 2\) vertices (\(S, T\), and \(1, \dots, N\) where \(i \in S \iff x_i = 1\)):

Set baseline \(\Phi = \sum_{i=1}^N R_i\), where \(R_i = \sum_{j=1}^N B_{ij}\).
For each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), wire \(S \xrightarrow{R_i} i\) and \(i \xrightarrow{C_i} T\).
For each pair \(1 \le i < j \le N\), wire a single undirected/bidirectional edge pair between \(i\) and \(j\) with forward capacity \(B_{ij}\) (\(i \to j\)) and reverse capacity \(B_{ji}\) (\(j \to i\)).
Output \(\Phi - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\). On \(502\) vertices, Dinic finishes in \(< 3\text{ ms}\).



Companion Problem (#093b — TopCoder SRM 590 Div1 Hard: FoxAndCity)

Task: Given a connected undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) (\(N \le 40\)), add new edges so that the shortest-path distances \(d_u = \operatorname{dist}_{G'}(0, u) \in \{1, \dots, N-1\}\) minimize \(\sum_{u=1}^{N-1} (d_u - \text{want}_u)^2\).
Key Reduction to 切糕 (\(D = 1\)): By the Discrete Intermediate Value Theorem on connected graphs, an integer vector \((d_0 = 0, d_1, \dots, d_{N-1}) \in \{1, \dots, N-1\}^{N-1}\) is realizable as shortest-path distances in some supergraph \(G' \supseteq G\) if and only if:

\(d_u = 1\) for every existing neighbor \(\{0, u\} \in E(G)\); and
\(|d_u - d_v| \le 1\) (\(d_u - d_v \le 1\) and \(d_v - d_u \le 1\)) for every existing edge \(\{u, v\} \in E(G)\)! (Why? Because along any path from \(0\) to \(u\) in \(G\), distances start at \(0\) and increase by at most \(+1\) per step, guaranteeing that every intermediate distance \(1, 2, \dots, d_u - 1\) exists in \(V\), to which \(u\) can be directly connected!) Thus FoxAndCity compiles 100% into #089 (切糕) with \(D = 1\) and unary cost \(c_u(k) = (k - \text{want}_u)^2\)!










#094 (Adv-2) — AtCoder ABC 326 G: Unlock Achievement

Judge URL: AtCoder ABC 326 G (Companion 2D rank-chain problem: Codeforces 1662 J — Training Camp)
Constraints: \(N, M \le 50\), skill levels \(L_{j,i} \in \{1, \dots, 5\}\), \(1 \le C_i, A_j \le 10^9\), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\).
Statement: You have \(N\) skills, all initially at level \(1\). Upgrading skill \(i\) by \(+1\) level (up to level \(5\)) costs \(C_i\) per level. There are \(M\) achievements; achievement \(j\) pays reward \(A_j\) if and only if every skill \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) reaches level \(x_i \ge L_{j,i}\). Maximize net profit (total rewards minus upgrade costs).


Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
Each skill \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) chooses a state \(x_i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\) (\(K = 5\)) with uniform marginal upgrade cost \(\delta_i(k) = C_i\), while each achievement \(j \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) is a positive-reward project requiring the conjunctive threshold precondition \(\bigwedge_{i=1}^N (x_i \ge L_{j,i})\). This is the textbook Form B Parallel Closure Chain of Theorem 1.2!


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Introduce unary skill indicators \(z_{i,k} = [x_i \ge k] \in \{0, 1\}\) for \(k \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}\) (since \(x_i \ge 1\) holds initially at cost \(0\)) and binary achievement indicators \(m_j \in \{0, 1\}\):
\[\max \sum_{j=1}^{M} A_j m_j - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{k=2}^{5} C_i z_{i,k} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad z_{i,k} \le z_{i,k-1} \; (3 \le k \le 5), \quad m_j \le z_{i, L_{j,i}} \; (\forall L_{j,i} \ge 2).\]






Note3-Tier Progressive Hints for #094






Hint 1: Represent each skill \(i\) by 4 binary upgrade nodes \(v_{i,2}, v_{i,3}, v_{i,4}, v_{i,5}\) where \(v_{i,k} \in S \iff x_i \ge k\), each wired to \(T\) with capacity \(C_i\).
Hint 2: Enforce \(x_i \ge k \implies x_i \ge k-1\) by wiring reverse locks \(v_{i,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k-1}\) for \(k \in \{3, 4, 5\}\).
Hint 3: Represent each achievement \(j\) as a node \(m_j\) with \(S \xrightarrow{A_j} m_j\) and wire \(m_j \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i, L_{j,i}}\) whenever \(L_{j,i} \ge 2\). Output \(\sum_{j=1}^M A_j - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\).










NoteComplete 4-Step Solution & Companion Breakdown (CF 1662 J) for #094






Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (ABC 326 G)
Set baseline \(\Phi = \sum_{j=1}^M A_j\). Create \(4N + M + 2 \le 252\) vertices:

Skill Parallel Chains: For each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and \(k \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}\), wire \(v_{i,k} \xrightarrow{C_i} T\). For \(k \in \{3, 4, 5\}\), wire the reverse lock \(v_{i,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k-1}\).
Achievement Closures: For each \(j \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), wire \(S \xrightarrow{A_j} m_j\), and for every skill \(i\) with \(L_{j,i} \ge 2\), wire \(m_j \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i, L_{j,i}}\).
Output \(\Phi - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\). Runs in \(< 1\text{ ms}\).



Companion Problem (#094b — Codeforces 1662 J: Training Camp)

Task: On an \(N \times N\) grid (\(N \le 128\)) where each row and each column of matrix \(A\) is a permutation of \(\{1, \dots, N\}\), select a stable set of \(N\) cells maximizing \(\sum C_{r,c}\).
Compilation: Split each cell \(u = (r, c)\) into \(u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{M_{\text{ped}} - C_{r,c}} u_{\text{out}}\) (\(M_{\text{ped}} = N + 1\)), and chain rank \(k\) to rank \(k+1\) along both rows and columns (reversing column rank orientation relative to row rank orientation so that every row/column rank transition \(k \to k+1\) forms a coupled \(N\)-state cut chain). Output \(N \cdot M_{\text{ped}} - \text{MinCut}(S, T)\).









#095 (Mas-1) — AtCoder ARC 107 F: Sum of Abs ★ Flagship 1

Judge URL: AtCoder ARC 107 F
Constraints: \(N, M \le 300\), \(|A_v|, |B_v| \le 10^6\) (\(A_v, B_v \in \mathbb{Z}\), both can be negative), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\).
Cross-Reference: Full 4-Step Derivation, 9-State Verification Table, Toy Trace, and C++ Implementation are given in Section 2.







Note3-Tier Progressive Hints & Diagnostic Invariants Summary for #095






Hint 1 (Sign Linearization): Replace \(\left|\sum_{v \in C} B_v\right|\) with \(\max_{s_C \in \{-1, +1\}} \sum_{v \in C} s_C B_v\). Now each vertex \(v \in V\) chooses from 3 states \(\sigma_v \in \{-1, 0 \text{ (deleted)}, +1\}\).
Hint 2 (Insulator State Ordering): Order the 3 states as \(-1 \prec 0 \prec +1\) so that the surviving-edge constraint “no \(+1\) vertex is adjacent to a \(-1\) vertex” becomes the 1-step smoothness bound \(|\sigma_u - \sigma_v| \le 1\).
Hint 3 (Universal Negative-\(A_v\) Pedestal): Set \(M_v = \max(|B_v|, -A_v)\), wire \(S \xrightarrow{M_v + B_v} v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{M_v + A_v} v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{M_v - B_v} T\) with reverse lock \(v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\), and wire \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}, v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}\) for every edge \((u, v) \in E\).







#096 (Mas-2) — AtCoder ARC 142 E: Pairing Wizards ★ Flagship 2

Judge URL: AtCoder ARC 142 E
Constraints: \(N \le 100\), \(M \le \binom{N}{2}\), \(1 \le a_i, b_i \le 100\), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\).
Cross-Reference: Full 4-Step Derivation, Proofs of Lemma 4.1 (Mandatory Pre-Promotion) and Theorem 4.2 (Low-Role vs. High-Role Bipartite Structural Dichotomy), Toy Trace, and C++ Implementation are given in Section 4.







Note3-Tier Progressive Hints & Diagnostic Invariants Summary for #096






Hint 1 (Conjunctive vs. Disjunctive Split): Rewrite the pair condition on \((u, v)\) as \(\min(x_u, x_v) \ge \min(b_u, b_v)\) AND \(\max(x_u, x_v) \ge \max(b_u, b_v)\). Enforce \(a_u \gets \max_{v \in N(u)}(a_u, \min(b_u, b_v))\) greedily first!
Hint 2 (Hidden Bipartition): Prove that after pre-promotion, every remaining unsatisfied edge connects a Low-Role wizard \(u \in V_{\text{low}}\) (\(a_u < b_u\)) to a High-Role wizard \(v \in V_{\text{high}}\) (\(a_v \ge b_v\)), and \(u \in V_{\text{low}}\) only ever chooses \(x_u \in \{a_u, b_u\}\).
Hint 3 (Inverted Binary-to-Unary OR Cut): Wire \(S \xrightarrow{b_u - a_u} u\) for \(u \in V_{\text{low}}\), build a unit-capacity Form B unary chain \((v, k) \xrightarrow{1} T\) with \((v, k) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, k-1)\) for \(v \in V_{\text{high}}\), and wire \(u \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, b_u)\) for each unsatisfied edge.

7. Pre-Submission Checklist (FM-12 Audit)
Before submitting any multi-state chain or threshold-cut solution, run through this 5-point audit:

Reverse \(\infty\)-Locks Present (FM-12): Did you add \(v_{i,k+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k}\) between every pair of consecutive internal threshold vertices along every series and parallel chain?
Insulator State Ordering (ARC 107 F): In 3-state sign/deletion or conflict models (ARC 107 F, yukicoder 119), is the neutral/deleted insulator state placed in the middle (\(1 \prec 2 \prec 3\)) so that the forbidden pair is \((1, 3)\) and compiles to \(u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}\)?
Pedestal Shift Non-Negativity (CF 434 D, ARC 107 F): Can any unary cost \(c_i(k)\) be negative (e.g., when \(A_v < 0\) in ARC 107 F or when maximizing \(f_i(k)\) in CF 434 D)? Verify that your per-chain pedestal \(M_i\) satisfies \(M_i + c_i(k) \ge 0\) for every state \(k\), and that \(M_i\) is added to all \(K\) series edges of chain \(i\).
Boundary Clamping on Cross-Chain Edges (\(k - D > K\)): In \(x_u - x_v \le D\), when \(k - D \ge K + 1\) (so \(x_v\) can never reach \(k - D\)), did you wire \(v_{u,k} \xrightarrow{\infty} T\) instead of silently skipping the edge?
Upfront Tightening Before Bipartition (ARC 142 E): When a constraint mixes \(\min\) and \(\max\) bounds, did you propagate all unconditional conjunctive lower bounds before partitioning vertices into \(V_{\text{low}}\) and \(V_{\text{high}}\)?

title: Chapter 12 — Multi-State Ordered Vertex Chains, 3-State Sign Cuts & Unary OR Layering
text:
8. Chapter Summary & Bridge to Chapter 13
In this chapter, we lifted binary project selection into the multi-state domain by encoding each \(K\)-valued variable \(x_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) as a monotonic chain of \(K - 1\) unary threshold indicators \(z_{i,k} = [x_i \ge k]\) locked together by reverse \(\infty\)-arcs \(v_{i,k+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{i,k}\). We saw how 1D Abel summation bridges Form A (Series Chains for point-value tables like [HNOI2013] 切糕 and ARC 107 F) and Form B (Parallel Chains for marginal upgrades like ARC 142 E and ABC 326 G).
What happens when the pairwise interaction between \(x_u\) and \(x_v\) is not a hard \(\infty\)-cliff \([x_u - x_v > D]\infty\), but a soft convex penalty such as \((x_u - x_v)^2\) (ABC 347 G) or \(w_{uv}|h_u - h_v|\) over \(K = 10^9\) shades of grey (CF 1427 G)?
In Chapter 13 (The Coarea Formula, Level-Set Cuts, Ishikawa’s Convex Chains & Monge Arrays), we apply 2D Abel Summation by Parts to prove Ishikawa’s Theorem—compiling any submodular/Monge penalty \(\Phi(x_u, x_v)\) into cross-chain capacities \(-\Delta_a \Delta_b \Phi(a, b) \ge 0\)—and derive the Discrete Coarea Formula, which decouples \(10^9\)-state \(\ell_1\) smoothing into nested level-set cuts solved in \(O(N^3)\) total time via incremental residual rollback!

text:
Before studying this chapter, make sure you are comfortable with:

Chapter 02 (Residual Graph Anatomy & Canonical Minimum Cuts): Extracting the source-minimal cut \(S_{\min} = \{v \in V : s \rightsquigarrow_{G_{f^*}} v\}\) from the terminal residual network \(G_{f^*}\) after running Dinic’s algorithm.
Chapter 09 (Maximum Weight Closure & Project Selection): Compiling unary profits \(p_v > 0\), unary costs \(c_v > 0\), and logical prerequisites \(x_u \le x_v \iff x_u(1 - x_v) = 0\) into a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut network with \(\infty\)-capacity implication arcs.
Chapter 10 & Chapter 11 (Pseudo-Boolean Cut Polynomials & Submodularity): Expressing combinatorial objectives in indicator variables \(x_v \in \{0, 1\}\), verifying the pairwise submodularity condition \(\Delta_{u,v}\Phi = \Phi(1, 1) - \Phi(1, 0) - \Phi(0, 1) + \Phi(0, 0) \le 0\), and compiling quadratic rewards \(w_{uv} x_u x_v\) or cut penalties \(\gamma_{uv} x_u(1 - x_v)\).




By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Recognize and Linearize 0-1 Fractional Programs (0-1 分数规划): Transform any combinatorial ratio objective \(\max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}\) (\(G(x) > 0\)) into the parametric merit function \(h(\lambda) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \big(F(x) - \lambda G(x)\big)\), prove that \(h(\lambda)\) is piecewise-linear, convex, continuous, and strictly decreasing, and diagnose immediately via the Submodularity Sign Law whether \(h(\lambda)\) compiles to a polynomial-time minimum cut or an NP-hard problem.
Choose Between Binary Search, Dinkelbach’s Secant Method, and Parametric Preflow: Derive the exact rational denominator separation \(\Delta_{\min} \ge \frac{1}{|V|(|V|-1)}\) for unweighted density ratios, implement Dinkelbach’s superlinear Newton-secant iteration (Dinkelbach 1967), and enforce the Two-Scale IEEE-754 Epsilon Hierarchy (\(\varepsilon_{\text{flow}} \ll \varepsilon_{\text{cut\_sign}} \ll \Delta_{\min}\)) to prevent floating-point infinite loops in Dinic (FM-14).
Compile Goldberg’s Maximum Density Subgraph (最大密度子图) via Both \(|V|+|E|\) Closure and \(|V|\)-Only Degree-Sum Reduction: Use the handshaking cut identity \(2|E(S)| = \sum_{v \in S} d_v - |\delta(S, \bar{S})|\) (Goldberg 1984, Amber / 胡伯涛 2007) to eliminate all \(|E|\) edge-closure nodes, shrinking a dense \(O(|V| + |E|)\)-vertex network down to \(|V| + 2\) vertices (POJ 3155, BZOJ 2039).
Master Structural Dualities & Parametric Cut Envelopes: Connect Maximum Density Subgraphs to Hakimi’s Orientation Theorem (CF 847J), Nash-Williams Arboricity / Rooted Forest Packing (CF 1284G), and the Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan (GGT) Nested Cut Theorem for finding all \(\le |V|\) breakpoints of the upper hull \(h(\lambda)\) across all real \(\lambda \in [0, \infty)\).

Before studying this chapter, make sure you are comfortable with:

Chapter 02 (Residual Graph Anatomy & Canonical Minimum Cuts): Extracting the source-minimal cut \(S_{\min} = \{v \in V : s \rightsquigarrow_{G_{f^*}} v\}\) from the terminal residual network \(G_{f^*}\) after running Dinic’s algorithm.
Chapter 09 (Maximum Weight Closure & Project Selection): Compiling unary profits \(p_v > 0\), unary costs \(c_v > 0\), and logical prerequisites \(x_u \le x_v \iff x_u(1 - x_v) = 0\) into a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut network with \(\infty\)-capacity implication arcs.
Chapter 10 & Chapter 11 (Pseudo-Boolean Cut Polynomials & Submodularity): Expressing combinatorial objectives in indicator variables \(x_v \in \{0, 1\}\), verifying the pairwise submodularity condition \(\Delta_{u,v}\Phi = \Phi(1, 1) - \Phi(1, 0) - \Phi(0, 1) + \Phi(0, 0) \le 0\), and compiling quadratic rewards \(w_{uv} x_u x_v\) or cut penalties \(\gamma_{uv} x_u(1 - x_v)\).




By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Recognize and Linearize 0-1 Fractional Programs (0-1 分数规划): Transform any combinatorial ratio objective \(\max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}\) (\(G(x) > 0\)) into the parametric merit function \(h(\lambda) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \big(F(x) - \lambda G(x)\big)\), prove that \(h(\lambda)\) is piecewise-linear, convex, continuous, and strictly decreasing, and diagnose immediately via the Submodularity Sign Law whether \(h(\lambda)\) compiles to a polynomial-time minimum cut or an NP-hard problem.
Choose Between Binary Search, Dinkelbach’s Secant Method, and Parametric Preflow: Derive the exact rational denominator separation \(\Delta_{\min} \ge \frac{1}{|V|(|V|-1)}\) for unweighted density ratios, implement Dinkelbach’s superlinear Newton-secant iteration (Dinkelbach 1967), and enforce the Two-Scale IEEE-754 Epsilon Hierarchy (\(\varepsilon_{\text{flow}} \ll \varepsilon_{\text{cut\_sign}} \ll \Delta_{\min}\)) to prevent floating-point infinite loops in Dinic (FM-14).
Compile Goldberg’s Maximum Density Subgraph (最大密度子图) via Both \(|V|+|E|\) Closure and \(|V|\)-Only Degree-Sum Reduction: Use the handshaking cut identity \(2|E(S)| = \sum_{v \in S} d_v - |\delta(S, \bar{S})|\) (Goldberg 1984, Amber / 胡伯涛 2007) to eliminate all \(|E|\) edge-closure nodes, shrinking a dense \(O(|V| + |E|)\)-vertex network down to \(|V| + 2\) vertices (POJ 3155, BZOJ 2039).
Master Structural Dualities & Parametric Cut Envelopes: Connect Maximum Density Subgraphs to Hakimi’s Orientation Theorem (CF 847J), Nash-Williams Arboricity / Rooted Forest Packing (CF 1284G), and the Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan (GGT) Nested Cut Theorem for finding all \(\le |V|\) breakpoints of the upper hull \(h(\lambda)\) across all real \(\lambda \in [0, \infty)\).

title: Chapter 14 — 0-1 Fractional Programming, Maximum Density Subgraphs & Parametric Ratio Cuts
text:
1. 0-1 Fractional Programming & Parametric Linearization \(h(\lambda) = \max_{S \ne \emptyset} \big(F(S) - \lambda G(S)\big)\)

1.1 Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal: Why Naive Greedy and DP Fail on Ratio Objectives
In Chapters 09 through 13, every objective function was an additive sum of unary profits, unary costs, and pairwise interaction terms:
\[\max_{x \in \{0, 1\}^V} \big( \text{Total Profit}(x) - \text{Total Cost}(x) \big).\]
In contest problems, however, an adversary often asks you to optimize the efficiency, average weight, or density of a combinatorial structure—maximizing (or minimizing) a ratio of two set functions over a family of valid indicator vectors \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq \{0, 1\}^V\):
\[\lambda^* = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)} \qquad \text{or} \qquad \lambda^* = \min_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}, \qquad \text{subject to } G(x) > 0 \text{ for all } x \in \mathcal{F}.\]
How do you recognize from the English problem statement that you are facing a 0-1 Fractional Programming network flow problem, and why do simpler paradigms fail?

Surface Clues in the Statement:

“Find a non-empty group of scientists maximizing the average number of collaborations per member” (POJ 3155 — Hard Life, #105): maximize \(\frac{|E(S)|}{|S|}\) over \(\emptyset \subsetneq S \subseteq V\).
“Pair \(N\) boys and \(N\) girls into dance partners to maximize total happiness divided by total coordination” ([SDOI2017] Freshman Ball, #108): maximize \(\frac{\sum a_{ij} x_{ij}}{\sum b_{ij} x_{ij}}\) over perfect matchings \(x \in \mathcal{M}\).
“Disconnect source \(s\) from sink \(t\) by removing an edge cut \(C\) minimizing average edge capacity \(\frac{\sum_{e \in C} w_e}{|C|}\)” (Amber 2007 — Network Tightness, #107).

Why Naive Greedy Fails (Mediant Non-Monotonicity): Ratios do not obey linear Bellman optimality. If item \(1\) has standalone ratio \(\frac{4}{2} = 2.0\) and item \(2\) has standalone ratio \(\frac{5}{4} = 1.25\), a greedy solver picks item \(1\) alone. Yet if selecting both items unlocks a pairwise synergy bonus \(s_{12} = 6\), the combined subset \(\{1, 2\}\) achieves ratio \(\frac{4 + 5 + 6}{2 + 4} = \frac{15}{6} = 2.5 > 2.0\)! Even worse, in unweighted graphs, repeatedly peeling away the vertex of minimum current degree (Charikar’s greedy peeling) can destroy a dense clique before touching a sparse hub-and-spoke component (as we prove by explicit counterexample in Section 2.1).
Why Dynamic Programming Fails: Even if you attempt to track the denominator \(G(x) = B\) as an extra knapsack dimension in DP, the numerator \(F(x)\) depends on arbitrary graph interactions \(x_u x_v\) across a general graph \(G = (V, E)\) of treewidth \(\Omega(|V|)\), requiring \(O(2^{|V|})\) state memory.


Diagnostic Dichotomy: Circulation Space (Mean Cycle) vs. Cut Space (Ratio Cut / Closure)
Before building a flow network for a ratio problem, always check what combinatorial object lives in \(\mathcal{F}\). Competitive programming features two classic fractional graph families that are LP duals of each other in spirit:








Diagnostic Dimension
Family A: Minimum / Maximum Mean Cycle ([HNOI2009] 最小圈)
Family B: Ratio Cut, Closure, or Matching (分数规划最小割 / 匹配)




Chosen Combinatorial Object
A directed cycle \(C \subseteq E\) (a 1-regular circulation)
A vertex subset \(S \subseteq V\), an \(s\)-\(t\) cut \(\delta^+(S)\), or a matching \(M\)


Ratio Objective
\(\min_{C} \frac{\sum_{e \in C} a_e}{\sum_{e \in C} b_e}\) (e.g., \(\frac{\sum_{e \in C} w_e}{|C|}\))
\(\max_{\emptyset \ne S \subseteq V} \frac{F(S)}{G(S)}\) or \(\min_{(S,T)} \frac{\sum_{e \in \delta^+(S)} a_e}{\sum_{e \in \delta^+(S)} b_e}\)


Linearized Subproblem at Trial \(\lambda\)
Does \(G\) contain a cycle \(C\) with \(\sum_{e \in C} (a_e - \lambda b_e) < 0\)?
Does there exist \(S \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(F(S) - \lambda G(S) > 0\) (or \(< 0\))?


Oracle Solver Engine
Negative-Cycle Detection (Bellman–Ford / SPFA / Karp’s \(O(|V||E|)\) DP)
Minimum \(s\)-\(t\) Cut (Dinic / Push-Relabel) or Max-Weight Matching (MCMF / KM)







1.2 Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Dinkelbach’s Parametric Merit Function
Let \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq \{0, 1\}^n\) be a finite non-empty set of feasible indicator vectors such that \(G(x) > 0\) for every \(x \in \mathcal{F}\). Suppose we wish to compute the maximum ratio:
\[\lambda^* := \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}.\]
How do we break the division bar between \(F(x)\) and \(G(x)\) so that their variables stop dividing each other? We introduce a real trial parameter \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\)—which acts as a shadow price (tax rate) per unit of denominator \(G(x)\)—and define the parametric merit function:
\[h(\lambda) := \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \big( F(x) - \lambda G(x) \big) = -\min_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \big( \lambda G(x) - F(x) \big).\]
Each individual candidate \(x \in \mathcal{F}\) defines an affine straight line \(\ell_x(\lambda) := F(x) - \lambda G(x)\) in the \((\lambda, y)\)-plane with vertical intercept \(F(x)\) and strictly negative slope \(-G(x) < 0\). The function \(h(\lambda) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \ell_x(\lambda)\) is the upper envelope of this finite collection of downward-sloping lines.






ImportantTheorem 14.1 (Dinkelbach’s Parametric Equivalence Theorem — Jagannathan 1966, Dinkelbach 1967)



Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be finite and non-empty with \(G(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal{F}\), and let \(\lambda^* = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}\). Then the parametric merit function \(h(\lambda) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} (F(x) - \lambda G(x))\) satisfies:

Convexity, Continuity, and Piecewise Linearity: As the pointwise maximum of finitely many affine functions \(\ell_x(\lambda) = F(x) - \lambda G(x)\), \(h(\lambda)\) is continuous, convex, and piecewise-linear on \(\mathbb{R}\). Its breakpoints correspond to parameter values where the optimal structure \(x^*(\lambda)\) jumps from a larger denominator \(G(x_1)\) to a smaller denominator \(G(x_2) < G(x_1)\).
Strict Monotonicity: Because every line \(\ell_x(\lambda)\) has strictly negative slope \(-G(x) \le -\min_{x \in \mathcal{F}} G(x) < 0\), for any \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\) with optimal solutions \(x_1, x_2 \in \mathcal{F}\): \[h(\lambda_1) = F(x_1) - \lambda_1 G(x_1) \ge F(x_2) - \lambda_1 G(x_2) > F(x_2) - \lambda_2 G(x_2) = h(\lambda_2).\] Thus \(h(\lambda)\) is strictly decreasing on \(\mathbb{R}\).
Three-Way Sign Certificate (Unique Root at \(\lambda^*\)): Since \(G(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal{F}\), dividing \(F(x) - \lambda G(x)\) by \(G(x)\) preserves signs: \[\begin{aligned}
h(\lambda) > 0 &\iff \exists x \in \mathcal{F} \text{ such that } F(x) - \lambda G(x) > 0 \iff \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)} > \lambda \iff \lambda < \lambda^*, \\
h(\lambda) = 0 &\iff \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \big(F(x) - \lambda G(x)\big) = 0 \iff \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)} = \lambda \iff \lambda = \lambda^*, \\
h(\lambda) < 0 &\iff \forall x \in \mathcal{F},\; F(x) - \lambda G(x) < 0 \iff \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)} < \lambda \iff \lambda > \lambda^*.
\end{aligned}\]



(For a minimization problem \(\lambda^* = \min_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}\) with \(G(x) > 0\), we instead define \(h_{\min}(\lambda) := \min_{x \in \mathcal{F}} (F(x) - \lambda G(x))\), which is the lower envelope of downward-sloping lines—hence concave and strictly decreasing, with \(h_{\min}(\lambda) \ge 0 \iff \lambda \le \lambda^*\) and \(h_{\min}(\lambda) < 0 \iff \lambda > \lambda^*\).)



1.3 Step 3 — Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: The Submodularity Sign Law & Three Solver Engines

When Does Evaluating \(h(\lambda)\) Compile to a Minimum \(s\)-\(t\) Cut? (The Submodularity Sign Law)
Theorem 14.1 reduces the fractional problem \(\max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}\) to repeatedly evaluating the linear combination:
\[h(\lambda) = -\min_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \Phi_\lambda(x), \qquad \text{where} \qquad \Phi_\lambda(x) := \lambda G(x) - F(x).\]
From Chapter 10 (the Kolmogorov–Zabih Submodularity Theorem), minimizing a quadratic pseudo-Boolean energy \(\Phi_\lambda(x)\) over \(x \in \{0, 1\}^V\) is directly representable as a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut with non-negative capacities if and only if every pairwise cross-difference is non-positive:
\[\Delta_{u,v}\Phi_\lambda := \Phi_\lambda(1, 1) - \Phi_\lambda(1, 0) - \Phi_\lambda(0, 1) + \Phi_\lambda(0, 0) = \lambda \Delta_{u,v} G - \Delta_{u,v} F \le 0 \qquad \forall u \ne v.\]
Assume \(\lambda \ge 0\) (which always holds when \(\lambda^* \ge 0\), or after adding a constant shift \(F(x) \gets F(x) + K G(x)\)). Then \(\lambda \Delta_{u,v} G - \Delta_{u,v} F \le 0\) holds unconditionally for every \(\lambda > 0\) whenever:

Numerator \(F(x)\) (to be maximized) is Supermodular (\(\Delta_{u,v} F \ge 0\)): e.g., internal subgraph edge weights \(\sum_{(u,v) \in E} w_{uv} x_u x_v\) (\(\Delta_{u,v} = +w_{uv} \ge 0\)), modular vertex profits \(\sum_{v \in V} p_v x_v\) (\(\Delta_{u,v} = 0\)), and negative boundary cut penalties \(-\sum_{(u,v) \in E} \gamma_{uv} x_u(1 - x_v)\) (\(\Delta_{u,v} = +\gamma_{uv} \ge 0\)).
Denominator \(G(x)\) (to be minimized) is Submodular (\(\Delta_{u,v} G \le 0\)): e.g., modular vertex costs \(\sum_{v \in V} q_v x_v\) (\(\Delta_{u,v} = 0\)) plus positive cut penalties \(\sum_{(u,v) \in E} d_{uv} x_u(1 - x_v)\) (\(\Delta_{u,v} = -d_{uv} \le 0\)).

This single algebraic sign check immediately separates tractable contest flow problems from famous NP-hard ratio cuts:

Comparing the Three Parametric Root-Finding Engines
Once we have an oracle that evaluates \(h(\lambda) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} (F(x) - \lambda G(x))\) (and returns the achieving structure \(x^*(\lambda) \in \mathcal{F}\)), we have three algorithms to locate the unique root \(\lambda^*\) where \(h(\lambda^*) = 0\):





flowchart LR
  subgraph BS["Engine 1: Binary Search"]
    B1["Midpoint: λ = (L + R) / 2"] --> B2["Run Min-Cut Oracle h(λ)"]
    B2 -->|"h(λ) > 0"| B3["L ← λ (save x*(λ))"]
    B2 -->|"h(λ) ≤ 0"| B4["R ← λ"]
  end
  subgraph DK["Engine 2: Dinkelbach's Secant Method"]
    D1["Start with valid x⁰ ∈ F, λ₀ = F(x⁰)/G(x⁰)"] --> D2["Find x^(k+1) = argmax (F(x) - λ_k G(x))"]
    D2 -->|"F(x^(k+1)) - λ_k G(x^(k+1)) > ε"| D3["Secant jump: λ_{k+1} = F(x^(k+1)) / G(x^(k+1))"]
    D2 -->|"≤ ε"| D4["Terminate: x^k is optimal!"]
  end







Engine 1: Binary Search with Exact Rational Separation \(\Delta_{\min}\)
Maintain a bracket \([L, R]\) guaranteed to contain \(\lambda^*\). At each midpoint \(\lambda = (L + R)/2\), evaluate \(h(\lambda)\): - If \(h(\lambda) > 0\) (feasible: there exists \(x \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\frac{F(x)}{G(x)} > \lambda\)), update \(L \gets \lambda\) and record \(x_{\text{best}} \gets x^*(\lambda)\). - If \(h(\lambda) \le 0\), update \(R \gets \lambda\).
How tight must the stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon = R - L\) be so that binary search is 100% exact (not merely an approximation)? Suppose \(F(x) \in \mathbb{Z}\) and \(G(x) \in \{1, 2, \dots, G_{\max}\}\) are integers. Any two distinct candidate ratios \(\frac{F_1}{G_1} \ne \frac{F_2}{G_2}\) satisfy:
\[\left| \frac{F_1}{G_1} - \frac{F_2}{G_2} \right| = \frac{|F_1 G_2 - F_2 G_1|}{G_1 G_2} \ge \frac{1}{G_{\max}(G_{\max} - 1)} > \frac{1}{2 G_{\max}^2}\]
(because when \(G_1 = G_2 = G\), the difference is at least \(\frac{1}{G} \ge \frac{1}{G_{\max}}\), and when \(G_1 \ne G_2\), \(\max(G_1, G_2) \le G_{\max}\) and \(\min(G_1, G_2) \le G_{\max} - 1\)). Therefore, running binary search until \(R - L < \frac{1}{2 G_{\max}^2}\) requires at most \(\lceil \log_2(2 F_{\max} G_{\max}^2) \rceil\) oracle calls and uniquely isolates the exact optimal rational fraction \(\lambda^* = \frac{F(x^*)}{G(x^*)}\)!


Engine 2: Dinkelbach’s Discrete Newton-Secant Method (Dinkelbach 1967)
Instead of bisecting \([L, R]\) blindly by \(1\) bit per step, Dinkelbach’s algorithm applies Newton’s root-finding method directly to the convex upper envelope \(h(\lambda)\):

Start with any feasible non-empty candidate \(x^{(0)} \in \mathcal{F}\) (for instance, a single edge and its two endpoints, or \(x^{(0)} = V\)), and set \(\lambda_0 = \frac{F(x^{(0)})}{G(x^{(0)})}\).
In iteration \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\):

Call the Min-Cut oracle at \(\lambda_k\) to find \(x^{(k+1)} = \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \big(F(x) - \lambda_k G(x)\big)\).
If \(h(\lambda_k) = F(x^{(k+1)}) - \lambda_k G(x^{(k+1)}) \le 0\) (within numerical tolerance), stop and return \(\lambda_k\) and \(x^{(k)}\).
Otherwise, follow the supporting line \(\ell_{x^{(k+1)}}(\lambda) = F(x^{(k+1)}) - \lambda G(x^{(k+1)})\) straight to its horizontal intercept: \[\lambda_{k+1} \gets \frac{F(x^{(k+1)})}{G(x^{(k+1)})} = \lambda_k + \frac{h(\lambda_k)}{G(x^{(k+1)})} > \lambda_k.\]








TipWhy Dinkelbach’s Method Strictly Decreases the Denominator \(G(x^{(k)})\) and Runs in 5–12 Steps



Because \(x^{(k)}\) achieves \(F(x^{(k)}) - \lambda_k G(x^{(k)}) = 0\) at \(\lambda_k = \frac{F(x^{(k)})}{G(x^{(k)})}\), while \(x^{(k+1)}\) achieves \(h(\lambda_k) = F(x^{(k+1)}) - \lambda_k G(x^{(k+1)}) > 0\), we have both:
\[h(\lambda_k) = F(x^{(k+1)}) - \lambda_k G(x^{(k+1)}) > 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad h(\lambda_{k+1}) \ge F(x^{(k+1)}) - \lambda_{k+1} G(x^{(k+1)}) = 0.\]
By convexity of \(h(\lambda)\) (slopes \(-G(x^*(\lambda))\) are monotonically increasing with \(\lambda\), so \(G(x^*(\lambda))\) is monotonically decreasing!), every non-terminal Dinkelbach step satisfies:
\[\lambda_0 < \lambda_1 < \dots < \lambda^* \qquad \text{and} \qquad G(x^{(1)}) > G(x^{(2)}) > \dots \ge 1.\]
When \(G(x) = |S| \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), Dinkelbach’s algorithm can take at most \(N\) iterations in the worst case, and because it is a Newton-secant method on a piecewise-linear convex curve, it converges superlinearly—requiring only \(5\) to \(12\) Dinic calls in practice vs. \(45\) to \(60\) calls for binary search! Even better, when \(F(x), G(x) \in \mathbb{Z}\), Dinkelbach’s oracle at \(\lambda_k = \frac{P_k}{Q_k}\) can be run in 100% exact 64-bit integer arithmetic by scaling all capacities by \(Q_k\): maximize \(Q_k F(x) - P_k G(x) \in \mathbb{Z}\)!




Engine 3: Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan (GGT) Parametric Preflow (1989)
When source capacities are non-decreasing and sink capacities are non-increasing in \(\lambda\) (or vice versa), the minimal optimal source sets \(S^*(\lambda)\) are nested: \(S^*(\lambda_1) \supseteq S^*(\lambda_2)\) for \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\). As we prove in Section 4, this allows finding all \(\le |V|\) breakpoints of the entire curve \(h(\lambda)\) in \(O(|V|)\) max-flow calls via Parametric Divide-and-Conquer Contraction (#111), or in the asymptotic time of a single Push-Relabel execution!





1.4 Step 4 — Broken-Gadget Counterexamples (FM-14) & The Two-Scale IEEE-754 Epsilon Hierarchy
Fractional min-cut problems are notorious in competitive programming for silent WA and TLE failures caused by three subtle traps, which we group under Failure Mode FM-14 (H-15):






WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexample FM-14a — The Trivial Empty Subgraph Trap (\(S = \emptyset\))



Suppose we want to maximize \(\frac{F(S)}{G(S)}\) over non-empty subsets \(\emptyset \subsetneq S \subseteq V\), where \(F(\emptyset) = 0\) and \(G(\emptyset) = 0\). When we linearize the objective into \(h(\lambda) = \max_{S \subseteq V} (F(S) - \lambda G(S))\) over all subsets \(S \subseteq V\) (which is what an unconstrained \(s\)-\(t\) minimum cut naturally optimizes), the empty set \(S = \emptyset\) always evaluates to:
\[F(\emptyset) - \lambda G(\emptyset) = 0 - \lambda \cdot 0 = 0 \qquad \text{for EVERY } \lambda \in \mathbb{R}!\]
What goes wrong if you ignore \(S = \emptyset\)?

Masking at \(\lambda = \lambda^*\) during Subgraph Reconstruction: At the exact optimal ratio \(\lambda = \lambda^*\), the true optimal non-empty subgraph \(S^*\) achieves \(F(S^*) - \lambda^* G(S^*) = 0\), which ties with \(S = \emptyset\)! Because the source-minimal cut \(S_{\min}\) returns the inclusion-minimal subset of \(V\) achieving the minimum cut, running Dinic at \(\lambda \ge \lambda^*\) returns \(S_{\min} = \emptyset\)!

Defensive Fix: Always reconstruct the vertex set \(S^*\) at the last feasible lower bound \(\lambda = L < \lambda^*\) (where \(F(S^*) - L \cdot G(S^*) > 0\) strictly beats \(S = \emptyset\) by at least \(\frac{1}{|V|}\)), or handle the zero-edge case \(|E| = 0\) (where \(\lambda^* = 0\)) explicitly by outputting any single vertex \(\{1\}\).

Negative Optimal Ratio (\(\lambda^* < 0\)) or Shifted Denominator (\(|S| - 1\)):

If every non-empty subset has \(F(S) < 0\) (e.g., all vertex profits are negative and must be offset), then for \(\lambda < 0\), \(\max_{\emptyset \ne S} (F(S) - \lambda G(S))\) can still be dominated by \(F(\emptyset) - \lambda G(\emptyset) = 0\).
In Nash-Williams Arboricity (#110), the denominator is \(G(S) = |S| - 1\) for \(|S| \ge 2\). Plugging \(S = \emptyset\) into \(|E(S)| - \lambda(|S| - 1)\) gives \(0 - \lambda(-1) = +\lambda > 0\), completely masking whether any valid \(|S| \ge 2\) violates the forest bound! To eliminate \(S = \emptyset\), you must pin a forced root vertex \(r \in S\) via \(s \xrightarrow{\infty} r\) (Section 3.3 and Problem #110).










WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexample FM-14b — Coarse Binary Search \(\varepsilon\) & Floating-Point Dinic Infinite Loops




Why \(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\) Fails at \(N = 100\): Consider two disjoint components in a graph on \(N = 100\) vertices: Component \(A\) has \(49\) edges on \(99\) vertices (or density \(\frac{48}{99}\)), and Component \(B\) has \(50\) edges on \(100\) vertices (or compare \(\frac{49}{99} \approx 0.494949\) vs. \(\frac{49.5}{100}\) in half-weighted graphs, or \(\frac{97}{99} = 0.979798\) vs. \(\frac{96}{98} = 0.979592\) whose difference is \(\frac{97 \times 98 - 96 \times 99}{99 \times 98} = \frac{2}{9702} \approx 2.06 \times 10^{-4}\); for general distinct fractions \(\frac{a}{99}\) and \(\frac{b}{100}\) such as \(\frac{49}{99}\) and \(\frac{50}{101}\), or \(\frac{98}{99}\) and \(\frac{99}{100}\), \(\frac{99}{100} - \frac{98}{99} = \frac{1}{9900} \approx 1.01 \times 10^{-4}\)!). Stopping binary search at \(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\) stops 10 times too early and extracts the wrong subgraph!
The Two-Scale IEEE-754 Epsilon Hierarchy: When running Dinic on double capacities, pushing flow along a bottleneck path executes e.cap -= pushed. In IEEE-754 64-bit double arithmetic (\(53\)-bit mantissa, machine epsilon \(\approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}\)), subtracting two nearly equal numbers leaves a phantom residual capacity of \(\approx 10^{-15}\).

If your Dinic BFS/DFS tests if (e.cap > 0), it treats \(10^{-15}\) as an unsaturated edge and loops infinitely!
Conversely, if your Dinic BFS/DFS uses the same tolerance EPS = 1e-5 as your outer binary search, Dinic ignores legitimate augmenting paths of capacity \(10^{-6}\) near \(\lambda^*\) and returns a corrupted minimum cut!
Mandatory Contract (H-15): Always separate the three scales by at least 2–3 orders of magnitude: \[\underbrace{\varepsilon_{\text{flow}} = 10^{-11}}_{\text{Dinic BFS/DFS: } \texttt{e.cap > EPS\_FLOW}} \;\ll\; \underbrace{\varepsilon_{\text{cut\_sign}} = 10^{-8}}_{\text{Sign check: } \texttt{h(lambda) > EPS\_CUT}} \;\ll\; \underbrace{\Delta_{\min} = \frac{1}{|V|(|V|-1)}}_{\text{Rational gap } (\ge 10^{-4} \text{ for } |V| \le 100)}.\]

2. Goldberg’s Maximum Density Subgraph (最大密度子图) — Edge-Vertex Closure vs. \(|V|\)-Only Degree-Sum Reduction

2.1 Problem Formulation & Why Charikar’s Greedy Peeling Only Gives a 2-Approximation
Given an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(N = |V|\) vertices and \(M = |E|\) edges, the Maximum Density Subgraph (MDS) problem (最大密度子图, Goldberg 1984; popularized in Chinese olympiad literature by Amber / 胡伯涛 in his 2007 national team paper 《最小割模型在信息学竞赛中的应用》) asks for a non-empty subset of vertices \(S \subseteq V\) maximizing the induced edge-to-vertex ratio:
\[\lambda^* = \max_{\emptyset \subsetneq S \subseteq V} D(S), \qquad \text{where} \qquad D(S) := \frac{|E(S)|}{|S|} \quad \text{and} \quad E(S) := \big\{ \{u, v\} \in E : u \in S \text{ and } v \in S \big\}.\]

Concrete Counterexample to Greedy Minimum-Degree Peeling (Charikar 2000)
Before constructing a flow network, every strong contestant asks: “Why can’t I just repeatedly delete a vertex of minimum current degree in \(G\), recording the highest density subgraph seen along the way?”
While Charikar (2000) proved that this \(O(N + M)\) greedy peeling algorithm is a \(2\)-approximation (\(D_{\text{peel}} \ge \frac{1}{2} \lambda^*\)), it fails to find the exact optimum even on simple graphs! Here is a concrete hand-checkable counterexample:

Construct \(G\) as two components (or connect them by a single bridge):

Component \(A\) (Dense Clique \(K_4\)): \(4\) vertices, all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) edges. Every vertex in \(A\) has degree \(3\), and its density is \(D(A) = \frac{6}{4} = \mathbf{1.50}\).
Component \(B\) (Bipartite Core \(K_{4, 4}\)): \(8\) vertices, \(16\) edges, EXCEPT we delete \(3\) edges of a matching so \(6\) vertices have degree \(3\) and \(2\) vertices have degree \(4\)? Not quite: in \(K_{4,4}\), every vertex has degree \(4 > 3\), and its density is \(D(B) = \frac{16}{8} = 2.0 > 1.5\). How do we give Component \(B\) a higher minimum degree than \(A\) at the start of peeling, while having a lower density than \(A\)?


Let us check if a single unweighted graph \(B\) can have \(\delta_{\min}(B) > 2 D(A)\): no, because the average degree of \(B\) is \(2 D(B) \ge \delta_{\min}(B)\), so if \(\delta_{\min}(B) \ge \delta_{\min}(A) = |A| - 1\) for a clique \(A = K_k\), then \(2 D(B) \ge k - 1 = 2 D(K_k)\)! That is why on a disjoint clique vs. another graph, the clique’s degree is \(2 D(K_k) = k - 1\).
Now attach leaves / hubs to \(A\) or look at how peeling breaks: Take Component \(A\) as \(K_5\) (\(5\) vertices, \(10\) edges, degree \(4\)) plus one extra vertex \(u_0\) connected to \(3\) vertices of \(K_5\): now \(A' = K_5 \cup \{u_0\}\) has \(6\) vertices and \(10 + 3 = 13\) edges, so its density is \(D(A') = \frac{13}{6} \approx \mathbf{2.1667}\), while \(u_0\) has degree \(3\)! Meanwhile, let Component \(B\) be \(K_{4,4}\) (\(8\) vertices, \(16\) edges), where every vertex has degree \(4 > 3\), and the maximum density of any subgraph of \(B\) is \(D(B) = \frac{16}{8} = \mathbf{2.00} < 2.1667\)!
If we tie-break or replace \(u_0\) in a weighted/multi-layered peeling (or if we connect \(K_d\) vertices to an external layer so that \(B\)’s core protects low-degree vertices until \(A\)’s vertices drop below \(B\)’s degree), in vertex-weighted or edge-weighted MDS, the failure is immediate and catastrophic: let Component \(A\) be a single edge \(e = \{1, 2\}\) of weight \(10\) on two vertices of cost \(1\) (weighted degree \(10\), density \(\frac{10}{2} = \mathbf{5.0}\)), and Component \(B\) be a star \(K_{1, 3}\) with center \(c\) (cost \(5\)) and \(3\) leaves \(\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3\) (cost \(1\) each), where each star edge has weight \(6\). In \(B\), every leaf has degree/cost ratio \(\frac{6}{1} = 6\), and the center has weighted degree \(18\) (or ratio \(\frac{18}{5} = 3.6\)). If peeling deletes minimum raw weighted degree, \(B\)’s leaves (\(6 < 10\)) are peeled first; if peeling deletes minimum degree-to-cost ratio, \(B\)’s center (\(\frac{18}{5} = 3.6 < 10\)) is deleted first, which immediately孤立s all three leaves in \(B\). Conversely, if \(B\)’s center has cost \(2.5\) (ratio \(\frac{18}{2.5} = 7.2\)) and each leaf has cost \(0.8\) (ratio \(\frac{6}{0.8} = 7.5\)), and \(A\) has edge weight \(7\) on two vertices of cost \(1\) (ratio \(7.0\), density \(\frac{7}{2} = \mathbf{3.5}\)), then every vertex in \(B\) has greedy ratio \(\ge 7.2 > 7.0\), so greedy peeling destroys \(A\) completely before touching \(B\), even though \(B\)’s total density is only \(\frac{18}{2.5 + 3(0.8)} = \frac{18}{4.9} \approx \mathbf{3.67}\) (or with \(4\) leaves of cost \(0.85\) and edge weight \(6.1\) and center cost \(3.0\): leaf ratio \(\frac{6.1}{0.85} = 7.17 > 7.0\), center ratio \(\frac{24.4}{3.0} = 8.13 > 7.0\), while \(B\)’s density is \(\frac{24.4}{3.0 + 3.4} = \frac{24.4}{6.4} = \mathbf{3.8125}\) vs. if \(A\) is \(K_3\) with edge weights \(3.6\) and vertex costs \(1\), where each vertex in \(A\) has weighted degree \(2 \times 3.6 = 7.2\) and \(A\)’s density is \(\frac{3 \times 3.6}{3} = \mathbf{3.60}\), and with \(K_4\) of edge weight \(2.35\): degree \(3 \times 2.35 = 7.05 < 7.17\), while \(A\)’s density is \(\frac{6 \times 2.35}{4} = \mathbf{3.525}\)—and for \(K_{10}\) with edge weight \(0.79\): degree \(9 \times 0.79 = 7.11 < 7.17\), while \(A\)’s density is \(\frac{45 \times 0.79}{10} = \mathbf{3.555}\), and for \(K_{20}\) with edge weight \(0.375\): degree \(19 \times 0.375 = 7.125 < 7.17\), while \(A\)’s density is \(\frac{190 \times 0.375}{20} = \mathbf{3.5625}\)…Wait: in \(K_k\), density is \(\frac{1}{2}\) of weighted degree! Why? Because \(\frac{\binom{k}{2} w}{k} = \frac{1}{2}(k-1)w = \frac{1}{2}\deg_w(v)\)! And in a star \(B\), each edge touches the center (cost \(c_0\)) and a leaf (cost \(c_1\)), so if \(\frac{w}{c_1} > d_A\) and \(\frac{L w}{c_0} > d_A\), then \(c_1 < \frac{w}{d_A}\) and \(c_0 < \frac{L w}{d_A}\), so \(B\)’s density is \(\frac{L w}{c_0 + L c_1} > \frac{L w}{\frac{L w}{d_A} + \frac{L w}{d_A}} = \frac{1}{2} d_A = D(A)\)! That’s actually a neat proof of Charikar’s 2-approximation factor \(\frac{1}{2}\)!).
How do we beat \(\frac{1}{2} d_A\) so \(D(A) > D(B)\) while every vertex in \(B\) has higher instantaneous degree than some vertex in \(A\)? In unweighted graphs, as we found above, take \(A' = K_5 \cup \{u_0\}\) where \(u_0\) has \(3\) edges into \(K_5\) (\(6\) vertices, \(13\) edges, \(D(A') = \frac{13}{6} \approx \mathbf{2.167}\), minimum degree \(\deg(u_0) = 3\)), and \(B = K_{4,4}\) (\(8\) vertices, \(16\) edges, \(D(B) = \mathbf{2.00}\), every vertex has degree \(4\))! Now if \(u_0\) is instead two vertices \(u_1, u_2\) adjacent to each other and to \(K_k\), or if we peel minimum degree on \(A\) where every vertex of \(A\) is part of a structure whose minimum degree is \(< 4\) while \(D(A) > 2\): wait—if \(A'\) has minimum degree \(3\) at \(u_0\), deleting \(u_0\) leaves \(K_5\) whose density is \(\frac{10}{5} = 2.00 < \frac{13}{6}\)! Wait: before \(u_0\) is deleted, \(A' \sqcup B\) has \(14\) vertices and \(13 + 16 = 29\) edges, so \(D(A' \sqcup B) = \frac{29}{14} \approx \mathbf{2.0714} < 2.1667\)! When greedy peeling starts on \(G = A' \sqcup B\):

Step 1: The unique vertex of minimum degree \(3\) is \(u_0 \in A'\). Before deleting \(u_0\), the current graph is \(A' \sqcup B\) with density \(\frac{29}{14} \approx \mathbf{2.0714}\).
Step 2: Greedy peeling deletes \(u_0\)! Now the remaining graph is \(K_5 \sqcup K_{4,4}\), where every vertex in both components has degree \(4\), and every remaining subgraph has density at most \(\frac{10}{5} = \frac{16}{8} = \mathbf{2.00}\)!
Result: Greedy peeling NEVER sees \(A'\) alone (because \(B\) is still present when \(u_0\) is deleted, diluting \(\frac{13}{6} \approx 2.1667\) down to \(\frac{29}{14} \approx 2.0714\), and as soon as \(u_0\) is deleted, \(A'\) is destroyed down to \(K_5\) of density \(2.00\))! Thus greedy peeling outputs \(\frac{29}{14} \approx 2.0714\) instead of the true optimum \(D(A') = \frac{13}{6} \approx 2.1667\)!



This 14-vertex unweighted counterexample (\(A' = K_5 \cup \{u_0\}\) disjoint from \(B = K_{4,4}\)) explains with 100% clarity why greedy peeling fails: an optimal subgraph \(A'\) can contain a slightly lower-degree vertex \(u_0\) (degree \(3 > 2.1667\)) that still raises \(A'\)’s average density, yet greedy peeling deletes \(u_0\) before stripping away a denser-looking distractor component \(B\) (\(K_{4,4}\), degree \(4\), density \(2.0\))!




2.2 Construction A: The \(|V| + |E|\) Bipartite Project-Selection Closure (Picard–Queyranne 1982)
At a fixed trial parameter \(\lambda \ge 0\), we want to evaluate:
\[h(\lambda) = \max_{S \subseteq V} \big( |E(S)| - \lambda |S| \big).\]

Step 2 (Algebraic Representation)
Introduce a binary vertex indicator \(x_v \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(x_v = 1 \iff v \in S\)) for each \(v \in V\) and a binary edge indicator \(y_e \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(y_e = 1 \iff e \in E(S)\)) for each edge \(e = \{u, v\} \in E\). By definition of induced subgraph \(E(S)\), we can claim the \(+1\) reward for edge \(e = \{u, v\}\) only if both endpoints \(u\) and \(v\) are selected in \(S\):
\[y_e = 1 \implies (x_u = 1 \text{ and } x_v = 1) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad y_e(1 - x_u) = 0 \text{ and } y_e(1 - x_v) = 0.\]
This is a textbook Maximum Weight Closure (Project Selection) problem from Chapter 09! Subtracting from the maximum possible edge reward \(|E| = M\), maximizing \(|E(S)| - \lambda |S|\) is equivalent to minimizing the closure cut polynomial:
\[\Phi_{\lambda}^{\text{closure}}(x, y) = \sum_{e \in E} 1 \cdot (1 - y_e) + \sum_{v \in V} \lambda x_v + \sum_{e = \{u, v\} \in E} \infty \cdot \big( y_e(1 - x_u) + y_e(1 - x_v) \big).\]


Step 3 (Mechanical Graph Compilation — Construction A)
Place \(y_e = 1, x_v = 1\) on the source side \(S_{\text{cut}}\) and \(y_e = 0, x_v = 0\) on the sink side \(T_{\text{cut}}\):

Source to Edge Nodes (\(s \to e\)): For every edge \(e \in E\), add a directed arc \(s \xrightarrow{1} e\) (severed when \(y_e = 0\), forfeiting \(+1\) edge count).
Edge Nodes to Endpoint Vertex Nodes (\(e \to u, e \to v\)): For every \(e = \{u, v\} \in E\), add two directed arcs \(e \xrightarrow{\infty} u\) and \(e \xrightarrow{\infty} v\) (enforcing \(y_e \le x_u\) and \(y_e \le x_v\)).
Vertex Nodes to Sink (\(v \to t\)): For every vertex \(v \in V\), add a directed arc \(v \xrightarrow{\lambda} t\) (severed when \(x_v = 1\), paying \(\lambda\) for including \(v \in S\)).

Then:
\[h(\lambda) = |E| - \operatorname{MinCut}_{\text{closure}}(\lambda), \qquad \text{so} \qquad \lambda < \lambda^* \iff \operatorname{MinCut}_{\text{closure}}(\lambda) < |E|.\]

Network Size: \(|V_{\text{flow}}| = |V| + |E| + 2\) vertices and \(|E_{\text{flow}}| = |V| + 3|E|\) directed arcs.
When to Use Construction A:

When \(|E|\) is sparse (\(|V|, |E| \le 5000\)) and capacities are small integers (e.g., CF 847J — Students Initiation, #106, where \(\lambda = K \in \mathbb{Z}\) makes Construction A a unit-network bipartite flow running in \(O((|V|+|E|)\sqrt{|V|+|E|})\)!).
When “edges” are \(k\)-uniform hyperedges (\(k \ge 3\)) or general shop-plant subsets \(P_j \subseteq V\) (HDU 5855, #112), where Construction B’s pairwise degree identity does not apply.






2.3 Construction B: Goldberg’s (1984) & Amber’s (2007) \(|V|\)-Only Degree-Sum Reduction
What if the graph \(G = (V, E)\) is dense—for example, \(N = 1000\) vertices and \(M = \binom{1000}{2} \approx 5 \times 10^5\) edges (as in [2009国家集训队] 人员雇佣 BZOJ 2039, #109)? Creating \(M = 5 \times 10^5\) edge nodes in Construction A builds a \(501,000\)-vertex flow network that will TLE inside a 50-step binary search.
Can we eliminate all \(M\) edge nodes so the flow network has only \(|V| + 2\) vertices?

Step 2 (Algebraic Representation — The Handshaking Cut-Degree Identity)
Consider any vertex subset \(S \subseteq V\) and its complement \(\bar{S} = V \setminus S\). If we sum the full degree \(d_v := \deg_G(v)\) of every vertex \(v \in S\), how many times is each edge of \(G\) counted?

Every internal edge \(e = \{u, v\} \in E(S)\) has both endpoints in \(S\), so it contributes \(+2\) to \(\sum_{v \in S} d_v\).
Every boundary (cut) edge \(e = \{u, v\} \in \delta(S, \bar{S})\) has exactly one endpoint in \(S\) and one endpoint in \(\bar{S}\), so it contributes \(+1\) to \(\sum_{v \in S} d_v\).
Every edge in \(E(\bar{S})\) contributes \(0\).

This gives the fundamental Cut-Degree Double-Counting Identity:
\[\sum_{v \in S} d_v = 2|E(S)| + |\delta(S, \bar{S})| \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad |E(S)| = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{v \in S} d_v - \frac{1}{2} |\delta(S, \bar{S})|.\]
Substitute this identity directly into \(h(\lambda) = \max_{S \subseteq V} (|E(S)| - \lambda |S|)\):
\[\begin{aligned}
|E(S)| - \lambda |S| &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{v \in S} d_v - \frac{1}{2} |\delta(S, \bar{S})| - \lambda \sum_{v \in S} 1 \\
&= -\frac{1}{2} \left( \sum_{v \in S} (2\lambda - d_v) + |\delta(S, \bar{S})| \right).
\end{aligned}\]
Pause and admire what just happened algebraically: - In Construction A, \(|E(S)| = \sum_{\{u,v\} \in E} x_u x_v\) was a sum of quadratic product terms, which forced us to introduce an auxiliary node \(y_e\) for every edge \(e \in E\). - By writing \(2 x_u x_v = x_u + x_v - |x_u - x_v|\), we converted all \(M\) quadratic rewards into modular unary vertex weights \(-d_v x_v\) plus standard undirected graph cut edges \(|x_u - x_v|\) directly between \(u\) and \(v\)!


Step 3 (Mechanical Graph Compilation — Amber’s Uniform \(+U\) Shift vs. Dynamic Sign-Splitting)
We want to find \(\min_{S \subseteq V} \Psi_\lambda(S)\), where:
\[\Psi_\lambda(S) := \sum_{v \in S} (2\lambda - d_v) + |\delta(S, \bar{S})| = \sum_{v \in V} (2\lambda - d_v) x_v + \sum_{\{u, v\} \in E} \big( x_u(1 - x_v) + x_v(1 - x_u) \big).\]
Notice a crucial detail: when \(2\lambda < d_v\), the unary coefficient \(2\lambda - d_v\) is negative! If we naively wired \(v \xrightarrow{2\lambda - d_v} t\), the capacity would be negative (Failure Mode FM-14). There are two clean ways to compile \(\Psi_\lambda(S)\) into non-negative capacities:

Method B1: Goldberg / Amber Uniform Pedestal Shift \(+U\) (H-15, Mandatory for Parametric Preflow)
Pick a constant pedestal \(U \ge \max_{v \in V} d_v\) (in practice, \(U = |E| = M\) or \(U = \max_v d_v\)). Add and subtract \(U\) on every vertex term by using the identity \(x_v - 1 = -(1 - x_v)\), or equivalently add the constant \(U \cdot |V| = \sum_{v \in V} U(x_v + (1 - x_v))\) to \(\Psi_\lambda(S)\):
\[U \cdot |V| + \Psi_\lambda(S) = \sum_{v \in V} U(1 - x_v) + \sum_{v \in V} \underbrace{(U + 2\lambda - d_v)}_{\ge 0} x_v + \sum_{\{u, v\} \in E} \big( x_u(1 - x_v) + x_v(1 - x_u) \big).\]
Every coefficient is now unconditionally non-negative for all \(\lambda \ge 0\)! This compiles immediately into the \(|V| + 2\)-vertex Goldberg–Amber network \(G_{\text{Goldberg}}(\lambda)\):





flowchart LR
  S(("Source s")) -->|"cap: U (cut if v ∉ S)"| U_node["Vertex u ∈ V"]
  S -->|"cap: U (cut if v ∉ S)"| V_node["Vertex v ∈ V"]
  U_node <-->|"undirected cap: 1 (both arcs u→v, v→u)"| V_node
  U_node -->|"cap: U + 2λ - d_u ≥ 0 (cut if u ∈ S)"| T(("Sink t"))
  V_node -->|"cap: U + 2λ - d_v ≥ 0 (cut if v ∈ S)"| T







Source Arcs (\(s \to v\)): For each \(v \in V\), add a directed arc \(s \xrightarrow{U} v\) (severed if \(v \notin S\), i.e., \(x_v = 0\)).
Sink Arcs (\(v \to t\)): For each \(v \in V\), add a directed arc \(v \xrightarrow{U + 2\lambda - d_v} t\) (severed if \(v \in S\), i.e., \(x_v = 1\)).
Internal Graph Arcs (\(u \leftrightarrow v\)): For each undirected edge \(\{u, v\} \in E\), add a bidirectional (undirected) edge of capacity \(1\) between \(u\) and \(v\) (i.e., \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\) and \(v \xrightarrow{1} u\), severed if \(|\{u, v\} \cap S| = 1\)).

For any vertex subset \(S \subseteq V\), the capacity of the \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((S \cup \{s\}, \bar{S} \cup \{t\})\) in \(G_{\text{Goldberg}}(\lambda)\) is:
\[\operatorname{Cap}_\lambda(S) = U \cdot |V| + 2\big(\lambda |S| - |E(S)|\big).\]
Therefore:
\[h(\lambda) = \max_{S \subseteq V} \big(|E(S)| - \lambda |S|\big) = \frac{U \cdot |V| - \operatorname{MinCut}_\lambda(s, t)}{2},\]
and a non-empty subgraph with density strictly greater than \(\lambda\) exists if and only if \(\operatorname{MinCut}_\lambda(s, t) < U \cdot |V|\)!


Method B2: Dynamic Sign-Splitting (Zero-Shift Optimization for Binary Search / Dinkelbach)
If you are rebuilding the network from scratch at each binary search or Dinkelbach step, you can avoid adding the shift \(U\) entirely by splitting vertices according to the sign of \(\beta_v(\lambda) := d_v - 2\lambda\):

If \(\beta_v(\lambda) > 0\) (i.e., \(d_v > 2\lambda\)): rewrite \(-\beta_v(\lambda) x_v = -\beta_v(\lambda) + \beta_v(\lambda)(1 - x_v)\), which wires \(s \xrightarrow{d_v - 2\lambda} v\).
If \(\beta_v(\lambda) \le 0\) (i.e., \(2\lambda \ge d_v\)): keep \((2\lambda - d_v) x_v \ge 0\), which wires \(v \xrightarrow{2\lambda - d_v} t\).
Undirected edges \(\{u, v\} \in E\) still get bidirectional capacity \(1\).
Then \(2 h(\lambda) = \sum_{v : d_v > 2\lambda} (d_v - 2\lambda) - \operatorname{MinCut}_\lambda(s, t)\).

Why keep both Method B1 and Method B2 in your toolkit? Method B2 has smaller capacities for standard binary search, whereas Method B1 (\(+U\) shift) keeps \(c(s \to v) = U\) independent of \(\lambda\) and makes \(c(v \to t) = U + 2\lambda - d_v\) monotonically increasing in \(\lambda\), which is the essential structural requirement for the Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan Parametric Preflow algorithm in Section 4!





2.4 Step 4 — Hand-Checkable Toy Trace (\(N = 4\) Paw Graph) & Three Broken-Gadget Counterexamples

Concrete Toy Trace on the \(N = 4\) Paw Graph
Let \(G = (V, E)\) be the 4-vertex “Paw Graph” with \(V = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) and \(M = 4\) edges: a triangle \(\{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\}, \{1, 3\}\) plus a pendant leaf edge \(\{3, 4\}\). - Degrees: \(d_1 = 2, d_2 = 2, d_3 = 3, d_4 = 1\). - Candidate densities: - Triangle \(S = \{1, 2, 3\}\): \(|E(S)| = 3, |S| = 3 \implies D(\{1, 2, 3\}) = \frac{3}{3} = 1.0\). - Whole graph \(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\): \(|E(S)| = 4, |S| = 4 \implies D(\{1, 2, 3, 4\}) = \frac{4}{4} = 1.0\). - Single edge \(S = \{1, 2\}\): \(D(\{1, 2\}) = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\).
Let us trace Method B1 (\(U = 4\), so \(U \cdot |V| = 16\)) at two trial parameters:

Trial \(\lambda = 0.8 < \lambda^* = 1.0\):

Source arcs: \(c(s \to v) = 4.0\) for all \(v \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\).
Sink arcs \(c(v \to t) = 4 + 1.6 - d_v = 5.6 - d_v\): \[c(1 \to t) = 3.6, \quad c(2 \to t) = 3.6, \quad c(3 \to t) = 2.6, \quad c(4 \to t) = 4.6.\]
Check cut \(S = \{1, 2, 3\}\) (\(\bar{S} = \{4\}\)): \[\operatorname{Cap}_{0.8}(\{1, 2, 3\}) = \underbrace{(3.6 + 3.6 + 2.6)}_{v \to t \text{ for } v \in S} + \underbrace{4.0}_{s \to 4 \text{ for } 4 \in \bar{S}} + \underbrace{1.0}_{\text{edge } 3 \to 4} = 9.8 + 4.0 + 1.0 = \mathbf{14.8} < 16.0.\]
Indeed, \(h(0.8) = \frac{16.0 - 14.8}{2} = +0.6 = 3 - 0.8 \times 3 > 0\)! And for \(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\), \(\operatorname{Cap}_{0.8}(V) = 3.6 + 3.6 + 2.6 + 4.6 = \mathbf{14.4} < 14.8\), giving \(h(0.8) = \frac{16.0 - 14.4}{2} = +0.8 = 4 - 0.8 \times 4 > 0\).

Trial \(\lambda = 1.1 > \lambda^* = 1.0\):

Sink arcs \(c(v \to t) = 4 + 2.2 - d_v = 6.2 - d_v\): \(c(1 \to t) = 4.2, c(2 \to t) = 4.2, c(3 \to t) = 3.2, c(4 \to t) = 5.2\).
Now \(\operatorname{Cap}_{1.1}(\{1, 2, 3\}) = (4.2 + 4.2 + 3.2) + 4.0 + 1.0 = 16.6 > 16.0\), and \(\operatorname{Cap}_{1.1}(V) = 16.8 > 16.0\). The minimum cut is \(S = \emptyset\) with \(\operatorname{Cap}_{1.1}(\emptyset) = 16.0 \implies h(1.1) = 0 \implies \lambda^* < 1.1\).




Three Classic Broken-Gadget Counterexamples in Maximum Density Subgraph

Using Directed Graph Edges Instead of Bidirectional Capacity-\(1\) Edges on Directed Input Graphs: Suppose the input graph \(G = (V, E)\) is directed, and the problem defines \(E(S) = \{(u \to v) \in E : u \in S \text{ and } v \in S\}\) as the set of directed arcs with both endpoints inside \(S\). A frequent blunder is adding only a directed arc \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\) in Goldberg’s \(|V|\)-only model.

Why It Breaks: Whether an arc is oriented \(u \to v\) or \(v \to u\), the indicator that both endpoints lie in \(S\) is \(x_u x_v\), which is 100% symmetric in \(u\) and \(v\)! In the degree identity \(\sum_{v \in S} (d_v^{\text{in}} + d_v^{\text{out}}) = 2|E(S)| + |\delta^+(S)| + |\delta^-(S)|\), both outgoing arcs \(\delta^+(S)\) and incoming arcs \(\delta^-(S)\) cross the boundary once. Therefore, even on a directed graph, Goldberg’s \(|V|\)-only reduction MUST use total degree \(d_v = d_v^{\text{in}} + d_v^{\text{out}}\) and undirected (bidirectional) capacity-\(1\) arcs \(u \leftrightarrow v\)!

Omitting Factor-of-\(2\) Scaling on \(\lambda\) or Edge Weights: In \(\sum_{v \in S} d_v = 2|E(S)| + |\delta(S, \bar{S})|\), every internal edge is counted twice in the degree sum. If you wire \(v \to t\) with capacity \(U + \lambda - d_v\) instead of \(U + 2\lambda - d_v\) (while keeping \(u \leftrightarrow v\) at capacity \(1\)), you are optimizing \(2|E(S)| - \lambda |S|\) instead of \(|E(S)| - \lambda |S|\), overestimating \(\lambda^*\) by a factor of \(2\)!
Applying Goldberg’s \(|V|\)-Only Identity to \(k\)-Uniform Hypergraphs (\(k \ge 3\)): Suppose each hyperedge \(e = \{u, v, w\} \in \mathcal{E}\) has size \(3\) and counts toward \(E(S)\) iff \(\{u, v, w\} \subseteq S\). In the hypergraph degree sum \(\sum_{v \in S} d_v = 3|E(S)| + 2|\delta_{2,1}(S)| + 1|\delta_{1,2}(S)|\), a hyperedge with \(2\) vertices in \(S\) and \(1\) in \(\bar{S}\) contributes \(+2\), whereas a hyperedge with \(1\) vertex in \(S\) and \(2\) in \(\bar{S}\) contributes \(+1\). Because an undirected graph cut on \(\{u, v, w\}\) cuts \(2\) edges in both the \(2\)-vs-\(1\) and \(1\)-vs-\(2\) splits, no pairwise graph gadget on \(V\) alone can distinguish \(|\delta_{2,1}(S)|\) from \(|\delta_{1,2}(S)|\)! For hyperedges of size \(k \ge 3\), you must use Construction A (\(|V| + |\mathcal{E}|\) Bipartite Closure).
