3. Generalized Density Ratios — Edge-Weighted, Vertex-Weighted, Minimum Ratio Cuts & Structural Dualities

3.1 Amber’s Master Weighted Density Model (最大密度子图推广模型, 胡伯涛 2007)
In advanced contest tasks, the numerator and denominator of a subgraph density ratio rarely consist of unweighted edge and vertex counts alone. Following Amber’s (胡伯涛 2007) unified classification, suppose we are given an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) equipped with four sets of weights:

Internal Edge Rewards \(w_e \ge 0\) (\(e \in E\)): Claimed if both endpoints of \(e = \{u, v\}\) belong to \(S\) (\(e \in E(S)\)).
Vertex Standalone Profits \(p_v \in \mathbb{R}\) (\(v \in V\)): Claimed (or paid, if \(p_v < 0\)) whenever \(v \in S\).
Boundary Cut Penalties \(\gamma_e \ge 0\) (\(e \in E\)): Deducted whenever exactly one endpoint of \(e = \{u, v\}\) belongs to \(S\) (\(e \in \delta(S, \bar{S})\)).
Vertex Denominator Weights \(q_v > 0\) (\(v \in V\)): Each vertex \(v \in S\) contributes \(q_v > 0\) to the denominator (e.g., setup time, headcount, or power consumption).

We seek a non-empty subset \(\emptyset \subsetneq S \subseteq V\) maximizing the generalized density ratio:
\[\lambda^* = \max_{\emptyset \subsetneq S \subseteq V} \frac{\sum_{e \in E(S)} w_e + \sum_{v \in S} p_v - \sum_{e \in \delta(S, \bar{S})} \gamma_e}{\sum_{v \in S} q_v}.\]

Step 2 (Algebraic Reduction to a \(|V|\)-Only Cut Polynomial)
At trial parameter \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\), the parametric merit function is:
\[h(\lambda) = \max_{S \subseteq V} \left( \sum_{e \in E(S)} w_e + \sum_{v \in S} (p_v - \lambda q_v) - \sum_{e \in \delta(S, \bar{S})} \gamma_e \right).\]
Define the weighted degree of each vertex \(v \in V\) with respect to internal edge rewards \(w_e\):
\[D_w(v) := \sum_{e \in E : e \ni v} w_e.\]
Just as in the unweighted case, summing \(D_w(v)\) over all \(v \in S\) counts every internal edge \(e \in E(S)\) twice (\(2 w_e\)) and every boundary edge \(e \in \delta(S, \bar{S})\) once (\(w_e\)):
\[\sum_{v \in S} D_w(v) = 2 \sum_{e \in E(S)} w_e + \sum_{e \in \delta(S, \bar{S})} w_e \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \sum_{e \in E(S)} w_e = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{v \in S} D_w(v) - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{e \in \delta(S, \bar{S})} w_e.\]
Substitute this into \(h(\lambda)\) and multiply by \(-2\) to convert maximization into minimization:
\[-2 h(\lambda) = \min_{S \subseteq V} \left( \sum_{v \in S} \big( 2\lambda q_v - 2p_v - D_w(v) \big) + \sum_{e = \{u, v\} \in \delta(S, \bar{S})} (w_e + 2\gamma_e) \right).\]


Step 3 (Mechanical Graph Compilation — Generalized \(|V|\)-Only Network)
Pick a uniform shift \(U \ge \max_{v \in V} (2p_v + D_w(v) - 2\lambda_{\min} q_v)\) so that every sink capacity is non-negative:

Source Arcs (\(s \to v\)): Capacity \(c(s \to v) = U\) for every \(v \in V\).
Sink Arcs (\(v \to t\)): Capacity \(c(v \to t) = U + 2\lambda q_v - 2p_v - D_w(v) \ge 0\) for every \(v \in V\).
Internal Undirected Edges (\(u \leftrightarrow v\)): Both directed arcs \(u \to v\) and \(v \to u\) receive capacity \(c(u \leftrightarrow v) = w_e + 2\gamma_e \ge 0\) for every \(e = \{u, v\} \in E\).

Then for any subset \(S \subseteq V\), the cut capacity is \(\operatorname{Cap}_\lambda(S) = U \cdot |V| - 2\big(F(S) - \lambda G(S)\big)\), so:
\[h(\lambda) > 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \operatorname{MinCut}_\lambda(s, t) < U \cdot |V|.\]






NoteNon-Fractional Corollary: Dense Synergy & Penalty Collapse ([2009国家集训队] 人员雇佣 BZOJ 2039, #109)



What if a problem has no fraction at all (\(\lambda\) is fixed, say \(\lambda = 1\)), and asks you to choose a subset of employees \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) (\(N \le 1000\)) to maximize:
\[\sum_{i \in S} (-A_i) + \sum_{\{i, j\} \subseteq S} 2 E_{ij} - \sum_{|\{i, j\} \cap S| = 1} E_{ij}?\]
Here \(w_{\{i,j\}} = 2 E_{ij}\) and \(\gamma_{\{i,j\}} = E_{ij}\). Even though this is a non-fractional closure problem from Chapter 09, a dense \(1000 \times 1000\) matrix has \(\binom{1000}{2} \approx 5 \times 10^5\) pairs! Instead of creating \(5 \times 10^5\) auxiliary closure vertices, we apply the exact identity above (or directly verify on all 4 truth assignments \((x_i, x_j) \in \{0, 1\}^2\)):
\[2 E_{ij} x_i x_j - E_{ij} |x_i - x_j| = E_{ij}(x_i + x_j) - 2 E_{ij} |x_i - x_j|.\]
This collapses the entire \(N \times N\) synergy matrix into a \(1002\)-vertex graph where \(s \to i\) has capacity \(\sum_{j \ne i} E_{ij}\), \(i \to t\) has capacity \(A_i\), and \(i \leftrightarrow j\) has bidirectional capacity \(2 E_{ij}\)!






3.2 Minimum Ratio \(s\)-\(t\) Edge Disconnection (网络严密性, #107) & Negative-Edge Severing
Suppose we are given a network \(G = (V, E)\) with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and two weights \((a_e, b_e)\) on every edge \(e \in E\) (\(a_e \ge 0, b_e > 0\)). We want to find an edge cut-set \(C \subseteq E\) whose removal disconnects \(s\) from \(t\) (no \(s \rightsquigarrow t\) path remains in \(G \setminus C\)), minimizing the ratio:
\[\lambda^* = \min_{C \in \mathcal{C}_{s,t}} \frac{\sum_{e \in C} a_e}{\sum_{e \in C} b_e}.\]
(In Amber’s 2007 problem 网络严密性, \(a_e = w_e\) is the edge capacity and \(b_e = 1\) for all \(e\), so \(\frac{\sum_{e \in C} w_e}{|C|}\) is the minimum average edge capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) disconnecting edge set!)

Step 2 & Step 3: Why Negative Modified Weights \(w_e(\lambda) \le 0\) Are Severed Greedily
At a trial parameter \(\lambda \ge 0\), each edge \(e \in E\) acquires the modified cut weight:
\[w_e(\lambda) := a_e - \lambda b_e.\]
We want to evaluate \(h_{\min}(\lambda) = \min_{C \in \mathcal{C}_{s,t}} \sum_{e \in C} w_e(\lambda)\) and check whether \(h_{\min}(\lambda) < 0\) (meaning \(\lambda > \lambda^*\)) or \(h_{\min}(\lambda) \ge 0\) (meaning \(\lambda \le \lambda^*\)).
What do we do when some edges have negative or zero modified weight \(w_e(\lambda) \le 0\)? - Recall that a disconnecting edge set \(C \in \mathcal{C}_{s,t}\) is any subset of edges \(C \subseteq E\) whose removal destroys all \(s \rightsquigarrow t\) paths. - Adding an extra edge \(e\) to \(C\) can never create a new \(s \rightsquigarrow t\) path—it only makes \(G \setminus C\) more disconnected! - Therefore, if an edge \(e \in E\) has \(w_e(\lambda) = a_e - \lambda b_e \le 0\), including \(e \in C\) both helps disconnect \(s\) from \(t\) and decreases (or leaves unchanged) the sum \(\sum_{e \in C} w_e(\lambda)\)!
This gives the exact mechanical compilation rule for Minimum Ratio Edge Disconnection:

Partition the edges at trial \(\lambda\) into two sets: \[E^-(\lambda) := \big\{ e \in E : a_e - \lambda b_e \le 0 \big\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad E^+(\lambda) := \big\{ e \in E : a_e - \lambda b_e > 0 \big\}.\]
Unconditionally sever all edges in \(E^-(\lambda)\) and accumulate their negative contribution: \[\operatorname{neg\_sum}(\lambda) := \sum_{e \in E^-(\lambda)} (a_e - \lambda b_e) \le 0.\]
On the remaining subgraph \(G^+(\lambda) = (V, E^+(\lambda))\) where every edge has strictly positive capacity \(c_e(\lambda) = a_e - \lambda b_e > 0\), run Dinic’s algorithm to compute \(\operatorname{MinCut}\big(G^+(\lambda)\big)\).
The exact value of the parametric merit function is: \[h_{\min}(\lambda) = \operatorname{neg\_sum}(\lambda) + \operatorname{MinCut}\big(G^+(\lambda)\big).\] If \(h_{\min}(\lambda) < 0\), then \(\lambda > \lambda^*\) (set \(R \gets \lambda\)); if \(h_{\min}(\lambda) \ge 0\), then \(\lambda \le \lambda^*\) (set \(L \gets \lambda\)).







WarningBroken-Gadget Trap: Clamping \(w_e(\lambda)\) to \(\max(0, a_e - \lambda b_e)\) vs. Strict Node-Partition Ratio Cuts




Why Clamping to \(0\) Fails: If you replace \(w_e(\lambda) < 0\) with \(0\) instead of adding \(w_e(\lambda)\) to \(\operatorname{neg\_sum}(\lambda)\), then \(\operatorname{MinCut}(G^+(\lambda)) \ge 0\) for every \(\lambda\), so \(h_{\min}(\lambda)\) can never become negative until \(E^+(\lambda)\) alone fails to connect \(s\) and \(t\)! That computes the maximum bottleneck edge ratio along paths, not the minimum ratio cut.
Edge-Set Disconnection \(C \subseteq E\) vs. Strict Vertex Partition \(\delta^+(S)\): Notice a subtle distinction when \(w_e(\lambda) < 0\): if an edge \(e = \{u, v\} \in E^-(\lambda)\) has both endpoints inside \(S\) (\(u \in S, v \in S\)) in the final cut of \(G^+(\lambda)\), then \(e\) is in the removed edge set \(C\), even though \(e \notin \delta(S, \bar{S})\). In network disconnection problems (网络严密性, #107), removing any superset \(C \supseteq \delta(S, \bar{S})\) is valid (and in fact, if \(b_e = 1\) for all \(e\), at \(\lambda = \lambda^*\) every edge has \(w_e(\lambda^*) = w_e - \lambda^*\), and can any edge have \(w_e < \lambda^*\)? Only if \(e\) belongs to the optimal cut \(C^*\), because if a minimal cut \(C_0\) had average \(> \lambda^*\) while some \(e \notin C_0\) had \(w_e < \lambda^*\), adding \(e\) to \(C_0\) reduces the average!). However, if a problem demands a strict vertex partition \(\delta(S, \bar{S})\) with arbitrary heterogeneous \(b_e\) where negative edges cannot be severed inside \(S\), then negative cut weights \(w_e(\lambda) < 0\) are supermodular (\(\Delta_{u,v} > 0\)) and NP-hard (Max-Cut)!







3.3 Structural Dualities: Hakimi’s Orientation Theorem & Nash-Williams Arboricity
Why does Goldberg’s Maximum Density Subgraph appear in problems that never mention “density” or “ratios” at all? Because by LP / Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality, the maximum density of an induced subgraph is the exact obstruction to orienting edges with bounded in/out-degree and to packing edges into forests!

1. Hakimi’s Orientation Theorem (1965) (Codeforces 847J — Students Initiation, #106)
Suppose we are given an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) and must orient every edge \(e = \{u, v\} \in E\) as either \(u \to v\) or \(v \to u\) so that each vertex \(v \in V\) has out-degree \(d^+(v) \le k_v\) (where \(k_v \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) is a given quota, or \(k_v = K\) for all \(v\) to minimize the maximum out-degree \(\max_{v \in V} d^+(v)\)).
When does a valid orientation exist? - Primal Flow Model (Construction A): Each undirected edge \(e = \{u, v\} \in E\) must choose one of its two endpoints to “charge” \(+1\) unit of out-degree. Wire \(s \xrightarrow{1} e\), \(e \xrightarrow{1} u\), \(e \xrightarrow{1} v\), and \(v \xrightarrow{k_v} t\). A valid orientation exists iff \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t) = |E|\). - Dual Minimum Cut Certificate: In this bipartite network, suppose a minimum cut puts a subset of vertex nodes \(S \subseteq V\) on the source side (\(x_v = 1\)) and \(\bar{S} = V \setminus S\) on the sink side (\(x_v = 0\)). - For every vertex \(v \in S\), we must sever \(v \xrightarrow{k_v} t\) at cost \(k_v\). - For every edge \(e = \{u, v\} \in E\), if both \(u \in S\) and \(v \in S\) (i.e., \(e \in E(S)\)), then \(e\) can stay on the source side without cutting \(e \to u\) or \(e \to v\); otherwise (if \(e \notin E(S)\)), we must sever \(s \xrightarrow{1} e\) at cost \(1\). - Thus the cut capacity associated with \(S \subseteq V\) is \((|E| - |E(S)|) + \sum_{v \in S} k_v\). - Requiring \(\operatorname{MinCut}(s, t) = |E|\) (which is achieved by \(S = \emptyset\)) is equivalent to requiring \((|E| - |E(S)|) + \sum_{v \in S} k_v \ge |E|\) for all \(S \subseteq V\)!






ImportantTheorem 14.2 (Hakimi’s Orientation Theorem, 1965)



An undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) admits an orientation with out-degrees \(d^+(v) \le k_v\) for all \(v \in V\) if and only if every subset \(S \subseteq V\) satisfies:
\[|E(S)| \le \sum_{v \in S} k_v.\]
In particular, setting \(k_v = K\) for all \(v \in V\), the minimum possible maximum out-degree over all orientations of \(G\) equals the ceiling of the Maximum Subgraph Density:
\[\min_{\text{orientations}} \max_{v \in V} d^+(v) = \left\lceil \max_{\emptyset \subsetneq S \subseteq V} \frac{|E(S)|}{|S|} \right\rceil.\]




2. Nash-Williams Forest Packing & Arboricity Theorem (1964) (#110)
The arboricity \(\Upsilon(G)\) of an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) is the minimum number of edge-disjoint forests needed to cover all edges \(E\). Since any forest on a non-empty vertex subset \(S \subseteq V\) with \(|S| \ge 2\) can contain at most \(|S| - 1\) edges, covering \(E(S)\) with \(k\) forests clearly requires \(|E(S)| \le k(|S| - 1)\) for every \(S \subseteq V\) with \(|S| \ge 2\). Nash-Williams (1964) proved that this necessary density condition is also sufficient:
\[\Upsilon(G) = \max_{\substack{S \subseteq V \\ |S| \ge 2}} \left\lceil \frac{|E(S)|}{|S| - 1} \right\rceil \le k \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \max_{\substack{S \subseteq V \\ |S| \ge 2}} \big( |E(S)| - k(|S| - 1) \big) \le 0.\]
How do we test whether \(\max_{|S| \ge 2} \big(|E(S)| - k|S| + k\big) \le 0\) using a minimum cut? - The Empty-Set Obstruction (FM-14a): Notice the \(+k\) term! If we simply maximize \(|E(S)| - k|S|\) over all subsets \(S \subseteq V\), the empty set \(S = \emptyset\) achieves \(|E(\emptyset)| - k|\emptyset| = 0\), whereas we need to check whether any non-empty \(S \ne \emptyset\) has \(|E(S)| - k|S| > -k\) (i.e., \(\min_{\emptyset \ne S \subseteq V} (k|S| - |E(S)|) < k\)). - Root-Pinning Compilation (H-15): Because any non-empty subset \(S \ne \emptyset\) must contain at least one vertex \(r \in V\), we can test non-emptiness by iterating over a pinned root vertex \(r \in V\): - Force \(r \in S\) (\(x_r = 1\)) by wiring \(s \xrightarrow{\infty} r\), and charge \(r\) zero sink penalty (\(c(r \to t) = U - d_r\) in Goldberg’s model, or \(c(r \to t) = 0\) in Construction A), while every other vertex \(v \ne r\) pays \(k\) (\(c(v \to t) = U + 2k - d_v\) in Goldberg’s model, or \(c(v \to t) = k\) in Construction A). - Then for a fixed root \(r \in V\), the network directly computes \(\max_{S \subseteq V : r \in S} \big(|E(S)| - k(|S| - 1)\big)\)! - Taking the maximum over all \(r \in V\) (at most \(|V|\) max-flow calls, or incrementally via root switching) decides whether \(\Upsilon(G) \le k\) in polynomial time!

section: 4. Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan Parametric Preflow & The Breakpoint Envelope
text:
4. Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan Parametric Preflow & The Breakpoint Envelope

4.1 Monotone Parametric Networks & The Nested Cut Theorem
Up to now, we have evaluated \(h(\lambda) = \max_{S \subseteq V} (|E(S)| - \lambda |S|)\) at a single value of \(\lambda\) to find the root \(\lambda^*\) where \(h(\lambda^*) = 0\).
Now consider a much deeper question (All-Lambda Parametric Density Envelope, #111):

Suppose we are given a graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(|V| \le 500\) and \(Q = 2 \times 10^5\) queries. Each query provides an arbitrary real tax rate \(\lambda_q \in [0, \infty)\) and asks for the maximum net value: \[h(\lambda_q) = \max_{S \subseteq V} \big( |E(S)| - \lambda_q |S| \big).\]

Running Dinic \(Q = 2 \times 10^5\) times is impossible. However, look at the geometry of \(h(\lambda)\): - Every subset \(S \subseteq V\) with \(|S| = k \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) defines a line \(\ell_S(\lambda) = |E(S)| - k \lambda\) of integer slope \(-k \in \{-N, \dots, 0\}\). - Among all subsets \(S \subseteq V\) of a fixed size \(|S| = k\), only one with the largest edge count \(|E(S)|\) can ever appear on the upper envelope \(h(\lambda)\). Since there are only \(N + 1\) possible integer slopes \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\), the upper envelope \(h(\lambda)\) is a piecewise-linear convex curve with at most \(N\) breakpoints!
Even better, Gallo, Grigoriadis, and Tarjan (1989) proved that in Goldberg’s \(+U\) shifted network \(G_{\text{Goldberg}}(\lambda)\) (where \(c_\lambda(s \to v) = U\) is non-increasing in \(\lambda\) and \(c_\lambda(v \to t) = U + 2\lambda - d_v\) is strictly increasing in \(\lambda\)), the source-minimal optimal cuts \(S_{\min}(\lambda)\) do not merely shrink in cardinality—they are inclusion-wise nested!






ImportantTheorem 14.3 (Parametric Cut Nesting Theorem — Eisner & Severance 1976; Gallo, Grigoriadis & Tarjan 1989)



In Goldberg’s network \(G_{\text{Goldberg}}(\lambda)\) (or any parametric network where \(c_\lambda(s \to v)\) is non-increasing in \(\lambda\), \(c_\lambda(v \to t)\) is strictly increasing in \(\lambda\), and internal capacities \(c(u \to v)\) are constant), let \(S(\lambda_1)\) be ANY minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut at parameter \(\lambda_1\) and \(S(\lambda_2)\) be ANY minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut at parameter \(\lambda_2\), where \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\). Then:

Cross-Parameter Submodularity: Both the union \(S(\lambda_1) \cup S(\lambda_2)\) is a minimum cut at \(\lambda_1\), and the intersection \(S(\lambda_1) \cap S(\lambda_2)\) is a minimum cut at \(\lambda_2\).
Strict Inclusion Nesting of Canonical Cuts: For the source-minimal canonical cuts \(S_{\min}(\lambda)\), if \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\), then: \[V \supseteq S_{\min}(0) \supseteq S_{\min}(\lambda_1) \supseteq S_{\min}(\lambda_2) \supseteq \dots \supseteq S_{\min}(\lambda^*) = \emptyset.\]

Proof: Let \(A = S(\lambda_1)\) and \(B = S(\lambda_2)\) with \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\). By submodularity of the cut capacity function \(\operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}\) at fixed \(\lambda_1\) and optimality of \(A\) at \(\lambda_1\):
\[0 \le \operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(A \cup B) - \operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(A) \le \operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(B) - \operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(A \cap B).\]
Now notice that the only edges whose capacities change between \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are the sink edges \(v \to t\), whose capacities increase by \(2(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) > 0\) for each \(v\). For any two sets \(B \supseteq A \cap B\), the difference \(\operatorname{Cap}_\lambda(B) - \operatorname{Cap}_\lambda(A \cap B)\) gains \(+2(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1)|B \setminus A|\) when \(\lambda\) increases from \(\lambda_1\) to \(\lambda_2\):
\[\operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_2}(B) - \operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_2}(A \cap B) = \big(\operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(B) - \operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(A \cap B)\big) + 2(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1)|B \setminus A|.\]
Since \(B\) is optimal at \(\lambda_2\), the left-hand side is \(\le 0\). Combining this with \(\operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(B) - \operatorname{Cap}_{\lambda_1}(A \cap B) \ge 0\) and \(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1 > 0\) forces:
\[2(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1)|B \setminus A| \le 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad |B \setminus A| = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad B \subseteq A! \qquad \blacksquare\]


Because \(V \supseteq S_1 \supsetneq S_2 \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq S_k = \emptyset\) is a strictly nested chain of subsets of \(V\), there are at most \(|V|\) distinct optimal subgraphs across the entire real half-line \(\lambda \in [0, \infty)\)! This chain of nested subgraphs is known in combinatorial optimization as the Principal Partition (or Density Decomposition) of \(G\).



4.2 Parametric Hull Divide-and-Conquer with Vertex Contraction (solve_hull)
How do we find all \(\le |V|\) optimal subsets on the upper envelope \(h(\lambda)\) in competitive programming? While the full Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan (GGT) algorithm maintains a single Push-Relabel preflow across increasing \(\lambda\), in contests with Dinic’s algorithm there is a remarkably clean, exact Divide-and-Conquer Contraction Algorithm (Eisner–Severance / GGT Contraction) that runs in \(O(|V|)\) Dinic calls on contracted subgraphs whose sizes sum to \(O(|V| + |E|)\) per recursion depth:

Boundary Initialization:

At \(\lambda_L = 0\), the optimal subset is \(S_L = V\) (with line \(\ell_{S_L}(\lambda) = |E| - |V|\lambda\)).
At \(\lambda_R = |E| + 1\), the optimal subset is \(S_R = \emptyset\) (with line \(\ell_{S_R}(\lambda) = 0 - 0\lambda\)).

Recursive Step solve_hull(S_L, S_R) (where \(S_R \subsetneq S_L\) and \(|S_L| > |S_R|\)):

Step 2a (Line Intersection): Compute the unique parameter \(\lambda_{\text{mid}}\) where the two known envelope lines \(\ell_{S_L}(\lambda) = |E(S_L)| - |S_L|\lambda\) and \(\ell_{S_R}(\lambda) = |E(S_R)| - |S_R|\lambda\) intersect: \[\lambda_{\text{mid}} = \frac{|E(S_L)| - |E(S_R)|}{|S_L| - |S_R|}.\]
Step 2b (Vertex Contraction using Nesting \(S_R \subseteq S^*(\lambda_{\text{mid}}) \subseteq S_L\)): By Theorem 14.3, the optimal subset \(S_{\text{mid}} := S_{\min}(\lambda_{\text{mid}})\) is guaranteed to satisfy \(S_R \subseteq S_{\text{mid}} \subseteq S_L\)! Therefore:

Every vertex \(u \in S_R\) is already locked into the source side \(s\) (contract \(S_R\) into \(s\)).
Every vertex \(w \in V \setminus S_L\) is already locked into the sink side \(t\) (contract \(V \setminus S_L\) into \(t\)).
We only need to create flow vertices for the active shell \(A = S_L \setminus S_R\)!

Step 2c (Exact Integer Scaling at \(\lambda_{\text{mid}} = P / Q\)): Let \(P = |E(S_L)| - |E(S_R)|\) and \(Q = |S_L| - |S_R|\). To avoid floating-point errors completely, scale Goldberg’s capacities by \(Q\): every active vertex \(v \in A\) gets \(s \to v\) of capacity \(Q \cdot U\), \(v \to t\) of capacity \(Q(U - d_v) + 2P\), and internal edges get capacity \(Q\).
Step 2d (Hull Vertex Test & Recursion): Extract \(S_{\text{mid}} = S_R \cup \{v \in A : s \rightsquigarrow_{G_f} v\}\). Check via exact 64-bit integer cross-multiplication whether \(S_{\text{mid}}\) lies strictly above the intersection of \(\ell_{S_L}\) and \(\ell_{S_R}\) at \(\lambda_{\text{mid}} = P/Q\): \[Q \cdot |E(S_{\text{mid}})| - P \cdot |S_{\text{mid}}| > Q \cdot |E(S_L)| - P \cdot |S_L|.\]

If true, \(S_{\text{mid}}\) is a new hull vertex with \(S_R \subsetneq S_{\text{mid}} \subsetneq S_L\)! Add \(\ell_{S_{\text{mid}}}\) to the hull and recurse on solve_hull(S_L, S_mid) and solve_hull(S_mid, S_R).
If false, \(\lambda_{\text{mid}}\) is an exact breakpoint where \(\ell_{S_L}\) hands off directly to \(\ell_{S_R}\), and no other optimal subset exists between \(\lambda_L\) and \(\lambda_R\)!









TipWhy Vertex Contraction Makes solve_hull Run in \(O(\log |V|)\) Full Max-Flow Equivalents



At any single level of the recursion tree of solve_hull, the active vertex shells \(A_i = S_{L,i} \setminus S_{R,i}\) are pairwise disjoint subsets of \(V\) (\(\sum_i |A_i| \le |V|\))! When we contract \(S_{R,i} \to s\) and \(V \setminus S_{L,i} \to t\): - Any edge with both endpoints inside \(S_{R,i}\) or both inside \(V \setminus S_{L,i}\) disappears completely. - Any edge from \(v \in A_i\) to \(S_{R,i}\) merges into the single source arc \(s \to v\). - Any edge from \(v \in A_i\) to \(V \setminus S_{L,i}\) merges into the single sink arc \(v \to t\). Consequently, the sum of vertices across an entire depth level of the recursion tree is \(\le |V|\), and the sum of active edges across a balanced recursion depth is \(O(|E| \log |V|)\)!

title: Chapter 14 — 0-1 Fractional Programming, Maximum Density Subgraphs & Parametric Ratio Cuts
text:
5. The 4-Step Fractional Cut Compilation Protocol
Whenever a problem asks you to optimize a ratio, density, or parametric threshold over a graph or combinatorial family, execute this 4-step mechanical protocol before writing a single line of code:

Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic & Ratio-vs-Bottleneck Triage:

Sum-of-Numerator over Sum-of-Denominator (Fractional Cut / Matching): Does the objective have the form \(\frac{\sum_{i} a_i}{\sum_{i} b_i}\) (like \(\frac{|E(S)|}{|S|}\) in POJ 3155 or \(\frac{\sum a_{ij} x_{ij}}{\sum b_{ij} x_{ij}}\) in [SDOI2017] 新生舞会)? Proceed to Dinkelbach / Binary Search + Min-Cut / Matching.
Minimum / Maximum over Elements (Bottleneck Peeling — NOT Flow!): Does the objective instead maximize \(\min_{v \in S} \frac{d_S(v)}{d_G(v)}\) (as in Codeforces 553D — Nudist Beach, where the strength of a subset \(S\) is the worst individual vertex’s fraction of neighbors inside \(S\))?

Crucial Diagnostic Contrast: For a bottleneck minimum \(\min_{v \in S} \frac{d_S(v)}{d_G(v)} \ge \lambda\), any vertex \(v\) with \(\frac{d_S(v)}{d_G(v)} < \lambda\) can never belong to ANY valid subset \(S\)! Therefore, bottleneck vertex-ratio problems are solved in \(O((|V| + |E|) \log |V|)\) by a priority-queue greedy peeling algorithm (repeatedly deleting the vertex with minimum current \(\frac{d_S(v)}{d_G(v)}\)), whereas sum-ratio Maximum Density Subgraph \(\frac{\sum_{v \in S} d_S(v)}{2|S|} = \frac{|E(S)|}{|S|}\) allows high-degree vertices to subsidize lower-degree vertices and requires \(s\)-\(t\) Minimum Cut!

Circulation vs. Cut Space: Is the feasible structure a directed cycle ([HNOI2009] 最小圈 \(\to\) Bellman–Ford / SPFA negative cycle) or a vertex subset / disconnecting cut / matching (\(\to\) Dinic / MCMF)?

Step 2 — Parametric Linearization & Submodularity Verification:

Write \(h(\lambda) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} (F(x) - \lambda G(x))\) (or \(\min\) for minimization).
Verify the Submodularity Sign Law: in the energy to be minimized \(\Phi_\lambda(x) = \lambda G(x) - F(x)\), check that every pairwise cross-difference satisfies \(\Delta_{u,v}\Phi_\lambda \le 0\) for \(\lambda > 0\).
If \(F(S)\) contains dense pairwise edge rewards \(\sum_{\{u,v\} \in E(S)} w_e\), apply Goldberg’s degree identity \(2 \sum_{e \in E(S)} w_e = \sum_{v \in S} D_w(v) - \sum_{e \in \delta(S, \bar{S})} w_e\) to eliminate all \(|E|\) edge-closure nodes.

Step 3 — Normal-Form Graph Compilation & Pedestal Shifting:

For Subgraph Density (#105, #109): Choose pedestal \(U = \max_{v \in V} (2p_v + D_w(v) - 2\lambda_{\min} q_v)\). Wire \(s \xrightarrow{U} v\), \(v \xrightarrow{U + 2\lambda q_v - 2p_v - D_w(v)} t\), and bidirectional \(u \xleftrightarrow{w_e + 2\gamma_e} v\).
For Disconnecting Ratio Cuts (#107): Sever all edges with \(w_e(\lambda) = a_e - \lambda b_e \le 0\) upfront into \(\operatorname{neg\_sum}(\lambda)\) and run Dinic on \(E^+(\lambda)\).
For Rooted / Non-Empty Constraints (#110): If \(F(\emptyset) - \lambda G(\emptyset) > 0\) (e.g., \(G(S) = |S| - 1\) in Nash-Williams arboricity), pin a root \(r \in S\) via \(s \xrightarrow{\infty} r\).

Step 4 — Two-Scale Precision Contract & Safe Reconstruction (FM-14):

Compute the minimum rational denominator separation \(\Delta_{\min} = \frac{1}{G_{\max}(G_{\max}-1)}\) (or use Dinkelbach’s exact integer scaling \(Q_k F(x) - P_k G(x)\)).
Enforce \(\varepsilon_{\text{flow}} = 10^{-11} \ll \varepsilon_{\text{cut\_sign}} = 10^{-8} \ll \Delta_{\min}\).
Reconstruct \(S^*\) from the residual reachability set \(S_{\min}(L)\) at the last feasible lower bound \(\lambda = L < \lambda^*\), never at \(\lambda = R \ge \lambda^*\) where \(S_{\min}(R) = \emptyset\).

7. Pre-Submission Verification Checklist (FM-14 Audit)
Before submitting any fractional programming or maximum density subgraph solution, audit your code against the five failure modes of FM-14 (H-15):









Failure Mode ID
Trap Name
What Goes Wrong
Defensive Rule (H-15)




FM-14a
Trivial Empty Subgraph Masking (\(S = \emptyset\))
Evaluating \(S_{\min}\) at \(\lambda \ge \lambda^*\) returns \(S = \emptyset\) because \(F(\emptyset) - \lambda G(\emptyset) = 0\) ties with \(S^*\); in Nash-Williams arboricity (\(G(S) = |S| - 1\)), \(S = \emptyset\) scores \(+k > 0\).
Reconstruct \(S^*\) strictly at the last feasible lower bound \(\lambda = L < \lambda^*\); handle \(M = 0\) upfront; pin a root \(s \xrightarrow{\infty} r\) when \(G(S) = |S| - 1\).


FM-14b
Unshifted Negative Sink Capacities (\(2\lambda - d_v < 0\))
Wiring \(v \xrightarrow{2\lambda - d_v} t\) without pedestal \(+U\) produces negative capacities when \(2\lambda < d_v\), corrupting Dinic.
Shift every vertex by \(+U\) (\(U = \max_v d_v\) or \(M\)): \(s \xrightarrow{U} v\) and \(v \xrightarrow{U + 2\lambda - d_v} t\), or use dynamic sign-splitting.


FM-14c
Coarse Binary Search Tolerance (\(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\))
Stopping binary search at \(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\) when \(N = 100\) fails to separate \(\frac{98}{99}\) from \(\frac{99}{100}\) (\(\Delta = \frac{1}{9900} \approx 1.01 \times 10^{-4}\)).
Stop binary search only when \(R - L < \frac{1}{2 G_{\max}(G_{\max}-1)}\) (or use Dinkelbach’s exact integer scaling \(Q_k F(x) - P_k G(x)\)).


FM-14d
Single-Epsilon Floating-Point Dinic Loop
Using cap > 0 in Dinic BFS/DFS loops infinitely on \(10^{-16}\) residuals; using cap > 1e-5 misses valid augmenting paths near \(\lambda^*\).
Enforce the Two-Scale Epsilon Hierarchy: EPS_FLOW = 1e-11 inside Dinic \(\ll\) EPS_CUT = 1e-8 in outer sign test \(\ll \Delta_{\min}\).


FM-14e
Clamping Negative Edges to \(0\) in Ratio Cuts
Replacing \(w_e(\lambda) = a_e - \lambda b_e < 0\) with \(\max(0, w_e(\lambda))\) in 网络严密性 (#107) ignores edges that reduce the ratio cut.
Sever all edges with \(w_e(\lambda) \le 0\) upfront and add their weights to neg_sum before running Dinic on \(E^+(\lambda)\).

text:
8. Chapter Summary & Bridge to Chapter 15

Dinkelbach’s Linearization: Any ratio maximization \(\max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{F(x)}{G(x)}\) (\(G(x) > 0\)) reduces to finding the unique root \(\lambda^*\) of the convex, continuous, strictly decreasing merit function \(h(\lambda) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}} (F(x) - \lambda G(x))\).
The Submodularity Sign Law: Evaluating \(h(\lambda)\) compiles to a polynomial-time minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut whenever \(\lambda G(x) - F(x)\) is submodular (\(\Delta_{u,v} F \ge 0\) and \(\Delta_{u,v} G \le 0\)).
Goldberg’s \(|V|\)-Only Degree-Sum Identity: By substituting \(2|E(S)| = \sum_{v \in S} d_v - |\delta(S, \bar{S})|\) and shifting by \(+U\), Maximum Density Subgraph (最大密度子图) eliminates all \(|E|\) edge-closure nodes, compiling into a \(|V| + 2\)-vertex network (POJ 3155, BZOJ 2039).
Structural Dualities & Parametric Envelopes: The dual of Maximum Density Subgraph governs Hakimi’s Orientation Theorem (CF 847J) and Nash-Williams Arboricity (#110), while the Parametric Cut Nesting Theorem (\(S_{\min}(\lambda_1) \supseteq S_{\min}(\lambda_2)\) for \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\)) enables finding all \(\le |V|\) breakpoints of \(h(\lambda)\) via Divide-and-Conquer Vertex Contraction (#111).
Bridge to Chapter 15 (Planar & Grid Network Duality): What happens when the graph \(G = (V, E)\) has \(|V|, |E| \approx 10^6\) vertices and edges—so large that even a single Dinic call on \(|V| + 2\) vertices TLEs—yet \(G\) is embedded in the plane ([BJWC2006] 狼抓兔子, [NOI2010] 海拔, [CSP-S 2021] 交通规划)? In Chapter 15, we cross from Direction A (building flow networks) to Direction B (eliminating flow engines via Planar Cycle–Cut Duality), turning minimum cuts on \(10^6\)-vertex planar grids into \(O(|V| \log |V|)\) Dual Dijkstra shortest paths!

title: Chapter 16 — Solving Max-Flow via Min-Cut DP, Global Min-Cut & Gomory–Hu Cut Trees
text:
Before studying this chapter, you should be comfortable with:

Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality & Residual Reachability (Chapter 1): The identity \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(S, T) = \min_{(V_S, V_T)} \operatorname{cap}(V_S, V_T)\) and the extraction of the canonical source-side cut \(V_S\) from the residual network \(G_f\).
Submodular Cut Polymatroids & Pseudo-Boolean Cut Polynomials (Chapter 10): Expressing an \(S\)-\(T\) cut as a binary indicator assignment \(\mathbf{x} \in \{0, 1\}^N\) minimizing \(E(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i p_i x_i + \sum_i s_i (1 - x_i) + \sum_{(i, j) \in E} c_{i,j} (1 - x_i) x_j\).
Residual Strongly Connected Components & Picard–Queyranne DAGs (Chapter 2): Identifying vital edges that belong to every minimum \(S\)-\(T\) cut via strongly connected components of \(G_f\).
Topological Cut Elimination on Planar Graphs (Chapter 15): The paradigm of bypassing augmenting-path solvers when graph geometry compresses the cut space.




By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Execute Direction B Flow Elimination (最大流转最小割 DP): When a maximum-flow problem has \(N \ge 10^4\)–\(5 \cdot 10^5\) vertices or online dynamic updates, invert the standard paradigm by writing the algebraic \(s\)-\(t\) cut cost \(C(S)\) and optimizing it directly via dynamic programming, convex slope-difference greedy (CF 724E), \((\min, +)\) tropical matrix multiplication on a Segment Tree (CF 1919F2), or prefix-suffix sweep-line Segment Trees (CF 903G).
Prove & Implement Stoer–Wagner Global Minimum Cut: Derive why the last two vertices \((s, t)\) visited by Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS) satisfy \(\lambda_{G}(s, t) = w(A \setminus \{t\}, t)\), and compute the global undirected minimum cut in \(O(VE + V^2 \log V)\) or \(O(V^3)\) time without constructing a flow network.
Prove Submodular Cut Uncrossing & Build Gomory–Hu Cut Trees (最小割树): Prove the Submodular Cut Uncrossing Lemma and the Ultrametric Triangle Inequality \(\lambda(u, w) \ge \min(\lambda(u, v), \lambda(v, w))\), and construct both a Flow-Equivalent Tree and a full Cut-Equivalent Gomory–Hu Tree in \(N - 1\) max-flow calls on the original uncontracted graph \(G\) via Gusfield’s (1990) Star-Splitting Algorithm.
Exploit Structural Extremal Properties of \(T_{\text{GH}}\): Use the Gomory–Hu tree to count distinct pairwise min-cuts (Luogu P4123), answer threshold cut queries (Luogu P3329), and construct Hamiltonian permutations maximizing adjacent min-cut sums (CF 343E).
Guard Against Cut-Compression Failure Modes (FM-16a & FM-16): Prevent bidirectional overcounting on directed prefix DAGs (FM-16a), supernode-contraction corruption in Gusfield’s algorithm (FM-16), and the invalid application of Gomory–Hu trees to directed graphs.

section: 1. Unifying Spine: Compressing an Exponential Cut Space (\(2^N \to \text{DP States or } N-1 \text{ Tree Edges}\))
text:
1. Unifying Spine: Compressing an Exponential Cut Space (\(2^N \to \text{DP States or } N-1 \text{ Tree Edges}\))
Across Chapters 9 through 14, we used the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem in Direction A (\(\text{Combinatorial Optimization} \to \text{Flow Solver}\)): we began with a non-flow optimization problem over \(2^N\) binary configurations, compiled its objective into the capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut, and handed the resulting graph to Dinic’s algorithm.
In this chapter, we confront the two fundamental scaling walls where Direction A breaks down:

The Single-Pair Scale Wall (\(N \ge 10^4 \text{ to } 5 \cdot 10^5\), or \(Q \ge 10^5\) Dynamic Updates): Suppose a problem explicitly asks for the maximum flow from \(s\) to \(t\), or compiles into an \(s\)-\(t\) cut network, on \(N = 10^4\) vertices with \(\binom{N}{2} \approx 5 \cdot 10^7\) complete DAG edges (CF 724E), or on a pipeline of \(N = 5 \cdot 10^5\) vertices with \(Q = 5 \cdot 10^5\) online capacity updates (CF 1919F2), or on a bipartite chain with \(M, Q = 2 \cdot 10^5\) cross-edges and updates (CF 903G). No augmenting-path solver can touch these constraints.
The All-Pairs Scale Wall (\(\binom{N}{2}\) Pairwise Minimum Cuts on \(N \le 850\) Vertices): Suppose we are given an undirected capacitated graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) with \(N = 850, M = 8500\) and must evaluate a function of the minimum cut \(\lambda_G(u, v) = \operatorname{MinCut}_G(u, v)\) across all \(\binom{N}{2} \approx 3.6 \cdot 10^5\) unordered pairs \(\{u, v\}\) (Luogu P4123, Luogu P3329, CF 343E), or find the global minimum cut over all \(2^{N-1} - 1\) non-trivial vertex partitions (POJ 2914). Running Dinic \(\binom{N}{2}\) times exceeds the time limit by three orders of magnitude.

What unifies the resolution of both walls is Cut-Space Compression—exploiting algebraic symmetry, bounded cut-interface width, or submodular uncrossing to collapse an exponential family of cuts into a compact polynomial representation:
\[
\text{Exponential Cut Space } \mathcal{C}(G) \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Symmetry / Treewidth / Submodular Uncrossing}} \quad \begin{cases} \text{Module 16A: Low-Width DP / Matrix / Sweep States} & (\text{Single } s\text{-}t \text{ Pair, } N \le 5 \cdot 10^5), \\[4pt] \text{Module 16B: } N - 1 \text{ Laminar Tree Edges in } T_{\text{GH}} & (\text{All } \binom{N}{2} \text{ Pairs, } N \le 850). \end{cases}
\]










Compression Axis
Underlying Mathematical Mechanism
Exponential Space Compressed
Compressed Representation
Canonical Complexity




Direction B: Uniform DAG Cut DP / Greedy (§2.2)
Cardinality decoupling \(\sum_{i \in S, j \notin S, i<j} c = \sum_{i \in S}(N-i)c - \binom{|S|}{2}c\)
\(2^N\) vertex partitions \((S, V \setminus S)\)
\(N+1\) cardinality states \(k = |S|\) (or sorted slope differences)
\(O(N^2)\) DP or \(O(N \log N)\) Greedy


Direction B: Dynamic Chain Matrix DP (§2.3)
Associativity of \(2 \times 2\) \((\min, +)\) tropical matrices
\(2^N\) cut sequences \((x_1, \dots, x_N) \in \{S, T\}^N\) under \(Q\) updates
Segment Tree of \(2 \times 2\) boundary-state matrices \(M_{[L, R]}\)
\(O((N + Q) \log N)\)


Direction B: Prefix-Suffix Chain Sweep (§2.4)
Monotone cut thresholds on forward-directed chains
\(2^{2N}\) cuts on coupled chains \(A_1 \to \dots \to A_N, B_1 \to \dots \to B_N\)

\(O((N + M + Q) \log N)\)


Global Undirected Min-Cut (Stoer–Wagner) (§3)

\(2^{N-1} - 1\) non-empty proper cuts \((S, V \setminus S)\)
\(N - 1\) last-pair \((s, t)\) phase cuts + vertex contractions
\(O(VE + V^2 \log V)\) or \(O(V^3)\)

Symmetric submodularity & Cut Uncrossing Lemma

\((N - 1) \cdot T_{\text{MaxFlow}}(N, M)\)

text:
2. Direction B Flow Elimination: Solving Max-Flow by Optimizing the Dual \(s\)-\(t\) Cut Directly (最大流转最小割 DP)

2.1 The Exact Algebraic \(s\)-\(t\) Cut Functional
Consider a directed flow network on vertex set \(\{s, t\} \cup \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\) with three families of non-negative capacities:

Source supply arcs: \(s \to i\) with capacity \(p_i \ge 0\) for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).
Sink demand arcs: \(i \to t\) with capacity \(s_i \ge 0\) for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\).
Internal transit arcs: \(i \to j\) with capacity \(c_{i,j} \ge 0\) for ordered pairs \((i, j)\).

By the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem, the maximum flow from \(s\) to \(t\) equals the minimum capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut. Any \(s\)-\(t\) cut is uniquely determined by the subset of internal vertices \(S \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\) placed on the source side (with \(s \in S_{\text{full}} = \{s\} \cup S\)), while the remaining vertices \(\bar{S} = \{1, \dots, N\} \setminus S\) are placed on the sink side (with \(t \in T_{\text{full}} = \{t\} \cup \bar{S}\)).
Let us count the exact capacity \(C(S)\) of the directed arcs severed by the partition \((S, \bar{S})\):

Severed source arcs (\(s \to i\)): Since \(s\) is on the source side, arc \(s \to i\) crosses from source side to sink side if and only if \(i \notin S\) (\(i \in \bar{S}\)), contributing \(\sum_{i \notin S} p_i\).
Severed sink arcs (\(i \to t\)): Since \(t\) is on the sink side, arc \(i \to t\) crosses from source side to sink side if and only if \(i \in S\), contributing \(\sum_{i \in S} s_i\).
Severed internal transit arcs (\(i \to j\)): A directed arc \(i \to j\) crosses from source side to sink side if and only if its tail lies in \(S\) (\(i \in S\)) and its head lies in \(\bar{S}\) (\(j \notin S\)), contributing \(\sum_{i \in S, j \notin S} c_{i,j}\).

Summing these three disjoint edge sets yields the Master Direction B Cut Equation:
\[
\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t) = \min_{S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}} C(S), \qquad C(S) = \sum_{i \notin S} p_i + \sum_{i \in S} s_i + \sum_{i \in S,\; j \notin S} c_{i,j}.
\]
When the internal transit arcs form a directed acyclic graph (DAG) respecting the natural vertex order \(1 < 2 < \dots < N\) (so \(c_{i,j} > 0\) only when \(i < j\)), the cross-term restricts to ordered pairs \(i < j\):
\[
C(S) = \sum_{i \notin S} p_i + \sum_{i \in S} s_i + \sum_{\substack{i \in S,\; j \notin S \\ 1 \le i < j \le N}} c_{i,j}.
\]
Equivalently, introducing binary state variables \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\) where \(x_i = 1 \iff i \in S\) (source side) and \(x_i = 0 \iff i \notin S\) (sink side), we seek to minimize the pseudo-Boolean polynomial:
\[
C(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i (1 - x_i) + \sum_{i=1}^N s_i x_i + \sum_{1 \le i < j \le N} c_{i,j}\, x_i (1 - x_j).
\]
Whenever the interaction matrix \((c_{i,j})\) has low rank, uniform structure, bounded bandwidth (path/tree), or monotone prefix thresholds, we can minimize \(C(\mathbf{x})\) over \(\{0, 1\}^N\) combinatorially—eliminating the flow solver entirely.



2.2 Uniform Prefix DAGs: From \(O(N^2)\) Cardinality DP to \(O(N \log N)\) Slope-Difference Greedy (CF 724E — Goods Transportation)
Suppose every earlier vertex \(i\) can ship goods to every later vertex \(j > i\) with the same uniform arc capacity \(c_{i,j} = c > 0\) for all \(1 \le i < j \le N\) (Codeforces 724E — Goods Transportation, where \(N \le 10^4\)).
Substituting \(c_{i,j} = c\) into the Master Direction B Cut Equation collapses the quadratic cross-term into a pure inversion-like pair count:
\[
C(S) = \sum_{i \notin S} p_i + \sum_{i \in S} s_i + c \cdot \big|\{(i, j) : 1 \le i < j \le N,\; i \in S,\; j \notin S\}\big|.
\]

Level 1 Compilation: \(O(N^2)\) Cardinality-Interface Dynamic Programming
Scan the vertices sequentially from \(i = 1\) to \(N\). When we decide whether to place vertex \(i\) into \(S\) (\(x_i = 1\)) or \(\bar{S}\) (\(x_i = 0\)), how much information about the prefix choices \((x_1, \dots, x_{i-1})\) do we need to charge all newly severed edges incident to \(i\)?

If we place \(i \in S\) (\(x_i = 1\)): we sever the sink arc \(i \to t\) of capacity \(s_i\). Do any arcs \(j \to i\) from earlier vertices \(j < i\) cross the cut? No: if \(j \in S\), both endpoints are in \(S\); if \(j \notin S\), the arc \(j \to i\) points from \(\bar{S}\) to \(S\) (backward across the cut!), which costs zero in a directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut.
If we place \(i \notin S\) (\(x_i = 0\)): we sever the source arc \(s \to i\) of capacity \(p_i\), and for every earlier vertex \(j < i\) that was placed in \(S\), the forward arc \(j \to i\) crosses from \(S\) to \(\bar{S}\) and is severed at cost \(c\)!

Notice the crucial structural invariant: the cost of placing \(i \notin S\) does not depend on which prefix vertices are in \(S\), but only on their cardinality \(k = \big|S \cap \{1, \dots, i-1\}\big|\)!
Define \(dp[i][k]\) as the minimum cut cost contributed by the prefix \(\{1, \dots, i\}\) (counting all source/sink arcs in \(\{1, \dots, i\}\) and all transit arcs \(u \to v\) with \(1 \le u < v \le i\)) given that \(\big|S \cap \{1, \dots, i\}\big| = k\). For each \(i = 1, \dots, N\) and \(0 \le k \le i\):
\[
dp[i][k] = \min\Big(\underbrace{dp[i-1][k] + p_i + k \cdot c}_{\text{place } i \notin S \text{ (sink side)}},\;\; \underbrace{dp[i-1][k-1] + s_i}_{\text{place } i \in S \text{ (source side)}}\Big),
\]
with base case \(dp[0][0] = 0\) and invalid states set to \(+\infty\). After \(N\) steps, \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t) = \min_{0 \le k \le N} dp[N][k]\) in \(O(N^2)\) time and \(O(N)\) rolling-array space.


Level 2 Compilation: Exact Algebraic Decoupling & \(O(N \log N)\) Slope-Difference Greedy
Can we compress the \(O(N^2)\) DP all the way to \(O(N \log N)\)? Yes—by counting the cross-pairs \(\{(i, j) : i < j, i \in S, j \notin S\}\) globally!
Fix the total cardinality \(k = |S|\). Every vertex \(i \in S\) has exactly \(N - i\) vertices \(j > i\) after it in total. Every such \(j > i\) lies either in \(\bar{S}\) (a cross-pair \(i \in S, j \notin S\)) or in \(S\) (an internal pair \(i \in S, j \in S\) with \(i < j\)). Summing over all \(i \in S\):
\[
\sum_{i \in S} (N - i) = \big|\{(i, j) : i < j,\; i \in S,\; j \notin S\}\big| + \big|\{(i, j) : i < j,\; i \in S,\; j \in S\}\big|.
\]
Look at the second term on the right-hand side: how many ordered pairs \((i, j)\) with \(i < j\) have both endpoints in \(S\)? Since \(|S| = k\), any two distinct elements of \(S\) form exactly one pair with \(i < j\), so that count is always \(\binom{k}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2}\), completely independent of which \(k\) indices form \(S\)!
Rearranging gives the exact Prefix-DAG Cross-Cut Identity:
\[
\big|\{(i, j) : 1 \le i < j \le N,\; i \in S,\; j \notin S\}\big| = \sum_{i \in S} (N - i) - \binom{|S|}{2}.
\]
Substitute this identity into \(C(S)\) and rewrite \(\sum_{i \notin S} p_i = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i - \sum_{i \in S} p_i\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(S) &= \sum_{i=1}^N p_i + \sum_{i \in S} (s_i - p_i) + c \left(\sum_{i \in S} (N - i) - \binom{|S|}{2}\right) \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^N p_i - \binom{|S|}{2} c + \sum_{i \in S} \underbrace{\big(s_i - p_i + (N - i)c\big)}_{w_i}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This equation is a minor miracle: once the cardinality \(k = |S|\) is fixed, the interactions between vertices in \(S\) vanish into the constant \(-\binom{k}{2}c\), and each vertex \(i \in S\) contributes an independent scalar weight \(w_i = s_i - p_i + (N - i)c\)! Therefore, for any fixed \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\), the optimal subset \(S\) of size \(k\) simply selects the \(k\) vertices with the smallest values of \(w_i\). Sorting \(w_{(1)} \le w_{(2)} \le \dots \le w_{(N)}\) reduces the \(5 \cdot 10^7\)-edge max-flow problem to a single prefix-sum sweep in \(O(N \log N)\) time:
\[
\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t) = \min_{0 \le k \le N} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^N p_i - \frac{k(k-1)}{2}c + \sum_{r=1}^k w_{(r)} \right].
\]






WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexample FM-16a: Undirected / Bidirectional Overcounting on a Directed Prefix DAG



A classic implementation bug when writing dp[i][k] or the algebraic sum for CF 724E is treating the transit arcs as undirected or charging \(c\) whenever \(i \in S\) and \(j \notin S\) for both \(i < j\) and \(i > j\):

The Buggy Recurrence: When placing \(i \in S\) (\(x_i = 1\)), a solver notices that \(i - 1 - (k - 1) = i - k\) earlier vertices in \(\{1, \dots, i-1\}\) were placed on the sink side \(\bar{S}\), and writes: \[dp_{\text{bug}}[i][k] = \min\big(dp_{\text{bug}}[i-1][k] + p_i + k \cdot c,\;\; dp_{\text{bug}}[i-1][k-1] + s_i + (i - 1 - (k - 1)) \cdot c\big).\]
Concrete Counterexample (\(N = 2, c = 10\)): Let \(p = [0, 100]\), \(s = [100, 0]\).

In the true directed graph, the only internal arc is \(1 \xrightarrow{10} 2\). If we set \(1 \notin S\) (\(1 \in \bar{S}\)) and \(2 \in S\), the severed arcs are \(s \to 1\) (\(p_1 = 0\)) and \(2 \to t\) (\(s_2 = 0\)), while the arc \(1 \to 2\) goes from \(\bar{S}\) to \(S\) (backward across the cut, paying \(0\)!). Thus the true minimum cut (and max-flow) is \(0\) (indeed, \(s \to 1\) has capacity \(0\) and \(2 \to t\) has capacity \(0\), so no positive flow can ever leave \(s\) or enter \(t\)!).
Under the buggy recurrence that charges \((i - k)c\) when \(2 \in S\) and \(1 \notin S\), the state \(S = \{2\}\) falsely pays \(c = 10\) for the non-existent reverse arc \(2 \to 1\), reporting a phantom flow of \(10\) on a network with zero capacity out of \(s\)!

Invariant to Enforce: In any directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut, an arc \(u \to v\) is severed if and only if \(u \in S\) and \(v \notin S\). Never charge arcs pointing from \(\bar{S}\) to \(S\).







2.3 Dynamic Pipeline Networks & \(2 \times 2\) \((\min, +)\) Tropical Matrix Segment Trees (CF 1919F1/F2 — Wine Factory)
Now suppose the internal transit network is a directed linear pipeline \(1 \xrightarrow{c_1} 2 \xrightarrow{c_2} \dots \xrightarrow{c_{N-1}} N\), where each node \(i\) has source supply \(s \xrightarrow{a_i} i\) and sink demand \(i \xrightarrow{b_i} t\), and we must process \(Q \le 5 \cdot 10^5\) online point updates to \((a_i, b_i, c_i)\) (Codeforces 1919F2 — Wine Factory (Hard Version)).
Let us apply the Master Direction B Cut Equation to this 1D chain. Assign each vertex \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) a binary cut label \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\), where we adopt the state convention:

State \(0\) (\(i \in \bar{S}\), sink side): Severs source arc \(s \to i\), paying \(a_i\).
State \(1\) (\(i \in S\), source side): Severs sink arc \(i \to t\), paying \(b_i\).
Pipe Transition (\(i \to i+1\) of capacity \(c_i\)): Because the pipe is directed from \(i\) to \(i+1\), it is severed if and only if \(x_i = 1\) (\(i \in S\)) and \(x_{i+1} = 0\) (\(i+1 \in \bar{S}\)), paying \(c_i\). All three other state transitions \((0 \to 0)\), \((0 \to 1)\), and \((1 \to 1)\) pay \(0\)!

Thus, the exact minimum cut of the pipeline is the minimum-cost path through a 2-state Markov chain of length \(N\):
\[
\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in \{0, 1\}^N} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^N \big(a_i [x_i = 0] + b_i [x_i = 1]\big) + \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} c_i [x_i = 1 \land x_{i+1} = 0] \right].
\]

Special Case (CF 1919F1): Infinite Pipe Capacities (\(c_i = \infty\))
When \(c_i = \infty\) for all \(1 \le i < N\), the transition \((x_i = 1 \to x_{i+1} = 0)\) is forbidden. Consequently, once the sequence \(\mathbf{x}\) enters state \(1\) (\(S\)), it can never return to state \(0\) (\(\bar{S}\)). Every finite-cost cut must consist of a prefix \(1 \dots k\) in state \(0\) (\(\bar{S}\)) followed by a suffix \(k+1 \dots N\) in state \(1\) (\(S\)) for some split index \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\):
\[
\operatorname{MaxFlow}_{c=\infty}(s, t) = \min_{0 \le k \le N} \left( \sum_{i=1}^k a_i + \sum_{i=k+1}^N b_i \right) = \sum_{i=1}^N b_i + \min_{0 \le k \le N} \sum_{i=1}^k (a_i - b_i).
\]
Maintaining prefix sums of \((a_i - b_i)\) in a Segment Tree resolves CF 1919F1 in \(O((N + Q) \log N)\) time.


General Case (CF 1919F2): Finite Pipe Capacities (\(c_i < \infty\)) via \((\min, +)\) Matrices
When \(c_i\) is finite, the optimal cut can alternate between \(0\) (\(\bar{S}\)) and \(1\) (\(S\)) arbitrarily many times. Define the tropical \((\min, +)\) matrix product \(A \otimes B\) of two \(2 \times 2\) matrices by:
\[
(A \otimes B)_{u, v} = \min_{w \in \{0, 1\}} \big(A_{u, w} + B_{w, v}\big), \qquad u, v \in \{0, 1\}.
\]
There are two equally clean ways to represent intervals in a Segment Tree:

Interval Endpoint-State Matrix \(D_{[L, R]}\) (Recommended for Implementation): For any contiguous subsegment \([L, R]\), let \(D_{[L, R]}(u, v)\) (\(u, v \in \{0, 1\}\)) be the minimum cut cost of all vertices and internal pipes strictly inside \([L, R]\) given that the left boundary vertex has state \(x_L = u\) and the right boundary vertex has state \(x_R = v\).

Single-vertex leaf \([i, i]\): Since \(x_i\) cannot simultaneously be \(0\) and \(1\), the off-diagonal entries are \(+\infty\): \[D_{[i, i]} = \begin{pmatrix} a_i & +\infty \\ +\infty & b_i \end{pmatrix}.\]
Merging \([L, M]\) and \([M+1, R]\) across pipe \(M \xrightarrow{c_M} M+1\): When \(x_M = x \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(x_{M+1} = y \in \{0, 1\}\), the connecting pipe \(M \to M+1\) adds \(c_M\) if and only if \((x, y) = (1, 0)\): \[D_{[L, R]}(u, v) = \min_{x \in \{0, 1\}} \min_{y \in \{0, 1\}} \Big( D_{[L, M]}(u, x) + D_{[M+1, R]}(y, v) + c_M \cdot [x = 1 \land y = 0] \Big).\]

Vertex-Plus-Outgoing-Pipe Transfer Matrix \(M_i\): Alternatively, absorb the outgoing pipe \(c_i\) (with \(c_N = 0\)) directly into vertex \(i\)’s transition matrix \(M_i(x_i, x_{i+1})\): \[M_i = \begin{pmatrix} a_i & a_i \\ b_i + c_i & b_i \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t) = \min_{u, v \in \{0, 1\}} \big(M_1 \otimes M_2 \otimes \dots \otimes M_N\big)_{u, v}.\]

Both formulations perform at most \(8\) to \(16\) additions and comparisons per Segment Tree node, solving dynamic max-flow on \(5 \cdot 10^5\) vertices in \(O((N + Q) \log N)\) time!




2.4 Coupled Forward Chains & Complete Bipartite Thresholds (CF 903G, ARC 125E, & Tree HLD-DDP)
The Direction B philosophy extends immediately to three further structural topologies that appear regularly in ICPC and OI competition:

Coupled Forward Chains (CF 903G — Yet Another MaxFlow Problem, #128): Suppose \(s = A_1 \xrightarrow{x_1} A_2 \xrightarrow{x_2} \dots \xrightarrow{x_{N-1}} A_N\) is a source chain, \(B_1 \xrightarrow{y_1} B_2 \xrightarrow{y_2} \dots \xrightarrow{y_{N-1}} B_N = t\) is a sink chain, and \(M \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) directed cross-edges \(A_u \xrightarrow{z_{uv}} B_v\) connect the two chains.

Why the Cut Space Collapses from \(2^{2N}\) to \(N^2\): Suppose a cut severs \(A_i \to A_{i+1}\) (so \(A_i \in S, A_{i+1} \in \bar{S}\)). If any later vertex \(A_k\) (\(k > i\)) were placed back in \(S\), it would only increase the number of severed cross-edges \(A_k \to B_v\) and chain edges without helping \(s = A_1\)! Formally, because all edges on \(A\) point forward from \(s = A_1\), replacing \(S_A\) by the contiguous prefix \(\{A_1, \dots, A_i\}\) (where \(i\) is the first index with \(A_{i+1} \notin S_A\)) never increases the cut capacity. By symmetry, \(T_B\) can always be chosen as a contiguous suffix \(\{B_{j+1}, \dots, B_N\}\).
Thus every minimal cut is indexed by a pair \((i, j) \in \{1, \dots, N\} \times \{0, \dots, N-1\}\) with cost: \[\operatorname{Cut}(i, j) = x_i + y_j + \sum_{u \le i,\; v > j} z_{uv} \qquad (x_N = y_0 = 0),\] which is precomputed for all \(i\) in \(O((N + M) \log N)\) via a sweep-line over \(i\) and a Lazy Range-Add Range-Min Segment Tree over \(j\)!

Complete Bipartite Degree-Sorted Cuts (AtCoder ARC 125E — Snack): Suppose \(s \to i\) has capacity \(A_i\) (\(1 \le i \le N\)), \(j \to t\) has capacity \(C_j\) (\(1 \le j \le M\)), and every pair \((i, j) \in \{1, \dots, N\} \times \{1, \dots, M\}\) has directed arc \(i \to j\) of capacity \(B_j\) (\(N, M \le 2 \cdot 10^5\)).

If we fix the cardinality \(k = |S_{\text{left}}| \in \{0, \dots, N\}\), each right vertex \(j\) either joins \(S\) (paying \(C_j\) on \(j \to t\)) or joins \(\bar{S}\) (paying \(k \cdot B_j\) on the \(k\) arcs from \(S_{\text{left}}\) to \(j\)), so right vertex \(j\) independently pays \(\min(C_j, k B_j)\)! Meanwhile, to minimize \(\sum_{i \notin S_{\text{left}}} A_i\), \(S_{\text{left}}\) must consist of the \(k\) left vertices with the largest \(A_i\): \[\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t) = \min_{0 \le k \le N} \left[ \sum_{r=k+1}^N A_{(r)} + \sum_{j=1}^M \min\big(C_j,\; k \cdot B_j\big) \right] \qquad (A_{(1)} \ge \dots \ge A_{(N)}).\]

Tree Networks via Dynamic DP (Tree Max-Flow, Checkpoint CP-IV #217): On an arbitrary tree \(T = (V, E)\) with source capacities \(a_u\), sink capacities \(b_u\), and undirected tree edge capacities \(c_{uv}\), the minimum cut is solved in \(O(N)\) time by a 2-state bottom-up Tree DP (dp[u][0] for \(u \in \bar{S}\), dp[u][1] for \(u \in S\)): \[dp[u][0] = a_u + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} \min\big(dp[v][0],\; dp[v][1] + c_{uv}\big), \qquad dp[u][1] = b_u + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} \min\big(dp[v][1],\; dp[v][0] + c_{uv}\big).\] Under online updates to \((a_u, b_u)\), Heavy-Light Decomposition (HLD) compiles each heavy chain into the exact same \(2 \times 2\) \((\min, +)\) matrix Segment Tree as CF 1919F2, answering dynamic tree max-flow queries in \(O(Q \log^2 N)\) time!

3. Global Undirected Minimum Cut: Stoer–Wagner & Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS)

3.1 The Global Minimum Cut Problem & The Dichotomy of a Vertex Pair
Let \(G = (V, E, w)\) be an undirected graph with \(N = |V|\) vertices, \(M = |E|\) edges, and non-negative edge weights \(w_{uv} = w_{vu} \ge 0\). For any subset \(S \subseteq V\), write \(\delta(S) = \{\{u, v\} \in E : u \in S, v \notin S\}\) for the boundary cut edges and \(c(\delta(S)) = \sum_{u \in S, v \notin S} w_{uv}\) for the cut capacity. For any two disjoint subsets \(X, Y \subseteq V\), write \(w(X, Y) = \sum_{x \in X, y \in Y} w_{xy}\).
The Global Minimum Cut Problem asks for a non-empty proper subset \(\emptyset \subsetneq S \subsetneq V\) minimizing \(c(\delta(S))\):
\[
\lambda(G) = \min_{\emptyset \subsetneq S \subsetneq V} c(\delta(S)) = \min_{\{u, v\} \subset V} \lambda_G(u, v),
\]
where \(\lambda_G(u, v) = \min_{S \subseteq V : u \in S, v \notin S} c(\delta(S))\) denotes the pairwise minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut.
Suppose we manage to pick any two distinct vertices \(s, t \in V\) for which we can easily compute their pairwise minimum cut \(\lambda_G(s, t)\). Then every global minimum cut \((S^*, V \setminus S^*)\) falls into one of two mutually exclusive cases:

Case 1 (\(S^*\) separates \(s\) and \(t\)): Then \(\lambda(G) = c(\delta(S^*)) = \lambda_G(s, t)\), which we just computed!
Case 2 (\(s\) and \(t\) lie on the same side of \(S^*\)): Then contracting \(s\) and \(t\) into a single supernode \(v_{st}\) (summing parallel edge weights \(w(v_{st}, u) = w(s, u) + w(t, u)\) for all \(u \notin \{s, t\}\) and deleting self-loops) preserves \(c(\delta(S^*))\) and every other cut that keeps \(s\) and \(t\) together: \[\lambda(G) = \min\Big(\lambda_G(s, t),\;\; \lambda\big(G / \{s, t\}\big)\Big).\]

Repeating this contraction \(N - 1\) times reduces \(G\) to a single vertex and guarantees finding \(\lambda(G)\)—provided we have a fast way to find some pair \((s, t)\) and its exact minimum cut \(\lambda_G(s, t)\) in each phase without running a max-flow algorithm!



3.2 Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS) & The Stoer–Wagner Theorem
In 1997, Mechthild Stoer and Frank Wagner proved a remarkable structural theorem (simplifying an earlier 1992 result of Nagamochi and Ibaraki): if we order the vertices of \(G\) by greedily pulling in the vertex most tightly connected to the already-visited prefix—an ordering called Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS)—then the last two vertices \(s = v_{N-1}\) and \(t = v_N\) of the ordering automatically satisfy \(\lambda_G(s, t) = c(\delta(\{t\})) = w(V \setminus \{t\}, t)\)!

Definition (Maximum Adjacency Ordering)
Fix an arbitrary starting vertex \(v_1 \in V\), and set \(A_1 = \{v_1\}\). For \(i = 2, 3, \dots, N\), define \(A_{i-1} = \{v_1, \dots, v_{i-1}\}\) and choose the next vertex \(v_i \in V \setminus A_{i-1}\) to maximize the total edge weight to \(A_{i-1}\):
\[
v_i \in \arg\max_{u \in V \setminus A_{i-1}} w(A_{i-1}, u).
\]
Notice that MAS is structurally identical to Prim’s Minimum Spanning Tree algorithm, except that the priority key of each unvisited vertex \(u \notin A_{i-1}\) is the sum \(w(A_{i-1}, u) = \sum_{x \in A_{i-1}} w_{xu}\) rather than \(\min_{x \in A_{i-1}} w_{xu}\).






ImportantTheorem 16.1 (Stoer–Wagner Theorem, 1997)



Let \(v_1, v_2, \dots, v_N\) be any Maximum Adjacency Ordering of an undirected non-negatively weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\), and let \(s = v_{N-1}\) and \(t = v_N\) be the last two vertices of the ordering. Then the singleton cut \((A_{N-1}, \{t\}) = (V \setminus \{t\}, \{t\})\) is an exact minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in \(G\):
\[
\lambda_G(s, t) = \min_{\substack{S \subseteq V \\ s \in S,\; t \notin S}} c(\delta(S)) = w(A_{N-1}, t).
\]




Complete Self-Contained Proof via Active-Vertex Cut Induction
Since \(s = v_{N-1} \in A_{N-1}\) and \(t = v_N \notin A_{N-1}\), the cut \((A_{N-1}, \{t\})\) is a valid \(s\)-\(t\) cut of capacity \(w(A_{N-1}, t)\), which immediately gives the upper bound \(\lambda_G(s, t) \le w(A_{N-1}, t)\).
To prove the reverse inequality \(\lambda_G(s, t) \ge w(A_{N-1}, t)\), fix any \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((C, \bar{C})\) with \(s = v_{N-1} \in C\) and \(t = v_N \in \bar{C}\). We must prove that \(c(\delta(C)) \ge w(A_{N-1}, v_N)\).
Call a vertex \(v_i\) (\(i \ge 2\)) active with respect to the cut \((C, \bar{C})\) if \(v_i\) and its immediate predecessor \(v_{i-1}\) in the MAS ordering lie on opposite sides of the cut \((C, \bar{C})\). Notice that since \(v_{N-1} \in C\) and \(v_N \in \bar{C}\), the last vertex \(v_N = t\) is always active!
For each vertex \(v_i\), let \(C_{v_i}\) denote the cut induced by \((C, \bar{C})\) on the prefix subgraph \(A_i = \{v_1, \dots, v_i\}\), so its capacity inside \(A_i\) is:
\[
c(C_{v_i}) = w\big(A_i \cap C,\; A_i \cap \bar{C}\big).
\]
Claim: For every active vertex \(v_i\), the prefix cut capacity satisfies:
\[
w(A_{i-1}, v_i) \le c(C_{v_i}).
\]
Proof of Claim by Induction on the Active Vertices:

Base Case (First active vertex \(v_i\)): Since \(v_i\) is the first active vertex, all predecessors \(v_1, \dots, v_{i-1}\) lie on the same side of \((C, \bar{C})\), while \(v_i\) lies on the opposite side! Therefore, inside \(A_i = A_{i-1} \cup \{v_i\}\), the cut \(C_{v_i}\) separates \(A_{i-1}\) from \(\{v_i\}\), which means every edge between \(A_{i-1}\) and \(v_i\) crosses \(C_{v_i}\): \[c(C_{v_i}) = w(A_{i-1}, v_i).\]
Inductive Step: Suppose the Claim holds for an active vertex \(v_i\), and let \(v_j\) (\(j > i\)) be the next active vertex after \(v_i\).

Because no vertex in \(\{v_{i+1}, \dots, v_{j-1}\}\) is active, all vertices in \(\{v_i, v_{i+1}, \dots, v_{j-1}\}\) lie on the same side of \((C, \bar{C})\) as \(v_i\), while \(v_j\) lies on the opposite side!
Consider the prefix \(A_{j-1} = A_{i-1} \cup \{v_i\} \cup (A_{j-1} \setminus A_i)\). We can decompose \(w(A_{j-1}, v_j)\) into two parts: \[w(A_{j-1}, v_j) = w(A_{i-1}, v_j) + w(A_{j-1} \setminus A_{i-1}, v_j).\]
First, at step \(i\) of MAS, both \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) were unvisited candidates outside \(A_{i-1}\), and MAS greedily selected \(v_i\) over \(v_j\)! Therefore: \[w(A_{i-1}, v_j) \le w(A_{i-1}, v_i) \le c(C_{v_i}) \qquad (\text{by the greedy choice of } v_i \text{ and IH}).\]
Second, every vertex in \(A_{j-1} \setminus A_{i-1} = \{v_i, \dots, v_{j-1}\}\) lies on the opposite side of \((C, \bar{C})\) from \(v_j\)! Thus all edges between \(A_{j-1} \setminus A_{i-1}\) and \(v_j\) are newly added cross-edges of the cut \(C_{v_j}\) that were not present in \(C_{v_i}\) (since \(j > i\)). Because edge weights are non-negative, the cut capacity inside \(A_j\) satisfies: \[c(C_{v_j}) \ge c(C_{v_i}) + w(A_{j-1} \setminus A_{i-1}, v_j).\]
Combining these two inequalities yields the inductive step: \[w(A_{j-1}, v_j) = w(A_{i-1}, v_j) + w(A_{j-1} \setminus A_{i-1}, v_j) \le c(C_{v_i}) + w(A_{j-1} \setminus A_{i-1}, v_j) \le c(C_{v_j}).\]


Applying the Claim to the final vertex \(v_N = t\) (which is always active and has \(A_N = V\), so \(c(C_{v_N}) = c(\delta(C))\)) gives:
\[
w(A_{N-1}, v_N) \le c(C_{v_N}) = c(\delta(C)).
\]
Since \((C, \bar{C})\) was an arbitrary \(s\)-\(t\) cut, \(\lambda_G(s, t) = w(A_{N-1}, v_N)\). \(\blacksquare\)




3.3 Algorithmic Contract, Complexity & Hand-Checkable Trace

Algorithmic Contract (Stoer–Wagner Global Minimum Cut)

Input: Undirected graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) with \(N = |V| \ge 2\) and non-negative weights \(w_e \ge 0\) (parallel edges summed into \(w_{uv}\)).
Execution:

Initialize \(\text{best\_cut} \gets +\infty\) and mark all \(N\) vertices as alive.
For phase \(r = 1, 2, \dots, N - 1\) (while \(k = N - r + 1 \ge 2\) vertices remain alive):

Run MAS on the \(k\) alive vertices to produce \(v_1, \dots, v_{k-1}, v_k\).
Set \(s \gets v_{k-1}\) and \(t \gets v_k\). Update \(\text{best\_cut} \gets \min\big(\text{best\_cut},\; w(A_{k-1}, t)\big)\).
Contract \(t\) into \(s\): mark alive[t] = false, and for every alive vertex \(u \neq s\), set \(w_{su} \gets w_{su} + w_{tu}\) and \(w_{us} \gets w_{us} + w_{ut}\).

Return \(\text{best\_cut}\).

Complexity:

Dense \(O(V^3)\) Array Implementation: Each of the \(V - 1\) phases runs \(O(V)\) iterations of scanning all alive vertices in \(O(V)\) time, taking \(O(V^3)\) time and \(O(V^2)\) space with an extraordinarily tiny constant factor (\(\approx \frac{1}{6} V^3\) additions, running in \(< 40\text{ ms}\) for \(V = 500\)).
Sparse \(O(VE + V^2 \log V)\) Heap Implementation: Using a Fibonacci heap (or \(O((V + E) \log V)\) per phase with a binary heap), the total time across \(V - 1\) phases is \(O(VE + V^2 \log V)\).




Hand-Checkable Toy Trace (\(N = 4\) Weighted Diamond)
Consider \(V = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) with edges \((1, 2) = 2\), \((1, 3) = 5\), \((2, 3) = 4\), \((2, 4) = 3\), \((3, 4) = 1\).

Phase 1 (\(4\) alive vertices \(\{1, 2, 3, 4\}\)):

Start at \(v_1 = 1\): keys to \(A_1 = \{1\}\) are \(w(1, 2) = 2, w(1, 3) = 5, w(1, 4) = 0\). Pick \(v_2 = 3\).
Now \(A_2 = \{1, 3\}\): keys are \(w(\{1, 3\}, 2) = 2 + 4 = 6\) and \(w(\{1, 3\}, 4) = 0 + 1 = 1\). Pick \(v_3 = 2\).
Last vertex is \(v_4 = 4\) with key \(w(\{1, 3, 2\}, 4) = 1 + 3 = 4\).
Phase 1 records \(\lambda(2, 4) = 4\) (cut \((\{1, 2, 3\}, \{4\})\)), and contracts \(t = 4\) into \(s = 2\): new edge weights are \((1, 2) = 2, (1, 3) = 5, (2, 3) = 4 + 1 = 5\).

Phase 2 (\(3\) alive vertices \(\{1, 2, 3\}\)):

Start at \(v_1 = 1\): keys are \(w(1, 2) = 2, w(1, 3) = 5\). Pick \(v_2 = 3\).
Last vertex is \(v_3 = 2\) with key \(w(\{1, 3\}, 2) = 2 + 5 = 7\).
Phase 2 records \(\lambda(3, 2) = 7\) (cut \((\{1, 3\}, \{2, 4\})\)), and contracts \(2\) into \(3\): new edge weight \((1, 3) = 5 + 2 = 7\).

Phase 3 (\(2\) alive vertices \(\{1, 3\}\)):

Start at \(v_1 = 1\), last vertex \(v_2 = 3\) with key \(w(1, 3) = 7\) (cut \((\{1\}, \{2, 3, 4\})\)).

Global Minimum Cut: \(\min(4, 7, 7) = \mathbf{4}\), achieved by separating \(\{4\}\) from \(\{1, 2, 3\}\).







NoteTheoretical Horizon: Karger’s \(\binom{N}{2}\) Bound & The DKL Cactus of All Global Minimum Cuts



How many distinct global minimum cuts of weight \(\lambda^* = \lambda(G)\) can an undirected connected graph \(G\) possess?

Karger’s \(\binom{N}{2}\) Theorem (1993): In any undirected graph with global minimum cut \(\lambda^*\), every vertex \(v\) has weighted degree \(\deg_w(v) \ge \lambda^*\), so total edge weight is \(W \ge \frac{N \lambda^*}{2}\). If we pick a random edge with probability proportional to \(w_e\) and contract it, any fixed global minimum cut \(C^*\) is hit with probability \(\le \frac{\lambda^*}{N \lambda^* / 2} = \frac{2}{N}\), surviving the first contraction with probability \(\ge \frac{N-2}{N}\). Telescoping across \(N - 2\) contractions down to \(2\) supernodes shows that \(C^*\) survives with probability \(\ge \prod_{n=3}^N \frac{n-2}{n} = \frac{2}{N(N-1)} = \binom{N}{2}^{-1}\). Because survival to the final 2-supernode multigraph is mutually exclusive for distinct cuts, \(G\) has at most \(\binom{N}{2}\) global minimum cuts (tight on the cycle \(C_N\))!
Dinits–Karzanov–Lomonosov (1976) Cactus \(\mathcal{K}(G)\) (最小割仙人掌): While a single tree cannot represent crossing global minimum cuts (such as cutting opposite pairs of edges on \(C_4\)), any two crossing global minimum cuts \((A, \bar{A})\) and \((B, \bar{B})\) must have empty diagonal edge sets \(w(A \cap B, \bar{A} \cap \bar{B}) = w(A \setminus B, B \setminus A) = 0\) and cycle-link weights \(\frac{\lambda^*}{2}\). Consequently, all global minimum cuts of \(G\) are represented by a canonical cactus graph \(\mathcal{K}(G)\) (where every edge lies in at most one simple cycle, bridges have weight \(\lambda^*\), and cycle edges have weight \(\frac{\lambda^*}{2}\)).
