text:
4. All-Pairs Minimum Cuts & Gusfield’s Gomory–Hu Cut Tree (最小割树)
What if we need not just the single global minimum cut \(\lambda(G)\), but the pairwise minimum cut \(\lambda_G(u, v) = \operatorname{MinCut}_G(u, v)\) for all \(\binom{N}{2}\) unordered pairs \(\{u, v\} \subset V\)?
In 1961, Ralph Gomory and T. C. Hu proved one of the crown jewels of combinatorial optimization: in any undirected capacitated graph \(G = (V, E, w)\), the \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairwise minimum cuts are completely encoded by a single weighted tree \(T_{\text{GH}}\) on the exact vertex set \(V\) (requiring zero extra Steiner vertices), constructible using only \(N - 1\) maximum-flow calls! Furthermore, in 1990, Dan Gusfield showed that all \(N - 1\) max-flow calls can be executed directly on the original unmodified graph \(G\) in a 15-line loop with zero vertex contractions.

4.1 Submodularity, Posimodularity, and the Ultrametric Triangle Inequality
Let \(f(S) = c(\delta(S)) = w(S, V \setminus S)\) be the undirected cut capacity function on \(G = (V, E, w)\) with \(w_{uv} \ge 0\). Because \(G\) is undirected, \(f\) is symmetric: \(f(S) = f(V \setminus S)\) for all \(S \subseteq V\).






ImportantTheorem 16.2 (Symmetric Submodularity & Posimodularity of Undirected Cuts)



For any two subsets \(A, B \subseteq V\) in an undirected graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) with \(w \ge 0\):

Submodularity: \[c(\delta(A)) + c(\delta(B)) \ge c(\delta(A \cap B)) + c(\delta(A \cup B)).\]
Posimodularity: \[c(\delta(A)) + c(\delta(B)) \ge c(\delta(A \setminus B)) + c(\delta(B \setminus A)).\]




Proof via Four-Quadrant Partition
Partition \(V\) into the four disjoint Venn-diagram quadrants:
\[
Q_1 = A \cap B, \qquad Q_2 = A \setminus B, \qquad Q_3 = V \setminus (A \cup B), \qquad Q_4 = B \setminus A.
\]
Expand both sides of the submodular inequality in terms of the six pairwise inter-quadrant edge sums \(w(Q_i, Q_j)\):

On the left-hand side, \(A = Q_1 \cup Q_2\) and \(B = Q_1 \cup Q_4\), so: \[\begin{aligned}
c(\delta(A)) &= w(Q_1, Q_3) + w(Q_1, Q_4) + w(Q_2, Q_3) + w(Q_2, Q_4), \\
c(\delta(B)) &= w(Q_1, Q_2) + w(Q_1, Q_3) + w(Q_4, Q_2) + w(Q_4, Q_3).
\end{aligned}\]
On the right-hand side, \(A \cap B = Q_1\) and \(A \cup B = V \setminus Q_3\), so: \[\begin{aligned}
c(\delta(A \cap B)) &= w(Q_1, Q_2) + w(Q_1, Q_3) + w(Q_1, Q_4), \\
c(\delta(A \cup B)) &= w(Q_1, Q_3) + w(Q_2, Q_3) + w(Q_4, Q_3).
\end{aligned}\]

Subtracting the right-hand side from the left-hand side cancels every term except the diagonal crossing between \(Q_2 = A \setminus B\) and \(Q_4 = B \setminus A\):
\[
c(\delta(A)) + c(\delta(B)) - c(\delta(A \cap B)) - c(\delta(A \cup B)) = 2\,w(A \setminus B,\; B \setminus A) \ge 0,
\]
which proves submodularity! Applying submodularity to \(A\) and \(\bar{B} = V \setminus B\) and using symmetry \(c(\delta(\bar{B})) = c(\delta(B))\) and \(c(\delta(A \cup \bar{B})) = c(\delta(V \setminus (A \cup \bar{B}))) = c(\delta(B \setminus A))\) immediately yields posimodularity:
\[
c(\delta(A)) + c(\delta(B)) - c(\delta(A \setminus B)) - c(\delta(B \setminus A)) = 2\,w(A \cap B,\; \bar{A} \cap \bar{B}) \ge 0. \quad \blacksquare
\]
Before proving Cut Uncrossing, observe a direct consequence of simple cut partitioning for any three vertices:






ImportantCorollary 16.3 (The Submodular Ultrametric Triangle Inequality)



For any three distinct vertices \(u, v, w \in V\) in an undirected graph \(G\):
\[
\lambda_G(u, w) \ge \min\big(\lambda_G(u, v),\;\; \lambda_G(v, w)\big).
\]
Equivalently, among the three pairwise minimum cuts \(\{\lambda_G(u, v), \lambda_G(v, w), \lambda_G(u, w)\}\), the two smallest values must be equal (there cannot be a unique minimum among the three!). Consequently, across all \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs, \(\lambda_G(u, v)\) can take at most \(N - 1\) distinct values.


Proof: Let \((S, \bar{S})\) be a minimum \(u\)-\(w\) cut with \(u \in S\), \(w \in \bar{S}\), and \(c(\delta(S)) = \lambda_G(u, w)\). Where does the third vertex \(v\) lie?

If \(v \in S\), then \((S, \bar{S})\) separates \(v \in S\) from \(w \in \bar{S}\), so it is a valid \(v\)-\(w\) cut: \(\lambda_G(u, w) = c(\delta(S)) \ge \lambda_G(v, w)\).
If \(v \in \bar{S}\), then \((S, \bar{S})\) separates \(u \in S\) from \(v \in \bar{S}\), so it is a valid \(u\)-\(v\) cut: \(\lambda_G(u, w) = c(\delta(S)) \ge \lambda_G(u, v)\).

In either case, \(\lambda_G(u, w) \ge \min(\lambda_G(u, v), \lambda_G(v, w))\). \(\blacksquare\)




4.2 The Submodular Cut Uncrossing Lemma
Why don’t we need to cross previous minimum cuts when finding new ones?






ImportantLemma 16.4 (The Cut Uncrossing Lemma — Gomory & Hu, 1961)



Let \((S, \bar{S})\) be any minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in an undirected graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) with \(s \in S\) and \(t \in \bar{S}\). For any two vertices \(u, v \in S\) that lie on the same side of \((S, \bar{S})\), there exists a minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut \((A, \bar{A})\) in \(G\) that does not cross \((S, \bar{S})\)—specifically, assuming \(u \in A\) and \(v \in \bar{A}\), whichever side of \((A, \bar{A})\) does not contain \(t\) is a subset of \(S\) (\(A \subseteq S\) or \(\bar{A} \subseteq S\)).



Proof via Submodularity and Posimodularity
Let \((B, \bar{B})\) be any minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut in \(G\), labeled so that \(u \in B\), \(v \in \bar{B}\), and \(c(\delta(B)) = \lambda_G(u, v)\). Since \(t \in \bar{S}\), the sink \(t\) lies either in \(\bar{B}\) or in \(B\):

Case 1 (\(t \in \bar{B}\), on the same side of \(B\) as \(v\)): Apply submodularity (Theorem 16.2(1)) to \(S\) and \(B\): \[c(\delta(S)) + c(\delta(B)) \ge c(\delta(S \cap B)) + c(\delta(S \cup B)).\] Examine the two sets on the right-hand side:

Since \(s \in S \subseteq S \cup B\) and \(t \notin S, t \notin B \implies t \notin S \cup B\), the cut \((S \cup B, \overline{S \cup B})\) separates \(s\) from \(t\)! Because \((S, \bar{S})\) is a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut, we must have: \[c(\delta(S \cup B)) \ge \lambda_G(s, t) = c(\delta(S)).\]
Subtracting \(c(\delta(S \cup B)) \ge c(\delta(S))\) from the submodular inequality forces: \[c(\delta(S \cap B)) \le c(\delta(B)) = \lambda_G(u, v).\]
Furthermore, since \(u \in S\) and \(u \in B\), we have \(u \in S \cap B\); and since \(v \notin B\), we have \(v \notin S \cap B\). Thus \(A = S \cap B \subseteq S\) separates \(u\) from \(v\), has capacity \(c(\delta(A)) = \lambda_G(u, v)\), and is completely contained inside \(S\)!

Case 2 (\(t \in B\), on the same side of \(B\) as \(u\)): Simply swap the roles of \(B\) and \(\bar{B}\) (applying submodularity to \(S\) and \(\bar{B}\), or equivalently posimodularity to \(S\) and \(B\)): since \(s \in S \cup \bar{B}\) and \(t \notin S \cup \bar{B}\), we have \(c(\delta(S \cup \bar{B})) \ge c(\delta(S))\), which forces \(c(\delta(S \cap \bar{B})) \le c(\delta(\bar{B})) = \lambda_G(u, v)\). Here \(\bar{A} = S \cap \bar{B} \subseteq S\) is an uncrossed minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut contained inside \(S\)! \(\blacksquare\)


Canonical Source-Side Uncrossing Without Case Distinction: What if we want \(A = S \cap B \subseteq S\) to work even when \(s \notin B\) and \(t \in B\)? Notice that if \((S, \bar{S})\) is the minimal source-side cut (the set of vertices reachable from \(s\) in \(G_f(s, t)\)), or more generally by symmetry of \(s\) and \(t\), if \(s \in B\) and \(t \in \bar{B}\) then Case 1 holds; if \(s \in \bar{B}\) and \(t \in B\), then swapping \(u \leftrightarrow v\) and \(B \leftrightarrow \bar{B}\) reduces back to Case 1; and if \(s, t\) lie on the same side of \(B\) (say \(s, t \in \bar{B}\)), then \(S \setminus B\) separates \(s \in S \setminus B\) from \(t \notin S \setminus B\), so posimodularity \(c(\delta(S)) + c(\delta(B)) \ge c(\delta(S \setminus B)) + c(\delta(B \setminus S))\) together with \(c(\delta(S \setminus B)) \ge c(\delta(S))\) gives \(c(\delta(B \setminus S)) \le c(\delta(B))\), where \(\overline{B \setminus S} \supseteq S\)! Thus in all four placements of \((s, t)\) relative to \((B, \bar{B})\), an uncrossed minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut exists.





4.3 Structure of the Gomory–Hu Tree & Gusfield’s (1990) 15-Line Algorithm

Definition (Flow-Equivalent Tree vs. Cut-Equivalent Gomory–Hu Tree)
Let \(T = (V, E_T, w_T)\) be a weighted tree on the vertex set \(V\) of \(G\). For every tree edge \(e = (x, y) \in E_T\), removing \(e\) from \(T\) splits \(V\) into two connected components \((C_x(e), C_y(e))\).

Flow-Equivalent Tree (Value Property): For all pairs \(u, v \in V\), the minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut value in \(G\) equals the minimum edge weight on the unique path \(P_T(u, v)\) between \(u\) and \(v\) in \(T\): \[\lambda_G(u, v) = \min_{e \in P_T(u, v)} w_T(e).\]
Gomory–Hu Tree (Value + Partition Property): In addition to the Value Property, for every tree edge \(e = (x, y) \in E_T\), the tree bipartition \((C_x(e), C_y(e))\) is an actual minimum \(x\)-\(y\) cut in \(G\) of capacity \(c_G(\delta(C_x(e))) = w_T(e) = \lambda_G(x, y)\). Consequently, for any pair \(u, v \in V\), removing the minimum-weight bottleneck edge \(e^* \in \arg\min_{e \in P_T(u, v)} w_T(e)\) from \(T\) yields an actual minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut partition in \(G\)!



Why \(N - 1\) Uncrossed Cuts Suffice
By Induction on \(N\) using the Cut Uncrossing Lemma (Lemma 16.4), we maintain a collection of supernodes (initially a single block \(V\)) connected by already-computed tree edges. At each step, we pick a block containing at least two vertices \(s, t\), compute a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((S, \bar{S})\) in \(G\), and split that block along \((S, \bar{S})\) into two sub-blocks connected by a tree edge \((s, t)\) of weight \(\lambda_G(s, t)\).
In 1990, Dan Gusfield discovered that we never need to contract supernodes in \(G\)! Instead, we represent the evolving tree using a simple parent array p[1..N] (initialized to a star p[2..N] = 1 rooted at vertex \(1\)) and split stars in \(N - 1\) iterations \(s = 2, 3, \dots, N\):
// Gusfield's (1990) 15-Line Gomory-Hu Cut Tree Construction
// Assumes: dinic_solve(s, t) resets all edge flows to 0 and returns MaxFlow_G(s, t),
//          and vis[u] == true iff u is reachable from s in the residual graph G_f(s, t).
vector<int> p(N + 1, 1);
vector<long long> w_tree(N + 1, 0);
p[1] = 0;

for (int s = 2; s <= N; ++s) {
    int t = p[s];
    w_tree[s] = dinic_solve(s, t);            // 1. Run s-t MaxFlow on the ORIGINAL graph G
    for (int u = s + 1; u <= N; ++u) {
        if (p[u] == t && vis[u]) {            // 2. ONLY re-parent u > s in t's current star
            p[u] = s;                         //    that lie on s's side of the cut!
        }
    }
    if (p[t] > 0 && vis[p[t]]) {              // 3. Cut-Equivalence Upgrade: if t's own parent
        p[s] = p[t];                          //    lies on s's side of the cut, invert (s, t)
        p[t] = s;                             //    so tree-edge removal matches the cut in G!
        swap(w_tree[s], w_tree[t]);
    }
}
// Resulting tree has N - 1 edges: (i, p[i]) with weight w_tree[i] for i = 2 .. N.


Why Gusfield’s Star-Splitting Works (And Why if (vis[p[t]]) Matters)
In iteration \(s \in \{2, \dots, N\}\), vertices \(\{1, \dots, s-1\}\) are the centers of the already-separated supernode blocks, while every unprocessed vertex \(u \in \{s, \dots, N\}\) is attached as a leaf (p[u] = center) to the unique supernode center in \(\{1, \dots, s-1\}\) whose block contains \(u\).

When we pick \(s\) and its current block center \(t = p[s] < s\), running \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}_G(s, t)\) on the original uncontracted graph \(G\) produces a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((S, \bar{S})\) with \(s \in S, t \in \bar{S}\) (vis[u] == 1 \(\iff u \in S\)).
Every future vertex \(u > s\) currently attached to \(t\) (p[u] == t) belongs to the supernode block being split by \((s, t)\). If \(u \in S\) (vis[u] == true), \(u\) moves into \(s\)’s new half of the block (p[u] = s); if \(u \in \bar{S}\), \(u\) stays in \(t\)’s half (p[u] = t).
What about the existing tree edge \((t, p[t])\) connecting \(t\)’s block to the rest of the tree? If \(p[t] \in S\) (vis[p[t]] == true), then the exterior component containing \(p[t]\) lies on the \(s\)-side of the cut \((S, \bar{S})\) rather than the \(t\)-side!

Without step 3 (if (vis[p[t]])): The tree leaves \((t, p[t])\) attached to \(t\) and attaches \(s\) as a leaf to \(t\). As Gusfield (1990) proved, this 3-line version still satisfies the Value Property (\(\lambda_G(u, v) = \min_{e \in P_T(u, v)} w_T(e)\) for all \(u, v\), i.e., a Flow-Equivalent Tree)!
With step 3 (if (vis[p[t]])): Whenever \(p[t] \in S\), we re-attach \(p[t]\) to \(s\) instead of \(t\) (p[s] = p[t]; p[t] = s; swap(w_tree[s], w_tree[t])), which guarantees by Lemma 16.4 that the resulting tree is a true Cut-Equivalent Gomory–Hu Tree (deleting any tree edge yields the exact physical cut partition in \(G\))!






4.4 Hand-Checkable Trace & Broken-Gadget Counterexamples (FM-16)

Hand-Checkable Trace of Gusfield’s Algorithm (\(N = 4\))
Let \(G\) have \(V = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) and undirected edges \((1, 2) = 3, (2, 3) = 4, (3, 4) = 5, (4, 1) = 2, (2, 4) = 1\).

Initialization: p = [_, 1, 1, 1, 1], w_tree = [_, 0, 0, 0, 0].
Iteration \(s = 2\) (\(t = p[2] = 1\)):

\(\operatorname{MaxFlow}_G(2, 1) = 5\), with residual reachable set \(S = \{2, 3, 4\}\) and \(\bar{S} = \{1\}\) (severing \((1,2)=3\) and \((1,4)=2\)).
Set w_tree[2] = 5. For \(u \in \{3, 4\}\), since p[u] == 1 and \(u \in S\), update p[3] = 2, p[4] = 2.

Iteration \(s = 3\) (\(t = p[3] = 2\)):

\(\operatorname{MaxFlow}_G(3, 2) = 7\), with \(S = \{3, 4\}\) and \(\bar{S} = \{1, 2\}\) (severing \((2,3)=4, (2,4)=1, (1,4)=2\) of total capacity \(4 + 1 + 2 = 7\), whereas \((\{3\}, \{1, 2, 4\})\) has capacity \(4 + 5 = 9\)).
Set w_tree[3] = 7. For \(u = 4\), since p[4] == 2 and \(4 \in S\), update p[4] = 3. Since \(p[t] = p[2] = 1 \notin S\), step 3 does not trigger.

Iteration \(s = 4\) (\(t = p[4] = 3\)):

\(\operatorname{MaxFlow}_G(4, 3) = 8\), with \(S = \{4\}\) and \(\bar{S} = \{1, 2, 3\}\) (severing \((3,4)=5, (2,4)=1, (1,4)=2\), total capacity \(5+1+2 = 8\)).
Set w_tree[4] = 8. Since \(p[3] = 2 \notin S\), step 3 does not trigger.

Final Gomory–Hu Tree: Path \(1 \stackrel{5}{\longleftrightarrow} 2 \stackrel{7}{\longleftrightarrow} 3 \stackrel{8}{\longleftrightarrow} 4\).

Check \(\lambda_G(2, 4)\): path \(2 - 3 - 4\) has bottleneck \(\min(7, 8) = 7\), and removing edge \((2, 3)\) gives partition \((\{1, 2\}, \{3, 4\})\) of capacity \(7\)!
Distinct pairwise min-cut values: \(\{5, 7, 8\}\) (\(3\) distinct values across \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) pairs).








WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexamples FM-16: The Three Classic Gomory–Hu Failures




Unconditional Re-Parenting Bug (Omitting p[u] == t in Gusfield’s Loop): Suppose a solver writes if (vis[u]) p[u] = s; without checking p[u] == t. Because the max-flow between \(s\) and \(t\) is computed on the uncontracted graph \(G\), the raw cut \((S, \bar{S})\) may cross another already-separated supernode block \(B'\)! Re-parenting vertices \(u \in B'\) that have p[u] != t tears apart previously constructed tree branches and destroys both the Value and Partition properties. Rule: Only vertices \(u > s\) currently belonging to \(t\)’s star (p[u] == t) may be re-parented to \(s\).
Subgraph Deletion / Naive Contraction Corruption (FM-16): In the recursive bucket version of Gomory–Hu (solve(vector<int> B)), when splitting bucket \(B\) into \(B_L = B \cap S\) and \(B_R = B \setminus S\), a common bug is running future max-flows on the induced subgraph \(G[B_L]\) (deleting \(V \setminus B_L\))! Deleting \(V \setminus B_L\) destroys valid flow paths between \(u, v \in B_L\) that route through \(V \setminus B_L\). In the example above, inside \(B_L = \{3, 4\}\), the induced edge is only \((3, 4) = 5\), missing the path \(3 - 2 - 4\) (\(1\)) and \(3 - 2 - 1 - 4\) (\(2\)) that raise \(\lambda_G(3, 4)\) from \(5\) to \(8\)! Always run Dinic on the entire original graph \(G\).
Applying Gomory–Hu to a Directed Graph (Failure of Symmetry & Posimodularity): Gomory–Hu trees exist only for undirected graphs. Consider the 3-vertex directed cycle \(1 \xrightarrow{10} 2 \xrightarrow{1} 3 \xrightarrow{10} 1\).

First, directed min-cuts are asymmetric: \(\lambda(1, 2) = 10\) (via \(1 \to 2\)), whereas \(\lambda(2, 1) = 1\) (limited by \(2 \to 3\)).
Second, even if you only look at \(\min(\lambda(u, v), \lambda(v, u))\) or outgoing cuts \(f(S) = c(\delta^+(S))\), posimodularity fails because \(f(S) \neq f(V \setminus S)\)! For \(A = \{1, 2\}\) (\(f(A) = c(2 \to 3) = 1\)) and \(B = \{2, 3\}\) (\(f(B) = c(3 \to 1) = 10\)), we have \(f(A) + f(B) = 11\), whereas \(A \setminus B = \{1\}\) (\(f(\{1\}) = c(1 \to 2) = 10\)) and \(B \setminus A = \{3\}\) (\(f(\{3\}) = c(3 \to 1) = 10\)) have \(f(A \setminus B) + f(B \setminus A) = 20 > 11\)! Directed all-pairs min-cuts require Schnorr’s (1979) \(N(N-1)\)-flow directed cut cactus, never Gusfield’s tree.

text:
5. The 4-Step Cut-Compression Diagnostic Protocol
Whenever a problem involves maximum flows or minimum cuts at a scale where standard single-run Dinic cannot directly answer the query—either because \(N, M, Q\) are too large for even one flow call (Module 16A), or because the query ranges over all \(\binom{N}{2}\) terminal pairs (Module 16B)—apply the following 4-Step Protocol:

Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Classify the Bottleneck)

Single \(s\)-\(t\) Pair, Huge \(N \ge 10^4\) or Online Queries \(Q \ge 10^5\) (Direction B Flow Elimination):

Does the problem ask for \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\) on a linear pipeline, tree, complete DAG \(i < j\), complete bipartite graph, or two coupled directed chains?
Action: Abandon augmenting paths. Switch to \(\operatorname{MinCut}(s, t) = \min_{S \subseteq V} C(S)\).

Undirected Graph, No Fixed Terminals, Global Disconnection (Stoer–Wagner):

Does the problem ask for \(\min_{\emptyset \subsetneq S \subsetneq V} c(\delta(S))\) with \(N \le 500\)?
Action: Run \(N - 1\) phases of Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS) + vertex contraction in \(O(N^3)\) or \(O(NM + N^2 \log N)\).

Undirected Graph, All-Pairs \(\binom{N}{2}\) Function of \(\lambda_G(u, v)\) (Gomory–Hu / Gusfield):

Does the problem ask to count pairs with \(\lambda_G(u, v) \le X\), count distinct values in \(\{\lambda_G(u, v)\}\), find a permutation maximizing \(\sum \lambda_G(p_i, p_{i+1})\), or test if a matrix \(M_{uv}\) is realizable as an all-pairs min-cut matrix (\(N \le 850\))?
Action: Build \(T_{\text{GH}}\) in \(N - 1\) Dinic runs on the uncontracted graph \(G\) via Gusfield’s star-splitting algorithm.




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic or Polyhedral Representation

For Direction B (Module 16A): Write down the exact directed cut polynomial: \[C(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i (1 - x_i) + \sum_{i=1}^N s_i x_i + \sum_{(i \to j) \in E} c_{i,j}\, x_i (1 - x_j), \qquad x_i = [i \in S] \in \{0, 1\}.\] Identify the interface width between prefix \(\{1, \dots, i\}\) and suffix \(\{i+1, \dots, N\}\):

Width \(1\) (Pipeline): Only \(x_i(1 - x_{i+1})\) appears \(\implies 2 \times 2\) \((\min, +)\) tropical matrix.
Symmetric Cardinality (Complete DAG): \(\sum_{i < j} x_i(1 - x_j) = \sum_{i \in S}(N - i) - \binom{|S|}{2} \implies O(N^2)\) DP or \(O(N \log N)\) sorted slope-difference greedy.
Monotone Prefix Chains: Only one edge \(A_i \to A_{i+1}\) and one edge \(B_j \to B_{j+1}\) are severed \(\implies\) 2D prefix-suffix sweep \((i, j)\).

For Gomory–Hu (Module 16B): Replace \(\lambda_G(u, v)\) with the tree path bottleneck: \[\lambda_G(u, v) = \min_{e \in P_{T_{\text{GH}}}(u, v)} w_T(e).\]



Step 3: Mechanical Compilation into Data Structures or Tree Traversals

Compile 1D Markov cut transitions into a Segment Tree of \(2 \times 2\) \((\min, +)\) matrices (CF 1919F2) or prefix-minimum Segment Tree (CF 1919F1, CF 903G).
Compile tree-bottleneck queries on \(T_{\text{GH}}\) into Kruskal/DSU edge-weight sorting (processing edges of \(T_{\text{GH}}\) from heaviest to lightest!).



Step 4: Broken-Gadget Audit (FM-16a & FM-16)

Verify that backward transit edges (\(x_i = 0, x_j = 1\) on \(i \to j\)) pay \(0\), never \(c_{i,j}\) (FM-16a).
Verify that Gusfield’s loop checks p[u] == t before re-parenting p[u] = s and resets all residual capacities to their original undirected weights before each of the \(N - 1\) Dinic runs (FM-16).

7. Pre-Submission Checklist (FM-16 & FM-16a Audit)
Before submitting any Direction B Min-Cut DP, Stoer–Wagner, or Gomory–Hu Cut Tree solution, run through this 6-point verification audit:

Directed Cut Asymmetry Audit (FM-16a): In any Direction B Min-Cut DP or \((\min, +)\) matrix transition (CF 724E, CF 1919F2, CF 903G), verify that a directed edge \(u \to v\) of capacity \(c_{uv}\) pays \(c_{uv}\) only when \(u \in S\) and \(v \in T\), and pays \(0\) when \(u \in T\) and \(v \in S\).
Boundary Index Completeness (k = 0 and k = N): In prefix-suffix cut parameterizations (CF 1919F1, CF 903G, ARC 125E), confirm that both extreme cuts—putting all vertices in \(S\) (k = 0 or i = N, \(x_N = 0\)) and putting all vertices in \(T\) (j = 0, \(y_0 = 0\))—are included in the DP or Segment Tree domain.
Gusfield Star-Splitting Scope Guard (FM-16): In Gusfield’s loop (for u = s+1 .. N), confirm that you check if (p[u] == t && vis[u]) p[u] = s; (or in a Cut-Equivalent tree over all \(u \neq s, t\), if (p[u] == t && vis[u])). Never re-parent vertices whose current parent is not \(t\).
Full Uncontracted Graph Reset in Gomory–Hu: Before each of the \(N - 1\) Dinic runs in Gusfield’s algorithm, reset all edge capacities back to their initial undirected capacities \((c, c)\) on the complete original graph \(G\)—never delete vertices outside the current bucket.
Undirected Graph Prerequisite for Gomory–Hu & Stoer–Wagner: Confirm that the input graph \(G\) is undirected (\(w_{uv} = w_{vu}\)). If \(G\) is directed, neither Stoer–Wagner nor Gomory–Hu applies.
Parallel Edge Accumulation in Stoer–Wagner: When reading edges into an adjacency matrix for Stoer–Wagner (POJ 2914) and when contracting \(t\) into \(s\), always accumulate g[u][v] += w rather than overwriting g[u][v] = w.

section: 8. Chapter Summary & Bridge to Part IV Checkpoint (CP-IV)
text:
8. Chapter Summary & Bridge to Part IV Checkpoint (CP-IV)

Chapter 16 Revision Summary

Direction B Flow Elimination (最大流转最小割 DP): When \(N \ge 10^4\) or dynamic queries \(Q \ge 10^5\) prohibit augmenting paths, replace \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\) with \(\min_{S \subseteq V} C(S)\) and compress the \(2^N\) cut space via cardinality DP (CF 724E), sorted slope-difference greedy (\(w_i = s_i - p_i + (N - i)c\)), \(2 \times 2\) \((\min, +)\) tropical matrix Segment Trees (CF 1919F2), or prefix-suffix sweep-line Segment Trees (CF 903G).
Stoer–Wagner Global Minimum Cut: By active-vertex cut induction along a Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS) ordering \(v_1, \dots, v_N\), the last two vertices \((s, t) = (v_{N-1}, v_N)\) satisfy \(\lambda_G(s, t) = w(A_{N-1}, t)\). Contracting \(s\) and \(t\) across \(N - 1\) phases computes \(\lambda(G)\) in \(O(VE + V^2 \log V)\) or \(O(V^3)\) time.
Gomory–Hu Cut Trees & Gusfield’s Star-Splitting (最小割树): By Symmetric Submodularity and the Cut Uncrossing Lemma, all \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairwise minimum cuts of an undirected graph are encoded as path bottlenecks on a single \(N\)-vertex tree \(T_{\text{GH}}\) built in \(N - 1\) Dinic calls on the uncontracted graph \(G\).




Part IV Two-Stage Blind Diagnostic Checkpoint (CP-IV: #217–#224)
This checkpoint tests your diagnostic mastery across all of Part IV (Chapters 14–16): 0-1 Fractional Programming & Maximum Density Subgraphs (Ch 14), Planar Dual Shortest Paths & Coarea Duality (Ch 15), and Direction B Min-Cut DP & Gomory–Hu Cut Trees (Ch 16)—mixed with 3 lookalike decoys that do not require network flow or cut compression!

Stage 1: Scrambled Blind Problem Statements (5 Genuine + 3 Decoys)

#217 (CP-IV-1): Given a tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(N \le 2 \cdot 10^5\) vertices where each vertex \(u\) has source capacity \(s \xrightarrow{a_u} u\), sink capacity \(u \xrightarrow{b_u} t\), and each tree edge \(\{u, v\}\) has undirected capacity \(c_{uv}\), compute \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\).
#218 (CP-IV-2): Given \(N \le 10^5\) items with values \(v_i > 0\) and weights \(w_i > 0\), select exactly \(K\) items to maximize \(\frac{\sum_{i \in S} v_i}{\sum_{i \in S} w_i}\).
#219 (CP-IV-3): Given an \(N \times M\) planar grid (\(N, M \le 600\)) where every horizontal and vertical edge has capacity \(c_e \ge 0\), \(s\) is the entire top row, and \(t\) is the entire bottom row, compute \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\).
#220 (CP-IV-4): Given an undirected weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) (\(N \le 2000, M \le 5000\)), answer \(Q \le 10^5\) queries asking for the maximum bottleneck capacity of a single simple path between \(u\) and \(v\).
#221 (CP-IV-5): Given an \(N \times N\) symmetric non-negative matrix \(M_{u,v}\) (\(N \le 1000\)), determine whether there exists an undirected capacitated graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) such that \(\operatorname{MinCut}_G(u, v) = M_{u,v}\) for all \(u \neq v\).
#222 (CP-IV-6): Given \(N \le 300\) projects with profits \(p_i > 0\), time costs \(t_i > 0\), and prerequisite dependencies \(u \to v\), find a non-empty closed set of projects \(C\) maximizing \(\frac{\sum_{i \in C} p_i}{\sum_{i \in C} t_i}\).
#223 (CP-IV-7): Given an undirected connected planar graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) (\(N \le 10^5\)) with positive edge weights \(w_e > 0\), find a spanning tree of \(G\) of minimum total weight.
#224 (CP-IV-8): Given a complete DAG on \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) (\(N \le 5000\)) where every forward arc \(i \to j\) (\(1 \le i < j \le N\)) has capacity \(b_j\) (depending on the destination \(j\)), \(s \to i\) has capacity \(p_i\), and \(i \to t\) has capacity \(s_i\), compute \(\operatorname{MaxFlow}(s, t)\).







NoteStage 2: Diagnostic Resolution & Decoy Elimination Key for CP-IV (#217–#224)













ID
Verdict
Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Explanation




#217
Genuine (Ch 16 §2.4)
Direction B Tree Min-Cut DP: At \(N = 2 \cdot 10^5\), Dinic is too slow, but \(\operatorname{MinCut}(s, t)\) on a tree is solved in \(O(N)\) time via 2-state bottom-up Tree DP (dp[u][0] for \(u \in T\), dp[u][1] for \(u \in S\))!


#218
DECOY (Binary Search + Sort)
Unconstrained 0-1 Fractional Knapsack: There are zero graph dependencies between items! Binary search \(\lambda\) and greedily pick the \(K\) items with the largest shifted weights \(v_i - \lambda w_i\) in \(O(N \log N \log V)\).


#219
Genuine (Ch 15 §2)
Top-to-Bottom Planar Grid Minimum Cut: Contracting the top row into \(s\) and the bottom row into \(t\) places both terminals on the outer boundary; run Planar Dual Dijkstra from the Left Outer Face \(S^*\) to the Right Outer Face \(T^*\) in \(O(NM \log(NM))\)!


#220
DECOY (Maximum Spanning Tree)
Single-Path Bottleneck \(\neq\) Gomory–Hu Cut Tree: A single path’s bottleneck capacity is maximized by the path minimum on the Maximum Spanning Tree (Kruskal in \(O(M \log M)\)), NOT \(N - 1\) max-flows!


#221
Genuine (Ch 16 §4.1)
Ultrametric Realizability of Gomory–Hu Cut Matrices: By Corollary 16.3, \(M\) is realizable as \(\lambda_G(u, v)\) iff \(M_{u,w} \ge \min(M_{u,v}, M_{v,w})\) for all \(u, v, w\), which holds iff \(M\) equals the path-bottleneck matrix of its own Maximum Spanning Tree \(T^*\) (checked in \(O(N^2)\))!


#222
Genuine (Ch 14 + Ch 09)
0-1 Fractional Project Selection: Binary search (or Dinkelbach) trial ratio \(\lambda > 0\); assign each project net weight \(w_i(\lambda) = p_i - \lambda t_i\) and solve Maximum Weight Closure (Ch 09) at each step.


#223
DECOY (Kruskal / Prim MST)
Minimum Spanning Tree: Planarity does not turn MST into a flow problem—Kruskal/Prim (or linear-time planar MST) solves it directly without cuts.


#224
Genuine (Ch 16 §2.2)
Head-Weighted Complete DAG Min-Cut DP: By Direction B (§2.2), \(C(S) = \sum_{i \notin S} p_i + \sum_{i \in S} s_i + \sum_{j \notin S} \big|S \cap \{1, \dots, j-1\}\big| \cdot b_j\). Scanning \(i = 1 \dots N\) and tracking \(k = \big|S \cap \{1, \dots, i\}\big|\) gives \(dp[i][k] = \min(dp[i-1][k] + p_i + k \cdot b_i,\; dp[i-1][k-1] + s_i)\) in \(O(N^2)\) time!










Bridge to Part V: Min-Cost Max-Flow (MCMF), Equation Differencing & LP Duality (Ch 17–Ch 21)
Across Parts I through IV (Chapters 1–16), every problem had a single scalar capacity per edge: we sought either a maximum flow or a minimum cut. Starting in Chapter 17 — Potentials, Reduced Costs, Primal–Dual Slope Convexity & Negative-Cycle Saturation, every edge acquires a second dimension—a unit cost \(w_e\)—opening the rich world of Min-Cost Max-Flow (MCMF), Johnson potentials, piecewise-linear convex slope curves \(C(f)\), equation differencing (差分约束与连续守恒方程差分), and Linear Programming Duality.

title: Chapter 18 — Separable Convex Costs, Marginal Edge Splitting & Tournament Triples
text:
Prerequisites: Chapter 17 (Min-Cost Flow Optimality, Johnson Potentials & Successive Shortest Paths). You should be fluent in the Residual Negative-Cycle Optimality Theorem (Theorem 17.2), Reduced-Cost Complementary Slackness (Theorem 17.3), Primal-Dual Successive Shortest Paths (SSP) with Johnson node potentials, and DAG / Fixed-Hop initialization for negative initial arc costs.






NoteLearning Objectives



By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Compile Separable Convex Costs into Linear Parallel Arcs (凸费用拆边): Transform any integer-valued flow variable \(f_e \in \{0, 1, \dots, U_e\}\) governed by a discrete convex cost function \(\Phi_e(f_e)\) into a bundle of parallel unit-capacity arcs with marginal costs \(\Delta \Phi_e(k) = \Phi_e(k) - \Phi_e(k-1)\), and prove via the Negative-Cycle Optimality Theorem why any min-cost flow automatically activates these arcs in exact prefix order \(1, 2, \dots, f_e\).
Bundle Piecewise-Linear Convex Brackets & \(\ell_1\) Deviations: Collapse \(U_e\) unit-capacity marginal arcs into \(K \ll U_e\) constant-slope interval arcs of capacity \(T_k - T_{k-1}\) for piecewise-linear tax/wage brackets ([SDOI2011] 工作安排) and 2-arc V-shaped \(\ell_1\) target penalties \(\alpha(f_0 - f)_+ + \beta(f - f_0)_+\).
Decouple Two-Variable Quadratic Ledgers ([JSOI2009] 球队收益): Eliminate coupled variables such as wins and losses (\(w_i + l_i = G_i\)) by pre-assuming a baseline outcome (all undecided games are losses) and deriving the unified single-variable convex marginal cost \(\Delta(w_i) = C_i(2w_i + 1) - D_i(2l_i - 1)\) with second difference \(2(C_i + D_i) \ge 0\).
Linearize Tournament 3-Cycles via Landau’s Theorem ([WC2007] 剪刀石头布): Prove the exact double-counting identity \(\#(\text{3-Cycles}) = \binom{N}{3} - \sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u}{2}\) and compile 3-cycle maximization into degree-convex min-cost flow with marginal costs \(0, 1, 2, \dots, N-2\).
Scale to Large Capacities & Large Horizon Graphs: Apply Edmonds–Karp \(2^k\) capacity bit-scaling (\(O(E \log U (E + V \log V))\)) when \(U \le 10^9\) forbids explicit unit-arc expansion, and Dynamic Lazy Edge Insertion (动态加边, [NOI2012] 美食节) when \(M \times P\) marginal slots are too numerous to pre-allocate.
Diagnose and Prevent Non-Convex Splitting Failures (FM-18 \(\leftrightarrow\) H-20): Prove why applying marginal edge splitting to a concave bulk-discount or fixed-charge function causes SSP to route flow through later, cheaper increments before earlier, expensive ones.

Linearize Tournament 3-Cycles via Landau’s Theorem ([WC2007] 剪刀石头布): Prove the exact double-counting identity \(\#(\text{3-Cycles}) = \binom{N}{3} - \sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u}{2}\) and compile 3-cycle maximization into degree-convex min-cost flow with marginal costs \(0, 1, 2, \dots, N-2\).
Scale to Large Capacities & Large Horizon Graphs: Apply Edmonds–Karp \(2^k\) capacity bit-scaling (\(O(E \log U (E + V \log V))\)) when \(U \le 10^9\) forbids explicit unit-arc expansion, and Dynamic Lazy Edge Insertion (动态加边, [NOI2012] 美食节) when \(M \times P\) marginal slots are too numerous to pre-allocate.
Diagnose and Prevent Non-Convex Splitting Failures (FM-18 \(\leftrightarrow\) H-20): Prove why applying marginal edge splitting to a concave bulk-discount or fixed-charge function causes SSP to route flow through later, cheaper increments before earlier, expensive ones.

section: 1. Separable Convex Cost Functions \(\Phi_e(f_e)\) & Marginal Increment Splitting (凸费用拆边)
text:
1. Separable Convex Cost Functions \(\Phi_e(f_e)\) & Marginal Increment Splitting (凸费用拆边)
In standard Min-Cost Max-Flow (Chapter 17), the total cost is strictly linear in the arc flows: \(\sum_{e \in E} c_e f_e\). Yet competitive programming problems frequently penalize congestion, workload imbalance, or pairwise collisions with non-linear objective functions:

Quadratic congestion or latency: \(\Phi_e(f_e) = a_e f_e^2 + b_e f_e\).
Pairwise conflict / transitive triple counting: \(\Phi_v(\deg^+(v)) = \binom{\deg^+(v)}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\deg^+(v)(\deg^+(v) - 1)\).
V-shaped \(\ell_1\) target tracking: \(\Phi_e(f_e) = c_e |f_e - f_e^{(0)}|\) or asymmetric shortage/surplus penalties \(\alpha_e \max(0, f_e^{(0)} - f_e) + \beta_e \max(0, f_e - f_e^{(0)})\).
Progressive tax or overtime wage brackets: piecewise-linear functions with increasing slopes across thresholds \(0 = T_0 < T_1 < \dots < T_K = U_e\).

Whenever the objective function is separable across edges (or vertex degrees) and convex on the integer lattice, we can compile the non-linear optimization problem directly into a standard linear MCMF instance without changing the solver at all.

1.1 The 4-Step Compilation for Convex Edge Costs
Let us apply the 4-Step English-to-Graph Compilation Protocol to a generic non-linear edge cost \(\Phi_e(f_e)\) defined on integer flows \(f_e \in \{0, 1, \dots, U_e\}\).

Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
You are optimizing an assignment, routing, or degree-constrained selection problem where the cost of using a resource \(f\) times grows faster than linearly—each additional unit of load on the same vertex or edge hurts at least as much as the previous unit. Typical English phrases include “the \(k\)-th item processed by machine \(i\) takes \(t_{i,k}\) time with \(t_{i,1} \le t_{i,2} \le \dots\)”, “total dissatisfaction is proportional to the square of the number of tasks assigned”, or “maximize the number of cyclic triples (rock-paper-scissors relationships)”. Naive greedy assignment fails because early routing choices lock in high marginal penalties for subsequent items, while dynamic programming fails because the state space must track the load vector across all \(N\) vertices simultaneously (\(O(U^N)\)).


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation (Marginal Differences)
Without Loss of Generality, normalize \(\Phi_e(0) = 0\) (if \(\Phi_e(0) \neq 0\), factor the constant \(\Phi_e(0)\) into a global base cost offset \(\text{BaseCost}\) and replace \(\Phi_e(f)\) by \(\Phi_e(f) - \Phi_e(0)\)). For each integer step \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, U_e\}\), define the \(k\)-th first forward difference (marginal cost):
\[
\Delta \Phi_e(k) \;:=\; \Phi_e(k) - \Phi_e(k - 1).
\]
By telescoping, for any integer flow \(f_e \in \{0, 1, \dots, U_e\}\), the non-linear cost is the exact prefix sum of its first \(f_e\) marginal increments:
\[
\Phi_e(f_e) \;=\; \Phi_e(0) + \sum_{k=1}^{f_e} \bigl(\Phi_e(k) - \Phi_e(k-1)\bigr) \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{f_e} \Delta \Phi_e(k).
\]
Now introduce \(U_e\) binary indicator variables \(x_{e,1}, x_{e,2}, \dots, x_{e,U_e} \in \{0, 1\}\), where \(x_{e,k} = 1\) means that the \(k\)-th unit of flow on edge \(e\) is active. If we can enforce the prefix activation invariant
\[
x_{e,1} \ge x_{e,2} \ge \dots \ge x_{e,U_e} \quad \text{and} \quad f_e = \sum_{k=1}^{U_e} x_{e,k},
\]
then the non-linear term \(\Phi_e(f_e)\) becomes the purely linear sum \(\sum_{k=1}^{U_e} \Delta \Phi_e(k) \, x_{e,k}\).


Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (Parallel Marginal Arc Bundle)
In a minimum-cost flow network, we do not need explicit constraint gadgets to enforce \(x_{e,1} \ge x_{e,2} \ge \dots \ge x_{e,U_e}\) provided the marginal costs are non-decreasing! We simply replace the single non-linear edge \(e = (u \to v)\) of capacity \(U_e\) with a bundle of \(U_e\) parallel directed arcs \(e_1, e_2, \dots, e_{U_e}\) from \(u\) to \(v\):
\[
e_k = (u \to v), \qquad \text{cap}(e_k) = 1, \qquad \text{cost}(e_k) = \Delta \Phi_e(k) \qquad (k = 1, 2, \dots, U_e).
\]





flowchart LR
    subgraph Original["Original Non-Linear Edge"]
        direction LR

    end
    subgraph Compiled["Compiled Parallel Marginal Bundle (U Arcs)"]
        direction LR

        u2 -->|"e_U: cap = 1, cost = Delta Phi(U)"| v2
    end
    Original ==>|"Delta^2 Phi(k) >= 0"| Compiled






Why does the solver never cheat by picking \(x_{e,2} = 1\) while leaving \(x_{e,1} = 0\)? We now prove that discrete convexity makes prefix activation an automatic consequence of residual negative-cycle optimality.






ImportantTheorem 18.1 (Convex Marginal Edge Splitting Invariant / Hazard H-20)



Let \(\Phi_e : \{0, 1, \dots, U_e\} \to \mathbb{R}\) with \(\Phi_e(0) = 0\) be discretely convex on the integer lattice, meaning its second difference is non-negative everywhere:
\[
\Delta^2 \Phi_e(k) \;:=\; \Delta \Phi_e(k+1) - \Delta \Phi_e(k) \;=\; \Phi_e(k+1) - 2\Phi_e(k) + \Phi_e(k-1) \;\ge\; 0 \qquad \forall\, 1 \le k < U_e,
\]
or equivalently, the marginal costs are monotonically non-decreasing:
\[
\Delta \Phi_e(1) \;\le\; \Delta \Phi_e(2) \;\le\; \dots \;\le\; \Delta \Phi_e(U_e).
\]
If edge \(e = (u \to v)\) is replaced by \(U_e\) parallel unit-capacity arcs \(e_1, \dots, e_{U_e}\) with linear costs \(\text{cost}(e_k) = \Delta \Phi_e(k)\), then for every total flow value \(f_e = \sum_{k=1}^{U_e} f(e_k) \in \{0, 1, \dots, U_e\}\):

Exact Cost Representation: The minimum linear cost of routing \(f_e\) units across the parallel bundle \(\{e_1, \dots, e_{U_e}\}\) is achieved by saturating the exact prefix \(f(e_1) = f(e_2) = \dots = f(e_{f_e}) = 1\) and \(f(e_{f_e+1}) = \dots = f(e_{U_e}) = 0\), yielding linear cost \(\sum_{k=1}^{f_e} \Delta \Phi_e(k) = \Phi_e(f_e)\).
Automatic Prefix Ordering under SSP: If the marginal costs are strictly increasing (\(\Delta \Phi_e(1) < \Delta \Phi_e(2) < \dots < \Delta \Phi_e(U_e)\)), every optimal integer min-cost flow in the expanded network satisfies \(f(e_1) \ge f(e_2) \ge \dots \ge f(e_{U_e})\). If weak inequalities hold (\(\Delta \Phi_e(k) = \Delta \Phi_e(k+1)\)), any optimal integer flow achieves the exact same cost \(\Phi_e(f_e)\) regardless of which tied arcs within the equal-cost plateau are chosen.



Proof. Suppose an integer flow \(f\) routes a total of \(f_e = \sum_{k=1}^{U_e} f(e_k)\) units from \(u\) to \(v\) across the bundle, and suppose for some indices \(1 \le k_1 < k_2 \le U_e\) the flow violates prefix order: \(f(e_{k_1}) = 0\) while \(f(e_{k_2}) = 1\).
Examine the residual network \(G_f\):

Because \(f(e_{k_1}) = 0 < 1 = \text{cap}(e_{k_1})\), the forward arc \(e_{k_1} = (u \to v)\) is residual with capacity \(1\) and cost \(+\Delta \Phi_e(k_1)\).
Because \(f(e_{k_2}) = 1 > 0\), the reverse arc \(\text{rev}(e_{k_2}) = (v \to u)\) is residual with capacity \(1\) and cost \(-\Delta \Phi_e(k_2)\).

Together, \(e_{k_1}\) and \(\text{rev}(e_{k_2})\) form a directed \(2\)-cycle \(C = (u \xrightarrow{e_{k_1}} v \xrightarrow{\text{rev}(e_{k_2})} u)\) in \(G_f\) of residual cost
\[
\text{cost}(C) \;=\; \Delta \Phi_e(k_1) - \Delta \Phi_e(k_2).
\]
Since \(k_1 < k_2\) and \(\Phi_e\) is discretely convex, \(\Delta \Phi_e(k_1) \le \Delta \Phi_e(k_2)\), so \(\text{cost}(C) \le 0\):

If \(\Delta \Phi_e(k_1) < \Delta \Phi_e(k_2)\), then \(\text{cost}(C) < 0\) is a strictly negative-cost residual cycle. By the Negative-Cycle Optimality Theorem (Chapter 17, Theorem 17.2), \(f\) cannot be a minimum-cost flow! Pushing \(1\) unit around \(C\) sets \(f(e_{k_1}) \gets 1\) and \(f(e_{k_2}) \gets 0\) without altering the net flow at any vertex, strictly decreasing the objective by \(\Delta \Phi_e(k_2) - \Delta \Phi_e(k_1) > 0\).
If \(\Delta \Phi_e(k_1) = \Delta \Phi_e(k_2)\), then \(\text{cost}(C) = 0\); swapping \(f(e_{k_1}) \gets 1, f(e_{k_2}) \gets 0\) leaves the objective value unchanged and equal to \(\sum_{k=1}^{f_e} \Delta \Phi_e(k) = \Phi_e(f_e)\).

Furthermore, during Primal-Dual SSP (Algorithm 17.1), all unsold parallel arcs \(e_k\) with \(f(e_k) = 0\) share the same endpoints \((u, v)\), so their reduced costs are \(\text{cost}^\pi(e_k) = \Delta \Phi_e(k) + \pi(u) - \pi(v)\). Whenever Dijkstra relaxes arcs out of \(u\), the smallest unsold index \(k\) minimizes \(\text{cost}^\pi(e_k)\) and is always selected first. \(\blacksquare\)




1.2 Standard Separable Convex Cost Catalog & Piecewise-Linear Interval Bundling
Rather than re-deriving finite differences from scratch during a contest, keep the following four canonical compilation patterns at your fingertips.

Pattern 1: Quadratic Congestion Cost \(\Phi(f) = a f^2 + b f + c\) (\(a > 0\))
Factor \(c = \Phi(0)\) into \(\text{BaseCost}\). For the \(k\)-th unit (\(k \ge 1\)):
\[
\Delta \Phi(k) \;=\; \bigl(a k^2 + b k\bigr) - \bigl(a(k-1)^2 + b(k-1)\bigr) \;=\; a(2k - 1) + b.
\]

Second difference: \(\Delta^2 \Phi(k) = \Delta \Phi(k+1) - \Delta \Phi(k) = 2a > 0\) (strictly convex).
Special Case (\(a = 1, b = 0, c = 0\), i.e., \(\Phi(f) = f^2\)): Since \(f^2 = 1 + 3 + 5 + \dots + (2f - 1)\), the \(U\) unit-capacity parallel arcs have odd-integer costs \(1, 3, 5, \dots, 2U - 1\).



Pattern 2: Binomial Pair-Counting \(\Phi(f) = \binom{f}{2}\) with Pre-Existing Load \(w_0\)
Suppose a vertex or bin already holds \(w_0 \ge 0\) fixed items before optimization begins, and receives \(f \in \{0, 1, \dots, U\}\) additional items. The total number of unordered pairs in the bin is \(\binom{w_0 + f}{2}\). Factoring \(\binom{w_0}{2}\) into \(\text{BaseCost}\), the variable cost is \(\Phi(f) = \binom{w_0 + f}{2} - \binom{w_0}{2}\). For the \(k\)-th additional item (\(k \ge 1\)):
\[
\Delta \Phi(k) \;=\; \binom{w_0 + k}{2} - \binom{w_0 + k - 1}{2} \;=\; w_0 + k - 1.
\]

Combinatorial Meaning: When the \(k\)-th new item enters the bin, there are already \(w_0 + k - 1\) items inside; the newcomer forms exactly \(w_0 + k - 1\) new pairs with those existing occupants!
Special Case (\(w_0 = 0\)): The marginal costs for \(k = 1, 2, 3, \dots, U\) are \(0, 1, 2, \dots, U - 1\). Notice that the first item costs \(0\) (a single item forms \(\binom{1}{2} = 0\) pairs).



Pattern 3: Piecewise-Linear Convex Brackets ([SDOI2011] 工作安排 Interval Bundling)
Suppose \(U \le 10^6\), so creating \(U\) unit-capacity arcs per vertex would blow up the graph size, but the marginal cost \(\Delta \Phi(k)\) is a step function that stays constant across \(K \ll U\) contiguous intervals (e.g., tax brackets or overtime wage tiers \(0 = T_0 < T_1 < T_2 < \dots < T_K = U\)):
\[
\Delta \Phi(k) \;=\; c_m \qquad \text{for all } k \in \{T_{m-1} + 1, \dots, T_m\}, \qquad \text{with } c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_K.
\]
Because the \(T_m - T_{m-1}\) unit arcs inside the \(m\)-th bracket all have the exact same endpoints \((u, v)\) and identical cost \(c_m\), we bundle them into a single directed arc!
\[
e^{(m)} = (u \to v), \qquad \text{cap}\bigl(e^{(m)}\bigr) = T_m - T_{m-1}, \qquad \text{cost}\bigl(e^{(m)}\bigr) = c_m \qquad (m = 1, 2, \dots, K).
\]
This reduces the arc count from \(O(U)\) to \(O(K)\) while preserving exact equivalence with Theorem 18.1: since \(c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_K\), SSP completely saturates bracket \(m\) (all \(T_m - T_{m-1}\) units) before routing a single unit through bracket \(m+1\).


Pattern 4: V-Shaped \(\ell_1\) Target Deviation \(\Phi(f) = \alpha(f_0 - f)_+ + \beta(f - f_0)_+\)
Suppose flow \(f \in [0, U]\) on edge \(e = (u \to v)\) has an ideal target \(f_0 \in [0, U]\). Falling short (\(f < f_0\)) incurs \(\alpha \ge 0\) per unit of shortage; exceeding \(f_0\) (\(f > f_0\)) incurs \(\beta \ge 0\) per unit of surplus (the symmetric case \(\Phi(f) = c|f - f_0|\) has \(\alpha = \beta = c\)).
Let us compute the marginal cost across the threshold \(f_0\):

For \(1 \le k \le f_0\) (reducing the shortage from \(f_0 - k + 1\) to \(f_0 - k\)): \(\Delta \Phi(k) = -\alpha\).
For \(f_0 < k \le U\) (increasing the surplus from \(k - 1 - f_0\) to \(k - f_0\)): \(\Delta \Phi(k) = +\beta\).

Since \(-\alpha \le +\beta\) whenever \(\alpha + \beta \ge 0\), \(\Phi(f)\) is piecewise-linear and convex with \(K = 2\) constant-slope brackets! Applying Pattern 3 (Interval Bundling) and factoring \(\Phi(0) = \alpha f_0\) into \(\text{BaseCost}\), we compile \(\Phi(f)\) into just two parallel arcs:

Below-Target Arc \(e_{\le}\): \((u \to v)\) with \(\text{cap}(e_{\le}) = f_0\) and \(\text{cost}(e_{\le}) = -\alpha\).
Above-Target Arc \(e_{>}\): \((u \to v)\) with \(\text{cap}(e_{>}) = U - f_0\) and \(\text{cost}(e_{>}) = +\beta\).

Alternative Non-Negative Re-Orientation: If you want to avoid the negative initial cost \(-\alpha\) on \(e_{\le}\), pre-send \(f_0\) units of flow along \(e_{\le}\) (adjusting the demand balances \(b(u) \gets b(u) - f_0\), \(b(v) \gets b(v) + f_0\) and cancelling \(\alpha f_0 - \alpha f_0 = 0\) from \(\text{BaseCost}\)). In the residual graph, the saturated arc \(e_{\le}\) flips into a reverse shortage arc \((v \to u)\) of capacity \(f_0\) and non-negative cost \(+\alpha\), alongside the forward surplus arc \((u \to v)\) of capacity \(U - f_0\) and non-negative cost \(+\beta\)!

1.3 Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Counterexample (FM-18 \(\leftrightarrow\) H-20)
Let us trace a concrete 2-path routing example under both a convex cost function and a concave (bulk-discount) cost function to see why convexity is an unbreakable contract.

Toy Trace A: Valid Convex Splitting (\(\Phi(f) = f^2\))
Suppose we must send \(F = 2\) units of flow from \(S\) to \(T\) across two parallel links \(A\) and \(B\), each with capacity \(U = 2\):

Link \(A\) has convex congestion cost \(\Phi_A(f_A) = f_A^2\), so \(\Delta \Phi_A(1) = 1\) and \(\Delta \Phi_A(2) = 3\).
Link \(B\) has convex congestion cost \(\Phi_B(f_B) = f_B^2 + 1 f_B\), so \(\Delta \Phi_B(1) = 2\) and \(\Delta \Phi_B(2) = 4\).

Compiling both links gives \(4\) unit-capacity arcs from \(S\) to \(T\):
\[
A_1: (\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=1), \quad B_1: (\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=2), \quad A_2: (\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=3), \quad B_2: (\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=4).
\]

Augmentation 1: SSP selects the minimum-cost arc \(A_1\) (\(\text{cost}=1\)), setting \(f_A = 1, f_B = 0\) and total cost \(1 = 1^2 + 0\).
Augmentation 2: The remaining residual arcs from \(S\) to \(T\) have costs \(\{2, 3, 4\}\). SSP selects \(B_1\) (\(\text{cost}=2\)) rather than \(A_2\) (\(\text{cost}=3\)), setting \(f_A = 1, f_B = 1\) and total cost \(1 + 2 = 3 = \Phi_A(1) + \Phi_B(1)\) (which beats routing both units on \(A\) for \(\Phi_A(2) = 4\)).







WarningBroken-Gadget Counterexample FM-18 (↔︎ Hazard H-20): The Concave Bulk-Discount / Fixed-Charge Trap



What happens if you apply marginal edge splitting to a concave (economies-of-scale) cost function?
Suppose a courier link \(e = (S \to T)\) of capacity \(U = 2\) charges a fixed setup fee plus a cheap per-unit rate, or offers a bulk discount:
\[
\Phi(0) = 0, \qquad \Phi(1) = 10, \qquad \Phi(2) = 12.
\]
The marginal increments are:
\[
\Delta \Phi(1) = \Phi(1) - \Phi(0) = 10, \qquad \Delta \Phi(2) = \Phi(2) - \Phi(1) = 2.
\]
Here \(\Delta^2 \Phi(1) = \Delta \Phi(2) - \Delta \Phi(1) = 2 - 10 = -8 < 0\), violating discrete convexity!
If a solver naively compiles \(e\) into two parallel unit-capacity arcs \(e_1 = (\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=10)\) and \(e_2 = (\text{cap}=1, \text{cost}=2)\) and asks for the minimum cost to send \(F = 1\) unit from \(S\) to \(T\):

What SSP Does: Dijkstra inspects the two parallel arcs \(e_1\) (cost \(10\)) and \(e_2\) (cost \(2\)). It greedily routes the \(1\) unit of flow through \(e_2\), leaving \(f(e_1) = 0\) and \(f(e_2) = 1\)!
The Corrupt Result: The solver reports a minimum cost of \(2\) for sending \(1\) unit of flow, whereas the true cost is \(\Phi(1) = \mathbf{10}\). In physical terms, the solver bought the “second item at 80% off” without ever buying the first item!
Why It Cannot Be Fixed in Polynomial Time: Minimum-cost flow with concave or fixed-charge edge costs (\(\Phi(f) = K \cdot [f > 0] + c \cdot f\)) is strongly NP-hard (it directly generalizes the Minimum Steiner Tree and Capacitated Facility Location problems via fixed setup costs). Whenever \(N\) or the number of concave edges is small (\(K \le 15\)), you must branch on \(2^K\) binary decisions or use DP; you can never split a concave edge into independent parallel linear arcs.

section: 2. Win–Loss Substitution & Coupled Quadratic Ledgers ([JSOI2009] 球队收益)
text:
2. Win–Loss Substitution & Coupled Quadratic Ledgers ([JSOI2009] 球队收益)
In many tournament and resource-allocation problems, the objective function appears to depend on two coupled variables per entity. The archetype is [JSOI2009] 球队收益 / 球队预算 (Team Revenue, Luogu P4307):

There are \(N\) teams in a league. Each team \(i\) currently has \(w_i^{(0)}\) wins and \(l_i^{(0)}\) losses, and is scheduled to play in \(\text{rem}_i\) additional undecided matches (out of \(M\) total remaining matches across the league).
At the end of the season, if team \(i\) finishes with \(w_i\) total wins and \(l_i\) total losses, the league management pays team \(i\) an expenditure of

\[
\text{Cost}_i(w_i, l_i) \;=\; C_i w_i^2 + D_i l_i^2,
\]
where \(C_i, D_i \ge 0\) are given per-team coefficients. We want to decide the winner of each of the \(M\) remaining matches to minimize total league expenditure \(\sum_{i=1}^N (C_i w_i^2 + D_i l_i^2)\).
At first glance, each match \(m = \{u, v\}\) affects four quantities: if \(u\) wins, \(w_u\) increases by \(1\) and \(l_v\) increases by \(1\); if \(v\) wins, \(w_v\) increases by \(1\) and \(l_u\) increases by \(1\). Because standard flow networks cannot simultaneously route “win flow” to \(u\) and “loss flow” to \(v\) on the same single unit of match supply, how do we decouple \(w_i\) and \(l_i\)?

2.1 The Conservation Invariant \(w_i + l_i = G_i\)
The key structural observation is that the total number of games played by team \(i\) is a fixed constant independent of match outcomes! Let \(G_i\) denote the total end-of-season games for team \(i\):
\[
G_i \;:=\; w_i^{(0)} + l_i^{(0)} + \text{rem}_i.
\]
Regardless of which matches team \(i\) wins or loses, its final win count \(w_i\) and final loss count \(l_i\) obey the exact linear conservation law:
\[
w_i + l_i \;=\; G_i \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad l_i \;=\; G_i - w_i.
\]
More concretely, let \(x_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, \text{rem}_i\}\) denote the number of additional wins team \(i\) earns among its \(\text{rem}_i\) remaining games, and let \(L_i := l_i^{(0)} + \text{rem}_i\) denote the number of losses team \(i\) would have if it lost every single remaining game. Then:
\[
w_i \;=\; w_i^{(0)} + x_i, \qquad l_i \;=\; L_i - x_i.
\]


2.2 Pre-Assuming Losses & Deriving the Coupled Marginal Cost
Substitute \(w_i = w_i^{(0)} + x_i\) and \(l_i = L_i - x_i\) into team \(i\)’s cost ledger to obtain a single-variable function \(\Phi_i(x_i)\):
\[
\Phi_i(x_i) \;=\; C_i\bigl(w_i^{(0)} + x_i\bigr)^2 + D_i\bigl(L_i - x_i\bigr)^2.
\]

Step 1 (Baseline Ledger at \(x_i = 0\) — Pre-Assume All Remaining Games Are Losses): When \(x_i = 0\) for all teams, the baseline cost is
\[
\text{BaseCost} \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N \Phi_i(0) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N \Bigl(C_i \bigl(w_i^{(0)}\bigr)^2 + D_i L_i^2\Bigr).
\]
Step 2 (Marginal Cost of the \(k\)-th Additional Win, \(k = 1, 2, \dots, \text{rem}_i\)): When team \(i\) wins its \(k\)-th remaining match, its win–loss record transitions from \((w, l) = (w_i^{(0)} + k - 1,\; L_i - k + 1)\) to \((w + 1,\; l - 1)\). Using the algebraic identities \((w + 1)^2 - w^2 = 2w + 1\) and \((l - 1)^2 - l^2 = -(2l - 1)\), the marginal change in team \(i\)’s cost is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta \Phi_i(k) \;&=\; \Phi_i(k) - \Phi_i(k - 1) \\
&=\; C_i \Bigl((w + 1)^2 - w^2\Bigr) + D_i \Bigl((l - 1)^2 - l^2\Bigr) \\
&=\; C_i (2w + 1) - D_i (2l - 1) \\
&=\; C_i \bigl(2(w_i^{(0)} + k - 1) + 1\bigr) - D_i \bigl(2(L_i - k + 1) - 1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 3 (Verifying Discrete Convexity): Let us check the second difference \(\Delta^2 \Phi_i(k) = \Delta \Phi_i(k + 1) - \Delta \Phi_i(k)\) as \(k\) increases by \(1\) (so \(w\) increases by \(1\) and \(l\) decreases by \(1\)):
\[
\Delta^2 \Phi_i(k) \;=\; \Delta \Phi_i(k+1) - \Delta \Phi_i(k) \;=\; 2C_i - (-2D_i) \;=\; 2(C_i + D_i) \;\ge\; 0.
\]
Because \(C_i, D_i \ge 0\), the marginal sequence \(\Delta \Phi_i(1) \le \Delta \Phi_i(2) \le \dots \le \Delta \Phi_i(\text{rem}_i)\) is guaranteed to be monotonically non-decreasing! Even though the loss term \(-D_i(2l - 1)\) can make early marginal costs \(\Delta \Phi_i(k)\) negative (when trading a loss for a win reduces the heavy \(D_i l^2\) penalty more than it increases \(C_i w^2\)), as \(k\) grows, \(w\) grows and \(l\) shrinks, so \(\Delta \Phi_i(k)\) strictly increases by \(2(C_i + D_i)\) at each step.
Step 4 (Eliminating Negative Initial Costs via Fixed-Hop DAG Potentials): Every augmenting path in the compiled network has length \(3\):
\[
S \;\xrightarrow{\text{cost } 0}\; \text{Match}_m \;\xrightarrow{\text{cost } 0}\; \text{Team}_i \;\xrightarrow{\text{cost } \Delta \Phi_i(k)}\; T.
\]
Because the initial graph is a 3-layer DAG, we can initialize exact Johnson potentials in \(O(N + M)\) time without SPFA (Chapter 17, Section 3.3):
\[
\pi(S) = 0, \qquad \pi(\text{Match}_m) = 0, \qquad \pi(\text{Team}_i) = 0, \qquad \pi(T) = \min\Bigl(0,\; \min_{1 \le i \le N} \Delta \Phi_i(1)\Bigr),
\]
or equivalently add a fixed-hop shift \(+K_{\text{shift}}\) to every \(\text{Team}_i \to T\) arc and subtract \(M \cdot K_{\text{shift}}\) from the final answer.



2.3 Hand-Checkable 3-Team Trace of Win–Loss Substitution
Suppose \(N = 3\) teams have current records \(w^{(0)} = (1, 0, 0)\), \(l^{(0)} = (0, 1, 0)\), cost weights \(C = (2, 1, 1)\), \(D = (1, 2, 1)\), and \(M = 2\) remaining games: Game 1 between \(\{1, 2\}\) and Game 2 between \(\{2, 3\}\).

Remaining game counts: \(\text{rem} = (1, 2, 1)\).
Pre-assumed loss counts \(L_i = l_i^{(0)} + \text{rem}_i\): \(L_1 = 0 + 1 = 1\), \(L_2 = 1 + 2 = 3\), \(L_3 = 0 + 1 = 1\).
Base Cost \(\text{BaseCost} = \sum (C_i (w_i^{(0)})^2 + D_i L_i^2)\):

Team 1: \(2(1^2) + 1(1^2) = 3\).
Team 2: \(1(0^2) + 2(3^2) = 18\).
Team 3: \(1(0^2) + 1(1^2) = 1\).
Total \(\text{BaseCost} = 3 + 18 + 1 = 22\).

Marginal Win Arcs \(\text{Team}_i \to T\) via \(\Delta \Phi_i(k) = C_i(2w + 1) - D_i(2l - 1)\):

Team 1 (\(\text{rem}_1 = 1\)): \(k = 1\) has \((w, l) = (1, 1) \implies \Delta \Phi_1(1) = 2(3) - 1(1) = +5\).
Team 2 (\(\text{rem}_2 = 2\)):

\(k = 1\) has \((w, l) = (0, 3) \implies \Delta \Phi_2(1) = 1(1) - 2(5) = -9\).
\(k = 2\) has \((w, l) = (1, 2) \implies \Delta \Phi_2(2) = 1(3) - 2(3) = -3\). (Check second difference: \(-3 - (-9) = +6 = 2(C_2 + D_2) = 2(1 + 2)\).)

Team 3 (\(\text{rem}_3 = 1\)): \(k = 1\) has \((w, l) = (0, 1) \implies \Delta \Phi_3(1) = 1(1) - 1(1) = 0\).

Optimal Routing of the \(M = 2\) Match Units:

Game 1 (\(\{1, 2\}\)): Compares \(\Delta \Phi_1(1) = +5\) vs \(\Delta \Phi_2(1) = -9\). Team 2 wins Game 1 (using arc \(k=1\) of Team 2, cost \(-9\)).
Game 2 (\(\{2, 3\}\)): Compares Team 2’s next marginal arc \(\Delta \Phi_2(2) = -3\) vs \(\Delta \Phi_3(1) = 0\). Team 2 also wins Game 2 (using arc \(k=2\) of Team 2, cost \(-3\)).

Final Minimum Cost: \(\text{BaseCost} + (-9) + (-3) = 22 - 12 = 10\). Verification: Final records are Team 1: \((1, 1)\) cost \(2(1)+1(1)=3\); Team 2: \((2, 1)\) cost \(1(4)+2(1)=6\); Team 3: \((0, 1)\) cost \(1(0)+1(1)=1\). Sum \(= 3 + 6 + 1 = 10\). Exact match!

section: 3. Landau’s Tournament Theorem & Maximizing Directed 3-Cycles ([WC2007] 剪刀石头布)
text:
3. Landau’s Tournament Theorem & Maximizing Directed 3-Cycles ([WC2007] 剪刀石头布)
A tournament on \(N\) players is a complete undirected graph \(K_N\) in which every edge \(\{u, v\}\) is assigned one of two orientations: either \(u \to v\) (\(u\) beats \(v\)) or \(v \to u\) (\(v\) beats \(u\)). In [WC2007] 剪刀石头布 (Rock-Paper-Scissors, Luogu P4249) and Codeforces 1264 E (Beautiful League), some match outcomes are already fixed while the remaining matches are undecided. We must orient every undecided match to maximize the number of directed 3-cycles (unordered triples \(\{u, v, w\}\) that form a rock-paper-scissors loop \(u \to v \to w \to u\) or \(u \to w \to v \to u\)).

3.1 Why Naive Direct Counting Fails—and How Complementary Counting Rescues It
If we try to count directed 3-cycles directly using indicator variables \(y_{uv} \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(y_{uv} = 1 \iff u \to v\), with \(y_{uv} + y_{vu} = 1\)), the condition that \(\{u, v, w\}\) forms a directed 3-cycle is the cubic polynomial
\[
y_{uv} y_{vw} y_{wu} + y_{uw} y_{wv} y_{vu} \;\in\; \{0, 1\}.
\]
Maximizing a sum of \(O(N^3)\) cubic products over \(O(N^2)\) variables cannot be modeled directly as a flow or cut problem: a single edge orientation \(y_{uv}\) participates in \(N - 2\) different triples simultaneously, and its contribution to triple \(\{u, v, w\}\) depends on the joint state of \(y_{vw}\) and \(y_{wu}\).
The breakthrough—originally due to Kendall and Babington Smith (1940) and popularized in competitive programming by [WC2007] 剪刀石头布—is to count the complement: which 3-player subsets \(\{u, v, w\}\) fail to form a directed 3-cycle?





flowchart LR
    subgraph Cyclic["Directed 3-Cycle: Out-Degrees (1, 1, 1)"]
        direction TB
        u1((u)) --> v1((v))
        v1 --> w1((w))
        w1 --> u1
    end
    subgraph Transitive["Transitive Triple: Out-Degrees (2, 1, 0)"]
        direction TB
        u2((u: deg+ = 2)) --> v2((v: deg+ = 1))
        u2 --> w2((w: deg+ = 0))
        v2 --> w2
    end












ImportantTheorem 18.2 (Complementary Triple Identity / Landau’s 3-Cycle Formula)



In any tournament \(T = (V, E)\) on \(N\) vertices where vertex \(u \in V\) has total out-degree (win count) \(w_u = \deg^+(u)\), the number of unordered 3-vertex subsets \(\{u, v, w\}\) that form a directed 3-cycle is given by the exact identity:
\[
\#(\text{3-Cycles}) \;=\; \binom{N}{3} \;-\; \sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u}{2}.
\]
Consequently, maximizing the number of directed 3-cycles in a partially completed tournament is equivalent to minimizing the separable degree-convex sum \(\sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u}{2}\).


Proof (By Double Counting Internal Out-Neighbor Pairs). Consider any unordered 3-vertex subset \(\tau = \{u, v, w\} \subseteq V\). Up to isomorphism, there are only two possible induced orientations on \(\tau\):

Directed 3-Cycle: Each vertex beats one member of \(\tau\) and loses to the other. The internal out-degrees within \(\tau\) are \((1, 1, 1)\). Thus, the number of pairs of vertices inside \(\tau\) beaten by the same member of \(\tau\) is
\[
\binom{1}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{1}{2} \;=\; 0 + 0 + 0 \;=\; 0.
\]
Transitive Triple: One dominant vertex beats both of the other vertices in \(\tau\), and one of those two beats the third. The internal out-degrees within \(\tau\) are \((2, 1, 0)\). Thus, the number of pairs of vertices inside \(\tau\) beaten by the same member of \(\tau\) is
\[
\binom{2}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{0}{2} \;=\; 1 + 0 + 0 \;=\; 1.
\]

Now let us count the set of dominated configurations \(\mathcal{D} = \bigl\{(u, \{v, w\}) : u \to v \text{ and } u \to w\bigr\}\) in two ways:

Grouped by the 3-subset \(\tau = \{u, v, w\}\): Every transitive triple \(\tau\) contributes exactly \(1\) element to \(\mathcal{D}\) (corresponding to its unique dominant vertex of internal out-degree \(2\)), while every directed 3-cycle \(\tau\) contributes \(0\) elements to \(\mathcal{D}\). Therefore, \(|\mathcal{D}| = \#(\text{Transitive Triples})\).
Grouped by the dominant vertex \(u \in V\): A fixed vertex \(u\) with out-degree \(w_u\) beats \(w_u\) opponents in total. Any unordered pair \(\{v, w\}\) chosen from those \(w_u\) beaten opponents forms a dominated configuration \((u, \{v, w\}) \in \mathcal{D}\). Therefore, vertex \(u\) contributes exactly \(\binom{w_u}{2}\) elements to \(\mathcal{D}\), so \(|\mathcal{D}| = \sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u}{2}\).

Since every 3-subset of \(V\) is either a directed 3-cycle or a transitive triple, subtracting \(|\mathcal{D}|\) from the total number of 3-subsets \(\binom{N}{3}\) yields
\[
\#(\text{3-Cycles}) \;=\; \binom{N}{3} - \#(\text{Transitive Triples}) \;=\; \binom{N}{3} - \sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u}{2}. \qquad \blacksquare
\]


3.2 Mechanical Graph Compilation for Tournament 3-Cycle Maximization
Suppose player \(u\) already has \(w_u^{(0)}\) fixed wins from decided matches, and there are \(M\) undecided matches \(m_1, \dots, m_M\) remaining. Let \(x_u \in \{0, 1, \dots, \text{rem}_u\}\) be the number of undecided matches that player \(u\) wins, so \(w_u = w_u^{(0)} + x_u\).
By Pattern 2 (Binomial Pair-Counting with Pre-Existing Load) from Section 1.2:

At \(x_u = 0\), player \(u\) already generates \(\binom{w_u^{(0)}}{2}\) transitive triples among their fixed wins. Thus \(\text{BaseTransitive} = \sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u^{(0)}}{2}\).
When player \(u\) wins their \(k\)-th undecided match (\(k = 1, 2, \dots, \text{rem}_u\)), their total win count rises from \(w_u^{(0)} + k - 1\) to \(w_u^{(0)} + k\), creating
\[
\Delta \Phi_u(k) \;=\; \binom{w_u^{(0)} + k}{2} - \binom{w_u^{(0)} + k - 1}{2} \;=\; w_u^{(0)} + k - 1
\]
new transitive triples!

Because \(\Delta^2 \Phi_u(k) = (w_u^{(0)} + k) - (w_u^{(0)} + k - 1) = 1 > 0\), this marginal sequence is strictly increasing and non-negative. We compile the tournament into a 3-layer MCMF network:

Source to Undecided Matches: For each undecided match \(m = \{u, v\}\) (\(1 \le m \le M\)), add arc \(S \to \text{Match}_m\) with \(\text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = 0\).
Match to Candidate Winners: For each undecided match \(m = \{u, v\}\), add two arcs \(\text{Match}_m \to \text{Player}_u\) and \(\text{Match}_m \to \text{Player}_v\), each with \(\text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = 0\). (Whoever receives the \(1\) unit of flow from \(\text{Match}_m\) wins that match!)
Player to Sink (Convex Marginal Bundle): For each player \(u \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and each \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \text{rem}_u\}\), add a parallel unit-capacity arc
\[
e_{u,k} = (\text{Player}_u \to T), \qquad \text{cap}(e_{u,k}) = 1, \qquad \text{cost}(e_{u,k}) = w_u^{(0)} + k - 1.
\]
Result Extraction: Run Primal-Dual SSP to route all \(M\) match units from \(S\) to \(T\). Because all initial arc costs are in \(\{0, 1, \dots, N-2\} \ge 0\), initial Johnson potentials are \(\pi \equiv 0\) (no SPFA needed!). If \(\text{MinCost}\) is the minimum cost returned by MCMF, the maximum number of directed 3-cycles is:
\[
\max \#(\text{3-Cycles}) \;=\; \binom{N}{3} \;-\; \sum_{u=1}^N \binom{w_u^{(0)}}{2} \;-\; \text{MinCost}.
\]
To reconstruct the tournament matrix, inspect the two outgoing arcs from each \(\text{Match}_m\): if \(\text{Match}_m \to \text{Player}_u\) carries flow \(1\), orient \(u \to v\); otherwise orient \(v \to u\).







TipSpace-Saving Variant: Implicit Complete-Graph Degree Elimination



When no matches are pre-decided (or when we only care about the win sequence \((w_1, \dots, w_N)\) rather than explicit match nodes), Landau’s Theorem (1953) states that a sequence \((w_1, \dots, w_N)\) is realizable as the out-degree sequence of a tournament if and only if \(\sum_{u \in S} w_u \ge \binom{|S|}{2}\) for all \(S \subseteq V\), with equality at \(S = V\). However, when arbitrary specific edges of \(K_N\) are pre-fixed ([WC2007] 剪刀石头布, \(N \le 100\)), \(M \le \binom{100}{2} = 4950\) is small enough that explicitly building the \(M\) match vertices is fast (\(V \le 5052\), \(E \le 20000\), runtime \(< 15\text{ ms}\) with Primal-Dual Dijkstra) and immediately gives the constructive edge orientations!




3.3 Hand-Checkable 4-Player Tournament Trace & The Two Classic Pitfalls
Let \(N = 4\) players \(\{1, 2, 3, 4\}\), so there are \(\binom{4}{3} = 4\) triples and \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) total matches. Suppose \(4\) matches are already decided:
\[
1 \to 2, \qquad 1 \to 3, \qquad 2 \to 3, \qquad 3 \to 4,
\]
and \(M = 2\) matches are undecided: \(m_1 = \{1, 4\}\) and \(m_2 = \{2, 4\}\).

Step 1 (Count Pre-Existing Wins \(w_u^{(0)}\) and Remaining Matches \(\text{rem}_u\)):

Player 1: beats \(\{2, 3\} \implies w_1^{(0)} = 2\), undecided \(\{1, 4\} \implies \text{rem}_1 = 1\).
Player 2: beats \(\{3\} \implies w_2^{(0)} = 1\), undecided \(\{2, 4\} \implies \text{rem}_2 = 1\).
Player 3: beats \(\{4\} \implies w_3^{(0)} = 1\), undecided \(\emptyset \implies \text{rem}_3 = 0\).
Player 4: beats \(\emptyset \implies w_4^{(0)} = 0\), undecided \(\{1, 4\}, \{2, 4\} \implies \text{rem}_4 = 2\).

Step 2 (Compute Baseline Transitive Triples \(\text{BaseTransitive} = \sum \binom{w_u^{(0)}}{2}\)): \(\binom{2}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{0}{2} = 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1\) (specifically, the already-decided transitive triple \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) where \(1\) beats both \(2\) and \(3\)).
Step 3 (Build Marginal Arcs \(\text{Player}_u \to T\) with cost \(w_u^{(0)} + k - 1\)):

Player 1 (\(w_1^{(0)} = 2, \text{rem}_1 = 1\)): \(k = 1\) has cost \(2 + 1 - 1 = \mathbf{2}\).
Player 2 (\(w_2^{(0)} = 1, \text{rem}_2 = 1\)): \(k = 1\) has cost \(1 + 1 - 1 = \mathbf{1}\).
Player 4 (\(w_4^{(0)} = 0, \text{rem}_4 = 2\)): \(k = 1\) has cost \(0 + 1 - 1 = \mathbf{0}\); \(k = 2\) has cost \(0 + 2 - 1 = \mathbf{1}\).

Step 4 (Route \(M = 2\) Match Units via SSP):

For \(m_1 = \{1, 4\}\): Player 1’s marginal win costs \(2\), while Player 4’s first marginal win (\(k=1\)) costs \(0\). Route \(m_1 \to \text{Player}_4 \to T\) at cost \(0\) (so \(4 \to 1\)).
For \(m_2 = \{2, 4\}\): Player 2’s marginal win (\(k=1\)) costs \(1\), and Player 4’s second marginal win (\(k=2\)) also costs \(1\) (tie!).

Case A (\(4 \to 2\), using Player 4’s \(k=2\) arc of cost \(1\)): Total \(\text{MinCost} = 0 + 1 = 1\). Final win counts: \(w = (2, 1, 1, 2)\), transitive triples \(= 1 + 1 = 2\), so \(\#(\text{3-Cycles}) = \binom{4}{3} - 2 = \mathbf{2}\) (namely \(1 \to 3 \to 4 \to 1\) and \(2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 2\)).
Case B (\(2 \to 4\), using Player 2’s \(k=1\) arc of cost \(1\)): Total \(\text{MinCost} = 0 + 1 = 1\). Final win counts: \(w = (2, 2, 1, 1)\), transitive triples \(= 1 + 1 = 2\), so \(\#(\text{3-Cycles}) = \mathbf{2}\) (namely \(1 \to 3 \to 4 \to 1\) and \(1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 1\)).









CautionTwo Classic Implementation Pitfalls in Tournament 3-Cycle MCMF




Pitfall 1 — Forgetting the Pre-Existing Win Offset \(w_u^{(0)}\): If you initialize every player’s marginal arc costs at \(0, 1, 2, \dots, \text{rem}_u - 1\) instead of \(w_u^{(0)}, w_u^{(0)} + 1, \dots, w_u^{(0)} + \text{rem}_u - 1\) (and instead route fixed wins through the network only after building the arcs), you will get the same result only if you also send \(w_u^{(0)}\) mandatory units of flow through \(\text{Player}_u \to T\). If you neither pre-saturate \(w_u^{(0)}\) units nor shift the marginal costs by \(+w_u^{(0)}\), then in the 4-player trace above, Player 1’s win against Player 4 would falsely appear to cost \(0\) instead of \(2\)! Shifting the marginal cost by \(w_u^{(0)}\) and adding \(\sum \binom{w_u^{(0)}}{2}\) to the baseline is cleaner and avoids routing \(O(N^2)\) already-decided games through the flow solver.
Pitfall 2 — Starting Marginal Costs at \(1\) Instead of \(0\): Because \(\binom{1}{2} - \binom{0}{2} = 0\), the very first win of a player with \(w_u^{(0)} = 0\) creates zero transitive triples! A common off-by-one bug is setting the \(k\)-th arc cost to \(w_u^{(0)} + k\) instead of \(w_u^{(0)} + k - 1\), which shifts every arc’s cost by \(+1\). (In a fixed-flow tournament where exactly \(M\) undecided games are routed, a uniform \(+1\) shift on all \(\text{Player}_u \to T\) arcs adds a constant \(+M\) to \(\text{MinCost}\), which will corrupt the final answer \(\#(\text{3-Cycles}) = \binom{N}{3} - \text{BaseTransitive} - \text{MinCost}\) by \(-M\)!)
