2. Weighted Matroid Intersection, Polymatroid Flows, and the Exact Boundary of Network Flow
Throughout Chapters 1–23, we compiled dozens of seemingly unrelated combinatorial constraints into Max-Flow, Min-Cut, and MCMF. Why did network flow succeed on Bipartite Matching (Ch 06), Nested Tree/Hierarchy Capacities (Ch 07), and Project Selection (Ch 09), yet fail when asked to find a Spanning Tree with degree bounds on all vertices or a Rainbow Spanning Tree (CF 1284G, CF 1556H)? The mathematical answer lies in Matroid Intersection Theory and Polymatroid Flows.

2.1 Matroids and the Four Competitive Programming Matroid Classes
A matroid is a pair \(\mathcal{M} = (E, \mathcal{I})\), where \(E\) is a finite ground set and \(\mathcal{I} \subseteq 2^E\) is a family of independent sets satisfying:

Non-emptiness: \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{I}\).
Hereditary Property: If \(I \in \mathcal{I}\) and \(J \subseteq I\), then \(J \in \mathcal{I}\).
Exchange Axiom: If \(I, J \in \mathcal{I}\) with \(|I| < |J|\), there exists \(e \in J \setminus I\) such that \(I \cup \{e\} \in \mathcal{I}\).

Equivalently, a matroid is uniquely determined by its rank function \(r : 2^E \to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\), \(r(S) = \max \{|I| : I \subseteq S, I \in \mathcal{I}\}\), which is monotone, normalized (\(r(\emptyset) = 0, r(S) \le |S|\)), and submodular:
\[
r(A) + r(B) \ge r(A \cup B) + r(A \cap B) \qquad \forall A, B \subseteq E
\]
Almost every matroid encountered in competitive programming belongs to one of four canonical classes:









Matroid Class
Ground Set \(E\)
Independence Condition \(I \in \mathcal{I}\)
Independence Oracle Cost




1. Partition Matroid
Disjoint groups \(E = \bigsqcup_{k=1}^p E_k\)
\(|I \cap E_k| \le c_k\) for all \(k = 1, \dots, p\)
\(O(1)\) per element (group counter)


2. Laminar Matroid
Nested family \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^E\) (\(A \cap B \in \{\emptyset, A, B\}\))
\(|I \cap A| \le c_A\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) (tree of subsets)
\(O(\text{depth}(\mathcal{F}))\)


3. Graphic Matroid
Edges \(E(G)\) of an undirected graph \(G\)
\(I\) is a forest (contains no cycle in \(G\))
\(O(|V|)\) or \(O(\alpha(|V|))\) via DSU / tree path


4. Linear (XOR) Matroid
Vectors \(v_e \in \mathbb{F}_2^d\) (or \(\mathbb{F}_p^d\))
\(\{v_e : e \in I\}\) are linearly independent
\(O(d)\) via Gaussian / XOR basis





2.2 Boundary 1: Why Partition \(\cap\) Partition and Laminar \(\cap\) Laminar ARE Network Flows
Suppose we want to find a maximum-weight (or maximum-cardinality) common independent set \(I \in \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\) of two matroids \(\mathcal{M}_1 = (E, \mathcal{I}_1)\) and \(\mathcal{M}_2 = (E, \mathcal{I}_2)\) on the same ground set \(E\).

Case A: Partition \(\cap\) Partition = Bipartite \(b\)-Matching (Ch 06): If \(\mathcal{M}_1\) partitions \(E = \bigsqcup_{u \in L} E_u\) with capacities \(c_u\) and \(\mathcal{M}_2\) partitions \(E = \bigsqcup_{v \in R} E'_v\) with capacities \(d_v\), then each element \(e \in E\) belongs to exactly one left group \(u(e) \in L\) and one right group \(v(e) \in R\). Representing \(e\) as a directed edge \(u(e) \to v(e)\) with capacity \(1\), the network \(S \xrightarrow{c_u} u \xrightarrow{e} v \xrightarrow{d_v} T\) enforces \(|I \cap E_u| \le c_u\) via flow conservation at \(u\) and \(|I \cap E'_v| \le d_v\) via flow conservation at \(v\).
Case B: Laminar \(\cap\) Laminar = Tree-Hierarchy Max-Flow / MCMF (Ch 07): Because a laminar family \(\mathcal{F}_1\) forms a rooted forest of subsets, flow conservation through the tree nodes of \(\mathcal{F}_1\) (from \(S\) down to leaves \(E\)) and up through the inverted tree nodes of \(\mathcal{F}_2\) (from leaves \(E\) up to \(T\)) enforces \(|I \cap A| \le c_A\) for all \(A \in \mathcal{F}_1 \cup \mathcal{F}_2\) simultaneously. The underlying constraint matrix is Totally Unimodular (TU) (Ch 20).
Case C: Polymatroid Flows & Edmonds’ Min-Cut Theorem: More generally, in a Polymatroid Network (Edmonds 1970, Lawler–Martel 1982), the bundle of edges exiting vertex \(u\) is constrained by a submodular rank function \(f(\delta^+(u)) \le r_u^+\), and the bundle entering \(u\) is constrained by \(f(\delta^-(u)) \le r_u^-\). By Edmonds’ Matroid Intersection Duality Theorem:
\[
\max_{I \in \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2} |I| = \min_{S \subseteq E} \Big( r_1(S) + r_2(E \setminus S) \Big)
\]
Notice that this is the exact submodular generalization of the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem! When \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are cut capacities or laminar tree capacities, a single static residual graph suffices because any swap inside a partition/laminar group can be routed through the group’s shared hub vertex \(u\).



2.3 Boundary 2: When Static Flow Networks Fail — Edmonds’ Augmenting Exchange Digraph
Why can we not represent a Graphic Matroid (forest constraint) or Linear XOR Matroid as a static flow gadget? In a partition matroid, if group \(E_u\) is at full capacity \(|I \cap E_u| = c_u\), inserting a new element \(y \in E_u \setminus I\) allows us to evict any existing element \(x \in I \cap E_u\) — the valid swaps \((x, y)\) depend only on static group membership, which a single hub vertex \(u\) can route. In a Graphic Matroid, however, adding a non-tree edge \(y = (a, b) \notin I\) creates a unique fundamental cycle \(C(I, y)\) in the current forest \(I\); we may only evict an edge \(x \in C(I, y) \setminus \{y\}\). Worse yet, which edges belong to \(C(I, y)\) changes dynamically every time the forest \(I\) changes! No fixed static graph of vertices and capacities can encode a state-dependent cycle membership relation.
Instead, Matroid Intersection rebuilds the residual exchange graph dynamically at every augmentation step!






ImportantAlgorithm 24.1 (Edmonds’ Weighted & Unweighted Matroid Intersection)



Given two matroids \(\mathcal{M}_1 = (E, \mathcal{I}_1)\) and \(\mathcal{M}_2 = (E, \mathcal{I}_2)\) with element weights \(w : E \to \mathbb{R}\) (to maximize \(\sum_{e \in I} w(e)\)), maintain a common independent set \(I \in \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\) (initially \(I = \emptyset\)). At each step, construct the bipartite Exchange Digraph \(G(I) = (I \sqcup (E \setminus I), A_1 \cup A_2)\):

Source Set \(X_1\) (\(\mathcal{M}_1\)-free insertions) and Sink Set \(X_2\) (\(\mathcal{M}_2\)-free insertions):
\[
X_1 = \{y \in E \setminus I : I \cup \{y\} \in \mathcal{I}_1\}, \qquad X_2 = \{y \in E \setminus I : I \cup \{y\} \in \mathcal{I}_2\}
\]
Exchange Arcs \(A_1\) (from \(I\) to \(E \setminus I\), governed by \(\mathcal{M}_1\)) and \(A_2\) (from \(E \setminus I\) to \(I\), governed by \(\mathcal{M}_2\)):
\[
A_1 = \big\{ (x \to y) : x \in I, \; y \in E \setminus I, \; (I \setminus \{x\}) \cup \{y\} \in \mathcal{I}_1 \big\}
\]
\[
A_2 = \big\{ (y \to x) : x \in I, \; y \in E \setminus I, \; (I \setminus \{x\}) \cup \{y\} \in \mathcal{I}_2 \big\}
\]
Shortest Augmenting Path & Symmetric Difference Update: Assign vertex weights \(\tilde{w}(y) = +w(y)\) for \(y \in E \setminus I\) and \(\tilde{w}(x) = -w(x)\) for \(x \in I\). Find an augmenting path \(P = (y_0, x_1, y_1, \dots, x_k, y_k)\) in \(G(I)\) from some \(y_0 \in X_1\) to some \(y_k \in X_2\) that maximizes total vertex weight \(\tilde{w}(P)\), breaking ties by minimum number of edges (shortest hop count)!

In the unweighted case (\(w(e) = 1\)), a simple BFS from \(X_1\) to \(X_2\) finds the shortest hop-count path \(P\).
In the weighted case, Bellman-Ford / SPFA finds the maximum-weight path with minimum hop count among tied maximum-weight paths.
Update \(I \gets I \oplus V(P) = (I \setminus \{x_1, \dots, x_k\}) \cup \{y_0, y_1, \dots, y_k\}\). Notice \(|I|\) increases by \(+1\). Stop when no \(X_1\)-to-\(X_2\) path exists.










WarningWhy Hop-Count Tie-Breaking Is Mandatory (Chordless Path Invariant)



Suppose a path \(P\) in \(G(I)\) has a shortcut chord \((x_i \to y_j) \in A_1\) or \((y_i \to x_j) \in A_2\) with \(i < j\). Then performing multiple simultaneous exchanges along \(P\) can violate independence in \(\mathcal{M}_1\) or \(\mathcal{M}_2\) (\(I \oplus V(P) \notin \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\))! Choosing a path of minimum hop count in the unweighted case (or maximum weight, then minimum hop count in the weighted case) mathematically guarantees that \(P\) has no shortcut chords of non-negative weight, which by the Strong Basis Exchange Lemma ensures \(I \oplus V(P) \in \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\).



Worked Contest Archetypes of Matroid Intersection (CF 1284G & CF 1556H)

[Hello 2020 / CF 1284G] Seollal (Unweighted Graphic \(\cap\) Partition Matroid):

English Disguise: Given an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 20\)) with 'O' and 'X' cells, place walls between adjacent 'O' cells so all 'O' cells stay connected, no cycle of 'O' cells exists (or equivalently, keep a spanning tree of 'O' cells), and every black 'O' cell (\((r+c) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\), except \((1,1)\)) has degree \(\ge 2\) in the kept subgraph.
Compilation: A subgraph is connected and has degree \(\ge 2\) at every required black vertex \(u\) if and only if it contains a spanning tree \(T\) where every required black vertex \(u\) has \(\deg_T(u) \ge 2\). Equivalently, if \(G\) has \(C\) connected components (usually \(1\)) and \(V_{\text{O}}\) vertices, we can instead select a forest \(I\) of size \(2|B|\) where every black vertex \(u \in B\) has at most 2 incident edges in \(I\), and then greedily extend \(I\) to a full spanning tree!

\(\mathcal{M}_1\) (Graphic Matroid): \(I \subseteq E\) contains no cycles in the grid graph.
\(\mathcal{M}_2\) (Partition Matroid): Partition edges by their incident black vertex \(u \in B\) (since the grid is bipartite, every edge touches at most one cell in \(B \setminus \{(1,1)\}\)!). Require \(|I \cap \delta(u)| \le 2\) for each \(u \in B\).
Run unweighted Matroid Intersection (BFS on \(G(I)\)); a valid solution exists iff \(\max |I| = 2|B|\).


[Deltix Round Summer 2021 / CF 1556H] DIY Tree (Weighted Graphic \(\cap\) Partition + \(2^{\binom{K}{2}}\) Enumeration):

English Disguise: Given a complete weighted graph on \(N \le 50\) vertices, find a minimum-weight spanning tree such that vertices \(1, 2, \dots, K\) (\(K \le 5\)) have degrees \(\le d_1, \dots, d_K\).
Why Naively Intersecting Degree Bounds on \(1 \dots K\) Fails: An edge \((u, v)\) with \(u \in \{1..K\}\) and \(v \in \{K+1..N\}\) touches only one degree-constrained vertex, so those edges form a Partition Matroid \(\mathcal{M}_2\). However, an edge \((u, v)\) with both \(u, v \in \{1..K\}\) touches two degree-constrained vertices!
Fix: Because \(K \le 5\), there are only \(\binom{K}{2} \le 10\) edges inside \(\{1, \dots, K\}\). Brute-force all \(2^{\binom{K}{2}} \le 1024\) acyclic subsets \(F_0\) of edges inside \(\{1, \dots, K\}\) (Bell(5) = 52 valid forests, or simply filter acyclic \(F_0\)). Once \(F_0\) is fixed, contract \(F_0\), decrement residual degree budgets \(d'_i = d_i - \deg_{F_0}(i)\), remove all remaining edges inside \(\{1, \dots, K\}\), and solve Minimum-Weight Matroid Intersection between \(\mathcal{M}_1\) (Graphic Matroid after contracting \(F_0\)) and \(\mathcal{M}_2\) (Partition Matroid on \(\{1, \dots, K\}\), since every remaining edge touches at most one vertex in \(\{1, \dots, K\}\)!).





2.4 Boundary 3: Why 3-Matroid Intersection Is NP-Hard & The “Flow Amnesia” Anti-Pattern
What happens when an English problem imposes three independent partition/matroid constraints on each chosen item \(e \in E\)?

NP-Hardness Barrier: Intersecting three Partition Matroids is 3-Dimensional Matching (3DM); intersecting a Graphic Matroid with two Partition Matroids (e.g., degree bounds \(\le 2\) on all vertices of a general graph) is Hamiltonian Path! Both are NP-hard.
The 3-Layer Flow Amnesia Trap (流量失忆): Novice solvers frequently attempt to solve 3-attribute matching \((a_e, x_e, b_e)\) by building a 3-layer flow network \(S \to A \to X \to B \to T\), adding edge \(a_e \to x_e\) and edge \(x_e \to b_e\) for each triple \(e = (a_e, x_e, b_e)\). Why this is broken: Vertex \(x \in X\) has Flow Amnesia! If triple \(e_1 = (a_1, x, b_1)\) adds \(a_1 \to x \to b_1\) and triple \(e_2 = (a_2, x, b_2)\) adds \(a_2 \to x \to b_2\), then a unit of flow from \(S \to a_1 \to x\) can exit along \(x \to b_2 \to T\), fabricating a hallucinated hybrid triple \((a_1, x, b_2) \notin E\)! A 3-layer network \(S \to A \to X \to B \to T\) is valid if and only if the problem allows arbitrary recombination at \(x\) (or each \(x \in X\) represents a single indivisible item with capacity \(1\) via vertex-splitting \(x_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} x_{\text{out}}\) where any \(a \in N^-(x)\) and any \(b \in N^+(x)\) form a valid choice, as in [SCOI2007] 修车 / [USACO07OPEN] Dining).

3. Combinatorial Game Invariants & The LGV Lemma Boundary
Even when a problem lives on a bipartite grid or asks for vertex-disjoint paths in a DAG, jumping straight into a flow solver without checking algebraic invariants can be fatal. In this section, we study two classic boundary phenomena:

Bipartite Parity Invariants Before Binary-Search Flow ([SCOI2012] 奇怪的游戏): Where a conservation law on \((r+c) \bmod 2\) either uniquely pins the target value \(X\) (making binary search invalid!) or proves that feasibility is monotone in \(X\).
The Lindström–Gessel–Viennot (LGV) Determinant Lemma ([NOI2021] 路径交点, CF 348D Turtles): Where the problem asks to count (or compute the parity of) \(K\)-tuples of vertex-disjoint DAG paths rather than simply finding one maximum-cardinality or minimum-cost tuple (Ch 02, Ch 14).


3.1 Chessboard Increment Invariants ([SCOI2012] 奇怪的游戏, Luogu P5038)

Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal
You are given an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 40\)) of initial non-negative integers \(a_{r,c}\). In one operation, you may pick any two orthogonally adjacent cells \((r_1, c_1)\) and \((r_2, c_2)\) and increment both by \(+1\). Find the minimum number of operations required to make all cells equal to some common final value \(X\), or report -1 if impossible.

Why Naive Binary Search Fails Immediately: Suppose \(N = 1, M = 3\) with initial grid \([1, 2, 1]\). Raising all cells to \(X = 2\) takes \(1 + 0 + 1 = 2\) cell increments (\(1\) operation on \((1,1)-(1,2)\)? No, that makes \([2, 3, 1]\)!). In fact, for \(X = 2\), the two black cells \((1,1)\) and \((1,3)\) need \((2-1) + (2-1) = 2\) increments, while the single white cell \((1,2)\) needs \(2 - 2 = 0\) increments — impossible because every domino operation increments one black cell and one white cell! Worse still, if \(X = 3\), black cells need \((3-1)+(3-1) = 4\) and white needs \(3-2 = 1\) (\(4 \ne 1\)). Feasibility is not monotonic in \(X\) when \(N \times M\) is odd!



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation (The Bipartite Parity Equation)
2-color the \(N \times M\) grid like a chessboard: let \(B = \{(r, c) : (r + c) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\}\) be the black cells and \(W = \{(r, c) : (r + c) \equiv 1 \pmod 2\}\) be the white cells. Let:
\[
c_B = |B|, \quad s_B = \sum_{u \in B} a_u, \qquad c_W = |W|, \quad s_W = \sum_{v \in W} a_v
\]
If all cells reach final value \(X \ge \max_{r,c} a_{r,c}\), then each cell \(u\) must be incremented exactly \(X - a_u \ge 0\) times. Since every operation increments one cell in \(B\) and one cell in \(W\), the total number of operations \(K(X)\) must simultaneously equal the sum of black deficits and the sum of white deficits:
\[
K(X) = \sum_{u \in B} (X - a_u) = c_B X - s_B = \sum_{v \in W} (X - a_v) = c_W X - s_W
\]
Rearranging terms yields the fundamental Linear Parity Invariant:
\[
(c_B - c_W) X = s_B - s_W
\]
This equation splits into two completely different algorithmic regimes depending on whether \(N \times M\) is odd or even:

Case 1: \(N \times M\) is Odd (\(c_B - c_W = 1\), assuming \((1,1) \in B\)): The invariant forces a unique candidate target value:
\[
X = s_B - s_W
\]
There is no monotonicity and no binary search! We simply check whether \(X \ge \max_{r,c} a_{r,c}\) and run one single Max-Flow for this exact \(X\). If that flow saturates \(K(X) = c_B X - s_B\), the answer is \(K(X)\); otherwise, the answer is -1.
Case 2: \(N \times M\) is Even (\(c_B = c_W\)): Now \(c_B - c_W = 0\), so the invariant requires \(s_B = s_W\) (if \(s_B \ne s_W\), output -1 immediately!). When \(s_B = s_W\), every \(X \ge \max a_{r,c}\) satisfies \(c_B X - s_B = c_W X - s_W\). Moreover, why is feasibility monotonic in \(X\)? Because when \(N \times M\) is even, the \(N \times M\) grid always admits a perfect domino tiling (a collection of \(c_B = c_W = NM/2\) disjoint adjacent pairs covering every cell once). If \(X\) is feasible, then firing every domino in the perfect tiling once increases every cell by \(+1\), proving that \(X + 1\) is also feasible! Thus we binary search \(X \in [\max a_{r,c}, \infty)\).



Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation (check(X))
To test whether a candidate \(X\) is achievable, let \(x_{uv} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) be the number of operations applied to adjacent pair \((u, v)\) with \(u \in B, v \in W\). We need:
\[
\sum_{v \in N(u)} x_{uv} = X - a_u \quad (\forall u \in B), \qquad \sum_{u \in N(v)} x_{uv} = X - a_v \quad (\forall v \in W)
\]
This is a standard Bipartite Supply-Demand Feasibility problem (Ch 06):

Source \(S \to u\) with capacity \(X - a_u\) for all \(u \in B\).
Directed edge \(u \to v\) with capacity \(\infty\) for all adjacent \(u \in B, v \in W\).
Directed edge \(v \to T\) with capacity \(X - a_v\) for all \(v \in W\).
Target \(X\) is feasible iff \(\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) = \sum_{u \in B} (X - a_u) = c_B X - s_B\).




3.2 Non-Intersecting DAG Paths & The LGV Lemma Boundary ([NOI2021] 路径交点, CF 348D)
Suppose we are given a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) \(G = (V, E)\) with \(K\) sources \(A = \{a_1, \dots, a_K\}\) and \(K\) sinks \(B = \{b_1, \dots, b_K\}\).

If the problem asks for the maximum number of vertex-disjoint paths from \(A\) to \(B\) (or minimum cost), we use Vertex-Split Max-Flow / MCMF (Ch 02, Ch 14): split each \(v \in V\) into \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}\).
What if the problem asks for the number of \(K\)-tuples of vertex-disjoint paths (or the signed parity of crossings, as in [NOI2021] 路径交点 Luogu P7736, or the count of non-intersecting lattice paths in CF 348D Turtles)? Max-Flow only finds one augmenting flow; it cannot count all valid path systems. Here we cross the boundary into Algebraic Combinatorics via the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot (LGV) Lemma.







ImportantTheorem 24.2 (Lindström–Gessel–Viennot Lemma, 1969 / 1985)



Let \(G = (V, E)\) be a finite edge-weighted Directed Acyclic Graph. For any path \(P\), define its weight \(\omega(P) = \prod_{e \in P} \omega(e)\) (for unweighted path counting, \(\omega(e) = 1\)). Let \(e(u, v) = \sum_{P : u \leadsto v} \omega(P)\) denote the total weight of all directed paths from \(u\) to \(v\). Given \(K\) sources \(A = (a_1, \dots, a_K)\) and \(K\) sinks \(B = (b_1, \dots, b_K)\), define the \(K \times K\) path-count matrix:
\[
M = \begin{bmatrix} e(a_1, b_1) & e(a_1, b_2) & \cdots & e(a_1, b_K) \\ e(a_2, b_1) & e(a_2, b_2) & \cdots & e(a_2, b_K) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ e(a_K, b_1) & e(a_K, b_2) & \cdots & e(a_K, b_K) \end{bmatrix}
\]
Then the determinant of \(M\) equals the signed weighted sum over all \(K\)-tuples of vertex-disjoint path systems \(\mathcal{P} = (P_1, \dots, P_K)\) where \(P_i : a_i \leadsto b_{\pi(i)}\) for some permutation \(\pi \in S_K\):
\[
\det(M) = \sum_{\pi \in S_K} \operatorname{sgn}(\pi) \sum_{\substack{\mathcal{P} = (P_1, \dots, P_K) \\ P_i : a_i \leadsto b_{\pi(i)} \\ P_i \cap P_j = \emptyset \; (\forall i \ne j)}} \prod_{i=1}^K \omega(P_i)
\]



Proof Sketch (The First-Intersection Path-Swapping Involution)
Expanding the determinant by Leibniz’s formula gives \(\det(M) = \sum_{\pi \in S_K} \operatorname{sgn}(\pi) \sum_{P_i : a_i \leadsto b_{\pi(i)}} \prod_{i=1}^K \omega(P_i)\), which sums over all path tuples (both vertex-disjoint and intersecting). For any path tuple \(\mathcal{P} = (P_1, \dots, P_K)\) that has at least one shared vertex, pick the lexicographically first intersecting vertex \(v\) along a fixed topological order of the DAG, and let \(i < j\) be the two smallest indices of paths passing through \(v\). Split \(P_i = P_i[a_i \leadsto v] \circ P_i[v \leadsto b_{\pi(i)}]\) and \(P_j = P_j[a_j \leadsto v] \circ P_j[v \leadsto b_{\pi(j)}]\), and swap their tails after \(v\):
\[
P'_i = P_i[a_i \leadsto v] \circ P_j[v \leadsto b_{\pi(j)}], \qquad P'_j = P_j[a_j \leadsto v] \circ P_i[v \leadsto b_{\pi(i)}]
\]
This mapping \(\Phi(\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{P}'\) is a weight-preserving, sign-reversing involution (\(\Phi(\Phi(\mathcal{P})) = \mathcal{P}\), \(\prod \omega(P'_k) = \prod \omega(P_k)\), and \(\pi' = \pi \circ (i \; j)\) so \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi') = -\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\)). Hence all intersecting path tuples cancel out in pairs, leaving only vertex-disjoint path tuples! \(\blacksquare\)


Two Canonical Consequences for Contest Problem Solving

Planar Non-Crossing Source/Sink Order (CF 348D Turtles): If \(G\) is a planar DAG (such as a grid where paths move right/down) and the sources \(a_1, \dots, a_K\) and sinks \(b_1, \dots, b_K\) lie on the boundary in order such that any path system for a non-identity permutation \(\pi \ne \text{id}\) must topologically cross (and therefore share a grid vertex), then every \(\pi \ne \text{id}\) has zero vertex-disjoint tuples! Thus \(\det(M)\) counts the exact number of non-intersecting path tuples \(P_i : a_i \leadsto b_i\).
Multi-Layer Planar Intersection Parity ([NOI2021] 路径交点, Luogu P7736): In [NOI2021] 路径交点, a layered graph has \(L\) layers (\(n_1 = n_L = K\)), with bipartite adjacency matrices \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{L-1}\) between consecutive layers where crossings of edges between layer \(t\) and \(t+1\) occur only at the endpoints or in the planar drawing. For any vertex-disjoint path system \(\mathcal{P}\) from layer \(1\) to layer \(L\) inducing permutation \(\pi \in S_K\), the parity of the total number of geometric edge crossings \(c(\mathcal{P})\) is governed by the inversion parity of \(\pi\): \((-1)^{c(\mathcal{P})} = \operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\)! Even better: if paths can intersect at intermediate layer vertices, the LGV involution cancels all vertex-intersecting tuples, and by the Cauchy–Binet / matrix multiplication identity, the total path matrix from layer \(1\) to layer \(L\) is simply the matrix product of the layer adjacency matrices:
\[
M = A_1 A_2 \cdots A_{L-1} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{Signed Answer} = \det(A_1 A_2 \cdots A_{L-1}) \pmod{998244353}
\]




3.3 Summary Table: Vertex-Split Flow vs. LGV Determinant vs. Matroid Intersection









Structural Feature
Vertex-Split Max-Flow / MCMF (Ch 02, Ch 14)
LGV Lemma (Ch 24.3)
Matroid Intersection (Ch 24.2)




Question Type
Find 1 optimal tuple of \(K\) disjoint paths (max size or min/max weight sum)
Count (or signed sum of) all tuples of \(K\) disjoint paths (\(\bmod P\))
Find 1 max-size / min-weight common independent set \(I \in \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\)


Graph Requirement
Directed or undirected (via vertex split \(v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}\))
Must be a DAG (cycles break path finiteness & involution)
Ground set \(E\) with any two matroid oracles

Any \(\pi \in S_K\) allowed (or fixed \(\pi\) only for \(K=2\) planar)
Sums \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\) over all \(\pi\); exact count if planar forces \(\pi = \text{id}\)
N/A (subforest + degree / color constraints)


Time Complexity
\(O(K \cdot M \log V)\) (MCMF) or \(O(M\sqrt{V})\) (Dinic)
\(O(K \cdot (V + M) + K^3)\) (DAG DP + Gaussian elimination)

4. The Master 3-Stage English-to-Flow Recognition Decision Tree & The 18-Class Disguise Dictionary
We now synthesize the entire 24-chapter curriculum into a unified 3-Stage Diagnostic Compiler. Whenever you read a competitive programming problem statement during a live contest, run it through these three stages in order.

4.1 Stage 1: Constraint-Scale Triage (\(N, M, V_{\max}\))
Before building any mathematical model, inspect the input dimensions \((N, M)\) and coordinate/capacity scale \(U\). They immediately eliminate \(80\%\) of candidate algorithms:

Trap to Avoid

\(2^N\) or small grid

Over-complicating a bitmask DP with MCMF


\(N \le 50 \sim 80\)
\(O(N^3 \sim N^4)\)
Weighted Matroid Intersection (CF 1284G, CF 1556H), General Graph Blossom (Ch 23), LP Simplex / Dual Circulation (Ch 19), Multicommodity / Parametric Flow

\(O(N^3)\)

\(O(M \sqrt{N})\)

Quadratic edge construction (\(O(N^2)\) edges \(\implies\) MLE/TLE); must compress intervals/prefixes (Ch 21)

Running explicit Dinic or MCMF directly on \(N = 10^5\) (TLE)





4.2 Stage 2: Structural Archetype Identification (The Master Decision Flowchart)
Once Stage 1 confirms that your target paradigm is either an explicit Flow/Cut/Matroid construction (\(N \le 5 \cdot 10^4\)) or a Flow-Eliminated Dual (\(N \ge 10^5\)), classify the mathematical relationship between variables using the following decision tree:

    F3A -->|"Potentials pi_v - pi_u <= c_e (Inverse SP / MST)"| Ch20["LP Dual of Shortest Path / MST -> MCMF (Ch 19–20)"]

4.3 Stage 3: The Complete 18-Class Disguise Dictionary (AL-01–AL-18)
The following master dictionary translates the 18 recurring English problem disguises across all 24 chapters into their exact intermediate algebraic representation and target chapter gadget:









Code
English Problem Disguise (Surface Clue)
Algebraic Intermediate Form
Target Compilation Gadget & Chapter




AL-01
“Select each item \(i \in \{0, 1\}\); picking \(u\) requires picking \(v\); maximize profit minus cost.”
\(\max \sum w_i x_i\) s.t. \(x_u - x_v \le 0\) (\(x_u(1 - x_v) = 0\))
Max-Weight Closure (Ch 09): \(w_i > 0 \Rightarrow S \xrightarrow{w_i} i\); \(w_i < 0 \Rightarrow i \xrightarrow{-w_i} T\); dependency \(u \to v\) (\(\infty\)).


AL-02
“Assign each node to class \(A\) or \(B\); if \(u \in A\) and \(v \in B\), pay penalty \(c_{uv}\).”
\(\min \sum c_i x_i + \sum d_i (1-x_i) + \sum c_{uv} x_u(1 - x_v)\)
2-Label Burn-Bury (Ch 10): Submodular (\(A+D \le B+C\)) \(\implies\) direct cut arc \(u \xrightarrow{B+C-A-D} v\).


AL-03
“Same side (\(u, v\) both \(A\) or both \(B\)) pays penalty; OR both picked gives bonus on a bipartite graph.”
Supermodular cost \(A + D > B + C\) on bipartite \(G = (L \sqcup R, E)\)
Bipartite Variable Inversion (Ch 10): Flip \(y_v = 1 - x_v\) for \(v \in R\); converts \(x_u x_v\) into \(x_u(1 - y_v)\).


AL-04
“Assign level \(x_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) with cost \(f_i(x_i)\) and \(|x_u - x_v| \le d\) (or \(x_u \le x_v + d\)).”
Unary indicators \(z_{i,t} = [x_i \ge t]\) with \(z_{i,t} \ge z_{i,t+1}\) and \(z_{u,t} \le z_{v,t-d}\)
Multi-State Threshold Chain / 切糕 (Ch 11): Vertical chain with reverse \(\infty\)-arcs; cross-links \(z_{u,t} \xrightarrow{\infty} z_{v,t-d}\).


AL-05
“Modify values \(y_i \to x_i \in \mathbb{R}\) to minimize \(\sum w_i |x_i - y_i|^p\) s.t. \(x_u \le x_v\) (or basis/tree optimality).”
Threshold slice \(x_i \in \{M, M+1\}\), \(\Delta_i(M) = f_i(M) - f_i(M+1)\)
\(L_p\) Isotonic Regression (Ch 24.1): 整体二分 + Max-Weight Closure on active \(V_{\text{cur}}\).


AL-06
“Cover all vertices/edges of a DAG using minimum number of paths; or find max independent set of incomparable nodes.”
Path cover = \(N - \text{MaxMatching}\) on split bipartite graph; Dilworth’s theorem
DAG Path Cover (Ch 06–Ch 07): Transitive closure + König / Hopcroft-Karp or Lower-Bound Flow (Ch 08).


AL-07
“Every edge/vertex must carry flow in \([l_e, u_e]\); check feasibility or minimize/maximize total flow.”
\(l_e \le f(e) \le u_e\), \(\sum_{\text{in}} f - \sum_{\text{out}} f = 0\)
Flow with Lower Bounds (Ch 08): Pre-saturate \(l_e\), track node imbalance \(M(v) = \text{in} - \text{out}\) via super-source \(S^*\) and super-sink \(T^*\).


AL-08
“Find \(K\) vertex-disjoint (or edge-disjoint) paths from \(S\) to \(T\) minimizing total weight.”
Node capacity \(1\) (\(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1, 0} v_{\text{out}}\)), flow value \(K\)
Vertex-Split MCMF (Ch 02, Ch 14): Split vertices; send \(K\) units of flow via shortest augmenting paths.


AL-09
“Count the number (or signed parity) of \(K\)-tuples of vertex-disjoint paths from \(A\) to \(B\) in a DAG.”
\(\det [e(a_i, b_j)]_{i,j=1}^K = \sum_{\pi} \operatorname{sgn}(\pi) N(\pi)\)
LGV Lemma (Ch 24.3): Compute \(e(a_i, b_j)\) by DAG DP, then Gaussian elimination in \(O(K^3)\).


AL-10
“Each worker \(j\) processes \(k\) tasks sequentially; waiting time of \(r\)-th task from the end scales by \(r \cdot t_{ij}\).”
Contribution of task at reverse position \(r \in \{1..N\}\) is \(r \cdot t_{ij}\)
Reverse-Time Slot Expansion (Ch 14, [SCOI2007] 修车): Create state \((j, r)\) with cost \(r \cdot t_{ij}\); dynamically insert \((j, r+1)\) (Ch 15).


AL-11
“Penalty for flow \(f\) on edge \(e\) is convex (e.g., \(a_e f^2\) or piecewise linear).”
\(f^2 = \sum_{k=1}^f (2k - 1)\) with marginal slopes \(1, 3, 5, \dots\)
Convex Marginal Edge Splitting (Ch 14–Ch 15): Parallel edges of cap \(1\) and non-decreasing costs \(f(k) - f(k-1)\).


AL-12
“Select intervals \([l_i, r_i]\) at cost \(c_i\) so every point \(t \in [1, T]\) is covered at least (or at most) \(d_t\) times.”
Slack \(s_t \ge 0\), take consecutive differences \(E_t - E_{t-1}\)
Equation Differencing Circulation (Ch 16, Ch 19): Each variable appears once as \(+1\) and once as \(-1\) \(\implies\) directed flow edge!


AL-13
“Reusable resource (napkins / Surgical tools): buy new at \(p\), fast-wash in \(d_1\) days at \(c_1\), slow-wash in \(d_2\) days at \(c_2\).”
Split day \(t\) into dirty supply \(t_{\text{dirty}}\) (\(+r_t\)) and clean demand \(t_{\text{clean}}\) (\(-r_t\))
Bipartite Time-Deferred MCMF (Ch 16, 餐巾计划): Forward edges \(t_{\text{dirty}} \to (t+d)_{\text{clean}}\) route reusable stock across time.


AL-14
“Modify edge weights \(w_e\) at minimum \(L_1\) cost so a given tree \(T\) becomes an MST (or a path becomes shortest).”
Tree vs. non-tree constraints \(w_e \le w_f\) for \(e \in P_T(f)\); LP dual
Inverse MST / Shortest Path LP Dual (Ch 19–Ch 20): Dualizes to bipartite matching / MCMF or \(L_1\) Isotonic Regression (Ch 24.1).


AL-15
“Edge \(u \to v\) connects to all \(v \in [L_u, R_u]\) (or 2D rectangle / tree path) with \(N, M \le 5 \cdot 10^4\).”
Factor clique \(U \times V\) through \(O(\log N)\) canonical data-structure nodes
DS-Accelerated Virtual Hub Graph (Ch 21): Segment-tree / binary-lifting / KD-tree internal hubs with \(\infty\) edges.


AL-16
“Match/assign \(N \ge 10^5\) items on a 1D line, cycle, or tree (mice & holes, gold miners, stock trading).”
Simulate residual augmenting paths and \(-w_e\) reverse edges via priority queues
Simulated MCMF / Slope Trick (Ch 22): Maintain min-heaps of candidate transitions and regret-undo transitions.


AL-17
“Check if a bipartite graph with \(N \ge 10^5\) interval/prefix neighborhoods has a perfect matching (or find max matching).”
Hall’s Marriage Theorem \(\max_{S} (|S| - |N(S)|) \le 0\) or Gale-Ryser prefix dominance
Hall Segment Tree / Parametric Cut (Ch 05, Ch 23): Sweep right endpoint \(R\) and maintain \(|S| - |N(S)|\) in a lazy segment tree.


AL-18
“Find a spanning tree (or forest) subject to color-group caps, black-vertex degree caps, or XOR independence.”
Common independent set \(I \in \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\) of Graphic/Linear and Partition matroids
Edmonds’ Matroid Intersection (Ch 24.2): Shortest hop-count (or max-weight + min-hop) augmenting path in \(G(I)\).





4.4 The Complete 26-Failure-Mode Audit Table (FM-01–FM-26)
Before submitting any flow, cut, matching, or matroid solution, verify that your construction is immune to the textbook’s 26 canonical failure modes:









ID
Chapter
Failure Mode Name
Root Cause & 1-Line Fix




FM-01
Ch 01
Missing Reverse Edge (cap = 0)
Omitting \(v \to u\) (cap = 0) prevents cancelling bad greedy paths; always insert paired edges at indices 2k, 2k+1.


FM-02
Ch 02
Undirected Edge Split Error
Adding two directed edges without sharing residual capacity or splitting vertex \(v\) instead of edge \(e\); use cap = C on both directions or proper directed pairs.


FM-03
Ch 03
Missing Current-Arc & Dead-Node Pruning
Resetting cur[u] only per BFS or forgetting if (pushed == 0) level[v] = -1 degrades Dinic to \(O(NM^2)\).


FM-04
Ch 04
Non-Unit Capacity in \(O(M\sqrt{V})\) Bound
Assuming Dinic is \(O(M\sqrt{V})\) when capacities are large; verify unit-network / bipartite hypothesis.


FM-05
Ch 05
Unoriented König Reconstruction
Taking reachable vertices in an unoriented graph instead of \(S\)-reachable in the directed residual network: \(\text{MVC} = (L \setminus R_S) \cup (R \cap R_S)\).


FM-06
Ch 06
Unsplit Vertex Capacity Collision
Putting capacity on incoming/outgoing arcs instead of splitting \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c_v} v_{\text{out}}\).


FM-07
Ch 07
Merging Disjoint vs. Overlapping Paths
Using direct DAG edges without transitive closure (or missing pass-through arc \(v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{out}}\)) confuses vertex-disjoint with general path cover.


FM-08
Ch 08
Unbalanced Loop Edge in Lower-Bound Flow
Forgetting the feedback edge \(T \xrightarrow{\infty} S\) when reducing \(s\)-\(t\) lower-bound flow to a circulation.


FM-09
Ch 09
Positive-Weight Cycle / Clique Blowup
Failing to contract SCCs or building \(O(|A|^2)\) pairwise edges instead of a single dummy hub \(v_A\).


FM-10
Ch 10
Supermodular Cut / Non-Bipartite Flip
Applying min-cut directly when \(A+D > B+C\), or applying Bipartite Variable Inversion on a graph with odd cycles.


FM-11
Ch 11
Missing Vertical \(\infty\) Reverse Chain Arcs
Omitting \(z_{i,t+1} \xrightarrow{\infty} z_{i,t}\) allows a multi-cut to sever the chain twice and represent a non-contiguous state set.


FM-12
Ch 12
Gomory-Hu Non-Terminal Weight Leak
Using arbitrary \(s\)-\(t\) min-cuts without contracting tree components or confusing Gomory-Hu cut values with all-pairs max-flow on directed graphs.


FM-13
Ch 13
Negative Cost Cycle in SSP MCMF
Running Dijkstra/SPFA SSP when the initial network has negative-cost cycles; use Negative-Cycle Cancellation (Ch 17) or lower-bound pre-saturation (Ch 18).


FM-14
Ch 14
Non-Convex Marginal Cost Splitting
Splitting edge capacities into parallel arcs when marginal costs are decreasing (\(c_1 > c_2\)); SSP picks the higher-index arc before the lower-index arc!


FM-15
Ch 15
Static Full-Expansion TLE / Wrong Johnson Update
Building all \(N \times M\) worker-slot vertices upfront instead of dynamic insertion, or updating Johnson potentials with residual costs instead of \(\pi_v \gets \pi_v + d_v\).


FM-16
Ch 16
Dirty-to-Clean Conservation Leak
Allowing unwashed dirty napkins to satisfy clean demand directly without passing through a wash-delay arc (餐巾计划).


FM-17
Ch 17
Primal-Dual Complementary Slackness Sign
Reversing the direction of a tight residual arc when reconstructing primal flows from dual potentials \(\pi\).


FM-18
Ch 18
Positive-Cost Lower-Bound Pre-Saturation
Forgetting to add \(\sum l_e c_e\) to the base cost or flipping \(M(v)\) when pre-saturating negative-cost edges (\(c_e < 0\)).


FM-19
Ch 19
Non-Consecutive Matrix Differencing
Applying equation differencing \(E_t - E_{t-1}\) when a column does not have the consecutive-ones property (produces \(>1\) positive and \(>1\) negative entry).


FM-20
Ch 20
Non-TU Integrality Assumption
Assuming an LP relaxation is automatically integral when the constraint matrix contains an odd hole or has \(\det \in \{\pm 2\}\).


FM-21
Ch 21
Bidirectional Hub Short-Circuit (流量短路)
Sharing a single segment-tree tree for both incoming and outgoing range edges (must build separate Out-Tree and In-Tree!).


FM-22
Ch 22
Missing Reverse-Regret Heap Insertion
Pushing a matched pair \((u, v)\) in Simulated MCMF without inserting the regret option \(2x_v - y_u\) into the opposite heap.


FM-23
Ch 23
Uncontracted Blossom Odd Cycle
Running bipartite Hopcroft-Karp on a non-bipartite graph or failing to shrink odd cycles into pseudonodes in Edmonds’ Blossom algorithm.


FM-24
Ch 24
Uncontracted 整体二分 Graph & Parity Blindness
Rebuilding the global \(N\)-node graph inside solve(V_cur, L, R) instead of contracting to \(V_{\text{cur}}\); or binary searching \(X\) when \(c_B \ne c_W\) in [SCOI2012] 奇怪的游戏.


FM-25
Ch 24
Chorded Path in Matroid Intersection
Augmenting along a path in \(G(I)\) that is not shortest in hop count (violates independence in \(\mathcal{M}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\)).


FM-26
Ch 24
3-Layer Flow Amnesia (流量失忆)
Routing 3-attribute items \((a_e, x_e, b_e)\) through \(S \to A \to X \to B \to T\) when multiple items share \(x \in X\), fabricating invalid hybrid triples \((a_1, x, b_2)\).

6. Pre-Submission Checklist (FM-24–FM-26 Audit)
Before submitting any problem from Chapter 24 or an unhinted contest problem, run through this 5-point checklist:

Graph Contraction in 整体二分 (FM-24a): Did you re-index the vertices of \(V_{\text{cur}}\) to \(0 \dots |V_{\text{cur}}| - 1\) so Dinic runs on \(|V_{\text{cur}}| + 2\) vertices, and did you drop all cross-edges between \(T_{\min}\) and \(S_{\min}\) before recursing?
Promotion Reward Sign (FM-24b): Did you verify \(\Delta_i(M) = f_i(M) - f_i(M+1)\) so that vertices with \(y_i > M\) (where moving up to \(M+1\) reduces cost) have \(\Delta_i(M) > 0\) and attach to \(S\)?
Bipartite Parity Check Before Binary Search (FM-24c): On any grid/bipartite increment game, did you check \((c_B - c_W) X = s_B - s_W\) before assuming \(X\) can be binary searched?
Chordless Shortest Path in Matroid Intersection (FM-25): In Edmonds’ Exchange Digraph \(G(I)\), are you breaking weight ties by minimum hop count (pair<cost, hops>) so that simultaneous exchanges along \(P\) never violate independence?
No 3-Layer Flow Amnesia (FM-26): If your flow network has 3 middle layers \(A \to X \to B\), did you confirm that flow entering \(x \in X\) from \(a_1\) is legally allowed to exit to any \(b_2 \in N^+(x)\)?

section: 7. Textbook Capstone Summary & Bridge to Part VI Checkpoint (CP-VI) and Synthesis Reserve
text:
7. Textbook Capstone Summary & Bridge to Part VI Checkpoint (CP-VI) and Synthesis Reserve
Congratulations! Over the course of 24 chapters, you have mastered the complete arc of Competitive Programming Network Flows, Minimum Cuts, Matchings, Min-Cost Circulations, Linear Programming Duality, Simulated Flows, Isotonic Regression, and Matroid Intersection:

Part I (Ch 01–Ch 04): Residual graphs, augmenting paths, Max-Flow Min-Cut duality, Dinic’s algorithm, and unit-network complexity laws.
Part II (Ch 05–Ch 08): Bipartite matching, Hall’s Marriage Theorem, König’s Theorem, DAG path covers, Dilworth’s antichains, and Flows with Lower Bounds.
Part III (Ch 09–Ch 12): Maximum-Weight Closure, 2-Label Burn-Bury (燃やす埋める), Bipartite Variable Inversion, Multi-State Threshold Chains (切糕), and Gomory-Hu Cut Trees.
Part IV (Ch 13–Ch 18): Successive Shortest Path MCMF, Johnson potentials, convex marginal cost splitting, dynamic edge insertion, time-expanded networks, and Min-Cost Circulations.
Part V (Ch 19–Ch 20): Linear Programming Duality, Equation Differencing (志愿者招募), Total Unimodularity, and Inverse Optimization.
Part VI (Ch 21–Ch 24): Data-Structure-Accelerated Flow Graphs, Simulated MCMF (Slope Trick / Regret Heaps), Edmonds’ Blossom Algorithm, \(L_p\) Isotonic Regression (保序回归), Weighted Matroid Intersection, the LGV Lemma, and the Master 3-Stage Recognition Compiler.

Next, test your diagnostic reflexes in the Part VI Checkpoint (CP-VI) and the 20-Problem Unhinted Cross-Chapter Synthesis Reserve (#193–#212), where problem statements appear with zero topic labels — just as they do on the ICPC World Finals and NOI/IOI contest floor!

Multilingual Bibliography & Seminal References

[ZH] 高睿泉 (Zhi-Rui Gao, 2018): 《浅谈保序回归问题》 (On Isotonic Regression Problems), Proceedings of the 2018 Chinese National Olympiad in Informatics (NOI) National Training Team Papers (国家集训队2018论文集). The foundational paper introducing 整体二分 + Maximum-Weight Closure for \(L_p\) Isotonic Regression and Inverse MST / Basis optimization in competitive programming.
[ZH] 胡伯涛 (Bo-Tao Hu / Amber, 2007): 《最小割模型在信息学竞赛中的应用》 (Applications of Minimum Cut Models in Olympiad in Informatics), 国家集训队2007论文集. Establishes the algebraic pseudo-Boolean compilation of closures, density subgraphs, and threshold cuts.
[EN] Jack Edmonds (1970): “Submodular Functions, Matroids, and Certain Polyhedra”, in Combinatorial Structures and Their Applications, Gordon and Breach, pp. 69–87. Proves the Matroid Intersection Duality Theorem and Polymatroid Min-Cut Theorem.
[EN] Bernt Lindström (1973) & Ira Gessel, Gérard Viennot (1985): “Binomial Determinants, Paths, and Hook Length Formulae”, Advances in Mathematics 58(3), pp. 300–321. The canonical reference for the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot determinant lemma on non-intersecting DAG path systems.
[EN] Ravindra K. Ahuja, Thomas L. Magnanti, and James B. Orlin (1993): Network Flows: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications, Prentice Hall. Comprehensive treatment of network simplex, parametric flows, inverse optimization, and matroid flows.
[JA] noshi91, maspypy, & tatyam (2019–2023): 「燃やす埋める問題と劣モジュラ関数」「マトロイド交差 (Matroid Intersection)」, Japanese competitive programming treatises unifying submodular cut compilation, Lovász extensions, and chordless exchange-graph augmentation.

title: Checkpoint II — Bipartite Matching, König–Hall–Dilworth Duality, and Decomposition
text:
In Chapters 05 through 08, you studied the four structural pillars of Part II:

Chapter 05 — Bipartite Matching & König’s Duality: Converting 2D assignment, prefix-sequential matching, and Minimum Vertex Cover (\(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\)) / Maximum Independent Set (\(\alpha(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\)) problems into unit bipartite networks.
Chapter 06 — Grid & Parity Matching, Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition & Games: Discovering hidden bipartiteness via coordinate parity invariants, decomposing vertices into essential (\(E\)), optional (\(O\)), and forbidden (\(N\)) classes, and solving two-player bipartite walk games (博弈).
Chapter 07 — Non-Graph Bipartite Reductions, 2D Line/Factor Incidence & \(b\)-Matching: Compiling non-graph arrays, prime factorizations, maximal H/V grid strips (Royal Guards), and degree-constrained 2-factors (Fox and Dinner) into bipartite incidence graphs.
Chapter 08 — Hall’s Marriage Theorem, Dilworth’s Poset Duality & Submodular Deficiency: Exploiting Hall’s deficiency formula \(\nu(G) = |L| - \max_{S \subseteq L}(|S| - |N(S)|)\) to eliminate explicit flow networks on structured intervals, and compiling DAG path covers and poset antichains via Dilworth’s theorem.

When you solve problems inside a specific chapter, the chapter title gives away the paradigm. In a live contest, nobody tells you whether a problem is a König vertex cover, a Dulmage–Mendelsohn game, a poset antichain, a Hall deficiency DP, or a non-flow 0-1 BFS decoy.



Pass 1 — Diagnostic Triage (15 minutes total for Section 1, 5 minutes per problem in Section 2): Read the raw, untagged problem statement and constraints. Without opening any callouts, write down:

Target Paradigm: Is this Maximum Matching (Ch 05), König MVC/MIS (Ch 05–06), Dulmage–Mendelsohn Game (Ch 06), Bipartite \(b\)-Matching / Incidence (Ch 07), Dilworth Poset Antichain / DAG Path Cover (Ch 08), Hall’s Deficiency (Ch 08), or a Non-Flow Decoy?
Left vs. Right Bipartition: What are the two disjoint vertex sets \(L\) and \(R\), and what invariant proves there are no odd cycles?
Primal vs. Dual Objective: Are you maximizing packed edges \(\nu(G)\), minimizing covering lines \(\tau(G)\), maximizing mutually compatible elements \(\alpha(G) = |V| - \nu(G)\), or decomposing a poset into chains?

Pass 2 — Progressive Hints (Hint 1 \(\to\) Hint 2): If your diagnostic stalls after 5 minutes, open Hint 1 (which reveals the structural bipartition or duality lens without giving away the graph wiring). Only open Hint 2 if you need the explicit algebraic-to-graph translation.
Pass 3 — Full 4-Step Compilation Audit: Compare your scratchpad against the Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution callout. Pay special attention to Step 4 (Broken Gadget Counterexamples), which audits the two signature Part II failure modes: omitting transitive closure before applying Dilworth (FM-07) and using standard \((r+c) \bmod 2\) checkerboard coloring on parity-preserving jumps (FM-08).

title: Checkpoint II — Bipartite Matching, König–Hall–Dilworth Duality, and Decomposition
text:
1. Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills
For each of the six miniature scenarios below, identify the exact Part II mechanism (Ch 05–Ch 08), the bipartition \((L, R)\), and any active failure mode (FM-07 or FM-08) in under 90 seconds before expanding the diagnostic key.


Drill 1.1 — Multi-Delegation Table Seating & Quota Assignment

Scenario (Luogu P3254 圆桌问题 / Luogu P2763 试题库问题): \(M \le 150\) delegations (delegation \(i\) has \(r_i\) members) must be seated across \(N \le 270\) dining tables (table \(j\) has capacity \(c_j\)) such that no two members of the same delegation sit at the same table. Determine if a valid seating exists and reconstruct the table assignment for every delegation.







TipDiagnostic Triage Key — Drill 1.1






Target Paradigm: Ch 07 (§7.3 Bipartite \(b\)-Matching / Gale–Ryser Multi-Allocation) & Ch 01 (§1.2).
Diagnostic Signal: Two disjoint entity classes (Delegations \(L\), Tables \(R\)) with vertex supply/demand caps \((r_i, c_j)\) and a pairwise uniqueness constraint (“at most one member of delegation \(i\) at table \(j\)”).
Algebraic & Graph Compilation: Let \(x_{i,j} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether delegation \(i\) sends a representative to table \(j\). We require \(\sum_{j=1}^N x_{i,j} = r_i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^M x_{i,j} \le c_j\). Wire \(S \xrightarrow{r_i} \text{Del}_i\), \(\text{Del}_i \xrightarrow{1} \text{Tab}_j\), and \(\text{Tab}_j \xrightarrow{c_j} T\). A valid seating exists iff \(\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) = \sum_{i=1}^M r_i\).
Critical Failure Guard: Setting the cross-edge capacity \(\text{Del}_i \to \text{Tab}_j\) to \(\infty\) instead of \(1\) destroys the uniqueness constraint and allows all \(r_i\) members of delegation \(i\) to crowd onto a single table.







Drill 1.2 — Prime-Sum Circular Dining Tables

Scenario (Codeforces 510 E — Fox And Dinner): Given \(N \le 200\) foxes with integer ages \(a_i \ge 2\), seat all \(N\) foxes around circular tables of size at least \(3\) such that every pair of adjacent foxes around any table hasages summing to a prime number.







TipDiagnostic Triage Key — Drill 1.2






Target Paradigm: Ch 06 (§6.1 Parity Bipartition) + Ch 07 (§7.3 Bipartite \(2\)-Factor Cycle Decomposition).
Diagnostic Signal: Every vertex in a collection of disjoint simple cycles has degree exactly \(2\), and since \(a_i \ge 2\), any prime sum \(a_i + a_j\) must be an odd prime (\(a_i + a_j \ge 4 > 2\)).
Algebraic & Graph Compilation: An odd prime sum requires one odd age and one even age! Partition the foxes into \(L = \{i : a_i \text{ is odd}\}\) and \(R = \{j : a_j \text{ is even}\}\). If \(|L| \neq |R|\), output Impossible. Otherwise, wire \(S \xrightarrow{2} u\) for \(u \in L\), \(v \xrightarrow{2} T\) for \(v \in R\), and \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\) whenever \(a_u + a_v\) is prime.
Why Cycles Have Length \(\ge 4\) Automatically: Because each cross-edge \(u \to v\) has capacity \(1\), the two incident edges chosen for any fox \(u\) must go to two distinct neighbors \(v_1 \neq v_2\), eliminating \(2\)-cycles. Since the graph is bipartite, every simple cycle has even length \(\ge 4 > 3\). Check \(\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) = N\) and extract cycles via DFS on saturated cross-edges.







Drill 1.3 — Laser Attack Devices on a Chessboard (FM-08 Audit)

Scenario (Luogu P4304 [TJOI2013] 攻击装置 vs. (±2, ±2) Bishop Traps): On an \(N \times N\) grid (\(N \le 200\)) with obstacles, place the maximum number of mutually non-attacking devices. Compare two rules:

Rule A: Device attacks \((\pm 1, \pm 2)\) and \((\pm 2, \pm 1)\) (standard knight jumps).
Rule B: Device attacks \((\pm 1, \pm 3)\) and \((\pm 3, \pm 1)\) (camel/giraffe jumps).








TipDiagnostic Triage Key — Drill 1.3






Target Paradigm: Ch 06 (§6.2 Coordinate-Parity Bipartite MIS: \(\alpha(G) = |V_{\text{free}}| - \nu(G)\)) and FM-08 (Broken Parity Invariant).
Algebraic Parity Audit:

Under Rule A, \(\Delta r + \Delta c \in \{\pm 1, \pm 3\}\) is always odd, so \((r + c) \bmod 2\) flips on every attack edge. Coloring by \((r + c) \bmod 2\) yields a valid bipartition.
Under Rule B, \(\Delta r + \Delta c \in \{0, \pm 2, \pm 4\}\) is always even! If you color by \((r + c) \bmod 2\), every attack edge connects two cells of the same color (FM-08 trap!). However, \(\Delta r \in \{\pm 1, \pm 3\}\) is always odd, so row parity \(r \bmod 2\) (and likewise \(c \bmod 2\)) strictly alternates on every attack edge!

Lesson: Never hardcode \((r + c) \bmod 2\) by reflex. Always compute the generator increments \((\Delta r, \Delta c)\) and find a linear functional \(\phi(r, c)\) (or bit-shifted parity \(\lfloor r/2^k \rfloor \bmod 2\)) that evaluates to \(1 \pmod 2\) on all step vectors.







Drill 1.4 — Mutually Unrelated String Antigens (FM-07 Audit)

Scenario (Codeforces 590 E — Birthday): Given \(N \le 750\) distinct strings of total length \(\sum |s_i| \le 10^7\) over {a, b}, select the maximum number of strings such that no chosen string is a contiguous substring of another chosen string, and print the chosen indices.







TipDiagnostic Triage Key — Drill 1.4






Target Paradigm: Ch 08 (§8.2 Dilworth’s Poset Maximum Antichain & constructive Kőnig extraction via Aho–Corasick).
Diagnostic Signal: The substring relation \(s_u \subseteq_{\text{sub}} s_v\) is reflexive, antisymmetric (on distinct strings), and transitive — it defines a strict poset \((P, \prec)\). “No chosen string is a substring of another” asks for a Maximum Antichain.
Critical FM-07 Guard: In the Aho–Corasick automaton, a single fail-link jump from \(s_v\) only finds the longest proper suffix of prefixes of \(s_v\) that appears in the dictionary. If you only add direct Aho–Corasick transitions without computing the transitive closure of the reachability DAG, a 3-chain \(s_x \prec s_y \prec s_z\) where \(s_x \to s_z\) is omitted allows the non-transitive path cover to undercount the antichain (FM-07)! You must collapse fail-tree ancestors to find direct dictionary predecessors for each prefix of \(s_v\), then run Floyd–Warshall (\(N \le 750\)) before bipartite matching.







Drill 1.5 — 3D Cuboid Chemical Disinfection

Scenario (Luogu P3231 [HNOI2013] 消毒): You are given a 3D grid of dimensions \(A \times B \times C\) containing infected cells \((x, y, z)\), where \(A \cdot B \cdot C \le 5000\). Sterilizing a sub-box of dimensions \(p \times q \times r\) costs \(\min(p, q, r)\) units of chemical. Find the minimum total cost to sterilize all infected cells.







TipDiagnostic Triage Key — Drill 1.5






Target Paradigm: Ch 07 (§7.1 Dimensional Slice Reduction) + Ch 05 (§5.2 König 2D Line Cover).
Diagnostic Signal: A slice of thickness \(1\) along any axis (\(1 \times B \times C\), \(A \times 1 \times C\), or \(A \times B \times 1\)) costs \(\min(1, \dots) = 1\), and any box of cost \(k\) can be decomposed into \(k\) unit-thickness planes! Thus we are covering 3D points \((x, y, z)\) with axis-parallel planes at cost \(1\) per plane.
Why 3D Line Cover Is NP-Hard — And How Constraints Rescue It: Minimum Vertex Cover on a 3-uniform hypergraph is NP-hard, but \(A \cdot B \cdot C \le 5000 \implies \min(A, B, C) \le \lfloor 5000^{1/3} \rfloor = 17\)!
Compilation: Permute coordinates so \(A \le 17\). Enumerate the bitmask \(S \subseteq \{0, \dots, A-1\}\) of \(x\)-planes sterilised directly (\(2^{17}\) masks). All remaining infected cells \((x, y, z)\) with \(x \notin S\) project onto a 2D \((y, z)\) grid, whose minimum plane cover is \(\nu(G_{y,z})\) by König’s Theorem (Ch 05)!







Drill 1.6 — Two-Player Token Walk on a Grid with Obstacles

Scenario (Luogu P4055 [JSOI2009] 游戏): An \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 100\)) has passable cells . and obstacles #. Alice places a token on a starting cell \(v_0\); then Bob and Alice alternate moving the token to an adjacent unvisited passable cell. The first player unable to move loses. Find all starting cells \(v_0\) from which Bob (the first mover) has a winning strategy.







TipDiagnostic Triage Key — Drill 1.6






Target Paradigm: Ch 06 (§6.3 Dulmage–Mendelsohn Essential Vertex Theorem & Joyner–Edmonds Bipartite Walk Game).
Diagnostic Signal: Impartial normal-play path-extension game on a bipartite graph (\(2\)-colored by \((r+c) \bmod 2\)).
Theorem & Compilation: Bob (first mover from \(v_0\)) has a winning strategy if and only if \(v_0\) belongs to EVERY maximum matching of \(G\) (\(v_0 \in E_L \cup E_R\) in the Dulmage–Mendelsohn decomposition).

Compute a maximum matching \(M^*\) on the \((r+c) \bmod 2\) bipartite graph.
Any unmatched vertex \(u\) can never be entered by a matched edge, so flood-fill alternating paths (unmatched \(\xrightarrow{\text{non-}M^*}\) matched \(\xrightarrow{M^*}\) matched) from all unmatched vertices in \(L\) and \(R\).
Every vertex not reached by this alternating BFS/DFS is essential (\(v_0 \in E\)) and is a winning start for Bob.
