title: Checkpoint II — Bipartite Matching, König–Hall–Dilworth Duality, and Decomposition
text:
2. Blind Checkpoint Problems (#201–#208)
Attempt each problem below under blind contest conditions before opening the progressive hints or the 4-step compilation key.


Problem #201 — Placing Rooks & Multi-Quota Incidence (Luogu P10937 / CH 6801 車的放置 & Luogu P1894 / P2763)

Problem Statement: You are given an \(N \times M\) chessboard (\(1 \le N, M \le 200\)) in which \(T\) specified cells \((r_k, c_k)\) are forbidden (muddy/damaged) and cannot hold a piece. Two rooks attack each other if they share the same row or the same column (forbidden cells do not block rook attacks).

Part A (Luogu P10937): Find the maximum number of mutually non-attacking rooks that can be placed on the non-forbidden cells of the board.
Part B (Multi-Quota Extension — Luogu P2763 试题库问题): Suppose instead that row \(r\) can hold at most \(1\) rook, column \(c\) requires exactly \(q_c \ge 1\) rooks, and you must reconstruct which rows are assigned to each column \(c\).








NoteHint 1 — Structural Recognition & Bipartition





Instead of viewing a cell \((r, c)\) as a vertex in a conflict graph of size \(N \times M = 40{,}000\), ask: what are the two orthogonal resources consumed when you place a rook at \((r, c)\)? Every rook consumes one row \(r \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and one column \(c \in \{1, \dots, M\}\).









NoteHint 2 — Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation





Introduce a binary indicator variable \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\) for each allowed cell \((r, c) \notin \mathcal{F}\). The non-attacking rules are linear degree bounds on the bipartite incidence graph between \(L = \{\text{Row}_1, \dots, \text{Row}_N\}\) and \(R = \{\text{Col}_1, \dots, \text{Col}_M\}\).









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #201






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Cues: Grid coordinates \((r, c)\) with \(N, M \le 200\), \(T\) forbidden cells, and global row/column mutual exclusion (“at most \(1\) rook per row and at most \(1\) rook per column”).
Why Naive DP / Conflict Graph Fails: Bitmask DP over columns takes \(O(N 2^M)\), which is impossible for \(M = 200\). Building a cell-conflict graph with \(V = NM \le 4 \times 10^4\) vertices and \(O(NM(N+M))\) edges loses the bipartite structure (a row of cells forms a clique!). The key shift is Rank-2 Coordinate-to-Edge Duality (Ch 05.1 / Ch 07.1): rows and columns are vertices; allowed cells are edges.



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(\mathcal{A} = (\{1..N\} \times \{1..M\}) \setminus \mathcal{F}\) be the set of allowed cells, and let \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether a rook is placed at \((r, c) \in \mathcal{A}\).
\[\max \sum_{(r,c) \in \mathcal{A}} x_{r,c} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{c : (r,c) \in \mathcal{A}} x_{r,c} \le 1 \;\; (\forall r), \qquad \sum_{r : (r,c) \in \mathcal{A}} x_{r,c} \le q_c \;\; (\forall c),\]
where \(q_c = 1\) in Part A and \(q_c \ge 1\) in Part B.


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Vertices: Source \(S\), Sink \(T\), Left row nodes \(L = \{R_1, \dots, R_N\}\), Right column nodes \(R = \{C_1, \dots, C_M\}\).
Arcs:

Row supply bound \(\sum_c x_{r,c} \le 1 \implies\) directed arc \(S \xrightarrow{1} R_r\) for each \(r \in \{1..N\}\).
Allowed cell decision \(x_{r,c} \in \{0, 1\} \implies\) directed arc \(R_r \xrightarrow{1} C_c\) for each \((r, c) \in \mathcal{A}\).
Column quota bound \(\sum_r x_{r,c} \le q_c \implies\) directed arc \(C_c \xrightarrow{q_c} T\) for each \(c \in \{1..M\}\).

Part A Output: \(\nu(G) = \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)\) in \(O(E \sqrt{V}) = O(NM \sqrt{N+M})\) via Hopcroft–Karp or Dinic.
Part B Output: Check \(\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) == \sum_{c=1}^M q_c\); if satisfied, for each column \(C_c\), collect all \(R_r\) whose arc \(R_r \to C_c\) carries flow \(1\) (residual capacity == 0).



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (\(N = M = 3\), forbidden \(\mathcal{F} = \{(1,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,3)\}\)):

Allowed edges: \(R_1 \to C_3\), \(R_2 \to \{C_1, C_2\}\), \(R_3 \to \{C_1, C_2\}\).
Augmenting paths saturate \(R_1 \to C_3\), \(R_2 \to C_1\), and \(R_3 \to C_2\), giving \(\nu(G) = 3\) rooks at \((1,3), (2,1), (3,2)\).

Broken Gadget Counterexample: Suppose a solver forgets to deduplicate input forbidden cells \((r_k, c_k)\) and instead subtracts \(1\) from a count matrix without clamping, adding duplicate parallel edges \(R_r \to C_c\) in Part B. Then a single cell \((r, c)\) could contribute \(2\) units of flow to column \(C_c\)’s quota \(q_c\), placing two rooks on the exact same cell! Always store a boolean grid forbidden[r][c] and emit at most one unit-capacity arc per \((r, c)\).








Problem #202 — Sequential Stage Clearance (Luogu P2319 [HNOI2006] 超级英雄)

Problem Statement: A game show consists of \(M\) sequential stages numbered \(1, 2, \dots, M\) (\(1 \le M \le 1000\)) and a pool of \(N\) distinct “Hint Keys” numbered \(0, 1, \dots, N-1\) (\(1 \le N \le 1000\)).

To clear stage \(i\), the contestant must use one of two specified Hint Keys \((u_i, v_i) \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}^2\) associated with stage \(i\).
Each Hint Key in \(\{0, \dots, N-1\}\) can be used at most once across the entire game.
The contestant plays stages strictly in order \(i = 1, 2, \dots, M\) and stops immediately at the first stage \(i\) that cannot be cleared (even if later stages \(j > i\) could still be cleared).

Compute the maximum number of consecutive stages \(K\) (\(0 \le K \le M\)) the contestant can clear starting from stage \(1\), and print the sequence of \(K\) Hint Keys used at stages \(1, 2, \dots, K\).







NoteHint 1 — Prefix Monotonicity vs. Offline Binary Search





Because the contestant must clear a contiguous prefix \(1, 2, \dots, K\) of stages, stages \(K+1, \dots, M\) must not steal keys from earlier stages. You could binary search \(K\) and run bipartite matching from scratch, but how does Kuhn’s augmenting-path algorithm behave when you insert left vertices \(i = 1, 2, \dots, M\) one by one?









NoteHint 2 — Incremental Kuhn Invariant & Reconstruction Trap





In Kuhn’s algorithm (find_augmenting_path(i)), augmenting from stage \(i\) can rearrange the key assignments among stages \(\{1, \dots, i-1\}\), but it never unmatches an already-matched stage \(j < i\)! Be careful at the end: if you store match_stage[key] = stage, how do you print the key chosen for each stage \(1 \dots K\) in order?









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #202






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Cues: Sequential stages \(i = 1, \dots, M\) (\(M \le 1000\)), each offering \(2\) candidate keys \((u_i, v_i) \in \{0..N-1\}^2\), each key usable at most once, stopping at the first unmatchable stage.
Why Greedy Fails: Choosing \(u_1\) at stage \(1\) might block stage \(2\) (which only accepts \((u_1, u_1)\)), whereas choosing \(v_1\) at stage \(1\) lets both stages pass. An augmenting path automatically “regrets” stage \(1\)’s choice from \(u_1\) to \(v_1\).



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For a prefix length \(K \in \{0, \dots, M\}\), we seek an injective map \(\pi : \{1, \dots, K\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}\) such that \(\pi(i) \in \{u_i, v_i\}\) for every \(1 \le i \le K\). By Berge’s Augmenting Path Theorem (Ch 05.1), the set of matchable left vertices in a bipartite graph is a matroid (transversal matroid): if \(\{1, \dots, i-1\}\) is matchable, then \(\{1, \dots, i\}\) is matchable iff there exists an \(M\)-augmenting path starting at stage \(i\) in the subgraph induced by \(\{1, \dots, i\} \cup \{0, \dots, N-1\}\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Bipartite Graph: Left vertices \(L = \{1, \dots, M\}\) (stages, added online), Right vertices \(R = \{0, \dots, N-1\}\) (Hint Keys). Each stage \(i \in L\) has at most \(2\) outgoing edges \(i \to u_i\) and \(i \to v_i\).
Online Incremental Kuhn Loop:

Initialize match_stage[0..N-1] = 0 and ans_key[1..M] = -1.
For \(i = 1, 2, \dots, M\):

Run a standard Kuhn DFS dfs(i) with visitation timestamp vis_key[k] == i.
Inside dfs(u): for each \(k \in \{u_u, v_u\}\), if vis_key[k] != current_step, mark vis_key[k] = current_step; if match_stage[k] == 0 or dfs(match_stage[k]) succeeds, set match_stage[k] = u, ans_key[u] = k, and return true.
If dfs(i) returns false, break immediately! Do not process stages \(i+1 \dots M\).

Print \(K = i - 1\) followed by ans_key[1] through ans_key[K].

Complexity: At most \(M\) DFS phases, each traversing at most \(2M\) edges \(\implies O(M^2)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (\(N = 3, M = 3\): Stage 1 has \((0, 1)\), Stage 2 has \((0, 0)\), Stage 3 has \((1, 1)\)):

\(i = 1\): dfs(1) matches Stage \(1 \to\) Key \(0\) (ans_key[1] = 0).
\(i = 2\): dfs(2) inspects Key \(0\) (held by Stage \(1\)), recurses dfs(1) which shifts Stage \(1 \to\) Key \(1\) (ans_key[1] = 1), and matches Stage \(2 \to\) Key \(0\) (ans_key[2] = 0).
\(i = 3\): dfs(3) inspects Key \(1 \to\) Stage \(1 \to\) Key \(0 \to\) Stage \(2 \to\) dead end. Returns false and stops. Output \(K = 2\), keys [1, 0].

Broken Gadget Counterexample:

Continuing the loop after dfs(i) fails: If Stage 3 fails ((1, 1)) and Stage 4 has (2, 2), continuing the loop matches Stage 4 to Key 2 and increments the count, violating the rule that the game terminates on the first failed stage!
Building the full \(M\)-stage Dinic network up front: Running Max-Flow on all \(M\) stages simultaneously allows Stage \(4\) to steal a key from Stage \(2\) if Stage \(4\) and Stage \(5\) together yield more total flow than Stage \(2\) alone. Incremental prefix insertion is mandatory.









Problem #203 — Exact Domino Tiling vs. Domino Cover (POJ 2446 Chessboard & POJ 3020 Antenna Placement)

Problem Statement: You are given an \(M \times N\) rectangular grid (\(1 \le M, N \le 32\)) from which \(K\) specific unit squares have been removed (holes).

Part A (POJ 2446 Chessboard): Determine whether the remaining \(MN - K\) intact squares can be tiled exactly by non-overlapping \(1 \times 2\) dominoes (so every intact square is covered by exactly one domino, and no domino covers a hole or extends outside the board).
Part B (Domino Cover Contrast — POJ 3020 Antenna Placement): Suppose instead that \(1 \times 2\) dominoes are allowed to overlap on intact squares (still forbidden from covering holes), and you want the minimum number of dominoes needed to cover all \(MN - K\) intact squares. How does the formula change?








NoteHint 1 — Parity Coloring & Necessary Cardinality Check





Every \(1 \times 2\) domino covers two orthogonally adjacent cells \((r, c)\) and \((r', c')\) with \(|r - r'| + |c - c'| = 1\). How does \((r + c) \bmod 2\) behave across those two cells? What immediately happens if the number of intact black squares \(|B|\) does not equal the number of intact white squares \(|W|\)?









NoteHint 2 — Perfect Matching vs. Gallai’s Minimum Edge Cover





In Part A, non-overlapping dominoes covering every intact cell correspond to a Perfect Matching (\(\nu(G) = |B| = |W|\)). In Part B, overlapping dominoes correspond to a Minimum Edge Cover \(\gamma(G)\) (selecting the minimum number of edges/singletons to cover all intact vertices). Express \(\gamma(G)\) in terms of \(|V_{\text{intact}}|\) and \(\nu(G)\)!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #203






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Cues: Grid of intact cells (\(MN \le 1024\)), local \(1 \times 2\) orthogonal adjacency (\(|r - r'| + |c - c'| = 1\)), and exact partitioning (Part A) vs. minimum covering (Part B).
Why Profile / Broken-Profile DP Is Unnecessary: Profile DP takes \(O(MN 2^{\min(M,N)})\), which is \(\approx 32 \cdot 1024 \cdot 2^{32} \approx 10^{14}\) operations for \(M = N = 32\) (TLE!). Because we only ask for existence (or minimum count) rather than the number of tilings, bipartite matching solves \(M, N \le 32\) in milliseconds.



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Color every intact cell \((r, c) \notin \mathcal{H}\) by its checkerboard parity:
\[B = \{(r, c) \notin \mathcal{H} : (r + c) \equiv 0 \pmod 2\}, \qquad W = \{(r, c) \notin \mathcal{H} : (r + c) \equiv 1 \pmod 2\}.\]
Let \(E\) be the set of orthogonal intact cell pairs \((u, v) \in B \times W\) with \(\|u - v\|_1 = 1\), and let \(x_{uv} \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether domino \((u, v)\) is placed.

Part A (Exact Disjoint Tiling): Every \(u \in B\) and \(v \in W\) must have degree exactly \(1\), which holds iff \(|B| = |W|\) and the maximum matching size satisfies \(\nu(G) = |B|\).
Part B (Minimum Overlapping Cover — Gallai’s Identity, Ch 05.3): Every matched edge in a maximum matching \(M^*\) covers two intact cells at cost \(1\), while the remaining \(|V_{\text{intact}}| - 2\nu(G)\) unmatched cells each require one additional domino of cost \(1\):

\[\gamma(G) = \nu(G) + \bigl(|V_{\text{intact}}| - 2\nu(G)\bigr) = |V_{\text{intact}}| - \nu(G).\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Vertices: Left set \(B\) (intact even-parity cells), Right set \(W\) (intact odd-parity cells). Total vertices \(|B| + |W| = MN - K \le 1024\).
Edges: For each \(u = (r, c) \in B\) and each of its \(4\) orthogonal neighbors \(v = (r + \Delta r, c + \Delta c)\) with \((\Delta r, \Delta c) \in \{(\pm 1, 0), (0, \pm 1)\}\), if \(v\) is in-bounds and intact, add directed edge \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\).
Part A Check: If \(|B| \neq |W|\), immediately return NO. Otherwise compute \(\nu(G)\) via Hopcroft–Karp / Dinic and return YES iff \(\nu(G) == |B|\).
Part B Check: Return \((|B| + |W|) - \nu(G)\).
Complexity: \(V \le 1024, E \le 2048 \implies O(E \sqrt{V}) \approx 6 \times 10^4\) operations.



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (\(2 \times 3\) board with holes at \((1,1)\) and \((2,3)\) — Opposite Corners Removed):

Remaining cells: \(B = \{(1,3), (2,2)\}\) (\(|B| = 2\)), \(W = \{(1,2), (2,1)\}\) (\(|W| = 2\)).
Edges: \((1,3) \to (1,2)\), \((2,2) \to (1,2)\), \((2,2) \to (2,1)\).
Maximum matching: \((1,3) \to (1,2)\) and \((2,2) \to (2,1)\), so \(\nu(G) = 2 = |B| \implies\) YES!
By contrast, on a \(4 \times 4\) board with opposite corners \((1,1)\) and \((4,4)\) removed (both in \(B\)), \(|B| = 6 \neq |W| = 8 \implies\) instant NO.

Broken Gadget Counterexample: Checking only \(\nu(G) == |B|\) without checking \(|B| == |W|\) in Part A! If a \(1 \times 3\) board has no holes and \((1,1), (1,3) \in W\) (\(|W| = 2\)) while \((1,2) \in B\) (\(|B| = 1\)), then \(\nu(G) = 1 == |B|\), yet cell \((1,3) \in W\) is left uncovered! Both \(|B| == |W|\) and \(\nu(G) == |B|\) are mandatory.








Problem #204 — Giraffe Placement on a Damaged Board (Luogu P5030 长脖子鹿放置)

Problem Statement: You are given an \(N \times M\) chessboard (\(1 \le N, M \le 200\)) with \(K\) forbidden cells that cannot hold a piece. A giraffe placed at cell \((r, c)\) attacks up to \(8\) cells at offsets:
\[(\Delta r, \Delta c) \in \{(\pm 1, \pm 3),\; (\pm 3, \pm 1)\}.\]
Forbidden cells do not block giraffe jumps. Find the maximum number of mutually non-attacking giraffes that can be placed on the non-forbidden cells of the board.







NoteHint 1 — Audit the Checkerboard Parity Trap (FM-08)





Test what happens to the standard knight coloring \((r + c) \bmod 2\) when a giraffe jumps by \((\Delta r, \Delta c) \in \{(\pm 1, \pm 3), (\pm 3, \pm 1)\}\). Since \(\Delta r + \Delta c \in \{0, \pm 2, \pm 4\}\) is even, \((r + c) \bmod 2\) is invariant under giraffe jumps! What simple coordinate parity does flip on every giraffe jump?









NoteHint 2 — Bipartite Maximum Independent Set





Every giraffe jump changes \(r\) by \(\pm 1\) or \(\pm 3\) (an odd integer) and changes \(c\) by \(\pm 3\) or \(\pm 1\) (also an odd integer). Therefore, coloring intact cells by row parity \(r \bmod 2\) (or column parity \(c \bmod 2\)) guarantees that every attack edge connects an even-row cell to an odd-row cell! Now apply König’s MIS formula.









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #204






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Cues: “Place the maximum number of mutually non-attacking pieces on an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 200\)) with forbidden cells” under fixed translation jumps \((\pm 1, \pm 3), (\pm 3, \pm 1)\).
Why It Is a Classic FM-08 Diagnostic Trap: Every competitive programmer memorizes \((r + c) \bmod 2\) from 骑士共存问题 (Luogu P3355, where knight jumps have \(|\Delta r| + |\Delta c| = 3\), odd). Here \(|\Delta r| + |\Delta c| = 4\) (even), so \((r + c) \bmod 2\) puts all attacking pairs on the same side of the bipartition!



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let \(V_{\text{free}}\) be the set of deduplicated non-forbidden cells (|V_free| = NM - |F|). For any giraffe jump \((r, c) \leftrightarrow (r', c')\), we have:
\[r' - r \in \{\pm 1, \pm 3\} \implies r' \equiv r + 1 \pmod 2.\]
Thus the conflict graph \(G = (V_{\text{free}}, E)\) is bipartite with parts:
\[L = \{(r, c) \in V_{\text{free}} : r \equiv 1 \pmod 2\}, \qquad R = \{(r, c) \in V_{\text{free}} : r \equiv 0 \pmod 2\}.\]
Selecting the maximum number of mutually non-attacking giraffes is the Maximum Independent Set \(\alpha(G)\) on the bipartite graph \(G\). By König’s Theorem (Ch 05.2 / Ch 06.2):
\[\alpha(G) = |V_{\text{free}}| - \tau(G) = |V_{\text{free}}| - \nu(G).\]


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Deduplication First: Input forbidden lists in Luogu P5030 can contain duplicate coordinates \((r_k, c_k)\)! Mark bad[r][c] = true and count \(|V_{\text{free}}|\) directly over \((r, c) \in [1..N] \times [1..M]\) where !bad[r][c].
Vertices: Source \(S\), Sink \(T\), Left set \(L\) (intact odd-row cells), Right set \(R\) (intact even-row cells).
Arcs:

For each \(u = (r, c) \in L\), add \(S \xrightarrow{1} u\).
For each \(v = (r', c') \in R\), add \(v \xrightarrow{1} T\).
For each \(u = (r, c) \in L\) and each of the \(8\) offsets \((\Delta r, \Delta c) \in \{(\pm 1, \pm 3), (\pm 3, \pm 1)\}\), if \(v = (r + \Delta r, c + \Delta c)\) is in-bounds and !bad[r + dr][c + dc], add directed edge \(u \xrightarrow{1} v\).

Output: \(|V_{\text{free}}| - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)\).
Complexity: \(V \le 4 \times 10^4, E \le 1.6 \times 10^5\); Dinic runs in \(O(E \sqrt{V}) \approx 3 \times 10^7\) operations (\(\approx 40\text{ ms}\)).



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (\(N = 2, M = 4\), no forbidden cells):

\(|V_{\text{free}}| = 8\); \(L = \{(1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (1,4)\}\) (row \(1\)), \(R = \{(2,1), (2,2), (2,3), (2,4)\}\) (row \(2\)).
Only \((\Delta r, \Delta c) = (+1, \pm 3)\) stays inside \(2 \times 4\): edges are \((1,1) \to (2,4)\) and \((1,4) \to (2,1)\).
Maximum matching \(\nu(G) = 2\), so \(\alpha(G) = 8 - 2 = 6\) giraffes (e.g., all cells except \((2,1)\) and \((2,4)\)).

Broken Gadget Counterexample (FM-08): Suppose a solver partitions cells by \((r + c) \bmod 2\) and only adds edges from even \((r+c)\) to odd \((r+c)\). Since \((1,1)\) has \(1+1=2\) (even) and \((2,4)\) has \(2+4=6\) (even), the conflict \((1,1) \leftrightarrow (2,4)\) connects two vertices in \(L\) and is completely dropped! The solver obtains \(\nu = 0\) and outputs \(8 - 0 = 8\), placing attacking giraffes at \((1,1)\) and \((2,4)\).








Problem #205 — Nested Bracket Depth & L-Corner Border Matching (Codeforces 1264 D2 & Codeforces 1404 E Bricks)

Problem Statement: This dual-track problem tests when a matching/cut duality collapses to a 1D split point versus a 2D bipartite conflict graph:

Track A — 1D Split-Point Duality (Codeforces 1264 D2 — Beautiful Bracket Sequence (Hard Version)): You are given a string \(s\) of length \(N \le 10^6\) consisting of (, ), and ?. The nested depth of a fixed bracket string is the maximum integer \(k\) such that there exists a subsequence of \(k\) opening brackets ( followed by \(k\) closing brackets ) (i.e., \(i_1 < \dots < i_k < j_1 < \dots < j_k\) with \(s[i_r] = \text{'('}\) and \(s[j_r] = \text{')'}\)). Sum the nested depth over all \(2^{\#?}\) ways to replace ? with ( or ), modulo \(998244353\).
Track B — 2D Bipartite Border Conflict (Codeforces 1404 E — Bricks): You are given an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 200\)) of black (#) and white (.) cells. Find the minimum number of non-overlapping \(1 \times k\) or \(k \times 1\) bricks needed to cover all black cells without covering any white cell.








NoteHint 1 — 1D Cut Split Point (Track A) vs. 2D Internal Borders (Track B)






Track A: View matching \(k\) (s on the left with \(k\) )s on the right as a maximum matching in a prefix-to-suffix bipartite graph. By König / Min-Cut duality, every valid configuration has a unique split index \(i \in \{1, \dots, N-1\}\) where the number of ( in \(s[1..i]\) equals the number of ) in \(s[i+1..N]\)!
Track B: Every \(1 \times 1\) black cell starts as \(1\) brick (total \(\#\text{black}\) bricks). Merging two adjacent black cells across a horizontal or vertical interior border reduces the brick count by \(1\), provided no cell simultaneously merges both horizontally and vertically (an L-corner!).










NoteHint 2 — Vandermonde Convolution (Track A) & Bipartite MIS on Borders (Track B)






Track A: At split point \(i\), if \(s[i] = \text{'('}\) (or ? fixed to (), the contribution of split \(i\) equals \(1\) for every completion where #(( in \(1..i-1\)) \(+ 1 =\) #($)in $i+1..N$). Sum this over the number of?` chosen via Vandermonde’s identity \(\sum_t \binom{A}{t}\binom{B}{C-t} = \binom{A+B}{C}\)!
Track B: Build a bipartite conflict graph where \(L =\) horizontal interior borders between two black cells, \(R =\) vertical interior borders between two black cells, and edges connect borders sharing a common black cell. Maximize compatible saved merges \(\alpha(G) = |V_{\text{borders}}| - \nu(G)\)!










TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #205






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Track A (CF 1264 D2): \(N \le 10^6\) immediately rules out explicit graph construction. However, matching \(k\) left (s with \(k\) right )s with \(i_k < j_1\) is a 1D interval cut (Ch 08.3): let \(L_i\) be the count of ( in \(s[1..i]\) and \(R_i\) be the count of ) in \(s[i..N]\). Since \(L_i\) increases by \(0\) or \(1\) and \(R_{i+1}\) decreases by \(0\) or \(1\) with \(L_{i} - R_{i+1}\) stepping by \(+1\) at every character, there is a unique index \(i\) where \(L_i = R_{i+1} = k^*\)!
Track B (CF 1404 E): \(N, M \le 200\) (\(NM \le 4 \times 10^4\)) with \(1 \times k\) and \(k \times 1\) strips signals Rank-2 Line-to-Vertex Bipartite Reduction (Ch 07.1).



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation

Track A (Exact Split-Point Decomposition): Instead of computing \(\max_i \min(L_i, R_{i+1})\), notice that \(k^* = \sum_{i=1}^{N} [s[i] == \text{'('} \text{ and } i \le i^*]\), where \(i^*\) is the unique split index satisfying \(L_{i^*} = R_{i^*+1}\). Equivalently, a character \(i\) is one of the \(k^*\) matched ( brackets iff \(s[i] = \text{'('}\) and #(( in \(1..i\)) \(\le\) #($)` in \(i+1..N\)). Let:

\(a =\) number of ( in \(s[1..i-1]\), \(x =\) number of ? in \(s[1..i-1]\);
\(b =\) number of ) in \(s[i+1..N]\), \(y =\) number of ? in \(s[i+1..N]\).

When \(s[i]\) is fixed to (, it is matched iff among the \(x\) left ?s (say \(u\) become () and \(y\) right ?s (say \(v\) become )), we have \(a + 1 + u \le b + v \iff (y - v) + u \le b - a - 1\). By Vandermonde’s identity, for any \(K = (y - v) + u\):
\[\sum_{\substack{u, v \\ u + (y - v) = K}} \binom{x}{u}\binom{y}{y - v} = \binom{x + y}{K} \implies \text{Valid completions for } i = \sum_{K = 0}^{b - a - 1} \binom{x + y}{K}.\]
Since \(x + y \in \{Q - 1, Q\}\) across all \(i\) (where \(Q = \#?\) in the whole string), we only need two prefix-sum arrays of binomial coefficients \(\sum_{K=0}^t \binom{Q}{K}\) and \(\sum_{K=0}^t \binom{Q-1}{K}\), giving \(O(N)\) total time!
Track B (2D Border-Saving MIS): Let \(H\) be the set of horizontal interior borders between \((r, c)\) and \((r+1, c)\) where both are #, and \(V\) be the set of vertical interior borders between \((r, c)\) and \((r, c+1)\) where both are #. Every chosen border saves \(1\) brick, and no cell \((r, c)\) can touch both a chosen \(h \in H\) and a chosen \(v \in V\):
\[\text{MinBricks} = \#\text{black} - \alpha(G_{H, V}) = \#\text{black} - \bigl(|H| + |V| - \nu(G_{H, V})\bigr).\]



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Track A (O(N) Algebraic Reduction): Precompute factorials up to \(N\) and prefix sums \(P_Q[t] = \sum_{k=0}^t \binom{Q}{k}\) and \(P_{Q-1}[t] = \sum_{k=0}^t \binom{Q-1}{k}\) in \(O(N)\) time; sweep \(i = 1 \dots N\) summing \(P_{x+y}[b - a - 1]\) whenever \(s[i] \in \{\text{'('}, \text{'?'}\}\).
Track B (O(NM \sqrt{NM}) Dinic Compilation):

Create a left vertex for each \(h \in H\) (\(S \xrightarrow{1} h\)) and a right vertex for each \(v \in V\) (\(v \xrightarrow{1} T\)).
For each black cell \((r, c)\), connect each incident horizontal border in \(\{h_{\text{up}}, h_{\text{down}}\} \cap H\) to each incident vertical border in \(\{v_{\text{left}}, v_{\text{right}}\} \cap V\) with capacity \(1\).
Output \(\#\text{black} - (|H| + |V| - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T))\).




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (Track B: \(2 \times 2\) all-black grid):

\(\#\text{black} = 4\), \(|H| = 2\) (left/right vertical pairs), \(|V| = 2\) (top/bottom horizontal pairs).
The 4 borders form a cycle \(C_4\) of L-corner conflicts; \(\nu(C_4) = 2\), \(\alpha(C_4) = 4 - 2 = 2\).
Minimum bricks \(= 4 - 2 = 2\) (either two \(1 \times 2\) horizontal bricks or two \(2 \times 1\) vertical bricks).

Broken Gadget Counterexample: In Track B, trying to match black cells directly into \(1 \times 2\) dominoes (POJ 2446 style) fails on a \(1 \times 3\) black strip: domino matching covers only \(2\) cells and leaves \(1\) cell uncovered (\(2\) bricks), whereas merging both vertical borders in \(V\) has zero conflicts with \(H = \emptyset\) and saves \(2\) merges, yielding \(3 - 2 = 1\) brick of size \(1 \times 3\)!








Problem #206 — Making a Divisibility Poset Bipartite (Codeforces 1630 F & Luogu P1263 Royal Guards)

Problem Statement: You are given \(N\) distinct positive integers \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_N\) (\(1 \le N \le 5 \times 10^4\), \(1 \le a_i \le 5 \times 10^4\)). Define an undirected graph \(G_0 = (V, E)\) on the \(N\) integers where an edge connects \(u\) and \(v\) (\(u \neq v\)) if and only if \(a_u \mid a_v\) or \(a_v \mid a_u\).
Find the minimum number of vertices to delete from \(G_0\) so that the induced subgraph on the remaining vertices is bipartite.







NoteHint 1 — When Is a Poset Comparability Graph Bipartite?





Divisibility \(a_u \mid a_v\) (\(a_u < a_v\)) is a strict partial order (poset)! If three remaining vertices form a 3-chain \(a_x \mid a_y \mid a_z\), then \((x, y)\), \((y, z)\), and \((x, z)\) are all edges in \(G_0\), forming a triangle \(K_3\) (not bipartite!). Conversely, if there is no 3-chain \(a_x \mid a_y \mid a_z\), can the comparability graph ever have an odd cycle?









NoteHint 2 — Role-Splitting Each Integer into Top (Source) vs. Bottom (Sink) (Ch 08.2)





A poset comparability graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no 3-chain \(x \prec y \prec z\) — which means every kept vertex \(u\) is either a minimal element (source, out-only) or a maximal element (sink, in-only) in the kept sub-poset, never both! Split each integer \(u\) into two candidate roles \((u_{\text{source}}, u_{\text{sink}})\) and formulate a Dilworth Maximum Antichain!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #206






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Cues: Distinct integers \(a_i \le 5 \times 10^4\), edges defined by \(a_u \mid a_v\), and “delete minimum vertices to make the graph bipartite.”
Why General Odd-Cycle Transversal Fails: Deleting minimum vertices to make a general graph bipartite (Odd Cycle Transversal) is NP-hard! The rescue is that \((V, \mid)\) is a transitive DAG (poset): any directed 3-path \(x \to y \to z\) automatically has the transitive shortcut \(x \to z\), creating a \(K_3\). Conversely, if no vertex has both an incoming edge and an outgoing edge, the kept vertices partition into sources (only outgoing edges) and sinks (only incoming edges), which is manifestly bipartite!



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Each kept vertex \(u\) must be assigned a role \(r_u \in \{\text{Top (source)}, \text{Bot (sink)}\}\):

Vertex \(u\) can be assigned at most one role: \((u, \text{Top})\) and \((u, \text{Bot})\) conflict.
If \(a_u \mid a_v\) (\(a_u < a_v\)), then we cannot keep both \(u\) and \(v\) unless \(u\) is a \(\text{Top}\) (source) and \(v\) is a \(\text{Bot}\) (sink). In particular:

\((u, \text{Bot})\) conflicts with \((v, \text{Top})\) and \((v, \text{Bot})\) (since \(u\) would have an outgoing edge \(u \to v\), violating \(u\)’s sink role);
\((v, \text{Top})\) conflicts with \((u, \text{Top})\) and \((u, \text{Bot})\) (since \(v\) would have an incoming edge \(u \to v\), violating \(v\)’s source role).


Define a new poset \(\mathcal{P}^*\) on \(2N\) elements \(\{(u, 0), (u, 1) : u \in V\}\) (where \((u, 0)\) means keeping \(u\) as a source and \((u, 1)\) means keeping \(u\) as a sink) with strict partial order \(\prec^*\):
\[(u, 0) \prec^* (u, 1) \quad (\forall u \in V), \qquad\text{and for all } a_u \mid a_v \;(a_u < a_v): \quad (u, 0) \prec^* (v, 0),\;\; (u, 1) \prec^* (v, 1),\;\; (u, 0) \prec^* (v, 1).\]
Check transitivity of \(\prec^*\):

\((u, 0) \prec^* (u, 1) \prec^* (v, 1) \implies (u, 0) \prec^* (v, 1)\) (present!);
\((u, 0) \prec^* (v, 0) \prec^* (w, 0) \implies (u, 0) \prec^* (w, 0)\) since \(a_u \mid a_v \mid a_w \implies a_u \mid a_w\) (present!).

Wait: in an antichain of \((\mathcal{P}^*, \prec^*)\):

\((u, 0) \prec^* (u, 1)\) forbids picking both roles for the same vertex \(u\);
If \(a_u \mid a_v\), then \((u, 0) \prec^* (v, 0)\), \((u, 1) \prec^* (v, 1)\), and \((u, 0) \prec^* (v, 1)\) forbid all role pairs except \(\{(u, 1), (v, 0)\}\) (keeping \(u\) as sink and \(v\) as source, so the directed edge \(u \to v\) has its tail in sinks and head in sources!).

Thus, maximum kept vertices in a bipartite subgraph \(=\) Maximum Antichain of \((\mathcal{P}^*, \prec^*)\)!


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
By Dilworth’s Theorem (Ch 08.1–08.2), since \(\prec^*\) is already transitively closed, the maximum antichain of the \(2N\)-element poset \(\mathcal{P}^*\) has size:
\[\alpha(\mathcal{P}^*) = 2N - \nu(G_{\text{bip}}), \qquad \text{MinDeletedVertices} = N - \alpha(\mathcal{P}^*) = \nu(G_{\text{bip}}) - N.\]

Bipartite Split Graph \(G_{\text{bip}}\):

Left vertices: \(L = \{(u, 0)_{\text{out}}, (u, 1)_{\text{out}} : u \in V\}\) (\(2N\) nodes);
Right vertices: \(R = \{(u, 0)_{\text{in}}, (u, 1)_{\text{in}} : u \in V\}\) (\(2N\) nodes).
For each \(u \in V\), add \((u, 0)_{\text{out}} \to (u, 1)_{\text{in}}\).
Enumerate multiples of each \(a_u\) via harmonic sieve (\(O(A \log A)\) where \(A = 5 \times 10^4\)). For each \(a_v = k \cdot a_u\) (\(k \ge 2\)) present in the input:

Add \((u, 0)_{\text{out}} \to (v, 0)_{\text{in}}\), \((u, 1)_{\text{out}} \to (v, 1)_{\text{in}}\), and \((u, 0)_{\text{out}} \to (v, 1)_{\text{in}}\) (this third edge is even redundant if we include \((u,0)\to(v,0)\to(v,1)\) in transitive closure, so including all 3 guarantees exact transitivity!).


Output: \(\text{MaxMatching}(G_{\text{bip}}) - N\).
Complexity: \(V_{\text{bip}} = 4N \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(E_{\text{bip}} \le 3 A \ln A + N \approx 1.7 \times 10^6\). Hopcroft–Karp runs in \(O(E \sqrt{V}) \approx 0.35\text{ s}\)! (Companion Note: Compare this role-splitting with Luogu P1263 [CEOI2002] Royal Guards, where obstacles split rows/columns into maximal contiguous segments \(H_{\text{seg}} \times V_{\text{seg}}\) before König matching.)



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (\(A = \{2, 4, 8\}\), a 3-chain \(2 \mid 4 \mid 8\)):

Here \(N = 3\), so \(\mathcal{P}^*\) has \(2N = 6\) elements.
Maximum matching on \(G_{\text{bip}}\) finds \(\nu(G_{\text{bip}}) = 4\) (leaving an antichain of size \(6 - 4 = 2\), e.g., \(\{(8, 0), (4, 1)\}\) corresponding to keeping \(\{4, 8\}\)).
Minimum deletions \(= \nu(G_{\text{bip}}) - N = 4 - 3 = 1\) (deleting \(2\), \(4\), or \(8\) leaves a single edge \(K_2\), which is bipartite).

Broken Gadget Counterexample (FM-07): Suppose a solver forgets the self-role link \((u, 0) \prec^* (u, 1)\) and only adds \((u, 0) \to (v, 1)\) for \(a_u \mid a_v\). Then for an isolated integer \(a_u\) (or the middle of a chain), the antichain picks both \((u, 0)\) and \((u, 1)\), counting vertex \(u\) twice in the kept subgraph! The intra-vertex chain \((u, 0) \prec^* (u, 1)\) is essential.








Problem #207 — Lexicographically Smallest Distance Permutation (Luogu P1963 [NOI2009] 变换序列)

Problem Statement: For two indices \(i, j \in \{0, 1, \dots, N-1\}\) on a circle of length \(N\) (\(1 \le N \le 10^4\)), define their circular distance as:
\[d(i, j) = \min\bigl(|i - j|,\; N - |i - j|\bigr).\]
Given \(N\) required circular distances \(D_0, D_1, \dots, D_{N-1}\), find a permutation \(T = (T_0, T_1, \dots, T_{N-1})\) of \(\{0, 1, \dots, N-1\}\) such that \(d(i, T_i) = D_i\) for every \(0 \le i < N\). If multiple valid permutations exist, output the lexicographically smallest sequence \((T_0, T_1, \dots, T_{N-1})\); if none exists, output No Answer.







NoteHint 1 — Degree-2 Candidate Graph & Lexicographic Order





For each \(i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}\), the equation \(d(i, T_i) = D_i\) yields at most two candidate targets in \(\{0, \dots, N-1\}\):
\[y_{i,1} = (i - D_i + N) \bmod N, \qquad y_{i,2} = (i + D_i) \bmod N.\]
Sort each vertex \(i\)’s adjacency list so that \(\min(y_{i,1}, y_{i,2})\) comes first and \(\max(y_{i,1}, y_{i,2})\) comes second. Now, in what order should you run Kuhn’s augmenting-path DFS over \(i\) so that \(T_0\) is minimized first, then \(T_1\), and so on?









NoteHint 2 — Why Forward Kuhn Fails & Reverse Kuhn (\(i = N-1 \downarrow 0\)) Works





When Kuhn’s algorithm runs dfs(i), it assigns \(i\) to its first valid neighbor \(y_{\min}\) and recursively pushes any previously matched vertex \(j\) along an augmenting path to \(j\)’s second choice! Therefore, the vertex processed last gets first priority on its preferred neighbor, while vertices processed earlier get displaced! To give \(i = 0\) highest priority, then \(i = 1\), etc., run the outer loop backwards from \(i = N-1\) down to \(0\)!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #207






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Cues: Construct a permutation \(T\) of \(\{0..N-1\}\) where each \(T_i\) belongs to a small candidate set \(\{y_{i,1}, y_{i,2}\}\) of size \(\le 2\), and minimize \((T_0, T_1, \dots, T_{N-1})\) lexicographically (\(N \le 10^4\)).
Why Standard Max-Flow + Edge Re-Testing Is Too Slow: Testing edges one by one with rollback takes \(O(N)\) flow runs. Here every left vertex has degree \(\le 2\), so the entire graph is a union of cycles and paths (\(E \le 2N\)), and Reverse-Order Kuhn DFS (Ch 05.1 / Ch 08.1) produces the lexicographically smallest perfect matching in a single pass!



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For each \(i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}\), define its ordered candidate tuple:
\[E(i) = \bigl(\min((i - D_i + N) \bmod N,\; (i + D_i) \bmod N),\;\; \max((i - D_i + N) \bmod N,\; (i + D_i) \bmod N)\bigr)\]
(deduplicated if \(D_i = 0\) or \(2D_i = N\)). We seek a bijection \(T : \{0..N-1\} \to \{0..N-1\}\) with \(T_i \in E(i)\) minimizing the vector \((T_0, T_1, \dots, T_{N-1})\) in dictionary order.


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Invariant of Reverse-Order Kuhn (\(i = N-1 \downarrow 0\)): Suppose we iterate \(i = N-1, N-2, \dots, 0\), and inside dfs(u) we always inspect \(u\)’s neighbors in increasing order \(y_{\text{small}}, y_{\text{large}}\):

When \(i\) is processed, dfs(i) tries \(y_{\text{small}}\) first.
Any augmenting path triggered by dfs(i) only visits vertices \(u > i\) (since vertices \(< i\) have not been matched yet!).
Thus, when we reach \(i = 0\), \(0\) claims its smallest feasible target in any perfect matching; inductively, each \(i\) claims its smallest target compatible with the already-optimal choices of \(\{0, \dots, i-1\}\) without ever disturbing a smaller index!

Algorithm:

For each \(i \in \{0..N-1\}\), build adj[i] sorted in increasing order.
Initialize match_left[0..N-1] = -1, match_right[0..N-1] = -1.
For \(i = N-1\) down to \(0\):

Run dfs(i) with visitation tag vis[y] == i.
If dfs(i) returns false, output No Answer and terminate.

Print match_right[0], match_right[1], ..., match_right[N-1].

Complexity: Since every left vertex has degree \(\le 2\), each connected component is a cycle or path; Kuhn’s algorithm takes \(O(N^2)\) worst-case time (and \(O(N)\) on average) with \(< 10\text{ ms}\) runtime for \(N = 10^4\).



Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (\(N = 4\), \(D = [1, 1, 1, 1]\)):

Sorted adjacency lists:

\(i = 0\): \([1, 3]\)
\(i = 1\): \([0, 2]\)
\(i = 2\): \([1, 3]\)
\(i = 3\): \([0, 2]\)

Reverse loop \(i = 3 \downarrow 0\):

\(i = 3\): matches \(3 \to 0\).
\(i = 2\): matches \(2 \to 1\).
\(i = 1\): tries \(0\) (held by \(3\)), pushes \(3 \to 2\), matches \(1 \to 0\).
\(i = 0\): tries \(1\) (held by \(2\)), pushes \(2 \to 3\), matches \(0 \to 1\).

Resulting permutation: \(T = [1, 0, 3, 2]\) (as opposed to \([3, 2, 1, 0]\)), which is the unique lexicographically smallest valid permutation!

Broken Gadget Counterexample: Running the outer loop forwards from \(i = 0\) to \(N-1\) on the exact same input:

\(i = 0\) matches \(1\); \(i = 1\) matches \(0\); \(i = 2\) tries \(1\), pushes \(i = 0\) from \(1\) to \(3\), and matches \(2 \to 1\); \(i = 3\) tries \(0\), pushes \(i = 1\) from \(0\) to \(2\), and matches \(3 \to 0\).
Forward Kuhn outputs \(T = [3, 2, 1, 0]\) — the lexicographically largest permutation instead of the smallest!









Problem #208 — Balanced Intervals on a Binary String (AtCoder AGC 056 C — 01 Balanced)

Problem Statement: We need to construct a 01-string \(S = s_1 s_2 \dots s_N\) of length \(N\) (\(2 \le N \le 10^6\)) satisfying \(M\) balance conditions (\(1 \le M \le 2 \times 10^5\)). The \(j\)-th condition specifies an interval \([L_j, R_j]\) (\(1 \le L_j < R_j \le N\), where \(R_j - L_j + 1\) is even) and requires that the substring \(s_{L_j} s_{L_j+1} \dots s_{R_j}\) contains an equal number of 0s and 1s.
It is guaranteed that at least one valid 01-string exists. Find the lexicographically smallest valid 01-string \(S\).







NoteHint 1 — Diagnostic Boundary Check (\(N = 10^6\) Rules Out Bipartite Matching!)





Can you match 0s and 1s inside each interval via bipartite flow? With \(N = 10^6\) and \(M = 2 \times 10^5\) overlapping intervals, any explicit matching graph TLEs. Instead, replace each 0 with \(-1\) and each 1 with \(+1\), and consider the prefix sum array \(P_0, P_1, \dots, P_N\)!









NoteHint 2 — Prefix-Sum Difference Constraints & Parity Coupling





Let \(P_i = \sum_{k=1}^i (2 s_k - 1) \in \mathbb{Z}\), where \(s_k \in \{0, 1\}\).

Step constraint: \(P_i - P_{i-1} \in \{-1, +1\}\) for each \(1 \le i \le N\).
Interval balance: \(P_{R_j} - P_{L_j - 1} = 0\) for each \(1 \le j \le M\).

Wait: \(P_i - P_{i-1} \in \{-1, +1\}\) looks non-convex because \(P_i - P_{i-1} \neq 0\), until you notice that \(P_i \equiv i \pmod 2\) is fixed! Since \(R_j - (L_j - 1)\) is even, every zero-weight edge preserves parity, so any integer solution to \(|P_i - P_{i-1}| \le 1\) automatically has \(|P_i - P_{i-1}| = 1\)!









TipFull 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #208






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Surface Cues: Construct the lexicographically smallest 01-string of length \(N \le 10^6\) subject to \(M \le 2 \times 10^5\) even-length interval balance equations.
Why It Is the Canonical Part II Diagnostic Boundary Decoy (Ch 08 \(\to\) Ch 21 Bridge): On the surface, “equal number of 0s and 1s in \([L_j, R_j]\)” sounds like pairing 0s and 1s (Ch 05–08). However, interval sum constraints on a 1D array always telescope under prefix sums \(P_i\), turning the problem into a System of Difference Constraints (Potential LP Dual, Ch 21) solvable in \(O(N + M)\) via 0-1 BFS! (Contrast this with Codeforces 653 D — Delivery Bears, where \(N \le 50\) and “equal weight \(w\) per bear” requires binary searching \(w\) and running integer Max-Flow with capacities \(\lfloor c_e / w \rfloor\).)



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Map '0' \(\mapsto -1\) and '1' \(\mapsto +1\), and let \(P_i = (\#\text{'1' in } 1..i) - (\#\text{'0' in } 1..i)\) with \(P_0 = 0\).

Parity Invariant: At every index \(i\), \(P_i \equiv i \pmod 2\). Since each interval \([L_j, R_j]\) has even length, \(R_j \equiv L_j - 1 \pmod 2\).
Relaxing \(\{-1, +1\}\) to \([-1, +1]\): Because every adjacent pair \((i-1, i)\) has opposite parity (\(i \not\equiv i-1 \pmod 2\)) and every zero-cost equality \(P_{R_j} = P_{L_j-1}\) connects vertices of the same parity, any integer assignment satisfying:
\[-1 \le P_i - P_{i-1} \le +1 \quad (\forall 1 \le i \le N) \qquad\text{and}\qquad P_{R_j} = P_{L_j - 1} \quad (\forall 1 \le j \le M)\]
automatically satisfies \(P_i \equiv i \pmod 2\), which forces \(P_i - P_{i-1} \neq 0 \implies P_i - P_{i-1} \in \{-1, +1\}\)!
Lexicographic Optimality: Choosing \(s_1 = \text{'0'}\) (\(P_1 = P_0 - 1\)), then \(s_2 = \text{'0'}\) (\(P_2 = P_1 - 1\)), etc., means making every prefix sum \(P_i\) as small as possible! In a difference-constraint system \(P_v - P_u \le w(u \to v)\) rooted at \(P_0 = 0\), the pointwise minimum valid potential vector (Wait: for \(P_1 \ge P_0 - 1\), minimizing \(P_i\) is symmetric to maximizing \(-P_i\)!). Let \(Q_i = \#\text{'0' in } 1..i - \#\text{'1' in } 1..i = -P_i\). To make \(S\) lexicographically smallest (as many '0's as early as possible), we want to maximize \(Q_1\), then \(Q_2\), …, i.e., compute the pointwise maximum valid potential \(Q_i\), which is the shortest path distance \(d(0, i)\) in the difference-constraint graph!



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
Let \(Q_i = -P_i\) with \(Q_0 = 0\). The constraints on \(Q\) are:

\(Q_i - Q_{i-1} \le 1\) and \(Q_{i-1} - Q_i \le 1 \implies\) undirected edge \((i-1) \leftrightarrow i\) of weight 1 for all \(1 \le i \le N\).
\(Q_{R_j} - Q_{L_j - 1} \le 0\) and \(Q_{L_j - 1} - Q_{R_j} \le 0 \implies\) undirected edge \((L_j - 1) \leftrightarrow R_j\) of weight 0 for all \(1 \le j \le M\).

By the triangle inequality of shortest paths, setting \(Q_i = \text{dist}(0, i)\) gives the maximum possible value of \(Q_i\) (and hence puts '0' at position \(i\) whenever \(Q_i = Q_{i-1} + 1\) is feasible!).

Algorithm:

Build the graph on vertices \(\{0, 1, \dots, N\}\) with \(N\) weight-\(1\) edges and \(M\) weight-\(0\) edges.
Run 0-1 BFS using a std::deque from source \(0\) to compute dist[0..N] in \(O(N + M)\) time.
For each \(i = 1, \dots, N\): if dist[i] == dist[i-1] + 1, output '0'; else (necessarily dist[i] == dist[i-1] - 1) output '1'.




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (\(N = 4, M = 1\), interval \([1, 2]\) balanced):

Edges of weight \(1\): \(0 \leftrightarrow 1 \leftrightarrow 2 \leftrightarrow 3 \leftrightarrow 4\).
Edge of weight \(0\): \(0 \leftrightarrow 2\) (since \(L_1 - 1 = 0, R_1 = 2\)).
0-1 BFS distances from \(0\):

dist[0] = 0, dist[2] = 0 (via \(0 \xrightarrow{0} 2\));
dist[1] = 1 (via \(0 \xrightarrow{1} 1\)), dist[3] = 1 (via \(2 \xrightarrow{1} 3\));
dist[4] = 2 (via \(3 \xrightarrow{1} 4\)).

Differences \(\Delta Q_i = \text{dist}[i] - \text{dist}[i-1]\):

\(i = 1\): \(1 - 0 = +1 \implies \text{'0'}\)
\(i = 2\): \(0 - 1 = -1 \implies \text{'1'}\)
\(i = 3\): \(1 - 0 = +1 \implies \text{'0'}\)
\(i = 4\): \(2 - 1 = +1 \implies \text{'0'}\)

Output: "0100" (interval \([1, 2]\) is "01", balanced, and positions \(3, 4\) greedily take '0').

Broken Gadget Counterexample: Defining \(P_i = \#\text{'1' in } 1..i\) (only counting '1's instead of \(\#\text{'0'} - \#\text{'1'}\)): then the step constraints are \(0 \le P_i - P_{i-1} \le 1\), which loses the parity invariant! A shortest-path solver can then set \(P_i - P_{i-1}\) to fractional or inconsistent values when zero-edges and negative-edges mix, requiring \(O(NM)\) Bellman–Ford instead of \(O(N + M)\) 0-1 BFS with non-negative weights \(\{0, 1\}\)!

3.2 Part II Failure Mode Self-Audit Checklist (FM-07, FM-08 & Constructive Readout Traps)
Before advancing to Part III, verify that you can state from memory both the algebraic cause and the mechanical fix for each of the following six Part II bugs:

FM-07 — Confusing Non-Transitive DAG Path Cover with Poset Antichain (Ch 08.1 vs. Ch 08.2):

Symptom: Your minimum path cover / maximum antichain size is strictly smaller (or larger) than the sample answer on a DAG where paths are allowed to “skip” already-visited vertices (Luogu P4298 祭祀, CF 590E Birthday).
Root Cause: Dilworth’s Theorem (\(\text{Max Antichain} = \text{Min Chain Cover} = |V| - \nu(G_{\text{bip}})\)) holds only on a transitive poset (\(u \prec v \land v \prec w \implies u \prec w\)). Without transitive closure, the bipartite graph \(G_{\text{bip}}\) only counts vertex-disjoint paths and cannot route two chains through a shared intermediate vertex.
Fix: If chains may share intermediate vertices (or if you need a Maximum Antichain), always compute the transitive closure (Floyd–Warshall / bitset DAG reachability) before running bipartite matching.

FM-08 — Reflexive \((r + c) \bmod 2\) Coloring on Parity-Preserving Jumps (Ch 06.2):

Symptom: Bipartite MIS outputs \(|V_{\text{free}}|\) (zero flow) or misses obvious conflicts (Luogu P5030 长脖子鹿放置, \((\pm 1, \pm 3)\) jumps, or \((\pm 2, \pm 2)\) jumps).
Root Cause: When \(\Delta r + \Delta c\) is even, \((r + c) \bmod 2\) does not change along an attack edge.
Fix: Test the step generators \((\Delta r, \Delta c)\) algebraically:

If \(\Delta r + \Delta c\) is odd: use \((r + c) \bmod 2\).
If \(\Delta r\) is odd and \(\Delta c\) is odd: use \(r \bmod 2\) (or \(c \bmod 2\)).
If \(\Delta r, \Delta c\) are multiples of \(2^k\): divide coordinates by \(2^k\) inside each \(\bmod 2^k\) residue class first (Ch 06.2).


Constructive Kőnig Vertex Cover / Independent Set Extraction Trap (Ch 05.2):

Symptom: You know the size \(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\), but taking {all matched vertices in L} gives a set that fails to cover some edges!
Fix: Start an alternating BFS/DFS from all unmatched vertices in \(L\) (traversing unmatched edges \(L \to R\) and matched edges \(R \to L\)). Then:
\[\text{MVC} = (L \setminus Z_L) \cup (R \cap Z_R), \qquad \text{MIS} = (L \cap Z_L) \cup (R \setminus Z_R).\]

Forward vs. Reverse Kuhn Order in Lexicographic Matching (Ch 05.1 / CP-II #207):

Symptom: You sorted each adjacency list in increasing order, but your matching is lexicographically largest or scrambled at early indices.
Fix: Because Kuhn’s augmenting DFS displaces previously matched vertices to make room for the currently queried vertex, you must process the highest-priority vertices last (iterate \(i = N-1\) down to \(0\)).

Dulmage–Mendelsohn Game Start Trap (Ch 06.3):

Symptom: Treating any vertex matched in one arbitrary maximum matching \(M^*\) as a winning start for the first player (Luogu P4055, Luogu P1971).
Fix: The first player wins from \(v_0\) iff \(v_0\) is matched in every maximum matching (\(v_0 \in E_L \cup E_R\)), which requires checking that no alternating path from an unmatched vertex can reach \(v_0\).

Duplicate Obstacle Coordinates in Grid MIS (Ch 06.2 / CP-II #204):

Symptom: Computing \(|V_{\text{free}}| = N \cdot M - K\) when the input lists the same forbidden cell \((r, c)\) multiple times.
Fix: Always deduplicate forbidden cells in a boolean array bad[r][c] and count |V_free| by iterating over the grid.

section: 4. Readiness Bridge to Part III — From Unweighted König Duality to the Minimum Cut Compiler (燃やす埋める)
text:
4. Readiness Bridge to Part III — From Unweighted König Duality to the Minimum Cut Compiler (燃やす埋める)
Throughout Part II (Ch 05–Ch 08), every decision was unweighted (or uniform-cost) and every conflict was a hard binary exclusion on a bipartite or poset structure:
\[\tau(G) = \nu(G), \qquad \alpha(G) = |V| - \nu(G).\]
What happens when the problem statement breaks out of the unweighted bipartite world along any of the following three axes?

Weighted Vertices & Implicational Dependencies (Ch 06 \(\to\) Ch 09 & Ch 11):

In Luogu P3355 骑士共存问题 (#042) and Luogu P5030 长脖子鹿放置 (#204), every cell had weight \(1\).
In Luogu P2774 方格取数问题 (#081, Ch 11.1), cell \((r, c)\) has profit \(w_{r,c} > 0\): replacing the unit capacities \(S \xrightarrow{1} u\) and \(v \xrightarrow{1} T\) by \(S \xrightarrow{w_u} u\) and \(v \xrightarrow{w_v} T\) (while locking conflict edges at \(u \xrightarrow{\infty} v\)) turns König’s Theorem into Weighted Bipartite Minimum Vertex Cover / Maximum Weight Independent Set via \(s\)-\(t\) Minimum Cut!
Even better: when implications \(x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1\) (u \xrightarrow{\infty} v) are placed on an arbitrary directed graph (not necessarily bipartite!), the exact same \(s\)-\(t\) Min-Cut gadget solves Picard’s Maximum-Weight Closure / Project Selection (最大权闭合子图, Ch 09) in polynomial time!

Soft Penalties & \(2 \times 2\) Payoff Matrices (Ch 07 \(\to\) Ch 10–Ch 11 燃やす埋める):

In Codeforces 1404 E — Bricks (#082 / #205 Track B), two adjacent borders sharing an L-corner were strictly forbidden from both being selected (\(\infty\) penalty).
What if choosing two adjacent items \((u, v)\) in the same class or different classes incurs a finite submodular cost table \(\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}\) with \(B + C \ge A + D\) (Ch 10), or a supermodular reward table \(A + D > B + C\) on a bipartite graph rescued by Bipartite Variable Inversion \(y_j = 1 - x_j\) (Ch 11, AtCoder AGC 038 F — Two Permutations)?

Multi-State Variables \(x_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) (Ch 08 \(\to\) Ch 12–Ch 13):

In Part III (Ch 12–Ch 13), we upgrade binary indicators \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\) to Unary Threshold Chains \(z_{i,1} \ge z_{i,2} \ge \dots \ge z_{i,K-1}\) (切糕 / K値燃やす埋める) and Coarea Level-Set Integrals (Codeforces 1427 G — One Billion Shades of Grey), compiling multi-valued convex optimization directly into \(s\)-\(t\) minimum cuts.


If you scored 6/6 on the Rapid-Fire Triage Drills and at least 6/8 on the Blind Checkpoint Problems #201–#208 without triggering FM-07 or FM-08, you are ready to enter Part III: The Minimum Cut Compiler (Ch 09–Ch 13).

title: Checkpoint IV — Part IV Blind Recognition: Fractional Cuts, Planar Duals, Min-Cut DP & Gomory–Hu Trees
text:
Chapters 14 through 16 elevated your minimum-cut toolkit along two major axes:

Parametric & Fractional Linearization (Ch 14): Transforming non-linear ratio objectives \(\max \frac{f(\mathbf{x})}{g(\mathbf{x})}\) into sequence-of-cuts feasibility tests \(F(\lambda) = \max [f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda g(\mathbf{x})] \ge 0\) via Dinkelbach’s root-finding algorithm — and compiled pairwise subgraph density \(|E(S)| - \lambda |S|\) into Goldberg’s positive-capacity shift network while separating sum-ratio density from bottleneck minimum-degree (\(k\)-core) peeling.
Structural & Topological Cut Compression (Ch 15 and Ch 16):Recognizing when running Dinic on \(N = 10^5\) or across \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs is fatal, and instead compiling cuts into planar dual shortest paths (\(O(N \log N)\)), Direction B Cut-State DP / Tropical Dynamic Segment Trees (\(O(N \log N)\) per update), Stoer–Wagner global min-cut (\(O(NM + N^2 \log N)\)), or Gomory–Hu / Gusfield cut trees (\(N - 1\) max-flows for all \(\binom{N}{2}\) undirected pairs).

In a live contest, the hardest decision in Part IV is triage before graph construction:

Does “maximize density” mean \(\frac{\sum_{e \in E(S)} w_e}{|S|}\) (which requires Dinkelbach + Goldberg’s \(s\)-\(t\) min-cut, Ch 14.2) or \(\min_{u \in S} \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\) (which is a bottleneck \(k\)-core property solved by \(O((N+M)\log N)\) greedy peeling, Ch 14.3)?
Does a ratio on a tree or general graph reduce to a \(0\)-\(1\) closure cut, a \(O(N K^2)\) tree knapsack DP, or a negative-cycle Bellman–Ford / SPFA test?
When capacities sit on a grid or planar embedding with \(N, M \le 10^6\), how do you orient the dual edges (FM-15) and pair outer-boundary segments when there are \(2k\) alternating terminals?
When a problem gives you an explicit flow network or cut formula with \(N = 2 \times 10^5\), how do you resist building the graph (Direction A) and instead compile the \(S/T\) partition directly into a DP or \((+, \min)\) tropical matrix product (Direction B, Ch 16.1)?




Pass 1 — Diagnostic Triage & Decoy Rejection (10 minutes per problem): Read the untagged problem statement, inspect the constraints (\(N, M, K, Q\)) and the algebraic form of the objective, and write down:

Primary Mechanism: 0-1 Fractional Cut / Dinkelbach (Ch 14.1), Goldberg Maximum Density Subgraph (Ch 14.2), Bottleneck Peeling / Cycle-Ratio (Ch 14.3), Planar Dual s-t / Multi-Terminal Cut (Ch 15.1–15.3), Planar Face / Enclosure Query (Ch 15.4), Direction B Min-Cut DP / Tropical Segment Tree (Ch 16.1), Stoer–Wagner Global Min-Cut (Ch 16.3), or Gomory–Hu Cut Tree (Ch 16.4).
Direction Choice: Are you compiling an algebraic objective into a flow network (Direction A), or compiling an intractable flow/cut problem into a dual shortest path, DP, or tree structure (Direction B)?

Pass 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Formulation (15 minutes per problem): Before drawing any vertex or edge, write the exact shifted cut polynomial, dual face potential system, tropical matrix transition, or cut-tree bottleneck invariant. Verify that every capacity is non-negative and that trivial cuts (\(S = \emptyset\)) are handled.
Pass 3 — Progressive Hint Unfolding & Failure-Mode Audit: Only unfold Hint 1 if your Pass 1 triage stalls. Only unfold Hint 2 if your Pass 2 algebra fails to compile cleanly. Compare your completed derivation against the Full 4-Step Solution and audit yourself against FM-14 through FM-16 in Section 3.

Does “maximize density” mean \(\frac{\sum_{e \in E(S)} w_e}{|S|}\) (which requires Dinkelbach + Goldberg’s \(s\)-\(t\) min-cut, Ch 14.2) or \(\min_{u \in S} \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\) (which is a bottleneck \(k\)-core property solved by \(O((N+M)\log N)\) greedy peeling, Ch 14.3)?
Does a ratio on a tree or general graph reduce to a \(0\)-\(1\) closure cut, a \(O(N K^2)\) tree knapsack DP, or a negative-cycle Bellman–Ford / SPFA test?
When capacities sit on a grid or planar embedding with \(N, M \le 10^6\), how do you orient the dual edges (FM-15) and pair outer-boundary segments when there are \(2k\) alternating terminals?
When a problem gives you an explicit flow network or cut formula with \(N = 2 \times 10^5\), how do you resist building the graph (Direction A) and instead compile the \(S/T\) partition directly into a DP or \((+, \min)\) tropical matrix product (Direction B, Ch 16.1)?




Pass 1 — Diagnostic Triage & Decoy Rejection (10 minutes per problem): Read the untagged problem statement, inspect the constraints (\(N, M, K, Q\)) and the algebraic form of the objective, and write down:

Primary Mechanism: 0-1 Fractional Cut / Dinkelbach (Ch 14.1), Goldberg Maximum Density Subgraph (Ch 14.2), Bottleneck Peeling / Cycle-Ratio (Ch 14.3), Planar Dual s-t / Multi-Terminal Cut (Ch 15.1–15.3), Planar Face / Enclosure Query (Ch 15.4), Direction B Min-Cut DP / Tropical Segment Tree (Ch 16.1), Stoer–Wagner Global Min-Cut (Ch 16.3), or Gomory–Hu Cut Tree (Ch 16.4).
Direction Choice: Are you compiling an algebraic objective into a flow network (Direction A), or compiling an intractable flow/cut problem into a dual shortest path, DP, or tree structure (Direction B)?

Pass 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Formulation (15 minutes per problem): Before drawing any vertex or edge, write the exact shifted cut polynomial, dual face potential system, tropical matrix transition, or cut-tree bottleneck invariant. Verify that every capacity is non-negative and that trivial cuts (\(S = \emptyset\)) are handled.
Pass 3 — Progressive Hint Unfolding & Failure-Mode Audit: Only unfold Hint 1 if your Pass 1 triage stalls. Only unfold Hint 2 if your Pass 2 algebra fails to compile cleanly. Compare your completed derivation against the Full 4-Step Solution and audit yourself against FM-14 through FM-16 in Section 3.

title: Checkpoint IV — Part IV Blind Recognition: Fractional Cuts, Planar Duals, Min-Cut DP & Gomory–Hu Trees
text:
Section 1: Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills
Before tackling the eight full blind problems, test your diagnostic reflexes on these six scenario drills. For each scenario, identify the trap/decoy, the correct Part IV mechanism, and the critical mathematical invariant before opening the solution callout.

Drill 1.1 — Sum-Ratio Subgraph Density vs. Bottleneck Degree Ratio

Scenario: You are given an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(N = 10^5\) vertices and \(M = 10^5\) edges. A subset of vertices \(B \subseteq V\) is forbidden. You must choose a non-empty subset \(S \subseteq V \setminus B\) to maximize:

Variant A: \(\frac{|E(S)|}{|S|}\), where \(E(S)\) is the set of edges with both endpoints in \(S\) (under smaller constraints \(N \le 1000, M \le 5000\)).
Variant B: \(\min_{u \in S} \frac{|\{v \in S : (u,v) \in E\}|}{\deg_G(u)}\) (under the full constraints \(N, M \le 10^5\)).

A teammate proposes running Dinkelbach binary search + Goldberg’s \(s\)-\(t\) min-cut on both variants. Critique this proposal.







NoteDrill 1.1 — Diagnostic Triage & Invariant






Decoy / Trap: Confusing the average internal degree objective \(\frac{2|E(S)|}{|S|}\) (sum-over-sum fractional program) with the minimum normalized internal degree objective \(\min_{u \in S} \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\) (bottleneck \(k\)-core objective). Running max-flow on Variant B with \(N = 10^5\) will TLE immediately, and worse, a min-cut cannot directly enforce a per-vertex minimum degree threshold without cascading deletions.
Correct Mechanism:

Variant A (Ch 14.2): Dinkelbach/binary search on \(\lambda\) + Goldberg’s shifted \(s\)-\(t\) minimum cut on \(V \setminus B\). Because \(|E(S)| = \sum_{\{u,v\} \in E} x_u x_v\) is a sum of supermodular pairwise rewards, maximizing \(|E(S)| - \lambda |S|\) is a project-selection closure problem solvable by Dinic in \(O(\text{MaxFlow}(N, M) \log N)\).
Variant B (Ch 14.3): Greedy Bottleneck Peeling (Generalized \(k\)-Core) in \(O((N + M) \log N)\). Start with \(S_0 = V \setminus B\) and repeatedly pop the vertex \(u \in S\) with the smallest current ratio \(\frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\) using a min-heap, recording the best active set seen across all \(N - |B|\) steps.

Key Proof Invariant (Variant B): For the optimal subset \(S^*\) achieving bottleneck ratio \(\lambda^*\), the very first vertex \(v \in S^*\) ever popped by the global greedy order has \(S^* \subseteq S_{\text{current}}\) at the moment \(v\) is popped, so its current ratio is at least \(\frac{\deg_{S^*}(v)}{\deg_G(v)} \ge \lambda^*\). Since \(v\) minimizes the current ratio across all of \(S_{\text{current}}\), the entire set \(S_{\text{current}}\) at that step achieves bottleneck ratio \(\ge \lambda^*\).






Drill 1.2 — Goldberg’s Unshifted Negative Capacity & The Trivial \(S = \emptyset\) Cut Trap (FM-14)

Scenario: To test whether there exists a non-empty subgraph \(S \subseteq V\) with \(\frac{|E(S)|}{|S|} > \lambda\), a contestant writes the cut objective \(\min_{S \subseteq V} \left(\lambda |S| - |E(S)|\right)\), substitutes \(|E(S)| = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{u \in S} \deg_G(u) - \frac{1}{2}|\delta(S)|\), and connects each vertex \(u\) to the sink \(t\) with capacity \(c(u, t) = \lambda - \frac{1}{2}\deg_G(u)\) and each undirected edge \((u,v)\) with capacity \(\frac{1}{2}\). Why does this fail in two distinct ways?







NoteDrill 1.2 — Diagnostic Triage & Invariant






Failure Mode 1 (Negative Capacities, FM-14a): Whenever \(2\lambda < \deg_G(u)\), the sink capacity \(c(u, t) = \lambda - \frac{1}{2}\deg_G(u)\) is strictly negative, violating the non-negative capacity precondition of Dinic’s algorithm.
Failure Mode 2 (Trivial \(S = \emptyset\) Minimum Cut, FM-14b): Even after shifting by a large constant \(U \ge \Delta(G)\) so that \(c(s, u) = U\), \(c(u, v) = 1\), and \(c(u, t) = U + 2\lambda - \deg_G(u) \ge 0\), the cut value for any \(S \subseteq V\) is: \[\text{cap}(S \cup \{s\}, \bar{S} \cup \{t\}) = U \cdot |V| + 2\left(\lambda |S| - |E(S)|\right)\] Putting \(S = \emptyset\) always yields cut capacity \(U \cdot |V| + 0\). If \(\lambda\) is larger than the maximum possible density \(\lambda^*\), then \(S = \emptyset\) is the unique global minimum cut of value \(U \cdot |V|\)! A solver who checks max_flow < U * N works only for strict inequality \(> \lambda\), and if \(S = \emptyset\) ties with a non-empty \(S\) at \(\lambda = \lambda^*\), reading the residual reachability from \(s\) must take the maximal \(s\)-side closure (or test \(\lambda - \varepsilon\)) so \(S \neq \emptyset\) is recovered.






Drill 1.3 — Directed Planar Dual Orientation & Boundary Short-Circuiting (FM-15)

Scenario: On an \(N \times N\) directed grid (\(N = 500\)) with source \(s = (0,0)\) at the top-left and sink \(t = (N,N)\) at the bottom-right, east/south edges have cost \(w_e\) and west/north edges have cost \(w'_e\). You split the outer face into \(s^*\) (bottom/left boundary) and \(t^*\) (top/right boundary) and build the dual graph \(G^*\). How do you orient the dual edge \(e^*\) for a primal directed edge \(e = (u \to v)\), and what goes wrong if you connect internal faces to \(s^*\) or \(t^*\) with undirected edges?







NoteDrill 1.3 — Diagnostic Triage & Invariant






Right-Hand Rule Orientation (FM-15a): Stand at \(u\) looking toward \(v\) along the directed primal edge \(e = (u \to v)\). If the \(s\)-side of the cut is to your left and the \(t\)-side is to your right when traversing the dual path from \(s^*\) to \(t^*\), then the forward primal edge \(e = (u \to v)\) crosses from the \(s\)-side to the \(t\)-side if and only if the directed dual edge \(e^*\) crosses \(e\) from left to right (clockwise \(90^\circ\) rotation) with weight \(c(e)\). The reverse primal edge \((v \to u)\) compiles to the opposite directed dual edge with weight \(c(v \to u)\).
Boundary Short-Circuiting (FM-15b): If you make the edges incident to \(s^*\) or \(t^*\) undirected (or reverse the right-hand rule on one boundary), a dual path can enter \(s^*\) from an internal face and exit \(s^*\) at another boundary cell for cost \(0\), teleporting across the boundary without cutting the primal boundary edges between them. Every dual edge leaving \(s^*\) must strictly enter the grid interior, and every dual edge entering \(t^*\) must strictly leave the grid interior.






Drill 1.4 — Direction A vs. Direction B on Dense Structured Networks

Scenario: You are given \(N = 2 \times 10^5\) vertices arranged in a line \(1, 2, \dots, N\). Each vertex \(i\) has source capacity \(p_i\) and sink capacity \(s_i\). Furthermore:

Variant A: For every pair \(1 \le i < j \le N\), there is a directed edge \(i \to j\) of uniform capacity \(c\).
Variant B: There is a directed edge \(i \to i+1\) of capacity \(c_i\), and you must handle \(Q = 2 \times 10^5\) point updates to \((p_i, s_i, c_i)\), printing the global \(s\)-\(t\) max-flow after each update.

Why is running Dinic (Direction A) impossible in both variants, and how does Direction B (Ch 16.1) solve each in \(O(N^2)\) (or \(O(N \log N)\)) and \(O(Q \log N)\)?







NoteDrill 1.4 — Diagnostic Triage & Invariant






Why Direction A Fails: Variant A has \(\binom{N}{2} \approx 2 \times 10^{10}\) edges; Variant B requires \(2 \times 10^5\) full max-flow runs on \(2 \times 10^5\) vertices.
Direction B Compilation (Ch 16.1): By Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality, the max-flow equals the minimum over all partitions \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(x_i = 1\) means \(i \in S\), \(x_i = 0\) means \(i \in T\)) of:

Variant A (CF 724E): If \(k\) vertices prior to \(i\) are placed in \(S\), placing \(i \in T\) cuts the source edge \(p_i\) plus all \(k\) edges from earlier \(S\)-vertices to \(i\), costing \(p_i + k \cdot c\). Placing \(i \in S\) cuts the sink edge \(s_i\). This compiles to a 1D DP where state \(k = \sum_{j < i} x_j\) tracks the number of \(S\)-vertices so far (in \(O(N^2)\), or \(O(N \log N)\) via slope trick since the transitions are convex).
Variant B (CF 1919F2): At each vertex \(i\), the cut contribution depends only on \((x_{i-1}, x_i) \in \{0, 1\}^2\): \[M_i = \begin{pmatrix} p_i & p_i \\ s_i + c_{i-1} & s_i \end{pmatrix}\] in the tropical \((+, \min)\) semiring! Maintaining the segment tree product \(M_1 \otimes M_2 \otimes \dots \otimes M_N\) answers each point-update max-flow query in \(O(\log N)\) time.







Drill 1.5 — Gomory–Hu Supernode Contraction vs. Directed Graphs (FM-16)

Scenario: A problem gives a graph with \(N = 400\) vertices and asks for \(\sum_{1 \le u < v \le N} \text{mincut}(u, v)\).

What happens if the graph is directed and you attempt to build a Gomory–Hu cut tree?
In an undirected graph, during step \(k\) of Gomory–Hu construction, you run \(s\)-\(t\) min-cut and obtain partition \((X, Y)\). A contestant discards all edges outside the current supernode and runs the next \(s\)-\(t\) flow on the induced subgraph of the supernode instead of contracting the exterior tree components into supernodes. Why does this produce wrong cuts?








NoteDrill 1.5 — Diagnostic Triage & Invariant






Failure Mode 1 (Directed Graphs Violate Symmetric Submodularity, FM-16a): In a directed graph, \(\lambda(u, v) \neq \lambda(v, u)\) in general, and directed cuts do not form a symmetric tree metric (though Schnorr 1979 constructs a directed cut packing for \(\min(\lambda(u,v), \lambda(v,u))\), standard Gomory–Hu trees for all-pairs \(\lambda(u,v)\) do not exist on directed graphs).
Failure Mode 2 (Deleting Exterior Components Instead of Contracting, FM-16b): Flow between two vertices \(u, v\) inside the current supernode \(V_i\) can legally route out of \(V_i\) into an already-split tree component \(C\) and re-enter \(V_i\) through another boundary edge! Deleting \(V \setminus V_i\) underestimates the true \(u\)-\(v\) cut in \(G\). You must either contract each connected component of \(T \setminus \{V_i\}\) into a single composite vertex (Gomory–Hu) or use Gusfield’s algorithm (Ch 16.4), which runs all \(N-1\) max-flows directly on the original unmodified graph \(G\)!






Drill 1.6 — Multi-Terminal Outerplanar Cuts vs. General Multiway Cut

Scenario: An undirected planar grid has \(N \times M\) vertices (\(N, M \le 500\)). In each of \(Q = 50\) queries, \(k \le 50\) terminal points are placed around the outer boundary of the grid, each colored either \(0\) (white) or \(1\) (black). You must find the minimum weight of grid edges to delete so no white terminal can reach any black terminal. A contestant recognizes “more than 2 terminals = NP-hard Multiway Cut” and gives up. Why is this problem solvable in \(O(k^2 N M \log(NM) + k^3)\) per query?







NoteDrill 1.6 — Diagnostic Triage & Invariant






Why General Multiway Cut Doesn’t Apply Here: All \(k\) terminals lie on the outer boundary of a planar graph, and there are only two terminal colors \(\{0, 1\}\).
Correct Mechanism (Ch 15.3, CSP-S 2021 交通规划): Walk clockwise around the outer boundary. Whenever two adjacent boundary terminals have different colors (\(0 \leftrightarrow 1\)), the outer face segment between them is a transition dual vertex where a separating cut curve must start or end. Since colors alternate around a cycle, there are an even number \(2r \le k\) of transition dual vertices \(v^*_1, v^*_2, \dots, v^*_{2r}\) in cyclic order!
Non-Crossing Catalan Matching: Any minimal cut separating white from black terminals corresponds in the planar dual \(G^*\) to a non-crossing perfect matching of \(\{v^*_1, \dots, v^*_{2r}\}\) via shortest paths in \(G^*\). Run \(2r\) Dijkstra passes from \(v^*_1, \dots, v^*_{2r}\) on \(G^*\), then run a \(O(r^3)\) circular interval DP: \[dp[l][r] = \min\left( \text{dist}_{G^*}(v^*_l, v^*_r) + dp[l+1][r-1], \min_{m} (dp[l][m] + dp[m+1][r]) \right)\]

title: Checkpoint IV — Part IV Blind Recognition: Fractional Cuts, Planar Duals, Min-Cut DP & Gomory–Hu Trees
text:
Section 2: Blind Checkpoint Problems (#217–#224)
Remember: do not unfold the hints or solutions until you have completed Pass 1 (Triage) and Pass 2 (Algebraic Formulation) on paper. Several slots pair two closely contrasting problems (Part A and Part B) so you can test your ability to distinguish near-identical surface narratives that compile to completely different algorithms.


Problem #217 — Fortress Ratios & Dual-Attribute Team Selection (CF 553D & Luogu P6577 / P3701)

Part A (Codeforces 553D — Nudist Beach, Judge Link)
You are given an undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(N\) cities and \(M\) bidirectional roads (\(1 \le N, M \le 10^5\)). Exactly \(K\) cities (\(1 \le K < N\)) are already occupied by fortresses and cannot be selected. You must choose a non-empty subset of non-fortress cities \(S \subseteq V \setminus F\) to maximize the weakest city’s fortification ratio in \(S\):
\[\max_{\emptyset \neq S \subseteq V \setminus F} \min_{u \in S} \frac{|\{v \in S : \{u, v\} \in E\}|}{\deg_G(u)}\]
where \(\deg_G(u)\) is the total number of roads incident to \(u\) in the original graph \(G\) (including roads to fortresses). Output the size \(|S|\) and the vertices of an optimal set \(S\).


Part B (Luogu P6577 — 【模板】二分图最大权完美匹配 / Luogu P3701 — 「伪模板」主席树, Judge Link (P6577), Judge Link (P3701))
To contrast with Part A’s bottleneck graph peeling:

Weighted Perfect Pairing Benchmark (P6577): Given a bipartite graph \(G = (L \cup R, E)\) with \(|L| = |R| = N \le 500\), \(M \le N^2\) edges, and edge weights \(w_{uv} \in [-10^9, 10^9]\), find a perfect matching of maximum total weight in \(O(N^3)\) time (tested as a rapid contrast: why does standard \(O(N^2 M)\) SPFA-based MCMF TLE on dense \(M = N^2\) graphs unless implemented with \(O(N^3)\) Hungarian / Kuhn–Munkres slack arrays?).
Role-Modified Combat Capacities (P3701): Two players each have \(N \le 100\) fighters. Each fighter has a combat class in \(\{\text{J}, \text{HK}, \text{W}, \text{YYY}, \text{E}\}\) and base stamina \(a_i\) (or \(b_j\)). Class interactions follow a rock-paper-scissors tournament matrix, except that each team’s 'J' fighters gain \(+1\) stamina bonus for every 'YYY' fighter on the same team, and player 1 can perform at most \(M\) global upgrades. Find the maximum number of victorious bouts player 1 can achieve.







NoteProblem #217 — Hint 1 (Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Rejection)






Part A (CF 553D): Look closely at the objective: it is \(\max_S \min_{u \in S} \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\), not \(\max_S \frac{\sum_{u \in S} \deg_S(u)}{\sum_{u \in S} \deg_G(u)}\). With \(N, M = 10^5\), running Goldberg’s max-density min-cut is both too slow and solves the wrong objective! What happens to the weakest vertex \(u = \arg\min_{v \in S} \frac{\deg_S(v)}{\deg_G(v)}\) if we try to improve the bottleneck ratio of \(S\)?
Part B (P6577 / P3701): In P6577, \(N = 500, M = 2.5 \times 10^5\) with negative weights requires augmenting along shortest paths while maintaining dual vertex potentials \(u_i + v_j \ge w_{ij}\) and per-right-vertex minimum slack \(\text{slack}[j] = \min_{i \in S} (u_i + v_j - w_{ij})\) in \(O(N)\) per step (\(O(N^3)\) total). In P3701, since the 'YYY' count on each side is fixed from the input, each fighter’s effective capacity is a known static integer \(a'_i\) (plus a shared pool of capacidad \(M\) from a throttled super-source \(s \to s'\) of capacity \(M\) to 'W'/'HK' fighters), reducing directly to bipartite max-flow!










NoteProblem #217 — Hint 2 (Intermediate Algebraic & Structural Model)






Part A (CF 553D): Define \(r_S(u) = \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\). Notice the monotonicity property: if \(A \subseteq B\), then for every \(u \in A\), \(r_A(u) \le r_B(u)\). Therefore, if we start with \(S_0 = V \setminus F\) and at step \(t\) remove the vertex \(u_t \in S_{t-1}\) that currently minimizes \(r_{S_{t-1}}(u)\), any hypothetical optimal subset \(S^* \subseteq S_0\) must be a subset of \(S_{t-1}\) right up until the first step \(t^*\) where a vertex \(v \in S^*\) is popped! At that exact step \(t^*\), every \(w \in S_{t^*-1}\) satisfies: \[r_{S_{t^*-1}}(w) \ge r_{S_{t^*-1}}(v) \ge r_{S^*}(v) \ge \min_{u \in S^*} r_{S^*}(u)\] So \(S_{t^*-1}\) is at least as good as \(S^*\)!










NoteProblem #217 — Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
In Part A (CF 553D), the problem asks to maximize a minimum vertex ratio \(\min_{u \in S} \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\) over \(N, M \le 10^5\). This is the canonical signature of Bottleneck Subgraph Peeling (Generalized \(k\)-Core) from Ch 14.3, which stands as the primary decoy against Goldberg’s sum-ratio Maximum Density Subgraph (Ch 14.2). No flow network is needed at all — or alternatively, one can binary search \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\) and run a cascade BFS/queue deletion of all vertices with \(\deg_S(u) < \lambda \deg_G(u)\) in \(O(N + M)\) per check.
In Part B (P6577 & P3701), P6577 tests the \(O(N^3)\) primal-dual Hungarian slack-maintenance optimization for dense bipartite weighted matching (\(M = N^2 = 2.5 \times 10^5\)), while P3701 tests recognizing when seemingly dynamic team buffs (“each 'J' gains \(+1\) life per 'YYY' on the team”) are actually static constants because the roster is fixed before combat.


Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation
For Part A (CF 553D), let \(x_u \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate \(u \in S\), with \(x_u = 0\) forced for \(u \in F\). For any fixed threshold \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\), a non-empty valid set \(S\) with \(\min_{u \in S} \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)} \ge \lambda\) exists if and only if the system of monotone implications: \[x_u = 1 \implies \sum_{v \in N(u)} x_v \ge \lceil \lambda \deg_G(u) \rceil\] has a non-zero solution. Because the right-hand side is monotone in \(\mathbf{x}\), the pointwise maximal solution is obtained by starting with \(x_u = [u \notin F]\) and iteratively setting \(x_u \gets 0\) whenever \(\sum_{v \in N(u)} x_v < \lambda \deg_G(u)\).
Even better, instead of binary searching \(\lambda\), we eliminate \(\lambda\) altogether via the Greedy Peeling Sequence:

Initialize \(S_0 = V \setminus F\) and compute \(\deg_{S_0}(u)\) for all \(u \in S_0\).
For \(t = 1, 2, \dots, |S_0|\):

Let \(u_t = \arg\min_{u \in S_{t-1}} \frac{\deg_{S_{t-1}}(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\), and record \(\lambda_{t-1} = \frac{\deg_{S_{t-1}}(u_t)}{\deg_G(u_t)}\).
Set \(S_t = S_{t-1} \setminus \{u_t\}\), and decrement \(\deg_S(v)\) for all neighbors \(v \in N(u_t) \cap S_t\).

Return the prefix \(S_{t^*}\) that maximizes \(\lambda_{t^*}\).



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

Priority Queue Peeling (CF 553D):

Store pairs \((\frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}, u)\) in a min-heap (using lazy deletion when \(\deg_S(v)\) decreases).
Each edge \((u, v)\) triggers at most one decrement when its earlier endpoint is popped, giving at most \(N + M\) heap pushes.
Total complexity: \(O((N + M) \log N)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space, avoiding floating-point precision loss from binary search by comparing fractions \(\frac{a_1}{b_1} < \frac{a_2}{b_2} \iff a_1 b_2 < a_2 b_1\) in 64-bit integers.

Slack-Array Hungarian (P6577) & Static-Buff Max-Flow (P3701):

In P6577, maintaining slack[j] for \(j \in R \setminus T\) updates in \(O(N)\) whenever a new left vertex \(i\) enters the alternating tree \(S\), bounding each phase to \(O(N^2)\) and total time to \(O(N^3)\).
In P3701, count \(c_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n [t_{1,i} = \text{YYY}]\) and \(c_2 = \sum_{j=1}^n [t_{2,j} = \text{YYY}]\). Add \(c_1\) to the capacity \(s \to i\) of each 'J' on side 1 and \(c_2\) to the capacity \(j \to t\) of each 'J' on side 2; route an intermediate node \(s_{\text{bonus}}\) with \(c(s, s_{\text{bonus}}) = M\) and \(c(s_{\text{bonus}}, i) = 1\) for upgradeable fighters \(i\), and connect \(i \to j\) with capacity \(1\) whenever fighter \(i\)’s class defeats fighter \(j\)’s class.




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (CF 553D): Let \(N = 4\), edges \((1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (2,4)\), and fortress \(F = \{1\}\). Degrees in \(G\): \(\deg_G = (1, 3, 2, 2)\).

Initial \(S_0 = \{2, 3, 4\}\). Internal degrees \(\deg_{S_0}\): \(\deg_{S_0}(2) = 2\) (edges to \(3,4\)), \(\deg_{S_0}(3) = 2\), \(\deg_{S_0}(4) = 2\).

If we select \(v_t\) (\(x_{v_t} = 1\)), we gain \(w_{v_t}(\lambda) = P_{v_t} - \lambda S_{v_t}\), increment the count \(j \to j+1\), and advance to \(t + 1\).
If we reject \(v_t\) (\(x_{v_t} = 0\)), no descendant of \(v_t\) can be selected, so we jump directly from \(t\) to \(t + \text{sz}[t]\) with weight change \(0\) and count change \(0\).

Part B (Luogu P4001): Each grid cell \((r, c)\) (\(1 \le r < N, 1 \le c < M\)) is split by its main diagonal \((r, c) - (r+1, c+1)\) into a lower-left triangle \(L(r, c)\) and an upper-right triangle \(U(r, c)\). Dual potentials \(d(f)\) satisfy \(d(s^*) = 0\) and \(d(f_2) \le d(f_1) + w_e\) for every primal edge \(e\) separating faces \(f_1, f_2\), with \(\text{mincut}(s, t) = d(t^*)\).



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

DFS-Order Linear DP (Luogu P4322):

Precompute preorder sequence id[1..N+1] and subtree sizes sz[1..N+1] once before the binary search.
Inside check(lambda) (35–40 iterations on \([0, 10^4]\)):

Initialize \(dp[1][0] = 0\), all other \(dp[t][j] = -\infty\).
For \(t = 1\) to \(N+1\) and \(j = 0\) to \(\min(t, K+1)\):

If \(j + 1 \le K + 1\): \(dp[t+1][j+1] \gets \max(dp[t+1][j+1], dp[t][j] + w_{\text{id}[t]}(\lambda))\) (for \(t = 1\), \(v_1 = 0\) is forced).
If \(t > 1\): \(dp[t + \text{sz}[t]][j] \gets \max(dp[t + \text{sz}[t]][j], dp[t][j])\).

Return \(dp[N+2][K+1] \ge 0\).

Total time: \(O(NK \log(\frac{\max P}{\varepsilon})) \approx 2500^2 \times 35 \approx 2.1 \times 10^8\) simple max/addition operations (\(\sim 0.15\text{ s}\) in C++).

Create \(2(N-1)(M-1) + 2\) dual vertices: \(s^* = 0\), \(t^* = 2(N-1)(M-1) + 1\), \(L(r, c) = 2((r-1)(M-1) + (c-1)) + 1\), and \(U(r, c) = L(r, c) + 1\).
Horizontal edges on row \(r\), column \(c\):

Top row \(r = 1\): connects \(U(1, c)\) to \(t^*\).
Bottom row \(r = N\): connects \(L(N-1, c)\) to \(s^*\).
Interior row \(1 < r < N\): connects \(L(r-1, c)\) to \(U(r, c)\).

Vertical edges on row \(r\), column \(c\):

Left column \(c = 1\): connects \(L(r, 1)\) to \(s^*\).
Right column \(c = M\): connects \(U(r, M-1)\) to \(t^*\).
Interior column \(1 < c < M\): connects \(U(r, c-1)\) to \(L(r, c)\).

Diagonal edges in cell \((r, c)\): connects \(L(r, c)\) to \(U(r, c)\).
Run Dijkstra from \(s^*\) to \(t^*\) (handle the degenerate \(N = 1\) or \(M = 1\) case by taking the minimum single edge weight).
