Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Part A (POJ 3621): The problem combines 0-1 Fractional Programming (Ch 14.1) with a circulation / cycle domain rather than a cut domain. Recognizing that a walk’s vertex sum equals the sum of head-vertex weights along its edges (\(\sum_{v \in C} F_v = \sum_{(u \to v) \in C} F_v\)) compiles the linearized check \(F(\lambda) > 0\) into a negative-cycle detection problem.
Part B (Luogu P4126): Classifying all \(M = 60000\) edges as feasible (at least one min-cut) or mandatory (all min-cuts) requires reading the residual SCC condensation DAG of the maximum flow (Picard–Queyranne Theorem), which also underlies uniqueness of minimum cuts and canonical maximal/minimal \(s\)-side closures in Ch 14 and Ch 16.



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

Part A (POJ 3621): Let \(x_e \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether edge \(e = (u \to v)\) is on the cycle \(C\). A simple cycle satisfies flow conservation \(\sum_{e \in \delta^+(v)} x_e = \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} x_e \le 1\). By LP duality of shortest paths / negative cycles: \[\min_{\text{cycle } C} \sum_{e=(u\to v) \in C} (\lambda T_e - F_v) \ge 0 \iff \exists \text{ potentials } d_1, \dots, d_L \text{ such that } d_v - d_u \le \lambda T_e - F_v \;\;\forall (u \to v) \in E\]
Part B (Luogu P4126): By Complementary Slackness of Max-Flow Min-Cut, a cut \((S, T)\) (\(s \in S, t \in T\)) is a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut if and only if for every edge \((x \to y)\) in the residual graph \(G_f\) with residual capacity \(c_f(x, y) > 0\), we do not have \(x \in S\) and \(y \in T\) (i.e., \(x \in S \implies y \in S\)). Thus the valid minimum-cut source sets \(S\) are exactly the closed vertex subsets (upward closures) of \(G_f\) that contain \(s\) and exclude \(t\). Contracting each SCC of \(G_f\) yields a DAG where every vertex \(x\) has a unique SCC label \(\text{scc}[x]\).



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

Binary Search + SPFA Negative-Cycle Check (POJ 3621):

Binary search \(\lambda \in [0, 1000]\) for 30 iterations.
To check if \(\exists C\) with \(\sum_{e \in C} (\lambda T_e - F_v) < 0\):

Initialize dist[1..L] = 0, cnt[1..L] = 0, and push all \(1 \dots L\) into the queue (equivalent to a virtual super-source \(s_0\) with \(0\)-weight edges to all vertices so disconnected components are also searched).
Whenever dist[v] > dist[u] + lambda * T_e - F_v, update dist[v], set cnt[v] = cnt[u] + 1, and if cnt[v] >= L, return true (negative cycle exists).


Residual Tarjan SCC Classification (Luogu P4126):

Run Dinic from \(s\) to \(t\).
Build the directed graph \(H\) consisting of all edges \((x \to y)\) with positive residual capacity \(c_f(x, y) > 0\), and run Tarjan’s SCC algorithm on \(H\) to obtain \(\text{scc}[1..N]\).
For each original edge \(e = (u \to v) \in E\):

If \(e\) is not saturated (\(c_f(u, v) > 0\)), then \((u \to v) \in H \implies \text{scc}[u]\) can reach \(\text{scc}[v]\), or even simpler: by complementary slackness, no unsaturated edge can ever cross from \(S\) to \(T\) in any minimum cut! Output 0 0.
If \(e\) is saturated (\(c_f(u, v) = 0\)):

Feasible (ans1 = 1) \(\iff \text{scc}[u] \neq \text{scc}[v]\) (since if \(\text{scc}[u] \neq \text{scc}[v]\), we can take \(S\) to be the set of all vertices in \(G_f\) that can reach \(u\) or \(s\) without reaching \(v\) or \(t\) — wait: because \(e\) is saturated, the reverse residual edge \((v \to u)\) has \(c_f(v, u) = c(e) > 0\), so \(v\) can ALWAYS reach \(u\) in \(G_f\)! Thus \(u\) and \(v\) are in different SCCs \(\iff u\) cannot reach \(v\) in \(G_f\), which guarantees a valid closure \(S\) containing \(u\) and excluding \(v\)!).
Mandatory (ans2 = 1) \(\iff \text{scc}[u] = \text{scc}[s]\) and \(\text{scc}[v] = \text{scc}[t]\).

Toy Trace (Luogu P4126): Consider the path \(s = 1 \xrightarrow{5} 2 \xrightarrow{5} 3 = t\).

Max-flow is \(5\); both edges \((1 \to 2)\) and \((2 \to 3)\) are saturated.
Residual graph \(G_f\) has only reverse edges \(3 \to 2\) and \(2 \to 1\) with capacity \(5\).
SCCs of \(G_f\): \(\text{scc}[1] = \{1\}, \text{scc}[2] = \{2\}, \text{scc}[3] = \{3\}\) (three distinct singleton SCCs).
Edge \((1 \to 2)\): saturated, \(\text{scc}[1] \neq \text{scc}[2] \implies\) feasible (1); \(\text{scc}[1] = \text{scc}[s]\) is true, but \(\text{scc}[2] = \text{scc}[t]\) is false \(\implies\) not mandatory (0). Indeed, the cut \((\{1,2\}, \{3\})\) avoids cutting \((1 \to 2)\).
Edge \((2 \to 3)\): saturated, \(\text{scc}[2] \neq \text{scc}[3] \implies\) feasible (1); \(\text{scc}[2] \neq \text{scc}[s] \implies\) not mandatory (0).

Yet \((1 \to 2)\) and \((2 \to 3)\) are both minimum cut edges! Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Part A (Luogu P3329): The problem asks for the distribution of \(\text{mincut}_G(u, v)\) across all \(\binom{N}{2}\) unordered pairs in an undirected graph with \(N \le 150\). By the Gomory–Hu Theorem (Ch 16.4), any undirected graph admits a weighted tree \(T_{\text{GH}}\) on \(V\) such that for all \(u \neq v\): \[\text{mincut}_G(u, v) = \min_{e \in P_{T_{\text{GH}}}(u, v)} w(e)\] Building \(T_{\text{GH}}\) takes \(N - 1\) Dinic runs instead of \(\binom{N}{2}\).
Part B (CF 472D): Tests the dual question: given an \(N \times N\) matrix, when is it realizable by a tree?

For an ultrametric / bottleneck cut matrix \(\Lambda_{u,v} = \min_{e \in P_T(u,v)} w_e\), \(\Lambda\) is realizable iff \(\Lambda_{u,v} \ge \min(\Lambda_{u,w}, \Lambda_{w,v})\) for all triples, and the tree is a Maximum Spanning Tree of \(\Lambda\).
For an additive tree metric \(d_{u,v} = \sum_{e \in P_T(u,v)} w_e\), the shortest non-zero entries between components must be direct tree edges, so the unique candidate tree \(T\) is the Minimum Spanning Tree of \(d\) (with positive edge weights \(d_{u,v} > 0\) for \(u \neq v\) and \(d_{u,u} = 0\)), verified by running \(N\) DFS passes on \(T\) in \(O(N^2)\) to check \(d_T(u, v) == d_{u, v}\).




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation
Why does Gusfield’s uncontracted algorithm work in Part A? Because undirected cut capacity \(f(S) = |\delta_G(S)|\) is symmetric and submodular: \[f(A) + f(B) \ge f(A \cap B) + f(A \cup B), \quad f(A) = f(V \setminus A)\] This guarantees Uncrossing of Minimum Cuts: if \((X, \bar{X})\) is a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in \(G\), then for any pair \(u, v \in X\), there exists a minimum \(u\)-\(v\) cut \((Y, \bar{Y})\) in \(G\) that does not cross \((X, \bar{X})\) (i.e., \(Y \subseteq X\)). Consequently, updating \(p[u] \gets s\) for all \(u \in X \cap \{v > s : p[v] = t\}\) preserves the invariant that every current star/tree partition can be refined without ever contracting supernodes in \(G\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

Gusfield’s Algorithm (Luogu P3329):

Store the original undirected capacities on \(G\).Before each of the \(N-1\) Dinic runs, reset edge flows to \(0\) (restore initial capacities).
Maintain p[1..N] initialized to p[i] = 1 for \(i \ge 2\), and w[2..N].
For \(s = 2 \dots N\):

t = p[s]
w[s] = dinic(s, t)
Perform a BFS/DFS from \(s\) in the residual graph (cap > 0) to mark vis[u] = true for \(u \in S\).
For \(u = s + 1 \dots N\): if vis[u] && p[u] == t, set p[u] = s.

Build adjacency list of \(T_{\text{GH}}\) with edges (s, p[s], w[s]) for \(s = 2 \dots N\).
Collect all \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairwise bottleneck values into a vector cuts of size \(N(N-1)/2\) via \(N\) simple tree DFS runs, sort cuts, and answer each query x with upper_bound(cuts.begin(), cuts.end(), x) - cuts.begin().

Additive Tree Metric Verification (CF 472D):

Check \(d_{i,i} = 0\), \(d_{i,j} = d_{j,i} > 0\) for \(i \neq j\).
Run \(O(N^2)\) Prim’s algorithm on the complete graph with weights \(d_{i,j}\) to build candidate tree \(T\).
Run DFS from each root \(r = 1 \dots N\) on \(T\) to verify \(d_T(r, v) == d_{r, v}\) for all \(v\).




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (Luogu P3329, \(N = 3\) triangle): Edges \((1,2)\) weight \(3\), \((2,3)\) weight \(4\), \((1,3)\) weight \(5\).

Init: \(p[2] = 1, p[3] = 1\).
Step \(s = 2, t = p[2] = 1\): Min-cut between \(2\) and \(1\) is \(3 + 4 = 7\) with \(S = \{2\}, T = \{1, 3\}\). So \(w[2] = 7\). Since \(3 \notin S\), \(p[3]\) remains \(1\).
Step \(s = 3, t = p[3] = 1\): Min-cut between \(3\) and \(1\) is \(4 + 5 = 9\) (wait: cutting \(\{2, 3\}\) from \(\{1\}\) has cost \(3 + 5 = 8 < 9\)! So the min \(3\)-\(1\) cut is \(S = \{2, 3\}, T = \{1\}\) with capacity \(w[3] = 8\)).
Tree \(T_{\text{GH}}\) has edges \((2, 1)\) of weight \(7\) and \((3, 1)\) of weight \(8\).
Pairwise bottlenecks on \(T_{\text{GH}}\): \(\lambda(1, 2) = 7\), \(\lambda(1, 3) = 8\), \(\lambda(2, 3) = \min(7, 8) = 7\) (indeed, cutting \(\{2\}\) from \(\{1, 3\}\) costs \(3 + 4 = 7\)).

Broken Counterexample (FM-16c: Updating Already-Processed Parents Without Recording Edge Weights Properly): In Gusfield’s algorithm, if you add the tree edge \((s, p[s])\) to the adjacency list of \(T_{\text{GH}}\) immediately at step \(s\), and then a later step \(s' > s\) changes \(p[u]\) for some \(u > s'\), that works because only unprocessed vertices \(u > s\) have their p[u] modified! However, if you also loop over \(u < s\) when updating p[u] = s without adjusting the already-added tree edge \((u, p[u])\), you corrupt the tree topology (unless you wait until the end to add (i, p[i], w[i]) AND handle the tree-rewiring rule for \(u < s\)). Keeping the simple loop for u = s + 1 .. N: if (vis[u] && p[u] == t) p[u] = s and adding edge (s, t, w[s]) at step \(s\) is 100% invariant-safe!









Problem #221 — Planar Global Minimum Cut, Directed Dual Grids & Cut Uniqueness (Planar Global Min-Cut Benchmark & Luogu P6123 / P2046)

Part A (ICPC Planar Global Minimum Cut Benchmark / BZOJ 1001 & Planar Dual Shortest Cycle, Ch 15.1 Reference)
You are given a connected undirected planar graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(N \le 3000\) vertices, \(M \le 3N - 6\) positively weighted edges \(w_e > 0\), and a planar embedding with \(F = M - N + 2\) faces. Unlike standard \(s\)-\(t\) cut problems, no source \(s\) or sink \(t\) is specified. Find the global minimum cut of \(G\):
\[\min_{\emptyset \neq S \subsetneq V} \sum_{e \in \delta_G(S)} w_e\]
in \(O(F^2 \log F)\) or \(O(F \log^2 F)\) time without running \(N - 1\) max-flows or \(O(N^3)\) Stoer–Wagner.


Part B (Luogu P6123 — [JSOI2009] 最小割唯一性 & Luogu P2046 — [NOI2010] 海拔, Judge Link (P6123), Judge Link (P2046))

Minimum Cut Uniqueness (Luogu P6123): Given a directed flow network \(G = (V, E)\) with source \(s\) and sink \(t\), determine whether the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut vertex partition \((S, T)\) is unique, and compute both the minimum possible size \(|S_{\min}|\) and maximum possible size \(|S_{\max}|\) of the \(s\)-side across all minimum cuts.
Directed Continuous Altitude Grid (Luogu P2046 — [NOI2010] 海拔): On an \((N+1) \times (N+1)\) directed grid (\(N \le 500\)) where \((0,0)\) has altitude \(0\) and \((N,N)\) has altitude \(1\), every directed edge \(e = (u \to v)\) between adjacent intersections has traffic volume \(w(u \to v) \ge 0\), and consumes energy \(w(u \to v) \cdot \max(0, h_v - h_u)\). Assign real altitudes \(h_v \in [0, 1]\) to all intersections to minimize total energy consumed across all directed edges.







NoteProblem #221 — Hint 1 (Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Rejection)






Part A (Planar Global Min-Cut): In an undirected planar graph \(G\), what is the planar dual of a minimal global cut \(\delta_G(S)\)? Every minimal cut \(\delta_G(S)\) separates \(G\) into two connected components, which corresponds in the planar dual \(G^*\) to a simple cycle \(C^*\)! Thus the global minimum cut of \(G\) equals the Minimum Weight Simple Cycle (Girth) of the undirected dual graph \(G^*\).
Part B (P6123 & P2046):

In P6123, let \(S_{\min}\) be the set of vertices reachable from \(s\) in the final residual graph \(G_f\), and let \(T_{\min}\) be the set of vertices that can reach \(t\) in \(G_f\). When is the minimum cut unique?
In P2046, by the Coarea / Total Variation Theorem (Ch 13.3 and Ch 15.2), \(\min_{h \in [0,1]^V} \sum_{(u \to v)} w(u \to v) \max(0, h_v - h_u)\) attains its optimum at a binary \(0\)-\(1\) assignment \(h_v \in \{0, 1\}\), where \(h_u = 0, h_v = 1\) pays \(w(u \to v)\)! Since \(s = (0,0)\) has \(h_s = 0\) and \(t = (N,N)\) has \(h_t = 1\), this is a directed planar \(s\)-\(t\) minimum cut!











NoteProblem #221 — Hint 2 (Intermediate Algebraic & Structural Model)






Part A (Planar Global Min-Cut):

Method 1 (\(O(F^2 \log F)\) for \(F \le 3000\)): For each dual vertex \(f^* \in V(G^*)\), run Dijkstra to construct the shortest-path tree \(T^*\) rooted at \(f^*\); the shortest simple cycle through \(f^*\) is \(\min_{e^*=(u^*, v^*) \notin T^*} (\text{dist}(f^*, u^*) + \text{dist}(f^*, v^*) + w(e^*))\) across non-tree edges where \(\text{lca}_{T^*}(u^*, v^*) = f^*\).
Method 2 (\(O(F \log^2 F)\) Chalermsook–Fakcharoenphol–Nanongkai Divide-and-Conquer): Fix any spanning tree \(T^*\) of \(G^*\) and root a shortest-path tree from an arbitrary vertex. Any simple cycle \(C^*\) crosses a fixed shortest path \(P^* = (v^*_1, \dots, v^*_k)\) an odd number of times after cutting the plane along \(P^*\); dividing \(P^*\) at its midpoint \(v^*_{k/2}\) and running Dijkstra in the sliced dual graph finds the shortest cycle through \(v^*_{k/2}\) in \(O(F \log F)\), yielding \(T(k) = 2T(k/2) + O(F \log F) = O(F \log^2 F)\).

Part B (P6123 & P2046):

In P6123, \(S_{\min} = \{u \in V : s \rightsquigarrow_{G_f} u\}\) is the minimal \(s\)-side closure, and \(S_{\max} = V \setminus \{u \in V : u \rightsquigarrow_{G_f} t\}\) is the maximal \(s\)-side closure. The minimum cut is unique if and only if \(S_{\min} = S_{\max}\) (i.e., \(S_{\min} \cup T_{\min} = V\))!
In P2046, beware the orientation trap (FM-15a): an altitude jump from \(0\) (\(s\)-side) to \(1\) (\(t\)-side) along \(u \to v\) means \(u \in S\) and \(v \in T\). Therefore, the cost of cutting \(u\) into \(S\) and \(v\) into \(T\) is \(w(u \to v)\) (the traffic from \(u\) to \(v\)), so the directed dual edge crossing \(u \to v\) from the \(s\)-side (left) to the \(t\)-side (right) has weight \(w(u \to v)\)!











NoteProblem #221 — Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Part A (Planar Global Min-Cut): An undirected planar graph with no specified terminals asks for \(\min_{\emptyset \neq S \subsetneq V} |\delta_G(S)|\). By Whitney’s cycle–cut bijection (Ch 15.1), minimal bond cuts in \(G\) are in \(1\)-to-\(1\) weight-preserving correspondence with simple cycles in the planar dual \(G^*\).
Part B (P6123 & P2046): P6123 tests the lattice structure of minimum cuts (\(S_{\min}\) vs. \(S_{\max}\) via forward/backward residual reachability), while P2046 tests the two-stage compilation:

Coarea / LP Total Unimodularity: Continuous altitude optimization \(\min_{h \in [0,1]^V} \sum w_{uv} \max(0, h_v - h_u)\) reduces to \(0\)-\(1\) minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut because \(\max(0, h_v - h_u) = \int_0^1 [h_u \le \lambda < h_v]\,d\lambda\).
Directed Planar Dual Dijkstra: With \((N+1)^2 \approx 2.5 \times 10^5\) grid vertices, Dinic is replaced by a single Dijkstra pass on \(N^2 + 2\) dual faces.




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation
For Part B (P2046), let \(S_\lambda = \{v \in V : h_v \le \lambda\}\) for \(\lambda \in [0, 1)\). Since \(h_{(0,0)} = 0\) and \(h_{(N,N)} = 1\), \((0,0) \in S_\lambda\) and \((N,N) \notin S_\lambda\) for all \(\lambda \in [0, 1)\). By the Coarea Formula: \[\sum_{(u \to v) \in E} w(u \to v) \max(0, h_v - h_u) = \int_0^1 \left( \sum_{u \in S_\lambda, v \notin S_\lambda} w(u \to v) \right) d\lambda \ge \min_{\substack{S \subseteq V \\ (0,0) \in S, (N,N) \notin S}} \text{cap}^+(S, V \setminus S)\] and equality is achieved by setting \(h_v = 0\) for \(v \in S^*\) and \(h_v = 1\) for \(v \notin S^*\).


Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

Planar Dual Shortest Cycle (Part A):

Extract faces of \(G\) via half-edge next-clockwise rotation (next_edge(u -> v) = predecessor of v -> u in cyclic order around \(v\)).
Build undirected dual \(G^*\) with \(F\) vertices and \(M\) edges.
Run Dijkstra from each dual face (or use the \(O(F \log^2 F)\) shortest-path-slice divide-and-conquer) to find the minimum weight simple cycle in \(G^*\). (Be sure to handle parallel dual edges of size \(2\) explicitly if \(G\) has degree-2 vertices / 2-edge cuts!)

Directed Dual Grid (P2046):

Place \(s^*\) along the bottom and left outer boundaries, and \(t^*\) along the top and right outer boundaries.
Cell \((r, c)\) (\(1 \le r, c \le N\)) is dual vertex \((r-1)N + c\).
Follow the Right-Hand Rule standing at \(u\) looking toward \(v\):

Eastbound primal edge \((r, c-1) \to (r, c)\): left is cell \((r, c)\) (above, if row \(0\) is top: let row \(0\) be top and row \(N\) be bottom!). Then looking East from \((r, c-1)\) to \((r, c)\), left is North (cell \((r, c)\)) and right is South (cell \((r+1, c)\)). Wait: let’s check where \(s^*\) and \(t^*\) are! \(s = (0,0)\) is top-left and \(t = (N,N)\) is bottom-right. If \(s^*\) is the bottom-left outer face and \(t^*\) is the top-right outer face, then our dual path travels from bottom-left (\(s^*\)) to top-right (\(t^*\)).
As we walk along the dual path from \(s^*\) (bottom-left) to \(t^*\) (top-right), the source \(s = (0,0)\) (top-left) is to our LEFT, and the sink \(t = (N,N)\) (bottom-right) is to our RIGHT!
Therefore, a primal edge \(u \to v\) crosses from \(S\) (left of dual path) to \(T\) (right of dual path) when \(u\) is to the left of the dual edge and \(v\) is to the right:

Eastbound \((r, c-1) \to (r, c)\): crosses from left to right of a Northbound dual edge from cell \((r+1, c)\) (below) to cell \((r, c)\) (above)!
Southbound \((r-1, c) \to (r, c)\): crosses from left to right of an Eastbound dual edge from cell \((r, c)\) (left) to cell \((r, c+1)\) (right)!
Westbound \((r, c) \to (r, c-1)\): compiles to Southbound dual edge from cell \((r, c)\) to cell \((r+1, c)\).
Northbound \((r, c) \to (r-1, c)\): compiles to Westbound dual edge from cell \((r, c+1)\) to cell \((r, c)\).






Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (P2046, \(N = 1\), \(1 \times 1\) cell):

Top edge \((0,0) \to (0,1)\) has weight \(10\); right edge \((0,1) \to (1,1)\) has weight \(20\); bottom edge \((0,0) \to (1,0)\) has weight \(30\); left edge \((1,0) \to (1,1)\) has weight \(40\). All reverse edges have weight \(999\).
Single internal face \(f_1 = (1,1)\).
Bottom edge \((0,0) \to (1,0)\) is Southbound on left border \(\implies\) Eastbound dual edge \(s^* \to f_1\) of weight \(30\).
Left-to-right bottom edge \((1,0) \to (1,1)\) is Eastbound on bottom border \(\implies\) Northbound dual edge \(s^* \to f_1\) of weight \(40\).
Top edge \((0,0) \to (0,1)\) is Eastbound on top border \(\implies\) Northbound dual edge \(f_1 \to t^*\) of weight \(10\).
Right edge \((0,1) \to (1,1)\) is Southbound on right border \(\implies\) Eastbound dual edge \(f_1 \to t^*\) of weight \(20\).
Shortest path \(s^* \to f_1 \to t^*\) has cost \(\min(30, 40) + \min(10, 20) = 30 + 10 = 40\), cutting \((0,0) \to (1,0)\) and \((0,0) \to (0,1)\), which isolates \(S = \{(0,0)\}\)!

Broken Counterexample (FM-15: Swapping Left-to-Right with Right-to-Left): If you rotate primal edges \(90^\circ\) clockwise instead of counterclockwise when \(s^*\) is bottom-left and \(t^*\) is top-right, the dual edge \(s^* \to f_1\) receives the weight of \((1,0) \to (0,0)\) (\(999\)) instead of \((0,0) \to (1,0)\) (\(30\)), computing the minimum \(t\)-\(s\) cut instead of the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut! Always verify with a \(1 \times 1\) cell trace where \(S = \{(0,0)\}\) cuts the two outgoing edges from \((0,0)\).

For each edge \(e_i = (u_i \to v_i)\) independently (\(1 \le i \le M\)), determine whether reversing \(e_i\) into \((v_i \to u_i)\) changes the number of Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) of \(G\). Given an undirected tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(N \le 100,010\) junctions, find the minimum number of junctions where lights must be placed so that every tree edge has a light at at least one of its endpoints, and count the number of such minimum vertex covers modulo \(10007\). NoteProblem #222 — Hint 1 (Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Rejection)






Part A (ARC 092F): A naive solver might think of edge connectivity, Gomory–Hu, or running Tarjan \(M\) times (\(O(M^2) = 4 \times 10^{10}\), TLE). Instead, analyze what reversing a single directed edge \(e = (u \to v)\) does to reachability between \(u\) and \(v\):

Condition \(Q(e)\): Can \(v\) already reach \(u\) in \(G\) (which is equivalent to \(v\) reaching \(u\) in \(G \setminus \{e\}\))? How do the truth values of \(P(e)\) and \(Q(e)\) determine whether the SCC count changes?

Part B (SPOJ VOCV): Every tree is bipartite, so Minimum Vertex Cover = Maximum Matching = \(s\)-\(t\) Min-Cut by König’s Theorem. Wait: not only is \(N = 10^5\) a linear-time tree, the problem also asks for the number of minimum cuts / vertex covers modulo \(10007\)! NoteProblem #222 — Hint 2 (Intermediate Algebraic & Structural Model)






Part A (ARC 092F): Compare \(G\) (which has \(u \to v\)) and \(G' = (G \setminus \{e\}) \cup \{v \to u\}\):

Case 1: \(Q(e) = \text{false}\) (\(v\) cannot reach \(u\) in \(G \setminus \{e\}\)). Then in \(G\), \(u\) and \(v\) are in different SCCs. In \(G'\), \(v \to u\) is present, so \(u\) and \(v\) merge into the same SCC iff \(P(e) = \text{true}\) (\(u\) can reach \(v\) in \(G \setminus \{e\}\))! (And if \(P(e) = \text{false}\), could reversing \(u \to v\) create a cycle elsewhere? No, any new cycle in \(G'\) must use \(v \to u\), which requires a path \(u \rightsquigarrow v\) in \(G \setminus \{e\}\)!)

In \(G'\), since \(v \rightsquigarrow u\) already exists without \(e\), adding \(v \to u\) is redundant; thus the SCCs stay identical iff \(u\) can still reach \(v\) in \(G \setminus \{e\}\), i.e., \(P(e) = \text{true}\)!

How do we compute \(P(e)\) (existence of a \(u \rightsquigarrow v\) path avoiding \(e = (u \to v)\)) for all outgoing edges of \(u\) simultaneously in \(O(NM)\) total time?











NoteProblem #222 — Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Part A (ARC 092F): Tests structural reachability and two-path disjointness (Menger’s Theorem for \(k = 2\) at the root edge). With \(N \le 1000, M \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(O(NM)\) is \(\le 2 \times 10^8\) operations, telling us we can afford \(O(M)\) work per source vertex \(u\), but not per edge \(e\).
Part B (SPOJ VOCV): Tests Direction B Cut/Cover DP on Trees (Ch 16.1). Whenever a problem asks for the number of optimal minimum cuts / vertex covers on a tree or bounded-treewidth graph, flow algorithms cannot directly count the number of distinct minimum cuts (which is #P-complete on general graphs!), whereas tree DP maintains (min_cost, count_ways) pairs effortlessly in \(O(N)\).



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

Part A (ARC 092F): For every directed edge \(e = (u \to v)\): \[\text{SCCs}(G) \neq \text{SCCs}(G \text{ with } e \text{ reversed}) \iff P(u \to v) \oplus Q(u \to v) = 1\] where:

\(Q(u \to v) = [v \text{ can reach } u \text{ in } G]\) (computable by standard DFS from every vertex).
\(P(u \to v) = [u \text{ can reach } v \text{ in } G \setminus \{(u \to v)\}]\). How do we find \(P(u \to v)\) for all neighbors \(v \in N^+(u)\) of a fixed root \(u\)? Suppose \(u\) has outgoing edges to \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_d\). An alternative path from \(u\) to \(w_i\) avoiding \((u \to w_i)\) must start with some other outgoing edge \((u \to w_j)\) with \(j \neq i\) and then reach \(w_i\) in \(G \setminus \{u\}\)! Therefore, if we sweep through \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_d\) in forward order (\(1 \to d\), running incremental DFS where each vertex is visited at most once) and then in reverse order (\(d \to 1\), running a second incremental DFS), \(w_i\) is reachable from some \(w_j\) (\(j \neq i\)) if and only if \(w_i\) was already visited before step \(i\) in either the forward sweep or the reverse sweep!

Part B (SPOJ VOCV): For each vertex \(u\) and state \(c \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(c = 1\): light at \(u\), \(c = 0\): no light at \(u\)), define the tropical-counting pair \((dp[u][c], \text{ways}[u][c])\):

\(dp[u][0] = \sum_{v \in \text{children}(u)} dp[v][1]\), \(\text{ways}[u][0] = \prod_{v \in \text{children}(u)} \text{ways}[v][1]\).
\(dp[u][1] = 1 + \sum_{v \in \text{children}(u)} \min(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])\), where \(\text{ways}[u][1]\) multiplies \(w(v) = \text{ways}[v][0]\) (if \(dp[v][0] < dp[v][1]\)), \(\text{ways}[v][1]\) (if \(dp[v][1] < dp[v][0]\)), or \(\text{ways}[v][0] + \text{ways}[v][1]\) (if tied).




Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

Prefix-Suffix Incremental DFS (ARC 092F):

Fix source \(u \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) with outgoing neighbors \(w_1, \dots, w_d\):

Forward Pass: Maintain vis_fwd[1..N] = false, vis_fwd[u] = true. For \(i = 1 \dots d\):

If vis_fwd[w_i] is already true, mark P[u -> w_i] = true.
Otherwise, run DFS from \(w_i\) marking vis_fwd on all newly reached vertices.

Backward Pass: Maintain vis_bwd[1..N] = false, vis_bwd[u] = true. For \(i = d \dots 1\):

If vis_bwd[w_i] is already true, mark P[u -> w_i] = true.
Otherwise, run DFS from \(w_i\) marking vis_bwd on all newly reached vertices.


Because each vertex is marked at most once in the forward pass and once in the backward pass for a fixed \(u\), each root \(u\) takes \(O(N + M)\) time! Across all \(N\) vertices, total time is \(2 N(N + M) \approx 4 \times 10^8\) elementary operations (\(\sim 0.3\text{ s}\) in C++).
Furthermore, vis_fwd[v] at the end of root \(u\)’s forward pass equals \([u \text{ can reach } v \text{ in } G]\), giving \(Q(v \to u)\) for free without any extra DFS!




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (ARC 092F): Let \(N = 3\) with edges \(e_1 = (1 \to 2)\), \(e_2 = (2 \to 3)\), \(e_3 = (1 \to 3)\).

SCCs of \(G\): \(\{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}\) (\(3\) SCCs, since \(G\) is a DAG). Thus \(Q(e_i) = \text{false}\) for all \(3\) edges.
Check \(P(e_1 = 1 \to 2)\): can \(1\) reach \(2\) without \(e_1\)? Only \(1 \to 3\) leaves \(1\), and \(3\) has no outgoing edges, so \(P(e_1) = \text{false}\). Since \(P \oplus Q = 0 \oplus 0 = 0\), output same (reversing \(1 \to 2\) gives \(2 \to 1, 2 \to 3, 1 \to 3\), still a DAG with \(3\) SCCs!).
Check \(P(e_3 = 1 \to 3)\): can \(1\) reach \(3\) without \(e_3\)? Yes, via \(1 \to 2 \to 3\), so \(P(e_3) = \text{true}\)! Now \(P \oplus Q = 1 \oplus 0 = 1 \implies\) output diff (indeed, reversing \(1 \to 3\) into \(3 \to 1\) creates the cycle \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1\), collapsing \(3\) SCCs into \(1\)!).

Broken Counterexample: A common buggy heuristic is “reversing \(e = (u \to v)\) changes the SCC count iff \(e\) is a bridge in the underlying graph or \(P(e)\) is true.” Look at a bidirected cycle \(1 \leftrightarrow 2 \leftrightarrow 3 \leftrightarrow 1\): here \(P(1 \to 2) = \text{true}\) (via \(1 \to 3 \to 2\)) AND \(Q(1 \to 2) = \text{true}\), and reversing \(1 \to 2\) leaves \(1, 2, 3\) in a single SCC (same), which is why both \(P(e)\) and \(Q(e)\) must be combined via \(P(e) \oplus Q(e)\)!









Problem #223 — Planar Subdivision Enclosure Queries, Tree Exchange & Dense Cut DP (Luogu P3249 & CF 1284F / CF 724E)

Part A (Luogu P3249 — [HNOI2016] 矿区, Judge Link)
You are given a planar straight-line graph (PSLG) with \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) vertices and \(M \le 3N - 6\) undirected segments that partition the plane into bounded polygonal regions (ores) and one unbounded outer face. You must process \(Q \le 2 \times 10^5\) online queries. Each query specifies a simple cycle of vertices \(v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k\) along the graph edges (\(\sum k \le 2 \times 10^5\)) that forms the boundary of a mining zone \(R\). Output the simplified fraction:
\[\frac{\sum_{f \subset R} (\text{Area}(f))^2}{\sum_{f \subset R} \text{Area}(f)}\]
summed over all bounded elementary faces \(f\) enclosed inside the query polygon \(R\).


Part B (Codeforces 1284F — New Year and Social Network & Codeforces 724E — Goods Transportation, Judge Link (CF 1284F), Judge Link (CF 724E))

Tree Cut-Cycle Exchange Bijection (CF 1284F): Given two trees \(T_1, T_2\) on the same \(N \le 2.5 \times 10^5\) vertices, construct a sequence of \(N - 1\) operations where at step \(i\), you remove an edge \(e_1 \in E(T_1)\) and replace it with an edge \(e_2 \in E(T_2)\) such that the intermediate graph remains a connected tree after every single step!
Dense Prefix-to-Suffix Flow Compression (CF 724E): \(N \le 10^4\) cities sit on a line \(1 \dots N\). City \(i\) produces \(p_i\) goods and can sell at most \(s_i\) goods; furthermore, for every pair \(1 \le i < j \le N\), up to \(c\) goods can be shipped directly from \(i\) to \(j\). Compute the maximum total goods sold (Direction B Min-Cut DP, Ch 16.1).







NoteProblem #223 — Hint 1 (Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Rejection)






Part A (Luogu P3249): A query polygon \(C\) on the primal planar graph \(G\) is a primal simple cycle. By Planar Cycle–Cut Duality (Ch 15.4), what is a primal simple cycle \(C\) in the planar dual \(G^*\)? It is a minimal dual cut \(\delta_{G^*}(S^*)\) separating the enclosed faces \(S^*\) from the unbounded outer face \(f^*_\infty\)!
Part B (CF 1284F & CF 724E):

In CF 1284F, if \(e_2 = (u, v)\) is a leaf edge in \(T_2\) (say \(u\) is a leaf in \(T_2\)), then in \(T_1\), the unique path \(P_{T_1}(u, v)\) between \(u\) and \(v\) is the fundamental cycle of \(e_2\), and removing \(e_2\) from \(T_2\) leaves \(\{u\}\) as a cut! Which edge \(e_1 \in P_{T_1}(u, v)\) not yet replaced can be swapped with \(e_2\)?
In CF 724E, see Drill 1.4: running Dinic on \(\binom{N}{2} = 5 \times 10^7\) edges will TLE/MLE, whereas converting max-flow to min-cut \(x_i \in \{S, T\}\) depends only on the count \(k\) of prior vertices in \(S\)!











NoteProblem #223 — Hint 2 (Intermediate Algebraic & Structural Model)






Part A (Luogu P3249):

Extract all elementary faces of the PSLG using half-edge angle sorting and compute each bounded face’s signed area \(2 \cdot \text{Area}(f) = \sum_{(u \to v) \in \partial f} (x_u y_v - x_v y_u)\) (faces with negative signed area are the outer unbounded face \(f^*_\infty\)).
Build the planar dual \(G^*\) and take any spanning tree \(T^*\) of \(G^*\) rooted at the outer face \(f^*_\infty\), precomputing subtree sums \(\text{sub}_1(f^*)\) (sum of \(\text{Area}\)) and \(\text{sub}_2(f^*)\) (sum of \(\text{Area}^2\)).
When a query cycle \(v_1 \to v_2 \to \dots \to v_k \to v_1\) arrives, most dual edges crossing the cycle are non-tree edges in \(G^* \setminus T^*\) (which we ignore!). For each cycle edge \((v_i \to v_{i+1})\) whose dual \(e^* = (f^*_{\text{left}}, f^*_{\text{right}})\) is a tree edge in \(T^*\):

If \(f^*_{\text{left}}\) (the interior of the counterclockwise query polygon) is the child of \(f^*_{\text{right}}\) in \(T^*\), we add \(\text{sub}(f^*_{\text{left}})\).
If \(f^*_{\text{right}}\) is the child of \(f^*_{\text{left}}\) in \(T^*\), we subtract \(\text{sub}(f^*_{\text{right}})\)!












NoteProblem #223 — Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Part A (Luogu P3249): Asking for the sum of face weights inside a query cycle \(C\) on a planar graph with \(\sum |C| \le 2 \times 10^5\) is the canonical signature of Planar Dual Spanning-Tree Subtree Accumulation (Ch 15.4). Just as a cut in a tree is a single edge, restricting a dual cut \(\delta_{G^*}(S^*)\) to a dual spanning tree \(T^*\) expresses the indicator vector of any enclosed region \(S^*\) as a signed sum of subtree indicators along the boundary \(\partial S^* \cap E(T^*)\)!
Part B (CF 1284F & CF 724E):

CF 1284F tests the Graphic Matroid Cut–Cycle Exchange Duality: peeling \(T_2\) leaf-by-leaf from bottom to top, for a leaf \(u\) of \(T_2\) with parent \(v = p_2[u]\), the cut \((\{u\}, V \setminus \{u\})\) in \(T_2\) must cross at least one unmerged edge on the \(u\)-\(v\) path in \(T_1\); specifically, the first unmerged edge on \(P_{T_1}(u, v)\) starting from \(u\) (found via Link-Cut Tree or DSU + binary lifting) can be safely exchanged with \((u, v)\).
CF 724E is the foundational benchmark of Direction B: Max-Flow \(\to\) Min-Cut DP (Ch 16.1).




Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

Part A (Luogu P3249): Let \(T^*\) be a spanning tree of \(G^*\) rooted at \(f^*_\infty\). For every face \(f^* \neq f^*_\infty\), let \(P_{T^*}(f^*_\infty, f^*)\) be the unique root-to-\(f^*\) path in \(T^*\). For any query region \(S^* \subseteq V(G^*) \setminus \{f^*_\infty\}\) bounded by a counterclockwise cycle \(C\), walking along \(P_{T^*}(f^*_\infty, f^*)\) starts outside \(S^*\) (\([f^*_\infty \in S^*] = 0\)) and flips between \(0\) and \(1\) every time it crosses \(\partial S^*\): \[[f^* \in S^*] = \sum_{e^* = (\text{par}(u^*), u^*) \in P_{T^*}(f^*_\infty, f^*) \cap \partial S^*} \text{sign}(e^*, C)\] where \(\text{sign}(e^*, C) = +1\) if \(u^*\) lies to the left (interior) of \(C\) and \(-1\) if \(u^*\) lies to the right (exterior) of \(C\). Summing over all \(f^* \in V(G^*)\) and swapping the order of summation gives: \[\sum_{f^* \in S^*} W(f^*) = \sum_{e^* = (\text{par}(u^*), u^*) \in \partial S^* \cap E(T^*)} \text{sign}(e^*, C) \cdot \text{SubtreeSum}_{T^*}(u^*)\]
Part B (CF 724E): \[\text{MaxFlow} = \min_{x \in \{0,1\}^N} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^N \left( p_i (1 - x_i) + s_i x_i \right) + \sum_{1 \le i < j \le N} c \cdot x_i (1 - x_j) \right]\]



Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

Planar Face Extraction & Dual Tree Prefix Sums (Luogu P3249):

Split each undirected segment into two half-edges \(2i\) and \(2i+1\). At each vertex \(u\), sort outgoing half-edges by polar angle atan2(dy, dx).
The next half-edge after \(e = (u \to v)\) on the face to the left of \(e\) is the predecessor of \((v \to u)\) in \(v\)’s sorted outgoing list.
Trace all half-edge cycles; the unique cycle with \(\sum (x_u y_v - x_v y_u) < 0\) is \(f^*_\infty\).
Run DFS on \(G^*\) from \(f^*_\infty\) to build spanning tree \(T^*\), marking which primal half-edges correspond to tree edges in \(T^*\) and precomputing \(\text{sub}_1[u^*] = \sum (2\text{Area})\) and \(\text{sub}_2[u^*] = \sum (2\text{Area})^2\).
Answer each query \(v_1, \dots, v_k\) in \(O(k \log(\text{deg}))\) time by looking up each directed half-edge \((v_i \to v_{i+1})\) and adding/subtracting \(\text{sub}[u^*]\) if it is a tree edge of \(T^*\).

1D Rolling DP (CF 724E):

Let \(dp[k]\) be the minimum cut cost after processing prefix \(1 \dots i\), given that \(k\) vertices in \(1 \dots i\) were placed in \(S\) (\(x_j = 1\)): \[dp_{\text{new}}[k] = \min\big( \underbrace{dp[k] + p_i + k \cdot c}_{x_i = 0 \text{ ($i \in T$)}},\; \underbrace{dp[k-1] + s_i}_{x_i = 1 \text{ ($i \in S$)}} \big)\]
Runs in \(O(N^2)\) time and \(O(N)\) memory.




Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (Luogu P3249): Suppose \(f^*_1\) (area \(4\)) and \(f^*_2\) (area \(6\)) are two adjacent unit squares, and the spanning tree \(T^*\) is \(f^*_\infty \to f^*_1 \to f^*_2\).

\(\text{sub}_1(f^*_2) = 6\), \(\text{sub}_1(f^*_1) = 4 + 6 = 10\).
Suppose a query asks for the cycle \(C\) enclosing only \(f^*_1\).
As \(C\) winds counterclockwise around \(f^*_1\):

On the outer edge between \(f^*_\infty\) and \(f^*_1\), \(f^*_1\) (the child) is inside \(C\), so we add \(+\text{sub}_1(f^*_1) = +10\).
On the shared edge between \(f^*_1\) and \(f^*_2\), \(f^*_2\) (the child) is outside \(C\) (to the right of \(C\)), so we subtract \(-\text{sub}_1(f^*_2) = -6\).

Net sum: \(10 - 6 = 4 = \text{Area}(f^*_1)\)!

Broken Counterexample (Luogu P3249): What if a query polygon is given in clockwise order instead of counterclockwise? Then every interior face lies to the right of the directed cycle edges, negating both the numerator and denominator! Taking the absolute value of the signed sum (or checking the sign of the denominator \(\sum \text{Area}(f) > 0\)) automatically protects against reversed polygon winding.









Problem #224 — Global Minimum Cut on Multigraphs & Degree-Constrained Spanning Trees (HDU 6081 & CF 1556H)

Part A (HDU 6081 — 度度熊的王国战略, Judge Link)
You are given an undirected multigraph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(N \le 3000\) vertices and \(M \le 10^5\) undirected edges with positive integer weights \(w_e\). Find the minimum weight of edges whose removal disconnects \(G\) into at least two non-empty components (the Global Minimum Cut of \(G\)).


Part B (Codeforces 1556H — DIY Tree, Judge Link)
You are given a complete undirected graph \(K_N\) on \(N \le 50\) vertices with edge weights \(w_{uv} \le 100\), and degree upper bounds \(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_K\) on the first \(K\) vertices (\(1 \le K \le \min(N, 5)\)). Find the minimum weight of a spanning tree \(T\) of \(K_N\) such that \(\deg_T(i) \le d_i\) for all \(1 \le i \le K\). (Contrast when degree-constrained subgraph problems compile to flow/matching vs. when they require Matroid Intersection or Fixed-Parameter Enumeration + Matroid Intersection!)






NoteProblem #224 — Hint 1 (Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Rejection)






Part A (HDU 6081): This is a non-planar undirected global minimum cut problem with \(N \le 3000, M \le 10^5\).

Observation 1 (Trivial Singleton Cuts): For any single vertex \(u\), \((\{u\}, V \setminus \{u\})\) is a valid global cut of capacity \(\deg_w(u) = \sum_{e \in \delta(u)} w_e\). Thus \(\min_{u \in V} \deg_w(u)\) is always an upper bound (and on random/contest testdata, often the exact answer or achievable after contracting heavy edges)!
Observation 2 (Heap-Accelerated Stoer–Wagner, Ch 16.3): Each Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS) phase of Stoer–Wagner runs in \(O((N + M) \log N)\) using a priority queue, giving \(O(N(N + M)\log N)\) worst-case time (and with Nagamochi–Ibaraki sparse certificates or component checks, runs in milliseconds).

Part B (CF 1556H): Notice that only \(K \le 5\) vertices have degree constraints! If \(K = 1\), it is trivial. If \(K \le 5\), what happens to edges that have both endpoints in \(\{1, \dots, K\}\) vs. edges that have at most one endpoint in \(\{1, \dots, K\}\)?










NoteProblem #224 — Hint 2 (Intermediate Algebraic & Structural Model)






Part A (HDU 6081): Review the Stoer–Wagner Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS) invariant (Ch 16.3):

Build set \(A\) starting from any vertex; at each step add \(v \notin A\) maximizing \(w(A, v) = \sum_{u \in A} w(u, v)\).
Let \(s\) and \(t\) be the second-to-last and last vertices added in the MAS ordering. Then the cut \((\{t\}, V \setminus \{t\})\) of weight \(w(V \setminus \{t\}, t)\) is a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in the current graph!
Record ans = min(ans, w(V \ {t}, t)), contract \(s\) and \(t\) into a single supernode, and repeat \(N - 1\) times.

Part B (CF 1556H):

There are at most \(\binom{K}{2} \le \binom{5}{2} = 10\) edges inside the constrained core \(C = \{1, \dots, K\}\). Any acyclic forest \(F_0\) inside \(C\) can be enumerated in \(2^{10} = 1024\) (or even fewer: \(6^3 < 250\) labeled forests on \(5\) vertices) ways!
Once the internal edges \(F_0 \subseteq E(C)\) are fixed, every remaining edge \(e \in E \setminus E(C)\) is incident to at most one vertex in \(C\)!
Therefore, choosing the remaining \(N - 1 - |F_0|\) edges to form:

A spanning tree when combined with \(F_0\) (Graphic Matroid \(\mathcal{M}_1\)), and
Having at most \(d_i - \deg_{F_0}(i)\) edges incident to each \(i \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) (Partition Matroid \(\mathcal{M}_2\)) is a Weighted Matroid Intersection problem (Ch 21.3) on at most \(N - 1\) elements (after pre-filtering outside edges to the MST of \(V \setminus C\))!












NoteProblem #224 — Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution






Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Part A (HDU 6081): Asks for the global minimum cut of an undirected graph with no specified \(s, t\). This is the direct domain of Stoer–Wagner’s Algorithm (Ch 16.3) and Nagamochi–Ibaraki Sparse Certificates.
Part B (CF 1556H): Serves as our Forward Bridge to Part V (Ch 21.3). Why can’t we solve degree-constrained spanning tree by Bipartite Matching or Max-Flow? Because the spanning tree (graphic matroid) constraint \(\mathcal{M}_1\) is non-bipartite! However, when we intersect \(\mathcal{M}_1\) (Graphic Matroid) with \(\mathcal{M}_2\) (Partition Matroid on \(\{1, \dots, K\}\)), any edge with two endpoints in \(\{1, \dots, K\}\) would belong to two parts of the partition (turning \(\mathcal{M}_2\) into an intersection of two matroids, i.e., 3-Matroid Intersection, which is NP-hard). Because \(K \le 5\), enumerating the forest \(F_0\) inside \(\{1, \dots, K\}\) reduces the remaining problem to clean 2-Matroid Weighted Intersection!



Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

Part A (Stoer–Wagner Proof Invariant, Ch 16.3): Let \(v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n\) be the MAS ordering (\(s = v_{n-1}, t = v_n\)). Call a vertex \(v_i\) active with respect to an \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((X, Y)\) if \(v_i\) and \(v_{i-1}\) lie on opposite sides of \((X, Y)\). By induction on active vertices using submodularity of \(w(A, \cdot)\), for every active \(v_i\): \[w(A_{i-1}, v_i) \le w(X \cap (A_{i-1} \cup \{v_i\}),\; Y \cap (A_{i-1} \cup \{v_i\}))\] Applying this to the last active vertex \(v_n = t\) gives \(w(A_{n-1}, t) \le w(X, Y)\) for every \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((X, Y)\)!
Part B (CF 1556H):

First, compute the Minimum Spanning Tree \(T_{\text{out}}\) of the unconstrained vertices \(\{K+1, \dots, N\}\) in \(O(N^2)\). Any edge inside \(\{K+1, \dots, N\}\) not in \(T_{\text{out}}\) is never needed, shrinking the candidate edge pool outside \(E(C)\) to at most \((N - K - 1) + K(N - K) \le 45 + 225 = 270\) edges!
For each valid forest \(F_0 \subseteq E(\{1, \dots, K\})\) obeying \(\deg_{F_0}(i) \le d_i\):

Find a minimum-weight common independent set \(I\) of size \(N - 1 - |F_0|\) in \(\mathcal{M}_1 / F_0\) (graphic matroid contracted by \(F_0\)) and \(\mathcal{M}_2\) (partition matroid where edge \((i, u)\) with \(i \le K < u\) has colour \(i\) with capacity \(d_i - \deg_{F_0}(i)\), and edges in \(T_{\text{out}}\) have colour \(0\) with capacity \(\infty\)).





Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

Heap-Based Stoer–Wagner (HDU 6081):

First check if the graph is already disconnected (\(0\)).
Maintain adjacency lists with Union-Find / contraction lists. In phase \(p = 1 \dots N-1\):

Push (w[v], v) into a std::priority_queue as \(w(A, v)\) increases.
Let \(s, t\) be the last two popped vertices; update ans = min(ans, w[t]).
Merge \(t\)’s adjacency list into \(s\) (combining parallel edges to the same neighbor).


Weighted Matroid Intersection (CF 1556H):

In each augmentation step from current independent set \(I\), build the exchange digraph on the \(m \le 270\) candidate edges:

Source set \(X_1 = \{e \notin I : I \cup \{e\} \in \mathcal{M}_1\}\), Sink set \(X_2 = \{e \notin I : I \cup \{e\} \in \mathcal{M}_2\}\).
For \(y \in I, x \notin I\): add \(y \to x\) if \(I \setminus \{y\} \cup \{x\} \in \mathcal{M}_1\); add \(x \to y\) if \(I \setminus \{y\} \cup \{x\} \in \mathcal{M}_2\).
Find the shortest (min-weight, then min-hops) path from \(X_1\) to \(X_2\) via SPFA/Bellman-Ford and take the symmetric difference \(I \gets I \triangle P\).





Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Toy Trace (Stoer–Wagner, \(N = 4\)): Two triangles \((1,2,3)\) and \((2,3,4)\) with heavy triangle edges \(10\) and a single bridge-like pair \((1,2)=10, (2,3)=10, (1,3)=10\) vs. \((3,4)=2, (2,4)=3\):

Start MAS at \(1\): \(A_1 = \{1\}\). Weights to \(A_1\): \(w(2)=10, w(3)=10, w(4)=0\).
Add \(2\): \(A_2 = \{1, 2\}\). Weights to \(A_2\): \(w(3) = 10+10 = 20, w(4) = 3\).
Add \(3\): \(A_3 = \{1, 2, 3\}\). Weight to \(A_3\): \(w(4) = 3 + 2 = 5\).
Last two vertices: \(s = 3, t = 4\), cut of \(t = 4\) is \(w(A_3, 4) = 5\). Contract \(3\) and \(4\) into supernode \(\{3,4\}\), and subsequent phases find cuts of size \(\ge 20\). Global min-cut is \(5\).

Broken Counterexample (CF 1556H): What if you do not enumerate the internal edges \(F_0\) inside \(\{1, \dots, K\}\) and instead put all \(\binom{N}{2}\) edges directly into the matroid intersection algorithm? An edge \((1, 2)\) between two constrained vertices consumes degree quota at both vertex \(1\) and vertex \(2\). The family of edge sets obeying degree bounds at all vertices simultaneously is a 2-matching / b-matching constraint (itself an intersection of two partition matroids if bipartite, or non-matroidal in general), so intersecting it with the Graphic Matroid \(\mathcal{M}_1\) breaks the 2-matroid exchange property and causes shortest augmenting paths to produce invalid degrees!

3.2 Failure Mode Self-Audit (FM-14 through FM-16)
Before moving on, verify that you can answer each of the following three structural audit questions from memory.

Audit 1 — FM-14: Goldberg’s Unshifted Negative Capacity & The Trivial \(S = \emptyset\) Cut Trap (Ch 14.2)

Self-Audit Question: In Goldberg’s Maximum Density Subgraph network for maximizing \(\frac{|E(S)|}{|S|}\), why do we add a large shift constant \(U \ge \Delta(G)\) to every source edge \(c(s, u) = U\) and sink edge \(c(u, t) = U + 2\lambda - \deg_G(u)\), and how do you guarantee that the residual \(s\)-side set \(S\) is non-empty (\(S \neq \emptyset\))?







ImportantFM-14 Self-Audit Verification






Why \(U \ge \Delta(G)\) is Mandatory: Without \(U\), the sink capacity \(2\lambda - \deg_G(u)\) is negative whenever \(\deg_G(u) > 2\lambda\), which invalidates Dinic’s non-negative capacity invariant. Adding \(U\) to both \(c(s, u)\) and \(c(u, t)\) adds exactly \(U\) to every vertex \(u\)’s contribution regardless of whether \(u \in S\) (cuts \(u \to t\)) or \(u \in \bar{S}\) (cuts \(s \to u\)), shifting every cut capacity by the constant \(+U \cdot |V|\) without changing the relative ordering of subsets \(S \subseteq V\).
Preventing the Trivial \(S = \emptyset\) Cut: Because \(S = \emptyset\) always yields cut capacity \(U \cdot |V| + 2(\lambda \cdot 0 - 0) = U \cdot |V|\), any \(\lambda > \lambda^*\) has \(S = \emptyset\) as the unique minimum cut. During binary search, test strict feasibility max_flow < U * N (with \(\varepsilon = \frac{1}{N(N-1)}\) spacing between distinct rational densities \(\frac{E_1}{V_1} \neq \frac{E_2}{V_2}\)), and reconstruct the subgraph at the last strictly feasible \(\lambda_{\text{low}} < \lambda^*\) where \(S_{\min} = \{u \in V : s \rightsquigarrow_{G_f} u\}\) is guaranteed to be non-empty!






Audit 2 — FM-15: Directed Planar Dual Orientation & Boundary Short-Circuiting (Ch 15.2–15.3)

Self-Audit Question: When converting a directed planar \(s\)-\(t\) cut network into a dual shortest-path problem from \(s^*\) to \(t^*\), how do you verify in \(30\) seconds on scratch paper that your \(90^\circ\) rotation direction is not backwards, and why must outer-boundary edges incident to \(s^*\) and \(t^*\) be strictly one-way (or carefully directed)?







ImportantFM-15 Self-Audit Verification






The \(1 \times 1\) Corner Cut Sanity Check: Always draw the \(1\)-vertex source cut \(S = \{s\}\) at the corner \(s = (0,0)\). The only primal edges in \(\delta^+(S)\) are the two outgoing edges from \((0,0)\): \((0,0) \to (0,1)\) and \((0,0) \to (1,0)\). Check that your dual graph routes \(s^* \to f_{(1,1)} \to t^*\) using the weights of those two outgoing edges from \((0,0)\), not the incoming edges \((0,1) \to (0,0)\) and \((1,0) \to (0,0)\)!
No Free Boundary Teleportation: Never connect internal faces to \(s^*\) with zero-weight reverse edges or allow a path to enter \(s^*\) and exit \(s^*\) at another boundary face. In a multi-terminal boundary problem (CSP-S 2021 交通规划, Ch 15.3), the outer boundary segments between adjacent same-colored terminals are blocked (or simply omitted as dual terminals); only the \(2r\) boundary intervals where terminal colors switch \(0 \leftrightarrow 1\) become active dual terminals \(v^*_1, \dots, v^*_{2r}\).






Audit 3 — FM-16: Gomory–Hu Undirected Precondition & Supernode Contraction (Ch 16.4)

Self-Audit Question: Why does a Gomory–Hu cut tree fail to exist on directed graphs, and why is Gusfield’s algorithm preferred over classical Gomory–Hu contraction in competitive programming implementations?







ImportantFM-16 Self-Audit Verification






Undirected Symmetry Requirement: On a directed cycle \(1 \xrightarrow{1} 2 \xrightarrow{1} 3 \xrightarrow{1} 1\), \(\text{mincut}(u, v) = 1\) for every ordered pair, yet any tree on 3 vertices has a leaf whose single incident edge must represent both \(\text{mincut}(u, v)\) and \(\text{mincut}(v, u)\) simultaneously — impossible when \(\text{mincut}(u, v) \neq \text{mincut}(v, u)\)! Furthermore, uncrossing of minimum cuts requires symmetric submodularity \(f(A) = f(V \setminus A)\).
Why Gusfield Beats Manual Supernode Contraction: Classical Gomory–Hu requires contracting the connected components of \(T \setminus \{V_i\}\) into supernodes before each max-flow call (and failing to contract — e.g., running max-flow only on the induced subgraph of \(V_i\) — produces wrong cuts because paths can detour through \(V \setminus V_i\)). Gusfield’s algorithm runs all \(N - 1\) Dinic calls on the original, unmodified graph \(G\), updating only the \(N\)-element parent array if (vis[u] && p[u] == t) p[u] = s in 8 lines of bug-free code.








3.3 Quarantined Part IV Template & Duplicate Problems (R-22 through R-29)
In accordance with the textbook’s zero-redundancy curation policy (PROBLEM_CURATION.md), eight bare templates, duplicate judge mirrors, and Part I circulation leftovers that often appear in external Part IV problem lists have been quarantined from the main problem sets. text:
Section 4: Readiness Bridge to Part V (Ch 17–Ch 21: Min-Cost Max-Flow, Equation Differencing & LP Duality)

4.1 Part IV Cut-Linearization & Structural Compression Cheat Sheet



Target Objective / Query
Algebraic Linearization / Dual Transformation
Compiled Solver & Complexity




0-1 Fractional Ratio \(\max \frac{\sum a_i x_i}{\sum b_i x_i}\)
\(F(\lambda) = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{F}} \sum (a_i - \lambda b_i) x_i \ge 0\)
Dinkelbach Newton step \(\lambda_{k+1} = \frac{f(\mathbf{x}^*)}{g(\mathbf{x}^*)}\) or Binary Search (Ch 14.1)


Maximum Density Subgraph \(\max_{\emptyset \neq S \subseteq V} \frac{\|E(S)\|}{\|S\|}\)
\(\min_{S \subseteq V} \big[ U\|V\| + \sum_{u \in S}(U + 2\lambda - \deg(u)) + \sum_{\bar{S}} U + \|\delta(S)\| \big]\)
Goldberg Shifted Network: \(c(s,u)=U\), \(c(u,v)=1\), \(c(u,t)=U+2\lambda-\deg(u)\) (Ch 14.2)


Bottleneck Degree Ratio \(\max_{\emptyset \neq S} \min_{u \in S} \frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\)
Monotone \(k\)-core implication \(u \in S \implies \deg_S(u) \ge \lambda \deg_G(u)\)
Greedy Priority-Queue Peeling of argmin \(\frac{\deg_S(u)}{\deg_G(u)}\) in \(O((N+M)\log N)\) (Ch 14.3)


Planar \(s\)-\(t\) Min-Cut (\(s, t\) on outer face)
Split outer face into \(s^*\) (left of \(s \to t\)) and \(t^*\) (right of \(s \to t\)); right-hand \(90^\circ\) rotation for directed edges
Single Dijkstra pass on \(G^*\) in \(O(F \log F)\) (Ch 15.1–15.2)


Planar \(2k\)-Boundary Bicolorable Cut
\(2r\) color-alternating boundary transitions \(v^*_1, \dots, v^*_{2r}\) around outer face
\(2r\) Dijkstra runs + Non-Crossing Catalan Interval DP in \(O(r F \log F + r^3)\) (Ch 15.3)


Planar Polygon Enclosure Sum \(\sum_{f \subset R} W(f)\)
Dual Spanning Tree \(T^*\) rooted at \(f^*_\infty\); signed subtree sum across \(\partial R \cap E(T^*)\)
Half-Edge Face Extraction + \(O(\|\partial R\| \log d)\) Tree Lookup (Ch 15.4)


Direction B Dynamic Line/Tree Cut (\(N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5\))
\(M_i = \begin{pmatrix} p_i & p_i \\ s_i + c_{i-1} & s_i \end{pmatrix}\) in \((+, \min)\) semiring
Dynamic DP / Tropical Segment Tree in \(O(Q \log N)\) (Ch 16.1)


Undirected Global Min-Cut (\(\min_{\emptyset \neq S \subsetneq V} \|\delta(S)\|\))
Maximum Adjacency Search (MAS): last two vertices \(s = v_{n-1}, t = v_n\) satisfy \(\lambda(s,t) = w(V \setminus \{t\}, t)\)
Stoer–Wagner Contraction in \(O(NM + N^2 \log N)\) (Ch 16.3)


All-Pairs Undirected Min-Cuts (\(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs)
Uncrossing submodular cuts form an ultrametric bottleneck tree \(\lambda_G(u,v) = \min_{e \in P_T(u,v)} w_e\)
Gusfield’s \(N-1\) Max-Flows on unmodified \(G\) (Ch 16.4)





4.2 What Changes in Part V? (From Feasibility & Cut Capacity to Cost-Driven Optimization)
Across Parts I through IV, every flow edge had only a capacity \(c(e)\) (plus an optional lower bound \(l(e)\)). If we wanted to optimize a linear objective over subsets or assignments, we had to encode all costs into cut capacities (\(s\)-\(t\) minimum cuts) or binary search on a threshold (\(\lambda\)).
In Part V (Ch 17–Ch 21), every edge \(e = (u \to v)\) gains an independent unit cost \(w(e)\) alongside its capacity \([l(e), u(e)]\), unlocking five transformative modelling paradigms:

Primal-Dual Potentials, Slope Convexity & Negative Cycles (Ch 17): Why the minimum-cost flow function \(C(f)\) is piecewise-linear and convex in the flow volume \(f\) (connecting directly to WQS binary search / Alien’s Trick in Part VI!), how Johnson potentials \(\pi_u\) maintain non-negative reduced costs \(w^\pi(u \to v) = w(u \to v) + \pi_u - \pi_v \ge 0\), and how lower bounds with costs compile into mandatory negative-cycle eliminations (UVa 10806, UOJ #455).
Convex Marginal Edge Splitting & Degree Penalties (Ch 18): Compiling separable convex costs \(\Phi(f_e)\) into parallel unit-capacity edges with non-decreasing marginal differences \(\Delta_k = \Phi(k) - \Phi(k-1)\), and modeling tournament triplets \(\binom{\text{deg}^+(u)}{2}\) in Landau’s theorem (Luogu P4249 剪刀石头布, WC2007).
The Equation Differencing Method (\(\Delta E_t = E_t - E_{t-1}\), Ch 19): Compiling linear systems of range inequalities \(L_t \le \sum_{i \in I_t} x_i \le R_t\) into exact flow conservation at vertices by taking consecutive row differences — turning interval coverage and employee scheduling problems (NOI2008 志愿者招募, CF 802C) into mechanical network compilations without guesswork.
Vertex-Disjoint Cycle Covers, Dynamic Server Activation & Hub Graphs (Ch 20): Modeling multi-vehicle routing, napkin/surgical-instrument sterilization delays (餐巾计划问题), and lazy waiting-multiplier queues (NOI2012 美食节).
LP Duality, Total Unimodularity & Polymatroid Intersection (Ch 21): Proving why all our flow and cut networks produce integer optima via Totally Unimodular (TU) constraint matrices, dualizing unfamiliar primal LPs into flow networks (ZJOI2013 防守战线), and extending beyond flow to Matroid & Polymatroid Intersection (as previewed in Problem #224B).

If you scored 18 / 24 or higher on Checkpoint IV and passed all three FM-14–FM-16 self-audits, you are ready to enter Chapter 17 — Min-Cost Max-Flow Foundations: Potentials, Convexity of the Cost Curve & Negative Cycles.

title: Checkpoint VI — Data-Structure Graphs, General Blossom Matching, Simulated MCMF, and Isotonic Regression
text:
Chapters 22 through 24 sit at the architectural frontier of competitive programming network flows. At this level, an explicit graph is either too dense to materialize (\(O(N^2)\) transitions across intervals, strings, or trees), non-bipartite (breaking standard flow reductions because odd cycles create half-integral LP vertices), too large for polynomial-time graph augmentation (\(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) with total flow \(F \le 10^{14}\), requiring regret-heap or slope-trick simulation of the residual network), or disguised as an order-constrained regression or matroid intersection problem.
This checkpoint tests your ability to read an untagged problem statement and choose the exact structural compilation before writing a single line of code:

Read the untagged constraints and surface cues first. Every problem below omits chapter tags in its statement. Ask yourself:

Does an explicit flow or matching network have \(O(N^2)\) edges that factor through 1D ranges, 2D dominance boxes, bitwise prefixes, or Suffix Automaton subtrees (Ch 22.1)?
Is the underlying pairing graph non-bipartite (Ch 22.2–22.4), and if so, are we seeking a maximum matching (Edmonds' Blossom / Tutte Matrix) or falling into an NP-hard vertex-cover / odd-cycle trap (FM-22)?
Does \(N \ge 10^5\) forbid explicit MCMF (Ch 23), meaning we must translate augmenting cycles and residual back-edges into priority-queue regret keys, RLE Leftist Heaps on trees, WQS penalty binary search, or convex cost-function ternary search (FM-23)?
Is the objective a convex deviation \(\sum w_v |x_v - y_v|^p\) subject to poset inequalities \(x_u \le x_v\) (Ch 24.1 Isotonic Regression), an intersection of two matroids (Ch 24.2), or a non-intersecting planar DAG path determinant (Ch 24.3 LGV Lemma vs. FM-24)?

Commit to a 4-Step Compilation Hypothesis before opening any collapsible callout:

Step 1 (Diagnostic Signal): Pinpoint the constraint bound and structural invariant that rules out naive DP, greedy, or raw Dinic/MCMF.
Step 2 (Algebraic / Logical Model): Write the indicator variables, dual potentials, residual path cost equations, or level-set slice cuts.
Step 3 (Mechanical Compilation): Specify the virtual hub topology, regret-heap state transitions, or closure cut capacities.
Step 4 (Toy Trace & Failure Guard): Test a 3–4 element trace and verify the boundary conditions (FM-22–FM-24).

Use the Progressive Hints Sparingly: Open Hint 1 only if you cannot identify the target paradigm after 5 minutes; open Hint 2 to verify the algebraic reduction or heap key formula; open the Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution to audit your complete derivation.

title: Checkpoint VI — Data-Structure Graphs, General Blossom Matching, Simulated MCMF, and Isotonic Regression
text:
1. Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills
Before tackling the eight full-scale checkpoint problems, test your diagnostic instincts on these six rapid-fire triage scenarios. Each drill contains a genuine frontier reduction paired against a classic lookalike decoy or failure mode (FM-22–FM-24).

Drill 1.1 — Range-to-Range Virtual Hub Sparsification (Ch 22.1)

Scenario: You are given \(N \le 5 \times 10^4\) weighted intervals \([l_i, r_i]\) with traversal cost \(c_i\). From interval \(i\), a path may transition to any interval \(j\) whose index lies in \([L_i, R_i]\). Find \(K \le 10\) vertex-disjoint paths from interval \(1\) to interval \(N\) of minimum total cost.







NoteHint 1 — Structural Bottleneck





Why does naive MCMF TLE, and why can you not simply run \(K\) independent shortest-path passes without a residual network?









NoteHint 2 — Hub Orientation





Do you need a Segment Tree Out-Tree (root-to-leaves), an In-Tree (leaves-to-root), or both? Count the exact number of virtual vertices and edges.









TipTriage Resolution & Compilation — Drill 1.1






Verdict: Genuine Ch 22.1 + Ch 17 (Segment Tree Out-Tree Sparsified Small-\(K\) MCMF).
Why Naive Fails: Wiring \(i_{\text{out}} \to j_{\text{in}}\) directly for all \(j \in [L_i, R_i]\) creates \(O(N^2) \approx 2.5 \times 10^9\) edges.
Mechanical Compilation:

Split each interval \(i\) into \(i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{ cost } c_i} i_{\text{out}}\) to enforce vertex-disjointness and charge \(c_i\).
Build a Segment Tree Out-Tree over indices \(1 \dots N\), where each internal node \(u\) connects downward to its children \(u \to \text{lc}(u)\) and \(u \to \text{rc}(u)\) with capacity \(\infty\) and cost \(0\), and each leaf \(j\) connects to \(j_{\text{in}}\) with \((\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0)\).
For each interval \(i\), decompose \([L_i, R_i]\) into \(O(\log N)\) canonical Segment Tree nodes \(u_1, \dots, u_k\) and wire \(i_{\text{out}} \to u_r\) with \((\text{cap } \infty, \text{cost } 0)\).
Because \(K \le 10\) is tiny and initial edge costs \(c_i \ge 0\) need no SPFA pass (or one DAG DP pass), run at most \(K = 10\) iterations of Primal–Dual Johnson Dijkstra in \(O(K \cdot N \log^2 N)\) time!

Failure Mode Guard (FM-22a): Never give internal Out-Tree downward edges unit capacity (\(1\)); multiple paths from different intervals \(i_1, i_2\) may share the same Segment Tree ancestor node \(u\) on their way to distinct leaves in \(u\)’s subtree.






Drill 1.2 — Non-Bipartite Matching vs. Vertex Cover & Tutte Pfaffians (Ch 22.2–22.4 & FM-22)

Scenario A: Given a general undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(N \le 500\) vertices and \(M \le 10^4\) edges, find the minimum size of a vertex subset \(S \subseteq V\) such that every edge \(uv \in E\) has at least one endpoint in \(S\).
Scenario B: Given the same graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(N \le 400, M \le 10^4\), find the size of a maximum matching \(\nu(G)\) AND identify every vertex \(v \in V\) that belongs to every maximum matching of \(G\).







NoteHint 1 — Bipartite vs. Non-Bipartite Duality





Does König’s Theorem (\(\tau(G) = \nu(G)\), minimum vertex cover equals maximum matching) hold when \(G\) contains odd cycles?









NoteHint 2 — Structural Characterization of Essential Vertices





In Scenario B, how does the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition \(V = D(G) \cup A(G) \cup C(G)\) (or the inverse of the symbolic skew-symmetric Tutte matrix \(T(G)\)) classify vertices that can avoid being matched in some maximum matching?









TipTriage Resolution & Compilation — Drill 1.2






Scenario A Verdict: DECOY / NP-Hard Trap (FM-22: General Graph Minimum Vertex Cover).

Diagnostic Proof: On a general graph with odd cycles, the LP relaxation of Minimum Vertex Cover has half-integral extreme points (\(x_v = 1/2\) on a triangle \(K_3\), giving LP value \(1.5\) while \(\nu(K_3) = 1\) and \(\tau(K_3) = 2\)). Minimum Vertex Cover on general graphs is NP-Complete; neither Max-Flow nor Edmonds’ Blossom can solve it!

Scenario B Verdict: Genuine Ch 22.3–22.4 (Gallai–Edmonds Decomposition / Tutte Matrix Inverse).

Method 1 (Combinatorial — Gallai–Edmonds Forest): Find one maximum matching \(M^*\) via Edmonds’ Blossom algorithm in \(O(V^3)\). Build the alternating Blossom forest rooted at all unmatched vertices \(R = V \setminus V(M^*)\) simultaneously. Every vertex \(v\) reached at an even distance from \(R\) (including \(R\) itself and all vertices inside contracted blossoms at even levels) belongs to \(D(G)\), meaning there exists an even-length alternating path from an unmatched vertex to \(v\) that shifts the matching to leave \(v\) exposed. Thus \(v\) belongs to every maximum matching if and only if \(v \notin D(G)\)!
Method 2 (Algebraic — Tutte Matrix over \(\mathbb{F}_p\)): Construct the \(N \times N\) skew-symmetric Tutte matrix \(T_{uv} = \pm \xi_{uv}\) for random \(\xi_{uv} \in \mathbb{F}_p\). By the Tutte–Berge and Schur-complement rank theorem, when \(G\) has a perfect matching, \(v\) can be exposed in a maximum matching of \(G \setminus \{v\}\) only if \(\operatorname{rank}(T) = N\) is impossible; in general, after augmenting \(G\) with \(\operatorname{def}(G) = N - 2\nu(G)\) universal dummy vertices connected to all \(v \in V\) so the augmented graph \(G'\) has a perfect matching, a vertex \(v \in V\) is inessential (\(v \in D(G)\)) if and only if there exists a dummy vertex \(d\) such that \((T(G')^{-1})_{v, d} \neq 0\) in a single \(O(N^3)\) matrix inversion!







Drill 1.3 — 1D Transportation: Prefix Balance vs. Regret Heap vs. WQS (Ch 23.1–23.2 & FM-23)

Scenario A: Given \(N \le 10^5\) points on a 1D line at \(x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_N\) with supplies \(a_i\) and demands \(b_i\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i = \sum_{i=1}^N b_i\), route all supplies to demands minimizing \(\sum_{i,j} f_{ij} |x_i - x_j|\).
Scenario B: Given \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) stock prices \(p_1, \dots, p_N\), perform at most \(K\) disjoint buy-then-sell transactions (\(i < j\), profit \(p_j - p_i\)) maximizing total profit.







NoteHint 1 — Conservation Across Cut Points





In Scenario A, since total supply equals total demand, how much net flow must cross the segment \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\) in every feasible routing that has no opposing flows?









NoteHint 2 — Concave Transaction Count





In Scenario B, what is the shape of \(f(k)\), the maximum profit using at most \(k\) transactions, as \(k\) varies from \(0\) to \(N/2\)?









TipTriage Resolution & Compilation — Drill 1.3






Scenario A Verdict: DECOY (\(O(N)\) Prefix Flow Conservation).

Diagnostic Proof: When \(\sum a_i = \sum b_i\) on a 1D line (or tree), any optimal routing never sends flow simultaneously left-to-right and right-to-left across the same segment \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\). Therefore, the exact flow across segment \(i \leftrightarrow i+1\) is deterministically fixed as \(\left|\sum_{k=1}^i (a_k - b_k)\right|\), giving total cost \(\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (x_{i+1} - x_i) \left|\sum_{k=1}^i (a_k - b_k)\right|\) in \(O(N)\) time with zero heaps! Regret heaps (Ch 23.3) are only needed when \(\sum_{\text{holes}} c_j > \sum_{\text{mice}} 1\) (unbalanced capacities where we must choose which holes absorb flow).

Scenario B Verdict: Genuine Ch 23.2 (WQS Binary Search + 1D Regret Heap / DP).

Mechanical Compilation: In the MCMF model where source supplies \(K\) units of flow along the time spine \(1 \to 2 \to \dots \to N\), each augmenting path corresponds to one transaction \([i, j]\) (or merging two adjacent transactions \([i_1, j_1], [i_2, j_2]\) into \([i_1, j_2]\) by cancelling the middle sell-buy pair). By MCMF augmenting-path monotonicity (Ch 17.2), the maximum profit \(f(k)\) is concave in \(k\). Apply WQS (Aliens) binary search on a per-transaction penalty \(\lambda \ge 0\), reducing the subproblem to unlimited transactions with fee \(\lambda\) in \(O(N \log(\max p_i))\) time!







Drill 1.4 — Tree \(L_2\) Isotonic Regression: 整体二分 + Closure vs. Slope Merge (Ch 24.1)

Scenario: Given a rooted tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(N \le 1000\) vertices, target values \(y_v \in \mathbb{R}\), and positive weights \(w_v > 0\), choose values \(x_v \in \mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(x_{\text{parent}(v)} \le x_v\) for every non-root vertex \(v\), minimizing the weighted \(L_2\) error \(\sum_{v \in V} w_v (x_v - y_v)^2\).







NoteHint 1 — Poset vs. Tree Topology





What is the directional derivative of \(w_v (x_v - y_v)^2\) at \(x_v = \lambda\), and why does thresholding \(z_v = [x_v > \lambda]\) turn the recursion into Maximum Weight Closure (Ch 09)?









NoteHint 2 — Exploiting Tree Structure





Because the poset is a tree rather than a general DAG, can you bypass Dinic entirely?









TipTriage Resolution & Compilation — Drill 1.4






Verdict: Genuine Ch 24.1 (Tree \(L_2\) Isotonic Regression).
General Poset Compilation (整体二分 / Parallel Binary Search + Dinic):

For any test threshold \(\lambda\), an optimal block average \(x_S^*\) exceeds \(\lambda\) if and only if choosing \(z_v = 1\) (meaning \(x_v > \lambda\)) subject to closure constraints \(u \preceq v \implies (z_u = 1 \implies z_v = 1)\) yields negative directional derivative \(\sum_{v: z_v=1} 2 w_v (\lambda - y_v) < 0\), i.e., positive weight \(\sum_{v: z_v=1} w_v (y_v - \lambda) > 0\).
For \(L_2\) loss, the unconstrained optimum of a pooled component \(S\) is the weighted mean \(\bar{y}_S = \frac{\sum_{v \in S} w_v y_v}{\sum_{v \in S} w_v}\), which can also be found exactly by testing midpoints in 整体二分.

Tree-Specific Fast Compilation (\(O(N \log N)\) Convex Piecewise-Quadratic Hull Merge):

Because \(T\) is a tree (not a general DAG), closure on a tree is solvable in linear time, and bottom-up Slope Trick / Leftist Heap merging maintains the derivative \(F'_u(x)\) of the subtree convex cost function in \(O(N \log N)\) time without any flow calls!







Drill 1.5 — Graphic \(\cap\) Partition Matroid Intersection vs. Max-Flow Boundary (Ch 24.2)

Scenario: Given an undirected multigraph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(|V| \le 100\) and \(M \le 500\) colored edges where color \(k\) may be used at most \(c_k\) times, find the maximum-cardinality subset \(I \subseteq E\) that forms an acyclic forest in \(G\) and obeys all color quotas (Rainbow Spanning Forest).







NoteHint 1 — Why Max-Flow Cannot Enforce Acyclicity





Can an \(S\)-\(T\) flow network enforce that a chosen subset of edges in a general graph \(G\) contains no cycles?









NoteHint 2 — The Two Matroids





Identify \(\mathcal{M}_1 = (E, \mathcal{I}_1)\) and \(\mathcal{M}_2 = (E, \mathcal{I}_2)\), and state how the bipartite exchange graph \(\mathcal{D}(I)\) is constructed at each augmentation step.









TipTriage Resolution & Compilation — Drill 1.5






Verdict: Genuine Ch 24.2 (Graphic Matroid \(\cap\) Partition Matroid Intersection).
Why Flow Fails: A bipartite flow network can intersect two Partition Matroids (left degree quotas \(\cap\) right degree quotas), because both rank functions factor through disjoint vertex stars. However, the Graphic Matroid \(\mathcal{M}_1 = (E, \{I \subseteq E : I \text{ is a forest}\})\) has circuits equal to simple cycles of arbitrary length in \(G\), which cannot be encoded as a flow conservation or min-cut constraint on a fixed network!
Mechanical Compilation:

Maintain current independent set \(I \in \mathcal{I}_1 \cap \mathcal{I}_2\).
Build the bipartite exchange graph on \(I \cup (E \setminus I)\):

Source set \(X_1 = \{e \in E \setminus I : I \cup \{e\} \text{ is a forest}\}\); for \(y \in (E \setminus I) \setminus X_1\), add directed edges \(x \to y\) for every \(x \in I\) on the fundamental tree cycle of \(y\) in \(I\).
Sink set \(X_2 = \{e \in E \setminus I : \text{cnt}_I(\text{color}(e)) < c_{\text{color}(e)}\}\); for \(y \in (E \setminus I) \setminus X_2\), add directed edges \(y \to x\) for every \(x \in I\) with \(\text{color}(x) = \text{color}(y)\).

Find a shortest \(X_1 \to X_2\) path \(P\) via BFS (shortest in hop count to prevent shortcutting chordal dependencies!) and update \(I \gets I \triangle V(P)\) in \(O(r \cdot M \cdot |V|)\) total time.







Drill 1.6 — Non-Intersecting Lattice Paths: LGV Determinant vs. MCMF (Ch 24.3 & FM-24)

Scenario: Given an \(N \times M\) grid (\(N, M \le 1000\)) with obstacles #, count the number of pairs of vertex-disjoint monotone right-down paths from \((1, 1)\) to \((N, M)\) (excluding the shared endpoints \((1,1)\) and \((N,M)\)) modulo \(10^9 + 7\) (Codeforces 348D — Turtles).







NoteHint 1 — Counting vs. Optimization





Max-Flow can decide if \(2\) disjoint paths exist (\(0\) or \(1\)), and MCMF can maximize weight along \(2\) disjoint paths, but what tool counts the number of disjoint path tuples modulo \(10^9 + 7\)?









NoteHint 2 — Planar Non-Crossing Guarantee





Why does every crossing permutation \(\sigma = (2\;1)\) between sources \(A_1 = (1, 2), A_2 = (2, 1)\) and sinks \(B_1 = (N-1, M), B_2 = (N, M-1)\) force the two paths to intersect on the grid?









TipTriage Resolution & Compilation — Drill 1.6






Verdict: Genuine Ch 24.3 (\(2 \times 2\) Lindström–Gessel–Viennot Determinant).
Mechanical Compilation:

Any two internal-vertex-disjoint paths from \((1, 1)\) to \((N, M)\) must leave \((1, 1)\) via \(A_1 = (1, 2)\) and \(A_2 = (2, 1)\) and enter \((N, M)\) via \(B_1 = (N-1, M)\) and \(B_2 = (N, M-1)\).
By grid planarity, any path from \(A_1 = (1, 2)\) (top-right) to \(B_2 = (N, M-1)\) (bottom-left) must cross any path from \(A_2 = (2, 1)\) (bottom-left) to \(B_1 = (N-1, M)\) (top-right). Thus the non-crossing condition (FM-24) holds strictly!
Run two \(O(NM)\) grid DPs from \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) to compute \(e(A_i, B_j) \bmod (10^9 + 7)\), the total number of monotone paths from \(A_i\) to \(B_j\), and return the \(2 \times 2\) LGV determinant: \[\det \begin{pmatrix} e(A_1, B_1) & e(A_1, B_2) \\ e(A_2, B_1) & e(A_2, B_2) \end{pmatrix} = e(A_1, B_1)e(A_2, B_2) - e(A_1, B_2)e(A_2, B_1) \pmod{10^9 + 7}.\]

Failure Mode Guard (FM-24): If the DAG is non-planar or \(A_1 \to B_2\) and \(A_2 \to B_1\) can bypass each other without sharing a vertex, \(\det M\) computes the signed sum \(N(\text{id}) - N((2\;1))\) rather than \(N(\text{id})\)!
