Syn-05 (#106) — Another Filling the Grid (Bipartite IE Collapse vs. Chirp-\(Z\) Evaluation)

Source: Codeforces 1228E — Another Filling the Grid
Bridged Chapters: Ch 08 (Bipartite Row/Column Inclusion–Exclusion) \(\times\) Ch 06 (Binomial Theorem Sum Collapse) \(\times\) Ch 16 (Bivariate Grid Series) \(\times\) Ch 07 (Chirp-\(Z\) Transform / Bluestein Identity)


Problem Statement
You have an \(n \times n\) grid and an integer \(K\). Each cell \((r, c)\) (\(1 \le r, c \le n\)) must be filled with an integer from \(\{1, 2, \dots, K\}\) such that:

The minimum value in every row is \(1\), and
The minimum value in every column is \(1\).

Count the number of valid \(n \times n\) grids modulo \(10^9 + 7\). (We analyze both the contest bound \(n \le 250\) and the strengthened FPS bound \(n \le 2 \times 10^5\).)


Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 250\) (strengthened version: \(1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\))
\(1 \le K \le 10^9\)
Modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\)
Required complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(n = 1, K = 5\): The single cell \((1, 1)\) must be \(1\). Output: \(1\).
\(n = 2, K = 2\): Each cell is in \(\{1, 2\}\). A row or column has minimum \(1\) iff it is not all \(2\)s.

Total \(2 \times 2\) grids: \(2^4 = 16\).
Using \(i\) bad rows (all \(2\)s) and \(j\) bad columns (all \(2\)s): the \(i + j\) rows/columns cover \(4 - (2-i)(2-j)\) cells forced to be \(2\), leaving \((2-i)(2-j)\) free cells with \(2\) choices each:

\((i, j) = (0, 0)\): \(\binom{2}{0}\binom{2}{0} 2^4 = 16\).
\((i, j) \in \{(1, 0), (0, 1)\}\): \(-2 \times \binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{0} 2^2 = -16\).
\((i, j) \in \{(2, 0), (0, 2)\}\): \(+2 \times \binom{2}{2}\binom{2}{0} 2^0 = +2\).
\((i, j) = (1, 1)\): \(+\binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{1} 2^1 = +8\).
\((i, j) \in \{(2, 1), (1, 2)\}\): \(-2 \times \binom{2}{2}\binom{2}{1} 2^0 = -4\).
\((i, j) = (2, 2)\): \(+\binom{2}{2}\binom{2}{2} 2^0 = +1\).

Total: \(16 - 16 + 2 + 8 - 4 + 1 = 7\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

A row (or column) has minimum \(1\) iff it does not have all entries in \(\{2, 3, \dots, K\}\). Thus a “bad” row (or column) is one whose entries all belong to the \((K-1)\)-element set \(\{2, \dots, K\}\). If we fix \(i\) bad rows and \(j\) bad columns, how many cells are forced into \(\{2, \dots, K\}\), and how many cells remain completely unconstrained in \(\{1, \dots, K\}\)?



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup


Perspective 1 (Row-Only IE / Binomial Collapse of 2D IE): In the 2D Inclusion–Exclusion sum over \(0 \le i, j \le n\), the exponent \((n-i)(n-j)\) is linear in \(j\) for each fixed \(i\)! Summing over \(j\) first using the Binomial Theorem \((a + b)^n = \sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j} a^{n-j} b^j\) collapses the entire \(O(n^2)\) double sum into a single \(O(n \log n)\) 1D sum (which also corresponds directly to doing IE on rows only while requiring every column to contain at least one \(1\) outside the \(i\) bad rows!).
Perspective 2 (Chirp-\(Z\) / Bluestein Identity on the Bilinear Exponent \((n-i)(n-j)\)): What if a grid problem has row/column weights \(A_i, B_j\) that are not binomial coefficients, so the inner sum over \(j\) cannot be collapsed by \((a+b)^n\)? The bilinear exponent \(q^{u v}\) with \(u = n - i\), \(v = n - j\) and \(q = K / (K-1)\) is rewritten via Bluestein’s identity \(u v = \binom{u+v}{2} - \binom{u}{2} - \binom{v}{2}\), turning the 2D sum into a single 1D convolution!




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

Starting from the 2D Inclusion–Exclusion formula:
\[\text{Ans} = \sum_{i=0}^n \sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^{i+j} \binom{n}{i} \binom{n}{j} K^{(n-i)(n-j)} (K-1)^{n^2 - (n-i)(n-j)}.\]

Perspective 1 Collapse: Factor \((K-1)^{n^2 - (n-i)(n-j)} = (K-1)^{n i} \cdot (K-1)^{(n-i) j}\) and sum over \(j\):

\[\text{Ans} = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \binom{n}{i} \Bigl( (K-1)^i \bigl( K^{n-i} - (K-1)^{n-i} \bigr) \Bigr)^n.\]

Perspective 2 Bluestein Convolution: For \(K > 1\), let \(q = K (K-1)^{-1} \bmod p\) and substitute \(u = n - i, v = n - j\) with \(q^{uv} = q^{\binom{u+v}{2}} q^{-\binom{u}{2}} q^{-\binom{v}{2}}\).








NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: Bipartite Row/Column IE & Binomial Theorem Sum Collapse (Ch 08 \(\times\) Ch 06)

The Diagnostic Signal
Let \(R_r\) be the bad event that row \(r\) contains no \(1\) (all its entries are in \(\{2, \dots, K\}\)), and \(C_c\) be the bad event that column \(c\) contains no \(1\). If we choose \(i\) bad rows and \(j\) bad columns:

The \((n-i)(n-j)\) cells in the intersection of the \((n-i)\) unchosen rows and \((n-j)\) unchosen columns are completely free (\(K\) choices per cell).
The remaining \(n^2 - (n-i)(n-j)\) cells lie in at least one chosen bad row or bad column, so each has \((K-1)\) choices.

By 2D Inclusion–Exclusion over all subsets of bad rows and bad columns:
\[\text{Ans} = \sum_{i=0}^n \sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^{i+j} \binom{n}{i} \binom{n}{j} K^{(n-i)(n-j)} (K-1)^{n^2 - (n-i)(n-j)}.\]


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Why evaluate an \(O(n^2)\) double sum when \(j\) appears in the exponent only linearly as \((n-i)(n-j)\)? Rewrite the exponent of \((K-1)\) as
\[n^2 - (n-i)(n-j) = n i + (n - i) j.\]
Now isolate everything depending on \(j\) inside the inner sum:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Ans} &= \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \binom{n}{i} (K-1)^{n i} \sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j} \left( K^{n-i} \right)^{n-j} \left( -(K-1)^{n-i} \right)^j \\
&= \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \binom{n}{i} (K-1)^{n i} \left( K^{n-i} - (K-1)^{n-i} \right)^n \\
&= \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \binom{n}{i} \Bigl( (K-1)^i \bigl( K^{n-i} - (K-1)^{n-i} \bigr) \Bigr)^n.
\end{aligned}\]
Notice the direct combinatorial meaning of this collapsed formula (1D Row-Only Inclusion–Exclusion):

Fix \(i\) rows to be bad (containing no \(1\)s).
Then for each of the \(n\) columns independently: the \(i\) entries in the bad rows each have \((K-1)\) choices, contributing \((K-1)^i\); the remaining \(n - i\) entries in the non-bad rows must contain at least one \(1\) so that the column has minimum \(1\), which happens in \(K^{n-i} - (K-1)^{n-i}\) ways!
Since the \(n\) columns are now completely independent given the \(i\) bad rows, raising the single-column count \((K-1)^i (K^{n-i} - (K-1)^{n-i})\) to the \(n\)-th power immediately gives the formula!

Evaluating the \(n+1\) terms takes \(O(n \log n)\) time (or \(O(n)\) using a linear sieve for \(m^n\)).




Perspective 2: Bluestein / Chirp-\(Z\) Transform on Bilinear Grid Sums (Ch 16 \(\times\) Ch 07)
What if the row and column weights are arbitrary arrays \(\alpha_i, \beta_j\) (for instance, when rows and columns have distinct target minimums or capacity constraints), so the Binomial Theorem no longer collapses the inner sum?
Assume \(K > 1\) (if \(K = 1\), every entry is \(1\) and the answer is \(1\)). Let \(u = n - i\), \(v = n - j\), and \(q = K (K - 1)^{-1} \bmod p\). Then the 2D sum has the canonical Chirp-\(Z\) bilinear form:
\[\text{Ans} = (K - 1)^{n^2} \sum_{u=0}^n \sum_{v=0}^n \underbrace{\left((-1)^{n-u} \binom{n}{u}\right)}_{A_u} \underbrace{\left((-1)^{n-v} \binom{n}{v}\right)}_{B_v} q^{u v}.\]
Applying Bluestein’s identity (Chapter 07)
\[u v = \binom{u + v}{2} - \binom{u}{2} - \binom{v}{2}\]
factors the coupled exponent \(q^{u v}\) into three univariate factors:
\[\text{Ans} = (K - 1)^{n^2} \sum_{s=0}^{2n} q^{\binom{s}{2}} \sum_{u + v = s} \left( A_u q^{-\binom{u}{2}} \right) \left( B_v q^{-\binom{v}{2}} \right),\]
which is a single polynomial convolution of length \(2n + 1\), solvable in \(O(n \log n)\) time for arbitrary sequences \(A_u, B_v\)!



Comparative Analysis: Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2








Dimension
Perspective 1 (1D Binomial Collapse / Row-Only IE)
Perspective 2 (Bluestein / Chirp-\(Z\) Convolution)




Time Complexity
\(O(n \log n)\) via binary exponentiation (or \(O(n)\) with linear sieve)
\(O(n \log n)\) via a single polynomial convolution


Space Complexity
\(O(n)\)
\(O(n)\)


When to Use
Whenever all columns (or rows) are symmetric so the inner sum is \(\sum_j \binom{n}{j} a^{n-j} b^j = (a+b)^n\)
Whenever rows and columns have heterogeneous weights \(A_u, B_v\) coupled by \(q^{u v}\)









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Division by Zero when \(K = 1\) in Ratio Factorizations



If you factor out \((K-1)^{n^2}\) and set \(q = K / (K - 1) \bmod p\), your code will divide by zero whenever \(K = 1\) (or \(K \equiv 1 \pmod p\))! By keeping the collapsed Perspective 1 base \(((K-1)^i (K^{n-i} - (K-1)^{n-i}))^n\) in polynomial form (with \(0^0 = 1\) at \(i = 0\)), the \(K = 1\) and \(K \equiv 1 \pmod p\) cases work seamlessly without division.




Algorithm Contract

Input: Integers \(n\) (\(1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\)) and \(K\) (\(1 \le K \le 10^9\)).
Output: Count of valid \(n \times n\) grids modulo \(p = 10^9 + 7\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(p = 10^9 + 7 > n\); convention \(0^0 = 1\) when \(K \equiv 1 \pmod p\) and \(i = 0\).
Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: For each \(0 \le i \le n\), the \(i\)-th summand equals \((-1)^i \binom{n}{i}\) times the exact number of grids where a fixed set of \(i\) rows contains no \(1\)s and every column contains at least one \(1\).









Syn-06 (#112) — Placing Rooks (Set Partition EGF vs. Rook Column IE)

Source: Codeforces 1342E — Placing Rooks
Bridged Chapters: Ch 04 (Set Partition EGF \(\operatorname{SET}_c(\operatorname{SET}_{\ge 1})\)) \(\times\) Ch 06 (Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind) \(\times\) Ch 08 (Column Inclusion–Exclusion & Binomial Inversion)


Problem Statement
Calculate the number of ways to place \(n\) rooks on an \(n \times n\) chessboard such that:

Every cell of the \(n \times n\) board is attacked by at least one rook (where a rook attacks its own cell and all cells in the same row or column), and
Exactly \(k\) pairs of rooks attack each other (two rooks attack each other iff they lie in the same row or column and there are no other rooks strictly between them).

Output the number of configurations modulo \(998244353\).


Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\)
\(0 \le k < \frac{n(n-1)}{2}\)
Modulus \(p = 998244353\)
Required complexity: \(O(n \log p)\) or \(O(n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(n = 3, k = 0\): Every row and column has \(1\) rook, so \(3! = 6\) ways.
\(n = 3, k = 1\): We need \(c = 3 - 1 = 2\) non-empty columns (and every row has \(1\) rook, OR every column has \(1\) rook and \(2\) non-empty rows).

Choose \(2\) columns out of \(3\): \(\binom{3}{2} = 3\) ways.
Surjectively map \(3\) rows onto \(2\) chosen columns: \(2^3 - 2 \cdot 1^3 = 6\) ways.
Multiply by \(2\) for row/column transpose symmetry: \(2 \times 3 \times 6 = 36\).

\(n = 3, k = 2\): \(c = 3 - 2 = 1\) non-empty column: \(2 \times \binom{3}{1} \times 1 = 6\).
\(n = 3, k \ge 3\): Impossible since \(c = n - k \le 0\). Output: \(0\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

For every cell of the \(n \times n\) board to be attacked, either every row contains at least one rook or every column contains at least one rook (otherwise an empty row and an empty column intersect at an unattacked cell!). Since there are only \(n\) rooks in total, “every row has at least one rook” forces every row to contain exactly \(1\) rook! Then no two rooks share a row, and within a column containing \(r \ge 1\) rooks, adjacent rooks along the column form exactly \(r - 1\) mutually attacking pairs.



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup

Summing \((r_j - 1)\) over all \(c\) non-empty columns gives \(\sum_{j=1}^c (r_j - 1) = n - c = k\), so there must be exactly \(c = n - k\) non-empty columns! (If \(k \ge n\), return \(0\); if \(k > 0\), multiply by \(2\) to account for the disjoint transpose case where every column has \(1\) rook and \(n - k\) rows are non-empty.)

Perspective 1 (Labeled Set Partition EGF): Assigning \(n\) distinct rows to \(c = n - k\) chosen non-empty columns is a labeled surjection \(\operatorname{SEQ}_c(\operatorname{SET}_{\ge 1}(x)) = (e^x - 1)^c\), which equals \(c! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\).
Perspective 2 (Empty-Column Inclusion–Exclusion): Among the \(c\) chosen columns, apply Inclusion–Exclusion over the subset of columns that remain empty.




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

For \(k \ge n\), the answer is \(0\). For \(k = 0\), the answer is \(n!\). For \(1 \le k \le n - 1\), let \(c = n - k\):
\[\text{Ans} = 2 \binom{n}{c} c! \begin{Bmatrix} n \\ c \end{Bmatrix} = 2 \binom{n}{c} \sum_{j=0}^{c} (-1)^{c - j} \binom{c}{j} j^n.\]







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: Set Partition EGF \(\operatorname{SET}_c(\operatorname{SET}_{\ge 1})\) & Stirling Numbers (Ch 04 \(\times\) Ch 06)

The Diagnostic Signal
First, classify how \(n\) rooks can cover all \(n^2\) cells:

Suppose row \(r_0\) is empty and column \(c_0\) is empty. Then cell \((r_0, c_0)\) is not attacked by any rook—contradiction!
Hence either all \(n\) rows are non-empty (so each of the \(n\) rows contains exactly one rook), or all \(n\) columns are non-empty (so each of the \(n\) columns contains exactly one rook).
When do both hold simultaneously? Only when every row AND every column contains \(1\) rook, which happens iff \(k = 0\) (giving \(n!\) permutation matrices). For \(k \ge 1\), the two cases (“one rook per row” vs. “one rook per column”) are disjoint and symmetric of equal size, contributing a factor of \(2\).



The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Assume each row \(1, \dots, n\) has exactly \(1\) rook, placed in column \(f(i) \in \{1, \dots, n\}\).

No two rooks share a row, so all attacking pairs are vertical.
In a column \(j\) that receives \(r_j \ge 1\) rooks, only adjacent rooks in that column attack each other (since rooks block lines of sight), creating exactly \(r_j - 1\) attacking pairs.
Summing over all \(c\) non-empty columns gives

\[k = \sum_{j=1}^c (r_j - 1) = \sum_{j=1}^c r_j - c = n - c \implies c = n - k.\]
If \(c \le 0\) (\(k \ge n\)), no valid configuration exists (\(0\) ways). For \(1 \le c \le n\):

Partition the \(n\) labeled rows into \(c\) non-empty unlabeled blocks: by Chapter 04’s \(\operatorname{SET}_c(\operatorname{SET}_{\ge 1}(x))\) construction, the EGF is \(\frac{(e^x - 1)^c}{c!}\), whose coefficient \(n! [x^n] \frac{(e^x - 1)^c}{c!} = \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) is the Stirling number of the second kind.
Assign the \(c\) non-empty blocks to \(c\) distinct columns out of \(n\) in \(n^{\underline{c}} = \binom{n}{c} c!\) ways.

Multiplying by \(2\) when \(k > 0\) gives:
\[\text{Ans} = 2^{[k > 0]} \binom{n}{n-k} (n-k)! \begin{Bmatrix} n \\ n - k \end{Bmatrix}.\]




Perspective 2: Empty-Column Inclusion–Exclusion Sieve (Ch 08)
Instead of passing through unlabeled blocks first, fix the subset \(C \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) of \(c = n - k\) columns that are allowed to contain rooks (\(\binom{n}{c}\) ways). Now we must count surjective functions \(f: \{1, \dots, n\} \to C\).
For any subset \(S \subseteq C\) of size \(c - j\) forced to be empty, the remaining \(j\) columns can receive rows arbitrarily in \(j^n\) ways. By Inclusion–Exclusion:
\[\lvert \operatorname{Surj}(n, c) \rvert = \sum_{j=0}^{c} (-1)^{c - j} \binom{c}{j} j^n.\]
Thus
\[\text{Ans} = 2^{[k > 0]} \binom{n}{n-k} \sum_{j=0}^{n-k} (-1)^{n-k-j} \binom{n-k}{j} j^n,\]
which evaluates in \(O(n \log n)\) (or \(O(n)\) with a linear sieve for \(j^n\)) for a single \(k\), while Perspective 1’s EGF convolution \((e^x - 1)^c\) or \(\left(\sum \frac{(-1)^i}{i!} x^i\right) \left(\sum \frac{j^n}{j!} x^j\right)\) computes the answers for all \(0 \le k < n\) simultaneously in \(O(n \log n)\) time!



Comparative Analysis: Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2








Dimension
Perspective 1 (Set Partition EGF & Stirling \(S_2\) Row NTT)
Perspective 2 (Direct Empty-Column IE)




Single-\(k\) Complexity
\(O(n)\) with linear sieve
\(O(n)\) with linear sieve (or \(O(n \log p)\) via modPow)


All-\(k\) Complexity (\(0 \le k < n\))
\(O(n \log n)\) via a single NTT convolution
\(O(n^2)\) if evaluated term-by-term without NTT


Conceptual Bridge
Identifies \(k = n - c\) as the cycle/forest rank of \(c\) linear chains on \(n\) vertices
Directly sieves non-empty columns from \(c^n\) unrestricted assignments









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Double-Counting \(k = 0\) by Multiplying by \(2\)



When \(k = 0\) (\(c = n\)), every row has \(1\) rook and every column has \(1\) rook simultaneously! Do not multiply by \(2\) when \(k = 0\); the factor of \(2\) applies strictly to \(1 \le k \le n - 1\) where the row-surjective and column-surjective configurations are disjoint.




Algorithm Contract

Input: Integers \(n\) (\(1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\)) and \(k\) (\(0 \le k < n(n-1)/2\)).
Output: Number of valid rook placements modulo \(p = 998244353\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(p = 998244353 > n\). If \(k \ge n\), return \(0\); if \(k = 0\), return \(n! \bmod p\).
Complexity: \(O(n \log p)\) (or \(O(n)\) with linear sieve) time and \(O(n)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: With \(c = n - k\), the inner alternating sum computes \(c! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ c \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\), the exact number of surjections from \(n\) rows onto \(c\) chosen columns.









Syn-07 (#142) — SDOI2014 Count Numbers (Aho–Corasick DP vs. Goulden–Jackson Cluster Matrix)

Source: Luogu P3311 — SDOI2014 数数
Bridged Chapters: Ch 05 (Automaton Rational Transfer Matrix & Digit DP) \(\times\) Ch 08 (Goulden–Jackson Multi-Pattern Cluster Method)


Problem Statement
You are given a positive integer \(N\) (as a decimal string of length \(\lvert N \rvert \le 1200\)) and a collection of \(m\) forbidden digit strings \(P_1, P_2, \dots, P_m \in \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}^+\). Count how many positive integers \(x \in [1, N]\) do not contain any \(P_i\) as a contiguous substring in their standard decimal representation (without leading zeros). Output the count modulo \(10^9 + 7\).


Constraints

\(1 \le \lvert N \rvert \le 1200\)
\(1 \le m \le 100\), \(\sum_{i=1}^m \lvert P_i \rvert \le 1500\), alphabet \(\Sigma = \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\) (\(\lvert \Sigma \rvert = 10\))
Modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\)
Required complexity: \(O(\lvert N \rvert \cdot \sum \lvert P_i \rvert \cdot \lvert \Sigma \rvert)\) via Perspective 1, or \(O(m^3 L + \lvert N \rvert m^2)\) for fixed-length blocks via Perspective 2.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(N = 20\), \(m = 2\), forbidden patterns \(P_1 = \text{"3"}\), \(P_2 = \text{"12"}\):

Positive integers in \([1, 20]\) are \(1, 2, \dots, 20\) (\(20\) integers).
Containing "3": \(3, 13\) (\(2\) integers).
Containing "12": \(12\) (\(1\) integer).
Valid integers: \(20 - 2 - 1 = 17\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

A decimal integer \(x \in [1, N]\) has a unique canonical string representation without leading zeros. By standard digit-prefix decomposition, the interval \([1, N]\) decomposes into:

All strings of length \(1 \le \ell < \lvert N \rvert\) starting with a non-zero digit \(d \in \{1, \dots, 9\}\), and
For each prefix \(N[1 \dots i-1]\) (provided \(N[1 \dots i-1]\) itself contains no forbidden pattern) and each digit \(d < N[i]\) (\(d \ge 1\) if \(i = 1\)), all completions of length \(\lvert N \rvert - i\) appended to \(N[1 \dots i-1] + d\).




Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup


Perspective 1 (Aho–Corasick Automaton Transfer Matrix & Digit DP): Build the Aho–Corasick trie-automaton on \(\{P_1, \dots, P_m\}\) with \(S \le \sum \lvert P_i \rvert + 1\) states, propagating the bad flag along failure links (bad[u] |= bad[fail[u]]). Then run Digit DP tracking (index, ac_state, is_tight, has_started).
Perspective 2 (Goulden–Jackson Multi-Pattern Cluster System): First reduce \(\{P_1, \dots, P_m\}\) to an antichain (removing any \(P_i\) that contains \(P_j\)). For unconstrained suffixes of length \(L\), instead of stepping through \(S = \sum \lvert P_i \rvert\) trie states, the Goulden–Jackson cluster matrix \((I + C(x))\) has dimension only \(m \times m\), where \(C_{i, j}(x)\) records the overlap suffixes of \(P_i\) that are prefixes of \(P_j\)!




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract


Perspective 1 (Aho–Corasick OGF): Removing all bad states from the \(S \times S\) transition matrix \(T\) leaves \(T_{\text{good}}\), and the number of valid completions of length \(L\) from state \(u\) is \([x^L] \mathbf{e}_u^\top (I - x T_{\text{good}})^{-1} \mathbf{1}\).
Perspective 2 (Goulden–Jackson \(m \times m\) System): Let \(\operatorname{Overlap}(P_i, P_j) = \sum_{k \in O(P_i, P_j)} x^{\lvert P_j \rvert - k}\). Then the OGF \(F(x)\) for avoiding \(\{P_1, \dots, P_m\}\) over \(\Sigma\) satisfies

\[F(x) = \frac{1}{1 - 10x + \sum_{i=1}^m w_i(x)}, \quad \text{where } (I + C(x)) \mathbf{w}(x) = (x^{\lvert P_1 \rvert}, \dots, x^{\lvert P_m \rvert})^\top.\]







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: Aho–Corasick Automaton Transfer Matrix & Digit DP (Ch 05)

The Diagnostic Signal
When \(\sum_{i=1}^m \lvert P_i \rvert \le 1500\) and \(\lvert N \rvert \le 1200\), the total number of prefixes across all patterns \(P_1, \dots, P_m\) is at most \(S \le 1501\). The Aho–Corasick automaton compresses the equivalence classes of all string prefixes modulo \(\{P_1, \dots, P_m\}\) into \(S\) states with deterministic transitions \(\delta(u, d)\) for \(d \in \{0, \dots, 9\}\).


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Automaton Construction & Bad-State Propagation:

Insert each \(P_i\) into a trie rooted at \(0\) and mark its terminal node bad[u] = true.
Run BFS to compute failure links fail[u] and deterministic transitions tr[u][d].
Crucially, a state \(u\) is forbidden if any of its suffixes is a forbidden pattern, so during BFS we propagate:


\[\text{bad}[u] \gets \text{bad}[u] \lor \text{bad}[\text{fail}[u]].\]

Precomputing Unconstrained Suffix Counts (Removing Redundant State Flags): Instead of carrying four booleans in the DP, precompute \(dp[\ell][u]\) = number of valid digit strings of length \(\ell\) (\(0 \le \ell \le \lvert N \rvert\)) starting from safe state \(u\):

\(dp[0][u] = 1\) for all \(u\) with \(\neg\text{bad}[u]\).
For \(\ell = 1, \dots, \lvert N \rvert\) and each safe state \(u\):


\[dp[\ell][u] = \sum_{\substack{d=0 \\ \neg\text{bad}[\text{tr}[u][d]]}}^{9} dp[\ell - 1][\text{tr}[u][d]].\]

Counting Valid Integers in \([1, N]\):

Shorter lengths \(1 \le \ell < \lvert N \rvert\): choose the first digit \(d \in \{1, \dots, 9\}\) (so no leading zeros!) and complete with \(\ell - 1\) digits:


\[\sum_{\ell = 1}^{\lvert N \rvert - 1} \sum_{\substack{d = 1 \\ \neg\text{bad}[\text{tr}[0][d]]}}^{9} dp[\ell - 1][\text{tr}[0][d]].\]

Same length \(\lvert N \rvert\): walk the digits \(N_1 N_2 \dots N_{\lvert N \rvert}\) along the automaton state \(u\) (starting at \(u = 0\)). At position \(i \in \{1, \dots, \lvert N \rvert\}\), for each digit \(d \in \{[i=1], \dots, N_i - 1\}\) with \(\neg\text{bad}[\text{tr}[u][d]]\), add \(dp[\lvert N \rvert - i][\text{tr}[u][d]]\). Then advance \(u \gets \text{tr}[u][N_i]\); if \(\text{bad}[u]\) becomes true, break early! If the walk finishes all \(\lvert N \rvert\) digits without hitting a bad state, add \(+1\) for \(N\) itself.





Perspective 2: Goulden–Jackson Multi-Pattern Cluster Method (Ch 08)
What if individual pattern lengths \(\lvert P_i \rvert\) are huge (say \(\sum \lvert P_i \rvert = 10^5\)), while the number of patterns \(m\) is small (\(m \le 20\))? Then the Aho–Corasick state space \(S = \sum \lvert P_i \rvert\) is too large for an \(O(\lvert N \rvert \cdot S)\) DP, whereas Goulden–Jackson reduces the system size from \(\sum \lvert P_i \rvert\) down to \(m\)!

Antichain Reduction: Remove any \(P_i\) that contains another \(P_j\) as a substring.
Cluster Matrix \(C(x)\): For each ordered pair \((P_i, P_j)\), let \(O(P_i, P_j)\) be the set of overlap lengths \(1 \le k < \min(\lvert P_i \rvert, \lvert P_j \rvert)\) where the suffix of \(P_i\) of length \(k\) equals the prefix of \(P_j\) of length \(k\). Define the overlap polynomial

\[C_{i, j}(x) = \sum_{k \in O(P_i, P_j)} x^{\lvert P_j \rvert - k}.\]
By the Goulden–Jackson Cluster Theorem (Chapter 08), the cluster weight generating functions \(\mathbf{w}(x) = (w_1(x), \dots, w_m(x))^\top\) satisfy the \(m \times m\) linear system
\[(I + C(x)) \mathbf{w}(x) = \begin{pmatrix} x^{\lvert P_1 \rvert} \\ \vdots \\ x^{\lvert P_m \rvert} \end{pmatrix}, \quad F(x) = \frac{1}{1 - 10x + \sum_{i=1}^m w_i(x)}.\]
Furthermore, for any prefix \(Q\) fixed by the digit-DP walk (such as \(N[1 \dots i-1] + d\)), a suffix completion creates a forbidden pattern either completely inside the suffix, or overlapping the boundary of \(Q\) via a non-empty suffix of \(Q\) that is a prefix of some \(P_j\), which is just a linear combination of the exact same cluster series \(w_j(x)\)!



Comparative Analysis: Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2








Dimension
Perspective 1 (Aho–Corasick Automaton DP)
Perspective 2 (Goulden–Jackson Cluster System)




State / Dimension Size
\(S = \sum_{i=1}^m \lvert P_i \rvert \le 1500\) trie states
\(m \le 100\) patterns (after antichain reduction)


Time Complexity
\(O(\lvert N \rvert \cdot S \cdot \lvert \Sigma \rvert) \approx 1.8 \times 10^7\) operations
\(O(m^2 \lvert N \rvert^2)\) or \(O(m^3 \lvert N \rvert \log \lvert N \rvert)\)


Best Regime
Small total pattern length \(\sum \lvert P_i \rvert \le 2000\), moderate \(m\)
Few patterns (\(m \le 15\)) of very large length \(\lvert P_i \rvert\), or huge query length \(\lvert N \rvert\)









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Failing to Propagate bad[u] |= bad[fail[u]] or Mishandling Leading Zeros




In Aho–Corasick, a pattern \(P_j\) may be a strict substring of another pattern \(P_i\)’s prefix without being a terminal trie node along that path. Always propagate bad[u] |= bad[fail[u]] in BFS order!
If "0" or "05" is a forbidden pattern, leading zeros of shorter numbers (\(x < 10^{\lvert N \rvert - 1}\)) must not be fed into the automaton from the root; start the automaton transitions only at the first non-zero digit of \(x\).





Algorithm Contract

Input: Decimal string \(N\) (\(\lvert N \rvert \le 1200\)) and \(m\) pattern strings \(P_1, \dots, P_m\) (\(\sum \lvert P_i \rvert \le 1500\)).
Output: Count of pattern-avoiding integers in \([1, N]\) modulo \(10^9 + 7\).
Algebraic Preconditions: None (pure ring arithmetic in \(\mathbb{Z} / (10^9 + 7)\mathbb{Z}\)).
Complexity: \(O(\sum \lvert P_i \rvert \cdot \lvert \Sigma \rvert)\) automaton build + \(O(\lvert N \rvert \cdot \sum \lvert P_i \rvert \cdot \lvert \Sigma \rvert)\) DP; \(O(\lvert N \rvert \cdot \sum \lvert P_i \rvert)\) or \(O(\sum \lvert P_i \rvert)\) rolling space.
Correctness Invariant: For every \(\ell \ge 0\) and safe state \(u\), \(dp[\ell][u]\) equals the number of strings \(w \in \Sigma^\ell\) such that no prefix of \(w\) visits a state \(v\) with \(\text{bad}[v] = \text{true}\) when starting at \(u\).









Syn-08 (#171) — TJOI2019 Sing, Dance, Rap, Basketball (Forbidden Block IE vs. 4-Variate Automaton PGF)

Source: Luogu P5339 — TJOI2019 唱、跳、rap和篮球
Bridged Chapters: Ch 08 (Disjoint Forbidden Block Inclusion–Exclusion) \(\times\) Ch 04 (Bounded-Occupancy EGF Convolution) \(\times\) Ch 14 (Automaton PGF) \(\times\) Ch 16 (Multivariate Diagonal)


Problem Statement
You have four types of students (\(1, 2, 3, 4\)) with available counts \(a, b, c, d\) respectively. Count the number of sequences of length \(n\) formed using at most \(a\) students of type \(1\), at most \(b\) of type \(2\), at most \(c\) of type \(3\), and at most \(d\) of type \(4\) (students of the same type are indistinguishable) such that the contiguous 4-element block \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) never appears anywhere in the sequence. Output the count modulo \(998244353\).


Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 1000\)
\(0 \le a, b, c, d \le 500\)
Modulus \(p = 998244353\)
Required complexity: \(O(n^2 \log n)\) via NTT or \(O(n^2)\) via sliding-window EGF maintenance; \(O(n)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(n = 4\), \((a, b, c, d) = (1, 1, 1, 1)\):

All \(4\) students must be used, forming \(4! = 24\) permutations of \((1, 2, 3, 4)\).
Only \(1\) sequence equals the forbidden block \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) itself.
Valid sequences: \(24 - 1 = 23\).

\(n = 4\), \((a, b, c, d) = (1, 1, 1, 0)\):

Total available students \(1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3 < 4 = n\). Impossible! Output: \(0\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Notice the zero-autocorrelation property of the forbidden pattern \(P = (1, 2, 3, 4)\): because all four symbols in \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) are distinct, two occurrences of \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) can never overlap! Therefore, any \(k\) occurrences of \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) in a sequence of length \(n\) are completely disjoint and consume exactly \(k\) symbols of each of the four types.



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup


Perspective 1 (Disjoint Block Inclusion–Exclusion + Bounded EGF): If we force \(k\) disjoint occurrences of \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) (\(0 \le k \le \min(a, b, c, d, \lfloor n/4 \rfloor)\)), contracting each block into a single super-token leaves \(n - 3k\) items, of which \(k\) are super-tokens (\(\binom{n-3k}{k}\) ways to place them) and the remaining \(n - 4k\) positions are filled using at most \(a - k, b - k, c - k, d - k\) of each type:

\[(n - 4k)! [x^{n - 4k}] E_{a-k}(x) E_{b-k}(x) E_{c-k}(x) E_{d-k}(x), \quad E_m(x) = \sum_{j=0}^m \frac{x^j}{j!}.\]

Perspective 2 (4-Variate Generating Function & Diagonal Collapse): In the 4-variate OGF over \((x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)\), the forbidden pattern \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) has no self-overlap, so the Goulden–Jackson / KMP denominator is \(1 - (x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4) + x_1 x_2 x_3 x_4\). Expanding \((1 - (S - u))^{-1}\) where \(S = x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4\) and \(u = x_1 x_2 x_3 x_4\) recovers the exact same sum over \(k\)!




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

For each \(0 \le k \le \min(a, b, c, d, \lfloor n/4 \rfloor)\):
\[\text{Ans} = \sum_{k=0}^{\min(a,b,c,d,\lfloor n/4 \rfloor)} (-1)^k \binom{n - 3k}{k} (n - 4k)! [x^{n - 4k}] \left( E_{a-k}(x) E_{b-k}(x) E_{c-k}(x) E_{d-k}(x) \right).\]
Even better: instead of multiplying 4 polynomials from scratch for each \(k\), pre-Split into two halves \(A_k(x) = E_{a-k}(x) E_{b-k}(x)\) and \(B_k(x) = E_{c-k}(x) E_{d-k}(x)\), which update from \(k\) to \(k+1\) in \(O(n)\) time (or compute the single dot product \(\sum_{i+j=n-4k} [x^i]A_k(x) [x^j]B_k(x)\) in \(O(n)\) per \(k\)), achieving strict \(O(n^2)\) time without NTT!







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: Disjoint Block Inclusion–Exclusion & Bounded EGF Splitting (Ch 08 \(\times\) Ch 04)

The Diagnostic Signal
Because the pattern \(P = (1, 2, 3, 4)\) consists of four distinct characters, its border polynomial is trivial (\(C_P(x) = 1\)): two occurrences of \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) cannot share any characters.


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Let \(k\) be the number of forced occurrences of \((1, 2, 3, 4)\), where \(0 \le k \le K_{\max} = \min(a, b, c, d, \lfloor n/4 \rfloor)\).

Choosing Positions for the \(k\) Blocks: Replace each forced block \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) by a single marker \(\star\). The sequence now has \(k\) markers \(\star\) and \(n - 4k\) normal positions, so there are \(n - 3k\) slots in total and \(\binom{n - 3k}{k}\) ways to place the \(k\) markers.
Filling the Remaining \(n - 4k\) Positions: The \(k\) blocks already used \(k\) students of each of the 4 types. The remaining \(n - 4k\) slots must be filled with \(c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4\) students of types \(1, 2, 3, 4\) such that

\[c_1 + c_2 + c_3 + c_4 = n - 4k, \quad 0 \le c_1 \le a - k, \; 0 \le c_2 \le b - k, \; 0 \le c_3 \le c - k, \; 0 \le c_4 \le d - k.\]
Since the number of ways to permute \((c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4)\) indistinguishable items of each type is \(\frac{(n - 4k)!}{c_1! c_2! c_3! c_4!}\), the truncated exponential polynomial \(E_m(x) = \sum_{j=0}^m \frac{x^j}{j!}\) turns this into a 4-way EGF product:
\[W(k) = (n - 4k)! [x^{n - 4k}] \left( E_{a-k}(x) E_{b-k}(x) E_{c-k}(x) E_{d-k}(x) \right).\]

Reducing \(O(n^2 \log n)\) to Pure \(O(n^2)\) via Meet-in-the-Middle EGF Halves: Notice that to extract the single coefficient \([x^{n-4k}](A_k(x) B_k(x))\) where \(A_k(x) = E_{a-k}(x) E_{b-k}(x)\) and \(B_k(x) = E_{c-k}(x) E_{d-k}(x)\):

Either compute \([x^i] A_k(x) = \sum_{j = \max(0, i - (b-k))}^{\min(i, a-k)} \frac{1}{j! (i - j)!} = \frac{1}{i!} \sum_j \binom{i}{j}\), which is a contiguous interval sum of row \(i\) of Pascal’s triangle!
Even simpler, when \(k\) increments to \(k + 1\), \(E_{a - (k+1)}(x) = E_{a - k}(x) - \frac{x^{a-k}}{(a-k)!}\), so \(A_{k+1}(x)\) differs from \(A_k(x)\) by just two shifted polynomials:
\[A_{k+1}(x) = A_k(x) - \frac{x^{a-k}}{(a-k)!} E_{b-k}(x) - \frac{x^{b-k}}{(b-k)!} E_{a-k-1}(x),\]
which updates all coefficients of \(A_k(x)\) and \(B_k(x)\) in \(O(n)\) time per \(k\), and then \([x^{n-4k}](A_k B_k) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-4k} A_k[i] B_k[n - 4k - i]\) takes \(O(n)\) time! Since \(k \le n/4\), total time is \(O(n^2)\) with tiny constant factor and zero NTT calls!






Perspective 2: 4-Variate Goulden–Jackson Rational OGF & Diagonal Extraction (Ch 14 \(\times\) Ch 16)
Consider the 4-variate generating function where \(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4\) mark the counts of types \(1, 2, 3, 4\), and \(t\) marks total length. Because the forbidden word \(1234\) has no proper borders, the Goulden–Jackson formula over \(\mathbb{Q}[[x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4, t]]\) is
\[\mathcal{G}(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4; t) = \frac{1}{1 - t(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4) + t^4 x_1 x_2 x_3 x_4}.\]
Expanding as a geometric series in \(t(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4) - t^4 x_1 x_2 x_3 x_4\):
\[[t^n] \mathcal{G} = \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/4 \rfloor} (-1)^k \binom{n - 3k}{k} (x_1 x_2 x_3 x_4)^k (x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4)^{n - 4k}.\]
Applying the bounded-exponent functional \(\sum_{c_1 \le a, c_2 \le b, c_3 \le c, c_4 \le d} [x_1^{c_1} x_2^{c_2} x_3^{c_3} x_4^{c_4}]\) shifts the upper bounds from \((a,b,c,d)\) to \((a-k, b-k, c-k, d-k)\) on the multinomial expansion of \((x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4)^{n-4k}\), reproducing Perspective 1’s formula algebraically in two lines!

Syn-09 (#173) — CTS2019 Random Cube (3D Poset IE vs. Continuous-Time Arrival Order)

Source: Luogu P5400 — CTS2019 随机立方体
Bridged Chapters: Ch 08 (Poset Inclusion–Exclusion) \(\times\) Ch 06 (At-Least-\(k\) Binomial Inversion) \(\times\) Ch 14 (Continuous-Time \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) Stopping-Time PGF) \(\times\) Ch 04 (Tree-Like Hook Product)


Problem Statement
An \(n \times m \times l\) 3D cube of \(V = n m l\) cells is filled with a uniformly random permutation of \(\{1, 2, \dots, n m l\}\). A cell \((x, y, z)\) is called a great cell (local maximum) if its value is strictly greater than the values of all \(n + m + l - 3\) other cells that share at least one coordinate with \((x, y, z)\)—that is, for all \((x', y', z') \neq (x, y, z)\) with \(x' = x\) or \(y' = y\) or \(z' = z\), \(\text{val}(x, y, z) > \text{val}(x', y', z')\).
Compute the probability that there are at least \(k\) great cells in the cube, modulo \(998244353\). (There are \(T \le 50\) test cases.)


Constraints

\(1 \le T \le 50\)
\(1 \le n, m, l \le 5 \times 10^6\), \(1 \le k \le 100\)
Modulus \(p = 998244353\)
Required complexity: \(O(\min(n, m, l) + \log p)\) per testcase, \(O(\min(n, m, l))\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(n = 1, m = 2, l = 2, k = 1\):

\(V = 1 \times 2 \times 2 = 4\) cells. Since \(n = 1\), EVERY pair of cells shares the \(x\)-coordinate \(x = 1\)!
Thus only the global maximum \(4\) can be a great cell, so there is always \(1\) great cell with probability \(1\). Output: \(1\).

\(n = 2, m = 2, l = 2, k = 2\):

\(D = \min(2, 2, 2) = 2\).
For \(j = 1\) chosen cell: the union of \(1\) cell’s slice neighborhood has size \(U_1 = 8 - (2-1)(2-1)(2-1) = 7\), so the probability it is great is \(\frac{1}{7}\), and across all \(8\) cells \(f_1 = 8 \cdot \frac{1}{7} = \frac{8}{7}\).
For \(j = 2\) chosen cells at non-sharing coordinates (\(2^{\underline{2}} 2^{\underline{2}} 2^{\underline{2}} = 8\) ordered pairs): probability is \(\frac{1}{8 \times 7} = \frac{1}{56}\), so \(f_2 = 8 \cdot \frac{1}{56} = \frac{1}{7}\) (or for unordered pairs, \(\frac{8}{2!} \cdot \frac{2!}{56} = \frac{1}{7}\)).
By at-least-\(k\) inversion for \(k = 2\): \(\Pr[\ge 2] = (-1)^{2-2} \binom{2-1}{2-1} f_2 = \frac{1}{7} \equiv 855638017 \pmod{998244353}\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Two distinct great cells \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2, z_2)\) can never share any coordinate (\(x_1 \neq x_2\), \(y_1 \neq y_2\), \(z_1 \neq z_2\)), because if they shared a coordinate, each would have to be strictly greater than the other! Thus at most \(D = \min(n, m, l)\) great cells can exist, and any set of \(j\) candidate great cells is specified by choosing \(j\) coordinates in each dimension (\(n^{\underline{j}} m^{\underline{j}} l^{\underline{j}} / j!\) unordered sets).



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup

For a fixed set of \(j\) pairwise non-sharing cells \(c_1, \dots, c_j\), how many cells in the \(n \times m \times l\) cube share at least one coordinate with \(\{c_1, \dots, c_j\}\)? The complement is an \((n - j) \times (m - j) \times (l - j)\) subcube! Thus the union of their slice neighborhoods has size \(U_j = n m l - (n - j)(m - j)(l - j)\).

Perspective 1 (Topological Tree-Like Hook Product + At-Least-\(k\) Binomial Inversion): Because \(c_1, \dots, c_j\) all share slices with overlapping cells, condition on the relative order of the values of \(c_1, \dots, c_j\) (\(j!\) symmetric orders, say \(\text{val}(c_1) > \text{val}(c_2) > \dots > \text{val}(c_j)\)). Then \(c_1\) must be the maximum of all \(U_j\) cells in the union of all \(j\) neighborhoods; once \(c_1\) and its exclusive slice-mates are removed, \(c_2\) must be the maximum of the remaining \(U_{j-1}\) cells in the union of \(\{c_2, \dots, c_j\}\)’s neighborhoods, and so on!
Perspective 2 (Continuous-Time \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) Arrival Process): Assign each cell an i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) arrival time \(T_c \sim \operatorname{Exp}(1)\) (where earliest arrival = largest value) and integrate the nested stopping times \(0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_j < \infty\).




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

Let \(D = \min(n, m, l)\) and \(U_i = n m l - (n - i)(m - i)(l - i)\) for \(1 \le i \le D\). The expected number of \(j\)-element subsets of great cells is
\[f_j = \frac{n^{\underline{j}} m^{\underline{j}} l^{\underline{j}}}{j!} \cdot j! \prod_{i=1}^{j} \frac{1}{U_i} = n^{\underline{j}} m^{\underline{j}} l^{\underline{j}} \prod_{i=1}^{j} \frac{1}{n m l - (n - i)(m - i)(l - i)}.\]
By At-Least-\(k\) Binomial Inversion (Chapter 06):
\[\Pr[\text{great cells} \ge k] = \sum_{j=k}^{D} (-1)^{j - k} \binom{j - 1}{k - 1} f_j.\]
Using Montgomery’s prefix-product batch inversion on \(U_1, \dots, U_D\), all \(f_1, \dots, f_D\) are computed in \(O(D + \log p)\) time with a single modular inverse!







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: 3D Poset Hook Product & At-Least-\(k\) Binomial Inversion (Ch 08 \(\times\) Ch 06 \(\times\) Ch 04)

The Diagnostic Signal
Let \(g_r\) be the probability that there are exactly \(r\) great cells, and let \(f_j = \sum_{r=j}^D \binom{r}{j} g_r\) be the expected number of \(j\)-subsets of great cells. By Binomial Inversion (Chapter 06), the tail probability \(\Pr[\text{great cells} \ge k] = \sum_{r=k}^D g_r\) is given by the kernel \((-1)^{j-k} \binom{j-1}{k-1}\):
\[\sum_{r=k}^{D} g_r = \sum_{j=k}^{D} (-1)^{j - k} \binom{j - 1}{k - 1} f_j.\]
How do we compute \(f_j\)? First, if two cells share any coordinate, they lie in a common slice, so at most one of them can be the maximum of that slice. Thus any \(j\) great cells must have pairwise distinct \(x\)-, \(y\)-, and \(z\)-coordinates, and there are
\[\frac{n^{\underline{j}} m^{\underline{j}} l^{\underline{j}}}{j!}\]
such unordered \(j\)-subsets of cells \(C = \{c_1, \dots, c_j\}\).


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Why isn’t the probability that all \(j\) cells in \(C\) are great simply a product of independent slice sizes? Because for \(r \neq s\), the slice neighborhood of \(c_r\) and the slice neighborhood of \(c_s\) intersect (for instance, at \((x_r, y_s, z_s)\))!
Whenever poset maximum conditions overlap symmetrically across \(j\) roots \(c_1, \dots, c_j\), break the overlap by conditioning on the relative order of the \(j\) roots:

There are \(j!\) linear orderings of the values of \(c_1, \dots, c_j\), all equally likely by symmetry. Fix the ordering \(\text{val}(c_j) > \text{val}(c_{j-1}) > \dots > \text{val}(c_1)\).
Let \(\mathcal{N}_i\) be the union of the slice neighborhoods of \(\{c_1, \dots, c_i\}\). A cell \((x, y, z)\) lies outside \(\mathcal{N}_i\) iff \(x \notin \{x_1, \dots, x_i\}\), \(y \notin \{y_1, \dots, y_i\}\), and \(z \notin \{z_1, \dots, z_i\}\), so \(\lvert \overline{\mathcal{N}_i} \rvert = (n - i)(m - i)(l - i)\) and

\[U_i = \lvert \mathcal{N}_i \rvert = n m l - (n - i)(m - i)(l - i).\]

Under the ordering \(\text{val}(c_j) > \text{val}(c_{j-1}) > \dots > \text{val}(c_1)\), the condition that every \(c_i\) beats its own slice neighborhood (given that \(c_{i+1}, \dots, c_j\) already beat theirs!) is equivalent to requiring that for each \(i = j, j-1, \dots, 1\), \(c_i\) has the single largest value among all \(U_i\) cells in \(\mathcal{N}_i\)!
Because \(\mathcal{N}_1 \subset \mathcal{N}_2 \subset \dots \subset \mathcal{N}_j\) is a strictly nested chain of subsets, the event that \(c_j = \max(\mathcal{N}_j)\), \(c_{j-1} = \max(\mathcal{N}_{j-1})\), \(\dots\), \(c_1 = \max(\mathcal{N}_1)\) has probability equal to the telescoping hook product:

\[\Pr[c_1, \dots, c_j \text{ all great}] = j! \prod_{i=1}^{j} \frac{1}{U_i}.\]
Multiplying by \(\frac{n^{\underline{j}} m^{\underline{j}} l^{\underline{j}}}{j!}\) cancels \(j!\) and yields:
\[f_j = n^{\underline{j}} m^{\underline{j}} l^{\underline{j}} \prod_{i=1}^{j} \frac{1}{n m l - (n - i)(m - i)(l - i)}.\]




Perspective 2: Continuous-Time \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) Arrival Integral (Ch 14)
Instead of discrete permutations of \(\{1, \dots, n m l\}\), assign each cell \(c\) an independent exponential random variable \(T_c \sim \operatorname{Exp}(1)\), and declare \(c\) to have a larger value than \(c'\) iff \(T_c < T_{c'}\) (earliest arrival wins).
Fix the arrival times \(0 < t_j < t_{j-1} < \dots < t_1 < \infty\) of the \(j\) cells \(c_j, \dots, c_1\). For each cell \(c \in \mathcal{N}_i \setminus \mathcal{N}_{i-1}\) (there are \(U_i - U_{i-1}\) such cells, whose earliest required dominator among \(\{c_1, \dots, c_j\}\) is \(c_i\) at time \(t_i\)), we must have \(T_c > t_i\), which happens with probability \(e^{-t_i}\). Integrating over the simplex \(0 < t_j < \dots < t_1 < \infty\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\Pr[c_1, \dots, c_j \text{ all great}] &= j! \int_{0 < t_j < \dots < t_1 < \infty} \prod_{i=1}^{j} e^{-(U_i - U_{i-1} - 1) t_i} e^{-t_i} \, dt_1 \cdots dt_j \\
&= j! \int_{0 < t_j < \dots < t_1 < \infty} \prod_{i=1}^{j} e^{-(U_i - U_{i-1}) t_i} \, dt_1 \cdots dt_j = j! \prod_{i=1}^{j} \frac{1}{U_i},
\end{aligned}\]
via the change of variables \(s_i = t_i - t_{i+1} > 0\), where \(\sum_{i=1}^j (U_i - U_{i-1}) t_i = \sum_{i=1}^j U_i s_i\) decouples the simplex integral into \(j\) independent integrals \(\int_0^\infty e^{-U_i s_i} ds_i = \frac{1}{U_i}\)!



Comparative Analysis: Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2








Dimension
Perspective 1 (Nested Poset Hook Product)
Perspective 2 (\(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) Simplex Integral)




Time Complexity
\(O(\min(n, m, l) + \log p)\) per testcase using prefix-product inversion
\(O(\min(n, m, l) + \log p)\) per testcase


Space Complexity
\(O(\min(n, m, l))\)
\(O(\min(n, m, l))\)


Generalizability
Applies to any nested chain of poset neighborhoods \(\mathcal{N}_1 \subset \dots \subset \mathcal{N}_j\)
Extends immediately to weighted arrival rates \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_c)\) where cells have non-uniform probabilities









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Calling modPow Inside the \(O(D)\) Loop (\(5 \times 10^6 \log p\) TLE)



With \(D = \min(n, m, l) \le 5 \times 10^6\) and \(T \le 50\), computing \(U_i^{-1} \bmod p\) via binary exponentiation for each \(i\) costs \(O(D \log p)\) and will TLE! Because we actually need the prefix products \(\prod_{i=1}^j U_i^{-1} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^j U_i\right)^{-1}\) (and binomial coefficients \(\binom{j-1}{k-1}\)), compute the prefix products \(P_j = \prod_{i=1}^j U_i \bmod p\) in \(O(D)\) time, invert only \(P_D^{-1}\) once in \(O(\log p)\) time, and sweep backwards \(P_{j-1}^{-1} = P_j^{-1} \cdot U_j \bmod p\) in \(O(D)\) total time!




Algorithm Contract

Input: \(n, m, l \le 5 \times 10^6\) and \(k \le 100\).
Output: \(\Pr[\text{great cells} \ge k] \bmod 998244353\).
Algebraic Preconditions: If \(k > D = \min(n, m, l)\), return \(0\). All \(U_i \equiv nml - (n-i)(m-i)(l-i) \pmod p\) must be non-zero mod \(p\).
Complexity: \(O(\min(n, m, l) + \log p)\) time per testcase and \(O(\min(n, m, l))\) auxiliary space.
Correctness Invariant: After the backward sweep, invPref[j] equals \(\prod_{i=1}^j U_i^{-1} \bmod p\), and \(f_j = n^{\underline{j}} m^{\underline{j}} l^{\underline{j}} \cdot \text{invPref}[j] \bmod p\).









Syn-10 (#182) — Twelvefold Way (Unlabeled Bosonic OGFs vs. Labeled Fermionic/Boltzmann EGFs)

Source: Luogu P5824 — 十二重计数法
Bridged Chapters: Ch 01 (Newton inv) \(\times\) Ch 02 (\(\ln / \exp\)) \(\times\) Ch 03 (Unlabeled MSET, Partition OGFs & Pentagonal Number Theorem) \(\times\) Ch 04 (Labeled SET EGFs) \(\times\) Ch 06 (Stirling \(S_2\) Row & Bell Numbers)


Problem Statement
Given \(n\) balls and \(m\) boxes, compute the number of ways to place all \(n\) balls into the \(m\) boxes under each of the 12 combinations of:

Balls: Distinguishable (Labeled / L) vs. Indistinguishable (Unlabeled / U)
Boxes: Distinguishable (Labeled / L) vs. Indistinguishable (Unlabeled / U)
Occupancy Constraint on each box: Unrestricted (Any) vs. Injective (\(\le 1\) ball per box) vs. Surjective (\(\ge 1\) ball per box).

Output all 12 answers modulo \(998244353\).


Constraints

\(1 \le n, m \le 2 \times 10^5\)
Modulus \(p = 998244353\)
Required complexity: \(O((n + m) \log(n + m))\) total time and \(O(n + m)\) space across all 12 subproblems.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
For \(n = 3\) balls, \(m = 2\) boxes:

I (L, L, Any): \(2^3 = 8\).
II (L, L, <=1): \(2^{\underline{3}} = 0\).
III (L, L, >=1): \(2! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 2 \times 3 = 6\).
IV (L, U, Any): \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} + \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 1 + 3 = 4\).
V (L, U, <=1): \([3 \le 2] = 0\).
VI (L, U, >=1): \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 3\).
VII (U, L, Any): \(\binom{3 + 2 - 1}{3} = \binom{4}{3} = 4\).
VIII (U, L, <=1): \(\binom{2}{3} = 0\).
IX (U, L, >=1): \(\binom{3 - 1}{2 - 1} = \binom{2}{1} = 2\).
X (U, U, Any): Partitions of \(3\) into \(\le 2\) parts: \(3, 2+1 \implies 2\).
XI (U, U, <=1): \([3 \le 2] = 0\).
XII (U, U, >=1): Partitions of \(3\) into \(= 2\) parts: \(2+1 \implies 1\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

View a placement of \(n\) balls into \(m\) boxes as a function \(f: N \to M\) from a domain of size \(n\) to a codomain of size \(m\), modded out by the symmetry group acting on the domain (\(S_n\) if balls are unlabeled, \(\{e\}\) if labeled) and on the codomain (\(S_m\) if boxes are unlabeled, \(\{e\}\) if labeled):

Perspective 1 (Labeled / Boltzmann EGF View — Rows I–VI): When balls are distinguishable (\(N\) is labeled), each box is a labeled subset of balls (\(\operatorname{SET}(x) = e^x\), \(\operatorname{SET}_{\le 1}(x) = 1 + x\), \(\operatorname{SET}_{\ge 1}(x) = e^x - 1\)).
Perspective 2 (Unlabeled / Bosonic OGF View — Rows VII–XII): When balls are indistinguishable (\(N\) is unlabeled), a box of size \(k\) is just the monomial \(x^k\), so labeled boxes multiply OGFs (\(\operatorname{SEQ}_m\)) while unlabeled boxes apply the Multiset/Euler Transform (\(\operatorname{MSET}_m\), conjugated to integer partitions with parts \(\le m\)).




Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup

All 12 cases reduce to three computational tiers:

Closed-form \(O(n + m)\) Binomial / Falling-Factorial evaluations: Cases I, II, V, VII, VIII, IX, XI.
Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) for \(0 \le k \le m\) (Cases III, IV, VI): A single NTT convolution of \(A(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n \frac{(-1)^i}{i!} x^i\) and \(B(x) = \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{j^n}{j!} x^j\) gives the entire row \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right\}, \dots, \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ \min(n, m) \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time!

Perspective 1: Labeled EGF & Stirling \(S_2\) Row Convolution (Cases I–VI, Ch 04 \(\times\) Ch 06)
When balls are distinguishable (Labeled), the \(n\) balls form a labeled set \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) partitioned among the boxes:

Cases I & II: Each ball independently chooses one of \(m\) labeled boxes (\(m^n\) ways), or chooses without replacement (\(m^{\underline{n}}\) ways).
Cases III, IV, VI: A non-empty box of labeled balls has EGF \(\operatorname{SET}_{\ge 1}(x) = e^x - 1\). Thus \(k\) unlabeled non-empty boxes have EGF \(\frac{(e^x - 1)^k}{k!}\), whose coefficient \(n! [x^n] \frac{(e^x - 1)^k}{k!} = \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) is the Stirling number of the second kind. Expanding \((e^x - 1)^k = \sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} e^{jx}\) and extracting \(n! [x^n]\) gives the Binomial Convolution for row \(n\) of Stirling numbers:

\[\begin{Bmatrix} n \\ k \end{Bmatrix} = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \frac{(-1)^{k - j}}{(k - j)!} \cdot \frac{j^n}{j!}.\]
Computing a single NTT product of \(A(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{\min(n,m)} \frac{(-1)^i}{i!} x^i\) and \(B(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n,m)} \frac{j^n}{j!} x^j\) modulo \(x^{\min(n,m)+1}\) immediately yields Cases III, IV, and VI in \(O(n \log n)\) time!



Perspective 2: Unlabeled OGF, Ferrers Conjugation & Logarithmic Euler Transform (Cases VII–XII, Ch 01 \(\times\) Ch 02 \(\times\) Ch 03)
When balls are indistinguishable (Unlabeled), a configuration is determined solely by the number of balls inside each box:

Cases VII, VIII, IX: Labeled boxes correspond to compositions \(c_1 + \dots + c_m = n\) with \(c_i \ge 0\) (\(\binom{n+m-1}{n}\)), \(c_i \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(\binom{m}{n}\)), or \(c_i \ge 1\) (\(\binom{n-1}{m-1}\)).
Cases X, XI, XII: When both balls and boxes are unlabeled, the box sizes can be sorted \(c_1 \ge c_2 \ge \dots \ge c_m \ge 0\), forming an integer partition of \(n\) into at most \(m\) parts (Case X) or exactly \(m\) positive parts (Case XII).

For Case XII, placing \(1\) ball in each of the \(m\) boxes first leaves \(n - m\) balls to partition into at most \(m\) parts: \(p_{=m}(n) = p_{\le m}(n - m)\) (with \(p_{=m}(n) = 0\) if \(n < m\)).
How do we compute \(P_m(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} p_{\le m}(n) x^n \bmod x^{n+1}\)? By Ferrers diagram conjugation (transposing rows and columns of the Young diagram), partitioning \(n\) into at most \(m\) parts is bijective to partitioning \(n\) into parts of size at most \(m\):


\[P_m(x) = \prod_{k=1}^{m} \frac{1}{1 - x^k} \bmod x^{n+1}.\]
Applying the Logarithmic Euler Transform (Chapters 02–03):
\[\ln P_m(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \ln \frac{1}{1 - x^k} = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor n / k \rfloor} \frac{x^{j k}}{j} \bmod x^{n+1}.\]
Populating the coefficients of \(\ln P_m(x)\) by a harmonic sieve takes \(O(n \log n)\) time, and a single polynomial \(\exp\) modulo \(x^{n+1}\) recovers all \(p_{\le m}(0), \dots, p_{\le m}(n)\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time!

Syn-11 (#172) — SNOI2017 Lost Answer (\(2\omega\)-Bit Prefix/Suffix OR-FWT vs. Divisor Lattice Boundary IE)

Source: Luogu P5366 — SNOI2017 遗失的答案
Bridged Chapters: Ch 24 (Bitwise OR-FWT / SOS Zeta & Möbius Transforms) \(\times\) Ch 08 (Divisor Lattice Boundary Inclusion–Exclusion)


Problem Statement
Given integers \(N, G, L\) and \(Q\) queries, in each query you are given an integer \(X\). Count the number of non-empty subsets \(S \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\) such that:

\(X \in S\),
\(\gcd(S) = G\), and
\(\operatorname{lcm}(S) = L\).

Output the answer for each query modulo \(10^9 + 7\).


Constraints

\(1 \le N, G, L, X \le 10^8\)
\(1 \le Q \le 10^5\)
Modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\)
Required complexity: \(O\bigl((D + Q) \cdot 2^{2\omega}\bigr)\) where \(\omega = \omega(L / G) \le 8\) (\(2^{2\omega} \le 65536\)) and \(D \le 768\) is the number of divisors of \(L / G\) in \([1, \lfloor N / G \rfloor]\).



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(N = 6, G = 1, L = 6\), query \(X = 2\):

Candidates in \(\{1, \dots, 6\}\) dividing \(6\) are \(\{1, 2, 3, 6\}\). Here \(L / G = 6 = 2^1 \cdot 3^1\) has \(\omega = 2\) prime factors (\(p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3\)).
Each divisor \(d \in \{1, 2, 3, 6\}\) gets a 4-bit boundary mask (v2 == 0, v2 == 1, v3 == 0, v3 == 1):

\(1 = 2^0 3^0 \implies \text{mask}(1) = (1, 0, 1, 0)_2 = 5\).
\(2 = 2^1 3^0 \implies \text{mask}(2) = (0, 1, 1, 0)_2 = 6\).
\(3 = 2^0 3^1 \implies \text{mask}(3) = (1, 0, 0, 1)_2 = 9\).
\(6 = 2^1 3^1 \implies \text{mask}(6) = (0, 1, 0, 1)_2 = 10\).

A subset \(S \subseteq \{1, 2, 3, 6\}\) containing \(X = 2\) has \(\gcd = 1\) and \(\operatorname{lcm} = 6\) iff the bitwise OR of the masks of elements in \(S\) equals \(1111_2 = 15\).
Since \(\text{mask}(2) = 0110_2\), the remaining elements \(S \setminus \{2\} \subseteq \{1, 3, 6\}\) must cover the missing bits \(1001_2\):

\(\text{mask}(3) = 1001_2\) already covers both missing bits! If \(3 \in S\), then \(1\) and \(6\) can be freely in or out (\(2^2 = 4\) subsets: \(\{2, 3\}, \{1, 2, 3\}, \{2, 3, 6\}, \{1, 2, 3, 6\}\)).
If \(3 \notin S\), we need both \(1\) (to cover bit \(1000_2\)) and \(6\) (to cover bit \(0001_2\)), giving \(1\) subset \(\{1, 2, 6\}\).

Total for \(X = 2\): \(4 + 1 = 5\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

First, if \(G \nmid L\), or \(G \nmid X\), or \(X \nmid L\), or \(X > N\), the answer is immediately \(0\). Otherwise, every element \(y \in S\) must satisfy \(G \mid y\) and \(y \mid L\) and \(y \le N\). Dividing everything by \(G\), let \(L' = L / G = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_\omega^{e_\omega}\). Since \(L' \le 10^8\) and \(2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdot 17 \cdot 19 \cdot 23 > 2 \times 10^8\), \(\omega \le 8\)! Furthermore, for each prime \(p_i\), \(\gcd = G \iff \min_{y \in S} v_{p_i}(y/G) = 0\), and \(\operatorname{lcm} = L \iff \max_{y \in S} v_{p_i}(y/G) = e_i\).



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup

Notice that interior prime powers \(0 < v_{p_i}(y/G) < e_i\) contribute nothing to achieving the minimum \(0\) or maximum \(e_i\)! Thus every valid divisor \(y\) of \(L\) (with \(G \mid y\) and \(y \le N\)) is completely characterized by a \(2\omega\)-bit mask \(M(y) \in [0, 2^{2\omega})\) recording for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, \omega\}\) whether \(v_{p_i}(y/G) = 0\) (bit \(2i-2\)) and whether \(v_{p_i}(y/G) = e_i\) (bit \(2i-1\)).

Perspective 1 (Prefix/Suffix OR-FWT + SOS Zeta Lookup): Group all valid divisors \(y\) sharing the same mask \(m\) (say \(c_m\) divisors). Excluding \(X\), picking a non-empty subset of a group \(m\) has \(2^{c_m} - 1\) ways to contribute mask \(m\). Compute the prefix OR-FWT and suffix OR-FWT over the \(\le D\) distinct masks so that for any query \(X\), removing \(X\)’s group and combining prefix \(\odot\) suffix via IFWT (or SOS Zeta evaluation) answers in \(O(1)\) per query after \(O(D \cdot 2^{2\omega})\) precomputation!
Perspective 2 (Divisor Lattice Boundary Inclusion–Exclusion): In the transformed FWT domain, each coordinate \(U \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, 2\omega - 1\}\) counts how many valid divisors \(y\) have \(M(y) \subseteq U\) (i.e., fail to satisfy any of the \(2\omega - \lvert U \rvert\) complement boundary conditions).




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

In the OR-FWT (SOS Zeta) domain, for any subset of bits \(U \subseteq \{0, \dots, 2\omega - 1\}\), let
\[\hat{C}[U] = \sum_{m \subseteq U} c_m\]
be the number of valid candidates \(y \le N\) (\(G \mid y \mid L\)) whose mask \(M(y)\) is a submask of \(U\). Then the number of subsets \(S\) containing \(X\) whose bitwise OR of masks is a submask of \(U\) is \(2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1}\) if \(M(X) \subseteq U\), and \(0\) otherwise! Applying SOS Möbius Inversion (IFWT) at the full mask \(\mathcal{U} = 2^{2\omega} - 1\):
\[\text{Ans}(X) = \sum_{M(X) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathcal{U}} (-1)^{\lvert \mathcal{U} \setminus U \rvert} 2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1}.\]
Precomputing the superset SOS transform of \((-1)^{\lvert \mathcal{U} \setminus U \rvert} 2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1}\) answers every query \(X\) in \(O(1)\) time after \(O(2\omega \cdot 2^{2\omega})\) precomputation!







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: \(2\omega\)-Bit Mask Reduction & Prefix/Suffix OR-FWT / Superset SOS (Ch 24)

The Diagnostic Signal
Why can we reduce divisors up to \(10^8\) to a bitmask DP? Because for any \(L / G \le 10^8\), the number of distinct prime factors \(\omega(L / G)\) is at most \(8\) (\(2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdot 17 \cdot 19 = 9{,}699{,}690 \le 10^8 < 2.23 \times 10^8\)).
For each prime factor \(p_i^{e_i} \parallel (L / G)\) (\(1 \le i \le \omega\)), a subset \(S\) achieves \(\gcd(S) = G\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(S) = L\) if and only if:

At least one \(y \in S\) has \(v_{p_i}(y / G) = 0\) (call this bit \(2i - 2\)), and
At least one \(y \in S\) has \(v_{p_i}(y / G) = e_i\) (call this bit \(2i - 1\)).

Therefore, each valid candidate \(y \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) with \(G \mid y\) and \(y \mid L\) maps to a \(2\omega\)-bit mask \(M(y) \in [0, 2^{2\omega})\), and a subset \(S\) containing \(X\) is valid iff
\[\bigcup_{y \in S} M(y) = \mathcal{U} = 2^{2\omega} - 1.\]


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Let us compare the two ways to use OR-FWT on the mask counts \(c_m = \lvert \{y \le N : G \mid y \mid L \text{ and } M(y) = m\} \rvert\):

Method 1A (Prefix/Suffix OR-FWT DP over the \(K \le 600\) Non-Empty Mask Groups): There are at most \(d(L / G) \le 768\) divisors of \(L / G\) (since \(\max_{x \le 10^8} d(x) = 768\)). Thus at most \(K \le 768\) masks \(m\) have \(c_m > 0\).

Each group \(m_j\) (\(1 \le j \le K\)) has polynomial \(P_j(x) = 1 + (2^{c_{m_j}} - 1) x^{m_j}\) in the OR-convolution ring.
Precompute prefix products \(\text{Pref}_j = P_1 *_{\text{OR}} \cdots *_{\text{OR}} P_j\) and suffix products \(\text{Suff}_j = P_j *_{\text{OR}} \cdots *_{\text{OR}} P_K\).
When \(X\) belongs to group \(j\), the remaining \(c_{m_j} - 1\) elements in group \(j\) plus \(X\) itself contribute \(2^{c_{m_j} - 1} x^{m_j}\), which we combine with \(\text{Pref}_{j-1}\) and \(\text{Suff}_{j+1}\) in \(O(2^{2\omega})\) per group!

Method 1B (Pointwise FWT / Superset SOS Collapse in \(O(2\omega \cdot 2^{2\omega})\) Total Precomputation + \(O(1)\) per Query!): Why maintain prefix and suffix arrays when \((1 + x^{M(y)})\) is invertible in the OR-FWT value domain? In the OR-FWT (SOS Zeta) domain, the transform of \(c_m\) is

\[\hat{C}[U] = \sum_{m \subseteq U} c_m \quad (U \subseteq \mathcal{U}).\]
For any fixed \(U \subseteq \mathcal{U}\), a subset \(S\) containing \(X\) has \(\bigcup_{y \in S} M(y) \subseteq U\) if and only if \(M(X) \subseteq U\) and all other elements of \(S \setminus \{X\}\) are chosen from the \(\hat{C}[U] - 1\) valid candidates (excluding \(X\)) whose masks are submasks of \(U\)! Thus, in the FWT value domain, the transformed array for query \(X\) is simply:
\[\hat{F}_X[U] = \begin{cases} 2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1} & \text{if } M(X) \subseteq U, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\]




Perspective 2: Divisor Lattice Boundary Inclusion–Exclusion & Superset SOS Lookup (Ch 08)
Applying the inverse OR-FWT (Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice \(2^{\mathcal{U}}\)) to extract the coefficient at the full mask \(\mathcal{U}\) gives:
\[\text{Ans}(X) = [x^{\mathcal{U}}] F_X(x) = \sum_{U \subseteq \mathcal{U}} (-1)^{\lvert \mathcal{U} \setminus U \rvert} \hat{F}_X[U] = \sum_{M(X) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathcal{U}} (-1)^{\lvert \mathcal{U} \setminus U \rvert} 2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1}.\]
Look closely at the right-hand side:

The summand \(g[U] = (-1)^{\lvert \mathcal{U} \setminus U \rvert} 2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1}\) (for \(\hat{C}[U] \ge 1\), or \(0\) for \(\hat{C}[U] = 0\)) does not depend on \(X\) at all!
And the sum over all \(U \supseteq M(X)\) is simply the Superset SOS Zeta Transform of \(g[U]\) evaluated at \(M(X)\)!

Therefore, our entire algorithm reduces to:

Factor \(L / G\), find all divisors \(\le N / G\), and accumulate \(c_{M(y)}\) in \(O(\sqrt{L/G} + d(L/G) \cdot \omega)\).
Run Submask SOS Zeta Transform on \(c\) to get \(\hat{C}[U] = \sum_{m \subseteq U} c_m\) in \(O(2\omega \cdot 2^{2\omega})\) time.
Set \(g[U] = (-1)^{\lvert \mathcal{U} \setminus U \rvert} 2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1}\) (for \(\hat{C}[U] \ge 1\)) and run Superset SOS Zeta Transform on \(g\) to get \(H[m] = \sum_{U \supseteq m} g[U]\) in \(O(2\omega \cdot 2^{2\omega})\) time.
For each of the \(Q\) queries \(X\): check if \(X \le N \land G \mid X \land X \mid L\); if so, output \(H[M(X)]\) in \(O(1)\) time!

\(O\bigl(2\omega \cdot 2^{2\omega}\bigr) \approx 16 \times 65536 \approx 10^6\) ops

\(O(\omega)\) (just compute \(M(X)\) and look up \(H[M(X)]\))


Space Complexity

\(O(2^{2\omega}) = 65536\) ints









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Evaluating \(2^{\hat{C}[U] - 1}\) when \(\hat{C}[U] = 0\)



When \(\hat{C}[U] = 0\), no valid candidate \(y\) has \(M(y) \subseteq U\), so no query \(X\) can satisfy \(M(X) \subseteq U\). If you blindly set \(g[U] = (-1)^{\lvert \mathcal{U} \setminus U \rvert} 2^{-1}\) when \(\hat{C}[U] = 0\) and then sum \(H[m] = \sum_{U \supseteq m} g[U]\), any \(m\) with \(\hat{C}[m] \ge 1\) only sums over supersets \(U \supseteq m\), all of which satisfy \(\hat{C}[U] \ge \hat{C}[m] \ge 1\)! Still, setting \(g[U] = 0\) whenever \(\hat{C}[U] = 0\) avoids needing \(2^{-1}\) altogether.




Algorithm Contract
