Syn-12 (#247) — Less Time, More Profit (Parametric Capacity Series vs. Poset Closure Min-Cut)

Source: HDU 5855 — Less Time, More Profit
Bridged Chapters: Ch 05 (Parametric Rational Series) \(\times\) Ch 06 (Taylor-Shifted Threshold Evaluation) \(\times\) Ch 08 (Poset Ideal / Picard–Queyranne Bipartite Closure)


Problem Statement
A company can build among \(N\) plants (\(1, \dots, N\)) to serve among \(M\) shops (\(1, \dots, M\)):

Building plant \(i\) (\(1 \le i \le N\)) costs \(pay_i\) and takes \(t_i\) time units. Multiple plants can be built in parallel, so building a subset \(P \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) of plants takes \(\max_{i \in P} t_i\) time and costs \(\sum_{i \in P} pay_i\).
Opening shop \(j\) (\(1 \le j \le M\)) yields revenue \(pro_j\), but requires a specified subset of prerequisite plants \(S_j \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) to all be built (\(S_j \subseteq P\)).

Find the minimum build time \(T_{\min}\) required to achieve a net profit of at least \(L\) (where net profit is \(\sum_{j \in Q} pro_j - \sum_{i \in P} pay_i\)), and among all valid configurations completing within time \(T_{\min}\), find the maximum possible net profit \(P_{\max}\). If no configuration achieves net profit \(\ge L\), output impossible.


Constraints

\(1 \le N, M \le 200\)
\(1 \le pay_i, pro_j \le 10^6\), \(1 \le t_i \le 10^9\), \(1 \le L \le 10^9\)
Required complexity: \(O\bigl(\log N \cdot \operatorname{MaxFlow}(N + M, N M)\bigr)\) time and \(O(N M)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(N = 2\) plants: Plant 1 (\(pay_1 = 3, t_1 = 2\)), Plant 2 (\(pay_2 = 4, t_2 = 5\)).
\(M = 2\) shops: Shop 1 (\(pro_1 = 6\), requires \(\{1\}\)), Shop 2 (\(pro_2 = 10\), requires \(\{1, 2\}\)).
Target \(L = 3\):

At time threshold \(T = 2\): only Plant 1 can be built (\(t_1 = 2 \le 2 < t_2 = 5\)). Building Plant 1 and opening Shop 1 gives profit \(6 - 3 = 3 \ge L\).
Thus \(T_{\min} = 2\) and \(P_{\max}(T = 2) = 3\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Notice that plants are built in parallel, so a time budget \(T\) simply restricts the allowed plant set to \(V(T) = \{i \in \{1, \dots, N\} : t_i \le T\}\). As \(T\) increases, the set of available plants \(V(T)\) grows monotonically (\(V(T_1) \subseteq V(T_2)\) for \(T_1 \le T_2\)), which means the maximum achievable profit \(f(T)\) is a monotonically non-decreasing step function of \(T\) that only jumps at the \(\le N\) distinct plant build times \(\{t_1, \dots, t_N\}\)!



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup


Perspective 1 (Parametric Time-Indexed Capacity Series): Sort the distinct build times \(T_{(1)} < T_{(2)} < \dots < T_{(K)}\) (\(K \le N\)). In the parametric polynomial ring where \(x^T\) tracks the activation time threshold of each plant/shop dependency, disallowing plant \(i\) for \(T < t_i\) is equivalent to setting its cost capacity to \(+\infty\) for \(T < t_i\) and \(pay_i\) for \(T \ge t_i\).
Perspective 2 (Picard–Queyranne Poset Ideal / Minimum-Cut Closure + Binary Search): For any fixed time threshold \(T\), choosing a subset of shops \(Q\) and their required plants \(P = \bigcup_{j \in Q} S_j\) is a Maximum Weight Closure problem on the bipartite implication poset:

Source \(s \to \text{shop } j\) with capacity \(pro_j\);
\(\text{shop } j \to \text{plant } i \in S_j\) with capacity \(+\infty\);
\(\text{plant } i \to \text{sink } t\) with capacity \(pay_i\) if \(t_i \le T\), or \(+\infty\) if \(t_i > T\) (or simply exclude any shop \(j\) that requires a plant with \(t_i > T\)).





Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

For a fixed time threshold \(T\), let \(Q(T) = \{j \in \{1, \dots, M\} : \max_{i \in S_j} t_i \le T\}\) be the shops whose prerequisite plants can all be completed within time \(T\), and \(P(T) = \{i \in \{1, \dots, N\} : t_i \le T\}\). In the closure flow network \(\mathcal{G}(T)\) on \(Q(T) \cup P(T)\):
\[f(T) = \sum_{j \in Q(T)} pro_j - \operatorname{MinCut}(\mathcal{G}(T)) = \sum_{j \in Q(T)} pro_j - \operatorname{MaxFlow}(\mathcal{G}(T)).\]
Since \(f(T)\) is monotonically non-decreasing in \(T\), binary search over the sorted array of distinct build times \(T_{(1)} < \dots < T_{(K)}\) (\(K \le N\)) in \(\le \lceil \log_2 N \rceil + 1 \le 8\) Dinic max-flow calls!







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: Parametric Time-Filtered Poset Ideals (Ch 05 \(\times\) Ch 06)

The Diagnostic Signal
Why is this problem placed in the Synthesis Reserve alongside generating function tools? Because on a bipartite implication poset \((Q \cup P, \preceq)\), every valid configuration is an order ideal (down-set) \(I \subseteq Q \cup P\): if \(j \in I \cap Q\) and \(i \in S_j\), then \(i \in I \cap P\).
In small-width posets, one enumerates order ideals via a transfer matrix or bivariate generating function \(\sum_{I} x^{\max_{i \in I} t_i} y^{\text{profit}(I)}\). However, when \(N, M \le 200\) and the implication graph is an arbitrary bipartite DAG without bounded treewidth, counting all ideals is #P-hard, whereas optimizing the maximum weight ideal at each threshold \(T\) is polynomial-time solvable via submodular minimization / network flow!


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Filter the poset by the time parameter \(T\):

Define the completion requirement of shop \(j\) as \(\tau_j = \max_{i \in S_j} t_i\).
Under time budget \(T\), any plant \(i\) with \(t_i > T\) cannot be built, and consequently any shop \(j\) with \(\tau_j > T\) cannot be opened.
Conversely, any subset of shops \(Q' \subseteq Q(T) = \{j : \tau_j \le T\}\) uses only plants in \(P' = \bigcup_{j \in Q'} S_j \subseteq P(T) = \{i : t_i \le T\}\), so its completion time is guaranteed to be \(\le T\)!
Therefore, the maximum profit achievable within time \(T\) is

\[f(T) = \max_{Q' \subseteq Q(T)} \left( \sum_{j \in Q'} pro_j - \sum_{i \in \bigcup_{j \in Q'} S_j} pay_i \right).\]
Because \(Q(T_1) \subseteq Q(T_2)\) whenever \(T_1 \le T_2\), the feasible family of shop subsets grows monotonically with \(T\), proving \(f(T_1) \le f(T_2)\).




Perspective 2: Picard–Queyranne Project Closure Minimum Cut & Binary Search (Ch 08)
To evaluate \(f(T)\) for a fixed threshold \(T\), construct a directed flow network \(\mathcal{G}(T)\) with source \(s\) and sink \(t\):

For each feasible shop \(j \in Q(T)\) (\(\tau_j \le T\)), add a directed edge \(s \to j\) with capacity \(pro_j\).
For each feasible plant \(i \in P(T)\) (\(t_i \le T\)), add a directed edge \(i \to t\) with capacity \(pay_i\).
For each \(j \in Q(T)\) and each prerequisite plant \(i \in S_j\), add a directed edge \(j \to i\) with capacity \(+\infty\).

Consider any \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((S, \bar{S})\) with finite capacity (\(s \in S, t \in \bar{S}\)):

Because edges \(j \to i\) have capacity \(+\infty\), no finite-capacity cut can have \(j \in S\) and \(i \in \bar{S}\). Thus if a shop \(j \in S \cap Q(T)\) is selected, all of its prerequisite plants \(i \in S_j\) must also lie in \(S \cap P(T)\)!
The capacity of the cut \((S, \bar{S})\) is

\[\operatorname{cap}(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{j \in Q(T) \setminus S} pro_j + \sum_{i \in P(T) \cap S} pay_i = \sum_{j \in Q(T)} pro_j - \left( \sum_{j \in Q(T) \cap S} pro_j - \sum_{i \in P(T) \cap S} pay_i \right).\]
Minimizing \(\operatorname{cap}(S, \bar{S})\) over all finite cuts simultaneously maximizes the net profit \(\sum_{j \in Q(T) \cap S} pro_j - \sum_{i \in P(T) \cap S} pay_i\):
\[f(T) = \sum_{j \in Q(T)} pro_j - \operatorname{MaxFlow}(\mathcal{G}(T)).\]
Binary searching over the sorted unique values of \(\{t_1, \dots, t_N\}\) finds the smallest \(T_{\min}\) with \(f(T_{\min}) \ge L\), and \(P_{\max} = f(T_{\min})\).



Comparative Analysis: Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2








Dimension
Perspective 1 (Parametric Threshold Filtration)
Perspective 2 (Picard–Queyranne Closure Cut + Dinic)




Role in Solution
Decouples the \(\max_{i \in P} t_i \le T\) bottleneck constraint from the additive profit objective
Evaluates the submodular poset ideal maximum \(f(T)\) in \(O(V^2 E)\) via Dinic’s algorithm


Time Complexity
\(O(N \log N)\) to sort thresholds and compute \(\tau_j\)
\(\le 8\) Dinic calls on \(V \le 402, E \le 40400\) (\(\approx 10^6\) ops total)









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Including Shops with Unbuildable Plants (\(t_i > T\)) in the Revenue Sum \(\sum pro_j\)



If you include all \(M\) shops in \(\sum_{j=1}^M pro_j\) and simply omit plants with \(t_i > T\) (or give them capacity \(0\)), a shop \(j\) requiring a forbidden plant \(i\) would be openable for free! Either exclude any shop \(j\) with \(\tau_j = \max_{i \in S_j} t_i > T\) from the graph and revenue sum altogether, or set the sink edge capacity of any plant \(i\) with \(t_i > T\) to \(+\infty\) so no finite cut can place \(i \in S\).




Algorithm Contract

Input: \(N, M \le 200\), target \(L \le 10^9\), plant arrays \((pay_i, t_i)\), and shop arrays \((pro_j, S_j)\).
Output: \((T_{\min}, f(T_{\min}))\) or impossible if \(f(\max_i t_i) < L\).
Algebraic Preconditions: Capacities \(pay_i, pro_j \ge 0\), using long long (\(64\)-bit integers) for \(\infty = 10^{15}\).
Complexity: \(O(\log N \cdot \operatorname{Dinic}(N + M, N M))\) time and \(O(N M)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: For any threshold \(T\), every finite-capacity cut \((S, \bar{S})\) in \(\mathcal{G}(T)\) corresponds bijectively to a valid closed project selection \(Q' = S \cap Q(T), P' = S \cap P(T)\) with completion time \(\le T\).









Syn-13 (#249) — CSES 1112 Required Substring (Goulden–Jackson Avoidance vs. First-Passage Hitting-Time PGF)

Source: CSES 1112 — Required Substring
Bridged Chapters: Ch 08 (Complementary Goulden–Jackson Pattern Avoidance) \(\times\) Ch 05 (Rational OGF & Bostan–Mori) \(\times\) Ch 14 (First-Passage Hitting-Time PGF & KMP Automaton)


Problem Statement
Given an integer \(n\) and a pattern string \(P\) of length \(m\) over the uppercase English alphabet \(\Sigma = \{\text{`A'}, \dots, \text{`Z'}\}\) (\(\sigma = \lvert \Sigma \rvert = 26\)), calculate the number of strings of length \(n\) over \(\Sigma\) that contain \(P\) as a contiguous substring at least once. Output the count modulo \(10^9 + 7\). (We cover both the CSES bound \(n \le 1000, m \le 100\) and the large-scale FPS bound \(n \le 10^{18}\) or \(n, m \le 2 \times 10^5\).)


Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 1000\), \(1 \le m = \lvert P \rvert \le 100\) (strengthened FPS version: \(n, m \le 2 \times 10^5\) or \(n \le 10^{18}\))
Alphabet size \(\sigma = 26\), modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\)
Required complexity: \(O(m + n \sigma)\) via KMP Automaton DP, or \(O(m + n \log m)\) / \(O(m \log m \log n)\) via Goulden–Jackson / First-Passage rational OGF.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(n = 3, m = 2, P = \text{"AB"}\), \(\sigma = 26\):

A string of length \(3\) contains "AB" either at positions \([1, 2]\) (\(26\) choices for position \(3\)) or at positions \([2, 3]\) (\(26\) choices for position \(1\)).
Since "AB" cannot overlap itself at shift \(1\), the intersection (both \([1, 2]\) and \([2, 3]\) equal "AB") is empty!
Total: \(26 + 26 = 52\).

\(n = 3, m = 2, P = \text{"AA"}\), \(\sigma = 26\):

Here "AA" has a period of length \(1\) (\(C_P(x) = 1 + x\)).
Positions \([1, 2] = \text{"AA"}\) (\(26\) ways) and positions \([2, 3] = \text{"AA"}\) (\(26\) ways) overlap on "AAA" (\(1\) way).
Total: \(26 + 26 - 1 = 51\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Every string \(w \in \Sigma^n\) either avoids \(P\) completely, or contains a unique first occurrence of \(P\) ending at some index \(k \in \{m, m+1, \dots, n\}\) (after which the remaining \(n - k\) characters in \(\Sigma^{n-k}\) are completely unconstrained, with \(\sigma^{n-k}\) choices). Both views are controlled by the autocorrelation (border) polynomial \(C_P(x) = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{B}(P)} x^{m - k}\), where \(\mathcal{B}(P)\) is the set of KMP border lengths \(1 \le k \le m\) such that \(P[1 \dots k] = P[m - k + 1 \dots m]\).



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup


Perspective 1 (Complementary Goulden–Jackson Single-Pattern Avoidance): By the Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method (Chapter 08), the OGF for strings avoiding \(P\) is \(A(x) = \frac{C_P(x)}{(1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m}\). Subtracting from all \(\sigma^n\) strings \(\frac{1}{1 - \sigma x}\) immediately gives the OGF for strings containing \(P\)!
Perspective 2 (First-Passage Hitting-Time OGF & KMP Automaton): Let \(F(x)\) be the OGF for strings whose first occurrence of \(P\) ends at the very end of the string. Appending \(P\) to an avoiding string \(A(x)\) creates a first occurrence of \(P\) inside the last \(m\) positions (tracked by \(C_P(x)\)), giving \(A(x) x^m = F(x) C_P(x)\) and \((1 - \sigma x) A(x) + F(x) = 1\). Multiplying \(F(x)\) by the unconstrained suffix generator \(\frac{1}{1 - \sigma x}\) yields the exact same rational OGF!




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

Let \(C_P(x) = 1 + \sum_{b \in \text{Borders}(P)} x^{m - b}\) (computed in \(O(m)\) time by KMP failure links \(b \gets \pi[b]\) starting from \(b = \pi[m]\)). Then the OGF for strings of length \(n\) containing \(P\) at least once is:
\[G(x) = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x} - \frac{C_P(x)}{(1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m} = \frac{x^m}{(1 - \sigma x)\bigl((1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m\bigr)}.\]







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: Complementary Goulden–Jackson Pattern Avoidance (Ch 08 \(\times\) Ch 05)

The Diagnostic Signal
Counting strings that contain \(P\) at least once is the exact complement of counting strings of length \(n\) that avoid \(P\) altogether:
\[\text{Ans}_n = \sigma^n - [x^n] A(x).\]


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
By the single-pattern Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method (Chapter 08), if we mark overlapping bad occurrences of \(P\) with weight \(-1\), any cluster of overlapping occurrences of \(P\) is generated by \(w(x)\) satisfying
\[(1 + C_{P, P}(x)) w(x) = x^m \implies w(x) = \frac{x^m}{C_P(x)},\]
where \(C_P(x) = 1 + C_{P, P}(x) = \sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}(P)} x^{m - b}\) sums \(x^{m - b}\) over all border lengths \(1 \le b \le m\) with \(P[1 \dots b] = P[m - b + 1 \dots m]\) (easily extracted in \(O(m)\) time by walking the KMP prefix function \(b = m, \pi[m], \pi[\pi[m]], \dots > 0\)).
Substituting \(w(x)\) into the cluster series \(A(x) = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x + w(x)}\) gives the rational generating function for \(P\)-avoiding strings:
\[A(x) = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x + \frac{x^m}{C_P(x)}} = \frac{C_P(x)}{(1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m}.\]
Subtracting \(A(x)\) from the all-strings OGF \(\frac{1}{1 - \sigma x}\) cancels \((1 - \sigma x) C_P(x)\) in the numerator:
\[G(x) = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x} - \frac{C_P(x)}{(1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m} = \frac{x^m}{(1 - \sigma x)\bigl((1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m\bigr)}.\]
Let us check our sample traces (\(n = 3, m = 2, \sigma = 26\)):

For \(P = \text{"AB"}\), \(C_P(x) = 1\): \(G(x) = \frac{x^2}{(1 - 26x)(1 - 26x + x^2)} = x^2 (1 + 26x + \cdots)(1 + 26x + \cdots) \implies [x^3] G(x) = 26 + 26 = 52\).
For \(P = \text{"AA"}\), \(C_P(x) = 1 + x\): \(G(x) = \frac{x^2}{(1 - 26x)((1 - 26x)(1 + x) + x^2)} = \frac{x^2}{(1 - 26x)(1 - 25x - 25x^2)} = x^2 (1 + 26x + \cdots)(1 + 25x + \cdots) \implies [x^3] G(x) = 26 + 25 = 51\). Both match our hand trace!





Perspective 2: First-Passage Hitting-Time PGF & KMP Automaton Transfer (Ch 14)
Can we derive the exact factor \(\frac{x^m}{(1 - \sigma x)((1 - \sigma x)C_P(x) + x^m)}\) directly from first-passage decomposition without Inclusion–Exclusion?
Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be the language of strings avoiding \(P\) (with OGF \(A(x)\)), and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the language of strings that contain \(P\) only once, as a suffix (the first-passage language, with OGF \(F(x)\)).

Every avoiding string extended by \(1\) character either remains in \(\mathcal{A}\) or enters \(\mathcal{F}\) for the first time (or is empty):

\[1 + \sigma x A(x) = A(x) + F(x) \implies (1 - \sigma x) A(x) + F(x) = 1.\]

Every string in \(\mathcal{A} \cdot P\) (obtained by appending \(P\) to an avoiding string, OGF \(A(x) x^m\)) contains its first occurrence of \(P\) ending at distance \(m - b\) from the end, where \(b \in \mathcal{B}(P)\) is the overlap border between that first occurrence and the suffix \(P\):

\[A(x) x^m = F(x) C_P(x).\]
Solving these two linear equations for \(F(x)\) immediately yields
\[F(x) = \frac{x^m}{(1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m}.\]
Finally, every string containing \(P\) at least once decomposes uniquely as a first-passage prefix \(u \in \mathcal{F}\) followed by an arbitrary suffix \(v \in \Sigma^*\) (generated by \(\frac{1}{1 - \sigma x}\)), so
\[G(x) = F(x) \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x} = \frac{x^m}{(1 - \sigma x)\bigl((1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m\bigr)}.\]
(Algorithmic Note): For \(n \le 1000, m \le 100\), either extract \([x^n] G(x)\) via the degree-\((m+1)\) linear recurrence defined by its denominator \(Q(x) = (1 - \sigma x)((1 - \sigma x)C_P(x) + x^m)\) in \(O(n m)\) time (with zero alphabet factor \(\sigma\)!), or build the \(m\)-state KMP automaton in \(O(m \sigma)\) and run the \(O(n m \sigma)\) DP; for \(n \le 10^{18}\), Bostan–Mori extracts \([x^n] G(x)\) in \(O(m \log m \log n)\) time!



Comparative Analysis: Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2








Dimension
Perspective 1 / 2 Rational Recurrence (\(Q(x)\))
Standard KMP Automaton DP




Time Complexity (\(n \le 1000, m \le 100\))
\(O(m + n \cdot \lvert \mathcal{B}(P) \rvert) \le O(n m)\) (completely independent of \(\sigma = 26\)!)
\(O((m + n m) \sigma)\) (\(26\times\) slower per state)


Time Complexity (\(n \le 10^{18}\))
\(O(m \log m \log n)\) via Bostan–Mori
\(O(m^3 \log n)\) via matrix exponentiation


Space Complexity
\(O(n + m)\) (or \(O(m)\) with Bostan–Mori)
\(O(m \sigma)\)









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Forgetting that Overlap Shifts are \(m - b\), Not \(b\)



When a border of \(P\) has length \(b \in \{1, \dots, m\}\), the second copy of \(P\) extends \(m - b\) characters beyond the first copy! Always accumulate \(x^{m - b}\) (so \(b = m\) gives \(x^0 = 1\)), never \(x^b\).




Algorithm Contract

Input: Integer \(n \ge 1\) and pattern string \(P\) of length \(m \ge 1\) over alphabet of size \(\sigma = 26\).
Output: \([x^n] G(x) \bmod 10^9 + 7\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \([x^0] \bigl((1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^m\bigr) = 1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\). If \(n < m\), return \(0\).
Complexity: \(O(m)\) KMP border extraction + \(O(n m)\) sparse linear recurrence (or \(O(m \log m \log n)\) Bostan–Mori); \(O(n + m)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: At each step \(t \ge m\), \(f_t = [x^t] F(x)\) equals the number of strings in \(\Sigma^t\) whose first occurrence of \(P\) ends at position \(t\), and \(\text{Ans}_n = \sum_{t=m}^n f_t \sigma^{n - t}\).









Syn-14 (#253) — Codeforces 961G Partitions (Linearity of Expectation vs. Pointed Bivariate Partition EGF)

Source: Codeforces 961G — Partitions
Bridged Chapters: Ch 14 (Linearity of Expectation / Indicator Decomposition) \(\times\) Ch 06 (Single-Term Stirling \(S_2\) Extraction) \(\times\) Ch 04 (Pointed Bivariate Partition EGF & Formal Differentiation)


Problem Statement
You are given \(n\) items with weights \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n\). The weight of a non-empty subset \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) is defined as
\[W(S) = \lvert S \rvert \sum_{i \in S} w_i.\]
The weight of a partition \(\mathcal{P} = \{S_1, S_2, \dots, S_k\}\) of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) into \(k\) non-empty disjoint subsets is \(\sum_{r=1}^k W(S_r)\). Sum the weights of all partitions of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) into \(k\) non-empty blocks, modulo \(10^9 + 7\).


Constraints

\(1 \le n, k \le 2 \times 10^5\)
\(1 \le w_i \le 10^9\)
Modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\)
Required complexity: \(O(k \log p)\) or \(O(k)\) time and \(O(k)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

\(n = 4, k = 2\), weights \(w = (1, 2, 3, 4)\) (\(\sum w_i = 10\)):

There are \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 7\) partitions of \(\{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) into \(2\) blocks:

Four \(1 + 3\) splits (e.g. \(\{1\} \cup \{2, 3, 4\}\)): in each, the singleton has size \(1\) and the triple has size \(3\). Across the 4 splits, each element \(i\) is a singleton \(1\) time (contributing \(1 \cdot w_i\)) and in a triple \(3\) times (contributing \(3 \cdot w_i\)), total \(10 w_i\).
Three \(2 + 2\) splits (e.g. \(\{1, 2\} \cup \{3, 4\}\)): in each, every block has size \(2\), so each element \(i\) contributes \(2 \cdot w_i\) in each of the 3 splits, total \(6 w_i\).

Total coefficient of each \(w_i\) is \(10 + 6 = 16 = \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} + 3 \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 7 + 3 \times 3 = 16\).
Total weight: \(16 \times (1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 160\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By symmetry and Linearity of Summation, every item \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) belongs to some unique block \(S \ni i\) of size \(\lvert S \rvert\), so its weight \(w_i\) is multiplied by \(\lvert S \rvert\) in that partition. Because the partition structure is completely symmetric with respect to the \(n\) item labels, the total sum must have the form
\[\text{Ans} = C(n, k) \sum_{i=1}^n w_i,\]
where \(C(n, k)\) is the sum of \(\lvert S_i \rvert\) (the size of the block containing a fixed item \(i\), say item \(1\)) over all \(k\)-block partitions of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\).



Hint 2 — Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2 Setup


Perspective 1 (Pair-Indicator Split): Write the size of the block \(S\) containing item \(i\) as \(\lvert S \rvert = 1 + \sum_{j \neq i} [j \in S]\).

The constant \(1\) (for \(i\) itself) is summed over all \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) partitions.
For each of the \(n - 1\) other items \(j \neq i\), gluing \(i\) and \(j\) into a single super-element leaves \(n - 1\) elements to be partitioned into \(k\) blocks in \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n - 1 \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) ways!

Perspective 2 (Pointed Bivariate Partition EGF): Sum \(\binom{n-1}{s-1} s \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n - s \\ k - 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) over the size \(s \ge 1\) of item \(1\)’s block by extracting \((n-1)! [x^{n-1}] \frac{\partial}{\partial u} \left( e^{u x} \frac{(e^x - 1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \right)\Big\vert_{u=1}\).




Hint 3 — Key Equations & Extraction Contract

Both perspectives collapse to the exact same two-Stirling-number identity:
\[C(n, k) = \begin{Bmatrix} n \\ k \end{Bmatrix} + (n - 1) \begin{Bmatrix} n - 1 \\ k \end{Bmatrix},\]
where each Stirling number \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} m \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} j^m\) is evaluated in \(O(k \log p)\) (or \(O(k)\) with a linear sieve) without even needing an FFT!







NoteComplete Dual-Perspective Derivation & Comparative Analysis






Perspective 1: Linearity of Expectation & Pair-Coincidence Decomposition (Ch 14 \(\times\) Ch 06)

The Diagnostic Signal
Expand the weight of a partition \(\mathcal{P} = \{S_1, \dots, S_k\}\) by decomposing the block size \(\lvert S_r \rvert = \sum_{j \in S_r} 1\):
\[\sum_{r=1}^k \lvert S_r \rvert \sum_{i \in S_r} w_i = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \left( 1 + \sum_{j \neq i} [j \text{ is in the same block as } i \text{ in } \mathcal{P}] \right).\]


The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
Summing over all \(\mathcal{P} \in \Pi(n, k)\) (partitions of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) into \(k\) non-empty blocks):

Diagonal contribution (\(j = i\)): In every partition \(\mathcal{P} \in \Pi(n, k)\), item \(i\) is in the same block as itself. There are \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) such partitions.
Off-diagonal contribution (\(j \neq i\)): Fix any ordered pair \((i, j)\) with \(j \neq i\) (for a fixed \(i\), there are \(n - 1\) choices for \(j\)). How many partitions \(\mathcal{P} \in \Pi(n, k)\) place \(i\) and \(j\) into the same block? Fuse \(i\) and \(j\) into a single composite element \(\{i, j\}\). Any partition of the resulting \(n - 1\) elements into \(k\) non-empty blocks corresponds bijectively to a partition of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) into \(k\) non-empty blocks where \(i\) and \(j\) share a block! Thus there are \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n - 1 \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) such partitions for each \(j \neq i\).

Combining both contributions immediately gives:
\[C(n, k) = \begin{Bmatrix} n \\ k \end{Bmatrix} + (n - 1) \begin{Bmatrix} n - 1 \\ k \end{Bmatrix}.\]




Perspective 2: Pointed Bivariate EGF & Operator Differentiation (Ch 04)
Alternatively, single out item \(1\) (the “pointed” element). If item \(1\)’s block has size \(s \ge 1\), we choose the other \(s - 1\) elements of its block in \(\binom{n-1}{s-1}\) ways, multiply by the block size \(s\), and partition the remaining \(n - s\) elements into \(k - 1\) non-empty blocks in \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n - s \\ k - 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) ways:
\[C(n, k) = \sum_{s=1}^{n} \binom{n - 1}{s - 1} s \begin{Bmatrix} n - s \\ k - 1 \end{Bmatrix}.\]
In the EGF ring, the pointed block of size \(s\) has generator \(\sum_{s \ge 1} s \frac{x^{s-1}}{(s-1)!} = \frac{d}{dx}(x e^x) = (1 + x) e^x\), while the remaining \(k - 1\) blocks have generator \(\frac{(e^x - 1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}\). Multiplying them gives the EGF for \(C(n, k)\) with respect to \(n - 1\):
\[\begin{aligned}
C(n, k) &= (n - 1)! [x^{n - 1}] \left( (1 + x) e^x \frac{(e^x - 1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \right) \\
&= (n - 1)! [x^{n - 1}] \left( e^x \frac{(e^x - 1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \right) + (n - 1)! [x^{n - 2}] \left( e^x \frac{(e^x - 1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \right).
\end{aligned}\]
Since \(\frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{(e^x - 1)^k}{k!} \right) = e^x \frac{(e^x - 1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}\), we have \(m! [x^m] \left( e^x \frac{(e^x - 1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \right) = (m + 1)! [x^{m+1}] \frac{(e^x - 1)^k}{k!} = \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} m + 1 \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\). Applying this at \(m = n - 1\) and \(m = n - 2\) gives
\[C(n, k) = \begin{Bmatrix} n \\ k \end{Bmatrix} + (n - 1) \begin{Bmatrix} n - 1 \\ k \end{Bmatrix}.\]
Notice how the differential identity \((1 + x) e^x = e^x + x e^x\) is the exact EGF dual of Perspective 1’s indicator split \(\lvert S \rvert = 1 + (\lvert S \rvert - 1)\)!
Using \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} m \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} j^m\), we can combine both Stirling evaluations into a single loop over \(0 \le j \le k\):
\[C(n, k) = \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^{k - j} \binom{k}{j} j^{n - 1} (j + n - 1) \quad (\text{for } n \ge 1).\]



Comparative Analysis: Perspective 1 vs. Perspective 2








Dimension
Perspective 1 (Pair-Coincidence Indicator Split)
Perspective 2 (Pointed Block EGF Differentiation)




Time Complexity
\(O(n + k \log p)\) (or \(O(n + k)\) with linear sieve)
\(O(n + k \log p)\)


Space Complexity
\(O(k)\)
\(O(k)\)


Generalizability
Easily handles arbitrary pair weights \(W(S) = \sum_{i, j \in S} A_{i, j}\)
Easily handles arbitrary block-size weight functions \(W(S) = f(\lvert S \rvert) \sum_{i \in S} w_i\) by replacing \((1+x)e^x\) with \(\sum_{s \ge 1} f(s) \frac{x^{s-1}}{(s-1)!}\)









WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Evaluating \(0^{n-1}\) at \(j = 0\) when \(n = 1\)



In the combined single-loop formula \(\sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} j^{n-1} (j + n - 1)\), when \(n = 1\) and \(k = 1\), the \(j = 0\) term has \(0^{1-1} \cdot (0 + 0) = 1 \cdot 0 = 0\), whereas \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} + 0 \cdot \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 1\)! Why? Because \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = [k = 0]\), whereas \(\sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} 0^{-1}\) is invalid at \(m = 0\). Either handle \(n = 1\) explicitly (if (n == 1) return k == 1 ? w[1] : 0;) or evaluate \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) and \((n-1)\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n-1 \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) with proper \(0^0 = 1\).




Algorithm Contract

Input: \(n, k \le 2 \times 10^5\) and weights \(w_1, \dots, w_n\).
Output: \(C(n, k) \left(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\right) \bmod 10^9 + 7\).
Algebraic Preconditions: If \(k > n\), return \(0\). If \(n = 1, k = 1\), return \(w_1 \bmod p\). For \(n \ge 2\), \(p = 10^9 + 7 > k\).
Complexity: \(O(n + k \log p)\) time and \(O(k)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: For \(n \ge 2\), the \(j\)-th summand equals \(\frac{(-1)^{k-j}}{j!(k-j)!} (j^n + (n-1) j^{n-1})\), summing over \(0 \le j \le k\) to \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\} + (n-1)\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n-1 \\ k \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\).

text:
3. Master Index & Architectural Synthesis of the 12 Revisited Dual-Perspective Flagship Problems (§5.2)
Beyond the 14 Synthesis Reserve problems above, the main 24-chapter curriculum intentionally revisits 12 flagship problems across two distinct chapters. Each problem is counted exactly once in the 254-problem partition (in its Primary Home Slot in Column 2) and is explicitly revisited as a worked comparative example in its Revisited Chapter (Column 5). Together, these twelve pairs teach how a problem first solved by a concrete combinatorial, inclusion–exclusion, or divide-and-conquer engine in an earlier chapter can be re-interpreted through a higher-level operator, residue, differential, or multivariate lens in a later chapter.

3.2 Worked Dual-Perspective Cross-Studies (Core 12 Architectural Threads)






NoteCross-Study A — Sparse ODEs vs. Dense NTT & Bostan–Mori (#101 CF 1096G, #040 ABC 300 Ex, #084 CF 438E)




#101 (CF 1096G — Lucky Tickets, Ch 02 [Int-1]):

Perspective 1 (Ch 02.4 \(O(NK)\) Sparse Power ODE): Because \(P(x) = \sum_{d=0}^9 x^d = \frac{1-x^{10}}{1-x}\), differentiating \(G(x) = P(x)^k\) yields \((1-x)(1-x^{10})G'(x) = k(1 - 10x^9 + 9x^{10})G(x)\), extracting all coefficients up to \(9k\) in \(O(k)\) scalar operations with zero NTTs.
Perspective 2 (Ch 01 / Ch 07 Cyclic NTT Power): Evaluate \(P(\omega_L^r)^k\) on a power-of-two NTT grid of length \(L > 9k\) and interpolate in \(O(N \log N)\) time.

#040 (ABC 300 Ex — Fibonacci: Revisited, Ch 05 [Adv-1]):

Perspective 1 (Ch 05.3 General Bostan–Mori): Extract \([x^{N-K}](1 - x - x^2 - \dots - x^K)^{-1}\) via parity splitting \(Q(x)Q(-x)\) in \(O(K \log K \log N)\) time.
Perspective 2 (Ch 02.4 \((1-x)\) Sparse Multiplier + Frobenius/Doubling): Multiply numerator and denominator by \((1-x)\) so \((1-x)Q(x) = 1 - 2x + x^{K+1}\) collapses to a 3-sparse trinomial, reducing each parity-halving or modular doubling step from \(O(K \log K)\) to \(O(K)\) when \(K\) is small or \(N\) is moderate!

#084 (CF 438E — The Child and Binary Tree, Ch 02 [Adv-2]):

Perspective 1 (Ch 02.3 Explicit Radical): Solve \(C(x)F(x)^2 - F(x) + 1 = 0\) via the rationalized quadratic formula \(F(x) = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4C(x)}} \bmod x^{M+1}\) using 1D sqrt and inv.
Perspective 2 (Ch 10.2 Direct Implicit Fréchet Newton Iteration): Apply \(F_{k+1} = F_k - \frac{C F_k^2 - F_k + 1}{2 C F_k - 1} \bmod x^{2^{k+1}}\) directly without square roots, which generalizes immediately to degree-\(d \ge 5\) tree equations where no radical formula exists.










NoteCross-Study B — Taylor Shift, Spectral Diagonalization & Laguerre IE (#094 CF 923E, #089 CF 840C)




#094 (CF 923E — Perpetual Subtraction, Ch 06 [Adv-1]):

Perspective 1 (Ch 06.3 Algebraic Taylor Shift): The transition \([x^j] P_{\text{next}}(x) = \sum_{i=j}^N \frac{[x^i]P(x)}{i+1}\) becomes diagonal after shifting \(G(y) = P(y+1)\): each coefficient \([y^k]G(y)\) simply multiplies by \((k+1)^{-1}\) per step, so \(M\) steps take two Taylor shifts \(P(x) \xrightarrow{x \mapsto y+1} G(y) \xrightarrow{\times (k+1)^{-M}} \widetilde{G}(y) \xrightarrow{y \mapsto x-1} P_M(x)\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time.
Perspective 2 (Ch 13.3 Eigenbasis Factorization): The upper-triangular matrix \(T_{j,i} = \frac{1}{i+1}[j \le i]\) is diagonalized by the Pascal matrix \(V_{i,j} = \binom{i}{j}\) (\(T = V \operatorname{diag}(1, \frac{1}{2}, \dots, \frac{1}{N+1}) V^{-1}\)), because \(V\) is the matrix representation of the formal shift operator \(\exp(D_x) : x^i \mapsto (x+1)^i\).

Perspective 1 (Ch 08.3 Connected-Component IE): Split \(c_i\) identical-class balls into \(b \in [1, c_i]\) blocks with signed EGF \(P_{c_i}(x) = \sum_{b=1}^{c_i} (-1)^{c_i-b} \binom{c_i}{b}\binom{c_i-1}{b-1} \frac{x^b}{b!}\) and multiply in \(O(N^2)\) DP.
Perspective 2 (Ch 19.3 Laguerre Polynomials & D&C NTT): Recognize \(P_{c}(x)\) as a shifted Laguerre polynomial and multiply \(\prod_{i=1}^m P_{c_i}(x)\) via a min-heap divide-and-conquer NTT tree in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time (scaling to \(N \le 2.5 \times 10^5\) in #028 ABC 260 Ex).

Perspective 1 (Ch 09.3–9.4 Online Relaxed Convolution): Solve \(F(x) = x \exp\!\left(\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{F(x^k)}{k}\right)\) or \(2 \times 2\) coupled functional systems coefficient-by-coefficient in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time using a 15-line RelaxedConvolution maintainer without computing Fréchet Jacobians.
Perspective 2 (Ch 10.2–10.3 Pólya & Coupled Jacobian Newton): Linearize with respect to the top-precision term \(F(x)\) (treating \(F(x^2), F(x^3), \dots\) as known constants at step \(2^k \to 2^{k+1}\)) or invert the \(2 \times 2\) Jacobian matrix \((I - J_G(F_k))^{-1}\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time.

Perspective 2 (Ch 21.3 All-\(n\) Kinoshita–Li revert & Ch 24.3 Pointed SPS \(\ln\)): When answers are required for all \(1 \le n \le N\) simultaneously (#016 fps_24_w), apply \(O(N \log^2 N)\) fast compositional inversion; when counting biconnected subgraphs of a fixed input graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(\lvert V \rvert \le 20\) (#207 UOJ 94), lift Tutte’s pointed block-cut \(\ln\) into the Set Power Series ring \(\mathcal{R}_V\) in \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time!










NoteCross-Study D — PGFs, Lattice Reflections, Furstenberg Diagonals & D-Finite ODEs (#156 Luogu P4548, #220 Luogu P3266, #058 ARC 136 F)




#156 (Luogu P4548 — 歌唱王国, Ch 14 [Int-1]):

Perspective 1 (Ch 14.2 Stopping-Time PGF & L’Hôpital Shift): Set up \((1-z)G(z) + F(z) = 1\) and \(G(z) + \sum_{b \in \text{Borders}(P)} m^{\lvert b \rvert - L} z^{L - \lvert b \rvert} F(z) = m^{-L} z^L G(z)\), then differentiate at \(z = 1\) to obtain \(F'(1) = \sum_{b \in \text{Borders}(P)} m^{\lvert b \rvert}\).
Perspective 2 (Ch 08.4 Goulden–Jackson Cluster Matrix & Ch 14.5 Optional Stopping Martingale): Evaluate the deterministic Goulden–Jackson avoidance OGF at \(x = z/m\), or run Li’s fair-casino betting martingale in \(O(L)\) KMP time.

#220 (Luogu P3266 — 骗我呢, Ch 15 [Int-1]):

Perspective 1 (Ch 15.1 Kelvin Alternating Reflection across Two Parallel Walls): Unfold the strip \(0 \le x - y \le M+1\) via alternating reflections across \(L_1: x - y = -1\) and \(L_2: x - y = M+2\), summing \(\binom{2N+M+1}{N - k(M+3)}\) in \(O(N/M)\) time.
Perspective 2 (Ch 15.3 Bivariate Kernel Method & Ch 05 Rational Transfer): Write the bounded step equation in \((K[y, y^{-1}])[[t]]\) and eliminate the two boundary series via the conjugate kernel roots \(y_1(t), y_2(t)\) (Chebyshev quotient \(U_{M+1} / U_{M+2}\)).

#058 (ARC 136 F — Flip Cells, CP-IV.6):

Perspective 1 (Ch 16.3–16.4 Bivariate Rational/Exponential Parity Walk): Formulate the \((r, c)\) parity-flip walk as a bivariate generating function and extract the target coefficient via formal residues.
Perspective 2 (Ch 18.2 Algebraic-to-D-Finite ODE Compilation): Differentiate the bivariate kernel/diagonal to compile a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients, then unroll the resulting P-recursive sequence recurrence in \(O(N)\) linear time!

title: 02 — Formal Calculus, 1D Newton Iteration (sqrt, ln, exp, pow) & The O(NK) Sparse Engine
text:
In Chapter 01, we built the algebraic foundations of the formal power series ring \(K[[x]]\): Cauchy convolution, valuation, formal topology, and multiplicative inversion via the degree-doubling recurrence \(G_{k+1} = G_k(2 - F G_k) \bmod x^{2^{k+1}}\). Yet inversion solves only linear equations \(F(x) G(x) = 1\). Most combinatorial structures and non-linear recurrences lead to richer algebraic or differential relations:
This chapter answers all four questions. We first define formal calculus—differentiation \(D_x\), the pointing operator \(\vartheta = x D_x\), and formal integration \(\int_0^x\)—purely as coefficient-shifting linear maps on \(K[[x]]\). We then audit characteristic-\(p\) obstructions, proving why division by \(1, 2, \dots, N\) separates \(p > N\) from \(p \le N\). Next, we lift linear inversion to 1D Newton-Raphson iteration on \(K[[x]]\), deriving the \(O(N \log N)\) engines for sqrt, ln, exp, and pow, alongside the two subtle modular arithmetic traps (Canonical Failure Modes #2 and #3) that break naive polynomial power templates. Finally, we construct the \(O(N \cdot K)\) Sparse Differential Equation Engine, showing how logarithmic derivatives let us compute \(P(x)^\alpha\), \(\exp P(x)\), \(\ln P(x)\), and \(\sqrt{P(x)}\) for \(K\)-sparse polynomials in pure \(O(N K)\) loops without a single Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT).

text:
2.1 Formal Differentiation \(D_x\), Pointing Operator \(\vartheta = x D_x\) & Formal Integration \(\int\)

Calculus Without Limits
In real or complex analysis, the derivative of a function \(f(x)\) is defined via the limit \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\). In a formal power series ring \(K[[x]]\) over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) or an arbitrary commutative ring \(K\), there is no Euclidean metric on \(K\), and dividing by a continuous increment \(h \to 0\) makes no sense.
Instead, what does term-by-term differentiation actually do to a sequence of coefficients \((a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)\)? It multiplies the \(n\)-th coefficient \(a_n\) by its index \(n\) and shifts it one position to the left (from \(x^n\) to \(x^{n-1}\)). We adopt this direct coefficient action as our definition.






NoteDefinition 2.1: Formal Derivative, Pointing Operator, and Formal Integral



Let \(K\) be a commutative ring with identity \(1_K\), and let \(A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n \in K[[x]]\).

Formal Derivative (\(D_x\)): The formal derivative map \(D_x : K[[x]] \to K[[x]]\) (also written \(A'(x)\) or \(\frac{d}{dx} A(x)\)) is the \(K\)-linear operator defined by \[D_x A(x) = A'(x) := \sum_{n \ge 1} n a_n x^{n-1} = \sum_{n \ge 0} (n+1) a_{n+1} x^n.\] Here \(n a_n\) denotes the scalar \((1_K + 1_K + \dots + 1_K) a_n\) (\(n\) times) in the ring \(K\). Notice that \(D_x\) requires no division in \(K\) and is well-defined over any commutative ring \(K\).
Pointing (Theta / Euler) Operator (\(\vartheta = x D_x\)): The pointing operator \(\vartheta : K[[x]] \to K[[x]]\) applies \(D_x\) and then multiplies by \(x\), preserving every monomial’s degree: \[\vartheta A(x) := x D_x A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} n a_n x^n.\] Combinatorially, if \(a_n\) counts unlabeled structures of size \(n\) (each built from \(n\) distinguishable atoms of weight \(1\)), then \(n a_n\) counts ways to choose a structure of size \(n\) and point at (distinguish) one of its \(n\) atoms.
Formal Integral (\(\int_0^x\)): Suppose \(A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n\) is truncated modulo \(x^N\). Provided the integers \(1, 2, \dots, N\) are invertible units in \(K\) (i.e., \(1, 2, \dots, N \in K^\times\)), the formal integral operator \(\int_0^x : K[[x]] / (x^N) \to K[[x]] / (x^{N+1})\) is defined by \[\int_0^x A(t)\,dt := \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \frac{a_n}{n+1} x^{n+1} \pmod{x^{N+1}}.\] By convention, the constant term \([x^0] \int_0^x A(t)\,dt\) is always set to \(0\).



Why is the unit condition \(1, 2, \dots, N \in K^\times\) attached to \(\int_0^x\) but not to \(D_x\)? Because multiplying \(a_n\) by \(n\) is always valid in any ring, whereas dividing \(a_n\) by \(n+1\) requires \((n+1)^{-1} \in K^\times\). When \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) is a prime field, \(1, 2, \dots, N \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) holds if and only if \(p > N\).


Algebraic Proofs of the Rules of Calculus
To use calculus safely over \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), we must verify that the familiar rules of differentiation—sum, product, power, quotient, and chain rule—hold as exact algebraic identities between coefficient sequences, without invoking limits.






TipTheorem 2.2: Rules of Formal Differentiation in \(K[[x]]\)



For any commutative ring \(K\) and any formal power series \(A(x), B(x) \in K[[x]]\):

\(K\)-Linearity: \(D_x(c A + d B) = c D_x A + d D_x B\) for all \(c, d \in K\).
Leibniz Product Rule: \(D_x(A(x) B(x)) = A'(x) B(x) + A(x) B'(x)\).
Power Rule: For every integer \(k \ge 1\), \(D_x(A(x)^k) = k A(x)^{k-1} A'(x)\).
Quotient Rule: If \(B(x) \in K[[x]]^\times\) (i.e., \([x^0] B(x) \in K^\times\)), then \[D_x\!\left(\frac{A(x)}{B(x)}\right) = \frac{A'(x) B(x) - A(x) B'(x)}{B(x)^2}.\]
Formal Chain Rule: If \(F(x) \in K[[x]]\) has strictly positive valuation \(\operatorname{val}(F) \ge 1\) (so \([x^0]F(x) = 0\) and the formal composition \(G(F(x))\) is a well-defined finite sum at every degree), then for every \(G(y) \in K[[y]]\), \[D_x\big(G(F(x))\big) = (D_y G)(F(x)) \cdot D_x F(x).\]



Proof (by Direct Coefficient Extraction):

Linearity is immediate from \([x^n] D_x(cA + dB) = (n+1)(c a_{n+1} + d b_{n+1}) = c(n+1)a_{n+1} + d(n+1)b_{n+1}\).
Product Rule: Extract the coefficient of \(x^n\) on the left-hand side of \(D_x(A \cdot B)\). By the definition of \(D_x\) and Cauchy convolution, \[[x^n] D_x(A(x) B(x)) = (n+1) [x^{n+1}](A(x) B(x)) = (n+1) \sum_{i+j=n+1} a_i b_j.\] Now split the multiplier \((n+1)\) into \((i + j)\) inside the sum: \[\sum_{i+j=n+1} (i + j) a_i b_j = \sum_{i+j=n+1} (i a_i) b_j + \sum_{i+j=n+1} a_i (j b_j).\] In the first sum, the \(i=0\) term vanishes because \(0 \cdot a_0 = 0\); re-indexing \(i' = i-1\) gives \(\sum_{i'+j=n} (i'+1) a_{i'+1} b_j = [x^n](A'(x) B(x))\). By symmetry, the second sum equals \([x^n](A(x) B'(x))\). Since the coefficients of \(x^n\) agree for all \(n \ge 0\), \(D_x(AB) = A'B + AB'\).
Power Rule: Follows by induction on \(k \ge 1\) using the Product Rule on \(A(x)^k = A(x)^{k-1} \cdot A(x)\).
Quotient Rule: First consider \(A(x) = 1\). Differentiating the identity \(B(x) \cdot B(x)^{-1} = 1\) via the Product Rule yields \(B'(x) B(x)^{-1} + B(x) D_x(B(x)^{-1}) = D_x(1) = 0\). Since \(B(x)\) is invertible, multiplying by \(B(x)^{-1}\) gives \(D_x(B(x)^{-1}) = -B'(x) / B(x)^2\). Applying the Product Rule to \(A(x) \cdot B(x)^{-1}\) then yields the general Quotient Rule.
Formal Chain Rule: Write \(G(y) = \sum_{k \ge 0} g_k y^k\). Because \(\operatorname{val}(F) \ge 1\), we have \(\operatorname{val}(F(x)^k) \ge k\), so the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(G(F(x))\) depends only on the finite truncation \(\sum_{k=0}^{n+1} g_k F(x)^k\). Applying linearity and the Power Rule to this finite sum modulo \(x^{n+1}\) gives \[D_x\big(G(F(x))\big) \equiv \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} g_k \cdot k F(x)^{k-1} F'(x) \equiv (D_y G)(F(x)) \cdot F'(x) \pmod{x^{n+1}}.\] Since this congruence holds for every \(n \ge 0\), the two series are identical in \(K[[x]]\). \(\blacksquare\)



The Fundamental Theorem of Formal Calculus
How do \(D_x\) and \(\int_0^x\) interact when \(1, 2, \dots, N \in K^\times\)?

Differentiating an integral recovers the exact series: For any \(A(x) \in K[[x]] / (x^N)\), \[D_x \left(\int_0^x A(t)\,dt\right) = D_x \left(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \frac{a_n}{n+1} x^{n+1}\right) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (n+1)\frac{a_n}{n+1} x^n = A(x) \pmod{x^N}.\]
Integrating a derivative recovers all terms of degree \(\ge 1\), zeroing out the constant term: For any \(F(x) = \sum_{n=0}^N f_n x^n\), \[\int_0^x F'(t)\,dt = \int_0^x \left(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (n+1) f_{n+1} t^n\right) dt = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_{n+1} x^{n+1} = F(x) - f_0 \pmod{x^{N+1}}.\]







ImportantThe Constant-of-Integration Rule



Whenever you solve a differential equation \(F'(x) = H(x)\) by integrating both sides, \(\int_0^x H(t)\,dt\) always has constant term \(0\). You must explicitly add back the initial condition \(f_0 = [x^0] F(x)\): \[F(x) \equiv [x^0]F(x) + \int_0^x F'(t)\,dt \pmod{x^{N+1}}.\]




Sequence-to-FPS Operator Dictionary & Index-Multiplier Alignment
One of the most frequent tasks in competitive programming is translating a recurrence with polynomial index coefficients (such as \((n+1) a_{n+1} = 3 n a_n + (n-1) a_{n-1}\)) into a differential equation on \(A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n\), or conversely, extracting a recurrence from a differential equation.

TipThe Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Index-Multiplier Alignment



The Diagnostic Signal: You encounter a linear or non-linear recurrence where each term \(a_{n-d}\) is multiplied by a linear or polynomial function of \(n\), such as \((n+1) a_{n+1} = \alpha a_n - (n-1) a_{n-1}\). Ordinary convolution cannot handle variable multipliers like \(n\), because Cauchy convolution only sees the difference of indices.
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Golden Rule of Index Alignment): Always rewrite every multiplier so that the integer multiplying \(a_m\) is its own index \(m\):

If you want to generate \(m a_m\) sitting at power \(x^n\), first look at \(A'(x) = \sum_{m \ge 1} m a_m x^{m-1}\), where \(m a_m\) sits at power \(x^{m-1}\).
Multiply \(A'(x)\) by whichever power of \(x\) shifts \(x^{m-1}\) to \(x^n\): specifically, multiply by \(x^{n - m + 1}\).

For \(m = n+1\): multiply \(A'(x)\) by \(x^0 = 1 \implies [x^n] A'(x) = (n+1) a_{n+1}\).
For \(m = n\): multiply \(A'(x)\) by \(x^1 = x \implies [x^n] (x A'(x)) = n a_n\).
For \(m = n-d\): multiply \(A'(x)\) by \(x^{d+1} \implies [x^n] (x^{d+1} A'(x)) = (n-d) a_{n-d}\).

What if the recurrence has \((n + c) a_{n-d}\) instead of \((n - d) a_{n-d}\)? Split the multiplier into the aligned index plus a constant remainder: \[(n + c) a_{n-d} = \underbrace{(n - d) a_{n-d}}_{[x^n]\big(x^{d+1} A'(x)\big)} + \underbrace{(c + d) a_{n-d}}_{(c+d)\,[x^n]\big(x^d A(x)\big)}.\]




Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): The Generalized Binomial Series via ODE
Suppose we want to compute the coefficients \(f_n = [x^n] F(x)\) of \(F(x) = (1 + x)^\alpha\) for an arbitrary scalar \(\alpha \in K\) (assuming \(1, 2, 3, 4 \in K^\times\)).

Form the Differential Equation: Differentiate \(F(x) = (1+x)^\alpha\) using the Power/Chain rule: \[F'(x) = \alpha (1+x)^{\alpha - 1}.\] Notice that \((1+x)^{\alpha-1}\) is just \(\frac{F(x)}{1+x}\). Multiply both sides by \((1+x)\) to clear the denominator and keep the polynomial sparse: \[(1 + x) F'(x) = \alpha F(x) \implies F'(x) + x F'(x) = \alpha F(x).\]
Extract \([x^n]\) using the Operator Dictionary:

\([x^n] F'(x) = (n+1) f_{n+1}\)
\([x^n] (x F'(x)) = n f_n\)
\([x^n] (\alpha F(x)) = \alpha f_n\) Combining these gives the 2-term recurrence: \[(n+1) f_{n+1} + n f_n = \alpha f_n \implies f_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha - n}{n+1} f_n.\]

Trace for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\) starting from \(f_0 = (1+0)^\alpha = 1\):

\(n = 0\): \(f_1 = \frac{\alpha - 0}{1} f_0 = \alpha\).
\(n = 1\): \(f_2 = \frac{\alpha - 1}{2} f_1 = \frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}{2}\).
\(n = 2\): \(f_3 = \frac{\alpha - 2}{3} f_2 = \frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)(\alpha - 2)}{6}\).
\(n = 3\): \(f_4 = \frac{\alpha - 3}{4} f_3 = \frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)(\alpha - 2)(\alpha - 3)}{24}\).


In four elementary steps—with no Taylor limits—formal differentiation and index alignment recover Newton’s generalized binomial coefficients \(\binom{\alpha}{n} = \frac{\alpha^{\underline{n}}}{n!}\).

section: 2.2 Characteristic-\(p\) Obstructions, The Frobenius Endomorphism & Lucas Breakdown
text:
2.2 Characteristic-\(p\) Obstructions, The Frobenius Endomorphism & Lucas Breakdown
In competitive programming, almost all generating function calculations happen over \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\) where \(p\) is a prime modulus. Most of the time, \(p = 998244353\) or \(10^9 + 7\) while \(N \le 5 \times 10^5\), so \(p > N\). However, a dedicated class of problems sets \(p\) to a small prime (\(p = 2, 3, 5, \text{ or } 10007 \le N\)). When \(p \le N\), the bridge between derivatives and integrals collapses. Understanding why it collapses—and what algebraic tools replace it—is essential.

Canonical Failure Mode #4: Characteristic-\(p\) Division Breakdown for \(p \le N\)






WarningCanonical Failure Mode #4: Characteristic-\(p\) Division Breakdown (\(p \le N\))



What Goes Wrong: Over \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), every multiple of \(p\) is \(0\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p\). When \(N \ge p\), the integer \(p\) is not invertible in \(\mathbb{F}_p\). Consequently:

Non-trivial Kernel of \(D_x\): Over \(\mathbb{Q}[[x]]\), \(F'(x) = 0\) implies \(F(x) = f_0\) is a constant series. Over \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), differentiating \(x^{kp}\) gives \(kp x^{kp-1} \equiv 0 \pmod p\) for every integer \(k \ge 1\)! Thus the kernel of \(D_x\) is the entire subring of \(p\)-th powers: \[\ker\big(D_x : \mathbb{F}_p[[x]] \to \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\big) = \mathbb{F}_p[[x^p]] = \left\{\sum_{k \ge 0} c_k x^{kp} : c_k \in \mathbb{F}_p\right\}.\] Differentiation completely destroys the coefficients \(f_p, f_{2p}, f_{3p}, \dots\), making it impossible to recover \(f_{kp}\) from \(F'(x)\) alone.
Cokernel Obstruction of \(\int_0^x\): In the formal integral \(\int_0^x A(t)\,dt = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{a_n}{n+1} x^{n+1}\), setting \(n = p - 1\) requires dividing \(a_{p-1}\) by \(p \equiv 0 \pmod p\). Even if \(a_{p-1} = 0\), the coefficient of \(x^p\) in any integrated series is indeterminate because \(D_x(x^p) = 0\).
Radius of Definition for \(\ln\), \(\exp\), and ODEs:

\(\ln(1 + x) = \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n} x^n\) crashes at \([x^p]\) because \(1/p\) does not exist in \(\mathbb{F}_p\).
\(\exp(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{x^n}{n!}\) crashes at \([x^p]\) because \(p! \equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Any ODE method (sparse_ln, sparse_exp, sparse_pow, or dense Newton exp) that divides by the loop index \(n\) at step \(n = p\) triggers a division-by-zero error when \(N \ge p\).


How to Diagnose & Remedy: Always check whether \(p > N\) before invoking \(\int_0^x\), \(\ln\), \(\exp\), or EGF division by \(n!\). When \(p \le N\), switch to derivative-free or Frobenius-aware tools (summarized in the Remedy Table at the end of this section).




The Frobenius Endomorphism: Turning the Obstacle into a Speedup
While characteristic \(p\) breaks integration at degree \(p\), it simultaneously grants \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\) an extraordinary algebraic symmetry that does not exist over \(\mathbb{Q}\) or \(\mathbb{R}\): raising a polynomial or formal power series to the \(p\)-th power requires zero convolutions!






TipTheorem 2.3: The Frobenius Endomorphism in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\)



Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\). Then: \[A(x)^p = A(x^p) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^{np} \quad \text{in } \mathbb{F}_p[[x]].\] More generally, for any integer \(k \ge 1\) and \(q = p^k\), \(A(x)^q = A(x^q)\).


Proof (Two-Step Verification):

Binomial Divisibility Lemma: For any \(1 \le j \le p-1\), the binomial coefficient \(\binom{p}{j} = \frac{p!}{j!(p-j)!}\) has a factor of \(p\) in the numerator, while neither \(j!\) nor \((p-j)!\) is divisible by the prime \(p\). Therefore, \(\binom{p}{j} \equiv 0 \pmod p\) for all \(1 \le j \le p-1\). Consequently, for any two series \(U, V \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), \[(U + V)^p = U^p + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \binom{p}{j} U^{p-j} V^j + V^p = U^p + V^p \quad \text{in } \mathbb{F}_p[[x]].\]
Coefficient Action via Fermat’s Little Theorem: Applying \((U+V)^p = U^p + V^p\) inductively to any finite truncation \(\sum_{n=0}^N a_n x^n\) (which determines \([x^m] A(x)^p\) for all \(m \le N\)) gives \[\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n\right)^p = \sum_{n \ge 0} (a_n x^n)^p = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n^p x^{np}.\] By Fermat’s Little Theorem, every element \(a_n \in \mathbb{F}_p\) satisfies \(a_n^p = a_n\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p\). Substituting \(a_n^p = a_n\) yields \(\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^{np} = A(x^p)\). Induction on \(k\) immediately gives \(A(x)^{p^k} = A(x^{p^k})\). \(\blacksquare\)







NoteCaution: General Ring vs. Prime Field \(\mathbb{F}_p\)



Notice the two distinct steps in the proof above:

In any commutative ring \(R\) of characteristic \(p\) (for instance, a polynomial ring \(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\) or a finite extension field \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\)), the Frobenius map raises each coefficient to its \(p\)-th power: \(\left(\sum a_n x^n\right)^p = \sum a_n^p x^{np}\).
Only when the coefficients lie in the prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\) does Fermat’s Little Theorem simplify \(a_n^p\) to \(a_n\), giving \(A(x)^p = A(x^p)\).




Algorithmic Application: Base-\(p\) Frobenius Decomposition of \(A(x)^K \bmod (p, x^N)\)
Suppose \(p \le N\) and we need to compute \(A(x)^K \bmod x^N\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\). We cannot use \(\exp(K \ln A(x))\) because \(\ln\) and \(\exp\) fail at degree \(p\). Instead, divide \(K\) by \(p\): write \(K = q p + r\) with \(0 \le r < p\), or expand \(K\) in base \(p\) as \(K = \sum_{i \ge 0} k_i p^i\) (\(0 \le k_i < p\)). By Theorem 2.3: \[A(x)^K = A(x)^{q p + r} = \big(A(x)^p\big)^q \cdot A(x)^r = A(x^p)^q \cdot A(x)^r \pmod p,\] and in full base-\(p\) form: \[A(x)^K = \prod_{i \ge 0} \Big(A\big(x^{p^i}\big)\Big)^{k_i} \pmod p.\] What makes \(A(x^p)^q \bmod x^N\) so fast? Every nonzero term in \(A(x^p)\) has degree divisible by \(p\)! Therefore, computing \(A(x^p)^q \bmod x^N\) is isomorphic to substituting \(y = x^p\) and computing \(A(y)^q \bmod y^{\lceil N/p \rceil}\) at one-\(p\)-th the degree!


Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4, p = 3\)): Computing \((1 + 2x + x^2)^7 \bmod (3, x^5)\)
Let \(A(x) = 1 + 2x + x^2 \in \mathbb{F}_3[[x]]\) and let us compute \(A(x)^7 \bmod x^5\) in \(\mathbb{F}_3\). Write the exponent \(7\) in base \(p = 3\): \(7 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1\). By the Frobenius Endomorphism (Theorem 2.3): \[A(x)^7 = \big(A(x)^3\big)^2 \cdot A(x)^1 = A(x^3)^2 \cdot A(x) \quad \text{in } \mathbb{F}_3[[x]].\]

Dilation step (\(A(x^3) \bmod x^5\)): Replace \(x\) by \(x^3\) in \(A(x) = 1 + 2x + x^2\) and truncate at \(x^4\): \[A(x^3) = 1 + 2x^3 + x^6 \equiv 1 + 2x^3 \pmod{x^5}.\]
Square the dilated series modulo \(x^5\): \[A(x^3)^2 \equiv (1 + 2x^3)^2 = 1 + 4x^3 + 4x^6 \equiv 1 + x^3 \pmod{x^5} \quad (\text{since } 4 \equiv 1 \pmod 3).\]
Multiply by \(A(x)^1 = 1 + 2x + x^2\) modulo \(x^5\): \[A(x)^7 \equiv (1 + x^3)(1 + 2x + x^2) = 1 + 2x + x^2 + x^3 + 2x^4 + x^5 \equiv 1 + 2x + x^2 + x^3 + 2x^4 \pmod{x^5}.\] Notice we never divided by \(3\), never called \(\ln\) or \(\exp\), and computed a 7th power by a trivial two-term shift!




The Lucas Obstruction to Exponential Generating Functions
Why does the Frobenius identity also govern binomial coefficients and Exponential Generating Functions (EGFs) modulo \(p\)? Consider \((1 + x)^n\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p[x]\). Writing \(n = \sum_{i \ge 0} n_i p^i\) in base \(p\) (\(0 \le n_i < p\)), Theorem 2.3 yields \[(1 + x)^n = \prod_{i \ge 0} \big((1 + x)^{p^i}\big)^{n_i} = \prod_{i \ge 0} \big(1 + x^{p^i}\big)^{n_i} \quad \text{in } \mathbb{F}_p[x].\] To extract the coefficient \([x^k](1 + x)^n = \binom{n}{k} \bmod p\), expand \(k = \sum_{i \ge 0} k_i p^i\) in base \(p\) (\(0 \le k_i < p\)). Since base-\(p\) representations are unique, the only way to form \(x^k\) by multiplying one term from each factor \((1 + x^{p^i})^{n_i}\) (whose degrees are \(0, p^i, 2p^i, \dots, n_i p^i < p^{i+1}\)) is to pick the \(x^{k_i p^i}\) term from the \(i\)-th factor! This proves Lucas’s Theorem: \[\binom{n}{k} \equiv \prod_{i \ge 0} \binom{n_i}{k_i} \pmod p.\]
What does Lucas’s Theorem mean for Exponential Generating Functions \(A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{a_n}{n!} x^n\) when \(p \le N\)?

Algebraic Breakdown: For \(n \ge p\), the denominator \(n!\) is \(0 \pmod p\), so \(\frac{a_n}{n!}\) cannot even be represented in \(\mathbb{F}_p\).
Combinatorial Breakdown (No Base-\(p\) Carries): Even if we keep \(a_n\) and \(b_m\) unscaled and look at the binomial convolution \(c_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} a_k b_{n-k} \pmod p\), Lucas’s Theorem says \(\binom{n}{k} \equiv 0 \pmod p\) whenever adding \(k\) and \(n-k\) in base \(p\) produces a carry in any digit position! Thus, binomial convolution modulo \(p\) disconnects into independent digit-wise convolutions across base-\(p\) digits, blocking the standard EGF mechanism.

2.3 1D Newton-Raphson Quadratic Convergence, sqrt, ln, exp, pow & Valuation Hazards
We now return to the standard competitive programming regime where \(1, 2, \dots, N \in K^\times\) (for instance, \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) with \(p > N\)). In Chapter 01, we computed \(F(x)^{-1} \bmod x^N\) by doubling the number of correct coefficients in each step: \(G_{k+1} = G_k(2 - F G_k) \bmod x^{2^{k+1}}\). That formula was not an isolated trick—it is a special case of 1D Newton-Raphson Iteration on the formal power series ring \(K[[x]]\).

The 3-Line Proof of 1D Newton-Raphson on \(K[[x]]\)
Suppose we have an unknown target series \(F(x) \in K[[x]]\) that satisfies an equation \(\Phi(F(x)) = 0 \pmod{x^N}\), where \(\Phi(G)\) is a smooth mapping on formal power series (such as \(\Phi(G) = G^2 - P(x)\) or \(\Phi(G) = \ln G - B(x)\)).






TipTheorem 2.4: 1D Newton-Raphson Quadratic Convergence in \(K[[x]]\)



Let \(\Phi(G)\) be a formal mapping with formal Fréchet derivative \(\Phi'(G) = \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial G}(G)\). Suppose we have an approximation \(G_k(x) \in K[[x]]\) that agrees with the true solution \(F(x)\) in its first \(2^k\) coefficients: \[F(x) - G_k(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^{2^k}}.\] Provided the constant term of the derivative is a unit, \([x^0]\Phi'(G_0) \in K^\times\) (which guarantees \(\Phi'(G_k)\) is invertible in \(K[[x]]\) for all \(k\)), the next iterate defined by \[G_{k+1}(x) := G_k(x) - \frac{\Phi(G_k(x))}{\Phi'(G_k(x))} \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}\] satisfies \(F(x) - G_{k+1}(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}\). That is, every Newton step exactly doubles the number of correct coefficients.


The 3-Line Proof:

Valuation Squaring: Since \(\operatorname{val}(F - G_k) \ge 2^k\), the square of their difference has valuation at least \(2 \cdot 2^k = 2^{k+1}\): \[\big(F(x) - G_k(x)\big)^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}.\]
First-Order Taylor Expansion: Expand \(\Phi(F)\) around \(G_k\) in powers of the perturbation \(\Delta = F - G_k\). Because \(\Delta^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}\), all terms of order \(\ge 2\) vanish modulo \(x^{2^{k+1}}\): \[0 \equiv \Phi(F) \equiv \Phi(G_k) + \Phi'(G_k)\big(F - G_k\big) \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}.\]
Solve for \(F\): Since \([x^0]\Phi'(G_k) = [x^0]\Phi'(G_0) \in K^\times\), the series \(\Phi'(G_k)\) is invertible modulo \(x^{2^{k+1}}\). Dividing by \(\Phi'(G_k)\) gives \[F(x) \equiv G_k(x) - \frac{\Phi(G_k(x))}{\Phi'(G_k(x))} \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}. \quad \blacksquare\]







NoteMaster Complexity Principle: Why Doubling Costs \(O(N \log N)\), Not \(O(N \log^2 N)\)



If each step of Newton iteration costs \(T(m) = c \cdot m \log m\) operations at length \(m = 2^k\), summing over \(m = 1, 2, 4, \dots, N\) yields a geometric series dominated by its final term: \[T_{\text{total}}(N) = \sum_{k=0}^{\lceil \log_2 N \rceil} T(2^k) \le c \left(N \log N + \frac{N}{2} \log N + \frac{N}{4} \log N + \dots\right) = 2c N \log N = O(N \log N).\] This single geometric-series property is why inv, sqrt, exp, and pow all run in \(O(N \log N)\) rather than \(O(N \log^2 N)\).




Primitive 1: Formal Square Root (sqrt)
Given \(P(x) \in K[[x]]\), we seek \(F(x) \in K[[x]]\) such that \(F(x)^2 \equiv P(x) \pmod{x^N}\).

The Diagnostic Signal: A quadratic formula \(\frac{-B \pm \sqrt{B^2 - 4AC}}{2A}\) from Catalan-like trees, lattice paths, or radical generating functions requires extracting the square root of a known series \(P(x)\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Unit Case \([x^0]P = p_0 \in K^\times\)): To find \(F\) with \(F^2 = P(x)\), treat \(P(x)\) as a fixed constant with respect to \(G\) and set \[\Phi(G) = G^2 - P(x) = 0 \implies \Phi'(G) = 2G.\] Crucial hypothesis: for \(\Phi'(G_0) = 2 g_0\) to be a unit in \(K\), we need \(2 \in K^\times\) (in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), this requires \(p > 2\), i.e., an odd prime) and \(g_0 \in K^\times\) where \(g_0^2 = p_0\). Substituting \(\Phi(G_k)\) and \(\Phi'(G_k)\) into Theorem 2.4 gives: \[G_{k+1} = G_k - \frac{G_k^2 - P}{2 G_k} = \frac{2 G_k^2 - G_k^2 + P}{2 G_k} = \frac{1}{2}\left(G_k + \frac{P(x)}{G_k}\right) \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}.\]
What if \([x^0]P(x) = 0\)? (Valuation Parity Shift): If \(P(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^N}\), then \(F(x) = 0\) is a valid square root. Otherwise, factor out the lowest nonzero power of \(x\): write \(P(x) = x^v \widetilde{P}(x)\) where \(v = \operatorname{val}(P) < N\) and \(\widetilde{p}_0 = [x^0]\widetilde{P}(x) \ne 0\). For \(F(x)^2 = x^v \widetilde{P}(x)\) to hold in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), the valuation \(v = 2 \operatorname{val}(F)\) must be even (\(v = 2m\)), and \(\widetilde{p}_0\) must be a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) (tested via Euler’s criterion \(\widetilde{p}_0^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod p\), with \(g_0 = \sqrt{\widetilde{p}_0} \bmod p\) found in \(O(\log p)\) time via Cipolla’s or Tonelli–Shanks’s algorithm). Then \[\sqrt{P(x)} \equiv x^m \sqrt{\widetilde{P}(x) \bmod x^{N - m}} \pmod{x^N}.\] Notice that because multiplying by \(x^m\) shifts degrees up by \(m\), we only need to compute \(\sqrt{\widetilde{P}(x)}\) to precision \(x^{N - m}\) (or \(x^{N - 2m}\) if we only trust the input \(P(x)\) modulo \(x^N\); in standard competitive programming library problems like Library Checker sqrt_of_formal_power_series, the input coefficients \(p_0, \dots, p_{N-1}\) are treated as exact up to \(x^N\) and \(\sqrt{\widetilde{P}}\) is computed modulo \(x^{N-m}\)).


Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): Computing \(\sqrt{1 - 4x} \bmod x^4\)
Let \(P(x) = 1 - 4x\) (the discriminant inside the Catalan generating function \(\frac{1 - \sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}\)).

Base case (\(2^0 = 1\)): \(p_0 = 1\), so choose \(G_0(x) = 1 \pmod x\).
Step \(k = 0 \to 1\) (\(\bmod x^2\)): \[G_1(x) \equiv \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1 - 4x}{1}\right) = \frac{1}{2}(2 - 4x) = 1 - 2x \pmod{x^2}.\]
Step \(k = 1 \to 2\) (\(\bmod x^4\)): First invert \(G_1(x) = 1 - 2x\) modulo \(x^4\): \[G_1(x)^{-1} = \frac{1}{1 - 2x} \equiv 1 + 2x + 4x^2 + 8x^3 \pmod{x^4}.\] Multiply by \(P(x) = 1 - 4x\) modulo \(x^4\): \[P(x) G_1(x)^{-1} \equiv (1 - 4x)(1 + 2x + 4x^2 + 8x^3) \equiv 1 - 2x - 4x^2 - 8x^3 \pmod{x^4}.\] Average with \(G_1(x) = 1 - 2x\): \[G_2(x) \equiv \frac{1}{2}\big((1 - 2x) + (1 - 2x - 4x^2 - 8x^3)\big) = 1 - 2x - 2x^2 - 4x^3 \pmod{x^4}.\] Let us hand-check by squaring \(G_2(x)\): \((1 - 2x - 2x^2 - 4x^3)^2 = 1 - 4x + (4 - 4)x^2 + (-8 + 8)x^3 + O(x^4) = 1 - 4x \pmod{x^4}\). Exact match!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: sqrt(P, N)




Input: Polynomial \(P(x)\) truncated modulo \(x^N\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (\(p > 2\) odd prime).
Preconditions: If \(P \not\equiv 0 \pmod{x^N}\) with \(v = \operatorname{val}(P) < N\) and \(P(x) = x^v \widetilde{P}(x)\), then \(v\) must be even (\(v = 2m\)) and \([x^0]\widetilde{P}\) must be a quadratic residue in \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (i.e., \((\widetilde{p}_0)^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod p\)). If either condition fails, no square root exists in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\).
Output: \(F(x) \bmod x^N\) satisfying \(F(x)^2 \equiv P(x) \pmod{x^N}\) (unique up to sign \(\pm F(x)\) once \([x^m]F = \sqrt{\widetilde{p}_0}\) is fixed).
Complexity: \(T_{\text{sqrt}}(N) \approx 2 T_{\text{inv}}(N) = O(N \log N)\) time, \(O(N)\) space (can be reduced to \(\frac{11}{6} E(N)\) by co-maintaining \(H_k = G_k^{-1} \bmod x^{2^{k-1}}\)).
Correctness Invariant: After iteration \(k\), \(G_k(x)^2 \equiv \widetilde{P}(x) \pmod{x^{2^k}}\), so \(\operatorname{val}(G_k^2 - \widetilde{P}) \ge 2^k\).






Primitive 2: Formal Logarithm (ln)






TipProposition 2.4 (ODE Characterization of Formal Exp and Log)



Let \(K\) be a commutative ring in which \(1, 2, \dots, N \in K^\times\) (in particular, \(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(K = \mathbb{F}_p\) with prime \(p > N\)). For any series \(A(x) \in K[[x]] / (x^{N+1})\) with \([x^0]A(x) = 1\), and any series \(B(x) \in K[[x]] / (x^{N+1})\) with \([x^0]B(x) = 0\): \[
G(x) = \ln A(x) \iff G'(x) = \frac{A'(x)}{A(x)} \text{ with } [x^0]G(x) = 0, \qquad F(x) = \exp(B(x)) \iff F'(x) = B'(x) F(x) \text{ with } [x^0]F(x) = 1.
\]


Given \(A(x) \in K[[x]]\) with constant term \([x^0]A(x) = 1\), we define its formal logarithm via the power series \(\ln(1 + u) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} u^k\) substituted at \(u = A(x) - 1\) (which has valuation \(\ge 1\)). How do we compute \(\ln A(x) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time?

The Diagnostic Signal: We want to convert an infinite product or an exponentiation \(A(x)^\alpha\) into an additive sum, or extract connected components from labeled graphs (\(C(x) = \ln G(x)\)).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Direct substitution into \(u - u^2/2 + u^3/3 - \dots\) would require \(N\) polynomial multiplications! Instead, apply the Formal Chain Rule (Theorem 2.2(5)) to differentiate \(G(x) = \ln(1 + u(x))\) where \(u(x) = A(x) - 1\): \[D_x G(x) = \left(\sum_{k \ge 1} (-1)^{k-1} u(x)^{k-1}\right) u'(x) = \frac{u'(x)}{1 + u(x)} = \frac{A'(x)}{A(x)}.\] Since \([x^0] G(x) = \ln(1 + 0) = 0\), applying the Fundamental Theorem of Formal Calculus (\(\int_0^x\)) recovers \(G(x)\) in one derivative, one inversion, one convolution, and one integral: \[\ln A(x) \equiv \int_0^x \frac{A'(t)}{A(t)}\,dt \pmod{x^N}.\]


Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): Computing \(\ln\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right) \bmod x^4\)
Let \(A(x) = \frac{1}{1-x} \equiv 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 \pmod{x^4}\).

Differentiate \(A(x) \bmod x^4 \to A'(x) \bmod x^3\): \[A'(x) \equiv 1 + 2x + 3x^2 \pmod{x^3}.\]
Invert \(A(x) \bmod x^3\): Since \(A(x) = (1-x)^{-1}\), its inverse is \(A(x)^{-1} \equiv 1 - x \pmod{x^3}\).
Multiply \(A'(x) \cdot A(x)^{-1} \bmod x^3\): \[A'(x) A(x)^{-1} \equiv (1 + 2x + 3x^2)(1 - x) = 1 + (2-1)x + (3-2)x^2 - 3x^3 \equiv 1 + x + x^2 \pmod{x^3}.\]
Integrate \(\int_0^x (1 + t + t^2)\,dt \bmod x^4\): \[\ln A(x) \equiv 0 + \frac{1}{1}x + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{3}x^3 = x + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{3}x^3 \pmod{x^4}.\]







NoteAlgorithm Contract: ln(A, N)




Input: \(A(x) \bmod x^N\) over \(K\).
Preconditions: \([x^0] A(x) = 1\) and \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), requires \(p \ge N\)). If \([x^0]A(x) \ne 1\), \(\ln A(x)\) is not defined as a formal power series over \(\mathbb{F}_p\)!
Output: \(G(x) = \ln A(x) \bmod x^N\) with \([x^0]G(x) = 0\).
Complexity: 1 call to inv of length \(N-1\) plus 1 NTT multiplication of length \(N-1\), costing \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
Correctness Invariant: \([x^{n-1}](A'(x) A(x)^{-1}) = n g_n\) for all \(1 \le n < N\); dividing by \(n \in K^\times\) uniquely determines \(g_n\).






Primitive 3: Formal Exponential (exp)
Given \(B(x) \in K[[x]]\) with constant term \([x^0] B(x) = 0\), we define its formal exponential via \(\exp(B(x)) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{B(x)^k}{k!}\). Because \(\operatorname{val}(B) \ge 1\), this sum is formally convergent whenever \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\).

The Diagnostic Signal: In labeled counting (Chapter 04), forming an unordered set of connected components translates to \(F(x) = \exp(B(x))\). In polynomial exponentiation or product-to-sum transforms, \(\prod_i F_i(x) = \exp\left(\sum_i \ln F_i(x)\right)\) requires recovering the product from its summed logarithm.
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: To solve \(F(x) = \exp(B(x))\), take the formal logarithm of both sides to linearize the unknown \(F\): \[\Phi(G) = \ln G(x) - B(x) = 0.\] What is the Fréchet derivative \(\Phi'(G) = \frac{\partial}{\partial G}(\ln G - B(x))\)? Here \(B(x)\) does not depend on \(G\), and \(\frac{d}{dG} \ln G = G^{-1}\). Plugging \(\Phi(G_k) = \ln G_k - B\) and \(\Phi'(G_k) = G_k^{-1}\) into 1D Newton-Raphson (Theorem 2.4) yields: \[G_{k+1}(x) = G_k(x) - \frac{\ln G_k(x) - B(x)}{G_k(x)^{-1}} = G_k(x)\Big(1 - \ln G_k(x) + B(x)\Big) \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}.\]


Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): Computing \(\exp\left(x + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{3}x^3\right) \bmod x^4\)
Let \(B(x) = x + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{3}x^3\). We expect \(\exp(B(x)) = \frac{1}{1-x} \equiv 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 \pmod{x^4}\).

Base case (\(2^0 = 1\)): Since \([x^0]B(x) = 0\), start with \(G_0(x) = \exp(0) = 1 \pmod x\).
Step \(k = 0 \to 1\) (\(\bmod x^2\)): Compute \(\ln G_0(x) \bmod x^2\): since \(G_0(x) = 1\), \(\ln(1) = 0 \pmod{x^2}\). Then \(G_1(x) \equiv 1 \cdot \big(1 - 0 + (x)\big) = 1 + x \pmod{x^2}.\)
Step \(k = 1 \to 2\) (\(\bmod x^4\)): First compute \(\ln G_1(x) = \ln(1 + x) \bmod x^4\): \[\ln(1 + x) = \int_0^x \frac{1}{1+t}\,dt = \int_0^x (1 - t + t^2)\,dt = x - \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{3}x^3 \pmod{x^4}.\] Now form \(1 - \ln G_1(x) + B(x) \bmod x^4\): \[1 - \left(x - \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{3}x^3\right) + \left(x + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{3}x^3\right) = 1 + x^2 \pmod{x^4}.\] Multiply by \(G_1(x) = 1 + x\) modulo \(x^4\): \[G_2(x) \equiv (1 + x)(1 + x^2) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 \pmod{x^4}.\] In just two iterations, all four coefficients \(1, 1, 1, 1\) are recovered!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: exp(B, N)




Input: \(B(x) \bmod x^N\) over \(K\).
Preconditions: \([x^0] B(x) = 0\) (i.e., \(\operatorname{val}(B) \ge 1\)) and \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), requires \(p \ge N\)). If \([x^0] B(x) \ne 0\), the infinite sum \(\sum_{k \ge 0} b_0^k / k!\) does not converge in the formal topology!
Output: \(F(x) = \exp(B(x)) \bmod x^N\) with \([x^0] F(x) = 1\).
Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space via Newton doubling (each step calls ln of size \(2^{k+1}\)). (Forward pointer: in Chapter 09 (§9.4), we will also see an alternative \(O(N \log^2 N)\) Divide-and-Conquer CDQ algorithm via \(F'(x) = B'(x) F(x)\) with much smaller constant factors for \(N \le 10^5\).)
Correctness Invariant: After step \(k\), \(\ln G_k(x) \equiv B(x) \pmod{x^{2^k}}\) and \([x^0]G_k(x) = 1\).






Primitive 4: General Formal Power (pow) & Two Canonical Failure Modes
Given an arbitrary polynomial \(P(x) \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x]] / (x^N)\) and an exponent \(\alpha\) (which might be a huge non-negative integer \(K \le 10^{18}\), a negative integer, or a rational number \(a/b \in \mathbb{Q}\)), how do we compute \(P(x)^\alpha \bmod x^N\) when \(p > N\)?






TipThe Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: General Formal Power pow(P, M, N)




The Diagnostic Signal: You need \([x^n] P(x)^M\) for \(n < N\) where the exponent \(M\) is large (\(M \le 10^{18}\) or given as a string of \(10^6\) digits) and \(P(x)\) is a dense polynomial that may start with leading zeros (\([x^0]P(x) = 0\)) or a non-unit constant term (\([x^0]P(x) = c \neq 1\)).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

If \([x^0]P(x) = 1\), we can immediately write \(P(x)^\alpha = \exp(\alpha \ln P(x)) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time, eliminating the \(\log M\) factor of binary exponentiation!
When \([x^0]P(x) \neq 1\), we cannot pass \(P(x)\) directly to ln. Instead, factor \(P(x)\) into three decoupled components:

Valuation \(v = \operatorname{val}(P)\): The index of the first nonzero coefficient \(c_v = [x^v] P(x) \ne 0\).
Leading scalar \(c_v \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\): Factor out \(c_v\) so the remaining series starts with \(1\).
Normalized monic series \(\widetilde{P}(x)\): Define \(\widetilde{P}(x) := c_v^{-1} x^{-v} P(x)\), which satisfies \([x^0]\widetilde{P}(x) = 1\).

Raise each of the three factors \(P(x) = x^v \cdot c_v \cdot \widetilde{P}(x)\) to the power \(\alpha\) separately: \[P(x)^\alpha = x^{v \alpha} \cdot c_v^\alpha \cdot \exp\big(\alpha \ln \widetilde{P}(x)\big) \pmod{x^N}.\]




Here lies one of the most notorious bug sources in competitive programming (Library Checker — Pow of Formal Power Series, where \(M \le 10^{18}\) while \(p = 998244353\)). Notice that the exponent \(\alpha\) appears in three different places on the right-hand side—and each of the three places lives in a completely different algebraic structure!






WarningCanonical Failure Mode #2: The 3-Way Modular Reduction Trap in \(P(x)^\alpha \bmod x^N\) for \(\alpha \ge p\)



What Goes Wrong: A coder reads the exponent \(M\) (say \(M = 10^{18}\)) and immediately reduces M %= 998244353 at the top of poly_pow(P, M). This single line causes three distinct Wrong Answers:

Bug A (\(0^0\) vs. \(0^p\)): If \(P(x) = 0\) and \(M = p = 998244353\), reducing \(M \bmod p\) turns \(M\) into \(0\), returning \(P(x)^0 = 1\) instead of \(0^p = 0\)!
Bug B (Valuation Shift Wrapping): If \(P(x) = x\) (\(v = 1\)) and \(M = p = 998244353\) with \(N = 10\), reducing \(M \bmod p = 0\) shifts by \(x^{1 \cdot 0} = 1\) instead of \(x^p \equiv 0 \pmod{x^{10}}\)!
Bug C (Fermat Exponent Mismatch): In the scalar factor \(c_v^M \bmod p\), the multiplicative group \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\) has order \(p - 1\), not \(p\)! Using \(c_v^{M \bmod p}\) instead of \(c_v^{M \bmod (p-1)}\) multiplies the entire output polynomial by the wrong constant whenever \(M \ge p\) and \(c_v \ne 1\).

The Exact 3-Way Reduction Rule: When computing \(P(x)^M \bmod x^N\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (\(p > N\)) for a non-negative integer \(M \ge 0\) (even if \(M\) is given as a \(10^6\)-digit string!):

Zero Exponent Guard (\(M = 0\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\)): Before anything else, if the unreduced integer \(M == 0\), immediately return the constant polynomial \(1 \bmod x^N\) (since \(P(x)^0 = 1\) even when \(P(x) = 0\)).
Zero Polynomial or Valuation Overflow Guard (True Integer \(\mathbb{Z}\) / __int128): Let \(v = \operatorname{val}(P)\). If \(P(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^N}\), or if \(v > 0\) and the true integer product \(v \cdot M \ge N\) (checked via M >= (N + v - 1) / v to prevent 64-bit overflow!), immediately return the zero polynomial \(0 \bmod x^N\).
Three Distinct Reductions of \(M\):

Degree Shift (\(x^{v M}\)): Uses the exact unreduced integer \(v \cdot M \in [0, N-1]\).
Leading Scalar (\(c_v^{M_{\text{exp}}} \bmod p\)): Uses \(M_{\text{exp}} = M \bmod (p - 1)\) by Fermat’s Little Theorem (\(c_v^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p\) for \(c_v \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\)).
Series Multiplier (\(M_{\text{mod}} \cdot \ln \widetilde{P}(x)\)): Uses \(M_{\text{mod}} = M \bmod p\) because the coefficients of \(\ln \widetilde{P}(x)\) live in the additive group of \(\mathbb{F}_p\).










NoteAlgorithm Contract: pow(P, M, N) — Dense Formal Power with 3-Way Modular Reduction




Input: Polynomial \(P(x) \bmod x^N\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\); non-negative integer exponent \(M \ge 0\) (supplied either as a 64-bit integer or as a multi-precision decimal string holding \((M_{\text{raw}}, M \bmod p, M \bmod (p-1))\)).
Preconditions: \(p \ge N\) so that ln and exp are well-defined up to degree \(N-1\).
Output: \(F(x) = P(x)^M \bmod x^N\).
Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space (1 call to ln and 1 call to exp of length \(N - vM\)).
Correctness Invariant: If \(M = 0\), returns \(1\); if \(P \equiv 0\) or \(vM \ge N\), returns \(0\); otherwise \(F(x) = x^{vM} \cdot c_v^{M \bmod (p-1)} \cdot \exp\big((M \bmod p) \ln \widetilde{P}(x)\big) \bmod x^N\) where \(\widetilde{P}(x) = c_v^{-1} x^{-v} P(x)\) has \([x^0]\widetilde{P} = 1\).



What if the exponent \(\alpha\) is not an integer, but a rational number \(\alpha = a / b \in \mathbb{Q}\) with \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) and \(b > 0\) (such as \(\alpha = 1/2\) for sqrt, \(\alpha = -1/2\) for inverse square root, or \(\alpha = 1/k\) for \(k\)-th roots)?






WarningCanonical Failure Mode #3: Rational Exponent \(P(x)^{a/b}\) Existence Failure



What Goes Wrong: A coder computes \(\alpha = a \cdot b^{-1} \bmod p \in \mathbb{F}_p\) and passes this modular integer into poly_pow(P, alpha), assuming that \(P(x)^{a/b} = \exp\big((a b^{-1} \bmod p) \ln P(x)\big)\) works whenever \(b \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Why It Fails: While \(\exp\big((a b^{-1} \bmod p) \ln \widetilde{P}(x)\big)\) is always well-defined for a normalized series \(\widetilde{P}(x)\) with \([x^0]\widetilde{P}(x) = 1\) (provided \(p \nmid b\) and \(p > N\)), the two outer factors \(x^{v \cdot (a/b)}\) and \(c_v^{a/b}\) are not automatically defined in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\):

Valuation Divisibility Obstruction: In \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), every monomial \(x^k\) must have an integer exponent \(k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\). You cannot divide the valuation \(v\) by \(b\) modulo \(p\)! For \(x^{v a / b}\) to be a legitimate monomial in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), \(b\) must divide \(v \cdot a\) as true integers in \(\mathbb{Z}\) (since \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), this is equivalent to \(b \mid v\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\)). For example, \(\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \notin \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\) even though \(1/2 \equiv (p+1)/2 \pmod p\) exists in \(\mathbb{F}_p\)!
Scalar \(b\)-th Residue Obstruction: In \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\), raising \(c_v\) to \(a/b\) means finding an element \(r \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) such that \(r^b \equiv c_v^a \pmod p\). This is not \(c_v^{a b^{-1} \bmod (p-1)}\) when \(\gcd(b, p-1) > 1\)! For instance, for \(a/b = 1/2\), \(2\) is not even invertible modulo \(p - 1\) (since \(p - 1\) is even); a square root of \(c_v\) exists in \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\) if and only if \(c_v^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod p\).

Exact Necessary and Sufficient Existence Criterion for \(P(x)^{a/b} \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x]] / (x^N)\) (\(\gcd(a,b)=1, b>0, p > N\)): Assuming \(P(x) = x^v c_v \widetilde{P}(x) \not\equiv 0 \pmod{x^N}\):

\(b \mid v\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) (with \(a \ge 0\), or \(v = 0\) if \(a < 0\) so negative powers of \(x\) do not appear);
\(c_v^a\) is a \(b\)-th power residue in \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (i.e., there exists \(r \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) with \(r^b \equiv c_v^a \pmod p\), which holds iff \((c_v^a)^{(p-1)/\gcd(b, p-1)} \equiv 1 \pmod p\));
For the normalized unit series \(\widetilde{P}(x)\) (\([x^0]\widetilde{P} = 1\)), \(\widetilde{P}(x)^{a/b} = \exp\big((a \cdot b^{-1} \bmod p) \ln \widetilde{P}(x)\big) \bmod x^{N - v a / b}\) is uniquely defined with constant term \(1\).
