title: 02 — Formal Calculus, 1D Newton Iteration (sqrt, ln, exp, pow) & The O(NK) Sparse Engine
section: 2.4 The Master \(O(N \cdot K)\) Sparse FPS Engine (sparse_div, sparse_ln, sparse_exp, sparse_pow, sparse_sqrt)
text:
2.4 The Master \(O(N \cdot K)\) Sparse FPS Engine (sparse_div, sparse_ln, sparse_exp, sparse_pow, sparse_sqrt)
Suppose a problem asks for the first \(N = 2 \times 10^5\) coefficients of \((1 + x + x^3)^{10^9} \bmod x^N\), or \(\exp(x + x^5 - 2x^{12}) \bmod x^N\), or \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 2x - 3x^2}} \bmod x^N\). Here, the input polynomial \(P(x)\) is \(K\)-sparse: it has at most \(K\) nonzero terms (with \(K \le 20\) or \(K \le 100\)).
Could we use the general \(O(N \log N)\) NTT engines (ln, exp, sqrt, pow) from Section 2.3? Yes, in \(O(N \log N)\) time with 6 to 15 NTT calls. Can we do dramatically better—computing the exact same answer in \(O(N \cdot K)\) time using a single 10-line for loop and zero NTTs?

The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad






TipThe Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Why Differentiating Preserves Sparsity



The Diagnostic Signal: You need to apply a non-linear FPS operation (inv, ln, exp, pow, sqrt) up to \(x^N\) where the input polynomial \(P(x)\) (or its numerator and denominator after multiplying by \(1-x\)) has only \(K \ll N\) nonzero terms, and \(p > N\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Why did our \(O(N \log N)\) algorithm for \(P(x)^\alpha = \exp(\alpha \ln P(x))\) require NTTs even when \(P(x) = 1 + x + x^3\) has only \(K = 3\) terms? Because as soon as we take the intermediate logarithm \(L(x) = \ln(1 + x + x^3)\), the series \(L(x)\) has \(\Theta(N)\) nonzero terms! Taking \(\ln\) destroys the sparsity of \(P(x)\).
How can we bypass the dense intermediate series \(\ln P(x)\) and relate \(F(x) = P(x)^\alpha\) directly to the sparse polynomial \(P(x)\)? Differentiate first, then clear the denominator!

Take the logarithmic derivative of \(F(x) = P(x)^\alpha\): \[\frac{F'(x)}{F(x)} = \alpha \frac{P'(x)}{P(x)}.\]
Cross-multiply by \(P(x)\) and \(F(x)\) to eliminate all divisions of series: \[P(x) F'(x) = \alpha P'(x) F(x).\] Look closely at this equation:


\(P(x)\) is \(K\)-sparse (at most \(K\) nonzero coefficients).
Therefore, its derivative \(P'(x)\) is also \(K\)-sparse (in fact, at most \(K-1\) nonzero coefficients)!
Consequently, when we extract the coefficient of \(x^{n-1}\) on both sides of \(P(x) F'(x) = \alpha P'(x) F(x)\), both convolutions sum over at most \(K\) nonzero terms! Solving for \(n f_n\) gives a direct \(O(K)\)-time recurrence for \(f_n\) from \(f_0, \dots, f_{n-1}\).



Let us derive the exact coefficient-by-coefficient recurrences for all five sparse primitives. Throughout this section, we represent a \(K\)-sparse series \(P(x)\) as a list of nonzero pairs \(\{(d, p_d) : d \ge 0, p_d \ne 0\}\) of size at most \(K\). Notice a critical distinction in ring preconditions: sparse_div requires NO division by the loop index \(n\) (only \(b_0 \in K^\times\), so it works over any commutative ring \(K\) and in all characteristics \(p \le N\)), whereas the differential-equation primitives (sparse_ln, sparse_exp, sparse_pow, sparse_sqrt) divide by \(n\) and therefore require \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (\(p \ge N\)).


1. Sparse Division (sparse_div): \(F(x) = \frac{A(x)}{B(x)} \bmod x^N\) (\(B\) is \(K\)-sparse, \(b_0 \in K^\times\), valid for ALL \(p\))

Cross-multiply to clear the denominator: \[B(x) F(x) = A(x).\]
Extract \([x^n]\) for \(n = 0, 1, \dots, N-1\): \[\sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(B) \\ 0 \le d \le n}} b_d f_{n-d} = a_n.\]
Isolate the \(d = 0\) term (\(b_0 f_n\)) and solve for \(f_n\) (requires only \(b_0^{-1} \in K^\times\), never divides by \(n\)!): \[f_n = b_0^{-1} \left(a_n - \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(B) \\ 1 \le d \le n}} b_d f_{n-d}\right).\]



2. Sparse Logarithm (sparse_ln): \(F(x) = \ln P(x) \bmod x^N\) (\(P\) is \(K\)-sparse, \(p_0 = 1\))

Differentiate and clear the denominator: \[F'(x) = \frac{P'(x)}{P(x)} \implies P(x) F'(x) = P'(x).\]
Multiply by \(x\) to align indices via the pointing operator \(\vartheta = x D_x\): \[P(x) \big(x F'(x)\big) = x P'(x).\]
Extract \([x^n]\) for \(n = 1, 2, \dots, N-1\), isolate \(d = 0\), drop \(d = n\), and divide by \(n\) (remembering \(f_0 = \ln(1) = 0\) and \(p_0 = 1\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 0 \le d \le n}} p_d \cdot (n - d) f_{n-d} &= n p_n
&& \text{(extract } [x^n] \text{ of the Cauchy product } P(x)\big(x F'(x)\big) = x P'(x)\text{)} \\[4pt]
p_0\, n\, f_n + \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 1 \le d \le n-1}} (n - d)\, p_d\, f_{n-d} + 0 &= n p_n
&& \text{(isolate } d = 0 \text{ and drop } d = n \text{ since } n - n = 0\text{)} \\[4pt]
f_n &= p_n - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 1 \le d \le n-1}} (n - d)\, p_d\, f_{n-d}.
&& \text{(use } p_0 = 1 \text{ and divide by } n \in K^\times\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]



3. Sparse Exponential (sparse_exp): \(F(x) = \exp P(x) \bmod x^N\) (\(P\) is \(K\)-sparse, \(p_0 = 0\))

Differentiate using the Chain Rule: \[F'(x) = P'(x) F(x) \implies x F'(x) = \big(x P'(x)\big) F(x).\]
Extract \([x^n]\) for \(n = 1, 2, \dots, N-1\) (starting from \(f_0 = \exp(0) = 1\)): \[n f_n = \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 1 \le d \le n}} d\, p_d\, f_{n-d} \implies f_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 1 \le d \le n}} d\, p_d\, f_{n-d}.\]



4. Sparse Power & Square Root (sparse_pow & sparse_sqrt): \(F(x) = P(x)^\alpha \bmod x^N\) (\(P\) is \(K\)-sparse, \(p_0 \in K^\times\))

Differentiate \(F(x) = P(x)^\alpha\) and clear the denominator: \[\frac{F'(x)}{F(x)} = \alpha \frac{P'(x)}{P(x)} \implies P(x) \big(x F'(x)\big) = \alpha \big(x P'(x)\big) F(x).\]
Extract \([x^n]\) for \(n = 1, 2, \dots, N-1\): On the left-hand side, \([x^n]\big(P(x) \cdot x F'(x)\big) = \sum_{d=0}^n p_d (n-d) f_{n-d}\). On the right-hand side, \([x^n]\big(\alpha x P'(x) \cdot F(x)\big) = \alpha \sum_{d=1}^n d p_d f_{n-d}\).
Separate the \(d = 0\) term on the left (\(p_0 \cdot n f_n\)) from \(1 \le d \le n\) and collect \(f_{n-d}\): \[p_0\, n\, f_n + \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 1 \le d \le n}} (n - d)\, p_d\, f_{n-d} = \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 1 \le d \le n}} \alpha\, d\, p_d\, f_{n-d}.\] Moving the sum to the right-hand side gives the Master Sparse Power Recurrence: \[f_n = \frac{1}{n \cdot p_0} \sum_{\substack{d \in \operatorname{supp}(P) \\ 1 \le d \le n}} \big((\alpha + 1) d - n\big)\, p_d\, f_{n-d} \quad (n \ge 1, \text{ with } f_0 = p_0^\alpha).\]

Notice how setting \(\alpha = \frac{1}{2} \equiv \frac{p+1}{2} \pmod p\) immediately gives sparse_sqrt, and setting \(\alpha = -\frac{1}{2} \equiv \frac{p-1}{2} \pmod p\) immediately gives sparse inverse square root!






NoteAlgorithm Contract: sparse_div(A, B, N), sparse_ln(P, N), sparse_exp(P, N)




Input: Dense dividend \(A(x) \bmod x^N\) and \(K\)-sparse divisor/argument \(B(x)\) or \(P(x)\) represented as a sorted list of nonzero pairs \(\{(d, p_d)\}\) of size \(\le K\).
Preconditions:

sparse_div: \(b_0 = [x^0]B(x) \in K^\times\) (requires NO division by \(n\); valid over any commutative ring \(K\) and in all characteristics \(p \le N\)!).
sparse_ln: \([x^0]P(x) = 1\) and \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (\(p \ge N\)).
sparse_exp: \([x^0]P(x) = 0\) and \(1, 2, \dots, N-1 \in K^\times\) (\(p \ge N\)).

Output: Dense coefficient array \(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{N-1}\) of \(A(x)/B(x)\), \(\ln P(x)\), or \(\exp P(x)\) modulo \(x^N\).
Complexity: \(O(N \cdot K)\) time and \(O(N)\) space, with zero NTTs.
Correctness Invariant: After step \(n\), \(F_{\le n}(x)\) satisfies \(B(x) F_{\le n}(x) \equiv A(x) \pmod{x^{n+1}}\) (sparse_div), \(P(x) x F'_{\le n}(x) \equiv x P'(x) \pmod{x^{n+1}}\) (sparse_ln), or \(x F'_{\le n}(x) \equiv x P'(x) F_{\le n}(x) \pmod{x^{n+1}}\) (sparse_exp).




Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\)): sparse_pow on \((1 + 2x + x^3)^\alpha \bmod x^4\)
Let \(P(x) = 1 + 2x + x^3\), so \(p_0 = 1\), and the nonzero sparse terms of degree \(d \ge 1\) are \((d=1, p_1=2)\) and \((d=3, p_3=1)\). Starting from \(f_0 = 1^\alpha = 1\):

\(n = 1\): Only \(d = 1 \le 1\) contributes: \[f_1 = \frac{1}{1 \cdot 1} \big((\alpha + 1)(1) - 1\big) \cdot 2 \cdot f_0 = 2\alpha.\]
\(n = 2\): Again only \(d = 1 \le 2\) contributes: \[f_2 = \frac{1}{2 \cdot 1} \big((\alpha + 1)(1) - 2\big) \cdot 2 \cdot f_1 = (\alpha - 1)(2\alpha) = 2\alpha(\alpha - 1).\]
\(n = 3\): Both \(d = 1\) and \(d = 3\) contribute: \[f_3 = \frac{1}{3 \cdot 1} \Big[\big((\alpha + 1)(1) - 3\big) \cdot 2 \cdot f_2 + \big((\alpha + 1)(3) - 3\big) \cdot 1 \cdot f_0\Big] = \frac{4\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}{3} + \alpha.\] Let us hand-check at \(\alpha = 2\): \((1 + 2x + x^3)^2 = 1 + 4x + 4x^2 + 2x^3 + 4x^4 + x^6\). Our trace formulas give \(f_1 = 4\), \(f_2 = 2(2)(1) = 4\), \(f_3 = 0 + 2 = 2\). Exact match!







NoteAlgorithm Contract & Reference Loop: sparse_pow(P, M, N)




Input: Polynomial \(P(x) \bmod x^N\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (\(p > N\)) with at most \(K\) nonzero terms; non-negative integer exponent \(M \ge 0\).
Preconditions: \(p > N\) so that \(1, 2, \dots, N-1\) are invertible in \(\mathbb{F}_p\). Apply the 3-Way Modular Reduction Guard (Failure Mode #2) first: if \(M == 0\), return \(1\); if \(P \equiv 0\) or \(v \cdot M \ge N\) (checked via M >= (N + v - 1) / v), return \(0\); otherwise normalize \(\widetilde{P}(x) = c_v^{-1} x^{-v} P(x)\) with sparse terms terms = {(d, p_d)} for \(d \ge 1\), set \(f_0 = c_v^{M \bmod (p-1)}\), \(\alpha = M \bmod p\), and shift the output by \(v \cdot M\).
Output: \(F(x) = P(x)^M \bmod x^N\).
Complexity: \(O(N \cdot K + N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space, with zero NTTs (using linear-time modular inverse precomputation inv[1..N-1]).
Correctness Invariant: After computing \(f_n\), the truncated series \(F_{\le n}(x)\) satisfies \(\widetilde{P}(x) x F'_{\le n}(x) \equiv (M \bmod p) x \widetilde{P}'(x) F_{\le n}(x) \pmod{x^{n+1}}\).

// Core O(N * K) recurrence for normalized P~(x) with [x^0]P~ = 1 (after 3-way shift/scalar guard)
f[0] = mod_pow(c_v, M % (p - 1), p);
long long alpha = M % p;
for (int n = 1; n < len; n++) {
    __int128 sum = 0;
    for (auto& [d, pd] : terms) { // terms: sorted {(d, p_d)} for d >= 1
        if (d > n) break;
        long long w = ((alpha + 1) % p * d - n % p + p) % p;
        sum += (__int128)w * pd % p * f[n - d];
    }
    f[n] = (sum % p) * inv[n] % p;
}





Hidden Sparsity: Rational Polynomials and the \((1 - x)\) Trick
What if a polynomial \(A(x)\) looks dense, such as \(A(x) = 1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^{d-1}\), and we need \(A(x)^K \bmod x^N\)? Applying sparse_pow directly to \(A(x)\) costs \(O(N d)\) time. However, multiplying and dividing by \((1 - x)\) turns \(A(x)\) into a ratio of two 2-sparse polynomials: \[A(x)^K = \left(\frac{1 - x^d}{1 - x}\right)^K = (1 - x^d)^K \cdot (1 - x)^{-K}.\] Here \((1 - x^d)^K\) has nonzero terms only at multiples of \(d\) (\(\binom{K}{j}(-1)^j x^{jd}\)), and \((1 - x)^{-K} = \sum_{m \ge 0} \binom{K + m - 1}{m} x^m\) is a 2-sparse negative power!
More generally, for any product of powers of sparse polynomials \(F(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m P_i(x)^{\alpha_i}\), taking the logarithmic derivative gives \[\frac{F'(x)}{F(x)} = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i \frac{P_i'(x)}{P_i(x)}.\] Clearing the common denominator \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m P_i(x)\) yields a single sparse linear ODE \(Q(x) F'(x) = R(x) F(x)\) whose sparsity is bounded by the product of the sparsities of \(P_i(x)\). (We will see this technique shine again in Chapter 05 on AtCoder ABC 300 Ex — Fibonacci: Revisited and in Chapter 18 on D-Finite / Holonomic sequences.)






TipRevisited Cross-Reference (#040 AtCoder ABC 300 Ex — Fibonacci: Revisited): Dense-to-Sparse Denominator Reduction via \((1-x)\)



In Chapter 5 (#040 AtCoder ABC 300 Ex — Fibonacci: Revisited), we encounter the \(K\)-step generalized Fibonacci recurrence \(F_n = \sum_{j=1}^K F_{n-j}\) with characteristic denominator \(Q(x) = 1 - x - x^2 - \dots - x^K\). Although \(Q(x)\) has \(K + 1\) nonzero terms (dense for large \(K\)), multiplying both numerator and denominator of \(P(x)/Q(x)\) by \((1 - x)\) collapses the denominator into the 3-sparse polynomial \[\widetilde{Q}(x) = (1 - x) Q(x) = 1 - 2x + x^{K+1}.\] Whenever you need all prefix coefficients \([x^0 \dots x^{N-1}] \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) for \(N \le 10^6\), applying sparse_div to \(\frac{(1-x)P(x)}{1 - 2x + x^{K+1}}\) runs in \(O(N)\) linear time with zero NTTs, whereas when \(N \le 10^{18}\) is a single huge index, Chapter 5’s Bostan–Mori engine extracts \([x^N]\) in \(O(K \log K \log N)\) time!

title: 02 — Formal Calculus, 1D Newton Iteration (sqrt, ln, exp, pow) & The O(NK) Sparse Engine
section: 2.5 Logarithmic Derivative (\(F'/F\)), Newton–Girard Power Sums & Radical Rationalization
text:
2.5 Logarithmic Derivative (\(F'/F\)), Newton–Girard Power Sums & Radical Rationalization
The logarithmic derivative operator \(\mathcal{L}(F) := \frac{F'(x)}{F(x)} = D_x \ln F(x)\) is one of the most versatile algebraic bridges in generating functions because it converts products into sums: \[\mathcal{L}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m F_i(x)^{\alpha_i}\right) = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i \frac{F_i'(x)}{F_i(x)}.\] Let us examine three high-impact applications of \(\mathcal{L}(F)\) and radical equations.

1. Harmonic Subset-Sum / Knapsack via Bucketed \(\ln / \exp\)
Suppose we have \(m\) items with positive integer weights \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_m \in \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\), and we want to compute the subset-sum generating function \[P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m (1 + x^{w_i})^{\alpha_i} \bmod x^{N+1}\] (for 0-1 knapsack, \(\alpha_i = 1\); for unbounded knapsack, \(\alpha_i = -1\) on \((1 - x^{w_i})\)).

The Diagnostic Signal: We have up to \(m \le 10^5\) factors of the binomial form \((1 \pm c x^{w_i})^{\alpha_i}\) modulo \(x^{N+1}\) (\(N \le 10^5\)), and many items may share the same weight \(w\).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Multiplying \(m\) polynomials one by one takes \(O(m N)\) time. Even a Divide-and-Conquer product tree takes \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time if we do not exploit the binomial structure \(1 \pm x^w\). Instead, take \(\ln P(x)\)! What is \(\ln(1 + x^w)\)? It is the standard alternating harmonic series evaluated at \(x^w\): \[\ln(1 + x^w) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} x^{kw}, \qquad \ln\left(\frac{1}{1 - x^w}\right) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{k} x^{kw}.\] Notice that \(\ln(1 + x^w) \bmod x^{N+1}\) has only \(\lfloor N / w \rfloor\) nonzero terms! Even better: if we first bucket items by weight, letting \(\text{cnt}[w] = \sum_{w_i = w} \alpha_i\) be the total multiplicity of weight \(w\), then we only need to loop over each distinct weight \(w \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) once and add its multiples \(kw \le N\): \[\ln P(x) \equiv \sum_{w=1}^N \text{cnt}[w] \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor N/w \rfloor} \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} x^{kw} \pmod{x^{N+1}}.\] The total number of loop iterations to build \(\ln P(x)\) is the harmonic sum \(\sum_{w=1}^N \lfloor N/w \rfloor = O(N \log N)\)! A single call to exp at the end recovers \(P(x) \bmod x^{N+1}\) in \(O(N \log N)\) total time.



2. Newton–Girard Power Sums via Logarithmic Derivative
Given \(m\) numbers \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m \in K\), how can we simultaneously compute the \(k\)-th power sums \[S_k := \sum_{i=1}^m a_i^k \quad \text{for all } k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, N\] in \(O(m \log^2 m + N \log N)\) time instead of the naive \(O(m N)\)?

The Diagnostic Signal: A problem asks for \(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i^k\) for all \(k \le N\), or asks for \(\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m (a_i + b_j)^k\) for all \(k \le N\) (which expands binomially into \(\sum_{r=0}^k \binom{k}{r} (\sum_i a_i^r)(\sum_j b_j^{k-r})\)).
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Where does \(a_i^k\) naturally appear as the coefficient of \(x^k\)? In the geometric series \(\frac{1}{1 - a_i x} = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_i^k x^k\)! Summing over all \(i = 1, \dots, m\) gives the Ordinary Generating Function of the power sums \(S_k\): \[S(x) := \sum_{k \ge 0} S_k x^k = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{1}{1 - a_i x} = m + \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{a_i x}{1 - a_i x}.\] How do we compute \(\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{a_i x}{1 - a_i x}\) without adding \(m\) fractions one by one? Recognise that \(\frac{-a_i}{1 - a_i x}\) is the logarithmic derivative of \((1 - a_i x)\)! Therefore: \[\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{a_i x}{1 - a_i x} = -x \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{-a_i}{1 - a_i x} = -x \frac{d}{dx} \ln \left(\prod_{i=1}^m (1 - a_i x)\right) = -\frac{x Q'(x)}{Q(x)},\] where \(Q(x) := \prod_{i=1}^m (1 - a_i x)\). This gives the complete two-stage algorithm:

Compute \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m (1 - a_i x)\) in \(O(m \log^2 m)\) time using a Divide-and-Conquer Product Tree (recursively multiplying left and right halves via NTT).
Truncate \(Q(x)\) modulo \(x^{N+1}\) and compute \(S(x) = m - x Q'(x) Q(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{N+1}\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time using one polynomial inversion (or -x * deriv(ln(Q))).








NoteAlgorithm Contract: Harmonic Subset-Sum Exp & Newton–Girard Power Sums




Input:

Harmonic Subset-Sum / Knapsack: \(m\) items with weights \(w_i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and exponents \(\alpha_i \in \mathbb{Z}\), target degree \(N\).
Newton–Girard Power Sums: \(m\) scalars \(a_1, \dots, a_m \in \mathbb{F}_p\), target exponent \(N\).

Preconditions: \(p > N\) so that \(1, 2, \dots, N \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (required by the harmonic series \(\sum x^{kw}/k\) and exp in Subset-Sum, and by ln if used in Newton–Girard; note that computing \(S(x) = m - x Q'(x) Q(x)^{-1}\) via inv directly does not even divide by \(k\)!).
Output:

Harmonic Subset-Sum: \(P(x) = \prod_{w=1}^N (1 \pm x^w)^{\text{cnt}[w]} \bmod x^{N+1}\).
Newton–Girard: \(S_k = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i^k \bmod p\) for all \(0 \le k \le N\).

Complexity: \(O(m + N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space for Harmonic Subset-Sum; \(O(m \log^2 m + N \log N)\) time and \(O(m + N)\) space for Newton–Girard.
Correctness Invariant: After the harmonic sweep over \(w \in [1, N]\) and \(k \in [1, \lfloor N/w \rfloor]\), \(L[n] = [x^n] \sum_{w=1}^N \text{cnt}[w] \ln(1 \pm x^w)\); in Newton–Girard, \([x^k](-x Q'(x) Q(x)^{-1}) = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i^k\) for all \(k \ge 1\).





3. Quadratic Equations & Radical Rationalization (Avoiding Valuation Precision Loss)
In combinatorial enumeration (such as weighted binary trees in Codeforces 438E, Catalan paths, or Motzkin paths), the generating function \(F(x)\) often satisfies a quadratic equation with polynomial coefficients: \[A(x) F(x)^2 + B(x) F(x) + C(x) = 0,\] where typically \(\operatorname{val}(A) \ge 1\) (so \(A(0) = 0\), e.g., \(A(x) = x D(x)\)), \([x^0] B(x) = -1\), and \([x^0] C(x) = 1\).
Suppose we solve for \(F(x)\) using the standard high-school quadratic formula: \[F(x) = \frac{-B(x) \pm \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}}{2 A(x)}.\] First, which sign (\(\pm\)) is correct? Look at \(x = 0\): since \(A(0) = 0\) and \(B(0) = -1\), choosing the \(+\) sign gives numerator \(-(-1) + \sqrt{1 - 0} = 2 \ne 0\) divided by denominator \(2 A(0) = 0\), which blows up (\(2/0 \notin K[[x]]\))! Choosing the \(-\) sign makes the numerator vanish at \(x = 0\): \(-(-1) - \sqrt{1} = 0\), cancelling the zero in \(2 A(x)\).
However, computing \(F(x) = \frac{-B(x) - \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}}{2 A(x)} \bmod x^N\) directly in code has a severe precision and invertibility hazard:

Because \(\operatorname{val}(A) = v \ge 1\), \(2 A(x)\) is not a unit in \(K[[x]]\)! To divide by \(2 A(x) = 2 x^v \widetilde{A}(x)\), you must shift the numerator down by \(x^v\)—which means you must compute \(\sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}\) to precision \(x^{N + v}\) instead of \(x^N\)! Worse still, if \(A(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^N}\) (for instance, in an edge case where all node weights exceed \(N\)), dividing by \(2 A(x)\) divides by zero!







TipThe Radical Rationalization Trick (Conjugate Multiplication)



Whenever \(A(0) = 0\), \(B(0) \in K^\times\), and \(C(0) \in K^\times\), rationalize the numerator by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate \(-B(x) + \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}\): \[\begin{aligned}
F(x) &= \frac{\big(-B(x) - \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}\big)\big(-B(x) + \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}\big)}{2 A(x) \big(-B(x) + \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}\big)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{B(x)^2 - \big(B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)\big)}{2 A(x) \big(-B(x) + \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}\big)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{2 C(x)}{-B(x) + \sqrt{B(x)^2 - 4 A(x) C(x)}} \pmod{x^N}.
\end{aligned}\] Why is this rationalized form strictly superior?

The non-unit factor \(2 A(x)\) cancels algebraically before any numerical division takes place!
At \(x = 0\) (where \(B(0) = -1, A(0) = 0\)), the new denominator has constant term \(-(-1) + \sqrt{1} = 2 \in K^\times\). It is always an invertible unit modulo \(x^N\), requiring zero extra precision beyond \(x^N\) and working seamlessly even when \(A(x) = 0\)!

2.6 Practice Ladder: 8 Curated Problems (4 Tiers)
We now apply every tool from this chapter across 8 canonical problems graded from Stepping Stone to Mastery. Try each problem using the progressive hints before expanding the full derivation.


Stepping Stone 1 (#238) — Sum of Powers (yukicoder 1145)

Source: yukicoder No. 1145 — Sum of Powers
Prerequisites: Divide-and-Conquer Product Tree, Logarithmic Derivative (ln / inv), Newton–Girard Identities (§2.5).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) integers \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N\) and a target exponent bound \(M\). For each integer \(k = 1, 2, \dots, M\), compute the power sum \[S_k = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i^k \bmod 998244353.\]

Constraints: \(1 \le N, M \le 2 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le A_i < 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N + M \log M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.
Sample Trace (\(N = 2, M = 3, A = [1, 2]\)): \(Q(x) = (1 - x)(1 - 2x) = 1 - 3x + 2x^2\), and \(-x Q'(x)/Q(x) = 3x + 5x^2 + 9x^3 + \dots\), matching \(S_1 = 1+2 = 3, S_2 = 1+4 = 5, S_3 = 1+8 = 9\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Evaluating \(\sum_{i=1}^N A_i^k\) directly for each \(k\) takes \(O(NM)\) time. Instead, pack the answers \(S_k\) into an Ordinary Generating Function \(S(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} S_k x^k\). What single rational fraction has \([x^k] = A_i^k\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By the geometric series formula, \(\sum_{k \ge 0} A_i^k x^k = \frac{1}{1 - A_i x}\). Summing over \(i = 1, \dots, N\) gives \[S(x) = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{1 - A_i x} = N + x \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{A_i}{1 - A_i x}.\] Notice that \(\frac{-A_i}{1 - A_i x} = \frac{d}{dx} \ln(1 - A_i x)\). How can you combine the sum of logarithms into a single polynomial product \(Q(x)\)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Define \(Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 - A_i x)\). Compute \(Q(x)\) of degree \(N\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time using a binary Divide-and-Conquer product tree (recursively multiplying \(\text{solve}(l, mid)\) and \(\text{solve}(mid+1, r)\) via NTT). Then truncate \(Q(x)\) modulo \(x^{M+1}\), compute \(\ln Q(x) \bmod x^{M+1}\) in \(O(M \log M)\), and extract \(S_k = -k [x^k] \ln Q(x) \pmod{998244353}\) for \(1 \le k \le M\).







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Forming the Generating Function: Let \(S(x) = \sum_{k=1}^M S_k x^k \bmod x^{M+1}\) be the generating function of the non-constant power sums. For each \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), the formal logarithm of \((1 - A_i x)\) is \[\ln(1 - A_i x) = -\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{A_i^k}{k} x^k.\] Summing this identity over all \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\) and using the additive property of the formal logarithm \(\sum_{i=1}^N \ln(1 - A_i x) = \ln\left(\prod_{i=1}^N (1 - A_i x)\right)\) gives \[\ln\left(\prod_{i=1}^N (1 - A_i x)\right) = -\sum_{k=1}^\infty \left(\sum_{i=1}^N A_i^k\right) \frac{x^k}{k} = -\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{S_k}{k} x^k.\]
Applying the Pointing Operator \(\vartheta = x D_x\): Let \(Q(x) := \prod_{i=1}^N (1 - A_i x)\), which is a polynomial of degree \(N\) with constant term \([x^0] Q(x) = 1\). Applying \(-x D_x\) to \(\ln Q(x)\) eliminates the denominator \(k\): \[-x D_x \ln Q(x) = -\frac{x Q'(x)}{Q(x)} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty S_k x^k.\] Equivalently, if we compute \(L(x) = \ln Q(x) \bmod x^{M+1}\), then for every \(1 \le k \le M\): \[S_k \equiv -k \cdot [x^k] L(x) \pmod{998244353}.\]



Boundary & Characteristic Audit

Since \(M \le 2 \times 10^5 < p = 998244353\), all integers \(1, 2, \dots, M\) are units in \(\mathbb{F}_p\), so \(\ln Q(x) \bmod x^{M+1}\) is well-defined.
\([x^0] Q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^N 1 = 1\), satisfying the unit precondition for ln and inv.
If \(N < M\), \(Q(x)\) has degree \(N < M\); we simply zero-pad \(Q(x)\) to length \(M + 1\) before inverting or taking ln. If \(N > M\), we truncate \(Q(x)\) modulo \(x^{M+1}\) after the D&C product tree finishes (or truncate intermediate D&C products to \(\min(\text{deg}, M)\)).



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

D&C Product Tree: Define build(l, r):

Base case \(l == r\): return the linear polynomial \(1 - A_l x\) of degree \(1\).
Recursive step: let \(mid = (l + r) / 2\), return \(\text{NTT\_mul}(\text{build}(l, mid), \text{build}(mid+1, r))\). At depth \(d\) of the recursion tree, the total degree across all nodes is \(N\), so each level costs \(O(N \log N)\) and all \(\lceil \log_2 N \rceil\) levels cost \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time.

Logarithmic Derivative Extraction: Resize \(Q(x)\) to \(M + 1\), compute \(H(x) = -x Q'(x) Q(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{M+1}\) in \(O(M \log M)\) time via a single inv call and one NTT multiplication, and output \([x^1]H(x), \dots, [x^M]H(x)\).







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #238 Power-Sum Extraction via D&C Product Tree & Logarithmic Derivative




Input & Preconditions: Array \(A[1\dots N]\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (\(p = 998244353\)), exponent bound \(M \ge 1\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(S_k = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i^k \bmod p\) for all \(1 \le k \le M\) via \(H(x) = -x Q'(x) Q(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{M+1}\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N + M \log M)\) time and \(O(N + M)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Each node \(u\) of the D&C product tree covering \([l, r]\) maintains the exact polynomial \(Q_u(x) = \prod_{i=l}^r (1 - A_i x)\) with \([x^0] Q_u(x) = 1\), and \(-x Q'(x) Q(x)^{-1} = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{A_i x}{1 - A_i x}\) holds as a formal power series identity in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Using \(-x Q'(x) Q(x)^{-1}\) directly avoids dividing by \(k\) and holds in arbitrary characteristic \(p\) (whereas calling ln(Q) requires \(p > M\)); if \(N < M\), zero-pad \(Q(x)\) to length \(M + 1\) before inverting, and if \(N > M\), truncate \(Q(x)\) modulo \(x^{M+1}\).











Stepping Stone 2 (#165) — 0-1 Subset Sum via Harmonic \(\ln / \exp\)

Source: Standard AtCoder / Luogu FPS 0-1 Subset Sum Benchmark (companion to Luogu P4389 — 付公主的背包 in Chapter 3)
Prerequisites: Harmonic Frequency Bucketing, Formal Logarithm \(\ln\), Formal Exponential \(\exp\) (§2.3, §2.5).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) items with positive integer weights \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_N \in \{1, 2, \dots, M\}\) and a capacity bound \(M\), where each item \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) can be chosen at most once (\(0\) or \(1\) time). For every target weight \(s = 1, 2, \dots, M\), compute the number of subsets of \(\{1, \dots, N\}\) whose weights sum to \(s\), modulo \(998244353\): \[[x^s] \prod_{i=1}^N (1 + x^{w_i}) \bmod 998244353.\]

Constraints: \(1 \le N, M \le 10^5\), \(1 \le w_i \le M\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N + M \log M)\) time and \(O(M)\) space.
Sample Trace (\(N = 3, M = 3, w = [1, 1, 2]\)): \(\prod_{i=1}^3 (1 + x^{w_i}) = (1 + x)^2(1 + x^2) = 1 + 2x + 2x^2 + 2x^3 + x^4\), so subset counts for \(s = 1, 2, 3\) are \((2, 2, 2)\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

In the Unbounded model, item \(i\) contributes the geometric factor \(\frac{1}{1 - x^{w_i}} = 1 + x^{w_i} + x^{2w_i} + \dots\); in the 0-1 model, item \(i\) contributes \((1 + x^{w_i})\). Thus we need \([x^s] \prod_{i=1}^N (1 - x^{w_i})^{-1} \bmod x^{M+1}\) (or \([x^s] \prod_{i=1}^N (1 + x^{w_i}) \bmod x^{M+1}\)). Why is naive \(O(NM)\) DP too slow, and what happens when we take \(\ln\) of the product?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Many items can share the same weight \(w \in \{1, \dots, M\}\). Let \(c_w = \#\{i : w_i = w\}\) be the frequency of weight \(w\). Then \[F_{\text{unbounded}}(x) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 - x^w)^{-c_w}, \qquad F_{0\text{-}1}(x) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 + x^w)^{c_w}.\] Take the formal logarithm \(\ln F(x) \bmod x^{M+1}\) using the explicit Taylor series \(\ln\left(\frac{1}{1 - x^w}\right) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{k} x^{kw}\) and \(\ln(1 + x^w) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} x^{kw}\).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Once weights are grouped into \(c_w\), the coefficient of \(x^{kw}\) receives \(+c_w / k\) (or \(+(-1)^{k-1} c_w / k\)) for each \(1 \le w \le M\) and \(1 \le k \le \lfloor M / w \rfloor\). Summing over all \(w\) and \(k\) takes \(\sum_{w=1}^M \lfloor M / w \rfloor = O(M \log M)\) operations. Finally, apply a single \(O(M \log M)\) Newton exp to recover \(F(x) \bmod x^{M+1}\).







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Combinatorial Specification to Generating Function:

In the Unbounded Knapsack (Luogu P4389) model, choosing \(k_i \ge 0\) copies of item \(i\) contributes weight \(k_i w_i\), represented by the factor \(\sum_{k_i \ge 0} x^{k_i w_i} = (1 - x^{w_i})^{-1}\). Across all \(N\) independent items, the generating function is \[F_{\text{unbounded}}(x) = \prod_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{1 - x^{w_i}} = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 - x^w)^{-c_w},\] where \(c_w = \sum_{i=1}^N [w_i = w]\) counts items of weight \(w\).
In the 0-1 Subset Sum model, each item \(i\) is picked \(0\) or \(1\) time, giving \[F_{0\text{-}1}(x) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 + x^{w_i}) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 + x^w)^{c_w}.\]

Logarithmic Transformation: Because \([x^0] F(x) = 1\) and \(M = 10^5 < p = 998244353\), we can write \(F(x) = \exp\big(L(x)\big) \bmod x^{M+1}\), where \(L(x) = \ln F(x) \bmod x^{M+1}\). Using the formal logarithm power series \(\ln(1 - u)^{-1} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{u^k}{k}\) and \(\ln(1 + u) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k-1} u^k}{k}\) at \(u = x^w\): \[L_{\text{unbounded}}(x) \equiv \sum_{w=1}^M c_w \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor M/w \rfloor} \frac{1}{k} x^{kw} \pmod{x^{M+1}},\] \[L_{0\text{-}1}(x) \equiv \sum_{w=1}^M c_w \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor M/w \rfloor} \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} x^{kw} \pmod{x^{M+1}}.\]



Boundary & Characteristic Audit

Why frequency bucketing is mandatory: If all \(N = 10^5\) items had \(w_i = 1\) and we added \(\ln(1 \pm x^{w_i})\) for each item \(i\) without bucketing, we would execute \(N \cdot M = 10^{10}\) operations (TLE)! Bucketing collapses identical weights into a single scalar multiplier \(c_w\), bounding the total work by the harmonic series \(\sum_{w=1}^M \frac{M}{w} \approx M \ln M\).
Characteristic check: \(p = 998244353 > M = 10^5\), so \(k^{-1} \bmod p\) exists for all \(1 \le k \le M\) and exp(L) is valid modulo \(x^{M+1}\).



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

Initialize array c[1..M] = 0 and accumulate c[w_i]++ in \(O(N)\) time.
Precompute modular inverses inv[1..M] in \(O(M)\) time using inv[i] = (p - p / i) * inv[p % i] % p.
Initialize L[0..M] = 0. For \(w = 1 \dots M\) (if \(c_w > 0\)), loop \(k = 1 \dots \lfloor M / w \rfloor\) and add \(c_w \cdot \text{inv}[k] \pmod p\) (or \((-1)^{k-1} c_w \cdot \text{inv}[k] \pmod p\)) to L[k * w].
Compute \(F = \text{exp}(L, M + 1)\) via 1D Newton iteration in \(O(M \log M)\) time, and print \(F[1], \dots, F[M]\).







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #165 Harmonic Frequency-Bucketed Knapsack (ln + exp)




Input & Preconditions: Positive integer weights \(w_1, \dots, w_N \ge 1\), capacity \(M < p\) (\(p = 998244353\)).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(F(x) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 - x^w)^{-c_w} \bmod x^{M+1}\) (unbounded) or \(\prod_{w=1}^M (1 + x^w)^{c_w} \bmod x^{M+1}\) (0-1 subset sum).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N + M \log M)\) time (\(O(M \log M)\) harmonic sieve + 1 Newton exp) and \(O(M)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing weight bucket \(w \in [1, W]\), \(L(x) \equiv \sum_{u=1}^W c_u \ln\big((1 - x^u)^{-1}\big) \pmod{x^{M+1}}\) (or \(\sum_{u=1}^W c_u \ln(1 + x^u) \pmod{x^{M+1}}\)) with \([x^0] L(x) = 0\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Omitting frequency bucketing \(c_w\) degrades the harmonic sum \(\sum_{w=1}^M \lfloor M/w \rfloor = O(M \log M)\) to \(O(NM)\) TLE when many items have small \(w_i\); zero weights \(w_i = 0\) must be factored out separately as \(2^{c_0}\) (0-1) since \(\ln(1 + x^0)\) has nonzero constant term.











Intermediate 1 (#101) — Lucky Tickets (Codeforces 1096G)

Source: Codeforces 1096G — Lucky Tickets
Prerequisites: The \(O(N \cdot K)\) Sparse Power Engine (sparse_pow), The \((1-x)\) Rational Trick, NTT pow (§2.3, §2.4).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
A ticket number is a string of \(n\) digits (where \(n\) is an even integer), and each digit is chosen from a given allowed subset \(D \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\) of size \(k = |D|\). Leading zeros are allowed. A ticket is called lucky if the sum of its first \(n/2\) digits equals the sum of its last \(n/2\) digits. Find the total number of lucky tickets modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(2 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\) (\(n\) is even), \(1 \le k \le 10\), allowed digits \(d_1, \dots, d_k \in \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\).
Required Complexity: Primary solution in \(O(N k)\) time with zero NTTs (where \(N = \frac{9n}{2} + 1 \le 9 \times 10^5\)); secondary solution in \(O(N \log N)\) via NTT.
Sample Trace (\(n = 2, D = \{0, 1\}\)): Here \(k = n/2 = 1\) and \(P(x) = 1 + x\). The sum of squares of coefficients of \(P(x)^1\) is \(1^2 + 1^2 = 2\) (tickets 00 and 11). For \(n = 4\) (\(k = 2\)), \(P(x)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2\), giving \(1^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 6\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(m = n / 2 \le 10^5\). The first \(m\) digits and the last \(m\) digits are chosen independently. If \(f_s\) is the number of ways for \(m\) digits from \(D\) to sum to \(s\), then the number of lucky tickets where both halves sum to \(s\) is \(f_s^2\), and the total answer is \(\sum_{s=0}^{9m} f_s^2 \bmod 998244353\). How is \(f_s\) expressed as the coefficient of a polynomial power?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

A single digit choice corresponds to the polynomial \(A(x) = \sum_{d \in D} x^d\). Choosing \(m\) independent digits yields \(F(x) = A(x)^m = \sum_{s=0}^{9m} f_s x^s\). Notice that \(A(x)\) has degree \(\le 9\) and at most \(k \le 10\) nonzero terms! Instead of running a size-\(2^{20}\) NTT, how can you compute all coefficients of \(F(x) = A(x)^m\) using a 10-line loop?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Apply sparse_pow from Section 2.4 directly to \(A(x)^m \bmod x^{d_{\max} m + 1}\)! Since \(A(x)\) has at most \(k \le 10\) nonzero terms and \(N = d_{\max} m + 1 \le 9 \times 10^5 < p = 998244353\), the recurrence \[f_s = \frac{1}{s \cdot a_0} \sum_{\substack{d \in D' \\ d \ge 1}} \big((m + 1) d - s\big) a_d f_{s-d}\] computes the entire array \(f_0, \dots, f_{9m}\) in at most \(9 \times 10^6\) loop iterations (\(\approx 15\text{ ms}\) in C++) with zero NTTs! (And if \(D = \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\), writing \(A(x) = \frac{1 - x^{10}}{1 - x}\) makes it a 2-sparse ratio!)







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Combinatorial Reduction to \(A(x)^m\): Let \(m = n / 2\). A half-ticket is a sequence \((c_1, \dots, c_m) \in D^m\) whose digit sum is \(s = c_1 + \dots + c_m\). The Ordinary Generating Function for a single digit is \[A(x) = \sum_{d \in D} x^d,\] so the OGF for the sum of \(m\) independent digits is \(F(x) = A(x)^m = \sum_{s=0}^{9m} f_s x^s\). Since a full ticket is lucky iff both halves share the same sum \(s\), the total number of lucky tickets is \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{s=0}^{9m} f_s^2 \pmod{998244353}.\]
Primary Method: The \(O(N k)\) Sparse Differential Equation Engine (Zero NTTs): Let \(d_{\min} = \min(D)\) and \(d_{\max} = \max(D)\). Factor out \(x^{d_{\min}}\) from \(A(x)\): \[\widetilde{A}(x) := x^{-d_{\min}} A(x) = 1 + \sum_{d \in D \setminus \{d_{\min}\}} x^{d - d_{\min}}.\] Because shifting every digit by \(-d_{\min}\) simply shifts every half-ticket sum by \(-m \cdot d_{\min}\) without changing the multiset of coefficient values \(\{f_s\}\), we have \(\sum_s f_s^2 = \sum_{s=0}^{N-1} \widetilde{f}_s^2\), where \(N = (d_{\max} - d_{\min}) m + 1 \le 9 \times 10^5\) and \[\widetilde{F}(x) = \widetilde{A}(x)^m = \sum_{s=0}^{N-1} \widetilde{f}_s x^s.\] Now differentiate \(\widetilde{F}(x) = \widetilde{A}(x)^m\) and multiply by \(x \widetilde{A}(x)\): \[\widetilde{A}(x) \big(x \widetilde{F}'(x)\big) = m \big(x \widetilde{A}'(x)\big) \widetilde{F}(x).\] Since \([x^0]\widetilde{A}(x) = 1\) and \([x^\delta]\widetilde{A}(x) = 1\) for each nonzero shift \(\delta \in \Delta := \{d - d_{\min} : d \in D, d > d_{\min}\}\) (where \(|\Delta| = k - 1 \le 9\)), extracting \([x^s]\) for \(s = 1, 2, \dots, N-1\) gives \[s \widetilde{f}_s + \sum_{\substack{\delta \in \Delta \\ \delta \le s}} (s - \delta) \widetilde{f}_{s - \delta} = m \sum_{\substack{\delta \in \Delta \\ \delta \le s}} \delta \widetilde{f}_{s - \delta} \implies \widetilde{f}_s = \frac{1}{s} \sum_{\substack{\delta \in \Delta \\ \delta \le s}} \big((m + 1)\delta - s\big) \widetilde{f}_{s - \delta},\] starting from \(\widetilde{f}_0 = 1\).
Special Case Bonus: The \((1-x)\) Rational Trick when \(D\) is an Arithmetic Progression: If \(D = \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\) (all 10 digits allowed), then \(A(x) = \frac{1 - x^{10}}{1 - x}\), so \[F(x) = (1 - x^{10})^m (1 - x)^{-m} = \left(\sum_{j=0}^m (-1)^j \binom{m}{j} x^{10j}\right) \left(\sum_{r \ge 0} \binom{m + r - 1}{r} x^r\right),\] which is the convolution of a series supported only at multiples of \(10\) with binomial coefficients!
Secondary Method: \(O(N \log N)\) NTT Binary / Logarithmic Exponentiation: Since \(p = 998244353 = 119 \cdot 2^{23} + 1\), we can also pad \(A(x)\) to the power of two \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(9m + 1) \rceil} \le 2^{20} = 1048576\), transform \(\hat{A} = \text{NTT}(A)\), raise each point value to the \(m\)-th power \(\hat{F}_i = (\hat{A}_i)^m \bmod p\) in \(O(L \log m)\) time, and apply \(\text{INTT}(\hat{F})\) in a single forward + inverse NTT pair!



Boundary & Characteristic Audit

If \(k = 1\), then \(\Delta = \emptyset\), \(N = 1\), \(\widetilde{f}_0 = 1\), and the formula immediately outputs \(1^2 = 1\).
\(N \le 9 \times 10^5 + 1 < 998244353\), so \(s^{-1} \bmod p\) exists for all \(1 \le s < N\).



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

Primary (\(O(N k)\) Sparse ODE): Precompute inv[1..N-1] in \(O(N)\) time, run the 2-nested loop over \(s \in [1, N-1]\) and \(\delta \in \Delta\) in \(O(N k)\) time (\(\le 8.1 \times 10^6\) operations), and sum \(\widetilde{f}_s^2 \bmod p\).







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #101 Lucky Tickets via Shifted sparse_pow




Input & Preconditions: Even length \(n \le 2 \times 10^5\) (\(m = n/2\)), digit set \(D \subseteq \{0,\dots,9\}\) of size \(k \le 10\), prime \(p = 998244353 > 9m\).
Postconditions (Output): Normalizes \(\widetilde{A}(x) = x^{-\min(D)} A(x)\) so \([x^0]\widetilde{A} = 1\), computes \(\widetilde{F}(x) = \widetilde{A}(x)^m\) up to degree \(N - 1 = (\max D - \min D)m\), and returns \(\sum_{s=0}^{N-1} \widetilde{f}_s^2 \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n k)\) time (zero NTTs) and \(O(n)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At iteration \(s \in [1, N-1]\), \(\widetilde{f}_0, \dots, \widetilde{f}_{s-1}\) are the exact coefficients of \(\widetilde{A}(x)^m \bmod x^s\), and \(\widetilde{f}_s\) is extracted in \(O(k)\) time from \([x^s]\big(\widetilde{A}(x) x \widetilde{F}'(x) - m x \widetilde{A}'(x) \widetilde{F}(x)\big) = 0\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(0 \notin D\), \([x^0] A(x) = 0\), so you must factor out \(x^{d_{\min}}\) (\(d_{\min} = \min D\)) before running sparse_pow to ensure \([x^0]\widetilde{A}(x) = 1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\); when \(k = 1\), \(N = 1\) and the loop is empty (\(\widetilde{f}_0 = 1\)).











Intermediate 2 (#222) — Lonely Senior Year (LOJ 6261 — 一个人的高三)

Source: LibreOJ #6261 — 一个人的高三
Prerequisites: Iterated Prefix Sums as \((1 - x)^{-K}\), Generalized Binomial Series (sparse_pow on \(1 - x\)), 3-Way Modular Reduction Trap, NTT Convolution (§2.1, §2.3, §2.4).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given a sequence \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{N-1}\) of length \(N\) and an integer \(K\). In one operation, the sequence \(A\) is replaced by its prefix-sum sequence \(A'_m = \sum_{i=0}^m A_i\) for \(0 \le m < N\). Find the resulting sequence \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{N-1}\) modulo \(998244353\) after performing this prefix-sum operation \(K\) times.

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(0 \le K \le 10^9\) (or up to \(10^{18}\)), \(0 \le A_i < 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space with a single NTT convolution (instead of \(O(N \log N \log K)\) binary exponentiation).
Sample Trace (\(N = 3, K = 2, A = [1, 1, 1]\)): Since \(A(x) = (1 - x)^{-1} \bmod x^3\), \(A^{(2)}(x) = A(x) \cdot (1 - x)^{-2} = (1 - x)^{-3} = 1 + 3x + 6x^2 + \dots\), giving \((1, 3, 6)\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Pack the sequence into an OGF \(A(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{N-1} A_m x^m \bmod x^N\). What polynomial multiplication corresponds to a single prefix-sum transformation \(A'_m = \sum_{i=0}^m A_i\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Since \(\frac{1}{1 - x} = 1 + x + x^2 + \dots\), multiplying \(A(x)\) by \((1 - x)^{-1}\) performs one prefix sum: \([x^m] \frac{A(x)}{1-x} = \sum_{i=0}^m A_i\). Therefore, applying the prefix-sum operation \(K\) times produces \[A^{(K)}(x) \equiv (1 - x)^{-K} A(x) \pmod{x^N}.\] How do we compute the coefficients \(b_m = [x^m](1 - x)^{-K}\) for \(0 \le m < N\) when \(K\) can be larger than \(p = 998244353\)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Because \(1 - x\) is 2-sparse, apply the sparse_pow recurrence (or generalized binomial series) to \(B(x) = (1 - x)^{-K} \bmod x^N\): \[b_0 = 1, \qquad b_m = \frac{(K \bmod p) + m - 1}{m} b_{m-1} \pmod p \quad (1 \le m < N).\] This computes \(B(x) \bmod x^N\) in \(O(N)\) linear time! One NTT convolution \(B(x) \cdot A(x) \bmod x^N\) then finishes the problem in \(O(N \log N)\) time.







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Translating Iterated Prefix Sums to \((1 - x)^{-K}\): Let \(A(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{N-1} A_m x^m \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x]] / (x^N)\). By Cauchy convolution with \(\frac{1}{1 - x} = \sum_{j \ge 0} x^j\), \[[x^m]\left(\frac{1}{1 - x} A(x)\right) = \sum_{i=0}^m 1 \cdot A_i = \sum_{i=0}^m A_i.\] By induction on \(K \ge 0\), applying the prefix-sum operator \(K\) times multiplies \(A(x)\) by \((1 - x)^{-K}\): \[A^{(K)}(x) \equiv (1 - x)^{-K} A(x) \pmod{x^N}.\]
Computing \(B(x) = (1 - x)^{-K} \bmod x^N\) via the Sparse ODE / Generalized Binomial Recurrence: Let \(B(x) = (1 - x)^{-K} = \sum_{m \ge 0} b_m x^m\). Differentiating gives \[B'(x) = K (1 - x)^{-K - 1} \implies (1 - x) B'(x) = K B(x).\] Extracting \([x^{m-1}]\) on both sides using the Operator Dictionary (\([x^{m-1}]B'(x) = m b_m\) and \([x^{m-1}](x B'(x)) = (m-1) b_{m-1}\)) yields: \[m b_m - (m - 1) b_{m-1} = K b_{m-1} \implies b_m = \frac{K + m - 1}{m} b_{m-1} \quad \text{for } m \ge 1,\] with initial condition \(b_0 = 1\). Unrolling this recurrence gives the closed-form generalized binomial coefficient \(b_m = \binom{K + m - 1}{m}\).



Boundary & Characteristic Audit (Canonical Failure Mode #2 Check)

What if \(K \ge p = 998244353\)? Notice that \(P(x) = 1 - x\) has valuation \(v = 0\) and constant term \(c_0 = 1\). Thus by our 3-Way Modular Reduction Rule (Section 2.3):

Shift \(v \cdot K = 0 \cdot K = 0\);
Scalar \(c_0^{-K} = 1^{-K} = 1\);
Series multiplier inside the ODE uses \(K_{\text{mod}} = K \bmod p\)! Indeed, in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\), \((1 - x)^{-K} = (1 - x)^{-(q p + r)} = (1 - x^p)^{-q} (1 - x)^{-r} \equiv (1 - x)^{-(K \bmod p)} \pmod{x^p}\). Since \(N \le 10^5 < p = 998244353\), reducing \(K \bmod p\) inside \(b_m = \frac{(K \bmod p) + m - 1}{m} b_{m-1} \bmod p\) is 100% exact for all \(0 \le m < N\)!

What if \(K = 0\)? Then \(K_{\text{mod}} = 0\), \(b_0 = 1\), and \(b_1 = \frac{0 + 1 - 1}{1} b_0 = 0 \implies b_m = 0\) for all \(m \ge 1\), so \(B(x) = 1\) and \(A^{(0)}(x) = A(x)\), as required.



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

Precompute inv[1..N-1] modulo \(p = 998244353\) in \(O(N)\) time.
Compute \(b_0 = 1\) and \(b_m = b_{m-1} \cdot ((K \bmod p) + m - 1) \bmod p \cdot \text{inv}[m] \bmod p\) for \(m = 1, \dots, N-1\) in \(O(N)\) time.
Multiply \(B(x)\) and \(A(x)\) modulo \(x^N\) using a single NTT convolution of length \(2^{\lceil \log_2(2N) \rceil}\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time, and output the first \(N\) coefficients.







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #222 \(K\)-Fold Prefix Sums via \((1 - x)^{-K}\)




Input & Preconditions: Array \(A[0\dots N-1] \in \mathbb{F}_p^N\) with \(N \le p\), non-negative integer \(K \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) (arbitrary size).
Postconditions (Output): Computes \(b_m = \binom{(K \bmod p) + m - 1}{m} \bmod p\) in \(O(N)\) time and returns \(A^{(K)}(x) = B(x) A(x) \bmod x^N\) via a single NTT convolution.
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: For each \(m \in [1, N-1]\), \(b_m = \frac{(K \bmod p) + m - 1}{m} b_{m-1} \bmod p\) satisfies \([x^{m-1}]\big((1 - x) B'(x) - K B(x)\big) \equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Canonical Failure Mode #2: because \(1 - x\) has valuation \(v = 0\) and constant term \(1\), \((1 - x)^{-K} \equiv (1 - x)^{-(K \bmod p)} \pmod{x^p}\), so \(K\) must be reduced modulo \(p\) (NOT modulo \(p - 1\)) before computing \((K \bmod p) + m - 1\); when \(K \equiv 0 \pmod p\), \(b_1 = 0 \implies b_m = 0\) for all \(1 \le m < N\).











Advanced 1 (#157) — Playing Games (Luogu P4705 — 玩游戏)

Source: Luogu P4705 — 玩游戏
Prerequisites: Binomial Decoupling (EGF Convolution), Newton–Girard Power Sums via \(-x \frac{d}{dx} \ln \prod(1 - a_i x)\), D&C Product Tree (§2.3, §2.5).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Alice has \(n\) cards with values \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\), and Bob has \(m\) cards with values \(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_m\). For each integer \(k = 1, 2, \dots, t\), if Alice chooses one card \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) uniformly at random and Bob chooses one card \(j \in \{1, \dots, m\}\) uniformly at random, compute the expected value of \((a_i + b_j)^k\) modulo \(998244353\): \[E_k = \frac{1}{n m} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m (a_i + b_j)^k \bmod 998244353.\]

Constraints: \(1 \le n, m, t \le 10^5\), \(0 \le a_i, b_j < 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O((n + m) \log^2(n + m) + t \log t)\) time and \(O(n + m + t)\) space.
Sample Trace (\(n = 1, m = 1, a = [1], b = [2], t = 2\)): There is \(n m = 1\) pair with sum \(a_1 + b_1 = 3\), so expected values for \(k = 1, 2\) are \((3^1, 3^2) = (3, 9)\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

The coupling between \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) sits inside \((a_i + b_j)^k\). How do you decouple a sum raised to the \(k\)-th power so that sums over \(i\) and sums over \(j\) become independent?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Expand \((a_i + b_j)^k\) using the Binomial Theorem and divide by \(k!\): \[\frac{1}{k!} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m (a_i + b_j)^k = \sum_{r=0}^k \left(\frac{1}{r!} \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^r\right) \left(\frac{1}{(k-r)!} \sum_{j=1}^m b_j^{k-r}\right).\] The right-hand side is a pure Cauchy convolution of two sequences \(F_r = \frac{S_r(a)}{r!}\) and \(G_s = \frac{S_s(b)}{s!}\), where \(S_r(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^r\) and \(S_s(b) = \sum_{j=1}^m b_j^s\) are the Newton–Girard power sums of \(a\) and \(b\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Use the algorithm from Stepping Stone 1 (#238 / §2.5) twice:

Build \(Q_A(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 - a_i x)\) via a D&C product tree in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) and extract \(S_r(a) = [x^r]\big(n - x Q'_A(x) Q_A(x)^{-1}\big)\) for \(0 \le r \le t\).
Build \(Q_B(x) = \prod_{j=1}^m (1 - b_j x)\) in \(O(m \log^2 m)\) and extract \(S_s(b)\) for \(0 \le s \le t\).
Scale \(F_r = S_r(a) / r!\) and \(G_s = S_s(b) / s!\), multiply \(H(x) = F(x) G(x) \bmod x^{t+1}\) via one NTT, and recover \(E_k = \frac{k!}{nm} [x^k] H(x) \pmod{998244353}\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Decoupling \((a_i + b_j)^k\) via Binomial Expansion: By the Binomial Theorem, \((a_i + b_j)^k = \sum_{r=0}^k \binom{k}{r} a_i^r b_j^{k-r} = k! \sum_{r=0}^k \frac{a_i^r}{r!} \frac{b_j^{k-r}}{(k-r)!}\). Exchanging the order of summation between \((i, j)\) and \(r\) separates the \(a_i\) sum from the \(b_j\) sum: \[\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m (a_i + b_j)^k = k! \sum_{r=0}^k \left(\frac{1}{r!} \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^r\right) \left(\frac{1}{(k-r)!} \sum_{j=1}^m b_j^{k-r}\right).\]
Newton–Girard Power Sums via Logarithmic Derivative: Define the power sums \(S_r(a) := \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^r\) (with \(S_0(a) = n\), since \(0^0 = 1\) in the binomial formula \((0 + b_j)^k = \sum_{r=0}^k \binom{k}{r} 0^r b_j^{k-r} = b_j^k\)) and \(S_s(b) := \sum_{j=1}^m b_j^s\) (with \(S_0(b) = m\)). As derived in Section 2.5, the Ordinary Generating Function of \(S_r(a)\) is \[\sum_{r=0}^t S_r(a) x^r = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{1 - a_i x} \equiv n - \frac{x Q'_A(x)}{Q_A(x)} \pmod{x^{t+1}}, \quad \text{where } Q_A(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 - a_i x).\] Similarly, \(\sum_{s=0}^t S_s(b) x^s \equiv m - \frac{x Q'_B(x)}{Q_B(x)} \pmod{x^{t+1}}\), where \(Q_B(x) = \prod_{j=1}^m (1 - b_j x)\).
EGF Convolution: Define the two exponential generating functions truncated modulo \(x^{t+1}\) (we will study Exponential Generating Functions and binomial convolutions systematically in Chapter 04, §4.1): \[F(x) = \sum_{r=0}^t \frac{S_r(a)}{r!} x^r, \qquad G(x) = \sum_{s=0}^t \frac{S_s(b)}{s!} x^s.\] Then for every \(1 \le k \le t\), \[E_k = \frac{k!}{n m} [x^k]\big(F(x) G(x)\big) \pmod{998244353}.\]



Boundary & Characteristic Audit

Zero card values (\(a_i = 0\) or \(b_j = 0\)): If \(a_i = 0\), the factor \(1 - a_i x = 1\) naturally contributes \(0\) to \(S_r(a)\) for \(r \ge 1\) and \(1\) to \(S_0(a) = n\). Setting \([x^0] F(x) = n\) and \([x^0] G(x) = m\) ensures \((0 + b_j)^k = b_j^k\) is counted accurately.
Characteristic check: \(\max(n, m, t) \le 10^5 < p = 998244353\), so \(n, m\), and \(k!\) are all invertible units in \(\mathbb{F}_p\).



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

Compute \(Q_A(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 - a_i x)\) and \(Q_B(x) = \prod_{j=1}^m (1 - b_j x)\) via Divide-and-Conquer product trees in \(O(n \log^2 n + m \log^2 m)\) time (as introduced in Chapter 01, §1.4 and studied further in Chapter 09, §9.1):

Poly build_prod(const vector<long long>& a, int l, int r) {
    if (l == r) return {1, (MOD - a[l] % MOD) % MOD};
    int mid = (l + r) >> 1;
    return multiply(build_prod(a, l, mid), build_prod(a, mid + 1, r));
}

Resize \(Q_A, Q_B\) to \(t + 1\), compute \(S_A(x) = n - x Q'_A(x) Q_A(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{t+1}\) and \(S_B(x) = m - x Q'_B(x) Q_B(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{t+1}\) in \(O(t \log t)\) time.
Divide \([x^r] S_A(x)\) by \(r!\) and \([x^s] S_B(x)\) by \(s!\), multiply \(F(x) \cdot G(x) \bmod x^{t+1}\) via NTT in \(O(t \log t)\) time, and multiply \([x^k](FG)\) by \(k! (nm)^{-1} \bmod p\).







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #157 Binomial Decoupling & Newton–Girard Power Sums




Input & Preconditions: Arrays \(a[1\dots n], b[1\dots m] \in \mathbb{F}_p\), target degree \(t < p\) (\(p = 998244353\), \(\gcd(nm, p) = 1\)).
Postconditions (Output): Decouples \(\sum_{i,j} (a_i + b_j)^k\) into the EGF product of \(S_r(a)/r!\) and \(S_s(b)/s!\), returning \(E_k = \frac{k!}{nm}[x^k](F(x)G(x)) \bmod p\) for \(1 \le k \le t\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O((n + m)\log^2(n + m) + t \log t)\) time and \(O(n + m + t)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: The divide-and-conquer product tree preserves \(Q_A(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 - a_i x)\) and \(Q_B(x) = \prod_{j=1}^m (1 - b_j x)\), from which logarithmic differentiation extracts \(S_A(x) \equiv n - x Q'_A(x) Q_A(x)^{-1} \pmod{x^{t+1}}\) and \(S_B(x) \equiv m - x Q'_B(x) Q_B(x)^{-1} \pmod{x^{t+1}}\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Zero card values (\(a_i = 0\) or \(b_j = 0\)) require setting \([x^0]F(x) = S_0(a) = n\) and \([x^0]G(x) = S_0(b) = m\) rather than \(0\); requires \(t < p\) so that \(1/r!\) and \(1/s!\) are valid in \(\mathbb{F}_p\).











Advanced 2 (#084) — The Child and Binary Tree (Codeforces 438E)

Source: Codeforces 438E — The Child and Binary Tree
Prerequisites: Symbolic Method for Binary Trees, Radical Rationalization, 1D Newton sqrt and inv (§2.3, §2.5).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given a set of \(n\) distinct positive integers \(C = \{c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n\}\) and a maximum weight bound \(m\). A good vertex-weighted rooted binary tree is a rooted binary tree (where each node has either \(0\) children, or both a left and a right child, each of which may be empty) in which every vertex is assigned a weight from \(C\). The total weight of a tree is the sum of the weights of its vertices. For each \(s = 1, 2, \dots, m\), find the number of good binary trees of total weight \(s\) modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n, m \le 10^5\), \(1 \le c_i \le 10^5\) (values \(c_i > m\) can be ignored).
Required Complexity: \(O(m \log m)\) time and \(O(m)\) space.
Sample Trace (\(n = 1, m = 3, C = \{1\}\)): Here \(C(x) = x\), so \(F(x) = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4x}} = 1 + x + 2x^2 + 5x^3 + \dots\) (Catalan numbers \(C_1 = 1, C_2 = 2, C_3 = 5\)).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(f_s\) be the number of good binary trees of total weight \(s\) (with \(f_0 = 1\) for the empty tree), and let \(F(x) = \sum_{s \ge 0} f_s x^s\) be their OGF. A non-empty binary tree consists of a root vertex of weight \(c \in C\), an ordered left subtree (possibly empty), and an ordered right subtree (possibly empty). How does this recursive structure translate into an algebraic equation for \(F(x)\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Let \(C(x) = \sum_{c \in C, c \le m} x^c\) be the generating function of allowed root weights. Then every non-empty tree is formed by choosing a root from \(C(x)\), a left subtree from \(F(x)\), and a right subtree from \(F(x)\), while the empty tree contributes \(1\): \[F(x) = 1 + C(x) F(x)^2 \iff C(x) F(x)^2 - F(x) + 1 = 0.\] Notice that \([x^0] C(x) = 0\) because all \(c_i \ge 1\)! If you use \(F(x) = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}}{2 C(x)}\), you cannot invert \(2 C(x)\) because \(C(0) = 0\). How do you eliminate \(C(x)\) from the denominator?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Apply the Radical Rationalization Trick from Section 2.5: multiply numerator and denominator by \(1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}\) to obtain \[F(x) = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}} \pmod{x^{m+1}}.\] Since \([x^0](1 - 4 C(x)) = 1\), compute \(S(x) = \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)} \bmod x^{m+1}\) via 1D Newton sqrt, add \(1\) to its constant term (so \([x^0](1 + S(x)) = 2 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\)), and invert \(1 + S(x)\) modulo \(x^{m+1}\) via 1D Newton inv!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Combinatorial Specification: Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the combinatorial class of vertex-weighted binary trees (including the empty tree \(\epsilon\) of weight \(0\)), and let \(\mathcal{C}\) be the class of single root vertices with weights in \(C \cap \{1, \dots, m\}\). Every tree in \(\mathcal{T}\) is either the empty tree \(\epsilon\), or a triple \((v, T_L, T_R) \in \mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{T} \times \mathcal{T}\). Translating the disjoint union (\(\sqcup \mapsto +\)) and Cartesian product (\(\times \mapsto \cdot\)) to Ordinary Generating Functions \(F(x) = \sum_{s \ge 0} f_s x^s\) and \(C(x) = \sum_{c \in C, c \le m} x^c\) yields \[F(x) = 1 + C(x) F(x)^2 \iff C(x) F(x)^2 - F(x) + 1 = 0.\]
Solving the Quadratic and Rationalizing the Denominator: By the quadratic formula with \(A(x) = C(x)\), \(B(x) = -1\), and constant term \(1\): \[F(x) = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}}{2 C(x)}.\] Since \(C(0) = 0\) and \(F(0) = f_0 = 1\), the \(+\) branch fails because its numerator at \(x = 0\) is \(1 + \sqrt{1} = 2 \ne 0\) while the denominator is \(2 C(0) = 0\). Selecting the \(-\) branch and multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}\) gives \[F(x) = \frac{\big(1 - \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}\big)\big(1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}\big)}{2 C(x) \big(1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}\big)} = \frac{4 C(x)}{2 C(x) \big(1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}\big)} = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}}.\]
Dual Perspective Preview (Chapter 10 Fréchet Newton Iteration): Could we also solve \(\Phi(F) = C(x) F^2 - F + 1 = 0\) directly by 1D Newton iteration without calling sqrt? Yes! Here \(\Phi'(F) = 2 C(x) F - 1\) has constant term \(-1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\), giving the direct iteration \[F_{k+1} = F_k - \frac{C F_k^2 - F_k + 1}{2 C F_k - 1} = \frac{C F_k^2 - 1}{2 C F_k - 1} \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}.\] We will generalize this implicit Newton technique to arbitrary polynomial and differential equations in Chapter 10.



Boundary & Characteristic Audit

What if all given weights \(c_i > m\), so \(C(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^{m+1}}\)? In the rationalized formula \(F(x) = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}}\), setting \(C(x) = 0\) gives \(\sqrt{1} = 1\) and \(F(x) = \frac{2}{1 + 1} = 1 \pmod{x^{m+1}}\), which outputs \(0\) for all \(1 \le s \le m\) without any division by zero!
\([x^0](1 - 4 C(x)) = 1\), so the square root always starts with \(1\), and \([x^0](1 + \sqrt{1 - 4 C(x)}) = 2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{998244353}\) is always invertible.



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

Build \(P(x) = 1 - 4 C(x) \bmod x^{m+1}\) in \(O(n + m)\) time.
Compute \(S(x) = \text{sqrt}(P, m + 1)\) via Newton sqrt in \(O(m \log m)\) time (using \(G_{k+1} = \frac{1}{2}(G_k + P G_k^{-1}) \bmod x^{2^{k+1}}\)).
Add \(1\) to \(S[0]\), compute \(F(x) = 2 \cdot \text{inv}(S, m + 1) \bmod x^{m+1}\) in \(O(m \log m)\) time, and output \(F[1], \dots, F[m]\).







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #084 Binary Tree OGF via Radical Rationalization (sqrt + inv)




Input & Preconditions: Positive root weights \(c_i \ge 1\) (\([x^0]C(x) = 0\)), target weight \(m \ge 1\), odd prime \(p = 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Evaluates \(F(x) = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4C(x)}} \bmod x^{m+1}\) with invertible denominator \([x^0](1 + \sqrt{1 - 4C(x)}) = 2 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n + m \log m)\) time and \(O(m)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Newton sqrt maintains \(S_k(x)^2 \equiv 1 - 4C(x) \pmod{x^{2^k}}\) with \([x^0]S_k = 1\), and Newton inv maintains \(F_k(x)(1 + S(x)) \equiv 2 \pmod{x^{2^k}}\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Dividing directly by \(2C(x)\) in \(\frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4C(x)}}{2C(x)}\) fails when \(\operatorname{val}(C) > 1\) or when all \(c_i > m\) (\(C(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^{m+1}}\)); rationalizing the numerator eliminates the \(C(x) = 0\) singularity completely.











Mastery 1 (#030) — Odd Sum (AtCoder ABC 267 Ex)

Source: AtCoder Beginner Contest 267 Ex — Odd Sum
Prerequisites: Bivariate Parity Bisection (Roots of Unity Filter), Frequency-Bucketed Harmonic \(\ln / \exp\) or D&C Product Tree (§2.3, §2.5).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) positive integers \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N\) and a target sum \(M\). Find the number of subsets of indices \(S \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\) such that:

The number of chosen elements \(|S|\) is odd; and
The sum of the chosen elements \(\sum_{i \in S} A_i\) equals \(M\).

Output the answer modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(1 \le M \le 10^6\), \(1 \le A_i \le 10\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N + M \log M)\) time via bucketed \(\ln/\exp\) (or \(O((M + N \log N) \log N)\) via D&C product tree), and cleanly generalizable even when the bound \(A_i \le 10\) is removed (\(A_i \le M\)).
Sample Trace (\(N = 3, M = 3, A = [1, 1, 2]\)): Odd-sized subsets summing to \(3\) must have size \(1\) (none, since \(3 \notin A\)) or size \(3\) (\(\{1, 1, 2\}\) sums to \(4 \ne 3\)). For \(M = 4\), the size-\(3\) subset \(\{1, 1, 2\}\) sums to \(4\), giving answer 1.



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Introduce two formal variables: \(x\) to track the weight sum \(\sum_{i \in S} A_i\), and \(y\) to track the subset size \(|S|\). Each item \(i\) contributes the factor \((1 + y x^{A_i})\), so the bivariate generating function is \(P(x, y) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 + y x^{A_i})\). How do you isolate only the terms where the exponent of \(y\) is odd?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Apply the Parity Bisection (2nd Roots of Unity Filter) on \(y\):

At \(y = +1\): \(P(x, 1) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 + x^{A_i})\) sums all subsets with weight \(+1\).
At \(y = -1\): \(P(x, -1) = \prod_{i=1}^N (1 - x^{A_i})\) gives weight \(+1\) to even-sized subsets and \(-1\) to odd-sized subsets! Subtracting the two cancels all even-sized subsets and doubles all odd-sized subsets: \[\text{Ans} = [x^M] \frac{P(x, 1) - P(x, -1)}{2} \pmod{998244353}.\]




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(c_w = \#\{i : A_i = w\}\) be the frequency of weight \(w\).

Since \(A_i \le 10\): There are at most \(10\) distinct weights \(w \in \{1, \dots, 10\}\)! Even better, for general \(A_i \le M\), we can compute both \(P(x, 1) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 + x^w)^{c_w} \bmod x^{M+1}\) and \(P(x, -1) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 - x^w)^{c_w} \bmod x^{M+1}\) in \(O(M \log M)\) time using Bucketed Harmonic \(\ln / \exp\) (just as in #165), or for \(A_i \le 10\) by expanding \((1 \pm x^w)^{c_w}\) directly as sparse polynomials and multiplying all 10 factors!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Bivariate Generating Function & Parity Filter: Define the bivariate polynomial \[P(x, y) := \prod_{i=1}^N (1 + y x^{A_i}) = \sum_{S \subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}} y^{|S|} x^{\sum_{i \in S} A_i}.\] We seek the coefficient of \(x^M\) restricted to odd powers of \(y\). For any integer \(k = |S|\), notice that \[\frac{1^k - (-1)^k}{2} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k \text{ is odd}, \\ 0 & \text{if } k \text{ is even}. \end{cases}\] Therefore, evaluating \(P(x, y)\) at \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\) reduces the bivariate problem to two univariate FPS evaluations: \[\text{Ans} = \frac{[x^M] P(x, 1) - [x^M] P(x, -1)}{2} \pmod{998244353}.\]
Method A (General \(A_i \le M\) via Harmonic Bucketed \(\ln / \exp\) in \(O(M \log M)\)): Group items by weight: let \(c_w = \sum_{i=1}^N [A_i = w]\). Then \[P(x, 1) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 + x^w)^{c_w}, \qquad P(x, -1) = \prod_{w=1}^M (1 - x^w)^{c_w}.\] Taking formal logarithms modulo \(x^{M+1}\) gives \[L_+(x) := \ln P(x, 1) \equiv \sum_{w=1}^M c_w \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor M/w \rfloor} \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k} x^{kw} \pmod{x^{M+1}},\] \[L_-(x) := \ln P(x, -1) \equiv -\sum_{w=1}^M c_w \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor M/w \rfloor} \frac{1}{k} x^{kw} \pmod{x^{M+1}}.\] Key observation: can we simplify even further and call exp only if needed, or exploit \(A_i \le 10\)?
Method B (Exploiting \(A_i \le 10\) via Direct Binomial Expansion + NTT in \(O(M \log M)\) with Zero exp Calls): Because \(A_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 10\}\), there are only \(10\) distinct values of \(w\)! For each \(w \in \{1, \dots, 10\}\), the polynomial \[Q_{w, \pm}(x) := (1 \pm x^w)^{c_w} = \sum_{j=0}^{c_w} (\pm 1)^j \binom{c_w}{j} x^{j w}\] is known explicitly in closed form in \(O(c_w)\) time! Multiplying the \(10\) polynomials \(Q_{1, +}(x), \dots, Q_{10, +}(x)\) modulo \(x^{M+1}\) (and similarly for \(Q_{w, -}(x)\)) requires at most \(9\) NTT multiplications of size \(\le M + 1\), running in \(O(M \log M)\) time without even needing Newton exp! (Even better: by our sparse_pow engine from Section 2.4, since \(P(x, \pm 1) = \prod_{w=1}^{10} (1 \pm x^w)^{c_w}\), you can also multiply the 10 binomial polynomials sequentially using D&C in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time, since the total degree \(\sum A_i \le 10 N \le 10^6\)!)



Boundary & Characteristic Audit

If \(M > \sum_{i=1}^N A_i\), then \([x^M] P(x, \pm 1) = 0\) and the answer is immediately \(0\).
\(p = 998244353 > M = 10^6\), so division by \(2\) and (in Method A) division by \(k \le M\) are valid in \(\mathbb{F}_p\).



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

Method A (General \(A_i \le M\)): Bucket \(c_w\), build \(L_+(x)\) and \(L_-(x)\) in \(O(M \log M)\) harmonic time, call exp twice to get \(P(x, 1)\) and \(P(x, -1)\) modulo \(x^{M+1}\) (or extract \([x^M]\)), and output \(\frac{P_+[M] - P_-[M]}{2} \bmod p\).
Method B (\(A_i \le 10\)): Precompute factorials up to \(N\), form the \(10\) polynomials \(Q_{w, +}(x)\) and \(Q_{w, -}(x)\) of degree \(\le \min(M, w c_w)\), multiply them via NTT, and output \(\frac{P_+[M] - P_-[M]}{2} \bmod p\).







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #030 Bivariate Parity Bisection & Bucketed Subset Sum




Input & Preconditions: Positive integer weights \(A_1, \dots, A_N \ge 1\), target sum \(M < p\) (\(p = 998244353\)).
Postconditions (Output): Evaluates \(P(x, \pm 1) = \prod_{w} (1 \pm x^w)^{c_w} \bmod x^{M+1}\) and returns \(\frac{1}{2}([x^M]P(x,1) - [x^M]P(x,-1)) \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N + M \log M)\) time and \(O(M)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: The 2nd roots-of-unity filter \(\frac{1}{2}(P(x, 1) - P(x, -1))\) cancels all even-cardinality subsets (\(1^{|S|} - (-1)^{|S|} = 0\)) and preserves every odd-cardinality subset with unit weight.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(A_i = 0\) were allowed, \((1 \pm x^0)^{c_0}\) would alter the constant term \([x^0]P(x, \pm 1) \ne 1\) and break ln in Method A (requiring 0-weight items to be factored out beforehand); when \(M > \sum A_i\), return \(0\) immediately.











Mastery 2 (#091) — Lust (Codeforces 891E)

Source: Codeforces 891E — Lust
Prerequisites: Linearity of Expectation, Telescoping Difference Identity, Exponential Generating Functions (EGFs), Pointing / Falling-Factorial Extraction (§2.1–§2.5).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(n\) integers \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\) and a number of operations \(k\). An accumulator variable res is initialized to \(0\). In each of the \(k\) operations, you choose an index \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) uniformly and independently at random, add the product of all \(n-1\) other elements \(\prod_{j \ne i} a_j\) to res, and then decrement \(a_i\) by \(1\) (\(a_i \leftarrow a_i - 1\)). Find the expected final value of res after \(k\) operations, modulo \(10^9 + 7\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 5000\), \(1 \le k \le 10^9\), \(0 \le a_i \le 10^9\), modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7\).
Required Complexity: \(O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.
Sample Trace (\(n = 2, k = 1, a = [2, 3]\)): With \(k = 1\) decrement, we either decrement \(a_1\) (\(2 \to 1\), gain \(3\)) or \(a_2\) (\(3 \to 2\), gain \(2\)), so expected gain is \(\frac{3 + 2}{2} = \frac{5}{2} \equiv 500000006 \pmod{10^9 + 7}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Look at what happens to the total product \(\Pi = \prod_{j=1}^n a_j\) during a single step when index \(i\) is decremented (\(a_i \leftarrow a_i - 1\)): \[\Pi_{\text{before}} - \Pi_{\text{after}} = a_i \prod_{j \ne i} a_j - (a_i - 1) \prod_{j \ne i} a_j = \prod_{j \ne i} a_j.\] The exact quantity added to res in each step is the decrease in the total product \(\prod_{j=1}^n a_j\)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By telescoping across all \(k\) steps, the final value of res on any sample path is simply \[\text{res} = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i - \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - c_i),\] where \(c_i \ge 0\) is the number of times index \(i\) was chosen across the \(k\) steps (\(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i = k\)). There are \(n^k\) equally likely sequences of \(k\) choices, and a tuple \((c_1, \dots, c_n)\) with \(\sum c_i = k\) occurs in \(\frac{k!}{c_1! c_2! \cdots c_n!}\) ways! How do you express \(\sum_{c_1 + \dots + c_n = k} \frac{k!}{c_1! \cdots c_n!} \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - c_i)\) using Exponential Generating Functions?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Notice that for a single factor \(i\), the EGF of the sequence \(m \mapsto (a_i - m)\) is \[\sum_{m \ge 0} (a_i - m) \frac{x^m}{m!} = a_i \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{x^m}{m!} - x \sum_{m \ge 1} \frac{x^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} = (a_i - x) e^x.\] Multiplying across all \(i = 1, \dots, n\) shows that the EGF of the \(n\)-fold multinomial sum is simply \[G(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - x) e^x = e^{n x} \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - x).\] Expand the degree-\(n\) polynomial \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - x) = \sum_{j=0}^n p_j x^j\) in \(O(n^2)\) time, and extract \(k! [x^k] \big(P(x) e^{nx}\big)\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

The Telescoping Invariant (Eliminating Step-by-Step Dependencies): Let \(a_i^{(t)}\) denote the value of the \(i\)-th element after \(t\) operations (\(0 \le t \le k\)). If the \(t\)-th operation selects index \(i_t\), then \(a_{i_t}^{(t)} = a_{i_t}^{(t-1)} - 1\) while \(a_j^{(t)} = a_j^{(t-1)}\) for all \(j \ne i_t\). Therefore, the amount added to res in step \(t\) is \[\Delta \text{res}_t = \prod_{j \ne i_t} a_j^{(t-1)} = a_{i_t}^{(t-1)} \prod_{j \ne i_t} a_j^{(t-1)} - \big(a_{i_t}^{(t-1)} - 1\big) \prod_{j \ne i_t} a_j^{(t-1)} = \prod_{j=1}^n a_j^{(t-1)} - \prod_{j=1}^n a_j^{(t)}.\] Summing \(\Delta \text{res}_t\) from \(t = 1\) to \(k\) telescopes all intermediate products, leaving only the initial product minus the final product: \[\text{res} = \sum_{t=1}^k \Delta \text{res}_t = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{(0)} - \prod_{i=1}^n a_i^{(k)} = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i - \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - c_i),\] where \(c_i\) is the total number of times index \(i\) was chosen during the \(k\) steps.
Multinomial Expectation via Exponential Generating Functions: Since each of the \(k\) operations chooses an index in \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) independently and uniformly at random, there are \(n^k\) equally likely outcome sequences, and a specific count vector \((c_1, \dots, c_n)\) with \(c_1 + \dots + c_n = k\) is produced by \(\frac{k!}{c_1! c_2! \cdots c_n!}\) sequences. Thus: \[\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - c_i)\right] = \frac{k!}{n^k} \sum_{\substack{c_1 + \dots + c_n = k \\ c_i \ge 0}} \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{a_i - c_i}{c_i!}.\] Notice that the inner sum is the exact coefficient of \(x^k\) in the Cauchy product of \(n\) Exponential Generating Functions \(G_i(x) := \sum_{c \ge 0} \frac{a_i - c}{c!} x^c\) (we will formalize Exponential Generating Functions and multinomial labeled products in Chapter 04, §4.1). Using the pointing identity \(c \frac{x^c}{c!} = x \frac{x^{c-1}}{(c-1)!}\) (or \(x D_x e^x = x e^x\)), each factor simplifies into a linear polynomial times \(e^x\): \[G_i(x) = a_i \sum_{c \ge 0} \frac{x^c}{c!} - x \sum_{c \ge 1} \frac{x^{c-1}}{(c-1)!} = (a_i - x) e^x.\] Multiplying \(G_1(x) \cdots G_n(x)\) gives \[G(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - x) e^x = e^{n x} \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - x).\]
Extracting \(k! [x^k] G(x)\) for Huge \(k \le 10^9\): Let \(P(x) := \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - x) = \sum_{j=0}^n p_j x^j\), which is a polynomial of degree \(n \le 5000\). Since \(e^{nx} = \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{n^m}{m!} x^m\), extracting \([x^k]\big(P(x) e^{nx}\big)\) only sums over \(0 \le j \le \min(n, k)\): \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - c_i)\right] &= \frac{k!}{n^k} [x^k]\left(\sum_{j=0}^n p_j x^j \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{n^m}{m!} x^m\right) \\[4pt]
&= \frac{k!}{n^k} \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} p_j \frac{n^{k - j}}{(k - j)!} = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} p_j \cdot \frac{k^{\underline{j}}}{n^j},
\end{aligned}\] where \(k^{\underline{j}} = \frac{k!}{(k-j)!} = k(k-1)\cdots(k-j+1)\) is the \(j\)-th falling factorial of \(k\)!



Boundary & Characteristic Audit

Why no division by \(k!\) is needed: Although \(k \le 10^9\) can be close to \(p = 10^9 + 7\), the ratio \(\frac{k!}{(k-j)!} = k(k-1)\cdots(k-j+1)\) cancels \((k-j)!\) algebraically into a pure product of \(j \le n \le 5000\) integers! Thus we never divide by any factorial, and the formula works over any prime modulus \(p \nmid n\).
Notice also that \(p_0 = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i\), so the \(j = 0\) term in the sum is \(p_0 \cdot \frac{k^{\underline{0}}}{n^0} = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i\), which cancels \(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i\) in \(\text{Ans} = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i - \mathbb{E}[\prod(a_i - c_i)]\), leaving \[\text{Ans} = -\sum_{j=1}^{\min(n, k)} p_j \cdot k^{\underline{j}} \cdot n^{-j} \pmod{10^9 + 7}.\]



Final Extraction Algorithm & Complexity

Initialize \(P^{(0)}(x) = p_0 = 1\) and \(p_1 = \dots = p_n = 0\). For \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\), update the coefficients of \(P(x) = \prod_{r=1}^n (a_r - x)\) in-place in descending degree order \(j = i, i - 1, \dots, 0\) via \(p_j \gets a_i p_j - p_{j-1}\) (with \(p_{-1} = 0\)) in \(O(n^2)\) total time. Loop Invariant: After outer step \(i\), \(\sum_{j=0}^i p_j x^j = \prod_{r=1}^i (a_r - x)\), and iterating \(j\) from \(i\) down to \(0\) guarantees \(p_{j-1}\) still holds its step-\((i-1)\) value when computing the new \(p_j\).
Compute \(n^{-1} \bmod (10^9 + 7)\) via Fermat’s Little Theorem, and accumulate \(k^{\underline{j}} \cdot n^{-j} \bmod (10^9 + 7)\) iteratively for \(j = 1, \dots, \min(n, k)\) in \(O(n)\) time.
Output \(\left(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i - \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, k)} p_j k^{\underline{j}} n^{-j}\right) \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).







NoteAlgorithm Contract: #091 Telescoping Multinomial EGF Extraction




Input & Preconditions: Array \(a[1\dots n]\) with \(n \le 5000\) and \(\gcd(n, p) = 1\), step count \(k \le 10^9\) (\(p = 10^9 + 7\)).
Postconditions (Output): Expands \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - x) = \sum_{j=0}^n p_j x^j\) and evaluates \(-\sum_{j=1}^{\min(n,k)} p_j k^{\underline{j}} n^{-j} \bmod p\) with zero factorial divisions.
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing the first \(m\) elements, the DP polynomial holds \(P_m(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m (a_i - x)\), while the telescoping invariant \(\sum_{t=1}^k \Delta \text{res}_t = \prod_{i=1}^n a_i - \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i - c_i)\) collapses the \(k\)-step Markov process into a single EGF coefficient \(k! [x^k](P_n(x) e^{nx})\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Never compute \(k!\) and \((k-j)!\) separately (which fails or TLEs for \(k \le 10^9\)); always accumulate the falling factorial \(k^{\underline{j}} = \prod_{r=0}^{j-1} (k - r) \bmod p\) directly and cap the loop at \(\min(n, k)\).

NoteChapter Overview & Algebraic Scope




Ambient Ring & Operators: The Exponential Generating Function (EGF) Ring \((K_{\text{exp}}[[x]], +, \star)\) equipped with the Hurwitz binomial convolution \((a \star b)_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} a_k b_{n-k}\), mapped isomorphically via the Borel–Laplace factorial scaling \(\mathcal{B}: a_n \mapsto \frac{a_n}{n!}\) to the standard formal power series ring \(K[[x]]\) whenever \(n! \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or prime \(p > N\)). Key operators include \(\operatorname{SEQ}\), \(\operatorname{SET}\) (\(\exp\)), \(\operatorname{CYC}\) (\(\ln\frac{1}{1-\cdot}\)), Pointing (\(\vartheta = x D_x\)), the Greene–Wilf Boxed Product (\(\widehat{C}'(x) = \widehat{A}'(x)\widehat{B}(x)\)), and the Prüfer Degree Transform.
Prerequisites: Chapter 01 (Truncated polynomial rings \(K[x]/(x^N)\), Cauchy convolution, polynomial inversion inv), Chapter 02 (Formal derivative \(D_x\), integral \(\int_0^x\), polynomial ln, exp, pow), and Chapter 03 (The unlabeled OGF symbolic method).
Learning Objectives:

Diagnose immediately whether a combinatorial specification lives in the unlabeled OGF world (\(A(x) = \sum a_n x^n\)) or the labeled EGF world (\(\widehat{A}(x) = \sum a_n \frac{x^n}{n!}\)).
Translate labeled composite structures (\(\operatorname{SEQ}\), \(\operatorname{SET}\), \(\operatorname{CYC}\), undirected cycles \(\operatorname{UCYC}_{\ge 3}\), and hyperbolic parity filters \(\cosh x, \sinh x\)) into \(O(N \log N)\) polynomial operations.
Invert the Exponential Formula \(\widehat{G}(x) = \exp(\widehat{C}(x))\) via \(\widehat{C}(x) = \ln \widehat{G}(x)\) to extract connected labeled graphs, bipartite graphs, and indecomposable components.
Apply the Greene–Wilf Boxed Product (\(\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{A}^{\square} \star \mathcal{B}\)) to model minimum-label pivot recurrences \(\binom{n-1}{k-1}\) and bypass characteristic-\(p\) division breakdowns (\(p \le N\)).
Convert degree-constrained labeled tree enumeration problems into EGF coefficient extraction via the Prüfer Sequence Bijection, while guarding against the canonical \(N = 1\) Boundary Trap (Failure Mode #16).
