Mastery 1 (#183) — Luogu P5827: 点双连通图计数 (Vertex-Biconnected Labeled Graphs)

Source: Luogu P5827
Prerequisites: Tutte’s Block-Cut Tree Equation & Log-Free Single-\(n\) Formula (§12.3), Formal Residue Integration by Parts (Ch 11.1).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given a positive integer \(n\), compute the number of simple undirected 2-vertex-connected (biconnected) labeled graphs on \(n\) vertices (connected graphs with no articulation points / cut-vertices) modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\), modulus \(p = 998244353\). (Note: for \(n = 1\), \(K_1\) has no cut-vertices so output \(1\); for \(n = 2\), \(K_2\) has no cut-vertices so output \(1\).)
Required Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.



Small Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n \le 5\))

\(n = 1\): \(\mathbf{1}\) (\(K_1\)).
\(n = 2\): \(\mathbf{1}\) (\(K_2\)).
\(n = 3\): \(\mathbf{1}\) (\(K_3\)).
\(n = 4\): \(\mathbf{10}\) (\(1\) copy of \(K_4\), \(6\) copies of \(K_4 - e\), and \(3\) four-cycles \(C_4\)).
\(n = 5\): \(\mathbf{238}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

We need the single count \(b_n\) at \(n \le 2 \times 10^5\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time without full polynomial composition inversion. If you root a connected graph at a vertex \(r\), how does \(r\) sit inside the biconnected blocks incident to \(r\), and what is attached to each non-root vertex of those blocks?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By Tutte’s Block-Cut Tree decomposition, the vertex-pointed connected EGF \(R(x) = x C'(x)\) satisfies \(R(x) = x \exp\!\big(B'(R(x))\big)\), where \(C(x) = \ln\!\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n} 2^{\binom{k}{2}} \frac{x^k}{k!}\right)\). Taking logarithms gives \(B'\big(x C'(x)\big) = \ln C'(x)\). Applying Ch 11 Lagrange Inversion to extract \([u^{n-1}] B'(u)\) with \(u = x C'(x)\) gives: \[[u^{n-1}] B'(u) = \frac{1}{n - 1} [x^{n-2}] \left( \big(\ln C'(x)\big)' \cdot C'(x)^{-(n-1)} \right).\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Notice that \(\big(\ln C'(x)\big)' \cdot C'(x)^{-(n-1)} = C''(x) C'(x)^{-n} = -\frac{1}{n-1} \frac{d}{dx}\big(C'(x)^{-(n-1)}\big)\). Using \([x^{n-2}] F'(x) = (n-1)[x^{n-1}] F(x)\) eliminates the outer logarithm and derivative completely, yielding \(b_n = -(n-2)! [x^{n-1}] \big(C'(x)^{-(n-1)}\big)\) for \(n \ge 2\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1: From All Graphs to Pointed Connected Graphs
Let \(G(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} 2^{\binom{k}{2}} \frac{x^k}{k!} \bmod x^{n+1}\) be the EGF of all simple labeled graphs on at most \(n\) vertices. By the Exp–Log Connected Component Bridge (Ch 04.3), the EGF of connected labeled graphs is: \[C(x) = \ln G(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} c_k \frac{x^k}{k!} \pmod{x^{n+1}}.\] Pointing a connected graph at a root vertex \(r\) multiplies the \(k\)-th coefficient by \(k\), giving \(R(x) = x C'(x)\), where: \[C'(x) = \frac{R(x)}{x} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} c_{k+1} \frac{x^k}{k!} \pmod{x^n}.\]


Step 2: Block-Cut Tree Equation and Formal Residue Extraction
For \(n = 1\), a single vertex \(K_1\) has no cut-vertices (\(b_1 = 1\)). For \(n \ge 2\), let \(B(u) = \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} b_k \frac{u^k}{k!}\) be the EGF of biconnected blocks. In any vertex-pointed connected graph \((G, r)\), the root \(r\) belongs to an unordered set of blocks incident to \(r\), and each of the \(k - 1\) non-root vertices in a block of size \(k\) roots an independent pointed connected graph \(u = R(x) = x C'(x)\): \[R(x) = x \exp\!\Big(B'\big(R(x)\big)\Big) \iff B'\big(x C'(x)\big) = \ln C'(x).\] Let \(u = R(x) = x C'(x)\). For \(n \ge 2\), by the Formal Residue Change-of-Variables Theorem (Ch 11.1): \[\begin{aligned}
[u^{n-1}] B'(u)
&= \frac{1}{n - 1} \operatorname{Res}_u \, B''(u) u^{-(n-1)} = \frac{1}{n - 1} \operatorname{Res}_x \, \frac{d}{dx}\Big(B'\big(R(x)\big)\Big) R(x)^{-(n-1)} \\
&= \frac{1}{n - 1} [x^{n-2}] \left( \frac{d}{dx}\big(\ln C'(x)\big) \cdot C'(x)^{-(n-1)} \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{n - 1} [x^{n-2}] \Big( C''(x) \, C'(x)^{-n} \Big) \\
&= -\frac{1}{(n - 1)^2} [x^{n-2}] \frac{d}{dx}\Big( C'(x)^{-(n-1)} \Big) \\
&= -\frac{1}{n - 1} [x^{n-1}] \Big( C'(x)^{-(n-1)} \Big).
\end{aligned}\] Multiplying by \((n - 1)!\) gives the exact count of biconnected labeled graphs on \(n \ge 2\) vertices: \[b_n = (n - 1)! [u^{n-1}] B'(u) = -(n - 2)! [x^{n-1}] \exp\!\Big(-(n - 1) \ln C'(x)\Big) \pmod{998244353}.\]
// O(n log n) Single-n Biconnected Graph Extraction (Luogu P5827)
if (n == 1) return 1;
Poly G(n + 1);
for (int k = 0; k <= n; ++k)
    G[k] = power(2, 1LL * k * (k - 1) / 2 % (MOD - 1)) * ifac[k] % MOD;
Poly C_prime = G.Ln(n + 1).Deriv(); // C'(x) of degree n - 1, [x^0]C'(x) = 1
Poly P = (C_prime.Ln(n) * (MOD - (n - 1))).Exp(n); // C'(x)^{-(n-1)} mod x^n
long long ans = (MOD - fac[n - 2]) * P[n - 1] % MOD;






NoteAlgorithm Contract




Input: Integer \(n \in [1, 2 \times 10^5]\) and prime modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Preconditions: \(p > n\); \([x^0] G(x) = 1\) and \([x^0] C'(x) = 1\).
Postconditions: Outputs \(b_n \bmod p\), the exact number of labeled 2-vertex-connected graphs on \(n\) vertices (with boundary check \(n = 1 \implies 1\)).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time (2 polynomial \(\ln\) calls and 1 polynomial \(\exp\) call of degree \(n\)) and \(O(n)\) space.
Core Invariant: Formal residue integration by parts reduces \(\operatorname{Res}_x (\ln C'(x))' R(x)^{-(n-1)}\) to \(-(n-1) [x^{n-1}] \big(C'(x)^{-(n-1)}\big)\) for all \(2 \le n < p\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le n\) (since \(n!\), \(1/(n-1)\), and the formal integration steps inside \(\ln\) and \(\exp\) up to degree \(n\) divide by zero modulo \(p\)), or if \(C'(x)\) is not truncated to degree \(n - 1\) before taking \(\ln C'(x)\).











Mastery 2 (#184) — Luogu P5828: 边双连通图计数 (2-Edge-Connected Labeled Graphs)

Source: Luogu P5828
Prerequisites: Bridge-Block Functional Equation \(E(x e^{R(x)}) = R(x)\) & Derivative-Free Single-\(n\) LIF (§12.4).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given a positive integer \(n\), compute the number of simple undirected 2-edge-connected (bridgeless) labeled graphs on \(n\) vertices (connected graphs with no bridge edges / cut-edges) modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 2 \times 10^5\), modulus \(p = 998244353\). (Note: for \(n = 1\), \(K_1\) has \(0\) edges and thus \(0\) bridges, so \(e_{2,1} = 1\); for \(n = 2\), \(K_2\) is a single bridge, so \(e_{2,2} = 0\).)
Required Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.



Small Hand-Checkable Trace (\(n \le 5\))

\(n = 1\): \(\mathbf{1}\) (\(K_1\) has \(0\) bridges).
\(n = 2\): \(\mathbf{0}\) (\(K_2\) is a bridge).
\(n = 3\): \(\mathbf{1}\) (\(K_3\)).
\(n = 4\): \(\mathbf{10}\) (same as biconnected graphs for \(n = 4\)).
\(n = 5\): \(\mathbf{253}\) (\(238\) biconnected graphs plus \(\binom{5}{1} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\binom{4}{2} = 15\) “bowtie” graphs consisting of two triangles sharing a single cut-vertex, which has no bridge edges!).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Contracting every 2-edge-connected component of a connected graph into a super-vertex turns the bridge edges into a tree of 2-ECCs. If we distinguish a root vertex \(r\), it belongs to a unique root 2-ECC \(H_0\); what hangs off each vertex \(v \in V(H_0)\) across the bridge edges incident to \(v\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Every vertex \(v \in V(H_0)\) (including \(r\)) sprouts an unordered set (\(\exp\)) of bridge edges leading to pointed connected components \(R(x) = x C'(x)\). Let \(E(z) = z B'_{\text{2-edge}}(z) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k \, e_{2,k} \frac{z^k}{k!}\) be the EGF of vertex-pointed 2-edge-connected graphs. Replacing every vertex \(z\) of the root 2-ECC by \(W(x) = x \exp(R(x))\) yields: \[E\big(W(x)\big) = R(x), \qquad W(x) = x \exp\!\big(R(x)\big) = x \exp\!\big(x C'(x)\big).\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Applying Ch 11 LIF to \(E(W(x)) = R(x)\) and integrating by parts for \(n \ge 2\) gives: \[[z^n] E(z) = \frac{1}{n} [x^{n-1}] \Big( R'(x) \exp\!\big(-n R(x)\big) \Big) = -\frac{1}{n} [x^n] \exp\!\big(-n R(x)\big).\] Multiply by \((n - 1)!\) to obtain \(e_{2,n} = -\frac{(n - 1)!}{n} [x^n] \exp\!\big(-n x C'(x)\big)\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step 1: Pointed Connected Graph EGF \(R(x) = x C'(x)\)
As in #183, form \(G(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} 2^{\binom{k}{2}} \frac{x^k}{k!} \bmod x^{n+1}\), compute \(C(x) = \ln G(x) \bmod x^{n+1}\) in \(O(n \log n)\) time, and apply the pointing operator \(\Theta = x D_x\) to obtain: \[R(x) = x C'(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} k \, c_k \frac{x^k}{k!} \pmod{x^{n+1}}.\]


Step 2: Bridge-Block Substitution and LIF Extraction
For \(n = 1\), output \(e_{2,1} = 1\). For \(n \ge 2\), let \(E(z) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k \, e_{2,k} \frac{z^k}{k!}\) be the EGF of vertex-pointed 2-edge-connected graphs. By Section 12.4, \(E(W(x)) = R(x)\) where \(W(x) = x \exp(R(x))\).
Applying Ch 11 Inverse Lagrange Inversion (Form 2) with \(\phi(x) = \frac{x}{W(x)} = \exp(-R(x))\): \[\begin{aligned}
[z^n] E(z)
&= \frac{1}{n} [x^{n-1}] \left( R'(x) \left(\frac{x}{W(x)}\right)^n \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{n} [x^{n-1}] \Big( R'(x) \exp\!\big(-n R(x)\big) \Big) \\
&= -\frac{1}{n^2} [x^{n-1}] \frac{d}{dx}\Big( \exp\!\big(-n R(x)\big) \Big) \\
&= -\frac{1}{n} [x^n] \exp\!\big(-n R(x)\big).
\end{aligned}\] Since \([z^n] E(z) = \frac{n \, e_{2,n}}{n!} = \frac{e_{2,n}}{(n - 1)!}\), multiplying both sides by \((n - 1)!\) yields the exact count of 2-edge-connected labeled graphs on \(n \ge 2\) vertices: \[e_{2,n} = -\frac{(n - 1)!}{n} [x^n] \exp\!\big(-n R(x)\big) = -\frac{(n - 1)!}{n} [x^n] \exp\!\big(-n x C'(x)\big) \pmod{998244353}.\]
// O(n log n) Single-n 2-Edge-Connected Graph Extraction (Luogu P5828)
if (n == 1) return 1;
Poly G(n + 1);
for (int k = 0; k <= n; ++k)
    G[k] = power(2, 1LL * k * (k - 1) / 2 % (MOD - 1)) * ifac[k] % MOD;
Poly R = G.Ln(n + 1);
for (int k = 0; k <= n; ++k) R[k] = R[k] * k % MOD; // R(x) = x C'(x)
Poly P = (R * (MOD - n)).Exp(n + 1);                // exp(-n R(x)) mod x^{n+1}
long long ans = (MOD - fac[n - 1]) * inv[n] % MOD * P[n] % MOD;






NoteAlgorithm Contract




Input: Integer \(n \in [1, 2 \times 10^5]\) and prime modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Preconditions: \(p > n\); \([x^0] G(x) = 1\) and \([x^0] R(x) = 0\).
Postconditions: Outputs \(e_{2,n} \bmod p\), the exact number of labeled 2-edge-connected graphs on \(n\) vertices (with boundary check \(n = 1 \implies 1, n = 2 \implies 0\)).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time (1 polynomial \(\ln\) call and 1 polynomial \(\exp\) call of degree \(n\)) and \(O(n)\) space.
Core Invariant: Under \(z = W(x) = x \exp(R(x))\), \([z^n] E(z) = -\frac{1}{n} [x^n] \exp(-n R(x))\) holds for all \(2 \le n < p\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le n\) (since \(n!\), \(1/n\), and the formal integration steps inside \(\ln\) and \(\exp\) up to degree \(n\) divide by zero modulo \(p\)), or if \(n = 1\) is evaluated via \(-\frac{1}{1}[x^1]\exp(-R(x)) = 1\) without accounting for the bridge-tree sign convention (which holds only for \(n \ge 2\)).

title: 14 — Probability Generating Functions, Renewal Stopping Times, Poissonization & Martingales
text:
In Chapters 01 through 13, our generating functions encoded deterministic enumeration sequences: \([x^n]A(x)\) counted unlabeled structures of size \(n\), and \(n!\,[x^n]\widehat{A}(x)\) counted labeled structures on \(n\) vertices. In this chapter we open Part IV (Probabilistic Generating Functions, Lattice Walks & Multivariate Series) by turning the formal power series ring \(K[[z]]\) into an algebraic engine for stochastic processes and random stopping times.
When a random process evolves step by step—tossing biased coins until one of \(m\) competing patterns appears, drawing coupons with multiplicity thresholds \(B_i\), flipping random switches on a hypercube until a target state is reached, or redistributing tokens among \(n\) piles until one player holds everything—computing the expected stopping time \(\mathbb{E}[T]\), its variance \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\), or the winning probabilities \(P_i\) via state-space Gaussian elimination often requires \(O(V^3)\) time over an exponentially large state space. Probabilistic Generating Functions (PGFs) collapse these infinite-horizon Markov chains into compact polynomial and exponential equations where \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\) are extracted by algebraic behavior at \(z = 1\).

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Formulate Stopping-Time & Survival PGFs (§14.1): Construct the stopping-time PGF \(F(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^T] = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T = n)z^n\) and the survival (tail) generating function \(G(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T > n)z^n\), derive the Stopping-Time Conservation Identity \(F(z) + (1 - z)G(z) = 1\), and extract falling factorial moments \(\mathbb{E}[T^{\underline{k}}] = F^{(k)}(1) = k G^{(k-1)}(1)\), ordinary moments \(\mathbb{E}[T^k] = [(\vartheta_z)^k F(z)]_{z=1}\), and variance \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2G'(1) + G(1) - G(1)^2\).
Eliminate \(0/0\) Indeterminate Forms via Formal Taylor Shift in \(K[t]/(t^3)\) (§14.2): Replace error-prone quotient-rule and L’Hôpital differentiations of rational PGFs \(F(z) = P(z)/Q(z)\) at \(z = 1\) with the Formal Jet Substitution \(z = 1 + t \bmod t^3\), factoring out the common valuation \(t^v\) (\(v = \operatorname{val}_t Q(1+t)\)) and inverting in \(K[t]/(t^3)\) in \(O(1)\) operations.
Execute First-Passage Renewal Deconvolution & Continuous-Time Poissonization (§14.3): Convert unconstrained visit generating functions \(H_{u \to v}(z)\) into first-passage PGFs \(F_{u \to v}(z) = H_{u \to v}(z) / H_{v \to v}(z)\), cancel the stationary simple pole at \(z = 1\) by multiplying numerator and denominator by \((1 - z)\), bridge coordinate-wise EGFs to OGFs via the Borel–Laplace Transform \(\mathcal{B}[e^{\lambda z}] = \frac{1}{1 - \lambda x}\), and pair Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion (Ch 08) with Poissonized truncated exponential EGFs \(\sum_{c < B_i} \frac{(p_i t)^c}{c!}\).
Master the Singing Kingdom KMP Border Theorem & Penney’s Game Correlation Systems (§14.4): Derive the exact polynomial relation between \(G(z)\) and \(F(z)\) by forcibly appending a target pattern \(S\) to surviving runs, extract \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\) over the KMP border chain \(\operatorname{Borders}(S)\) in \(O(L)\) time, and solve multi-pattern competing stopping games in \(O(m^2 L + m^3)\) via the Guibas–Odlyzko correlation matrix.
Deploy Martingale Optional Stopping & Separable Potential Drift Duality (§14.4): Re-derive string stopping times via Li’s fair-casino martingale and Doob’s Optional Stopping Theorem, construct additively separable potentials \(\Phi(a_1, \dots, a_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(a_i)\) with unit drift \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta \Phi \mid X_t] = -1\) for symmetric multi-pile processes, reduce the resulting tridiagonal balance equations to first-difference recurrences \(g(x) = f(x+1) - f(x)\), and connect \(\phi_u = -\widetilde{H}'_{u \to t}(1)\) to the Poisson drift equation \((I - P)\phi = e_t - \pi_t \mathbf{1}\).

This chapter builds directly on four foundational modules from Parts I and II:

Chapter 04: Labeled Symbolic Method & EGFs: Exponential generating functions \(\widehat{A}(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n \frac{z^n}{n!}\), independent labeled tuple products, and the hyperbolic parity filters \(\cosh(z) = \frac{e^z + e^{-z}}{2}\) and \(\sinh(z) = \frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{2}\).
Chapter 05: Rational GFs, Euclidean Division & Bostan–Mori: Rational power series \(P(z)/Q(z) \in K(z)\), transfer-matrix resolvents \((I - zT)^{-1}\), and partial-fraction decompositions.
Chapter 06: Binomial Sums, Stirling Numbers & Taylor Shift: Converting between falling factorials \(n^{\underline{k}}\) and ordinary powers \(n^k\) via Stirling numbers of the second kind \(\left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\}\), and the \(O(N \log N)\) polynomial Taylor Shift \(P(z) \mapsto P(1 + t)\).

title: 14 — Probability Generating Functions, Renewal Stopping Times, Poissonization & Martingales
section: 14.1 PGF Fundamentals, Tail-Sum Conservation & Factorial Moments
text:
14.1 PGF Fundamentals, Tail-Sum Conservation & Factorial Moments

Concrete Combinatorial Setup: Counting by When the Process Stops
Suppose a randomized algorithm or stochastic game runs in discrete steps \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) until a target stopping condition \(\mathcal{E}\) occurs for the first time. Let \(T \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \cup \{\infty\}\) denote the stopping time—the exact step index at which the process halts. At every step \(n \ge 0\), the probability mass of all possible trajectories partitions cleanly into two disjoint sets of histories:

Terminating histories (\(T = n\)): Trajectories that were still active after step \(n - 1\) and satisfy the stopping condition \(\mathcal{E}\) for the very first time at step \(n\). We denote their probability by \[f_n = \mathbb{P}(T = n) \qquad (n \ge 0).\]
Surviving (active) histories (\(T > n\)): Trajectories that have not yet triggered \(\mathcal{E}\) at any of steps \(0, 1, \dots, n\), and therefore continue to step \(n + 1\). We denote their probability by \[g_n = \mathbb{P}(T > n) \qquad (n \ge 0).\]

We package these two sequences into two ordinary generating functions in \(\mathbb{Q}[[z]]\) (or \(\mathbb{F}_p[[z]]\) when all step probabilities have denominators coprime to \(p\)):

The Probabilistic Generating Function (PGF) of the stopping time \(T\): \[F(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^T] = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T = n) z^n = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n z^n.\]
The Survival (or Tail) Generating Function of the active trajectories: \[G(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T > n) z^n = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} g_n z^n.\]

Whenever the process halts with probability \(1\) (\(\mathbb{P}(T < \infty) = 1\)), evaluating \(F(z)\) at \(z = 1\) sums the probabilities of all mutually exclusive halting steps: \[F(1) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T = n) = \mathbb{P}(T < \infty) = 1.\]


Single-Step Derivation of the Stopping-Time Conservation Identity
Why do we introduce both \(F(z)\) and \(G(z)\) instead of working with \(F(z)\) alone? Because in combinatorial applications (such as pattern matching, coupon collection, and random walks), describing a surviving state in \(G(z)\) is often much simpler than describing a first-hit state in \(F(z)\), and the two series are locked together by a universal algebraic identity.

** Diagnostic Signal**: Whenever a problem asks for the expected stopping time \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) or variance \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\) of a process whose “still running after \(n\) steps” configurations are easier to characterize than its “stopped at step \(n\) for the first time” configurations, introduce both \(F(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T = n)z^n\) and \(G(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T > n)z^n\).
** Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad**: How are \(f_n\) and \(g_n\) related at step \(n\)? Every trajectory that is still alive after step \(n - 1\) (mass \(g_{n-1}\)) either stops at step \(n\) (mass \(f_n\)) or stays alive after step \(n\) (mass \(g_n\)). Translating \(g_{n-1} = f_n + g_n\) into generating functions will let us eliminate \(F(z)\) or \(G(z)\) at will.

Let us execute this derivation step by step:

Base case at step \(n = 0\): Before any step is taken, the total probability mass is \(1\). At \(n = 0\), a trajectory either stops immediately at step \(0\) (probability \(f_0 = \mathbb{P}(T = 0)\)) or survives past step \(0\) (probability \(g_0 = \mathbb{P}(T > 0)\)): \[f_0 + g_0 = 1.\]
Conservation of probability mass at step \(n \ge 1\): The event \(\{T > n - 1\}\) (surviving step \(n - 1\)) is the disjoint union of \(\{T = n\}\) (stopping at step \(n\)) and \(\{T > n\}\) (surviving step \(n\)). Therefore, for every integer \(n \ge 1\): \[f_n + g_n = g_{n-1} \qquad (n \ge 1).\]
Summing over all \(n \ge 0\) with weight \(z^n\): Multiply the \(n = 0\) equation by \(z^0 = 1\), multiply each \(n \ge 1\) equation by \(z^n\), and add them over all \(n \ge 0\): \[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n z^n + \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} g_n z^n = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} g_{n-1} z^n.\]
Re-indexing the right-hand sum: Factor \(z\) out of the right-hand sum and substitute \(m = n - 1 \ge 0\): \[F(z) + G(z) = 1 + z \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} g_m z^m = 1 + z G(z).\]
Collecting the \(G(z)\) terms: Subtract \(z G(z)\) from both sides to obtain the Stopping-Time Conservation Identity: \[\boxed{F(z) + (1 - z) G(z) = 1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad G(z) = \frac{1 - F(z)}{1 - z}.}\]



Factorial Moments, Ordinary Moments & Variance Extraction
In the formal power series ring \(K[[z]]\), the formal derivative operator \(D_z = \frac{d}{dz}\) maps \(z^n \mapsto n z^{n-1}\). Applying \(D_z\) \(k\) times to \(F(z)\) pulls down the \(k\)-th falling factorial \(n^{\underline{k}} = n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\): \[F^{(k)}(z) = \sum_{n=k}^{\infty} n^{\underline{k}} f_n z^{n-k}.\] When \(F(z)\) (and its derivatives) converge at \(z = 1\)—or when \(F(z)\) is a rational function whose pole at \(z = 1\) has been cancelled so \(z = 1\) is regular—evaluating \(F^{(k)}(z)\) at \(z = 1\) yields the \(k\)-th factorial moment of \(T\): \[F^{(k)}(1) = \sum_{n=k}^{\infty} n^{\underline{k}} \mathbb{P}(T = n) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\underline{k}}\right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[T(T-1)\cdots(T-k+1)\right].\]
Now let us differentiate the conservation identity \(F(z) = 1 - (1 - z)G(z)\) \(k\) times with respect to \(z\) for \(k \ge 1\). Because \((1 - z)\) has degree \(1\), its first derivative is \(-1\) and all higher derivatives vanish. By the Leibniz product rule: \[F^{(k)}(z) = -(1 - z) G^{(k)}(z) + k G^{(k-1)}(z) \qquad (k \ge 1).\] Setting \(z = 1\) annihilates the \((1 - z) G^{(k)}(1)\) term and leaves a direct bridge between the derivatives of \(F\) and \(G\): \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\underline{k}}\right] = F^{(k)}(1) = k G^{(k-1)}(1) \qquad (k \ge 1).}\]
Specializing to \(k = 1\) and \(k = 2\) gives the fundamental formulas of competitive programming probability:

First Moment (Expected Stopping Time) & Tail-Sum Formula (\(k = 1\)): \[\mathbb{E}[T] = F'(1) = G(1) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T > n).\] Notice what \(G(1) = \sum_{n \ge 0} g_n\) says combinatorially: every step \(n \ge 0\) in which the process is still alive (\(T > n\)) contributes \(+1\) to the total lifespan \(T\), confirming \(T = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbf{1}[T > n]\).
Second Factorial Moment (\(k = 2\)): \[\mathbb{E}[T(T - 1)] = F''(1) = 2 G'(1) = 2 \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n \, \mathbb{P}(T > n).\]
Variance in Terms of \(F(z)\) and \(G(z)\): Since \(T^2 = T(T - 1) + T\), linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb{E}[T^2] = \mathbb{E}[T(T - 1)] + \mathbb{E}[T] = F''(1) + F'(1)\). Subtracting \(\mathbb{E}[T]^2 = F'(1)^2\) yields: \[\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(T) = F''(1) + F'(1) - F'(1)^2 = 2 G'(1) + G(1) - G(1)^2.}\]
Arbitrary \(k\)-th Ordinary Moments via the Euler Operator \(\vartheta_z = z D_z\) (Ch 06): Whereas \(D_z^k\) extracts falling factorials \(n^{\underline{k}}\), applying the Euler differential operator \(\vartheta_z = z \frac{d}{dz}\) (which maps \(z^n \mapsto n z^n\)) \(k\) times pulls down \(n^k\) directly: \[\left(\vartheta_z^k F\right)(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n^k f_n z^n \implies \mathbb{E}[T^k] = \left.\left(\vartheta_z^k F\right)(z)\right|_{z=1}.\] By the Stirling operator identity \(\vartheta_z^k = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} z^j D_z^j\) established in Chapter 06, evaluating at \(z = 1\) converts factorial moments into ordinary moments: \[\mathbb{E}[T^k] = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} F^{(j)}(1) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} j \, G^{(j-1)}(1) \qquad (k \ge 1).\]







NoteBridge to Moment & Cumulant Generating Functions (\(z = e^t\))



Substituting \(z = e^t\) into the PGF \(F(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^T]\) converts the Euler operator \(\vartheta_z = z \frac{d}{dz}\) into ordinary differentiation \(\frac{d}{dt}\), producing the Moment Generating Function (MGF): \[M_T(t) = F(e^t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tT}] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}[T^k] \frac{t^k}{k!}.\] Because \(M_T(0) = F(1) = 1\), its formal logarithm \(K_T(t) = \ln F(e^t) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \kappa_k \frac{t^k}{k!}\) is well-defined in \(\mathbb{Q}[[t]]\) and is called the Cumulant Generating Function. Expanding \(\ln(1 + (M_T(t) - 1))\) up to \(t^2\) gives \[K_T(t) = \ln\!\left(1 + \mathbb{E}[T] t + \mathbb{E}[T^2] \frac{t^2}{2!} + O(t^3)\right) = \mathbb{E}[T] t + \left(\mathbb{E}[T^2] - \mathbb{E}[T]^2\right) \frac{t^2}{2!} + O(t^3),\] so the first cumulant is \(\kappa_1 = \mathbb{E}[T]\) and the second cumulant is \(\kappa_2 = \operatorname{Var}(T)\). Because \(\ln(F_1(e^t) F_2(e^t)) = \ln F_1(e^t) + \ln F_2(e^t)\), all cumulants \(\kappa_k\) are additive across independent random variables.




Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace: Geometric Stopping Time & Small Coefficient Verification
Let us verify the entire §14.1 pipeline on a concrete process where every coefficient can be checked by hand. Suppose each step \(n \ge 1\) succeeds with probability \(p \in (0, 1)\) and fails with probability \(q = 1 - p\), and \(T \ge 1\) is the step of the first success.

Coefficients for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\):

At \(n = 0\): \(f_0 = \mathbb{P}(T = 0) = 0\), and \(g_0 = \mathbb{P}(T > 0) = 1\) (since \(f_0 + g_0 = 1\)).
At \(n = 1\): \(f_1 = p\), and \(g_1 = q\) (check: \(f_1 + g_1 = p + q = 1 = g_0\)).
At \(n = 2\): \(f_2 = qp\), and \(g_2 = q^2\) (check: \(f_2 + g_2 = q(p + q) = q = g_1\)).
In general, for \(n \ge 1\), \(f_n = q^{n-1}p\) and \(g_n = q^n\).

Closed-form generating functions: \[F(z) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p q^{n-1} z^n = \frac{pz}{1 - qz}, \qquad G(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} q^n z^n = \frac{1}{1 - qz}.\]
Verifying conservation \(F(z) + (1 - z)G(z) = 1\): \[F(z) + (1 - z)G(z) = \frac{pz + (1 - z)}{1 - qz} = \frac{1 - (1 - p)z}{1 - qz} = \frac{1 - qz}{1 - qz} = 1.\]
Extracting expectation and variance via \(G(z)\): Since \(1 - q = p\), evaluating \(G(z) = (1 - qz)^{-1}\) and \(G'(z) = q(1 - qz)^{-2}\) at \(z = 1\) gives: \[\mathbb{E}[T] = G(1) = \frac{1}{1 - q} = \frac{1}{p}, \qquad G'(1) = \frac{q}{(1 - q)^2} = \frac{q}{p^2},\] \[\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2G'(1) + G(1) - G(1)^2 = \frac{2q}{p^2} + \frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{p^2} = \frac{2(1 - p) + p - 1}{p^2} = \frac{1 - p}{p^2} = \frac{q}{p^2}.\] Notice that differentiating \(G(z) = (1 - qz)^{-1}\) once was noticeably cleaner than differentiating \(F(z) = pz(1 - qz)^{-1}\) twice by the quotient rule!

section: 14.2 Formal Taylor Shift \(z = 1 + t \bmod t^3\) for \(0/0\) Pole Cancellation
text:
14.2 Formal Taylor Shift \(z = 1 + t \bmod t^3\) for \(0/0\) Pole Cancellation

The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad
In finite-state Markov chains, string automata, and renewal processes, solving a system of linear equations over \(\mathbb{Q}(z)\) (or simplifying a sum of partial fractions) expresses the stopping-time PGF as a rational function \[F(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)},\] where \(P(z), Q(z) \in K[z]\) are polynomials (or truncated series).

** Diagnostic Signal: You have derived a rational PGF \(F(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)}\) and need \(\mathbb{E}[T] = F'(1)\) or \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = F''(1) + F'(1) - F'(1)^2\), but** substituting \(z = 1\) gives \(P(1) = 0\) and \(Q(1) = 0\) because an uncancelled factor \((1 - z)^v\) (\(v \ge 1\)) divides both numerator and denominator.
** Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Why is \((1 - z)\) dividing both \(P(z)\) and \(Q(z)\)? For instance, in §14.3 we will see that unnormalized visit series \(H(z)\) have a simple pole at \(z = 1\); clearing denominators across \(m\) states introduces \((1 - z)^v\) into both \(P(z)\) and \(Q(z)\). If we try to compute \(F'(1)\) via the quotient rule \(F'(z) = \frac{P'(z)Q(z) - P(z)Q'(z)}{Q(z)^2}\), plugging in \(z = 1\) gives \(\frac{0}{0}\)! Worse, applying L’Hôpital’s rule to \(F''(z) = \frac{d^2}{dz^2}\left(\frac{P(z)}{Q(z)}\right)\) when \(P(1) = Q(1) = 0\) requires differentiating up to order \(v + 2\). How do we cancel the root at \(z = 1\) algebraically** and extract \(F(1), F'(1), F''(1)\) in one stroke? Instead of differentiating in \(z\) and then substituting \(z = 1\), we substitute \(z = 1 + t\) first! In the local coordinate \(t = z - 1\), Taylor’s theorem says \[F(1 + t) = F(1) + F'(1) t + \frac{F''(1)}{2!} t^2 + O(t^3).\] Furthermore, a shared root at \(z = 1\) of multiplicity \(v\) becomes a shared monomial factor \(t^v\) in \(P(1 + t)\) and \(Q(1 + t)\), which we can strip by shifting indices before performing a 3-term formal power series division modulo \(t^3\)!







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: The \(0/0\) Quotient-Rule & L’Hôpital Trap at \(z = 1\)




The Trap: Attempting to evaluate \(F'(1) = \frac{P'(1)Q(1) - P(1)Q'(1)}{Q(1)^2}\) when \(Q(1) \equiv 0 \pmod p\). In modular arithmetic over \(\mathbb{F}_p\), inv(Q(1)) either returns \(0\) (via Fermat’s Little Theorem qpow(0, p - 2) == 0) or triggers a division-by-zero assertion, silently corrupting \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\). Even when \(v = 1\) is cancelled manually by L’Hôpital’s rule (\(F(1) = P'(1)/Q'(1)\)), computing \(F'(1)\) and \(F''(1)\) via repeated L’Hôpital quotients requires up to \(Q^{(3)}(1)\) and \(P^{(3)}(1)\) with intricate cross-terms.
The Remedy: Never apply the quotient rule or manual L’Hôpital differentiation to \(P(z)/Q(z)\) at \(z = 1\). Always expand \(P(1 + t)\) and \(Q(1 + t)\) in the jet ring \(K[t]/(t^{v+3})\), strip their shared \(t\)-adic valuation \(v = \operatorname{val}_t Q(1 + t)\) by shifting \(p_j = [t^{v+j}]P(1+t)\) and \(q_j = [t^{v+j}]Q(1+t)\) for \(j \in \{0, 1, 2\}\), and divide in \(K[t]/(t^3)\).





Single-Step Derivation of the 3-Term Formal Quotient Engine in \(K[t]/(t^3)\)
Let \(P(z), Q(z) \in K[z]\) be polynomials of degree at most \(N\) over a field \(K\) of characteristic \(p = 0\) or \(p > N\) (or \(p > v + 2\) if \(P(1+t), Q(1+t)\) are constructed directly in \(t\)).

Step 1 (Taylor Shift to \(z = 1 + t\)): Using the polynomial Taylor Shift engine from Chapter 06 (or direct coefficient accumulation when \(P\) and \(Q\) have sparse/structured forms), write: \[\widetilde{P}(t) = P(1 + t) = \sum_{j=0}^{N} \tilde{p}_j t^j, \qquad \widetilde{Q}(t) = Q(1 + t) = \sum_{j=0}^{N} \tilde{q}_j t^j,\] where \(\tilde{p}_j = \frac{P^{(j)}(1)}{j!} = \sum_{n=j}^{N} \binom{n}{j} [z^n]P(z)\) and \(\tilde{q}_j = \frac{Q^{(j)}(1)}{j!} = \sum_{n=j}^{N} \binom{n}{j} [z^n]Q(z)\).
Step 2 (Valuation Cancellation): Let \(v = \operatorname{val}_t(\widetilde{Q}(t)) = \min\{j \ge 0 : \tilde{q}_j \neq 0\}\) be the \(t\)-adic valuation of the denominator. Because \(F(z) = P(z)/Q(z)\) is regular at \(z = 1\) with \(F(1) = 1\), \(\widetilde{P}(t)\) must also vanish to order at least \(v\) at \(t = 0\) (\(\tilde{p}_0 = \dots = \tilde{p}_{v-1} = 0\)) and satisfy \(\tilde{p}_v = \tilde{q}_v \neq 0\). Dividing both \(\widetilde{P}(t)\) and \(\widetilde{Q}(t)\) by \(t^v\) in the Laurent field \(K((t))\) leaves two series with nonzero constant terms: \[p_0 + p_1 t + p_2 t^2 + O(t^3) = t^{-v}\widetilde{P}(t), \qquad q_0 + q_1 t + q_2 t^2 + O(t^3) = t^{-v}\widetilde{Q}(t),\] where \(p_r = \tilde{p}_{v+r}\) and \(q_r = \tilde{q}_{v+r}\) for \(r \in \{0, 1, 2\}\), and \(q_0 \in K^\times\) is invertible.
Step 3 (3-Term Formal Division in \(K[t]/(t^3)\)): We seek \(F(1 + t) \equiv c_0 + c_1 t + c_2 t^2 \pmod{t^3}\) such that \[\left(q_0 + q_1 t + q_2 t^2\right)\left(c_0 + c_1 t + c_2 t^2\right) \equiv p_0 + p_1 t + p_2 t^2 \pmod{t^3}.\] Comparing coefficients of \(t^0\), \(t^1\), and \(t^2\) one power at a time gives:

\([t^0]\) equation: \(q_0 c_0 = p_0 \implies c_0 = \frac{p_0}{q_0} = 1\) (confirming proper probability normalization \(F(1) = 1\)).
\([t^1]\) equation: \(q_0 c_1 + q_1 c_0 = p_1 \implies c_1 = \frac{p_1 - c_0 q_1}{q_0} = \frac{p_1 - q_1}{q_0}\).
\([t^2]\) equation: \(q_0 c_2 + q_1 c_1 + q_2 c_0 = p_2 \implies c_2 = \frac{p_2 - c_0 q_2 - c_1 q_1}{q_0} = \frac{p_2 - q_2}{q_0} - \frac{q_1(p_1 - q_1)}{q_0^2}\).

Step 4 (Reading off \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\)): Since \(F(1 + t) = 1 + F'(1) t + \frac{F''(1)}{2} t^2 + O(t^3) = 1 + c_1 t + c_2 t^2 + O(t^3)\), matching coefficients of \(t^1\) and \(t^2\) yields \(F'(1) = c_1\) and \(F''(1) = 2c_2\). Therefore: \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = c_1 = \frac{p_1 - q_1}{q_0}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(T) = 2c_2 + c_1 - c_1^2.}\]



Hand-Checkable Worked Example: Pole-Cancelled Rational PGF (\(N = 3\))
Suppose a 3-state Markov chain for coin tossing until HH (with an uneliminated absorbing-state factor \((1 - z)\) in both numerator and denominator) produces the unreduced rational PGF \[F(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)} = \frac{z^2(1 - z)}{(4 - 2z - z^2)(1 - z)} = \frac{z^2 - z^3}{4 - 6z + z^2 + z^3}.\] Notice that plugging in \(z = 1\) gives \(P(1) = 1 - 1 = 0\) and \(Q(1) = 4 - 6 + 1 + 1 = 0\), a \(0/0\) indeterminate form. Let us apply the 4-step Formal Jet Engine by hand:

Substitute \(z = 1 + t\):

Numerator: \[\widetilde{P}(t) = (1 + t)^2 - (1 + t)^3 = (1 + 2t + t^2) - (1 + 3t + 3t^2 + t^3) = -t - 2t^2 - t^3.\]
Denominator: \[\widetilde{Q}(t) = 4 - 6(1 + t) + (1 + t)^2 + (1 + t)^3 = 4 - (6 + 6t) + (1 + 2t + t^2) + (1 + 3t + 3t^2 + t^3) = -t + 4t^2 + t^3.\]

Cancel common valuation \(v = 1\): Both \(\widetilde{P}(t)\) and \(\widetilde{Q}(t)\) have valuation \(v = 1\). Dividing both by \(t^1\) gives \[p_0 + p_1 t + p_2 t^2 = -1 - 2t - t^2, \qquad q_0 + q_1 t + q_2 t^2 = -1 + 4t + t^2,\] so \((p_0, p_1, p_2) = (-1, -2, -1)\) and \((q_0, q_1, q_2) = (-1, 4, 1)\).
Extract \(c_0, c_1, c_2\) in \(K[t]/(t^3)\):

\(c_0 = \frac{p_0}{q_0} = \frac{-1}{-1} = 1\) (confirming \(F(1) = 1\)).
\(c_1 = \frac{p_1 - q_1}{q_0} = \frac{-2 - 4}{-1} = 6 \implies \mathbb{E}[T] = 6\).
\(c_2 = \frac{p_2 - q_2 - c_1 q_1}{q_0} = \frac{-1 - 1 - 6(4)}{-1} = \frac{-26}{-1} = 26 \implies \mathbb{E}[T(T-1)] = 2c_2 = 52\).

Compute variance: \[\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2c_2 + c_1 - c_1^2 = 52 + 6 - 36 = 22.\] In just three lines of polynomial arithmetic in \(K[t]/(t^3)\), we cancelled the \(0/0\) singularity and obtained both \(\mathbb{E}[T] = 6\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 22\).







TipAlgorithm Contract: Formal Jet Moment Extractor (jet_moments_at_one)




Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Shifted Taylor coefficient arrays \(\tilde{p}[0 \dots N]\) and \(\tilde{q}[0 \dots N]\) representing \(P(1+t) = \sum_{j=0}^{N} \tilde{p}_j t^j\) and \(Q(1+t) = \sum_{j=0}^{N} \tilde{q}_j t^j\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\), with common zero-multiplicity \(v = \operatorname{val}_t(\widetilde{Q}) \in [0, N - 2]\).
Preconditions:

\(v = \min\{j \in [0, N] : \tilde{q}[j] \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\}\) exists with \(v + 2 \le N\).
\(\tilde{p}[j] \equiv 0 \pmod p\) for all \(0 \le j < v\), and \(\tilde{p}[v] \equiv \tilde{q}[v] \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) (so \(\lim_{z \to 1} F(z) = 1\)).
Characteristic condition: \(p > N\) if \(\tilde{p}, \tilde{q}\) are computed from \(P(z), Q(z)\) via \(O(N \log N)\) binomial Taylor shift (Ch 06), or \(p > 2\) if \(\tilde{p}, \tilde{q}\) are constructed directly in \(t\) modulo \(t^3\).

Postconditions (Output): Pair \((\mathbb{E}[T], \operatorname{Var}(T)) \in \mathbb{F}_p^2\) where \(\mathbb{E}[T] = c_1 = \frac{p_1 - q_1}{q_0}\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2c_2 + c_1 - c_1^2\) with \(c_2 = \frac{p_2 - q_2 - c_1 q_1}{q_0}\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space if full polynomial Taylor shift is needed; \(O(\log p)\) time and \(O(1)\) space once the 3-term reduced jets \((p_0, p_1, p_2)\) and \((q_0, q_1, q_2)\) are extracted.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Shifting \(z = 1 + t\) is a ring automorphism of \(K[z]\) mapping the ideal \((z - 1)^k\) to \((t^k)\), and after stripping \(t^v\), the relation \(\left(\sum_{j=0}^{2} c_j t^j\right)\left(\sum_{j=0}^{2} q_j t^j\right) \equiv \sum_{j=0}^{2} p_j t^j \pmod{t^3}\) holds in \(K[t]/(t^3)\) with \(q_0 \in K^\times\).

// Extracts (E[T], Var(T)) mod p from shifted jets P(1+t), Q(1+t) after stripping t^v
pair<Mint, Mint> jet_moments_from_reduced(Mint p0, Mint p1, Mint p2,
                                          Mint q0, Mint q1, Mint q2) {
    assert(q0 != 0 && p0 == q0); // Precondition: q0 in K^x and F(1) = p0/q0 = 1
    Mint inv_q0 = q0.inv();
    Mint c1 = (p1 - q1) * inv_q0;               // E[T] = F'(1)
    Mint c2 = (p2 - q2 - c1 * q1) * inv_q0;     // E[T(T-1)] / 2 = F''(1) / 2
    Mint var_T = 2 * c2 + c1 - c1 * c1;         // Var(T) = F''(1) + F'(1) - F'(1)^2
    return {c1, var_T};
}

14.3 Renewal First-Passage Deconvolution (\(F = H_{0 \to E} / H_{E \to E}\)) & Continuous-Time Poissonization

Part A: First-Passage Renewal Deconvolution & The \((1-z)\) Pole Cancellation Trick
In many random walk and toggle problems—such as flipping switches on an \(n\)-dimensional hypercube ([ZJOI2019] 开关), flipping cells in a grid (ARC 136 F), or moving 3 particles on \(\mathbb{Z}\) until they meet (ABC 289 Ex)—computing the probability \(f_n = \mathbb{P}(T_{u \to v} = n)\) that the process reaches a target state \(v\) from initial state \(u\) at step \(n\) for the first time seems to require tracking the entire history to forbid earlier visits at steps \(1, \dots, n - 1\).

** Diagnostic Signal: It is easy to compute the unconstrained visit probability** \(h_{u \to v, n} = \mathbb{P}(X_n = v \mid X_0 = u)\) of being at state \(v\) at step \(n\) (regardless of whether \(v\) was visited earlier)—either via coordinate-wise EGF products, Walsh–Hadamard / eigenvalues, or binomial convolutions—and the process is Markovian (time-homogeneous) upon reaching \(v\).
** Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: How are unconstrained visits to \(v\) related to the first** visit to \(v\)? Every walk that starts at \(u\) and stands on \(v\) at step \(n\) must have visited \(v\) for the very first time at some uniquely determined step \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}\). After reaching \(v\) at step \(k\), the remaining \(n - k\) steps form an unconstrained walk from \(v\) back to \(v\) of length \(n - k\)! Because a convolution in \(n\) becomes a product of OGFs, this partitions \(H_{u \to v}(z)\) into \(F_{u \to v}(z) \cdot H_{v \to v}(z)\).

Let us write out this Renewal First-Passage Decomposition step by step:

Define the three OGFs:

Unconstrained visit OGF from \(u\) to \(v\): \(H_{u \to v}(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(X_n = v \mid X_0 = u) z^n\).
Unconstrained return OGF from \(v\) to \(v\): \(H_{v \to v}(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(X_n = v \mid X_0 = v) z^n\) (note that \([z^0]H_{v \to v}(z) = 1\)).
First-passage PGF from \(u\) to \(v\): \(F_{u \to v}(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T_{u \to v} = n) z^n\).

Partition the event \(\{X_n = v\}\) by the first hitting step \(T_{u \to v} = k\): Since \(\{T_{u \to v} = 0\}, \{T_{u \to v} = 1\}, \dots, \{T_{u \to v} = n\}\) partition the event \(\{X_n = v\}\), the Markov property at step \(k\) gives: \[\mathbb{P}(X_n = v \mid X_0 = u) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \mathbb{P}(T_{u \to v} = k) \cdot \mathbb{P}(X_n = v \mid X_k = v) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \mathbb{P}(T_{u \to v} = k) \cdot \mathbb{P}(X_{n-k} = v \mid X_0 = v).\]
Translate the discrete convolution into \(K[[z]]\): Multiplying by \(z^n\) and summing over \(n \ge 0\) recognizes the right-hand side as the Cauchy product of \(F_{u \to v}(z)\) and \(H_{v \to v}(z)\): \[H_{u \to v}(z) = F_{u \to v}(z) \cdot H_{v \to v}(z).\]
Invert \(H_{v \to v}(z)\): Because \([z^0]H_{v \to v}(z) = \mathbb{P}(X_0 = v \mid X_0 = v) = 1 \in K^\times\) is always a unit in \(K[[z]]\), \(H_{v \to v}(z)\) is formally invertible (Ch 01), giving the Renewal First-Passage Formula: \[\boxed{F_{u \to v}(z) = \frac{H_{u \to v}(z)}{H_{v \to v}(z)}.}\]







WarningFailure Modes & Remedies: Renewal Deconvolution Traps




Trap 1 (Confusing Any-Visit \(H_{u \to v}(z)\) with First-Passage \(F_{u \to v}(z)\) & Evaluating \(H_{v \to v}(1)\) Directly):

What Goes Wrong: Computing the unconstrained visit OGF \(H_{u \to v}(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(X_n = v \mid X_0 = u) z^n\) via FWT / EGF and attempting to evaluate \(H'_{u \to v}(1)\) directly, or attempting to divide \(H'_{u \to v}(1) / H_{v \to v}(1)\) without clearing the \((1 - z)^{-1}\) pole.
Why It Fails: In a recurrent Markov chain without absorption at \(v\), the target state \(v\) is visited infinitely often! Both \(H_{u \to v}(z)\) and \(H_{v \to v}(z)\) have a simple pole \(\frac{\pi_v}{1 - z}\) at \(z = 1\) (so \(H_{u \to v}(1) = H_{v \to v}(1) = \infty\), or a division-by-zero error \(\frac{1}{1 - 1} \bmod p\)). Furthermore, \(H_{u \to v}(z)\) overcounts trajectories by every subsequent return to \(v\).
Remedy: First divide out returns via \(F_{u \to v}(z) = \frac{H_{u \to v}(z)}{H_{v \to v}(z)}\), and then multiply both numerator and denominator by \((1 - z)\) to define the pole-cancelled series \(\widetilde{H}_{u \to v}(z) = (1 - z)H_{u \to v}(z)\) and \(\widetilde{H}_{v \to v}(z) = (1 - z)H_{v \to v}(z)\) before evaluating at \(z = 1 + t \bmod t^3\).

Trap 2 (Asymmetric Multi-Target Sets Break Single-Series Renewal Deconvolution):

What Goes Wrong: Suppose the stopping condition is reaching any state in a target subset \(\mathcal{T} \subseteq V\) with \(|\mathcal{T}| \ge 2\). Writing \(H_{u \to \mathcal{T}}(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(X_n \in \mathcal{T} \mid X_0 = u)z^n\) and dividing by \(H_{\mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{T}}(z)\) fails if different states \(w, w' \in \mathcal{T}\) have different future return series \(H_{w \to \mathcal{T}}(z) \neq H_{w' \to \mathcal{T}}(z)\): \[H_{u \to \mathcal{T}}(z) = \sum_{w \in \mathcal{T}} F_{u \to w}^{\text{first in }\mathcal{T}}(z) \, H_{w \to \mathcal{T}}(z),\] which does not factor into \(F_{u \to \mathcal{T}}(z) \cdot H_{\mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{T}}(z)\)!
Remedy: You may apply scalar division \(F_{u \to \mathcal{T}}(z) = H_{u \to \mathcal{T}}(z) / H_{\text{return}}(z)\) if and only if Target Return Symmetry holds: there is a single series \(H_{\text{return}}(z)\) such that \(H_{w \to \mathcal{T}}(z) = H_{\text{return}}(z)\) for every \(w \in \mathcal{T}\) (for example, by translation invariance in ABC 289 Ex or row/column permutation symmetry in ARC 136 F). When \(\mathcal{T}\) is asymmetric and small (\(|\mathcal{T}| = m \le 300\)), set up an \(m \times m\) matrix renewal system over \(w \in \mathcal{T}\) instead (as in Penney’s Game, §14.4).





The EGF-to-OGF Borel Transform Bridge & \((1-z)\) Pole Cancellation
How do we apply \(F_{u \to v}(z) = H_{u \to v}(z) / H_{v \to v}(z)\) when the walk length is unbounded and we want \(\mathbb{E}[T_{u \to v}] = F'_{u \to v}(1)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T_{u \to v})\)?
In independent-coordinate toggle problems (such as flipping \(n\) switches where switch \(i\) is flipped at each step with probability \(p_i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i = 1\)), the number of steps distributed across the \(n\) coordinates in an \(m\)-step walk is a labeled tuple (Ch 04), so the natural generating function that factors across coordinates \(i = 1, \dots, n\) is the Exponential Generating Function (EGF): \[\widehat{H}_{u \to v}(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(X_m = v \mid X_0 = u) \frac{x^m}{m!} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \left(\frac{e^{p_i x} + (-1)^{u_i \oplus v_i} e^{-p_i x}}{2}\right).\] Expanding this finite product (via a 1D knapsack DP over the discrete exponents) expresses both \(\widehat{H}_{u \to v}(x)\) and \(\widehat{H}_{v \to v}(x)\) as linear combinations of exponentials: \[\widehat{H}_{u \to v}(x) = \sum_{\lambda} c_{\lambda} e^{\lambda x}, \qquad \widehat{H}_{v \to v}(x) = \sum_{\lambda} d_{\lambda} e^{\lambda x},\] where the eigenvalues \(\lambda \in [-1, 1]\) are rational multiples of \(1/P\) (\(P = \sum A_i\)).
To pass from the EGF \(\widehat{H}(x)\) to the OGF \(H(z)\) needed by the renewal equation \(F(z) = H_{u \to v}(z) / H_{v \to v}(z)\), we apply the Borel–Laplace Transform \(\mathcal{B}: K[[x]] \to K[[z]]\), defined coefficient-wise by multiplying \(\frac{x^m}{m!}\) by \(m!\) (or analytically by \(\mathcal{B}[\widehat{H}](z) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \widehat{H}(zt)\,dt\)): \[\mathcal{B}\!\left[e^{\lambda x}\right](z) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} m! \left[x^m\right] \left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^k x^k}{k!}\right) z^m = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} (\lambda z)^m = \frac{1}{1 - \lambda z}.\] By linearity, applying \(\mathcal{B}\) term by term converts the exponential sums into partial-fraction rational OGFs: \[H_{u \to v}(z) = \sum_{\lambda} \frac{c_{\lambda}}{1 - \lambda z}, \qquad H_{v \to v}(z) = \sum_{\lambda} \frac{d_{\lambda}}{1 - \lambda z}.\]
Now look closely at what happens at \(z = 1\):

For an ergodic Markov chain (or up to parity), the unique maximum eigenvalue is \(\lambda = 1\), with coefficient \(c_1 = d_1 = \pi_v > 0\) equal to the stationary weight of state \(v\) (e.g., \(\pi_v = 2^{-n}\) on the \(n\)-cube).
Therefore, at \(z = 1\), the \(\lambda = 1\) summand \(\frac{\pi_v}{1 - z}\) diverges in both \(H_{u \to v}(z)\) and \(H_{v \to v}(z)\): every recurrent state is visited infinitely many times in an infinite walk, so \(\sum_{m \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(X_m = v) = \infty\)!

How do we remove this \(\infty / \infty\) singularity at \(z = 1\)? Multiply both numerator and denominator of \(F_{u \to v}(z) = \frac{H_{u \to v}(z)}{H_{v \to v}(z)}\) by \((1 - z)\)! Define the pole-cancelled visit series: \[\widetilde{H}_{u \to v}(z) = (1 - z) H_{u \to v}(z) = c_1 + (1 - z) \sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{c_{\lambda}}{1 - \lambda z}, \qquad \widetilde{H}_{v \to v}(z) = (1 - z) H_{v \to v}(z) = d_1 + (1 - z) \sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{d_{\lambda}}{1 - \lambda z}.\] Now every summand with \(\lambda \neq 1\) has a non-vanishing denominator \(1 - \lambda \neq 0\) at \(z = 1\)! Substituting the §14.2 formal Taylor shift \(z = 1 + t \bmod t^3\) (so \(1 - z = -t\)) and expanding each denominator modulo \(t^2\) via \(\frac{1}{1 - \lambda(1 + t)} = \frac{1}{(1 - \lambda) - \lambda t} = \frac{1}{1 - \lambda} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \frac{\lambda}{1 - \lambda} t} \equiv \frac{1}{1 - \lambda} + \frac{\lambda}{(1 - \lambda)^2} t \pmod{t^2}\) immediately expands \(\widetilde{H}_{u \to v}(1 + t)\) and \(\widetilde{H}_{v \to v}(1 + t)\) in \(K[t]/(t^3)\): \[\widetilde{H}_{u \to v}(1 + t) = c_1 - t \sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{c_{\lambda}}{(1 - \lambda) - \lambda t} \equiv \pi_v - \left(\sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{c_{\lambda}}{1 - \lambda}\right) t - \left(\sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{c_{\lambda} \lambda}{(1 - \lambda)^2}\right) t^2 \pmod{t^3}.\] Applying the 3-term formal quotient formula from §14.2 (\(p_0 = q_0 = \pi_v\), \(p_1 = -\sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{c_\lambda}{1 - \lambda}\), \(q_1 = -\sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{d_\lambda}{1 - \lambda}\)) gives the Pole-Cancelled Renewal Expectation & Variance Formulas: \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{u \to v}] = \frac{p_1 - q_1}{\pi_v} = \frac{1}{\pi_v} \sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{d_{\lambda} - c_{\lambda}}{1 - \lambda},}\] and with \(p_2 = -\sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{c_\lambda \lambda}{(1 - \lambda)^2}\) and \(q_2 = -\sum_{\lambda \neq 1} \frac{d_\lambda \lambda}{(1 - \lambda)^2}\), the second factorial moment is \(\mathbb{E}[T_{u \to v}(T_{u \to v}-1)] = 2c_2 = 2\frac{p_2 - q_2 - \mathbb{E}[T_{u\to v}] q_1}{\pi_v}\).


Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace: 2-Switch Walk ([ZJOI2019] 开关 at \(n = 2\))
Suppose \(n = 2\) switches start at \(u = (0, 0)\) and we want the first-hit expectation and variance to reach \(v = (1, 1)\), where each step flips switch \(1\) with probability \(1/2\) and switch \(2\) with probability \(1/2\).

EGF products:

Reaching \(v = (1, 1)\) requires both switches to be flipped an odd number of times: \[\widehat{H}_{u \to v}(x) = \left(\frac{e^{x/2} - e^{-x/2}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} e^{x} - \frac{2}{4} e^{0 \cdot x} + \frac{1}{4} e^{-x}.\]
Returning to \(v = (1, 1)\) requires both switches to be flipped an even number of times: \[\widehat{H}_{v \to v}(x) = \left(\frac{e^{x/2} + e^{-x/2}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} e^{x} + \frac{2}{4} e^{0 \cdot x} + \frac{1}{4} e^{-x}.\] Thus the eigenvalues are \(\lambda \in \{1, 0, -1\}\) with \(\pi_v = c_1 = d_1 = \frac{1}{4}\), \((c_0, d_0) = (-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})\), and \((c_{-1}, d_{-1}) = (\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{4})\).

Evaluate the pole-cancelled jets at \(z = 1 + t \bmod t^3\):

First-order coefficients \(p_1, q_1\): \[p_1 = -\left(\frac{-1/2}{1 - 0} + \frac{1/4}{1 - (-1)}\right) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{3}{8}, \qquad q_1 = -\left(\frac{1/2}{1 - 0} + \frac{1/4}{1 - (-1)}\right) = -\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{8} = -\frac{5}{8}.\] Hence \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \frac{p_1 - q_1}{\pi_v} = \frac{3/8 - (-5/8)}{1/4} = \frac{1}{1/4} = 4\).
Second-order coefficients \(p_2, q_2\) (only \(\lambda = -1\) contributes to \(\frac{\lambda}{(1-\lambda)^2} = \frac{-1}{4}\) since \(\lambda = 0\) has numerator \(0\)): \[p_2 = -\left(\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{-1}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{16}, \qquad q_2 = -\left(\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{-1}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{16}.\] Hence \(c_2 = \frac{p_2 - q_2 - \mathbb{E}[T] q_1}{\pi_v} = \frac{0 - 4(-5/8)}{1/4} = 10\), so \(\mathbb{E}[T(T-1)] = 20\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 20 + 4 - 4^2 = 8\). Let us check by elementary Markov chain states! From distance \(2\) (\((0,0)\)), \(1\) step always moves to distance \(1\); from distance \(1\), with prob \(1/2\) we reach \((1,1)\) and with prob \(1/2\) we return to \((0,0)\). Thus \(T = 2G\) where \(G \sim \operatorname{Geom}(1/2)\), which indeed has \(\mathbb{E}[T] = 2(2) = 4\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 4 \operatorname{Var}(G) = 4(2) = 8\)!








NoteAlgorithm Contract: Pole-Cancelled Renewal First-Passage Moment Extractor




Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Spectral expansion arrays \(c[-S \dots S]\) and \(d[-S \dots S]\) of the unconstrained hit EGF \(\widehat{H}_{u \to v}(x) = \sum_{k=-S}^{S} c_k e^{(k/S)x}\) and return EGF \(\widehat{H}_{v \to v}(x) = \sum_{k=-S}^{S} d_k e^{(k/S)x}\), where \(S = \sum_{i=1}^n A_i \ge 1\) and index \(k = S\) corresponds to the stationary eigenvalue \(\lambda_S = 1\).
Preconditions:

The Markov chain is ergodic (or ergodic on the reachable parity component) so the \(\lambda = 1\) pole is simple and \(c_S = d_S = \pi_v \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).
For all \(-S \le k < S\), \(1 - \frac{k}{S} = \frac{S - k}{S} \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) (holds whenever \(2S < p\)).
Target Return Symmetry: Every state \(w\) in the target set \(\mathcal{T}\) has the exact same return EGF \(\widehat{H}_{w \to \mathcal{T}}(x) = \widehat{H}_{v \to v}(x)\).

Postconditions (Output): First-passage expectation \(\mathbb{E}[T_{u \to v}] = \frac{1}{\pi_v} \sum_{k=-S}^{S-1} \frac{d_k - c_k}{1 - k/S} \pmod p\) (and variance \(\operatorname{Var}(T_{u \to v}) \bmod p\) via the second-order pole-cancelled jet).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n S)\) time and \(O(S)\) space to build \(c[-S \dots S]\) and \(d[-S \dots S]\) via 1D knapsack DP, plus \(O(S)\) time (with linear-time modular inverses) to accumulate the pole-cancelled sum.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing the first \(i\) coordinates with partial weight sum \(S_i = \sum_{j=1}^i A_j\), the DP array stores the exact coefficients of \(\prod_{j=1}^i \frac{e^{(A_j/S)x} \pm e^{-(A_j/S)x}}{2}\) on the symmetric support \([-S_i, S_i]\).







Part B: Continuous-Time Poissonization, Truncated Exponential EGFs & Min–Max IE
Let us now turn to the second major PGF engine of §14.3: Generalized Coupon Collection with Multiplicity Thresholds (AGC 038 E — Gachapon, Luogu P4707 — 重返现世, UOJ 390 — 百鸽笼).
Suppose there are \(N\) items; at each discrete step, item \(i\) is drawn independently with probability \(p_i = A_i / S\) (\(\sum_{i=1}^N p_i = 1\)), and item \(i\) requires at least \(B_i \ge 1\) copies. Let \(T_i\) be the discrete step at which item \(i\) receives its \(B_i\)-th copy. We want to compute:

The expected time until all items meet their quota: \(T_{\text{all}} = \max_{1 \le i \le N} T_i\), or
The expected time until at least \(k\) items meet their quota: \(T_{(k)} = \operatorname{kthmin}_{1 \le i \le N} T_i = \operatorname{Kthmax}_{1 \le i \le N} T_i\) where \(K = N - k + 1\).
** Diagnostic Signal: The stopping condition is a conjunction** (“every item \(i\) has \(\ge B_i\) copies”, i.e. \(\max_i T_i\)) or a \(k\)-out-of-\(N\) threshold, and the item probabilities \(p_i = A_i/S\) and quotas \(B_i\) have moderate total sums (\(\sum A_i \le 400\), \(\sum B_i \le 400\)).
** Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad**: Why is \(\max_{i \in [N]} T_i\) hard while \(\min_{i \in T} T_i\) is easy?

First, by Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion (Ch 08), we convert any maximum (or \(K\)-th maximum) of stopping times into a linear combination of subset minimums \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{i \in T} T_i]\): \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{i \in [N]} T_i\right] = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq [N]} (-1)^{|T|-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{i \in T} T_i\right],\] and more generally for the \(K\)-th largest stopping time (\(K = N - k + 1\)): \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\operatorname{Kthmax}_{i \in [N]} T_i\right] = \sum_{\substack{T \subseteq [N] \\ |T| \ge K}} (-1)^{|T|-K} \binom{|T|-1}{K-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{i \in T} T_i\right].\]
Now fix a non-empty subset \(T \subseteq [N]\), and let \(T_{\min}(T) = \min_{i \in T} T_i\) be the first step at which some item \(i \in T\) reaches \(B_i\) copies. How do we compute \(\mathbb{E}[T_{\min}(T)]\)? There are two completely equivalent ways to derive the exact same EGF formula—the Discrete Conditioning View and the Continuous-Time Poissonization View—and seeing both makes the identity unforgettable:



View 1: Discrete Active-Subset Conditioning + Tail-Sum Identity

Filter out steps outside \(T\): At each step, the drawn item falls into \(T\) with probability \[P_T = \sum_{i \in T} p_i = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{i \in T} A_i.\] Draws that land outside \(T\) (probability \(1 - P_T\)) do not change the counts of any item in \(T\). Since each hit inside \(T\) takes an expected \(\frac{1}{P_T}\) total steps (by Wald’s identity / geometric waiting time between hits inside \(T\)), if \(M_T\) is the number of hits inside \(T\) until some \(i \in T\) reaches \(B_i\) copies, then \[\mathbb{E}[T_{\min}(T)] = \frac{1}{P_T} \mathbb{E}[M_T] = \frac{1}{P_T} \sum_{K=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(M_T > K).\]
Count surviving \(K\)-hit sequences inside \(T\) via Truncated Exponential EGF: Conditioned on landing inside \(T\), each step chooses item \(i \in T\) with conditional probability \(\frac{p_i}{P_T}\). The event \(\{M_T > K\}\) holds if and only if, after \(K\) hits inside \(T\), every item \(i \in T\) has appeared \(c_i < B_i\) times (with \(\sum_{i \in T} c_i = K\)). By the labeled tuple construction (Ch 04), summing the multinomial probability over all valid tuples \((c_i)_{i \in T}\) is the coefficient of \(\frac{x^K}{K!}\) in the product of truncated exponential EGFs: \[\mathbb{P}(M_T > K) = \sum_{\substack{\sum_{i \in T} c_i = K \\ 0 \le c_i < B_i}} \frac{K!}{\prod_{i \in T} c_i!} \prod_{i \in T} \left(\frac{p_i}{P_T}\right)^{c_i} = \frac{K!}{P_T^K} [x^K] \prod_{i \in T} \left(\sum_{c=0}^{B_i - 1} \frac{(p_i x)^c}{c!}\right).\]
Multiply by \(\frac{1}{P_T}\) and sum over \(K \ge 0\): \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{i \in T} T_i\right] = \sum_{K=0}^{\sum_{i \in T}(B_i - 1)} K! \left(\frac{1}{P_T}\right)^{K+1} [x^K] \prod_{i \in T} \left(\sum_{c=0}^{B_i - 1} \frac{(p_i x)^c}{c!}\right).}\]



View 2: Continuous-Time Poissonization & Laplace Integral
Instead of drawing one item at each discrete tick \(n = 1, 2, \dots\), imagine that draws arrive according to a continuous-time Poisson process of total rate \(\lambda = 1\) (so the time between consecutive draws is \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) with mean \(1\)). By Wald’s identity, the expected continuous time \(\mathbb{E}[\tau]\) until the stopping condition holds equals the expected discrete number of draws \(\mathbb{E}[T]\)!
By the Poisson Thinning Theorem, splitting a rate-\(1\) Poisson process where each arrival is assigned to bin \(i\) with probability \(p_i\) produces \(N\) mutually independent Poisson processes of rates \(p_1, p_2, \dots, p_N\). At continuous time \(t \ge 0\), the number of items in bin \(i\) is \(N_i(t) \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(p_i t)\) independently across all \(i\), so the probability that bin \(i\) has strictly fewer than \(B_i\) items at time \(t\) is: \[\mathbb{P}(N_i(t) < B_i) = e^{-p_i t} \sum_{c=0}^{B_i - 1} \frac{(p_i t)^c}{c!}.\] Because the bins are independent in continuous time, the probability that every bin \(i \in T\) has fewer than \(B_i\) items at time \(t\) is simply the product over \(i \in T\): \[\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\min}(T) > t) = \prod_{i \in T} \mathbb{P}(N_i(t) < B_i) = e^{-P_T t} \prod_{i \in T} \left(\sum_{c=0}^{B_i - 1} \frac{(p_i t)^c}{c!}\right).\] Integrating \(\mathbb{E}[\tau_{\min}(T)] = \int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}(\tau_{\min}(T) > t)\,dt\) and applying the Euler gamma/Laplace integral \[\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{t^K}{K!} e^{-P_T t} \, dt = \frac{1}{P_T^{K+1}}\] term-by-term to \([t^K] \prod_{i \in T} \sum_{c=0}^{B_i-1} \frac{(p_i t)^c}{c!}\) reproduces the exact same boxed formula in a single integral!


Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace: 2-Item Threshold Collection (\(B_1 = 2, B_2 = 1\))
Suppose \(N = 2\) items have equal draw probabilities \(p_1 = p_2 = \frac{1}{2}\), and we need \(B_1 = 2\) copies of item \(1\) and \(B_2 = 1\) copy of item \(2\). What is \(\mathbb{E}[\max(T_1, T_2)]\)?

Subset \(T = \{1\}\): \(P_{\{1\}} = \frac{1}{2}\), truncated EGF is \(1 + \frac{1}{2}x\) (\(K \in \{0, 1\}\)): \[\mathbb{E}[T_1] = 0! \left(\frac{1}{1/2}\right)^1 (1) + 1! \left(\frac{1}{1/2}\right)^2 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 2 + 2 = 4.\]
Subset \(T = \{2\}\): \(P_{\{2\}} = \frac{1}{2}\), truncated EGF is \(1\) (\(K = 0\)): \[\mathbb{E}[T_2] = 0! \left(\frac{1}{1/2}\right)^1 (1) = 2.\]
Subset \(T = \{1, 2\}\): \(P_{\{1, 2\}} = 1\), truncated EGF product is \(\left(1 + \frac{1}{2}x\right)(1) = 1 + \frac{1}{2}x\) (\(K \in \{0, 1\}\)): \[\mathbb{E}[\min(T_1, T_2)] = 0! \left(\frac{1}{1}\right)^1 (1) + 1! \left(\frac{1}{1}\right)^2 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}.\]
Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion: \[\mathbb{E}[\max(T_1, T_2)] = \mathbb{E}[T_1] + \mathbb{E}[T_2] - \mathbb{E}[\min(T_1, T_2)] = 4 + 2 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{9}{2}.\] Let us check directly: item \(1\) alone takes expected \(4\) steps; the only way \(T_2 > T_1\) is if the first two draws are both item \(1\) (probability \((1/2)^2 = 1/4\)), after which waiting for item \(2\) takes \(2\) more expected steps, giving \(4 + \frac{1}{4}(2) = \frac{9}{2}\). Exact match!







NoteAlgorithm Contract: Poissonized Min–Max / All-Targets Stopping-Time Extractor




Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Number of item types \(N \ge 1\), integer weight array \(A[1 \dots N]\) with \(A_i \ge 1\) and \(S = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i\), and integer quota array \(B[1 \dots N]\) with \(B_i \ge 1\) and \(B_{\text{tot}} = \sum_{i=1}^N (B_i - 1)\).
Preconditions:

\(1 \le A_i\) and \(1 \le S < p\), so every subset weight sum \(a = A_T = \sum_{i \in T} A_i \in [1, S]\) is invertible modulo \(p\).
\(\max_i (B_i - 1) < p\) and \(B_{\text{tot}} < p\), so all factorials \(c!\) (\(0 \le c < B_i\)) and \(K!\) (\(0 \le K \le B_{\text{tot}}\)) are invertible modulo \(p\).

Postconditions (Output): Expected stopping time \(\mathbb{E}[\max_{1 \le i \le N} T_i] = S \sum_{a=1}^{S} \sum_{K=0}^{B_{\text{tot}}} \text{dp}[a][K] \cdot K! \cdot a^{-(K+1)} \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O\big(S \cdot (\sum B_i)^2\big)\) (or \(O\big(N \cdot S \cdot B_{\text{tot}}\big)\) with prefix-sum loop bounds) time and \(O(S \cdot B_{\text{tot}})\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing the first \(i\) items with running sums \(S_A = \sum_{j=1}^i A_j\) and \(S_B = \sum_{j=1}^i (B_j - 1)\), the 2D table entry \(\text{dp}[a][K]\) (\(0 \le a \le S_A\), \(0 \le K \le S_B\)) equals \([y^a x^K] \left(-\prod_{j=1}^{i} \left(1 - y^{A_j} \sum_{c=0}^{B_j-1} \frac{A_j^c}{c!} x^c\right)\right)\).
