section: 14.4 The Singing Kingdom KMP Border Theorem, Multi-Pattern Correlation Systems & Doob’s Optional Stopping Martingale
text:
14.4 The Singing Kingdom KMP Border Theorem, Multi-Pattern Correlation Systems & Doob’s Optional Stopping Martingale

Part A: Single-Pattern Hitting Time (The Singing Kingdom) & KMP Border Polynomial
Suppose characters from an alphabet \(\Sigma\) are generated independently one by one, where letter \(c \in \Sigma\) is chosen at each step with probability \(p_c \in (0, 1)\) (\(\sum_{c \in \Sigma} p_c = 1\); in the uniform case on an alphabet of size \(\sigma = |\Sigma|\), \(p_c = \frac{1}{\sigma}\)). Given a target pattern string \(S = s_1 s_2 \dots s_L\) of length \(L\), the process halts at the exact step \(T\) when \(S\) appears as a contiguous substring (hence as the suffix of the generated string) for the first time. How do we compute \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\) in \(O(L)\) time?

** Diagnostic Signal**: We are generating random characters until a target string \(S[1 \dots L]\) (or one of \(m\) target strings \(S_1, \dots, S_m\)) appears as a suffix for the first time.
** Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Why is the Goulden–Jackson / KMP automaton transfer matrix not needed here? Let \(F(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T = n)z^n\) be the stopping-time PGF and \(G(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T > n)z^n\) be the survival GF of all trajectories \(w\) that have not yet** produced \(S\). What happens if we take a surviving trajectory \(w\) (which does not contain \(S\)) and forcibly append the entire pattern \(S = s_1 s_2 \dots s_L\) to the end of \(w\)? On the one hand, the appended string \(w \cdot S\) certainly ends with \(S\), so the stopping condition must be triggered somewhere during the appending of those \(L\) characters! On the other hand, because \(w\) itself was \(S\)-free, the first occurrence of \(S\) in \(w \cdot S\) must end at some position \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, L\}\) inside the appended copy of \(S\). If it ends at the \(k\)-th appended character, then the last \(k\) characters of the stopped string are \(s_1 s_2 \dots s_k\) (a prefix of \(S\) of length \(k\)), while by definition of stopping they must also equal \(s_{L-k+1} \dots s_L\) (the suffix of \(S\) of length \(k\))! A length \(k \in \{1, \dots, L\}\) whose prefix \(S[1 \dots k]\) equals the suffix \(S[L-k+1 \dots L]\) is precisely a KMP border of \(S\)!

Let us formalize this Forced-Appending Bijection as a single-step derivation in \(K[[z]]\):

Definition of the Border Set \(\operatorname{Borders}(S)\): Define the set of all non-empty border lengths of \(S\): \[\operatorname{Borders}(S) = \left\{ k \in \{1, 2, \dots, L\} \;\middle|\; S[1 \dots k] = S[L - k + 1 \dots L] \right\}.\] Note that \(k = L\) is always in \(\operatorname{Borders}(S)\). Using the standard 1-indexed KMP failure table \(\pi[1 \dots L]\) (computable in \(O(L)\) time), \(\operatorname{Borders}(S)\) is enumerated in decreasing order by iterating \(k = L, \pi[L], \pi[\pi[L]], \dots\) while \(k > 0\).
Weight of Forcibly Appending \(S\) to \(G(z)\): Each surviving string \(w\) of length \(n\) has probability weight \(\mathbb{P}(w) z^n\) in \(G(z)\). Appending the specific characters \(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_L\) multiplies its weight by \(\prod_{t=1}^{L} (p_{s_t} z)\). Summing over all surviving strings \(w\) gives the total generating function of forcibly appended trajectories: \[\text{LHS}(z) = G(z) \prod_{t=1}^{L} \left(p_{s_t} z\right).\]
Partitioning by the Exact First-Stop Offset \(k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)\): Every trajectory \(w \cdot S\) where \(w\) is \(S\)-free contains \(S\) for the first time ending at a unique index \(n + k\) with \(1 \le k \le L\). For this to happen at offset \(k\):

The prefix \(w \cdot s_1 \dots s_k\) is a valid halting trajectory (it stops for the first time at step \(n + k\)), which is generated by \(F(z)\).
The overlap condition \(S[1 \dots k] = S[L - k + 1 \dots L]\) requires \(k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)\). Conversely, for every halting trajectory \(u\) (which ends with \(S\)) and every \(k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)\), stripping the last \(k\) characters of \(u\) leaves an \(S\)-free prefix \(w\) such that \(w \cdot S\) hits \(S\) for the first time at \(u = w \cdot s_1 \dots s_k\), followed by the remaining \(L - k\) deterministic characters \(s_{k+1} \dots s_L\)! Because those remaining \(L - k\) characters \(s_{k+1} \dots s_L\) carry weight \(\prod_{t=k+1}^{L} (p_{s_t} z)\), summing over all \(k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)\) gives the exact bijection: \[\boxed{G(z) \prod_{t=1}^{L} \left(p_{s_t} z\right) = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \prod_{t=k+1}^{L} \left(p_{s_t} z\right).}\]

Dividing by \(\prod_{t=1}^{L} (p_{s_t} z)\) to Isolate \(G(z)\): Notice how dividing both sides by \(\prod_{t=1}^{L} (p_{s_t} z) = \left(\prod_{t=1}^{k} p_{s_t} z\right)\left(\prod_{t=k+1}^{L} p_{s_t} z\right)\) cancels the suffix product \(\prod_{t=k+1}^{L} (p_{s_t} z)\) on the right-hand side and leaves the reciprocal of the prefix product \(\prod_{t=1}^{k} (p_{s_t} z)\): \[\boxed{G(z) = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} z^{-k} \prod_{t=1}^{k} p_{s_t}^{-1}.}\]
Extracting Expected Stopping Time \(\mathbb{E}[T] = G(1)\): Setting \(z = 1\) and using \(F(1) = 1\) and \(\mathbb{E}[T] = F'(1) = G(1)\) from §14.1 yields the Singing Kingdom KMP Border Theorem: \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = G(1) = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \prod_{t=1}^{k} p_{s_t}^{-1}, \qquad \text{and for uniform } p_c = \frac{1}{\sigma}: \quad \mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k.}\]
Extracting Stopping-Time Variance \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\): Let \(W_k = \prod_{t=1}^k p_{s_t}^{-1}\) be the reciprocal prefix probability of border \(k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)\) (so \(W_k = \sigma^k\) in the uniform case), and let \(E = G(1) = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} W_k\). Differentiating \(G(z) = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} W_k z^{-k}\) at \(z = 1\) via the product rule gives: \[G'(1) = F'(1) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} W_k + F(1) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} (-k) W_k = E^2 - \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k W_k.\] Substituting \(G(1) = E\) and \(2G'(1) = 2E^2 - 2\sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k W_k\) into \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2G'(1) + G(1) - G(1)^2\) yields the String Hitting-Time Variance Formula: \[\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(T) = \mathbb{E}[T]^2 + \mathbb{E}[T] - 2 \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k \prod_{t=1}^{k} p_{s_t}^{-1}.}\]







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: The Non-Uniform Prefix vs. Suffix Cancellation Trap




The Trap: When letter probabilities \(p_c\) are non-uniform, a classic error is to guess that a border of length \(k\) contributes the reciprocal probability of the length-\(k\) suffix \(\prod_{t=L-k+1}^{L} p_{s_t}^{-1}\), or that for a pair of strings \((S_i, S_j)\) with overlap \(S_i[L_i - k + 1 \dots L_i] = S_j[1 \dots k]\), it doesn’t matter whether we use \(S_i\)’s prefix or \(S_j\)’s prefix.
Concrete Counterexample: Take \(S = \texttt{ABA}\) (\(L = 3\)) with \(p_{\texttt{A}} = \frac{1}{3}\) and \(p_{\texttt{B}} = \frac{2}{3}\). Here \(\operatorname{Borders}(\texttt{ABA}) = \{1, 3\}\). For \(k = 1\), \(S[1\dots 1] = S[3\dots 3] = \texttt{A}\) matches, but what if we have two competing strings \(S_1 = \texttt{BA}\) and \(S_2 = \texttt{AB}\) where \(S_1\)’s suffix of length \(k=1\) (\(\texttt{A}\)) matches \(S_2\)’s prefix of length \(k=1\) (\(\texttt{A}\))? When forcibly appending \(S_2 = \texttt{AB}\) to \(G(z)\), we multiply \(G(z)\) by \(p_{\texttt{A}} p_{\texttt{B}} z^2\), and the remaining tail of \(S_2\) after the length-\(k\) overlap is \(S_2[k+1 \dots L_2] = \texttt{B}\) (weight \(p_{\texttt{B}} z\)). Dividing by \(\prod_{t=1}^{L_2} (p_{S_2[t]} z)\) cancels the tail of \(S_2\) and leaves \(\prod_{t=1}^{k} p_{S_2[t]}^{-1}\)—the reciprocal of the prefix of the appended string \(S_2\) (which equals the suffix of the stopping string \(S_1\), not the prefix of \(S_1\)!).
The Remedy: Always remember which factor cancels: appending \(S_j\) leaves the tail \(S_j[k+1 \dots L_j]\) on the RHS, so dividing by the full weight of \(S_j\) leaves \(\prod_{t=1}^{k} p_{S_j[t]}^{-1}\) (the reciprocal of the length-\(k\) prefix of \(S_j\), which is identical to the length-\(k\) suffix of \(S_i\)).






Part B: Multi-Pattern Competing Stopping Times (Penney’s Game & Guibas–Odlyzko Linear System)
Now suppose \(m\) players choose patterns \(S_1, S_2, \dots, S_m\) of lengths \(L_1, \dots, L_m\) (where no pattern \(S_i\) is a contiguous substring of any \(S_j\) for \(i \neq j\), as otherwise \(S_j\) could never win before \(S_i\)). Characters are generated at random until one of the \(m\) patterns appears as a suffix for the first time, halting the game and declaring that pattern the winner. How do we find the winning probability \(P_i = \mathbb{P}(S_i \text{ wins})\) for every \(i = 1, \dots, m\), as well as the expected game duration \(\mathbb{E}[T]\)?

Decompose \(F(z)\) by the winning pattern: For each \(i \in \{1, \dots, m\}\), let \(F_i(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T = n \text{ and } S_i \text{ wins}) z^n\) be the PGF of trajectories won by \(S_i\). Then the total stopping-time PGF is \(F(z) = \sum_{i=1}^m F_i(z)\), and evaluating at \(z = 1\) gives: \[P_i = F_i(1), \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m} P_i = F(1) = 1, \qquad \mathbb{E}[T] = F'(1) = G(1).\]
Define the Directed Overlap / Correlation Set \(\mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)\): For any ordered pair of patterns \((S_i, S_j)\), let \(\mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)\) be the set of non-empty overlap lengths \(k\) such that the suffix of \(S_i\) of length \(k\) equals the prefix of \(S_j\) of length \(k\): \[\mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j) = \left\{ k \in \{1, \dots, \min(L_i, L_j)\} \;\middle|\; S_i[L_i - k + 1 \dots L_i] = S_j[1 \dots k] \right\}.\]
Forcibly Append \(S_j\) to \(G(z)\) for Each \(j = 1, \dots, m\): Take any surviving string \(w\) counted by \(G(z)\) (which contains none of \(S_1, \dots, S_m\)) and forcibly append \(S_j\). The game must halt at some first occurrence of some pattern \(S_i\) (\(1 \le i \le m\)) ending at offset \(k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)\) inside the appended copy of \(S_j\), followed by the remaining \(L_j - k\) characters \(S_j[k+1 \dots L_j]\): \[G(z) \prod_{t=1}^{L_j} \left(p_{S_j[t]} z\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} F_i(z) \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} \prod_{t=k+1}^{L_j} \left(p_{S_j[t]} z\right) \qquad (1 \le j \le m).\]
Divide by \(\prod_{t=1}^{L_j} (p_{S_j[t]} z)\) and Evaluate at \(z = 1\): Setting \(z = 1\) produces \(m\) linear equations in the \(m + 1\) unknowns \(P_1, \dots, P_m\) and \(G(1) = \mathbb{E}[T]\), which together with \(\sum_{i=1}^m P_i = 1\) form a non-singular \((m + 1) \times (m + 1)\) linear system: \[\boxed{\sum_{i=1}^{m} C_{i, j} P_i - G(1) = 0 \quad (1 \le j \le m), \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m} P_i = 1,}\] where the Guibas–Odlyzko correlation coefficient \(C_{i, j}\) is \[C_{i, j} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} \prod_{t=1}^{k} p_{S_j[t]}^{-1} \qquad \left(\text{or } C_{i, j} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} \sigma^k \text{ in the uniform case}\right).\]


Hand-Checkable Worked Example: Penney’s Game (HHT vs. HTT on a Fair Coin, \(\sigma = 2\))
Suppose Player 1 chooses \(S_1 = \texttt{HHT}\) and Player 2 chooses \(S_2 = \texttt{HTT}\), and a fair coin (\(\sigma = 2\)) is tossed until one pattern appears. Despite both patterns having individual expected hitting time \(2^3 = 8\) when played alone, let us compute who wins when they compete head-to-head:

Compute the \(2 \times 2\) correlation overlaps \(\mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)\):

\(\mathcal{O}(\texttt{HHT}, \texttt{HHT}) = \{3\} \implies C_{1, 1} = 2^3 = 8\).
\(\mathcal{O}(\texttt{HHT}, \texttt{HTT}) = \{2\}\) (since suffix \(\texttt{HT}\) of \(S_1\) matches prefix \(\texttt{HT}\) of \(S_2\)) \(\implies C_{1, 2} = 2^2 = 4\).
\(\mathcal{O}(\texttt{HTT}, \texttt{HHT}) = \emptyset\) (suffixes \(\texttt{T}, \texttt{TT}, \texttt{HTT}\) of \(S_2\) do not match prefixes \(\texttt{H}, \texttt{HH}, \texttt{HHT}\) of \(S_1\)) \(\implies C_{2, 1} = 0\).
\(\mathcal{O}(\texttt{HTT}, \texttt{HTT}) = \{3\} \implies C_{2, 2} = 2^3 = 8\).

Write the \((2 + 1) \times (2 + 1)\) linear system: \[\begin{cases}
8 P_1 + 0 P_2 = G(1) & (j = 1: \text{append } \texttt{HHT}), \\
4 P_1 + 8 P_2 = G(1) & (j = 2: \text{append } \texttt{HTT}), \\
P_1 + P_2 = 1. &
\end{cases}\]
Solve by hand: Comparing the first two equations gives \(8 P_1 = 4 P_1 + 8 P_2 \implies 4 P_1 = 8 P_2 \implies P_1 = 2 P_2\). Combined with \(P_1 + P_2 = 1\), we obtain: \[P_1 = \frac{2}{3}, \qquad P_2 = \frac{1}{3}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[T] = G(1) = 8 P_1 = \frac{16}{3}.\] Even though both \(\texttt{HHT}\) and \(\texttt{HTT}\) have the exact same solitary hitting time \(8\), \(\texttt{HHT}\) beats \(\texttt{HTT}\) two-thirds of the time because any path heading toward \(\texttt{HTT}\) must pass through \(\texttt{HT}\) (\(C_{1,2} = 4\)), which \(\texttt{HHT}\) frequently intercepts first!







NoteRevisited Dual-Perspective Cross-Reference — From Goulden–Jackson Clusters (Ch 08 §8.4) to Guibas–Odlyzko Martingales (Ch 14 §14.4)



In Chapter 08 §8.4 (The Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method), we counted words avoiding a reduced forbidden set \(\mathcal{B} = \{S_1, \dots, S_m\}\) over an alphabet of size \(\sigma\) by solving the \((m+1) \times (m+1)\) cluster linear system in the formal variable \(x\). Under the probabilistic substitution \(x = \frac{z}{\sigma}\), the Goulden–Jackson avoidance OGF \(F_{\text{GJ}}\!\left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)\) is identically the survival generating function \(G(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathbb{P}(T > n) z^n\) of §14.1, and the Goulden–Jackson overlap polynomial \(\operatorname{Corr}(S_i, S_j; x)\) evaluated at \(x = \frac{1}{\sigma}\) (multiplied by \(\sigma^{|S_j|}\)) becomes the exact Guibas–Odlyzko martingale payout \(C_{i, j} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} \sigma^k\)! Evaluating the Ch 08 cluster matrix at \(z = 1\) therefore bypasses rational polynomial inversion completely and collapses directly to the scalar Penney’s Game system above.






Part C: Two Martingale Bridges — Fair Casino Gamblers & Separable Potential Drift Duality
Why did the KMP border sum \(\sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \prod_{t=1}^k p_{s_t}^{-1}\) and the Guibas–Odlyzko system \(\sum_{i=1}^m C_{i,j} P_i = G(1)\) take such clean linear forms at \(z = 1\)? And how do we compute expected stopping times for multi-pile token processes (like CF 1349D — Slime and Biscuits) where there are \(n \le 10^5\) piles and no simple 1D EGF factorization exists?
Both questions are answered by the Martingale Optional Stopping Engine, which forms an exact algebraic dual to PGF differentiation at \(z = 1\).

Bridge 1: Li’s Fair Casino Martingale & Doob’s Optional Stopping Theorem
A discrete-time stochastic process \((M_n)_{n \ge 0}\) adapted to the history \((X_1, \dots, X_n)\) is called a martingale if \(\mathbb{E}[|M_n|] < \infty\) and its conditional one-step drift is zero everywhere: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[M_{n+1} - M_n \;\middle|\; X_1, \dots, X_n\right] = 0 \qquad (\forall n \ge 0).\] By Doob’s Optional Stopping Theorem, if \(T\) is a stopping time such that \(\mathbb{E}[T] < \infty\) and the one-step increments \(|M_{n+1} - M_n|\) are uniformly bounded on \(\{T > n\}\) (which always holds on a finite state space with exponentially decaying tail \(\mathbb{P}(T > n) = O(\rho^n)\), \(\rho < 1\)), then the expected value of \(M_T\) at the random stopping time \(T\) equals its initial value \(M_0\): \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[M_T] = \mathbb{E}[M_0].}\]
Let us see how H. Li’s (1980) Fair Casino Construction derives the Singing Kingdom and Penney’s Game formulas in 30 seconds:

The Casino Rules (Betting on Pattern \(S = s_1 \dots s_L\)): Before each step \(n = 1, 2, \dots\), a new gambler \(n\) walks into a fair casino with initial capital \(\$1\).

Gambler \(n\) bets their entire \(\$1\) that the \(n\)-th character will be \(s_1\). Because \(s_1\) occurs with probability \(p_{s_1}\), fair odds pay \(p_{s_1}^{-1}\) per dollar: if \(X_n = s_1\), Gambler \(n\) now holds \(\$p_{s_1}^{-1}\); otherwise Gambler \(n\) goes broke (\(\$0\)) and leaves.
If Gambler \(n\) survived step \(n\), then at step \(n + 1\) they bet their entire fortune \(\$p_{s_1}^{-1}\) that \(X_{n+1} = s_2\) at fair odds \(p_{s_2}^{-1}\) (growing to \(\$p_{s_1}^{-1} p_{s_2}^{-1}\) on success, or \(\$0\) on failure), and so on up to \(s_L\).

Zero-Drift Martingale Invariant: Because every single bet is fair (\(\mathbb{E}[\text{payout}] = p_c \cdot p_c^{-1} + (1 - p_c) \cdot 0 = 1\)), the casino’s net profit is a martingale! Specifically, after \(n\) steps, let \(W_n\) be the total fortune held by all gamblers currently in the casino. Since \(n\) gamblers have entered with \(\$1\) each (total entry fees \(\$n\)), the net wealth process \[M_n = W_n - n \qquad (n \ge 0, \;\; M_0 = 0)\] is a martingale!
Evaluating \(W_T\) at the Stopping Time \(T\): At the exact moment \(T\) when the generated string ends with \(S_i\) (say in Penney’s Game, where our gamblers bet on \(S_j\)), which gamblers are still alive and holding money in the casino? A gambler who entered \(k\) steps ago (for \(1 \le k \le L_j\)) has survived all \(k\) of their bets \(S_j[1], \dots, S_j[k]\) if and only if the last \(k\) characters of the stopped string \(S_i\) equal \(S_j[1 \dots k]\)—that is, \(k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)\)! And that gambler holds exactly \(\prod_{t=1}^k p_{S_j[t]}^{-1}\) dollars. Therefore, conditioned on \(S_i\) winning at step \(T\), the total casino payout at time \(T\) is deterministically \(C_{i, j} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} \prod_{t=1}^k p_{S_j[t]}^{-1}\). Applying Doob’s Optional Stopping Theorem \(\mathbb{E}[M_T] = \mathbb{E}[W_T - T] = 0\) immediately gives \[\mathbb{E}[T] = \mathbb{E}[W_T] = \sum_{i=1}^{m} P_i C_{i, j},\] reproducing the Guibas–Odlyzko system (and for \(m = 1\), \(\mathbb{E}[T] = C_{1, 1} = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \prod_{t=1}^k p_{s_t}^{-1}\)) without a single derivative!




Bridge 2: Separable Martingale Potentials, Poisson Drift Duality & Tridiagonal Order Reduction
What if the process is not a string automaton, but a symmetric multi-pile game on an enormous state space \(\Omega\)—such as \(n\) players holding \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\) biscuits with \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = S\) (CF 1349D — Slime and Biscuits), where at each step a random biscuit is transferred to another player until one player holds all \(S\) biscuits?

** Diagnostic Signal: You have a symmetric Markov process on tuples \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) with a conserved sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = S\) (or active components merging/splitting symmetrically), stopping when a single coordinate reaches \(S\). The number of partition states is far too large for Gaussian elimination, and** the one-step transition probabilities of a single coordinate \(a_i = x\) depend only on \(x\), \(n\), and \(S\).
** Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: By Doob’s Optional Stopping Theorem, if we can construct a potential function** \(\Phi: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) on the state space such that every non-terminal state \(X_t = (a_1, \dots, a_n)\) has constant expected one-step drift \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Phi(X_{t+1}) - \Phi(X_t) \;\middle|\; X_t\right] = -1,\] then \(M_t = \Phi(X_t) + t\) is a martingale! If moreover every terminal state \(X_T\) (a permutation of \((S, 0, \dots, 0)\)) has the same terminal potential \(\Phi_{\text{end}}\), then \(\mathbb{E}[M_T] = \mathbb{E}[M_0]\) immediately gives: \[\mathbb{E}[\Phi(X_T) + T] = \Phi(X_0) \implies \boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = \Phi(X_0) - \Phi_{\text{end}}.}\] How do we construct \(\Phi(a_1, \dots, a_n)\) without solving a system over all partitions of \(S\)? Exploit symmetry and additive separability: seek \(\Phi(a_1, \dots, a_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(a_i)\) for a single 1D function \(f: \{0, 1, \dots, S\} \to K\)! Then \(\mathbb{E}[\Phi(X_{t+1}) - \Phi(X_t) \mid X_t] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[f(a_i') - f(a_i) \mid a_i]\). How do we make a sum of \(n\) single-pile drifts equal \(-1\) for every tuple \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = S\)? Because \(\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{a_i}{S} = 1\) (and equivalently \(\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{S - a_i}{S(n - 1)} = 1\)) holds identically on the hyperplane \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = S\), we can rewrite the right-hand side \(-1\) as \(-\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{S - a_i}{S(n - 1)}\) (or \(-\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{a_i}{S}\)) and equate the \(i\)-th summands term-by-term!

Let us execute this Separable Potential & First-Difference Reduction step by step:

Single-Pile Drift Equation: Suppose a pile of size \(x \in \{0, 1, \dots, S - 1\}\) transitions in one step to \(x - 1\) with probability \(p^-(x)\), to \(x + 1\) with probability \(p^+(x)\), and stays at \(x\) otherwise. Requiring the single-pile drift to equal \(-w(x)\) (where \(\sum_{i=1}^n w(a_i) = 1\) whenever \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = S\), e.g. \(w(x) = \frac{S - x}{S(n - 1)}\) or \(w(x) = \frac{x}{S} - c\)) gives the 1D tridiagonal balance equation: \[p^-(x)\big(f(x - 1) - f(x)\big) + p^+(x)\big(f(x + 1) - f(x)\big) = -w(x) \qquad (0 \le x < S).\]
Order Reduction via First Differences \(g(x) = f(x + 1) - f(x)\): Notice that \(f\) appears only through its adjacent differences! Define the first-difference sequence \[g(x) = f(x + 1) - f(x) \qquad (0 \le x < S), \qquad \text{with } f(0) = 0 \text{ and } f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{x-1} g(j).\] Substituting \(f(x + 1) - f(x) = g(x)\) and \(f(x - 1) - f(x) = -g(x - 1)\) collapses the second-order tridiagonal system for \(f\) into a first-order two-term recurrence for \(g\): \[\boxed{p^+(x) \, g(x) - p^-(x) \, g(x - 1) = -w(x) \qquad (0 \le x < S).}\] Since \(p^-(0) = 0\) (an empty pile cannot lose a token), the \(x = 0\) equation immediately determines \(g(0) = -\frac{w(0)}{p^+(0)}\), and each subsequent \(g(1), g(2), \dots, g(S - 1)\) is computed in \(O(1)\) time by a single forward sweep!
Recovering \(\mathbb{E}[T]\): Since every terminal state has one pile of size \(S\) and \(n - 1\) piles of size \(0\), its terminal potential is \(\Phi_{\text{end}} = f(S) + (n - 1)f(0) = f(S)\). Thus \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(a_i) - f(S) \quad (\text{for drift } -1), \qquad \text{or } f(S) - \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(a_i) \quad (\text{for drift } +1).}\]







NoteAlgorithm Contract: Separable Potential & Optional Stopping Extractor




Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Number of piles \(n \ge 2\), initial pile sizes \(a[1 \dots n]\) with \(a_i \in [0, S]\) and conserved total sum \(S = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i \ge 1\), and single-pile transition probabilities \(p^+(x), p^-(x)\) and drift weight \(w(x)\) for \(x \in [0, S - 1]\).
Preconditions:

\(p^-(0) = 0\) and \(p^+(x) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) for all \(0 \le x < S\) (holds whenever \(S < p\) and \(n - 1 < p\)).
Partition-of-unity condition: \(\sum_{i=1}^n w(a_i) = 1\) for every configuration \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = S\).
The stopping time \(T\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[T] < \infty\) with bounded one-step increments \(|\Phi(X_{t+1}) - \Phi(X_t)| \le 2 \max_{0 \le x < S} |g(x)| < \infty\) (Doob’s Optional Stopping validity).

Postconditions (Output): First-difference array \(g[0 \dots S-1]\), potential array \(f[0 \dots S]\) with \(f[0] = 0\), and expected stopping time \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n f[a_i] - f[S]\right) \bmod p\) (for drift \(-1\), or \(f[S] - \sum_{i=1}^n f[a_i] \bmod p\) for drift \(+1\)).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n + S)\) time (using linear-time modular inverses up to \(S\)) and \(O(S)\) auxiliary space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: For every \(0 \le x < S\), the prefix sum \(f[x + 1] = \sum_{j=0}^{x} g[j]\) satisfies the exact second-order single-pile balance equation \(p^+(x)(f[x+1] - f[x]) + p^-(x)(f[x-1] - f[x]) = \pm w(x)\).









NoteOperator Duality (Elegia’s Theorem): Why Renewal Pole Cancellation and Martingale Potentials Are Identical



Why can problems like [ZJOI2019] 开关, CF 1349D — Slime and Biscuits, and CF 1479E — School Clubs be solved both by the §14.3 PGF Renewal Quotient \(F_{u \to t}(z) = \widetilde{H}_{u \to t}(z) / \widetilde{H}_{t \to t}(z)\) and by the §14.4 Martingale Potential method?
Let \(P\) be the transition matrix of an ergodic Markov chain with stationary distribution \(\pi\). The matrix of unconstrained visit OGFs is the resolvent \(H(z) = \sum_{m \ge 0} z^m P^m = (I - zP)^{-1}\), and the pole-cancelled matrix \(\widetilde{H}(z) = (1 - z)H(z)\) satisfies \[(I - zP)\widetilde{H}(z) = (1 - z)I.\] Differentiating both sides with respect to \(z\) at \(z = 1\) (where \(\widetilde{H}_{v \to t}(1) = \pi_t\) for all \(v\)) gives \[(I - P)\widetilde{H}'(1) - P\widetilde{H}(1) = -I \implies (I - P)\!\left(-\widetilde{H}'(1)\right) = I - \mathbf{1}\pi^T.\] Looking at column \(t\) (corresponding to target state \(t\)), the vector \(\phi_u = -\widetilde{H}'_{u \to t}(1)\) satisfies the Poisson Drift Equation: \[(I - P)\phi = e_t - \pi_t \mathbf{1} \Longleftrightarrow \mathbb{E}[\phi(X_1) - \phi(X_0) \mid X_0 = u] = \pi_t - \mathbf{1}[u = t].\] Dividing \(\phi_u - \phi_t\) by \(\pi_t\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[T_{u \to t}] = \frac{\phi_u - \phi_t}{\pi_t} = \frac{\widetilde{H}'_{t \to t}(1) - \widetilde{H}'_{u \to t}(1)}{\pi_t}\)! Thus:

Renewal PGF Deconvolution (§14.3) solves the Poisson drift equation in the spectral / generating-function domain by diagonalizing \(P\) via EGF products and differentiating \(\widetilde{H}(z)\) at \(z = 1\).
The Martingale Potential Method (§14.4) solves the exact same Poisson drift equation in the time / state-space domain by exploiting symmetry \(\Phi = \sum_{i=1}^n f(a_i)\) and reducing the tridiagonal difference equation to \(g(x) = f(x+1) - f(x)\).

title: 14 — Probability Generating Functions, Renewal Stopping Times, Poissonization & Martingales
text:
14.5 4-Tier 8-Problem Practice Ladder
Every problem below is self-contained and ordered strictly by conceptual dependency (2 Stepping Stones, 2 Intermediate, 2 Advanced, 2 Mastery). Use the visible \(N \le 4\) sample trace to verify your combinatorial model before opening the progressive hints.


Stepping Stone 1 (#115) — Codeforces 1392H: ZS Shuffles Cards

Source: Codeforces Global Round 10, Problem H
Prerequisite Tags: Stopping-Time PGF & Tail-Sum Identity (§14.1), Renewal Epoch Decomposition (§14.3), Binomial Sums (Ch 06).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
A deck contains \(n\) numbered cards (\(1, 2, \dots, n\)) and \(m\) identical jokers (\(n + m\) cards in total), shuffled uniformly at random. You maintain a set \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) of collected numbered cards, initially \(S = \emptyset\).
In each round (epoch), you draw cards one by one from the top of the deck without replacement:

If you draw a numbered card \(x \in \{1, \dots, n\}\), you add \(x\) to \(S\) (\(S \leftarrow S \cup \{x\}\)) and continue drawing from the deck.
If you draw a joker, the current round ends immediately: you take all cards drawn during this round, shuffle them back into the remaining deck to form a fresh uniformly random permutation of all \(n + m\) cards, and start the next round (keeping your set \(S\)).

At the moment a joker is drawn (ending the round), if \(S = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\), the game stops; otherwise all drawn cards are reshuffled back into the deck and the next round begins. Compute the expected total number of card draws (including jokers) until the game stops, modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n, m \le 2 \times 10^6\), time limit \(2.0\text{ s}\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(n + m)\) time and \(O(n + m)\) (or \(O(1)\) auxiliary) space.



Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n = 2, m = 1\))
With \(n = 2\) numbered cards and \(m = 1\) joker (\(3\) cards total):

Single-epoch length \(\mathbb{E}[L]\): In any permutation of \(2\) numbered cards and \(1\) joker, each of the \(2\) numbered cards precedes the lone joker with probability \(\frac{1}{m + 1} = \frac{1}{2}\). Including the joker itself (\(+1\) draw), the expected number of cards drawn in one round is \(\mathbb{E}[L] = 1 + \frac{2}{2} = 2\).
Number of rounds \(\mathbb{E}[R]\): In one round, the joker is at position \(1, 2,\) or \(3\) with probability \(1/3\) each, revealing \(0, 1,\) or \(2\) numbered cards. By Min–Max IE (or conditioning on \(|S|\)):

For a subset \(T \subseteq \{1, 2\}\) of size \(k = 1\), card \(x \in T\) is drawn in a round with probability \(\frac{1}{m+1} = \frac{1}{2}\), so \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{x \in T} R_x] = 2\).
For \(T = \{1, 2\}\) (\(k = 2\)), at least one of the \(2\) cards precedes the \(m = 1\) joker unless the joker is first among all \(k + m = 3\) cards (probability \(\frac{m}{k+m} = \frac{1}{3}\)), so a round hits \(T\) with probability \(\frac{k}{k+m} = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{x \in \{1,2\}} R_x] = \frac{3}{2}\).
By Min–Max IE, \(\mathbb{E}[R] = \binom{2}{1}(2) - \binom{2}{2}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = 4 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{5}{2}\).

Total expected draws: By Wald’s Renewal Identity, \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \mathbb{E}[R] \cdot \mathbb{E}[L] = \frac{5}{2} \cdot 2 = 5 \equiv 5 \pmod{998244353}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Notice that whenever a joker is drawn, all cards drawn in that round are reshuffled back into the deck, resetting the deck’s permutation while preserving your collected set \(S\). This divides the process into rounds (epochs). Are the epoch length \(L_r\) (cards drawn in round \(r\)) and the stopping round \(R\) (the first round after which \(S = \{1, \dots, n\}\)) coupled, or can the expected total draws \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) be factored into two simpler expectations?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By Wald’s Identity (since the event \(\{R \ge r\}\) depends only on rounds \(1, \dots, r-1\) and is independent of the fresh shuffle in round \(r\)), total expected draws factor as \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \mathbb{E}[R] \cdot \mathbb{E}[L]\):

Expected cards per round \(\mathbb{E}[L]\): By linearity of expectation among the \(n\) numbered cards and \(m\) jokers, any fixed numbered card \(x\) appears before all \(m\) jokers with probability \(\frac{1}{m + 1}\). Adding \(+1\) for the joker that ends the round gives \(\mathbb{E}[L] = 1 + \frac{n}{m + 1} = \frac{n + m + 1}{m + 1}\).
Expected number of rounds \(\mathbb{E}[R]\): Apply Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion (Ch 08 / §14.3) over the \(n\) numbered cards! Let \(R_x\) be the round in which card \(x\) is drawn for the first time, so \(R = \max_{1 \le x \le n} R_x\). For a subset \(T \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) of size \(k = |T|\), what is the probability \(p_k\) that a single round draws at least one card from \(T\) before the first joker?




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Among the \(k\) cards in \(T\) and the \(m\) jokers (\(k + m\) cards whose relative order is uniformly random), a round misses all of \(T\) if and only if the very first of these \(k + m\) cards is one of the \(m\) jokers (probability \(\frac{m}{k + m}\)). Therefore, a round hits \(T\) with probability \(p_k = 1 - \frac{m}{k + m} = \frac{k}{k + m}\), so \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{x \in T} R_x] = \frac{1}{p_k} = \frac{k + m}{k} = 1 + \frac{m}{k}\). Sum over all \(\binom{n}{k}\) subsets of size \(k\) (or use the identity \(\sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} \frac{1}{k} = H_n\)) to simplify \(\mathbb{E}[R]\) to a clean \(O(n)\) harmonic sum!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Renewal Factorization into Rounds \(\mathbb{E}[R]\) and Epoch Length \(\mathbb{E}[L]\)
Although the number of cards \(L_r\) drawn in round \(r\) is correlated with how many new elements are added to \(S\) during round \(r\), notice that for every round \(r \ge 1\), the event \(\{R \ge r\}\) (meaning the game did not stop at the end of round \(r - 1\), so \(S \neq \{1, \dots, n\}\) before round \(r\) begins) is determined purely by rounds \(1, \dots, r - 1\) and is therefore independent of the fresh shuffle in round \(r\)! Consequently, writing total draws as \(T = \sum_{r=1}^{\infty} L_r \cdot \mathbf{1}[R \ge r]\) and taking expectations gives Wald’s Identity: \[\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{r=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[L_r \cdot \mathbf{1}[R \ge r]\right] = \sum_{r=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}[L_r] \, \mathbb{P}(R \ge r) = \mathbb{E}[L] \sum_{r=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(R \ge r) = \mathbb{E}[L] \cdot \mathbb{E}[R].\]


2. Expected Length of a Single Round \(\mathbb{E}[L]\)
In a single round, we draw until the first of the \(m\) jokers appears. Consider any one of the \(n\) numbered cards, say card \(x\). In the uniformly random relative order of the \(m + 1\) cards \(\{x\} \cup \{\text{all } m \text{ jokers}\}\), card \(x\) is the very first of these \(m + 1\) cards with probability \(\frac{1}{m + 1}\). By linearity of expectation across all \(n\) numbered cards plus the \(1\) joker that terminates the round: \[\mathbb{E}[L] = 1 + \sum_{x=1}^{n} \frac{1}{m + 1} = 1 + \frac{n}{m + 1} = \frac{n + m + 1}{m + 1}.\]


3. Expected Number of Rounds \(\mathbb{E}[R]\) via Two Dual Bridges
Let \(R_x \ge 1\) be the index of the first round in which numbered card \(x\) is drawn before a joker. The game ends at round \(R = \max_{1 \le x \le n} R_x\).

Method A (Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion + Binomial Harmonic Identity): By Min–Max IE (§14.3): \[\mathbb{E}[R] = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq [n]} (-1)^{|T|-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{x \in T} R_x\right].\] Fix a subset \(T \subseteq [n]\) of size \(k = |T|\). In each round, \(\min_{x \in T} R_x\) is triggered if at least one of the \(k\) cards in \(T\) appears before all \(m\) jokers. Among the \(k + m\) cards in \(T \cup \{\text{jokers}\}\), the first card belongs to \(T\) with probability \(p_k = \frac{k}{k + m}\). Because rounds are independent, \(\min_{x \in T} R_x \sim \operatorname{Geom}(p_k)\) with PGF \(F_k(z) = \frac{p_k z}{1 - (1 - p_k)z}\) and expectation \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{x \in T} R_x] = F'_k(1) = \frac{1}{p_k} = \frac{k + m}{k} = 1 + \frac{m}{k}\). Summing over all \(\binom{n}{k}\) subsets of size \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) and splitting \(1 + \frac{m}{k}\) using \(\sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k-1}\binom{n}{k} = 1 - (1 - 1)^n = 1\) gives: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[R] &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} \left(1 + \frac{m}{k}\right) \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} + m \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} \frac{1}{k} \\
&= 1 + m \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} \frac{1}{k}.
\end{aligned}\] Recall the standard binomial-harmonic identity \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} \frac{1}{k} = H_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i}\) (provable by integrating \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} x^{k-1} = \frac{1 - (1 - x)^n}{x}\) from \(0\) to \(1\)). Thus: \[\mathbb{E}[R] = 1 + m \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i} = 1 + m H_n.\]
Method B (Direct Markov Conditioning on \(i = n - |S|\) Missing Cards): Whenever \(i \ge 1\) numbered cards remain uncollected, a round collects at least one of them with probability \(\frac{i}{i + m}\); conditioned on collecting at least one, the relative order of those \(i\) missing cards and \(m\) jokers still has the same distribution! In fact, each of the \(n\) numbered cards has a \(\frac{m}{i + m}\) chance of having a joker appear immediately before the \(i\)-th last new card is discovered, immediately yielding \(\mathbb{E}[R] = 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{m}{i}\).



4. Final Formula & Algorithm Contract
Combining \(\mathbb{E}[L]\) and \(\mathbb{E}[R]\) yields the closed-form answer: \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = \left(1 + \frac{n}{m + 1}\right) \left(1 + m \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i}\right) \pmod{998244353}.}\]

Input & Preconditions: Integers \(n, m \in [1, 2 \times 10^6]\) representing \(n\) numbered cards and \(m\) jokers; prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > \max(n, m + 1)\), so all modular inverses \(\operatorname{inv}[1 \dots \max(n, m+1)] \bmod p\) are well-defined.
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \frac{n + m + 1}{m + 1}\left(1 + m H_n\right) \bmod 998244353\).
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Harmonic sum index \(i\) runs over \(1 \le i \le n\), and linear modular inverse table is precomputed up to \(\max(n, m + 1)\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n + m)\) time and \(O(n + m)\) space using the linear modular inverse table \(\operatorname{inv}[i] = (p - \lfloor p/i \rfloor) \operatorname{inv}[p \bmod i] \bmod p\) (or \(O(n \log p)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After iteration \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\), the harmonic accumulator holds \(H_i = \sum_{k=1}^{i} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{i}{k} \frac{1}{k} = \sum_{j=1}^{i} \frac{1}{j} \bmod p\), which equals the expected number of rounds per joker when \(i\) numbered cards remain.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Because the game only checks whether \(S = \{1, \dots, n\}\) when a joker is drawn to end the round, the final round still requires drawing \(1\) joker (\(+1\) in \(\mathbb{E}[R] = 1 + m H_n\) and \(+1\) in \(\mathbb{E}[L] = 1 + \frac{n}{m+1}\)); omitting either \(+1\) undercounts the terminating joker draw.









Stepping Stone 2 (#026) — AtCoder Beginner Contest 242 Ex: Random Painting

Source: AtCoder ABC 242 Ex
Prerequisite Tags: Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion over Stopping Times (§14.3), Geometric PGFs (§14.1), Interval-Gap Dynamic Programming (Ch 08).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
There are \(N\) points numbered \(1, 2, \dots, N\) on a number line, all initially unpainted, and \(M\) segments \([L_1, R_1], [L_2, R_2], \dots, [L_M, R_M]\) with \(1 \le L_j \le R_j \le N\).
At each step, you choose one of the \(M\) segments uniformly at random (independently with probability \(1/M\) each) and paint all integer points in \([L_j, R_j]\). Compute the expected number of steps until all \(N\) points are painted, modulo \(998244353\) (it is guaranteed that every point \(1 \dots N\) is covered by at least one segment).

Constraints: \(1 \le N, M \le 400\), \(1 \le L_j \le R_j \le N\), time limit \(2.0\text{ s}\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O(N^2 (N + M))\) time and \(O(N^2 + N M)\) space.



Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(N = 3, M = 3\))
Suppose \(N = 3\) and the \(M = 3\) segments are \(I_1 = [1, 2]\), \(I_2 = [2, 3]\), and \(I_3 = [2, 2]\).

For any non-empty subset of points \(T \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}\), let \(c(T)\) be the number of segments that miss \(T\) completely (contain no point of \(T\)). Then \(M - c(T)\) segments hit \(T\), so \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{x \in T} T_x] = \frac{M}{M - c(T)}\):

\(T = \{1\}\): missed by \(I_2 = [2,3]\) and \(I_3 = [2,2]\) (\(c = 2\)), so \(\mathbb{E}[T_1] = \frac{3}{3 - 2} = 3\).
\(T = \{3\}\): missed by \(I_1 = [1,2]\) and \(I_3 = [2,2]\) (\(c = 2\)), so \(\mathbb{E}[T_3] = \frac{3}{3 - 2} = 3\).
\(T = \{1, 3\}\): missed only by \(I_3 = [2, 2]\) which lies strictly inside the gap \((1, 3)\) (\(c = 1\)), so \(\mathbb{E}[\min(T_1, T_3)] = \frac{3}{3 - 1} = \frac{3}{2}\).
Any subset \(T\) containing point \(2\) (\(T \in \{\{2\}, \{1,2\}, \{2,3\}, \{1,2,3\}\}\)) hits all 3 segments (\(c = 0\)), so \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{x \in T} T_x] = \frac{3}{3} = 1\), and their alternating sum \(\sum_{S \subseteq \{1,3\}} (-1)^{|S|} (1) = (1 - 1)^2 = 0\) cancels completely!

Summing by Min–Max IE gives \(\mathbb{E}[\max_{x} T_x] = 3 + 3 - \frac{3}{2} + 0 = \frac{9}{2} \equiv 499122181 \pmod{998244353}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(T_x\) be the step at which point \(x \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) is painted for the first time, so the game ends at \(\max_{1 \le x \le N} T_x\). Should you apply Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion to the \(M\) segments or to the \(N\) points, and why does choosing the \(N\) points make the “missed segment” condition decompose cleanly into disjoint intervals?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Apply Min–Max IE to the \(N\) points: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{1 \le x \le N} T_x\right] = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}} (-1)^{|T|-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{x \in T} T_x\right].\] For a subset of points \(T \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\), let \(c(T)\) be the number of segments \([L_j, R_j]\) that contain no point of \(T\) (\([L_j, R_j] \cap T = \emptyset\)). Then at each step, the chosen segment hits \(T\) with probability \(\frac{M - c(T)}{M}\), so \(\min_{x \in T} T_x\) is a geometric stopping time with expectation \(\frac{M}{M - c(T)}\). Why is \(c(T)\) easy to compute by dynamic programming over the sorted elements \(i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_r\) of \(T\)? Because a segment \([L_j, R_j]\) misses \(T\) if and only if it lies strictly between two consecutive chosen points of \(T\) (with dummy boundary points \(i_0 = 0\) and \(i_{r+1} = N + 1\))!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Precompute \(\operatorname{cnt}[l][r]\) = the number of input segments \([L_j, R_j]\) such that \(l \le L_j \le R_j \le r\) (using a 2D prefix sum in \(O(N^2 + M)\) time). Define \(\text{dp}[i][k]\) as the sum of \((-1)^{|T|-1}\) over all non-empty subsets \(T \subseteq \{1, \dots, i\}\) whose maximum element is \(i\) and that miss a total of \(k \in \{0, \dots, M\}\) segments on \([1, i - 1]\). Transition from the previous element \(j \in \{0, \dots, i - 1\}\) by adding \(\operatorname{cnt}[j + 1][i - 1]\) to \(k\) and flipping the sign!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion Reduction to Missed-Segment Counts
Let \(T_x\) be the step at which point \(x \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) is first covered. By Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion (§14.3): \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{1 \le x \le N} T_x\right] = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq [N]} (-1)^{|T|-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{x \in T} T_x\right].\] For a non-empty subset \(T \subseteq [N]\), let \(c(T) = \#\{j \in [M] : [L_j, R_j] \cap T = \emptyset\}\) be the number of segments disjoint from \(T\). Since every point in \([N]\) is covered by at least one segment and \(T \neq \emptyset\), at least one segment intersects \(T\), so \(0 \le c(T) \le M - 1\). At each step, the probability of picking a segment that intersects \(T\) is \(p(T) = \frac{M - c(T)}{M}\). Thus \(\min_{x \in T} T_x\) has PGF \(F_T(z) = \frac{p(T) z}{1 - (1 - p(T))z}\) and expectation: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{x \in T} T_x\right] = F'_T(1) = \frac{M}{M - c(T)}.\]


2. Interval-Gap Decomposition of \(c(T)\)
Write the elements of \(T\) in increasing order as \(1 \le i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_r \le N\), and augment them with sentinel boundaries \(i_0 = 0\) and \(i_{r+1} = N + 1\). A segment \([L_j, R_j] \subseteq [1, N]\) contains no point of \(T\) if and only if there exists a unique index \(t \in \{0, 1, \dots, r\}\) such that \([L_j, R_j]\) is contained entirely inside the open gap \((i_t, i_{t+1})\), i.e., \(i_t + 1 \le L_j \le R_j \le i_{t+1} - 1\). Therefore, letting \(\operatorname{cnt}[l][r]\) denote the number of segments \([L_j, R_j]\) satisfying \(l \le L_j \le R_j \le r\) (with \(\operatorname{cnt}[l][r] = 0\) if \(l > r\)), the missed-segment count decomposes additively across the \(r + 1\) consecutive gaps: \[c(T) = \sum_{t=0}^{r} \operatorname{cnt}[i_t + 1][i_{t+1} - 1].\]


3. Polynomial / Knapsack DP over the Last Selected Point
We compute \(\operatorname{cnt}[l][r]\) for all \(1 \le l \le r \le N\) in \(O(N^2 + M)\) time via 2D inclusion–exclusion: \[\operatorname{cnt}[l][r] = \operatorname{exact}[l][r] + \operatorname{cnt}[l + 1][r] + \operatorname{cnt}[l][r - 1] - \operatorname{cnt}[l + 1][r - 1].\] Next, define \(\text{dp}[i][k]\) for \(1 \le i \le N\) and \(0 \le k \le M\) as the signed sum \(\sum (-1)^{|T|-1}\) over all subsets \(T \subseteq [i]\) with \(\max(T) = i\) whose prefix gaps \((0, i_1), (i_1, i_2), \dots, (i_{r-1}, i)\) contain a total of \(k\) segments:

Base case (\(i_1 = i\), meaning \(T = \{i\}\) of size \(1\), sign \((-1)^{1-1} = +1\)): \[\text{dp}[i]\big[\operatorname{cnt}[1][i - 1]\big] \mathrel{+}= 1.\]
Transitions from previous point \(j \in \{1, \dots, i - 1\}\): Let \(g = \operatorname{cnt}[j + 1][i - 1]\). Appending \(i\) to a subset ending at \(j\) increases \(|T|\) by \(1\) (flipping the sign by \(-1\)) and adds \(g\) missed segments: \[\text{dp}[i][k + g] \mathrel{-}= \text{dp}[j][k] \qquad (0 \le k \le M - g).\]
Final Extraction (closing the suffix gap \((i, N + 1)\)): For a subset \(T\) with \(\max(T) = i\), adding the final gap \(\operatorname{cnt}[i + 1][N]\) gives its total missed segments \(c(T) = k + \operatorname{cnt}[i + 1][N]\): \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{1 \le x \le N} T_x\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{k=0}^{M - 1 - \operatorname{cnt}[i+1][N]} \text{dp}[i][k] \cdot \frac{M}{M - \left(k + \operatorname{cnt}[i + 1][N]\right)} \pmod{998244353}.\]



4. Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Number of points \(N \in [1, 400]\), number of segments \(M \in [1, 400]\), and \(1\)-indexed segment endpoints \([L_j, R_j] \subseteq [1, N]\) for \(j = 1, \dots, M\).
Preconditions: Every point \(x \in [N]\) is covered by at least one segment, ensuring \(k + \operatorname{cnt}[i+1][N] \le M - 1 < M\) for all reachable states with \(\text{dp}[i][k] \neq 0\), and \(M < 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\mathbb{E}[\max_{1 \le x \le N} T_x] \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N^2 + M)\) time to build \(\operatorname{cnt}[l][r]\) and \(O(N^2 M)\) time for the \(O(N^2)\) gap transitions over degree-\(M\) polynomials; \(O(N^2 + NM)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After completing outer index \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{M} \text{dp}[i][k] u^k = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq [i], \max(T)=i} (-1)^{|T|-1} u^{\sum_{t=0}^{r-1} \operatorname{cnt}[i_t+1][i_{t+1}-1]}\) encodes the exact generating polynomial of prefix-missed segments for all subsets ending at \(i\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: If some point \(x \in [N]\) is covered by zero segments, a subset \(T = \{x\}\) avoids all \(M\) segments (\(k(T) = M\)), causing the geometric denominator \(M - k(T) = 0\) to diverge (\(\mathbb{E}[\max T_x] = \infty\)) and triggering division by zero in \(\operatorname{inv}[M - k_{\text{tot}}]\).









Intermediate 1 (#156) — Luogu P4548: [CTSC2006] 歌唱王国 (The Singing Kingdom + Variance Extension)

Source: Luogu P4548 — CTSC 2006
Prerequisite Tags: Singing Kingdom KMP Border Theorem (§14.4), Stopping-Time Conservation Identity (§14.1), KMP Prefix Function \(\pi[1 \dots L]\).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
In the Singing Kingdom, the alphabet has size \(\sigma\) (consisting of integers \(1, 2, \dots, \sigma\)). At each step, the citizens sing one character chosen uniformly and independently at random from \(\{1, \dots, \sigma\}\) (each with probability \(1/\sigma\)).
Given \(Q\) independent test cases, each specifying a target anthem \(S = s_1 s_2 \dots s_L\) of length \(L\), the singing stops at the exact step \(T\) when \(S\) appears as a contiguous substring for the first time. For each test case, compute:

The expected stopping time \(\mathbb{E}[T] \bmod 10^4\) (printed as a 4-digit zero-padded integer, as required by Luogu P4548), and
The exact stopping-time variance \(\operatorname{Var}(T) \bmod 998244353\) in \(O(L)\) time.


Constraints: \(\sigma \le 10^5\), \(Q \le 50\), \(L \le 10^5\), time limit \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Required Complexity: \(O(L)\) time and \(O(L)\) space per testcase.



Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(\sigma = 2, S = \texttt{ABA}, L = 3\))
Let \(\sigma = 2\) and \(S = (1, 2, 1)\) (\(L = 3\)):

KMP failure table: \(\pi[1] = 0\), \(\pi[2] = 0\) (\(s_1 \neq s_2\)), \(\pi[3] = 1\) (\(s_1 = s_3 = 1\)).
Border chain: Starting at \(k = L = 3\) and following \(k \leftarrow \pi[k]\) while \(k > 0\) gives \(\operatorname{Borders}(S) = \{3, 1\}\).
Expected stopping time: \[\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{k \in \{1, 3\}} 2^k = 2^1 + 2^3 = 2 + 8 = 10 \quad (\text{printed as } \texttt{0010} \bmod 10^4).\]
Variance: \[\operatorname{Var}(T) = \mathbb{E}[T]^2 + \mathbb{E}[T] - 2 \sum_{k \in \{1, 3\}} k \cdot 2^k = 10^2 + 10 - 2\big(1 \cdot 2^1 + 3 \cdot 2^3\big) = 110 - 2(2 + 24) = 110 - 52 = 58.\]



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Instead of building an \(L\)-state KMP Markov chain and solving a linear system, consider the stopping-time PGF \(F(z)\) and survival GF \(G(z)\). What happens combinatorially if you take any non-terminated string \(w\) counted by \(G(z)\) and forcibly append the entire pattern \(S = s_1 \dots s_L\) to the end of \(w\)? Where can the very first occurrence of \(S\) inside \(w \cdot S\) end?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By §14.1, \((1 - z)G(z) = 1 - F(z)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[T] = F'(1) = G(1)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2G'(1) + G(1) - G(1)^2\). When we forcibly append \(S = s_1 \dots s_L\) to any \(w\) counted by \(G(z)\) (multiplying \(G(z)\) by \((z / \sigma)^L\)), the resulting string \(w \cdot S\) must hit \(S\) for the first time at some border length \(k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)\), leaving \(L - k\) remaining characters of \(S\): \[G(z) \left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)^L = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)^{L-k} \Longleftrightarrow G(z) = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k z^{-k}.\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


Evaluate \(G(z)\) at \(z = 1\) (using \(F(1) = 1\)) to get \(\mathbb{E}[T] = G(1) = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k\).
Differentiate \(G(z) = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k z^{-k}\) at \(z = 1\) (using \(F'(1) = G(1)\)) to get \(G'(1) = G(1)^2 - \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k \sigma^k\), and plug into \(\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2G'(1) + G(1) - G(1)^2\). Compute \(\pi[1 \dots L]\) in \(O(L)\) via KMP and walk \(k = L, \pi[L], \dots > 0\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. PGF Conservation & Forced-Appending Equation
Let \(F(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T = n)z^n\) and \(G(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T > n)z^n\). By the Stopping-Time Conservation Identity (§14.1): \[F(z) + (1 - z)G(z) = 1, \qquad F(1) = 1, \qquad \mathbb{E}[T] = F'(1) = G(1), \qquad F''(1) = 2G'(1).\] Every surviving string \(w\) counted by \(G(z)\) has no occurrence of \(S\). Forcibly appending \(S = s_1 s_2 \dots s_L\) multiplies \(G(z)\) by \(\left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)^L\). Because \(w\) is \(S\)-free, the first occurrence of \(S\) in \(w \cdot S\) must end at the \(k\)-th appended character for some \(k \in \{1, \dots, L\}\), which happens if and only if \(S[1 \dots k] = S[L - k + 1 \dots L]\) (\(k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)\)) and the prefix \(w \cdot s_1 \dots s_k\) is a valid stopping trajectory in \(F(z)\), followed by the remaining \(L - k\) characters \(s_{k+1} \dots s_L\) (weight \(\left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)^{L-k}\)): \[G(z) \left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)^L = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)^{L-k}.\] Dividing both sides by \(\left(\frac{z}{\sigma}\right)^L\) isolates \(G(z)\): \[G(z) = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k z^{-k}.\]


2. Extracting \(\mathbb{E}[T]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\) at \(z = 1\)

Expectation: Substituting \(z = 1\) and \(F(1) = 1\) yields: \[\mathbb{E}[T] = G(1) = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k.\]
Variance: Differentiating \(G(z) = F(z) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k z^{-k}\) with respect to \(z\) at \(z = 1\) gives: \[G'(1) = F'(1) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k - F(1) \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k \sigma^k = G(1)^2 - \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k \sigma^k.\] Therefore: \[\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2G'(1) + G(1) - G(1)^2 = G(1)^2 + G(1) - 2 \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k \sigma^k.\]



3. Algorithm Contract & Concise KMP Border Traversal

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Alphabet size \(\sigma \in [1, 10^5]\) and \(1\)-indexed pattern \(S[1 \dots L]\) of length \(L \in [1, 10^5]\).
Preconditions: Characters \(S[i] \in \{1, \dots, \sigma\}\) are drawn i.i.d. uniformly with probability \(1/\sigma > 0\), so \(F(1) = 1\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\mathbb{E}[T] \bmod 10^4\) (formatted with %04d) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T) \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(L)\) time and \(O(L)\) space per testcase.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Walking \(k = L, \pi[L], \pi[\pi[L]], \dots > 0\) visits the exact set of border lengths \(\operatorname{Borders}(S) = \{1 \le k \le L : S[1 \dots k] = S[L - k + 1 \dots L]\}\) in strictly decreasing order, accumulating \(B_S(1) = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} \sigma^k\) and \(-B'_S(1) = \sum_{k \in \operatorname{Borders}(S)} k \sigma^k\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: If \(\sigma \equiv 0 \pmod M\) (e.g., \(\sigma\) is a multiple of \(10\) under \(M = 10^4\)), all border powers \(\sigma^k \bmod M\) vanish for \(k \ge 4\), which is algebraically valid since no division by \(\sigma\) occurs; however, using \(0\)-indexed KMP links without a sentinel or forgetting the full-pattern border \(k = L\) omits the dominant \(\sigma^L\) term.

// Compute 1-indexed KMP border array pi[1..L] and accumulate E[T] and Var(T)
vector<int> pi = kmp_prefix_function(S); // Standard O(L) 1-indexed KMP border array
Mint E = 0, weighted_sum = 0;
for (int k = L; k > 0; k = pi[k]) {
    E += pow_sigma[k];                      // sigma^k
    weighted_sum += Mint(k) * pow_sigma[k]; // k * sigma^k
}

Intermediate 2 (#071) — AtCoder Grand Contest 038 E: Gachapon

Source: AtCoder AGC 038 E
Prerequisite Tags: Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion + Continuous-Time Poissonization / Truncated Exponential EGFs (§14.3), 2D Knapsack Convolution (Ch 04).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
A gachapon machine contains \(N\) types of toys. At each draw, toy \(i\) (\(1 \le i \le N\)) is generated independently with probability \(p_i = \frac{A_i}{S}\), where \(S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} A_i\).
You draw toys repeatedly until for every \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), you have obtained at least \(B_i\) copies of toy \(i\). Compute the expected total number of draws, modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 400\), \(A_i, B_i \ge 1\), \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} A_i \le 400\), \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} B_i \le 400\), time limit \(2.0\text{ s}\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O\big(N \cdot (\sum A_i) \cdot (\sum B_i)\big)\) time and \(O\big((\sum A_i)(\sum B_i)\big)\) space.



Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(N = 2, A = (1, 1), B = (2, 1)\))
Here \(S = A_1 + A_2 = 2\), so \(p_1 = p_2 = \frac{1}{2}\), and we need \(B_1 = 2\) copies of toy 1 and \(B_2 = 1\) copy of toy 2. Using the raw-\(A_i\) EGF scaling \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{i \in T} T_i] = S \sum_{K \ge 0} \frac{K!}{A_T^{K+1}} [x^K] \prod_{i \in T} \sum_{c=0}^{B_i-1} \frac{A_i^c}{c!} x^c\):

\(T = \{1\}\) (\(A_T = 1, c_1 \in \{0, 1\}\)):

\(K = 0\): \(0! \cdot \frac{1^0}{0!} \cdot \frac{2}{1^1} = 2\).
\(K = 1\): \(1! \cdot \frac{1^1}{1!} \cdot \frac{2}{1^2} = 2\). Total \(\mathbb{E}[T_1] = 2 + 2 = 4\).

\(T = \{2\}\) (\(A_T = 1, c_2 = 0\)): \(0! \cdot \frac{1^0}{0!} \cdot \frac{2}{1^1} = 2\).
\(T = \{1, 2\}\) (\(A_T = 2, c_1 + c_2 \in \{0, 1\}\)):

\(K = 0\): \(0! \cdot 1 \cdot \frac{2}{2^1} = 1\).
\(K = 1\): \(1! \cdot 1 \cdot \frac{2}{2^2} = \frac{1}{2}\). Total \(\mathbb{E}[\min(T_1, T_2)] = \frac{3}{2}\).

Alternating sum: \(4 + 2 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{9}{2} \equiv 499122181 \pmod{998244353}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(T_i\) be the step at which toy \(i\) reaches \(B_i\) copies, so we seek \(\mathbb{E}[\max_{1 \le i \le N} T_i]\). Notice the unusually small sum constraints \(\sum_{i=1}^N A_i \le 400\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^N B_i \le 400\). If you convert \(\max_{i} T_i\) into an alternating sum over subsets \(T \subseteq [N]\) of \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{i \in T} T_i]\), what are the only two aggregate parameters of a subset \(T\) and a survival configuration \((c_i)_{i \in T}\) (\(0 \le c_i < B_i\)) that determine its contribution?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion and §14.3 Part B, writing \(A_T = \sum_{i \in T} A_i\), \(p_i = A_i / S\), and \(P_T = A_T / S\), the factors of \(S^{-K}\) in \(\prod_{i \in T} (A_i/S)^{c_i}\) and \(P_T^{-(K+1)} = (S/A_T)^{K+1}\) cancel down to a single factor of \(S\): \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{i \in T} T_i\right] = S \sum_{K=0}^{\sum_{i \in T}(B_i - 1)} \frac{K!}{A_T^{K+1}} [x^K] \prod_{i \in T} \left(\sum_{c=0}^{B_i - 1} \frac{A_i^c}{c!} x^c\right).\] Notice that \((-1)^{|T|-1} = -\prod_{i \in T} (-1)\)! This means we can attach a factor of \(-1\) to each toy \(i \in T\) and compute the subset sum over all \(2^N - 1\) non-empty subsets \(T\) using a 2D knapsack DP over the two small aggregate parameters \((A_T, K)\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Maintain a 2D array \(\text{dp}[a][k]\) where \(a = A_T \in [0, \sum A_i]\) and \(k = K \in [0, \sum (B_i - 1)]\), initialized to \(\text{dp}[0][0] = -1\) (so multiplying by \(-1\) for each chosen item \(i \in T\) produces \((-1)^{|T|-1}\)). When processing item \(i\), transition from \((a, k)\) to \((a + A_i, k + c)\) for \(0 \le c < B_i\) with weight \(-\frac{A_i^c}{c!}\). By tightening the inner loop bounds to current prefix sums \(\sum_{j < i} A_j\) and \(\sum_{j < i} (B_j - 1)\), what is the exact total number of DP transitions?







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Min–Max IE + Truncated Exponential EGF Formula
Let \(T_i\) be the step at which toy \(i\) reaches \(B_i\) copies. By Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion and the §14.3 Part B Poisson / Active-Subset Theorem: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{1 \le i \le N} T_i\right] = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq [N]} (-1)^{|T|-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{i \in T} T_i\right].\] For a fixed non-empty subset \(T \subseteq [N]\), let \(A_T = \sum_{i \in T} A_i\). Conditioned on a draw landing in \(T\) (which happens with probability \(P_T = \frac{A_T}{S}\), so each hit in \(T\) takes \(\frac{S}{A_T}\) expected total draws), toy \(i \in T\) is chosen with conditional probability \(\frac{A_i}{A_T}\). The event that after \(K\) hits in \(T\), every toy \(i \in T\) still has \(c_i < B_i\) copies has probability: \[\mathbb{P}(M_T > K) = \frac{K!}{A_T^K} [x^K] \prod_{i \in T} \left(\sum_{c=0}^{B_i - 1} \frac{A_i^c}{c!} x^c\right).\] Multiplying by \(\frac{S}{A_T}\) and summing over all \(T \neq \emptyset\) and \(K \ge 0\) gives: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{1 \le i \le N} T_i\right] = S \sum_{a=1}^{S} \sum_{K=0}^{B_{\text{tot}}} \frac{K!}{a^{K+1}} \left( \sum_{\substack{\emptyset \neq T \subseteq [N] \\ A_T = a}} (-1)^{|T|-1} [x^K] \prod_{i \in T} \sum_{c=0}^{B_i - 1} \frac{A_i^c}{c!} x^c \right),\] where \(B_{\text{tot}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (B_i - 1) < 400\).


2. 2D Knapsack DP over \((A_T, K)\)
Write \((-1)^{|T|-1} = -\prod_{i \in T} (-1)\). Define \(\text{dp}[a][k]\) after processing the first \(i\) toys to be: \[\text{dp}[a][k] = -\sum_{\substack{T \subseteq [i] \\ A_T = a}} [x^k] \prod_{j \in T} \left( -\sum_{c=0}^{B_j - 1} \frac{A_j^c}{c!} x^c \right).\]

Initialization: \(\text{dp}[0][0] = -1\), all other \(\text{dp}[a][k] = 0\).
Transition for toy \(i = 1, \dots, N\): Let \(S_A\) and \(S_B\) be the running sums of \(A_j\) and \(B_j - 1\) for \(j < i\). Iterate \(a\) from \(S_A\) down to \(0\), \(k\) from \(S_B\) down to \(0\) (skipping \(\text{dp}[a][k] = 0\)), and \(c\) from \(0\) to \(B_i - 1\): \[\text{dp}[a + A_i][k + c] \mathrel{-}= \text{dp}[a][k] \cdot \frac{A_i^c}{c!}.\] Then update \(S_A \mathrel{+}= A_i\) and \(S_B \mathrel{+}= B_i - 1\).
Final Summation: \[\text{Ans} = S \sum_{a=1}^{S} \sum_{k=0}^{S_B} \text{dp}[a][k] \cdot k! \cdot a^{-(k+1)} \pmod{998244353}.\]



3. Algorithm Contract & Complexity Analysis

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Number of toys \(N \in [1, 400]\), \(1\)-indexed weights \(A_1, \dots, A_N \ge 1\) with \(S = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \le 400\), and quotas \(B_1, \dots, B_N \ge 1\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^N B_i \le 400\).
Preconditions: \(A_i \ge 1\) and \(S \le 400 < 998244353\), so \(a \in \{1, \dots, S\}\) and \(c! \in \{1!, \dots, 400!\}\) are all invertible modulo \(998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\mathbb{E}[\max_{1 \le i \le N} T_i] \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: In step \(i\), the loop over \(k \in [0, S_B]\) and \(c \in [0, B_i - 1]\) performs \((S_B + 1) B_i\) operations for each \(a \in [0, S_A]\). Since \(\sum_{i=1}^N S_B B_i \le \left(\sum B_i\right)^2\), total time is \(O\big((\sum A_i)(\sum B_i)^2\big)\) (\(\approx \frac{1}{4} \cdot 400^3 = 1.6 \times 10^7\) fused multiply-adds) and space is \(O\big((\sum A_i)(\sum B_i)\big)\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing prefix \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), \(\text{dp}[a][k] = -[y^a x^k] \prod_{j=1}^{i} \left(1 - y^{A_j} \sum_{c=0}^{B_j - 1} \frac{A_j^c}{c!} x^c\right) \bmod p\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if any \(A_i = 0\) with \(B_i \ge 1\) (infinite waiting time \(\mathbb{E}[\max T_i] = \infty\)), or if \(p \le \max(\sum A_i, \sum B_i)\) (where either the Laplace denominator \(a^{k+1}\) for \(a \in [1, \sum A_i]\) or the factorial \(k!\) for \(k \le \sum(B_i - 1)\) vanishes modulo \(p\)).









Advanced 1 (#148) — Luogu P3706: [SDOI2017] 硬币游戏 (Penney’s Game)

Source: Luogu P3706 — SDOI 2017
Prerequisite Tags: Multi-Pattern Competing Stopping-Time PGF Linear System (§14.4 Part B), String Hashing / KMP Overlap Matrix, Gaussian Elimination.


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
In a game played by \(n\) classmates, each classmate \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) chooses a distinct binary string \(S_i \in \{\texttt{H}, \texttt{T}\}^m\) of the exact same length \(m\).
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly (\(\mathbb{P}(\texttt{H}) = \mathbb{P}(\texttt{T}) = \frac{1}{2}\)), generating an infinite sequence of characters. The game halts at the exact toss \(T\) when one of the \(n\) strings \(S_1, \dots, S_n\) appears as a contiguous substring (suffix) for the first time, and that classmate wins. (Since all \(S_i\) are distinct and have the same length \(m\), no \(S_i\) can be a substring of \(S_j\) for \(i \neq j\), so the winner is always unique.)
Compute the winning probability \(P_i\) of each classmate \(i = 1, \dots, n\), accurate to \(6\) decimal places.

Constraints: \(1 \le n, m \le 300\), all \(S_i\) are distinct strings of length \(m\), time limit \(1.0\text{ s}\).
Required Complexity: \(O(n^2 m + n^3)\) time and \(O(n^2 + nm)\) space.



Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n = 3, m = 3\): HTT, HTH, HHH)
Suppose \(n = 3, m = 3\) with \(S_1 = \texttt{HTT}\), \(S_2 = \texttt{HTH}\), \(S_3 = \texttt{HHH}\) (\(\sigma = 2\)):

Correlation matrix \(C_{i, j} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} 2^k\):

Row \(i = 1\) (\(\texttt{HTT}\)): suffixes \(\texttt{T}, \texttt{TT}, \texttt{HTT}\) only match \(\texttt{HTT}\) at \(k = 3 \implies C_{1, 1} = 8, C_{1, 2} = 0, C_{1, 3} = 0\).
Row \(i = 2\) (\(\texttt{HTH}\)):

vs \(S_1 = \texttt{HTT}\): suffix \(\texttt{HT}\) (\(k = 2\)) matches prefix \(\texttt{HT} \implies C_{2, 1} = 4\).
vs \(S_2 = \texttt{HTH}\): suffixes \(k \in \{1, 3\}\) (\(\texttt{H}, \texttt{HTH}\)) match \(\implies C_{2, 2} = 2^1 + 2^3 = 10\).
vs \(S_3 = \texttt{HHH}\): suffix \(\texttt{H}\) (\(k = 1\)) matches prefix \(\texttt{H} \implies C_{2, 3} = 2\).

Row \(i = 3\) (\(\texttt{HHH}\)):

vs \(S_1 = \texttt{HTT}\): suffix \(\texttt{H}\) (\(k = 1\)) matches prefix \(\texttt{H} \implies C_{3, 1} = 2\).
vs \(S_2 = \texttt{HTH}\): suffix \(\texttt{H}\) (\(k = 1\)) matches prefix \(\texttt{H} \implies C_{3, 2} = 2\).
vs \(S_3 = \texttt{HHH}\): suffixes \(k \in \{1, 2, 3\}\) all match \(\implies C_{3, 3} = 2 + 4 + 8 = 14\).


Linear system (\(\sum_{i=1}^3 C_{i, j} P_i = G(1)\) and \(P_1 + P_2 + P_3 = 1\)): \[8P_1 + 4P_2 + 2P_3 = G(1), \qquad 10P_2 + 2P_3 = G(1), \qquad 2P_2 + 14P_3 = G(1).\] From the last two: \(8P_2 = 12P_3 \implies P_2 = \frac{3}{2}P_3\), so \(G(1) = 17 P_3\). Then \(8P_1 = 17P_3 - 6P_3 - 2P_3 = 9P_3 \implies P_1 = \frac{9}{8}P_3\). Normalizing \(P_1 + P_2 + P_3 = \left(\frac{9}{8} + \frac{12}{8} + \frac{8}{8}\right)P_3 = \frac{29}{8}P_3 = 1\) gives \(P_1 = \frac{9}{29} \approx 0.310345\), \(P_2 = \frac{12}{29} \approx 0.413793\), \(P_3 = \frac{8}{29} \approx 0.275862\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(F_i(z)\) be the PGF of trajectories where string \(S_i\) wins, and let \(G(z)\) be the survival GF of trajectories where none of \(S_1, \dots, S_n\) has appeared yet. What are the \(n + 1\) scalar unknowns at \(z = 1\)? They are \(P_1 = F_1(1), P_2 = F_2(1), \dots, P_n = F_n(1)\), together with \(G(1) = \mathbb{E}[T]\).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By §14.4 Part B, forcibly appending string \(S_j\) (\(1 \le j \le n\)) to every surviving string in \(G(z)\) and evaluating at \(z = 1\) gives the \(j\)-th linear equation: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} C_{i, j} P_i - G(1) = 0, \qquad \text{where } C_{i, j} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} 2^k,\] and \(\mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j) = \{1 \le k \le m : S_i[m - k + 1 \dots m] = S_j[1 \dots k]\}\). Combine these \(n\) equations with \(\sum_{i=1}^n P_i = 1\).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


To avoid floating-point overflow when \(m = 300\) (\(2^{300} \approx 2 \times 10^{90}\), which fits in double up to \(2^{1023}\) or can be normalized by multiplying the forced-appending equation by \(2^{-m}\) so weights are \(2^{k - m} \in [2^{-m}, 1]\)!), scale \(C'_{i, j} = 2^{-m} C_{i, j} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} 2^{k - m}\) and replace \(G(1)\) by \(g' = 2^{-m} G(1)\).
Compute \(\mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)\) for all \(n^2\) pairs in \(O(n^2 m)\) time using polynomial rolling hashes (or KMP on each \(S_j\)), and solve the \((n + 1) \times (n + 1)\) linear system in \(O(n^3)\) using Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting.








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Multi-Pattern Forced Appending System Scaled by \(2^{-m}\)
Let \(F_i(z)\) (\(1 \le i \le n\)) be the PGF of stopping with winner \(S_i\), and let \(G(z)\) be the survival GF. As proved in §14.4 Part B, forcibly appending \(S_j\) to \(G(z)\) yields: \[G(z) \left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^m = \sum_{i=1}^{n} F_i(z) \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} \left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{m - k} \qquad (1 \le j \le n).\] Rather than multiplying by \(2^m\) (which produces numbers of size \(2^{300}\)), simply set \(z = 1\) directly in this equation! Letting \(P_i = F_i(1)\) and \(g' = 2^{-m} G(1)\), we obtain \(n\) well-conditioned linear equations with coefficients in \([0, 2]\): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_{j, i} P_i - g' = 0 \qquad (1 \le j \le n), \qquad \text{where } A_{j, i} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} 2^{-(m - k)}.\] Appending the \((n + 1)\)-st probability conservation equation \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i = 1\] completes the \((n + 1) \times (n + 1)\) linear system for \((P_1, \dots, P_n, g')\).


2. Computing All \(n^2\) Overlap Sets in \(O(n^2 m)\)
Using 64-bit double-modulus polynomial rolling hashes (or building the KMP failure array \(\pi_j[1 \dots m]\) for each pattern \(S_j\) and feeding \(S_i[1 \dots m]\) through \(S_j\)’s KMP automaton to reach final state \(q\), then walking \(k = q, \pi_j[q], \dots > 0\)), we check \(S_i[m - k + 1 \dots m] = S_j[1 \dots k]\) for each \(k \in \{1, \dots, m\}\) in \(O(1)\) per \((i, j, k)\).


3. Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Number of players \(n \in [1, 300]\), pattern length \(m \in [1, 300]\), and \(1\)-indexed distinct binary strings \(S_1, \dots, S_n \in \{\texttt{H}, \texttt{T}\}^m\).
Preconditions: All \(S_i\) are distinct and of equal length \(m\), so no \(S_i\) is a factor of \(S_j\) (\(i \neq j\)), guaranteeing a unique \((n+1) \times (n+1)\) nonsingular Guibas–Odlyzko linear system.
Postconditions (Output): Returns winning probabilities \((P_1, \dots, P_n)\) printed to \(6\) decimal places, with \(\sum_{i=1}^n P_i = 1\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n^2 m)\) time to construct the \(n \times n\) overlap matrix \(A\) via rolling hashes or KMP, plus \(O(n^3)\) time for Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting; \(O(n^2 + nm)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Scaling the forced-appending equations by \(2^{-m}\) sets \(A_{j, i} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{O}(S_i, S_j)} 2^{-(m - k)} \in [0, 2]\) with diagonal entries \(A_{j, j} \ge 1\) (\(k = m \in \mathcal{O}(S_j, S_j)\)) and auxiliary variable \(g' = 2^{-m} G(1)\), preventing floating-point overflow (\(2^{300}\)) or underflow throughout Gaussian elimination.
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Unscaled coefficients \(2^k\) for \(m = 300\) approach \(2^{300} \approx 2 \times 10^{90}\) (causing severe ill-conditioning or overflow if squared, and outright IEEE-754 double overflow if \(m \ge 1024\)); if patterns can have unequal lengths where \(S_i\) is a substring of \(S_j\), player \(j\) can never win (\(P_j = 0\)) and redundant rows must be pruned before elimination.









Advanced 2 (#209) — UOJ 390: [UNR #3] 百鸽笼 (Pigeonhole Cages)

Source: UOJ 390 — UNR #3
Prerequisite Tags: Active-Set Equivalence, Subset Inclusion–Exclusion (Ch 08), Continuous-Time Poissonization / Truncated Exponential EGF Borel Integral (§14.3).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
There are \(n\) pigeonholes numbered \(1, 2, \dots, n\), all initially empty. Pigeonhole \(i\) has capacity \(a_i \ge 1\).
In each step, let \(U \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) be the set of currently non-full pigeonholes (those currently holding strictly fewer than \(a_j\) pigeons). As long as \(U \neq \emptyset\), one pigeonhole is chosen uniformly at random from \(U\) (each with probability \(1/|U|\)) and receives \(1\) pigeon.
For each pigeonhole \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\), compute the probability that pigeonhole \(i\) is the last pigeonhole among all \(n\) to become full, modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 30\), \(1 \le a_i \le 30\) (so \(S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \le 900\)), time limit \(2.0\text{ s}\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Required Complexity: \(O\big(n^3 (\sum a_i)^2\big)\) (or \(O\big(n^2 (\sum a_i)^2\big)\) with rollback DP) time and \(O(n \sum a_i)\) space.



Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n = 2, a = (2, 1)\))
Suppose \(n = 2\) with capacities \(a_1 = 2\) and \(a_2 = 1\):

Direct step trace:

Initially both \(\{1, 2\}\) are non-full (\(|U| = 2\)).
With probability \(1/2\), step 1 picks hole \(2\), making hole \(2\) full immediately; then hole \(1\) is guaranteed to be the last to become full!
With probability \(1/2\), step 1 picks hole \(1\) (now hole \(1\) has \(1 < 2\) pigeons, so \(U = \{1, 2\}\) still has size \(2\)). At step 2, with prob \(1/2\) hole \(2\) is picked (so hole \(1\) finishes last), and with prob \(1/2\) hole \(1\) is picked (making hole \(1\) full first, so hole \(2\) finishes last).
Thus \(\mathbb{P}(\text{hole } 1 \text{ last}) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{4}\), and \(\mathbb{P}(\text{hole } 2 \text{ last}) = \frac{1}{4}\).

EGF Borel trace for \(i = 1\) (\(a_1 = 2\)):

Subset \(T = \emptyset\) (\(|T| = 0, K = 0\)): \((-1)^0 \binom{0+2-1}{2-1} \left(\frac{1}{1}\right)^{2} = 1\).
Subset \(T = \{2\}\) (\(|T| = 1, c_2 = 0 < a_2 = 1 \implies K = 0\)): \((-1)^1 \binom{0+2-1}{2-1} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = -\frac{1}{4}\).
Sum: \(1 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}\). Exact match!




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

In the problem statement, the transition probability \(\frac{1}{|U|}\) changes dynamically whenever a pigeonhole becomes full and drops out of \(U\). Why can we replace this dynamic process by an infinite static process where at every step we pick one of the \(n\) pigeonholes uniformly at random (with probability \(1/n\) each) and allow already-full pigeonholes to keep receiving dummy pigeons, defining \(T_j\) as the step at which pigeonhole \(j\) receives its \(a_j\)-th pigeon?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

In the static process, any step that lands on an already-full pigeonhole is simply a self-loop on the set of non-full pigeonholes; conditioning on landing inside the non-full set \(U\) picks each \(j \in U\) uniformly with probability \(\frac{1}{|U|}\)! Therefore, the probability distribution of the relative order in which the \(n\) pigeonholes reach their thresholds \(a_j\) is 100% identical in both processes! Now fix pigeonhole \(i\). We want \(\mathbb{P}(T_i > T_j \text{ for all } j \neq i)\). By Inclusion–Exclusion over the subset \(T \subseteq [n] \setminus \{i\}\) of pigeonholes that violate this condition (i.e. \(T_j > T_i\) for all \(j \in T\)): \[\mathbb{P}(\text{hole } i \text{ is last}) = \sum_{T \subseteq [n] \setminus \{i\}} (-1)^{|T|} \mathbb{P}\!\left(T_j > T_i \text{ for all } j \in T\right).\] Notice that the event \(\{T_j > T_i \text{ for all } j \in T\}\) depends only on steps that land in \(T \cup \{i\}\) (an active set of size \(|T| + 1\))!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Conditioned on steps landing in \(T \cup \{i\}\) (each with probability \(\frac{1}{|T| + 1}\)), \(T_j > T_i\) holds for all \(j \in T\) if and only if, at the exact step when \(i\) receives its \(a_i\)-th pigeon, every \(j \in T\) has received \(0 \le c_j < a_j\) pigeons. If \(K = \sum_{j \in T} c_j\) is the total pigeons in \(T\) before \(i\)’s \(a_i\)-th pigeon, there are \(K + a_i\) total steps in \(T \cup \{i\}\) (with the last step fixed to \(i\)), so the probability of a tuple \((c_j)_{j \in T}\) is: \[\frac{(K + a_i - 1)!}{(a_i - 1)! \prod_{j \in T} c_j!} \left(\frac{1}{|T| + 1}\right)^{K + a_i} = \frac{(K + a_i - 1)!}{(a_i - 1)! \left(|T| + 1\right)^{K + a_i}} [x^K] \prod_{j \in T} \left(\sum_{c=0}^{a_j - 1} \frac{x^c}{c!}\right).\] Maintain the 2D EGF knapsack over \((|T|, K)\) and use DP rollback (removing item \(i\) from the full \(n\)-item DP in \(O(n \cdot a_i \cdot \sum a_j)\)) to solve for all \(n\) pigeonholes in \(O(n^2 (\sum a_j)^2)\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






1. Equivalence to Uniform Continuous-Time Poissonization
Consider \(n\) independent Poisson processes of rate \(\lambda = 1\), one for each pigeonhole \(j \in \{1, \dots, n\}\). At any moment when \(U \subseteq [n]\) is the set of non-full pigeonholes, by the memorylessness and competing-exponentials property of Poisson processes, the next arrival among \(U\) is equally likely to occur in any pigeonhole \(j \in U\) (probability \(1/|U|\))! Therefore, if \(\tau_j\) is the continuous time at which pigeonhole \(j\) receives its \(a_j\)-th arrival (an \(\operatorname{Erlang}(a_j, 1)\) random variable with density \(f_j(t) = \frac{t^{a_j - 1}}{(a_j - 1)!} e^{-t}\) and survival function \(\mathbb{P}(\tau_j > t) = e^{-t} \sum_{c=0}^{a_j - 1} \frac{t^c}{c!}\)), the probability that pigeonhole \(i\) is the last to fill is: \[P_i = \mathbb{P}\!\left(\tau_i > \tau_j \text{ for all } j \neq i\right) = \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{t^{a_i - 1}}{(a_i - 1)!} e^{-t} \prod_{j \neq i} \left(1 - e^{-t} \sum_{c=0}^{a_j - 1} \frac{t^c}{c!}\right) dt.\]


2. Expanding the Subset Product via Inclusion–Exclusion
Expanding the product over \(j \neq i\) as a sum over subsets \(T \subseteq [n] \setminus \{i\}\) gives: \[P_i = \sum_{T \subseteq [n] \setminus \{i\}} (-1)^{|T|} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{t^{a_i - 1}}{(a_i - 1)!} e^{-(|T| + 1)t} \prod_{j \in T} \left(\sum_{c=0}^{a_j - 1} \frac{t^c}{c!}\right) dt.\] Letting \(m = |T| \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}\) and \(K = \sum_{j \in T} c_j \in \{0, \dots, \sum_{j \neq i}(a_j - 1)\}\), and evaluating the Laplace integral \(\int_{0}^{\infty} t^{K + a_i - 1} e^{-(m + 1)t} \, dt = \frac{(K + a_i - 1)!}{(m + 1)^{K + a_i}}\) yields: \[\boxed{P_i = \sum_{m=0}^{n-1} \sum_{K=0}^{S} \operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m][K] \cdot \binom{K + a_i - 1}{a_i - 1} \cdot \frac{K!}{(m + 1)^{K + a_i}},}\] where \(\operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m][K]\) is the coefficient of \(x^K\) in the signed EGF subset sum over \([n] \setminus \{i\}\): \[\operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m][K] = [y^m x^K] \prod_{j \neq i} \left(1 - y \sum_{c=0}^{a_j - 1} \frac{x^c}{c!}\right).\]


3. Rollback EGF Knapsack in \(O(n^2 S^2)\)
Instead of running the \((n - 1)\)-item knapsack from scratch \(n\) times in \(O(n^3 S^2)\), we first compute the full \(n\)-item 2D polynomial product \[D(y, x) = \prod_{j=1}^{n} \left(1 - y \sum_{c=0}^{a_j - 1} \frac{x^c}{c!}\right)\] in \(O(n^2 S^2)\) time. Then, for each \(i = 1, \dots, n\), we obtain \(\operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m][K]\) by dividing \(D(y, x)\) by \(\left(1 - y \sum_{c=0}^{a_i - 1} \frac{x^c}{c!}\right)\) in a single forward pass over \(m = 0, \dots, n - 1\): \[\operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m][K] = D[m][K] + \sum_{c=0}^{\min(K, a_i - 1)} \operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m - 1][K - c] \cdot \frac{1}{c!}.\]


4. Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Number of pigeonholes \(n \in [1, 30]\) and \(1\)-indexed capacities \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in [1, 30]\), with maximum survival degree \(S = \sum_{j=1}^n (a_j - 1) \le 870\).
Preconditions: \(n + \sum_{j=1}^n a_j \le 930 < 998244353\), so all factorials \(K!\) and powers \((m + 1)^{-(K + a_i)}\) are invertible modulo \(998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(P_1, \dots, P_n \bmod 998244353\), satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^n P_i \equiv 1 \pmod{998244353}\).
Time & Space Complexity: Building \(D(y, x)\) takes \(O(n S \cdot \max a_i) = O(n S^2)\) operations; each of the \(n\) rollbacks takes \(O(n S a_i)\) operations, summing to \(O(n S^2) = O\big(n (\sum a_i)^2\big)\) total time and \(O(n S)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: During the rollback for item \(i\), the recurrence \(\operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m][K] = D[m][K] + \sum_{c=0}^{\min(K, a_i - 1)} \operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m - 1][K - c] \frac{1}{c!}\) maintains \(\sum_{m, K} \operatorname{dp}^{(-i)}[m][K] y^m x^K = D(y, x) \cdot \left(1 - y \sum_{c=0}^{a_i - 1} \frac{x^c}{c!}\right)^{-1} \bmod y^n\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le \max\big(n, \sum_{j=1}^n a_j\big)\) (where either the Laplace base \(m + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p\) or the factorial \((K + a_i - 1)!\) divides by zero modulo \(p\)), or if the rollback loop over \(m\) runs in decreasing instead of increasing order (\(m = 1 \dots n - 1\)), which fails to invert the \(1 - y E_{a_i}(x)\) factor.
