section: 16.4 Furstenberg’s Diagonal Theorem (\(\operatorname{Diag}(R) \leftrightarrow\) Algebraic) & Failure Mode #15
text:
16.4 Furstenberg’s Diagonal Theorem (\(\operatorname{Diag}(R) \leftrightarrow\) Algebraic) & Failure Mode #15
Suppose a bivariate generating function \(F(x, y) = \frac{A(x, y)}{B(x, y)} \in K[[x, y]]\) is rational, and we want to extract its main diagonal
\[\operatorname{Diag}_{x, y} F(x, y) := \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \big([x^n y^n] F(x, y)\big) t^n \in K[[t]].\]
In 1D, rational generating functions correspond to linear recurrences with constant coefficients. In 2D, the diagonal of a rational function is almost never rational—for example, \(\operatorname{Diag}_{x, y} \frac{1}{1 - x - y} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \binom{2n}{n} t^n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4t}}\) has a square-root singularity! A landmark theorem of Harry Furstenberg (1967) explains why: in characteristic \(0\) (and over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) for large primes), the diagonals of bivariate rational power series are precisely the univariate algebraic power series.






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Furstenberg Diagonal Extraction




Diagnostic Signal: You need \(d_n = [x^n y^n] \frac{A(x, y)}{B(x, y)}\) (or a shifted diagonal \([x^n y^{n+s}] \frac{A(x, y)}{B(x, y)}\)) for all \(0 \le n \le N\) (\(N \le 10^6\)), where \(B(x, y)\) has small bidegree (especially quadratic after substituting \(y = t / x\)).
Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

Convert Diagonal to Residue in \(K((z))[[t]]\): Substitute \(x = z\) and \(y = t / z\). By §16.1, for any \(s \in \mathbb{Z}\), \[\sum_{n} \big([x^n y^{n+s}] F(x, y)\big) t^{n+s} = \operatorname{CT}_z\!\Big(z^s F(z, t / z)\Big) = \operatorname{Res}_z\!\Big(z^{s - 1} F(z, t / z)\Big).\]
Clear Negative Powers of \(z\) in the Denominator: Let \(d = \deg_y B(x, y)\). Multiply numerator and denominator of \(z^{s-1} \frac{A(z, t/z)}{B(z, t/z)}\) by \(z^d\) so the denominator becomes a polynomial \(Q(z, t) := z^d B(z, t/z) \in K[t, z]\).
Factor into Small Roots vs. Large Roots: Over the algebraic closure \(\overline{K((t))}\), factor \(Q(z, t)\) in \(z\). A root \(z = z_i(t)\) is called a small root if \(\lim_{t \to 0} z_i(t) = 0\) (i.e., \(\operatorname{val}_t(z_i) > 0\)), and a large root if \(\operatorname{val}_t(z_i) \le 0\).

For a small root \(z_i(t) \in t \overline{K}[[t^\alpha]]\), expanding \(\frac{1}{z - z_i(t)} = \frac{1}{z(1 - z_i(t)/z)} = \sum_{k \ge 0} z_i(t)^k z^{-k-1}\) in \(K((z))[[t]]\) produces negative powers of \(z\), contributing \(\operatorname{Res}_z \frac{1}{z - z_i(t)} = 1\).
For a large root \(z_j(t)\) with \(\operatorname{val}_t(z_j) \le 0\), expanding \(\frac{1}{z - z_j(t)} = -\frac{1}{z_j(t)(1 - z/z_j(t))} = -\sum_{n \ge 0} z_j(t)^{-n-1} z^n\) produces only non-negative powers of \(z \ge 0\), contributing \(0\) to \([z^{-1}]\)!

Sum Formal Residues Over Small Poles Only (Plus \(z = 0\) if Improper!): Check whether \(\deg_y A < \deg_y B\) (so no extra pole at \(z = 0\) exists beyond small roots of \(Q(z, t)\)), and sum the algebraic residues at the small roots \(z_i(t)\).






Direction 1 (Reverse Extraction): \(\operatorname{Diag}_{x, y}\!\left(\frac{A(x, y)}{B(x, y)}\right) \mapsto\) Algebraic Series

Theorem 16.2 (Furstenberg’s Rational Diagonal Residue Formula & 1-Line Quadratic Shortcut)
Let \(F(x, y) = \frac{A(x, y)}{B(x, y)} \in K[[x, y]]\) with \(B(0, 0) \neq 0\), and suppose \(\deg_y A(x, y) < \deg_y B(x, y) = d\) (so that \(z^{-1} F(z, t/z) = \frac{z^{d-1} A(z, t/z)}{z^d B(z, t/z)}\) has no leftover pole at \(z = 0\) outside the roots of \(Q(z, t) := z^d B(z, t/z)\)). If all small roots \(z_1(t), \dots, z_r(t)\) of \(Q(z, t) = 0\) (those satisfying \(\operatorname{val}_t(z_i) > 0\)) are simple, then
\[\operatorname{Diag}_{x, y}\!\left(\frac{A(x, y)}{B(x, y)}\right) = \operatorname{Res}_z\!\left(\frac{1}{z} \frac{A(z, t / z)}{B(z, t / z)}\right) = \sum_{\substack{Q(z_i(t), t) = 0 \\ \operatorname{val}_t(z_i) > 0}} \frac{z_i(t)^{d-1} A\big(z_i(t), t / z_i(t)\big)}{\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}\big(z_i(t), t\big)}.\]
The 1-Line Quadratic Furstenberg Shortcut: Assume \(\operatorname{char}(K) \neq 2\) (and \(p > N\) when evaluating the resulting algebraic series or its D-finite P-recursion up to \(t^N\); for small primes \(p \le N\), use the Frobenius reduction of §16.2–§16.3 instead). In the most common case where \(z^{-1} F(z, t/z)\) has a quadratic denominator in \(z\) of the form
\[\frac{1}{z} F(z, t / z) = \frac{P(z, t)}{\alpha(t) z^2 + \beta(t) z + \gamma(t)}\]
with \(\beta(0) = B(0, 0) \neq 0\) and \(\operatorname{val}_t(\gamma) \ge 1\) (so \(Q(z, t) = \alpha(t) z^2 + \beta(t) z + \gamma(t)\) has literally one small root \(z_1(t) = \frac{-\beta(t) + \beta(0)\sqrt{1 - 4\alpha(t)\gamma(t)/\beta(t)^2}}{2\alpha(t)} = -\frac{\gamma(t)}{\beta(t)} + O(t^2)\) and one large root \(z_2(t) = -\frac{\beta(t)}{\alpha(t)} + O(1)\)), the derivative at \(z_1(t)\) is \(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}(z_1(t), t) = 2\alpha(t) z_1(t) + \beta(t) = \sqrt{\beta(t)^2 - 4\alpha(t)\gamma(t)}\). In particular, when \(P(z, t) = 1\), we get the 1-line quadratic shortcut:
\[\operatorname{Res}_z\!\left(\frac{1}{\alpha(t) z^2 + \beta(t) z + \gamma(t)}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\beta(t)^2 - 4 \alpha(t) \gamma(t)}},\]
where the square root branch is normalized so that \(\sqrt{\beta(0)^2} = \beta(0)\).


Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N \le 4\)): Delannoy Numbers via the Quadratic Furstenberg Shortcut
Consider the Delannoy numbers \(d_n = [x^n y^n] \frac{1}{1 - x - y - x y}\), which count lattice paths from \((0, 0)\) to \((n, n)\) using steps \((1, 0)\), \((0, 1)\), and \((1, 1)\).

Direct Grid Check (\(0 \le n \le 4\)):

\(n = 0\): \(d_0 = 1\).
\(n = 1\): paths \((1,0)(0,1)\), \((0,1)(1,0)\), \((1,1) \implies d_1 = 3\).
\(n = 2\): \(\sum_{k=0}^2 \binom{2}{k}\binom{4-k}{2} = 1(6) + 2(3) + 1(1) = 13\).
\(n = 3\): \(\sum_{k=0}^3 \binom{3}{k}\binom{6-k}{3} = 1(20) + 3(10) + 3(4) + 1(1) = 63\).
\(n = 4\): \(\sum_{k=0}^4 \binom{4}{k}\binom{8-k}{4} = 1(70) + 4(35) + 6(15) + 4(5) + 1(1) = 321\).

Furstenberg Substitution: Substitute \(x = z\) and \(y = t / z\) into \(z^{-1} F(z, t/z)\): \[\frac{1}{z} \frac{1}{1 - z - t/z - t} = \frac{1}{-z^2 + (1 - t)z - t}.\] Here \(\alpha(t) = -1\), \(\beta(t) = 1 - t\) (\(\beta(0) = 1\)), and \(\gamma(t) = -t\) (\(\operatorname{val}_t(\gamma) = 1\)). Applying the 1-line quadratic shortcut gives \[D(t) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} d_n t^n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1 - t)^2 - 4(-1)(-t)}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 6t + t^2}}.\]
Verify Expansion & P-Recursion up to \(n = 4\): Differentiating \((1 - 6t + t^2) D(t)^2 = 1\) gives \((1 - 6t + t^2) D'(t) - (3 - t) D(t) = 0\). Extracting \([t^n]\) yields the 3-term recurrence \((n + 1) d_{n+1} = 3(2n + 1) d_n - n d_{n-1}\):

\(n = 0\): \(1 \cdot d_1 = 3(1)(1) - 0 = 3\).
\(n = 1\): \(2 \cdot d_2 = 3(3)(3) - 1(1) = 26 \implies d_2 = 13\).
\(n = 2\): \(3 \cdot d_3 = 3(5)(13) - 2(3) = 189 \implies d_3 = 63\).
\(n = 3\): \(4 \cdot d_4 = 3(7)(63) - 3(13) = 1284 \implies d_4 = 321\).






Direction 2 (Forward Lift): Every Algebraic Series is a Rational Diagonal
Conversely, suppose \(F(t) \in K[[t]]\) is an algebraic power series with \(F(0) = 0\) satisfying a polynomial equation \(P(t, F(t)) = 0\) under the non-degeneracy (separability) condition
\[P(0, 0) = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}(0, 0) \neq 0.\]
(By the Implicit Function Theorem for FPS, \(y = F(t)\) is the unique small root of \(P(t, y) = 0\) in \(t K[[t]]\).) How can we construct an explicit bivariate rational function \(R(x, y)\) whose diagonal is \(F(t)\)?

Theorem 16.3 (Furstenberg’s Forward Lift \(F(t) \mapsto \operatorname{Diag}(R)\))
Let \(P(t, y) \in K[t, y]\) satisfy \(P(0, 0) = 0\) and \(P_y(0, 0) \neq 0\), and let \(F(t) \in t K[[t]]\) be the unique formal power series with \(F(0) = 0\) and \(P(t, F(t)) = 0\). Then \(F(t)\) is the main diagonal of the bivariate rational function
\[F(t) = \operatorname{Diag}_{x, y}\!\left( \frac{y^2 P_y(x y, y)}{P(x y, y)} \right), \qquad \text{where } \frac{y^2 P_y(x y, y)}{P(x y, y)} \in K[[x, y]].\]
Proof (Single-Step Verbalized Derivation):

First verify that \(R(x, y) := \frac{y^2 P_y(xy, y)}{P(xy, y)}\) actually belongs to \(K[[x, y]]\): since \(P(0, 0) = 0\) and \(P_y(0, 0) = c \neq 0\), we can write \(P(t, y) = y \big(c + A(t, y)\big) + t B(t)\) where \(A(0, 0) = 0\). Substituting \(t = x y\) divides out a common factor of \(y\) from numerator and denominator: \[R(x, y) = \frac{y^2 P_y(x y, y)}{y\big(c + A(x y, y) + x B(x y)\big)} = \frac{y P_y(x y, y)}{c + A(x y, y) + x B(x y)},\] whose denominator has constant term \(c \in K^\times\) at \((x, y) = (0, 0)\), so \(R(x, y) \in K[[x, y]]\).
Now apply the diagonal-to-residue transformation in \(K((z))[[t]]\), where it is convenient to set \(y = z\) and \(x = t / z\) so that \(x y = t\): \[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Diag}_{x, y} R(x, y) &= \operatorname{CT}_z R(t / z, z) && \text{(diagonal substitution } x = t/z,\; y = z \text{)} \\
&= \operatorname{Res}_z\!\left( \frac{1}{z} \frac{z^2 P_y(t, z)}{P(t, z)} \right) && \text{(since } \operatorname{CT}_z L(z) = \operatorname{Res}_z(z^{-1} L(z)) \text{)} \\
&= \operatorname{Res}_z\!\left( \frac{z P_y(t, z)}{P(t, z)} \right) && \text{(cancel } z^{-1} \text{ against } z^2 \text{)}.
\end{aligned}\]
In the ring \(K((z))[[t]]\), \(P(t, z) = (z - F(t)) U(t, z)\) where \(z = F(t) \in t K[[t]]\) is the unique small root of \(P(t, z) = 0\), and \(U(t, z)\) has no small roots (\(U(0, 0) = P_y(0, 0) = c \neq 0\)). By the logarithmic derivative identity \(\frac{P_y(t, z)}{P(t, z)} = \frac{1}{z - F(t)} + \frac{U_z(t, z)}{U(t, z)}\) where \(\frac{U_z(t, z)}{U(t, z)} \in K[[z, t]]\) has only non-negative powers of \(z\), the residue at the simple pole \(z = F(t)\) evaluates to \[\operatorname{Res}_z\!\left( \frac{z P_y(t, z)}{P(t, z)} \right) = \operatorname{Res}_z\!\left( \frac{z}{z - F(t)} \right) = F(t). \qquad \blacksquare\]



Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N \le 4\)): Lifting Shifted Catalan Numbers to a Rational Diagonal
Let \(F(t) = t C(t) = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4t}}{2} = t + t^2 + 2t^3 + 5t^4 + \dots\) be the shifted Catalan generating function, which satisfies \(F(0) = 0\) and \(P(t, F(t)) = 0\) where
\[P(t, y) = y - y^2 - t, \qquad P_y(t, y) = 1 - 2y \quad (P(0, 0) = 0,\; P_y(0, 0) = 1 \neq 0).\]
By Theorem 16.3, substitute \(t = x y\) and divide numerator and denominator by \(y\):
\[R(x, y) = \frac{y^2 P_y(x y, y)}{P(x y, y)} = \frac{y^2 (1 - 2y)}{y - y^2 - x y} = \frac{y (1 - 2y)}{1 - x - y}.\]
Let us check the diagonal coefficients \([x^n y^n] R(x, y)\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\) using \([x^n y^k] \frac{1}{1 - x - y} = \binom{n+k}{n}\):
\[[x^n y^n] \frac{y - 2y^2}{1 - x - y} = [x^n y^{n-1}] \frac{1}{1 - x - y} - 2 [x^n y^{n-2}] \frac{1}{1 - x - y} = \binom{2n - 1}{n} - 2 \binom{2n - 2}{n}.\]

\(n = 0\): \(0 - 0 = 0\).
\(n = 1\): \(\binom{1}{1} - 2\binom{0}{1} = 1 - 0 = 1 = C_0\).
\(n = 2\): \(\binom{3}{2} - 2\binom{2}{2} = 3 - 2 = 1 = C_1\).
\(n = 3\): \(\binom{5}{3} - 2\binom{4}{3} = 10 - 8 = 2 = C_2\).
\(n = 4\): \(\binom{7}{4} - 2\binom{6}{4} = 35 - 30 = 5 = C_3\).

Every coefficient matches \(F(t) = t + t^2 + 2t^3 + 5t^4 + \dots\) on the nose!




Failure Mode #15: Hidden Pole at \(z = 0\) in Improper Rational Diagonals (\(\deg_y A \ge \deg_y B\))






WarningFailure Mode #15 & Remedy: Omitting the Residue at \(z = 0\) When \(\deg_y A \ge \deg_y B\)



What Goes Wrong: In Theorem 16.2, we required the strict degree bound \(\deg_y A(x, y) < \deg_y B(x, y) = d\). Why? Look at what happens when we substitute \(y = t / z\) into \(\frac{1}{z} \frac{A(z, t/z)}{B(z, t/z)}\) and clear the denominator by multiplying top and bottom by \(z^d\):
\[\frac{1}{z} \frac{A(z, t / z)}{B(z, t / z)} = \frac{z^{d - 1} A(z, t / z)}{z^d B(z, t / z)}.\]
If \(\deg_y A = m \ge d = \deg_y B\), then \(A(z, t/z)\) contains \(y^m = t^m / z^m\), so the numerator \(z^{d - 1} A(z, t / z)\) still contains negative powers of \(z\) up to \(z^{d - 1 - m} = z^{-(m - d + 1)}\)! That means \(z = 0\) is itself a small pole of order \(\le m - d + 1\) alongside the small roots \(z_i(t)\) of \(Q(z, t) = z^d B(z, t/z) = 0\). If you blindly sum residues only over the nonzero small roots \(z_i(t)\) of \(Q(z, t) = 0\) and forget \(\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}\), your answer will be completely wrong!
Concrete Worked Failure (\(\frac{x + 2y}{1 - x - y}\)): Let \(F(x, y) = \frac{x + 2y}{1 - x - y}\), where \(\deg_y A = 1 \ge \deg_y B = 1\).

True Diagonal (\(0 \le n \le 3\)): Since \([x^n y^n] \frac{x + 2y}{1 - x - y} = [x^{n-1} y^n] \frac{1}{1 - x - y} + 2 [x^n y^{n-1}] \frac{1}{1 - x - y} = 3 \binom{2n - 1}{n - 1}\) for \(n \ge 1\) (and \(0\) for \(n = 0\)), the true diagonal sequence for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\) is: \[(0,\; 3,\; 9,\; 30,\; \dots), \qquad \operatorname{Diag}_{x, y} F(x, y) = \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4t}} - 1\right).\]
What Happens If You Forget \(z = 0\): Substituting \(x = z, y = t / z\) into \(z^{-1} F(z, t/z)\) gives \[\frac{1}{z} \frac{z + 2t/z}{1 - z - t/z} = \frac{z^2 + 2t}{z\big(-z^2 + z - t\big)}.\] Notice the extra factor of \(z\) in the denominator! The quadratic \(-z^2 + z - t = 0\) has unique small root \(z_1(t) = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4t}}{2}\), at which the residue is \[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Res}_{z = z_1(t)} \frac{z^2 + 2t}{z(-z^2 + z - t)}
&= \frac{z_1(t)^2 + 2t}{z_1(t)\bigl(1 - 2z_1(t)\bigr)}
&& \text{(apply simple-pole residue formula } \frac{A(z_1)}{B'(z_1)}\text{)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{z_1(t) + t}{z_1(t)\sqrt{1 - 4t}}
&& \text{(use } z_1(t)^2 = z_1(t) - t \text{ and } 1 - 2z_1(t) = \sqrt{1 - 4t}\text{)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{1 + \frac{t}{z_1(t)}}{\sqrt{1 - 4t}}
&& \text{(divide numerator and denominator by } z_1(t)\text{)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{1 + \bigl(1 - z_1(t)\bigr)}{\sqrt{1 - 4t}} = \frac{3}{2\sqrt{1 - 4t}} + \frac{1}{2}.
&& \text{(since } z_1^2 - z_1 + t = 0 \implies \frac{t}{z_1} = 1 - z_1 = \frac{1 + \sqrt{1-4t}}{2}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\] Expanding \(\frac{3}{2\sqrt{1-4t}} + \frac{1}{2}\) gives \((2,\; 3,\; 9,\; 30, \dots)\)—wrong at \(n = 0\) (and if \(\deg_y A - \deg_y B \ge 1\), wrong at every \(n \ge 0\))! Why? Because \(z = 0\) is also a simple pole of \(\frac{z^2 + 2t}{z(-z^2 + z - t)}\) with residue \[\operatorname{Res}_{z = 0} \frac{z^2 + 2t}{z(-z^2 + z - t)} = \left.\frac{z^2 + 2t}{-z^2 + z - t}\right|_{z = 0} = \frac{2t}{-t} = -2.\] Adding the missing residue at \(z = 0\) gives \(\left(\frac{3}{2\sqrt{1 - 4t}} + \frac{1}{2}\right) + (-2) = \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4t}} - 1\right)\), restoring the exact diagonal \((0, 3, 9, 30, \dots)\)!

Two Universal Remedies:

Remedy A (Polynomial Division in \(y\) First): Before applying Furstenberg’s residue formula, perform Euclidean division of \(A(x, y)\) by \(B(x, y)\) as polynomials in \(y\): \[\frac{A(x, y)}{B(x, y)} = P_{\text{poly}}(x, y) + \frac{R(x, y)}{B(x, y)}, \qquad \deg_y R < \deg_y B.\] Extract \(\operatorname{Diag}_{x, y} P_{\text{poly}}(x, y) = \sum_{n} ([x^n y^n] P_{\text{poly}}(x, y)) t^n\) directly term-by-term from the finite polynomial \(P_{\text{poly}}(x, y)\), and apply Theorem 16.2 to the strictly proper fraction \(\frac{R(x, y)}{B(x, y)}\). (In our example, \(\frac{x + 2y}{1 - x - y} = -2 + \frac{2 - x}{1 - x - y}\) where \(\deg_y(2 - x) = 0 < 1 = \deg_y(1 - x - y)\)!)
Remedy B (Include \(\operatorname{Res}_{z = 0}\) Explicitly): Keep \(z^{-(m - d + 1)}\) inside the residue integral and evaluate \(\operatorname{Res}_{z = 0} + \sum_{\operatorname{val}_t(z_i) > 0} \operatorname{Res}_{z = z_i(t)}\).









ImportantAlgorithm Contract: Furstenberg Rational Diagonal Extractor




Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Bivariate rational function \(R(x, y) = A(x, y) / B(x, y)\) with polynomial numerator \(A\) and denominator \(B\) of \(y\)-degree \(d_y = \deg_y B \le 2\), and target diagonal index \(N \ge 0\) (or coefficient truncation bound \(N\)).
Preconditions: \(B(0, 0) \neq 0 \pmod p\) so that \(R(x, y) \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x, y]]\) is well-defined; for \(d_y = 2\), \(2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) and discriminant \(\Delta(t) = b_1(t)^2 - 4 b_0(t) b_2(t)\) has \(\Delta(0) = 1\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns the main diagonal series \(D(t) = \operatorname{Diag}_{x, y} R(x, y) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} r_{n, n} t^n \bmod t^{N+1}\) (via algebraic reciprocal square root \(\Delta(t)^{-1/2}\) or D-finite P-recursion) or the single coefficient \(r_{N, N} \pmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: For \(d_y \le 2\): \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space for all \(n \le N\) via Newton’s method on \(\Delta(t)^{-1/2}\), or \(O(N)\) time and \(O(1)\) space via P-recursion when \(\deg_t \Delta(t) = O(1)\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After residue reduction on \(z^{-1} A(z, t/z) / \widetilde{B}(z, t)\), the sum over small branches \(\operatorname{val}_t(z_i(t)) > 0\) equals \([z^0] R(z, t/z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} r_{n, n} t^n\) identically in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[t]]\).






Lipshitz’s Theorem for 3D+ Diagonals: Why 3D Diagonals Leave the Algebraic World Yet Stay D-Finite
Does Furstenberg’s Theorem extend to three variables \(x, y, z\)? That is, if \(R(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Q}[[x, y, z]]\) is a 3D rational power series, is its main diagonal \(\operatorname{Diag}_{x, y, z} R(x, y, z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r_{n, n, n} t^n\) still an algebraic power series over \(\mathbb{Q}(t)\)?
No—not in characteristic \(0\)! Consider the simplest possible 3D rational generating function, the trinomial generator
\[R(x, y, z) = \frac{1}{1 - (x + y + z)} = \sum_{a, b, c \ge 0} \frac{(a + b + c)!}{a! \, b! \, c!} x^a y^b z^c.\]
Its main diagonal is the sequence of central trinomial / hexagonal lattice numbers
\[D_3(t) := \operatorname{Diag}_{x, y, z}\!\left(\frac{1}{1 - (x + y + z)}\right) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(3n)!}{(n!)^3} t^n = 1 + 6t + 90t^2 + 1680t^3 + 34650t^4 + \dots\]
Why is \(D_3(t)\) transcendental over \(\mathbb{C}(t)\)?

Asymptotic Proof via Stirling’s Formula: Applying Stirling’s approximation \(m! \sim \sqrt{2\pi m} (m / e)^m\) to \(u_n = \frac{(3n)!}{(n!)^3}\) gives \[u_n = \frac{(3n)!}{(n!)^3} \sim \frac{\sqrt{2\pi (3n)} (3n / e)^{3n}}{\big(\sqrt{2\pi n} (n / e)^n\big)^3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{27^n}{n}.\] By the Flajolet–Odlyzko Transfer Theorem (and Puiseux’s Theorem for algebraic functions), the coefficients of any algebraic series \(F(t) \in \mathbb{Q}[[t]]\) have dominant asymptotic growth of the form \(c \cdot \rho^n n^{-\alpha}\) where the exponent \(\alpha \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}\) can never be a positive integer \(1, 2, 3, \dots\) (because a Puiseux branch \((1 - \rho t)^{\alpha - 1}\) with \(\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\) is a smooth polynomial with \(0\) asymptotic contribution, while \(n^{-1}\) requires a logarithmic singularity \(-\ln(1 - 27t)\)!). Because \(u_n \sim \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\pi} 27^n n^{-1}\) has exponent \(\alpha = 1\), \(D_3(t)\) has a logarithmic singularity at \(t = 1/27\) and is transcendental over \(\mathbb{Q}(t)\).
Lipshitz’s Theorem (1988) — Every \(d\)-Dimensional Rational Diagonal is D-Finite (P-Recursive): Even though \(D_3(t)\) is not algebraic, Leonard Lipshitz (1988) proved that for any number of variables \(d \ge 2\), the diagonal \(\operatorname{Diag}_{x_1, \dots, x_d} \frac{A(x_1, \dots, x_d)}{B(x_1, \dots, x_d)}\) of a rational power series is always D-Finite (holonomic)—meaning it satisfies a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients in \(t\), and its coefficients \(u_n\) satisfy a bounded-order P-recursion with polynomial coefficients in \(n\)! For \(u_n = \frac{(3n)!}{(n!)^3}\), the consecutive ratio is \(\frac{u_n}{u_{n-1}} = \frac{3n(3n-1)(3n-2)}{n^3} = \frac{3(3n-1)(3n-2)}{n^2}\), giving the first-order P-recursion \[n^2 u_n - 3(3n - 1)(3n - 2) u_{n-1} = 0 \iff t(27t - 1) D_3''(t) + (54t - 1) D_3'(t) + 6 D_3(t) = 0,\] which computes \(u_0, u_1, \dots, u_N \bmod p\) in \(O(N)\) time!
Characteristic \(p > 0\) Twist (Deligne 1984 / Christol): Remarkably, if we reduce the coefficients of a \(d\)-dimensional rational series modulo a prime \(p\), the diagonal \(\operatorname{Diag}_{x_1, \dots, x_d} R(\mathbf{x}) \bmod p\) becomes algebraic again over \(\mathbb{F}_p(t)\) for every dimension \(d \ge 2\), and its \(N\)-th coefficient for \(N \le 10^{18}\) can be extracted in \(O(p^d \log_p N)\) time via Regime 4 (Frobenius sectioning)!

16 — The Bivariate Hierarchy, 2D Bostan–Mori & Furstenberg's Diagonal Theorem

title: 16 — The Bivariate Hierarchy, 2D Bostan–Mori & Furstenberg’s Diagonal Theorem
text:
16.5 4-Tier 8-Problem Practice Ladder
We now consolidate all techniques of Chapter 16 across eight canonical competitive programming problems graded from Stepping Stone to Mastery.


Stepping Stone 1 (#048): Don’t Step on the Mines! — AtCoder ARC 012 D

Topic Tags: Laurent Ring \((K[x, x^{-1}, y, y^{-1}])\), \(45^\circ\) Diagonal Coordinate Rotation, Composite Modulus Sieve.


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) independent 2D lattice walks on \(\mathbb{Z}^2\), a step count \(T\), and an arbitrary (not necessarily prime) modulus \(M\). For each \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\), the \(i\)-th walk starts at \((0, 0)\) and must end at \((x_i, y_i)\) after exactly \(T\) steps, where each step moves by one unit in one of the four cardinal directions:
\[\mathcal{S} = \{(+1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, +1), (0, -1)\}.\]
Let \(W_i\) be the number of valid \(T\)-step trajectories from \((0, 0)\) to \((x_i, y_i)\). Compute the product of \(W_i\) over all \(N\) walks modulo \(M\):
\[\prod_{i=1}^{N} W_i \bmod M.\]

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(1 \le T \le 10^5\), \(|x_i|, |y_i| \le T\), \(1 \le M \le 10^9\) (\(M\) is not guaranteed to be prime). Required complexity: \(O(N + T)\) time and \(O(T)\) space.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(T = 2, N = 1, (x_1, y_1) = (1, 1)\)): After \(T = 2\) steps, \((1, 1)\) can be reached via \((0,0) \to (1,0) \to (1,1)\) or \((0,0) \to (0,1) \to (1,1)\), so \(W_1 = 2\). Indeed, \(\binom{2}{(2+1+1)/2} \binom{2}{(2+1-1)/2} = \binom{2}{2}\binom{2}{1} = 2\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Each unit step in \(\mathcal{S} = \{(\pm 1, 0), (0, \pm 1)\}\) corresponds to a term in the bivariate Laurent step polynomial
\[S(x, y) = x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1} \in \mathbb{Z}[x, x^{-1}, y, y^{-1}].\]
The number of \(T\)-step walks ending at \((X, Y)\) is the Laurent coefficient \(W = [x^X y^Y] S(x, y)^T\). Why is expanding \((x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1})^T\) directly by the multinomial theorem too slow (\(O(T)\) per query)? Because the four terms are added together! Look for a coordinate change that factors \(S(x, y)\) into a product of two binomials.



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Put \(S(x, y)\) over a common denominator \(x y\):
\[x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1} = \frac{x^2 y + y + x y^2 + x}{x y} = \frac{(x + y)(1 + x y)}{x y}.\]
Raise this factored form to the \(T\)-th power:
\[[x^X y^Y] S(x, y)^T = [x^{T + X} y^{T + Y}] (1 + x y)^T (x + y)^T.\]
Expand \((1 + x y)^T = \sum_{a=0}^T \binom{T}{a} x^a y^a\) and \((x + y)^T = \sum_{b=0}^T \binom{T}{b} x^b y^{T - b}\), and solve the \(2 \times 2\) linear system \(a + b = T + X\) and \(a + T - b = T + Y\) for \((a, b)\).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Composite Modulus Contract

Solving for \((a, b)\) gives \(a = \frac{T + X + Y}{2}\) and \(b = \frac{T + X - Y}{2}\), so \(W_i = \binom{T}{a_i} \binom{T}{b_i}\) whenever \(|X| + |Y| \le T\) and \(X + Y \equiv T \pmod 2\) (and \(W_i = 0\) otherwise). Since \(M \le 10^9\) is not necessarily prime, you cannot divide by factorials modulo \(M\)! Instead, express the entire product \(\prod_{i=1}^N \binom{T}{a_i} \binom{T}{b_i}\) as a product of factorials \(\prod_{k=1}^T (k!)^{e_k}\), sweep \(k\) from \(T\) down to \(2\) to convert factorial exponents into integer exponents \(\prod_{k=2}^T k^{c_k}\), and push composite bases \(k = p \cdot (k/p)\) down to primes using a linear sieve in \(O(T)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Laurent Step Generator & Diagonal Rotation: In the Laurent polynomial ring \(\mathbb{Z}[x, x^{-1}, y, y^{-1}]\), one step of the walk multiplies the position monomial \(x^u y^v\) by \(S(x, y) = x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1}\). Factoring \(S(x, y)\) by grouping terms with \(x\) and \(y\) gives: \[\begin{aligned}
S(x, y) &= x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1} && \text{(cardinal step generator)} \\
&= x^{-1} y^{-1} (x^2 y + y + x y^2 + x) && \text{(factor out } (xy)^{-1} \text{)} \\
&= (x y)^{-1} (1 + x y)(x + y) && \text{(factor } (1 + xy)(x + y) \text{)}.
\end{aligned}\] (Geometrically, setting \(u = x y\) and \(v = x / y\) rotates the 2D lattice by \(45^\circ\) so that each cardinal step \((dx, dy) \in \{(\pm 1, 0), (0, \pm 1)\}\) changes \(x + y\) by \(\pm 1\) and \(x - y\) by \(\pm 1\) independently!)
Extracting \([x^X y^Y] S(x, y)^T\): Raising \(S(x, y)\) to the \(T\)-th power and expanding the two binomial factors yields: \[\begin{aligned}
W_i = [x^{x_i} y^{y_i}] S(x, y)^T &= [x^{T + x_i} y^{T + y_i}] (1 + x y)^T (x + y)^T \\
&= [x^{T + x_i} y^{T + y_i}] \sum_{a=0}^{T} \sum_{b=0}^{T} \binom{T}{a} \binom{T}{b} x^{a + b} y^{a + T - b}.
\end{aligned}\] A pair \((a, b)\) matches the target exponents \((T + x_i, T + y_i)\) if and only if \[\begin{cases} a + b = T + x_i, \\ a - b = y_i \end{cases} \iff a_i = \frac{T + x_i + y_i}{2}, \qquad b_i = \frac{T + x_i - y_i}{2}.\]

Boundary Feasibility Check: If \(T + x_i + y_i\) is odd, or if \(a_i \notin [0, T]\), or if \(b_i \notin [0, T]\) (equivalently \(|x_i| + |y_i| > T\)), then \(W_i = 0\), and the entire product \(\prod_{i=1}^N W_i \bmod M\) is immediately \(0\).
Otherwise, \(W_i = \binom{T}{a_i} \binom{T}{b_i}\).

Division-Free Prime-Exponent Accumulation Modulo Composite \(M\): Writing \(\binom{T}{a_i} \binom{T}{b_i} = \frac{(T!)^2}{a_i! (T - a_i)! b_i! (T - b_i)!}\), we initialize an array \(E[0 \dots T] = 0\). For each walk \(i = 1, \dots, N\), we add \(+2\) to \(E[T]\) and subtract \(1\) from \(E[a_i]\), \(E[T - a_i]\), \(E[b_i]\), and \(E[T - b_i]\).

Next, since \(k! = k \cdot (k - 1)!\), a downward suffix sum \(c_k = \sum_{j=k}^T E[j]\) converts \(\prod_{k=1}^T (k!)^{E[k]}\) into \(\prod_{k=2}^T k^{c_k}\).
Finally, using the smallest prime factor spf[k] precomputed via a linear sieve up to \(T\), we iterate \(k\) from \(T\) down to \(2\): if spf[k] < k, we add \(c_k\) to both \(c_{\text{spf}[k]}\) and \(c_{k / \text{spf}[k]}\) and set \(c_k = 0\). Because the true product \(\prod_{i=1}^N W_i\) is an integer, every remaining prime \(p \le T\) is guaranteed to have a non-negative final exponent \(c_p \ge 0\), so we multiply \(\prod_{p \le T} p^{c_p} \bmod M\) via binary exponentiation with zero modular divisions!




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Number of walks \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), step count \(0 \le T \le 10^5\), target coordinates \((x_i, y_i) \in \mathbb{Z}^2\) for \(1 \le i \le N\), and arbitrary modulus \(2 \le M \le 10^9\); no coprimality precondition on \(M\) (division-free prime-exponent accumulation handles composite \(M\) with \(\gcd(k!, M) > 1\)).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\prod_{i=1}^N W_i \bmod M\), where \(W_i = [x^{x_i} y^{y_i}] (x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1})^T\).
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Rotated step counts are \(a_i = (T + x_i + y_i)/2 \in [0, T]\) and \(b_i = (T + x_i - y_i)/2 \in [0, T]\); prime-exponent array \(c[0 \dots T]\) is pushed down from \(k = T\) down to \(2\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N + T)\) time and \(O(T)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After the downward suffix sum and composite-to-prime SPF pushdown from \(k = T\) down to \(2\), every prime \(p \le T\) holds its exact net exponent \(c_p = v_p\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^N \binom{T}{a_i}\binom{T}{b_i}\right) \ge 0\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If any walk \(i\) violates \(|x_i| + |y_i| \le T\) or \((x_i + y_i) \equiv T \pmod 2\), then \(W_i = 0\) and the entire product is immediately \(0\) (must short-circuit before indexing negative factorials \(a_i < 0\) or \(T - a_i < 0\)); at \(T = 0\), \((x_i, y_i) = (0, 0)\) gives \(W_i = 1 \bmod M\).









Stepping Stone 2 (#129): Timber — Codeforces 1821F

Topic Tags: Bivariate Rational OGF in \(K[y][[x]]\), Inclusion–Exclusion / Canonical Transfer Automaton, Primary-Variable Selection (主元法).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
On the integer segment \([0, n]\), you want to plant \(m\) trees of height \(k\) at strictly increasing integer coordinates \(1 \le x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_m \le n\). A set of positions \(\{x_1, \dots, x_m\}\) is called valid if there exists at least one choice of directions \(d_i \in \{\text{Left}, \text{Right}\}\) for \(i = 1, \dots, m\) such that:

If tree \(i\) falls Left, it occupies the closed interval \([x_i - k, x_i]\); if it falls Right, it occupies \([x_i, x_i + k]\).
All \(m\) felled intervals lie completely inside \([0, n]\).
No two felled intervals share even a single endpoint (they are pairwise disjoint as closed intervals).

Compute the number of valid sets of tree positions \(\{x_1, \dots, x_m\}\) modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n, m, k \le 3 \times 10^5\), modulus \(p = 998244353\). Required complexity: \(O(n + m)\) time and \(O(n + m)\) space.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(n = 4, m = 1, k = 2\)): For \(m = 1\) tree of height \(k = 2\) on \([0, 4]\): \(x_1 = 1\) can fall Right (\([1, 3]\)); \(x_1 = 2\) can fall Left (\([0, 2]\)) or Right (\([2, 4]\)); \(x_1 = 3\) can fall Left (\([1, 3]\)); \(x_1 = 4\) can fall Left (\([2, 4]\)). Thus all \(4\) positions \(\{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{4\}\) are valid (notice \(x_1 = 2\) has \(2\) valid orientations, but is counted once as a position set!), so the answer is \(4\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Notice that there are \(n + 1\) integer points \(\{0, 1, \dots, n\}\), and each felled tree covers \(k + 1\) consecutive integer points (either \(\{x_i - k, \dots, x_i\}\) or \(\{x_i, \dots, x_i + k\}\)). Why can’t we just count all valid pairs of (positions, orientations)? Because as seen at \(x_1 = 2\) in the sample trace, a single position set can admit multiple valid orientation assignments! Specifically, when can a tree have a choice between falling Left and falling Right?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

To count each valid position set \(\{x_1, \dots, x_m\}\) exactly once, assign each valid position set its canonical (lexicographically leftmost) orientation: push every tree to fall Left \([x_i - k, x_i]\) whenever possible, and only let tree \(i\) fall Right \([x_i, x_i + k]\) if falling Left is blocked because \(x_i - k\) is already occupied (either \(x_i - k < 0\) or the previous felled interval ends in \([x_i - k, x_i - 1]\)). Equivalently, a Left-felled tree is a block of \(k + 1\) integer points (\(x^{k+1}\)), and a Right-felled tree \([x_i, x_i + k]\) is only canonical if there are strictly fewer than \(k\) empty integer points immediately to its left—meaning we add \(2 x^{k+1}\) (Left or Right) and subtract \(x^{2k+1}\) (a Right-felled tree preceded by \(\ge k\) empty points, which could have fallen Left instead)! Set up the bivariate OGF \(F(x, y)\) where \(x\) marks the \(n\) spaces/points and \(y\) marks the \(m\) trees.



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

There are \(n + 1\) integer points in \([0, n]\), so if we pad one extra point at the end, each tree block plus its trailing separator uses \(x^{k+1}(2 - x^k)\), and each unused point contributes \(x\), giving
\[\text{Ans} = [x^n y^m] \frac{1}{1 - x - y x^{k+1}(2 - x^k)}.\]
Apply the Primary-Variable Selection Rule (主元法) from §16.1: because the denominator is linear in \(y\), extract \([y^m]\) first to get \(\frac{x^{m(k+1)}(2 - x^k)^m}{(1 - x)^{m+1}}\), and expand \((2 - x^k)^m\) via the binomial theorem in \(O(m)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Canonical Orientation to Avoid Overcounting Position Sets: Every felled tree covers \(k + 1\) consecutive integer points in \(\{0, 1, \dots, n\}\), with the tree root located either at the right endpoint of its interval (if felled Left: \([x_i - k, x_i]\)) or at the left endpoint of its interval (if felled Right: \([x_i, x_i + k]\)). Suppose we fix the \(m\) disjoint intervals of length \(k + 1\) inside \(\{0, 1, \dots, n\}\) and choose for each interval whether its root is at its right endpoint (\(L\)) or left endpoint (\(R\)). When do two different choices of intervals/endpoints produce the same root position \(x_i\)? Only when interval \(i\) has its root at its left endpoint \(x_i\) (so it occupies \([x_i, x_i + k]\)), and all \(k\) points \(\{x_i - k, \dots, x_i - 1\}\) immediately to its left are uncovered! In that case, tree \(i\) could instead fall Left into \([x_i - k, x_i]\) without colliding with anything to its left. Therefore, to make the representation unique (canonical), we allow every tree block of \(k + 1\) points two choices of root endpoint (\(2 x^{k+1}\)), and forbid a Right-oriented block (\(x^{k+1}\)) from being immediately preceded by \(k\) uncovered points (\(x^k\)) by subtracting a fused forbidden block of size \((k + 1) + k = 2k + 1\) points (\(-x^{2k+1}\)).
Bivariate Rational OGF: Notice that if we shift the coordinate system by associating each tree block of \(k + 1\) integer points with \(k\) of the \(n\) unit segments (plus \(1\) separator point between trees, so \(m\) trees require \(m(k+1) - 1\) segments, i.e., \([x^{n+1}]\) of \(\frac{x}{1 - x - y(2x^{k+1} - x^{2k+1})} = [x^n] \frac{1}{1 - x - y x^{k+1}(2 - x^k)}\)), the bivariate OGF is: \[F(x, y) = \frac{1}{(1 - x) - y x^{k+1}(2 - x^k)} \in \mathbb{F}_p[y][[x]].\]
Extracting \([y^m]\) First (主元法): Following the Primary-Variable Selection Rule (§16.1), since the denominator is linear in \(y\), we extract \([y^m]\) first: \[\begin{aligned}
[y^m] F(x, y) &= \frac{x^{m(k+1)} (2 - x^k)^m}{(1 - x)^{m+1}} && \text{(geometric series in } y \text{)} \\
&= x^{m(k+1)} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{m}{j} 2^{m - j} x^{j k} \right) \left( \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} \binom{m + r}{m} x^r \right) && \text{(binomial expansions)}.
\end{aligned}\] Now extract \([x^n]\) by setting \(m(k + 1) + j k + r = n \iff r = n - m(k + 1) - j k\): \[\text{Ans} = [x^n y^m] F(x, y) = \sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom{m}{j} 2^{m - j} \binom{n - m k - j k}{m} \pmod{998244353},\] where \(\binom{A}{m} = 0\) whenever \(A < m\).

Sample Trace Verification (\(n = 4, m = 1, k = 2\)):

\(j = 0\): \((-1)^0 \binom{1}{0} 2^1 \binom{4 - 2 - 0}{1} = 2 \cdot 2 = 4\).
\(j = 1\): \((-1)^1 \binom{1}{1} 2^0 \binom{4 - 2 - 2}{1} = -1 \cdot \binom{0}{1} = 0\).
Total: \(4 + 0 = 4\).





Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Segment length \(1 \le n \le 3 \times 10^5\), tree count \(1 \le m \le 3 \times 10^5\), and tree height \(1 \le k \le 3 \times 10^5\).
Preconditions: Prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > \max(n, m)\) so factorials up to \(\max(n, m)\) are invertible.
Postconditions (Output): Returns \([x^n y^m] \big(1 - x - y x^{k+1}(2 - x^k)\big)^{-1} \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n + m)\) time and \(O(n + m)\) space using precomputed factorials up to \(\max(n, m)\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After summing \(0 \le j \le j_0\), the partial sum equals \([x^n] (1 - x)^{-(m+1)} x^{m(k+1)} \sum_{j=0}^{j_0} (-1)^j \binom{m}{j} 2^{m-j} x^{j k} \bmod p\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Multiply m * (k + 1) in 64-bit integer arithmetic (1LL * m * (k + 1)) before comparing against \(n\), since \(m, k \le 3 \times 10^5\) overflows 32-bit signed int; fails if \(p \le \max(n, m)\) because inverse factorials hit division by zero modulo \(p\).









Intermediate 1 (#025): Teleporting Takahashi — AtCoder ABC 240 G

Topic Tags: Trivariate Laurent Ring, 1D-vs-2D Variable Decoupling, \(45^\circ\) Rotated 2D Walk Factor.


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Takahashi is in 3D space \(\mathbb{Z}^3\), initially at \((0, 0, 0)\). In one teleportation step, he moves by \(\pm 1\) along exactly one of the three coordinate axes:
\[\mathcal{S}_3 = \{(\pm 1, 0, 0), (0, \pm 1, 0), (0, 0, \pm 1)\}.\]
Count the number of \(N\)-step trajectories starting at \((0, 0, 0)\) and ending at \((X, Y, Z)\), modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 10^7\), \(|X|, |Y|, |Z| \le 10^7\), modulus \(p = 998244353\). Required complexity: \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(N = 3, (X, Y, Z) = (2, 0, -1)\)): To reach \((2, 0, -1)\) in \(3\) steps, Takahashi must take two \(+x\) steps and one \(-z\) step, which can be ordered in \(\frac{3!}{2! 1!} = 3\) ways.



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

The 3D step Laurent polynomial is
\[S_3(x, y, z) = x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1} + z + z^{-1},\]
and we want \([x^X y^Y z^Z] S_3(x, y, z)^N\). Why can’t we factor \(S_3(x, y, z)\) into three linear factors the way we factored \(S_2(x, y) = x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1} = (xy)^{-1}(1+xy)(x+y)\) in Stepping Stone 1? Because in 3D, a cross-polytope (octahedron) has \(6\) vertices, whereas a product of \(3\) binomials has \(2^3 = 8\) vertices! Since 3D cannot factor completely, how can we combine 1D binomial expansion with our 2D factorization?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Split \(S_3(x, y, z)\) into the 1D \(z\)-step generator \(z + z^{-1}\) and the 2D \((x, y)\)-step generator \(S_2(x, y) = x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1}\):
\[S_3(x, y, z)^N = \Big( (z + z^{-1}) + (x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1}) \Big)^N = \sum_{k=0}^{N} \binom{N}{k} \big(z + z^{-1}\big)^k \big(x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1}\big)^{N - k}.\]
Notice that \(z\) only appears in the first factor and \((x, y)\) only appear in the second factor!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

For each fixed number of \(z\)-steps \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}\):

The \(z\)-factor contributes \([z^Z](z + z^{-1})^k = \binom{k}{(k + Z)/2}\) (when \(k \ge |Z|\) and \(k \equiv Z \pmod 2\)).
By Stepping Stone 1 (#048), the \((x, y)\)-factor of length \(m = N - k\) contributes \([x^X y^Y] S_2(x, y)^m = \binom{m}{(m + X + Y)/2} \binom{m}{(m + X - Y)/2}\) (when \(m \ge |X| + |Y|\) and \(m \equiv X + Y \pmod 2\)). Precompute factorials up to \(N = 10^7\) and sum over \(k\) in \(O(N)\) time!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Decoupling 3D into \(1\text{D} \oplus 2\text{D}\): In \(\mathbb{F}_p[x, x^{-1}, y, y^{-1}, z, z^{-1}]\), group the 6 step directions into \(z\)-axis steps and \((x, y)\)-plane steps: \[\begin{aligned}
[x^X y^Y z^Z] \big(x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1} + z + z^{-1}\big)^N &= \sum_{k=0}^{N} \binom{N}{k} \Big([z^Z] (z + z^{-1})^k\Big) \Big([x^X y^Y] (x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1})^{N - k}\Big).
\end{aligned}\] In words, \(\binom{N}{k}\) chooses which \(k\) of the \(N\) time steps move along the \(z\)-axis, \([z^Z](z + z^{-1})^k\) counts 1D walks of length \(k\) ending at \(Z\), and \([x^X y^Y] S_2(x, y)^{N - k}\) counts 2D walks of length \(m = N - k\) ending at \((X, Y)\).
Closed Form for Each Summand:

First check global parity and Manhattan distance: if \(|X| + |Y| + |Z| > N\) or \((X + Y + Z) \not\equiv N \pmod 2\), the answer is \(0\).
Otherwise, for any \(k \in [|Z|, N - |X| - |Y|]\) with \(k \equiv Z \pmod 2\), let \(m = N - k\). Then \(m \equiv N - Z \equiv X + Y \pmod 2\) and \(m \ge |X| + |Y|\) hold automatically, so: \[[z^Z] (z + z^{-1})^k = \binom{k}{\frac{k + Z}{2}}, \qquad [x^X y^Y] S_2(x, y)^m = \binom{m}{\frac{m + X + Y}{2}} \binom{m}{\frac{m + X - Y}{2}}.\]

Final \(O(N)\) Summation: \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{\substack{|Z| \le k \le N - |X| - |Y| \\ k \equiv Z \pmod 2}} \binom{N}{k} \binom{k}{\frac{k + Z}{2}} \binom{N - k}{\frac{N - k + X + Y}{2}} \binom{N - k}{\frac{N - k + X - Y}{2}} \pmod{998244353}.\]

Sample Trace Verification (\(N = 3, X = 2, Y = 0, Z = -1\)): The range for \(k\) is \(|-1| \le k \le 3 - 2 - 0 \implies k = 1\). The single term \(k = 1\) (\(m = 2\)) gives \(\binom{3}{1} \binom{1}{0} \binom{2}{2} \binom{2}{2} = 3 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 3\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Walk length \(1 \le N \le 10^7\) and target coordinates \((X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{Z}^3\) with \(|X|, |Y|, |Z| \le 10^7\).
Preconditions: Prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > N\) so factorials up to \(N\) are invertible.
Postconditions (Output): Returns \([x^X y^Y z^Z] (x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1} + z + z^{-1})^N \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space (precomputing fact and inv_fact up to \(N = 10^7\)).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Each loop iteration \(k \in [|Z|, N - |X| - |Y|]\) with \(k \equiv Z \pmod 2\) accumulates the exact number of 3D trajectories that take \(k\) steps along the \(z\)-axis and \(N - k\) steps in the \((x, y)\)-plane.
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le N\) (where inv_fact[N] divides by zero modulo \(p\)), or if the parity and Manhattan guard \(|X| + |Y| + |Z| > N\) or \((X + Y + Z) \not\equiv N \pmod 2\) is omitted (which causes negative indices in binomial coefficient lookups).









Intermediate 2 (#232): Bivariate Walk with Bounded Height & Weight — QOJ 4815

Topic Tags: 2D Bostan–Mori (Regime 1 Truncated Ring & Regime 2 Root-of-Unity Evaluation), Transfer Matrix Determinant.


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given a directed graph (possibly with multi-edges and self-loops) on \(d\) vertices \(\{1, 2, \dots, d\}\), where each directed edge \(e = (u \to v)\) carries a non-negative integer weight \(w(e) \in \{0, 1, \dots, c\}\). Summarizing all edges from \(u\) to \(v\) defines a polynomial adjacency matrix \(A(y) \in \mathbb{F}_p[y]^{d \times d}\) with \((u, v)\)-entry \(A_{u, v}(y) = \sum_{e: u \to v} y^{w(e)}\).
Given a huge walk length \(N \le 10^{18}\) and a maximum weight threshold \(K\), compute for every \(k = 0, 1, \dots, K\) the number of directed walks of length exactly \(N\) from vertex \(1\) to vertex \(d\) whose total edge weight is exactly \(k\), modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le d \le 15\), \(1 \le N \le 10^{18}\), \(0 \le K \le 10^4\), \(\deg_y A_{u, v}(y) \le c\), modulus \(p = 998244353\). Required complexity: \(O(d K \log(d K) \log N + d^3 K \log K)\) time.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(d = 2, N = 2, K = 2\)): Suppose \(A(y) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & y \\ 1 & y \end{pmatrix}\). Then \(I - x A(y) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - x & -x y \\ -x & 1 - x y \end{pmatrix}\) has determinant \(Q(x, y) = (1 - x)(1 - x y) - x^2 y = 1 - x(1 + y)\) and \((1, 2)\)-cofactor \(P(x, y) = x y\). Thus \([x^2] \frac{x y}{1 - x(1 + y)} = y(1 + y) = y + y^2\), giving counts \((w_0, w_1, w_2) = (0, 1, 1)\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By the transfer-matrix method, the generating function of walks of length \(N\) and weight \(k\) from vertex \(1\) to vertex \(d\) is the \((1, d)\)-entry of the matrix inverse \((I - x A(y))^{-1}\):
\[\sum_{N=0}^{\infty} \big(A(y)^N\big)_{1, d} x^N = \big((I - x A(y))^{-1}\big)_{1, d} = \frac{P(x, y)}{Q(x, y)},\]
where \(Q(x, y) = \det(I - x A(y))\) has \(x\)-degree \(\le d\) and \(Q(0, y) = \det(I) = 1\), while \(P(x, y) = (-1)^{1+d} \det\big((I - x A(y))_{\setminus (d, 1)}\big)\) has \(x\)-degree \(< d\). Since \(N \le 10^{18}\) is huge and \(d \le 15, K \le 10^4\), which regimes of §16.2 apply?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

First, how do we compute the bivariate polynomials \(P(x, y) \bmod y^{K+1}\) and \(Q(x, y) \bmod y^{K+1}\) without doing polynomial matrix elimination explicitly? Choose an NTT length \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(K + 1) \rceil}\) (or \(L > d c\) if \(d c \le K\)). For each root of unity \(y_r = \omega_L^r\) (\(0 \le r < L\)), \(A(\omega_L^r) \in \mathbb{F}_p^{d \times d}\) is a scalar matrix! We can compute the characteristic polynomial \(Q(x, \omega_L^r) = \det(I - x A(\omega_L^r))\) and adjugate entry \(P(x, \omega_L^r)\) at \(d + 1\) values of \(x\) (or via Hessenberg reduction / Gaussian elimination) in \(O(d^3)\) time per root \(r\), then interpolate in \(y\) modulo \(y^{K+1}\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Once \(P(x, y) \bmod y^{K+1}\) and \(Q(x, y) \bmod y^{K+1}\) are known (with \(\deg_x P < \deg_x Q \le d\) and \(Q(0, y) = 1\)), apply Regime 1 (Truncated Auxiliary Ring) of §16.2: run 1D Bostan–Mori in \(x\) over the coefficient ring \(R = \mathbb{F}_p[y]/(y^{K+1})\) by Kronecker-packing \((x, y) \mapsto x \cdot (2K + 1) + y\) into a 1D NTT of size \(\le 2^{\lceil \log_2(2 d (2K + 1)) \rceil}\), truncating modulo \(y^{K+1}\) after each of the \(\lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor + 1\) steps!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Rational Walk Generating Function in \(K[y][[x]]\): Let \(A(y) \in \mathbb{F}_p[y]^{d \times d}\) be the polynomial adjacency matrix truncated modulo \(y^{K+1}\). By Cramer’s rule over the commutative ring \(R[[x]]\) where \(R = \mathbb{F}_p[y]/(y^{K+1})\), \[\sum_{N=0}^{\infty} \big(A(y)^N \bmod y^{K+1}\big)_{1, d} x^N = \frac{P(x, y)}{Q(x, y)} \pmod{y^{K+1}},\] where \(Q(x, y) = \det(I_d - x A(y)) \bmod y^{K+1}\) has \(\deg_x Q \le d\) and \([x^0] Q(x, y) = 1\), and \(P(x, y)\) is the \((d, 1)\)-cofactor of \(I_d - x A(y) \bmod y^{K+1}\) with \(\deg_x P \le d - 1\).
Constructing \(P(x, y)\) and \(Q(x, y) \bmod y^{K+1}\) via Root Evaluation: To avoid polynomial arithmetic inside Gaussian elimination, notice that if we truncate \(A(y) \bmod y^{K+1}\), then in \(\det(I_d - x A(y)) \bmod y^{K+1}\) we only ever need \(y\) modulo \(y^{K+1}\) (or if we evaluate at \(y_r = \omega_L^r\) where \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(d \cdot \min(c, K) + 1) \rceil}\), we recover \(P(x, y)\) and \(Q(x, y)\) exactly and then truncate \(\bmod y^{K+1}\); alternatively, to work directly \(\bmod y^{K+1}\) when \(c > K\), compute \((I_d - x A(y))^{-1} \bmod x^{2d}\) by solving \((I_d - x A(y)) v(x, y) = e_d \bmod (x^{2d}, y^{K+1})\) at \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(2dK + 1) \rceil}\) roots of unity and run Berlekamp–Massey!). Specifically, for each \(x_s = \omega_{2d}^s\) (\(0 \le s < 2d\)) and \(y_r = \omega_L^r\), Gaussian elimination on \(I_d - x_s A(y_r) \in \mathbb{F}_p^{d \times d}\) gives \(\det(I_d - x_s A(y_r))\) and the \((1, d)\)-entry of \((I_d - x_s A(y_r))^{-1} \det(I_d - x_s A(y_r))\) in \(O(d^3)\) scalar operations. Interpolating in \((x, y)\) and truncating \(\bmod y^{K+1}\) produces \(P(x, y)\) and \(Q(x, y)\) of bidegree \((\le d, \le K)\).
2D Bostan–Mori in \(R[[x]]\) (\(R = \mathbb{F}_p[y]/(y^{K+1})\)): While \(N > 0\):

Pack \(P(x, y)\) and \(Q(x, y)\) via the Kronecker map \((i, j) \mapsto i(2K + 1) + j\) into 1D arrays of length \(\le (d + 1)(2K + 1)\), and compute \(U(x, y) = P(x, y) Q(-x, y)\) and \(V(x^2, y) = Q(x, y) Q(-x, y)\) using 1D NTT of length \(M = 2^{\lceil \log_2((2d + 1)(2K + 1)) \rceil}\).
Unpack the 1D product: discard any term with \(j = I \bmod (2K + 1) > K\) (this performs the exact truncation \(\bmod y^{K+1}\)!), set \(P_{\text{next}}(x, y) = \sum_{i=0}^{d-1} [x^{2i + (N \bmod 2)}] U(x, y) \cdot x^i\), \(Q_{\text{next}}(x, y) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} [x^{2i}] V(x^2, y) \cdot x^i\), and \(N \gets \lfloor N / 2 \rfloor\). When \(N = 0\), since \([x^0] Q(x, y) = 1\) is preserved at every step (\(V(0, y) = Q(0, y)^2 = 1^2 = 1\)), the polynomial \(P(0, y) = \sum_{k=0}^K w_k y^k\) immediately gives all \(K + 1\) answers!




Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Vertex count \(1 \le d \le 15\), walk length \(1 \le N \le 10^{18}\), weight threshold \(0 \le K \le 10^4\), and polynomial adjacency matrix \(A(y) \bmod y^{K+1}\).
Preconditions: \([x^0] Q(x, y) = \det(I_d) = 1 \in \big(\mathbb{F}_p[y]/(y^{K+1})\big)^\times\), and NTT prime \(p = 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \([x^N y^k] \big((I - x A(y))^{-1}\big)_{1, d} \bmod 998244353\) for all \(0 \le k \le K\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(d K \log(d K) \log N + d^3 K \log K)\) time and \(O(d K)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After each halving step \(N \gets \lfloor N / 2 \rfloor\), \([x^N] \frac{P(x, y)}{Q(x, y)} \pmod{y^{K+1}}\) is invariant, with \(\deg_x P < \deg_x Q \le d\) and \(Q(0, y) = 1\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: During Gaussian elimination over \(\mathcal{R} = \mathbb{F}_p[y]/(y^{K+1})\), pivot selection must prefer a polynomial with non-zero constant term \([y^0]M_{r, c}(y) \neq 0\) (a unit in \(\mathcal{R}\)); if all remaining rows have \(y^v \mid M_{r, c}(y)\), factor out the common shift \(y^v\) before calling Newton polynomial inversion.









Advanced 1 (#237): Generalized Delannoy & Chebyshev Diagonal Sum — yukicoder No. 1080

Topic Tags: Furstenberg’s Diagonal Theorem (§16.4), 1-Line Quadratic Shortcut, D-Finite 3-Term P-Recursion, Gaussian Integer Extension \(\mathbb{F}_p[i]\).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given an integer \(N \le 10^6\) and parameters \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{F}_p\) defining the generalized bivariate Delannoy rational generating function
\[F(x, y) = \frac{1}{1 - a x - b y - c x y} \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x, y]].\]
Compute all main diagonal coefficients
\[d_n = [x^n y^n] \frac{1}{1 - a x - b y - c x y} \pmod{998244353} \qquad \text{for } n = 0, 1, \dots, N.\]
(In yukicoder No. 1080, the target Chebyshev rational diagonal sum \(\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n+k}{2k} c^k\) and \(T_n + i U_n\) reduce over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) via \(i \equiv 3^{(p-1)/4} \pmod p\) to extracting these exact quadratic diagonal coefficients \(d_0, \dots, d_N\).)

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 10^6\), \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{F}_{998244353}\). Required complexity: \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(a = 1, b = 1, c = 1, N = 3\)): As traced in §16.4, for \(a = b = c = 1\) we obtain the standard Delannoy sequence \((d_0, d_1, d_2, d_3) = (1, 3, 13, 63)\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Expanding \(\frac{1}{1 - ax - by - cxy} = \sum_{n, m} d_{n, m} x^n y^m\) directly gives \(d_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} \binom{2n-k}{n} a^{n-k} b^{n-k} c^k\), which takes \(O(N)\) time for a single \(n\), or \(O(N^2)\) for all \(0 \le n \le N\) (and \(O(N \log N)\) via 1D NTT convolution). How can we compute all \(d_0, d_1, \dots, d_N\) in strictly linear \(O(N)\) time with zero FFTs? Reach for Furstenberg’s Diagonal Theorem (Theorem 16.2)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Substitute \(x = z\) and \(y = t / z\) into \(\frac{1}{z} F(z, t/z)\) inside \(K((z))[[t]]\):
\[\frac{1}{z} \frac{1}{1 - a z - b(t / z) - c t} = \frac{1}{-a z^2 + (1 - c t) z - b t}.\]
Apply the 1-Line Quadratic Furstenberg Shortcut (Theorem 16.2) with \(\alpha(t) = -a\), \(\beta(t) = 1 - c t\), and \(\gamma(t) = -b t\) to obtain the closed-form 1D algebraic generating function \(D(t) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty d_n t^n\).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

By Theorem 16.2,
\[D(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1 - c t)^2 - 4 a b t}} = \Big(1 - 2(c + 2 a b) t + c^2 t^2\Big)^{-1/2}.\]
Let \(\Delta(t) = 1 - 2(c + 2ab) t + c^2 t^2\). Differentiate \(\Delta(t) D(t)^2 = 1\) with respect to \(t\) to get \(2 \Delta(t) D'(t) + \Delta'(t) D(t) = 0\), and extract \([t^n]\) to obtain a 3-term linear recurrence computing \(d_0, \dots, d_N\) in \(O(N)\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Diagonal-to-Residue Transformation in \(K((z))[[t]]\): Let \(D(t) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} d_n t^n = \operatorname{Diag}_{x, y} \frac{1}{1 - a x - b y - c x y}\). Under \((x, y) \mapsto (z, t/z)\), we have \(\deg_y(1) = 0 < 1 = \deg_y(1 - ax - by - cxy)\), so there is no hidden pole at \(z = 0\) (Failure Mode #15 does not trigger). Thus: \[\begin{aligned}
D(t) &= \operatorname{CT}_z \frac{1}{1 - a z - b(t / z) - c t} && \text{(diagonal substitution)} \\
&= \operatorname{Res}_z \frac{1}{-a z^2 + (1 - c t) z - b t} && \text{(multiply top and bottom by } z^{-1} \text{)}.
\end{aligned}\]
Residue at the Unique Small Root \(z_1(t)\): The quadratic denominator \(Q(z, t) = -a z^2 + (1 - c t) z - b t\) has \(\beta(0) = 1 \neq 0\) and \(\gamma(t) = -b t \in t K[[t]]\), so it possesses a unique small root \[z_1(t) = \frac{(1 - c t) - \sqrt{(1 - c t)^2 - 4 a b t}}{2a} = b t + O(t^2) \in t K[[t]].\] Evaluating \(\frac{1}{\partial_z Q(z_1(t), t)} = \frac{1}{-2a z_1(t) + (1 - c t)}\) yields the algebraic generating function: \[D(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1 - c t)^2 - 4 a b t}} = \Big(1 - 2(c + 2 a b) t + c^2 t^2\Big)^{-1/2}.\]
Converting the Algebraic Equation to an \(O(N)\) 3-Term P-Recursion: Set \(\Delta(t) = 1 - 2(c + 2ab) t + c^2 t^2\) so that \(D(t) = \Delta(t)^{-1/2}\). Differentiating \(\ln D(t) = -\frac{1}{2} \ln \Delta(t)\) gives: \[\frac{D'(t)}{D(t)} = -\frac{\Delta'(t)}{2 \Delta(t)} = \frac{(c + 2 a b) - c^2 t}{1 - 2(c + 2 a b) t + c^2 t^2} \iff \Big(1 - 2(c + 2 a b) t + c^2 t^2\Big) D'(t) - \Big((c + 2 a b) - c^2 t\Big) D(t) = 0.\] Extracting the coefficient of \(t^n\) from this differential equation gives a single-step equality for \(d_{n+1}\): \[(n + 1) d_{n+1} - 2 n (c + 2 a b) d_n + (n - 1) c^2 d_{n-1} - (c + 2 a b) d_n + c^2 d_{n-1} = 0,\] which simplifies to the clean 3-term linear recurrence: \[d_{n+1} = \frac{(2n + 1)(c + 2 a b) \, d_n - n c^2 \, d_{n-1}}{n + 1} \pmod{998244353}, \qquad d_0 = 1, \quad d_1 = c + 2 a b.\]



Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Target bound \(1 \le N \le 10^6 < p = 998244353\) and parameters \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{F}_p\).
Preconditions: Prime \(p > N\) and \(2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) so that \(n + 1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) for all \(0 \le n < N\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns all diagonal coefficients \(d_0, d_1, \dots, d_N \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space (using linear-time modular inverses \(\operatorname{inv}[1 \dots N]\)).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At step \(n\), \(d_0, \dots, d_n\) satisfy \(\Delta(t) D'(t) - \frac{1}{2}\Delta'(t) D(t) \equiv 0 \pmod{t^n}\).
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(p \le N\) (since the D-finite recurrence divides by \(n + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p\) at \(n = p - 1\)), or if \(a \equiv 0 \pmod p\) makes \(\Delta_1 = 0\) and the boundary condition \(d_1 = (b + c) d_0\) is not initialized before starting the \(n \ge 1\) loop.

Advanced 2 (#074): Yet Another ABC String — AtCoder AGC 058 D

Topic Tags: Trivariate Rational Generating Function, Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method, Elementary Symmetric Decoupling (\(s = x + y + z, u = x y z\)).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given three positive integers \(A, B, C\). Count the number of strings of length \(N = A + B + C\) consisting of exactly \(A\) copies of 'A', \(B\) copies of 'B', and \(C\) copies of 'C' that do not contain any of the three cyclic triples "ABC", "BCA", or "CAB" as a contiguous substring of length \(3\), modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le A, B, C \le 10^6\), modulus \(p = 998244353\). Required complexity: \(O(A + B + C)\) time and \(O(A + B + C)\) space.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(A = 1, B = 1, C = 1\)): There are \(3! = 6\) permutations of "A", "B", "C". Among them, "ABC", "BCA", "CAB" are forbidden, while "ACB", "BAC", "CBA" are valid, so the answer is \(3\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(x, y, z\) mark the counts of 'A', 'B', and 'C' respectively. We want the trivariate coefficient \([x^A y^B z^C] F(x, y, z)\) of the generating function \(F(x, y, z)\) of words avoiding the forbidden set \(\mathcal{F} = \{\text{`"ABC"`}, \text{`"BCA"`}, \text{`"CAB"`}\}\). In §16.4, we saw that a general 3D rational diagonal is transcendental and requires Lipshitz’s P-recursion. Why is this specific 3D rational function much simpler? Look at how the three forbidden words in \(\mathcal{F}\) can overlap with each other!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

If two words in \(\mathcal{F} = \{\text{`"ABC"`}, \text{`"BCA"`}, \text{`"CAB"`}\}\) overlap, the combined word must be a contiguous substring of the infinite periodic string "ABCABCABC..." of length \(L \ge 3\)! Apply Inclusion–Exclusion (the Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method): inside a maximal periodic block of length \(L \ge 3\), each forbidden triple of length \(3\) can start at positions \(1, 2, \dots, L - 2\). Verify that the sum of \((-1)^{\# \text{chosen triples}}\) over all subsets of triples whose union covers the entire block of length \(L\) is:

\(-1\) if \(L \equiv 0 \pmod 3\) (\(L = 3k\), which has monomial \((xyz)^k\) for each of the \(3\) starting letters, contributing \(-3(xyz)^k\)),
\(+1\) if \(L \equiv 1 \pmod 3\) (\(L = 3k + 1\), which has monomials \(x(xyz)^k, y(xyz)^k, z(xyz)^k\), contributing \(+(x + y + z)(xyz)^k\)),
\(0\) if \(L \equiv 2 \pmod 3\)!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Summing the cluster weights over \(k \ge 1\) gives the cluster generator \(C(x, y, z) = \frac{(-3 + x + y + z) x y z}{1 - x y z}\), so
\[F(x, y, z) = \frac{1}{1 - (x + y + z) - C(x, y, z)} = \frac{1 - x y z}{1 - (x + y + z) + 2 x y z}.\]
Notice that \(F(x, y, z)\) depends only on \(s = x + y + z\) and \(u = x y z\)! Expand \(\frac{1 - u}{1 - s + 2u} = (1 - u) \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{(-2u)^k}{(1 - s)^{k+1}}\) in powers of \(u = x y z\). Since \(u^k = x^k y^k z^k\) simply shifts \((A, B, C) \mapsto (A - k, B - k, C - k)\), and \([x^{A-k} y^{B-k} z^{C-k}] (1 - s)^{-(k+1)}\) is a single trinomial coefficient times a binomial coefficient, the entire 3D extraction collapses to a 1D sum of length \(\min(A, B, C)\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Goulden–Jackson Cluster Weight on Periodic Chains "ABCABC...": To count words avoiding \(\mathcal{F} = \{\text{`"ABC"`}, \text{`"BCA"`}, \text{`"CAB"`}\}\) by Inclusion–Exclusion, we mark an arbitrary subset of occurrences of forbidden triples in a word, each with weight \(-1\). Maximal connected components of overlapping marked triples are called clusters. Because "ABC" is uniquely determined by its first letter (A must be followed by B, B by C, C by A), any cluster of length \(L \ge 3\) is a prefix of length \(L\) of "ABCABC...", "BCABCA...", or "CABCAB...". In a periodic chain of length \(L \ge 3\), a subset of triples covers all \(L\) characters if and only if it includes the first triple \([1, 3]\), the last triple \([L - 2, L]\), and has no gap \(> 3\) between consecutive starts (so each step between consecutive starts is \(+1\) or \(+2\)). Thus the net Inclusion–Exclusion weight \(w_L\) for a fixed starting letter satisfies the transfer series: \[\sum_{L=3}^{\infty} w_L t^L = -t^3 \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (-t - t^2)^r = \frac{-t^3}{1 + t + t^2} = \frac{-t^3(1 - t)}{1 - t^3} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \big(-t^{3k} + t^{3k+1}\big).\]

When \(L = 3k\), the word has \(k\) 'A's, \(k\) 'B's, and \(k\) 'C's regardless of which of the \(3\) letters it starts with, contributing \(3 \cdot (-1) (x y z)^k = -3(x y z)^k\).
When \(L = 3k + 1\), the word has \(k\) full triples plus \(1\) extra copy of its starting letter, contributing \(+(x + y + z)(x y z)^k\). Summing over \(k \ge 1\) gives the cluster generating function \[C(x, y, z) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \big(-3 + (x + y + z)\big) (x y z)^k = \frac{\big(-3 + (x + y + z)\big) x y z}{1 - x y z}.\]

Closed-Form Trivariate Rational Function: Every word with marked clusters is a sequence of single letters (\(s = x + y + z\)) and clusters (\(C(x, y, z)\)). Setting \(s = x + y + z\) and \(u = x y z\): \[F(x, y, z) = \frac{1}{1 - s - C(x, y, z)} = \frac{1}{1 - s - \frac{(-3 + s) u}{1 - u}} = \frac{1 - u}{(1 - s)(1 - u) - (-3 + s) u} = \frac{1 - u}{1 - s + 2 u}.\]
Decoupling \([x^A y^B z^C]\) via Expansion in \(u = x y z\): Rewrite the denominator as \((1 - s) + 2u = (1 - s)\big(1 + \frac{2u}{1 - s}\big)\) and expand in a geometric series in \(u\): \[\frac{1 - u}{1 - s + 2 u} = (1 - u) \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-2)^j u^j}{(1 - s)^{j + 1}} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} u^k \left( \frac{(-2)^k}{(1 - s)^{k + 1}} - \frac{(-2)^{k - 1}}{(1 - s)^k} \right),\] where for \(k = 0\) the second term inside the parentheses is \(0\). Now extract \([x^A y^B z^C]\) term-by-term. Since \(u^k = x^k y^k z^k\), for any integer \(r \ge 1\): \[\begin{aligned}
[x^A y^B z^C] \frac{u^k}{(1 - s)^r} &= [x^{A-k} y^{B-k} z^{C-k}] (1 - (x + y + z))^{-r} \\
&= \binom{(N - 3k) + r - 1}{r - 1} \frac{(N - 3k)!}{(A - k)! \, (B - k)! \, (C - k)!},
\end{aligned}\] where \(N = A + B + C\). Substituting \(r = k + 1\) and \(r = k\) and factoring out \((-2)^{k-1}\) yields the exact \(O(\min(A, B, C))\) formula: \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Ans} &= \sum_{k=0}^{\min(A, B, C)} \left( (-2)^k \binom{N - 2k}{k} - (-2)^{k - 1} \binom{N - 2k - 1}{k - 1} \right) \frac{(N - 3k)!}{(A - k)! \, (B - k)! \, (C - k)!} \\
&= \sum_{k=0}^{\min(A, B, C)} (-2)^{k - 1} \left( -2 \binom{N - 2k}{k} - \binom{N - 2k - 1}{k - 1} \right) \frac{(N - 3k)!}{(A - k)! \, (B - k)! \, (C - k)!} \pmod{998244353},
\end{aligned}\] with the convention \(\binom{N - 1}{-1} = 0\) at \(k = 0\).

Sample Trace Verification (\(A = B = C = 1, N = 3\)):

\(k = 0\): \((-2)^0 \binom{3}{0} \frac{3!}{1!1!1!} = 6\).
\(k = 1\): \(\big((-2)^1 \binom{1}{1} - (-2)^0 \binom{0}{0}\big) \frac{0!}{0!0!0!} = (-2 - 1) \cdot 1 = -3\).
Sum: \(6 - 3 = 3\).





Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Positive integers \(1 \le A, B, C \le 10^6\) (\(N = A + B + C \le 3 \times 10^6\)); prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > N\) so factorials up to \(N\) are invertible.
Postconditions (Output): Returns \([x^A y^B z^C] \frac{1 - xyz}{1 - (x+y+z) + 2xyz} \bmod 998244353\).
Index & Truncation Boundaries: Summation index \(k\) runs over \(0 \le k \le \min(A, B, C)\) so that \(A - k, B - k, C - k \ge 0\) and \(N - 3k \ge 0\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(A + B + C)\) time and \(O(A + B + C)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After summing \(0 \le k \le k_0\), the partial sum equals \([x^A y^B z^C]\) of the truncated \(u\)-series \(\sum_{k=0}^{k_0} u^k \big((-2)^k (1-s)^{-(k+1)} - (-2)^{k-1}(1-s)^{-k}\big) \bmod p\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: At \(k = 0\), the second binomial term \(\binom{N - 1}{-1}\) must evaluate to \(0\) (do not index inv_fact[-1]); at \(k = \min(A, B, C)\) when \(A = B = C\), \(N - 2k - 1 = k - 1\) gives \(\binom{k - 1}{k - 1} = 1\), whereas \(\binom{-1}{-1}\) does not occur since \(k \ge 1\).

Primary Perspective (Chapter 08, §8.2 & §8.4): Construct the cluster generating function \(C(x, y, z) = \frac{(-3 + x + y + z)xyz}{1 - xyz}\) via the Goulden–Jackson Cluster Method and Inclusion–Exclusion on periodic overlap chains.

Mastery 1 (#240): Remix Sum (Digits-Sum-Mod-10 Convolution) — yukicoder No. 1783

Topic Tags: Hybrid Cyclic/Truncated Tensor Algebra, Multidimensional Radix-10 DFT, Twisted Kronecker \(T\)-Variate FPS Power (§16.3).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(N\) base-10 integers \(A_1, \dots, A_N \in [0, 10^K - 1]\) (each padded with leading zeros to \(K\) base-10 digits), a huge tuple length \(M \le 10^{18}\), and a binary string \(C_1 C_2 \dots C_K \in \{0, 1\}^K\) specifying the addition rule at each digit position \(r \in \{1, \dots, K\}\):

If \(C_r = 0\) (Cyclic Modulo-10 Addition), the \(r\)-th digits of two numbers add modulo \(10\) without carry (\(z_r^{i} \cdot z_r^{j} = z_r^{(i + j) \bmod 10}\), i.e., in \(\mathbb{F}_P[z_r] / (z_r^{10} - 1)\)).
If \(C_r = 1\) (Truncated Addition), the \(r\)-th digits add as integers, and any tuple whose \(r\)-th digit sum is \(\ge 10\) is discarded (\(z_r^i \cdot z_r^j = 0\) if \(i + j \ge 10\), i.e., in \(\mathbb{F}_P[z_r] / (z_r^{10})\)).

For every \(v \in [0, 10^K - 1]\), compute the number of ordered \(M\)-tuples \((i_1, \dots, i_M) \in \{1, \dots, N\}^M\) whose digitwise sum under rules \(C_1, \dots, C_K\) equals \(v\), modulo the prime \(P = 120586241\).

Constraints: \(1 \le K \le 5\) (\(10^K \le 10^5\)), \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(1 \le M \le 10^{18}\), modulus \(P = 120586241 = 2^{20} \cdot 115 + 1\). Required complexity: \(O(10^K K^2 \log 10 + 10^{K+1} K)\) time and \(O(K \cdot 10^K)\) space.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(K = 1, C_1 = 1, N = 2, A = \{0, 1\}, M = 3\)): Since \(K = 1\) and \(C_1 = 1\) (truncated mod \(z_1^{10}\)), \(F(z_1) = 1 + z_1\), and \(F(z_1)^3 = (1 + z_1)^3 = 1 + 3z_1 + 3z_1^2 + z_1^3 \bmod z_1^{10}\), giving counts \((1, 3, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)\) for \(v = 0, \dots, 9\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Let \(\mathcal{T} = \{r \in \{1, \dots, K\} : C_r = 1\}\) be the set of \(T = |\mathcal{T}|\) truncated digit dimensions, and let \(\mathcal{C} = \{1, \dots, K\} \setminus \mathcal{T}\) be the \(K - T\) cyclic digit dimensions. We need to compute \(F(z_1, \dots, z_K)^M\) in the hybrid tensor product ring
\[\mathcal{A} = \left( \bigotimes_{r \in \mathcal{C}} \frac{\mathbb{F}_P[z_r]}{(z_r^{10} - 1)} \right) \otimes \left( \bigotimes_{r \in \mathcal{T}} \frac{\mathbb{F}_P[z_r]}{(z_r^{10})} \right).\]
Why did the problem author choose the unusual prime modulus \(P = 120586241\) instead of \(998244353\)? Factor \(P - 1 = 120586240 = 2^{20} \cdot 5 \cdot 23\)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Because \(10 \mid (P - 1)\) and \(2^{20} \mid (P - 1)\), the prime field \(\mathbb{F}_P\) contains both a primitive \(10\)-th root of unity \(\omega_{10} = g^{(P-1)/10} \bmod P\) (for radix-10 cyclic DFT!) and primitive \(2^{20}\)-th roots of unity (for standard binary NTT)! By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, applying a \((K - T)\)-dimensional radix-10 DFT along the cyclic dimensions \(r \in \mathcal{C}\) diagonalizes \(\bigotimes_{r \in \mathcal{C}} \mathbb{F}_P[z_r]/(z_r^{10} - 1)\) into \(10^{K - T}\) completely independent \(T\)-variate truncated polynomial rings \(\mathcal{R}_T = \mathbb{F}_P[u_1, \dots, u_T] / (u_1^{10}, \dots, u_T^{10})\), each of volume \(V = 10^T\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

On each of the \(10^{K - T}\) decoupled fibers, we have a \(T\)-variate truncated FPS \(F_\omega(u_1, \dots, u_T) \in \mathcal{R}_T\) of volume \(V = 10^T\), and we need \(F_\omega^M \in \mathcal{R}_T\):

If the constant term \(c_0 = F_\omega(\mathbf{0}) \neq 0\), normalize \(\widetilde{F}_\omega = c_0^{-1} F_\omega\) and compute \(c_0^M \exp(M \ln \widetilde{F}_\omega)\) in \(O(T \cdot 10^T \log(10^T))\) time using our Twisted Kronecker + Radial Euler Derivation \(\mathfrak{D}\) engine from §16.3 (since \(P = 120586241 > 10^5 \ge V\), \(\mathfrak{D}^{-1}\) is always valid!).
What if \(F_\omega(\mathbf{0}) = 0\)? (See the Failure Mode callout in §16.3!) Because \(u_1^{10} = \dots = u_T^{10} = 0\), any polynomial in \(\mathcal{R}_T\) with zero constant term satisfies \(\operatorname{deg}_{\text{total}} \ge 1\), so \(F_\omega^M = 0\) whenever \(M > 9 T\)! Thus if \(F_\omega(\mathbf{0}) = 0\) and \(M > 9 T\), output \(0\) immediately; if \(M \le 9 T \le 45\), compute \(F_\omega^M\) via binary exponentiation with \(\cdot_\chi\) in \(\le 6\) multiplications!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Why \(P = 120586241\) Enables Hybrid Radix-10 DFT \(\oplus\) Twisted Kronecker NTT: Each input number \(A_j\) (\(1 \le j \le N\)) with base-10 digits \((d_{j, 1}, \dots, d_{j, K}) \in \{0, \dots, 9\}^K\) contributes a monomial \(z_1^{d_{j, 1}} \cdots z_K^{d_{j, K}}\) to the generating polynomial \(F(z_1, \dots, z_K)\). Because \(P - 1 = 120586240\) is divisible by \(10\), we find a primitive root \(g\) of \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times\) (here \(g = 3\) works since \(3^{(P-1)/2} \equiv -1\), \(3^{(P-1)/5} \not\equiv 1\), \(3^{(P-1)/23} \not\equiv 1 \pmod P\)) and set \(\omega_{10} = g^{(P-1)/10} \bmod P\). For each cyclic dimension \(r \in \mathcal{C}\) (\(C_r = 0\)), evaluating \(z_r\) at \(1, \omega_{10}, \omega_{10}^2, \dots, \omega_{10}^9\) via a 1D length-10 DFT along axis \(r\) takes \(10^2 \cdot 10^{K-1} = 10^{K+1}\) operations per cyclic axis, establishing the ring isomorphism: \[\mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\sim} \prod_{\boldsymbol{\alpha} \in \{0, \dots, 9\}^{K - T}} \frac{\mathbb{F}_P[u_1, \dots, u_T]}{(u_1^{10}, \dots, u_T^{10})}.\]
\(T\)-Variate Truncated Power \(F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^M\) on Each Fiber via Twisted Kronecker (§16.3): Fix one frequency slice \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} \in \{0, \dots, 9\}^{K - T}\), giving a packed array \(F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}[0 \dots 10^T - 1]\) of size \(V = 10^T\) with mixed radices \(N_r = 10^r\) and grading \(\chi(I) = \big(\sum_{r=1}^{T-1} \lfloor I / 10^r \rfloor\big) \bmod T\).

Case 1 (\(F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}[0] = c_0 \neq 0 \pmod P\)): Since \(P = 120586241 > 10^5 \ge V\), every \(I \in \{1, \dots, V - 1\}\) is invertible modulo \(P\). Using the Radial Euler Derivation \(\mathfrak{D}(F)[I] = I \cdot F[I]\) from §16.3:

Scale \(\widetilde{F} = c_0^{-1} F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\) so \(\widetilde{F}[0] = 1\).
Compute \(\ln \widetilde{F} = \mathfrak{D}^{-1}\big(\mathfrak{D}(\widetilde{F}) \cdot_\chi \widetilde{F}^{-1}\big)\) in \(O(T V \log V)\) time.
Multiply \(\ln \widetilde{F}\) by \(M \bmod P\), compute \(H = \exp(M \ln \widetilde{F})\) via Newton doubling on \(H_{2m} = H_m \cdot_\chi (1 - \ln H_m + M \ln \widetilde{F})\), and scale by \(c_0^M \bmod P\) (with \(M \bmod (P - 1)\) in the scalar exponent!).

Case 2 (\(F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}[0] = 0 \pmod P\)): Every nonzero term in \(F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(u_1, \dots, u_T)\) has total degree \(i_1 + \dots + i_T \ge 1\). Since \(u_1^{10} = \dots = u_T^{10} = 0\) in \(\mathcal{R}_T\), the maximum nonzero total degree in \(\mathcal{R}_T\) is \(9 T\).

If \(M > 9 T\), then \(F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^M = 0\) identically in \(\mathcal{R}_T\)!
If \(M \le 9 T \le 45\), compute \(F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^M\) directly by binary exponentiation using \(\cdot_\chi\) in \(\lfloor \log_2 M \rfloor + 1 \le 6\) multiplications!


Inverse Radix-10 DFT: After powering all \(10^{K - T}\) fibers, apply the \((K - T)\)-dimensional inverse length-10 DFT (using \(\omega_{10}^{-1}\) and multiplying by \(10^{-(K - T)} \bmod P\)) to recover the final coefficients for all \(v \in [0, 10^K - 1]\).



Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Digit count \(1 \le K \le 5\) (\(10^K \le 10^5\)), array size \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), tuple length \(1 \le M \le 10^{18}\), carry mask \(C \in \{0, 1\}^K\), and input integers \(A_1, \dots, A_N \in [0, 10^K - 1]\).
Preconditions: Prime \(P = 120586241 = 2^{20} \cdot 115 + 1\) satisfies \(10 \mid (P - 1)\), \(2^{20} \mid (P - 1)\), and \(P > 10^K\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \([z^{\mathbf{v}}] F(\mathbf{z})^M \bmod 120586241\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) for all \(0 \le v < 10^K\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O\big(10^{K-T} \cdot (T \cdot 10^T \log(10^T) + T^2 \cdot 10^T) + (K - T) \cdot 10^{K+1}\big) = O(K^2 10^K \log 10)\) time and \(O(K 10^K)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After the \((K - T)\)-dimensional radix-10 DFT, each frequency fiber \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} \in \{0, \dots, 9\}^{K-T}\) evolves independently in \(\mathbb{F}_P[u_1, \dots, u_T]/(u_1^{10}, \dots, u_T^{10})\) under \(\chi\)-twisted Kronecker arithmetic.
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(10 \nmid (P - 1)\) (so no primitive 10-th root of unity \(\omega_{10} \in \mathbb{F}_P^\times\) exists for the radix-10 DFT axes), or if \(P(\mathbf{u})[0] = 0\) on a fiber where \(P(\mathbf{u}) \not\equiv 0\) and the leading valuation monomial \(\mathbf{u}^{\mathbf{v}_0}\) is not factored out before applying \(\exp(M \ln(\cdot))\) or binary exponentiation.









Mastery 2 (#214): 【集训队互测2021】三维立体混元劲 — UOJ 596

Topic Tags: 3-Variate EGF Logarithm \(\ln G(x, y, z)\), Twisted Kronecker Substitution (\(d = 3\), \(\chi(I) = \big(\lfloor I/(A+1) \rfloor + \lfloor I/((A+1)(B+1)) \rfloor\big) \bmod 3 = \big(b + (B+2)c\big) \bmod 3\)), Radial Euler Derivation \(\mathfrak{D}\).


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are counting connected labeled 3-colored graphs (or equivalent 3-type coupled labeled structures governed by the 3-variate Exponential Formula \(C(x, y, z) = \ln G(x, y, z)\)) with \(a\) Red vertices, \(b\) Green vertices, and \(c\) Blue vertices for all \(0 \le a \le A\), \(0 \le b \le B\), \(0 \le c \le C\), modulo \(998244353\).
Specifically, given dimension bounds \(A, B, C \le 50\) (or total grid volume \(V = (A + 1)(B + 1)(C + 1) \le 1.5 \times 10^5\)) and edge fugacity weights \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \lambda_{rg}, \lambda_{gb}, \lambda_{br}) \in \mathbb{F}_p^6\) defining the disconnected 3-colored graph EGF
\[G(x, y, z) = \sum_{a=0}^{A} \sum_{b=0}^{B} \sum_{c=0}^{C} \alpha^{\binom{a}{2}} \beta^{\binom{b}{2}} \gamma^{\binom{c}{2}} \lambda_{rg}^{a b} \lambda_{gb}^{b c} \lambda_{br}^{c a} \frac{x^a}{a!} \frac{y^b}{b!} \frac{z^c}{c!},\]
compute the connected 3-colored graph counts \(c_{a, b, c} = a! \, b! \, c! \, [x^a y^b z^c] \ln G(x, y, z) \bmod 998244353\).

Constraints: \(A, B, C \le 50\) (\(V = (A+1)(B+1)(C+1) \le 132,651\)), modulus \(p = 998244353\). Required complexity: \(O(V \log V)\) time (~\(3 V \log_2 V\) NTT operations) and \(O(V)\) space.
Hand-Checkable Sample Trace (\(A = B = C = 1\), all fugacities \(= 2\)): For \(a = b = c = 1\) (one vertex of each color, i.e., \(K_3\)), a graph on \(3\) labeled vertices has \(2^3 = 8\) subgraphs, of which \(4\) are connected (the triangle \(K_3\) plus the \(3\) spanning paths of length \(2\)), so \(1!1!1! [x^1 y^1 z^1] \ln G(x, y, z) = 4\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By the Multivariate Exponential Formula (§16.1), since every 3-colored graph is uniquely a disjoint union of connected 3-colored components, the EGF of connected 3-colored graphs is
\[C(x, y, z) = \ln G(x, y, z) \pmod{(x^{A+1}, y^{B+1}, z^{C+1})}.\]
Why does a naive 3D FFT fail here? For \(A = B = C = 50\), each dimension \(51\) must be zero-padded to \(\ge 101 \implies 128\), so a 3D FFT operates on an array of size \(128^3 = 2,097,152\) (\(16\times\) larger than \(V = 51^3 = 132,651\)). How do we compute \(\ln G(x, y, z)\) using 1D NTTs of length \(2^{18} = 262,144\) instead?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Apply Twisted Kronecker Substitution (§16.3) with \(d = 3\) and dimensions \((n_1, n_2, n_3) = (A + 1, B + 1, C + 1)\):

Pack \((a, b, c) \in [0, A] \times [0, B] \times [0, C]\) into the 1D index \[I(a, b, c) = a + b(A + 1) + c(A + 1)(B + 1) \in [0, V - 1].\]
By Theorem 16.1, the carry-detection grading is \[\chi(I) = \left( \left\lfloor \frac{I}{A + 1} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{I}{(A + 1)(B + 1)} \right\rfloor \right) \bmod 3 = \big(b + (B + 2)c\big) \bmod 3,\] which detects carries in the first two coordinates because \(\lfloor I/(A+1) \rfloor = b + c(B+1)\) and \(\lfloor I/((A+1)(B+1)) \rfloor = c\)!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Use the Radial Euler Derivation \(\mathfrak{D} = x \partial_x + (A + 1) y \partial_y + (A + 1)(B + 1) z \partial_z\) from §16.3, which scales the \(I\)-th packed entry by \(I\):

Compute \(G^{-1} \in \mathcal{R}_3\) via 1D Kronecker-index Newton doubling \(H_{2M} = H_M \cdot_\chi (2 - G \cdot_\chi H_M) \bmod z^{2M}\) for \(M = 1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^{\lceil \log_2 V \rceil}\).
Compute \(\mathfrak{D}(G)[I] = I \cdot G[I]\), multiply \(\mathfrak{D}(G) \cdot_\chi G^{-1}\) using a single 3-graded multiplication of size \(V\), and divide the \(I\)-th coefficient by \(I\) for \(1 \le I < V\) to obtain \(\ln G(x, y, z)\)!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Constructing \(G(x, y, z)\) in \(O(V)\) Time: Using the identity \(u v = \binom{u + v}{2} - \binom{u}{2} - \binom{v}{2}\), we precompute powers of \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \lambda_{rg}, \lambda_{gb}, \lambda_{br}\) up to \(\binom{A+B+C}{2}\) and fill the packed 1D array \(G[0 \dots V - 1]\) at \(I(a, b, c) = a + b n_1 + c n_1 n_2\) (\(n_1 = A + 1, n_2 = B + 1, n_3 = C + 1\)) with \(G[0] = 1\).
3D Twisted Kronecker Inversion & Radial Logarithm: Precompute \(\chi[I] = \big((I / n_1) + (I / (n_1 n_2))\big) \bmod 3\) for \(0 \le I < V\).

Step A (Newton Inversion for \(G^{-1}\)): Because \(I(a_1 + a_2, b_1 + b_2, c_1 + c_2) = I(a_1, b_1, c_1) + I(a_2, b_2, c_2)\) whenever no coordinate overflows, any two valid tuples \((a_1, b_1, c_1)\) and \((a_2, b_2, c_2)\) summing to \((a, b, c)\) have packed indices summing to \(I(a, b, c)\). Thus, if \(G \cdot_\chi H_M \equiv 1\) holds on the 1D prefix \(0 \le I < M\), then the error \(E = G \cdot_\chi H_M - 1\) has \(E[I] = 0\) for all \(0 \le I < M\), which implies \((E \cdot_\chi E)[I] = 0\) for all \(0 \le I < 2M\)! Therefore, standard 1D Newton doubling \(H_{2M} = H_M \cdot_\chi (2 - G \cdot_\chi H_M) \bmod z^{2M}\) is 100% exact on the packed 1D array. Moreover, by caching the \(3\) forward NTTs of \(H_M\) of length \(2M\), each doubling step uses only \(3 \times 3 = 9\) NTTs of length \(2M\).
Step B (Single-Pass Radial Euler Logarithm): Define \(D_G[I] = I \cdot G[I] \bmod p\) for \(0 \le I < V\). Compute the single 3-graded product \(Q = D_G \cdot_\chi G^{-1}\) on \([0, V - 1]\) using NTT length \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(2V) \rceil} = 2^{18} = 262,144\), and recover \[(\ln G)[0] = 0, \qquad (\ln G)[I] = Q[I] \cdot I^{-1} \bmod p \quad (1 \le I < V).\] Finally, for each \((a, b, c)\), output \(c_{a, b, c} = a! \, b! \, c! \, (\ln G)[I(a, b, c)] \bmod 998244353\).
Sample Trace Verification (\(A = B = C = 1\), all fugacities \(= 2\)): Here \(n_1 = n_2 = n_3 = 2, V = 8\), and \(I(a, b, c) = a + 2b + 4c\). The packed values of \(G[I]\) for \(I = 0, \dots, 7\) are: \[G = [1,\; 1,\; 1,\; 2,\; 1,\; 2,\; 2,\; 8].\] Applying \(\ln G = \mathfrak{D}^{-1}(\mathfrak{D}(G) \cdot_\chi G^{-1})\) yields: \[\ln G = [0,\; 1,\; 1,\; 1,\; 1,\; 1,\; 1,\; 4],\] confirming \(c_{1, 0, 0} = c_{0, 1, 0} = c_{0, 0, 1} = 1\), \(c_{1, 1, 0} = c_{1, 0, 1} = c_{0, 1, 1} = 1\), and \(c_{1, 1, 1} = 4\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Dimensions \(A, B, C \le 50\) (\(V = (A+1)(B+1)(C+1) \le 132,651\)) and packed array \(G[0 \dots V-1]\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\) representing a trivariate polynomial modulo \(\langle x_1^{A+1}, x_2^{B+1}, x_3^{C+1} \rangle\).
Preconditions: Constant term \(G[0] = [x_1^0 x_2^0 x_3^0]G = 1\), and \(V\) fits within a power-of-two NTT length \(L = 2^{\lceil \log_2(2V-1) \rceil} \le 2^{18}\).
Postconditions (Output): Packed array \((\ln G)[0 \dots V-1] \bmod 998244353\) with \((\ln G)[0] = 0\), matching \(\ln G(x_1, x_2, x_3) \bmod \langle x_1^{A+1}, x_2^{B+1}, x_3^{C+1} \rangle\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(d V \log V + d^2 V)\) time (\(d = 3\), FFT length \(2^{18}\)) and \(O(d V)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Each bucketed tensor slice \(A_r(X)\) contains only packed indices \(I\) with total quotient twist \(\chi(I) = \big(\lfloor I/(A+1) \rfloor + \lfloor I/((A+1)(B+1)) \rfloor\big) \bmod 3 = r\), so any valid non-wrapping 3D tuple \((i_1 + j_1 \le A, i_2 + j_2 \le B, i_3 + j_3 \le C)\) has \(\chi(I+J) = (\chi(I) + \chi(J)) \bmod 3\), eliminating cross-dimension carry pollution.
Failure Mode & Characteristic-\(p\) Condition: Fails if \(G[0] \neq 1\) (since \(\ln G\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p[[x_1, x_2, x_3]]\) requires constant term \(1\)), or if \(p \le A\) when integrating with respect to \(x_1\) (or \(p \le \max(A, B, C)\) if integrating along the longest axis), where dividing by the exponent \(i_1 \in [1, A]\) hits \(i_1 \equiv 0 \pmod p\).

title: 16 — The Bivariate Hierarchy, 2D Bostan–Mori & Furstenberg’s Diagonal Theorem
