§20.5 Complete 8-Problem 4-Tier Practice Ladder


Stepping Stone 1 (#050) — Đa Thức / Polynomial (AtCoder ARC 033 D)

Source: AtCoder Regular Contest 033 D — 多項式 (Polynomial)
Canonical ID: #050 (5B#D1)
Prerequisites: Consecutive-grid Lagrange interpolation (§20.4 Part B), prefix/suffix products.


Problem Statement
There is an unknown polynomial \(P(x)\) of degree at most \(N\) with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}_p\) where \(p = 10^9 + 7\). You are given the \(N + 1\) point values \(A_0 = P(0), A_1 = P(1), \dots, A_N = P(N) \pmod{10^9 + 7}\), and an integer \(T\). Compute \(P(T) \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).


Constraints

\(1 \le N \le 10^5\)
\(0 \le A_i < 10^9 + 7\) for \(0 \le i \le N\)
\(0 \le T \le 10^9\)
Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\) (requires \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space).



Sample Trace (\(N = 2, T = 4\))
Suppose \(N = 2\), \(A = [P(0), P(1), P(2)] = [1, 3, 7]\) (corresponding to \(P(x) = 1 + x + x^2\)), and \(T = 4\).

Prefix products \(\text{pref}_i = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(4 - j)\): \(\text{pref}_0 = 1, \text{pref}_1 = 4, \text{pref}_2 = 4 \cdot 3 = 12\).
Suffix products \(\text{suff}_i = \prod_{j=i+1}^2(4 - j)\): \(\text{suff}_2 = 1, \text{suff}_1 = 2, \text{suff}_0 = 3 \cdot 2 = 6\).
Numerators \(\text{num}_i = \text{pref}_i \cdot \text{suff}_i\): \(\text{num} = [6, 8, 12]\).
Denominators \(\text{den}_i = (-1)^{2-i} i! (2-i)!\): \(\text{den} = [2, -1, 2]\).
Sum: \(P(4) = 1 \cdot \frac{6}{2} + 3 \cdot \frac{8}{-1} + 7 \cdot \frac{12}{2} = 3 - 24 + 42 = 21\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

You are given \(N + 1\) values of a degree-\(N\) polynomial on the consecutive integer grid \(x = 0, 1, \dots, N\), and you only need to evaluate \(P(x)\) at a single query point \(x = T\). Because \(m = 1\), you do not even need an NTT—you only need to evaluate the Lagrange interpolation sum at \(x = T\) in \(O(N)\) time without dividing by zero when \(T \le N\).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Write the Lagrange basis polynomial at \(x_i = i\): \[
\ell_i(T) = \frac{\prod_{j \ne i} (T - j)}{\prod_{j \ne i} (i - j)} = \frac{\left(\prod_{j=0}^{i-1} (T - j)\right) \left(\prod_{j=i+1}^N (T - j)\right)}{(-1)^{N - i}\, i!\, (N - i)!}.
\] Notice that by writing the numerator as the product of a prefix product \(\text{pref}[i] = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(T - j)\) and a suffix product \(\text{suff}[i] = \prod_{j=i+1}^N(T - j)\), you never divide by \((T - i)\), so the formula works even when \(0 \le T \le N\) (or you can return \(A_T\) directly when \(T \le N\)).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to \(N\) in \(O(N + \log p)\) time, compute \(\text{pref}[0 \dots N]\) and \(\text{suff}[0 \dots N]\) in two \(O(N)\) sweeps, and accumulate \(\sum_{i=0}^N A_i \cdot \text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i] \cdot (-1)^{N-i} \text{inv\_fact}[i] \cdot \text{inv\_fact}[N-i] \bmod p\).







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Uniqueness of Degree-\(N\) Polynomial: A polynomial \(P(x) \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]\) of degree at most \(N\) is uniquely determined by its values at \(N + 1\) distinct points \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{F}_p\) (since \(N < 10^9 + 7 = p\), the residues \(0, 1, \dots, N\) are distinct modulo \(p\)).
Lagrange Basis Decomposition: By Lagrange’s interpolation formula, \[
P(T) = \sum_{i=0}^N A_i \prod_{\substack{0 \le j \le N \\ j \ne i}} \frac{T - j}{i - j}.
\]
Denominator Factorization: For a fixed \(i \in \{0, \dots, N\}\), split the denominator product at \(j = i\): \[
\prod_{j=0}^{i-1} (i - j) = i(i - 1) \cdots 1 = i!, \qquad \prod_{j=i+1}^N (i - j) = (-1)( -2 ) \cdots (-(N - i)) = (-1)^{N - i} (N - i)!.
\]
Prefix-Suffix Numerator Split (Avoiding \(0/0\)): Define \[
\text{pref}[i] = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1} (T - j) \bmod p, \qquad \text{suff}[i] = \prod_{j=i+1}^N (T - j) \bmod p.
\] These satisfy the recurrences \(\text{pref}[0] = 1\), \(\text{pref}[i] = \text{pref}[i-1] \cdot (T - i + 1) \bmod p\), and \(\text{suff}[N] = 1\), \(\text{suff}[i] = \text{suff}[i+1] \cdot (T - i - 1) \bmod p\).
Final Linear Sum: Combining numerator and denominator yields \[
P(T) \equiv \sum_{i=0}^N A_i \cdot \text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i] \cdot (-1)^{N - i}\, (i!)^{-1}\, ((N - i)!)^{-1} \pmod p.
\] (Boundary Case \(0 \le T \le N\)): If \(0 \le T \le N\), then for every \(i \ne T\), either \(\text{pref}[i]\) or \(\text{suff}[i]\) contains the factor \((T - T) = 0\), while for \(i = T\), \(\text{pref}[T] \cdot \text{suff}[T] = T! (-1)^{N-T} (N - T)!\), so the formula automatically returns \(A_T\).



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integer \(N \ge 1\), array \(A[0 \dots N]\) of length \(N + 1\) with \(A[i] = P(i) \bmod p\), and evaluation point \(T \ge 0\); prime modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7 > N\).
Postconditions (Output): Single integer \(P(T) \bmod p \in [0, p - 1]\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N + \log p)\) time and \(O(N)\) auxiliary space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After \(i\) steps of the prefix/suffix sweeps, \(\text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i] = \prod_{0 \le j \le N, j \ne i} (T - j) \bmod p\) without performing any division by \((T - i)\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Computing \(\prod_{j=0}^N (T - j)\) globally and dividing by \((T - i) \bmod p\) crashes with \(0/0\) whenever \((T \bmod p) \in [0, N]\); using \(\text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i]\) avoids division by \((T - i)\) completely.









Stepping Stone 2 (#197) — [NOIP2020] 微信步数 / WeChat Steps (Luogu P7116)

Source: Luogu P7116 — [NOIP2020] 微信步数 (WeChat Steps)
Canonical ID: #197 (5B#D7)
Prerequisites: Polynomial degree of hyperrectangle volume, prefix sums of polynomials, consecutive-grid Lagrange evaluation (§20.4 Part B).


Problem Statement
A walker starts at an initial grid cell \((x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k)\) inside a \(k\)-dimensional box \([1, w_1] \times [1, w_2] \times \dots \times [1, w_k]\) (\(1 \le x_i \le w_i\)). The walker repeatedly executes a periodic sequence of \(n\) steps: the \(r\)-th step (\(1 \le r \le n\)) adds \(d_r \in \{-1, +1\}\) to coordinate \(c_r \in \{1, \dots, k\}\). A walk terminates on the first step it leaves \([1, w_1] \times \dots \times [1, w_k]\). Sum the total number of steps taken before leaving the box over all \(\prod_{i=1}^k w_i\) starting cells, modulo \(10^9 + 7\), or output \(-1\) if at least one starting cell never leaves the box.


Constraints

\(1 \le k \le 10\), \(1 \le n \le 5 \times 10^5\), \(1 \le w_i \le 10^9\)
\(1 \le c_r \le k\), \(d_r \in \{-1, +1\}\)
Modulus: \(10^9 + 7\). Time limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\) (requires \(O(n k + k^2)\) time).



Sample Trace (\(k = 1, w_1 = 5, n = 2\), steps: \(+1, +1\))
Here \(k = 1, w_1 = 5, n = 2\), and each period moves \(+2\) in dimension \(1\) (\(\Delta_1 = 2\)).

Before step \(1\): all \(5\) cells survive (\(+5\)).
Period \(q = 0\): after step \(r = 1\) (\(+1\)), span is \(1\), so \(5 - 1 = 4\) cells survive (\(+4\)); after step \(r = 2\) (\(+2\)), span is \(2\), so \(5 - 2 = 3\) cells survive (\(+3\)).
Period \(q = 1\): at \(r = 1\), span is \(1 + 2 = 3 \implies 5 - 3 = 2\) cells survive (\(+2\)); at \(r = 2\), span is \(2 + 2 = 4 \implies 5 - 4 = 1\) cell survives (\(+1\)).
Period \(q = 2\): at \(r = 1\), span reaches \(5 \implies 0\) cells survive.
Total steps = \(5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15\) (matching exit steps \(5, 4, 3, 2, 1\) from \(x_1 = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\)).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

By tail-sum expectation (double counting), the sum of exit steps over all starting cells equals \(\sum_{t \ge 0} (\text{number of starting cells still inside the box after } t \text{ steps})\). Because coordinates evolve independently, the set of surviving starting cells after \(t\) steps is a \(k\)-dimensional box whose side length in dimension \(i\) is \(\max\big(0,\; w_i - (\max_{0 \le s \le t} \delta_i(s) - \min_{0 \le s \le t} \delta_i(s))\big)\), where \(\delta_i(s)\) is the net displacement in dimension \(i\) after \(s\) steps.



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Let \(t = q n + r\) where \(q \ge 1\) is the period index and \(1 \le r \le n\) is the step offset inside the period. After the first full period (\(q = 0\)), the running maximum and minimum in dimension \(i\) have already reached their envelope, so for every subsequent period \(q \ge 1\), the span \(S_i(q n + r) = \max_{0 \le s \le qn+r} \delta_i(s) - \min_{0 \le s \le qn+r} \delta_i(s)\) grows strictly linearly in \(q\): \[
S_i(q n + r) = L_i(r) + (q - 1) \cdot |\delta_i(n)| \quad (q \ge 1),
\] where \(L_i(r) = S_i(n + r)\) is the span at step \(r\) of period \(q = 1\), and \(\Delta_i = |\delta_i(n)|\) is the net drift per period in dimension \(i\).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

For a fixed step \(r \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) (or equivalently, summing the linear coefficients over all \(r \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) first!), the number of surviving cells at period \(q \ge 1\) while all \(k\) dimensions remain positive (\(q \le Q_{\max}\)) is a polynomial in \(q\) of degree at most \(k\): \[
P_r(q) = \prod_{i=1}^k \big(w_i - L_i(r) - (q - 1)\Delta_i\big).
\] Even better: instead of interpolating \(P_r(q)\) for each \(r\) separately (which would cost \(O(n k^2)\)), expand or maintain the coefficients of \((q - 1)^0, \dots, (q - 1)^k\) as \(r\) advances from \(1\) to \(n\) (only one factor changes at step \(r\)!), or evaluate the prefix sum \(\sum_{q=1}^{Q_{\max}} q^d\) for \(0 \le d \le k\) once using consecutive-grid Lagrange interpolation on \(k + 2\) points in \(O(k^2)\)!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Tail-Sum Reformulation: A starting cell \(\mathbf{x} \in \prod_{i=1}^k [1, w_i]\) exits on step \(T(\mathbf{x}) \ge 1\) if and only if it survives steps \(0, 1, \dots, T(\mathbf{x}) - 1\). Therefore: \[
\sum_{\mathbf{x}} T(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{t = 0}^{\infty} \prod_{i=1}^k \max\!\big(0,\; w_i - S_i(t)\big),
\] where \(S_i(t) = \max_{0 \le s \le t} \delta_i(s) - \min_{0 \le s \le t} \delta_i(s)\) is the peak-to-trough range of dimension \(i\) up to time \(t\).
Infinite Walk Criterion: The walk is infinite (return \(-1\)) if and only if after one full period (\(t = n\)), \(S_i(n) < w_i\) for all \(1 \le i \le k\) and the net period displacement vector is zero (\(\delta_i(n) = 0\) for all \(1 \le i \le k\)).
Separating Period \(q = 0\) from Periodic Regime \(q \ge 1\):

Simulate \(t = 0, 1, \dots, n\) directly in \(O(n k)\) time, adding \(\prod_{i=1}^k \max(0, w_i - S_i(t))\) to the answer. If any dimension reaches \(S_i(t) \ge w_i\) during \(t \le n\), terminate immediately.
For \(t = q n + r\) with \(q \ge 1\) and \(1 \le r \le n\), let \(\Delta_i = |\delta_i(n)|\) and let \(L_i(r) = S_i(n + r)\) (obtained by simulating one more period \(n + 1 \dots 2n\)). Because every extremum after \(t \ge n\) simply shifts the extremum of the previous period by \(\delta_i(n)\), we have \[
S_i(q n + r) = L_i(r) + (q - 1)\Delta_i \quad \text{for all } q \ge 1.
\]

Summing over \(q = 1, \dots, Q(r)\) via Power Sums / Lagrange Interpolation: At step offset \(r\), the box remains non-empty for \(1 \le q \le Q(r)\), where \[
Q(r) = 1 + \min_{\substack{1 \le i \le k \\ \Delta_i > 0}} \left\lfloor \frac{w_i - L_i(r) - 1}{\Delta_i} \right\rfloor
\] (with \(Q(r) = 0\) if \(w_i \le L_i(r)\) for some \(i\)). Observe that as \(r\) goes from \(1\) to \(n\), \(L_i(r)\) increases by at most \(1\) at the single coordinate \(i = c_r\). Even simpler: \(Q(r)\) can only take two values across all \(r \in \{1, \dots, n\}\)—namely \(Q_{\min}\) and \(Q_{\min} + 1\)! Specifically, let \(Q_{\text{full}} = \min_{i : \Delta_i > 0} \lfloor (w_i - S_i(n) - 1) / \Delta_i \rfloor\) be the number of complete periods after \(q = 0\) before any dimension can possibly hit \(0\). Or for each \(r\), expand the degree-\(k\) polynomial in \(x = q - 1\): \[
P_r(x) = \prod_{i=1}^k \big((w_i - L_i(r)) - \Delta_i x\big) = \sum_{d=0}^k c_{r, d} x^d \pmod p
\] in \(O(k^2)\) (or \(O(k)\) by dividing out the old factor for \(c_r\) and multiplying the new one), and multiply \(c_{r, d}\) by the precomputed power sum \(S_d(Q(r) - 1) = \sum_{x=0}^{Q(r)-1} x^d \bmod p\), which is a polynomial of degree \(d + 1 \le k + 1\) evaluated at \(X = Q(r) - 1\) via Stepping Stone 1 (consecutive-grid Lagrange interpolation on \(0, 1, \dots, k + 1\)) in \(O(k)\) time!



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Dimension \(k \in [1, 10]\), period length \(n \in [1, 5 \times 10^5]\), box widths \(w[1 \dots k]\), and step pairs \((c_r, d_r)\) for \(1 \le r \le n\); prime modulus \(p = 10^9 + 7 > k + 2\).
Postconditions (Output): Total steps over all starting cells modulo \(10^9 + 7\), or \(-1\) if unbounded.
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n k + k^2 \log p)\) time and \(O(n + k^2)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After step \(r\) of period \(q = 1\), \(L_i(r) = S_i(n + r)\) satisfies \(S_i(q n + r) = L_i(r) + (q - 1)\Delta_i\) for all \(q \ge 1\) and \(1 \le i \le k\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Check whether \(\Delta_i = 0\) for all \(1 \le i \le k\) while \(w_i > S_i(n)\) for all \(i\) (returning \(-1\) for infinite walk before dividing by \(\Delta_i\)); consecutive-grid Lagrange interpolation on \(\{0, 1, \dots, k + 1\}\) requires \(p > k + 1\), and when \(X = Q(r) - 1 \in \{0, \dots, k + 1\}\) falls on a grid node, return the sample value directly to avoid \(0/0\).









Intermediate 1 (#127) — Koxia and Bracket (Codeforces 1770G)

Source: Codeforces Good Bye 2022 (CF 1770 G) — Koxia and Bracket
Canonical ID: #127 (5B#B8)
Prerequisites: Transposed polynomial multiplication (mulT, §20.2), Divide-and-Conquer DP over active balance windows.


Problem Statement
You are given a bracket string \(S\) of length \(N\) consisting of '(' and ')'. Let \(k\) be the minimum number of character deletions required to transform \(S\) into a valid (balanced) bracket sequence. Compute the number of distinct subsets of indices of size \(k\) whose deletion makes \(S\) a valid bracket sequence, modulo \(998244353\).


Constraints

\(1 \le N \le 2.5 \times 10^5\)
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\) (NTT-friendly prime).
Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\) (requires \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space).



Sample Trace (\(S = \text{")())(("}\), \(N = 6\))
Prefix balances of \(S = \text{")())(("}\) are \(b = [0, -1, 0, -1, -2, -1, 0]\), with global minimum \(b_{\min} = -2\) at position \(p^* = 4\) (")())" has \(b_4 = -2\), and suffix "((" has reversed balance \(-2\)).

Left prefix \(S[1..4] = \text{")())"}\): must delete \(2\) closing brackets ')' while keeping prefix balance \(\ge 0\). Valid deletions of \(2\) ')' from positions \(\{1, 3, 4\}\): deleting \(\{1, 3\}\) leaves "()", deleting \(\{1, 4\}\) leaves "()", so \(2\) ways (deleting \(\{3, 4\}\) leaves ")(", invalid).
Right suffix \(S[5..6] = \text{"(("}\): must delete both '(', giving \(1\) way.
Total valid minimum-deletion subsets: \(2 \times 1 = 2\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Assign \(+1\) to '(' and \(-1\) to ')', and let \(b_i = \sum_{j=1}^i s_j\) be the prefix balance (\(b_0 = 0\)), with global minimum \(b_{\min} = \min_{0 \le i \le N} b_i\). Any minimum deletion deletes exactly \(-b_{\min}\) closing brackets ')' and \(b_N - b_{\min}\) opening brackets '('. Crucially, if \(p^*\) is an index achieving \(b_{p^*} = b_{\min}\), all deleted ')' must come from the prefix \(S[1 \dots p^*]\) and all deleted '(' must come from the suffix \(S[p^* + 1 \dots N]\)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By reversing the suffix \(S[p^*+1 \dots N]\) and swapping '(' \(\leftrightarrow\) ')', both halves reduce to the same problem: given a string where we are only allowed to delete ')', count the ways to reach the final mandatory balance while never letting the current balance drop below \(0\). Between consecutive ')' characters, a block of \(c_i\) opening brackets '(' simply shifts the polynomial state by \(x^{c_i}\). At each ')', we either keep it (shift by \(x^{-1}\)) or delete it (shift by \(x^0\)), which multiplies the state by \((x^{-1} + 1)\) followed by zeroing out any negative power \([x^{-1}]\).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

In a naive DP, the state polynomial has degree up to \(N\), making each step \(O(N)\). However, over any segment \([L, R]\) of ')' blocks in a Divide-and-Conquer tree, the net balance only changes by \(O(R - L + 1)\) relative to the prefix minimum of the segment! Specifically, at every step \(i\), any state below the minimum required balance \(\text{low}_i\) is zeroed out, and over a segment \([L, R]\) of length \(\ell = R - L + 1\), only the window \([\text{low}_L - \ell,\; \text{low}_R + \ell]\) of length \(O(\ell)\) can both enter \([L, R]\) and survive to \(R\). Use D&C with mulT / NTT over windows of size \(O(R - L + 1)\) to advance the DP in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) total time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Splitting at the Global Minimum Balance \(p^*\): Let \(b_i\) be the prefix sum of \(+1\)/\(-1\) weights and let \(p^* \in [0, N]\) minimize \(b_{p^*}\).

In \(S[1 \dots p^*]\), we must delete \(k_L = -b_{p^*}\) closing brackets ')' and \(0\) opening brackets '(' so that the running balance never drops below \(0\) and ends at \(0\) at \(p^*\).
In the reversed, complemented suffix \(S'[1 \dots N - p^*]\), we must delete \(k_R = b_N - b_{p^*}\) closing brackets ')' and \(0\) opening brackets '(' under the exact same rule. Since the two halves are independent, the total count is \(\text{Ways}(S[1 \dots p^*]) \times \text{Ways}(S'[1 \dots N - p^*]) \bmod 998244353\).

Formulating the One-Sided Deletion DP as Windowed Polynomial Shifts: In a string of length \(M\) where we only delete ')' and must delete all excess ')' (so the final balance is \(0\)), let \(d_i\) be the number of deletions made in the first \(i\) characters. Since all '(' are kept, the current balance after \(i\) characters is \(b_i + d_i \ge 0\), which forces the lower bound \[
d_i \ge \max(0, -b_i) =: \text{low}_i, \qquad \text{and also } d_i \le \text{cnt}_{')'}(1 \dots i).
\] More simply, track the DP indexed by the number of kept ')' characters \(u_i\) in \(S[1 \dots i]\):

At an '(' character, \(u_i\) does not change.
At the \(m\)-th ')' character (which occurs after \(a_m\) opening brackets '(' have been seen in total), we can either delete it (\(u_m = u_{m-1}\)) or keep it (\(u_m = u_{m-1} + 1\)), provided \(u_m \le a_m\) (so balance \(a_m - u_m \ge 0\)). Thus, at the \(m\)-th ')' (\(1 \le m \le K\)), the state polynomial \(D_m(x) = \sum_{u=0}^{a_m} \text{dp}_m[u] x^u\) updates via: \[
D_m(x) = \big(D_{m-1}(x) \cdot (1 + x)\big) \bmod x^{a_m + 1},
\] and at the end we want \([x^{a_K}] D_K(x)\) (since final balance is \(0 \implies u_K = a_K\)).

Divide-and-Conquer with mulT / Active Window Truncation: Notice that across a segment of ')' steps \(m \in [L, R]\) of length \(\ell = R - L + 1\), each step multiplies by \((1 + x)\) and caps the degree at \(a_m\) (which is non-decreasing: \(a_L \le a_{L+1} \le \dots \le a_R\)).

Because each step increases the degree of \(x\) by at most \(1\), any term \(x^u\) entering at \(m = L - 1\) with \(u < a_L - \ell\) can reach degree at most \(u + \ell < a_L \le a_m\), so it never hits the upper boundary \(a_m\) during \([L, R]\)!
Conversely, inside \([L, R]\), only degrees \(u \in [a_L - \ell,\; a_R]\) (a window of size \((a_R - a_L) + \ell + 1\)) interact with the boundary \(a_m\).
Better yet: over the entire prefix \(1 \dots K\), \(\sum (a_R - a_L)\) across a single level of the D&C tree telescopes to \(a_K \le N\), and \(\sum \ell = K \le N\)! Therefore, on each D&C interval \([L, R]\), we shift the active polynomial slice \(D_{L-1}[a_L - \ell \dots a_{L-1}]\) down by \(a_L - \ell\), recurse on \([L, M]\) and \([M+1, R]\) (while pushing the non-boundary low-degree part across \([L, R]\) via a single multiplication by \((1 + x)^\ell\) or transposed mulT), and sum the work at each tree level to \(O((a_K + K) \log N) = O(N \log N)\), yielding \(O(N \log^2 N)\) total time!




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Bracket string \(S[1 \dots N]\) of length \(N \le 2.5 \times 10^5\); prime modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Number of minimum-deletion valid bracket subsequences modulo \(998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N)\) auxiliary space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Entering D&C node \([L, R]\) of length \(\ell = R - L + 1\), the active polynomial slice tracks degrees \([ \max(0, a_L - \ell),\; a_{L-1} ]\) of length \(\le (a_R - a_L) + \ell + 1\), whose sum across all disjoint intervals at depth \(d\) is bounded by \(a_K + K \le N\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(S\) has no closing brackets to delete in a half (\(K = 0\)), return \(1\) immediately for that half; when multiple indices achieve the global minimum prefix balance \(b_{\min}\), splitting at any single minimum index \(p^*\) yields the same canonical partition without double counting because no deleted ')' can lie to the right of \(p^*\) and no deleted '(' can lie to the left of \(p^*\).









Intermediate 2 (#167) — [十二省联考2019] 字符串问题 / String Problem (Luogu P5284)

Source: Luogu P5284 — [十二省联考2019] 字符串问题 (String Problem)
Canonical ID: #167 (5B#B5)
Prerequisites: DAG fan-out / addition gate duality (§20.1), Suffix Automaton / Suffix Tree parent tree, topological DP.


Problem Statement
You are given a string \(S\) of length \(|S|\) over lowercase English letters, \(n_a\) substrings of \(S\) designated as Type-A strings \(A_1, \dots, A_{n_a}\) (specified by \([la_i, ra_i]\)), and \(n_b\) substrings designated as Type-B strings \(B_1, \dots, B_{n_b}\) (specified by \([lb_j, rb_j]\)). There are \(m\) explicit directed edges from Type-A strings to Type-B strings (\(A_{x_k} \to B_{y_k}\)). In addition, every Type-B string \(B_j\) has an implicit directed edge \(B_j \to A_i\) to every Type-A string \(A_i\) that contains \(B_j\) as a prefix (\(|A_i| \ge |B_j|\) and \(A_i[1 \dots |B_j|] = B_j\)). The weight of each \(A_i\) is its length \(|A_i|\), and the weight of each \(B_j\) is \(0\). Find the maximum total weight of a walk in this directed graph, or output \(-1\) if there is a walk of infinitely large weight (i.e., a directed cycle reachable from an \(A_i\) or containing an \(A_i\)).


Constraints

\(\sum |S|, \sum n_a, \sum n_b, \sum m \le 2 \times 10^5\) across testcases.
Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\) (requires \(O((|S| + n_a + n_b + m)\log |S|)\) time and \(O(|S| + n_a + n_b + m)\) space).



Sample Trace (\(S = \text{"abaa"}\), \(A_1 = \text{"aba"}, A_2 = \text{"ab"}\), \(B_1 = \text{"a"}, B_2 = \text{"aba"}\))
Suppose explicit edges are \(A_1 \to B_1\) and \(A_2 \to B_2\):

Implicit prefix edges: \(B_1 = \text{"a"}\) is a prefix of both \(A_1 = \text{"aba"}\) and \(A_2 = \text{"ab"}\), so \(B_1 \to A_1\) and \(B_1 \to A_2\). \(B_2 = \text{"aba"}\) is a prefix of \(A_1 = \text{"aba"}\), so \(B_2 \to A_1\).
Notice the cycle \(A_1 \to B_1 \to A_1\): since \(|A_1| = 3 > 0\), we can repeat this cycle infinitely many times, so the output is \(-1\). If \(A_1 \to B_1\) were removed, the longest path would be \(A_2 \to B_2 \to A_1\) with weight \(|A_2| + |A_1| = 2 + 3 = 5\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Naive graph construction adds up to \(n_a \cdot n_b = 4 \times 10^{10}\) implicit edges \(B_j \to A_i\) whenever \(B_j\) is a prefix of \(A_i\). In the Suffix Tree of \(S\) (constructed as the parent tree of the Suffix Automaton of the reversed string \(S^R\)), \(B_j\) is a prefix of \(A_i\) if and only if the locus of \(A_i\) is in the subtree of the locus of \(B_j\) (or at the same node with \(|A_i| \ge |B_j|\)). This is a tree-subtree fan-out broadcast from \(B_j\) to all \(A_i\) in its subtree!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Apply the DAG Gate Compression / Transposition Principle (§20.1) to factor the \(O(n_b \cdot n_a)\) bipartite fan-out edges through a linear-size auxiliary spine on the Suffix Tree:

Build the Suffix Automaton (SAM) on \(S^R\); its link tree is the exact Suffix Tree of \(S\).
For each substring \(S[l \dots r]\) (representing the suffix \(S[l \dots |S|]\) truncated to length \(L = r - l + 1\)), start at the SAM node for prefix \(S^R\) up to \(l\) and use binary lifting on the SAM link tree to jump to the highest ancestor \(u\) with \(\text{len}(u) \ge L\).
Within a single SAM node \(u\), multiple \(A_i\) and \(B_j\) may land with various lengths \(L \in (\text{len}(\text{link}(u)), \text{len}(u)]\). Sort all strings landing at node \(u\) by length (placing \(B_j\) before \(A_i\) on ties \(|B_j| = |A_i|\)) and chain them with a suffix-spine of auxiliary nodes so each \(B_j\) only needs one outgoing edge to reach all longer \(A_i\) in node \(u\) and all descendants of \(u\)!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Specifically, at each SAM node \(u\), create an entry hub \(\text{in}[u]\) and an exit hub \(\text{out}[u]\) (or chain the sorted \(B_j\) and \(A_i\) at node \(u\) directly): connect \(\text{out}[\text{link}(u)] \to \text{in}[u]\), connect each \(B_j\) at node \(u\) to the suffix of longer \(A_i\)’s at node \(u\) and to \(\text{out}[u]\), and run Kahn’s topological sort + longest-path DP on the resulting \(O(|S| + n_a + n_b)\)-vertex, \(O(|S| + n_a + n_b + m)\)-edge DAG. If the topological sort visits fewer than \(V\) vertices, a cycle exists and we output \(-1\).







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Prefix Relation as Suffix-Tree Subtree Dominance: Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the link tree of the Suffix Automaton built on \(S^R\). Every node \(u \in \mathcal{T}\) represents an equivalence class of substrings of \(S\) sharing the same start-position set, with maximum length \(\text{len}(u)\). For any substring \(P = S[l \dots r]\) of length \(L = r - l + 1\), its locus \(u(P) \in \mathcal{T}\) is the unique ancestor of the prefix node \(\text{pos}[l]\) satisfying \(\text{len}(\text{link}(u)) < L \le \text{len}(u)\), found in \(O(\log |S|)\) via binary lifting. Then \(B_j\) is a prefix of \(A_i\) if and only if:

Either \(u(A_i)\) is a strict descendant of \(u(B_j)\) in \(\mathcal{T}\), or
\(u(A_i) = u(B_j)\) and \(|A_i| \ge |B_j|\).

Factoring the Subtree Fan-Out via Spine Nodes: At each node \(u \in \mathcal{T}\), collect all Type-A and Type-B strings with locus \(u\), and sort them in non-decreasing order of length, breaking ties of equal length by placing Type-B before Type-A. Create a chain of auxiliary hub nodes \(h_{u, 1}, h_{u, 2}, \dots, h_{u, k_u}\) corresponding to the sorted list at node \(u\), plus a base hub \(h_{u, 0}\) (entered from \(\text{link}(u)\)) and a tail hub \(h_{u, k_u + 1}\):

Add directed \(0\)-weight edges along the spine: \(h_{u, 0} \to h_{u, 1} \to \dots \to h_{u, k_u} \to h_{u, k_u + 1}\).
For every child \(v\) of \(u\) in \(\mathcal{T}\), add a \(0\)-weight edge \(h_{u, k_u + 1} \to h_{v, 0}\).
If the \(t\)-th sorted item at node \(u\) is a Type-B string \(B_j\), add a \(0\)-weight edge \(B_j \to h_{u, t}\).
If the \(t\)-th sorted item at node \(u\) is a Type-A string \(A_i\), add a \(0\)-weight edge \(h_{u, t} \to A_i\).
Add the \(m\) explicit edges \(A_{x_k} \to B_{y_k}\) directly, and assign vertex weight \(|A_i|\) to each \(A_i\) (and \(0\) to all other nodes).

Exact Equivalence Proof: A Type-B node \(B_j\) at position \((u, t)\) can reach \(h_{u, t'}\) for all \(t' \ge t\) (which includes all \(A_i\) at node \(u\) with \(|A_i| \ge |B_j|\) because Type-B precedes Type-A on ties) as well as \(h_{u, k_u + 1}\), which flows down to \(h_{v, 0}\) and hence to all \(A_i\) in the strict subtree of \(u\). Conversely, no shorter string or non-descendant can be reached. Thus the reachability relation from \(B\) to \(A\) is \(100\%\) preserved while reducing the edge count from \(O(n_a n_b)\) to \(O(|S| + n_a + n_b + m)\)!
Topological Sort & Longest Path DP: Compute in-degrees of all \(V \le 2|S| + 2(n_a + n_b)\) vertices and run Kahn’s algorithm:

Initialize \(\text{dp}[v] = \text{weight}(v)\) for all \(v\).
Along each edge \(u \to v\), relax \(\text{dp}[v] \gets \max(\text{dp}[v], \text{dp}[u] + \text{weight}(v))\).
If the number of popped vertices is \(< V\), a cycle exists (and since every cycle in this bipartite-plus-DAG graph alternates through at least one \(A_i\) with \(|A_i| \ge 1\), it has positive weight), so output \(-1\); otherwise output \(\max_v \text{dp}[v]\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: String \(S[1 \dots |S|]\), Type-A intervals \([la_i, ra_i]_{i=1}^{n_a}\), Type-B intervals \([lb_j, rb_j]_{j=1}^{n_b}\), and \(m\) directed edges \((x_k, y_k)\) with \(1 \le la_i \le ra_i \le |S|\) and \(1 \le lb_j \le rb_j \le |S|\).
Postconditions (Output): Maximum total length of Type-A strings on a valid walk, or \(-1\) if a cycle exists.
Time & Space Complexity: \(O((|S| + n_a + n_b)\log |S| + m)\) time and \(O(|S| + n_a + n_b + m)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At each Suffix Tree node \(u\), sorting strings by \((\text{length}, \text{is\_Type\_A})\) ensures \(B_j \to h_{u, t}\) reaches \(A_i\) at \((u, t')\) if and only if \(t' \ge t \iff |A_i| \ge |B_j|\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When \(|A_i| = |B_j|\) at the same SAM node \(u\), placing Type-B strictly before Type-A in the comparator is mandatory so that \(B_j\) can transition to an identical-length \(A_i\); also clear all SAM transitions, binary-lifting tables, and adjacency lists up to the exact allocated node count between testcases.









Advanced 1 (#208) — \(a^{-1} + b\) problem (UOJ 182)

Source: UOJ #182 — a^-1 + b problem
Canonical ID: #208 (5B#B12)
Prerequisites: Möbius transformations (\(PGL_2\)), Logarithmic derivative \(P'(x)/P(x)\), Division-free Transposed Multipoint Evaluation (eval, §20.3).


Problem Statement
You are given an array of \(n\) elements \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{F}_p\) (\(p = 998244353\)) and a sequence of \(m\) global operations of two types:

1 x: Add \(x\) to every element (\(a_i \gets (a_i + x) \bmod p\) for all \(1 \le i \le n\)).
2: Replace every element by its modular inverse (\(a_i \gets a_i^{-1} \bmod p\) for all \(1 \le i \le n\); it is guaranteed that \(a_i \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) whenever Operation 2 is executed).

After each of the \(m\) operations, output the sum of all \(n\) elements \(\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right) \bmod 998244353\).


Constraints

\(1 \le n, m \le 6 \times 10^4\)
\(0 \le a_i, x < 998244353\)
Time limit: \(3.0\text{ s}\) (requires \(O((n + m) \log^2(n + m))\) time and \(O((n + m) \log(n + m))\) space).



Sample Trace (\(n = 2, a = [1, 2]\), Operations: 1 1, then 2, then 1 3)

Initial: \(a = [1, 2]\).
Step 1 (1 1): \(a_i \gets a_i + 1 \implies a = [2, 3]\), sum \(= 5\).
Step 2 (2): \(a_i \gets a_i^{-1} \implies a = [2^{-1}, 3^{-1}] = [\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}]\), sum \(= \frac{5}{6} \equiv 831870295 \pmod{998244353}\).
Step 3 (1 3): \(a_i \gets a_i + 3 \implies\) sum \(= \frac{5}{6} + 2 \cdot 3 = \frac{41}{6} \equiv 831870301 \pmod{998244353}\). In Möbius form \(a_i^{(k)} = \frac{\alpha_k a_i + \beta_k}{\gamma_k a_i + \delta_k}\): at Step 2, \(a_i^{(2)} = \frac{0 \cdot a_i + 1}{1 \cdot a_i + 1} = \frac{1}{a_i + 1}\), which evaluates \(\sum_{i=1}^2 \frac{1}{a_i + 1} = \frac{P'(1)}{P(1)}\) where \(P(x) = (x+1)(x+2) = x^2 + 3x + 2\) and \(P'(x) = 2x + 3\), giving \(\frac{P'(1)}{P(1)} = \frac{5}{6}\)!



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Both operations \(z \mapsto z + x\) and \(z \mapsto 1/z\) are linear fractional (Möbius) transformations on the projective line \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)\), represented by \(2 \times 2\) matrices: \[
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\] Thus after step \(k\) (\(1 \le k \le m\)), the \(i\)-th element is \(a_i^{(k)} = \frac{\alpha_k a_i + \beta_k}{\gamma_k a_i + \delta_k}\) for a known \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} \alpha_k & \beta_k \\ \gamma_k & \delta_k \end{bmatrix}\) independent of \(i\).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

When \(\gamma_k \equiv 0 \pmod p\), the transformation is purely linear: \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^{(k)} = \frac{\alpha_k}{\delta_k} \sum_{i=1}^n a_i + n \frac{\beta_k}{\delta_k}\). When \(\gamma_k \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\), perform polynomial division of \(\alpha_k a_i + \beta_k\) by \(\gamma_k a_i + \delta_k\) to isolate \(a_i\) in the denominator: \[
\frac{\alpha_k a_i + \beta_k}{\gamma_k a_i + \delta_k} = \frac{\alpha_k}{\gamma_k} + \frac{\beta_k \gamma_k - \alpha_k \delta_k}{\gamma_k^2 \left(a_i + \frac{\delta_k}{\gamma_k}\right)}.
\] Summing over \(i = 1, \dots, n\) shows that we only need to evaluate the rational sum \[
S(e_k) := \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{a_i + e_k} \quad \text{at the query point } e_k = \frac{\delta_k}{\gamma_k} \bmod p.
\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Define the degree-\(n\) polynomial \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (x + a_i)\). By logarithmic differentiation, \[
\frac{P'(x)}{P(x)} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{x + a_i} = S(x).
\] Build \(P(x)\) in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) via a bottom-up subproduct tree, compute its formal derivative \(P'(x)\) in \(O(n)\), and run two calls to Division-Free Transposed Multipoint Evaluation (eval, §20.3) to evaluate both \(P(e_k)\) and \(P'(e_k)\) at all \(m\) query points \(e_1, \dots, e_m\) simultaneously in \(O((n + m) \log^2(n + m))\) time!







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Matrix Composition of Möbius Transformations: Maintain the cumulative \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(M_k = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_k & \beta_k \\ \gamma_k & \delta_k \end{bmatrix}\) initialized to \(M_0 = I_2\):

On Operation 1 x: left-multiply \(M_k = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} M_{k-1}\).
On Operation 2: left-multiply \(M_k = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} M_{k-1}\). By associativity of Möbius transformations, \(a_i^{(k)} = \frac{\alpha_k a_i + \beta_k}{\gamma_k a_i + \delta_k} \pmod p\) for all \(1 \le i \le n\) and \(1 \le k \le m\).

Reduction to Logarithmic Derivative Evaluation:

Case 1 (\(\gamma_k \equiv 0 \pmod p\)): Since \(\det M_k = \pm 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\), we have \(\delta_k \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\), and \[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^{(k)} = \delta_k^{-1} \left( \alpha_k \sum_{i=1}^n a_i + n \beta_k \right) \bmod p,
\] which is answered in \(O(1)\) using the precomputed initial sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\).
Case 2 (\(\gamma_k \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\)): Let \(e_k = \delta_k \gamma_k^{-1} \bmod p\). Then \[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^{(k)} = n \alpha_k \gamma_k^{-1} + (\beta_k \gamma_k - \alpha_k \delta_k) \gamma_k^{-2} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{e_k + a_i} \bmod p.
\] Since the problem guarantees \(a_i^{(k')}\) is never \(0\) before an inversion step, \(\gamma_k a_i + \delta_k \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) for all \(1 \le i \le n\), which guarantees \(e_k + a_i \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\), i.e., \(P(e_k) = \prod_{i=1}^n (e_k + a_i) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).

Shared Subproduct Tree & Transposed eval for \(P(e_k)\) and \(P'(e_k)\):

Build the subproduct tree over leaves \(1 + a_i x\) (\(1 \le i \le n\)) in \(O(n \log^2 n)\) to obtain \(P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (x + a_i)\) of degree \(n\), and differentiate term-by-term to obtain \(P'(x)\) of degree \(n - 1\).
Build a second subproduct tree over the query points \(Q_{\text{leaf}(k)}(x) = 1 - e_k x\) for all steps \(k\) with \(\gamma_k \ne 0\) (\(K \le m\)).
Compute \(Q_{\text{root}}(x)^{-1} \bmod x^{n+1}\) once at the root, run eval_down on \(P(x)\) and eval_down on \(P'(x)\) sharing the exact same subproduct tree \(Q_u(x)\) and root inverse!
Batch-invert all \(P(e_k)\) in \(O(K + \log p)\) time and compute \(S(e_k) = P'(e_k) \cdot P(e_k)^{-1} \bmod p\).




Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Array \(a[1 \dots n]\) and \(m\) operations \((\text{type}_k, x_k)\) for \(1 \le k \le m\); prime modulus \(p = 998244353\), with \(e_k + a_i \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) whenever \(\gamma_k \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\).
Postconditions (Output): Array of \(m\) sums \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^{(k)} \bmod p\) for \(1 \le k \le m\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O((n + m)\log^2(n + m))\) time and \(O((n + m)\log(n + m))\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Because \(P(e_k) = \prod_{i=1}^n (e_k + a_i) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\), \(P'(e_k) / P(e_k) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^n (e_k + a_i)^{-1} \pmod p\) holds without poles at every query step \(k\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(\gamma_k \equiv 0 \pmod p\) (the Möbius transformation at step \(k\) is affine, \(c = 0\)), evaluating \(S(e_k)\) is unnecessary and \(e_k = \delta_k \gamma_k^{-1}\) is undefined; always branch on \(\gamma_k = 0\) and use the affine sum formula \(\alpha_k \sum_{i=1}^n a_i + n \beta_k \bmod p\) directly.









Advanced 2 (#202) — [KrOI2021] Feux Follets (Luogu P7440)

Source: Luogu P7440 — [KrOI2021] Feux Follets
Canonical ID: #202 (5B#B13)
Prerequisites: Tellegen’s Principle on Divide-and-Conquer trees (§20.1–§20.3), Transposed Middle Product (mulT), Stirling / Falling-Factorial / Binomial D&C.


Problem Statement & Constraints
You are given an integer \(N\), root parameters \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{N-1} \in \mathbb{F}_{998244353}\), and a linear-functional coefficient array \(c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{N-1} \in \mathbb{F}_{998244353}\). For each prefix polynomial \[
Q_j(x) = \prod_{i=0}^{j-1} (x + a_i) \qquad (0 \le j < N, \quad Q_0(x) = 1),
\] define the output sequence \(b_0, b_1, \dots, b_{N-1}\) by the linear functional pairing: \[
b_j = \sum_{k=0}^{j} c_k \, [x^k] Q_j(x) \pmod{998244353} \qquad \text{for all } j = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1,
\] and symmetrically for the leave-one-out subproduct basis \(P_{\text{leaf}(i)}(x) = 1 + a_i x\), define \(z_i = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k \, [x^k] \prod_{j \ne i}(1 + a_j x) \pmod{998244353}\). Compute all \(N\) dual linear forms modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 10^5\), \(0 \le a_i, c_i < 998244353\), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\), Modulo \(998244353\).



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Input: \(N = 3\), \(a = (1, 2, 3)\), \(c = (c_0, c_1, c_2) = (2, 3, 5)\).
Prefix Polynomials \(Q_j(x) = \prod_{i=0}^{j-1} (x + a_i)\):

\(Q_0(x) = 1\),
\(Q_1(x) = x + 1\),
\(Q_2(x) = (x + 1)(x + 2) = x^2 + 3x + 2\).

Direct Evaluation of \(b_j = \sum_{k=0}^{j} c_k [x^k] Q_j(x)\):

\(b_0 = c_0 [x^0] Q_0(x) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2\),
\(b_1 = c_0 [x^0] Q_1(x) + c_1 [x^1] Q_1(x) = 2(1) + 3(1) = 5\),
\(b_2 = c_0 [x^0] Q_2(x) + c_1 [x^1] Q_2(x) + c_2 [x^2] Q_2(x) = 2(2) + 3(3) + 5(1) = 18\).

Top-Down mulT Trace: Root covector \(C_{[0, 3)}(x) = 2 + 3x + 5x^2\).

Left child \([0, 2)\): \(\deg < 2 \implies C_{[0, 2)}(x) = C_{[0, 3)}(x) \bmod x^2 = 2 + 3x\).

Leaf \(j = 0\): \(C_{[0, 1)}(x) = 2 \implies b_0 = 2\).
Leaf \(j = 1\): \(C_{[1, 2)}(x) = \operatorname{mulT}_1(1 + x, 2 + 3x) = 2(1) + 3(1) = 5 \implies b_1 = 5\).

Right child \([2, 3)\): Multiply in transpose by \(Q_{[0, 2)}(x) = (x+1)(x+2) = 2 + 3x + x^2\): \[C_{[2, 3)}(x) = \operatorname{mulT}_1(2 + 3x + x^2, 2 + 3x + 5x^2) = 2(2) + 3(3) + 1(5) = 18 \implies b_2 = 18.\]

Leave-One-Out Subproduct Trace (\(c = [1, 2, 1]\)): Start at root with \(\hat{A}_{\text{root}} = [1, 2, 1]\), push to \(\{0, 1\}\) via \(\operatorname{mulT}([1, 2, 1], [1, 3], 2) = [7, 5]\) (yielding \(z_0 = 17, z_1 = 12\)) and to Leaf \(2\) via \(\operatorname{mulT}([1, 2, 1], [1, 3, 2], 1) = [9] = z_2\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Whenever a problem asks you to compute \(N\) outputs \(z_0, \dots, z_{N-1}\) where each \(z_i = \langle \mathbf{c}, \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{e}_i) \rangle\) is the inner product of a fixed coefficient mask \(\mathbf{c}\) with the polynomial generated by a unit impulse at leaf \(i\) of a Divide-and-Conquer tree, computing each \(z_i\) separately would take \(O(N^2)\). Instead, recognize that \(\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{L}^\top \mathbf{c}\) is the exact transpose of the bottom-up D&C polynomial combination \(\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{L} \mathbf{w}\)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Write the primal bottom-up D&C recurrence explicitly first! In the primal circuit, each leaf \(i\) starts with a small polynomial \(A_i(x)\) of degree \(O(1)\) determined by \(w_i\), and each internal node \(u\) covering \([l, r]\) combines its left and right children via polynomial multiplications: \[
A_u(x) = A_{\text{left}(u)}(x) \cdot P_{\text{right}(u)}(x) + A_{\text{right}(u)}(x) \cdot P_{\text{left}(u)}(x)
\] (or a triangular \(2 \times 2\) polynomial matrix transition \(V_u = M_{\text{right}} V_{\text{left}}\)). By Tellegen’s Principle (§20.1), reverse the tree traversal from bottom-up to top-down: initialize the root covector \(\hat{A}_{\text{root}} = \mathbf{c}\) of length \(N\), and at each node \(u\) covering \([l, r]\), push \(\hat{A}_u\) to the left and right children using mulT!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

What is the single most critical invariant for keeping the top-down transposed D&C in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) instead of \(O(N^2 \log N)\)? Degree-Window Truncation: In the primal circuit, the polynomial \(A_{\text{left}(u)}(x)\) at child node \(\text{left}(u)\) has degree strictly less than \(s_L = \text{mid} - l + 1\). Therefore, in the transposed top-down circuit, the covector \(\hat{A}_{\text{left}(u)} = \operatorname{mulT}\big(\hat{A}_u, P_{\text{right}(u)}, s_L\big)\) must be truncated to length \(s_L = \text{mid} - l + 1\)! Never pass a full length-\(N\) array down the tree.







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Primal Bottom-Up D&C Formulation: Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the segment tree over \([0, N-1]\). At each node \(u\) covering \([l, r]\) of length \(s_u = r - l + 1\), precompute the auxiliary subproduct polynomials \(P_u(x)\) (of degree \(s_u\), length \(s_u + 1\)) bottom-up via \(P_u(x) = P_{\text{left}(u)}(x) \cdot P_{\text{right}(u)}(x)\) in \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time. In the primal map \(\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})\), leaf \(i\) holds \(A_{\text{leaf}(i)}(x) = w_i\), and each internal node \(u\) computes \[
A_u(x) = \mathcal{M}_{P_{\text{right}(u)}}\big(A_{\text{left}(u)}(x)\big) + \mathcal{M}_{P_{\text{left}(u)}}\big(A_{\text{right}(u)}(x)\big)
\] of degree \(< s_u\). If the root also applies a global polynomial transform (such as a Taylor shift, Stirling transform, or multiplication by \(G(x) \bmod x^N\)), that is a single root operator \(\mathcal{R}\) applied after \(A_{\text{root}}(x)\) is formed: \(\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{R}\big(A_{\text{root}}\big)\).
Transposing the Circuit Top-Down (\(\mathcal{L}^\top \mathcal{R}^\top \mathbf{c}\)): Given the target linear functional covector \(\mathbf{c} = (c_0, \dots, c_{N-1})^\top\):

Step \(1^\top\) (Transpose Root Operator): Compute \(\hat{A}_{\text{root}} = \mathcal{R}^\top(\mathbf{c})\) of length \(N\) in \(O(N \log N)\) time (using a single mulT).
Step \(2^\top\) (Top-Down Tree Push via mulT): At every internal node \(u\) covering \([l, r]\) with midpoint \(m = \lfloor(l+r)/2\rfloor\), the input covector \(\hat{A}_u\) has length \(s_u = r - l + 1\). Since \(\deg P_{\text{right}(u)} = r - m\) (length \(r - m + 1\)) and \(\deg A_{\text{left}(u)} < m - l + 1\), the transpose of \(\mathcal{M}_{P_{\text{right}(u)}}\) is \[
\hat{A}_{\text{left}(u)} = \operatorname{mulT}\!\big(\hat{A}_u,\; P_{\text{right}(u)},\; m - l + 1\big),
\] and symmetrically, \[
\hat{A}_{\text{right}(u)} = \operatorname{mulT}\!\big(\hat{A}_u,\; P_{\text{left}(u)},\; r - m\big).
\]
Step \(3^\top\) (Leaf Extraction): At each leaf \(l = r = i\), \(\hat{A}_{\text{leaf}(i)}\) has length \(1\), and its sole entry \(\hat{A}_{\text{leaf}(i)}[0]\) equals \(z_i = (\mathcal{L}^\top \mathcal{R}^\top \mathbf{c})_i\).

Complexity Proof: At depth \(d\) of the segment tree, the lengths \(s_u = r - l + 1\) of all disjoint nodes \(u\) sum to \(N\). Each node \(u\) performs two mulT calls of FFT size \(< 2 s_u\), costing \(O(s_u \log s_u)\). Summing over all \(O(\log N)\) levels yields \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N \log N)\) space.



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integer \(N \le 10^5\), covector array \(c[0 \dots N-1]\), and leaf transition polynomials \(P_{\text{leaf}(i)}(x)\) for \(0 \le i < N\); prime modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Postconditions (Output): Array \(z[0 \dots N-1]\) where \(z[i] = \langle \mathbf{c}, \mathcal{R}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{e}_i) \rangle \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N \log^2 N)\) time and \(O(N \log N)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At every tree node \(u\) covering \([l, r]\), the dual covector \(\hat{A}_u\) is truncated to exact length \(r - l + 1\) and satisfies \(\langle \hat{A}_u, A_u \rangle = \langle \hat{A}_{\text{left}(u)}, A_{\text{left}(u)} \rangle + \langle \hat{A}_{\text{right}(u)}, A_{\text{right}(u)} \rangle\) for all primal polynomials \(A_{\text{left}(u)}, A_{\text{right}(u)}\) with \(\deg A_{\text{left}} \le m - l\) and \(\deg A_{\text{right}} \le r - m - 1\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Failing to truncate the child covector \(\hat{A}_{\text{left}(u)}\) to length \(m - l + 1\) (and \(\hat{A}_{\text{right}(u)}\) to length \(r - m\)) after each mulT call causes the covector length to stay \(\Omega(N)\) at all levels, blowing up the runtime to \(O(N^2 \log N)\).









Mastery 1 (#181) — N-Step Shift (Luogu P5668)

Source: Luogu P5668 — N-Step Shift
Canonical ID: #181 (5B#D8)
Prerequisites: Shift of Sampling Points (连续点值平移, §20.4 Part B), P-recursive polynomial doubling (§20.4 Part C), Multipoint Evaluation (§20.3).


Problem Statement & Constraints
Let \(F(x)\) be a polynomial of degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\), specified by its \(d + 1\) point evaluations \(F(0), F(1), \dots, F(d)\) on consecutive integers. Given a step count \(K = 2^t\) (or general integer \(K \ge 1\)) and query shift \(c \in \mathbb{F}_{998244353}\), define the \(K\)-step rising product polynomial of degree \(D = K d\): \[
P_K(x) = \prod_{j=0}^{K-1} F(x + j).
\] Using Shift of Sampling Points (§20.4) to maintain all intermediate polynomials purely by their point values on consecutive integers \(\{0, 1, \dots, k d\}\) without converting back to monomial coefficients, compute the shifted point-value window \(P_K(c), P_K(c + 1), \dots, P_K(c + K d)\) modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le d \cdot K \le 10^5\), \(0 \le c < 998244353\), Time Limit \(2.0\text{ s}\), Modulo \(998244353\).



Concrete Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))

Input: Degree \(d = 1\) with \(F(0) = 1, F(1) = 3\) (so \(F(x) = 2x + 1\)), step count \(K = 2\), query shift \(c = 2\).
Step 1 (Degree Extension \(k = 1 \to 2\)):

Initially we have \(P_1(x) = F(x)\) of degree \(1\) at \(x \in \{0, 1\}\): \(P_1(0) = 1, P_1(1) = 3\).
To multiply \(P_1(x)\) and \(P_1(x + 1)\) (whose product \(P_2(x)\) has degree \(2\)), first extend \(P_1\) from \(\{0, 1\}\) to \(\{2\}\) via shift_of_sampling_points([1, 3], c = 2, m = 1), giving \(P_1(2) = 5\), so \(P_1(0..2) = [1, 3, 5]\).
Next, evaluate \(P_1(x + 1)\) on \(x \in \{0, 1, 2\}\) (via shift_of_sampling_points([1, 3], c = 1, m = 3) or array shift since \(1 \in \mathbb{Z}\)), giving \(P_1(1..3) = [3, 5, 7]\).
Multiply pointwise on \(x \in \{0, 1, 2\}\): \[P_2(0) = 1 \cdot 3 = 3, \quad P_2(1) = 3 \cdot 5 = 15, \quad P_2(2) = 5 \cdot 7 = 35.\] (Check: \(P_2(x) = (2x + 1)(2x + 3) = 4x^2 + 8x + 3\) gives \(3, 15, 35\) at \(x = 0, 1, 2\).)

Step 2 (Query Shift \(c = 2\)):

Call shift_of_sampling_points([3, 15, 35], c = 2, m = 3) to obtain \(P_2(2..4) = [35, 63, 99]\).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Unrolling \(N\) steps of a polynomial recurrence \(\mathbf{v}_{k} = M(k) \mathbf{v}_{k-1}\) where each entry of the \(r \times r\) transition matrix \(M(x)\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(\le \delta\) requires computing the rising matrix product \(\mathcal{M}_N(x) = M(x + N) M(x + N - 1) \cdots M(x + 1)\).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Each entry of the \(d\)-step product matrix \(\mathcal{M}_d(x) = M(x + d) \cdots M(x + 1)\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree at most \(D = \delta d\). Therefore, \(\mathcal{M}_d(x)\) is completely determined by its values on the \(D + 1\) consecutive grid points \(t = 0, 1, \dots, D\) (where \(x = v \cdot t\) for giant-step stride \(v = \lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\)). To double the step count from \(d\) to \(2d\), use the associativity identity \[
\mathcal{M}_{2d}(v t) = \mathcal{M}_d(v t + d) \cdot \mathcal{M}_d(v t).
\]



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

At step \(d\) (with current polynomial degree \(D = \delta d\)), each of the \(r^2\) matrix entries is stored as an array of \(D + 1\) values at \(t = 0, 1, \dots, D\).

Apply shift_of_sampling_points with offset \(c_1 = D + 1\) and length \(m_1 = D\) to extend each entry to \(t = 0, 1, \dots, 2D\).
Apply shift_of_sampling_points with offset \(c_2 = d \cdot v^{-1} \bmod p\) and length \(m_2 = 2D + 1\) to obtain \(\mathcal{M}_d(v t + d)\) for \(t = 0, 1, \dots, 2D\).
Multiply the \(r \times r\) matrices \(\mathcal{M}_d(v t + d) \cdot \mathcal{M}_d(v t)\) pointwise at each \(t \in [0, 2D]\)!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Polynomial Degree Bound of the \(d\)-Step Transfer Matrix: Let \(M(x) \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]^{r \times r}\) have polynomial entries of degree \(\le \delta\). For any integer \(d \ge 1\), the \(d\)-step transfer matrix \[
\mathcal{M}_d(x) := M(x + d) M(x + d - 1) \cdots M(x + 1)
\] has polynomial entries of degree at most \(D = \delta d\). Fix a giant-step stride \(v \ge 1\) (\(\gcd(v, p) = 1\)) and define the rescaled matrix polynomial \(\mathcal{H}_d(t) := \mathcal{M}_d(v t)\), whose entries also have degree \(\le D = \delta d\) in \(t\).
Point-Value Doubling Recurrence (\(d \to 2d\) and \(2d \to 2d + 1\)): Suppose we know the \(r \times r\) matrices \(\mathcal{H}_d(0), \mathcal{H}_d(1), \dots, \mathcal{H}_d(D)\). Since \(\deg \mathcal{H}_{2d} \le 2D\), we need \(\mathcal{H}_{2d}(t)\) for \(t = 0, 1, \dots, 2D\). By definition, \[
\mathcal{H}_{2d}(t) = \mathcal{M}_{2d}(v t) = \mathcal{M}_d(v t + d) \cdot \mathcal{M}_d(v t) = \mathcal{H}_d\!\left(t + d v^{-1}\right) \cdot \mathcal{H}_d(t).
\]

First, for each \((i, j) \in [1, r]^2\), call shift_of_sampling_points on the degree-\(D\) sequence \(\mathcal{H}_d(0 \dots D)_{i,j}\) with shift \(c_1 = D + 1\) and count \(m_1 = D\) to obtain \(\mathcal{H}_d(D + 1 \dots 2D)_{i,j}\).
Second, call shift_of_sampling_points on \(\mathcal{H}_d(0 \dots D)_{i,j}\) with shift \(c_2 = d v^{-1} \bmod p\) and count \(m_2 = 2D + 1\) to obtain \(\mathcal{H}_d(t + d v^{-1})_{i,j}\) for \(0 \le t \le 2D\).
Note that the Lagrange denominator weights \((-1)^{D-k}/(k!(D-k)!)\) and the shifted inverse kernel \(B[t] = (c - D + t)^{-1}\) depend only on \(D\) and \(c\), not on \((i, j)\)! Thus the forward NTT of \(B\) is computed once per shift and shared across all \(r^2\) matrix entries.
Finally, for each \(t \in [0, 2D]\), perform one \(r \times r\) matrix multiplication \(\mathcal{H}_{2d}(t) = \mathcal{H}_d(t + d v^{-1}) \cdot \mathcal{H}_d(t)\) in \(O(r^3)\) time.
If advancing \(d \to d + 1\), extend the grid by \(\delta\) more points via shift_of_sampling_points and left-multiply each \(\mathcal{H}_d(t)\) by \(M(v t + d + 1)\).

Giant-Step Contraction: Once \(d = v = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor\), multiply \(\mathcal{H}_v(v - 1) \cdots \mathcal{H}_v(1) \mathcal{H}_v(0) \mathbf{v}_0\) and apply the remaining \(N - v^2 < 2v + 1\) single steps \(M(k)\) directly.



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Step count \(N\), matrix dimension \(r\), degree bound \(\delta\), polynomial matrix \(M(x) \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]^{r \times r}\), and initial vector \(\mathbf{v}_0 \in \mathbb{F}_p^r\); prime modulus \(p = 998244353 > \delta \sqrt{N}\).
Postconditions (Output): Final state vector \(\mathbf{v}_N = M(N) M(N-1) \cdots M(1) \mathbf{v}_0 \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O\big(r^2 \delta \sqrt{N} \log(\delta N) + r^3 \delta \sqrt{N}\big)\) time and \(O(r^2 \delta \sqrt{N})\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At the end of doubling step \(d\), the stored table \(\mathcal{H}_d[0 \dots \delta d]\) equals the exact point evaluations \(\mathcal{M}_d(v t) \bmod p\) of the degree-\(\delta d\) matrix polynomial \(\prod_{j=1}^d M(v t + j)\) at \(t = 0, 1, \dots, \delta d\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Recomputing the Lagrange denominator weights and the forward NTT of the shifted inverse kernel \(B[t] = (c - D + t)^{-1}\) separately for each of the \(r^2\) matrix entries adds a factor of \(r^2\) to the kernel setup; compute the kernel’s DFT once per shift and reuse it across all \(r^2\) entries, and always guard against \(c + j \equiv k \pmod p\) overlap singularities in shift_of_sampling_points.









Mastery 2 (#217) — 快速阶乘算法 / Fast Factorial (LOJ 161 / Luogu P5282)

Source: LibreOJ #161 (快速阶乘算法) / Luogu P5282 (快速阶乘算法)
Canonical ID: #217 (5B#D11)
Prerequisites: Shift of Sampling Points (连续点值平移, §20.4 Part B), Block Polynomial Doubling (§20.4 Part C), Overlap Singularity Handling.


Problem Statement
Given positive integers \(N\) and a prime \(P\) (for standard NTT mode \(P = 998244353\), or arbitrary prime \(P \le 2^{31} - 1\) using 3-prime NTT / MTT), compute \(N! \bmod P\) in \(O(\sqrt{P} \log P)\) time.


Constraints

\(1 \le N < P \le 2^{31} - 1\) (with up to \(T \le 5\) testcases)
Time limit: \(1.0\text{ s}\)–\(2.0\text{ s}\) (requires \(O(\sqrt{N} \log N)\) time and \(O(\sqrt{N})\) space).



Sample Trace (\(N = 10, P = 998244353\))
With \(N = 10\), \(v = \lfloor\sqrt{10}\rfloor = 3\):

Start \(d = 1\): \(H_1(t) = G_1(3t) = 3t + 1\) for \(t \in \{0, 1\}\), so \(H_1 = [G_1(0), G_1(3)] = [1, 4]\).
Double \(d = 1 \to 2\):

Shift 1 (\(c_1 = 2, m_1 = 1\)): \(H_1(2) = G_1(6) = 7\), extending \(H_1(0 \dots 2) = [1, 4, 7]\).
Shift 2 (\(c_2 = 1 \cdot 3^{-1} \bmod P\), \(m_2 = 3\)): evaluates \(G_1(3t + 1) = 3t + 2\) at \(t = 0, 1, 2\), yielding \([2, 5, 8]\).
Pointwise product: \(H_2(0 \dots 2) = [1 \cdot 2,\; 4 \cdot 5,\; 7 \cdot 8] = [2, 20, 56]\).

Increment \(d = 2 \to 3\):

Shift \(H_2(0 \dots 2)\) to \(t = 3\): \(H_2(3) = G_2(9) = 10 \cdot 11 = 110\), so \(H_2(0 \dots 3) = [2, 20, 56, 110]\).
Multiply by \((3t + 3)\) for \(t = 0, 1, 2, 3\): \(H_3(0 \dots 3) = [2 \cdot 3,\; 20 \cdot 6,\; 56 \cdot 9,\; 110 \cdot 12] = [6, 120, 504, 1320]\).

Giant steps (\(t = 0, 1, 2\)): \(H_3(0) \cdot H_3(1) \cdot H_3(2) = 6 \cdot 120 \cdot 504 = 362880 = 9!\).
Tail (\(j = 10\)): \(362880 \times 10 = 3628800 = 10!\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

When \(N \ge P\), \(N! \equiv 0 \pmod P\) immediately. When \(N > (P - 1)/2\), Wilson’s Theorem \((P - 1)! \equiv -1 \pmod P\) allows us to reduce \(N!\) to the inverse of \((P - 1 - N)!\): \[
N! \equiv \frac{(-1)^{P - N}}{(P - 1 - N)!} \pmod P,
\] which cuts \(N\) to at most \(P / 2\) before we even start! Then for \(v = \lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\), we need \(G_v(k v) = \prod_{j=1}^v (k v + j) \bmod P\) for \(0 \le k < v\).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Define \(H_d(t) = G_d(v t) = \prod_{j=1}^d (v t + j)\), a polynomial in \(t\) of degree \(d\). At each binary step of \(v\), we maintain the array of \(d + 1\) point values \(H_d(0), H_d(1), \dots, H_d(d)\). To go from \(d\) to \(2d\) (or \(2d + 1\) if the current bit of \(v\) is \(1\), let \(\text{bit} \in \{0, 1\}\)):

Shift \(H_d(0 \dots d)\) to \(c_1 = d + 1\) with length \(m_1 = d + \text{bit}\) to obtain \(H_d(0 \dots 2d + \text{bit})\).
Shift \(H_d(0 \dots d)\) to \(c_2 = d \cdot v^{-1} \bmod P\) with length \(m_2 = 2d + 1 + \text{bit}\) to obtain \(H_d(t + d v^{-1})\) for \(0 \le t \le 2d + \text{bit}\).
Multiply pointwise: \(H_{2d}(t) = H_d(t) \cdot H_d(t + d v^{-1}) \bmod P\).
If \(\text{bit} = 1\), multiply each \(H_{2d}(t)\) by \((v t + 2d + 1) \bmod P\) for \(0 \le t \le 2d + 1\).




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Why is Shift 2 (\(c_2 = d \cdot v^{-1} \bmod P\)) guaranteed not to hit the Overlap Singularity Trap when \(2v^2 < P\)? Because \(c_2 + t \equiv s \pmod P\) for \(0 \le t \le 2d + 1\) and \(0 \le s \le d\) would imply \(d + v(t - s) \equiv 0 \pmod P\), where \(0 < |d + v(t - s)| \le v + v(2v + 1) = 2v^2 + 2v < P\) for \(N \le P/2\)! Still, wrapping shift_of_sampling_points with the general overlap-splitting guard (§20.4 Part B) makes it \(100\%\) bulletproof for all \(N, P\).







NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Wilson’s Theorem Reflection for \(N > P / 2\): If \(N \ge P\), return \(0\). If \(N > (P - 1) / 2\), since \((P - 1)! \equiv -1 \pmod P\) and \(\prod_{k = N + 1}^{P - 1} k \equiv (-1)^{P - 1 - N} (P - 1 - N)! \pmod P\), we have \[
N! \equiv (-1)^{P - N} \big((P - 1 - N)!\big)^{-1} \pmod P.
\] Thus we may assume \(N \le (P - 1) / 2\). If \(N\) is small (\(N \le 256\)), compute \(N! \bmod P\) directly by a simple loop.
Binary Doubling on Sampling Points \(H_d(0 \dots d)\): Set \(v = \lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\). Start at the highest set bit of \(v\) with \(d = 1\) and \(H_1 = [1,\; v + 1]\). For each subsequent bit \(\text{bit} \in \{0, 1\}\) of \(v\) from top to bottom:

Let \(D_{\text{next}} = 2d + \text{bit}\).
Call 1: Extend \(H_d[0 \dots d]\) by calling shift_of_sampling_points(H_d, d + 1, d + bit) to get \(H_d[d + 1 \dots D_{\text{next}}]\), and concatenate to form \(L[0 \dots D_{\text{next}}]\).
Call 2: Call shift_of_sampling_points(H_d, d * inv(v) % P, D_next + 1) to get \(R[0 \dots D_{\text{next}}]\) where \(R[t] = G_d(v t + d) \bmod P\).
Combine: Set \(H_{\text{next}}[t] = L[t] \cdot R[t] \bmod P\) for \(0 \le t \le D_{\text{next}}\).
Odd Increment (\(\text{bit} = 1\)): For \(0 \le t \le D_{\text{next}}\), multiply \(H_{\text{next}}[t]\) by \((v t + 2d + 1) \bmod P\).
Update \(d \gets D_{\text{next}}\) and \(H_d \gets H_{\text{next}}\).

Final Assembly: Once \(d = v\), multiply the first \(v\) block values \(\text{ans} = \prod_{t=0}^{v-1} H_v[t] \bmod P = (v^2)! \bmod P\), and multiply by the remaining tail \(\prod_{k = v^2 + 1}^N k \bmod P\). (Arbitrary Prime \(P \le 2^{31} - 1\)): Inside shift_of_sampling_points, perform the single polynomial convolution of length \(\le 4v \le 2 \times 10^5\) using a 3-prime NTT (e.g., primes \(998244353, 1004535809, 469762049\) with Chinese Remainder Theorem reconstruction) so that all arithmetic modulo \(P\) remains \(100\%\) exact!



Algorithm Contract

Input & Preconditions: Integer \(N \ge 0\) and prime modulus \(P \ge 2\) (for arbitrary \(P \le 2^{31} - 1\), use 3-prime NTT inside shift_of_sampling_points).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(N! \bmod P \in [0, P - 1]\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(\sqrt{\min(N, P - N)} \log P)\) time and \(O(\sqrt{\min(N, P - N)})\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing a prefix of the binary representation of \(v\) with value \(d\), the array \(H_d[0 \dots d]\) has length \(d + 1\) and satisfies \(H_d[t] \equiv \prod_{j=1}^d (v t + j) \pmod P\) for all \(0 \le t \le d\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: If \(N \ge P\), return \(0\) immediately; if \(N > (P - 1)/2\), apply Wilson’s reflection \(N! \equiv (-1)^{P - N} ((P - 1 - N)!)^{-1} \pmod P\) first so that \(2 v^2 + 2v < P\) and shift_of_sampling_points never divides by \(0 \pmod P\) in the Lagrange kernel.

Pre-Submission Checklist for Chapter 20 Engines

mulT Input Truncation: Did you truncate or bound the first argument \(C\) of \(\operatorname{mulT}(C, B, n)\) to length at most \(n + m - 1\) before zero-padding to the FFT length \(L \ge n + m - 1\)? (Leaving nonzero elements at indices \(\ge n + m - 1\) causes cyclic wrap-around to spill past index \(m - 2\) and corrupt the output window \([m-1, n+m-2]\).)
Top-Down eval Degree Trimming: At every node \(u\) of the top-down multipoint evaluation or transposed D&C tree covering \([l, r]\), did you pass the exact target length \(s = r - l + 1\) to mulT?
Shift of Sampling Points Overlap Guard: Before inverting \(c - d + t \pmod p\) in shift_of_sampling_points, did you reduce \(c \bmod p\) and split out any index \(k \in [0, m-1]\) where \((c + k) \bmod p \in [0, d]\) by copying \(F((c+k) \bmod p)\) directly?
Characteristic Check (\(p > d\)): Did you verify that the prime modulus \(p\) satisfies \(p > d\) so that the Lagrange denominator \(i! (d - i)! \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\) is invertible?




Quarantined Footnotes & Historical Notes

Tellegen’s Theorem (1952) & Algebraic Complexity (Baur–Strassen / Kaltofen / Bostan–Lecerf–Schost): Originally discovered by Bernard Tellegen in electrical network theory (conservation of virtual power across topologically dual circuits), the transposition principle was brought into algebraic complexity by Fiduccia, Bordewich, Kaltofen, and systematized for polynomial algorithms (including the middle product mulT and division-free multipoint evaluation) by Bostan, Lecerf, and Schost (2003), “Tellegen’s Principle into Practice”.
Curriculum Reference Registry & Verification Benchmarks (R-26, R-27, R-30): The transposed middle-product and division-free multipoint evaluation algorithms in this chapter correspond to R-26 (Bostan, Lecerf, and Schost (2003) — Tellegen’s Principle into Practice) and R-27 (CP-Algorithms — Multipoint Evaluation and Interpolation), verified against the Library Checker benchmark R-30 (multipoint_evaluation) and shift_of_sampling_points (shift_of_sampling_points_of_polynomial).

Learning Objectives:

Distinguish \(O(N^2)\) Naive Subtree Convolution from \(\Theta(N^2 \log N)\) Unbalanced NTT Merging: Prove the \(\binom{N}{2}\) Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) pair bound for naive subtree knapsack (\(O(NK)\)), and demonstrate why replacing inner loops with NTT still degrades to \(\Theta(N^2 \log N)\) on path and caterpillar trees unless the tree topology is re-balanced.

Eliminate Dynamic DP Division-by-Zero via Zero-Divisor Pairs (Failure Mode #10): Maintain light-child point-value products under dynamic vertex updates in \(\mathbb{F}_p\) by lifting each frequency into the multiplicative group of pairs \((a, c) \equiv a \cdot 0^c\) (\(a \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times, c \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\)), preventing permanent state corruption when an intermediate factor hits \(0 \pmod p\).

22.1 Subtree Size Convolution Bounds (\(O(N^2)\)) vs. Arbitrary-Degree Polynomial Merging (\(O(N \log^2 N)\))

The Concrete Combinatorial Model
Suppose we are given a rooted tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(N = |V|\) vertices rooted at \(r = 1\). For each vertex \(u \in V\), let \(T_u\) denote the subtree rooted at \(u\), and let \(\text{sz}[u] = |T_u|\) denote its vertex count. In a wide class of tree counting problems—such as counting independent sets of size \(k\), \(k\)-matchings, connected induced subgraphs, or antichains—the dynamic programming state at vertex \(u\) is naturally packaged as a polynomial (or truncated formal power series) in \(K[x]\) whose degree is bounded by \(\text{sz}[u]\):
\[F_u(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\text{sz}[u]} f_{u,k} x^k,\]
where \(f_{u,k} = [x^k] F_u(x)\) counts the number of valid configurations inside \(T_u\) of size (or weight) \(k\). When \(u\) merges the independent choices from its children \(v_1, v_2, \dots, v_d \in \text{child}(u)\), the transition multiplies their generating functions:
\[F_u(x) \leftarrow \text{Combine}\!\left(x, \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} F_v(x)\right).\]
Before reaching for Fast Fourier Transform / Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) engines, every competitive programmer must first understand the exact boundary between the classical \(O(N^2)\) naive subtree knapsack and the \(O(N \log^2 N)\) Heavy-Light polynomial architecture.



Theorem 22.1 (The \(\binom{N}{2}\) Subtree Knapsack Bound and \(O(NK)\) Truncation)
Suppose we compute the product \(\prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} F_v(x)\) at every vertex \(u \in T\) using the naive quadratic polynomial multiplication loop, maintaining an accumulator polynomial \(A_u(x)\) whose current degree is \(\text{cur\_sz}\) and multiplying it by the next child’s polynomial \(F_v(x)\) of degree \(\text{sz}[v]\):
// Naive subtree knapsack accumulator merge at vertex u (<= 15 lines)
vector<mint> A = {1}; // cur_sz = 0 initially (counts vertex u alone)
int cur_sz = 1;
for (int v : child[u]) {
    vector<mint> next_A(min(K, cur_sz + sz[v]) + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i <= min(K, cur_sz); ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j <= min(K, sz[v]) && i + j <= K; ++j)
            next_A[i + j] += A[i] * F[v][j];
    A = move(next_A);
    cur_sz += sz[v];
}

Untruncated Bound (\(K = N\)): The total number of inner-loop scalar multiplications A[i] * F[v][j] across the entire tree \(T\) is exactly \(\binom{N}{2} = \frac{N(N-1)}{2} = \Theta(N^2)\) (plus lower-order boundary terms for \(i=0\) or \(j=0\)).
Capacity-Truncated Bound (\(K \le N\)): If every polynomial is truncated modulo \(x^{K+1}\) (keeping only degrees \(0 \le k \le K\)), the total number of inner-loop operations across the entire tree is \(O(NK)\).


Proof by Bijective Double Counting
Consider the untruncated case \(K = N\). When vertex \(u\) merges a child \(v \in \text{child}(u)\) into its running accumulator \(A_u(x)\), the degree of \(A_u(x)\) equals the total number of vertices in \(T_u\) already processed (namely \(u\) itself plus all previously merged subtrees \(T_{v'}\) for \(v'\) preceding \(v\) in \(\text{child}(u)\)), while the degree of \(F_v(x)\) equals \(\text{sz}[v] = |T_v|\).
Therefore, the number of inner-loop iterations \((i, j)\) with \(1 \le i \le \text{cur\_sz}\) and \(1 \le j \le \text{sz}[v]\) equals:
\[\text{cur\_sz} \times \text{sz}[v] = \left|\{w_1 \in T_u \text{ already processed}\}\right| \times \left|\{w_2 \in T_v\}\right|.\]
Each such pair \((w_1, w_2)\) of vertices in \(T\) has \(\operatorname{LCA}(w_1, w_2) = u\), and is counted exactly once throughout the entire DFS—specifically, at the unique moment when the child subtree \(T_v\) containing \(w_2\) is merged into the accumulator at \(u = \operatorname{LCA}(w_1, w_2)\) that already contains \(w_1\). Summing over all \(u \in V\) and all children \(v \in \text{child}(u)\) bijectively partitions the set of all unordered vertex pairs \(\{w_1, w_2\} \subseteq V\):
\[\sum_{u \in V} \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \text{cur\_sz}_{u,v} \cdot \text{sz}[v] = \binom{N}{2} = \frac{N(N-1)}{2}.\]
For the capacity-truncated case \(K \le N\), the merge between an accumulator of size \(s_1 = \text{cur\_sz}\) and a child of size \(s_2 = \text{sz}[v]\) performs \(\min(s_1, K) \cdot \min(s_2, K)\) operations. We split all merges across the tree into three disjoint cases:

Case 1 (\(s_1 \ge K\) and \(s_2 \ge K\)): Both merged components contain at least \(K\) vertices. Treating components of size \(\ge K\) as macro-nodes in a binary merge tree, there are at most \(\lfloor N/K \rfloor\) disjoint subtrees of size \(\ge K\), so at most \(\lfloor N/K \rfloor - 1\) merges can occur between two components both of size \(\ge K\). Each such merge costs \(K^2\), contributing at most \((N/K) \cdot K^2 = NK\).
Case 2 (\(s_1 < K\) and \(s_2 < K\)): The merge cost is \(s_1 \cdot s_2\), which equals the number of vertex pairs \((w_1, w_2)\) between the two components whose merged component still has size \(< 2K\). Each vertex can participate in at most \(2K\) such pairs before its component size exceeds \(2K\), contributing at most \(2NK\) overall.
Case 3 (One of \(s_1, s_2\) is \(\ge K\) and the other is \(< K\)): Without loss of generality \(s_1 \ge K\) and \(s_2 < K\). The merge cost is \(K \cdot s_2\). Every vertex in the smaller component \(T_v\) (of size \(s_2 < K\)) is absorbed into a component of size \(\ge K\); once inside a component of size \(\ge K\), that vertex can never belong to the smaller side (\(< K\)) of a Case 3 merge again! Thus each vertex \(w \in V\) is charged at most \(K\) once in its lifetime, contributing at most \(NK\).

Summing all three cases proves that capacity-\(K\) tree knapsack runs in \(O(NK)\) time and \(O(NK)\) space without any FFT/NTT machinery. \(\blacksquare\)






ImportantAlgorithm Contract: Truncated Subtree Knapsack Convolution (\(O(NK)\) / \(O(N^2)\))




Input & Preconditions: A rooted tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(N\) vertices, integer capacity \(K \in [1, N]\), and at each vertex \(u\) a base polynomial \(F_u^{(0)}(x)\) of degree \(\le 1\) (initializing \(\text{sz}[u] = 1\)).
Postconditions (Output): Computes for every vertex \(u \in V\) the truncated subtree polynomial \(F_u(x) \bmod x^{\min(\text{sz}[u], K) + 1}\) of degree \(\le \min(\text{sz}[u], K)\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(NK)\) time (\(O(N^2)\) when \(K = N\)) and \(O(NK)\) space across the entire tree without FFT/NTT.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Before merging child \(v\) into \(u\), \(\text{sz}[u]\) equals the exact number of vertices merged into \(u\)’s prefix of children so far, and the loop bounds \(i \in [0, \min(\text{sz}[u], K)]\), \(j \in [0, \min(\text{sz}[v], K - i)]\) evaluate the exact truncated product \(F_u^{\text{old}}(x) F_v(x) \bmod x^{\min(\text{sz}[u] + \text{sz}[v], K) + 1}\) before updating \(\text{sz}[u] \gets \text{sz}[u] + \text{sz}[v]\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Updating \(\text{sz}[u] \gets \text{sz}[u] + \text{sz}[v]\) before the nested loop or iterating \(i\) up to \(K\) without clamping to \(\text{sz}[u]\) destroys the LCA pair-counting bound and degrades the runtime from \(O(NK)\) to \(\Theta(N K^2)\) (or \(\Theta(N^3)\) when \(K = N\)).







Why Naive NTT Tree DP Still Degrades to \(\Theta(N^2 \log N)\)
When \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) and we need the entire polynomial \(F_{\text{root}}(x)\) up to degree \(N\) (i.e., \(K = N\)), \(O(N^2)\) is far too slow. A natural first instinct is to replace the nested for loop in the DP with an \(O((d_1 + d_2) \log(d_1 + d_2))\) NTT multiplication.
Why does this fail? Unlike the naive loop—where multiplying a polynomial of degree \(N-1\) by a polynomial of degree \(1\) takes \(O(N \cdot 1) = O(N)\) time—an NTT convolution of degree \(d_1\) and degree \(d_2\) must transform both operands to length \(2^{\lceil \log_2(d_1 + d_2 + 1) \rceil}\), taking \(\Theta((d_1 + d_2) \log(d_1 + d_2))\) time even when \(\min(d_1, d_2) = 1\)!
We encounter two distinct geometric bottlenecks on trees:

Horizontal Bottleneck (High-Degree Star Vertex): If vertex \(u\) has \(d\) leaf children \(v_1, \dots, v_d\) each of degree \(1\), merging them sequentially one by one via NTT costs \(\sum_{i=1}^d i \log i = \Theta(d^2 \log d)\).

Fix: As learned in Chapter 9, merging the children of \(u\) in a Min-Heap (Huffman) priority queue ordered by polynomial degree reduces the horizontal merge at \(u\) to \(O(D_u \log^2 D_u)\) where \(D_u = \sum_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \text{sz}[v]\).

Vertical Bottleneck (Long Path / Caterpillar Spine): Suppose \(T\) is a simple path \(1 - 2 - 3 - \dots - N\) (or a caterpillar where every spine vertex \(u_i\) has one leaf child and one spine child \(u_{i+1}\)). At vertex \(u_i\), \(\text{sz}[u_{i+1}] = N - i\). Even if there is only one child (or one leaf child of degree \(1\)), computing \(F_{u_i}(x)\) from \(F_{u_{i+1}}(x)\) via a polynomial multiplication of size \(N - i\) at every step \(i = N-1, N-2, \dots, 1\) costs: \[\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} \Theta((N - i) \log(N - i)) = \Theta(N^2 \log N).\]

Notice the irony: on a path of length \(N\), naive quadratic multiplication takes \(O(N^2)\) (or \(O(N)\) if each step only shifts/adds a constant), whereas sequential bottom-up NTT takes \(\Theta(N^2 \log N)\)!



Concrete Hand-Checkable Trace (\(N = 4\) Tree Independent Set Polynomials)
Before formalizing the Heavy-Light architecture, let us trace the Tree Independent Set Polynomial on a 4-vertex tree \(T\) rooted at \(1\), with edges \((1,2), (2,3), (1,4)\) (so \(1\) has children \(2\) and \(4\), and \(2\) has child \(3\)).
We want to compute \(F_1(x) = \sum_{k=0}^4 f_k x^k\), where \(f_k\) is the number of independent sets of \(T\) of size \(k\). At each vertex \(u\), we track two polynomials:

\(F_{u,0}(x)\): independent sets of \(T_u\) where \(u\) is not selected (\(u \notin I\)). If \(u \notin I\), each child \(v \in \text{child}(u)\) may either be selected or not: \[F_{u,0}(x) = \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \bigl(F_{v,0}(x) + F_{v,1}(x)\bigr).\]
\(F_{u,1}(x)\): independent sets of \(T_u\) where \(u\) is selected (\(u \in I\), contributing factor \(x^1\)). If \(u \in I\), no child \(v\) may be selected: \[F_{u,1}(x) = x \prod_{v \in \text{child}(u)} F_{v,0}(x).\]

Let us trace all 4 vertices by hand:

Leaves \(u = 3\) and \(u = 4\) (\(\text{child}(u) = \emptyset\), empty product \(= 1\)): \[F_{3,0}(x) = 1, \quad F_{3,1}(x) = x, \qquad F_{4,0}(x) = 1, \quad F_{4,1}(x) = x.\]
Vertex \(u = 2\) (sole child \(v = 3\)): \[F_{2,0}(x) = F_{3,0}(x) + F_{3,1}(x) = 1 + x, \qquad F_{2,1}(x) = x \cdot F_{3,0}(x) = x.\] Total in \(T_2 = \{2, 3\}\): \(F_2(x) = F_{2,0}(x) + F_{2,1}(x) = 1 + 2x\) (\(1\) empty set, \(2\) singletons \(\{2\}, \{3\}\), and \(0\) pairs since \((2,3) \in E\)).
Root \(u = 1\) (children \(v \in \{2, 4\}\)): \[F_{1,0}(x) = \bigl(F_{2,0}(x) + F_{2,1}(x)\bigr)\bigl(F_{4,0}(x) + F_{4,1}(x)\bigr) = (1 + 2x)(1 + x) = 1 + 3x + 2x^2,\] \[F_{1,1}(x) = x \cdot F_{2,0}(x) F_{4,0}(x) = x(1 + x)(1) = x + x^2.\] Summing gives the global independent set polynomial of \(T\): \[F_1(x) = F_{1,0}(x) + F_{1,1}(x) = 1 + 4x + 3x^2.\]

Hand Verification:

\(k = 0\): \(\emptyset\) (\(1\) set).
\(k = 1\): \(\{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{4\}\) (\(4\) sets).
\(k = 2\): non-adjacent pairs among \((1,2), (2,3), (1,4)\) are \(\{1,3\}, \{2,4\}, \{3,4\}\) (\(3\) sets).
\(k = 3\): any 3 vertices include either \(\{1,2\}\) or \(\{2,3\}\) or \(\{1,4\}\), so \(0\) sets.




The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad






TipDiagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Spine vs. Off-Spine Separation




The Diagnostic Signal: You have a bottom-up Tree DP where each vertex \(u\) computes one or a constant number \(c\) of polynomials \(\mathbf{F}_u(x) = (F_{u,0}(x), \dots, F_{u,c-1}(x))^T\) of degree \(O(\text{sz}[u])\), and \(N \le 2 \times 10^5\) prevents \(O(N^2)\) knapsack.
The Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad:

Why did bottom-up NTT fail on a path? Because at every vertex \(u\) on the spine, we multiplied a huge polynomial \(F_{\text{heavy}(u)}(x)\) (of degree \(\approx \text{sz}[u]\)) with a tiny polynomial from the remaining children (of degree \(\text{sz}[u] - 1 - \text{sz}[\text{heavy}(u)]\)).
Fix the imbalance by singling out the heavy child \(h_u = \arg\max_{v \in \text{child}(u)} \text{sz}[v]\) at every non-leaf vertex \(u\), and calling all other children \(v \in \text{light}(u) = \text{child}(u) \setminus \{h_u\}\) light children.
In our Independent Set recurrence, separate \(h_u\) from \(\text{light}(u)\): \[L_{u,0}(x) = \prod_{v \in \text{light}(u)} \bigl(F_{v,0}(x) + F_{v,1}(x)\bigr), \qquad L_{u,1}(x) = x \prod_{v \in \text{light}(u)} F_{v,0}(x).\] Once \(L_{u,0}(x)\) and \(L_{u,1}(x)\) are known, the dependency of \(\mathbf{F}_u(x)\) on the heavy child \(\mathbf{F}_{h_u}(x)\) is a linear \(2 \times 2\) polynomial matrix transition: \[\begin{pmatrix} F_{u,0}(x) \\ F_{u,1}(x) \end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} L_{u,0}(x) & L_{u,0}(x) \\ L_{u,1}(x) & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{M_u(x)} \begin{pmatrix} F_{h_u, 0}(x) \\ F_{h_u, 1}(x) \end{pmatrix}.\]
Now the entire heavy chain \(u_1 \to u_2 \to \dots \to u_k\) (where \(u_k\) is a leaf with \(F_{u_k,0}(x) = L_{u_k,0}(x) = 1\) and \(F_{u_k,1}(x) = L_{u_k,1}(x) = x\)) reduces to an associative matrix product \(M_{u_1}(x) M_{u_2}(x) \cdots M_{u_{k-1}}(x) \mathbf{F}_{u_k}(x)\), which we can balance by weight-balanced divide-and-conquer!
