Advanced 1 (#110) — Wise Men (Hard Version)

Source: Codeforces 1326F2 — Wise Men (Hard Version)
Prerequisites: Partition-Indexed Subset Convolution, Ranked Zeta Space & Superset Möbius Inversion (§24.1, §24.2)


Problem Statement
There are \(n\) wise men numbered \(1, \dots, n\), and a symmetric binary adjacency matrix \(G \in \{0, 1\}^{n \times n}\) indicating which pairs of wise men know each other. For each of the \(n!\) permutations \(p = (p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n)\) of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\), we form a binary string \(s(p) = s_1 s_2 \dots s_{n-1} \in \{0, 1\}^{n-1}\) of length \(n - 1\), where \(s_i = 1\) if \(p_i\) and \(p_{i+1}\) know each other (\(G_{p_i, p_{i+1}} = 1\)), and \(s_i = 0\) otherwise.
For every binary string \(w \in \{0, 1\}^{n-1}\), compute the number of permutations \(p\) such that \(s(p) = w\). (Output all \(2^{n-1}\) exact integer counts in \(64\)-bit integers int64_t.)


Constraints

\(2 \le n \le 18\)
\(G_{i,j} \in \{0, 1\}\), \(G_{i,i} = 0\), \(G_{i,j} = G_{j,i}\)
Exact 64-bit integer output (no modulus!)
Time limit: \(4.0\text{ s}\), Memory limit: \(512\text{ MB}\)

Sample Trace (\(n = 3\), edges \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 3)\)):

Path counts \(P_k(S)\) for \(S = \{1, 2, 3\}\):

Partition \(\lambda = (3)\) (one path of length 3): \(1 \to 2 \to 3\) and \(3 \to 2 \to 1\), so \(Z_{(3)} = 2\).
Partition \(\lambda = (2, 1)\) (path of length 2 on \(T\) and length 1 on \(V \setminus T\)): for \(T = \{1,2\}\), \(2 \times 1 = 2\); for \(T = \{2,3\}\), \(2 \times 1 = 2\); for \(T = \{1,3\}\), \(0\). Sum \(Z_{(2,1)} = 4\).
Partition \(\lambda = (1, 1, 1)\): \(1! \times 3! = 6\).

Mapping partitions to masks \(w \in \{00_2, 01_2, 10_2, 11_2\}\) of 1-runs (Superset Zeta \(\widehat{A}_w\)):

\(\widehat{A}_{11} = Z_{(3)} = 2\); \(\widehat{A}_{10} = \widehat{A}_{01} = Z_{(2,1)} = 4\); \(\widehat{A}_{00} = Z_{(1,1,1)} = 6\).

Superset IFMT gives \(A_{11} = 2\), \(A_{10} = 4 - 2 = 2\), \(A_{01} = 4 - 2 = 2\), \(A_{00} = 6 - 4 - 4 + 2 = 0\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

Directly requiring \(s_i = 0\) (two adjacent vertices do not know each other) is awkward, whereas requiring \(s_i = 1\) (an edge is present) simply chains consecutive vertices into directed paths in \(G\)! Apply Superset Zeta Transform on the \((n-1)\)-bit pattern \(w\): requiring \(s(p) \supseteq w\) means every maximal contiguous block of \(1\)s in \(w\) of length \(L - 1\) forces a directed path of \(L\) vertices in \(G\).



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Notice that the number of ways to cover \(V\) with disjoint directed paths of vertex sizes \(L_1, L_2, \dots, L_r\) (where \(\sum L_i = n\)) depends only on the unordered integer partition \(\lambda = (L_1 \ge L_2 \ge \dots \ge L_r) \vdash n\), NOT on the order of the blocks! For \(n = 18\), there are \(2^{17} = 131072\) masks \(w\), but only \(p(18) = 385\) integer partitions of \(18\)!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


Use standard \(O(n^2 2^n)\) Hamiltonian path DP to compute \(P_{|S|}(S)\), the number of directed paths spanning subset \(S\).
Apply the \(O(n 2^n)\) Fast Zeta Transform to each rank \(k = 1, \dots, n\): \(\widehat{P}_k(M) = \sum_{S \subseteq M, |S|=k} P_k(S)\).
Backtrack over all \(p(n) \le 385\) partitions \(\lambda = (L_1, \dots, L_r) \vdash n\), maintaining the pointwise product \(\prod_{i=1}^r \widehat{P}_{L_i}(M)\) and evaluating the top-mask IFZT sum \(\sum_{M} (-1)^{n - |M|} \prod_i \widehat{P}_{L_i}(M)\) in \(O(2^n)\) per partition.
Assign each mask \(w \in [0, 2^{n-1}-1]\) the value of its run-length partition \(\lambda(w)\), and run an \(O((n-1) 2^{n-1})\) Superset IFMT!








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Mathematical Derivation
For each pattern mask \(w \in \{0, 1\}^{n-1}\), let \(A_w\) be the number of permutations \(p\) with \(s(p) = w\), and let \(\widehat{A}_w = \sum_{w' \supseteq w} A_{w'}\) be its Superset Zeta Transform: the number of permutations \(p\) such that \(p_i\) and \(p_{i+1}\) know each other whenever bit \(i\) of \(w\) is \(1\) (with no restriction when bit \(i\) of \(w\) is \(0\)).
Decompose the \((n-1)\)-bit mask \(w\) by splitting at every \(0\)-bit. This partitions the \(n\) positions \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) into maximal contiguous segments of sizes \(L_1, L_2, \dots, L_r\) (\(\sum_{i=1}^r L_i = n\)), where a segment of \(L_i\) vertices corresponds to \(L_i - 1\) consecutive \(1\)-bits in \(w\). A permutation \(p\) satisfies \(s(p) \supseteq w\) if and only if it partitions the vertex set \(V\) into an ordered tuple of disjoint subsets \((S_1, S_2, \dots, S_r)\) with \(|S_i| = L_i\), and forms a valid directed path in \(G[S_i]\) on each subset \(S_i\)!
For each \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) and \(S \subseteq V\) with \(|S| = k\), let \(P_k(S)\) be the number of directed Hamiltonian paths spanning \(S\). Then in the Set Power Series ring \(\mathcal{R}_n\):
\[
\widehat{A}_w = [\mathbf{x}^V] \prod_{i=1}^r \left(\sum_{|S| = L_i} P_{L_i}(S) \mathbf{x}^S\right).
\]
Because \(\mathcal{R}_n\) is commutative, this product depends only on the sorted integer partition \(\lambda(w) = \operatorname{sort}(L_1, \dots, L_r) \vdash n\)! For \(n = 18\), the number of partitions is \(p(18) = 385 \ll 2^{17} = 131072\).
Let \(\widehat{P}_k(M) = \sum_{S \subseteq M, |S| = k} P_k(S)\) be the Fast Zeta Transform of the rank-\(k\) slice. Because \(\sum L_i = n\), any overlapping union \(\bigcup_{i=1}^r S_i\) with \(|S_i| = L_i\) has cardinality strictly less than \(n\), so its contribution to the full mask \(V\) vanishes under IFZT! Thus, for every partition \(\lambda = (L_1, \dots, L_r) \vdash n\), we evaluate the top-mask IFZT directly by inclusion-exclusion:
\[
Z_\lambda = [\mathbf{x}^V] \prod_{i=1}^r P_{L_i}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{M=0}^{2^n - 1} (-1)^{n - \operatorname{popcount}(M)} \prod_{i=1}^r \widehat{P}_{L_i}(M).
\]
We compute \(P_k(S)\) in \(O(n^2 2^n)\) via standard bitmask path DP, transform each rank \(k\) in \(O(n 2^n)\), DFS over the \(p(n) = 385\) partitions maintaining the running pointwise product array prod[M] in \(385 \times 2^{18} \approx 10^8\) multiplications, fill \(\widehat{A}_w = Z_{\lambda(w)}\), and finish with a Superset IFMT on \(\widehat{A}\) in \(O(n 2^{n-1})\)!
// DFS over integer partitions lambda of n, maintaining pointwise product in Zeta space
void dfs_part(int rem, int max_L, vector<int>& cur, const vector<ll>& prod) {
    if (rem == 0) {
        ll sum = 0;
        for (int M = 0; M < (1 << n); ++M)
            sum += ((n - __builtin_popcount(M)) & 1) ? -prod[M] : prod[M];
        part_val[cur] = sum; return;
    }
    for (int L = min(rem, max_L); L >= 1; --L) {
        vector<ll> nxt(1 << n);
        for (int M = 0; M < (1 << n); ++M) nxt[M] = prod[M] * P_hat[L][M];
        cur.push_back(L); dfs_part(rem - L, L, cur, nxt); cur.pop_back();
    }
}


Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: \(2 \le n \le 18\), \(n \times n\) symmetric adjacency matrix \(G\).
Preconditions: Exact 64-bit signed arithmetic int64_t (since \(18! \approx 6.4 \times 10^{15} < 2^{63} - 1\) and no divisions are needed).
Postconditions (Output): Outputs \(2^{n-1}\) exact integers \(A_w\) for \(w \in [0, 2^{n-1}-1]\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O\big((n^2 + p(n)) 2^n\big)\) time and \(O(n 2^n)\) space, where \(p(18) = 385\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: At each DFS node with partial partition \((L_1, \dots, L_j)\), prod[M] holds \(\prod_{i=1}^j \widehat{P}_{L_i}(M)\), and at leaves (\(\sum L_i = n\)), the alternating sum over \(M\) extracts the exact disjoint-union coefficient \([\mathbf{x}^V] \prod_i P_{L_i}(\mathbf{x})\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Because the problem requires exact \(64\)-bit integers without a modulus, do not reduce modulo \(998244353\); use int64_t (long long) or uint64_t throughout (safe since \(\sum_w A_w = 18! \approx 6.40 \times 10^{15} < 2^{63} - 1\)), and note that a contiguous segment of \(L\) vertices corresponds to \(L - 1\) consecutive 1-bits in the \((n - 1)\)-bit mask \(w\).









Advanced 2 (#207) — [集训队互测2015] 胡策的统计

Source: UOJ 94 — 胡策的统计
Prerequisites: Pointed Vertex-by-Vertex Biconnected SPS \(\ln\), SPS \(\exp\) & Divided Powers (§24.3, Callout #9)


Problem Statement
You are given a simple undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. A non-empty induced or spanning subgraph \(H = (S, E_H)\) (\(S \subseteq V, E_H \subseteq E[S]\)) is called biconnected if it is connected and contains no articulation point (no vertex \(v \in S\) whose removal disconnects \(H\); in particular, a single vertex \(|S| = 1\) and a single edge \(|S| = 2\) are biconnected).

First, for every non-empty subset \(S \subseteq V\), compute the number of biconnected spanning subgraphs \(B_S\) on \(S\).
Second, compute the total weight over all ordered partitions of \(V\) into \(k \ge 1\) vertex-disjoint biconnected spanning subgraphs (equivalently, \([\mathbf{x}^V] \frac{1}{1 - B(\mathbf{x})}\) in \(\mathcal{R}_n\)), modulo \(998244353\).



Constraints

\(1 \le n \le 15\)
\(0 \le m \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2}\)
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\)
Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\), Memory limit: \(256\text{ MB}\)

Sample Trace (\(n = 3\), triangle \(K_3\) with \(3\) edges):

Total subgraphs \(F_S = 2^{e(S)}\): \(F_1 = 1\), \(F_2 = 2\), \(F_{\{1,2,3\}} = 8\).
Connected subgraphs \(C = \ln F\): \(C_1 = 1\), \(C_2 = 1\), \(C_{\{1,2,3\}} = 4\) (the triangle plus \(3\) paths of \(2\) edges).
Sequential pointed \((n-1)\)-variable \(\ln\) for \(v = 1, 2, 3\):

At \(v = 1\): \(C^{(1)} = 1 + x_2 + x_3 + 4 x_2 x_3\). Taking \(\ln C^{(1)}\) in \(\mathcal{R}_{\{2,3\}}\) subtracts \(x_2 \cdot x_3\) (the path \(2 - 1 - 3\) where \(1\) is a cut vertex!), updating \(C_{\{1,2,3\}} \leftarrow 4 - 1 = 3\).
At \(v = 2\): subtracts the path \(1 - 2 - 3\), updating \(C_{\{1,2,3\}} \leftarrow 3 - 1 = 2\).
At \(v = 3\): subtracts the path \(1 - 3 - 2\), updating \(C_{\{1,2,3\}} \leftarrow 2 - 1 = 1\) (only the \(3\)-cycle \(K_3\) remains!).

Thus \(B_1 = 1, B_2 = 1, B_{\{1,2,3\}} = 1\). Finally, \([\mathbf{x}^V](1 - B(\mathbf{x}))^{-1} = 1(B_{\{1,2,3\}}) + 2!\cdot 3(B_2 B_1) + 3!\cdot 1(B_1^3 / 3!) = 1 + 6 + 6 = 13\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

To find the number of biconnected spanning subgraphs \(B_S\) for every \(S \subseteq V\) on a fixed graph \(G\) (\(n \le 15\)), start with \(F_S = 2^{e(S)}\), take the \(n\)-variable SPS logarithm \(C(\mathbf{x}) = \ln F(\mathbf{x})\) to isolate connected subgraphs, and then ask: how do we strip away connected subgraphs that have an articulation point?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Fix a vertex \(v \in V\). In any connected graph \(H\) on \(T \cup \{v\}\) (\(T \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}\)), deleting \(v\) partitions \(T\) into connected pieces \(T_1 \sqcup \dots \sqcup T_k = T\) that were attached to \(v\) and had no edges between distinct \(T_i\) and \(T_j\). That means the pointed \((n-1)\)-variable SPS \(C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{T \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}} C_{T \cup \{v\}} \mathbf{x}^T \in \mathcal{R}_{V \setminus \{v\}}\) is the exponential of connected graphs on \(T_i \cup \{v\}\) where \(v\) is not an articulation point!



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


Compute \(C = \ln F\) in \(\mathcal{R}_n\) in \(O(n^2 2^n)\).
For each \(v = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1\): extract the \((n-1)\)-variable SPS \(C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x})\) on masks \(T \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}\) (note \(C^{(v)}_\varnothing = C_{\{v\}} = 1\)), replace \(C^{(v)}\) with \(\ln C^{(v)}\) in \(\mathcal{R}_{V \setminus \{v\}}\) in \(O(n^2 2^{n-1})\), and write the coefficients back into \(C_{T \cup \{v\}}\).
After all \(n\) vertices are processed, \(B_S = C_S\) holds the exact number of biconnected spanning subgraphs on \(S\). Compute \((1 - B(\mathbf{x}))^{-1}\) in \(\mathcal{R}_n\) in \(O(n^2 2^n)\) to obtain \([\mathbf{x}^V](1 - B(\mathbf{x}))^{-1}\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Mathematical Derivation
Let \(F_S = 2^{e(S)}\) be the number of spanning subgraphs on \(S \subseteq V\). Taking the Set Power Series logarithm in \(\mathcal{R}_n\):
\[
C(\mathbf{x}) = \ln F(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{in } \mathcal{R}_n
\]
yields \(C_S\), the number of connected spanning subgraphs on \(S\).
Now we must eliminate all connected subgraphs that contain at least one articulation point (cut vertex). Order the vertices \(V = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}\). Suppose that after step \(v - 1\), \(C_S\) counts connected spanning subgraphs on \(S\) in which none of the vertices in \(S \cap \{0, \dots, v-1\}\) is an articulation point.
Consider how a graph \(H\) counted by \(C_{T \cup \{v\}}\) (where \(T \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}\)) behaves when we delete vertex \(v\):

Deleting \(v\) splits \(H \setminus \{v\}\) into \(k \ge 1\) connected components on disjoint vertex subsets \(T_1 \sqcup T_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup T_k = T\).
For each piece \(T_i\), the induced subgraph \(H[T_i \cup \{v\}]\) is connected, \(v\) is not an articulation point of \(H[T_i \cup \{v\}]\), and furthermore no vertex \(u \in T_i \cap \{0, \dots, v-1\}\) can be an articulation point of \(H[T_i \cup \{v\}]\) if and only if \(u\) was not an articulation point of \(H\)!
Conversely, gluing \(k\) such \(v\)-blocks \(H_i\) on \(T_i \cup \{v\}\) at vertex \(v\) creates no new cycles between distinct \(T_i\), so a vertex \(u \neq v\) is an articulation point of the union \(H\) if and only if \(u\) is an articulation point of its own piece \(H_i\)!

Therefore, in the \((n-1)\)-variable Set Power Series ring \(\mathcal{R}_{V \setminus \{v\}}\), the pointed series
\[
C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{T \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}} C_{T \cup \{v\}} \mathbf{x}^T \quad \big(\text{with } C^{(v)}_\varnothing = C_{\{v\}} = 1\big)
\]
is the exact subset exponential of the subgraphs on \(T \cup \{v\}\) in which \(v\) is not an articulation point! Updating
\[
C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x}) \leftarrow \ln_{\mathcal{R}_{V \setminus \{v\}}} C^{(v)}(\mathbf{x})
\]
and writing its coefficients back to \(C_{T \cup \{v\}}\) strips away all graphs where \(v\) is an articulation point. After repeating this for \(v = 0, 1, \dots, n-1\), no vertex in \(V\) can be an articulation point, so \(B(\mathbf{x}) = C(\mathbf{x})\) is the exact SPS of biconnected spanning subgraphs! Finally, an ordered sequence of \(k\) disjoint biconnected components partitioning \(V\) has generating function \(\sum_{k \ge 0} B(\mathbf{x})^k = (1 - B(\mathbf{x}))^{-1}\) in \(\mathcal{R}_n\).
vector<mint> C = sps_ln(F, n); // Step 1: connected subgraphs on V
for (int v = 0; v < n; ++v) {  // Step 2: strip cut vertex v via (n-1)-var SPS ln
    vector<mint> Cv(1 << (n - 1));
    for (int T = 0; T < (1 << (n - 1)); ++T) {
        int full_T = (T & ((1 << v) - 1)) | ((T >> v) << (v + 1)) | (1 << v);
        Cv[T] = C[full_T];
    }
    Cv = sps_ln(Cv, n - 1); // C_{\{v\}} = 1 is the constant term Cv[0]
    for (int T = 0; T < (1 << (n - 1)); ++T) {
        int full_T = (T & ((1 << v) - 1)) | ((T >> v) << (v + 1)) | (1 << v);
        C[full_T] = Cv[T];
    }
}
vector<mint> ans_sps = sps_inv_one_minus(C, n); // Step 3: (1 - B(x))^{-1}


Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: \(1 \le n \le 15\), undirected edge list \(E\) of size \(m\).
Preconditions: \(F_\varnothing = 1\) and \(C_{\{v\}} = 1\) for all \(v \in V\); \(1, \dots, n \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (\(p = 998244353\)).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \([\mathbf{x}^V](1 - B(\mathbf{x}))^{-1} \bmod 998244353\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(n^3 2^n)\) time (\(15\) calls to \(14\)-variable SPS \(\ln\), \(\approx 15 \cdot 14^2 \cdot 2^{14} \approx 4.8 \times 10^7\) ops) and \(O(n 2^n)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After iteration \(v \in [0, n-1]\), for every non-empty \(S \subseteq V\), C[S] equals the number of connected spanning subgraphs on \(S\) whose set of articulation points is disjoint from \(\{0, 1, \dots, v\}\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: In the pointed \((n-1)\)-variable logarithm at vertex \(v\), the empty subset \(T = \varnothing \subseteq V \setminus \{v\}\) corresponds to the single-vertex subgraph \(\{v\}\) with \(C^{(v)}_\varnothing = C_{\{v\}} = 1\) (so \(\ln C^{(v)}\) is well-defined with constant term \(0\)), and both \(|S| = 1\) (single vertex) and \(|S| = 2\) (single edge \(K_2\)) have no articulation points and remain biconnected (\(B_S = 1\)).









Mastery 1 (#231) — 幂数 (Powerful Numbers)

Source: LibreOJ 6729 — 幂数
Prerequisites: Dirichlet Ring \(\mathcal{D}_f\), Bell Series Division & Powerful Number Perturbation (§24.4)


Problem Statement
Let \(f, g : \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1} \to \mathbb{F}_p\) be two multiplicative functions such that \(f(1) = g(1) = 1\) and \(f(p) = g(p)\) at every prime \(p\). Given a positive integer \(N \le 10^{11}\), an \(O(1)\) (or \(O(\sqrt{x})\)-cached) prefix-sum oracle for \(G(x) = \sum_{n=1}^x g(n) \bmod p\), and prime-power evaluators for \(f(p^k)\) and \(g(p^k)\) (\(k \ge 1\)), compute the prefix sum
\[
S(N) = \sum_{n=1}^N f(n) \bmod p
\]
in \(O(\sqrt{N})\) time by expressing \(f = h *_D g\) in the Dirichlet ring \(\mathcal{D}_f\), proving via Bell series that \(h = f *_D g^{-1}\) vanishes outside the \(O(\sqrt{N})\) powerful numbers \(d \le N\) (\(p \mid d \implies p^2 \mid d\)), and summing \(h(d) G(\lfloor N / d \rfloor)\) over all powerful numbers \(d \le N\).


Constraints

\(1 \le N \le 10^{11}\) (or up to \(10^{13}\))
Number of powerful numbers \(\le N\) is \(\le \frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)} \sqrt{N} \approx 2.17 \sqrt{N}\) (\(\le 6.8 \times 10^5\) at \(N = 10^{11}\))
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\) or \(10^9 + 7\)
Time limit: \(2.0\text{ s}\), Memory limit: \(256\text{ MB}\)

Sample Trace (\(N = 12\), \(f(p) = 1\), \(f(p^k) = 2\) for \(k \ge 2\), and \(g(n) = 1\) for all \(n\)):

At every prime \(p\): \(B_p(f; x) = 1 + x + 2x^2 + 2x^3 + \dots\) and \(B_p(g; x) = \frac{1}{1 - x}\) (with prefix sum \(G(x) = x\)).
Bell series quotient: \(B_p(h; x) = B_p(f; x)(1 - x) = (1 + x + 2x^2 + 2x^3 + \dots)(1 - x) = 1 + x^2\).
Thus \(h(p) = 0\), \(h(p^2) = 1\), and \(h(p^k) = 0\) for \(k \ge 3\). The powerful numbers \(\le 12\) with \(h(d) \neq 0\) are \(d \in \{1, 4, 9\}\) with \(h(1) = h(4) = h(9) = 1\).
Prefix sum: \(\sum_{n=1}^{12} f(n) = h(1) G(12) + h(4) G(3) + h(9) G(1) = 12 + 3 + 1 = 16\) (matching direct evaluation where \(f(n) = 1\) except at \(n \in \{4, 8, 9, 12\}\) where \(f(n) = 2\)).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

When \(f\) and \(g\) are multiplicative and agree on all primes (\(f(p) = g(p)\)), their Bell series at every prime \(p\) agree up to degree \(1\): \(B_p(f; x) \equiv B_p(g; x) \pmod{x^2}\). What does that imply about the degree-1 term of their quotient \(B_p(h; x) = B_p(f; x) B_p(g; x)^{-1}\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Because \(B_p(f; x) = 1 + f(p) x + f(p^2) x^2 + \dots\) and \(B_p(g; x) = 1 + g(p) x + g(p^2) x^2 + \dots\) with \(f(p) = g(p)\), their ratio \(B_p(h; x) = B_p(f; x) / B_p(g; x)\) has \([x^1] B_p(h; x) = f(p) - g(p) = 0\)! Since \(h\) is multiplicative and \(h(p) = 0\) for every prime \(p\), \(h(n) = \prod_{p^k \parallel n} h(p^k) = 0\) whenever any prime divides \(n\) to the first power (\(k = 1\)).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


Sieve all primes \(p \le \sqrt{N}\).
For each prime \(p \le \sqrt{N}\) (or in \(O(\log^2 N)\) globally if \(h(p^k)\) is a polynomial in \(p^k\)), compute \(h(p^k)\) for \(2 \le k \le \lfloor \log_p N \rfloor\) via the \(O(k^2)\) Bell series recurrence \(h(p^k) = f(p^k) - \sum_{j=1}^k g(p^j) h(p^{k-j})\).
DFS over all powerful numbers \(d = \prod p_i^{k_i} \le N\) (choosing only exponents \(k_i \ge 2\) on primes \(p_i \le \sqrt{N / d_{\text{cur}}}\)), accumulating \(h(d) G(\lfloor N / d \rfloor) \bmod p\).








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Mathematical Derivation
Since \(f\) and \(g\) are multiplicative with \(f(1) = g(1) = 1\), both are units in the Dirichlet ring \(\mathcal{D}_f\), and their Dirichlet quotient \(h = f *_D g^{-1}\) is also multiplicative. At each prime \(p\), the Bell series satisfy:
\[
B_p(h; x) = \frac{B_p(f; x)}{B_p(g; x)} = \frac{1 + f(p) x + f(p^2) x^2 + \dots}{1 + g(p) x + g(p^2) x^2 + \dots} \quad \text{in } \mathbb{F}_p[[x]].
\]
Extracting \([x^1]\) from \(B_p(h; x) B_p(g; x) = B_p(f; x)\) gives:
\[
h(p) + g(p) h(1) = f(p) \implies h(p) = f(p) - g(p) = 0.
\]
For higher prime powers \(k \ge 2\), the truncated polynomial inversion recurrence in \(\mathbb{F}_p[x]/(x^{E+1})\) gives:
\[
h(p^k) = f(p^k) - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} g(p^j) h(p^{k-j}) - g(p^k).
\]
Because \(h\) is multiplicative and \(h(p) = 0\) for every prime \(p\), any integer \(n = \prod p_i^{e_i}\) with at least one exponent \(e_i = 1\) has \(h(n) = \prod h(p_i^{e_i}) = 0\). Thus \(\operatorname{supp}(h)\) is contained in the powerful numbers:
\[
\mathcal{P}(N) = \left\{ d \le N : p \mid d \implies p^2 \mid d \right\}.
\]
Every powerful number \(d\) can be written uniquely as \(d = a^2 b^3\) with \(b\) square-free, so \(|\mathcal{P}(N)| \le \sum_{b=1}^{\lfloor N^{1/3} \rfloor} \sqrt{N / b^3} = O(\sqrt{N})\). Expanding \(f = h *_D g\) on the prefix sum \(\sum_{n=1}^N f(n)\) yields:
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N f(n) = \sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{d \mid n} h(d) \, g\!\left(\frac{n}{d}\right) = \sum_{\substack{d \in \mathcal{P}(N)}} h(d) \, G\!\left(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{d} \right\rfloor\right).
\]
// DFS over all O(sqrt(N)) powerful numbers d <= N, accumulating h(d) * G(N / d)
void dfs_pn(int idx, ll d, mint hd) {
    ans += hd * G_prefix(N / d);
    for (int i = idx; i < (int)primes.size(); ++i) {
        ll p = primes[i];
        if (d > N / (p * p)) break;
        ll pk = p * p;
        for (int k = 2; d <= N / pk; ++k) {
            if (h_pk[i][k].val() != 0) dfs_pn(i + 1, d * pk, hd * h_pk[i][k]);
            if (pk > N / p) break;
            pk *= p;
        }
    }
}


Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: Integer \(1 \le N \le 10^{11}\), prime-power evaluators for \(f(p^k), g(p^k)\) with \(f(p) = g(p)\), and fast prefix-sum oracle \(G(\lfloor N/d \rfloor)\).
Preconditions: \(f(1) = g(1) = 1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) and \(f(p) = g(p)\) for all primes \(p \le \sqrt{N}\).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \(\sum_{n=1}^N f(n) \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(\sqrt{N})\) time and \(O(\sqrt{N})\) space to sieve primes up to \(\sqrt{N}\), precompute \(h(p^k)\) via Bell series division, and traverse all powerful numbers \(d \le N\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Each DFS state (idx, d, hd) visits a unique powerful number \(d\) whose prime factors have indices \(< \text{idx}\) (or is extended by \(p_i^k\) with \(i \ge \text{idx}\) and \(k \ge 2\)), with hd \(= \prod_{p^k \parallel d} h(p^k)\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: When stepping prime powers pk *= p in the recursive DFS over powerful numbers \(d \le N\), always guard against 64-bit integer overflow using division (if (d > N / (p * p)) break; and if (pk > N / p) break;) before multiplying, since \(p^k\) or \(d \cdot p^k\) can exceed \(2^{63} - 1\) when \(N = 10^{11}\) and \(p \approx 3 \times 10^5\).









Mastery 2 (#038) — A Nameless Counting Problem

Source: AtCoder Beginner Contest 288 Ex — A Nameless Counting Problem
Prerequisites: Bitwise XOR Cancellation, Parity Decomposition, Digit DP & EGF-to-OGF Hyperbolic Substitution (§24.1, §24.3)


Problem Statement
Given three non-negative integers \(M, N, X\), find the number of non-decreasing sequences of \(N\) integers \(0 \le A_1 \le A_2 \le \dots \le A_N \le M\) such that their bitwise XOR sum equals \(X\):
\[
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_N = X.
\]
Output the answer modulo \(998244353\).


Constraints

\(0 \le M < 2^{30}\)
\(1 \le N \le 200\)
\(0 \le X < 2^{30}\)
Modulus: \(p = 998244353\)
Time limit: \(4.0\text{ s}\), Memory limit: \(1024\text{ MB}\)

Sample Trace (\(M = 2, N = 2, X = 1\)):

Non-decreasing pairs \(0 \le A_1 \le A_2 \le 2\) with \(A_1 \oplus A_2 = 1\):

Unordered pairs of distinct elements in \([0, 2]\) with XOR \(1\): only \(\{0, 1\}\) (since \(0 \oplus 1 = 1\), \(0 \oplus 2 = 2\), \(1 \oplus 2 = 3\)).
Since any duplicate pair \((v, v)\) cancels under XOR (\(v \oplus v = 0\)), every non-decreasing sequence of length \(N = 2\) with XOR \(1\) must consist of \(k = 2\) odd-multiplicity values \(\{0, 1\}\) and \(0\) even-multiplicity pairs!
Thus \((A_1, A_2) = (0, 1)\) is the unique solution (answer \(= 1\)).




Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model

In any multiset of \(N\) integers \(\{A_1 \le A_2 \le \dots \le A_N\}\), the bitwise XOR \(A_1 \oplus \dots \oplus A_N\) depends only on the parity of the frequency of each value \(v \in [0, M]\)! Specifically, if \(k\) distinct values \(v_1 < v_2 < \dots < v_k\) appear an odd number of times and all other values appear an even number of times, then \(N \equiv k \pmod 2\) and the remaining \((N - k)/2\) pairs of identical elements can be assigned freely to any values in \([0, M]\)!



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Compare two generating functions in the XOR group algebra \(\mathbb{F}_p[\mathbb{Z}_2^{30}]\):

The OGF of multisets (what the problem asks for): each value \(v \in [0, M]\) contributes \(1 + x^v u + u^2 + x^v u^3 + \dots = \frac{1 + x^v u}{1 - u^2}\), giving \(\prod_{v=0}^M \frac{1 + x^v u}{1 - u^2} = (1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)} \prod_{v=0}^M (1 + x^v u)\).
The EGF of ordered tuples \(T_j\) in \([0, M]^j\) (easy to count via Digit DP): each value \(v \in [0, M]\) contributes \(\cosh(z) + x^v \sinh(z) = \cosh(z)(1 + x^v \tanh(z))\), giving \(\cosh(z)^{M+1} \prod_{v=0}^M (1 + x^v \tanh(z))\).




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract


Use MSB-to-LSB Digit DP in \(O(N^2 \log M)\) to compute \(T_j\) for \(0 \le j \le N\): the number of ordered \(j\)-tuples in \([0, M]^j\) with XOR \(X\).
Substitute \(z = \operatorname{artanh}(u) = \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{u^{2m+1}}{2m+1}\) into the EGF \(\sum_{j=0}^N T_j \frac{z^j}{j!} \bmod u^{N+1}\). Since \(\cosh(\operatorname{artanh}(u)) = (1 - u^2)^{-1/2}\), multiplying the composed polynomial by \((1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)/2}\) produces \([x^X] \prod_{v=0}^M \frac{1 + x^v u}{1 - u^2}\)! Extract \([u^N]\) in \(O(N^2)\) polynomial operations.








NoteComplete Derivation & Solution






Mathematical Derivation
Every non-decreasing sequence \(0 \le A_1 \le A_2 \le \dots \le A_N \le M\) is uniquely identified by the multiplicity \(c_v \ge 0\) of each value \(v \in [0, M]\), where \(\sum_{v=0}^M c_v = N\). Because \(v \oplus v = 0\) in the XOR group \((\mathbb{Z}_2^{30}, \oplus)\), a value \(v\) with multiplicity \(c_v\) contributes \(x^v\) to the XOR product if \(c_v\) is odd, and \(x^0 = 1\) if \(c_v\) is even.
Therefore, in the formal power series ring \(\mathbb{F}_p[\mathbb{Z}_2^{30}][[u]]\) over the XOR group algebra, the bivariate OGF of non-decreasing sequences is:
\[
\Phi(x, u) = \prod_{v=0}^M \left(1 + x^v u + u^2 + x^v u^3 + \dots\right) = (1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)} \prod_{v=0}^M \left(1 + x^v u\right),
\]
and we seek \([x^X u^N] \Phi(x, u)\).
On the other hand, let \(T_j\) be the number of ordered \(j\)-tuples \((B_1, \dots, B_j) \in [0, M]^j\) (with repetition allowed) such that \(B_1 \oplus \dots \oplus B_j = X\). By the exponential formula for labeled sequences, the EGF of ordered tuples in \(\mathbb{F}_p[\mathbb{Z}_2^{30}][[z]]\) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Psi(x, z) &= \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \left(\sum_{v=0}^M x^v\right)^j \frac{z^j}{j!} = \exp\!\left(\sum_{v=0}^M x^v z\right) = \prod_{v=0}^M \exp(x^v z) \\
&= \prod_{v=0}^M \left(\sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{z^{2m}}{(2m)!} x^0 + x^v \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{z^{2m+1}}{(2m+1)!}\right) \\
&= \prod_{v=0}^M \big(\cosh(z) + x^v \sinh(z)\big),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality holds because \((x^v)^2 = x^{v \oplus v} = 1\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p[\mathbb{Z}_2^{30}]\)! Factoring out \(\cosh(z)\) from each of the \(M + 1\) terms yields:
\[
\Psi(x, z) = \cosh(z)^{M+1} \prod_{v=0}^M \big(1 + x^v \tanh(z)\big).
\]
Now substitute \(z = \operatorname{artanh}(u) = u + \frac{u^3}{3} + \frac{u^5}{5} + \dots \in \mathbb{F}_p[[u]]\) (valid up to \(u^N\) since \(N \le 200 < p\)). Using the identity \(\cosh(\operatorname{artanh}(u)) = (1 - u^2)^{-1/2}\) and extracting \([x^X]\) on both sides gives:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} T_j \frac{\operatorname{artanh}(u)^j}{j!} = (1 - u^2)^{-\frac{M+1}{2}} [x^X] \prod_{v=0}^M \left(1 + x^v u\right).
\]
Comparing this with \(\Phi(x, u) = (1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)} \prod_{v=0}^M (1 + x^v u)\), we need only multiply by an extra factor of \((1 - u^2)^{-\frac{M+1}{2}}\) to obtain the exact OGF of our problem:
\[
\text{Ans} = [u^N] \left((1 - u^2)^{-\frac{M+1}{2}} \sum_{j=0}^N T_j \frac{\operatorname{artanh}(u)^j}{j!}\right) \pmod{998244353}.
\]
To compute \(T_0, \dots, T_N\) in \(O(N^2 \log M)\): run a Digit DP from bit \(b = 29\) down to \(0\) tracking how many of the \(j\) elements remain tight to \(M\). Even simpler: classify the \(j\) elements by the highest bit \(b\) where at least one element drops strictly below \(M_b = 1\); below bit \(b\), that loose element’s bits are completely free in \(\{0, 1\}\), so the XOR of bit \(b' < b\) is automatically satisfied in exactly \(2^{j-1}\) ways per bit!
// Given T[0..N] (ordered j-tuples in [0, M]^j with XOR = X from O(N^2 log M) Digit DP):
vector<mint> A(N + 1), B(N + 1); // B(u) = artanh(u) = u + u^3/3 + u^5/5 + ...
for (int i = 1; i <= N; i += 2) B[i] = inv_small[i];
vector<mint> pw(N + 1, 0); pw[0] = 1;
for (int j = 0; j <= N; ++j) {
    mint c = T[j] * ifac[j];
    for (int i = 0; i <= N; ++i) A[i] += c * pw[i];
    pw = poly_mul_trunc(pw, B, N); // O(N^2) truncated multiplication
}
// Multiply A(u) by (1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)/2} and extract A[N]


Algorithm Contract

Input & Exact Index Boundaries: \(0 \le M, X < 2^{30}\), \(1 \le N \le 200\), modulus \(p = 998244353\).
Preconditions: \(1, 2, \dots, N \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (\(N \le 200 < 998244353\)).
Postconditions (Output): Returns \([u^N]\big((1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)/2} \sum_{j=0}^N T_j \frac{\operatorname{artanh}(u)^j}{j!}\big) \bmod p\).
Time & Space Complexity: \(O(N^2 \log M + N^3)\) time and \(O(N^2)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Because \(\prod_{v=0}^M (\cosh z + x^v \sinh z)\big|_{z = \operatorname{artanh}(u)} = (1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)/2} \prod_{v=0}^M (1 + x^v u)\), multiplying by \((1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)/2}\) produces \(\prod_{v=0}^M \frac{1 + x^v u}{1 - u^2}\), whose \([x^X u^N]\) coefficient is the exact count of \(N\)-element multisets in \([0, M]\) with XOR \(X\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Because \(M < 2^{30}\) can be much larger than \(N \le 200\), when computing the generalized binomial coefficients of \((1 - u^2)^{-(M+1)/2}\), reduce the exponent \((M + 1) \bmod p\) before multiplying rising factorial terms, and ensure \(2^{-1} \bmod p\) is used when halving \((M + 1)\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p\).











NoteImplementation Verification Footnote (Quarantined Research Templates R-07, R-08, R-50, R-51 & R-52)



During the adversarial audit of the preliminary research notes for this chapter, five legacy code snippets were quarantined and replaced by the clean C++ engines in §24.1–§24.4:

R-07 / R-08 (fwt_or, fwt_and, fwt_xor): Verified that the butterfly updates in §24.1 (a[i + j + k] += sgn * a[i + j] for OR, a[i + j] += sgn * a[i + j + k] for AND, and u + v, u - v scaled by \(2^{-1}\) for XOR) match the exact Zeta, Möbius, and Walsh-Hadamard character matrices.
R-50 (subset_conv): Re-derived in §24.2 using flat cache-friendly indexing A[mask * (n + 1) + k] and explicit rank-cleaning C_S = [t^{|S|}] C_S(t) so higher-rank garbage never contaminates subsequent subset convolutions.
R-51 (sps_ln, sps_exp_msb, sps_compose): Replaced naive full-rank ODE loops where appropriate with the division-free MSB split (sps_exp_msb) and Elegia’s Taylor shift pyramid (sps_compose) in §24.3, eliminating division preconditions and halving the constant factor.
R-52 (dgf_exp, dgf_ln): Grounded in §24.4 via the completely additive prime-multiplicity derivation \((\vartheta f)(n) = \Omega(n) f(n)\), explicitly guarding \(\Omega(1) = 0\) and documenting the characteristic precondition \(p > \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor\).

title: Blind Checkpoint II: Part II Diagnostic Arena (Chapters 05–08)
text:
When solving problems at the end of a specific textbook chapter, you benefit from chapter-title leakage: if a problem appears at the end of Chapter 07 (Roots of Unity, Multiplicative Indexing, 3-Prime NTT & Chirp-\(Z\)), you already know before reading a single sentence that you should look for a roots-of-unity filter, primitive-root discrete log, or Chirp-\(Z\) transform. In a live ICPC regional or high-rated online contest, no such label exists. A problem asking for a sum over \(2^q\) bracket completions, a bilinear form with \(c^{i^2 j^3}\), or a count of permutations with a prescribed win-loss margin arrives completely unadorned.
This Blind Topic-Group Checkpoint (CP-II) tests your ability to diagnose and route problems across all of Part II (Chapters 05–08) while retaining fluency with the foundational algebraic engines of Part I (Chapters 01–04):

Part I Foundations (Chapters 01–04): Formal power series rings \(K[[x]]\), Newton engines (inv, ln, exp, sqrt, pow), divide-and-conquer / online CDQ NTT, Ordinary Generating Functions (OGFs), and Exponential Generating Functions (EGFs, including labeled trees and Prüfer sequences).
Chapter 05: Rational Generating Functions, Linear Recurrences, Berlekamp–Massey, and the Bostan–Mori Algorithm.
Chapter 06: Binomial Sums, Vandermonde / Egorychev Coefficient Extraction ([x^n]), Falling Factorial Bases, Polynomial Taylor Shift \(F(x + c)\), Stirling Numbers, Faulhaber Power Sums, Multiplicative Euler Sieve for \(i^k\), and \(O(k)\) Consecutive Lagrange Interpolation.
Chapter 07: Roots of Unity Filters, Primitive-Root Multiplicative Indexing, Arbitrary-Modulo 3-Prime NTT (Garner CRT), and Bluestein’s Chirp-\(Z\) Transform (CZT).
Chapter 08: Sieve Methods, Inclusion–Exclusion (IE), Binomial Inversion (“At Least \(k\)” \(\leftrightarrow\) “Exactly \(k\)”), Ferrers-Board Rook Polynomials, Run-Length Transfer, and Goulden–Jackson Pattern Autocorrelation.







ImportantRecommended Workflow for Maximum Diagnostic Training




Stage 1 (Cold Diagnostic Read): Read each problem statement (CP-II.1 through CP-II.8) without opening any collapsible blocks. Give yourself 10–15 minutes per problem to write down on scratch paper:

Which chapter and section (Ch 01–Ch 08) owns the core reduction;
The exact generating function, inversion kernel, or polynomial identity that decouples the indices;
Any modular arithmetic, valuation, or boundary-case pitfalls (\(n=1\), \(k=0\), \(p \le N\), non-NTT primes).

Progressive Unmasking: If you get stuck on routing, open Hint 1 (Diagnostic Signal) first. Only open Hint 2 (Target Chapter Routing) after you have committed to a hypothesis. Use Hint 3 to verify your algebraic reduction and edge-case checklist before reading the Complete Derivation, Algorithm Contract & Complexity Analysis.
Stage 2 (Post-Mortem Audit): After solving or studying all eight problems, open the Master Diagnostic Routing Key at the bottom of the page to compare your diagnostic triggers against the canonical routing table.

title: Blind Checkpoint II: Part II Diagnostic Arena (Chapters 05–08)
section: The 3-Axis Part II Diagnostic Rubric (No Spoilers)
text:
The 3-Axis Part II Diagnostic Rubric (No Spoilers)
When faced with an unlabeled counting or summation problem, run it through three orthogonal diagnostic axes before writing down any algebra:

Axis 1: Constraint & Query Scale (\(N, K, S\) vs. Modulus \(P\))
The raw numerical magnitudes of the input parameters eliminate impossible techniques immediately:

Tiny Dimension + Astronomical Target (e.g., \(n \le 20\), target degree \(\ge 10^{12}\)):

Dense polynomial arithmetic up to the target degree is impossible. Look for a sparse product of \(n\) factors that expands into \(2^n\) monomials, paired with an \(O(n)\) closed-form coefficient extraction on the remaining dense series.

Moderate Dimension (\(N \le 2000\)) + Arbitrary / Non-NTT Prime (\(10^9+7, 10^9+9\)):

\(O(N^2)\) dynamic programming or \(O(N^2)\) precomputed binomial sums fit comfortably within 1 second without needing NTT. Look for a 2D combinatorial state space or a double sum that either runs in \(O(N^2)\) directly or collapses to \(O(N)\) via binomial absorption.

Quasilinear Scale (\(N \le 10^5\) or \(10^6\)) + Prime Modulus:

\(O(N^2)\) is strictly TLE. Any double sum \(\sum_{i,j}\) must be decoupled into a 1D convolution \(\sum_{u+v=w} A_u B_v\) or collapsed in \(O(N)\) linear time via an algebraic identity.

Huge Evaluation Point (\(N \le 10^9\)) + Moderate Parameter (\(K \le 10^6\)):

Iterating up to \(N\) is impossible, yet \(K\) is small enough for \(O(K)\) linear space and time. Check whether the target quantity \(F(N)\) is a polynomial or rational function in \(N\) of degree \(O(K)\) that can be reconstructed from \(O(K)\) small sample values.








NoteOptional Pre-Flight Reference: The 3-Axis Diagnostic Decision Tree (Consult After Stage 1 Cold Read)






Axis 2: Algebraic Coupling Shape
Look at how the summation indices \((i, j, k)\) interact inside the summand:








Coupling Pattern
Structural Signature
Candidate Decoupling Tool




Difference + Index
\(\sum_k f(j-k) g(k)\) or \(\binom{j}{k} (-1)^{j-k} k^i\)
Factor \(\binom{j}{k} = \frac{j!}{k!(j-k)!}\) and apply 1D NTT Cauchy Convolution.


Complementary Upper Indices
\(\sum_k \binom{x}{k-L} \binom{y}{k-R}\)
Flip one binomial via \(\binom{y}{k-R} = \binom{y}{y+R-k}\) so lower indices sum to \(y+R-L\), then apply Vandermonde’s Identity.


Bilinear Exponent
\(\sum_{i,j} a_i b_j c^{\phi(i)\psi(j)} \pmod p\)
Bucket \(I = \phi(i) \bmod (p-1)\), \(J = \psi(j) \bmod (p-1)\) and apply Bluestein’s Chirp-\(Z\) Identity \(IJ = \binom{I+J}{2} - \binom{I}{2} - \binom{J}{2}\).


Upper-Triangular Binomial Kernel
\(g_j = \sum_{m=j}^n \binom{m}{j} f_m\)
Invert via Binomial Inversion \(f_k = \sum_{j=k}^n (-1)^{j-k} \binom{j}{k} g_j\).


Prescribed Multiplicities in a Sequence
Sequence of length \(L\) where item \(i\) appears \(c_i\) times
Extract \([x^L] L! \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{x^{c_i}}{c_i!} = \frac{L!}{\prod_{i=1}^n c_i!}\) via Multinomial EGF.





Axis 3: Combinatorial Obstruction Keyword
Translate verbal constraints in the problem statement directly into algebraic operators:

“At most \(f_i\) items from box \(i\)”: Bounded geometric series \(\frac{1 - x^{f_i+1}}{1 - x}\).
“Exactly \(K\) occurrences / wins / matches”: Usually intractable to count directly because forbidding the remaining \(N-K\) positions from accidentally matching creates global dependencies. Relax to “designate at least \(j \ge K\) occurrences” (\(g_j\)), complete the remaining \(N-j\) elements freely, and recover \(f_K\) via Binomial Inversion.
“Number of labeled trees with prescribed degrees \(d_1, \dots, d_n\)”: Biject via Prüfer sequences to words of length \(n-2\) over alphabet \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) where label \(i\) appears \(d_i - 1\) times.
“Maximum nested depth of a bracket subsequence”: By split-point duality, equals \(\max_{0 \le i \le n} \min(\text{count of } \texttt{(} \text{ in } s[1..i],\, \text{count of } \texttt{)} \text{ in } s[i+1..n])\), occurring at the unique split point \(i\) where prefix \(\texttt{(}\) count equals suffix \(\texttt{)}\) count.

Stage 1: Spoiler-Free Blind Problem Set (CP-II.1 to CP-II.8)

Problem CP-II.1 (#085) — Devu and Flowers

Source: Codeforces 451E — Devu and Flowers


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Devu wants to decorate his garden with flowers. He has \(n\) boxes of flowers, numbered \(1\) through \(n\). All flowers inside a single box have the same color, and flowers in different boxes have distinct colors. Box \(i\) contains \(f_i\) indistinguishable flowers of color \(i\).
Devu wants to select a multiset of exactly \(s\) flowers in total from the \(n\) boxes. Two selections are considered distinct if and only if there is at least one box \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) from which they take a different number of flowers. That is, we wish to count the number of integer tuples \((x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)\) satisfying \[
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = s \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \le x_i \le f_i \quad \text{for all } 1 \le i \le n.
\] Output this count modulo \(10^9 + 7\).

Input Constraints:

\(1 \le n \le 20\)
\(0 \le s \le 10^{14}\)
\(0 \le f_i \le 10^{12}\) for each \(1 \le i \le n\)
Modulus: \(P = 10^9 + 7\) (prime)

Sample Trace (\(n = 2, s = 3, f = [1, 2]\)): The only integer pair \((x_1, x_2)\) satisfying \(x_1 + x_2 = 3\) with \(0 \le x_1 \le 1\) and \(0 \le x_2 \le 2\) is \((1, 2)\), so the output is 1.
Target Complexity: \(O(n 2^n)\) or \(O(2^n \log P)\) time, \(O(n)\) space.



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal (What to look for in the constraints)

Before looking for a generating function, ask what makes the upper bounds \(0 \le x_i \le f_i\) annoying compared to \(x_i \ge 0\). Because \(n \le 20\) is tiny while \(s \le 10^{14}\) is huge, any DP over the sum \(s\) is impossible. How can you trade the \(n\) upper-bound constraints \(x_i \le f_i\) for a small collection of simpler unbounded problems?



Hint 2 — Target Chapter Routing & Initial Setup


Primary Routing: Chapter 06 (§6.1 Bounded Compositions & Negative Binomial Extraction) and Chapter 08 (§8.1 Subset Inclusion–Exclusion).
Generating Function Setup: In \(K[[x]]\), the choice of \(x_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, f_i\}\) flowers from box \(i\) corresponds to the finite geometric polynomial \[
1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^{f_i} = \frac{1 - x^{f_i + 1}}{1 - x}.
\] Multiplying across all \(n\) independent boxes gives the Ordinary Generating Function for the number of valid selections of size \(s\): \[
\text{Ans} = [x^s] \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1 - x^{f_i + 1}}{1 - x} = [x^s] \left( \prod_{i=1}^n \left(1 - x^{f_i + 1}\right) \right) (1 - x)^{-n}.
\]




Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Reduction & Edge Cases


Separating the Sparse Numerator from the Dense Denominator:

The numerator \(N(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 - x^{f_i+1})\) is a product of \(n \le 20\) binomials, so expanding it yields at most \(2^n\) nonzero terms indexed by subsets \(T \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\): \[
N(x) = \sum_{T \subseteq [n]} (-1)^{\lvert T \rvert} x^{d(T)}, \qquad \text{where } d(T) = \sum_{i \in T} (f_i + 1).
\]
The denominator \((1 - x)^{-n} = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \binom{m + n - 1}{n - 1} x^m\) has known coefficients for arbitrarily large \(m\).

Critical Modular Edge Case (\(s - d(T) \ge P\)): Because \(m = s - d(T)\) can be as large as \(10^{14} \gg P = 10^9 + 7\), you cannot precompute factorials up to \(m\). However, the lower index of \(\binom{m + n - 1}{n - 1}\) is \(n - 1 \le 19 < P\). Therefore, compute the falling factorial directly: \[
\binom{m + n - 1}{n - 1} \equiv \frac{\prod_{j=1}^{n-1} \big((m + j) \bmod P\big)}{(n - 1)!} \pmod P.
\] (Note: Over \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(\binom{M}{k} = \frac{M(M-1)\cdots(M-k+1)}{k!}\) is an exact integer equality, and since \(\gcd(k!, P) = 1\) for \(k = n - 1 < P\), reducing the numerator and denominator modulo \(P\) in the localization ring \(\mathbb{Z}_{(P)}\) of rationals with denominator coprime to \(P\) is 100% exact for all integers \(M \ge 0\).)








NoteComplete Derivation, Algorithm Contract & Complexity Analysis






1. Combinatorial Model & Generating Function Formulation
We are counting weak compositions of \(s\) into \(n\) parts \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) subject to upper capacity bounds \(0 \le x_i \le f_i\). In the formal power series ring \(\mathbb{Q}[[x]]\), let \(x^{x_i}\) record the contribution of box \(i\) to the total flower count. Since box \(i\) can contribute any integer amount in \(\{0, 1, \dots, f_i\}\), its generating polynomial is \[
P_i(x) = \sum_{x_i=0}^{f_i} x^{x_i} = \frac{1 - x^{f_i + 1}}{1 - x}.
\] Here \(1 - x\) has constant term \([x^0](1 - x) = 1 \in \mathbb{Q}^\times\), so \((1 - x)^{-1}\) is a well-defined formal power series. Multiplying \(P_i(x)\) over \(i = 1, \dots, n\), the coefficient of \(x^s\) in the product counts all valid tuples \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\): \[
\text{Ans} = [x^s] \prod_{i=1}^n P_i(x) = [x^s] \left( \prod_{i=1}^n \left(1 - x^{f_i + 1}\right) \right) (1 - x)^{-n}.
\]


2. Step-by-Step Coefficient Extraction (Distributivity + Negative Binomial Series)
We expand the finite product and the negative binomial series separately:

Numerator Expansion (Combinatorial Meaning: Violated Box Capacities): By the distributive law of multiplication across \(n\) factors, choosing the \(-x^{f_i+1}\) term for a subset of boxes \(T \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) and the \(1\) term for \([n] \setminus T\) gives \[
\prod_{i=1}^n \left(1 - x^{f_i + 1}\right) = \sum_{T \subseteq [n]} (-1)^{\lvert T \rvert} x^{d(T)}, \qquad d(T) := \sum_{i \in T} (f_i + 1).
\] Combinatorially, \(d(T)\) is the minimum number of flowers required to violate the capacity bound (\(x_i \ge f_i + 1\)) simultaneously for every box \(i \in T\).
Denominator Expansion (Unbounded Stars and Bars): By the negative binomial theorem in \(\mathbb{Q}[[x]]\), \[
(1 - x)^{-n} = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \binom{-n}{m} (-1)^m x^m = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \binom{m + n - 1}{n - 1} x^m.
\]
Cauchy Product Extraction at \([x^s]\): Applying the linearity of the coefficient extraction operator \([x^s]\): \[
\begin{aligned}
[x^s] \left( \sum_{T \subseteq [n]} (-1)^{\lvert T \rvert} x^{d(T)} \right) (1 - x)^{-n}
&= \sum_{T \subseteq [n]} (-1)^{\lvert T \rvert} [x^{s - d(T)}] (1 - x)^{-n} \\
&= \sum_{\substack{T \subseteq [n] \\ d(T) \le s}} (-1)^{\lvert T \rvert} \binom{s - d(T) + n - 1}{n - 1}.
\end{aligned}
\] Note that whenever \(d(T) > s\), the required degree \(s - d(T)\) is strictly negative, and since \((1 - x)^{-n} \in \mathbb{Q}[[x]]\) has no negative powers of \(x\), its coefficient is \(0\).



3. Hand-Checkable Concrete Trace (\(n = 2, s = 3, f = [1, 2]\))
Let \(n = 2\) boxes with capacities \(f_1 = 1, f_2 = 2\), and target \(s = 3\). Directly listing valid pairs \((x_1, x_2)\) with \(x_1 + x_2 = 3\), \(0 \le x_1 \le 1\), \(0 \le x_2 \le 2\):

\((x_1, x_2) = (1, 2)\) is the only valid solution, so the answer must be \(1\).

Let us verify the formula over the \(2^2 = 4\) subsets \(T \subseteq \{1, 2\}\), where \(f_1 + 1 = 2\) and \(f_2 + 1 = 3\):

\(T = \emptyset\): \(d(\emptyset) = 0 \le 3\), sign \(+1\), contribution \(+\binom{3 - 0 + 1}{1} = +\binom{4}{1} = +4\).
\(T = \{1\}\): \(d(\{1\}) = 2 \le 3\), sign \(-1\), contribution \(-\binom{3 - 2 + 1}{1} = -\binom{2}{1} = -2\).
\(T = \{2\}\): \(d(\{2\}) = 3 \le 3\), sign \(-1\), contribution \(-\binom{3 - 3 + 1}{1} = -\binom{1}{1} = -1\).
\(T = \{1, 2\}\): \(d(\{1, 2\}) = 2 + 3 = 5 > 3\), skipped (contribution \(0\)).

Summing the contributions: \(4 - 2 - 1 + 0 = 1\), matching our manual count.






WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Evaluating \(\binom{M}{k} \bmod P\) When \(M \ge P\) vs. Negative Remainder Bugs




Do Not Confuse \(M < 0\) with \(M \equiv r \pmod P\): The condition \(d(T) \le s\) is an exact integer inequality in \(\mathbb{Z}\) (representing \([x^{s-d(T)}]\) for a non-negative exponent), not a modular condition. You must test if (d_T <= s) using 64-bit signed integers (long long) before reducing \(s - d(T)\) modulo \(P\). If you reduce \(s - d(T) \pmod P\) when \(d(T) > s\), the polynomial \(\frac{M^{\underline{n-1}}}{(n-1)!}\) will evaluate at a negative integer \(M < 0\) where the algebraic polynomial \(\binom{M}{n-1}\) is nonzero even though \([x^{s-d(T)}](1-x)^{-n} = 0\)!
Valid Division by \((n-1)!\): Because \(n \le 20 < P = 10^9 + 7\), \((n-1)!\) is a unit in \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times\). In the localization \(\mathbb{Z}_{(P)}\), the identity \(\binom{M}{n-1} = \frac{M(M-1)\cdots(M-n+2)}{(n-1)!}\) holds identically for all integers \(M \ge 0\), so reducing \((M - j) \bmod P\) inside the numerator product and multiplying by \(\big((n-1)!\big)^{-1} \bmod P\) is exact even when \(M \ge P\).





4. Algorithm Contract

Input: Integer \(n \in [1, 20]\), integer \(s \in [0, 10^{14}]\), array \(f[1..n]\) with \(f_i \in [0, 10^{12}]\).
Output: Number of bounded integer tuples \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) summing to \(s\), modulo \(10^9 + 7\).
Core Invariant: Each bitmask \(\text{mask} \subseteq [n]\) represents the subset of boxes forced to violate their capacity bound (\(x_i \ge f_i + 1\)) with exact integer threshold \(d(\text{mask}) = \sum_{i \in \text{mask}} (f_i + 1) \le s\).
Precomputation: Compute \(\text{invFact} = \left((n - 1)!\right)^{P - 2} \bmod P\) in \(O(n + \log P)\) time.
Subset Iteration: For each bitmask \(\text{mask} \in [0, 2^n - 1]\):

Compute \(d = \sum_{i : \text{bit } i \in \text{mask}} (f_i + 1)\) in 64-bit integer arithmetic (long long; maximum value \(20 \times (10^{12} + 1) \approx 2 \times 10^{13} < 2^{63} - 1\)).
If \(d > s\), continue to the next mask.
Let \(M = s - d + n - 1\). Compute \(\text{num} = \prod_{j=0}^{n-2} \big((M - j) \bmod P\big) \bmod P\), and \(\text{term} = \text{num} \cdot \text{invFact} \bmod P\).
If \(\text{popcount}(\text{mask})\) is odd, subtract \(\text{term}\) from \(\text{ans} \bmod P\); otherwise add \(\text{term}\) to \(\text{ans} \bmod P\).

Complexity: \(O(n 2^n)\) time (or \(O(2^n)\) using Gray-code / DFS subset sum transitions and \(O(n)\) binomial evaluation), \(O(n)\) auxiliary space.









Problem CP-II.2 (#152) — [HEOI2016 / TJOI2016] Summation

Source: Luogu P4091 — [HEOI2016 / TJOI2016] 求和


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given a positive integer \(n\), evaluate the double sum \[
f(n) = \sum_{i=0}^n \sum_{j=0}^i \left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\} 2^j \, j! \pmod{998244353},
\] where \(\left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\}\) denotes the Stirling number of the second kind (the number of ways to partition a set of \(i\) labeled elements into \(j\) non-empty unlabeled subsets, with the standard boundary conventions \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 1\) and \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} i \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 0\) for \(i \ge 1\)).

Input Constraints:

\(1 \le n \le 10^5\)
Modulus: \(P = 998244353\) (prime)

Sample Trace (\(n = 2\)): The row sums for \(i = 0, 1, 2\) are \(1\), \(0 + 2 = 2\), and \(0 + 2 + 8 = 10\), giving \(f(2) = 1 + 2 + 10 = 13\).
Target Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time, \(O(n)\) space.



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal (What to look for in the constraints)

Look at the inner sum \(\sum_{j=0}^i \left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\} 2^j j!\). Instead of evaluating \(\left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\}\) directly via an \(O(n^2)\) DP triangle, ask: what combinatorial structure on \(i\) labeled elements partitions them into \(j\) non-empty blocks and orders those \(j\) blocks (accounting for \(j!\)), and how does that help you decouple the row index \(i\) from the column index \(j\)?



Hint 2 — Target Chapter Routing & Initial Setup


Primary Routing: Chapter 06 (§6.4 Stirling Numbers, Falling Factorials & NTT Row/Column Convolution) and Chapter 08 (§8.1 Surjection Inclusion–Exclusion).
Initial Algebraic Setup:

Because \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} i \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 0\) whenever \(j > i\), we can extend the inner summation limit of \(j\) from \(i\) to \(n\) without changing the value of the sum, and then swap the \(i\) and \(j\) sums: \[
f(n) = \sum_{j=0}^n 2^j \sum_{i=0}^n j! \left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\}.
\]
Recall the explicit Inclusion–Exclusion (or EGF convolution) formula for the number of surjections \(j! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} i \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) from an \(i\)-element set onto a \(j\)-element set: \[
j! \left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\} = \sum_{k=0}^j (-1)^{j-k} \binom{j}{k} k^i.
\]





Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Reduction & Edge Cases


Decoupling \((j - k)\) and \(k\) via Geometric Series: Substitute the surjection formula into \(f(n)\) and expand \(\binom{j}{k} = \frac{j!}{k!(j-k)!}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
f(n) &= \sum_{j=0}^n 2^j j! \sum_{k=0}^j \frac{(-1)^{j-k}}{(j-k)!} \cdot \frac{1}{k!} \left( \sum_{i=0}^n k^i \right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Closed-Form Inner Geometric Sum \(S(k) = \sum_{i=0}^n k^i\): For each fixed \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}\), the innermost sum over \(i\) no longer depends on \(j\)! It is a simple geometric progression of length \(n + 1\): \[
S(k) := \sum_{i=0}^n k^i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k = 0 \text{ (using } 0^0 = 1\text{)}, \\ n + 1 & \text{if } k = 1, \\ \dfrac{k^{n+1} - 1}{k - 1} & \text{if } k \ge 2. \end{cases}
\]
Final Convolution Shape: Define two degree-\(n\) polynomials \(A(x)\) and \(B(x)\) with coefficients \[
A_r = \frac{(-1)^r}{r!}, \qquad B_k = \frac{S(k)}{k!}.
\] Then the inner sum over \(k\) is literally the Cauchy convolution \([x^j]\big(A(x) B(x)\big)\), and \(f(n) = \sum_{j=0}^n 2^j j! [x^j]\big(A(x) B(x)\big)\).








NoteComplete Derivation, Algorithm Contract & Complexity Analysis






1. The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Diagnostic Signal: We have a double sum \(\sum_{i=0}^n \sum_{j=0}^i \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} i \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^j j!\) with \(n \le 10^5\) modulo \(998244353\). In single-row Stirling problems, we fix \(i = n\) and compute \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} n \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\}_{j=0}^n\) via a single NTT using \([x^j] \left(\sum_r \frac{(-1)^r}{r!} x^r\right)\left(\sum_k \frac{k^n}{k!} x^k\right)\). Here, \(i\) is not fixed—it is summed from \(0\) to \(n\).
Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Because convolution is a linear operator on the sequence \(B_k^{(i)} = \frac{k^i}{k!}\), summing the output of the convolution over \(i = 0, \dots, n\) is identical to summing the input polynomial \(B^{(i)}(x)\) over \(i = 0, \dots, n\) before performing the convolution! That replaces \(n+1\) separate NTTs with a single NTT on the summed geometric series \(\sum_{i=0}^n k^i\).



2. Step-by-Step Algebraic Derivation

Domain Extension (Zero-Padding the Upper Triangle): For any \(0 \le i < j \le n\), a set of \(i\) elements cannot be partitioned into \(j > i\) non-empty subsets, so \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} i \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 0\). Extending the upper limit of \(j\) from \(i\) to \(n\): \[
f(n) = \sum_{i=0}^n \sum_{j=0}^n \left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\} 2^j \, j!.
\]
EGF / Inclusion–Exclusion Expansion of \(j! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} i \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\): The quantity \(j! \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} i \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) counts ordered \(j\)-tuples of non-empty subsets partitioning \([i]\) (i.e., surjective functions \([i] \twoheadrightarrow [j]\)). In the EGF world, a single non-empty bin has EGF \(e^x - 1\), so \(j\) ordered bins have EGF \((e^x - 1)^j\): \[
j! \left\{ \begin{matrix} i \\ j \end{matrix} \right\} = i! [x^i] (e^x - 1)^j = i! [x^i] \sum_{k=0}^j (-1)^{j-k} \binom{j}{k} e^{kx} = \sum_{k=0}^j (-1)^{j-k} \binom{j}{k} k^i,
\] where \(0^0 = 1\) (since \(e^{0 \cdot x} = 1 = 1 x^0 + 0 x^1 + \dots\)).
Swapping Summations & Factoring the Binomial Coefficient: Substitute this identity into \(f(n)\), write \(\binom{j}{k} = \frac{j!}{k!(j-k)!}\), and bring the \(i\)-sum inside the \(k\)-sum: \[
\begin{aligned}
f(n) &= \sum_{j=0}^n 2^j \sum_{i=0}^n \sum_{k=0}^j (-1)^{j-k} \frac{j!}{k!(j-k)!} k^i \\
&= \sum_{j=0}^n 2^j j! \sum_{k=0}^j \frac{(-1)^{j-k}}{(j-k)!} \cdot \frac{1}{k!} \left( \sum_{i=0}^n k^i \right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Evaluating the Geometric Progression \(S(k) = \sum_{i=0}^n k^i\):

For \(k = 0\): \(S(0) = 0^0 + 0^1 + \dots + 0^n = 1 + 0 + \dots + 0 = 1\).
For \(k = 1\): \(S(1) = \sum_{i=0}^n 1 = n + 1\).
For \(2 \le k \le n\): Since \(k - 1 \in \{1, \dots, n - 1\}\) and \(n \le 10^5 < P = 998244353\), \(k - 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod P\) is invertible in \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times\), yielding \[
S(k) = \frac{k^{n+1} - 1}{k - 1} \pmod P.
\]

1D Cauchy Convolution: Define formal power series \(A(x), B(x) \in \mathbb{F}_P[[x]]\) truncated to degree \(n\): \[
A(x) = \sum_{r=0}^n \frac{(-1)^r}{r!} x^r, \qquad B(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{S(k)}{k!} x^k.
\] Then the inner sum over \(k\) is \([x^j]\big(A(x) B(x)\big)\), and \[
f(n) = \sum_{j=0}^n 2^j \, j! \, [x^j]\big(A(x) B(x)\big) \pmod P.
\]



3. Hand-Checkable Concrete Trace (\(n = 2\))
Let \(n = 2\). By direct enumeration from the definition:

\(i = 0\): \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^0 0! = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1\).
\(i = 1\): \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^0 0! + \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^1 1! = 0 + 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 2\).
\(i = 2\): \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^0 0! + \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^1 1! + \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} 2^2 2! = 0 + 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 4 \cdot 2 = 10\).
Total \(f(2) = 1 + 2 + 10 = 13\).

Now trace the convolution formula for \(n = 2\):

Geometric sums: \(S(0) = 1\), \(S(1) = 2 + 1 = 3\), \(S(2) = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7\).
Polynomials truncated to \(x^2\): \[
A(x) = 1 - x + \frac{1}{2}x^2, \qquad B(x) = 1 + 3x + \frac{7}{2}x^2.
\]
Product \(C(x) = A(x)B(x) \bmod x^3\):

\(C_0 = 1 \cdot 1 = 1\).
\(C_1 = 1 \cdot 3 + (-1) \cdot 1 = 2\).
\(C_2 = 1 \cdot \frac{7}{2} + (-1) \cdot 3 + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 = 4 - 3 = 1\).

Weighted sum \(\sum_{j=0}^2 2^j j! C_j\): \[
(1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1) + (2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2) + (4 \cdot 2 \cdot 1) = 1 + 4 + 8 = 13.
\]







WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: The \(k = 0\) and \(k = 1\) Singularities in \(S(k) = \frac{k^{n+1}-1}{k-1}\)




Division by Zero at \(k = 1\): The rational formula \(\frac{k^{n+1}-1}{k-1}\) divides by \(k - 1 = 0\) when \(k = 1\). Always branch explicitly: set S[1] = n + 1.
Miscomputing \(0^0\) at \(k = 0\): In formal power series \(e^{0 \cdot x} = 1 = \sum_{i \ge 0} \frac{0^i}{i!} x^i\), the convention \(0^0 = 1\) is mandatory so that \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 1\) is included. If you set \(S(0) = 0\) instead of \(S(0) = 1\), you drop the \(i = 0, j = 0\) term and your answer will be off by \(1\).





4. Algorithm Contract

Input: Integer \(n \in [1, 10^5]\).
Output: \(f(n) \bmod 998244353\).

1. The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Diagnostic Signal: We want to sum \(\max_{0 \le i \le n} \min\big(L_T(i), R_T(i)\big)\) over all \(2^q\) completions \(T\) of \(s\). Whenever a problem asks for the sum of a max or min over \(2^q\) configurations, we must convert the non-linear max into a linear sum of indicator variables so that we can swap the sum over configurations with the sum over indices.

Case 2 (\(T[i] = \texttt{)}\)): The prefix gains no (, so \(L_T(i) = L_T(i-1)\), while the suffix loses one ), so \(R_T(i) = R_T(i-1) - 1\). Thus \(\Delta_T(i) = \Delta_T(i-1) - (-1) = \Delta_T(i-1) + 1\).

For \(i > i^*\), \(L_T(i) \ge L_T(i^*)\) and \(R_T(i) \le R_T(i^*)\), so \(\min(L_T(i), R_T(i)) = R_T(i) \le R_T(i^*)\).

\] For a fixed split index \(i \in \{1, \dots, n - 1\}\), inspect the pattern \(s\):

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
Given two integers \(n\) and \(k\), evaluate the power sum \[
S_k(n) = \sum_{i=1}^n i^k = 1^k + 2^k + 3^k + \dots + n^k \pmod{10^9 + 7}.

\(1 \le n \le 10^9\)
\(0 \le k \le 10^6\)

Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal (What to look for in the constraints)

Consider \(S_k(x) = \sum_{i=1}^x i^k\) as a function of the upper limit \(x\). When \(x\) increases by \(1\), the discrete difference \(S_k(x) - S_k(x - 1) = x^k\) is a polynomial of degree \(k\). What does this imply about the algebraic form of \(S_k(x)\), and how many sample values \(S_k(0), S_k(1), \dots\) uniquely determine it for any \(x = n\)?



Hint 2 — Target Chapter Routing & Initial Setup


Primary Routing: Chapter 06 (§6.4 Faulhaber’s Power Sums, Multiplicative Euler Sieve for \(i^k\) & \(O(k)\) Consecutive Lagrange Interpolation).
Polynomial Degree via Finite Differences: Define \(S_k(0) = 0\) and \(S_k(x) = \sum_{i=1}^x i^k\) for integers \(x \ge 1\). Its forward difference is \[
\Delta S_k(x) = S_k(x + 1) - S_k(x) = (x + 1)^k,
\] which is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(k\). Because taking the forward difference \(\Delta\) lowers the degree of any polynomial by \(1\), \(S_k(x)\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(d = k + 1\)!
Sampling Strategy: A polynomial of degree \(d = k + 1\) is uniquely determined by its values at \(d + 1 = k + 2\) consecutive integer points \(x = 0, 1, 2, \dots, k + 1\) (or \(x = 1, 2, \dots, k + 2\)).




Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Reduction & Edge Cases


\(O(k)\) Consecutive-Node Lagrange Interpolation Formula: Given sample values \(y_i = S_k(i)\) at nodes \(x_i = i\) for \(i = 0, 1, \dots, d\) (where \(d = k + 1\)), the Lagrange interpolation formula at \(x = n > d\) is \[
S_k(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} y_i \prod_{\substack{0 \le j \le d \\ j \neq i}} \frac{n - j}{i - j}.
\] Notice how the numerator and denominator simplify for consecutive nodes \(j = 0, 1, \dots, d\):

Denominator: For \(j < i\), the product of \((i - j)\) is \(i \cdot (i - 1) \cdots 1 = i!\). For \(j > i\), the product of \((i - j)\) is \((-1)(-2)\cdots(-(d - i)) = (-1)^{d - i} (d - i)!\).
Numerator: Define prefix products \(\text{pref}[i] = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1} (n - j)\) and suffix products \(\text{suff}[i] = \prod_{j=i+1}^{d} (n - j)\). Then \(\prod_{j \neq i} (n - j) = \text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i]\).

When \(k = 0\), \(i^0 = 1\) for \(1 \le i \le n\) (and \(S_0(0) = 0\)), so \(S_0(n) = n\) has degree \(1 = k + 1\).
When \(n \le k + 1\), \((n - j)\) vanishes at \(j = n\), so simply return the precomputed sample \(y_n\) directly before building prefix/suffix products!

1. Why \(S_k(n)\) Is a Degree-\((k+1)\) Polynomial in \(n\)
Let \(V_{k+1}\) be the \((k+2)\)-dimensional \(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector space of polynomials in \(x\) of degree at most \(k + 1\), and let \(V_{k+1}^0 = \{P \in V_{k+1} : P(0) = 0\}\) be the \((k+1)\)-dimensional subspace of polynomials with zero constant term. Consider the forward difference operator \(\Delta : V_{k+1}^0 \to V_k\) defined by \((\Delta P)(x) = P(x + 1) - P(x)\).

For any monomial \(x^m\) (\(m \ge 1\)), \(\Delta(x^m) = (x + 1)^m - x^m = m x^{m-1} + \binom{m}{2} x^{m-2} + \dots + 1\) has leading term \(m x^{m-1} \neq 0\) in characteristic \(0\) (and in \(\mathbb{F}_P\) whenever \(m \le k + 1 < P\)).
Therefore, \(\Delta : V_{k+1}^0 \to V_k\) is a linear isomorphism!
Since \((x + 1)^k \in V_k\), there exists a unique polynomial \(F_k(x) \in V_{k+1}^0\) such that \(F_k(x + 1) - F_k(x) = (x + 1)^k\) for all \(x\). By telescoping from \(x = 0\) to \(n - 1\), \(F_k(n) = \sum_{i=1}^n i^k = S_k(n)\) for every integer \(n \ge 0\).

Because \(k \le 10^6\) and \(P = 10^9 + 7 > k + 1\), all denominators \(1, 2, \dots, k + 1\) in the polynomial coefficients of \(F_k(x)\) are units in \(\mathbb{F}_P^\times\), so \(F_k(x) \bmod P\) is a well-defined polynomial in \(\mathbb{F}_P[x]\) of degree \(d = k + 1\).

F_k(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} y_i \, \ell_i(n), \qquad \text{where } \ell_i(n) = \prod_{\substack{0 \le j \le d \\ j \neq i}} \frac{n - j}{i - j}.
\] Splitting the product over \(j \in \{0, \dots, d\} \setminus \{i\}\) into \(j < i\) and \(j > i\):

Numerator: \[
\prod_{j=0}^{i-1} (n - j) \cdot \prod_{j=i+1}^{d} (n - j) = \text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i],
\] where \(\text{pref}[0] = 1\), \(\text{pref}[i] = \text{pref}[i-1] \cdot (n - (i - 1))\) for \(1 \le i \le d\), and \(\text{suff}[d] = 1\), \(\text{suff}[i] = \text{suff}[i+1] \cdot (n - (i + 1))\) for \(d - 1 \ge i \ge 0\).
Denominator: \[
\prod_{j=0}^{i-1} (i - j) \cdot \prod_{j=i+1}^{d} (i - j) = (i \cdot (i-1) \cdots 1) \cdot \big((-1)(-2)\cdots(-(d-i))\big) = (-1)^{d-i} \, i! \, (d - i)!.
\]

Combining these pieces gives the division-free per-term evaluation: \[
F_k(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} (-1)^{d - i} \, y_i \cdot \text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i] \cdot \text{invFact}[i] \cdot \text{invFact}[d - i] \pmod P.
\]

\(y_0 = 0\), \(y_1 = 1^2 = 1\), \(y_2 = 1 + 4 = 5\), \(y_3 = 5 + 9 = 14\).
For \(n = 4\), the node differences \((4 - j)\) for \(j = 0, 1, 2, 3\) are \(4, 3, 2, 1\).

\(i = 0\): \(y_0 = 0 \implies \text{term}_0 = 0\).
\(i = 1\): \((-1)^{3-1} y_1 \frac{(4-0)(4-2)(4-3)}{1! \, 2!} = (+1) \cdot 1 \cdot \frac{4 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}{2} = +4\).
\(i = 2\): \((-1)^{3-2} y_2 \frac{(4-0)(4-1)(4-3)}{2! \, 1!} = (-1) \cdot 5 \cdot \frac{4 \cdot 3 \cdot 1}{2} = -30\).
\(i = 3\): \((-1)^{3-3} y_3 \frac{(4-0)(4-1)(4-2)}{3! \, 0!} = (+1) \cdot 14 \cdot \frac{4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2}{6} = +56\).

WarningFailure Mode & Remedy: Characteristic Collapse (\(P \le k + 1\)) & \(0/0\) when \(n \le d\)

4. Algorithm Contract

Input: \(n \in [1, 10^9]\), \(k \in [0, 10^6]\), prime \(P = 10^9 + 7\).
Output: \(S_k(n) = \sum_{i=1}^n i^k \bmod P\).
Core Invariant: \(F_k(x) = \sum_{i=1}^x i^k\) is the unique polynomial of degree \(d = k + 1\) with \(F_k(0) = 0\) and forward difference \(\Delta F_k(x) = (x + 1)^k\), determined by \(d + 1\) consecutive evaluations \(y_0, \dots, y_d\).
Step 1 (\(O(k)\) Multiplicative Sieve for \(m^k\) and Sample Values \(y_0..y_d\)): Set \(d = k + 1\), \(y_0 = 0\), \(\text{pw}[1] = 1\). Run a linear sieve up to \(d\): for each prime \(p \le d\), compute \(\text{pw}[p] = p^k \bmod P\) in \(O(\log k)\) time, and for composite \(m = i \cdot p\), set \(\text{pw}[i \cdot p] = \text{pw}[i] \cdot \text{pw}[p] \bmod P\). Accumulate \(y_i = (y_{i-1} + \text{pw}[i]) \bmod P\). (Since \(\pi(d) = O(k / \log k)\), the total time for all prime exponentiations is \(O\!\left(\frac{k}{\log k} \cdot \log k\right) = O(k)\)!)
Step 2 (Short-Circuit): If \(n \le d\), return \(y_n\).
Step 3 (\(O(k)\) Lagrange Evaluation):

Precompute \(\text{invFact}[0..d]\) in \(O(d)\) time.
Compute \(\text{pref}[0..d]\) and \(\text{suff}[0..d]\) in \(O(d)\) time.
Sum \((-1)^{d-i} y_i \cdot \text{pref}[i] \cdot \text{suff}[i] \cdot \text{invFact}[i] \cdot \text{invFact}[d-i] \bmod P\) for \(0 \le i \le d\).

Complexity: \(\Theta(k)\) time and \(\Theta(k)\) space.









Problem CP-II.5 (#100) — Epic Convolution

Source: Codeforces 1054H — Epic Convolution


Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given two integer arrays \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}\) and \(b_0, b_1, \dots, b_{m-1}\), together with an integer base \(c\). Evaluate the bilinear sum \[
S = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} a_i \, b_j \, c^{i^2 j^3} \pmod{490019}.
\] Here \(0^0 = 1\), so whenever \(i = 0\) or \(j = 0\), the exponent \(i^2 j^3 = 0\) and \(c^{i^2 j^3} = c^0 = 1\).

Input Constraints:

\(1 \le n, m \le 10^5\)
\(0 \le a_i, b_j \le 490018\)
\(1 \le c \le 490018\)
Modulus: \(P = 490019\) (prime, with \(P - 1 = 490018 = 2 \times 491 \times 499\))

Sample Trace (\(P = 5, c = 2, a = [1, 2, 1], b = [1, 1, 2]\)): For \(i, j \in \{0, 1, 2\}\), the row sums for \(i = 0, 1, 2\) are \(4, 10, 4\), giving \(4 + 10 + 4 = 18 \equiv 3 \pmod 5\).

Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal (What to look for in the constraints)

Why did the problem setter choose the bizarre modulus \(P = 490019\) instead of \(998244353\) or \(10^9 + 7\)? First, confirm that \(P = 490019\) is prime (\(\sqrt{490019} \approx 700\), and \(P - 1 = 490018 = 2 \times 491 \times 499\)). Because \(P\) is prime and \(1 \le c \le P - 1\), Fermat’s Little Theorem guarantees \(c^{P-1} \equiv 1 \pmod P\). Therefore, the huge exponent \(i^2 j^3\) only matters modulo \(P - 1 = 490018\)! Even better, the product \(i^2 j^3 \bmod (P - 1)\) separates into a function of \(i\) alone (\(I = i^2 \bmod (P - 1)\)) times a function of \(j\) alone (\(J = j^3 \bmod (P - 1)\)).



Hint 2 — Target Chapter Routing & Initial Setup


Primary Routing: Chapter 07 (§7.3 Bluestein’s Chirp-\(Z\) Transform & Index-Calculus Reductions).
Step 1 (Exponent Bucketing modulo \(P - 1\)): Since \(c \not\equiv 0 \pmod P\), for every \(i, j\) we have \[
c^{i^2 j^3} \equiv c^{(i^2 \bmod (P-1)) \cdot (j^3 \bmod (P-1))} \pmod P.
\] Define two bucketed arrays \(A[0..P-2]\) and \(B[0..P-2]\) of length \(M = P - 1 = 490018\) by accumulating \[
A_I = \sum_{\substack{0 \le i < n \\ i^2 \bmod (P-1) = I}} a_i \pmod P, \qquad B_J = \sum_{\substack{0 \le j < m \\ j^3 \bmod (P-1) = J}} b_j \pmod P.
\] Now the original sum becomes a clean bilinear form in \(I\) and \(J\): \[
S = \sum_{I=0}^{P-2} \sum_{J=0}^{P-2} A_I \, B_J \, c^{I \cdot J} \pmod P.
\]




Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Reduction & Edge Cases

How do you turn the multiplicative exponent \(I \cdot J\) into an additive convolution index \(I + J\)? You have two canonical routes from Chapter 07:

Route 1 (Bluestein’s Chirp-\(Z\) Identity — Direct 1D Convolution): Use the triangular-number identity \[
I \cdot J = \binom{I + J}{2} - \binom{I}{2} - \binom{J}{2}.
\] Because \(\binom{k}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2}\) is an integer for every integer \(k \ge 0\), no division by \(2\) modulo \(P - 1\) is needed! Rewrite \(c^{IJ}\) as \[
c^{IJ} = c^{\binom{I+J}{2}} \cdot c^{-\binom{I}{2}} \cdot c^{-\binom{J}{2}} \pmod P.
\] Then \(S = \sum_{K=0}^{2P-4} c^{\binom{K}{2}} \sum_{I+J=K} \left(A_I c^{-\binom{I}{2}}\right)\left(B_J c^{-\binom{J}{2}}\right) \pmod P\), which is a single 1D polynomial multiplication of degree \(P - 2 = 490017\)! (Since \(P = 490019\) is small, max coefficient before mod is \((P-1) P^2 \approx 1.18 \times 10^{17} < 2^{57}\), or after modding inputs by \(P\), max convolution sum is \(490018 \times 490018^2 \approx 1.17 \times 10^{17}\), which fits inside a 2-prime NTT or long double / split-radix FFT!)
Route 2 (CRT + 2D Index-Calculus over \(P - 1 = 2 \times 491 \times 499\)): Notice why \(P - 1 = 2 \times 491 \times 499\) was chosen: \(491\) and \(499\) are both primes! You can separate the \(i = 0\) or \(j = 0\) terms (or indices divisible by \(491\) or \(499\)), and map \(\mathbb{Z}_{491}^\times \times \mathbb{Z}_{499}^\times\) via primitive roots to a \(2 \times 490 \times 498\) 3D cyclic convolution of tiny length \(\approx 2.4 \times 10^5\). However, Route 1 (Bluestein’s CZT) avoids all zero-divisor casework of \(491 \mid I\) and \(499 \mid I\) completely!








NoteComplete Derivation, Algorithm Contract & Complexity Analysis






1. The Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Diagnostic Signal: The summand contains \(c^{i^2 j^3} \pmod P\) where \(P = 490019\) is a moderate prime (\(P \approx 5 \times 10^5\)). Whenever a prime modulus \(P \le 10^6\) appears with a variable exponent, Fermat’s Little Theorem (\(c^{P-1} \equiv 1 \pmod P\)) compresses the exponent space from \(\mathbb{Z}\) down to \(\mathbb{Z}_{P-1}\).
Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Once we compress \(I = i^2 \bmod (P - 1)\) and \(J = j^3 \bmod (P - 1)\), we have \[
S = \sum_{I=0}^{P-2} \sum_{J=0}^{P-2} A_I B_J c^{I J} \pmod P.
\] To convert the product \(IJ\) in the exponent into a sum \(I + J\) suitable for Cauchy convolution, we cannot simply write \(2IJ = (I+J)^2 - I^2 - J^2\) and divide the exponent by \(2\) modulo \(P - 1\), because \(P - 1 = 490018\) is even (\(\gcd(2, P - 1) = 2 \neq 1\), so \(2^{-1} \bmod (P - 1)\) does not exist!). Instead, we use Bluestein’s Binomial Identity over the integers \(\mathbb{Z}\): \[
I \cdot J = \binom{I + J}{2} - \binom{I}{2} - \binom{J}{2} \qquad \text{for all } I, J \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}.
\] Why does this bypass the parity obstruction? Because for every integer \(k\), \(k(k-1)\) is an even integer in \(\mathbb{Z}\), so \(\binom{k}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2} \in \mathbb{Z}\) is already an exact integer before we ever reduce modulo \(P - 1\)!



2. Step-by-Step Algebraic Derivation

Fermat Reduction & Bucketing: Since \(1 \le c \le P - 1\) and \(P = 490019\) is prime, \(\gcd(c, P) = 1\) and \(c^{P-1} \equiv 1 \pmod P\). For each \(0 \le i < n\) and \(0 \le j < m\), let \[
I(i) = i^2 \bmod (P - 1), \qquad J(j) = j^3 \bmod (P - 1).
\] Then \(i^2 j^3 \equiv I(i) J(j) \pmod{P - 1}\), so \(c^{i^2 j^3} \equiv c^{I(i) J(j)} \pmod P\). Grouping terms with the same values of \(I \in [0, P-2]\) and \(J \in [0, P-2]\) gives \[
A_I = \sum_{I(i) = I} a_i \bmod P, \qquad B_J = \sum_{J(j) = J} b_j \pmod P.
\]
Bluestein Decoupling: For any \(I, J \in \{0, 1, \dots, P - 2\}\), the identity \(\binom{I+J}{2} = \frac{(I+J)(I+J-1)}{2} = \frac{I(I-1)}{2} + \frac{J(J-1)}{2} + IJ = \binom{I}{2} + \binom{J}{2} + IJ\) holds in \(\mathbb{Z}\). Since \(c \in \mathbb{F}_P^\times\) is invertible modulo \(P\), let \(c^{-1} = c^{P-2} \bmod P\). Then in \(\mathbb{F}_P\): \[
c^{IJ} \equiv c^{\binom{I+J}{2} \bmod (P-1)} \cdot (c^{-1})^{\binom{I}{2} \bmod (P-1)} \cdot (c^{-1})^{\binom{J}{2} \bmod (P-1)} \pmod P.
\] Define modified coefficient arrays \(\widetilde{A}_I\) and \(\widetilde{B}_J\) for \(0 \le I, J \le P - 2\): \[
\widetilde{A}_I = A_I \cdot (c^{-1})^{\binom{I}{2} \bmod (P-1)} \bmod P, \qquad
\widetilde{B}_J = B_J \cdot (c^{-1})^{\binom{J}{2} \bmod (P-1)} \bmod P.
\]
Cauchy Convolution: Let \(\widetilde{C}(x) = \widetilde{A}(x) \widetilde{B}(x) = \sum_{K=0}^{2P-4} \widetilde{C}_K x^K\), where \(\widetilde{C}_K = \sum_{I+J=K} \widetilde{A}_I \widetilde{B}_J\). Then \[
S = \sum_{K=0}^{2P-4} \left( \widetilde{C}_K \bmod P \right) \cdot c^{\binom{K}{2} \bmod (P-1)} \pmod P.
\]



3. Hand-Checkable Concrete Trace (\(P = 5, c = 2, n = m = 3\))
Suppose we work with toy prime \(P = 5\) (\(P - 1 = 4\)), base \(c = 2\) (\(c^{-1} \equiv 3 \pmod 5\)), and arrays \(a = [1, 2, 1]\), \(b = [1, 1, 2]\) for \(i, j \in \{0, 1, 2\}\).

\(i = 0\) (\(a_0 = 1, i^2 = 0\)): \(1 \cdot (1 \cdot 2^0 + 1 \cdot 2^0 + 2 \cdot 2^0) = 4\).
\(i = 1\) (\(a_1 = 2, i^2 = 1\)): \(2 \cdot (1 \cdot 2^0 + 1 \cdot 2^1 + 2 \cdot 2^8) = 2 \cdot (1 + 2 + 2 \cdot 1) = 10 \equiv 0 \pmod 5\).
\(i = 2\) (\(a_2 = 1, i^2 = 4 \equiv 0 \pmod 4\)): \(1 \cdot (1 \cdot 2^0 + 1 \cdot 2^4 + 2 \cdot 2^{32}) = 1 \cdot (1 + 1 + 2) = 4\).
