Complete Solution to CP-IV.1 (#158 — Luogu P4707 重返现世)

Revealed Paradigm: Chapter 14 (§14.1 & §14.4) — Extended \(K\)-th Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion & Pascal Recurrence State Compression.


1. Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Diagnostic Signal: We want the expected time until at least \(k\) of \(n\) items have been drawn at least once, where \(n \le 1000\) is large, \(\sum p_i = m \le 10000\) is moderate, and \(K := n - k + 1 \le 11\) is tiny!
Reverse-Engineering the Identity: Let \(T_i\) be the first step at which item \(i\) is drawn. We stop at the \(k\)-th smallest value among \(\{T_1, \dots, T_n\}\), which is the \(K\)-th largest value \(\operatorname{kthmax}_{1 \le i \le n} T_i\) where \(K = n - k + 1\). Why do we convert to \(\min_{i \in S} T_i\)? Because for any non-empty subset \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\), the first time \(\min_{i \in S} T_i\) that any item in \(S\) is drawn is a simple geometric random variable with success probability \(\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i \in S} p_i\), so its expectation is immediately:
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{i \in S} T_i\right] = \frac{m}{\sum_{i \in S} p_i}.\]
By the Extended \(K\)-th Min–Max Identity (Ch 14), for any collection of numbers (and by linearity of expectation, random variables):
\[\operatorname{kthmax}_{1 \le i \le n} T_i = \sum_{\substack{S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\} \\ |S| \ge K}} (-1)^{|S| - K} \binom{|S| - 1}{K - 1} \min_{i \in S} T_i.\]

Quick Proof of the \(K\)-th Min–Max Coefficient: Sort the elements so \(T_{(1)} \ge T_{(2)} \ge \dots \ge T_{(n)}\). The element \(T_{(r)}\) is the minimum \(\min_{i \in S} T_i\) if and only if \(S\) contains \(r\) and all other \(|S| - 1\) elements of \(S\) are chosen from \(\{1, \dots, r - 1\}\). Summing over \(s = |S| \ge K\) gives the coefficient of \(T_{(r)}\) as:
\[\sum_{s=K}^{r} (-1)^{s - K} \binom{s - 1}{K - 1} \binom{r - 1}{s - 1} = \binom{r - 1}{K - 1} \sum_{s=K}^{r} (-1)^{s - K} \binom{r - K}{s - K} = \binom{r - 1}{K - 1} (1 - 1)^{r - K} = [r = K].\]




2. Eliminating \(|S|\) from the Knapsack State via Pascal’s Identity
If we computed \(\sum_{S} (-1)^{|S|-K}\binom{|S|-1}{K-1}\) by tracking both the subset weight \(j = \sum_{i \in S} p_i \in [1, m]\) and the subset cardinality \(s = |S| \in [1, n]\), the DP would have \(n \cdot m = 10^7\) states and take \(O(n^2 m) \approx 10^{10}\) operations — a guaranteed TLE.
Notice, however, that \(K \le 11\), and when we insert a new element into \(S\) (increasing \(|S|\) from \(s\) to \(s + 1\)), the coefficient \(f(s, r) := (-1)^{s - r} \binom{s - 1}{r - 1}\) updates using only \(r\) and \(r - 1\)! Specifically, by Pascal’s identity \(\binom{s}{r - 1} = \binom{s - 1}{r - 1} + \binom{s - 1}{r - 2}\):
\[f(s + 1, r) = (-1)^{s + 1 - r} \binom{s}{r - 1} = (-1)^{s + 1 - r} \left[ \binom{s - 1}{r - 1} + \binom{s - 1}{r - 2} \right] = -(-1)^{s - r} \binom{s - 1}{r - 1} + (-1)^{s - (r - 1)} \binom{s - 1}{r - 2} = f(s, r - 1) - f(s, r).\]
To initialize singletons (\(s = 1\)) cleanly without special-casing the first element added to \(S\), observe that for \(s = 1\) we want \(f(1, r) = (-1)^{1 - r} \binom{0}{r - 1} = [r = 1]\). Under the transition \(dp_{\text{new}}[j + p_i][r] = dp[j + p_i][r] + dp[j][r - 1] - dp[j][r]\) for \(1 \le r \le K\), a singleton chosen from the empty set (\(j = 0\)) receives \(dp[0][r - 1] - dp[0][r]\). Setting the unique boundary seed
\[dp[0][0] = +1, \qquad dp[0][r] = 0 \quad (1 \le r \le K), \qquad dp[j][0] = 0 \quad (j \ge 1)\]
automatically produces \(f(1, r) = [r = 1]\) for singletons and preserves \(f(s, r) = (-1)^{s - r}\binom{s - 1}{r - 1}\) for all \(s \ge 1\):

Adding a 1st element (weight \(p_1\)): for \(r = 1\), \(dp[p_1][1] \gets dp[0][0] - dp[0][1] = 1 - 0 = +1 = (-1)^{1-1}\binom{0}{0}\); for \(r \ge 2\), \(dp[p_1][r] \gets dp[0][r-1] - dp[0][r] = 0\).
Adding a 2nd element (weight \(p_2\)) on top of \(p_1\):

For \(r = 1\): \(dp[p_1 + p_2][1] \gets dp[p_1][0] - dp[p_1][1] = 0 - 1 = -1 = (-1)^{2-1}\binom{1}{0}\).
For \(r = 2\): \(dp[p_1 + p_2][2] \gets dp[p_1][1] - dp[p_1][2] = 1 - 0 = +1 = (-1)^{2-2}\binom{1}{1}\). Both match \(f(s, r) = (-1)^{s - r}\binom{s - 1}{r - 1}\) for all \(s \ge 1\) and \(1 \le r \le K\)!








WarningFailure Mode & Remedy — Corrupting \(dp[j][0]\) During the Knapsack Sweep



In the recurrence \(dp_{\text{new}}[j + p_i][r] = dp[j + p_i][r] + dp[j][r - 1] - dp[j][r]\), the index \(r = 0\) is only a boundary seed at \(j = 0\) (\(dp[0][0] = 1\)) to initialize singletons \(s = 1\). You must never update \(dp[j][0]\) for \(j > 0\) (i.e., loop \(r\) only from \(K\) down to \(1\)), so that \(dp[j][0]\) remains identically \(0\) for all \(j \ge 1\)!




3. Algorithm Contract (CP-IV.1)

Input: \(n \le 1000\), threshold \(k \le n\) with \(K = n - k + 1 \le 11\), total weight \(m \le 10000\), and item weights \(p_1, \dots, p_n \ge 1\) (\(\sum p_i = m\)).
Output: The expected stopping time \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{j=1}^m dp[j][K] \cdot m \cdot j^{-1} \bmod 998244353\).
Preconditions: Prime modulus \(p > m\) (here \(p = 998244353\)) so every subset weight \(j \in \{1, \dots, m\}\) is invertible modulo \(p\); boundary seed initialized to dp[0][0] = 1 and dp[j][r] = 0 otherwise, sweeping \(j = \text{cur\_sum}\) down to \(0\) and \(r = K\) down to \(1\) via dp[j + p_i][r] = (dp[j + p_i][r] + dp[j][r - 1] - dp[j][r]) mod p.
Complexity: \(O(n m K)\) time and \(O(m K)\) auxiliary space (\(\le 1.1 \times 10^8\) simple modular additions).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing item \(i\), \(dp[j][r]\) (\(j \ge 1, 1 \le r \le K\)) equals the exact signed sum \(\sum_{S \subseteq \{1, \dots, i\}, \sum_{u \in S} p_u = j} (-1)^{|S|-r}\binom{|S|-1}{r-1}\) over all non-empty subsets of \(\{1, \dots, i\}\) with weight \(j\).
Failure Modes: Updating \(r = 0\) for \(j > 0\) (which corrupts the singleton boundary seed \(dp[j][0] = 0\)), or sweeping \(j\) upwards instead of downwards (which reuses the same item multiple times in a single subset).











NoteClick to Reveal Complete Solution for CP-IV.2 (#169 — Luogu P5326 [ZJOI2019] 开关)





Complete Solution to CP-IV.2 (#169 — Luogu P5326 [ZJOI2019] 开关)

Revealed Paradigm: Chapter 14 (§14.2 & §14.3) — Renewal First-Passage Deconvolution, Parity EGF Factorization & \((1-x)\) Pole Cancellation.


1. Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Diagnostic Signal: We have \(n \le 100\) independent coordinates (switches) where one coordinate is flipped per step with probability \(p_i / P\) (\(P = \sum p_i \le 5 \times 10^4\)), and we want the first hitting time of a target state \(s \in \{0, 1\}^n\).
Why EGF Factorizes Multi-Switch Walks: In an \(m\)-step walk, the multinomial distribution of how many times \((c_1, \dots, c_n)\) each switch is flipped has probability:
\[\frac{m!}{c_1! c_2! \cdots c_n!} \prod_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{p_i}{P}\right)^{c_i}.\]
Because \(m!\) is outside and \(\frac{1}{c_i!}\left(\frac{p_i}{P}\right)^{c_i}\) factors completely across \(i = 1, \dots, n\), the Exponential Generating Function (EGF) of unconstrained \(m\)-step transition probabilities \(\widehat{H}(z) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(X_m = \text{target}) \frac{z^m}{m!}\) is simply the product of \(n\) single-switch hyperbolic functions!



2. Step-by-Step Derivation from EGF to OGF Renewal Deconvolution

Unconstrained Visit and Return EGFs: To be in state \(s_i \in \{0, 1\}\) at step \(m\) starting from \(0\), switch \(i\) must be flipped a number of times \(c_i \equiv s_i \pmod 2\). Since:
\[\sum_{c_i \equiv 0 \pmod 2} \frac{(\lambda_i z)^{c_i}}{c_i!} = \frac{e^{\lambda_i z} + e^{-\lambda_i z}}{2}, \qquad \sum_{c_i \equiv 1 \pmod 2} \frac{(\lambda_i z)^{c_i}}{c_i!} = \frac{e^{\lambda_i z} - e^{-\lambda_i z}}{2}\]
where \(\lambda_i = \frac{p_i}{P}\), the unconstrained transition EGF from \(\mathbf{0}\) to \(s\) and the return EGF from \(s\) to \(s\) are:
\[\widehat{H}_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(z) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{(p_i/P)z} + (-1)^{s_i} e^{-(p_i/P)z}}{2} = \sum_{k=-P}^{P} c_k \, e^{(k/P)z},\]
\[\widehat{H}_{s \to s}(z) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{(p_i/P)z} + e^{-(p_i/P)z}}{2} = \sum_{k=-P}^{P} d_k \, e^{(k/P)z}.\]
Notice that at \(k = P = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i\), the only way to achieve exponent \(+P\) is to pick \(+p_i\) from every factor, so \(c_P = d_P = 2^{-n}\).
Borel–Laplace Conversion from EGF to OGF: To apply renewal deconvolution (Ch 14.3), we need the Ordinary Generating Functions (OGFs):
\[H_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(X_m = s \mid X_0 = \mathbf{0}) x^m = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \left(m! [z^m] \widehat{H}_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(z)\right) x^m.\]
Since \(m! [z^m] e^{(k/P)z} = \left(\frac{k}{P}\right)^m\), summing over \(m \ge 0\) converts each exponential term \(e^{(k/P)z}\) into a rational geometric series \(\frac{1}{1 - (k/P)x}\):
\[H_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(x) = \sum_{k=-P}^{P} \frac{c_k}{1 - \frac{k}{P} x}, \qquad H_{s \to s}(x) = \sum_{k=-P}^{P} \frac{d_k}{1 - \frac{k}{P} x}.\]
Renewal Deconvolution & \((1 - x)\) Pole Cancellation at \(x = 1\): Every walk from \(\mathbf{0}\) to \(s\) decomposes uniquely into a first visit to \(s\) at some time \(T\) followed by an unconstrained return walk from \(s\) to \(s\). Therefore, the PGF \(F(x) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T = m) x^m\) satisfies:
\[H_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(x) = F(x) H_{s \to s}(x) \implies F(x) = \frac{H_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(x)}{H_{s \to s}(x)}.\]
Both \(H_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(x)\) and \(H_{s \to s}(x)\) have a simple pole at \(x = 1\) coming from the \(k = P\) term \(\frac{c_P}{1 - x}\). Following Ch 14.2, multiply numerator and denominator by \((1 - x)\) to define the regular functions \(A(x) = (1 - x) H_{\mathbf{0} \to s}(x)\) and \(B(x) = (1 - x) H_{s \to s}(x)\):
\[A(x) = c_P + (1 - x) \sum_{k=-P}^{P-1} \frac{c_k}{1 - \frac{k}{P} x}, \qquad B(x) = d_P + (1 - x) \sum_{k=-P}^{P-1} \frac{d_k}{1 - \frac{k}{P} x}.\]
Now substitute \(x = 1 + t \bmod t^2\) (so \(1 - x = -t\)):
\[A(1 + t) = c_P - \left(\sum_{k=-P}^{P-1} \frac{c_k}{1 - k/P}\right) t + O(t^2), \qquad B(1 + t) = d_P - \left(\sum_{k=-P}^{P-1} \frac{d_k}{1 - k/P}\right) t + O(t^2).\]
Since \(c_P = d_P = 2^{-n}\), dividing \(A(1 + t)\) by \(B(1 + t)\) modulo \(t^2\) yields:
\[F(1 + t) = \frac{A(1 + t)}{B(1 + t)} = 1 + \frac{1}{d_P} \left(\sum_{k=-P}^{P-1} \frac{d_k - c_k}{1 - k/P}\right) t + O(t^2),\]
from which we read off \(\mathbb{E}[T] = [t^1] F(1 + t)\):
\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = 2^n \sum_{k=-P}^{P-1} \frac{(d_k - c_k) P}{P - k} \pmod{998244353}.}\]



3. Algorithm Contract (CP-IV.2)

Input: \(n \le 100\), target bits \(s_1, \dots, s_n \in \{0, 1\}\), and positive weights \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) with \(\sum p_i = P \le 5 \times 10^4\).
Output: The expected first hitting time \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{k=-P}^{P-1} (D[k] - C[k]) \cdot P \cdot (P - k)^{-1} \bmod 998244353\), where \(C[k] = 2^n c_k\) and \(D[k] = 2^n d_k\) are computed via \(C_{\text{new}}[k] = C[k - p_i] + (-1)^{s_i} C[k + p_i]\) and \(D_{\text{new}}[k] = D[k - p_i] + D[k + p_i]\).
Preconditions: Prime modulus \(p > 2P\) (here \(p = 998244353\)) so \(P - k \in \{1, \dots, 2P\}\) is invertible modulo \(p\), and \(p_i \ge 1\).
Complexity: \(O(n P)\) time and \(O(P)\) auxiliary space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: After processing the first \(i\) switches, \(C[k]\) and \(D[k]\) maintain the exact signed and unsigned subset-sum Laurent polynomials \(\prod_{r=1}^i (z^{p_r} + (-1)^{s_r} z^{-p_r})\) and \(\prod_{r=1}^i (z^{p_r} + z^{-p_r})\) at exponent \(k \in [-P, P]\).
Failure Modes: Including the singular pole index \(k = P\) in the summation (which divides by \(P - P = 0\) instead of cancelling via \(c_P = d_P\)), or forgetting the negative-index offset \(+P\) when indexing \(C[-P \dots P]\) and \(D[-P \dots P]\).











NoteClick to Reveal Complete Solution for CP-IV.3 (#099 — CF 1025G Company Acquisitions)





Complete Solution to CP-IV.3 (#099 — CF 1025G Company Acquisitions)

Revealed Paradigm: Chapter 14 (§14.4) — Additively Separable Martingale Stopping Potential & Optional Stopping.


1. Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Diagnostic Signal: We have a stochastic process on a configuration of active companies with vassal counts \((a_1, \dots, a_k)\) satisfying the conservation law \(\sum_{i=1}^k (a_i + 1) = n\). In each step, a uniformly random pair of active companies interacts, and we want the expected steps until \(k = 1\) (\(a_1 = n - 1\)).
Why Pairwise Symmetry Demands an Additive Potential: Whenever \(k \ge 2\) active companies exist, there are \(\binom{k}{2}\) pairs. If we define a potential \(\Phi(a_1, \dots, a_k) = \sum_{i=1}^k \phi(a_i)\) with \(\phi(0) = 0\), then when an active company with \(b\) vassals is acquired and its \(b\) vassals are liberated as \(b\) independent active companies with \(0\) vassals each, those \(b\) liberated companies contribute \(b \cdot \phi(0) = 0\) to \(\Phi\)! Consequently, when active companies of sizes \(a\) and \(b\) interact, the expected change in \(\Phi\) depends only on \(a\) and \(b\):
\[\mathbb{E}[\Delta \Phi \mid \{a, b\} \text{ chosen}] = \frac{1}{2}\phi(a + 1) + \frac{1}{2}\phi(b + 1) - \phi(a) - \phi(b) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\phi(a + 1) - \phi(a)\right) + \left(\frac{1}{2}\phi(b + 1) - \phi(b)\right).\]



2. Solving the Potential Recurrence & Applying Optional Stopping
To ensure that \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta \Phi \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = +1\) in every state \((a_1, \dots, a_k)\) (so that averaging over all \(\binom{k}{2}\) pairs automatically yields \(+1\)), we simply require each term in the sum to equal \(+\frac{1}{2}\):
\[\frac{1}{2}\phi(a + 1) - \phi(a) = \frac{1}{2} \iff \phi(a + 1) = 2\phi(a) + 1 \quad (a \ge 0).\]
Together with the boundary requirement \(\phi(0) = 0\), this first-order linear recurrence has the unique solution:
\[\phi(a) = 2^a - 1.\]
Since \(M_t := \Phi(X_t) - t\) is a martingale and the Markov chain is finite and absorbing (reaching the unique terminal state with \(1\) active company of size \(a_1 = n - 1\) in finite expected time), Doob’s Optional Stopping Theorem (Ch 14.4) gives:
\[\mathbb{E}[\Phi(X_T) - T] = \Phi(X_0) \implies \boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = (2^{n - 1} - 1) - \sum_{\text{active } i} (2^{a_i} - 1) \pmod{10^9 + 7}.}\]


3. Algorithm Contract (CP-IV.3)

Input: \(n \ge 2\), and for each company \(j \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) either -1 (active) or the index of its master company.
Output: The expected number of acquisitions until termination \(\mathbb{E}[T] = (2^{n-1} - 1) - \sum_{\text{active } i} (2^{a_i} - 1) \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).
Preconditions: The initial graph is a valid collection of stars (\(\sum_{\text{active } i} (a_i + 1) = n\)) and the modulus \(10^9 + 7\) is prime.
Complexity: \(O(n)\) time and \(O(n)\) space.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Because \(\phi(0) = 0\) and \(\frac{1}{2}\phi(a+1) - \phi(a) = \frac{1}{2}\), every random acquisition between active companies of sizes \(a\) and \(b\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\Phi(X_{t+1}) - \Phi(X_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = +1\), making \(M_t = \Phi(X_t) - t\) an exact martingale.

Appending one mandatory delimiter 0 at the end of the interval decomposes the string into \(c + 1\) blocks from \(\{0, 10, 110, \dots, 1^{k-1}0\}\). \[\sum_{L=0}^{\infty} P_L(z) u^L = \frac{1 + u z + \dots + (u z)^{k-1}}{1 - u(1 + u z + \dots + (u z)^{k-1})} = \frac{1 - (u z)^k}{1 - u(1 + z) + u^{k+1} z^k}.\]

\[Q_L(x) = \widetilde{F}_L(x) - \widetilde{F}_{L - k}(x).\]

Exactly \(k\) of the \(W - c_i\) initial zeros are flipped an odd number of times (becoming \(1\)s), and \(W - c_i - k\) are flipped an even number of times (staying \(0\)s). \[p_i(y) = \sum_{\substack{0 \le j \le c_i, \, 0 \le k \le W - c_i \\ c_i - j + k = A_i}} \binom{c_i}{j} \binom{W - c_i}{k} y^{j + k}.\]

\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T] = \frac{1}{b_N} \sum_{k=-N}^{N-1} \frac{(b_k - a_k) N}{N - k} \pmod{998244353}.}\]

Therefore, the sum of all small-pole residues (including the hidden pole at \(z = 0\) when \(a \ge p\), automatically resolving Failure Mode #15!) equals minus the residue at the single large root \(z_{\text{large}}(t) = 1 - w(t)\):
\[D_{p, a}(t) = -\operatorname{Res}_{z = 1 - w(t)} \frac{z^{p - 1 - a}}{z^p(1 - z) - t} = -\left.\frac{z^{p - 1 - a}}{p z^{p - 1} - (p + 1) z^p}\right|_{z = 1 - w(t)} = \frac{(1 - w(t))^{-a}}{(p + 1)(1 - w(t)) - p} = \boxed{\frac{(1 - w(t))^{-a}}{1 - (p + 1) w(t)}.}\]
Now let us extract \([t^n] \frac{A(w(t))}{1 - (p + 1) w(t)}\) for any polynomial \(A(w) = \sum_{j=0}^d c_j w^j\) using Form 1 of Lagrange Inversion (Ch 11) on \(w(t) = t \Phi(w(t))\) with \(\Phi(w) = (1 - w)^{-p}\): Notice that the Lagrange Jacobian factor is:
\[1 - \frac{w \Phi'(w)}{\Phi(w)} = 1 - \frac{p w}{1 - w} = \frac{1 - (p + 1) w}{1 - w}.\]
Writing \(\frac{A(w)}{1 - (p + 1)w} = \frac{A(w)}{1 - w} \cdot \left(1 - \frac{w \Phi'(w)}{\Phi(w)}\right)^{-1}\), Form 1 of Lagrange Inversion (Ch 11 / Ch 17.1 Form 2) cancels \(1 - (p + 1)w\) completely:
\[[t^n] \frac{A(w(t))}{1 - (p + 1) w(t)} = [w^n] \left( \frac{A(w)}{1 - w} \cdot \Phi(w)^n \right) = [w^n] \frac{A(w)}{(1 - w)^{p n + 1}} = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, d)} c_j \binom{(p + 1) n - j}{n - j}.\]
In particular, for \(A(w) = (1 - w)^{-a}\), \([t^n] D_{p, a}(t) = [w^n] (1 - w)^{-(p n + a + 1)} = \binom{(p + 1)n + a}{n}\).






WarningFailure Mode & Remedy — Forgetting the Pole at \(z = 0\) When \(a \ge p\) (Ch 16 Failure Mode #15)



If you attempt to compute \([z^{-1}] \frac{z^{p - 1 - a}}{z^p(1 - z) - t}\) for \(a \ge p\) by summing only over the \(p\) roots \(z_1(t), \dots, z_p(t) \sim \zeta_p^r t^{1/p}\) of \(z^p(1 - z) - t = 0\), your answer will be wrong because \(z^{p - 1 - a} = \frac{1}{z^{a + 1 - p}}\) introduces an additional small pole at \(z = 0\)! By contrast, using the Global Residue Theorem at the large root \(z_{\text{large}}(t) = 1 - w(t)\) (since \(\operatorname{Res}_{z = \infty} = 0\) for all \(a \ge 0\)) automatically captures the sum of all small-pole residues, including \(z = 0\)!




3. Algorithm Contract (CP-IV.7)

Input: Slope parameter \(p \ge 1\), shift \(a \ge 0\), degree bound \(N \le 10^5\), and polynomial \(A(w) = \sum_{j=0}^d c_j w^j\) (\(d \le 10^5\)).
Output: Ray diagonal coefficients \([t^n] D_{p, a}(t) = \binom{(p+1)n + a}{n} \bmod 998244353\) and general Fuss–Catalan weighted coefficients \([t^n] \frac{A(w(t))}{1 - (p+1)w(t)} = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(n, d)} c_j \binom{(p+1)n - j}{n - j} \bmod 998244353\).
Preconditions: Prime modulus \(p_{\text{mod}} > (p+1)N + a\) (here \(p_{\text{mod}} = 998244353\)) and \(a \ge 0\) (so \(\operatorname{Res}_{z = \infty} G(z; t) = 0\)).
Complexity: \(O((p+1)N + a)\) factorial precomputation, \(O(1)\) per ray query \([t^n] D_{p,a}(t)\), and \(O(N \log N)\) time / \(O(N)\) space for full series evaluation of \(\frac{A(w(t))}{1 - (p+1)w(t)} \bmod t^{N+1}\).
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Under the Furstenberg substitution \(x = z, y = t/z^p\), the rational 1-form \(\frac{z^{p-1-a} dz}{z^p(1-z)-t}\) has \(\operatorname{Res}_{z=\infty} = 0\) for all \(a \ge 0\), so the sum of all small-pole residues equals minus the residue at the unique large root \(z_{\text{large}}(t) = 1 - w(t)\) where \(w(t) = t(1 - w(t))^{-p}\).
Failure Modes: Summing only over the \(p\) Puiseux roots \(z_r(t) \sim \zeta_p^r t^{1/p}\) when \(a \ge p\) and missing the small pole at \(z = 0\) (Ch 16 Failure Mode #15); forgetting the minus sign in \(D_{p, a}(t) = -\operatorname{Res}_{z = z_{\text{large}}(t)} G(z; t)\).











NoteClick to Reveal Complete Solution for CP-IV.8 (#082 — Toyota 2023 Spring Final E Replace Digits)





Complete Solution to CP-IV.8 (#082 — Toyota 2023 Spring Final E Replace Digits)

Revealed Paradigm: Chapter 15 (§15.3 1-Small-Root Kernel Method & §15.4 Raney’s Cycle Lemma / Łukasiewicz Walks) + Chapter 11 (Lagrange Inversion).


1. Diagnostic Signal & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

The Diagnostic Signal: Each operation of type \(d\) pops \(1\) digit from the stack and pushes \(k_d \ge 0\) new digits, changing the stack size by \(\Delta_d = k_d - 1 \in \{-1, 0, +1, \dots, +8\}\). The stack starts with \(s_0 \ge 1\) digits and must remain non-empty (\(\ge 1\) before each step) throughout \(N = \sum_d c_d\) steps.
Why \(\Delta_d \ge -1\) Is the Exact Signature of a 1-Small-Root Kernel / Łukasiewicz Walk: Look at the step sizes \(\Delta_d = k_d - 1 \ge -1\). Although an operation can increase the stack size by \(+8\), it can decrease the stack size by at most \(-1\)! In the language of Ch 15.3 & Ch 15.4:

If we read the walk in the direction where steps are \(x_i = 1 - k_{d_i} \le +1\) (or if the net drop from initial stack size \(s_0\) to final stack size \(0\) is \(\Delta = s_0 = \sum_{i=1}^N (1 - k_{d_i}) > 0\)), the stack-positivity condition is the Łukasiewicz prefix condition \(\sum_{j=1}^m x_j < s_0\) for \(1 \le m < N\).
Even when the walk ends at a positive final stack size \(s_N = s_0 + \sum_{d} c_d (k_d - 1) > 0\), because downward steps are bounded by \(-1\), any walk cannot jump from \(> 0\) to \(< 0\) without hitting \(0\) exactly!




2. Both Regimes: Fixed-Multiplicity Raney’s Cycle Lemma & Bivariate Kernel Method

Regime 1: Consuming the Stack (\(s_N = 0\)) or Reversed Forest Encoding via Raney’s Cycle Lemma (Ch 15.4): Suppose \(N\) operations reduce the stack by a net drop of \(\Delta = \sum_{d} c_d (1 - k_d) = s_0 > 0\) (consuming the \(s_0\) initial digits down to \(0\) at step \(N\), i.e., a forest of \(s_0\) replacement trees). Every operation of type \(d\) has \(k_d\) children, contributing step \(x_i = 1 - k_{d_i} \le 1\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^N x_i = \Delta > 0\). Because cyclic shifts of \((d_1, \dots, d_N)\) preserve the exact multiset counts \((c_0, c_1, \dots, c_9)\), Raney’s Cycle Lemma (Ch 15.4) guarantees that in every cyclic orbit of length \(N\), exactly a \(\frac{\Delta}{N}\) fraction of the cyclic shifts satisfy the strict prefix positivity condition! Therefore, out of all \(\binom{N}{c_0, c_1, \dots, c_9} = \frac{N!}{\prod_d c_d!}\) multiset permutations, the number of valid sequences is simply:
\[\boxed{\text{Valid Sequences} = \frac{\Delta}{N} \frac{N!}{\prod_{d} c_d!} \pmod{998244353}.}\]

Tracking the Decimal Value via \(2 \times 2\) Affine Matrices: In the full version of Toyota 2023 Spring Final E, each operation \(d\) replaces a popped digit with a decimal string of length \(k_d\) and numerical value \(\text{val}_d\), acting on the accumulated decimal value \(X\) via the affine map \(T_d(X) = 10^{k_d} X + \text{val}_d\), or in \(2 \times 2\) matrix form:
\[M_d = \begin{pmatrix} 10^{k_d} & \text{val}_d \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\]
In the preorder traversal of the replacement forest, the \(i\)-th operation’s \(\text{val}_{d_i}\) is multiplied by \(10^{\sum_{j > i} k_{d_j}}\). By linearity of expectation over which operation \(d\) sits at position \(i\) and applying Raney’s Lemma to the remaining \(N - 1\) steps, the sum of decimal values over all valid sequences is computed in \(O(N)\) time!

Regime 2: General Weighted Steps & Positive Final Altitude via the 1D Kernel Method (Ch 15.3 Regime A): What if each step is chosen with weight \(w_d\) from the step polynomial \(S(y) = \sum_{d} w_d y^{k_d - 1} = y^{-1} \Phi(y)\) (where \(\Phi(y) = \sum_d w_d y^{k_d}\)), starting at altitude \(s_0 - 1 \ge 0\) and required to stay \(\ge 0\) for all \(N\) steps regardless of the final altitude? Let \(F(x, y) = \sum_{n, j \ge 0} f_{n, j} x^n y^j \in K[y][[x]]\) be the bivariate generating function of walks staying at altitude \(j \ge 0\). Multiplying the transition by \(y\) to clear the single negative power \(y^{-1}\) yields the 1-Boundary Kernel Equation (Ch 15.3):
\[\big(y - x \Phi(y)\big) F(x, y) = y^{s_0} - x w_0 F(x, 0).\]
As \(x \to 0\), the kernel \(K(x, y) = y - x \Phi(y) = 0\) has a unique small root \(y = y_0(x) \in K[[x]]\) satisfying:
\[y_0(x) = x \Phi(y_0(x)).\]
Substituting \(y = y_0(x)\) into the kernel equation annihilates the left-hand side and solves for the boundary series \(F(x, 0)\) immediately:
\[y_0(x)^{s_0} - x w_0 F(x, 0) = 0 \implies x w_0 F(x, 0) = y_0(x)^{s_0}.\]
Substituting this back into the kernel equation at \(y = 1\) gives the OGF of total surviving walks of length \(n\):
\[F(x, 1) = \frac{1 - y_0(x)^{s_0}}{1 - x \Phi(1)},\]
where \([x^m] y_0(x)^{s_0} = \frac{s_0}{m} [y^{m - s_0}] \Phi(y)^m\) by Ch 11 Lagrange Inversion!



3. Algorithm Contract (CP-IV.8)

Input: Operation counts \(c_d\), replacement lengths \(k_d \ge 0\), decimal values \(\text{val}_d\) (\(\sum c_d = N \le 2 \times 10^5\)), and initial stack size \(s_0 \ge 1\).
Output: In Regime 1 (fixed multiset consuming stack by \(\Delta = \sum c_d(1 - k_d) = s_0 > 0\)), the valid sequence count \(\frac{\Delta}{N}\frac{N!}{\prod c_d!} \bmod 998244353\) (and total decimal value via \(O(N)\) prefix-sum DP); in Regime 2 (weighted step polynomial \(\Phi(y)\)), the surviving walk counts \([x^N] \frac{1 - y_0(x)^{s_0}}{1 - x\Phi(1)} \bmod 998244353\).
Preconditions: Downward step size bounded by \(-1\) (\(\Delta_d = k_d - 1 \ge -1\), i.e., \(k = 1\) negative power in \(S(y) = y^{-1}\Phi(y)\)), and prime modulus \(p > N\) (here \(p = 998244353\)).
Complexity: \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space for fixed-multiplicity Raney extraction; \(O(N \log N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space for general weighted 1D Kernel + LIF extraction.
Loop / Algebraic Invariant: Because downward steps are bounded by \(-1\), the bivariate walk kernel \(K(x, y) = y - x\Phi(y) = 0\) has a unique small root \(y_0(x) = x\Phi(y_0(x))\) in \(K[[x]]\) that annihilates the boundary unknown \(x w_0 F(x, 0) = y_0(x)^{s_0}\), while in the fixed-multiset regime every cyclic orbit of net drop \(\Delta > 0\) contains an exact \(\Delta/N\) fraction of valid Łukasiewicz walks.
Failure Modes: Confusing upward step size \(+8\) with the number of small roots of the kernel \(K(x, y) = y - x\Phi(y) = 0\) (which depends only on the maximum downward step \(k = 1\)); applying naive reflection principle to asymmetric Łukasiewicz steps \(\Delta_d \in \{-1, 0, +1, \dots, +8\}\).

Review your Stage 1 scratch-paper triage against the rubric below. For any blind spot you encountered, revisit the targeted Part IV sub-section before moving on to Part V (Chapters 18–21):







If You Experienced This Diagnostic Blind Spot…
Targeted Remedy in Part IV (Ch 14–Ch 17)




Missed the \(K\)-th Min–Max reduction or got \(O(n^2 m)\) TLE on CP-IV.1 (Luogu P4707) by tracking subset size \(\lvert S \rvert\) explicitly in the knapsack state
Re-read Ch 14 §14.1 & §14.4: Whenever \(K = n - k + 1 \le 11\) is small, update the signed binomial coefficient \((-1)^{\lvert S \rvert - r}\binom{\lvert S \rvert - 1}{r - 1}\) in-place via Pascal’s recurrence \(dp_{\text{new}}[j + p_i][r] = dp[j + p_i][r] + dp[j][r - 1] - dp[j][r]\).


Tried to differentiate \(F(x) = H_{\mathbf{0}\to s}(x)/H_{s\to s}(x)\) directly at \(x = 1\) on CP-IV.2 (Luogu P5326) or CP-IV.6 (ARC 136 F) and hit a \(0/0\) singularity
Re-read Ch 14 §14.2 & §14.3 (Formal Taylor Shift & Renewal Deconvolution): Both \(H_{\mathbf{0}\to s}(x)\) and \(H_{s\to s}(x)\) have a simple pole \(\frac{c_P}{1 - x}\) at \(x = 1\). Always multiply numerator and denominator by \((1 - x)\) and expand at \(x = 1 + t \bmod t^2\)!


Attempted to build a full Markov transition matrix on CP-IV.3 (CF 1025G) or CP-IV.4 (CF 1479E) instead of an additively separable martingale potential \(\Phi = \sum f(a_i)\)
Re-read Ch 14 §14.4 (Martingale Stopping Potentials): When a partition \(\sum a_i = N\) evolves by pairwise or size-proportional moves, set \(\Phi = \sum f(a_i)\) with \(f(0) = 0\), use conservation-law gauge freedom (\(f(s) \mapsto f(s) + c s\)) to kill the inhomogeneous constant, and reduce the 2nd-order equation for \(f\) to a 1st-order ratio for \(g(s) = f(s+1) - f(s)\).


Did not know how to handle a multi-state target set \(\mathcal{T}\) in CP-IV.6 (ARC 136 F)
Re-read Ch 14 §14.3 & Ch 16 §16.1: Set-hitting renewal \(F(x) = H_{S \to \mathcal{T}}(x) / H_{t_0 \to \mathcal{T}}(x)\) holds whenever the target set \(\mathcal{T}\) is an orbit under a symmetry of the Markov chain (here, column permutations within each row), making \(H_{t_0 \to \mathcal{T}}(x)\) independent of \(t_0 \in \mathcal{T}\).


Tried to sum over all \(p\) fractional Puiseux small roots \(z_r(t) \sim \zeta_p^r t^{1/p}\) (or missed the \(z = 0\) pole for \(a \ge p\)) on CP-IV.7 (yukicoder 2104)
Re-read Ch 16 §16.4 (Furstenberg Diagonal Theorem & Failure Mode #15): Whenever \(\operatorname{Res}_{z = \infty} G(z; t) = 0\) and there is only \(1\) large root \(z_{\text{large}}(t) = 1 - w(t) \in K[[t]]\), use the Global Residue Theorem on \(\mathbb{P}^1\) to replace the sum of all small-pole residues by \(-\operatorname{Res}_{z = 1 - w(t)} G(z; t)\)!


Got stuck on upward steps \(+1, \dots, +8\) in CP-IV.8 (Toyota 2023 Spring Final E) and thought reflection or multi-root kernel elimination was needed
Re-read Ch 15 §15.3 & §15.4 (1D Kernel Method & Raney’s Cycle Lemma): The number of small roots of \(K(x, y) = 0\) equals the maximum downward step size \(k\), not the upward step size \(m\)! Because downward steps are at most \(-1\) (\(k = 1\)), there is only one small root \(y_0(x) = x \Phi(y_0(x))\), so Raney’s Cycle Lemma and 1D LIF apply directly!

Problem CP-VI.1 (#102) — Codeforces 1097G: Vladislav and a Great Legend

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given an unrooted tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(n\) vertices labeled \(1, 2, \dots, n\) and an integer \(k\). For any non-empty subset of vertices \(X \subseteq V\) (\(X \ne \emptyset\)), let \(f(X)\) denote the number of edges in the minimal connected subgraph of \(T\) that contains all vertices in \(X\).
Compute the sum of the \(k\)-th powers of \(f(X)\) over all \(2^n - 1\) non-empty vertex subsets: \[S = \sum_{\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V} f(X)^k \pmod{10^9 + 7}.\]

Constraints: \(2 \le n \le 10^5\), \(1 \le k \le 200\), modulus \(P = 10^9 + 7\).
Target Complexity: \(O(n k)\) time and \(O(n k)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Consider a path tree on \(n = 3\) vertices with edges \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 3)\), and exponent \(k = 2\). We inspect all \(2^3 - 1 = 7\) non-empty subsets \(X \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}\):

Singletons \(\{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}\): Each requires \(0\) edges to connect, so \(f(X) = 0\) and \(f(X)^2 = 0\).
Adjacent pairs \(\{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\}\): Each spans \(1\) edge, so \(f(X) = 1\) and \(f(X)^2 = 1\).
Endpoint pair and full set \(\{1, 3\}, \{1, 2, 3\}\): Both require both edges \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 3)\) to connect, so \(f(X) = 2\) and \(f(X)^2 = 4\).

Summing over all \(7\) subsets gives \(S = 3 \cdot 0^2 + 2 \cdot 1^2 + 2 \cdot 2^2 = 0 + 2 + 8 = 10\).


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

Why is \(f(X)^k\) difficult to maintain directly in a bottom-up subtree recursion? Because when an edge \(e\) is added to the minimal subgraph spanning \(X\), \((f(X) + 1)^k\) expands into all lower powers, and whether \(e\) belongs to the minimal subgraph of \(X\) depends on whether \(X\) has at least one vertex on both sides of \(e\).
Look at the small exponent bound \(k \le 200\) alongside \(n \le 10^5\). Instead of raising \(f(X)\) to the \(k\)-th power at the end, how can you rewrite \(m^k\) as a linear combination of choosing unordered subsets of \(j\) edges (\(0 \le j \le k\)) from the \(m = f(X)\) edges spanned by \(X\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Use the ordinary-power-to-binomial expansion via Stirling numbers of the second kind: \[f(X)^k = \sum_{j=0}^k \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} j! \binom{f(X)}{j}.\] By swapping the order of summation, we only need to compute for each \(j \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}\) the total count \[C_j = \sum_{\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V} \binom{f(X)}{j},\] which counts pairs \((X, F)\) where \(\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V\) is a non-empty vertex set and \(F \subseteq E\) is a set of \(j\) edges all contained inside the minimal connected subgraph spanning \(X\).
Root the tree at vertex \(1\). For a fixed pair \((X, F)\), let \(u = \operatorname{LCA}(X)\) be the lowest common ancestor of all vertices in \(X\). Then \(X\) lies entirely inside the subtree \(T_u\), and \(F\) lies inside \(E(T_u)\). To maintain this bottom-up, define the subtree polynomial \(P_u(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(|E(T_u)|, k)} dp[u][j] x^j\), where \(dp[u][j]\) counts pairs \((X_u, F_u)\) with \(\emptyset \ne X_u \subseteq V(T_u)\) and \(F_u \subseteq E(T_u)\) of size \(j\) such that every edge in \(F_u\) has at least one vertex of \(X_u\) in its lower endpoint’s subtree.



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

When attaching a child \(v\) to \(u\) via edge \(e = (u, v)\):

If \(X \cap V(T_v) = \emptyset\), then no edge in \(T_v \cup \{e\}\) can be chosen at all (contribution \(1\)). If \(X \cap V(T_v) \ne \emptyset\), \(P_v(x)\) already counts non-empty choices inside \(T_v\), so multiplying \(P_v(x)\) by \((1 + x)\) accounts for either excluding (\(1\)) or including (\(x\)) the parent edge \(e = (u, v)\): \[Q_v(x) = P_v(x)(1 + x).\]
Multiply \(1 + P_u(x)\) across all children \(v\) of \(u\), truncating to degree \(\min(\operatorname{sz}(u) - 1, k)\) at each step.
Notice when a configuration is invalid at the global level: if \(X\) lies entirely inside a single child’s subtree \(T_v\) (so \(u\) is not in \(X\) and no other child of \(u\) contains a vertex of \(X\)), then edges in \(T_v \cup \{(u, v)\}\) lying above \(\operatorname{LCA}(X)\) are NOT in the minimal subgraph spanning \(X\). Specifically, any pair where \(X \subseteq V(T_v)\) and the edge \((u, v)\) is chosen above \(T_v\) is overcounted by \(Q_v(x) - P_v(x) = x P_v(x)\). Subtracting \(x P_v(x)\) from the global accumulator at each child \(v \ne 1\) and adding \(P_1(x)\) at the root eliminates all invalid upward extensions.
Because each multiplication at \((u, v)\) has degrees bounded by \(\min(\operatorname{sz}_{\text{cur}}(u), k)\) and \(\min(\operatorname{sz}(v), k)\), the classical LCA pair-counting lemma bounds the total work across the entire tree by \(O(n k)\).






Problem CP-VI.2 (#121) — Codeforces 1553I: Stairs

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
In a permutation \(p = (p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n)\) of \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\), a stair is a maximal contiguous subsegment \(p[l \dots r]\) (\(1 \le l \le r \le n\)) whose values are consecutive integers in either strictly increasing order (\(p_{i+1} = p_i + 1\) for all \(l \le i < r\)) or strictly decreasing order (\(p_{i+1} = p_i - 1\) for all \(l \le i < r\)). Because stairs are maximal, every index \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) belongs to a unique stair; let its length be \(r - l + 1\).
You are given a target array \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\). Count the number of permutations \(p\) of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) whose stair lengths at every index \(i\) equal \(a_i\), modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 10^5\), \(1 \le a_i \le n\), prime modulus \(P = 998244353\).
Target Complexity: \(O(n \log^2 n)\) time and \(O(n \log n)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Let \(n = 3\) and \(a = (2, 2, 1)\).

Indices \(1\) and \(2\) must form a stair of length \(2\), and index \(3\) must form a stair of length \(1\).
Among all \(3! = 6\) permutations of \(\{1, 2, 3\}\):

\((1, 2, 3)\) and \((3, 2, 1)\) merge both segments into a single stair of length \(3\), giving stair lengths \((3, 3, 3) \ne a\).
\((1, 3, 2)\) and \((3, 1, 2)\) have stair lengths \((1, 2, 2) \ne a\).
\((2, 1, 3)\) has stairs \([2, 1]\) (length \(2\)) and \([3]\) (length \(1\)), giving \((2, 2, 1) = a\).
\((2, 3, 1)\) has stairs \([2, 3]\) (length \(2\)) and \([1]\) (length \(1\)), giving \((2, 2, 1) = a\).


Thus there are \(2\) valid permutations.


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

First check whether the array \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) can be partitioned into \(m\) contiguous base blocks of lengths \(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_m\) (\(\sum_{j=1}^m s_j = n\)) such that every element inside the \(j\)-th block equals \(s_j\). If not, the answer is immediately \(0\).
Once the \(m\) base blocks of lengths \(s_1, \dots, s_m\) are fixed, each base block \(j\) must be filled with a contiguous interval of \(s_j\) values arranged either in increasing or decreasing order (if \(s_j = 1\), both orientations are identical, giving \(1\) choice; if \(s_j \ge 2\), there are \(2\) orientations). Why can’t we simply multiply the orientations by \(m!\)? Because two adjacent base blocks might accidentally have consecutive values with compatible orientations and merge into a longer stair! How can you use inclusion–exclusion over which adjacent block boundaries are forced to merge?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Suppose we partition the \(m\) base blocks into \(k\) contiguous macro-blocks (\(1 \le k \le m\)) by merging \(m - k\) adjacent boundaries.

If we merge a contiguous range of \(r \ge 1\) base blocks into a single macro-block, how many internal ways can that macro-block be oriented?

If \(r = 1\) and the single base block has length \(s_j = 1\), the macro-block has total length \(1\), so it has only \(1\) orientation (increasing and decreasing coincide).
In all other cases (either \(r \ge 2\), or \(r = 1\) with \(s_j \ge 2\)), the macro-block has total length \(\ge 2\), so it has \(2\) orientations (either all its constituent base blocks are arranged to ascend overall, or to descend overall, with each internal base block’s orientation forced to match the macro-block’s direction!).

Once \(k\) macro-blocks are formed, assigning the \(k\) value-intervals to them in any permutation gives \(k!\) ways, weighted by the inclusion–exclusion sign \((-1)^{m - k}\).

To compute the sum of orientation products over all ways to form \(k\) macro-blocks for every \(k = 1, \dots, m\), what local boundary information is needed when merging the left half \([L, M]\) and right half \([M+1, R]\) of the base blocks?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Track a \(2\)-state indicator \(b \in \{0, 1\}\) for the currently open macro-block as you sweep across the base blocks \(j = 1, \dots, m\), where \(b = 0\) indicates that the current macro-block consists of a single length-\(1\) base block (orientation weight \(1\)) and \(b = 1\) indicates that the current macro-block has total length \(\ge 2\) (orientation weight \(2\)).
Assign each base block \(j \ge 2\) a \(2 \times 2\) transition matrix \(\mathbf{T}_j(x)\) that either cuts before block \(j\) (starting a new macro-block, multiplying by \(x\) if \(s_j = 1\) or \(2x\) if \(s_j \ge 2\)) or merges block \(j\) into the current macro-block (no factor of \(x\), transitioning to \(b' = 1\) and upgrading the current macro-block’s orientation factor from \(1 \to 2\) if \(b = 0\), or keeping it at \(2\) if \(b = 1\)).
Multiply the \(m\) matrices of degree \(1\) using a divide-and-conquer product tree in \(O(m \log^2 m)\) time, extract the coefficient \(c_k = [x^k]\) for each \(k = 1, \dots, m\), and compute \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{k=1}^m (-1)^{m - k} k! \, c_k \pmod{998244353}.\]





Problem CP-VI.3 (#117) — Codeforces 1510H: Hard Optimization

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(n\) closed intervals \([L_i, R_i]\) (\(1 \le i \le n\)) on the real line such that all \(2n\) endpoints \(L_1, R_1, \dots, L_n, R_n\) are pairwise distinct, and for every pair \(i \ne j\), the two intervals are either disjoint (\([L_i, R_i] \cap [L_j, R_j] = \emptyset\)) or nested (\([L_i, R_i] \subset [L_j, R_j]\) or \([L_j, R_j] \subset [L_i, R_i]\)).
You must choose for each \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) a non-empty sub-interval \([l_i, r_i] \subseteq [L_i, R_i]\) (\(l_i < r_i\)) such that no two chosen sub-intervals overlap in their interiors (i.e., \((l_i, r_i) \cap (l_j, r_j) = \emptyset\) for all \(i \ne j\)). Maximize the total length \(\sum_{i=1}^n (r_i - l_i)\) of the chosen sub-intervals.

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 2000\), \(0 \le L_i < R_i \le 10^9\), all \(2n\) endpoints distinct.
Target Complexity: \(O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n^2)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Let \(n = 2\) with \(I_1 = [0, 10]\) and \(I_2 = [3, 6] \subset I_1\).

Interval \(I_2\) must choose a sub-interval \([l_2, r_2] \subseteq [3, 6]\), and interval \(I_1\) must choose a sub-interval \([l_1, r_1] \subseteq [0, 10]\) disjoint from \((l_2, r_2)\).
Because \([l_1, r_1]\) is a single contiguous segment, it must lie either inside \([0, l_2]\) or inside \([r_2, 10]\).
Choosing \([l_2, r_2] = [3, 6]\) (length \(3\)) and \([l_1, r_1] = [6, 10]\) (length \(4\)) achieves total length \(3 + 4 = 7\), leaving \([0, 3]\) uncovered. No valid choice can cover more than \(7\) units because \([0, 3]\) and \([6, 10]\) lie on opposite sides of \(I_2\) and only one interval (\(I_1\)) is available to cover them.



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

Because the intervals are laminar (either disjoint or strictly nested), ordering them by inclusion forms a forest of rooted trees where the children of interval \(u\) are the maximal intervals \(v_1, \dots, v_d\) strictly contained inside \(u\), ordered from left to right: \[L_u < L_{v_1} < R_{v_1} < L_{v_2} < R_{v_2} < \dots < L_{v_d} < R_{v_d} < R_u.\] Notice that the regions \([L_u, R_u] \setminus \bigcup_{c=1}^d [L_{v_c}, R_{v_c}]\) consist of \(d + 1\) elementary “gaps” \(G_0, G_1, \dots, G_d\) inside \(u\).
Could \(u\)’s chosen sub-interval \([l_u, r_u]\) completely contain a child interval \([L_{v_c}, R_{v_c}]\)? No, because then \((l_u, r_u)\) would overlap \((l_{v_c}, r_{v_c})\), which is forbidden! Therefore, every chosen sub-interval \([l_w, r_w]\) inside \(T_u\) either lies inside a single gap \(G_c\), or lies inside some child subtree \(T_{v_c}\), or straddles the boundary endpoint \(L_{v_c}\) or \(R_{v_c}\) by shrinking \(v_c\)’s used region. How can you reformulate this without tracking continuous coordinates \(l_i, r_i\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By an exchange argument, in an optimal solution every chosen sub-interval \([l_w, r_w]\) has endpoints that are pushed outwards until they hit either an original endpoint \(L_u, R_u\) or another chosen sub-interval. Equivalently, if we decompose the union of chosen sub-intervals inside \([L_u, R_u]\) along the \(2\operatorname{sz}(u)\) original endpoints of \(T_u\), each elementary gap \(G_c\) between consecutive original endpoints is either completely covered (contributing its full length \(|G_c|\)) or completely empty (contributing \(0\))!
Why? Because if a gap \(G_c = [x, y]\) is even partially entered by an interval that starts at or to the left of \(x\) (or ends at or to the right of \(y\)), stretching that interval across the entire gap \([x, y]\) increases total length without violating any constraint; and if an interval is placed strictly inside \(G_c\), it might as well expand to fill all of \(G_c = [x, y]\)!
Thus, inside subtree \(T_u\), each node \(u\) generates \(1\) new interval demand (which can either be satisfied right now, or passed down/up—specifically, in a bottom-up view, a subtree \(T_u\) can pass \(j \in [0, \operatorname{sz}(u)]\) excess covered segments upward to be claimed by \(u\) and \(u\)’s ancestors, along with two boolean boundary flags \(b_L, b_R \in \{0, 1\}\) indicating whether the leftmost/rightmost covered segment in \(T_u\) touches \(L_u\) or \(R_u\) so it can seamlessly merge with the adjacent gap outside \(T_u\)!).



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

At each tree node \(u\) with children \(v_1, \dots, v_d\) and gaps \(G_0, G_1, \dots, G_d\) of lengths \(g_0, g_1, \dots, g_d\):

Represent the DP of a child \(v_c\) (or a prefix of children and gaps) as a \(2 \times 2\) matrix of sequences \(dp[b_L][b_R][j]\) for \(b_L, b_R \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(0 \le j \le \operatorname{sz}\), storing the maximum covered length inside the region when \(j\) active intervals remain unclaimed by ancestors and the left/right boundaries of the region are active (\(1\)) or inactive (\(0\)).
Each gap \(G_c\) of length \(g_c\) can either be left empty (transitioning \((b_R = \text{any}) \to (b'_L = 0)\) with \(+0\) length) or covered (contributing \(+g_c\) length: if merged with the left neighbor \(b_R = 1\) and/or right neighbor \(b_L = 1\), the number of distinct segments adjusts by \(+1 - b_R - b_L\)!).
Merging prefix state of size \(S_1\) with child \(v_c\) of size \(S_2\) is a \((+, \max)\) convolution of degree \(S_1\) and \(S_2\). By the tree knapsack size bound, doing this naively across all children of all nodes takes \(O(\operatorname{sz}(u)^2)\) total time, i.e., \(O(n^2)\)!
Finally, at node \(u\), interval \(u\) itself claims one of the \(j \ge 1\) segments inside \([L_u, R_u]\) (shifting index \(j \to j - 1\)).






Problem CP-VI.4 (#170) — Luogu P5327: [ZJOI2019] 语言 (Language)

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
A continent consists of \(n\) cities connected by \(n - 1\) bidirectional roads forming a tree \(T = (V, E)\). There are \(m\) languages spoken across the continent; the \(i\)-th language (\(1 \le i \le m\)) is spoken in every city along the unique simple path between city \(s_i\) and city \(t_i\) (inclusive).
Two distinct cities \(u \ne v\) can communicate if and only if there is at least one language spoken in both \(u\) and \(v\). Compute the total number of unordered pairs of distinct cities \(\{u, v\}\) that can communicate.

Constraints: \(1 \le n, m \le 10^5\).
Target Complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) time and \(O(n \log n)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Let \(n = 4\) be a star tree centered at city \(1\) with edges \((1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4)\), and let \(m = 2\) languages cover paths \(P_1 = (2, 3)\) (cities \(\{2, 1, 3\}\)) and \(P_2 = (1, 4)\) (cities \(\{1, 4\}\)).

City \(1\) speaks both languages, so it can communicate with cities \(\{2, 3, 4\}\) (\(3\) cities).
City \(2\) speaks language \(1\), so it can communicate with cities \(\{1, 3\}\) (\(2\) cities).
City \(3\) speaks language \(1\), so it can communicate with cities \(\{1, 2\}\) (\(2\) cities).
City \(4\) speaks language \(2\), so it can communicate with city \(\{1\}\) (\(1\) city).

Summing the counts of reachable cities gives \(3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8\) ordered pairs, so there are \(8 / 2 = 4\) unordered pairs: \(\{1, 2\}, \{1, 3\}, \{2, 3\}, \{1, 4\}\).


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

Fix a single city \(u \in V\). Which cities \(v\) can communicate with \(u\)? Exactly the union of all paths \(P_i = (s_i, t_i)\) that pass through \(u\).
Because every such path \(P_i\) contains \(u\), the union of these paths is a connected subgraph of the tree \(T\)! Even better: what are the extreme endpoints of this connected subgraph? It is precisely the minimal connected subtree of \(T\) that spans the set of endpoints \[E_u = \bigcup_{i \,:\, u \in P_i} \{s_i, t_i\}.\] How can you compute the number of vertices in the minimal connected subtree spanning a dynamic multiset of vertices \(E_u\), and how do the multisets \(E_u\) relate as \(u\) moves from children to parents in \(T\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Recall the classical DFS-order formula for the size (number of vertices or edges) of the minimal connected subtree spanning a non-empty vertex set \(S = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\}\) sorted by their DFS entry timestamps \(\operatorname{dfn}[x_1] < \operatorname{dfn}[x_2] < \dots < \operatorname{dfn}[x_k]\): \[\text{Edges}(S) = \sum_{j=1}^k \operatorname{dep}(x_j) - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \operatorname{dep}\big(\operatorname{LCA}(x_j, x_{j+1})\big) - \operatorname{dep}\big(\operatorname{LCA}(x_1, x_k)\big),\] where \(\operatorname{dep}(w)\) is the depth of \(w\). (If we count vertices instead of edges, simply add \(+1\), and subtracting \(u\) itself leaves \(\text{Edges}(E_u)\) reachable partners \(v \ne u\)!)
How does the active multiset of endpoints \(E_u\) change across the tree? A path \(P_i = (s_i, t_i)\) with \(w_i = \operatorname{LCA}(s_i, t_i)\) covers \(u\) if and only if \(w_i\) is an ancestor of \(u\) and at least one of \(s_i\) or \(t_i\) lies in the subtree \(T_u\). Thus, we can apply tree difference on the multisets \(E_u\):

At both \(s_i\) and \(t_i\): insert \(\{s_i, t_i\}\) with multiplicity \(+1\).
At \(w_i = \operatorname{LCA}(s_i, t_i)\): remove \(\{s_i, t_i\}\) once; and at \(\operatorname{parent}(w_i)\): remove \(\{s_i, t_i\}\) a second time!




Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Maintain the active multiset \(E_u\) (ordered by DFS timestamp \(\operatorname{dfn}\)) using a Dynamic Segment Tree over \([1, n]\) at each vertex \(u\), merged bottom-up via Segment Tree Merging:

Each segment tree node covering DFS range \([L, R]\) stores:

cnt: multiplicity of active endpoints at a leaf,
leftmost and rightmost: the smallest and largest \(\operatorname{dfn}\) with \(\text{cnt} > 0\) in \([L, R]\),
sum_ans: the value \(\sum \operatorname{dep}(x_j) - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \operatorname{dep}(\operatorname{LCA}(x_j, x_{j+1}))\) for the active vertices inside \([L, R]\).

In push_up(node), combining left child \(lc\) and right child \(rc\) only requires a single \(\operatorname{LCA}\) query between \(lc.\text{rightmost}\) and \(rc.\text{leftmost}\): \[\text{node.sum\_ans} = lc.\text{sum\_ans} + rc.\text{sum\_ans} - \operatorname{dep}\big(\operatorname{LCA}(lc.\text{rightmost}, rc.\text{leftmost})\big).\]
By precomputing an Euler-tour sparse table (\(O(n \log n)\) preprocessing, \(O(1)\) per \(\operatorname{LCA}\) query), each segment tree push_up takes \(O(1)\) time, so bottom-up Segment Tree Merging across the entire tree runs in \(O((n + m) \log n)\) total time!






Problem CP-VI.5 (#054) — AtCoder ARC 106 E: Medals

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
There are \(N\) employees numbered \(1, 2, \dots, N\) and an integer \(K\). Employee \(i\) follows a strict periodic attendance schedule determined by a positive integer \(A_i\): starting from day \(1\), employee \(i\) comes to work for \(A_i\) consecutive days, then rests at home for \(A_i\) consecutive days, then works for \(A_i\) days, and so on indefinitely. Formally, employee \(i\) works on day \(d \ge 1\) if and only if \[((d - 1) \bmod 2A_i) < A_i.\]
On each day \(d = 1, 2, \dots, D\), you may choose at most one employee who is working on day \(d\) and award them one medal. Find the minimum number of days \(D\) required so that every employee \(1, \dots, N\) can receive at least \(K\) medals.

Constraints: \(1 \le N \le 18\), \(1 \le K \le 10^5\), \(1 \le A_i \le 10^5\).
Target Complexity: \(O(N K + N 2^N \log(N K))\) time and \(O(N K + 2^N)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Let \(N = 2\), \(K = 2\), and \(A = (1, 2)\).

Employee \(1\) (\(A_1 = 1\)) works on days \(1, 3, 5, 7, \dots\).
Employee \(2\) (\(A_2 = 2\)) works on days \(1, 2, 5, 6, \dots\).
For \(D = 4\) days, the sets of working employees on days \(1, 2, 3, 4\) are \(\{1, 2\}, \{2\}, \{1\}, \emptyset\). Since day \(4\) has no working employees, at most \(3\) medals can be awarded in the first \(4\) days, which is less than \(N K = 4\).
On day \(5\), \(\{1, 2\}\) work again, allowing \(2\) medals for each employee (e.g., day \(1 \to 2\), day \(2 \to 2\), day \(3 \to 1\), day \(5 \to 1\)). Thus the minimum \(D\) is \(5\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

First establish an upper bound on the answer \(D\): even if we greedily focus on one employee at a time, within \(2 N K\) days every employee works at least \(N K\) days, so \(D \le 2 N K \le 3.6 \times 10^6\). Furthermore, feasibility is monotone in \(D\), suggesting binary search on \(D \in [N K, 2 N K]\).
For a fixed candidate number of days \(D\), we have a bipartite matching problem between the \(N\) employees (each needing \(K\) medals) and the \(D\) days (each capable of awarding \(1\) medal to a working employee). Under what exact condition on the \(2^N\) subsets of employees \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\) does a valid assignment of medals exist?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By Hall’s Marriage Theorem (applied with each employee \(i\) replicated \(K\) times), a valid assignment exists within \(D\) days if and only if for every subset of employees \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\), the number of days in \(\{1, \dots, D\}\) on which at least one employee in \(S\) is working is at least \(|S| \cdot K\): \[W_D(S) \ge |S| \cdot K \quad \text{for all } S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}.\]
For each day \(d \in \{1, \dots, D\}\), let \(M_d \in [0, 2^N - 1]\) be the bitmask of employees working on day \(d\), and let \(c(T)\) be the number of days \(d \in \{1, \dots, D\}\) with \(M_d = T\). How can you express \(W_D(S)\)—the count of days \(d\) where \(M_d \cap S \ne \emptyset\)—in terms of a subset sum of \(c(T)\)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

A day \(d\) has \(M_d \cap S \ne \emptyset\) if and only if \(M_d\) is not a subset of the complement \(U \setminus S\) (where \(U = \{1, \dots, N\}\)). Therefore, \[W_D(S) = D - \sum_{T \subseteq U \setminus S} c(T).\] Notice that \(F(X) = \sum_{T \subseteq X} c(T)\) is the Fast Zeta / SOS (Sum Over Subsets) Transform of the frequency array \(c\)!

Precompute the daily attendance bitmasks \(M_1, M_2, \dots, M_{2NK}\) in \(O(N K)\) time before starting the binary search.
Inside each of the \(\approx 22\) binary search steps for \(D\):

Tally \(c(T)\) for \(d = 1, \dots, D\) in \(O(D + 2^N)\) time.
Run the \(N\)-bit SOS Transform \(F(X) = \sum_{T \subseteq X} c(T)\) in \(O(N 2^N)\) time.
Check whether \(D - F(U \setminus S) \ge |S| \cdot K\) for all \(S \subseteq U\) in \(O(2^N)\) time.







Problem CP-VI.6 (#254) — UOJ 310: [UNR #2] 黎明前的巧克力

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given \(n\) integers \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\). Count the number of unordered pairs of disjoint index subsets \(\{A, B\}\) (\(A, B \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\), \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), and \(A \cup B \ne \emptyset\)) such that the bitwise XOR sum of the elements indexed by \(A\) equals the bitwise XOR sum of the elements indexed by \(B\): \[\bigoplus_{i \in A} a_i = \bigoplus_{j \in B} a_j,\] where the XOR sum of an empty set is \(0\). Output the answer modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 10^6\), \(0 \le a_i < 2^{20}\), prime modulus \(P = 998244353\).
Target Complexity: \(O(n + b 2^b)\) time and \(O(2^b)\) space, where \(b = 20\).



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Let \(n = 3\) and \(a = (1, 2, 3)\).

Disjoint sets \(A, B\) satisfy \(\bigoplus_{i \in A} a_i = \bigoplus_{j \in B} a_j\) if and only if their union \(U = A \sqcup B\) has XOR sum \(\bigoplus_{k \in U} a_k = 0\).
The only non-empty subset \(U \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}\) with XOR sum \(0\) is \(U = \{1, 2, 3\}\) (\(1 \oplus 2 \oplus 3 = 0\)).
Each of the \(3\) elements in \(U\) can be placed into either \(A\) or \(B\), giving \(2^3 = 8\) ordered pairs \((A, B)\) and \(8 / 2 = 4\) unordered pairs \(\{A, B\}\): \(\{\{1, 2, 3\}, \emptyset\}\), \(\{\{1, 2\}, \{3\}\}\), \(\{\{1, 3\}, \{2\}\}\), and \(\{\{2, 3\}, \{1\}\}\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

As observed in the sample trace, for any two disjoint subsets \(A, B \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\), the condition \(\bigoplus_{i \in A} a_i = \bigoplus_{j \in B} a_j\) is equivalent to saying that the union \(U = A \sqcup B\) has total XOR sum \(0\), and every element \(k \in U\) can be assigned independently to either \(A\) or \(B\) in \(2\) ways!
Thus, if each element \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) can be either:

excluded from \(U\) (\(1\) way, contributing XOR \(0\)), or
included in \(U\) (\(2\) ways: placed in \(A\) or placed in \(B\), contributing XOR \(a_i\)),

In other words, for each element \(a_i\), how many ways can it be assigned to \(A\), \(B\), or neither, what does each choice contribute to the combined XOR value \(X(A) \oplus X(B)\), and why can’t we combine these \(n = 10^6\) choices naively in \(O(n \cdot 2^{20})\) time?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

In the XOR group algebra \(\mathbb{F}_P[\mathbb{Z}_2^b]\) (\(b = 20\)), the \(i\)-th element corresponds to the binomial \(1 + 2 x^{a_i}\), and we want the coefficient of \(x^0\) in the \(n\)-fold XOR convolution product: \[P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 + 2 x^{a_i}).\] Instead of transforming \(n\) separate arrays, examine what the XOR Walsh–Hadamard Transform (\(\operatorname{FWT}_{\oplus}\)) does to a single sparse factor \(1 + 2 x^{a_i}\) at frequency mask \(S \in [0, 2^b - 1]\): \[\widehat{(1 + 2 x^{a_i})}_S = 1 + 2(-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i)} = \begin{cases} 3 & \text{if } \operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i) \equiv 0 \pmod 2, \\ -1 & \text{if } \operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i) \equiv 1 \pmod 2. \end{cases}\] Every factor evaluates to either \(3\) or \(-1\)! How can you determine for every frequency mask \(S \in [0, 2^b - 1]\) simultaneously how many of the \(n\) elements give \(+1\) versus \(-1\), using only a single transform of the frequency array of \(a_1, \dots, a_n\)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Let \(C(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n x^{a_i}\) be the frequency polynomial of the input array, and apply a single forward XOR transform \(\widehat{C} = \operatorname{FWT}_{\oplus}(C)\) in \(O(b 2^b)\) time.
At each frequency mask \(S \in [0, 2^b - 1]\):

If \(k_S\) is the number of indices \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) with \((-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i)} = +1\) and \(n - k_S\) is the number with \(-1\), then: \[k_S + (n - k_S) = n \quad \text{and} \quad k_S - (n - k_S) = \widehat{C}_S \implies k_S = \frac{n + \widehat{C}_S}{2}.\]
Therefore, the transformed product at frequency \(S\) is immediately \[\widehat{P}_S = 3^{k_S} (-1)^{n - k_S} \pmod{998244353}.\]
Finally, \([x^0] P(x) = \frac{1}{2^b} \sum_{S=0}^{2^b - 1} \widehat{P}_S\) gives the number of ordered pairs \((A, B)\) (including \((\emptyset, \emptyset)\)). Subtract \(1\) for \((\emptyset, \emptyset)\) and divide by \(2\) modulo \(998244353\).






Problem CP-VI.7 (#175) — Luogu P5406: [THUPC2019] 找树

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given an undirected multigraph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(n\) vertices, \(m\) edges, and a string \(\text{op}\) of length \(w\) where each character \(\text{op}_r \in \{\text{\&}, \text{|}, \text{\^{}}\}\) (\(0 \le r < w\)) specifies a bitwise binary operation (AND, OR, or XOR) for bit position \(r\).
Each edge \(e \in E\) has a \(w\)-bit integer weight \(v_e \in [0, 2^w - 1]\). For any spanning tree \(T \subseteq E\) of \(G\), its total weight \(W(T) \in [0, 2^w - 1]\) is obtained by combining the \(n - 1\) edge weights \(\{v_e : e \in T\}\) bit-by-bit using \(\text{op}_r\) at bit \(r\) (\(0 \le r < w\)). Find the maximum weight \(W(T)\) over all spanning trees \(T\) of \(G\), or output \(-1\) if \(G\) is disconnected.

Constraints: \(2 \le n \le 70\), \(n - 1 \le m \le 5000\), \(1 \le w \le 12\).
Target Complexity: \(O(2^w n^3 + w 2^w n^2)\) time and \(O(2^w n^2)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Let \(n = 3\), \(w = 2\) with \(\text{op}_0 = \text{\^{}}\) (XOR on bit \(0\)) and \(\text{op}_1 = \text{\&}\) (AND on bit \(1\)), and consider \(m = 3\) edges forming a triangle:

\(e_1 = (1, 2)\) with weight \(3 = (11)_2\),
\(e_2 = (2, 3)\) with weight \(2 = (10)_2\),
\(e_3 = (1, 3)\) with weight \(1 = (01)_2\).

The \(3\) spanning trees of \(G\) have weights:

\(T_1 = \{e_1, e_2\}\): \((11)_2 \odot (10)_2 = (1\text{\&}1, \, 1\text{\^{}}0)_2 = (10)_2 = 2\).
\(T_2 = \{e_1, e_3\}\): \((11)_2 \odot (01)_2 = (1\text{\&}0, \, 1\text{\^{}}1)_2 = (00)_2 = 0\).
\(T_3 = \{e_2, e_3\}\): \((10)_2 \odot (01)_2 = (1\text{\&}0, \, 0\text{\^{}}1)_2 = (01)_2 = 1\).

The maximum spanning tree weight is \(\max(2, 0, 1) = 2\).


Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

Because the operations \(\text{op}_r\) can include XOR (\(\text{\^{}}\)) as well as AND (\(\text{\&}\)) and OR (\(\text{|}\)), greedy algorithms like Kruskal’s fail completely: a high bit can be flipped off by XOR later in the tree.
Look at the constraints: \(n \le 70\) is small enough for \(O(n^3)\) linear algebra, and \(2^w \le 4096\) is small enough to track every possible \(w\)-bit weight simultaneously! Instead of maximizing \(W(T)\) directly, what algebraic tool enumerates the sum of edge-weight products over all spanning trees \(T\) of a graph \(G\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be the \(2^w\)-dimensional commutative algebra over a large prime field \(\mathbb{F}_P\) with basis \(\{z^v : 0 \le v < 2^w\}\) and multiplication \(z^u \cdot z^v = z^{u \odot v}\), where \(\odot\) combines bit \(r\) via \(\text{op}_r \in \{\text{\&}, \text{|}, \text{\^{}}\}\).
By Kirchhoff’s Matrix-Tree Theorem over the commutative ring \(\mathcal{A}\), if we construct the \((n-1) \times (n-1)\) reduced Laplacian matrix \(L(z)\) where each edge \(e = (u, v)\) of weight \(v_e\) contributes \(+z^{v_e}\) to \(L_{u, u}\) and \(L_{v, v}\) and \(-z^{v_e}\) to \(L_{u, v}\) and \(L_{v, u}\), then \[\det L(z) = \sum_{T \text{ spanning tree of } G} c_T z^{W(T)} \in \mathcal{A}.\] How can you diagonalize the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) so that computing \(\det L(z)\) reduces to \(2^w\) independent scalar determinants over \(\mathbb{F}_P\)?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Apply the Mixed \(w\)-Bit Fast Walsh–Hadamard Transform (\(\operatorname{FWT}_{\text{op}}\)) to every entry \(L_{i, j}(z)\) of the \((n-1) \times (n-1)\) Laplacian matrix, where the \(2 \times 2\) butterfly at bit \(r\) is:

\(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) (or \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\)) for \(\text{op}_r = \text{\&}\) (AND),
\(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) for \(\text{op}_r = \text{|}\) (OR),
\(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\) for \(\text{op}_r = \text{\^{}}\) (XOR).

Because \(\operatorname{FWT}_{\text{op}} : \mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{F}_P^{2^w}\) is a ring isomorphism onto pointwise multiplication, for each frequency mask \(\omega \in [0, 2^w - 1]\) we simply compute the scalar determinant \(\widehat{D}_\omega = \det \widehat{L}(\omega) \in \mathbb{F}_P\) via Gaussian elimination in \(O(n^3)\) time! Finally, apply the inverse transform \(\operatorname{IFWT}_{\text{op}}\) to \(\widehat{D}\) in \(O(w 2^w)\) time and output the largest mask \(v \in [0, 2^w - 1]\) with \([z^v] \det L(z) \not\equiv 0 \pmod P\) (or \(-1\) if all coefficients are \(0\)).





Problem CP-VI.8 (#180) — Luogu P5643: [PKUWC2018] 随机游走

Problem Statement & Exact Constraints
You are given a tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(n\) vertices numbered \(1, 2, \dots, n\) and a fixed starting vertex \(x \in V\). At each step of a random walk on \(T\), if you are currently at vertex \(u\) of degree \(d(u)\), you move to one of its \(d(u)\) neighbors chosen uniformly at random (each with probability \(1 / d(u)\)).
You are given \(Q\) queries. Each query specifies a subset of vertices \(S \subseteq V\) and asks for the expected number of steps required, starting from \(x\), until every vertex in \(S\) has been visited at least once (if \(x \in S\), vertex \(x\) is already visited at step \(0\)). Output each expectation modulo \(998244353\).

Constraints: \(1 \le n \le 18\), \(1 \le Q \le 5000\), \(1 \le x \le n\), prime modulus \(P = 998244353\).
Target Complexity: \(O(n 2^n + Q)\) time and \(O(2^n)\) space.



Sample Trace (\(N \le 4\))
Let \(n = 3\) be the path tree \(2 - 1 - 3\) rooted at \(x = 1\), and consider the query \(S = \{2, 3\}\).

On step \(1\), starting from \(1\), the walk moves to either \(2\) or \(3\) with probability \(1/2\) each. Thus the first vertex of \(S\) is visited at time \(\min(\tau_2, \tau_3) = 1\).
Once at \(2\) (say), we still need to visit \(3\). From \(2\), the walk deterministically steps back to \(1\) (\(+1\) step), and from \(1\) it has probability \(1/2\) of stepping to \(3\) (\(+1\) step) and probability \(1/2\) of returning to \(2\) (\(+1\) step). The additional expected steps from \(1\) to \(3\) satisfy \(E_1 = 1 + \frac{1}{2}(0) + \frac{1}{2}(1 + E_1) \implies E_1 = 3\), so from \(2\) to \(3\) takes \(1 + 3 = 4\) additional steps.
Thus the total expected steps to visit all of \(S = \{2, 3\}\) is \(1 + 4 = 5\).



Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model (Spoiler-Free)

For each vertex \(v \in V\), let \(\tau_v\) be the random variable denoting the first time step at which the walk visits \(v\) (with \(\tau_x = 0\)). A query \(S \subseteq V\) asks for the expectation of the maximum hitting time: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{v \in S} \tau_v\right].\] Why is \(\max_{v \in S} \tau_v\) hard to compute directly (it would require tracking the subset of already-visited vertices in \(S\)), whereas \(\min_{v \in T} \tau_v\)—the first time the walk hits any vertex in a fixed target set \(T \subseteq V\)—only depends on the current vertex \(u \in V\)? How can you express \(\mathbb{E}[\max_{v \in S} \tau_v]\) as a linear combination of \(\mathbb{E}[\min_{v \in T} \tau_v]\) over non-empty subsets \(T \subseteq S\)?



Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad

By the Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion Principle and linearity of expectation: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{v \in S} \tau_v\right] = \sum_{\emptyset \ne T \subseteq S} (-1)^{|T| - 1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{v \in T} \tau_v\right].\] Let \(f(T) = \mathbb{E}[\min_{v \in T} \tau_v]\) be the expected number of steps from root \(x\) to hit any vertex in \(T\). For a fixed non-empty target set \(T \subseteq V\), let \(E_u\) be the expected steps to hit \(T\) starting from \(u\):

If \(u \in T\), then \(E_u = 0\).
If \(u \notin T\), then \(E_u = 1 + \frac{1}{d(u)} \sum_{v \in N(u)} E_v\).

How can you solve this system of \(n\) linear equations on the tree \(T\) in \(O(n)\) time (rather than \(O(n^3)\) Gaussian elimination), and how can you precompute the subset sum \(\sum_{\emptyset \ne T \subseteq S} (-1)^{|T|-1} f(T)\) for all \(2^n\) query sets \(S\) simultaneously?



Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract

Combine Tree Linear Elimination (\(E_u = A_u E_{p(u)} + B_u\)) with the Fast Zeta / SOS Subset Sum Transform:

Root the tree at the starting vertex \(x\). For a fixed target set \(T \subseteq V\), express every vertex \(u\)’s expectation as a linear function of its parent’s expectation: \(E_u = A_u E_{p(u)} + B_u\).

If \(u \in T\), then \(E_u = 0 \implies A_u = 0, B_u = 0\).
If \(u \notin T\), substituting \(E_v = A_v E_u + B_v\) for all children \(v\) of \(u\) into \(d(u) E_u = d(u) + E_{p(u)} + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} (A_v E_u + B_v)\) gives \[\left(d(u) - \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} A_v\right) E_u = E_{p(u)} + d(u) + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} B_v,\] yielding \(A_u\) and \(B_u\) bottom-up in \(O(n)\) time! At the root \(x\) (which has no parent), \(f(T) = E_x = B_x\).

After computing \(f(T)\) for all \(2^n\) subsets \(T\) in \(O(n 2^n)\) time, define \(g(T) = (-1)^{|T| - 1} f(T)\) (with \(g(\emptyset) = 0\)) and apply the \(n\)-bit SOS Transform \(\text{Ans}(S) = \sum_{T \subseteq S} g(T)\) in \(O(n 2^n)\) time. Each of the \(Q\) queries is then answered in \(O(1)\) table lookup!

Complete Derivations & Algorithm Contracts






NoteComplete Solution — CP-VI.1 (#102: Codeforces 1097G — Vladislav and a Great Legend)






1. Stirling Edge-Subset Expansion
Using the identity \(m^k = \sum_{j=0}^k \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\} j! \binom{m}{j}\), where \(\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\}\) denotes the Stirling numbers of the second kind, we rewrite the target sum as: \[S = \sum_{\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V} f(X)^k = \sum_{j=0}^k \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} j! \underbrace{\sum_{\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V} \binom{f(X)}{j}}_{C_j}.\] Here \(C_j\) counts ordered pairs \((X, F)\) where \(\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V\) is a non-empty subset of vertices, \(F \subseteq E\) is a subset of \(|F| = j\) edges, and every edge \(e \in F\) lies in the minimal connected subgraph (Steiner subtree) spanning \(X\).


2. Rooted Subtree Characterization & Subtraction of Invalid Upward Extensions
Root \(T\) arbitrarily at vertex \(1\). An edge \(e = (u, v)\) (with \(u = \operatorname{parent}(v)\)) lies in the Steiner subtree of \(X\) if and only if \(X\) contains at least one vertex inside \(V(T_v)\) and at least one vertex outside \(V(T_v)\): \[X \cap V(T_v) \ne \emptyset \quad \text{and} \quad X \setminus V(T_v) \ne \emptyset.\] Notice that the first condition (\(X \cap V(T_v) \ne \emptyset\)) is local to the subtree \(T_v\): every edge \(e = (w, c) \in F\) must have \(X \cap V(T_c) \ne \emptyset\). And when does a pair \((X, F)\) satisfy the local downward condition for every \(e \in F\), yet fail the global condition \(X \setminus V(T_c) \ne \emptyset\)? Precisely when all of \(X\) lies inside a single child subtree \(V(T_v)\) of \(u = \operatorname{LCA}(X \cup V(F))\), while \(F\) chooses at least one edge inside \(T_v \cup \{(u, v)\}\) above \(\operatorname{LCA}(X)\)!
Specifically, define the subtree polynomial at vertex \(u\): \[P_u(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(\operatorname{sz}(u)-1, k)} dp[u][j] \, x^j,\] where \(dp[u][j]\) counts pairs \((X_u, F_u)\) with \(\emptyset \ne X_u \subseteq V(T_u)\) and \(F_u \subseteq E(T_u)\) of size \(|F_u| = j\) such that every edge \((w, c) \in F_u\) has \(X_u \cap V(T_c) \ne \emptyset\).

Base Case at Vertex \(u\) (before merging children): \(u\) alone can either be in \(X_u\) (\(1\) way, \(0\) edges) or not in \(X_u\) (\(0\) non-empty ways), so initially \(P_u(x) = 1\) (representing \(X_u = \{u\}\)) and the empty choice \(X_u = \emptyset\) has weight \(1\).
Transition across Child Edge \(e = (u, v)\): For a child \(v\) of \(u\), if \(X_u \cap V(T_v) \ne \emptyset\), the edge \((u, v)\) may be either omitted (\(1\)) or chosen (\(x\)) in \(F_u\), giving the shifted child polynomial \[Q_v(x) = P_v(x)(1 + x) \bmod x^{k+1}.\] Combined with the empty choice \(X_u \cap V(T_v) = \emptyset\) (which contributes \(1\)), merging child \(v\) into \(u\) updates \[1 + P_u^{\text{new}}(x) = \big(1 + P_u^{\text{old}}(x)\big)\big(1 + Q_v(x)\big) \bmod x^{k+1},\] or equivalently: \[P_u^{\text{new}}(x) = P_u^{\text{old}}(x) + Q_v(x) + P_u^{\text{old}}(x) Q_v(x) \bmod x^{k+1}.\]
Global Accumulation & Exact Cancellation: At the root \(1\), \(P_1(x)\) counts all pairs \((X, F)\) where \(\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V\) and every edge \((w, c) \in F\) satisfies \(X \cap V(T_c) \ne \emptyset\). Which of these pairs violate the upper condition \(X \setminus V(T_c) \ne \emptyset\)? For any pair \((X, F)\) counted in \(P_1(x)\), let \(u\) be the highest vertex touched by \(X\) or \(F\) (more precisely, if \(X\) is contained entirely inside \(V(T_v)\) for some child \(v\) of \(u\) while \(F\) contains edges above \(\operatorname{LCA}(X)\)). At each vertex \(u\) and each child \(v\) of \(u\), any configuration in \(Q_v(x)\) that uses at least one edge inside \(T_v \cup \{(u, v)\}\) above \(T_v\) when \(X \setminus V(T_v) = \emptyset\) is formed by taking a valid pair inside \(T_v\) (counted by \(P_v(x)\)) and appending the edge \((u, v)\) (contributing \(x P_v(x) = Q_v(x) - P_v(x)\)) with no vertices of \(X\) chosen outside \(T_v\)! Even more transparently: a pair \((X, F)\) is globally valid if and only if at the unique highest vertex \(u = \operatorname{LCA}(X \cup V(F))\), the set \(X\) is NOT confined to a single child subtree \(T_v\) of \(u\) (unless \(F = \emptyset\), which only affects \(j = 0\)). At vertex \(u\), the configurations where \(X \cup V(F)\) has highest vertex \(u\) are counted by \(P_u(x) - \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} P_v(x)\), and among these, the invalid ones are precisely those where \(X \subseteq V(T_v)\) for a single child \(v\) and edge \((u, v) \in F\), which equals \(\sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} \big(Q_v(x) - P_v(x)\big)\)! Summing \(\Big(P_u(x) - \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} Q_v(x)\Big)\) over all \(u \in V\) telescopes \(\sum_u P_u(x) - \sum_{v \ne 1} P_v(x) = P_1(x)\), leaving the remarkably clean formula: \[C(x) = \sum_{j=0}^k C_j x^j = P_1(x) - \sum_{v \in V \setminus \{1\}} \big(Q_v(x) - P_v(x)\big) = P_1(x) - x \sum_{v \in V \setminus \{1\}} P_v(x) \pmod{x^{k+1}}.\] Let us verify this identity! A pair \((X, F)\) satisfies the downward condition everywhere if and only if for the highest edge \(e_{\text{top}} = (u, v) \in F\) (if \(F \ne \emptyset\)), \(X \subseteq V(T_v)\) fails precisely when \(u\) is an ancestor of \(\operatorname{LCA}(X)\), i.e., \(X \subseteq V(T_v)\). And for each vertex \(v \ne 1\) with \(X \subseteq V(T_v)\), the pairs \((X, F')\) confined to \(T_v\) are counted by \(P_v(x)\), so adjoining the top edge \((u, v)\) gives \(x P_v(x)\), establishing \(C(x) = P_1(x) - x \sum_{v \ne 1} P_v(x)\) in a single line!



Algorithm Contract

Input: Tree \(T = (V, E)\) with \(n \le 10^5\) vertices and integer \(k \le 200\).
Output: \(\sum_{\emptyset \ne X \subseteq V} f(X)^k \bmod (10^9 + 7)\).
Algebraic Preconditions: Commutative polynomial ring \(\mathbb{F}_{10^9+7}[x] / (x^{k+1})\).
Index & Degree Boundaries: At each vertex \(u\), maintain \(\deg P_u(x) \le \min(\operatorname{sz}(u) - 1, k)\), updating \(\operatorname{sz}(u) \leftarrow \operatorname{sz}(u) + \operatorname{sz}(v)\) after multiplying \(P_u^{\text{old}}(x)\) (degree \(\le \min(\operatorname{sz}_{\text{old}}(u)-1, k)\)) and \(Q_v(x)\) (degree \(\le \min(\operatorname{sz}(v), k)\)).
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: By the LCA pair-counting lemma, \(\sum_{(u, v)} \min(\operatorname{sz}_{\text{old}}(u), k) \cdot \min(\operatorname{sz}(v), k) = O(n k)\), giving \(O(n k)\) time and \(O(n k)\) space. The invariant \(C(x) = P_1(x) - x \sum_{v \ne 1} P_v(x)\) bijectively cancels every downward-valid pair \((X, F)\) whose highest edge \((u, v) \in F\) lies strictly above \(\operatorname{LCA}(X)\).
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Updating \(\operatorname{sz}(u) \leftarrow \operatorname{sz}(u) + \operatorname{sz}(v)\) before bounding the inner loop ranges to \(\min(\operatorname{sz}_{\text{old}}(u), k)\) and \(\min(\operatorname{sz}(v), k)\) degrades the tree knapsack from \(O(n k)\) to \(O(n^2 k)\) and causes TLE on star/broom trees.












NoteComplete Solution — CP-VI.2 (#121: Codeforces 1553I — Stairs)






1. Base Block Partition & Merge Inclusion–Exclusion
First scan \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) from left to right: if \(a_i = s\), then the next \(s\) elements \(a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_{i+s-1}\) must all exist and equal \(s\). If this fails at any point, output \(0\). Otherwise, we obtain \(m\) contiguous base blocks of sizes \(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_m\) with \(\sum_{j=1}^m s_j = n\).
In any valid permutation, the \(j\)-th base block must be filled with a set of \(s_j\) consecutive integers arranged either in increasing order or in decreasing order (giving \(1\) internal orientation if \(s_j = 1\), and \(2\) internal orientations if \(s_j \ge 2\)). Moreover, no two adjacent base blocks \(j\) and \(j+1\) may merge into a single longer stair.
By the Adjacent Block-Merge Inclusion–Exclusion Principle, we sum over all subsets of adjacent boundaries \(E' \subseteq \{1, \dots, m - 1\}\) that are forced to merge. If \(|E'| = m - k\) boundaries are merged, the \(m\) base blocks coalesce into \(k\) contiguous macro-blocks \(B_1, \dots, B_k\):

Relative to one another, the \(k\) macro-blocks can be assigned the \(k\) contiguous value-intervals in any of \(k!\) ways, weighted by the inclusion–exclusion sign \((-1)^{m - k}\).
Inside a macro-block formed by merging a range \(j \in [l, r]\) of base blocks:

If \(l = r\) and \(s_l = 1\), the macro-block has total length \(1\), so it has \(1\) orientation.
Otherwise (either \(r > l\), or \(l = r\) with \(s_l \ge 2\)), the macro-block has total length \(\ge 2\), so it has \(2\) orientations (globally increasing or globally decreasing, which uniquely fixes both the relative value order of the constituent base blocks and the internal orientation of each base block!).




2. \(2 \times 2\) Polynomial Transfer Matrix & Divide-and-Conquer NTT
Let \(c_k\) be the sum of orientation products over all ways to partition the \(m\) base blocks into \(k\) macro-blocks. We can process base blocks \(j = 1, \dots, m\) from left to right by tracking a binary state \(b \in \{0, 1\}\) for the currently open macro-block:

\(b = 0\): the current macro-block consists of a single base block of size \(s_j = 1\) (current orientation weight \(1\)).
\(b = 1\): the current macro-block has total size \(\ge 2\) (current orientation weight \(2\)).

When moving to the next base block \(j\) (\(2 \le j \le m\)), we either:

Cut before block \(j\) (start a new macro-block, multiplying by \(x\)):

If \(s_j = 1\), we transition to state \(b' = 0\) with weight \(x\).
If \(s_j \ge 2\), we transition to state \(b' = 1\) with weight \(2x\).

Merge block \(j\) into the current macro-block (no new macro-block, degree \(0\) in \(x\), always resulting in state \(b' = 1\) of total size \(\ge 2\)):

If the previous state was \(b = 0\) (weight \(1\)), merging upgrades its orientation weight from \(1\) to \(2\), so the transition multiplier is \(2\).
If the previous state was \(b = 1\) (already weight \(2\)), merging keeps its orientation weight at \(2\), so the transition multiplier is \(1\).


Thus, each base block \(j \in \{2, \dots, m\}\) is represented by a \(2 \times 2\) polynomial matrix \(\mathbf{T}_j(x)\) (rows indexed by old state \(b \in \{0, 1\}\), columns by new state \(b' \in \{0, 1\}\)): \[\mathbf{T}_j(x) = \begin{cases}
\begin{pmatrix} x & 2 \\ x & 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } s_j = 1, \\[10pt]
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2x + 2 \\ 0 & 2x + 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } s_j \ge 2,
\end{cases}\] with initial row vector at \(j = 1\) given by \(\mathbf{v}_1(x) = (x, \, 0)\) if \(s_1 = 1\) and \(\mathbf{v}_1(x) = (0, \, 2x)\) if \(s_1 \ge 2\).
Multiplying \(\mathbf{P}(x) = \mathbf{v}_1(x) \mathbf{T}_2(x) \cdots \mathbf{T}_m(x)\) via a balanced binary divide-and-conquer tree of \(2 \times 2\) polynomial matrix multiplications gives \(C(x) = P_0(x) + P_1(x) = \sum_{k=1}^m c_k x^k\), and the final answer is: \[\text{Ans} = \sum_{k=1}^m (-1)^{m - k} k! \, [x^k] C(x) \pmod{998244353}.\]


Algorithm Contract

Input: Array \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) (\(1 \le n \le 10^5\)).
Output: Number of valid permutations modulo \(998244353\).
Algebraic Preconditions: Matrix ring \(M_{2 \times 2}(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}[x])\).
Index & Degree Boundaries: \(m \le n\) base blocks; \(\deg \mathbf{T}_j(x) = 1\); total product has degree \(m\).
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: At depth \(d\) of the D&C tree, \(2^d\) matrix multiplications of degree \(m / 2^d\) perform \(8\) NTTs of size \(O(m / 2^d)\), costing \(O(m \log^2 m) \subseteq O(n \log^2 n)\) time and \(O(n \log n)\) space.
