1. Laminar Containment Forest & Elementary Gap Decomposition
Sort the \(n\) intervals by increasing left endpoint \(L_i\). Because the intervals are laminar with distinct endpoints, each interval \(u\) directly contains a sequence of child intervals \(v_1, v_2, \dots, v_d\) ordered from left to right: \[L_u < L_{v_1} < R_{v_1} < L_{v_2} < R_{v_2} < \dots < L_{v_d} < R_{v_d} < R_u.\] Add a virtual super-root if there are multiple top-level intervals. The \(2n\) original endpoints partition \([L_u, R_u]\) into the child intervals \([L_{v_c}, R_{v_c}]\) and \(d + 1\) elementary gaps: \[G_0 = [L_u, L_{v_1}], \quad G_1 = [R_{v_1}, L_{v_2}], \quad \dots, \quad G_d = [R_{v_d}, R_u],\] with lengths \(g_c = |G_c| > 0\).
By pushing endpoints of chosen sub-intervals \([l_i, r_i]\) to original endpoints \(L_w, R_w\), every elementary gap \(G_c\) is either completely covered by a single chosen sub-interval \([l_w, r_w]\) or completely uncovered. Why? If two chosen sub-intervals met inside the interior of \(G_c\), one of them could be shrunk to an endpoint of \(G_c\) while the other expands across \(G_c\), preserving total length \(\sum (r_i - l_i)\) without creating any new overlap. Thus the union of chosen sub-intervals is a union of elementary gaps, and every chosen sub-interval \([l_w, r_w]\) is a contiguous run of covered elementary gaps inside \([L_w, R_w]\).


2. Bottom-Up \(2 \times 2\) Boundary-State Tree Knapsack
Inside a subtree \(T_u\), each of the \(\operatorname{sz}(u)\) intervals \(w \in T_u\) must be assigned a distinct non-empty covered sub-interval \([l_w, r_w] \subseteq [L_w, R_w]\). As we sweep across \([L_u, R_u]\) from left to right (alternating \(G_0, T_{v_1}, G_1, T_{v_2}, \dots, T_{v_d}, G_d\)), some covered segments inside \(T_u\) have already been claimed by intervals \(w \in T_u\), while \(j\) covered segments remain unclaimed so they can be claimed by \(u\) or by strict ancestors of \(u\) (or extended across adjacent gaps!).
Notice how many unclaimed segments can coexist at the boundary of \(T_u\): because at most one ancestor’s sub-interval can cross \(L_u\) and at most one can cross \(R_u\), any other unclaimed segment strictly inside \((L_u, R_u)\) can never be extended further, so it serves as a finished segment waiting to be claimed by \(u\) or an ancestor of \(u\). Since \(T_u\) plus its ancestors can claim at most \(\operatorname{sz}(u)\) segments originating inside \(T_u\), we only need to track \(0 \le j \le \operatorname{sz}(u)\) unclaimed segments!
Define at each node \(u\) the \(2 \times 2\) state table \[dp_u[b_L][b_R][j] \quad (b_L, b_R \in \{0, 1\}, \; 0 \le j \le \operatorname{sz}(u)),\] representing the maximum covered length inside \([L_u, R_u]\) after all intervals \(w \in T_u\) (including \(u\) itself) have claimed their sub-intervals, leaving \(j\) unclaimed segments for strict ancestors of \(u\), where \(b_L = 1\) (resp. \(b_R = 1\)) iff the leftmost (resp. rightmost) point \(L_u\) (resp. \(R_u\)) belongs to an unclaimed segment that may continue outside \([L_u, R_u]\).

Sweeping across \(G_0, T_{v_1}, G_1, \dots, T_{v_d}, G_d\) inside \(u\):

Single Gap \(G_c\) of length \(g_c\): Represented by a \(2 \times 2\) table \(M_{G_c}[b_L][b_R][j]\) where:

Leaving \(G_c\) uncovered: \(M_{G_c}[0][0][0] = 0\).
Covering \(G_c\) as an unclaimed segment: \(M_{G_c}[1][1][1] = g_c\).

Concatenating two adjacent regions \(A\) and \(B\): When region \(A\) (state \((b_L, m, j_1)\)) abuts region \(B\) (state \((m', b_R, j_2)\)) at a shared point:

If \(m = 1\) and \(m' = 1\), we can either fuse the two boundary segments into a single contiguous segment (resulting in \(j = j_1 + j_2 - 1\) unclaimed segments) or split them at the boundary endpoint so they remain two separate adjacent segments (\(j = j_1 + j_2\)).
Otherwise (\(m = 0\) or \(m' = 0\)), the unclaimed segment count is simply \(j = j_1 + j_2\). This is a \((+, \max)\) convolution of sizes \(\operatorname{sz}(A)\) and \(\operatorname{sz}(B)\).


Claiming Interval \(u\)’s Own Sub-Interval: Once the full region \([L_u, R_u]\) has been assembled into \(F_u[b_L][b_R][j]\) (\(0 \le j \le \operatorname{sz}(u)\)), interval \(u\) itself must claim one of the \(j \ge 1\) unclaimed segments inside \([L_u, R_u]\)!

If \(u\) claims an interior segment (or a boundary segment that terminates at \(L_u\) or \(R_u\)), \(j\) decreases to \(j - 1\), and if the claimed segment was the left/right boundary (\(b_L = 1\) or \(b_R = 1\)), that boundary flag resets to \(0\) (since \(u\)’s sub-interval cannot extend outside \([L_u, R_u]\)!): \[dp_u[b'_L][b'_R][j - 1] \stackrel{\max}{\longleftarrow} F_u[b_L][b_R][j] \quad \text{for } b'_L \le b_L, \; b'_R \le b_R, \; j \ge 1.\]


(To reconstruct the actual intervals \([l_i, r_i]\) as required by CF 1510H, store backpointers at each \((+, \max)\) merge and gap decision.)

Input: \(n \le 2000\) laminar intervals \([L_i, R_i]\).
Output: Maximum total length \(\sum_{i=1}^n (r_i - l_i)\) (and the intervals \([l_i, r_i]\)).
Algebraic Preconditions: Tropical semiring \((\mathbb{Z} \cup \{-\infty\}, \max, +)\) over \(2 \times 2\) boundary matrices.
Index & Degree Boundaries: At node \(u\), \(j \in [0, \operatorname{sz}(u)]\); after \(u\) claims its segment, \(j \in [0, \operatorname{sz}(u) - 1]\), so at every tree root the final answer is \(dp_{\text{root}}[0][0][0]\).
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: Merging child \(v_c\) of size \(\operatorname{sz}(v_c)\) into a running prefix of size \(S\) costs \(O(S \cdot \operatorname{sz}(v_c))\), which sums over all pairs of vertices to \(\binom{n}{2} = O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n^2)\) space.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Initialize all unreachable \((+, \max)\) DP states to \(-\infty\) (e.g., -1e9) rather than \(0\) so invalid boundary-flag combinations cannot be selected, and add a virtual super-root if the input intervals form a forest of multiple top-level intervals.

1. Reachable Set as a Minimal Steiner Subtree
Fix a city \(u \in V\), and let \(\mathcal{P}_u = \{i \in \{1, \dots, m\} : u \in P_i\}\) be the set of languages spoken at \(u\). The set of cities \(v\) that can communicate with \(u\) is the union of the paths \(P_i = (s_i, t_i)\) for \(i \in \mathcal{P}_u\).
Because every path \(P_i\) (\(i \in \mathcal{P}_u\)) is connected and passes through the common vertex \(u\), their union \(\bigcup_{i \in \mathcal{P}_u} P_i\) is a connected subtree of \(T\) whose leaves are a subset of the endpoint multiset \[E_u = \bigcup_{i \in \mathcal{P}_u} \{s_i, t_i\}.\] Conversely, since \(u\) lies on every path \(P_i\) (\(i \in \mathcal{P}_u\)), the unique path between any two endpoints in \(E_u\) is contained in \(\bigcup_{i \in \mathcal{P}_u} P_i\). Therefore, \(\bigcup_{i \in \mathcal{P}_u} P_i\) is identical to the minimal connected subtree (Steiner subtree) spanning \(E_u\)! Furthermore, the number of cities \(v \ne u\) in this subtree is simply the number of edges in the Steiner subtree of \(E_u\).


2. DFS-Order Steiner Size & Bottom-Up Segment Tree Merging
Root \(T\) at vertex \(1\), and compute the DFS entry order \(\operatorname{dfn}[w] \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) and depth \(\operatorname{dep}(w)\) of every vertex \(w\). Precompute an Euler-tour RMQ table so that \(\operatorname{LCA}(x, y)\) can be answered in \(O(1)\) time.
If the distinct vertices in \(E_u\) are \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\) sorted by \(\operatorname{dfn}[x_1] < \operatorname{dfn}[x_2] < \dots < \operatorname{dfn}[x_k]\), the number of edges in the minimal subtree spanning \(E_u\) is: \[\text{Edges}(E_u) = \sum_{j=1}^k \operatorname{dep}(x_j) - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \operatorname{dep}\big(\operatorname{LCA}(x_j, x_{j+1})\big) - \operatorname{dep}\big(\operatorname{LCA}(x_1, x_k)\big).\]
To maintain the multiset \(E_u\) across all \(u \in V\):

For each path \(P_i = (s_i, t_i)\) with \(w_i = \operatorname{LCA}(s_i, t_i)\), \(P_i\) covers \(u\) iff at least one of \(s_i, t_i\) lies in \(T_u\) and \(w_i\) is an ancestor of \(u\). Thus we apply tree difference:

At \(s_i\): add \(+1\) to the multiplicity of \(\operatorname{dfn}[s_i]\) and \(+1\) to \(\operatorname{dfn}[t_i]\).
At \(t_i\): add \(+1\) to \(\operatorname{dfn}[s_i]\) and \(+1\) to \(\operatorname{dfn}[t_i]\).
At \(w_i\): add \(-1\) to \(\operatorname{dfn}[s_i]\) and \(-1\) to \(\operatorname{dfn}[t_i]\).
At \(\operatorname{parent}(w_i)\) (if \(w_i \ne 1\)): add \(-1\) to \(\operatorname{dfn}[s_i]\) and \(-1\) to \(\operatorname{dfn}[t_i]\).

Maintain at each vertex \(u\) a dynamic segment tree over \(\operatorname{dfn} \in [1, n]\). Each segment tree node stores:

cnt: total multiplicity at a leaf,
L_v, R_v: the vertex with the smallest and largest \(\operatorname{dfn}\) having \(\text{cnt} > 0\) in the node’s range (\(0\) if empty),
val: \(\sum \operatorname{dep}(x_j) - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \operatorname{dep}(\operatorname{LCA}(x_j, x_{j+1}))\) over active vertices in the node’s range.

In push_up(p) from children lc and rc: \[\text{p.val} = \text{lc.val} + \text{rc.val} - \big[\text{lc.R\_v} \ne 0 \land \text{rc.L\_v} \ne 0\big] \cdot \operatorname{dep}\big(\operatorname{LCA}(\text{lc.R\_v}, \text{rc.L\_v})\big).\]
Merge children’s segment trees into \(u\)’s segment tree bottom-up, apply \(u\)’s point updates at \(w_i\) / \(\operatorname{parent}(w_i)\), and query the root rt[u] of \(u\)’s segment tree: \[\text{Edges}(E_u) = \text{rt}[u].\text{val} - \operatorname{dep}\big(\operatorname{LCA}(\text{rt}[u].\text{L\_v}, \text{rt}[u].\text{R\_v})\big).\]
Sum \(\text{Edges}(E_u)\) over all \(u \in V\) and divide by \(2\).



Algorithm Contract

Input: Tree \(T\) on \(n \le 10^5\) vertices and \(m \le 10^5\) paths \((s_i, t_i)\).
Output: Number of unordered pairs \(\{u, v\}\) covered by at least one path.
Algebraic Preconditions: Monoid of DFS-ordered active vertex chains equipped with \(O(1)\) Euler-tour RMQ \(\operatorname{LCA}\).
Index & Degree Boundaries: \(O(m)\) point updates of \(\pm 1\) on \(\operatorname{dfn} \in [1, n]\); empty tree (rt[u].L_v == 0) contributes \(0\).
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: \(O(m)\) insertions generate \(O(m \log n)\) segment tree nodes; each overlapping node merge takes \(O(1)\) time and destroys one node, running in \(O((n + m) \log n)\) time and \(O((n + m) \log n)\) space.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Because \(u\) itself is always included in \(E_u\) whenever \(\mathcal{P}_u \ne \emptyset\), an empty segment tree at \(u\) (rt[u].L_v == 0) must contribute \(0\) edges; also divide the global sum \(\sum_{u \in V} \text{Edges}(E_u)\) by \(2\) using integer division (ans / 2), since the problem asks for the exact 64-bit integer count rather than a modular residue.

1. Upper Bound on \(D\) & Hall’s Marriage Theorem
Within any \(2 A_i\) consecutive days, employee \(i\) works on exactly \(A_i\) days (at least half the days). Thus, within \(2 N K\) days, every employee works on at least \(N K\) days, so we can trivially give \(K\) medals to each of the \(N\) employees in turn. Hence the minimum number of days satisfies \[N K \le D \le 2 N K \le 3.6 \times 10^6.\]
For a fixed candidate \(D\), construct a bipartite graph where the left side has \(N\) employee nodes (each with demand \(K\)), the right side has \(D\) day nodes \(d \in \{1, \dots, D\}\) (each with capacity \(1\)), and an edge connects employee \(i\) to day \(d\) iff employee \(i\) works on day \(d\). By Hall’s Marriage Theorem, a valid assignment of \(K\) medals per employee exists if and only if for every subset of employees \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}\), the number of days \(W_D(S)\) in \(\{1, \dots, D\}\) on which at least one employee in \(S\) works satisfies: \[W_D(S) \ge |S| \cdot K \quad \text{for all } S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}.\]


2. Fast Zeta (SOS) Transform on Complement Masks
Let \(U = \{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}\) be the full set of employees. For each day \(d \in \{1, \dots, 2 N K\}\), precompute the bitmask \(M_d \in [0, 2^N - 1]\) of employees working on day \(d\).
For a candidate \(D\), let \(c(T)\) be the count of days \(d \in \{1, \dots, D\}\) such that \(M_d = T\). A day \(d\) has \(M_d \cap S \ne \emptyset\) if and only if \(M_d\) is not a subset of the complement mask \(U \setminus S\): \[W_D(S) = D - \sum_{T \subseteq U \setminus S} c(T).\] Computing \(F(X) = \sum_{T \subseteq X} c(T)\) for all \(X \subseteq U\) is a single \(N\)-bit Fast Zeta / SOS Transform \(F = \operatorname{FZT}_{\text{OR}}(c)\) (iterating \(b = 0, \dots, N - 1\) and accumulating \(F[\text{mask}] \mathrel{+}= F[\text{mask} \oplus 2^b]\) whenever bit \(b\) of \(\text{mask}\) is \(1\)). We then check \(D - F[(2^N - 1) \oplus S] \ge \operatorname{popcount}(S) \cdot K\) for all \(S \in [1, 2^N - 1]\). Binary searching \(D \in [N K, 2 N K]\) takes \(\lceil \log_2(N K) \rceil \le 22\) iterations.


Algorithm Contract

Input: \(N \le 18\), \(K \le 10^5\), \(A_1, \dots, A_N \le 10^5\).
Output: Minimum days \(D\) such that all \(N\) employees can receive \(K\) medals.
Algebraic Preconditions: Subset lattice \((\mathcal{P}(U), \subseteq)\) over \(\mathbb{Z}\).
Index & Degree Boundaries: Precompute \(M_d\) for \(1 \le d \le 2 N K\); binary search range \([N K, 2 N K]\).
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: Precomputing \(M_d\) takes \(O(N K)\) time (by marking intervals of length \(A_i\) for each \(i\)); each binary search check takes \(O(N K + N 2^N)\) time, giving \(O((N K + N 2^N) \log(N K))\) time and \(O(N K + 2^N)\) space.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Check Hall’s condition \(D - F[(2^N - 1) \oplus S] \ge \operatorname{popcount}(S) \cdot K\) for all non-empty masks \(S \in [1, 2^N - 1]\), and note that the maximum answer \(D \le 2 N K = 3.6 \times 10^6\) requires 64-bit integers when multiplying \(|S| \cdot K\) if \(K\) is large.

1. Reformulation in the XOR Group Ring
Two disjoint subsets \(A, B \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) satisfy \(\bigoplus_{i \in A} a_i = \bigoplus_{j \in B} a_j\) if and only if their disjoint union \(U = A \sqcup B\) satisfies \(\bigoplus_{k \in U} a_k = 0\). Conversely, any subset \(U \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}\) with XOR sum \(0\) can be partitioned into an ordered pair of disjoint subsets \((A, B)\) with \(A \sqcup B = U\) in \(2^{|U|}\) ways (each element \(k \in U\) goes to \(A\) or \(B\)).
Therefore, in the XOR group algebra \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}[\mathbb{Z}_2^b]\) (\(b = 20\)) where monomials multiply via \(x^u \cdot x^v = x^{u \oplus v}\), the number of ordered pairs \((A, B)\) of disjoint subsets with equal XOR sum is the coefficient of \(x^0\) in \[P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n \big(1 + 2 x^{a_i}\big).\]


2. Small-Support Walsh–Hadamard Eigenvalue Trick
Applying the \(b\)-bit XOR Fast Walsh–Hadamard Transform (\(\operatorname{FWT}_{\oplus}\)) turns XOR convolution into pointwise multiplication. For a single factor \(1 + 2 x^{a_i}\), its transform at frequency mask \(S \in [0, 2^b - 1]\) is: \[\widehat{(1 + 2 x^{a_i})}_S = 1 + 2(-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i)} \in \{3, -1\}.\] Specifically, the value is \(3\) if \(\operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i)\) is even, and \(-1\) if \(\operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i)\) is odd.
To find how many \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) give \(+1\) versus \(-1\) at each frequency \(S\) without transforming \(n\) polynomials separately, form the single frequency polynomial \[C(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n x^{a_i}\] and compute \(\widehat{C} = \operatorname{FWT}_{\oplus}(C)\) in \(O(b 2^b)\) time. At frequency \(S\), let \(k_S\) be the number of indices \(i\) with \((-1)^{\operatorname{popcount}(S \ \& \ a_i)} = +1\). Then: \[\begin{cases}
k_S + (n - k_S) = n, \\
k_S - (n - k_S) = \widehat{C}_S,
\end{cases}
\implies k_S = \frac{n + \widehat{C}_S}{2}.\] Hence the Walsh–Hadamard spectrum of \(P(x)\) at frequency \(S\) is immediately: \[\widehat{P}_S = 3^{k_S} (-1)^{n - k_S} \pmod{998244353}.\] By the inverse XOR transform at index \(0\), \([x^0] P(x) = 2^{-b} \sum_{S=0}^{2^b - 1} \widehat{P}_S\). Subtracting \(1\) (to remove the empty pair \(A = B = \emptyset\)) and multiplying by \(2^{-1} \bmod 998244353\) (for unordered pairs \(\{A, B\}\)) yields the final answer: \[\text{Ans} = \frac{[x^0] P(x) - 1}{2} \pmod{998244353}.\]


Algorithm Contract

Input: \(n \le 10^6\) integers \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in [0, 2^{20} - 1]\).
Output: Number of unordered non-empty disjoint subset pairs \(\{A, B\}\) with equal XOR sum modulo \(998244353\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}) = 998244353 \ne 2\), so \(2^{-b}\) and \(2^{-1}\) exist. Perform the forward \(\operatorname{FWT}_{\oplus}\) of \(C(x)\) over standard 64-bit integers int64_t (not modulo \(998244353\)!) so that \(k_S = (n + \widehat{C}_S) / 2 \in [0, n]\) is an exact integer exponent for \(3^{k_S}\).
Index & Degree Boundaries: \(b = 20\), \(2^b = 1{,}048{,}576\); precompute powers \(3^0, 3^1, \dots, 3^n \bmod 998244353\) in \(O(n)\) time.
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: One \(O(b 2^b)\) integer \(\operatorname{FWT}_{\oplus}\) and \(O(n + 2^b)\) linear scans achieve \(O(n + b 2^b)\) time and \(O(n + 2^b)\) space.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Do NOT reduce \(\widehat{C}_S\) modulo \(998244353\) during the forward \(\operatorname{FWT}_{\oplus}\) of the frequency array \(C\), because \(\widehat{C}_S \in [-n, n]\) is needed as an exact integer to compute the exponent \(k_S = (n + \widehat{C}_S) / 2\) (whereas by Fermat’s Little Theorem, exponents must be reduced modulo \(P - 1\), not \(P\)).

1. Matrix-Tree Theorem over the Mixed Bitwise Group Algebra
Fix a large prime \(P\) (e.g., \(P = 998244353\) or \(10^9 + 9\)) so that non-zero spanning tree counts do not vanish modulo \(P\), and consider the \(2^w\)-dimensional commutative ring \[\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{F}_P[z^0, z^1, \dots, z^{2^w - 1}] \quad \text{with} \quad z^u \cdot z^v = z^{u \odot v},\] where \(u \odot v\) combines the \(r\)-th bits of \(u\) and \(v\) via \(\text{op}_r \in \{\text{\&}, \text{|}, \text{\^{}}\}\) for each \(0 \le r < w\).
Construct the \(n \times n\) Laplacian matrix \(L(z) \in M_{n \times n}(\mathcal{A})\) of the multigraph \(G\): for each edge \(e = (u, v) \in E\) with weight \(v_e\), add \(+z^{v_e}\) to \(L_{u, u}(z)\) and \(L_{v, v}(z)\), and add \(-z^{v_e}\) to \(L_{u, v}(z)\) and \(L_{v, u}(z)\). By Kirchhoff’s Matrix-Tree Theorem (which holds over any commutative ring \(\mathcal{A}\)), the determinant of the \((n-1) \times (n-1)\) principal minor \(L^{(n)}(z)\) (deleting row \(n\) and column \(n\)) equals: \[D(z) = \det L^{(n)}(z) = \sum_{T \text{ spanning tree of } G} \prod_{e \in T} z^{v_e} = \sum_{v=0}^{2^w - 1} c_v \, z^v,\] where \(c_v \bmod P\) is the number of spanning trees of \(G\) whose combined bitwise weight is \(v\).


2. Diagonalization via Mixed \(w\)-Bit Fast Walsh–Hadamard Transform
Because \(\mathcal{A} \cong \bigotimes_{r=0}^{w-1} \mathcal{A}_r\) is a tensor product of \(w\) independent \(1\)-bit commutative algebras, the Mixed \(w\)-Bit Fast Walsh–Hadamard Transform \(\operatorname{FWT}_{\text{op}} : \mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{F}_P^{2^w}\) applies at bit \(r\) (\(0 \le r < w\)) the \(2 \times 2\) butterfly matrix: \[M_r = \begin{cases}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } \text{op}_r = \text{\&}, \\[10pt]
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } \text{op}_r = \text{|}, \\[10pt]
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } \text{op}_r = \text{\^{}},
\end{cases}
\qquad
M_r^{-1} = \begin{cases}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } \text{op}_r = \text{\&}, \\[10pt]
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } \text{op}_r = \text{|}, \\[10pt]
\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{if } \text{op}_r = \text{\^{}}.
\end{cases}\]
Since \(\operatorname{FWT}_{\text{op}}\) is an algebra isomorphism onto \(\mathbb{F}_P^{2^w}\) with pointwise addition and multiplication, it commutes with polynomial expressions such as the determinant: \[\widehat{D}(\omega) = \det\!\big(\widehat{L^{(n)}}(\omega)\big) \quad \text{for every } \omega \in \{0, 1, \dots, 2^w - 1\}.\]
Thus the algorithm proceeds in three clean steps:

Apply \(\operatorname{FWT}_{\text{op}}\) of length \(2^w\) to each of the \((n-1)^2\) entries of \(L^{(n)}(z)\) (using symmetry \(L_{i, j} = L_{j, i}\) to transform only \(\binom{n}{2}\) entries) in \(O(w 2^w n^2)\) time.
For each frequency \(\omega \in [0, 2^w - 1]\), compute the scalar determinant \(\widehat{D}(\omega) = \det \widehat{L^{(n)}}(\omega) \bmod P\) via Gaussian elimination in \(O(n^3)\) time.
Apply \(\operatorname{IFWT}_{\text{op}}\) to \(\widehat{D}\) in \(O(w 2^w)\) time to recover \(c_v = [z^v] D(z) \bmod P\), and return the largest \(v \in [0, 2^w - 1]\) with \(c_v \ne 0\) (or \(-1\) if no such \(v\) exists).



Algorithm Contract

Input: Multigraph \(G\) with \(n \le 70\), \(m \le 5000\), bit-width \(w \le 12\), operation string \(\text{op} \in \{\text{\&}, \text{|}, \text{\^{}}\}^w\), and edge weights \(v_e \in [0, 2^w - 1]\).
Output: Maximum spanning tree weight \(v \in [0, 2^w - 1]\), or \(-1\) if \(G\) is disconnected.
Algebraic Preconditions: Prime modulus \(P = 998244353 > 2\) (so \(2^{-1} \bmod P\) exists for XOR inversion and \(P\) exceeds the maximum spanning tree count on small graphs or acts as a randomized Schwartz–Zippel modulus).
Index & Degree Boundaries: \((n-1) \times (n-1)\) minor; \(2^w \le 4096\) frequencies.
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: \(\binom{n}{2}\) transforms of size \(2^w\) plus \(2^w\) Gaussian eliminations of size \(n - 1\) take \(O(2^w n^3 + w 2^w n^2)\) time and \(O(2^w n^2)\) space.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Because \(G\) is a multigraph, parallel edges between \(u\) and \(v\) must be accumulated (+= / -=) rather than overwritten in the Laplacian matrix \(L(z)\), and self-loops \(u = v\) must be ignored; if all \(2^w\) coefficients of \(D(z)\) are \(0 \bmod P\), output \(-1\).












NoteComplete Solution — CP-VI.8 (#180: Luogu P5643 — [PKUWC2018] 随机游走)






1. Min–Max Inclusion–Exclusion Reduction
Let \(\tau_v\) be the first hitting time of vertex \(v\) starting from root \(x\). For any query subset \(S \subseteq V\), the time until all vertices in \(S\) have been visited is \(\max_{v \in S} \tau_v\). Applying the Min–Max Identity \(\max_{v \in S} \tau_v = \sum_{\emptyset \ne T \subseteq S} (-1)^{|T| - 1} \min_{v \in T} \tau_v\) and taking expectations gives: \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{v \in S} \tau_v\right] = \sum_{\emptyset \ne T \subseteq S} (-1)^{|T| - 1} f(T), \quad \text{where } f(T) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\min_{v \in T} \tau_v\right].\] Here \(f(T)\) is the expected number of steps, starting from \(x\), to hit at least one vertex in \(T\).


2. \(O(n)\) Tree Linear Elimination for Fixed Target Set \(T\)
Root the tree \(T_{\text{tree}}\) at the starting vertex \(x\). For a fixed non-empty target subset \(T \subseteq V\), let \(E_u\) be the expected number of steps to hit \(T\) starting from \(u\). The Markov chain transitions satisfy:

If \(u \in T\): \(E_u = 0\).
If \(u \notin T\): \(E_u = 1 + \frac{1}{d(u)} \Big(E_{p(u)} + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} E_v\Big)\), where \(p(u)\) is the parent of \(u\) (omitted if \(u = x\)) and \(\text{ch}(u)\) is the set of children of \(u\).

We prove by bottom-up induction on the tree that every vertex \(u\) satisfies a linear relation \[E_u = A_u E_{p(u)} + B_u:\]

Target vertices (\(u \in T\)): Since \(E_u = 0\) regardless of \(E_{p(u)}\), we have \(A_u = 0\) and \(B_u = 0\).
Non-target vertices (\(u \notin T\)): Assuming \(E_v = A_v E_u + B_v\) has already been computed for every child \(v \in \text{ch}(u)\), substitute these into \(u\)’s equation: \[d(u) E_u = d(u) + [u \ne x] E_{p(u)} + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} \big(A_v E_u + B_v\big).\] Collecting the \(E_u\) terms on the left gives: \[\left(d(u) - \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} A_v\right) E_u = [u \ne x] E_{p(u)} + d(u) + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} B_v.\] Setting \(D_u = \big(d(u) - \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} A_v\big)^{-1} \bmod 998244353\), we obtain in \(O(\deg(u))\) time: \[A_u = [u \ne x] \cdot D_u \bmod P, \qquad B_u = D_u \cdot \left(d(u) + \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} B_v\right) \bmod P.\]

At the root \(x\), \(A_x = 0\) and \(f(T) = E_x = B_x\)! Thus \(f(T)\) is computed in \(O(n)\) time per subset \(T\), and across all \(2^n - 1\) non-empty subsets \(T \subseteq V\) in \(O(n 2^n)\) total time.


3. Fast Zeta (SOS) Transform for \(O(1)\) Query Lookup
Define the signed array \(g(T) = (-1)^{|T| - 1} f(T) \bmod 998244353\) for \(T \ne \emptyset\) and \(g(\emptyset) = 0\). Then for every query subset \(S \subseteq V\): \[\text{Ans}(S) = \sum_{T \subseteq S} g(T) \pmod{998244353}.\] Applying the \(n\)-bit Fast Zeta / SOS Transform to \(g\) precomputes \(\text{Ans}(S)\) for all \(2^n\) subsets \(S\) in \(O(n 2^n)\) time, allowing each of the \(Q\) queries to be answered in \(O(1)\) time.


Algorithm Contract

Input: Tree on \(n \le 18\) vertices, root \(x\), and \(Q \le 5000\) query subsets \(S \subseteq V\).
Output: \(\mathbb{E}[\max_{v \in S} \tau_v] \bmod 998244353\) for each query \(S\).
Algebraic Preconditions: \(\mathbb{F}_{998244353}\); since \(T \ne \emptyset\) is reachable from every vertex \(u \notin T\) on a finite tree, the spectral radius of the transient submatrix is strictly less than \(1\) in \(\mathbb{R}\), guaranteeing \(d(u) - \sum_{v \in \text{ch}(u)} A_v \not\equiv 0 \pmod{998244353}\).
Index & Degree Boundaries: \(T \in [1, 2^n - 1]\); if \(x \in T\), then immediately \(f(T) = E_x = 0\).
Complexity & Correctness Invariant: \(2^n\) bottom-up tree passes of \(O(n)\) plus one \(n\)-bit SOS transform take \(O(n 2^n + Q)\) time and \(O(2^n)\) space.
Failure Modes & Edge Cases: Whenever the starting vertex \(x\) belongs to the target subset \(T\), the walk hits \(T\) in \(0\) steps (\(f(T) = E_x = 0\)), and for any vertex \(u \in T\) we must set \(A_u = B_u = 0\) rather than applying the non-target transition.

title: FPS Notation, Operators & 16 Failure Modes
text:
Base Ring & Coefficient Conventions

\(\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) denotes the nonnegative integers; \([0, n)\) denotes integer indices \(0, \dots, n-1\). Empty sums are \(0\), empty products are \(1\), and the unique empty combinatorial object has size \(0\) and contributes \(1 \cdot x^0\).
\([P]\) is the Iverson indicator of proposition \(P\) (\(1\) if \(P\) holds, \(0\) otherwise); this is distinct from the linear coefficient-extraction functional \([x^n]F(x)\).
\(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}\) is the ring of residues modulo \(m\); \(\mathbb{F}_p\) is a prime field of characteristic \(p\); \(\mathbb{F}_q\) denotes a finite field of prime-power order \(q = p^r\).
Division by \(a \in K\) means multiplication by \(a^{-1}\) and requires \(a \in K^\times\) (a unit in \(K\)). Over \(\mathbb{F}_p\), \(a \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times \iff a \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\); over \(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}\), \(a \in (\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})^\times \iff \gcd(a, m) = 1\).
For nonzero \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), \(v_p(n)\) denotes the \(p\)-adic exponent of prime \(p\) dividing \(n\), with \(v_p(0) = +\infty\).
\(\mathcal{M}(N)\) (or \(M(N)\)) denotes the arithmetic cost of multiplying two polynomials of degree \(< N\); over an NTT-friendly prime modulus, \(\mathcal{M}(N) = O(N \log N)\).

section: Hadamard Products, Diagonals, Differential & Transposed Operators
text:
Hadamard Products, Diagonals, Differential & Transposed Operators

Hadamard Product \(F \odot G\): Termwise (coefficient-wise) product of two univariate series: \[(F \odot G)(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \bigl([x^n]F(x)\bigr)\bigl([x^n]G(x)\bigr) x^n.\]
Constant-Term & Diagonal Operator \(\operatorname{Diag}_{x,y}\): For \(F(x,y) = \sum_{i,j \ge 0} f_{i,j} x^i y^j\), the main diagonal is extracted via the Laurent substitution \(x = u, y = t/u\) in \(K[[t]]((u))\): \[\operatorname{Diag}_{x,y} F(x,y) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_{n,n} t^n = [u^0] F(u, t/u) = \operatorname{Res}_{u=0} \frac{1}{u} F(u, t/u).\]
Euler Differential Operator \(\vartheta\) (and Pointing \(\Theta\), \(\vartheta_x = x D_x\), \(\Theta_x = x \partial_x\)): \[\vartheta = \Theta = x \frac{d}{dx}, \qquad \vartheta^k\!\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n x^n\right) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n^k f_n x^n = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} x^j F^{(j)}(x).\]
Weyl Algebra \(K[x]\langle D \rangle\) & Shift Algebra \(K[n]\langle E_n \rangle\): Non-commutative operator rings governed by the Leibniz commutation relations: \[D x - x D = 1 \quad \text{in } K[x]\langle D \rangle, \qquad E_n n - (n + 1) E_n = 0 \quad \text{in } K[n]\langle E_n \rangle,\] connected on coefficients via \([x^n]\bigl(x^a D^b F(x)\bigr) = (n - a + 1)^{\overline{b}} f_{n - a + b}\).
Tellegen Transposed Multiplication (Middle Product mulT / \(\operatorname{mulT}(C, B)\) / \(\operatorname{mul}^T\)): Given \(B(x)\) of degree \(< m\) and \(C(x)\) of degree \(< m + n - 1\), the transposed multiplication \(\operatorname{mulT}(C, B) = T_B^\top \mathbf{c}\) (also written \(\operatorname{mul}^T(B, C)\)) is the linear transpose of \(A \mapsto A \cdot B\) on the dual space \(K[x]_{<n+m-1}^* \to K[x]_{<n}^*\): \[[x^i]\operatorname{mulT}(C, B) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} b_j c_{i+j} = [x^i]\bigl(B(x^{-1}) C(x)\bigr) \qquad (0 \le i < n).\]
\(q\)-Pochhammer Symbol & Gaussian \(q\)-Binomial Coefficient: \[(a; q)_n = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (1 - a q^i), \qquad (a; q)_0 = 1, \qquad \begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q = \binom{n}{k}_q = \frac{(q; q)_n}{(q; q)_k (q; q)_{n-k}}.\]
Set Power Series Ring \(\mathcal{R}_n\) & Dirichlet Ring \(\mathcal{D}_f\): \[\mathcal{R}_n = K[x_1, \dots, x_n]/(x_1^2, \dots, x_n^2), \qquad \mathcal{D}_f(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{f(n)}{n^s}, \qquad (\vartheta_{\Omega} f)(n) = \Omega(n) f(n).\]

Symbol / Operator
Mathematical Definition & Canonical Meaning

\([x^n] F(x)\), \([x^k y^m] F(x,y)\)
Coefficient extraction: \([x^n] \sum f_k x^k := f_n\); multivariate \([x^k y^m] F(x,y) := [x^k]\big([y^m] F(x,y)\big) = f_{k,m}\)
None (pure \(K\)-linear functional)


\(F(x) \bmod x^N\)
Degree truncation: projection onto \(R[x]/(x^N)\), keeping terms \(x^0, \dots, x^{N-1}\)
None


\(\deg(P)\)
Degree of a polynomial \(P \in R[x]\), with \(\deg(0) := -\infty\)
\(P\) is a finite polynomial


\(\nu(F) = \operatorname{val}(F) = \operatorname{ord}_x(F)\)
Formal (\(\mathfrak{m}\)-adic) valuation: \(\min\{n \in \mathbb{Z} : [x^n]F(x) \neq 0\}\), with \(\nu(0) := +\infty\) (written \(\operatorname{val}_x(F)\) or \(\operatorname{ord}_x(F)\) when the variable is emphasized)
None


\(D F(x) = F'(x)\)
Formal derivative: \(\sum_{n \ge 1} n f_n x^{n-1}\)
None


\(\int F(x)\,dx\)
Formal integral: \(\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{f_n}{n+1} x^{n+1}\) (constant term \(0\))
\(1, 2, \dots, N \in R^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) = 0\) or \(p > N\))


\(\vartheta = x D\) (or \(\vartheta_x = x D_x\), \(\Theta_x = x \partial_x\))
Theta / Euler pointing operator: \(\vartheta F(x) = x F'(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} n f_n x^n\)
None


\(E\) (or \(E_n\)) and \(\Delta = E - I\)
Forward shift operator (\(E f_n = f_{n+1}\)) and forward difference operator (\(\Delta f_n = f_{n+1} - f_n\))
None


\(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} F(x) = \operatorname{Res}_x F(x)\)
Formal residue (also written \(\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} F(x)\,dx\)): \([x^{-1}] F(x)\) for \(F(x) \in K((x))\)
\(F(x) \in K((x))\) is a formal Laurent series


\(\operatorname{Diag}_{x,y} F(x,y)\)
Bivariate diagonal operator: \(\sum_{n \ge 0} ([x^n y^n] F(x,y)) t^n\)
\(F(x,y) \in K[[x,y]]\) (or diagonally summable Laurent series)


\(\operatorname{mulT}(C, B) = T_B^\top \mathbf{c}\)
Transposed multiplication (middle product) on the dual space \(K[x]_{<n+m-1}^* \to K[x]_{<n}^*\): \([x^i]\operatorname{mulT}(C, B) := \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} b_j c_{i+j}\)
None


\(x^{\underline{k}}\), \(x^{\overline{k}}\)
Falling factorial \(x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)\) and rising factorial \(x(x+1)\cdots(x+k-1)\)
None


\(\left\{ \begin{matrix} n \\ k \end{matrix} \right\}\), \(\left[ \begin{matrix} n \\ k \end{matrix} \right]\), \(\left\langle \begin{matrix} n \\ k \end{matrix} \right\rangle\)
Stirling numbers of the second kind, unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind, and Eulerian numbers (Karamata notation)
None


\(\begin{bmatrix} n \\ k \end{bmatrix}_q\), \((a; q)_n\)
Gaussian \(q\)-binomial coefficient \(\frac{(q;q)_n}{(q;q)_k (q;q)_{n-k}}\) and \(q\)-Pochhammer symbol \(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1 - a q^j)\)
None (polynomial in \(q\))


\(*_{\text{or}}\), \(*_{\text{and}}\), \(*_{\text{xor}}\), \(*_{\text{sub}}\)
Bitwise OR, AND, XOR convolutions on \(K^{2^n}\) and subset convolution on \(K[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}]/(x_0^2,\dots,x_{n-1}^2)\)
\(*_{\text{xor}}\) inversion requires \(2 \in K^\times\) (\(\operatorname{char}(K) \neq 2\))

title: FPS Notation, Operators & 16 Failure Modes
text:
The 16 Global Algebraic Failure Modes (#1–#16)
Every algorithm contract in the 24-chapter FPS textbook cross-references these canonical failure modes:



Failure Mode
Hazard Name & Algebraic Trigger
Exact Defensive Remedy & Target Chapter




Failure Mode #1
Precision Loss in Shifted Division \(B(x)/A(x) \bmod x^N\) when \(\nu(A) = v \ge 1\)
Dividing by \(x^v\) shifts degree \(N+v-1\) down to \(N-1\); always compute both \(A(x)\) and \(B(x)\) to precision \(\bmod x^{N+v}\) before shifting (Ch 01.4).


Failure Mode #2
3-Way Modular Reduction Trap in \(P(x)^\alpha \bmod x^N\) when \(\alpha \ge p\)
(1) Shift \(v \cdot \alpha\) in true integer __int128 (return \(0\) if \(v > 0\) and \(v\alpha \ge N\)); (2) leading scalar \(c_v^{\alpha \bmod (p-1)}\) by Fermat; (3) series exponent \((\alpha \bmod p)\ln \widetilde{P}\) (Ch 02.3).


Failure Mode #3
Rational Exponent \(P(x)^{a/b}\) Existence Failure (\(\gcd(a,b)=1\))
\(P(x)^{a/b} \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]\) exists iff \(b \mid (v \cdot a)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) and the leading coefficient \(c_v\) is a \(b\)-th residue in \(\mathbb{F}_p^\times\) (Ch 02.3).


Failure Mode #4
Characteristic-\(p\) Transcendental Breakdown (\(\ln, \exp, \int\)) when \(p \le N\)
\(\int x^{p-1}dx = x^p/p\) divides by \(0 \bmod p\); replace \(\ln/\exp\) with algebraic inv, Bostan–Mori, Frobenius \(A(x)^p \equiv A(x^p) \pmod p\), or Boxed Products (Ch 02.2, Ch 04.3).


Failure Mode #5
Lagrange Inversion \(1/n\) Breakdown when \(p \mid n\)
Classical LIF \(\frac{1}{n}[u^{n-1}]H'(u)\Phi(u)^n\) divides by \(n \equiv 0 \pmod p\); always use Derivative-Free Residue LIF (Form 2): \([u^n]H(u)(\Phi(u) - u\Phi'(u))\Phi(u)^{n-1}\) (Ch 11.2).


Failure Mode #6
Compositional Inverse (revert) Breakdown when \(p \le N\)
Route A (noshi91 Power Projection + pow) divides by \(1, \dots, N-1\); switch to Route B (Newton Iteration + Kinoshita–Li compose), which divides only by \(2\) and \(f_1\) (Ch 21.4).


Failure Mode #7
2D Obstinate Kernel Over-Subtraction & Newton–Girard Symmetric Function Asymmetry (\(p_k \leftrightarrow e_k\)) when \(p \le N\)
Subtracting \(F(x,0)+F(0,y)\) double-counts \(F(0,0)\) (\(\to +F(0,0)\)); for \(E(t) = \sum_{k \ge 0} e_k t^k\), \(e_k \to p_k\) via \(P(t) = -t E'(-t)/E(-t)\) uses only inv (\(e_0=1\)) and is 100% division-free in all characteristics \(p\); \(p_k \to e_k\) divides by \(k\) and fails for \(p \le N\) (Ch 17.3).


Failure Mode #8
Vanishing Indicial Polynomial \(I(n^*) \equiv 0 \pmod p\) in P-Recursive Unrolling
Supply initial value if \(I(n^*) = 0\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\); lift the recurrence to the \(p\)-adic quotient ring \(\mathbb{Z}/p^{V+1}\mathbb{Z}\) (\(u \cdot p^e\)) where \(V = \sum_{I(n)\equiv 0} v_p(I(n))\) (Ch 18.4).


Failure Mode #9
Gaussian \(q\)-Binomial Pole when \(\operatorname{ord}_p(q) = d \le n\)
Direct \((q;q)_n\) division hits \(1 - q^d \equiv 0 \pmod p\); apply the \(q\)-Lucas Theorem \(\begin{bmatrix} n_1 d + n_0 \\ k_1 d + k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q \equiv \binom{n_1}{k_1}\begin{bmatrix} n_0 \\ k_0 \end{bmatrix}_q \pmod p\) (Ch 23.2).


Failure Mode #10
Dynamic Division by Zero in Point-Value / Tree-DP Products
When a light child evaluates to \(F_v(\omega_r) \equiv 0 \pmod p\), maintain each frequency state in the Zero-Divisor Monoid \((a, c) \equiv a \cdot 0^c\) (\(a \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times, c \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\)) (Ch 22.3).


Failure Mode #11
Missing \(m\)-th Root of Unity in Filter (单位根反演) when \(m \nmid (p-1)\)
Do not search for a scalar \(\omega_m \in \mathbb{F}_p\); compute modulo the Cyclotomic Polynomial \(\Phi_m(\omega)\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p[\omega]/(\Phi_m(\omega))\) (Ch 07.4).


Failure Mode #12
Bluestein Chirp-Z Square-Root Failure (\(c^{1/2} \notin \mathbb{F}_p\)) & \(c=0\) Trap
Never use \(ij = \frac{1}{2}((i+j)^2 - i^2 - j^2)\); always use Bluestein’s Binomial Identity \(ij = \binom{i+j}{2} - \binom{i}{2} - \binom{j}{2}\), and branch on \(c = 0\) (Ch 07.3).


Failure Mode #13
Full-Online Self-Convolution Asymmetry Bug at \(l > 0\)
In cdq(l, r) for \(f_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f_i f_{n-i}\), convolve \(f[0..m]^2\) at \(l=0\), but convolve \(2 \cdot f[l..m] \times f[0..r-l]\) at \(l > 0\) (Ch 09.2).


Failure Mode #14
Negative-Integer \(\alpha = -d\) Pole in Generalized \(\alpha\)-Euler Transform
Split \(F(y) = F_{\le d}(y) + y^{d+1} F_{>d}(y)\) before applying \((1-x)^{-\alpha}\) so the tail shifts \(\alpha \mapsto 1 > 0\) (Ch 06.4).


Failure Mode #15
Hidden Pole at \(z = 0\) in Improper Rational Diagonals (\(\deg_y A \ge \deg_y B\))
Substituting \(y = t/z\) introduces \(z^{\deg_y B - \deg_y A - 1}\); include \(\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}\) or perform polynomial division in \(y\) first (Ch 16.4).


Failure Mode #16
Catalan Negative Upper-Index Trap (\(k=0\)) & Prüfer \(N=1\) Trap
Isolate \(k=0\) before \(\binom{2k-1}{k} = \binom{2k-1}{k-1}\) (\(\binom{-1}{0}=1 \neq \binom{-1}{-1}=0\)), and handle \(N=1\) before \((N-2)!\) Prüfer extraction (Ch 04.4, Ch 11.3).

Weekly Study Rhythm & Blind Checkpoint Protocol

Session A — Theory & Scratchpad (90 min): Reproduce the chapter’s central algebraic derivations on paper and verify the small hand-worked examples through degree \(3\) or \(4\). Do not move to problems until you can state why each division is valid and which of the 16 Global Failure Modes applies.
Session B — Stepping Stones & Intermediate Ladder (2 h): Solve SS-1, SS-2, Int-1, and Int-2 from the chapter’s 8-problem ladder. Record which statement clue triggered the generating function model.
Session C — Advanced & Mastery Ladder (2.5–3 h): Attempt Adv-1, Adv-2, Mas-1, and Mas-2. Write down the target complexity in \(\mathcal{M}(N)\) and verify characteristic-\(p\) and valuation-shift preconditions before coding.
Part Gate — Two-Stage Blind Checkpoint (CP-I–CP-VI): At the end of each Part, attempt the 8 blind checkpoint problems without topic labels:

Stage 1 (10 minutes per problem, no hints): Classify the algebraic object (OGF vs. EGF vs. PGF vs. Laurent residue vs. bivariate diagonal vs. SPS) and write the target functional equation.
Stage 2 (Full solve): Solve at least 6 of 8 blind problems before advancing to the next Part.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Here is a situation every competitive programmer recognizes. You are solving a problem about an array, you notice a pattern in the samples, you code the pattern, and you get Wrong answer on test 7. The implementation is perfect. The pattern was false.
Now compare that with a different failure. You reduce the problem to “find the smallest \(x\) with \(Kx \equiv -S \pmod N\)”, you call your extended-Euclid routine, and you get Wrong answer on test 3 because a solution exists only when \(\gcd(K,N)\) divides \(S\) — a condition you never checked, because nobody told you it was there.
Both bugs have the same cause: a claim was used without being proved, and the claim was false or incomplete. No amount of stress testing reliably finds these, because the wrong claim is usually right on small cases; that is precisely why it looked convincing.
This chapter is about the small set of habits that catch such bugs before you write code: saying exactly what you are claiming, knowing which direction of an “if and only if” you actually need, proving that a loop makes progress, and counting a set of objects in two different ways to check yourself. None of it requires a mathematics degree. All of it is the working language of every later chapter.
